Bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the distal 6 cm of the fibula
Tenderness over the base of the second metatarsal
items.e: Ottawa Ankle Rules mandate radiographs if there is pain in the malleolar zone AND bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm), or an inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately and in the emergency department.

items.q: A professional football player presents with pain over the anterior syndesmosis following an external rotation and dorsiflexion injury. Which clinical examination is considered the most sensitive for diagnosing this 'high ankle' sprain?
items.e: The external rotation stress test (Kleiger test) is the most sensitive clinical test for identifying syndesmotic (high ankle) injuries, which typically occur from external rotation and dorsiflexion forces.

items.q: A 48-year-old patient with Takakura stage 3A varus ankle osteoarthritis (medial gutter obliteration with preserved lateral joint space) is being considered for joint-preserving surgery. Which procedure is most appropriate for this patient?
items.e: Supramalleolar osteotomy (SMOT) is indicated for asymmetric (varus or valgus) ankle OA where at least 50% of the joint surface is preserved (Takakura 2-3A), as it realigns the mechanical axis to the preserved side.

items.q: What is the most common complication associated with total ankle replacement (TAR) performed through a standard anterior approach?
o: Aseptic loosening of the talar component
items.e: Wound complications are the most common issue following TAR via the anterior approach, occurring in approximately 5-15% of cases due to the thin soft-tissue envelope over the anterior ankle.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a Hawkins Type III talar neck fracture. The talar body is extruded posteromedially. Regarding the management of this injury, which of the following is true?
o: ORIF must be performed within 6 hours to reduce the risk of AVN
The reduction of the dislocations is a surgical emergency to protect the skin
Timing of definitive fixation is the primary determinant of revascularization
Primary talectomy is the treatment of choice for Type III injuries
items.e: According to studies by Vallier and Lindvall, the timing of definitive ORIF does not influence the rate of AVN. However, the urgent reduction of dislocations (subtalar and ankle) is a surgical emergency because the extruded body puts the skin at risk of necrosis.

items.q: To intraoperatively assess the reduction of a talar neck fracture and ensure no varus malalignment is present, which specific radiographic view is most useful?
items.e: The Canale view (15-degree pronation of the foot with a 75-degree cephalad-tilted AP) is the best radiographic view to visualize the talar neck and assess for varus malunion or medial comminution.

items.q: A patient returns for follow-up 8 weeks after a talar neck fracture. An AP radiograph of the ankle shows a subchondral lucent band in the talar dome. This finding (Hawkins sign) implies:
o: Disuse osteopenia indicating the need for weight-bearing
Active revascularization and a good prognosis
items.e: The Hawkins sign is a subchondral radiolucent band in the talar dome seen at 6-8 weeks, representing bone resorption in the presence of an intact blood supply. It is a good prognostic sign indicating revascularization.

items.q: In a lateral subtalar (peritalar) dislocation that is irreducible by closed means, which structure is the most common block to reduction?
items.e: In lateral subtalar dislocations, the tibialis posterior tendon is the most common structure that becomes interposed, preventing closed reduction. In medial dislocations, the extensor digitorum brevis or the talar head buttonholing through the capsule are more common blocks.

items.q: In a diabetic patient with medial arterial calcification (Mönckeberg sclerosis) yielding an ankle-brachial index (ABI) greater than 1.3, which of the following objective measurements is associated with successful wound healing?
o: Transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2) greater than 15 mmHg
Ankle systolic pressure greater than 50 mmHg
items.e: In calcified, non-compressible vessels, ABI is falsely elevated. A toe pressure greater than 40 mmHg (normal is over 70 mmHg) or a transcutaneous oxygen tension (TcPO2) greater than 30–40 mmHg is associated with wound healing.

items.q: According to Brodsky's anatomical classification of Charcot neuroarthropathy, which type involves the tibiotalar joint, is considered the most unstable, and carries the worst prognosis?
items.e: Brodsky Type 3A involves the tibiotalar joint (ankle); it is the most unstable pattern, prone to severe varus/valgus deformity and malleolar ulceration, and has the worst prognosis. Type 1 involves the tarsometatarsal/naviculocuneiform joints, Type 2 involves hindfoot joints, and Type 3B involves the calcaneal tuberosity.

items.q: A neuropathic diabetic patient undergoes percutaneous triple-hemisection Achilles tendon lengthening (Hoke technique) to offload a recurrent forefoot plantar ulcer. What is the principal complication of overlengthening the tendon?
o: Heel (calcaneal) ulceration from a calcaneus gait
Complete loss of active ankle dorsiflexion
Rupture of the tibialis anterior tendon
items.e: Achilles lengthening reduces forefoot plantar pressure and ulcer recurrence, but overlengthening weakens push-off and produces a calcaneus gait with excessive heel loading, leading to heel ulcers.

items.q: An MRI of a 32-year-old male with chronic medial ankle pain reveals a deep, cup-shaped osteochondral lesion on the posteromedial aspect of the talar dome. This lesion is most likely:
o: Associated with a high ankle sprain
A lateral process fracture of the talus
items.e: Medial osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT) are typically posteromedial, deeper, cup-shaped, and often atraumatic. Lateral lesions are usually anterolateral, shallow/wafer-like, and clearly associated with trauma.

items.q: During ORIF of a calcaneal fracture, which anatomical structure is considered the 'constant fragment' because it remains attached to the talus by the deltoid and interosseous ligaments?
items.e: The sustentaculum tali (superomedial fragment) is known as the 'constant fragment' as it remains attached to the talus via the deltoid and interosseous ligaments. It serves as a stable point for reduction of the other fragments.

items.q: A 40-year-old patient has a Sanders Type IV calcaneal fracture with extreme comminution of the posterior facet. What is the most appropriate primary surgical management according to current consensus?
o: Non-operative management with early range of motion
ORIF via a sinus tarsi approach
Primary subtalar arthrodesis with ORIF to restore calcaneal shape
Percutaneous pinning using the Essex-Lopresti manoeuvre
items.e: Sanders Type IV fractures are highly comminuted (four or more parts) and have poor outcomes with ORIF alone. Primary subtalar arthrodesis, combined with ORIF to restore the height and width of the calcaneal body, is the preferred treatment.

items.q: A 28-year-old male presents with multiple dense bony lumps on his jaw and skull. Radiographs show mature cortical bone lesions. What is the most crucial next step in management to address potential systemic associations?
items.e: Multiple osteomas, especially of the jaw, are a hallmark of Gardner syndrome (FAP). Because colonic polyps in these patients have a near 100% malignant potential, colonoscopy is a vital screening step.

items.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a dull ache in his sacrum that is not significantly relieved by aspirin. CT shows a 2.5 cm expansile lytic lesion with a thin rim of reactive bone and internal mineralisation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Osteoblastoma is histologically similar to osteoid osteoma but is larger (>1.5-2 cm), more common in the spine/sacrum, and typically presents with pain that is less responsive to NSAIDs.

items.q: A 16-year-old boy has a suspicious permeative lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis. After plain radiographs, which investigation is most critical to evaluate for skip lesions and define the anatomic extent for surgical planning?
o: MRI of the whole bone including adjacent joints
items.e: MRI of the whole bone is the investigation of choice to identify skip lesions (discontinuous tumour foci in the same bone) and define soft tissue and marrow involvement before biopsy.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman with a known distal femoral osteochondroma notices that it has continued to enlarge and ache since skeletal maturity. MRI shows a 2.5 cm thick, irregular cartilage cap without destruction of the host bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Growth after skeletal maturity, new pain and a cartilage cap thicker than 2 cm in an adult are red flags for malignant transformation of an osteochondroma into secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma.

items.q: Which mutation is most commonly associated with enchondroma, Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome?
items.e: IDH1/IDH2 mutations are found in enchondromas and the enchondromatoses Ollier/Maffucci, and in about half of central chondrosarcomas.

items.q: A 12‑year‑old boy has a lytic lesion in the proximal epiphysis of the femur showing chondroblast‑like cells on histology. Which of the following is a characteristic genetic abnormality of this tumour?
items.e: Chondroblastoma harbours a H3F3B K36M mutation (formerly H3.3), a hallmark of this tumour.

items.q: On X‑ray a hand lesion shows punctate, popcorn‑like calcification within an intramedullary cavity. The most likely diagnosis is
items.e: The classic “popcorn” stippled calcification is characteristic of intramedullary enchondroma.

items.q: A 45-year-old has an intramedullary cartilage lesion of the proximal femur with ring-and-arc calcification and new pain at rest. Which radiological feature most favours atypical cartilaginous tumour/low-grade chondrosarcoma over enchondroma?
o: Deep endosteal scalloping involving more than two-thirds of cortical thickness
items.e: Deep endosteal scalloping (>2/3 of cortex), cortical breach, periosteal reaction, soft-tissue mass, size >5 cm and pain at rest favour chondrosarcoma; ring-and-arc calcification only indicates a cartilage matrix.

items.q: A 9-year-old presents with a painful thigh swelling, intermittent fever and raised ESR. Radiographs show a permeative lytic lesion of the femoral diaphysis with a large soft-tissue mass. Which small round cell tumour is most likely?
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is the commonest small round cell tumour of bone between 5 and 20 years and often presents with fever, raised ESR and a permeative diaphyseal lesion with a soft-tissue mass. Neuroblastoma metastases occur mostly under 5 years, while lymphoma and myeloma are tumours of adults.

items.q: Which feature distinguishes small cell osteosarcoma from Ewing sarcoma on histology?
items.e: Small cell osteosarcoma produces osteoid; Ewing sarcoma does not, and both may be CD99‑positive.

items.q: A 54-year-old man has a painless, enlarging mass in the posterior thigh. Which ultrasound feature most strongly raises suspicion of a soft-tissue sarcoma requiring referral to a sarcoma centre?
o: Superficial, compressible lesion less than 3 cm
Homogeneous hyperechoic lesion parallel to the skin
Anechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement
Heterogeneous, internally vascular lesion deep to the deep fascia
items.e: Red flags for sarcoma are size >5 cm, location deep to the deep fascia, increasing size, pain and heterogeneous internal vascularity; homogeneous hyperechoic superficial lesions are typical of lipomas and anechoic lesions of cysts.

items.q: A 60-year-old has a deep 15 cm thigh mass. MRI shows a predominantly fatty lesion with thick septa (>2 mm) and non-fatty nodular areas. Which molecular finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Thick septa and nodular non-fatty areas in a large deep fatty mass suggest atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma, confirmed by MDM2 amplification on FISH. FUS-DDIT3 defines myxoid liposarcoma and SS18-SSX synovial sarcoma.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman has a 7 cm calf mass. Biopsy shows an undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma with 22 mitoses per 10 high-power fields and 60% tumour necrosis. What is the FNCLCC histological grade?
o: Cannot be graded without tumour size
items.e: Differentiation score 3 (undifferentiated), mitotic score 3 (20 or more per 10 HPF) and necrosis score 2 (50% or more) total 8; FNCLCC totals of 6-8 are Grade 3. Size is a staging, not grading, parameter.

items.q: After initial ultrasound, which investigation is of choice for local staging of a suspected deep soft-tissue sarcoma of the thigh?
items.e: Contrast-enhanced MRI best defines tumour size, compartment and relationship to neurovascular structures and bone, guiding biopsy and resection; CT chest is used for systemic staging.

items.q: A 6 cm deep thigh mass is suspected to be a sarcoma. Which principle of biopsy is correct?
o: The biopsy should pass through an intermuscular plane to avoid contaminating muscle
The tract should traverse a single compartment in line with the planned resection so it can be excised en bloc
A transverse incision should be preferred for cosmesis
The biopsy is ideally done at the referring hospital before referral to a sarcoma centre
items.e: The biopsy tract is contaminated, so it must traverse a single compartment, avoid neurovascular structures and intermuscular planes, and lie in line with the planned incision so it can be excised en bloc; biopsy should be done at the treating sarcoma centre.

items.q: A 68-year-old man with prostate cancer has thoracic back pain worse at night. AP radiograph shows absence of the left pedicle outline at T7 while the spinous process and right pedicle are preserved. What is this sign called?
items.e: Loss of one pedicle outline on the AP radiograph gives the 'winking owl' sign of spinal metastasis, as deposits in the posterior vertebral body extend into the pedicle. Picture-frame vertebra is seen in Paget disease and rugger-jersey spine in renal osteodystrophy.

items.q: Which of the following is the most common metabolic complication in patients with skeletal metastases?
items.e: Hypercalcaemia, from osteoclastic bone resorption and tumour-secreted PTHrP, occurs in about 10-30% of patients with advanced cancer and is the commonest metabolic complication of bone metastases.

items.q: A 71‑year‑old male presents with painful, weight‑bearing fracture of the distal femur. Imaging shows an expansile, lytic lesion that has eroded the cortex. Which primary tumour is most likely responsible?
items.e: Renal cell carcinoma produces hypervascular, expansile lytic lesions that often present with cortical blow‑out.

items.q: When a metastatic bone lesion is suspected, which laboratory value should be checked to rule out a multiple myeloma masquerading as a solitary metastasis?
o: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains
items.e: Protein electrophoresis with free light chains detects monoclonal gammopathy, distinguishing myeloma from true metastasis.

items.q: Which agent is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL used to reduce skeletal-related events in osteolytic metastases?
items.e: Denosumab binds RANKL and prevents osteoclast formation and activation; zoledronic acid is a bisphosphonate, and teriparatide is contraindicated in skeletal malignancy.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 8 years ago has a solitary painful lytic lesion in the proximal femoral diaphysis with an impending fracture. What should be done before prophylactic fixation?
o: Intramedullary nailing straight away, sending reamings for histology
Radiotherapy to the lesion and observation
Staging investigations and biopsy to confirm metastasis
items.e: A solitary bone lesion, even with a history of carcinoma, may be a primary sarcoma or a second malignancy; staging and biopsy must confirm metastasis before nailing, which would contaminate the whole canal if the lesion were a sarcoma.

items.q: A 16-year-old has a painful distal femoral swelling suspicious for a primary bone sarcoma. What is the correct sequence of investigations?
o: Plain radiographs, MRI of the whole bone, CT chest and bone scan, then biopsy
Plain radiographs, biopsy, MRI, then CT chest
MRI, biopsy, plain radiographs, then CT chest
Biopsy, plain radiographs, MRI, then CT chest
items.e: Staging should be completed before biopsy because biopsy haematoma and oedema distort the MRI; radiographs come first, then MRI of the whole bone, then CT chest and bone scan or PET-CT, and finally biopsy at the treating centre.

items.q: For initial systemic staging of Ewing sarcoma, which investigation is more sensitive than Tc-99m bone scintigraphy for detecting bone metastases?
items.e: FDG PET-CT is more sensitive than bone scintigraphy for osseous metastases in Ewing sarcoma and is used for systemic staging along with CT chest and bone marrow assessment.

items.q: After an open incisional biopsy of a suspected bone sarcoma, if a drain is needed, where should it exit?
o: Through the adjacent joint to decompress haematoma
Through a separate stab incision well away from the wound
Through the opposite compartment of the limb
In line with and close to the end of the biopsy incision
items.e: The drain tract is contaminated by tumour, so it must exit in line with and close to the biopsy incision so it can be excised with the biopsy tract at definitive surgery; meticulous haemostasis reduces the need for a drain.

items.q: The lytic bone lesions of multiple myeloma are most likely to be missed on which investigation?
items.e: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic response, so Tc-99m bone scans are often falsely negative; whole-body low-dose CT, whole-body MRI or PET-CT are recommended instead.

items.q: Which organism is most commonly responsible for acute septic arthritis in an otherwise healthy, sexually active 25-year-old man?
items.e: In sexually active young adults Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the commonest cause of acute septic arthritis, often with migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions.

items.q: Besides Staphylococcus aureus, which organism is classically associated with osteomyelitis and septic arthritis of the sternoclavicular, sacroiliac and pubic symphysis joints in intravenous drug users?
items.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is classically linked to axial osteoarticular infection in IV drug users. Salmonella is associated with sickle cell disease, Pasteurella with animal bites and Eikenella with human bites.

items.q: After removal of an external fixator pin with persistent discharge, a radiograph shows a radiolucent zone surrounding a ring of dense bone around the pin track. This is called:
items.e: A ring sequestrum is an annulus of dead cortical bone around a pin track from thermal necrosis during drilling and infection; it is treated by curettage or over-drilling of the track.

items.q: A 25‑year‑old woman from Delhi presents with a 4‑month history of painless swelling over the right knee, mild pain on movement, and a cold‑looking sinus on the medial side of the joint. X‑ray shows juxta‑articular osteoporosis and marginal erosions but the joint space is still largely preserved. Which laboratory test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
items.e: GeneXpert (CBNAAT) on synovial tissue rapidly detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance, the preferred test for extrapulmonary TB in India.

items.q: A 10-year-old with tuberculosis of the hip in the stage of synovitis will typically show which attitude and limb-length finding?
o: Flexion, adduction, internal rotation with apparent shortening
Flexion, abduction, external rotation with apparent lengthening
Flexion, adduction, internal rotation with true lengthening
Extension, abduction, internal rotation with apparent lengthening
items.e: In the stage of synovitis the hip lies in flexion, abduction and external rotation (maximum capsular volume) with apparent lengthening; in the stages of arthritis it becomes flexion, adduction and internal rotation with apparent and true shortening.

items.q: During first-line antitubercular therapy for spinal tuberculosis, a patient develops drug-induced hepatitis. Which first-line drug is the most hepatotoxic and is usually the last to be reintroduced, or omitted?
items.e: Pyrazinamide carries the highest risk of hepatotoxicity among first-line drugs; after the hepatitis settles, rifampicin and then isoniazid are reintroduced sequentially, while pyrazinamide is often omitted and treatment prolonged.

items.q: In chronic kidney disease‑related bone disorder (renal osteodystrophy) the characteristic laboratory abnormality is:
o: High phosphate, low calcium, very high PTH, low 1,25‑OH₂D
Low phosphate, high calcium, very low PTH, high 1,25‑OH₂D
Low phosphate, low calcium, high PTH, high 1,25‑OH₂D
High phosphate, low calcium, high PTH, high 1,25‑OH₂D
items.e: CKD causes phosphate retention and reduced 1α‑hydroxylase activity, leading to low 1,25‑OH₂D and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: A diabetic patient has a plantar ulcer with surrounding erythema extending 3 cm beyond the ulcer margin and a plantar abscess, but temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and white cell count are normal. What is the IDSA/IWGDF infection severity?
items.e: Infection with erythema more than 2 cm from the ulcer or involving deeper tissues (abscess, osteomyelitis, fasciitis) without systemic inflammatory response signs is moderate (IWGDF grade 3); mild is limited to skin and subcutis with erythema 0.5-2 cm, and severe requires SIRS.

items.q: A diabetic patient is undergoing transmetatarsal amputation for forefoot gangrene. Which additional procedure reduces the risk of late equinus deformity and ulceration at the distal stump?
o: Peroneus longus to peroneus brevis transfer
items.e: Loss of the metatarsal heads shortens the forefoot lever against an intact triceps surae, so equinus and distal stump ulceration are common; tendo-Achilles lengthening or gastrocnemius recession is routinely added.

items.q: After a Chopart (midtarsal) amputation, which soft-tissue balancing is required to prevent equinovarus deformity of the residual hindfoot?
o: Tendo-Achilles lengthening or tenotomy with transfer of tibialis anterior to the talar neck
Peroneus longus tenodesis to the calcaneus
No balancing, as all extrinsic tendon insertions are preserved
items.e: Chopart amputation removes the insertions of the ankle dorsiflexors and evertors, leaving the triceps surae and tibialis posterior unopposed; Achilles lengthening or tenotomy plus reattachment of tibialis anterior to the talar neck prevents equinovarus.

items.q: What is the characteristic late complication of a Syme ankle disarticulation?
o: Painful neuroma of the sural nerve
Posterior and medial migration of the heel pad
Stress fracture of the distal tibia
items.e: Instability and migration of the heel pad off the end of the tibia is the typical complication of Syme amputation; it is reduced by tenodesis of the Achilles tendon or fixing the heel pad to the distal tibia.

items.q: A 24-year-old footballer has persistent anterolateral ankle pain after an inversion sprain. Arthroscopy shows a separate distal fascicle of the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament abrading the anterolateral talar dome. This structure is called:
items.e: Bassett's ligament is an accessory distal fascicle of the AITFL that can impinge on the anterolateral talar dome; Wolin's meniscoid lesion is hyalinised scar tissue in the lateral gutter, and the Stieda process is an elongated posterolateral talar process.

items.q: Long-term follow-up (over 20 years) after tibiotalar arthrodesis most consistently shows:
o: Progressive arthritis of the ipsilateral subtalar and midfoot joints
Late non-union of the fusion in most patients
Recurrent valgus deformity of the knee
items.e: Coester and colleagues showed that after ankle arthrodesis the ipsilateral subtalar and transverse tarsal joints develop progressive arthritis at long-term follow-up because of increased stress on the adjacent joints.

items.q: Compared with open ankle arthrodesis, arthroscopic ankle arthrodesis is least suitable for which patient?
o: A rheumatoid patient with poor-quality skin
A 60-year-old with post-traumatic arthritis and minimal deformity
A patient with severe coronal deformity and major talar bone loss
A diabetic patient with normal foot perfusion
items.e: Arthroscopic arthrodesis gives similar or better union with less wound morbidity and faster recovery, but it cannot correct large coronal deformities or deal with major bone loss, which need an open approach.

items.q: Compared with an anatomic Broström repair, non-anatomic tenodesis procedures for lateral ankle instability that use the peroneus brevis (Watson-Jones, Evans, Chrisman-Snook) are mainly criticised because they:
o: Have a higher rate of recurrent instability in the first year
Restrict subtalar motion and alter hindfoot kinematics
items.e: Non-anatomic tenodeses sacrifice a dynamic evertor and cross the subtalar joint in a non-physiological line, causing subtalar stiffness and altered kinematics, so anatomic repair or reconstruction is preferred.

items.q: On CT, an osteochondral lesion of the talus is completely detached but remains in its bed without displacement. What is its Berndt and Harty stage?
items.e: Berndt and Harty: stage I subchondral compression, II partially detached fragment, III completely detached but non-displaced, IV detached and displaced.

items.q: A 35-year-old falls from a ladder and sustains a displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture. Which associated injury must be specifically excluded?
items.e: Axial loading from a fall causes associated lumbar or thoracolumbar spine fractures in about 10% of calcaneal fractures, and contralateral calcaneal fractures are also common.

items.q: A 30-year-old has lateral midfoot pain after an inversion-plantarflexion twist, with tenderness about 2 cm anterior and inferior to the ATFL just distal to the sinus tarsi. Ankle radiographs are normal. Which injury is most likely being missed?
o: Fracture of the lateral process of the talus
Avulsion fracture of the anterior process of the calcaneus
Fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal
items.e: Anterior process fractures are avulsions by the bifurcate ligament during inversion and plantarflexion; tenderness lies distal to the sinus tarsi and the fracture is best seen on a lateral oblique foot view or CT.

items.q: In Buckley's multicentre RCT of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures, which group of patients did better with non-operative treatment?
o: Patients with a higher initial Böhler angle
items.e: Overall outcomes were similar, but patients receiving workers' compensation did better without surgery, whereas women, younger patients, those with light workloads and less severe fractures did better with ORIF; non-operative patients more often needed late subtalar fusion.

items.q: Night pain relieved by NSAIDs in osteoid osteoma is due to high levels of which mediator produced by the nidus?
items.e: The nidus produces very high levels of prostaglandin E2 (via COX-1 and COX-2) and contains unmyelinated nerve fibres, explaining nocturnal pain that responds dramatically to aspirin and NSAIDs.

items.q: A child with a photosensitive poikilodermatous facial rash, sparse hair, short stature and radial ray defects has a high risk of osteosarcoma. Which gene is mutated?
items.e: Rothmund-Thomson syndrome is caused by RECQL4 helicase mutations and carries a high risk of osteosarcoma; RB1 causes hereditary retinoblastoma, TP53 Li-Fraumeni syndrome and WRN Werner syndrome.

items.q: A radiograph of the forearm shows irregular cortical hyperostosis flowing along one side of the radius into the carpus, resembling wax dripping down a candle. Diagnosis?
items.e: Melorheostosis produces 'dripping candle wax' cortical hyperostosis in a sclerotomal distribution, often with pain, stiffness and soft-tissue contracture; osteopoikilosis gives multiple periarticular bone islands and osteopathia striata linear metaphyseal striations.

items.q: An incidental radiograph shows numerous small, round, symmetric sclerotic foci clustered around the ends of long bones and the pelvis; the patient also has dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata. Which gene is mutated?
items.e: Osteopoikilosis and Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome result from loss-of-function mutations in LEMD3; SOST causes sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease, CLCN7 osteopetrosis, and LRP5 high bone mass or osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.

items.q: A 72-year-old with long-standing polyostotic Paget disease develops new constant pain in the humerus and a rapidly enlarging mass. Radiographs show a destructive lytic area with cortical breach within pagetic bone. Most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Sarcomatous change occurs in under 1% of patients with Paget disease, usually osteosarcoma of the pelvis, femur or humerus, heralded by new pain, a mass and cortical destruction; prognosis is very poor.

items.q: A 20-year-old has a 2 cm surface lesion of the proximal humeral metaphysis with cortical saucerisation, sharp sclerotic buttresses at its margins and chondroid matrix, without perpendicular spiculation. Diagnosis?
items.e: Periosteal chondroma is a small (usually under 3 cm) juxtacortical cartilage tumour that scallops the cortex with well-defined buttresses; periosteal osteosarcoma is larger and diaphyseal with perpendicular spiculation, and an osteochondroma shows medullary continuity.

items.q: A 5-year-old has a hard, painless swelling on the medial ankle. Radiographs show an irregular osteocartilaginous mass arising from the medial half of the talus, with a similar lesion of the medial distal femoral epiphysis on the same side. Diagnosis?
items.e: Trevor disease is an osteochondroma-like overgrowth of an epiphysis or tarsal bone, typically affecting the medial side of one lower limb; hereditary multiple exostoses arise from metaphyses.

items.q: A 35-year-old man has a well-defined lytic lesion of the femoral head epiphysis. Biopsy shows cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, scattered osteoclast-type giant cells and woven bone. Diagnosis and treatment?
o: Clear cell chondrosarcoma; wide en bloc resection
items.e: Clear cell chondrosarcoma is a low-grade epiphyseal chondrosarcoma of adults, most often in the proximal femur, that mimics chondroblastoma; curettage leads to recurrence, so wide en bloc resection is required.

items.q: Secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change is most commonly found in association with which lesion?
items.e: About a third of ABCs are secondary, arising within another lesion, most commonly giant cell tumour, followed by chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma and fibrous dysplasia; secondary ABCs lack the USP6 rearrangement of primary ABC.

items.q: In a randomised trial by Varshney et al., percutaneous sclerotherapy for primary aneurysmal bone cyst achieved healing comparable to intralesional curettage. Which agent was injected?
items.e: Repeated percutaneous polidocanol injection gave healing similar to curettage with less morbidity, making sclerotherapy useful especially for difficult sites such as the pelvis and spine.

items.q: Biopsy of a ground-glass intramedullary femoral lesion shows irregular curvilinear woven-bone trabeculae ('Chinese letters') in a fibrous stroma without osteoblastic rimming. Which mutation is characteristic?
items.e: Fibrous dysplasia is caused by activating GNAS mutations; trabeculae lacking osteoblastic rimming distinguish it from osteofibrous dysplasia, and absence of MDM2 amplification separates it from low-grade central osteosarcoma.

items.q: Ewing sarcoma arising from the soft tissues of the chest wall is eponymously known as:
items.e: Askin tumour is Ewing sarcoma of the thoracopulmonary region carrying the EWSR1 fusion; Codman tumour is an old name for chondroblastoma and Pancoast tumour is an apical lung carcinoma.

items.q: A 3-year-old has periorbital ecchymoses, an abdominal mass and multiple lytic skeletal lesions. Which urine test supports the likely diagnosis?
items.e: Metastatic neuroblastoma, the commonest skeletal metastasis in children under 5, secretes catecholamines whose metabolites VMA and HVA are raised in urine; 'raccoon eyes' reflect orbital metastases.

items.q: A 4-year-old has a limp, night pain and fatigue. Radiographs show transverse radiolucent bands across the metaphyses of the distal femur and proximal tibia. Most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Lucent metaphyseal 'leukaemic lines' with bone pain and constitutional symptoms suggest ALL, which can mimic JIA or osteomyelitis; lead poisoning and osteopetrosis cause dense metaphyseal bands.

items.q: Langerhans cell histiocytosis lesions, including solitary eosinophilic granuloma of bone, most frequently carry which mutation?
items.e: About half of LCH lesions carry BRAF V600E and most others have MAPK-pathway mutations such as MAP2K1, establishing LCH as a myeloid neoplasm; GNAS is fibrous dysplasia and IDH1 enchondroma.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman has a slow-growing, highly vascular deep thigh mass and later develops brain metastases. Histology shows nests of cells with PAS-positive, diastase-resistant crystals. Which genetic alteration is characteristic?
items.e: Alveolar soft part sarcoma has the ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion from der(17)t(X;17), PAS-positive crystals and a tendency for lung and brain metastases; SS18-SSX is synovial sarcoma and EWSR1-ATF1 clear cell sarcoma.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a slowly enlarging multinodular plaque on the trunk. Biopsy shows a storiform CD34-positive spindle cell tumour infiltrating fat in a honeycomb pattern. For unresectable disease, which targeted agent is used?
items.e: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans carries the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion, so unresectable or metastatic disease responds to imatinib, which blocks PDGF receptor signalling; wide or Mohs excision is the primary treatment.

items.q: A 28-year-old has a 2 cm forearm mass that appeared and enlarged over three weeks. Biopsy shows plump fibroblasts in a 'tissue-culture-like' pattern with extravasated red cells and mitoses but no atypia, and a USP6 rearrangement. Diagnosis?
items.e: Nodular fasciitis is a rapidly growing, self-limiting pseudosarcomatous proliferation in young adults driven by MYH9-USP6 fusion; it may regress and simple excision is curative.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with long-standing arm lymphoedema after mastectomy and axillary clearance develops purple nodules on the arm. Likely diagnosis?
items.e: Stewart-Treves syndrome is an angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphoedema, classically after mastectomy; it is aggressive and needs early wide excision or amputation.

items.q: Isolated limb perfusion for unresectable extremity soft-tissue sarcoma, used to permit limb salvage, delivers which combination?
items.e: Hyperthermic isolated limb perfusion with high-dose TNF-alpha and melphalan in a circuit isolated from the systemic circulation can shrink locally advanced extremity sarcomas to allow limb-sparing resection.

items.q: A thigh 'lipoma' was shelled out at a general hospital and histology shows a high-grade sarcoma with involved margins. What is the appropriate next step?
o: Staging, then wide re-excision of the scar and tumour bed at a sarcoma centre
items.e: After an unplanned excision residual tumour is often present, so patients need local and systemic staging followed by wide re-excision of the scar, tracts and tumour bed, usually with radiotherapy, at a sarcoma centre.

items.q: After intramedullary nailing of an impending pathological femoral fracture from breast cancer, what is recommended to reduce local progression and reoperation?
o: Postoperative external beam radiotherapy covering the whole implant
Prophylactic nailing of the contralateral femur
items.e: Postoperative radiotherapy to the whole operative field and implant length reduces tumour progression, fixation failure and reoperation and improves function (Townsend et al.).

items.q: A patient with lung cancer has back pain and new bilateral leg weakness; MRI confirms metastatic spinal cord compression. Which drug should be started immediately?
items.e: High-dose dexamethasone reduces vasogenic cord oedema and is started immediately in metastatic cord compression, followed by definitive surgery and/or radiotherapy.

items.q: According to Gainor and Buchert, pathological fractures from which primary tumour have the lowest likelihood of union?
items.e: Union of pathological fractures was most likely with myeloma and least likely with lung carcinoma, reflecting short survival and tumour biology; union also depends on survival beyond 6 months.

items.q: A Tc-99m bone scan in a man with prostate cancer shows intense, diffuse skeletal uptake with absent renal and bladder activity. This appearance is called:
items.e: A superscan shows diffusely high skeletal uptake with faint or absent kidneys because tracer is avidly taken up by bone; it occurs with diffuse osteoblastic metastases and metabolic bone disease.

items.q: During biopsy of a suspected proximal humeral sarcoma, which route is preferred?
o: Through the anterior third of the deltoid muscle
Through the rotator interval into the joint
items.e: The biopsy should pass through the anterior deltoid so the tract can be excised en bloc with the resection; the deltopectoral interval would contaminate the pectoralis major and cephalic vein, and the joint must not be entered.

items.q: Why does acute haematogenous osteomyelitis of the proximal femur in an infant under 18 months frequently cause septic arthritis and epiphyseal damage?
o: Transphyseal vessels still cross the physis
The periosteum is thick and firmly adherent
The physis is avascular cartilage that infection cannot cross
items.e: Before about 18 months, transphyseal vessels connect the metaphysis and epiphysis, allowing infection into the epiphysis and joint; the intra-articular proximal femoral metaphysis further favours spread to the hip.

items.q: An infant had untreated septic arthritis of the hip. Years later the femoral head and neck are destroyed, leaving a mobile, unstable hip. This sequel is called:
items.e: Tom Smith arthritis is destruction of the femoral head and neck from septic arthritis in infancy, leaving pseudarthrosis and instability; early arthrotomy and antibiotics prevent it.

items.q: A 12-year-old has acute femoral osteomyelitis with severe sepsis, multifocal disease, a large subperiosteal abscess, deep vein thrombosis and septic pulmonary emboli. Which Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor is classically associated with this picture?
items.e: PVL-positive S. aureus, often community-acquired MRSA, causes severe musculoskeletal infection with extensive abscesses, multifocal disease, venous thrombosis and septic emboli, needing aggressive drainage and antibiotics.

items.q: A 30-year-old with active pulmonary tuberculosis develops symmetrical polyarthritis of the knees, ankles and hands. Synovial fluid is sterile with negative AFB and GeneXpert, and the arthritis resolves on antitubercular therapy without joint damage. Diagnosis?
items.e: Poncet disease is a reactive, sterile polyarthritis accompanying active tuberculosis elsewhere; it settles with antitubercular treatment and causes no joint destruction.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a painful, progressively stiff shoulder with marked deltoid wasting, no swelling or abscess, and erosion of the humeral head. Biopsy shows caseating granulomas. This dry form of tuberculous shoulder is called:
items.e: Caries sicca is the dry, atrophic form of shoulder tuberculosis in adults, with pain, stiffness and wasting but no pus or sinus, often ending in fibrous ankylosis.

items.q: In tuberculosis of the upper cervical spine (C1-C3), a cold abscess most commonly presents as:
o: A swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck
A swelling in the supraclavicular fossa
items.e: Cold abscesses from the upper cervical vertebrae collect behind the prevertebral fascia in the retropharyngeal space, causing dysphagia, dyspnoea or a posterior pharyngeal bulge; lower cervical abscesses track to the posterior triangle.

items.q: A child has severe rickets, alopecia, low serum calcium and phosphate and markedly raised serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. What is the defect?
items.e: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 is end-organ resistance from vitamin D receptor mutations, so calcitriol is very high and alopecia is common; type 1 (CYP27B1 deficiency) has low calcitriol and responds to calcitriol.

items.q: Autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets is caused by a mutation that makes which protein resistant to proteolytic cleavage?
items.e: ADHR results from gain-of-function FGF23 mutations at its cleavage site, raising intact FGF23 and causing renal phosphate wasting; XLH is due to PHEX and autosomal recessive forms to DMP1 or ENPP1.

items.q: A child with hypophosphataemic rickets has hypercalciuria, raised serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and low FGF23. Which disorder is this?
items.e: HHRH results from loss of the renal NaPi-IIc cotransporter (SLC34A3); FGF23 is suppressed so calcitriol rises and causes hypercalciuria. It is treated with phosphate alone, as added calcitriol would worsen the hypercalciuria.

items.q: Which biochemical pattern distinguishes X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets from nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets?
o: Low phosphate, normal calcium, normal or mildly raised PTH and inappropriately normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Low calcium, low phosphate, markedly raised PTH and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
High phosphate, low calcium and high PTH
Low alkaline phosphatase with normal phosphate
items.e: In XLH, excess FGF23 causes renal phosphate wasting with normal calcium, near-normal PTH and inappropriately normal calcitriol; nutritional rickets shows low 25(OH)D and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and low ALP suggests hypophosphatasia.

items.q: A 15-month-old fed only boiled milk is irritable, refuses to bear weight and has bleeding gums. Radiographs show a dense metaphyseal line, a lucent band beneath it and a sclerotic ring around the epiphyseal ossification centres. Diagnosis?
items.e: Vitamin C deficiency gives the dense Frankel line, the lucent Trümmerfeld zone, Pelkan spurs and the Wimberger ring around epiphyses, with subperiosteal haemorrhage causing pseudoparalysis.

items.q: A systematic review assessed the diagnostic accuracy of serum cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) for rheumatoid arthritis. The pooled sensitivity was 0.72 and the pooled specificity was 0.68. Which interpretation aligns with these figures?
o: COMP is a highly reliable screening test for RA
COMP should replace anti‑CCP antibodies in diagnosis
COMP provides moderate discrimination but is not definitive
The low specificity indicates a high false‑positive rate beyond acceptable limits
items.e: Sensitivity of 0.72 and specificity of 0.68 mean the test correctly identifies about 72 % of RA cases but misclassifies 32 % of healthy individuals, reflecting moderate accuracy.

items.q: In meta‑analysis, heterogeneity among studies is often quantified by the I² statistic. An I² of 85% indicates:
o: Substantial heterogeneity suggesting differing study effects
items.e: An I² above 75% is generally interpreted as substantial heterogeneity, implying that differences in effect sizes are more likely due to real variation than chance.

items.q: A cohort study reports that patients undergoing total knee replacement have a 5% mortality rate at 30 days, while the matched non‑operative cohort shows 2%. The difference is statistically significant with a p‑value of 0.04. What does this tell us about the operative group's risk?
o: Operative patients have conclusively higher mortality risk
The operative group shows a higher risk but causality cannot be confirmed
Mortality rates are clinically identical despite statistical difference
The 0.04 p‑value indicates no meaningful difference
items.e: A statistically significant p‑value indicates a likely real difference, but cohort studies cannot definitively prove causation.

items.q: A recent RCT compared platelet‑rich plasma (PRP) injections with corticosteroids for Achilles tendinopathy. The 12‑month follow‑up showed no difference in VISA‑Ach score between groups (p=0.73). Which of the following best describes the study’s outcome?
o: There is no evidence of superiority of either treatment
The study was under‑powered to detect a clinically relevant difference
items.e: A p‑value of 0.73 means we cannot reject the null hypothesis; thus neither treatment shows superiority over the other.

items.q: In evidence‑based orthopaedics, the number needed to treat (NNT) for a new ankle‑foot orthosis to prevent one re‑injury over a year is 25. How should a clinician interpret this number?
o: 25 patients must receive the orthosis to reduce one re‑injury
Only 1 in 25 patients will be harmed
The orthosis has a 25% risk of failure
items.e: NNT quantifies how many patients need to be treated to achieve one beneficial outcome; thus 25 patients treated prevent one re‑injury.

items.q: A systematic review pooled data from 10 trials evaluating bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell therapy for cartilage repair. The relative risk of improvement versus control was 1.34 with a 95% CI of 1.01–1.78. What conclusion is appropriate?
o: The therapy offers a small but statistically significant benefit
The CI indicates a lack of precision rendering the result unreliable
items.e: The CI excludes 1, indicating statistical significance; the relative risk >1 gives a modest benefit but not a large reduction.

items.q: A prospective cohort study uses propensity score matching to compare outcomes of surgical fixation versus watchful waiting for occult femoral neck fractures. Which statement best reflects the role of propensity scores?
o: They allow randomization in observational data
They balance measured covariates between groups
They increase the sample size automatically
items.e: Propensity scores match patients on observed characteristics, creating comparable groups in non‑randomised studies.

items.q: An evidence‑based guideline recommends intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures unless the patient has a contraindication. What type of evidence underpins this guideline?
items.e: The recommendation is based on high‑quality Level I randomized trials demonstrating superior union and lower complication rates with IM nailing.

items.q: In a randomized controlled trial comparing two fixation methods for femoral shaft fractures, the investigators reported that 8% of patients in the control group and 3% in the experimental group developed a complication. The absolute risk reduction (ARR) is:
Which of the following statements best describes the role of the Perren strain theory in fracture healing?
o: High interfragmentary strain always promotes union
Low strain (<2%) allows the formation of primary bone
Strain values above 10% are ideal for secondary bone healing
Strain has no influence on bone remodeling once a plate is fixed
items.e: The theory states that strain <2% permits primary union; higher strain favors secondary healing.

items.q: The sample size calculation for a superiority trial requires a power of 80 % and a two‑sided alpha of 0.05. Which of the following is *not* a necessary component of the calculation?
o: Effect size (difference in means or proportions)
Standard deviation or event probability in each arm
items.e: Drop‑out rate is factored in post‑calculation; the core formula uses effect size, variance, alpha, and power.

items.q: In a level‑of‑evidence hierarchy, a systematic review of seven adequately powered randomized controlled trials occupies which level?
items.e: Systematic reviews of RCTs represent the highest evidence level (I).

items.q: A study reports that the sensitivity of serum cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) for early osteoarthritis is 78 %. Specificity is 65 %. Which statistical metric would best describe its overall discriminative ability?
items.e: AUC summarizes diagnostic accuracy independent of disease prevalence.

items.q: A 3‑month post‑operative MRI shows a mean T2 relaxation time of 45 ms in the femoral cartilage beyond the healing plate. According to current consensus, a T2 value above 40 ms suggests:
items.e: Elevated T2 indicates increased water content, correlating with cartilage matrix breakdown.

items.q: When performing a meta‑analysis that includes both randomized and non‑randomized studies, the heterogeneity statistic I² above what threshold typically indicates substantial inconsistency?
items.e: I² >60 % is generally considered substantial heterogeneity.

items.q: In a randomized controlled trial of two bone‑healing augmentations, the investigators used a two‑tailed t‑test with a significance level of 0.05 to compare the union rates. A type I error in this context means:
o: Rejecting the null hypothesis when the hemostatic agent truly increases union rates.
Rejecting the null hypothesis when the augment truly has no effect.
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the augment truly has no effect.
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the augment truly increases union rates.
items.e: A type I error is a false positive – declaring a difference when none exists.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old male presents with a migratory knee pain that has worsened after a recent episode of cellulitis. A serum C‑reactive protein of 120 mg/L is observed. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm septic arthritis?
o: Joint aspiration with Gram stain and culture
items.e: Synovial fluid analysis is the gold standard for septic arthritis; imaging is ancillary.

items.q: A 21‑year‑old runner develops a palpable, firm mass in the paratesticular region. Ultrasound reveals a homogeneous hypoechoic lesion highly vascular on Doppler. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?
items.e: Malignant mixed germ‑cell tumours arise intra‑scrotally; paratesticular masses are usually cysts, sarcomas or benign tumours.

items.q: The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for a knee‑score patient‑reported outcome is 7 points. If you design a trial to detect this MCID with 90 % power at α = 0.05, which of the following sample size formulas is appropriate?
items.e: The standard two‑sided formula: n = [(Zα/2+Zβ)×σ/Δ]² for comparing two means.

items.q: In a prospective cohort study examining postoperative delirium in elderly hip fracture patients, which confounder is most likely to influence both exposure (analgesia type) and outcome?
items.e: Functional status affects analgesic choice and delirium risk; BMI, smoking, and gender are less direct.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old patient has an MRI‑only shoulder arthroscopy set‑up. The operating surgeon prefers a beam‑type imaging system. Which of the following best characterizes the dose‑area product (DAP) for this case?
o: High, because the system uses wide‑beam collimation
Low, because the system is free‑hand and allows minimal exposure
Moderate, as patient distance is fixed but beam focus is narrow
Very high, as MRI generators require strong static fields
items.e: Beam‑type systems produce lower DAP compared with biplanar fluoroscopy when using short‑circuit pathways.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old man presents with painless enlargement of the skull, hearing loss, and a markedly raised serum alkaline phosphatase of 850 IU/L while calcium and phosphate remain normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Elevated ALP with normal calcium and coarse, irregular skull bone appearance are classic for Paget’s disease. Hyperparathyroidism would raise calcium, metastatic disease often shows lytic lesions, and myeloma presents with hypercalcaemia and lytic bone lesions.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman on long‑term alendronate therapy complains of aching thigh pain. Radiographs reveal a focal lesion in the femoral diaphysis with a mixed lytic and sclerotic appearance and a sharply defined zone of transition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Suppressed bone turnover leading to atypical femoral fracture
items.e: Bisphosphonate use is associated with atypical femoral fractures characterised by a transverse, non‑stress fracture with a sclerotic zone of transition. Paget’s presents with enlarged, lytic‑sclerotic lesions but not a transverse fracture. Osteonecrosis and osteosarcoma have different imaging hallmarks.

items.q: Which of the following laboratory findings is most specific for diagnosing active Paget disease of bone?
items.e: Serum alkaline phosphatase is the most reliable marker of disease activity in Paget’s. Calcium and vitamin D remain normal, and while bone resorption markers rise, ALP is the standard screening test.

items.q: A 70‑year‑old man with known Paget disease is being evaluated for a new, painful swelling in the pelvis. Pelvic MRI shows a large, heterogeneous, hyperintense lesion on T2‑weighted images with a well‑defined margin. Which complication is most likely?
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
items.e: The imaging and clinical situation suggest an osteosarcoma arising in Paget’s bone, a recognised malignant transformation. Spinal stenosis and avascular necrosis are indirect complications, and reversible paralysis is not a classic presentation.

items.q: Which of the following is the first‐line pharmacologic treatment for pain and disease progression in Paget disease of bone?
items.e: Zoledronic acid, a potent bisphosphonate, is the preferred agent for controlling pain and halting histologic progression in Paget’s disease. Denosumab is effective but less commonly used.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman presents with foot pain and a history of vitamin D‑deficiency rickets. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is least likely to be present?
items.e: Rickets is characterised by elevated ALP due to increased bone turnover; low calcium, phosphate, and 25‑hydroxy vitamin D are typical. A low ALP would be unexpected.

items.q: In a patient with established Paget disease of bone, the most common clinical complication that can develop over time is:
items.e: Paget’s disease predisposes to debilitating vertebral fractures due to structurally altered bone. While osteosarcoma is a known complication, fractures are far more common.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old man with widespread bone pain and a markedly raised ALP receives a diagnosis of Paget disease. He also reports hearing loss. Which subunit of the bone‑forming osteoblast is primarily responsible for the increased bone turnover seen in this disease?
items.e: RANKL, expressed by osteoblasts and stromal cells, stimulates osteoclast differentiation and activity, driving the high remodeling rate seen in Paget’s disease. DKK1, sclerostin, and PTHrP are involved in other bone disorders.

items.q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for early detection of Paget disease involving the spine?
items.e: Bone scintigraphy shows increased uptake in the disease‑active areas of the spine in early stages, often before lytic or sclerotic changes appear on X‑ray or CT.

items.q: A 47‑year‑old male is crushed by a falling ladder and sustains a comminuted tibial plateau fracture with a prominent fracture fragment displaced into the medial tibial plateau. Which surgical approach gives the best exposure for open reduction and internal fixation while preserving neurovascular integrity?
o: Medial parapatellar approach with short medial incision
Lateral Kocher’s approach with a 10‑cm incision
Anterolateral approach via the extensor compartment
Medial subvastus approach via a short incision over the 1st metatarsal base
items.e: The Medial Parapatellar approach allows direct access to the medial and central plateau, facilitates lag screw placement, and keeps the neurovascular bundles of the popliteal fossa safe.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old female falls from a height and has a right tibial pilon fracture classified as AO type B3. What is the primary determinant for choosing between a primary ORIF and a staged external fixator followed by delayed internal fixation?
o: Patient’s soft‑tissue condition at the time of injury
Degree of axial alignment on the initial X‑ray
Presence of a mid‑posterior tibial plateau depression
Bone mineral density of the tibia
items.e: Soft‑tissue status—particularly swelling and skin tenting—guides the initial decision; a compromised soft‑tissue envelope favors early temporary fixation and delayed definitive ORIF.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a classic feature of a post‑traumatic subtalar arthritis following an intra‑articular pilon fracture?
o: Pain radiating to the proximal tibia
items.e: Pain radiating to the proximal tibia is atypical for subtalar arthritis; the other options describe classic post‑traumatic subtalar pain patterns.

items.q: In a pilon fracture, the ‘pilon sign’ seen on a weight‑bearing ankle radiograph indicates:
o: A bony callus bridging the fracture after initial healing
A high vertical impaction of the tibial plafond into the talus
A comminution of the fibular head extending to the talus
A fracture of the peroneal head protruding into the ankle joint
items.e: The ‘pilon sign’ represents a vertical impaction of the articular surface—typical of a type? pilon fracture—showing the weight of the body forces onto the distal tibial articular cartilage.

items.q: The primary goal of a 90° fixation angle in a tibial plateau fracture is:
o: To distract the fragment and reduce comminution
To provide optimal contact across the articular surface
To maintain the anteroposterior offset of the femorotibial joint
To align the fibular head with the tibial plafond
items.e: A 90° angle of the plate to the tibial shaft maximises contact across the articular surface while providing stable fixation of the plateau fragment.

items.q: A patient with a closed tibial plateau fracture (AO 41-B3) presents with a soft‑tissue blister over the medial malleolus. The best immediate management is:
o: Apply a hinged external fixator and arrange ORIF in 2‑3 weeks
Perform a temporary cast and start antibiotics
Initiate a reverse‑biceps approach with debridement
items.e: Blisters indicate severe swelling; initial temporary external fixation stabilises the fracture while allowing soft‑tissue recovery before definitive ORIF.

items.q: Which implant is preferred for fixation of an osteochondral fracture of the lateral tibial plateau in a young adult with a crush mechanism?
o: Two 3‑mm lag screws placed in an anterior‑posterior direction
A large 6‑mm cannulated screw across the fragment
A 5‑mm quasi‑parallel screw from the medial side
items.e: Two small lag screws placed in an anteroposterior direction provide compression across the cartilage–bone interface while preserving the subchondral bone.

items.q: In the management of a comminuted pilon fracture with a viable soft‑tissue envelope, the medium‑term prognosis (≤2 yrs) is mainly dependent on:
o: The initial fracture displacement in the coronal plane
Whether the articular surface is restored to <2‑mm step off
The size of the fibula shortening
items.e: Restoring the articular surface to <2 mm is crucial for preventing early posttraumatic osteoarthritis—the chief determinant of medium‑term outcome.

items.q: The mechanical axis of a tibial component in a balanced TKA should ideally lie where in relation to the tibial plateau?
o: Through the centre of the medial tibial plateau
Through the centre of the lateral tibial plateau
Through the centre of the tibial plateau (mid‑line)
Through the midpoint of the tibial tubercle
items.e: The goal is neutral mechanical alignment; the tibial component should align the mechanical axis through the centre of the tibial plateau, ensuring equal load distribution on medial and lateral sides.

items.q: During TKA for a fixed flexion deformity, posterior osteophytes are removed and the posterior capsule is released. A residual flexion contracture persists with a tight extension gap but a well-balanced flexion gap. What is the next step?
o: Resect an additional 2 mm of distal femur
Resect additional bone from the posterior femoral condyles
items.e: Distal femoral resection enlarges only the extension gap, correcting a contracture without altering a balanced flexion gap. Posterior condylar resection and increased tibial slope mainly enlarge the flexion gap, and a thicker insert would tighten extension further.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical indicator of a ‘balanced’ knee during a flexion gap assessment in TKA?
o: Equal medial and lateral gap widths at 90° flexion
A 5° gap difference favoring the medial side
A stable gap when varus stress is applied
items.e: A 5° medial bias indicates a lax medial side or over‑resection of the lateral side, implying the gap is not balanced.

items.q: A patient with previous high tibial osteotomy now presents for revision TKA. The surgeon notices significant medial tibial osteophytes and a varus malalignment of 8°. What is the most appropriate first surgical step to achieve proper mechanical alignment?
o: Resect the medial condyle more than the lateral
Use a tibial stem to offset varus
Re‑section the medial tibial plateau to equal tibial slope
items.e: Over‑resection of the medial tibial plateau restores neutral mechanical alignment by removing the varus‑inducing bone and osteophytes.

items.q: Which intra‑operative measurement device is most reliable for confirming neutral mechanical axis in a TKA without computer navigation?
o: A spacer block with pre‑measured dimensions
A graded K-wire placed through the femoral condyles
A calibrated alignment rod through the tibial tubercle
A robotic arm with optical tracking
items.e: A calibrated alignment rod centered on the tibial tubercle and passing through the mid‑line of the tibial plateau is the classic method for checking neutral mechanical axis.

items.q: After a primary TKA, a 72‑year‑old patient reports chronic medial knee pain. Radiographs show a slight medial overhang of the tibial component. What is the most likely cause?
o: Medial tibial component overhang leading to soft‑tissue irritation
items.e: Medial overhang can irritate the medial retinaculum and meniscus, producing chronic medial pain; correcting the component position typically resolves the issue.

items.q: A surgeon chooses a posterior-stabilised TKA in a patient with a deficient posterior cruciate ligament. Which component adjustment best prevents tibial over‑extension and posterior subluxation?
o: Add lateral slope to the tibial component
Insert a larger cam on the femoral component
items.e: A larger femoral cam engages the tibial post throughout the range of motion, preventing posterior subluxation when the PCL is absent.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a painful spinal deformity. Radiographs show a non-structural scoliosis of the lumbar spine. A CT scan reveals a 1.2 cm radiolucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis in the posterior elements of the L3 vertebra. Regarding this condition, where is the lesion typically located in relation to the deformity?
o: On the convex side at the apex of the curve
On the concave side at the apex of the curve
At the base of the curve on the convex side
At the base of the curve on the concave side
items.e: Osteoid osteoma of the spine typically involves the posterior elements and causes a painful, non-structural scoliosis. The lesion is characteristically located on the concave side at the apex of the scoliosis curve.

items.q: Which of the following is considered the most important adverse prognostic factor for a patient newly diagnosed with conventional osteosarcoma of the distal femur?
o: Presence of detectable metastases at diagnosis
Huvos necrosis grade of less than 90%
items.e: According to the prognostic table, the presence of metastases at diagnosis is the most important adverse factor, with 5-year survival dropping to 20-30% compared to 65-70% for localized disease.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a slow-growing, painless mass on the posterior aspect of her distal femur. Radiographs show a dense, lobulated surface mass with a 'string sign' (a radiolucent cleavage line between the tumor and the cortex). Which molecular finding is most characteristic of this lesion?
items.e: The description (posterior distal femur, string sign, low grade) fits parosteal osteosarcoma. Parosteal osteosarcoma and low-grade central osteosarcoma are characterized by MDM2 and CDK4 amplification.

items.q: According to Mankin's principles for the biopsy of musculoskeletal sarcomas, which of the following is a mandatory requirement for a correctly performed biopsy?
o: The biopsy tract must pass through intermuscular planes to avoid muscle damage
The biopsy tract must be placed in line with the planned definitive incision
Drains, if used, should be brought out through a separate stab incision far from the biopsy site
A transverse incision should be used to allow better visualization of neurovascular bundles
items.e: Mankin's rules state that the biopsy tract must be in line with the definitive incision so it can be excised en bloc with the tumor. It should go through a single muscle compartment and avoid intermuscular planes and neurovascular bundles.

items.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a dull ache in his lower back that is poorly responsive to aspirin. Imaging shows a 3 cm expansile lytic lesion in the sacrum with secondary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) changes. Which of the following features most likely distinguishes this from an osteoid osteoma?
o: Location in the posterior elements of the spine
Size of the lesion being greater than 2 cm
items.e: Osteoblastomas are histologically similar to osteoid osteomas but are larger (typically >1.5-2 cm), show progressive growth, and respond poorly to NSAIDs. Both occur in posterior elements and show intense uptake on bone scan.

items.q: A patient with osteosarcoma has completed neoadjuvant chemotherapy and undergone wide resection. The pathologist reports 94% tumor necrosis in the resected specimen. According to the Huvos grading system, this patient is classified as a:
items.e: Huvos Grade III is defined as 90-99% necrosis and Grade IV is 100% necrosis. Both Grade III and IV are considered 'good responders' to chemotherapy.

items.q: A 25-year-old man is found to have multiple dense lamellar bone lesions on his facial bones and skull. Given the association with Gardner syndrome, what is the most appropriate next step in his clinical evaluation?
o: Genetic testing for the RECQL4 gene
Colonoscopy to screen for familial adenomatous polyposis
Evaluation for poikiloderma and radial ray defects
items.e: Multiple osteomas of the jaw or skull are associated with Gardner syndrome (APC gene). Because the associated colonic polyps have near 100% malignant potential, these patients should undergo colonoscopy.

items.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with knee pain and a joint effusion. Radiographs show a well-defined lytic lesion in the distal femoral epiphysis with a thin sclerotic rim. MRI demonstrates extensive marrow and soft tissue oedema surrounding the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Chondroblastoma is a classic epiphyseal lesion in skeletally immature patients (age 10-25). A radiographic hallmark is the thin sclerotic rim, and MRI typically shows extensive perilesional oedema out of proportion to the lesion size.

items.q: In a patient with Hereditary Multiple Exostoses (HME), radiographs show a short ulna, radial bowing, and a dislocated radial head. No osteochondroma is visible at the proximal radius. According to the Masada classification of forearm deformities, this is classified as:
items.e: Masada Type IIb is defined by radial head dislocation secondary to a short ulna (usually due to a distal ulnar lesion) in the absence of a proximal radial osteochondroma.

items.q: According to the WHO 2020 classification of bone tumours, what is the correct terminology for a grade 1 chondrosarcoma located in the femur?
items.e: The WHO 2020 classification uses the term 'atypical cartilaginous tumour (ACT)' for grade 1 cartilage tumours in the appendicular skeleton (long bones of limbs); the term 'grade 1 chondrosarcoma' is reserved for the axial skeleton (pelvis, scapula, skull base).

items.q: Which of the following molecular markers is specifically associated with the diagnosis of chondroblastoma?
items.e: H3F3B K36M (H3.3) is the specific driver mutation for chondroblastoma. EXT1/EXT2 is associated with osteochondroma, IDH mutations with enchondroma/chondrosarcoma, and HEY1-NCOA2 with mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.

items.q: Which radiological feature most strongly suggests a diagnosis of an atypical cartilaginous tumour (ACT) over a solitary enchondroma in the proximal humerus?
o: Endosteal scalloping involving more than two-thirds of the cortical thickness
Lack of a soft tissue mass
items.e: While both can have rings-and-arcs calcification, deep endosteal scalloping (greater than two-thirds of the cortical thickness or length of the lesion) is a key indicator of locally aggressive behavior favoring ACT/chondrosarcoma over enchondroma.

items.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a painful, well-defined lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the proximal femur. He is skeletally mature. Histology reveals clear cells with osteoclast-like giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Clear cell chondrosarcoma is a low-grade malignant subtype that characteristically involves the epiphysis of the proximal femur or proximal humerus in adults (age 25-50). It is considered the adult equivalent/mimic of chondroblastoma.

items.q: A 28-year-old female presents with an eccentric, lytic lesion of the distal radius reaching the subchondral bone. On histology, the lesion contains numerous multinucleated giant cells and mononuclear stromal cells. Which of the following is correct regarding the pathogenesis of this lesion?
o: The multinucleated giant cells are the neoplastic component
The neoplastic cells typically carry an H3F3A G34W mutation
The stromal cells express RANK while giant cells express RANKL
The lesion originates from the diaphysis and migrates to the epiphysis
items.e: In Giant Cell Tumour (GCT), the mononuclear stromal cells are the neoplastic component and express RANKL, which recruits reactive RANK-expressing osteoclast-like giant cells. Over 90% of GCTB cases harbor the H3F3A (H3.3) G34W mutation.

items.q: A 15-year-old presents with an expansile, eccentric 'blow-out' lesion of the proximal tibial metaphysis with multiple fluid-fluid levels on MRI. Which genetic finding would confirm this as a primary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC)?
items.e: Primary ABC is a true neoplasm characterized by USP6 gene rearrangements (commonly CDH11-USP6). Secondary ABCs, which occur within other lesions like GCT, lack this translocation.

items.q: A 30-year-old male is diagnosed with a Campanacci Grade II giant cell tumour of the distal femur. The surgeon considers neoadjuvant denosumab. According to current consensus, why might denosumab be avoided if the lesion is already suitable for curettage?
o: It increases the risk of benign pulmonary implants
It causes immediate malignant transformation to secondary GCT
It leads to a thick sclerotic rim that increases local recurrence after curettage
It is only FDA approved for skeletally immature patients
items.e: Denosumab promotes significant bone formation and a thick sclerotic rim. This makes it difficult to define the tumor margins during curettage and can hide residual neoplastic stromal cells, leading to higher local recurrence rates.

items.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a well-defined, geographic lytic lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis that has a thin sclerotic rim. Using the Lodwick classification, this margin is classified as:
items.e: Lodwick Grade IA represents a geographic lesion with a well-defined, sclerotic rim, indicating a slow-growing, benign process like a Non-Ossifying Fibroma (NOF) or Simple Bone Cyst (UBC).

items.q: A 32-year-old male presents with a multiloculated 'soap-bubble' lytic lesion in the anterior cortex of the tibial diaphysis. Biopsy reveals epithelial nests in a fibro-osseous stroma that stain positive for keratin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant lesion typically found in the anterior tibial diaphysis of adults. It is distinguished from osteofibrous dysplasia by the presence of keratin-positive epithelial nests.

items.q: A 3-year-old child presents with irritability, a palpable abdominal mass, and symmetric permeative lytic lesions in the metaphyses of both distal femurs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: In children under 5 years, metastatic neuroblastoma is the most common cause of bone metastases, often presenting with an adrenal mass and symmetric metaphyseal involvement. Ewing sarcoma peak incidence is in the second decade (10-20 years).

items.q: A 14-year-old male presents with a painful diaphyseal lesion of the femur. Biopsy reveals sheets of small round blue cells that are PAS positive and show strong membranous staining for CD99. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most likely to be found?
items.e: The clinical and immunohistochemical profile (CD99 positive, PAS positive) describes Ewing sarcoma. Its genetic hallmark is the t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation, resulting in the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion transcript in over 90% of cases.

items.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with thigh pain, a tender mass, and a low-grade fever. Radiographs show a permeative lytic lesion in the femoral diaphysis with lamellated 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction. Laboratory studies show an elevated ESR and white blood cell count. What is the most likely prognostic factor for this patient?
o: The specific type of EWSR1 fusion transcript
items.e: The clinical picture is classic for Ewing sarcoma. The presence of detectable metastases at diagnosis (found in 20-25% of patients) is the most important adverse prognostic factor.

items.q: A 52-year-old male presents with a large soft-tissue mass surrounding the humerus. Radiographs show a permeative pattern with minimal periosteal reaction, but MRI shows extensive marrow replacement. Biopsy shows the cells are CD45 and CD20 positive. What is the most appropriate definitive management for the primary lesion?
o: En bloc wide resection with endoprosthetic replacement
Amputation at the level of the surgical neck
High-dose radiotherapy (60 Gy) as the sole treatment
items.e: The patient has primary lymphoma of bone (adult, CD20/CD45 positive, minimal periosteal reaction). Surgery has no role in tumour removal for lymphoma; management is chemotherapy (R-CHOP) often followed by consolidation radiotherapy.

items.q: A 65-year-old male with known multiple myeloma presents with severe back pain. A technetium-99m bone scan is performed and shows no increased uptake in the spine despite radiographic evidence of multiple 'punched-out' lytic lesions. What is the underlying mechanism for this 'cold' bone scan?
o: The lesions are located in areas of low blood flow
Tumour cells secrete DKK1 and sclerostin which suppress osteoblasts
Myeloma cells primarily activate the RANKL pathway in osteocytes
items.e: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic and often appear 'cold' on bone scans because there is a lack of osteoblastic activity. Myeloma cells secrete DKK1 and sclerostin, which suppress osteoblasts, preventing the reactive bone formation required for bone scan uptake.

items.q: Which of the following is the current standard chemotherapy regimen for localized Ewing sarcoma, based on the COG AEWS0031 and Euro Ewing 2012 trials?
o: Vincristine, Doxorubicin, and Cyclophosphamide (VDC) every 3 weeks
Interval-compressed VDC alternating with Ifosfamide and Etoposide (IE) every 2 weeks
VIDE (Vincristine, Ifosfamide, Doxorubicin, Etoposide) for 6 cycles
Vincristine, Actinomycin D, and Cyclophosphamide (VAC) for 9 months
items.e: The North American COG AEWS0031 and European Euro Ewing 2012 trials established that interval-compressed VDC/IE (given every 2 weeks) is superior to 3-week cycles and VIDE induction, showing better event-free survival.

items.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with proptosis and periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'). Evaluation reveals an abdominal mass and elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). If bone marrow biopsy shows small round cells with Homer Wright rosettes, which genetic finding is associated with a poor prognosis?
items.e: The clinical features (raccoon eyes, VMA, rosettes) indicate neuroblastoma. MYCN amplification is a well-known genetic marker associated with a poor prognosis in neuroblastoma.

items.q: Regarding local control in Ewing sarcoma, which of the following statements is true?
o: Definitive radiotherapy is preferred over surgery for all pelvic tumours
Surgery is preferred when a wide margin can be achieved with acceptable function
Postoperative radiotherapy is only indicated if there is a good histological response
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is radiosensitive, but surgery is preferred for local control when a wide margin is achievable because it typically yields lower local recurrence rates and avoids the late risks of radiation, such as secondary sarcomas.

items.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly enlarging mass in the forearm. Histology reveals a malignant mesenchymal tumour. According to the source notes, what is the most common histological subtype of soft-tissue sarcoma in the paediatric age group?
items.e: In children, the commonest soft-tissue sarcoma (STS) is rhabdomyosarcoma. In contrast, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) and liposarcoma are the most common subtypes in the adult population.

items.q: In the transition from the AJCC 7th to the 8th edition staging system for soft-tissue sarcomas of the trunk and extremities, which of the following parameters was removed from the T-staging criteria?
o: Presence of regional lymph node metastasis
items.e: Tumour depth (superficial vs deep) was removed from the AJCC 8th edition staging for trunk and extremity sarcomas, although it remains a prognostic factor and a clinical 'red flag'.

items.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a painful mass in the popliteal fossa. Radiographs show faint stippled calcification within the soft tissue. Biopsy reveals a translocation t(X;18)(p11;q11). Which of the following is a characteristic feature of this tumour?
o: It is frequently intra-articular in location
It is associated with a high rate of regional lymph node metastasis
It is highly resistant to ifosfamide-based chemotherapy
It is the most common soft-tissue sarcoma in patients over 60 years
items.e: Synovial sarcoma is part of the 'SCARE' mnemonic (Synovial, Clear cell, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, Epithelioid) for sarcomas with a higher propensity for lymph node metastasis. Despite its name, it is rarely intra-articular.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with a 4 cm, asymptomatic desmoid-type fibromatosis in the deltoid muscle. According to the 2020 global consensus (Desmoid Tumor Working Group), what is the recommended first-line approach?
o: Wide local excision with 2 cm margins
items.e: The 2020 global consensus recommends active surveillance as the first-line management for most asymptomatic or non-threatening desmoid tumours, as many stabilize or regress spontaneously.
