items.q: In glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, the randomised trial by Saag et al. (NEJM 2007) comparing teriparatide with alendronate showed that teriparatide:
o: Produced greater BMD gains and fewer new vertebral fractures
items.e: Glucocorticoids mainly suppress bone formation, so the anabolic agent teriparatide outperformed alendronate in BMD gain and vertebral fracture reduction; oral bisphosphonates remain first-line for most patients.

items.q: The International Osteoporosis Foundation recommends which pair of bone turnover markers as reference markers?
items.e: Serum C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX, resorption) and procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (P1NP, formation) are the reference markers, useful for monitoring treatment adherence and response.

items.q: Zoledronic acid 5 mg for osteoporosis is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is below:
items.e: Zoledronate and oral bisphosphonates are not recommended below a creatinine clearance of 30–35 mL/min because of nephrotoxicity and possible adynamic bone; denosumab can be used with careful calcium monitoring.

items.q: The most important early adverse effect to monitor when giving denosumab to a patient with advanced chronic kidney disease is:
items.e: Denosumab is not renally cleared, but severe and occasionally fatal hypocalcaemia can occur in advanced CKD, so calcium and vitamin D must be replete and calcium checked in the first weeks.

items.q: Oral alendronate should be taken:
o: After an overnight fast with plain water, remaining upright for at least 30 minutes before food
With orange juice to improve absorption
items.e: Bisphosphonate absorption is under 1% and is abolished by food, calcium and drinks other than water; staying upright reduces oesophagitis.

items.q: A 25-year-old woman has wrist pain; MRI shows osteonecrosis of the entire scaphoid with no history of fracture. This idiopathic condition is called:
items.e: Preiser disease is non-traumatic avascular necrosis of the scaphoid; Kienböck affects the lunate, Freiberg the second metatarsal head and Köhler the navicular in children.

items.q: A 15-year-old girl has forefoot pain; radiographs show flattening and sclerosis of the second metatarsal head. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Freiberg infraction is osteonecrosis of the (usually second) metatarsal head, most often in adolescent girls, linked to a long second ray and repetitive loading; most respond to offloading.

items.q: A commercial diver has shoulder pain; radiographs show juxta-articular osteonecrosis of the humeral head. The underlying mechanism of dysbaric osteonecrosis is:
o: Nitrogen bubble formation occluding intraosseous vessels during decompression
items.e: In Caisson disease, nitrogen dissolved in fatty marrow forms bubbles on rapid decompression, occluding vessels; the humeral head, femoral head and distal femur are typical sites.

items.q: Six weeks after starting antitubercular therapy for spinal TB with good compliance, an HIV-negative patient's paravertebral cold abscess enlarges while he feels systemically better. GeneXpert showed rifampicin-sensitive disease. The most likely explanation is:
items.e: A paradoxical reaction (transient worsening of lesions after starting ATT due to immune recovery) is common in osteoarticular TB; ATT is continued, with drainage or steroids if needed, after excluding resistance and non-compliance.

items.q: In a diabetic foot, which MRI finding favours osteomyelitis over an acute Charcot neuroarthropathy?
o: Periarticular marrow oedema centred on the tarsometatarsal joints
The 'ghost sign': bone outline lost on T1 but reappearing after contrast
items.e: In osteomyelitis the infected bone appears to vanish on T1 and reappears on post-contrast or T2 images (ghost sign), usually adjacent to an ulcer; Charcot changes are periarticular, midfoot-centred and not contiguous with an ulcer.

items.q: Which first-line antitubercular drug commonly causes hyperuricaemia and may precipitate gout?
items.e: Pyrazinamide (via pyrazinoic acid) reduces renal urate excretion and frequently raises serum urate; ethambutol has a lesser effect, and both are causes of drug-induced gout.

items.q: In infants with rickets, radiographic changes are best seen at which site?
items.e: The fastest-growing metaphyses show the changes best: the wrist (distal ulna and radius) in infants and the knee in older children, with cupping, fraying, splaying and widened physes.

items.q: A 2-year-old has severe rickets and total alopecia. Calcium is low, 25(OH)D normal and 1,25(OH)2D markedly raised. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: End-organ resistance from vitamin D receptor mutations (VDDR type 2A) gives very high 1,25(OH)2D, and alopecia marks more severe forms; treatment needs very high-dose calcitriol and calcium, sometimes IV.

items.q: In uncomplicated acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children, randomised evidence (Peltola) supports a total antibiotic course of about:
o: 3 weeks with early switch to oral therapy
items.e: Short IV therapy (2–4 days) followed by oral antibiotics for a total of about 20 days was as effective as 30 days for culture-positive childhood osteomyelitis, provided clinical response and CRP normalise.

items.q: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children most commonly begins in the metaphysis because:
o: Sluggish flow in looping sinusoidal vessels and relative lack of phagocytes favour bacterial settling
The physis is the primary site of entry
Periosteum is absent at the metaphysis
items.e: Terminal metaphyseal capillaries loop into large venous sinusoids with slow turbulent flow and few phagocytes, so blood-borne bacteria settle there, often after minor trauma.

items.q: A child with sickle cell disease has a painful swollen limb with fever. Which feature most helps distinguish osteomyelitis from a bone infarct (vaso-occlusive crisis)?
o: Subperiosteal fluid on ultrasound at presentation
Persistent fever with rising CRP and a positive blood culture
items.e: Infarction is far more common than infection; persistent high fever, rising inflammatory markers and positive cultures favour osteomyelitis (Salmonella or S. aureus), while imaging alone overlaps considerably.

items.q: Teriparatide carries a historical labelling warning (since removed by the FDA in 2020) because in rats it caused:
items.e: High-dose lifelong teriparatide caused osteosarcoma in rats, so it is avoided in patients with increased baseline risk (Paget disease, unexplained raised ALP, open epiphyses, prior skeletal radiation).

items.q: Romosozumab, a sclerostin antibody, carries a warning to avoid it in patients who in the past year have had:
items.e: In the ARCH trial romosozumab had more serious cardiovascular events than alendronate, so it should not be started within a year of MI or stroke; it is given monthly for 12 months, then an antiresorptive.

items.q: A 24‑year‑old vegetarian woman presents with knee pain and a radiological ‘subchondral sclerosis’ of the femoral condyles. Serum calcium is 9.5 mg/dL, phosphate 2.4 mg/dL, 25‑OH vitamin D 28 ng/mL. Which of the following best explains her metabolic bone disorder?
o: Hypophosphataemic osteomalacia due to dietary deficiency
items.e: The low phosphate and near‑normal calcium with mild vitamin D insufficiency in a vegetarian points to osteomalacia from dietary phosphorus/ vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D‑resistance rickets would show elevated 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia.

items.q: A 66‑year‑old woman on long‑term alendronate therapy presents with a subtrochanteric fracture after a low‑energy fall. Which underlying metabolic abnormality is most likely contributing to this fracture pattern?
o: Osteoclast hyperactivity due to bisphosphonate non‑compliance
Age‑related decreased bone turnover leading to micro‑damage accumulation
items.e: Bisphosphonates suppress bone turnover; over time, micro‑damage accumulates, especially in the subtrochanteric region, predisposing to atypical fractures. The other options describe secondary causes not linked to bisphosphonate treatment.

items.q: A 48‑year‑old man with chronic kidney disease on haemodialysis presents with pain in the humerus. Radiographs show subperiosteal bone resorption in the radial aspects of the middle phalanges and scalloping of the cortical bone of the radius. Which metabolic disturbance is this classic radiographic sign most associated with?
o: Hypovitaminosis D from insufficient sun exposure
items.e: Subperiosteal resorption along radial aspects of phalanges and cortical scalloping are classic for secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD, reflecting bone over‑resorption by PTH.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old man with a history of long‑term corticosteroid use complains of progressive hip pain. MRI shows a subchondral bone marrow edema and a focal cortical thinning on the femoral head with a well‑defined sclerotic border. Which of the following diagnoses is least likely?
o: Steroid‑induced avascular necrosis of the femoral head
items.e: Paget disease involves widespread lytic‑blastic activity and usually affects the pelvis and long bones, not a focal femoral head lesion in a steroid user. The other three are common in this context.

items.q: A 52‑year‑old woman with untreated hyperparathyroidism demonstrates a classic ‘salt and pepper’ appearance of the skull and a ‘floating’ vertebral body on spine radiographs. Which of the following laboratory findings would most likely be present?
o: High serum calcium and low phosphate
Low serum calcium and high phosphate
Normal calcium, high alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate
items.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism raises serum calcium and lowers phosphate due to PTH‑mediated phosphaturia. The classical radiologic picture reflects bone turnover changes.

items.q: In a patient with Paget disease of bone treated with zoledronic acid, which of the following adverse effects would most strongly warrant monitoring of serum calcium?
o: Hypocalcaemia due to oversuppression of bone resorption
items.e: Zoledronic acid can cause transient hypocalcaemia by inhibiting osteoclasts; close monitoring of serum calcium is advised. Osteonecrosis and fractures are clinical concerns but not calcium‑related.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman presents with pain in the left hip, claudication for 1 year, and a humeral “boxing‑glove” hand. Radiographs reveal lytic lesions in the tibia and a diffuse osteopenia on the pelvis. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to stage the disease?
items.e: Tc‑99m bone scan is the gold standard for detecting and staging Paget’s disease due to its sensitivity for high bone turnover.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding teriparatide therapy in a patient with metastatic bone disease is true?
o: It should be given continuously for 24 months
Contraindicated in patients with a history of osteosarcoma
Is effective in treating spinal cord compression
items.e: Teriparatide is contraindicated in any patient with a history of primary bone tumour such as osteosarcoma because it is an anabolic agent that may stimulate tumour growth.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man with chronic renal failure and secondary hyperparathyroidism develops a bone pain crisis. His serum calcium is 9.6 mg/dL, phosphate 5.2 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 980 IU/L. Which of the following is the best initial step?
items.e: CALCIMIMETICS lower PTH and reduce bone turnover; they are first‑line for secondary hyperparathyroidism in kidney failure.

items.q: A 22‑year‑old patient sustains an OTA 43‑P2 tibial pilon fracture (Pauwels type III). After initial debridement, the most appropriate next step to optimize articular congruity is:
o: Perform an open reduction and internal fixation with a medial buttress plate
Perform a closed reduction and cast immobilisation
items.e: Pauwels type III pilon fractures need stable articular surface restoration; an open‑reduction internal fixation with a medial buttress plate provides optimal support and alignment.

items.q: Which of the following is the investigation of choice for assessing articular step‑off >2 mm in a tibial plateau fracture?
items.e: CT with thin slices accurately quantifies articular step‑off and is the preferred imaging for surgical planning of tibial plateau fractures.

items.q: A 19‑year‑old male falls from a height and sustains a bicondylar tibial plateau fracture with dorsal rim deficiency seen on CT. What intra‑operative imaging is most useful to confirm reduction?
items.e: Both AP and lateral fluoroscopic views are required intra‑operatively to verify articular congruity and varus/valgus alignment in bicondylar plateau fractures.

items.q: Posterior tibial plateau fractures with a step‑off >4 mm often require which additional material to restore articular surface?
items.e: Orthopaedic guidelines recommend autologous bone graft for large articular voids (>4 mm) in posterior plateau fractures to achieve stable fixation and prevent collapse.

items.q: A 27‑year‑old patient with a tibial plateau fracture involving the medial condyle (Schatzker IV) also has a 3 cm tibial cortical defect post‑debridement. The most appropriate method to manage the defect is:
o: Internal fixation with a bone plate and osteotomy
Metaphyseal bone grafting with a structural allograft
items.e: A structural allograft fills large metaphyseal defects and provides immediate load transfer when internal fixation is stable.

items.q: In an OTA 43‑P1 eminence fracture of the tibial articular surface, the preferred fixation device is:
items.e: Headless compression screws provide compression across the fracture line without a prominent head, suitable for intra‑articular eminence fractures.

items.q: The 'hinge' construct in high‑energy tibial pilon fractures is primarily designed to allow:
o: Early motion while protecting the articular surface
items.e: Hinge fixation permits controlled axial loading and early motion while protecting the fractured articular surface during healing.

items.q: After a road‑traffic accident, a 38‑year‑old male has a burst fracture at L2 with 40% loss of anterior vertebral body height. Plain radiographs show the fracture cleft filled with loose bone fragments. Which part of the Denis three‑column model is most likely disrupted?
o: All three columns are always involved in burst fractures
items.e: Mid‑column disruption is typical of burst fractures; the anterior column is also often compromised but the question asks for the most likely.

items.q: In the 'middle path regimen' for spinal tuberculosis proposed by the Indian Academy of Neurology, the decision to operate is primarily based on
o: Extent of kyphosis >30° irrespective of symptoms
items.e: Surgery is reserved for those with neurologic compromise or risk of paralysis, not merely for deformity or abscess size.

items.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate first‑line antitubercular regimen for a patient with confirmed spinal TB not yet on therapy?
o: HRZE for 2 months followed by HR for 10 months
items.e: The standard 2‑month intensive phase with HRZE, then 10 months of HR, totals 12 months and is evidence‑based.

items.q: A CT scan of the thoracic spine in a suspected case of skeletal TB shows the classic ‘Rahman sign’. Which structure is involved?
o: Antero‑posterior shift of the vertebral body
A sparing of the disc space with vertebral body destruction
Circumferential destruction with no disc involvement
items.e: The Rahman sign describes caseating vertebral bodies with relatively preserved disc spaces, typical of TB.

items.q: The most common site of spinal tuberculosis in patients from high‑prevalence areas is
items.e: The thoracic spine is affected in about 55–70 % of spinal TB cases.

items.q: In spinal tuberculosis, the most common location of vertebral involvement is:
items.e: The majority of spinal TB lesions affect the thoracic vertebrae, particularly the thoracolumbar junction (T11–L1).

items.q: According to the Pott's disease classification, a single vertebral body destroyed by TB with < 50% collapse and no kyphosis is?
items.e: Grade 1 disease involves single vertebra with mild destruction, < 50% collapse and no significant deformity.

items.q: In the WHO guidelines for multidrug‑resistant TB treatment, the first injectable agent of choice is:
items.e: Amikacin is preferred as the first‑line injectables in MDR‑TB because of its higher efficacy and lower ototoxicity compared to capreomycin, kanamycin, or streptomycin.

items.q: The most sensitive imaging modality for early vertebral infection in a child is:
items.e: MRI detects bone marrow edema and early abscesses before x‑ray changes appear, making it the gold standard for early spinal infection in children.

items.q: Which organism is most commonly isolated from an abscess in spinal TB?
items.e: The abscess fluid in spinal TB is almost always due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis; bacterial abscesses are atypical.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old male with Pott’s spine presents with a cold abscess in the anterior chest wall. The most appropriate drainage technique is:
items.e: Ultrasound‑guided needle aspiration is minimally invasive, effective for cold abscesses, and preserves the posterior spinal column.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognised indication for early surgery in spinal TB?
items.e: Early surgery is indicated for neuro deficit, progressive deformity or large abscess; mild pain alone does not warrant surgery.

items.q: The ‘modified British Society for Research on Spinal TB (BST) score’ considers which factor as most critical for predicting residual kyphosis?
items.e: Pre‑operative kyphosis angle is the strongest predictor of post‑treatment residual deformity in the BST scoring system.

items.q: Under India's NTEP, a CBNAAT (GeneXpert/Truenat) test on tissue from suspected spinal tuberculosis detects resistance to which drug, used as the surrogate marker for MDR-TB?
items.e: CBNAAT detects M. tuberculosis and rpoB mutations conferring rifampicin resistance; rifampicin resistance is taken as a surrogate for MDR-TB and changes the regimen, while isoniazid resistance needs a line probe assay.

items.q: In a balanced TKA, the mechanical axis of the tibial component should lie relative to the distal tibial joint line how?
o: 0.5 mm lateral to the tibial plateau mid‑line
1 mm medial to the tibial plateau mid‑line
2 mm medial to the tibial plateau mid‑line
Right on the tibial plateau mid‑line
items.e: The tibial component is ideally positioned along the mechanical axis, i.e., on the plateau’s mid‑line to avoid varus/valgus imbalance.

items.q: The mechanical axis of a balanced knee after TKA should ideally lie in which of the following locations?
o: 3 mm medial to the tibial plateau mid‑line
3 mm lateral to the tibial plateau mid‑line
5 mm lateral to the tibial plateau mid‑line
items.e: A balanced knee requires the tibial component to align with the mechanical axis, i.e., the tibial plateau mid‑line.

items.q: Regarding tibial component alignment, which of the following statements is correct?
o: An 8° opening angle in a medial opening‑wedge HTO places the tibial component in slight deep flexion
A neutral mechanical axis alignment ensures a 5° external rotation of the tibial component
A varus bias of 2° is recommended for knees with pre‑operative valgus deformity
The tibial component should be placed 5 mm distal to the joint line to avoid tibial slope correction
items.e: A 2° varus bias in the tibial component helps neutralise a pre‑existing valgus knee, improving weight distribution.

items.q: Which of the following is a key surgical principle for achieving a balanced knee in TKA?
o: Use intraoperative skin tension as a guide
Preserve the posterior cruciate ligament if possible
Perform the femoral cut only after the tibial cut
Reconstruct the medial collateral ligament in all patients
items.e: Preserving the PCL (in a PCL‑retaining TKA) allows the knee to regain its natural kinematics and aids in achieving balance.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a varus MADT of 12° undergoes a conventional TKA. In the femoral component positioning, the goal is to balance the flexion and extension gaps with a 3‑mm posterior condylar offset. Which of the following statements about the posterior condylar axis (PCA) is true?
o: The PCA should be placed 3° distal to the joint line
The PCA is most reliably identified on a lateral radiograph of the knee in full extension
The PCA is parallel to the line of the posterior femoral condyles in 90° flexion
The PCA is used to set the rotation of the tibial component
items.e: The PCA is defined by the posterior femoral condyles in 90° flexion; a 3‑mm offset is restored by aligning the femoral component so that the flexion and extension gaps are equal in 3‑mm increments.

items.q: A 76‑year‑old man undergoes a re‑TKA after a septic loosening of the tibial component. During the operation, the surgeon uses a computer navigation system to restore mechanical alignment. Which of the following is a potential pitfall that can still lead to a gap imbalance despite navigation?
o: Inaccurate placement of the reference marker on the tibial plateau
Over‑resection of the medial tibial plateau
items.e: Navigation only corrects bone cuts; if the reference marker is misplaced, the entire navigation axis becomes erroneous, leading to a misaligned component and gap imbalance.

items.q: In a patient with a 10° valgus deformity, the surgeon performs an opening‑wedge high tibial osteotomy and subsequently plans a TKA. What intra‑operative bone cut is critical to preserve the mechanical axis while maintaining soft‑tissue balance?
o: Performing the osteotomy on the medial side by 5 mm
Adding a 4° posterior slope on the tibial plateau
Making a 7° distal rotation of the femoral component
Closing the tibial plate to exact 5° of valgus
items.e: A medial opening‑wedge by ~5 mm restores the mechanical axis to neutral; this length is chosen to compensate for the valgus deformity while keeping soft tissues intact.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman has a patellar clunk syndrome 18 months after a CR TKA. Pre‑operative imaging shows a well‑aligned implant. Which intra‑operative action is most likely to have caused the clunk?
o: Over‑tightening of the patellar tendon slackness
Inadequate patellar resurfacing with a low‑profile component
items.e: An inadequate patellar resurfacing with a low‑profile component allows the patella to impinge on the intercondylar notch during flexion, producing the clunk syndrome.

items.q: In a patient with a bent withdrawal ligament, the surgeon chooses a PS TKA instead of a CR design. What intra‑operative observation confirms the need for a PS implant?
o: A posterior pivot of the femur during flexion
Loss of extension due to a stiff posterior capsule
A tight medial collateral ligament in flexion
A high posterior tibial slope of 12°
items.e: The necessity of a PS implant is confirmed when the posterior cruciate is torn or associated with tibial plateau imbalance, leading to a posterior pivot that needs a cam‑post mechanism.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman has a painless hard swelling behind the knee. Radiographs show a lobulated mass, densely ossified centrally, on the posterior surface of the distal femoral metaphysis, separated from the cortex by a thin radiolucent line. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Parosteal osteosarcoma is a low-grade surface osteosarcoma of young adults that classically involves the posterior distal femur, with dense central ossification and a 'string sign' cleavage plane; myositis ossificans matures peripherally rather than centrally.

items.q: Periosteal osteosarcoma, an intermediate-grade surface tumour of the tibial or femoral diaphysis, shows which predominant histological pattern?
items.e: Periosteal osteosarcoma is predominantly chondroblastic, arising on the diaphyseal surface with perpendicular 'sunburst' spiculation and Codman triangles.

items.q: A high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femur has broken through the cortex into the surrounding soft tissue. There are no metastases. What is the Enneking (MSTS) stage?
items.e: Enneking stage II means high grade, and B means extracompartmental extension; stage III requires metastasis.

items.q: During open biopsy of a lytic bone lesion, the cortical window should be made in which shape to reduce the risk of fracture?
o: A line of multiple small drill holes
items.e: An oval window with rounded ends minimises stress concentration; the defect may be plugged with cement or haemostatic material to limit haematoma spread.

items.q: A metastatic deposit in the phalanx of a finger (acral metastasis) most commonly arises from which primary?
items.e: Metastases distal to the elbow and knee are rare, and lung carcinoma is the commonest primary, probably because tumour emboli enter the systemic arterial circulation directly.

items.q: Which lesion typically appears purely lytic on radiographs and may be 'cold' on technetium bone scan, so that a skeletal survey or MRI is preferred?
items.e: Myeloma suppresses osteoblast activity, so lytic lesions show little tracer uptake; prostate and carcinoid deposits are typically osteoblastic.

items.q: A patient with a spinal metastasis has a Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) of 9. How is this classified?
items.e: SINS 0-6 is stable, 7-12 potentially unstable and 13-18 unstable; a score of 7 or more warrants surgical consultation.

items.q: Which prognostic scoring system for spinal metastases includes the patient's Karnofsky performance status?
items.e: The revised Tokuhashi score includes general condition (KPS), number of spinal and extraspinal bone metastases, visceral metastases, primary site and neurology; the Tomita score uses only primary tumour growth rate, visceral metastases and bone metastases.

items.q: In Campanacci radiographic grading of giant cell tumour, grade III means:
o: Indistinct borders with cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension
Well-defined margin with an intact sclerotic rim
items.e: Campanacci grades are I (latent, well-marginated), II (active, thinned expanded cortex) and III (aggressive, cortical breach with soft-tissue mass).

items.q: The commonest translocation in CIC-rearranged undifferentiated round cell sarcoma, an Ewing-like tumour with a worse prognosis, is:
items.e: CIC-DUX4 sarcoma most often carries t(4;19), and less often t(10;19); t(11;22) is Ewing sarcoma, t(X;18) synovial sarcoma and t(2;13) alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

items.q: A large, deep fatty mass in the thigh has thick septa. Which test best distinguishes atypical lipomatous tumour from benign lipoma?
items.e: Atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma has MDM2 (12q15) amplification, which lipomas lack; t(12;16) defines myxoid liposarcoma.

items.q: A midline sacral tumour in a 60-year-old shows physaliphorous cells in a myxoid matrix. Which nuclear immunostain confirms the diagnosis?
items.e: Nuclear brachyury expression is specific for notochordal tumours and confirms chordoma, which is treated by en bloc resection, often with high-dose particle radiotherapy.

items.q: Diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumour (pigmented villonodular synovitis) is driven by overexpression of which ligand, the target of the oral drug pexidartinib?
items.e: A CSF1 translocation in a minority of neoplastic synovial cells causes CSF1 overexpression, which recruits CSF1R-bearing macrophages; pexidartinib is a CSF1R inhibitor approved for unresectable disease.

items.q: A patient with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a plexiform neurofibroma that has recently become painful and is growing rapidly. Which investigation best helps detect malignant transformation before biopsy?
items.e: NF1 patients have a lifetime MPNST risk of about 8-13%; high FDG uptake (raised SUVmax) separates MPNST from benign neurofibroma and guides biopsy of the most avid area.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman has a slowly growing, poorly defined firm mass deep to the inferior angle of the scapula, noticed only on shoulder flexion. MRI shows interlaced fibrous and fatty tissue. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Elastofibroma dorsi is a benign fibroelastic pseudotumour between the chest wall and the inferior scapular angle in elderly people, often bilateral; its fat-interlaced fibrous pattern on MRI is diagnostic and it needs no treatment if asymptomatic.

items.q: Abaloparatide, an anabolic agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis, is an analogue of:
items.e: Abaloparatide is a synthetic PTHrP(1-34) analogue given daily subcutaneously; teriparatide is PTH(1-34) and romosozumab is an anti-sclerostin antibody.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman has received denosumab every 6 months for 6 years and now wishes to stop. What is recommended to prevent rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures?
o: Stop without further treatment; the effect persists for years
Start a bisphosphonate (for example zoledronic acid) about 6 months after the last dose
Give a single dose of vitamin D 600,000 IU
items.e: Denosumab's effect is reversible, and stopping it causes a rebound rise in bone turnover with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures; a bisphosphonate is given as consolidation when it is stopped.

items.q: In advanced tuberculosis of the hip, erosion of the superior acetabular rim allows the femoral head to migrate upwards and backwards. What is this radiological appearance called?
items.e: Destruction of the posterosuperior acetabulum with upward displacement of the femoral head into the eroded area gives the 'wandering acetabulum' of advanced tuberculous arthritis of the hip.

items.q: A 45-year-old non-smoker without systemic disease has chronic tibial osteomyelitis. The only adverse host factor is dense radiation fibrosis and scarring of the overlying soft tissue. What is the Cierny-Mader physiological host class?
items.e: Cierny-Mader B hosts are compromised locally (scarring, radiation fibrosis, vascular disease, lymphoedema) or systemically (diabetes, renal or liver failure, immunosuppression, smoking); C hosts are those in whom treatment is worse than the disease.

items.q: In the Cierny-Mader anatomical classification, type III (localised) osteomyelitis is defined as:
o: Full-thickness cortical sequestration that leaves the bone stable after debridement
Infection confined to the medullary canal
Infection of the outer cortical surface only
Permeative circumferential involvement that makes the bone unstable
items.e: Type I is medullary, II superficial, III localised (full-thickness cortical sequestrum but stable after debridement) and IV diffuse (unstable before or after debridement).

items.q: A child of short stature has dense brittle bones, persistently open anterior fontanelle, an obtuse mandibular angle and resorption of the terminal phalanges. Mutation of which gene is responsible?
items.e: Pyknodysostosis is an autosomal recessive osteosclerosis caused by cathepsin K deficiency, which impairs osteoclast collagen degradation, and acro-osteolysis is a hallmark.

items.q: A 12-year-old with leg pain and a waddling gait has symmetrical fusiform cortical thickening of the diaphyses of the femora and tibiae, sparing the epiphyses. Which gene is mutated?
items.e: Camurati-Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia) is an autosomal dominant TGFB1 mutation causing symmetrical diaphyseal hyperostosis, limb pain and muscle weakness.

items.q: An infant has severe generalised osteosclerosis, pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly and progressive visual loss from optic nerve compression. What is the only curative treatment?
items.e: Malignant infantile (autosomal recessive) osteopetrosis, most often due to TCIRG1 mutation, reflects defective osteoclasts derived from haematopoietic precursors, so HSCT is the only cure.

items.q: An adult with recurrent fractures has 'sandwich' vertebrae with dense endplates and a 'bone-within-bone' appearance of the pelvis. Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (Albers-Schonberg disease) is caused by mutation of:
items.e: ADO type II results from dominant-negative CLCN7 chloride channel mutations that impair osteoclast acidification; carbonic anhydrase II deficiency causes recessive osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis.

items.q: The Japanese Investigation Committee (JIC) classification of osteonecrosis of the femoral head is based on:
o: Percentage of femoral head surface collapse
Location of the necrotic zone relative to the weight-bearing portion of the acetabulum
Presence of a crescent sign and acetabular involvement
items.e: JIC types A, B, C1 and C2 describe how much of the weight-bearing area (on the AP view) the necrotic zone occupies; lesions extending lateral to the acetabular edge (C2) carry the highest risk of collapse.

items.q: In the modified Kerboul method, the arcs of femoral head necrosis on mid-coronal and mid-sagittal MRI are added. Above which combined necrotic angle is the risk of collapse high?
items.e: A combined necrotic angle under 190 degrees has a low risk of collapse and above 240 degrees a high risk, which helps choose between joint-preserving surgery and arthroplasty.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has sudden severe medial knee pain while walking, worse at night, with no steroid or alcohol use. MRI shows a low-signal subchondral line in the weight-bearing medial femoral condyle with extensive marrow oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (formerly SONK)
Bone bruise from meniscal root avulsion only
items.e: So-called spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee is now regarded as a subchondral insufficiency fracture in elderly, often osteopenic women; it is often associated with medial meniscal root tears.

items.q: Which feature favours secondary (for example steroid-associated) osteonecrosis of the knee over a subchondral insufficiency fracture?
o: Bilateral, multifocal lesions extending into the metaphysis in a patient under 45
A single small lesion of the medial femoral condyle in an elderly woman
Sudden onset of pain after minimal activity
items.e: Secondary osteonecrosis affects younger patients with risk factors, is often bilateral and multifocal (both condyles, tibial plateau, other joints) and can extend into the metaphysis, unlike the single subchondral lesion of SIFK.

items.q: A previously healthy farmer from a tropical region has a painful, woody-hard swollen thigh for 2 weeks with fever. Ultrasound shows an intramuscular fluid collection in the vastus lateralis. Which stage of pyomyositis is this, and what is the usual organism?
items.e: Pyomyositis progresses from an invasive (phlegmonous) stage to a suppurative stage, when pus forms and drainage is needed, and then to a late septic stage; Staphylococcus aureus causes about 90% of tropical cases.

items.q: During bedside exploration of suspected necrotising fasciitis of the leg, which finding on the 'finger test' supports the diagnosis?
o: Brisk bleeding with firm adherence of fascia to fat
Easy blunt finger dissection along the fascial plane with no bleeding and greyish 'dishwater' fluid
Thick yellow pus localised in the subcutaneous fat
Crepitus localised to the skin only
items.e: Loss of resistance to finger dissection along the deep fascia, absent bleeding and thin dishwater fluid indicate necrotising fasciitis and call for immediate radical debridement.

items.q: A 40-year-old with palmoplantar pustulosis has painful swelling of the anterior chest wall. Bone scan shows increased uptake around both sternoclavicular joints and the manubrium (a 'bull's head' pattern). What is the diagnosis?
items.e: SAPHO (synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis) characteristically causes anterior chest wall hyperostosis and osteitis, giving the bull's head appearance on scintigraphy.

items.q: What is the recommended antibiotic treatment of brucellar spondylitis?
o: Doxycycline with an aminoglycoside or rifampicin for at least 12 weeks
items.e: Brucellar spondylitis needs prolonged combination therapy (typically doxycycline plus streptomycin or gentamicin at the start, or plus rifampicin), usually for at least 3 months, because relapse is common with shorter courses.

items.q: A vertebral body shows destruction confined to its centre with the adjacent discs preserved, mimicking a tumour on MRI. Biopsy confirms tuberculosis. Which pattern of spinal tuberculosis is this, and what deformity can follow?
o: Paradiscal type; disc-space collapse with kyphosis
Anterior subperiosteal type; scalloping of several vertebrae
Central type; concertina collapse resembling vertebra plana
items.e: Central vertebral TB spreads through the body from Batson's plexus or the nutrient artery, spares the disc and may collapse the body uniformly, mimicking neoplasm or vertebra plana, so biopsy is essential.

items.q: Before starting pegloticase for refractory tophaceous gout, which condition must be excluded because it can cause severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia?
items.e: Pegloticase is a recombinant uricase that converts urate to allantoin and generates hydrogen peroxide; in G6PD deficiency this causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, so screening is mandatory.

items.q: The Thacher Rickets Severity Score grades nutritional rickets using radiographs of which sites?
items.e: The Thacher score (0-10) rates metaphyseal fraying, cupping and growth-plate lucency at the distal radius and ulna and at the distal femur and proximal tibia, and is used to monitor healing.

items.q: A toddler with premature loss of primary teeth (with roots intact), bowing and fractures has a low serum alkaline phosphatase. Raised levels of which substrate support the diagnosis of hypophosphatasia?
items.e: Deficient tissue-nonspecific ALP (ALPL mutation) causes its natural substrates, pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, inorganic pyrophosphate and phosphoethanolamine, to accumulate; pyrophosphate inhibits mineralisation.

items.q: Long-term phenytoin or carbamazepine therapy can cause osteomalacia mainly by:
o: Inducing hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that increase vitamin D catabolism
items.e: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants speed up hepatic breakdown of vitamin D to inactive metabolites, lowering 25(OH)D; affected patients need monitoring and vitamin D supplementation.

items.q: A man on long-term tenofovir disoproxil for HIV develops bone pain and pseudofractures, with hypophosphataemia, glycosuria with normal blood glucose, and aminoaciduria. What is the mechanism of his osteomalacia?
o: Proximal renal tubulopathy (acquired Fanconi syndrome) causing phosphate wasting
items.e: Tenofovir disoproxil is toxic to proximal tubular mitochondria, causing Fanconi syndrome with renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemic osteomalacia; switching to tenofovir alafenamide or another drug is advised.

items.q: In a 35-year-old premenopausal woman, how should a DXA result be interpreted, according to ISCD guidance?
o: Using the Z-score; a value of -2.0 or lower is 'below the expected range for age'
Using the T-score; -2.5 or lower is osteoporosis
Using the T-score; -1.0 to -2.5 is osteopenia
items.e: In premenopausal women, men under 50 and children, the Z-score (comparison with age-matched controls) is used, and osteoporosis cannot be diagnosed on densitometry alone.

items.q: What did the two sham-controlled randomised trials published in NEJM in 2009 (Buchbinder; Kallmes) show about vertebroplasty for painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures?
o: Vertebroplasty gave superior pain relief at 1 month
No significant benefit over a sham procedure in pain or disability
Higher rates of adjacent-level fracture than kyphoplasty
items.e: Both trials found that vertebroplasty was no better than a sham procedure for pain and function, which tempered its routine use, although later trials in acute fractures gave mixed results.

items.q: A sexually active 22-year-old has migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrist extensors and a few painless pustules on the limbs. Which organism is most likely?
items.e: Disseminated gonococcal infection presents with the triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgia (or purulent monoarthritis); it is treated with ceftriaxone, and swabs of mucosal sites raise the culture yield.

items.q: According to the international consensus definition of fracture-related infection (FRI), which finding is a confirmatory criterion?
o: Phenotypically indistinguishable pathogens in at least two separate deep tissue or implant samples
items.e: Confirmatory FRI criteria are a fistula, sinus or wound breakdown communicating with bone or implant, purulent drainage or pus, the same pathogen in at least two deep samples, and microorganisms on histopathology; raised inflammatory markers and fever are only suggestive.

items.q: Which property is essential for an antibiotic to be mixed into PMMA bone cement for a spacer or beads?
o: Thermal stability, with availability as a powder
items.e: The antibiotic must survive the exothermic polymerisation of PMMA (thermostable), be available as a powder, be water-soluble enough to elute and have a broad bactericidal spectrum; vancomycin, gentamicin and tobramycin are typical.

items.q: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is associated with which metabolic abnormality, which should be looked for in younger patients?
items.e: Secondary CPPD occurs with haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia; low magnesium (a cofactor of pyrophosphatases) favours crystal formation.

items.q: In the CARES trial (NEJM 2018) of patients with gout and established cardiovascular disease, febuxostat compared with allopurinol was associated with:
o: Lower rates of gout flares and mortality
items.e: Febuxostat was non-inferior for the composite cardiovascular endpoint but had higher cardiovascular and all-cause death, so allopurinol is preferred first line, especially in patients with cardiovascular disease.

items.q: Colchicine controls acute crystal arthritis mainly by:
o: Binding tubulin and inhibiting microtubule polymerisation in neutrophils
items.e: By binding tubulin, colchicine disrupts microtubules, which impairs neutrophil migration and NLRP3 inflammasome activation; it has no effect on serum urate.

items.q: Monosodium urate crystals provoke acute gouty inflammation mainly through NLRP3 inflammasome activation and release of which cytokine, the target of anakinra and canakinumab?
items.e: Crystals phagocytosed by macrophages activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and caspase-1, which release IL-1 beta; IL-1 blockers are used for flares when colchicine, NSAIDs and steroids are unsuitable.

items.q: Which imaging technique can non-invasively identify and colour-code monosodium urate deposits in and around joints and tendons by material decomposition?
items.e: Dual-energy CT separates urate from calcium by its attenuation at two energy levels, which helps diagnose gout when aspiration is negative or not feasible and quantifies tophus burden.

items.q: A 40-year-old has acute neck pain, painful swallowing and low-grade fever. Lateral radiograph shows prevertebral soft-tissue swelling with amorphous calcification anterior to C1-C2. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
o: Calcific tendinitis of longus colli; NSAIDs, as it is self-limiting
items.e: Acute calcific tendinitis of the longus colli is hydroxyapatite deposition in its superior oblique fibres; CT shows the calcification without a rim-enhancing abscess, and it resolves in 1-2 weeks with NSAIDs.

items.q: A 45-year-old has had shoulder pain for 9 months despite physiotherapy and a subacromial injection. Ultrasound shows a dense 15 mm calcific deposit in the supraspinatus. Which minimally invasive treatment is most appropriate next?
o: Ultrasound-guided needle barbotage (lavage) of the deposit
items.e: Ultrasound-guided barbotage fragments and aspirates the calcium, usually with a subacromial steroid injection, and gives faster relief than injection alone; arthroscopic removal is reserved for failures.

items.q: In the randomised trial by Reid et al. (NEJM 2018) of women aged 65 or over with osteopenia (T-score -1.0 to -2.5), zoledronic acid 5 mg every 18 months:
o: Had no effect on fractures because BMD was not osteoporotic
Reduced the risk of fragility fractures compared with placebo
items.e: Over 6 years, zoledronate reduced non-vertebral and vertebral fragility fractures in osteopenic women, showing that treatment can be justified by fracture risk and not by T-score alone.

items.q: The FREEDOM trial established which effect of denosumab 60 mg every 6 months in postmenopausal osteoporosis?
o: Reduction of new vertebral, hip and non-vertebral fractures compared with placebo
Superiority to teriparatide in vertebral fracture reduction
Reduction of mortality after hip fracture
items.e: Over 3 years, denosumab reduced new vertebral fractures by about 68%, hip fractures by about 40% and non-vertebral fractures by about 20%; the mortality benefit after hip fracture was shown with zoledronate (HORIZON-RFT).

items.q: In the VERO trial of postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis and prevalent vertebral fractures, teriparatide compared with risedronate:
o: Was equivalent for all fracture outcomes
items.e: Teriparatide roughly halved new vertebral fractures and also reduced clinical fractures compared with risedronate, supporting anabolic-first treatment in very high-risk patients.

items.q: The FLEX trial compared continuing alendronate to 10 years with stopping after 5 years. Continuation reduced:
items.e: Continuing alendronate lowered clinical vertebral fractures but not non-vertebral or hip fractures, which supports a drug holiday after 5 years in lower-risk women.

items.q: What is the main role of a fracture liaison service in an orthopaedic department?
o: Coordinating theatre lists for hip fracture surgery
Systematically identifying patients with fragility fractures and starting osteoporosis assessment and treatment to prevent further fractures
items.e: A coordinator-based fracture liaison service closes the treatment gap after a fragility fracture by organising DXA, falls assessment and drug treatment, and reduces refracture rates.

items.q: On a transiliac bone biopsy after tetracycline double labelling, which combination confirms osteomalacia?
o: Increased osteoid seam width with a prolonged mineralisation lag time
Reduced osteoid with a normal mineral apposition rate
Increased osteoclast number with peritrabecular fibrosis
Thin trabeculae with normal osteoid and mineralisation
items.e: Two timed tetracycline labels measure the mineral apposition rate; osteomalacia shows wide, excess osteoid seams with delayed mineralisation, whereas osteoporosis has normal mineralisation with reduced bone mass.

items.q: A patient on long-term haemodialysis taking calcium-based binders and calcitriol has bone pain and fractures. Intact PTH and bone-specific ALP are low, and biopsy shows very low bone formation without excess osteoid. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Adynamic bone disease is a low-turnover renal osteodystrophy, often from oversuppression of PTH; osteitis fibrosa is high turnover with high PTH, and osteomalacia shows excess unmineralised osteoid.

items.q: In the Cruess classification of humeral head osteonecrosis, the appearance of a subchondral crescent sign with the articular surface still largely spherical is stage:
items.e: Cruess stages are I (MRI changes only), II (sclerosis, sphericity preserved), III (crescent sign or subchondral fracture), IV (articular collapse) and V (glenoid involvement).

items.q: Which supplement is given with isoniazid during treatment of osteoarticular tuberculosis to prevent peripheral neuropathy?
items.e: Isoniazid increases pyridoxine excretion and antagonises it, causing peripheral neuropathy, especially in malnourished, diabetic, alcoholic, HIV-positive or pregnant patients; pyridoxine 10-25 mg daily prevents this.

items.q: A 60-year-old with tibial osteomyelitis and a sinus that has drained for 30 years develops increased pain, bleeding and a fungating, foul-smelling lesion at the sinus opening. Biopsy will most likely show:
items.e: Marjolin ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic sinus tract or scar, usually after decades; it needs biopsy and often amputation because the bone is invaded.

items.q: The 'Hong Kong operation' for spinal tuberculosis, described by Hodgson and Stock, consists of:
o: Radical anterior debridement and strut bone grafting
items.e: Hodgson's procedure is radical anterior excision of the diseased vertebrae, abscess and sequestra, followed by anterior strut grafting, which gives decompression with early fusion and less kyphosis.

items.q: What was the principal conclusion of the Medical Research Council Working Party trials on spinal tuberculosis?
o: Radical anterior surgery is mandatory in all patients
Plaster jackets with prolonged bed rest are essential
Ambulatory chemotherapy with short-course isoniazid- and rifampicin-based regimens was effective for most patients
items.e: The MRC trials showed that outpatient chemotherapy (6-9 month regimens with isoniazid and rifampicin) without routine bed rest or plaster gave good results, with surgery reserved for specific indications.

items.q: Which approach allows drainage of a thoracic paravertebral cold abscess and limited anterolateral decompression without a formal thoracotomy?
items.e: Costotransversectomy removes the medial rib and transverse process to reach the paravertebral space posterolaterally; laminectomy alone is contraindicated because it destabilises an anteriorly diseased spine.

items.q: The major virulence factor of Clostridium perfringens in gas gangrene, which causes myonecrosis and haemolysis, is alpha-toxin, which is a:
items.e: Alpha-toxin is a lecithinase that destroys cell membranes, causing myonecrosis, haemolysis and shock; treatment is urgent radical debridement with penicillin and clindamycin.

items.q: What did the OVIVA trial (NEJM 2019) show for adults with bone and joint infection, including implant-related infection?
o: Intravenous therapy was superior for implant infections
Oral antibiotics in the first 6 weeks were non-inferior to intravenous antibiotics
Two weeks of therapy was as good as six weeks
items.e: OVIVA found treatment failure at one year was similar with appropriate oral or IV antibiotics during the first 6 weeks, with fewer line complications and shorter stays in the oral group.

items.q: Sonication of an explanted prosthesis in suspected periprosthetic joint infection improves diagnosis because it:
o: Removes the need for tissue cultures
Dislodges biofilm-embedded bacteria from the implant surface, increasing culture sensitivity
items.e: Low-frequency ultrasound releases sessile biofilm bacteria into fluid for culture, which increases sensitivity, especially when antibiotics were given before surgery.

items.q: Trabecular bone score (TBS), increasingly used alongside DXA, is:
o: A measure of cortical thickness at the femoral neck
A biochemical index of bone turnover
A grey-level texture index from lumbar spine DXA images that reflects microarchitecture and adjusts FRAX
items.e: TBS is calculated from the lumbar DXA image and predicts fracture risk independently of BMD; it is especially useful in diabetes and glucocorticoid use, and can adjust the FRAX probability.

items.q: In the Genant semiquantitative method of grading vertebral fractures, a moderate (grade 2) fracture has a vertebral height reduction of about:
items.e: Genant grades are 1 (mild, 20-25%), 2 (moderate, 25-40%) and 3 (severe, more than 40%) loss of anterior, middle or posterior height.

items.q: Which antihypertensive agent has a uricosuric effect and is preferred in hypertensive patients with gout?
items.e: Losartan inhibits the URAT1 transporter and lowers serum urate modestly, whereas thiazide and loop diuretics raise urate and precipitate gout.

items.q: The Steinberg (University of Pennsylvania) staging of femoral head osteonecrosis differs from Ficat staging mainly by:
o: Quantifying lesion size (A, B, C) by percentage of femoral head involved
items.e: Steinberg stages 0-VI include MRI and add a size grade, A (under 15%), B (15-30%) or C (over 30%) head involvement, which improves prognostic value.

items.q: Sugioka's transtrochanteric anterior rotational osteotomy for osteonecrosis of the femoral head aims to:
o: Shorten the femoral neck to unload the hip
Revascularise the head with a fibular graft
Fuse the hip in a functional position
Rotate the necrotic segment out of the weight-bearing zone and bring intact posterior head under load
items.e: Rotating the head about the neck axis moves the anterosuperior necrotic segment away from the weight-bearing area; it suits young patients with limited lesions and an adequate intact posterior segment.

items.q: Hernigou's technique for early (pre-collapse) femoral head osteonecrosis combines core decompression with:
o: Implantation of autologous bone marrow concentrate containing mesenchymal stem cells
items.e: Core decompression with injection of concentrated iliac-crest bone marrow aims to repopulate the necrotic zone with osteoprogenitor cells and has shown lower progression to collapse than decompression alone in early disease.

items.q: A 50-year-old has progressive symmetrical peripheral neuropathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin hyperpigmentation and a sclerotic lesion in the iliac bone. Serum shows a lambda monoclonal protein. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: POEMS (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein, skin changes) is a plasma cell disorder with sclerotic bone lesions and raised VEGF; the monoclonal protein is almost always lambda.

items.q: A 55-year-old has a single lytic lesion of the T10 vertebral body. Biopsy shows monoclonal plasma cells, and bone marrow, skeletal survey/PET and calcium, renal function and haemoglobin are all normal. What is the treatment of choice?
items.e: Solitary plasmacytoma of bone is highly radiosensitive and is treated with local radiotherapy, with surgery only for instability or neurological compromise; many patients later progress to myeloma, so follow-up is lifelong.

items.q: In sporadic desmoid-type fibromatosis, which CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutation is associated with a higher risk of recurrence after surgery?
items.e: Sporadic desmoids carry CTNNB1 exon 3 mutations, and S45F predicts recurrence more than T41A; desmoids in FAP arise from germline APC mutation instead.

items.q: A 55-year-old with long-standing knee osteoarthritis has recurrent painless effusions. MRI shows frond-like synovial proliferation with fat signal on all sequences and no blooming on gradient echo. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Lipoma arborescens is villous lipomatous synovial proliferation, usually in the suprapatellar pouch, and follows fat signal; PVNS shows haemosiderin blooming and chondromatosis shows cartilage nodules.

items.q: A farmer from a sheep-rearing region has a slowly expanding, multiloculated lytic lesion of the pelvis without periosteal reaction. MRI shows many small cysts like a bunch of grapes. What is the most likely diagnosis and the main treatment challenge?
o: Hydatid disease of bone; high recurrence because complete excision is difficult
items.e: Osseous echinococcosis (most often spine and pelvis) spreads as multivesicular cysts through the bone without a capsule, so it recurs often; treatment is wide excision where possible with long-term albendazole.

items.q: A diabetic rice farmer from coastal Odisha has fever and septic arthritis of the knee with multiple splenic abscesses. Cultures grow a Gram-negative bacillus with bipolar 'safety-pin' staining. Which is the recommended initial antibiotic?
o: Ceftazidime or meropenem, followed by co-trimoxazole eradication
items.e: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) is endemic in India and South-East Asia, affects diabetics and causes bone and joint infection with visceral abscesses; it needs intensive IV ceftazidime or meropenem followed by months of co-trimoxazole.

items.q: An infant has bilateral symmetrical erosion of the medial proximal tibial metaphyses on radiographs, with periostitis of multiple long bones. This 'Wimberger sign' suggests:
items.e: Focal destruction of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis (Wimberger sign) is characteristic of congenital syphilis; the Wimberger ring around the epiphysis is a different sign seen in scurvy.

items.q: A lateral spine radiograph of an adult with sickle cell disease shows central, step-like depressions of the vertebral endplates with preserved peripheral margins. What causes this 'H-shaped' (Lincoln log) vertebra?
o: Infarction of the central endplate supplied by end-arteries, with preserved peripheral growth
items.e: Microvascular occlusion of the central endplate end-arteries stops central growth while the periphery, with collateral supply, grows normally, producing H-shaped vertebrae that are almost pathognomonic of sickle cell disease.

items.q: A child has short stature, round face, short fourth and fifth metacarpals and subcutaneous ossification, with hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and raised PTH. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Pseudohypoparathyroidism 1a is end-organ resistance to PTH from maternally inherited GNAS inactivation, so calcium is low and phosphate high despite raised PTH, with the Albright osteodystrophy phenotype.

items.q: A child with rickets has a low 25-hydroxyvitamin D that does not rise despite adequate vitamin D supplements, but responds to calcifediol. Mutation of which gene is responsible (vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1B)?
items.e: CYP2R1 encodes hepatic vitamin D 25-hydroxylase, so 25(OH)D stays low; type 1A is CYP27B1 (1-alpha-hydroxylase, treated with calcitriol) and type 2A is VDR resistance.

items.q: Chondromyxoid fibroma, a lobulated eccentric metaphyseal lesion of the proximal tibia in young adults, is characterised by rearrangement of which gene?
items.e: Chondromyxoid fibroma shows recurrent GRM1 rearrangements causing overexpression of metabotropic glutamate receptor 1; USP6 rearrangement is typical of primary aneurysmal bone cyst.

items.q: Primary synovial chondromatosis is now regarded as a neoplasm, with recurrent fusion of which genes?
items.e: FN1-ACVR2A (and related ACVR2A) fusions are found in most cases of primary synovial chondromatosis and its malignant counterpart; CSF1 rearrangement is the driver of tenosynovial giant cell tumour.

items.q: A 14-year-old has a small round blue cell sarcoma of the soft tissue that is CD99-positive but lacks EWSR1 rearrangement. Molecular testing shows a CIC-DUX4 fusion. Compared with Ewing sarcoma, this tumour:
o: Has a better prognosis and responds well to Ewing chemotherapy
Is a benign lesion treated by excision alone
Has a worse prognosis with poorer response to Ewing-type chemotherapy
items.e: CIC-rearranged sarcoma is now a separate entity in the WHO classification; it is aggressive, often in soft tissue of young adults, and responds less well than Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: Myxoid liposarcoma differs from most other soft-tissue sarcomas in its marked:
o: Sensitivity to radiotherapy, often shrinking considerably after preoperative irradiation
Resistance to all chemotherapy, including trabectedin
items.e: Myxoid liposarcoma is unusually radiosensitive and also responds to trabectedin, reflecting its FUS-DDIT3-driven biology.

items.q: In Enneking's classification of surgical margins, a margin passing through the reactive zone around a sarcoma is termed:
items.e: Intralesional enters the tumour, marginal passes through the reactive zone (risk of satellite lesions), wide passes through normal tissue within the compartment, and radical removes the entire compartment.

items.q: In the classic study by Mankin and colleagues on biopsy of musculoskeletal tumours, problems such as diagnostic errors, wound complications and changes in treatment plan were:
o: Equally frequent wherever the biopsy was done
More frequent with core needle biopsy than open biopsy at the treating centre
Several times more frequent when the biopsy was done at a referring institution rather than the treating centre
Unrelated to the subsequent need for amputation
items.e: Mankin's studies (1982, 1996) showed biopsy-related problems were far more frequent when done outside the treating centre and sometimes changed treatment to amputation, so biopsy should be done where definitive surgery will be performed.

items.q: In the AJCC 8th edition staging of appendicular bone sarcomas, the size threshold that separates T1 from T2 primary tumours is:
items.e: For appendicular skeleton, trunk, skull and facial bones, T1 is 8 cm or less and T2 more than 8 cm; T3 denotes discontinuous tumours in the same bone.

items.q: Mifamurtide, approved in Europe as an adjunct to postoperative chemotherapy for resected non-metastatic high-grade osteosarcoma, acts by:
o: Blocking the mTOR pathway in tumour cells
Activating monocytes and macrophages as a liposomal muramyl tripeptide (NOD2 ligand)
items.e: Mifamurtide (liposomal MTP-PE) mimics a bacterial cell-wall component and activates macrophages to kill tumour cells; the INT-0133 trial suggested improved overall survival when added to chemotherapy.

items.q: In the Enneking and Dunham classification of pelvic resections, a periacetabular resection is classified as:
items.e: Type I is iliac, type II periacetabular, type III pubis and ischium (obturator ring), and type IV involves the sacroiliac region and sacral ala; combinations are written as I+II and so on.

items.q: A 40-year-old has multiple lytic lesions in contiguous bones of the foot and nodules in the liver. Biopsy shows cords of epithelioid endothelial cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles in a myxohyaline stroma. Which fusion confirms the diagnosis?
items.e: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a malignant vascular tumour, often multifocal, that carries WWTR1-CAMTA1 in about 90% (YAP1-TFE3 in a minority); CAMTA1 immunostaining is a useful surrogate.

items.q: Radium-223 dichloride improved overall survival in the ALSYMPCA trial. For which patients is it indicated?
o: Breast cancer with lytic bone metastases
Castration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases and no known visceral metastases
Renal cell carcinoma with a solitary bone metastasis
items.e: Radium-223 is an alpha-emitting calcium mimetic that concentrates at sites of high bone turnover; ALSYMPCA showed longer survival and delayed skeletal events in castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone-only metastases.

items.q: For uncomplicated painful bone metastases, a single 8 Gy fraction of radiotherapy compared with a multi-fraction course (such as 30 Gy in 10) gives:
o: Similar pain relief, but a higher rate of retreatment
Higher rates of pathological fracture and cord compression
Better pain relief and lower retreatment rates
items.e: Randomised trials and meta-analyses show equivalent overall and complete pain response with a single 8 Gy fraction, at the cost of more retreatment (about 20% vs 8%); it is convenient for patients with limited life expectancy.

items.q: Nuclear expression of SATB2 on a small core biopsy of a malignant bone tumour indicates:
items.e: SATB2 is a transcription factor of osteoblastic lineage that helps identify neoplastic osteoid-forming cells; brachyury marks chordoma and S100/SOX9 cartilaginous tumours.

items.q: What is the main advantage of a non-invasive expandable endoprosthesis after resection of a distal femoral osteosarcoma in a 9-year-old?
o: It eliminates the risk of aseptic loosening
It allows sporting activity without restriction
It can be lengthened with an external electromagnetic field without repeated surgery or anaesthesia
items.e: Non-invasive growing prostheses are lengthened in clinic by a rotating external magnetic field, compensating for lost growth while avoiding the infection risk of repeated open lengthening procedures.

items.q: Nirogacestat, which prolonged progression-free survival in progressing desmoid tumours in the DeFi trial, is a:
o: Gamma-secretase inhibitor that blocks Notch signalling
items.e: Nirogacestat is an oral gamma-secretase inhibitor; DeFi (NEJM 2023) showed improved progression-free survival and symptoms in desmoid tumours, with ovarian dysfunction as a notable side effect.

items.q: During en bloc sacrectomy for a sacral chordoma, preservation of which nerve roots gives the best chance of retaining near-normal bladder and bowel control?
o: Both S3 roots (with S1 and S2)
items.e: Bilateral preservation of S1-S3 allows near-normal sphincter function in most patients; preserving only bilateral S2 retains continence in about half, and unilateral resection of sacral roots is usually well tolerated.

items.q: An adult has a large, deep, fatty mass of the thigh with thick septa; FISH shows MDM2 amplification and there is no dedifferentiated component. What is the usual surgical treatment?
o: Marginal excision, accepting a low risk of local recurrence
items.e: Atypical lipomatous tumour of the limbs is locally aggressive but does not metastasise; marginal excision is generally adequate, and dedifferentiation is rare in the extremities.

items.q: In the trial by Stopeck and colleagues (J Clin Oncol 2010) in women with breast cancer and bone metastases, denosumab compared with zoledronic acid:
o: Had a higher rate of osteonecrosis of the jaw that led to early stopping
Delayed the time to the first skeletal-related event
items.e: Denosumab was superior to zoledronic acid in delaying first on-study skeletal-related events (by about 18%), with no difference in survival; it is not renally excreted but causes more hypocalcaemia.

items.q: The PRISM trial in Paget disease of bone compared intensive bisphosphonate therapy aimed at normalising alkaline phosphatase with symptom-directed treatment. It showed:
o: Less progression of deafness with intensive therapy
No clinical benefit of intensive therapy in fractures, orthopaedic surgery, bone pain or quality of life
items.e: PRISM (Langston et al., JBMR 2010) found that suppressing bone turnover to normal gave no advantage over treating symptoms, so bisphosphonates in Paget disease are given mainly for bone pain.

items.q: In free vascularised fibular grafting for femoral head osteonecrosis (Urbaniak technique), the peroneal vessels of the graft are anastomosed to:
o: The superficial femoral artery and vein
The deep circumflex iliac artery and vein
The medial circumflex femoral artery directly beneath the femoral head
The ascending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery and its venae comitantes
items.e: Through a lateral approach, a core track is made into the necrotic head, the fibula is inserted, and its peroneal vessels are joined to the ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex vessels.

items.q: Odanacatib reduced osteoporotic fractures in the LOFT trial but was never marketed. Its mechanism and the reason for withdrawal were:
o: Cathepsin K inhibition; increased risk of stroke
RANKL inhibition; osteonecrosis of the jaw
items.e: Odanacatib inhibits cathepsin K, the osteoclast collagenase, reducing resorption with less suppression of formation; development stopped in 2016 because of an increased stroke risk.

items.q: Why does DXA overestimate the true gain in bone mineral density in a patient treated with strontium ranelate?
o: Strontium increases bone size rather than density
Strontium has a higher atomic number than calcium and attenuates X-rays more
Strontium causes soft-tissue calcification over the spine
items.e: Strontium is incorporated into bone and, being heavier than calcium, absorbs more X-ray energy, so about half of the measured BMD rise is artefactual; its use is now restricted because of cardiovascular risk.

items.q: In the ACTIVE trial, compared with teriparatide, abaloparatide was associated with:
o: No reduction of vertebral fractures versus placebo
An increased rate of non-vertebral fractures
items.e: Abaloparatide, a PTHrP(1-34) analogue, reduced vertebral and non-vertebral fractures against placebo, and caused hypercalcaemia less often than teriparatide (about 3% vs 6%).

items.q: A man with alcoholic cirrhosis sustains a minor leg abrasion while wading in seawater. Within 24 hours he has septic shock with haemorrhagic bullae spreading up the leg. The most likely organism is:
items.e: Vibrio vulnificus causes fulminant necrotising soft-tissue infection with haemorrhagic bullae in people with liver disease after seawater exposure or raw shellfish; treatment is urgent debridement with doxycycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin.

items.q: After digit replantation, medicinal leeches are applied for venous congestion. Prophylaxis against which gut symbiont of the leech is recommended?
items.e: Aeromonas hydrophila lives in the leech gut and can cause severe wound infection; prophylaxis with a fluoroquinolone or co-trimoxazole is given while leeches are used.

items.q: A gardener pricked by a rose thorn develops an ulcerated nodule on the finger followed by a chain of painless nodules along the lymphatics of the forearm. The appropriate treatment is:
o: Wide surgical excision of all nodules
items.e: Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, spreads along lymphatics; itraconazole for several months is first-line.

items.q: A patient on long-term haemodialysis has an acute knee effusion. Synovial fluid shows bipyramidal (envelope-shaped) crystals. These are most likely:
items.e: Calcium oxalate crystals are bipyramidal and occur in end-stage renal disease and primary hyperoxaluria; urate crystals are needle-shaped and CPP crystals rhomboid.

items.q: Nitisinone, used to slow ochronotic arthropathy in alkaptonuria, works by:
o: Inhibiting 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, reducing homogentisic acid production
Increasing renal excretion of homogentisic acid
items.e: Nitisinone blocks the enzyme upstream of homogentisic acid formation, lowering HGA levels; the SONIA 2 trial showed slowed disease progression, with raised tyrosine as a side effect.

items.q: After parathyroidectomy for severe primary hyperparathyroidism with osteitis fibrosa cystica, a patient develops severe hypocalcaemia lasting several days despite a normal residual parathyroid. The most likely explanation is:
o: Accidental removal of all parathyroid tissue
Hungry bone syndrome from rapid remineralisation of the skeleton
items.e: Hungry bone syndrome causes prolonged hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia and hypomagnesaemia after parathyroidectomy as demineralised bone avidly takes up minerals; high preoperative ALP is a risk factor.

items.q: After the monsoon in India, a 45-year-old has abrupt high fever, a maculopapular rash and severe, disabling symmetrical polyarthralgia of the hands, wrists and ankles. Six months later the joint pain persists. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Chikungunya, an Aedes-borne alphavirus, causes prominent polyarthralgia that becomes chronic in a substantial proportion, sometimes resembling rheumatoid arthritis; dengue causes myalgia without chronic arthritis.

items.q: An infant develops osteomyelitis of the proximal tibia months after BCG vaccination, and BCG osteitis is confirmed. Which drug should be omitted from treatment because the organism is intrinsically resistant to it?
items.e: BCG is an attenuated Mycobacterium bovis strain, which is naturally resistant to pyrazinamide, so treatment uses isoniazid and rifampicin (often with ethambutol).

items.q: A 30-year-old primigravida develops severe back pain in the first weeks after delivery while breastfeeding. Imaging shows several vertebral compression fractures and low BMD with no other cause. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Pregnancy and lactation-associated osteoporosis usually presents with multiple vertebral fractures in late pregnancy or early lactation, often in a first pregnancy; management includes stopping breastfeeding, calcium and vitamin D, and sometimes teriparatide.

items.q: A child with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets has been on conventional therapy with oral phosphate and calcitriol for years. Which complication requires periodic renal ultrasound?
items.e: Conventional therapy can cause nephrocalcinosis and secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism; burosumab, an anti-FGF23 antibody, avoids these and is now preferred where available.

items.q: Which agent is given with doxorubicin in children with osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma to reduce the risk of cardiomyopathy?
items.e: Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator and topoisomerase II-beta modulator, reduces anthracycline cardiotoxicity; mesna protects the bladder from ifosfamide and leucovorin rescues normal cells from methotrexate.

items.q: A child receiving high-dose methotrexate for osteosarcoma develops acute kidney injury with toxic plasma methotrexate levels despite leucovorin and hydration. Which agent rapidly lowers plasma methotrexate?
items.e: Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) cleaves methotrexate into inactive metabolites and is used when renal dysfunction delays clearance; leucovorin is continued alongside.

items.q: A patient receiving high-dose ifosfamide for a sarcoma becomes confused and drowsy on the second day of infusion. Besides stopping the infusion, which treatment is used for ifosfamide encephalopathy?
items.e: Ifosfamide encephalopathy is attributed to chloroacetaldehyde; methylene blue (and thiamine) is used for treatment and prophylaxis, whereas mesna prevents haemorrhagic cystitis.

items.q: In the trial by Raje and colleagues (Lancet Oncol 2018) in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, denosumab compared with zoledronic acid:
o: Was inferior in preventing skeletal-related events
Was non-inferior for time to first skeletal-related event, with fewer renal adverse events
Eliminated the need for radiotherapy to bone lesions
items.e: Denosumab was non-inferior to zoledronic acid for skeletal events in myeloma and had less renal toxicity, making it useful when renal function is impaired.

items.q: The Tikhoff-Linberg procedure for a sarcoma of the shoulder girdle differs from a forequarter amputation in that it:
o: Removes the entire upper limb with the scapula
Is used only for benign lesions
Resects the scapula, lateral clavicle and proximal humerus while preserving the forearm and hand
items.e: Tikhoff-Linberg is an interscapulothoracic limb-salvage resection that keeps a functional hand and elbow, provided the brachial plexus and axillary vessels can be preserved.

items.q: After resection of a proximal humeral sarcoma in a child, the 'clavicula pro humero' reconstruction involves:
o: Rotating the clavicle down on its sternoclavicular hinge and fixing its distal end to the humeral remnant
Replacing the humerus with a vascularised fibula from the opposite leg
Fusing the humeral remnant to the scapula
Implanting a modular endoprosthesis with a growing mechanism
items.e: The clavicle, kept on its sternoclavicular joint and blood supply, is turned down to bridge the defect to the humeral shaft, giving a biological, growing strut for a stable shoulder.

items.q: For a standard external hemipelvectomy, the skin and muscle flap used to close the wound is usually:
o: An anterior flap based on the deep circumflex iliac vessels
A posterior flap of gluteus maximus based on the inferior gluteal vessels
items.e: The classic hemipelvectomy uses a long posterior gluteal flap; when the buttock is involved by tumour, an anterior myocutaneous flap based on the superficial femoral vessels is used instead.

items.q: The study by Townsend and colleagues (J Clin Oncol 1994) on surgical fixation of pathological fractures from bone metastases showed that postoperative radiotherapy:
o: Improved limb function and reduced the need for a second operation
Increased infection rates and implant failure
items.e: Patients given postoperative radiotherapy after fixation were more likely to regain normal use of the limb and had fewer reoperations, supporting routine radiotherapy to the whole operated field.

items.q: On T1-weighted MRI, a well-defined fusiform intermuscular mass of the thigh is outlined by a thin rim of fat at its upper and lower poles. This 'split-fat' sign suggests:
items.e: Nerve sheath tumours arise in the intermuscular fat around neurovascular bundles, so a rim of fat surrounds them; the target sign and an entering or exiting nerve are other clues.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a slowly growing mass in the thigh that is strongly FDG-avid on PET-CT. MRI shows a lipomatous mass with prominent vessels, and histology shows multivacuolated granular cells resembling brown fat. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Hibernoma is a benign tumour of brown fat; its mitochondria-rich cells take up FDG avidly and can mimic sarcoma, but marginal excision is curative.

items.q: What is the usual treatment of lung metastases present at diagnosis in Ewing sarcoma, after systemic chemotherapy?
items.e: Whole-lung irradiation (about 15-18 Gy) after chemotherapy improves outcome in Ewing sarcoma with pulmonary metastases, reflecting its radiosensitivity; surgery is used for selected residual nodules.

items.q: The Papineau technique for chronic osteomyelitis with a bone defect consists of:
o: Closed suction-irrigation with antibiotics for 3 weeks
Radical excision, then open cancellous bone grafting onto a healthy granulation bed, followed by skin cover
Antibiotic cement spacer then autograft into an induced membrane
items.e: Papineau's open cancellous grafting excises infected bone, allows granulation tissue to form, then packs cancellous autograft into the open wound, which epithelialises or is skin-grafted later.

items.q: A 4-year-old has painless, hard, rapidly enlarging periarticular masses around the hips and shoulders. Radiographs show lobulated calcified masses. Serum phosphate is high with normal calcium and renal function. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Hyperphosphataemic familial tumoral calcinosis results from loss of FGF23 action (GALNT3, FGF23 or KL mutations), increasing renal phosphate reabsorption and causing periarticular calcium phosphate deposits.

items.q: Which congenital finding, present at birth, is the earliest clue to fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva before any soft-tissue ossification appears?
o: Short, malformed great toes with hallux valgus
items.e: Malformed great toes are present in nearly all patients with FOP (ACVR1 R206H); recognising them avoids biopsy and intramuscular injections, which trigger flare-ups.

items.q: A man who had a splenectomy is bitten by his dog and within 48 hours has septic shock with purpura. Which organism is classically responsible?
items.e: Capnocytophaga canimorsus from dog saliva causes fulminant sepsis in asplenic patients and those with alcohol misuse; amoxicillin-clavulanate prophylaxis is advised after dog bites in these patients.

items.q: When vancomycin is used for surgical prophylaxis in arthroplasty, when should the infusion begin?
items.e: Vancomycin needs a slow infusion (over about 60 minutes or more), so it is started within 120 minutes before incision; cefazolin is given within 60 minutes.

items.q: What is the recommended daily total calcium intake (diet plus supplements) for a postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis?
items.e: Guidelines advise about 1000-1200 mg/day of calcium for women over 50, preferably from diet, with vitamin D of 800-1000 IU; higher intakes add renal stone risk without benefit.
