o: Lateral hip pain from greater trochanteric pain syndrome
Abductor weakness from a short lever arm
items.e: Over-restoring offset tightens the iliotibial band over the trochanter causing lateral pain; too little offset weakens the abductors and increases impingement and dislocation.

items.q: When templating a THA on an AP pelvic radiograph, the inferomedial edge of the acetabular component is usually placed at the:
items.e: The teardrop marks the medial and inferior limits of the true acetabulum, restoring the anatomical centre of rotation.

items.q: Radiographic leg-length discrepancy after THA is usually measured on an AP pelvis as the vertical distance from a line joining both:
o: Iliac crests to the greater trochanters
Ischial tuberosities to the knee joint lines
Sacroiliac joints to the femoral heads
items.e: The inter-teardrop (or inter-ischial) line is the pelvic reference, and the corresponding point on each lesser trochanter gives the femoral reference.

items.q: After an uncomplicated THA, a patient feels the operated leg is longer, but measured true leg lengths are equal and the pelvis is tilted from an abduction contracture. The best initial management is:
o: An immediate shoe raise on the opposite side
Revision to shorten the femoral neck
Reassurance and physiotherapy to stretch the contracture, as apparent lengthening usually settles
items.e: Apparent (functional) discrepancy from pelvic obliquity usually resolves over months as soft tissues settle; true discrepancy is bony and does not.

items.q: In the Hartofilakidis classification of hip dysplasia in adults, a high dislocation (type C) means:
o: The femoral head has migrated superoposteriorly out of the true acetabulum without contact with it
A dysplastic acetabulum still containing the head
A head articulating with a false acetabulum that overlaps the true one
Protrusio of the head into the pelvis
items.e: Type A dysplasia: head within the true acetabulum; B low dislocation: false acetabulum overlapping the true one; C high dislocation: no contact with the true acetabulum.

items.q: In THA for developmental dysplasia, the proximal femur typically has a:
o: Narrow canal with excessive anteversion, needing a modular or cemented stem to control version
items.e: Dysplastic femora are small, straight and excessively anteverted; modular stems or cemented stems let the surgeon set version independently of canal shape.

items.q: Before THA in active Paget disease of the hip, preoperative bisphosphonate treatment is mainly used to reduce:
o: Intraoperative blood loss from hypervascular pagetic bone
items.e: Active Paget bone is highly vascular; controlling disease activity preoperatively reduces bleeding (and may reduce HO). Deformity may also need osteotomy.

items.q: After THA with medial cement extrusion through the acetabular floor, a patient has weakness of hip adduction and numbness over the medial thigh. The nerve involved is the:
items.e: The obturator nerve runs on the quadrilateral plate; cement or screws breaching the medial wall injure it, causing adductor weakness and medial thigh sensory loss.

items.q: On a postoperative AP pelvic radiograph, acetabular component inclination is measured as the angle between the line across the cup opening and the:
items.e: Radiographic inclination (abduction) uses the inter-teardrop (or inter-ischial) line as the horizontal reference; Lewinnek's target is 40 plus or minus 10 degrees.

items.q: Medialising the acetabular centre of rotation in THA reduces the joint reaction force mainly by:
o: Shortening the body-weight lever arm relative to the abductor lever arm
items.e: Joint reaction force depends on the ratio of the body-weight moment arm to the abductor moment arm; medialising the hip centre shortens the former, reducing the force the abductors must generate.

items.q: Placing the acetabular component in a high hip centre (superior and lateral to the anatomical centre) in THA tends to:
o: Increase joint reaction force and impair abductor function
items.e: A superolateral centre lengthens the body-weight moment arm and shortens the abductors, raising joint reaction force, wear and instability.

items.q: In the anterolateral (Watson-Jones) approach, damage to the inferior branch of the superior gluteal nerve mainly denervates:
items.e: The inferior branch of the superior gluteal nerve continues anteriorly to supply TFL; the interval between TFL and gluteus medius is therefore not a true internervous plane.

items.q: Compared with primary THA for osteoarthritis, THA performed after previous acetabular fracture fixation has higher rates of:
items.e: Post-traumatic THA has scarring, retained hardware, bone defects and avascular segments, so infection, HO and loosening are more common.

items.q: In primary THA, intravenous tranexamic acid has been shown to:
o: Reduce blood loss at the cost of a doubled DVT rate
Reduce blood loss and transfusion without increasing venous thromboembolism
items.e: Meta-analyses and the AAOS/AAHKS guideline support tranexamic acid in arthroplasty: less blood loss and transfusion without a rise in VTE.

items.q: Which Gruen zone of a femoral stem on the AP radiograph corresponds to the medial calcar region?
items.e: Gruen zones 1-7 run from the lateral greater trochanter (1) down to the stem tip (4) and up to the medial calcar (7); stress shielding typically affects zones 1 and 7.

items.q: At Camper's chiasma, where FDP passes through the split in FDS, the two FDS slips decussate at the level of the:
items.e: FDS divides over the proximal phalanx; the slips pass around FDP, rejoin as Camper's chiasma and insert on the middle phalanx, while FDP continues to the distal phalanx.

items.q: Why can most people flex the DIP joint of the index finger independently, but not of the middle, ring and little fingers?
o: The index FDS inserts on the distal phalanx
Only the index finger has a vinculum longum
The index FDP has a separate muscle belly, whereas the ulnar three share a common belly
The index finger lumbrical is supplied by the ulnar nerve
items.e: The ulnar three FDP tendons arise from a common belly (hence the quadriga effect), while the index has an independent belly.

items.q: When testing FDS function of the little finger, an apparently absent FDS should be interpreted cautiously because:
o: Little finger FDS is supplied by the ulnar nerve
FDS of the little finger inserts on the distal phalanx
The test requires flexion of the MCP joint only
FDS to the little finger is absent or functionally linked to the ring finger in about 15-20% of people
items.e: Little finger FDS is congenitally absent or tethered to the ring FDS in a significant minority, so failure to flex the PIP joint in isolation is not proof of laceration.

items.q: In the thumb, which pulley is the most important biomechanically for preventing bowstringing of flexor pollicis longus?
items.e: The thumb has A1, oblique and A2 pulleys; the oblique pulley over the proximal phalanx is the key restraint (it is preserved during trigger thumb release).

items.q: Which annular pulley of a finger lies over the proximal interphalangeal joint?
items.e: A1, A3 and A5 overlie the MCP, PIP and DIP joints respectively, while A2 and A4 arise from the shafts of the proximal and middle phalanges.

items.q: Within the digital flexor sheath, the main source of nutrition for the flexor tendons is:
items.e: Diffusion from synovial fluid is the dominant nutritional pathway within the sheath; the vincula provide a segmental vascular supply with avascular watershed zones.

items.q: In a Leddy-Packer type II FDP avulsion, the tendon retracts only to the level of the PIP joint because:
o: The lumbrical holds the tendon at the PIP joint
A bony fragment catches at the A4 pulley
The vinculum longum remains intact and tethers it
items.e: In type II the long vinculum is intact, preserving some blood supply and limiting retraction, so repair is possible up to about 6 weeks. In type III a bony fragment catches at A4.

items.q: A Leddy-Packer type III FDP avulsion has a large bony fragment held at the A4 pulley. The usual treatment is:
o: Open reduction and fixation of the fragment
Splinting the DIP joint in flexion for 6 weeks
items.e: The large fragment limits retraction to the middle phalanx and the tendon remains attached, so fixing the fragment restores FDP function.

items.q: In a Leddy-Packer type IV injury, the FDP avulsion fracture fragment is present but the tendon has also pulled off the fragment. Treatment requires:
o: Fixation of the bony fragment and separate reattachment of the tendon to the distal phalanx
Excision of the fragment and acceptance of the deficit
items.e: Type IV combines a bony avulsion with tendon avulsion from that fragment, so both the fracture and the tendon must be addressed.

items.q: A flexor tendon laceration in the palm between the distal edge of the carpal tunnel and the A1 pulley is in zone III. A feature of this zone is that:
o: Both tendons lie in a tight fibro-osseous sheath
The median nerve is almost always cut
The lumbrical muscles originate from FDP here
items.e: Zone III contains the lumbrical origins and lies outside the fibro-osseous sheath, so results are better than in zone II.

items.q: A glass injury at the volar wrist divides multiple flexor tendons, the median and ulnar nerves and the ulnar artery ('spaghetti wrist'). This is flexor zone:
items.e: Zone V is proximal to the carpal tunnel; zone IV is within the carpal tunnel, and zone III lies in the palm.

items.q: In a zone II flexor tendon repair, each core suture should ideally take purchase in the tendon at about what distance from the cut end?
items.e: Core purchase of about 7-10 mm gives the best holding strength; shorter bites pull out, and longer ones add little and increase bulk.

items.q: Compared with a volarly placed core suture, a dorsally placed core suture in a flexor tendon repair is:
o: Weaker and more prone to gap formation
Equivalent but more likely to cause adhesions
items.e: Dorsal placement of the core suture within the tendon gives greater repair strength, and the volar surface remains smoother for gliding.

items.q: The main mechanical benefits of adding a running epitendinous suture to a core flexor tendon repair are:
o: Increased repair strength and reduced gapping, with a smoother gliding surface
Elimination of the need for postoperative splinting
items.e: The epitendinous suture tidies the repair and adds roughly 10-50% to its strength while reducing gap formation and gliding resistance.

items.q: Gap formation at a flexor tendon repair site is considered clinically important when it exceeds about:
items.e: Gaps over about 3 mm reduce the accrual of strength and are associated with rupture and adhesion formation.

items.q: After a zone II flexor tendon repair, the strength of the repair falls in the early weeks, and ruptures most commonly occur:
o: Only after return to heavy labour at 6 months
items.e: Tendon ends soften in the inflammatory phase, so the repair is weakest during roughly days 5-21; most ruptures occur around days 7-14.

items.q: During a zone II flexor repair, a bulky repair catches on the A2 pulley. Which step is acceptable without causing significant bowstringing?
o: Excising the entire A2 and A4 pulleys
Venting (partially releasing) up to about two-thirds of the A2 pulley
Excising A2 and leaving A4 intact while also dividing A3
items.e: Partial release of A2 (up to about two-thirds) or of the whole A4 alone allows gliding without functionally significant bowstringing.

items.q: After a zone II flexor tendon repair, the dorsal blocking splint usually holds:
o: Wrist extended 45 degrees, MCP joints extended and IP joints flexed
Wrist fully flexed, MCP joints extended and IP joints extended
Wrist neutral to slight flexion, MCP joints flexed about 50-70 degrees and IP joints extended
Wrist neutral, MCP joints extended and IP joints flexed 90 degrees
items.e: The position relaxes the repair while keeping the IP joints extended to prevent PIP flexion contracture.

items.q: The Kleinert rehabilitation protocol after flexor tendon repair is based on:
o: Purely passive motion by the therapist (no active movement)
Active extension against rubber-band traction that passively flexes the finger
items.e: Kleinert used rubber bands from the nail to the splint: the patient actively extends and the band passively flexes. Duran used controlled passive motion.

items.q: After a 4-strand zone II flexor tendon repair with an epitendinous suture, which rehabilitation approach generally gives the best final range of motion?
o: Immobilisation in a cast for 4 weeks
items.e: Strong multistrand repairs tolerate early active motion (for example the Saint John or Manchester short splint regimens), which reduces adhesions and gives better motion.

items.q: Eight months after a zone II flexor tendon repair, a patient has full passive but limited active finger flexion, and the soft tissues are supple. The most appropriate step is:
items.e: Adhesions are the commonest complication; tenolysis is done after about 3-6 months once soft tissues are mature and passive motion is full, followed by immediate active motion.

items.q: On day 10 after a zone II FDP repair, a patient feels a snap and loses active DIP flexion. The usual management is:
items.e: Early recognised ruptures are re-explored and re-repaired; late ruptures with scarring may need grafting or staged reconstruction.

items.q: After a flexor tendon graft, a patient's PIP joint paradoxically extends when he tries to flex the finger. This 'lumbrical-plus' finger results from:
o: A graft that is too short (quadriga)
Adhesion of FDS to the proximal phalanx
A graft that is too long, so FDP pull is transmitted through the lumbrical to the extensor apparatus
items.e: When FDP is lax distal to the lumbrical origin, contraction pulls the lumbrical, which extends the IP joints via the lateral bands. Treatment is lumbrical release or correcting graft tension.

items.q: Before planning a palmaris longus tendon graft, its presence can be confirmed by opposing the thumb to the little finger with the wrist flexed. This is the:
items.e: Palmaris longus is absent in about 15% of people; Schaeffer's test makes the tendon stand out at the wrist. Plantaris or toe extensors are alternatives.

items.q: In two-stage (Hunter) flexor tendon reconstruction, the tendon graft is usually inserted at the second stage after about:
items.e: The silicone rod is left for about 3 months to form a mature pseudosheath, through which the graft is then passed.

items.q: In Boyes' preoperative classification for flexor tendon grafting, grade 1 indicates:
o: Minimal scarring with mobile joints and no trophic changes (good prognosis)
items.e: Boyes grade 1 is good; grades 2-5 add scarring, joint damage, nerve injury and multiple-digit involvement, each worsening the prognosis.

items.q: The posterior interosseous nerve, which can be divided during wrist denervation, lies on the floor of which dorsal extensor compartment?
items.e: The terminal PIN runs on the floor of the fourth compartment on the radial side, supplying sensory fibres to the wrist capsule.

items.q: Intersection syndrome causes pain and crepitus on the dorsoradial forearm about 4-8 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle, where:
o: The first-compartment muscles (APL and EPB) cross over the second-compartment tendons (ECRL and ECRB)
EPL crosses over ECRL and ECRB distal to Lister's tubercle
ECU subluxes over the ulnar head
items.e: Intersection syndrome is a tenosynovitis of the second compartment where APL and EPB cross it proximally; De Quervain's is more distal at the radial styloid.

items.q: Persistent symptoms after release of the first dorsal compartment for De Quervain's tenosynovitis are most often due to:
o: Division of the superficial radial nerve
Failure to release a separate EPB subcompartment
items.e: A separate fibro-osseous subsheath for EPB is common; if it is not identified and released, symptoms persist.

items.q: After a laceration over the dorsum of the hand proximal to the juncturae tendinum, a patient can still extend the affected finger at the MCP joint. The most likely explanation is:
o: The interossei extend the MCP joint
The lumbrical extends the MCP joint
Juncturae tendinum from adjacent EDC tendons transmit extension
The sagittal band extends the MCP joint independently
items.e: Juncturae link the EDC tendons distally, so a proximal EDC laceration can be masked; careful exploration is needed.

items.q: When harvesting extensor indicis proprius for a tendon transfer, it is identified at the MCP joint as the tendon lying:
o: Radial to the EDC tendon of the index finger
Ulnar to the EDC tendon of the index finger
items.e: EIP and EDM both lie ulnar to the corresponding EDC tendon, which helps identify them for transfer (for example EIP to EPL).

items.q: With the PIP joint held in extension, the DIP joint cannot be passively flexed, but it flexes easily when the PIP joint is flexed. This indicates tightness of the:
items.e: The oblique retinacular ligament passes volar to the PIP axis and dorsal to the DIP axis, linking the two joints; its tightness is assessed by this Haines-Zancolli manoeuvre.

items.q: In boutonniere deformity, the lateral bands sublux volar to the PIP joint axis because of attenuation of the:
items.e: The triangular ligament links the lateral bands dorsally over the middle phalanx; when it stretches, the bands fall volarly and become PIP flexors.

items.q: In swan-neck deformity, the lateral bands sublux dorsally over the PIP joint. The structure that normally prevents this dorsal subluxation is the:
items.e: The transverse retinacular ligament tethers the lateral bands to the volar plate at the PIP joint; laxity allows dorsal subluxation and PIP hyperextension.

items.q: The lumbrical muscles are unique because they:
o: Insert on the volar plate of the MCP joint
Are all supplied by the median nerve
Extend the MCP joint and flex the IP joints
Originate from a flexor tendon (FDP) and insert into the extensor apparatus, relaxing their own antagonist
items.e: Lumbricals arise from FDP and insert on the radial lateral band, so their contraction slackens FDP distally; they flex the MCP joint and extend the IP joints.

items.q: An extensor tendon laceration over the dorsum of a metacarpal shaft is in extensor zone:
items.e: Odd zones lie over joints (I DIP, III PIP, V MCP, VII wrist); zone VI is the metacarpal and IV the proximal phalanx.

items.q: Extensor tendon lacerations in zone VII are particularly prone to which problem after repair?
items.e: Zone VII lies under the extensor retinaculum; repairs here tend to adhere, and partial retinacular release may be needed.

items.q: A carpenter cuts the dorsum of the DIP joint with a chisel, dividing the terminal extensor tendon. In Doyle's classification this open mallet injury is type:
items.e: Doyle I is closed (with or without small avulsion); II is a laceration at or proximal to the DIP joint; III is deep abrasion with loss of skin and tendon; IV is a mallet fracture.

items.q: At week 4 of continuous splinting for a closed tendinous mallet finger, the patient removes the splint and lets the DIP joint flex. The correct advice is to:
o: Continue for the remaining 2 weeks only
Stop splinting and accept the lag
Restart the full period of continuous extension splinting
items.e: Any flexion during the full-time period disrupts the healing terminal tendon, so the 6-8 week full-time splinting period starts again.

items.q: A patient presents 8 weeks after a closed tendinous mallet injury with a 30-degree DIP extensor lag and no swan-neck deformity. The usual first treatment is:
o: Continuous DIP extension splinting for 6-8 weeks
Terminal tendon reconstruction with a graft
items.e: Extension splinting remains effective even when presentation is delayed (up to about 3 months) and is tried before surgery.

items.q: A chronic untreated mallet finger has produced a supple swan-neck deformity. A simple soft-tissue procedure to rebalance the extensor mechanism is:
o: Volar plate release at the PIP joint
items.e: Releasing the central slip transfers extensor pull to the lateral bands and DIP joint, correcting PIP hyperextension. Terminal tendon tenotomy is used for chronic boutonniere.

items.q: A closed acute boutonniere injury is splinted with the PIP joint in extension for 6 weeks while the DIP joint is left free and actively flexed. DIP flexion is encouraged mainly to:
o: Pull the lateral bands dorsally and prevent oblique retinacular ligament tightness
Stretch the volar plate of the PIP joint
items.e: Active DIP flexion draws the lateral bands distally and dorsally, stopping them becoming fixed volar to the PIP axis.

items.q: A patient with a chronic boutonniere deformity has a fixed 40-degree PIP flexion contracture. Before any extensor reconstruction, the first step is to:
o: Restore full passive PIP extension with splinting or serial casting
items.e: Reconstruction is pointless with a fixed contracture; most chronic cases improve with splinting, and surgery is considered only once passive extension is restored.

items.q: A chronic boutonniere deformity with full passive PIP extension remains troublesome because of fixed DIP hyperextension. A simple procedure to improve DIP flexion is:
o: Terminal extensor tendon tenotomy over the middle phalanx (Dolphin)
items.e: Dividing the terminal tendon proximal to the oblique retinacular ligament insertion lets the DIP joint flex while the ORL maintains some extension.

items.q: After a PIP hyperextension injury, a patient has a fixed PIP flexion contracture with normal DIP joint motion and no DIP hyperextension. This is:
o: Pseudoboutonniere deformity from volar plate scarring
items.e: Pseudoboutonniere follows volar plate injury; unlike boutonniere the central slip is intact and the DIP joint is not hyperextended.

items.q: A boxer has acute painful ulnar subluxation of the middle finger EDC tendon with an extension lag at the MCP joint 1 week after a punch. The first-line treatment is:
o: Cast immobilisation of the wrist only
Relative motion (yoke) splint holding the MCP joint in relative extension for about 6 weeks
items.e: Acute radial sagittal band injuries usually heal with splinting; surgical repair or centralisation is reserved for chronic or failed cases.

items.q: In a clenched-fist (fight bite) injury over the MCP joint, the organism classically resistant to clindamycin and first-generation cephalosporins is:
items.e: Eikenella, a human oral commensal, is sensitive to penicillins, so co-amoxiclav is the usual choice. Pasteurella is associated with cat and dog bites.

items.q: A small laceration over the third MCP joint after a punch appears superficial with the fingers extended. Why should the wound be examined and explored with the fist clenched?
o: Skin, tendon and capsule wounds align only in the clenched position, revealing joint penetration
The sagittal band can be tested only in flexion
The digital nerve is visible only in flexion
items.e: With the fingers extended the tendon wound retracts proximally from the skin wound, concealing joint penetration; assume the joint is involved and explore.

items.q: A relative motion extension (yoke) splint for a zone V-VI extensor repair works by:
o: Holding all fingers in full flexion
Holding the injured finger's MCP joint about 15-20 degrees more extended than the adjacent fingers
Immobilising the wrist in 45 degrees of flexion
Blocking the IP joints in extension only
items.e: The yoke reduces tension on the repaired EDC while allowing early active motion of all fingers.

items.q: A clean laceration divides about 30% of the cross-section of an FDP tendon in zone II, with no triggering. The usual management is:
o: Trim or bevel the cut edge without a core suture and mobilise early
items.e: Partial lacerations of less than about 50-60% are generally not core-repaired; trimming prevents catching on pulleys, and early motion follows.

items.q: A rugby player presents 3 months after an untreated FDP avulsion of the ring finger. He has full PIP flexion through an intact FDS, and the DIP joint is stable. The most common sensible management is:
o: Excision of FDS and single-stage FDP graft in all cases
Accept the deficit, or perform DIP tenodesis or arthrodesis if the joint is unstable
items.e: Late FDP repair is not possible after retraction and contracture; most patients function well with FDS, and grafting through an intact FDS risks harming PIP motion.

items.q: A patient cannot extend the thumb at the IP joint after a wrist fracture. Which test specifically isolates EPL function?
o: Lifting the thumb off the table with the palm flat (retropulsion)
Thumb IP extension with the hand in any position
items.e: Thumb IP extension can be produced by intrinsics through the extensor hood; retropulsion of the thumb above the plane of the palm specifically tests EPL.

items.q: Water accounts for approximately what proportion of the wet weight of normal adult articular cartilage?
items.e: Water forms about 65-80% of the wet weight of articular cartilage, held in the matrix by the negatively charged proteoglycans; collagen forms 10-20% and proteoglycans 10-15%.

items.q: Within the heterotypic collagen fibril of articular cartilage, which collagen type cross-links the surfaces of type II fibrils?
items.e: Type IX collagen is covalently bound to the surface of type II fibrils and cross-links them (the II-IX-XI network); type X is confined to the calcified zone and hypertrophic physis.

items.q: Which collagen type is concentrated in the pericellular matrix immediately surrounding articular chondrocytes and rises early in osteoarthritis?
items.e: Type VI collagen forms the thin pericellular matrix around chondrocytes and increases early in OA; type II makes up the bulk of the interterritorial matrix.

items.q: The glycosaminoglycan side chains carried on the aggrecan core protein are:
items.e: Aggrecan carries chondroitin sulfate (4- and 6-) and keratan sulfate chains; hyaluronic acid is the backbone to which many aggrecan molecules attach, not a side chain.

items.q: With normal ageing of articular cartilage, which glycosaminoglycan increases in concentration?
o: Hyaluronic acid within aggrecan side chains
items.e: Keratan sulfate rises with age while chondroitin-4 sulfate falls and chondroitin-6 sulfate stays roughly constant, so the chondroitin:keratan ratio falls with ageing (it rises in OA).

items.q: How does the concentration of chondroitin-6 sulfate in articular cartilage change with normal ageing?
o: It disappears completely after the fifth decade
items.e: Chondroitin-6 sulfate stays about the same with age; chondroitin-4 sulfate decreases and keratan sulfate increases.

items.q: The deep (radial) zone of articular cartilage is characterised by:
o: Highest proteoglycan content, lowest water content and collagen fibres perpendicular to the surface
Highest water content and collagen parallel to the surface
Type X collagen and hydroxyapatite with hypertrophic cells
items.e: The deep zone has the most proteoglycan, the least water, the largest fibrils oriented perpendicular to the surface and chondrocytes in vertical columns, so it resists compression; the calcified zone (type X) lies below the tidemark.

items.q: The lamina splendens of articular cartilage is best described as:
o: The basophilic line between uncalcified and calcified cartilage
The cement line between calcified cartilage and subchondral bone
The chondrocyte-rich layer of the middle zone
An acellular film of fine fibrils covering the superficial zone
items.e: The lamina splendens is a thin acellular layer of fine collagen fibrils lying on top of the superficial (tangential) zone; the basophilic line separating deep and calcified cartilage is the tidemark.

items.q: The thickest articular cartilage in the human body, reaching about 5-7 mm, is found on the:
items.e: Cartilage is thickest where contact stresses are highest; the patella has the thickest articular cartilage in the body (up to about 5-7 mm).

items.q: Which regional compartment of the articular cartilage matrix is the largest and contributes most to its mechanical properties?
items.e: The matrix is divided into pericellular (thin, type VI), territorial and interterritorial regions; the interterritorial region forms the bulk and gives cartilage its mechanical properties.

items.q: The principal energy pathway of adult articular chondrocytes is:
items.e: Chondrocytes live in a low oxygen tension, avascular environment and rely mainly on anaerobic glycolysis; they have a low metabolic rate.

items.q: Which growth factor is regarded as the main anabolic factor for chondrocytes present in synovial fluid?
items.e: IGF-1 is the principal anabolic factor in synovial fluid stimulating matrix synthesis; IL-1 beta and TNF-alpha are catabolic cytokines.

items.q: Sprifermin, investigated as a disease-modifying drug for knee osteoarthritis by increasing cartilage thickness, is a recombinant form of:
items.e: Sprifermin is recombinant human FGF-18, an anabolic factor for chondrocytes studied as an intra-articular disease-modifying OA drug.

items.q: Degradation of aggrecan in osteoarthritic cartilage is mediated mainly by which enzyme family?
items.e: Aggrecanases ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5 cleave aggrecan (ADAMTS-5 dominant in animal models); cathepsin K is the osteoclast collagenase, and lysyl oxidase forms collagen cross-links.

items.q: The naturally occurring inhibitors that limit matrix metalloproteinase activity in cartilage are:
items.e: TIMPs (together with plasminogen activator inhibitor) are the natural inhibitors of MMPs; an imbalance in favour of MMPs drives cartilage breakdown in OA.

items.q: A 30-year-old's knee is immobilised in a cast for 8 weeks. The expected early change in the articular cartilage is:
o: Irreversible loss of type II collagen with tidemark duplication
Proteoglycan loss with softening that is largely reversible on remobilisation
Increased stiffness from advanced glycation end-product accumulation
Hypertrophy of the superficial zone with increased proteoglycan
items.e: Immobilisation removes the cyclic loading that pumps nutrients, causing proteoglycan loss, softening and thinning that are largely reversible early; collagen is lost only with prolonged insult.

items.q: Salter's experimental work showed that continuous passive motion after a full-thickness articular cartilage defect in animals:
o: Caused delamination of the repair tissue
Improved healing, with more hyaline-like repair tissue
Had no effect compared with immobilisation
Produced mainly bone rather than cartilage in the defect
items.e: Salter's CPM experiments demonstrated better healing of full-thickness defects with a more hyaline-like repair tissue than with immobilisation or intermittent active motion.

items.q: When a constant compressive load is applied to articular cartilage, the deformation progressively increases with time as fluid is exuded. This viscoelastic behaviour is called:
items.e: Creep is increasing deformation under a constant load; stress relaxation is the fall in stress under a constant deformation.

items.q: Articular cartilage is held at a fixed compressive deformation and the measured stress falls progressively with time. This phenomenon is:
items.e: Stress relaxation is the time-dependent decrease in stress at constant strain, reflecting fluid redistribution in the biphasic matrix; creep is deformation increasing under constant load.

items.q: The permeability of articular cartilage:
o: Is inversely related to proteoglycan content and falls as the tissue is compressed
Increases as the tissue is compressed
Is directly proportional to proteoglycan content
Is highest in the deep zone
items.e: Proteoglycans restrict fluid flow, so permeability is inversely related to their content, and strain-dependent permeability falls with compression, trapping fluid and protecting the matrix.

items.q: The coefficient of friction of a normal synovial joint is approximately:
items.e: Synovial joints have a coefficient of friction of about 0.002-0.04, lower than any man-made bearing; metal-on-polyethylene is about 0.05-0.15.

items.q: During dynamic joint motion, the main lubrication mode in which deformation of cartilage increases the contact area and traps a fluid film between the surfaces is:
items.e: Elastohydrodynamic lubrication, where the compliant cartilage deforms to enlarge contact and trap fluid, is regarded as the main mode during dynamic motion; boundary lubrication by lubricin dominates at low speed and high load.

items.q: At heel strike, the articular surfaces of the knee approach each other perpendicularly, and the fluid being squeezed out of the gap supports the load. This mechanism is called:
items.e: Squeeze-film lubrication occurs when surfaces approach perpendicularly, generating pressure in the fluid as it is squeezed out; hydrodynamic lubrication requires tangential sliding of non-parallel surfaces.

items.q: In 'boosted' lubrication of synovial joints:
o: Fluid is squeezed out of the cartilage into the joint space under load
A monolayer of lubricin bonds to each surface
A fluid wedge forms between non-parallel sliding surfaces
Solvent passes into the cartilage, leaving a concentrated hyaluronic acid-protein gel pooled between the surfaces
items.e: Boosted lubrication describes water and small solutes entering the cartilage under load so that concentrated hyaluronate-protein gel is left between the surfaces; fluid exuding from cartilage is weeping lubrication.

items.q: A child with congenital flexion contractures of the fingers, early non-inflammatory joint failure, coxa vara and pericardial effusion most likely has a mutation in the gene encoding:
items.e: Camptodactyly-arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis syndrome results from PRG4 mutations causing loss of lubricin, the boundary lubricant, with early joint failure.

items.q: Microscopic damage that accumulates in articular cartilage from repetitive cyclic loading, even when lubrication is adequate, is termed:
items.e: Fatigue wear results from accumulated microdamage from cyclic loading regardless of lubrication; adhesive and abrasive wear are forms of interfacial wear between surfaces.

items.q: Accumulation of pentosidine and other advanced glycation end-products in ageing articular cartilage causes the tissue to become:
items.e: AGEs form non-enzymatic collagen cross-links with age, increasing stiffness and brittleness and linking ageing to OA risk; softening, increased permeability and hydration are features of OA.

items.q: Compared with normal cartilage, the modulus of elasticity of osteoarthritic articular cartilage is:
o: Increased in tension but unchanged in compression
items.e: OA cartilage is softer, with decreased stiffness and increased permeability due to proteoglycan loss and collagen network disruption; ageing cartilage, in contrast, becomes stiffer.

items.q: At arthroscopy, a femoral condyle chondral lesion shows fragmentation and fissuring over an area 2 cm in diameter, without exposed bone. The Outerbridge grade is:
items.e: Outerbridge grade 3 is fragmentation and fissuring over 1.3 cm (half an inch) in diameter; grade 2 is under 1.3 cm and grade 4 is erosion to exposed subchondral bone.

items.q: Under the ICRS classification, a chondral lesion extending deeper than 50% of the cartilage thickness but not penetrating the subchondral bone is:
items.e: ICRS grade 3 (severely abnormal) lesions extend beyond 50% depth (3a-3d); grade 2 is under 50% depth and grade 4 extends through the subchondral bone.

items.q: During arthroscopic microfracture of a femoral condyle defect, awl perforations are recommended to be placed approximately how far apart?
items.e: Holes are placed about 3-4 mm apart, perpendicular to the surface, preserving bridges of subchondral plate between them so that the plate is not weakened.

items.q: In mosaicplasty (osteochondral autograft transfer) for a femoral condyle defect, donor plugs are usually harvested from the:
o: Central weight-bearing area of the lateral femoral condyle
Margins of the femoral trochlea or intercondylar notch
items.e: Plugs are taken from relatively non-weight-bearing areas such as the trochlear margins or intercondylar notch; donor-site morbidity limits the size of defect that can be treated.

items.q: Fresh osteochondral allografts for large femoral condyle defects should ideally be implanted within about how long after harvest to maintain chondrocyte viability?
items.e: Chondrocyte viability falls with storage time, so fresh allografts are generally implanted within about 28 days of harvest; frozen grafts lose chondrocyte viability.

items.q: The commonest complication of first-generation autologous chondrocyte implantation using a periosteal patch is:
items.e: Periosteal patch hypertrophy causing catching and requiring debridement was the commonest problem with first-generation ACI, leading to collagen membrane (second-generation) and matrix-seeded (MACI) techniques.

items.q: A 26-year-old footballer has a symptomatic 5 cm2 full-thickness medial femoral condyle defect with a stable, well-aligned knee, normal menisci and a previously failed microfracture. The most appropriate procedure is:
items.e: ACI/MACI suits larger defects (about 2-10 cm2) in young active patients and after failed marrow stimulation; repeat microfracture gives fibrocartilage with poor durability in large defects.

items.q: A 35-year-old with a 3 cm2 medial femoral condyle full-thickness chondral defect has 8 degrees of varus mechanical alignment. Cartilage restoration should be combined with:
items.e: Uncorrected malalignment overloads the repair and causes failure, so a varus knee with a medial defect needs a valgus-producing HTO at the same time; a distal femoral varus osteotomy would add to medial overload.

items.q: The synovial intima permits free exchange between blood and synovial fluid because it:
o: Has a continuous endothelium with tight junctions
Is a single layer of keratinised epithelium
Lacks a basement membrane and tight junctions
items.e: The intima is 1-4 cells thick with no basement membrane or tight junctions, overlying a highly vascular subintima with fenestrated capillaries, which allows ready diffusion.

items.q: Which of the following intra-articular surfaces of the knee is NOT covered by synovial membrane?
o: Articular cartilage of the femoral condyles
Inner surface of the joint capsule
items.e: Synovium lines the capsule, pouches, bursae and tendon sheaths but does not cover articular cartilage or the meniscal articular surfaces.

items.q: Normal synovial fluid does not clot when aspirated because it:
o: Contains high concentrations of heparin from mast cells
Has a high hyaluronic acid concentration that inhibits thrombin
Contains no fibrinogen or clotting factors
Has a very low calcium concentration
items.e: Synovial fluid is a plasma dialysate from which large proteins such as fibrinogen are excluded; in inflammation, fibrinogen enters and the fluid may clot.

items.q: The viscosity of normal synovial fluid falls as the rate of shear increases. This property, which depends on hyaluronic acid, is described as:
items.e: Synovial fluid is non-Newtonian and thixotropic owing to hyaluronic acid, so viscosity falls with increasing shear rate; dilute or degraded hyaluronate in inflammation gives a poor string sign.

items.q: The upper limit of the white cell count in normal synovial fluid is approximately:
items.e: Normal synovial fluid has fewer than about 200 WBC/mm3 with under 25% neutrophils; 200-2,000 is non-inflammatory.

items.q: A 68-year-old with a chronically swollen knee has clear, viscous yellow aspirate with 800 WBC/mm3 and 15% neutrophils, and no crystals. This is most consistent with:
items.e: A count of 200-2,000 WBC/mm3 with under 25% neutrophils is non-inflammatory fluid, typical of OA, trauma, AVN or neuropathic joints; RA and gout give inflammatory counts above 2,000.

items.q: A 45-year-old diabetic presents with a 2-day history of a hot, swollen knee. Aspiration shows turbid fluid with 110,000 WBC/mm3, 95% neutrophils and low glucose. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Synovial WBC over 50,000/mm3 with over 75-90% neutrophils and low glucose indicates septic arthritis; RA usually gives 2,000-50,000 WBC.

items.q: Aspiration of a tense haemarthrosis after a knee injury shows fat globules floating on the blood. This finding indicates:
items.e: Fat globules come from marrow fat escaping through a fracture into the joint, so a lipohaemarthrosis indicates an intra-articular fracture.

items.q: A 50-year-old man has an acutely swollen first MTP joint. Compensated polarised light microscopy of the aspirate shows needle-shaped crystals that are yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis. These crystals are:
items.e: Gout crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent, appearing yellow when parallel to the compensator; CPPD crystals are rhomboid, weakly positive and blue when parallel.

items.q: Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals in synovial fluid, as in Milwaukee shoulder, are best identified with:
o: Polarised light microscopy showing strong negative birefringence
Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence
items.e: BCP crystals are too small to be seen individually and are not birefringent; they form clumps that stain with Alizarin red. Congo red with apple-green birefringence identifies amyloid.

items.q: Bipyramidal, positively birefringent crystals in the synovial fluid of a patient on long-term dialysis are most likely:
items.e: Calcium oxalate crystals are bipyramidal and positively birefringent and occur in chronic renal failure; cholesterol crystals are flat notched plates seen in chronic effusions.

items.q: According to the 2018 ICM definition, which synovial fluid threshold is a minor criterion for chronic periprosthetic knee or hip infection?
items.e: For chronic PJI (beyond about 6 weeks), ICM 2018 uses synovial WBC over 3,000/mm3 and PMN over 80%; the higher thresholds (over 10,000 and 90%) apply to acute postoperative infection.

items.q: A 40-year-old with recurrent diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour of the knee after two open synovectomies has unresectable disease causing severe morbidity. The approved targeted systemic drug acts by inhibiting:
items.e: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour is driven by CSF1 overexpression from a translocation; pexidartinib, a CSF1R inhibitor, is approved for symptomatic unresectable disease.

items.q: In a normally aligned lower limb on a standing long-leg radiograph, the mechanical axis (centre of the femoral head to the centre of the ankle) typically passes:
o: Just medial to the centre of the knee
Through the lateral third of the lateral compartment
Medial to the medial tibial plateau
items.e: The normal mechanical axis passes just medial to the knee centre, giving an overall alignment of about 0-3 degrees of varus; passing medial to the whole plateau indicates marked varus.

items.q: The anatomical axis of the femur differs from its mechanical axis by approximately:
items.e: Because the femoral shaft is offset from the head, the anatomical axis lies about 5-7 degrees valgus to the mechanical axis, which is why the distal femoral cut is set at that angle to the intramedullary rod.

items.q: With mechanical alignment TKA using an intramedullary femoral guide, the distal femoral cut is set at what angle relative to the anatomical axis, so that it is perpendicular to the mechanical axis?
items.e: The intramedullary rod follows the anatomical axis, so a 5-7 degree valgus setting produces a cut perpendicular to the mechanical axis; a 0 degree cut would leave the femoral component in varus.

items.q: In the native knee, the proximal tibial joint line is oriented relative to the tibial mechanical axis in approximately:
o: 3 degrees of varus (medial proximal tibial angle about 87 degrees)
items.e: The native tibial plateau sits in about 3 degrees of varus (MPTA about 87 degrees); mechanical alignment deliberately cuts it perpendicular, which kinematic alignment avoids.

items.q: The 'anatomical alignment' concept of TKA described by Hungerford aimed for:
o: Restoration of each patient's pre-arthritic limb alignment
A joint line in about 3 degrees of varus with an overall neutral limb
Tibial and femoral cuts both perpendicular to their mechanical axes
Deliberate residual varus of 5 degrees in all knees
items.e: Anatomical alignment cut the tibia in about 3 degrees of varus and the femur in matching valgus so the limb was neutral but the joint line oblique like the native knee; restoring each patient's own alignment is kinematic alignment.

items.q: The chief practical difference between kinematic alignment and mechanical alignment TKA in soft-tissue handling is that kinematic alignment:
o: Aims for minimal or no collateral ligament releases
Requires routine release of the superficial MCL
Relies on routine lateral retinacular release
items.e: Kinematic alignment resurfaces the pre-arthritic joint so native ligament tension is restored with few releases, whereas mechanical alignment corrects to neutral and balances with releases.

items.q: How many alignment phenotypes are described in the CPAK (Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee) classification?
items.e: CPAK combines three categories of arithmetic HKA (varus, neutral, valgus) with three of joint line obliquity (apex distal, neutral, apex proximal), giving nine phenotypes.

items.q: Regarding robotic and computer-navigated TKA, the best-supported current statement is that they:
o: Have proven better 10-year survival than conventional TKA
Abolish the need for soft-tissue balancing
Reduce coronal alignment outliers, but clear superiority in clinical outcome or survival is not proven
Increase alignment outliers compared with manual instruments
items.e: Navigation and robotics improve the accuracy of component alignment and reduce outliers, but randomised trials and registries have not shown consistent clinical or survival benefit.

items.q: The classic coronal alignment target for mechanical alignment TKA, associated in older series with better implant survival, is:
o: Neutral within plus or minus 8 degrees
Neutral hip-knee-ankle angle within plus or minus 3 degrees
7 degrees of valgus of the mechanical axis
items.e: Older series linked a mechanical axis within 3 degrees of neutral with lower failure, although the strength of this association with modern implants is debated.

items.q: Using measured resection in a varus arthritic knee, the proximal tibial cut is usually referenced at about 8-10 mm below the:
o: Deepest point of the medial plateau defect
Tip of the medial tibial spine
items.e: The resection equal to implant thickness (about 8-10 mm) is measured from the less worn, higher plateau; taking 8-10 mm below the deepest defect would remove excessive bone.

items.q: In a posterior-stabilised TKA, the tibial cut is usually given less posterior slope than in a cruciate-retaining TKA, mainly because excessive slope in a PS knee:
o: Opens the flexion gap and risks flexion instability and post impingement
Causes anterior notching of the femur
Tightens the extension gap and causes recurvatum
Increases patellar maltracking through tibial internal rotation
items.e: With the PCL sacrificed, extra slope loosens the flexion gap (risking cam jump) and can cause post impingement; CR knees use more slope to allow PCL-mediated flexion.

items.q: For the intramedullary femoral alignment guide in TKA of a typical knee, the entry hole is placed:
o: At the centre of the lateral femoral condyle
Through the trochlear groove at its proximal end only
Just medial and anterior to the PCL origin in the intercondylar notch
items.e: The entry point slightly medial and anterior to the femoral PCL origin best aligns the rod with the femoral canal; a poorly placed entry point alters the coronal angle of the distal cut.

items.q: The 'surgical' transepicondylar axis used for femoral component rotation joins the lateral epicondyle to the:
items.e: The surgical TEA runs from the lateral epicondylar prominence to the sulcus of the medial epicondyle (deep MCL origin); the clinical TEA uses the medial prominence instead.

items.q: Whiteside's anteroposterior axis is an unreliable rotational landmark for the femoral component in which situation?
o: Varus knee with a normal trochlea
Hypoplastic lateral femoral condyle with a normal trochlea
items.e: Whiteside's line runs from the deepest point of the trochlear groove to the centre of the notch, so a dysplastic trochlea makes it inaccurate; it is actually helpful when the lateral condyle is hypoplastic.

items.q: In measured resection, the femoral component is externally rotated about 3 degrees relative to the posterior condylar axis because:
o: The lateral posterior condyle is normally larger than the medial
The medial posterior femoral condyle is normally larger than the lateral
The tibial cut is made in 3 degrees of valgus
The patella sits medial to the trochlea
items.e: The larger medial posterior condyle makes the posterior condylar axis internally rotated relative to the TEA; external rotation by about 3 degrees restores a rectangular flexion gap after a perpendicular tibial cut.

items.q: In the gap-balancing technique for femoral component rotation, rotation is set by:
o: Rotating the femoral cutting block so the flexion gap is rectangular with the ligaments tensioned after the tibial cut
Aligning the component to the posterior condylar axis without external rotation
Aligning it to the medial third of the tibial tubercle
Matching the rotation of the patellar button
items.e: Gap balancing tensions the collaterals in flexion after the tibial cut and rotates the femoral cut parallel to it, creating a rectangular flexion gap; measured resection instead uses bony landmarks.

items.q: According to Berger's CT study, a combined (femoral plus tibial) component internal rotation of about 7-17 degrees after TKA was associated with:
o: Early patellar dislocation or patellar component failure
items.e: Berger found combined internal rotation of 1-4 degrees produced tilt, 3-8 degrees subluxation and 7-17 degrees early dislocation or patellar failure.

items.q: The investigation of choice to measure femoral and tibial component rotation in a painful TKA suspected of malrotation is:
items.e: CT allows measurement of femoral component rotation relative to the surgical TEA and tibial component rotation relative to the tubercle; a skyline view shows tilt but cannot quantify rotation.

items.q: Notching of the anterior femoral cortex during TKA is clinically important because it:
o: Reduces torsional strength of the distal femur and predisposes to supracondylar periprosthetic fracture
items.e: Biomechanical studies show anterior notching reduces torsional strength by around 30-40 percent, increasing the risk of supracondylar fracture.

items.q: With an anterior-referencing femoral instrument system, choosing a smaller femoral size mainly:
o: Removes more anterior cortex, causing notching
Removes more posterior condyle, loosening the flexion gap
items.e: Anterior referencing fixes the anterior cut, so the size difference comes off the posterior condyles; downsizing therefore enlarges the flexion gap.

items.q: A disadvantage of posterior-referencing femoral sizing instruments in TKA is the risk of:
o: Anterior notching or overstuffing of the patellofemoral joint
A loose flexion gap when downsizing
Elevation of the joint line in extension
items.e: Posterior referencing restores posterior condylar offset, so any size mismatch is taken at the anterior cut, risking notching (if undersized) or patellofemoral overstuffing (if oversized).

items.q: Which bone cut in TKA affects ONLY the extension gap?
items.e: The tibial cut affects both gaps, the posterior condylar cut affects only flexion, and the distal femoral cut affects only extension.

items.q: During TKA the knee is equally loose in both flexion and extension but the gaps are rectangular. The simplest correction is:
items.e: Symmetrical laxity in both gaps is managed by filling both with a thicker insert; upsizing the femur only corrects the flexion gap.

items.q: During TKA the flexion gap is balanced but the knee is loose in extension. Which correction addresses this without changing the flexion gap?
o: Distal femoral augmentation to bring the femoral component distally
items.e: Only the distal femoral level changes the extension gap alone; adding distal femur (augments) fills it, whereas a thicker insert alone would tighten flexion too.

items.q: During TKA the extension gap is balanced but the knee is loose in flexion. An appropriate correction is to:
o: Upsize the femoral component, adding posterior augments if needed
items.e: A larger femoral component (posterior augments) fills the flexion gap only; more tibial resection or slope would loosen flexion further.

items.q: Elevation of the joint line in TKA is generally considered acceptable only up to about:
items.e: Keeping the joint line within about 8 mm of native avoids mid-flexion instability and pseudo-patella baja with patellofemoral problems.

items.q: In a fixed varus knee undergoing TKA, the first step in medial soft-tissue balancing is:
o: Subperiosteal release of the superficial MCL from the tibia
Removal of medial tibial and femoral osteophytes
items.e: Osteophytes tent the medial capsule and MCL, so they are removed first; releases then proceed stepwise from deep MCL to the posteromedial corner and superficial MCL.

items.q: During medial release for a varus knee in TKA, the posteromedial capsule and semimembranosus insertion are released when the medial side is tight mainly in:
items.e: The posterior structures (posteromedial capsule, semimembranosus, posterior oblique fibres) tighten in extension, whereas the anterior fibres of the superficial MCL are tight in flexion.

items.q: The 'medial tibial reduction osteotomy' used for varus knees in TKA consists of:
o: A medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy
Release of the superficial MCL from the femur
Downsizing and lateralising the tibial tray and removing the uncovered medial tibial bone
Resecting more distal medial femoral condyle
items.e: Reducing the medial tibial overhang shortens the medial side and slackens the MCL without formal ligament release.

items.q: 'Pie-crusting' in TKA balancing refers to:
o: Subperiosteal stripping of a ligament from bone
Multiple small stab incisions in a tight ligament or capsule to lengthen it gradually
Drilling the sclerotic tibial bed before cementing
Serial osteophyte removal with a rongeur
items.e: Multiple needle or blade punctures (e.g. of the superficial MCL or the lateral structures) lengthen a tight structure progressively while keeping its continuity.

items.q: In a fixed valgus knee undergoing TKA, the iliotibial band is released mainly when the lateral side is tight in:
items.e: The ITB tightens in extension, whereas the popliteus is tight in flexion and the LCL in both.

items.q: Ranawat type II valgus knee deformity is defined as:
o: A correctable valgus with intact medial structures
A severe osseous deformity after osteotomy with an incompetent medial side
Valgus due solely to lateral tibial plateau fracture malunion
A fixed valgus deformity with an attenuated medial soft-tissue sleeve
items.e: Type I is correctable with intact medial tissues, type II is fixed with attenuated medial structures (may need more constraint) and type III is a severe osseous deformity with incompetent medial structures needing a constrained implant.

items.q: Which situation is a classic indication for a posterior-stabilised rather than cruciate-retaining TKA?
o: Mild varus with an intact PCL
Unicompartmental osteoarthritis in a young patient
Good preoperative range of motion with no deformity
items.e: After patellectomy the weakened extensor mechanism makes a CR knee prone to anteroposterior instability, so PCL substitution with a cam-post is favoured.

items.q: Fluoroscopic kinematic studies of cruciate-retaining TKA have shown which abnormal motion pattern?
o: Excessive femoral rollback beyond the native knee
Paradoxical anterior sliding of the femur on the tibia during flexion
Pure hinge motion with no rotation
items.e: Many CR knees show paradoxical anterior femoral translation in flexion instead of normal rollback, one reason for congruent and medial-pivot designs.

items.q: A complication specific to mobile-bearing TKA designs is:
o: Cam jump in a fixed-bearing CR knee
items.e: Mobile bearings can rotate out of position (spinout), particularly with flexion gap laxity; long-term survival is not proven to differ from fixed bearings.

items.q: The principle of using the least constraint necessary in TKA is based on the fact that more constrained implants:
o: Cannot be used with cemented fixation
Produce more anterior knee pain because of a thicker patella
Transfer more stress to the fixation interfaces, increasing loosening
items.e: Constraint resists varus-valgus and rotational forces through the implant rather than the soft tissues, loading the bone-cement-implant interfaces and increasing aseptic loosening.

items.q: A 60-year-old with post-polio paralysis has knee arthritis with severe genu recurvatum and weak quadriceps. The most appropriate TKA implant is:
items.e: Neuromuscular recurvatum tends to recur because the soft tissues stretch, so a linked rotating hinge with an extension stop is used.

items.q: The KAT (Knee Arthroplasty Trial) and meta-analyses on patellar resurfacing in TKA have shown that resurfacing mainly:
o: Markedly improves functional scores at 10 years
Increases revision for anterior knee pain
Reduces reoperation for anterior knee pain, with little difference in functional scores
items.e: Resurfacing reduces secondary resurfacing procedures for anterior knee pain, but patient-reported function is similar; inflammatory arthritis favours routine resurfacing.

items.q: To improve patellar tracking in TKA, the patellar button is preferably placed:
o: Lateralised on the cut patellar surface
Medialised on the cut patellar surface
Centred exactly regardless of patellar shape
Superiorly placed to lower the patella
items.e: Medialising the button recreates the medial apex of the patellar ridge and reduces the lateral pull; lateral placement promotes maltracking.

items.q: The 'no thumb' test in TKA is used to assess:
o: Patellar tracking through the arc of motion without medial digital pressure
Flexion gap tension with spacer blocks
Tibial component rotation against the tubercle
items.e: The patella should track centrally in the trochlea through flexion without the surgeon's thumb holding it medially; failure prompts a check of rotation and possibly lateral release.

items.q: To reduce the risk of patellar fracture when resurfacing the patella in TKA, the residual patellar bone thickness should generally be at least:
items.e: Leaving less than about 12 mm of bone after the cut weakens the patella and increases fracture risk; the composite thickness should restore the native thickness.

items.q: A patient has 75 degrees of flexion 6 weeks after an uncomplicated primary TKA despite physiotherapy. Infection has been excluded. The usual next step is:
o: Continue physiotherapy and review at 1 year
items.e: Flexion below about 90 degrees at 6-12 weeks is treated by manipulation under anaesthesia, which is most effective within about 12 weeks; arthroscopic or open arthrolysis and revision are later options.

items.q: Six weeks after TKA, a patient has a displaced supracondylar femoral fracture above a well-fixed cruciate-retaining femoral component. In the Lewis-Rorabeck classification this is type:
o: III, requiring revision to a distal femoral replacement
II, usually treated by fixation with a locking plate or retrograde nail
II, requiring revision to a stemmed femoral component
items.e: Type I is undisplaced with a stable prosthesis, type II displaced with a stable prosthesis (fixation; a retrograde nail needs an open-box design) and type III has a loose prosthesis needing revision.

items.q: The Felix classification of periprosthetic fractures around TKA applies to fractures of the:
o: Femoral shaft above a hip stem
items.e: Felix classifies tibial periprosthetic fractures by location and implant stability; Lewis-Rorabeck is for the supracondylar femur and Goldberg/Ortiguera-Berry for the patella.

items.q: During the proximal tibial cut in TKA, the popliteal artery is at greatest risk because it lies:
o: Directly behind the posterior capsule, close to the posterior tibia and slightly lateral to the midline
Within the substance of the PCL
Anterior to the popliteus muscle at the joint line
items.e: The popliteal artery lies behind the posterior capsule, only about 9 mm behind the tibia in flexion and slightly lateral to midline, so saws must be protected posteriorly and laterally.

items.q: A patient needing TKA has two old longitudinal scars over the knee. Which incision should generally be used?
o: The most lateral usable previous incision
A new midline incision between the scars regardless of the bridge width
A transverse incision joining both scars
items.e: The skin blood supply comes predominantly from the medial side, so using the most lateral scar avoids leaving a poorly perfused lateral flap; skin bridges of about 5-6 cm are preferred.

items.q: A complete patellar tendon rupture after TKA with poor-quality tissue is most reliably reconstructed with:
o: Immobilisation in a cylinder cast for 6 weeks
Extensor mechanism allograft or synthetic mesh reconstruction, with a medial gastrocnemius flap if needed
items.e: Primary repair after TKA has a high failure rate, so augmentation or reconstruction with allograft or synthetic mesh is preferred; the medial gastrocnemius flap adds soft-tissue cover and extensor support.

items.q: In the work-up of an unexplained painful primary TKA, the first condition that must be excluded is:
o: Periprosthetic joint infection, with ESR, CRP and aspiration
items.e: Infection must be excluded first because it changes management completely; instability, malrotation, loosening, patellar problems and referred pain are considered afterwards.

items.q: On a weight-bearing AP radiograph, the upper limit of the normal hallux valgus angle is about:
items.e: A hallux valgus angle (first metatarsal to proximal phalanx axis) under about 15° is normal. 9° is the upper limit of the normal first-second intermetatarsal angle, not the HVA.

items.q: The distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA) in hallux valgus is generally considered abnormal when it exceeds about:
items.e: A DMAA above about 10° indicates lateral tilt of the first metatarsal head articular surface; this matters because soft-tissue correction alone would leave an incongruent joint.

items.q: Which weight-bearing measurements place a hallux valgus deformity in the severe category?
items.e: Severe hallux valgus is usually defined as HVA over 40° and IMA over 16–20°. The other combinations are mild or moderate.

items.q: In hallux valgus, a first MTP joint is described as 'congruent' when:
o: The articular surfaces of the metatarsal head and phalangeal base are parallel
The proximal phalanx is laterally subluxed on the metatarsal head
The sesamoids lie lateral to the metatarsal head
items.e: A congruent joint has parallel articular surfaces with the deformity built into the head (increased DMAA); an incongruent joint has lateral subluxation of the phalanx on the head.

items.q: The Hardy and Clapham grading on a weight-bearing AP radiograph describes:
o: Position of the medial sesamoid relative to the first metatarsal axis
items.e: Hardy and Clapham grade the tibial sesamoid position relative to the metatarsal axis (grades 1–7); poor sesamoid reduction is linked to recurrence.

items.q: On a weight-bearing AP radiograph of a bunion, the lateral edge of the first metatarsal head looks rounded instead of angular (the 'round sign'). This indicates:
o: Avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head
items.e: A rounded lateral head contour reflects first metatarsal pronation; unaddressed pronation is a recognised cause of recurrence after correction.

items.q: In a patient with hallux valgus and coexisting metatarsus adductus, the measured intermetatarsal angle tends to be:
items.e: Metatarsus adductus brings the lesser metatarsals medially, so the 1–2 IMA appears smaller than the true deformity; correction is harder and recurrence higher.

items.q: Amputation of which digit is a recognised cause of secondary hallux valgus?
items.e: Loss of the second toe removes the lateral buttress of the hallux, which then drifts into valgus.

items.q: In juvenile hallux valgus, family history is common and transmission is most often:
o: Absent; it is always acquired from footwear
items.e: Juvenile hallux valgus is familial in most cases with a predominantly maternal pattern of transmission.

items.q: In a distal chevron (Austin) osteotomy, the V-shaped cut is oriented with its apex:
o: Distal, at the centre of the metatarsal head
items.e: The chevron is a V-shaped cut through the metatarsal head with its apex distal; the capital fragment is shifted laterally, usually up to about one third to half of the head width.

items.q: Why does a proximal first metatarsal osteotomy correct a larger intermetatarsal angle than a distal chevron osteotomy?
o: It allows a larger lateral release
Angular correction at the base produces greater displacement of the head distally
items.e: A small angular correction at the base gives a large lateral displacement of the metatarsal head because of the long lever arm, so proximal osteotomies suit moderate to severe IMAs.

items.q: The Ludloff osteotomy for hallux valgus is:
o: An oblique diaphyseal osteotomy running from dorsal-proximal to plantar-distal
A V-shaped osteotomy of the metatarsal head
A medial closing wedge of the proximal phalanx
A dorsal closing wedge of the proximal phalanx
items.e: The Ludloff is an oblique shaft osteotomy from dorsal-proximal to plantar-distal, rotated around a proximal screw to close the IMA; the Mau osteotomy runs in the opposite direction.

items.q: The Keller procedure for hallux valgus consists of:
o: Resection of the base of the proximal phalanx
items.e: Keller resection arthroplasty excises the base of the proximal phalanx; it is reserved for elderly low-demand patients because of cock-up deformity, transfer metatarsalgia and weak push-off.

items.q: A 78-year-old woman had a Keller resection arthroplasty 3 years ago. The most characteristic late deformity of the hallux is:
o: Mallet deformity of the IP joint
items.e: Loss of the short flexor insertion with base excision allows the toe to ride up in a cock-up deformity; transfer metatarsalgia is another common sequel.

items.q: Simple medial eminence excision (Silver bunionectomy) on its own is rarely used today mainly because of:
o: Avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head
items.e: Removing the bump does not correct the IMA or the joint subluxation, so the deformity recurs; it is used only as a component of other procedures.

items.q: For first MTP arthrodesis, the recommended sagittal position of the hallux relative to the floor is about:
items.e: About 10–15° of dorsiflexion to the floor (roughly 20–25° to the metatarsal shaft) with 10–15° of valgus and neutral rotation allows toe-off without IP joint overload.

items.q: A 60-year-old with severe hallux valgus (IMA 17°) has a first MTP arthrodesis without a metatarsal osteotomy. What usually happens to the intermetatarsal angle?
o: It increases because of loss of joint motion
It is unchanged and needs a later Lapidus
items.e: A first MTP fusion in correct valgus reduces the IMA spontaneously, so an additional basal osteotomy is usually unnecessary.

items.q: A 12-year-old girl has a painful but mild juvenile hallux valgus. The recommended general approach is:
o: Delay osteotomy until skeletal maturity, because recurrence is high
items.e: Juvenile hallux valgus recurs frequently after surgery in the growing foot, so correction is usually deferred to maturity; guided growth is an option in selected cases.

items.q: Guided growth for juvenile hallux valgus with metatarsus primus varus uses hemiepiphysiodesis of the:
o: Medial side of the distal first metatarsal
Medial side of the proximal phalanx
Lateral side of the proximal phalanx
Lateral side of the proximal first metatarsal physis
items.e: The first metatarsal physis is at its base; tethering its lateral side lets medial growth reduce the intermetatarsal angle.

items.q: A 50-year-old has a flexible hallux varus with a normal joint after bunion surgery. Which reconstruction is appropriate?
o: Tenodesis or transfer using extensor hallucis brevis or longus
items.e: Flexible postoperative hallux varus without arthritis is corrected by EHB tenodesis or a split EHL transfer; rigid or arthritic cases need first MTP fusion.

items.q: During bunion surgery, removing the medial eminence medial to the sagittal sulcus ('staking' the metatarsal head) predisposes to:
items.e: Over-resection of the medial eminence leaves no medial articular buttress and the phalanx drifts medially, causing hallux varus.

items.q: After a bunion operation through a medial incision, a patient has a painful neuroma and numbness of the dorsomedial hallux. The nerve injured is a branch of the:
items.e: The dorsomedial cutaneous nerve of the hallux is the terminal medial branch of the superficial peroneal nerve and lies at risk in the dorsomedial incision.

items.q: The most common complication after hallux valgus surgery is:
o: Avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head
items.e: Recurrence (roughly 10–25%) is the commonest complication, linked to undercorrected IMA, unrecognised DMAA, pronation, hypermobility and poor sesamoid reduction.

items.q: The approximate non-union rate after a modified Lapidus (first tarsometatarsal) arthrodesis is:
items.e: First TMT fusion non-union is reported in about 5–10%; other issues are shortening with transfer metatarsalgia and dorsiflexion malunion.

items.q: In the original McBride procedure, which step was mainly responsible for postoperative hallux varus?
items.e: Removing the lateral sesamoid eliminates the lateral restraint, so the hallux drifts into varus; the modified McBride preserves the sesamoid.

items.q: The earliest pathoanatomical change in the development of hallux valgus is:
o: Attenuation of the medial capsule and medial sesamoid ligament
items.e: Medial capsular and sesamoid ligament attenuation allows the phalanx to drift laterally, after which the adductor and long tendons act as deforming forces.

items.q: In established hallux valgus, the flexor and extensor hallucis longus tendons:
o: Remain central and protect against deformity
Become medial and act as correctors
Bowstring laterally and increase the valgus deformity
items.e: As the hallux drifts laterally, the long flexor and extensor tendons lie lateral to the joint axis and their pull worsens the valgus deformity.

items.q: In hallux valgus, the hallux usually rotates into:
o: Pronation (eversion), with the nail facing medially
Supination with the nail facing laterally
items.e: The hallux pronates as abductor hallucis slips plantarward; the toenail faces medially.

items.q: Hallux rigidus is characterised by:
o: A dorsal osteophyte of the first metatarsal head limiting dorsiflexion
A medial eminence with lateral deviation
items.e: Hallux rigidus is first MTP arthritis with a dorsal osteophyte ('dorsal bunion') that blocks dorsiflexion, causing pain at push-off; it is the commonest arthritis in the foot.

items.q: In the Coughlin and Shurnas classification of hallux rigidus, grade 0 denotes:
o: Joint space narrowing with pain at extremes
Mid-range pain with a positive grind test
Stiffness of the joint with a normal radiograph
items.e: Grade 0 is reduced dorsiflexion with normal radiographs; grades 1–3 add osteophytes and narrowing and grade 4 adds mid-range pain.

items.q: In a cheilectomy for hallux rigidus, how much of the metatarsal head is typically removed with the dorsal osteophyte?
items.e: Excising the dorsal osteophyte with the dorsal 25–30% of the head decompresses the joint and restores dorsiflexion without destabilising it.

items.q: A Moberg osteotomy, sometimes added to cheilectomy for hallux rigidus, is a:
o: Dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx
Medial closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx
Plantarflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal
Shortening osteotomy of the first metatarsal neck
items.e: A dorsal closing wedge of the proximal phalanx shifts the arc of motion into dorsiflexion, helping toe-off; the Akin is the medial closing wedge.

items.q: A shoe modification that limits first MTP motion and relieves hallux rigidus pain is a:
o: Morton's extension (carbon-fibre plate under the hallux)
items.e: A stiff carbon-fibre Morton's extension, or a rocker sole, reduces painful dorsiflexion at toe-off.

items.q: A silicone first MTP implant inserted years ago is failing. The characteristic complication of silicone joint implants is:
items.e: Wear debris from silicone implants provokes a foreign-body synovitis with lytic cysts and subsidence, so they have a high failure rate.

items.q: A 15-year-old athlete has first MTP pain and stiffness. In adolescent hallux rigidus, the usual underlying lesion is:
o: Freiberg infraction of the second metatarsal
Osteochondral lesion of the first metatarsal head
items.e: Adolescent hallux rigidus is typically associated with an osteochondritis dissecans-type lesion of the first metatarsal head, unlike the degenerative adult form.

items.q: A mallet toe is defined by isolated flexion deformity at the:
items.e: A mallet toe is DIP flexion from FDL contracture; flexible cases respond to FDL tenotomy at the DIP level.

items.q: A hammer toe, the commonest lesser toe deformity, consists of:
o: MTP hyperextension with PIP and DIP flexion
Flexion of the PIP joint with a neutral or slightly extended MTP joint
Varus rotation of the toe under its neighbour
items.e: Hammer toe is PIP flexion with the MTP neutral or mildly extended, most often of the second toe; MTP hyperextension plus PIP and DIP flexion is a claw toe.

items.q: A 3-year-old has a flexible third toe that is flexed and rotated into varus under the second toe. The preferred surgical treatment if it remains symptomatic is:
items.e: Congenital curly toe is due to FDL tightness and responds well to simple flexor tenotomy; many improve spontaneously.

items.q: In the Girdlestone-Taylor procedure for a flexible claw toe, the flexor digitorum longus tendon is:
o: Split and transferred to the dorsal extensor hood of the proximal phalanx
items.e: Transferring the split FDL dorsally to the extensor hood converts it into an MTP flexor and IP extender, substituting for the weak intrinsics.

items.q: A DuVries arthroplasty for a fixed hammer toe involves:
o: Resection of the head and neck of the proximal phalanx
Resection of the base of the proximal phalanx
Shortening osteotomy of the metatarsal neck
items.e: The DuVries procedure is a PIP resection arthroplasty (condylectomy of the proximal phalanx head) for fixed deformities; PIP arthrodesis is the alternative.

items.q: The most common complication of a Weil osteotomy of a lesser metatarsal is:
o: Avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head
Floating toe (toe that fails to touch the ground)
items.e: Floating toe follows plantar depression of the head and dorsal shift of the MTP axis, which turns the interossei into MTP extensors.

items.q: A Weil osteotomy of the second metatarsal is made:
o: As a dorsal closing wedge at the head
Obliquely through the neck, roughly parallel to the sole, and the head is translated proximally
As a V-shaped cut with lateral shift
items.e: An oblique cut from dorsal-distal to plantar-proximal, close to parallel with the weight-bearing surface, allows proximal translation that shortens the metatarsal and decompresses the MTP joint.

items.q: A clinical test for second MTP instability, in which the proximal phalanx is translated dorsally on the stabilised metatarsal head, is the:
o: Vertical drawer (Lachman) test of the MTP joint
items.e: Dorsal translation of the phalanx beyond about 50% of the joint indicates plantar plate insufficiency; Mulder's test is for interdigital neuroma.

items.q: For primary metatarsalgia, a metatarsal pad should be placed:
o: Just proximal to the painful metatarsal heads
Directly under the painful metatarsal heads
items.e: A pad placed proximal to the heads lifts and offloads them; placing it directly under the heads increases pressure.

items.q: A discrete, well-localised intractable plantar keratosis under a lesser metatarsal head is usually caused by:
o: A prominent plantar (fibular) condyle of the metatarsal head
items.e: A discrete IPK lies under a prominent condyle and can be treated by plantar condylectomy; a diffuse callosity reflects a long or plantarflexed metatarsal.

items.q: A 50-year-old with forefoot overload has a positive Silfverskiöld test. The Strayer procedure for this involves:
o: Percutaneous triple hemisection of the Achilles tendon
items.e: Strayer recession divides the gastrocnemius aponeurosis distal to the muscle bellies, relieving isolated gastrocnemius contracture while preserving soleus power.

items.q: Pathologically, a Morton (interdigital) neuroma is:
o: A schwannoma of the plantar digital nerve
Perineural fibrosis of the common plantar digital nerve
items.e: It is not a true neoplasm but perineural fibrosis and degeneration of the common digital nerve beneath the deep transverse metatarsal ligament.

items.q: In a patient with Morton neuroma, spreading apart of the toes adjacent to the affected web space on standing is called:
items.e: Sullivan sign is divergence of the adjacent toes caused by the mass in the web space; Mulder click is elicited by mediolateral compression.

items.q: The SI unit of absorbed radiation dose, defined as one joule of energy deposited per kilogram of tissue, is the:
items.e: Absorbed dose is measured in gray (1 Gy = 1 J/kg = 100 rad). The sievert is used for equivalent and effective dose, which include weighting factors for radiation type and tissue sensitivity.

items.q: To compare the whole-body cancer risk of a CT abdomen with that of a bone scan, the most appropriate dose quantity is:
o: Absorbed dose to the skin, in milligray
Exposure in air, in coulombs per kilogram
items.e: Effective dose sums the equivalent doses to each organ multiplied by tissue weighting factors, giving a single estimate of stochastic risk that can be compared across modalities. Activity and skin dose do not account for which organs are irradiated.

items.q: When converting absorbed dose to equivalent dose, the radiation weighting factor applied to alpha particles is:
items.e: Alpha particles have a radiation weighting factor of 20 because of their dense ionisation, whereas X-rays and gamma rays have a factor of 1.

items.q: Which of the following is a deterministic (tissue reaction) effect of ionising radiation?
items.e: Deterministic effects have a dose threshold and their severity rises with dose; cataract is the classic example relevant to fluoroscopy users. Cancers and heritable effects are stochastic.

items.q: According to the 2011 ICRP statement, the threshold absorbed dose to the lens of the eye for radiation-induced cataract is now considered to be about:
