items.e: ICRP lowered the cataract threshold to about 0.5 Gy in 2011, and at the same time cut the occupational lens dose limit from 150 to 20 mSv per year.

items.q: Stochastic effects of radiation, such as cancer induction, are characterised by:
o: A clear threshold below which no effect occurs
No threshold, with the probability (not the severity) of the effect rising with dose
Severity that increases in proportion to dose
items.e: Stochastic effects follow the linear no-threshold model: any dose carries some risk, and higher doses make the effect more likely but not more severe. Thresholds and dose-dependent severity describe deterministic effects.

items.q: The current ICRP occupational dose limit for the lens of the eye of a radiation worker is:
o: 50 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
items.e: The lens limit was reduced from 150 mSv to 20 mSv per year (averaged over 5 years, no single year over 50 mSv) in 2011, making lead glasses important for high-volume fluoroscopy users.

items.q: The annual effective dose limit recommended by ICRP for members of the general public is:
items.e: The public limit is 1 mSv per year, compared with 20 mSv per year (averaged over 5 years) for radiation workers.

items.q: The ICRP equivalent dose limit for the skin, hands and feet of an occupationally exposed orthopaedic surgeon is:
items.e: The extremity and skin limit is 500 mSv per year. The surgeon's hands usually receive the highest dose because they come close to or into the primary beam.

items.q: An orthopaedic registrar declares her pregnancy to the radiation protection officer. For the remainder of the pregnancy, the dose to the fetus should not exceed:
items.e: After declaration, the fetal dose limit is 1 mSv for the rest of the pregnancy, the same as for a member of the public; she can usually continue to work with appropriate shielding and monitoring.

items.q: Although the occupational effective dose limit is 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years, the maximum permitted in any single year is:
items.e: ICRP allows up to 50 mSv in any one year provided the 5-year average stays at or below 20 mSv per year.

items.q: A woman who is 11 weeks pregnant needs imaging after trauma. The gestational period during which the fetus is most vulnerable to radiation-induced microcephaly and intellectual disability is:
items.e: Organogenesis of the CNS makes 8 to 15 weeks the period of greatest risk for neurological effects. In the first 2 weeks the effect is all-or-none (loss or normal development).

items.q: Exposure of an embryo to a significant radiation dose in the first two weeks after conception typically results in:
o: An all-or-none effect: either loss of the pregnancy or normal development
Childhood leukaemia as the main risk
items.e: Before implantation the embryo either fails or recovers completely because surviving cells are still totipotent. Neurological malformation risk peaks at 8 to 15 weeks.

items.q: A pregnant trauma patient needs a CT of the abdomen and pelvis. The fetal dose below which no increase in malformation or fetal loss has been shown (ACOG) is about:
items.e: Fetal doses under about 50 mGy (5 rad) have not been associated with malformations or fetal loss; a CT abdomen-pelvis gives roughly 10 to 25 mGy, so necessary imaging should not be withheld.

items.q: In a diagnostic X-ray tube, most of the useful X-ray photons are produced by:
o: Characteristic radiation from inner-shell electron transitions
Bremsstrahlung, as electrons are decelerated by the nuclei of the tungsten target
Radioactive decay of the anode material
items.e: Braking (bremsstrahlung) radiation produces a continuous spectrum and is the main source of the beam; characteristic radiation contributes discrete peaks only.

items.q: Of the kinetic energy of electrons striking the anode of an X-ray tube, approximately what fraction is converted to heat?
items.e: Only about 1% of the energy becomes X-rays; the rest is heat, which is why the tungsten anode rotates to spread the heat load.

items.q: Increasing the peak kilovoltage (kVp) of a radiograph while keeping other factors constant will:
o: Increase beam penetration and reduce image contrast
Increase image contrast between bone and soft tissue
Reduce the energy of the photons in the beam
items.e: kVp controls beam quality; higher energy photons penetrate more, Compton scatter increases and the image becomes greyer with less contrast. mAs controls photon quantity.

items.q: If the tube current-time product (mAs) is doubled while kVp is unchanged, the patient dose:
items.e: mAs governs the number of photons, so dose rises in direct proportion to it, whereas kVp changes beam energy.

items.q: The photoelectric effect is the main reason bone appears white against soft tissue on a radiograph. Its probability is roughly proportional to:
o: Photon energy alone, independent of atomic number
Electron density of the tissue only
The cube of atomic number divided by the cube of photon energy (Z³/E³)
The square of the distance from the source
items.e: Photoelectric absorption rises steeply with atomic number (calcium, iodine, lead) and falls steeply with energy, which explains both image contrast and why it dominates at low kVp.

items.q: Aluminium filtration placed in the path of the X-ray beam at the tube is used primarily to:
o: Remove high-energy photons to improve contrast
Remove low-energy photons that would add skin dose without contributing to the image
items.e: Low-energy photons are absorbed in superficial tissue and never reach the detector, so removing them lowers patient skin dose. Scatter reaching the detector is reduced by grids and collimation.

items.q: On a hip radiograph taken for arthroplasty templating, magnification of the hip will increase if:
o: The distance between the hip and the detector increases
A 25 mm calibration ball is placed at the level of the hip
items.e: Magnification rises with object-to-detector distance and falls with longer source-to-image distance; a calibration marker at the level of the bone allows correction, typically for 15 to 20% magnification.

items.q: During percutaneous scaphoid fixation, a surgeon keeps his gloved fingers in the primary beam, believing lead-impregnated gloves protect him. The main problem with this practice is that:
o: Lead gloves fully block the beam, so the image is lost
Automatic brightness control increases tube output, raising dose to the hand and the patient
Lead gloves increase Compton scatter only to the image intensifier
It reduces the dose to the hand to an acceptable level, so there is no problem
items.e: Lead gloves give false security: the ABC system compensates for the attenuating glove by increasing output, and the hand also receives the full primary beam. Hands should be kept out of the beam.

items.q: When taking a horizontal lateral fluoroscopic view of the hip with a C-arm, where should the surgeon stand to minimise scatter exposure?
o: On the X-ray tube side of the patient
On the image intensifier (detector) side of the patient
Distance does not matter as long as a lead apron is worn
items.e: Most scatter arises where the beam enters the patient, on the tube side, so the surgeon should stand on the detector side and step back during screening.

items.q: Which of the following C-arm practices increases radiation dose to both patient and staff?
o: Using pulsed fluoroscopy at a low frame rate
Collimating the beam to the area of interest
Using last-image hold to review a position
items.e: Magnification modes increase dose rate; pulsed fluoroscopy, collimation and last-image hold are standard ALARA measures that reduce it.

items.q: A lead apron of 0.5 mm lead equivalent worn during fluoroscopy attenuates approximately what proportion of scattered radiation?
items.e: A 0.5 mm Pb-equivalent apron stops about 95% or more of scatter at diagnostic energies; it is not complete protection, so time and distance still matter.

items.q: In fluoroscopy-heavy orthopaedic procedures such as distal locking of a femoral nail, which part of the surgeon's body typically receives the highest radiation dose?
items.e: The hands are nearest the beam and are often in or close to it during targeting, so ring dosimeters are recommended; the extremity limit is 500 mSv per year.

items.q: Narrowing the X-ray beam with collimation during fluoroscopy has which combination of effects?
o: Lower patient dose but more scatter to staff
Higher image contrast but higher patient dose
Lower patient dose, less scatter to staff and a sharper image
No effect on scatter, only on field size
items.e: Collimation reduces the irradiated volume, so less scatter is produced, dose falls and contrast improves through reduced fog.

items.q: For surgeons, the most important source of occupational radiation exposure during fluoroscopy is:
o: Leakage radiation from the image intensifier
items.e: Compton scatter changes photon direction and spreads radiation around the theatre; it is also the main cause of image fog.

items.q: On a CT scan, a well-defined soft-tissue mass in the thigh has an attenuation of -90 Hounsfield units. This value indicates that the lesion is composed mainly of:
items.e: Fat measures about -100 to -50 HU; water is 0 HU, acute blood about +50 to +80 HU and bone several hundred HU or more.

items.q: In the Hounsfield scale used in CT, the reference value of 0 HU is assigned to:
items.e: HU express attenuation relative to water (0 HU), with air at -1000 HU and dense cortical bone at +1000 HU or more.

items.q: In helical CT, increasing the pitch (table movement per rotation divided by beam width) while other parameters remain constant will:
o: Increase the dose and improve resolution
Shorten the scan and lower the dose at the cost of spatial resolution
items.e: A higher pitch covers the volume faster with fewer overlapping rotations, reducing dose but also z-axis resolution.

items.q: When reviewing a CT for a subtle tibial plateau fracture line, the radiologist chooses a bone window. Compared with a soft-tissue window, a bone window has:
o: A narrow window width and a low window level
A narrow window width and a high window level
The same width but a lower level
A wide window width and a high window level
items.e: Bone windows display a wide range of HU (about 1500-2000) centred high (about +300 to +500), so cortical and trabecular detail are visible; soft-tissue windows are narrow and centred near +40.

items.q: For postoperative CT of a fracture fixed with a plate, which implant material produces the least streak artefact?
items.e: Titanium has a lower atomic number and density, causing less beam hardening and photon starvation; stainless steel and cobalt-chrome produce more severe streaking.

items.q: A dual-energy CT scanner can reduce metal artefact around a hip arthroplasty mainly by:
o: Generating virtual monochromatic images at high keV
Increasing the slice thickness to 10 mm
items.e: Virtual monochromatic reconstructions at high energy reduce beam hardening; lowering mAs would worsen photon starvation and thick slices lose detail.

items.q: The dose-length product (DLP) displayed on a CT scanner console is calculated as:
o: Effective dose divided by body weight
CTDIvol multiplied by the scan length
items.e: DLP (mGy·cm) is the volume CT dose index times the irradiated length, and can be converted to an approximate effective dose with region-specific factors.

items.q: Bone mineral density reported by DEXA is expressed as an areal density in:
items.e: DEXA measures mineral content over the projected area, so it is affected by bone size; volumetric density (mg/cm³) requires quantitative CT.

items.q: The DEXA T-score expresses a patient's bone mineral density as the number of standard deviations from the mean of:
o: Healthy young adults of the same sex at peak bone mass
People of the same age and sex
The general population of all ages
items.e: The T-score compares with young-adult peak bone mass and is used for postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over; the Z-score compares with age- and sex-matched controls.

items.q: A 35-year-old premenopausal woman on long-term corticosteroids has a lumbar spine DEXA. Which result should guide interpretation?
o: The T-score, with -2.5 or lower diagnosing osteoporosis
The Z-score, with -2.0 or lower reported as below the expected range for age
The T-score, with -1.0 to -2.5 diagnosing osteopenia
Absolute BMD alone, as scores do not apply under 50
items.e: In premenopausal women, men under 50 and children, Z-scores are used; -2.0 or lower prompts a search for secondary causes such as steroids. WHO T-score categories apply to postmenopausal women and older men.

items.q: A 64-year-old postmenopausal woman has a femoral neck T-score of -1.8 and no fractures. By WHO criteria this is:
items.e: A T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 is osteopenia; -2.5 or lower is osteoporosis, and severe osteoporosis additionally requires a fragility fracture.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman has a total hip T-score of -2.7 and a previous low-energy distal radius fracture. Her WHO category is:
o: Osteoporosis without the 'severe' qualifier, because wrist fractures do not count
items.e: A T-score of -2.5 or lower together with one or more fragility fractures defines severe (established) osteoporosis.

items.q: A 78-year-old man has a lumbar spine T-score of +0.5 but a femoral neck T-score of -2.9. The most likely reason for the discrepancy is:
o: Degenerative osteophytes, facet arthritis or aortic calcification falsely raising spinal BMD
Hip osteoarthritis falsely lowering hip BMD
Calibration error that invalidates both results
Osteomalacia, which affects only the hip
items.e: Spinal degenerative change, vertebral compression fractures and aortic calcification add mineral to the projected area and spuriously elevate lumbar BMD in older people, so the hip is more reliable.

items.q: In a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism, which additional DEXA site is recommended because it is rich in cortical bone, the bone PTH preferentially affects?
items.e: PTH excess preferentially thins cortical bone, best shown at the one-third radius; this site is also used when the spine or hip cannot be measured or in very obese patients.

items.q: Each 1 standard deviation reduction in BMD measured by DEXA increases the risk of fracture by approximately:
o: It has no consistent relationship with fracture risk
items.e: Fracture risk roughly doubles for each SD fall in BMD, with the strongest gradient for hip BMD predicting hip fracture.

items.q: On serial DEXA scans, a change in BMD should be regarded as real only if it exceeds the least significant change, which is calculated as about:
o: 2.77 times the precision error of the machine
items.e: The least significant change (2.77 × precision error at 95% confidence) defines a true change; scans should be done on the same machine for valid comparison.

items.q: Trabecular bone score (TBS), derived from a lumbar spine DEXA image, provides:
o: An index of trabecular microarchitecture from grey-level texture, adding to BMD in fracture risk
A measure of cortical thickness of the femoral neck
The 10-year probability of hip fracture without needing clinical risk factors
items.e: TBS analyses pixel grey-level variation to estimate microarchitecture and can adjust FRAX; it is not a density measurement.

items.q: The Larmor (precession) frequency of hydrogen protons is proportional to the magnetic field strength. At 3 tesla it is approximately:
items.e: The gyromagnetic ratio of hydrogen is about 42.6 MHz per tesla, giving about 64 MHz at 1.5 T and about 128 MHz at 3 T.

items.q: An MRI sequence uses a short repetition time (TR) and a short echo time (TE). On this sequence:
o: Fluid is bright and fat is intermediate (T2-weighted)
Both fat and fluid are suppressed
Fat is bright and fluid is dark (T1-weighted)
Fat is dark and fluid very bright (STIR)
items.e: Short TR/short TE gives T1 weighting, in which fat with its short T1 is bright; this is ideal for anatomy and marrow replacement.

items.q: A sequence with a long TR and a short TE, commonly used for high-resolution imaging of the menisci and articular cartilage, is:
items.e: Long TR minimises T1 effects and short TE minimises T2 effects, so contrast reflects proton density; it gives excellent detail of menisci, cartilage and labrum.

items.q: On a T1-weighted MRI of the lumbar spine in a 60-year-old, the vertebral marrow is darker than the adjacent intervertebral discs. This suggests:
o: Marrow replacement, for example by tumour, myeloma or infection
items.e: Normal adult marrow is fatty and brighter than disc and muscle on T1; marrow darker than these suggests infiltration. Haemangiomas and Modic 2 changes are fat-rich and bright on T1.

items.q: A 3-year-old has several lytic lesions in the long bones and skull, with irritability and weight loss. Considering age as the main clue, which malignant cause is most likely?
items.e: Under 5 years, malignant bone lesions are usually metastatic neuroblastoma or leukaemia (with LCH as a benign mimic); osteosarcoma and Ewing peak at 5-25 years.

items.q: In a 68-year-old with a solitary destructive lytic bone lesion, which diagnosis is statistically the most likely?
items.e: Over 40, metastasis is the commonest malignant bone lesion, followed by myeloma, but a solitary lesion still needs staging and biopsy because it could be a primary sarcoma.

items.q: Under NICE NG12, a child with unexplained bone pain or swelling should be offered:
o: A very urgent plain radiograph within 48 hours
Routine referral to orthopaedics within 18 weeks
items.e: NG12 recommends a very urgent X-ray within 48 hours for children and young people with unexplained bone swelling or pain.

items.q: Under NICE NG12, an adult with an unexplained soft-tissue lump that is increasing in size should have:
o: An urgent direct-access ultrasound within 2 weeks
items.e: Ultrasound within 2 weeks is the first step; if it suggests sarcoma the patient is referred on the suspected cancer pathway to a sarcoma service.

items.q: In Enneking's four radiographic questions about a bone lesion, 'What is the bone doing to the lesion?' assesses the:
o: Periosteal and sclerotic reaction of the host bone
items.e: The four questions are: where is it, what is it doing to the bone (margin, cortex), what is the bone doing to it (periosteal and sclerotic response) and what clues are within it (matrix).

items.q: A lytic bone lesion has a geographic pattern with an ill-defined margin, without moth-eaten or permeative destruction. Its Lodwick-Madewell grade is:
items.e: IA is geographic with sclerosis, IB geographic and well defined without sclerosis, IC geographic with an ill-defined margin; II adds moth-eaten or permeative areas, and III is purely moth-eaten or permeative.

items.q: A Codman triangle on a radiograph of a long bone is best interpreted as:
o: A sign of an aggressive process that may also be seen in infection, not specific for malignancy
A sign of a slow-growing benign lesion
items.e: A Codman triangle forms when periosteum is lifted faster than it can ossify; it occurs in osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis.

items.q: A metaphyseal lesion shows 'rings and arcs' calcification. This matrix indicates a:
items.e: Ring-and-arc, popcorn or stippled calcification indicates chondroid matrix (enchondroma, chondrosarcoma); cloud-like ivory density indicates osteoid; ground-glass suggests fibrous dysplasia.

items.q: When planning the level of bone resection for a distal femoral osteosarcoma, which MRI sequence best shows the intramedullary extent of tumour?
items.e: On T1-weighted images, marrow fat is bright and tumour dark, giving the most accurate marrow extent; T2 and STIR overestimate it because of peritumoral oedema.

items.q: For a suspected osteoid osteoma of the femoral neck, which investigation best demonstrates the nidus?
items.e: CT is the best test for localising the nidus; bone scan is sensitive (double density sign) but less precise, and MRI may be confused by surrounding oedema.

items.q: What is the single most useful investigation for establishing the likely diagnosis of a bone lesion?
items.e: Radiographs show location, margins, periosteal reaction and matrix, which drive the differential diagnosis; MRI is for local staging.

items.q: A 60-year-old with a destructive lytic lesion has a normal Tc-99m bone scan apart from that lesion. Which primary is particularly likely to give falsely cold bone scan lesions?
items.e: Aggressive purely lytic metastases (renal cell, thyroid) and myeloma provoke little osteoblastic response and may be cold on bone scan; prostate metastases are typically hot.

items.q: Which soft-tissue sarcoma in the SCARE group, besides synovial, clear cell, epithelioid sarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma, also has a notable rate of regional lymph node spread?
items.e: SCARE = Synovial, Clear cell, Angiosarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, Epithelioid sarcoma; these need nodal assessment, unlike most sarcomas, which spread to the lungs.

items.q: In a teenager with osteosarcoma, which pair of serum markers when raised at diagnosis is associated with a worse prognosis?
items.e: High ALP and LDH reflect tumour burden and are adverse prognostic factors in osteosarcoma; LDH is also adverse in Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: In a 65-year-old with multiple lytic lesions, the recommended laboratory screen for myeloma includes:
o: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains
Bence Jones protein by urine dipstick only
items.e: Electrophoresis with immunofixation plus serum free light chain assay detects nearly all myeloma, including light-chain-only disease; calcium and creatinine are also checked.

items.q: In the Rougraff protocol for a skeletal lesion of unknown origin in an adult (history, examination, bloods, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and bone scan), the most common primary identified is:
items.e: This protocol identifies the primary in about 85% of cases; lung is the commonest, followed by kidney.

items.q: A 62-year-old with no known cancer has a pathological fracture through a solitary lytic femoral shaft lesion. Why should the fracture not be nailed before a tissue diagnosis?
o: Nailing is never possible in pathological fractures
If it is a primary sarcoma, reaming and nailing spread tumour along the whole canal and may force amputation
The fracture will always heal in a cast
items.e: A solitary lesion may be a primary sarcoma; intramedullary instrumentation contaminates the entire femur, ruining limb salvage options.

items.q: In Mankin's studies of the hazards of biopsy, an unnecessary amputation resulted from a badly performed biopsy in about:
items.e: Mankin reported major diagnostic errors in about 18%, changes of treatment in about 18-19% and unnecessary amputation in about 4-5%, with problems much commoner at referring hospitals.

items.q: Fine-needle aspiration cytology is generally considered adequate for:
o: Confirming local recurrence or metastasis of a known, previously diagnosed tumour
Primary diagnosis and grading of a suspected sarcoma
Molecular subtyping of a new round cell tumour
items.e: FNA yields cells without architecture and too little tissue for grading or molecular tests, so it is not recommended for primary sarcoma diagnosis.

items.q: Excisional biopsy of a soft-tissue mass is acceptable as the first procedure when the mass is:
o: Deep to the fascia and over 5 cm
Small (under about 3 cm) and superficial, where a wide excision would not compromise later treatment
In the popliteal fossa abutting the neurovascular bundle
items.e: Small superficial lesions can be excised with a margin; large or deep lesions need imaging and a planned core biopsy at a sarcoma centre.

items.q: Two image-guided core biopsies of a suspected bone sarcoma are non-diagnostic and discordant with the imaging. The next appropriate step is:
o: Open incisional biopsy at the treating centre
Observation with repeat MRI in 6 months
items.e: Open incisional biopsy gives the most tissue and highest accuracy and is used when needle biopsy fails or disagrees with imaging.

items.q: In a cartilage tumour of a long bone, which radiographic feature most favours chondrosarcoma over enchondroma?
o: Size under 2 cm in a hand phalanx
Deep endosteal scalloping involving more than two-thirds of the cortical thickness
items.e: Endosteal scalloping over two-thirds of the cortex, cortical breach, periosteal reaction, a soft-tissue mass and pain suggest chondrosarcoma; histology alone may undergrade it.

items.q: For an open biopsy of a suspected distal femoral sarcoma, the recommended route is:
o: Through vastus medialis or lateralis on the side of the tumour, avoiding the suprapatellar pouch and rectus femoris
Through the rectus femoris tendon in the midline
Through the suprapatellar pouch to reach the metaphysis
A transverse incision over the popliteal fossa
items.e: Going through a vastus keeps the tract in one compartment and avoids contaminating the knee joint, the quadriceps tendon and the neurovascular bundle.

items.q: For biopsy of a suspected proximal tibial sarcoma, the tract should usually be placed:
o: Anteromedially, medial to the tibial crest, avoiding the patellar tendon and knee joint
Through the anterior compartment muscles laterally
items.e: The subcutaneous anteromedial tibia allows a tract that can be excised with the medial gastrocnemius flap approach used for reconstruction.

items.q: The preferred route for biopsy of a suspected proximal femoral sarcoma is:
o: Direct lateral, through the vastus lateralis just distal to the greater trochanter
Posterior through gluteus maximus and the sciatic nerve region
items.e: A lateral tract through vastus lateralis lies in the line of the definitive resection incision and avoids the hip joint and femoral vessels.

items.q: For a suspected primary tumour of a thoracolumbar vertebral body, the usual biopsy technique is:
o: Lateral transpsoas biopsy through the retroperitoneum
Open biopsy through the intervertebral disc
CT-guided transpedicular biopsy from a posterior approach
items.e: A posterior transpedicular (or costotransverse in the thorax) tract can be excised with the posterior approach used for later en bloc resection.

items.q: During an open biopsy of a limb tumour performed under tourniquet, the tourniquet should be:
o: Released before wound closure to achieve meticulous haemostasis
Kept inflated until the dressing is applied
items.e: A haematoma carries tumour cells and widens contamination, so the tourniquet is released and bleeding controlled before closure; exsanguination is by elevation only.

items.q: After making a cortical window during open biopsy of a bone tumour, the hole is often plugged with bone wax or PMMA mainly to:
o: Prevent a tumour-laden haematoma escaping into the soft tissues
items.e: Plugging the window limits bleeding from the medullary cavity into the soft tissues, which would spread tumour cells.

items.q: A 19-year-old runner has shin pain with a lamellated periosteal reaction on the posteromedial tibial diaphysis. MRI shows a transverse linear low-signal band with marrow oedema. The best step is:
o: Treat as a stress fracture and avoid biopsy, which could mimic osteosarcoma
items.e: Stress fractures are 'don't touch' lesions: healing callus can look malignant on histology. The MRI fracture line makes the diagnosis.

items.q: After an unplanned excision of a high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma, re-excision of the tumour bed finds residual tumour in about:
items.e: Residual tumour is present in about 50% of re-excisions, which is why wide re-excision (often with radiotherapy) is standard after restaging.

items.q: An asymptomatic non-ossifying fibroma with a sclerotic rim found incidentally in a 12-year-old is Enneking benign stage 1 (latent). The usual management is:
items.e: Latent lesions are inactive and often heal spontaneously; treatment is needed only for symptoms or a high fracture risk.

items.q: A primary aneurysmal bone cyst confined within an expanded but intact cortex is an Enneking stage 2 (active) lesion. The usual treatment is:
o: Intralesional curettage, often with an adjuvant, and grafting
items.e: Active benign lesions grow but are limited by natural barriers; curettage is usually enough, while stage 3 lesions need extended curettage or resection.

items.q: A parosteal osteosarcoma confined to the posterior distal femoral surface without soft-tissue breach is low grade and intracompartmental. Its Enneking stage and usual treatment are:
o: IIB; neoadjuvant chemotherapy and wide resection
items.e: Low-grade intracompartmental tumours are stage IA and need a wide margin; chemotherapy is not given for low-grade parosteal osteosarcoma.

items.q: A low-grade sarcoma lies in the femoral triangle. Because this space has no natural fascial barriers, its Enneking stage is:
items.e: The femoral triangle, axilla, antecubital and popliteal fossae, mid-hand, mid-foot and paraspinal/pelvic spaces are extracompartmental by definition, so a low-grade tumour there is IB.

items.q: A high-grade osteosarcoma is entirely within the medullary canal with an intact cortex and no metastases. Its Enneking stage is:
items.e: High grade (G2) intracompartmental (T1) without metastasis is IIA; most osteosarcomas break through the cortex and present as IIB.

items.q: Under AJCC 8th edition for appendicular bone sarcoma, a 6 cm low-grade central chondrosarcoma without nodal or distant spread is stage:
items.e: T1 (8 cm or less), N0, M0, low grade (G1 or GX) is stage IA; over 8 cm or skip lesions with low grade is IB.

items.q: Under AJCC 8th edition for appendicular bone sarcoma, a high-grade osteosarcoma with a skip lesion in the same bone and no metastases is stage:
items.e: Discontinuous tumours in the primary bone are T3; T3 with high grade, N0, M0 is stage III.

items.q: In the AJCC 8th edition, the T category of primary bone tumours of the pelvis is defined differently from the appendicular skeleton because it is based on:
o: Tumour size cut-off of 8 cm only
The number of pelvic segments involved and extraosseous extension
items.e: Pelvic and spinal bone tumours have their own T definitions based on segments involved, extraosseous extension and vessel involvement, rather than size alone.

items.q: The FNCLCC grading of soft-tissue sarcoma is based on the sum of scores for:
o: Tumour differentiation, mitotic count and tumour necrosis
Mitotic count, Ki-67 and nuclear atypia
Necrosis, vascular invasion and margin status
items.e: Differentiation (1-3), mitoses per 10 HPF (1-3) and necrosis (0-2) are summed: 2-3 grade 1, 4-5 grade 2, 6-8 grade 3.

items.q: A soft-tissue sarcoma scores 2 for differentiation, 2 for mitotic count and 1 for necrosis on FNCLCC. Its grade is:
items.e: A total of 5 falls in the 4-5 band, which is grade 2.

items.q: For a localised soft-tissue sarcoma, the most important single prognostic factor for distant metastasis is:
o: Location in the upper versus lower limb
items.e: Grade best predicts metastatic risk; size and depth also contribute, and margin status mainly predicts local recurrence.

items.q: After neoadjuvant chemotherapy for osteosarcoma, the resection specimen shows 95% tumour necrosis. In the Huvos grading this is:
items.e: Huvos I: little necrosis; II: 50-89%; III: 90-99%; IV: 100%. A necrosis of 90% or more defines a good responder.

items.q: In non-metastatic osteosarcoma treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and resection, the strongest prognostic factor is:
o: Histological necrosis of the tumour after chemotherapy
items.e: Chemotherapy-induced necrosis of 90% or more (Huvos III-IV) predicts much better survival than poor response.

items.q: The Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini (WBB) staging system for spinal tumours is mainly used to:
o: Plan the feasibility and route of en bloc resection by mapping tumour sectors and layers
items.e: WBB divides the vertebra into 12 radial zones and 5 tissue layers to plan en bloc resection; SINS scores instability and Tokuhashi estimates survival.

items.q: Biopsy of a deep thigh mass shows a monophasic spindle-cell tumour. Which molecular finding confirms synovial sarcoma?
items.e: Synovial sarcoma carries t(X;18) SS18-SSX1/2; EWSR1-FLI1 is Ewing sarcoma, MDM2 amplification is well-differentiated liposarcoma and FUS-DDIT3 is myxoid liposarcoma.

items.q: Biopsy of an epiphyseal lytic lesion in a 15-year-old shows chondroblasts with 'chicken-wire' calcification. Which mutation supports the diagnosis?
items.e: Chondroblastoma carries H3F3B K36M; H3F3A G34W is characteristic of giant cell tumour, IDH mutations of enchondroma/chondrosarcoma and GNAS of fibrous dysplasia.

items.q: Molecular testing that shows a USP6 gene rearrangement in a blood-filled expansile bone lesion supports:
items.e: USP6 rearrangement defines primary ABC (and nodular fasciitis) and helps distinguish it from secondary ABC change in other tumours and from telangiectatic osteosarcoma.

items.q: In a patient with Ollier disease, biopsy of an enlarging cartilage lesion would be expected to show mutations in:
items.e: Enchondromas and chondrosarcomas in Ollier and Maffucci syndromes carry somatic IDH1/IDH2 mutations; EXT1/EXT2 underlie multiple hereditary exostoses.

items.q: A child with a history of bilateral retinoblastoma is at increased risk of osteosarcoma because of a germline mutation in:
items.e: Germline RB1 mutation predisposes to osteosarcoma; TP53 (Li-Fraumeni) and RECQL4 (Rothmund-Thomson) are other hereditary causes.

items.q: An above-knee amputation is performed for a distal tibial sarcoma, but the cut passes through tumour extending into the proximal tibia. Using Enneking's terminology the margin is:
items.e: Margins are defined by the plane of dissection relative to tumour, not by the operation type; an amputation through tumour is still intralesional.

items.q: In Enneking's classification, a radical margin is achieved when:
o: The tumour is removed with a cuff of normal tissue within the compartment
The entire anatomical compartment containing the tumour is removed
The plane passes through the reactive zone
The tumour is curetted and the cavity cauterised
items.e: Radical margins remove the whole compartment (extracompartmental dissection); wide margins remove the tumour with a cuff of normal tissue but can leave skip lesions.

items.q: After a wide (but not radical) resection of a high-grade sarcoma, which residual disease could theoretically remain in the compartment?
o: Satellite nodules in the reactive zone
items.e: A wide margin goes through normal tissue beyond the reactive zone, removing satellites, but skip lesions elsewhere in the compartment may remain; a marginal margin leaves satellites.

items.q: A resected sarcoma specimen shows tumour cells at the inked margin on microscopy but no gross residual disease. Its residual tumour classification is:
items.e: R0 = no microscopic residual; R1 = microscopic residual (positive margin); R2 = macroscopic residual tumour.

items.q: The main insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon, the primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch, is on the:
o: Plantar aspect of the medial cuneiform only
items.e: Tibialis posterior inserts chiefly into the navicular tuberosity, with slips to the cuneiforms, cuboid and bases of metatarsals 2-4. The sustentaculum tali is a pulley for FHL, not the tibialis posterior insertion.

items.q: During heel rise, contraction of tibialis posterior inverts the hindfoot and converts the midfoot into a rigid lever for push-off mainly by:
o: Plantarflexing the first ray through the medial cuneiform
Making the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joint axes non-parallel, locking the transverse tarsal joint
Tightening the plantar fascia through the windlass mechanism
Everting the subtalar joint so that the Chopart axes become parallel
items.e: Hindfoot inversion makes the TN and CC axes diverge, locking Chopart's joint into a rigid lever. Eversion makes the axes parallel and unlocks the midfoot (flexible for shock absorption).

items.q: Degenerative tendinosis of the tibialis posterior tendon in progressive collapsing foot deformity is typically located:
o: At the musculotendinous junction in the mid-calf
At the bony insertion into the navicular
Just behind and distal to the medial malleolus, in a hypovascular zone
items.e: The tendon has a hypovascular watershed where it turns around the posterior and distal medial malleolus; this is where degeneration and tears occur.

items.q: The principal antagonist of tibialis posterior, whose unopposed pull contributes to hindfoot valgus and forefoot abduction when tibialis posterior fails, is:
items.e: Peroneus brevis is the main evertor and directly opposes tibialis posterior; when TP fails, the brevis abducts and everts the foot unopposed.

items.q: Failure of which part of the spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament complex is most important in the development of progressive collapsing foot deformity?
items.e: The superomedial band forms a hammock supporting the talar head and is the most important static restraint; its failure allows plantarflexion and medial uncovering of the talar head. The bifurcate ligament is a lateral structure.

items.q: In a patient with flexible flatfoot from tibialis posterior dysfunction, the forefoot must be assessed for compensatory forefoot varus (supination). The correct position for this assessment is with the:
o: Patient standing in full hindfoot valgus
Subtalar joint held in neutral, observing the plane of the metatarsal heads
Ankle in maximal plantarflexion and the knee extended
items.e: Forefoot supination is unmasked only when the hindfoot valgus is corrected to subtalar neutral; a fixed forefoot varus then needs a medial column procedure (e.g. Cotton osteotomy) in addition to hindfoot correction.

items.q: A patient with a flatfoot cannot perform a single-limb heel rise. On a double-limb heel rise the heel moves from valgus into varus. This indicates that:
o: The deformity is rigid and needs arthrodesis
items.e: Hindfoot inversion during a double heel rise shows that the subtalar joint is mobile, i.e. a flexible deformity suitable for joint-sparing reconstruction.

items.q: A 54-year-old woman with stage II tibialis posterior dysfunction has limited ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended that improves substantially when the knee is flexed (positive Silfverskiöld test). The soft-tissue procedure that should accompany her reconstruction is:
items.e: Improvement with knee flexion localises the contracture to the gastrocnemius, which is treated by isolated gastrocnemius recession; a Hoke Achilles lengthening is for a combined gastrocnemius-soleus contracture.

items.q: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing flatfoot has moved from medial ankle pain to pain on the lateral side below the fibula. The most likely cause of the lateral pain is:
o: Peroneus longus rupture at the cuboid tunnel
Calcaneofibular (subfibular) impingement from progressive hindfoot valgus
items.e: As the hindfoot collapses into valgus, the calcaneus abuts the fibula and the sinus tarsi is compressed, producing lateral pain in later stages of PCFD.

items.q: On a weight-bearing lateral radiograph of an adult flatfoot, which measurement is characteristically DECREASED?
items.e: Calcaneal pitch (normally about 20-30 degrees) falls as the arch collapses. The lateral talocalcaneal, talonavicular coverage and AP talo-first metatarsal angles all increase in flatfoot.

items.q: In flexible adult flatfoot reconstruction, talonavicular uncoverage of more than about 40% on the weight-bearing AP radiograph is the usual indication to add:
o: Cotton osteotomy of the medial cuneiform
items.e: Marked forefoot abduction (large TN uncoverage) is corrected by lengthening the lateral column (Evans or CC distraction arthrodesis); the Cotton osteotomy addresses forefoot varus, not abduction.

items.q: The radiographic view used to measure coronal hindfoot alignment relative to the tibial axis in a patient with flatfoot is the:
items.e: The Saltzman view is a weight-bearing posteroanterior view angled 20 degrees that shows the calcaneus relative to the tibial shaft. Harris-Beath shows the subtalar facets for coalition, Broden the posterior facet, and Canale the talar neck.

items.q: A 63-year-old woman with a long-standing flatfoot now has valgus tilting of the talus within the ankle mortise on a weight-bearing AP ankle radiograph, which corrects with manual pressure. In the Myerson modification of Johnson and Strom, this is:
items.e: Stage IV means ankle valgus from deltoid failure; it is IVA when flexible (correctable, no tibiotalar arthritis) and IVB when rigid or arthritic.

items.q: On weight-bearing CT of a patient with progressive collapsing foot deformity, which finding is a recognised early marker of peritalar subluxation?
o: Uncoverage (subluxation) of the middle facet of the subtalar joint
Fracture of the anterior process of the calcaneus
items.e: Weight-bearing CT shows the calcaneus rotating under the talus; middle facet uncoverage and subfibular impingement are markers of peritalar subluxation.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman has 6 weeks of medial ankle pain and swelling along the tibialis posterior tendon. She can perform a single-limb heel rise with pain and her foot alignment is normal. The appropriate first-line management is:
o: Flexor digitorum longus transfer with medialising calcaneal osteotomy
Corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath
Immobilisation in a walking boot or cast, followed by an arch-supporting orthosis
items.e: This is stage I (tenosynovitis with normal alignment), treated non-operatively; tenosynovectomy is reserved for failure. Steroid injection into the TP sheath risks rupture.

items.q: After hindfoot correction for flexible flatfoot, the forefoot remains in fixed supination. The first tarsometatarsal joint is stable without plantar gapping. The procedure of choice for this residual deformity is:
o: Plantarflexion opening-wedge osteotomy of the medial cuneiform (Cotton)
Dorsiflexion closing-wedge osteotomy of the first metatarsal
items.e: With a stable first TMT joint, a Cotton osteotomy plantarflexes the medial column joint-sparingly. Lapidus is preferred when the first TMT joint is unstable or arthritic; a dorsiflexion osteotomy would worsen the deformity.

items.q: In a flexible flatfoot, the medial column shows hypermobility with plantar gapping at the first tarsometatarsal joint on the lateral radiograph. The preferred medial column procedure is:
o: Cotton osteotomy of the medial cuneiform
items.e: Instability at the first TMT joint itself is corrected by arthrodesing it in plantarflexion (Lapidus); a Cotton osteotomy does not stabilise a hypermobile TMT joint.

items.q: A 61-year-old woman has a flexible flatfoot and valgus talar tilt in the mortise that corrects passively, with preserved tibiotalar joint space. The appropriate operative plan is:
o: Deltoid ligament reconstruction combined with correction of the hindfoot deformity
Isolated deltoid ligament reconstruction without foot correction
items.e: Flexible stage IV disease needs deltoid reconstruction protected by realignment of the foot; deltoid reconstruction alone fails if the valgus foot is left uncorrected. Pantalar fusion is for rigid arthritic deformity.

items.q: In the 2020 consensus classification of progressive collapsing foot deformity, the overall Stage (1 or 2) of the deformity is determined by:
o: Whether the tibialis posterior is ruptured on MRI
The number of joints with arthritis
Whether the deformity is flexible or rigid
items.e: Stage 1 is flexible and stage 2 is rigid; the classes A-E describe which components of the deformity are present.

items.q: Flexor digitorum longus is preferred for transfer to the navicular in flexible flatfoot reconstruction, but it must be combined with bony correction mainly because:
o: It has only about one-third the strength of tibialis posterior
It is out of phase with tibialis posterior
It lies anterior to the ankle axis
Its harvest causes loss of lesser toe flexion
items.e: FDL is in phase and adjacent to TP but much weaker (roughly 30%), so a medialising calcaneal osteotomy is added to protect it. Toe flexion is preserved by FHL interconnections.

items.q: After harvesting the flexor digitorum longus for transfer to the navicular, active flexion of the lesser toes is largely preserved because:
o: Quadratus plantae alone flexes the toes
The lumbricals flex the interphalangeal joints
Flexor digitorum brevis is attached to the FDL stump
Interconnections from flexor hallucis longus to the FDL slips distal to the knot of Henry
items.e: The FHL sends slips to the FDL distal to the master knot of Henry, so tenodesing the distal FDL stump to FHL keeps lesser toe flexion.

items.q: In a medialising displacement calcaneal osteotomy for flexible flatfoot, the posterior tuberosity is usually shifted medially by about:
items.e: A shift of about 1 cm (roughly 8-12 mm) moves the Achilles line of pull medial to the subtalar axis; larger shifts risk tibial nerve compression in the tarsal tunnel.

items.q: A 58-year-old develops burning plantar paraesthesia after a large medialising calcaneal osteotomy. The most likely explanation is:
o: Tibial nerve compression in the tarsal tunnel due to the medial shift
Sural nerve transection at the lateral incision
items.e: Large medial translation of the tuberosity reduces tarsal tunnel volume and can compress the tibial nerve, producing plantar symptoms. The sural nerve supplies the lateral foot, not the plantar surface.

items.q: The Evans lateral column lengthening osteotomy is performed:
o: Through the calcaneal tuberosity posterior to the posterior facet
Through the cuboid at its waist
Through the neck of the talus
Through the anterior calcaneus about 1-1.5 cm proximal to the calcaneocuboid joint, between the anterior and middle facets
items.e: Evans cuts the anterior process of the calcaneus parallel to the CC joint, between the anterior and middle facets, and inserts a tricortical wedge to abduct-correct the forefoot.

items.q: An alternative to the Evans osteotomy for lengthening the lateral column, particularly when the calcaneocuboid joint is arthritic, is:
items.e: CC distraction bone-block arthrodesis lengthens the lateral column while fusing an arthritic CC joint. A Dwyer closing wedge shortens the lateral side and is used for hindfoot varus.

items.q: A 59-year-old woman with tenosynovitis of the tibialis posterior tendon asks for an injection. The main reason to avoid corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath is:
o: Risk of plantar fat pad atrophy
items.e: Steroid injection into the TP sheath is associated with rupture and progression of deformity; fat pad atrophy is a complication of heel injection for plantar fasciitis.

items.q: A 79-year-old frail woman has a symptomatic rigid flatfoot from long-standing tibialis posterior insufficiency and is unfit for surgery. The most appropriate support is:
o: A custom lace-up leather and polypropylene ankle-foot orthosis (Arizona-type brace)
items.e: Rigid or advanced deformities need an AFO that controls the hindfoot and ankle (e.g. Arizona brace); UCBL inserts and arch supports are for flexible deformities.

items.q: For a flexible flatfoot, a foot orthosis should include a medial arch support combined with:
o: A recess under the first metatarsal head
items.e: A medial heel wedge resists hindfoot valgus. A lateral heel wedge, lateral forefoot post and first metatarsal recess are cavovarus orthotic features.

items.q: During triple arthrodesis for rigid flatfoot, the hindfoot should be positioned in:
o: About 15 degrees of valgus with forefoot abduction
About 5 degrees of valgus with a plantigrade forefoot
Neutral to slight varus with forefoot supination
About 10 degrees of varus with a plantarflexed first ray
items.e: Slight valgus (about 5 degrees) with neutral forefoot rotation and abduction gives a plantigrade, stable foot; varus malposition overloads the lateral foot and is poorly tolerated.

items.q: The most common site of non-union after triple arthrodesis is the:
o: Posterior facet of the subtalar joint
items.e: The TN joint, with its curved surface and limited exposure, is the commonest site of non-union after triple arthrodesis.

items.q: The commonest long-term problem after a well-healed triple arthrodesis is:
o: Stress fracture of the calcaneal tuberosity
Degenerative arthritis of adjacent joints such as the ankle and naviculocuneiform joints
items.e: Loss of hindfoot motion increases stress on the ankle and midfoot, leading to adjacent joint arthritis in long-term follow-up.

items.q: An advantage of performing triple (or double) arthrodesis for severe rigid valgus flatfoot through a single medial incision is that it:
o: Avoids lateral wound complications when the tight lateral skin is stretched during correction
Allows the calcaneocuboid joint to be prepared more completely
Eliminates the risk of talonavicular non-union
items.e: Correcting severe valgus stretches the lateral skin; a medial approach avoids a lateral incision under tension. The CC joint is not easily prepared medially, which is why double (TN + subtalar) fusion is often done.

items.q: Subtalar arthroereisis (sinus tarsi implant) for flexible flatfoot is mainly used in:
o: Elderly patients with rigid stage III deformity
Children and adolescents with symptomatic flexible flatfoot
Patients with stage IV ankle valgus
items.e: Arthroereisis blocks excessive subtalar eversion and is used mainly in paediatric flexible flatfoot; it has only a limited, adjunctive role in adults and is contraindicated in rigid or arthritic feet.

items.q: The commonest form of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease causing bilateral cavovarus feet (CMT1A) is due to:
o: Mutation of the MPZ gene on chromosome 1q
Duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17p
Point mutation of the GJB1 gene on the X chromosome
Mutation of the frataxin gene on chromosome 9q
items.e: CMT1A, the commonest type, is an autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathy caused by PMP22 duplication on 17p11.2. Frataxin (GAA repeat) causes Friedreich ataxia, GJB1 causes CMTX.

items.q: In Charcot-Marie-Tooth cavovarus foot, the muscle imbalance responsible for hindfoot varus and forefoot adduction is:
o: Weak tibialis anterior overpowered by peroneus longus
Weak gastrocnemius overpowered by tibialis anterior
Weak peroneus brevis overpowered by tibialis posterior
Weak intrinsics overpowered by extensor digitorum longus
items.e: Peroneus brevis weakens early and tibialis posterior is spared, pulling the hindfoot into varus and the forefoot into adduction; the TA-PL imbalance produces the plantarflexed first ray instead.

items.q: In a cavovarus foot, the 'tripod effect' refers to:
o: Weight shared equally between the heel and first and fifth metatarsal heads in a normal foot
Lateral ankle instability caused by a short fibula
A rigidly plantarflexed first ray forcing the hindfoot into varus on weight bearing
Clawing of the toes from intrinsic weakness
items.e: When the plantarflexed first metatarsal head strikes the ground first, the foot rolls into supination and the hindfoot is driven into varus: forefoot-driven hindfoot varus.

items.q: Standing with the feet parallel and viewed from the front, the medial heel pad is visible on one side. This 'peek-a-boo' heel sign indicates:
items.e: In a normally aligned foot, the heel is hidden behind the forefoot; a visible medial heel pad from the front denotes hindfoot varus, typical of cavovarus foot.

items.q: In a 26-year-old with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, the hindfoot varus does not correct on the Coleman block test. In addition to forefoot procedures, the bony correction required is:
o: Lateralising or lateral closing-wedge (Dwyer) calcaneal osteotomy
Cotton osteotomy of the medial cuneiform
items.e: Failure of the varus to correct means a fixed hindfoot component, which needs a calcaneal osteotomy that moves the heel laterally (Dwyer or Z-type), or arthrodesis if rigid and arthritic.

items.q: A calcaneal pitch angle of 40 degrees on a weight-bearing lateral radiograph of a patient with residual poliomyelitis indicates:
items.e: A calcaneal pitch above about 30 degrees indicates calcaneocavus, typically due to weak triceps surae (polio, myelomeningocele). Normal pitch is roughly 20-30 degrees.

items.q: On a lateral weight-bearing radiograph of a cavus foot, the angle between the long axis of the calcaneus and the long axis of the first metatarsal is known as the:
items.e: The Hibbs (calcaneal-first metatarsal) angle decreases in cavus (under about 150 degrees). Böhler and Gissane angles assess calcaneal fractures; Kite angle is the AP talocalcaneal angle.

items.q: A 12-year-old with spina bifida has a calcaneocavus foot with weak triceps surae. Which procedure should be avoided?
o: Tibialis anterior transfer to the calcaneus
items.e: In calcaneocavus the triceps surae is already weak; lengthening the Achilles would worsen push-off and the calcaneus deformity. Transfers to the calcaneus augment plantarflexion.

items.q: In forefoot-driven cavovarus from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, transfer of the peroneus longus to the peroneus brevis achieves:
o: Removal of the deforming plantarflexion force on the first ray while augmenting eversion
items.e: The peroneus longus plantarflexes the first ray; transferring it to the weak brevis removes that force and strengthens eversion, opposing hindfoot varus.

items.q: A 30-year-old with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease has a flexible cavovarus foot and foot drop with grade 5 tibialis posterior power. The tendon transfer that restores active dorsiflexion is:
o: Peroneus longus transfer to the base of the second metatarsal
Flexor hallucis longus transfer to the navicular
Extensor hallucis longus transfer to the first metatarsal neck
Tibialis posterior transfer through the interosseous membrane to the lateral cuneiform
items.e: TP is often spared in CMT and is a deforming force; routing it anteriorly through the interosseous membrane to the dorsum (lateral/middle cuneiform) both removes a varus force and restores dorsiflexion. EHL to the first metatarsal neck is the Jones transfer for the clawed hallux.

items.q: A 19-year-old has flexible claw deformities of the lesser toes that correct with pressure under the metatarsal heads. The tendon procedure that corrects this by converting a toe flexor into a metatarsophalangeal flexor is:
o: Hibbs transfer of EDL to the cuboid
Jones transfer of EHL to the first metatarsal
items.e: Girdlestone-Taylor transfers FDL to the dorsal extensor hood (proximal phalanx), so it flexes the MTP joint and extends the IP joints in flexible claw toes.

items.q: A patient has cavus with the apex of the deformity in the midfoot and a fixed deformity. A dorsally based closing-wedge osteotomy through the navicular-cuneiform and cuboid is known as the:
items.e: The Cole midfoot osteotomy removes a dorsal wedge at the apex of midfoot cavus. Dwyer is a calcaneal osteotomy for varus, Evans lengthens the lateral column, and Cotton plantarflexes the medial cuneiform.

items.q: In a young patient with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and correctable cavovarus, triple arthrodesis is avoided as a primary operation mainly because:
o: The subtalar joint cannot be fused in CMT
Long-term results show a high rate of ankle and midfoot degenerative arthritis
items.e: Triple arthrodesis in CMT gives poor long-term results with adjacent joint arthritis, so joint-sparing osteotomies and tendon transfers are preferred while the deformity is flexible.

items.q: The orthosis appropriate for a flexible forefoot-driven cavovarus foot includes:
o: A medial heel wedge and medial arch support
A rigid medial longitudinal arch with a UCBL heel cup
A lateral forefoot post with a recess under the first metatarsal head
A rocker sole with a medial flare
items.e: Allowing the first metatarsal to drop into a recess and posting the lateral forefoot reproduces the Coleman block effect and lets the flexible hindfoot evert.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of patients presenting with symptomatic pes cavus have an underlying neurological disorder?
items.e: Around two-thirds of cavus feet have a neurological cause (CMT commonest), so a full neurological examination and appropriate investigations are mandatory.

items.q: During single-leg stance, the hip abductors balance body weight about the femoral head acting as the fulcrum. This arrangement is an example of a:
o: Pulley system with a fixed axle
items.e: In a first-class lever the fulcrum (femoral head) lies between the effort (abductors on the greater trochanter) and the load (body weight acting medially). The biceps at the elbow, by contrast, is a third-class lever.

items.q: When a person rises onto tiptoe, the fulcrum is at the metatarsophalangeal joints, body weight acts through the ankle and the triceps surae pulls on the calcaneus. This is a:
o: Lever with the fulcrum at the ankle joint
items.e: In a second-class lever the load lies between the fulcrum (MTP joints) and the effort (Achilles insertion), giving a mechanical advantage. Third-class levers, such as biceps at the elbow, are the commonest in the body.

items.q: A motorcyclist strikes an object at twice the velocity of a comparable low-speed collision with the same mass. The kinetic energy delivered to the limb is increased approximately:
o: Unchanged, because mass is the same
items.e: Kinetic energy = half x mass x velocity squared, so doubling velocity quadruples energy. This is why high-velocity injuries cause disproportionate comminution and soft-tissue damage.

items.q: On a stress-strain curve for an implant metal, toughness is represented by the:
o: Slope of the linear elastic portion
Total area under the curve up to the point of failure
items.e: Toughness is the energy absorbed per unit volume before fracture, i.e. the area under the stress-strain curve. The slope of the elastic portion is the modulus (stiffness), and the peak stress is the ultimate tensile strength.

items.q: A surgeon contours a 3.5 mm reconstruction plate to the pelvic brim, and it keeps its new shape after the bending irons are removed. The plate has been deformed into its:
o: Plastic region, beyond the yield point
Elastic region, below the proportional limit
Region of fatigue below the endurance limit
items.e: Permanent deformation occurs only after the yield point, in the plastic region. Elastic deformation is fully recoverable; repeated back-and-forth bending also introduces fatigue damage, especially in notch-sensitive titanium.

items.q: For a ceramic femoral head, the material property that most directly explains its superior resistance to third-body scratching is its:
items.e: Hardness is resistance to surface indentation and scratching; ceramics are the hardest bearing materials. Their fracture toughness, by contrast, is low, which is why they are brittle.

items.q: Poisson's ratio of a material is defined as the ratio of:
o: Stress to strain in the elastic region
Yield stress to ultimate tensile stress
items.e: When a material is stretched it narrows; Poisson's ratio is transverse strain divided by axial strain. Stress divided by strain in the elastic region is Young's modulus, and shear stress over shear strain is the shear modulus.

items.q: Cortical bone tested along the long axis of the osteons is stronger and stiffer than the same bone tested across them. This dependence of mechanical properties on loading direction is called:
items.e: Anisotropic materials (bone, ligament, cartilage) have properties that vary with loading direction, while most metals are isotropic. Viscoelasticity refers to time- and rate-dependent behaviour, not direction-dependent behaviour.

items.q: Adult cortical bone is strongest under which mode of loading?
items.e: Bone is strongest in compression, weaker in tension and weakest in shear. Torsion produces failure in tension along a 45-degree helix, giving a spiral fracture.

items.q: When a tendon is loaded and then unloaded, the unloading curve lies below the loading curve and the enclosed area represents energy dissipated as heat. This viscoelastic phenomenon is:
items.e: Hysteresis is the energy lost within a loading-unloading cycle of a viscoelastic tissue. Creep is increasing deformation under constant load, and stress relaxation is falling stress under constant deformation.

items.q: Serial casting for an equinus contracture holds the tissues at a fixed length so that the tension within them gradually falls, allowing further correction at the next cast. The property exploited is:
items.e: When strain (length) is held constant, the stress in a viscoelastic tissue declines over time: stress relaxation. Creep is the complementary behaviour when load, rather than length, is held constant.

items.q: In bone-ligament-bone specimens, the ACL loaded at a slow strain rate most typically fails by:
items.e: Bone is more rate-sensitive than ligament; at slow loading the bone is relatively weaker and the insertion avulses, whereas fast loading stiffens bone and the ligament tends to fail mid-substance.

items.q: A skier's boot binding fails to release and the tibia is subjected to a pure twisting load. The expected fracture pattern is:
o: Short oblique with a butterfly fragment on the tension side
items.e: Torsion creates tensile stresses along a 45-degree helix, so bone fails in a spiral. Bending gives a transverse fracture, often with a butterfly fragment on the compression side.

items.q: A tibial diaphysis is broken by a three-point bending load from a car bumper striking the leg. If a butterfly fragment forms, it is characteristically located on the:
o: Compression (concave) side, which is the side of impact
Anterior surface regardless of the direction of force
Posterior surface regardless of the direction of force
items.e: In three-point bending the struck side becomes concave and is compressed, while the opposite convex cortex fails first in tension with a transverse crack; as the crack enters the compression side it splits obliquely, leaving a butterfly fragment on the impact (compression) side.

items.q: Displaced fractures of the patella, olecranon and base of the fifth metatarsal due to muscle pull are typically transverse because the bone fails under:
items.e: Pure tensile loading produces transverse fracture lines perpendicular to the load, as in avulsion and traction injuries. Compression produces oblique or crush patterns, and torsion produces spiral fractures.

items.q: Compared with cortical bone, cancellous bone can tolerate approximately how much strain before failure?
o: Up to about 2%, versus about 75% for cortical bone
About 10%, the same as cortical bone
Up to about 75%, versus about 2% for cortical bone
Less than 1%, because it is more porous
items.e: Cortical bone is stiff and fails at about 2% strain, whereas porous cancellous bone can undergo very large strains (up to about 75%) before failure, making it a good energy absorber.

items.q: The compressive strength of cancellous bone is roughly proportional to the square of its apparent density. If osteoporosis halves the apparent density of a vertebral body, its compressive strength falls to approximately:
items.e: Strength is proportional to density squared, so halving density gives (0.5) squared = 0.25 of the original strength. This explains why modest losses of bone mass produce large rises in fracture risk.

items.q: In ageing long bones the cortex thins, yet bending strength is partly preserved. The main mechanical reason is:
o: Endosteal apposition thickens the cortex from inside
Increased mineralisation raises the elastic modulus
Periosteal apposition increases the diameter, raising the area moment of inertia
Conversion of lamellar to woven bone increases toughness
items.e: Bending and torsional rigidity depend on the distribution of bone around the neutral axis (proportional to radius to the fourth power), so slow periosteal expansion compensates for endosteal resorption.

items.q: When a cortical window must be made in a diaphysis for biopsy, which shape minimises the reduction in bone strength?
o: A rectangular hole with square corners
An oval hole with rounded ends
Several small separate holes joined by a saw cut
items.e: Sharp corners concentrate stress, and a long slot creates an open-section defect that drastically reduces torsional strength. An oval or round window with rounded ends minimises the stress riser.

items.q: Twelve months after reamed nailing of a tibial shaft fracture, radiographs show abundant 'elephant foot' callus with a persistent lucent gap. According to Perren's strain theory, the best explanation and treatment is:
o: Inadequate biology; add bone graft without changing fixation
Excessive stiffness; dynamise by removing all locking screws and leave the nail
Excessive interfragmentary strain; improve stability, for example by exchange nailing or compression plating
Infection; remove the nail and apply a cement spacer
items.e: Hypertrophic non-union indicates good biology but strain above about 10% so only fibrous or granulation tissue bridges the gap. Increasing stability lowers strain and allows the callus to mineralise.

items.q: A simple transverse humeral shaft fracture with a 1 mm gap is fixed with a long locked bridging plate leaving the gap unreduced and unloaded. The risk of delayed union arises because:
o: The construct is too rigid for any callus to form
Bridging plates cannot be used in the upper limb
All motion is concentrated in a tiny gap, producing high interfragmentary strain
items.e: Strain equals change in gap width divided by original gap width; a small gap with motion has very high strain. Bridging works for comminuted zones because movement is spread over many fragments, while simple patterns need anatomical reduction and compression.

items.q: A double-lead (dual-thread) screw has a thread pitch of 1.25 mm. How far does it advance with one full revolution?
items.e: Lead is the distance a screw advances per revolution; in a single-lead screw lead equals pitch, but a double-lead screw has two thread starts and advances twice the pitch per turn.

items.q: To obtain maximal interfragmentary compression from a single lag screw across an oblique fracture, the screw should be directed:
o: Perpendicular to the long axis of the bone
At 15 degrees to the long axis
items.e: A lag screw perpendicular to the fracture plane generates the greatest compression without shear; a screw perpendicular to the long axis best resists axial loading, so in practice surgeons often bisect the two angles.

items.q: In osteoporotic metaphyseal bone, a locking plate construct that fails under cyclic loading most characteristically does so by:
o: Sequential toggling and loosening of individual screws
Simultaneous cut-out of the whole screw-plate construct en bloc
Breakage of the plate at the first empty hole away from the fracture
Fretting corrosion of the screw heads causing gross osteolysis
items.e: Because each locked screw is fixed at an angle to the plate, the construct behaves as a single unit and the bone around all screws fails together. Conventional plates fail by sequential screw loosening once plate-bone friction is lost.

items.q: Femoral shaft plates are placed on the lateral (anterolateral) surface mainly because this surface:
o: Is the compression side and needs buttressing
Has the thickest cortex for screw purchase
Avoids the profunda femoris perforators completely
Is the tension side of the femur under physiological load
items.e: The femur bends with its lateral cortex in tension; a plate applied on the tension side acts as a tension band, converting tensile forces into compression at the fracture.

items.q: In a Weber B lateral malleolar fracture, a plate applied to the posterior surface of the distal fibula, with the fracture spike lying under it, acts mainly as a:
o: Compression plate with eccentrically placed screws
items.e: The posterior antiglide plate prevents the distal fragment from sliding proximally and posteriorly along the oblique fracture, resisting shear in the way a buttress does in metaphyseal fractures.

items.q: An oblique tibial fracture is fixed with an interfragmentary lag screw, and a plate is added with screws in neutral position to protect the lag screw from bending and torsion. The plate is functioning as a:
items.e: A lag screw alone cannot withstand functional loads; a neutralisation plate shields it from bending, rotational and axial forces. Bridging plates span comminution without lag screws.

items.q: According to AO recommendations for bridge plating of a diaphyseal fracture, which combination of plate span width ratio and screw density is preferred?
o: Plate span width ratio below 1 and screw density close to 1
Plate span width ratio greater than about 2-3 and screw density below about 0.4-0.5
Plate length equal to the fracture length and every hole filled
Plate span width ratio of 1.5 and three screws immediately adjacent to the fracture
items.e: Long plates with few, well-spaced screws distribute load and increase working length, lowering stress in the plate. Filling every hole close to the fracture stiffens the construct and concentrates stress at the fracture.

items.q: Far cortical locking screws are designed to:
o: Reduce stiffness at the near cortex, allowing more symmetric interfragmentary motion and callus
Increase pull-out strength in the far cortex by using a larger thread diameter
Convert a locking plate into a compression plate
Lock into the plate at variable angles
items.e: Standard locked plates are very stiff at the near cortex, producing asymmetric motion and less callus under the plate. Far cortical locking screws engage only the far cortex, reducing stiffness and promoting more uniform callus.

items.q: Increasing the diameter of a solid intramedullary nail from 10 mm to 12 mm (same material) increases its bending stiffness by approximately:
items.e: Bending stiffness of a solid cylinder is proportional to radius to the fourth power; (12/10) to the fourth power is about 2.07, so stiffness roughly doubles with a 2 mm larger nail.

items.q: If the working length of an intramedullary nail across a fracture is doubled, its bending stiffness is reduced to approximately:
items.e: Bending stiffness of a nail is inversely proportional to the square of its working length, whereas torsional stiffness is inversely proportional to working length, so doubling the working length halves torsional and quarters bending stiffness.

items.q: In the SPRINT trial of reamed versus unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures, the main finding was:
o: A clear benefit of unreamed nailing in closed fractures
A significant reduction in infection with reaming in open fractures
A possible benefit of reaming in closed fractures, with no significant difference in open fractures
Higher rates of compartment syndrome with reaming in closed fractures
items.e: SPRINT found fewer events (mainly fewer dynamisations for delayed union) with reamed nailing in closed fractures but no difference in open fractures. Reaming did not increase infection.

items.q: A static-locked femoral nail shows delayed union of an axially stable transverse fracture at 4 months. Removing the proximal or distal static screws to allow controlled axial loading is called:
items.e: Dynamisation converts a static construct into a dynamic one so that weight-bearing compresses the fracture, stimulating healing in axially stable patterns. Exchange nailing replaces the nail with a larger reamed one.

items.q: To make a unilateral external fixator stiffer, the single change with the greatest effect is to:
o: Increase the distance between the bar and the bone
Move the pins in each fragment closer together
Use unicortical rather than bicortical pins
items.e: Pin bending stiffness is proportional to radius to the fourth power, so increasing pin diameter has the largest effect. Moving the bar further from bone, clustering pins and unicortical pins all reduce stiffness.

items.q: Which pin arrangement within each fragment gives the stiffest unilateral external fixator?
o: One pin close to the fracture and one far from it ('near-near, far-far')
Both pins clustered close to the fracture
Both pins clustered at the far end of the fragment
Pins at equal distance from the joint regardless of the fracture
items.e: Spreading pins widely within each fragment, with the inner pins close to the fracture, maximises the effective lever arm and stiffness of the frame.

items.q: When applying a circular (Ilizarov-type) fixator, which combination increases stability of the bone-wire construct?
o: Tensioned wires (about 90-130 kg) crossing close to 90 degrees
Untensioned wires crossing at about 20 degrees
Fewer, thinner wires on larger-diameter rings
Wires crossing in parallel planes to avoid neurovascular structures
items.e: Ring stability rises with wire tension, wire diameter, number of wires and a crossing angle near 90 degrees, and falls with larger ring diameter. Narrow crossing angles allow the bone to translate along the wires.

items.q: Doubling the diameter of a monofilament stainless steel cerclage wire increases its tensile strength by approximately:
items.e: Tensile strength of a wire depends on cross-sectional area, which is proportional to radius squared. Bending stiffness, by contrast, varies with radius to the fourth power.

items.q: Tension band wiring of a transverse patellar fracture converts distraction into compression across the articular surface most effectively when the knee is:
o: Flexed, so the quadriceps and patellar tendon pull against the anterior wire loop
Held in full extension in a cylinder cast
Hyperextended to tighten the posterior capsule
items.e: The anterior wire on the tension side resists distraction as the knee flexes, so muscle forces compress the fracture at the articular (posterior) surface. This is the Pauwels tension band principle.

items.q: A patient with right hip osteoarthritis is advised to use a walking stick. To reduce the load on the right hip most effectively, the stick should be held in the:
o: Either hand, as the effect is identical
Right hand while carrying a bag in the left
items.e: A cane in the contralateral hand acts on a long lever arm from the affected hip and markedly reduces the abductor force and joint reaction force. Bags should be carried in the ipsilateral hand.

items.q: A patient with a painful left total hip replacement must carry a heavy suitcase. To minimise the left hip joint reaction force, the suitcase should be carried in the:
o: Right hand with a stick in the left hand
Both hands in front of the body
items.e: A load in the ipsilateral hand shifts the centre of gravity towards the affected hip and reduces the abductor demand; a load in the contralateral hand acts on a long lever arm and greatly increases the joint reaction force.

items.q: During total hip arthroplasty, which change in implant position reduces the hip joint reaction force?
o: Lateralising the acetabular centre of rotation
Distalising the greater trochanter without changing offset
items.e: Medialising the cup shortens the body-weight lever arm, and increasing femoral offset lengthens the abductor lever arm; both reduce the abductor force required and so the joint reaction force.

items.q: A patient with a painful hip leans the trunk over the affected hip during stance (abductor lurch). Mechanically this:
o: Lengthens the body-weight lever arm and increases abductor force
Moves the centre of gravity towards the hip, reducing abductor force and joint reaction force
Increases the abductor lever arm by elevating the pelvis
Has no effect on the hip joint reaction force
items.e: Leaning over the stance hip shortens the body-weight moment arm so the abductors need to generate less force; this compensatory Trendelenburg (antalgic) lurch lowers hip loading.

items.q: In a knee with neutral mechanical alignment, approximately what proportion of the tibiofemoral load during stance passes through the medial compartment?
items.e: The adduction moment during gait loads the medial compartment more, so about 60-70% of load passes medially even in a neutral knee; varus malalignment increases this further.

items.q: Patellofemoral joint reaction force is greatest during which activity?
o: Standing with the knee locked in extension
items.e: Patellofemoral load rises with knee flexion and quadriceps force: about 0.5 times body weight walking, about 3-3.5 times on stairs and up to about 7-8 times in deep squatting.

items.q: The main biomechanical function of the patella is to:
o: Increase the tibiofemoral contact area in flexion
Act as the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation
Reduce the patellofemoral joint reaction force in deep flexion
Increase the moment arm of the extensor mechanism, especially near full extension
items.e: By displacing the quadriceps tendon anteriorly, the patella lengthens the extensor lever arm; patellectomy substantially reduces extension strength (often quoted about 25-50%).

items.q: In the terminal 15-20 degrees of knee extension the tibia rotates externally on the femur to 'lock' the knee. The muscle that initiates unlocking at the start of flexion is:
items.e: The screw-home mechanism externally rotates the tibia in terminal extension; popliteus internally rotates the tibia (or externally rotates the femur) to unlock it.

items.q: In the extended elbow under axial load, the approximate distribution of force across the joint is:
o: About 50% through each articulation regardless of position
Almost all through the proximal radioulnar joint
items.e: Most axial load is transmitted from the hand to the radius and across the radiocapitellar joint (commonly quoted about 60%), which is why the radial head is important after Essex-Lopresti injuries.

items.q: According to Nachemson's in vivo measurements of L3 intradiscal pressure, which posture produces the highest pressure?
o: Sitting, leaning forward while holding a weight
items.e: Intradiscal pressure is lowest supine, higher standing, higher still sitting than standing, and highest when sitting and flexing forward with a load in the hands.

items.q: In 316L stainless steel, the letter 'L' indicates:
o: Low carbon content, which reduces susceptibility to corrosion
Lamellar grain structure for increased ductility
Low nickel content for hypersensitive patients
items.e: Reducing carbon limits chromium carbide precipitation at grain boundaries, preserving chromium for the passive oxide layer and reducing corrosion. 316L still contains about 13-15% nickel.

items.q: A patient with a failed metal-on-metal hip develops cardiomyopathy, hypothyroidism, peripheral neuropathy and hearing loss. The most likely cause is systemic toxicity from:
items.e: Systemic cobalt toxicity (arthroprosthetic cobaltism) causes cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, auditory and visual disturbance and hypothyroidism; it has been reported with metal-on-metal bearings and with ceramic head fracture revised to a metal head.

items.q: On axial CT of a shoulder with primary osteoarthritis, the glenoid shows central wear with the humeral head medialised so that a line joining the anterior and posterior glenoid rims cuts through the humeral head. There is no posterior subluxation. Walch type?
items.e: Walch A2 is a major central erosion with medialisation (the rim line transects the head); A1 is minor central erosion, and B types involve posterior subluxation or posterior wear.
