items.q: In the modified Walch classification, a monoconcave glenoid with posterior bone loss, retroversion over about 15° and/or posterior humeral head subluxation over 70%, without a biconcavity, is type:
items.e: B3 is monoconcave and retroverted from posterior erosion; B2 is the biconcave glenoid with a posterior neoglenoid, and C is dysplastic (not erosive) retroversion.

items.q: Which Walch glenoid type describes glenoid anteversion or anterior humeral head subluxation?
items.e: Type D was added in the modified Walch classification for anteverted glenoids or anterior subluxation; C is dysplastic retroversion over 25°.

items.q: Glenoid version on axial CT is classically measured (Friedman method) as the angle between the glenoid face and a line perpendicular to the:
o: Long axis of the humeral shaft
Line joining the coracoid tip to the acromion
Transepicondylar axis of the distal humerus
Line from the medial tip of the scapula to the centre of the glenoid
items.e: Friedman's method uses the scapular axis, drawn from the medial tip of the scapular body to the glenoid centre, as the reference for version.

items.q: In primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, the range of motion that is typically lost earliest and most markedly is:
items.e: Contracture of the anterior capsule and subscapularis with posterior head subluxation causes characteristic loss of external rotation.

items.q: The 'goat's beard' osteophyte seen on the AP radiograph in primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis is located at the:
o: Inferior margin of the humeral head
items.e: A large inferior humeral head osteophyte (goat's beard) is typical of primary OA; acromial changes suggest cuff tear arthropathy instead.

items.q: A 68-year-old with Walch B2 osteoarthritis and an intact cuff has 18° of glenoid retroversion. The surgeon plans anatomic TSA. Asymmetric (high-side) reaming alone is generally considered safe for correcting up to about:
o: Any amount, provided the cuff is intact
items.e: Eccentric reaming beyond about 10–15° removes too much bone and medialises the joint line; larger corrections need augmented components, bone graft or a reverse prosthesis.

items.q: A 74-year-old has primary OA with a Walch B3 glenoid, 28° retroversion and 80% posterior subluxation, but an intact rotator cuff. Which option is most reliable?
o: Anatomic TSA with a standard non-augmented glenoid
items.e: Severe posterior bone loss and subluxation in the elderly make anatomic glenoid fixation unreliable; RTSA is favoured, while hemiarthroplasty leaves posterior glenoid erosion progressing.

items.q: The main reason anatomic TSA is preferred to humeral hemiarthroplasty for primary glenohumeral OA is that hemiarthroplasty leads to:
o: Progressive painful glenoid erosion and inferior pain relief
Higher rates of humeral stem loosening
items.e: With hemiarthroplasty the native arthritic glenoid continues to erode, giving worse pain relief and more revisions; notching is a reverse-prosthesis problem.

items.q: In the original Grammont reverse shoulder design, the humeral neck-shaft angle was about:
items.e: The Grammont design had a 155° inclination, which increased scapular notching; newer designs use 135–145° to reduce notching and improve rotation.

items.q: In bony increased-offset reverse shoulder arthroplasty (BIO-RSA), lateralisation of the centre of rotation is achieved by:
o: An autologous humeral head bone graft placed under the baseplate
Medialising the baseplate into the glenoid vault
items.e: BIO-RSA uses a cylinder of humeral head autograft beneath the baseplate to lateralise the glenoid side; a lower neck-shaft angle lateralises the humeral side instead.

items.q: Which glenoid-side technical factor reduces scapular notching after RTSA?
o: Placing the baseplate high with superior tilt
Medialising the glenosphere by deep reaming
Using a larger-diameter glenosphere placed low on the glenoid
items.e: Inferior placement, inferior tilt, lateralisation and a larger glenosphere let the cup clear the scapular neck in adduction; superior tilt and medialisation increase notching.

items.q: On radiographs after RTSA, a notch in the inferior scapular neck that reaches the inferior baseplate screw but does not extend over it is Sirveaux grade:
items.e: Sirveaux grade 1 is limited to the pillar, grade 2 contacts the inferior screw, grade 3 extends over the screw and grade 4 extends under the baseplate.

items.q: A 70-year-old with cuff tear arthropathy has a positive hornblower's sign and an external rotation lag. MRI shows fatty atrophy of the infraspinatus and teres minor. To restore active external rotation, RTSA should be combined with:
o: Lower trapezius transfer alone without RTSA
items.e: External rotation after RTSA depends on the teres minor; when it is absent, a L'Episcopo-type latissimus dorsi (± teres major) transfer restores it. Pectoralis major transfer is for subscapularis deficiency.

items.q: A positive hornblower's sign (inability to hold the arm in external rotation at 90° abduction) indicates deficiency of:
items.e: Hornblower's sign tests the teres minor; its absence predicts poor external rotation after RTSA.

items.q: Which is the single non-negotiable requirement for a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty to function?
o: A functioning deltoid with an intact axillary nerve
items.e: RTSA relies entirely on the deltoid to elevate the arm; subscapularis and teres minor improve stability and rotation but are not mandatory.

items.q: Pseudoparalysis of the shoulder is best defined as:
o: Loss of both active and passive elevation from capsular contracture
Weakness of elevation from an axillary nerve palsy
Active forward elevation under 90° with preserved passive elevation, without a neurological cause
Painful arc between 60° and 120° of abduction
items.e: Pseudoparalysis is loss of active elevation despite full passive motion due to a massive cuff tear; it is a key indication for RTSA.

items.q: A 66-year-old has a massive irreparable cuff tear and early glenohumeral arthritis. Active elevation is 150°, the coracoacromial arch is intact and he wants to keep lifting moderate loads. A recognised option, instead of RTSA, is:
o: Anatomic TSA with a cemented polyethylene glenoid
Arthroscopic acromioplasty and coracoacromial ligament release
Hemiarthroplasty with an extended-coverage (CTA) humeral head
items.e: A CTA head hemiarthroplasty suits younger or lower-demand patients with preserved elevation and an intact CA arch; anatomic TSA would loosen (rocking horse) and CA release risks anterosuperior escape.

items.q: A 72-year-old with a massive cuff tear has anterosuperior escape of the humeral head on attempted elevation (Seebauer IIB). Which previous procedure is most likely to have contributed?
o: Distal clavicle excision through a superior approach without CA release
items.e: Loss of the coracoacromial arch removes the last restraint to superior migration in a cuff-deficient shoulder, producing anterosuperior escape (Seebauer IIB).

items.q: In the Seebauer classification of cuff tear arthropathy, type IIB is characterised by:
o: Decentred, unstable head with anterosuperior escape through an incompetent coracoacromial arch
Centred head with minimal superior migration
Decentred head with limited superior translation and intact arch
items.e: Seebauer type I is centred (IA stable, IB medialised), IIA is decentred with limited superior translation, and IIB is decentred with anterosuperior escape.

items.q: Radiographs of a shoulder with a chronic massive cuff tear show the undersurface of the acromion has become concave, but there is no glenohumeral joint space narrowing. Hamada grade?
items.e: Hamada grade 3 adds acetabularisation of the acromion to a narrowed acromiohumeral interval; grade 4 involves glenohumeral narrowing and grade 5 humeral head collapse.

items.q: In the Hamada classification of massive cuff tears, grade 5 corresponds to:
o: Acromiohumeral interval of 5 mm or less
Humeral head collapse (cuff tear arthropathy with osteonecrosis-like collapse)
items.e: Grade 5 is collapse of the humeral head; grades 2–4 describe AHI narrowing, acetabularisation and glenohumeral arthritis respectively.

items.q: 'Femoralisation' of the humeral head in cuff tear arthropathy refers to:
o: Rounding off of the greater tuberosity so the proximal humerus resembles a femoral head
Medial migration of the head into the glenoid
Collapse of the humeral head from osteonecrosis
Inferior subluxation of the head from deltoid atony
items.e: Wear against the acromion rounds the greater tuberosity, while the acromion becomes concave (acetabularisation).

items.q: An 80-year-old woman has a large, recurrent, blood-stained shoulder effusion with rapid destruction of the joint and a massive cuff tear. Aspirate shows basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Milwaukee shoulder is a hydroxyapatite-associated destructive arthropathy in elderly women with large haemorrhagic effusions; CPPD would show rhomboid positively birefringent crystals.

items.q: Neer's original explanation for cuff tear arthropathy included a 'nutritional' factor. This refers to:
o: Vitamin D deficiency causing subchondral collapse
Leakage of synovial fluid through the cuff defect, depriving the cartilage of nutrition and pressure
Avascularity of the humeral head after anterior circumflex artery injury
items.e: Neer proposed mechanical (superior migration, instability) and nutritional (loss of a closed joint with fluid leakage and disuse) factors causing cartilage atrophy and collapse.

items.q: An acromiohumeral interval of under about 5 mm on a true AP radiograph most strongly suggests:
items.e: AHI under 7 mm suggests a cuff tear and under 5 mm a massive tear with superior head migration.

items.q: A 75-year-old woman has a displaced four-part proximal humerus fracture-dislocation. She lives independently. Compared with hemiarthroplasty, reverse shoulder arthroplasty with tuberosity repair gives:
o: More reliable forward elevation with fewer revisions
Better external rotation in every case
Lower rates of infection and instability
Results that depend more on tuberosity healing
items.e: RTSA function relies on the deltoid, not tuberosity union, so elevation is more predictable; tuberosity repair still improves external rotation.

items.q: In reverse shoulder arthroplasty for a four-part proximal humerus fracture in a 78-year-old, repairing the tuberosities around the stem is recommended mainly because tuberosity healing:
o: Is essential to prevent axillary nerve injury
Improves active external rotation and elevation
items.e: Although RTSA does not depend on tuberosity union, healed tuberosities (with teres minor and infraspinatus attached) improve rotation and elevation.

items.q: The PROFHER trial compared surgery with non-operative treatment for displaced proximal humerus fractures involving the surgical neck in adults. It found:
o: Superior outcomes with locking plate fixation
No significant difference in Oxford Shoulder Score at 2 years
items.e: PROFHER (JAMA 2015) showed no significant benefit of surgery over sling treatment at 2 years for most displaced surgical neck fractures.

items.q: In the Cruess classification of humeral head osteonecrosis, which stage generally needs a total shoulder replacement rather than hemiarthroplasty or resurfacing?
items.e: Cruess stage V has secondary glenoid arthritis, so a glenoid component is added; stages III–IV with an intact glenoid suit hemiarthroplasty or resurfacing.

items.q: A 30-year-old on long-term steroids has collapse of the humeral head (Cruess stage IV) with a normal glenoid and intact cuff. Preferred arthroplasty?
o: Anatomic TSA with a cemented glenoid
items.e: With an intact glenoid in a young patient, replacing only the humeral side avoids glenoid wear and loosening concerns; RTSA is not indicated with an intact cuff in the young.

items.q: Boileau's classification of proximal humerus fracture sequelae: which type is the surgical neck non-union, which does poorly with anatomic arthroplasty and is now usually managed with RTSA?
items.e: Boileau types 1 (head collapse/necrosis) and 2 (locked dislocation) are intracapsular; type 3 (surgical neck non-union) and type 4 (severe tuberosity malunion) are extracapsular and do poorly with anatomic implants unless osteotomy is done.

items.q: A 50-year-old had a Putti–Platt repair for anterior instability 20 years ago. He now has pain and markedly restricted external rotation. Radiographs show posterior glenoid wear and posterior subluxation. Diagnosis?
o: Hardware arthropathy from a loose suture anchor
items.e: Over-tightening the anterior structures limits external rotation and forces the head posteriorly, causing posterior wear (capsulorrhaphy arthropathy).

items.q: In the anterosuperior (Neviaser–Mackenzie) approach for reverse shoulder arthroplasty, the deltoid split should not extend more than about how far distal to the acromion to protect the axillary nerve?
items.e: The anterior branch of the axillary nerve runs about 5–7 cm below the acromion; splitting the deltoid further risks denervating the anterior deltoid.

items.q: Compared with the deltopectoral approach, the superolateral (deltoid-splitting) approach for RTSA has been associated with:
o: Lower dislocation rates but more difficult inferior glenoid exposure
Higher dislocation rates but easier inferior glenoid exposure
Easier extension for humeral shaft fractures
items.e: The superolateral approach preserves the subscapularis (less instability) but makes inferior baseplate placement harder, increasing the risk of notching; it does not extend well distally.

items.q: During a deltopectoral approach for shoulder arthroplasty, the cephalic vein is usually:
o: Retracted medially with the pectoralis major
Ligated routinely at the clavipectoral fascia
Found deep to the conjoint tendon
items.e: Most of its tributaries come from the deltoid, so the cephalic vein is usually taken laterally with the deltoid to reduce bleeding.

items.q: During the deltopectoral approach, excessive medial retraction of the conjoint tendon most endangers the musculocutaneous nerve, which usually enters coracobrachialis about how far below the coracoid?
o: At the level of the deltoid insertion
items.e: The nerve typically pierces coracobrachialis about 5 cm below the coracoid tip, but can be as close as 3 cm, so vigorous retraction can cause a traction palsy.

items.q: During inferior capsular release in shoulder arthroplasty, which nerve is most at risk as it passes below the subscapularis and capsule?
items.e: The axillary nerve runs along the inferior border of subscapularis and the inferior capsule into the quadrilateral space; protect it during inferior release.

items.q: A lesser tuberosity osteotomy is sometimes chosen for subscapularis management during anatomic TSA because it:
o: Avoids any need for postoperative restriction of external rotation
Eliminates the risk of anterior instability
Allows bone-to-bone healing of the subscapularis
Preserves the anterior circumflex artery to the humeral head
items.e: Osteotomy healing can be checked radiographically and is bone-to-bone; external rotation is still protected early after surgery.

items.q: Six months after anatomic TSA via a deltopectoral approach with subscapularis tenotomy, a patient has weakness of internal rotation, increased passive external rotation and anterior instability. Which test is most useful to confirm the cause?
items.e: Subscapularis failure after TSA gives anterior instability and weakness; belly-press and lift-off tests assess subscapularis.

items.q: In early rehabilitation after anatomic TSA through a subscapularis tenotomy, the movement usually restricted for about 6 weeks is:
o: Passive forward elevation in the scapular plane
items.e: Limiting external rotation protects the subscapularis repair, whose failure causes anterior instability.

items.q: After a successful RTSA for cuff tear arthropathy, active forward elevation typically reaches about:
o: 90° only, with no improvement in rotation
items.e: RTSA reliably restores elevation to roughly 120–140°, but rotation (especially internal rotation behind the back) remains limited.

items.q: Which feature distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis of the glenohumeral joint from primary OA on CT?
o: Posterior glenoid wear with a biconcave glenoid
Central glenoid erosion with medialisation of the joint line
items.e: Inflammatory arthritis erodes the glenoid centrally (medialisation) with little osteophyte formation, while OA wears posteriorly with osteophytes.

items.q: In a patient with rheumatoid arthritis planned for shoulder arthroplasty, which preoperative assessment is particularly important for anaesthetic safety?
o: Nerve conduction studies of the axillary nerve
Flexion-extension radiographs of the cervical spine
DEXA scan of the proximal humerus
items.e: Atlantoaxial instability is common in RA and must be excluded before intubation and positioning.

items.q: A key benefit of a stemless (metaphyseal-fixation) humeral component in anatomic TSA compared with a stemmed implant is:
o: Superior fixation in osteoporotic metaphyseal bone
Preservation of humeral bone stock and easier revision
items.e: Stemless implants save diaphyseal bone and avoid stem-related periprosthetic fracture; they need good metaphyseal bone, so are unsuitable for osteoporosis or fractures.

items.q: Which patient factor is most strongly associated with Cutibacterium acnes periprosthetic shoulder infection?
items.e: C. acnes colonises sebaceous, hair-bearing skin around the shoulder and axilla more heavily in men, making male sex a consistent risk factor.

items.q: Which skin preparation measure has been shown to reduce Cutibacterium acnes load on the skin before shoulder arthroplasty?
o: Alcohol hand rub applied to the shoulder only on the day of surgery
Topical benzoyl peroxide applied for a few days before surgery
Shaving the axilla with a razor the night before
Oral doxycycline for 6 weeks before surgery
items.e: Benzoyl peroxide penetrates sebaceous glands and reduces C. acnes colonisation; standard chlorhexidine alone does not eradicate it from deeper dermal structures.

items.q: Months after a well-functioning RTSA, the patient develops sudden acromial pain and loss of active elevation after minor effort. Which surgical factor increases the risk of this complication?
o: Using a lateralised humeral insert to reduce deltoid tension
Placing the glenosphere low on the glenoid
items.e: Acromial and scapular spine stress fractures follow increased deltoid tension from over-lengthening or lateralisation, especially with osteoporosis.

items.q: Which is the most important risk factor for dislocation after RTSA through a deltopectoral approach?
o: An irreparable subscapularis with a medialised implant
items.e: Instability after RTSA is linked to subscapularis deficiency, inadequate soft-tissue tension and medialised designs; lateralisation improves tension and stability.

items.q: A 78-year-old falls 3 weeks after RTSA and has an anterior dislocation of the prosthesis. After closed reduction, the shoulder redislocates easily. The usual next step is:
o: Revision to increase soft-tissue tension (thicker insert, larger glenosphere or spacer)
Sling immobilisation in extension and internal rotation for 6 weeks
items.e: Recurrent instability after RTSA usually reflects inadequate tension; revision increases humeral length or offset. Extension, adduction and internal rotation are the dislocating position.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of the surface of the talus is covered by articular cartilage?
items.e: Roughly three-fifths of the talus is articular, leaving limited surface for vascular entry; together with the absence of muscle attachments this explains its vulnerable blood supply.

items.q: Which statement about the soft-tissue attachments of the talus is correct?
o: Tibialis posterior inserts on the talar head
No muscle or tendon attaches to it
Extensor digitorum brevis arises from the talar neck
The plantaris inserts on the posterior process
items.e: The talus has no muscle or tendon attachments; it is held only by ligaments and capsule, so its vessels enter through limited non-articular areas (neck, tarsal canal and sinus, deltoid region).

items.q: The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs in a groove on the posterior talus lying between the:
o: Lateral process and the talar head
Talar neck and the sustentaculum tali
Medial and lateral tubercles of the posterior process
Posterior facet and the middle facet
items.e: The FHL groove separates the posteromedial and posterolateral tubercles of the posterior process; FHL then passes beneath the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus.

items.q: The artery of the tarsal sinus, supplying the lateral part of the talar body, is derived from branches of the:
items.e: The artery of the tarsal sinus is formed from the perforating peroneal and dorsalis pedis (lateral tarsal) branches; the artery of the tarsal canal comes from the posterior tibial artery.

items.q: Beneath the talar neck, the arteries of the tarsal canal and tarsal sinus join to form:
items.e: The tarsal canal and tarsal sinus arteries anastomose beneath the neck, forming a sling from which branches enter the body; a displaced neck fracture disrupts this supply.

items.q: The superior (dorsal) aspect of the talar head and neck receives its blood supply mainly from branches of the:
o: Posterior tibial artery via the deltoid branch
Peroneal artery via the posterior malleolar branch
items.e: Dorsalis pedis branches supply the superior neck and head; the body depends mainly on the tarsal canal artery (posterior tibial) and its deltoid branch.

items.q: The term 'aviator's astragalus' refers to a talar neck fracture produced mainly by:
o: Direct blow to the dorsum of the foot
Forced dorsiflexion of the foot with axial load
Twisting external rotation with the foot planted
items.e: Forced dorsiflexion drives the talar neck against the anterior lip of the tibia, as seen when aircraft rudder bars were driven into the pilot's feet in crashes.

items.q: A displaced talar neck fracture is associated with dislocation of the subtalar, tibiotalar and talonavicular joints. In the Canale-Kelly modification of Hawkins' classification this is type:
items.e: Type IV adds talonavicular subluxation or dislocation to the type III pattern (subtalar and ankle dislocation); AVN risk approaches 100%.

items.q: Vallier subdivided Hawkins type II talar neck fractures into IIA and IIB. What distinguishes IIB, and why does it matter?
o: The subtalar joint is dislocated rather than subluxed, with a higher AVN rate
The fracture is open, with higher infection rate
There is talar body comminution, with higher non-union
The ankle joint is also subluxed, requiring malleolar osteotomy
items.e: IIA has a subluxed subtalar joint, IIB a dislocated one; Vallier found osteonecrosis much more often in IIB, reflecting greater disruption of the remaining vessels.

items.q: In a Hawkins type III talar neck fracture, the talar body is most often extruded in which direction?
items.e: The body usually extrudes posteromedially, between the posterior tibia and the Achilles tendon, where it can compress the neurovascular bundle and threaten the skin.

items.q: Studies by Vallier and Lindvall on displaced talar neck fractures found that delaying definitive internal fixation (after any dislocation is reduced):
o: Doubled the rate of osteonecrosis after 6 hours
Did not significantly increase the rate of osteonecrosis
items.e: Time to definitive ORIF did not influence AVN; the emergency is reduction of dislocations and skin protection, after which fixation can wait for soft tissues.

items.q: For fixation of a talar neck fracture, screws inserted from posterior to anterior (from the posterolateral talus) compared with anterior-to-posterior screws are:
o: Biomechanically stronger and placed more perpendicular to the fracture
items.e: Posterior-to-anterior screws are better aligned with the neck axis and perpendicular to the fracture, giving greater stiffness; they are inserted via a posterolateral approach lateral to FHL.

items.q: In a talar neck fracture with dorsomedial comminution, a small plate is often applied along the medial or lateral neck rather than relying on compression screws. Its purpose is to:
o: Bridge the comminution and prevent shortening and varus collapse
Compress the fracture and close the comminuted gap
items.e: Lag screws across a comminuted medial neck shorten it and produce varus; a bridging (position) plate holds length and alignment.

items.q: A talar neck fracture heals in varus malalignment. The resulting foot posture is:
o: Hindfoot varus with forefoot adduction and lateral border overload
Fixed equinus with no change in coronal alignment
Pes planus with medial arch collapse
items.e: Varus malunion locks the subtalar joint in inversion, reducing eversion and causing forefoot adduction with weight bearing on the lateral column.

items.q: During open reduction of a talar body fracture via a medial malleolar osteotomy, which structure must be preserved to protect the remaining blood supply?
o: Deltoid ligament attachments to the talus
items.e: The deltoid branch of the tarsal canal artery runs within the deltoid ligament; preserving it may protect the last vascular supply to the body.

items.q: A 30-year-old has collapse of the talar body from avascular necrosis after a neck fracture. In the Blair fusion, the tibia is fused to the:
o: Calcaneus with an intramedullary nail, excising the talus
Navicular and cuboid with a fibular strut
Talar neck and head with an anterior sliding tibial graft
items.e: The Blair procedure excises the necrotic body and slides an anterior tibial graft into the talar head-neck, preserving limb length and some hindfoot motion.

items.q: Eight weeks after fixation of a talar neck fracture, no subchondral lucency is visible in the talar dome on the AP ankle radiograph. The correct interpretation is:
o: Osteonecrosis is possible but not certain; MRI can clarify
Osteonecrosis has definitely occurred and collapse is inevitable
Union has failed and revision is required
The fracture has healed with a normal blood supply
items.e: The Hawkins sign is a good prognostic sign when present, but its absence does not guarantee AVN; MRI is more informative.

items.q: A patient has osteonecrosis of the talar body after a neck fracture but the dome has not collapsed. Which statement is correct?
o: The body can revascularise by creeping substitution without collapse
The fracture will not unite until revascularisation is complete
items.e: AVN of the talus does not always progress to collapse; the body may revascularise by creeping substitution, and the fracture can still unite. Protected weight bearing is debated.

items.q: A snowboarder's lateral process of talus fracture is severely comminuted on CT with small fragments only. The best definitive treatment of symptomatic fragments is:
items.e: Small or comminuted lateral process fragments that cannot be fixed are excised; large displaced fragments (over about 1 cm) are fixed and undisplaced ones treated in a cast.

items.q: A footballer has posterolateral ankle pain after forced plantarflexion. Radiographs show an ossicle behind the talus. Which feature favours an acute Shepherd fracture rather than an os trigonum?
o: A similar ossicle in the opposite ankle
A broad fibrous interface on MRI without oedema
items.e: An os trigonum is smooth and fully corticated and often bilateral; a Shepherd (lateral tubercle) fracture has rough uncorticated edges and marrow oedema.

items.q: A fracture of the lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process (Shepherd fracture) is usually caused by:
o: Forced plantarflexion compressing it between the tibia and calcaneus
Avulsion by the anterior talofibular ligament
items.e: Extreme plantarflexion impinges the posterior process between the posterior tibial plafond and calcaneus (or the posterior talofibular ligament avulses it).

items.q: Medial subtalar dislocation accounts for about 80% of subtalar dislocations. The clinical appearance of the foot is:
o: Everted and abducted, like an acquired flatfoot
Inverted and medially displaced, like an acquired clubfoot
Plantarflexed with the forefoot dorsally displaced
Shortened with the heel displaced anteriorly
items.e: In medial (inversion) dislocation the foot sits medially in an inverted, 'acquired clubfoot' position; lateral dislocation gives an 'acquired flatfoot' appearance.

items.q: A medial subtalar dislocation cannot be reduced closed. The talar head is most likely trapped by:
o: The extensor digitorum brevis or extensor retinaculum
items.e: In medial dislocations the talar head buttonholes through EDB, the extensor retinaculum or talonavicular capsule (peroneal tendons are another block); tibialis posterior blocks lateral dislocations.

items.q: During closed reduction of a subtalar dislocation, the knee is kept flexed to:
o: Relax the hamstrings and tibial nerve
items.e: Knee flexion relaxes the gastrocnemius-Achilles unit; the deformity is accentuated, then reversed with heel traction.

items.q: After successful closed reduction of a subtalar dislocation, the next most useful investigation is:
o: Stress radiographs of the subtalar joint
items.e: Associated osteochondral and process fractures are found in over half of cases and are often missed on radiographs; CT identifies them and intra-articular fragments.

items.q: Compared with medial subtalar dislocation, lateral subtalar dislocation is:
o: Higher energy, more often open, with a worse prognosis
items.e: Lateral dislocations are less common, higher energy, more often open or associated with fractures, and have worse outcomes.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an open total talar extrusion; the talus is found in the wound with no soft-tissue attachment. After thorough debridement, the preferred management is:
o: Discarding the talus and inserting a cement spacer permanently
Reimplantation of the talus with stabilisation
items.e: Reimplantation after meticulous cleaning preserves height and alignment and has fewer complications than talectomy, even though AVN is almost certain.

items.q: Calcaneal fractures make up approximately what proportion of tarsal fractures, and what proportion are intra-articular?
items.e: The calcaneus is the commonest tarsal bone fractured (about 60%), and about three-quarters of these fractures involve the subtalar joint.

items.q: Which calcaneal articular facet is the largest and carries most body weight?
items.e: The posterior facet is the main weight-bearing subtalar surface and the target of reduction in intra-articular fractures.

items.q: During ORIF of a sustentacular fragment, a screw that is too long can injure which tendon running directly beneath the sustentaculum tali?
items.e: FHL runs in a groove on the undersurface of the sustentaculum; over-long lateral-to-medial screws can irritate or tether it.

items.q: In the classic axial-load calcaneal fracture, the primary fracture line is produced by which structure acting as a wedge?
items.e: The lateral process of the talus drives into the angle of Gissane, splitting the calcaneus into a superomedial (sustentacular) and superolateral (tuberosity) fragment.

items.q: In the Essex-Lopresti classification, what defines a tongue-type calcaneal fracture?
o: The posterior facet is a separate depressed fragment behind the primary line
The fracture involves only the anterior process
The fracture splits the sustentaculum from the body
The secondary fracture line exits through the posterior tuberosity, so the posterior facet stays attached to it
items.e: In tongue-type fractures the posterior facet remains attached to a tongue of tuberosity; in joint-depression type the facet is a separate fragment driven into the body.

items.q: A missed compartment syndrome of the foot after a calcaneal fracture typically leads to:
items.e: Ischaemic contracture of the intrinsic muscles (calcaneal compartment) produces claw toes, stiffness and neuropathic pain.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph, Böhler's angle is formed by a line from the highest point of the anterior process to the highest point of the posterior facet and a second line from the highest point of the posterior facet to the:
o: Superior edge of the posterior tuberosity
items.e: Böhler's angle (normal about 20-40 degrees) reflects calcaneal height and posterior facet position; it falls when the facet is depressed.

items.q: The critical angle of Gissane on the lateral radiograph is formed by:
o: The long axis of the talus and the calcaneal inclination
The plantar calcaneus and the fifth metatarsal
Two cortical struts: one along the posterior facet and one running to the anterior process
The posterior facet and the Achilles insertion
items.e: Gissane's angle (about 95-105 degrees) lies beneath the lateral process of the talus between strong cortical struts; it increases when the posterior facet is depressed.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph of an intra-articular calcaneal fracture, a 'double density' sign indicates:
o: Intact posterior facet with lateral wall blowout
A depressed and rotated posterior facet fragment
items.e: The depressed lateral part of the posterior facet sits below and is rotated relative to the medial part, producing two articular outlines.

items.q: Which radiograph best shows varus angulation, widening and shortening of the calcaneal tuberosity after a fracture?
items.e: The axial Harris heel view shows tuberosity alignment and heel width; Broden views show the posterior facet.

items.q: On coronal CT through the posterior facet, a calcaneal fracture has several lines but no displacement greater than 2 mm. Sanders type and treatment:
items.e: Sanders type I includes all undisplaced fractures (displacement under 2 mm), regardless of the number of fracture lines, and is treated non-operatively.

items.q: In Sanders' classification, the letters A, B and C describe the location of the posterior facet fracture lines. A 'C' line is:
o: Most lateral, close to the lateral wall
Central, through the middle of the facet
Most medial, near the sustentaculum and hardest to see and reduce from a lateral approach
items.e: Lines run lateral (A) to medial (C); C lines are hardest to visualise and reduce through lateral approaches, and outcomes are poorer.

items.q: In Sanders' series, which fracture type had the most predictable good results after ORIF?
items.e: Two-part posterior facet fractures (type II) did best after ORIF; type III were intermediate and type IV poor, leading to consideration of primary fusion.

items.q: After an intra-articular calcaneal fracture, ORIF through a lateral approach is usually delayed until the:
o: Skin wrinkles return, typically 7-14 days after injury
Fracture blisters have scarred over, typically at 6 weeks
Swelling has fully resolved on ultrasound
Fracture has early callus at 3 weeks
items.e: A positive wrinkle test indicates the swelling has subsided enough to reduce wound complications; operating earlier through oedematous skin increases dehiscence.

items.q: Before calcaneal ORIF, the patient has blood-filled fracture blisters over the lateral heel. These blisters indicate:
o: Superficial epidermal injury that can be ignored
Deeper dermal injury, and incisions through them should be avoided
items.e: Haemorrhagic blisters indicate dermal-epidermal separation at a deeper level than clear blisters; incisions through them heal poorly.

items.q: The main advantage of the sinus tarsi (minimally invasive) approach over the extensile lateral approach for Sanders II-III fractures is:
o: Better access to the sustentacular fragment
Ability to use a larger plate
Fewer wound complications with comparable reduction
Lower risk of subtalar arthritis due to complete joint exposure
items.e: The sinus tarsi approach reduces wound dehiscence (about 2-5% vs 10-25%) while achieving similar posterior facet reduction for most fractures.

items.q: The UK Heel Fracture Trial (HeFT, Griffin et al. 2014) of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures found that operative fixation compared with non-operative care:
o: Improved function at 2 years with fewer late fusions
Improved outcomes only in Sanders IV fractures
Gave no better patient-reported outcome at 2 years and had more complications
items.e: HeFT (extensile lateral ORIF vs non-operative) showed no functional benefit at 2 years and a higher complication and reoperation rate in the surgical group.

items.q: In Buckley's Canadian RCT (2002) of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures, patients treated non-operatively were about 5.5 times more likely to need:
items.e: Overall outcomes were similar, but non-operative patients more often needed late subtalar fusion for arthritis.

items.q: Which subgroup benefited from operative treatment in Buckley's 2002 calcaneal fracture trial?
o: Patients with Böhler angle below 0 degrees
items.e: Women, younger patients, those not on compensation, lighter workers, Böhler angle 0-14 degrees and simple (Sanders II) patterns did better with surgery.

items.q: A patient has lateral hindfoot pain beneath the fibula 2 years after a non-operatively treated calcaneal fracture; subtalar joint is not arthritic. CT shows lateral wall bulging abutting the fibula with peroneal tendon stenosis. Best surgical option:
o: Lateral wall exostectomy with peroneal tendon decompression
items.e: This is Stephens-Sanders type I malunion: lateral wall blowout causing subfibular and peroneal impingement, treated by exostectomy and peroneal decompression.

items.q: In the Stephens-Sanders classification of calcaneal malunion, type III (lateral wall exostosis, subtalar arthritis and calcaneal body malalignment, usually varus) is treated with:
o: Subtalar fusion with a calcaneal osteotomy to correct alignment
items.e: Type I: exostectomy; type II: exostectomy plus subtalar fusion; type III: add a calcaneal osteotomy to correct varus.

items.q: A 9-year-old falls from a tree and sustains a calcaneal fracture. Compared with adults, paediatric calcaneal fractures are:
o: More often extra-articular and usually managed non-operatively
More often Sanders IV and fused primarily
More likely to need emergency fixation
items.e: Children's calcaneal fractures are more commonly extra-articular, lower energy and remodel well, so most are treated non-operatively.

items.q: An isolated displaced fracture of the sustentaculum tali can cause restricted great toe motion by entrapping the:
items.e: FHL runs directly under the sustentaculum; displaced fragments can tether it, and fixation is advised when displaced.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM preoperative scoring system for periprosthetic joint infection, which minor criterion is worth 3 points?
o: Synovial WBC above 3,000 cells/µL or leukocyte esterase ++
items.e: Synovial WBC/leukocyte esterase and alpha-defensin each score 3; PMN% scores 2, while ESR and synovial CRP score only 1 point each.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM minor criteria for chronic periprosthetic infection, serum ESR scores 1 point when it exceeds:
items.e: ESR above 30 mm/h scores 1 point; serum CRP above 10 mg/L or D-dimer above 860 ng/mL scores 2 points.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM definition, the serum CRP threshold that scores as a minor criterion for chronic PJI is above:
items.e: Serum CRP above 1 mg/dL (10 mg/L) scores 2 points for chronic PJI; the much higher 100 mg/L threshold applies only in the early postoperative period.

items.q: Synovial fluid CRP is one of the 2018 ICM minor criteria. It scores 1 point above:
items.e: Synovial CRP above 6.9 mg/L carries 1 point; it is a low-weight criterion compared with synovial WBC or alpha-defensin (3 points each).

items.q: For chronic hip or knee PJI, the 2018 ICM synovial polymorphonuclear percentage threshold (worth 2 points) is above:
items.e: Synovial PMN above 80% scores 2 points in chronic PJI; in the first 6 weeks after surgery a higher cut-off of about 90% is used.

items.q: In the early postoperative period (within about 6 weeks of arthroplasty), the serum CRP level suggestive of acute PJI is above approximately:
items.e: Surgery itself raises CRP, so the threshold for acute postoperative PJI is about 100 mg/L rather than the 10 mg/L used for chronic infection.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM intraoperative criteria, positive histology for PJI is defined as:
o: More than 5 neutrophils per high-power field in at least 5 high-power fields
More than 10 lymphocytes per high-power field in at least 10 fields
Any neutrophil seen in a single high-power field
Presence of plasma cells and foreign-body giant cells
items.e: Over 5 neutrophils per HPF in 5 or more HPFs (frozen or permanent section) scores 3 intraoperative points; lymphocytes and giant cells are typical of aseptic wear reactions.

items.q: A painful TKA has a preoperative ICM minor score of 3. At revision there is no purulence and all cultures are negative, but histology shows more than 5 neutrophils per HPF in 5 fields. Using the combined ICM score, the joint is classified as:
items.e: Positive histology adds 3 points to the preoperative score of 3, giving 6, which meets the threshold for infection even without positive cultures.

items.q: A patient with a painful THA has a 2018 ICM preoperative minor score of 4 and no major criterion. How is this interpreted?
o: Not infected; proceed with aseptic revision
Infected only if alpha-defensin is also positive
Possibly infected; intraoperative findings are needed to decide
items.e: A preoperative score of 2-5 is inconclusive, so intraoperative histology, purulence and cultures are added; 6 or more is infected and 0-1 is not infected.

items.q: Which of the following alone confirms PJI under the 2018 ICM definition?
o: A single positive culture of Staphylococcus epidermidis
Serum CRP of 80 mg/L three months after surgery
Two positive periprosthetic cultures of the same organism
items.e: Two cultures growing the same organism (or a sinus tract) are major criteria; alpha-defensin is a 3-point minor criterion and a single culture may be a contaminant.

items.q: The time limit for debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR) in early PJI is based mainly on:
o: Maturation of bacterial biofilm on the implant within about 3-4 weeks
The time needed for osseointegration of uncemented implants
The duration of the normal postoperative rise in CRP
The elution period of antibiotics from bone cement
items.e: Once the biofilm matures, sessile bacteria become highly resistant to antibiotics and host defences, so implant retention is reserved for infections caught before this stage.

items.q: The 'race for the surface' concept, describing competition between host tissue cells and bacteria to colonise an implant, was proposed by:
items.e: Gristina described the race for the surface; if host cells integrate first the implant resists colonisation, whereas bacterial adhesion leads to biofilm formation.

items.q: Which pair of organisms together accounts for the majority of periprosthetic hip and knee infections?
items.e: Staphylococci cause roughly 50-60% of PJI; C. acnes is characteristic of shoulder arthroplasty and gram-negative organisms are less common.

items.q: The most common reason for culture-negative periprosthetic joint infection is:
items.e: Prior antibiotics are the leading cause of culture-negative PJI; fastidious, fungal or mycobacterial organisms are rarer causes, which is why antibiotics are stopped at least 2 weeks before aspiration.

items.q: A patient listed for TKA received an intra-articular corticosteroid injection. The usual recommended minimum interval between the injection and arthroplasty to limit infection risk is about:
items.e: Intra-articular steroid injection within about 3 months of arthroplasty is associated with increased PJI risk, so surgery is usually deferred beyond this window.

items.q: Which laboratory value indicates malnutrition that increases the risk of periprosthetic infection?
items.e: Albumin under 3.5 g/dL, transferrin under 200 mg/dL and total lymphocyte count under 1,500/mm³ are markers of malnutrition linked to wound complications and PJI.

items.q: A 68-year-old MRSA nasal carrier is having a primary THA. Vancomycin prophylaxis should be started:
items.e: Vancomycin needs a long infusion and should start within 120 minutes of incision; cefazolin is given within 60 minutes.

items.q: During a prolonged revision arthroplasty, intraoperative cefazolin should be re-dosed after about:
o: 4 hours, or sooner if blood loss exceeds about 1,500 mL
Never, as a single dose covers any operation
items.e: Cefazolin is re-dosed roughly every 4 hours (about two half-lives) or after major blood loss to maintain tissue concentrations.

items.q: Current guidance on the duration of antibiotic prophylaxis after primary total joint arthroplasty is to stop it:
o: When the wound has healed at 2 weeks
items.e: Prolonging prophylaxis beyond 24 hours adds no protection and increases resistance and C. difficile risk.

items.q: Which skin antiseptic for arthroplasty has been shown to reduce surgical site infection more than aqueous povidone-iodine?
items.e: Chlorhexidine-alcohol preparation outperformed povidone-iodine in surgical site infection trials and is the preferred skin preparation.

items.q: A patient screened before TKA is a nasal Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) carrier. The recommended decolonisation is:
o: Nasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine body washes
No action, as carriage does not affect infection risk
items.e: S. aureus carriage is a modifiable risk factor; short-course nasal mupirocin plus chlorhexidine washes reduce staphylococcal surgical site infection.

items.q: How should hair be removed from the operative site before arthroplasty, if needed?
o: Razor shaving in the anaesthetic room
items.e: Razor shaving causes skin microabrasions that become colonised; clipping close to the time of surgery carries the lowest infection risk.

items.q: In the Tsukayama classification of prosthetic joint infection, type IV refers to:
o: Positive intraoperative cultures at revision for presumed aseptic failure
Early postoperative infection within the first month
Late chronic infection with an insidious onset
Acute haematogenous infection of a well-functioning joint
items.e: Type I is early postoperative, II late chronic, III acute haematogenous and IV positive intraoperative cultures, usually treated with about 6 weeks of antibiotics.

items.q: At revision TKA for presumed aseptic loosening, 1 of 5 tissue cultures grows coagulase-negative staphylococcus. Preoperative CRP, ESR and aspirate were normal, there was no pus and histology was negative. The best interpretation is:
o: Chronic PJI requiring a two-stage revision
Probable contaminant; the joint does not meet the definition of PJI
items.e: A single positive culture scores only 2 points; with negative other markers the combined score stays low, so a low-virulence isolate is regarded as contamination.

items.q: The main benefit of sonicating explanted arthroplasty components is that it:
o: Dislodges biofilm bacteria from the implant, increasing culture yield (especially after prior antibiotics)
Sterilises the implant so it can be re-used
items.e: Low-frequency ultrasound releases sessile bacteria from the biofilm, improving culture sensitivity compared with periprosthetic tissue culture alone.

items.q: When joint aspiration is inconclusive, which nuclear medicine study has the best accuracy for diagnosing PJI?
o: Labelled leukocyte scan combined with bone marrow (sulphur colloid) imaging
items.e: Plain bone scans remain positive for a year or more after arthroplasty and are non-specific; combined leukocyte-marrow imaging distinguishes infection from marrow packing.

items.q: A leukocyte esterase strip test is planned on a blood-stained knee aspirate. To make the result readable, the fluid should be:
o: Diluted with an equal volume of saline
items.e: Red cells interfere with the colorimetric reading; centrifugation removes them so the supernatant can be tested.

items.q: A well-functioning TKA becomes acutely painful and swollen after a skin infection. DAIR is reasonable for acute haematogenous infection if symptoms have been present for less than about:
items.e: DAIR is suitable for acute haematogenous PJI with a short symptom duration (under about 3 weeks), well-fixed implants and healthy soft tissues; earlier is better.

items.q: Four weeks after primary THA, a patient has an acute PJI. Which finding makes DAIR inappropriate?
o: Radiographic loosening of the femoral stem
items.e: DAIR requires well-fixed implants; a loose component cannot be retained and needs exchange arthroplasty.

items.q: After DAIR for an acute PJI caused by Escherichia coli, which oral agent is preferred for its activity against gram-negative biofilm?
items.e: Fluoroquinolones are the biofilm-active choice for gram-negative PJI with retained implants; rifampicin plays this role for staphylococci.

items.q: After DAIR with retained components for staphylococcal PJI, the usual total duration of antibiotic therapy recommended by IDSA is about:
o: 3 months for the hip and 6 months for the knee
6 weeks for the hip and 2 weeks for the knee
items.e: IDSA recommends rifampicin-based combination therapy for about 3 months after hip DAIR and 6 months after knee DAIR.

items.q: A patient had DAIR for acute PJI after TKA 8 months ago. Infection has recurred, the implants remain fixed and there is now a sinus. The best treatment for a fit patient is:
o: A second DAIR with polyethylene exchange
Arthroscopic washout and 6 weeks of antibiotics
Oral antibiotics until the sinus closes
items.e: Repeat DAIR has poor results and a sinus indicates chronic infection, so component removal with one- or two-stage exchange is required.

items.q: Arthroscopic washout of an acutely infected TKA is discouraged mainly because it:
o: Does not permit thorough debridement and exchange of the modular polyethylene insert
Always spreads infection to the hip
items.e: Exchange of modular parts and open radical debridement are key to DAIR success; arthroscopic lavage has higher failure rates.

items.q: Which of the following is a component of the KLIC score for predicting DAIR failure in early postoperative PJI?
items.e: KLIC = Kidney failure, Liver cirrhosis, Index surgery (revision or fracture), Cemented prosthesis and CRP over 115 mg/L; male sex, COPD and age over 80 belong to CRIME80 for late acute PJI.

items.q: One-stage exchange with antibiotic-loaded cement for infected arthroplasty was popularised by Buchholz at:
items.e: Buchholz's ENDO-Klinik developed single-stage exchange using antibiotic-loaded cement, while two-stage exchange became the North American standard.

items.q: Which finding most favours two-stage over one-stage exchange for chronic PJI?
o: Methicillin-sensitive S. aureus identified on aspiration
No organism identified before surgery (culture-negative infection)
items.e: One-stage exchange is best suited to a known organism with known sensitivities, good soft tissues and a healthy host; unknown organisms favour a staged approach.

items.q: Which antibiotic combination is most commonly added to cement for a high-dose spacer in two-stage revision?
items.e: Vancomycin and aminoglycosides are heat-stable powders that elute well from PMMA and cover the common organisms; rifampicin interferes with cement polymerisation.

items.q: Before the second stage of a two-stage revision for PJI, which statement about confirming eradication of infection is correct?
o: No single test reliably confirms eradication; ESR/CRP trends and aspiration are interpreted together
A normal ESR alone confirms eradication
A negative aspirate after 2 days off antibiotics excludes persistent infection
Alpha-defensin is invariably negative once infection is cured
items.e: Inflammatory markers may remain raised and aspirates may be falsely negative with a spacer in situ, so the decision combines trends, aspiration and intraoperative findings.

items.q: A randomised trial by Frank et al. studied patients after re-implantation in two-stage exchange for PJI. It showed that:
o: Stopping all antibiotics at re-implantation reduced resistance without affecting failure
Lifelong rifampicin was needed to prevent recurrence
IV antibiotics were superior to oral antibiotics after re-implantation
A further 3 months of oral antibiotics reduced treatment failure
items.e: Extended oral antibiotic prophylaxis for 3 months after the second stage significantly reduced failure from infection.

items.q: The OVIVA trial (2019) on bone and joint infection, including PJI, showed that:
o: IV antibiotics halved the failure rate compared with oral therapy
Oral antibiotics were non-inferior to IV antibiotics during the first 6 weeks
12 weeks of antibiotics was superior to 6 weeks
Rifampicin monotherapy was effective with retained implants
items.e: OVIVA found oral therapy non-inferior to IV therapy with fewer line complications; the 12- vs 6-week comparison was the DATIPO trial.

items.q: The DATIPO trial (2021) on antibiotic duration for PJI found that:
o: 6 weeks was non-inferior to 12 weeks for all surgical strategies
2 weeks was sufficient after two-stage exchange
Oral therapy was inferior to IV therapy
12 weeks of antibiotics resulted in fewer persistent infections than 6 weeks
items.e: DATIPO failed to show non-inferiority of 6 weeks; 12 weeks gave lower rates of persistent infection after DAIR, one-stage or two-stage exchange.

items.q: A 66-year-old has recurrent knee PJI after two failed two-stage revisions, with extensor mechanism loss and large bone defects. He wishes to keep walking on his own leg. The most suitable salvage is:
o: Permanent resection arthroplasty of the knee
Knee arthrodesis (for example with an intramedullary nail)
Lifelong suppression with a loose infected implant
items.e: Arthrodesis provides a stable, infection-free limb when reconstruction is no longer feasible; resection arthroplasty of the knee gives poor function and amputation is reserved for uncontrolled sepsis.

items.q: Excision arthroplasty of the hip, removing the components and leaving a pseudarthrosis, is known as:
items.e: Girdlestone resection is a salvage option for uncontrolled hip PJI or unfit patients; function is limited but infection control is good.

items.q: Long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy for PJI is most appropriate for:
o: A fit 55-year-old with early postoperative infection
Any patient after successful two-stage revision
A patient with a sinus tract who is fit for exchange
A frail patient unfit for further surgery with a retained infected implant
items.e: Suppression controls symptoms without eradicating biofilm infection and is reserved for patients who cannot or will not undergo definitive surgery.

items.q: A healthy patient with a well-functioning THA is due for a dental extraction. Current AAOS/ADA guidance on antibiotic prophylaxis is:
o: Routine prophylaxis is not recommended; consider it only for selected immunocompromised patients
Amoxicillin before all dental procedures for life
Prophylaxis for the first 10 years after arthroplasty
IV vancomycin before any dental procedure
items.e: Evidence does not support routine dental prophylaxis in arthroplasty patients; good oral hygiene is emphasised.

items.q: A Candida periprosthetic knee infection is confirmed. The preferred surgical strategy is:
o: Two-stage exchange with an antifungal-loaded spacer and prolonged antifungal therapy
items.e: Fungal PJI has poor outcomes; staged exchange with amphotericin- or voriconazole-loaded cement and long systemic antifungals is recommended.

items.q: A patient on warfarin starts rifampicin for staphylococcal PJI with retained implants. The expected interaction is:
o: Rising INR and bleeding risk due to enzyme inhibition
Falling INR due to enzyme induction, needing a higher warfarin dose
items.e: Rifampicin is a potent cytochrome P450 inducer that accelerates warfarin metabolism, so the INR must be monitored closely.

items.q: A patient receiving prolonged linezolid for MRSA PJI should be monitored mainly for:
items.e: Linezolid courses longer than about 2 weeks cause dose-related myelosuppression (and neuropathy), so blood counts are checked weekly.

items.q: Ten days after THA, the wound continues to drain despite local care and compression. The best management is:
o: Early surgical debridement with modular component exchange and deep cultures
Superficial swab and dry dressing only
items.e: Persistent drainage beyond about 5-7 days should be treated surgically; empirical antibiotics without cultures mask infection and lower diagnostic yield.

items.q: In a painful metal-on-metal hip with adverse local tissue reaction, synovial cell counts for PJI should be performed:
o: After adding chlorhexidine to the sample
Manually, because metal debris falsely raises automated counts
items.e: Metal particles and debris are counted as cells by automated analysers, so a manual count is required in metallosis.

items.q: The 2021 European Bone and Joint Infection Society (EBJIS) definition classifies periprosthetic infection into:
o: Infection unlikely, infection likely and infection confirmed
Stages I to IV by anatomy and host
Early, delayed and late by timing
Types A, B and C by host status
items.e: EBJIS uses three tiers based on clinical, laboratory, histological and microbiological features, unlike the ICM point score.

items.q: A diabetologist screens a patient's feet with a biothesiometer. Above which vibration perception threshold is the patient considered to have significant neuropathy with a high ulcer risk?
items.e: A vibration perception threshold over 25 V on biothesiometry indicates loss of protective sensation and a markedly raised ulcer risk; lower values are within or near the normal range.

items.q: Vibration sense in routine diabetic foot screening is tested with a tuning fork of which frequency?
items.e: The 128 Hz tuning fork applied to the hallux interphalangeal joint is used for vibration sense; 256/512 Hz forks are used for hearing tests (Rinne/Weber).

items.q: Which foot finding in a long-standing diabetic is a direct manifestation of autonomic neuropathy?
o: Inability to feel a 10 g monofilament
Dry, cracked skin due to loss of sweating
items.e: Sudomotor (autonomic) neuropathy causes anhidrosis with dry, fissured skin that admits infection; clawing is motor, monofilament loss is sensory and absent pulses reflect arterial disease.

items.q: Diabetic motor neuropathy raises plantar forefoot pressure mainly through:
o: Tibialis posterior dysfunction causing a flat foot
Peroneus brevis weakness causing heel varus
Intrinsic muscle weakness causing claw toes and distal displacement of the plantar fat pad
Quadriceps weakness causing a crouch gait
items.e: Intrinsic minus clawing drives the metatarsal heads plantarward and pulls the protective fat pad distally, exposing the heads to high pressure and ulceration.

items.q: Peripheral arterial disease in diabetes most characteristically affects which arterial segment?
o: Infrarenal aorta and common iliac arteries
Digital arteries of the toes in isolation
items.e: Diabetic PAD is typically distal (crural/infrapopliteal), often with relative sparing of the pedal arteries, which allows distal bypass targets.

items.q: In the vascular assessment of a diabetic foot, a toe-brachial index below which value is considered abnormal?
items.e: A toe-brachial index under about 0.7 indicates arterial insufficiency; toe vessels are less affected by medial calcification, making the TBI more reliable than the ABI.

items.q: Which factor is the strongest single predictor of a new foot ulcer in a person with diabetes?
o: A previous foot ulcer or amputation
items.e: Prior ulceration or amputation carries the highest risk of (re)ulceration; this is why it places the patient in the highest IWGDF risk category.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of lower-limb amputations in people with diabetes are preceded by a foot ulcer?
items.e: Around 85% of diabetic amputations follow a foot ulcer, so ulcer prevention and early treatment are the key to amputation prevention.

items.q: The 5-year mortality after a major lower-limb amputation in a diabetic patient is approximately:
items.e: Five-year mortality after major diabetic amputation is about 50-70%, worse than many cancers, reflecting coexisting cardiovascular and renal disease.

items.q: The lifetime risk of developing a foot ulcer in a person with diabetes is approximately:
items.e: The lifetime risk of diabetic foot ulceration is quoted as about 15-25% (some recent estimates are higher), which justifies annual screening of all diabetics.

items.q: Limited joint mobility in diabetes, contributing to stiff joints and Achilles contracture with forefoot overload, is caused by:
o: Amyloid deposition in the joint capsule
items.e: Advanced glycation end-products cross-link collagen, stiffening skin, capsules and tendons; equinus then increases forefoot plantar pressure.

items.q: A diabetic has dry gangrene confined to the second and third toes with no gangrene of the rest of the foot. What is the Wagner grade?
items.e: Wagner grade 4 is localised (toe or forefoot) gangrene; grade 5 is gangrene of the whole foot; grade 3 is deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis.

items.q: A diabetic with loss of protective sensation has a healed ulcer scar and a prominent bunion, but the skin is intact. What is the Wagner grade?
items.e: Wagner grade 0 is the at-risk foot with intact skin (pre-ulcerative lesion, deformity or healed ulcer); grade 1 is a superficial ulcer.

items.q: The main criticism of the Wagner classification of diabetic foot ulcers is that it:
o: Does not grade ischaemia and infection separately from depth
items.e: Wagner is a depth-and-gangrene scale; infection and ischaemia are not independently scored, which led to the University of Texas, SINBAD and WIfI systems.

items.q: A University of Texas grade 3, stage D diabetic foot ulcer is one that:
o: Reaches tendon or capsule and is infected but not ischaemic
Penetrates to bone or joint and is both infected and ischaemic
Is superficial and ischaemic but not infected
Penetrates to bone but is clean and well perfused
items.e: UT grade (0-3) is depth, with 3 reaching bone/joint; stage A clean, B infected, C ischaemic, D infected and ischaemic.

items.q: In the University of Texas diabetic ulcer classification, which component better predicts the risk of amputation?
o: The stage (presence of infection and/or ischaemia)
The ulcer site on the foot
The ulcer area in square centimetres
items.e: In Armstrong and Lavery's validation, amputation risk rose more with stage (infection and ischaemia, worst in D) than with increasing depth grade.

items.q: The SINBAD system, recommended by the IWGDF for communication between health professionals, scores site, ischaemia, neuropathy, bacterial infection, area and:
items.e: SINBAD = Site, Ischaemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial infection, Area and Depth; each scores 0 or 1, giving a total of 0-6.

items.q: The Society for Vascular Surgery WIfI classification of the threatened limb grades:
o: Weight-bearing, inflammation, fragmentation and instability in Charcot foot
Wound, ischaemia and foot infection, to estimate amputation risk and benefit of revascularisation
Wagner grade, infection and functional impairment after amputation
Wound width, induration and fluctuance to decide on abscess drainage
items.e: WIfI scores Wound, Ischaemia and foot Infection (each 0-3) and stratifies 1-year amputation risk and the likely benefit of revascularisation.

items.q: A diabetic has an infected plantar ulcer with cellulitis, temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 115/min and white cell count 17,000/µL. Under the IWGDF/IDSA scheme, the infection is:
items.e: Any local infection with signs of systemic inflammatory response (two or more SIRS criteria) is classified as severe (PEDIS grade 4), mandating admission and IV antibiotics.

items.q: The probe-to-bone test has its highest positive predictive value for diabetic foot osteomyelitis when:
o: Used in a high-prevalence setting such as inpatients with infected ulcers
Applied to superficial ulcers under 1 cm²
Combined with a superficial swab culture
items.e: Predictive values depend on prevalence: a positive probe-to-bone test is highly predictive where osteomyelitis is common, whereas a negative test is most useful (high NPV) in low-prevalence settings.

items.q: How long after the onset of diabetic foot osteomyelitis do changes typically become visible on plain radiographs?
items.e: Radiographic signs (periosteal reaction, cortical erosion, osteolysis) lag by about 10-14 days and need 30-50% bone loss, so early radiographs may be normal.

items.q: On MRI of a diabetic forefoot, which finding is most specific for osteomyelitis?
o: Confluent low T1 signal replacing the normal marrow fat
items.e: High STIR/T2 signal is sensitive but nonspecific (reactive oedema); confluent marrow replacement on T1 is the most specific sign of osteomyelitis.

items.q: A diabetic with a cardiac pacemaker needs imaging for suspected forefoot osteomyelitis. Which nuclear study is most specific for infection?
items.e: Labelled white cell scanning (with marrow imaging, or FDG-PET/CT) is used when MRI is contraindicated; a three-phase bone scan is sensitive but positive in Charcot, fracture and after surgery.

items.q: In a diabetic with a forefoot ulcer, which ESR value most strongly suggests underlying osteomyelitis?
items.e: An ESR over 70 mm/h raises the likelihood of osteomyelitis in a diabetic foot ulcer; lower elevations are nonspecific.

items.q: Which specimen best guides antibiotic choice in an infected diabetic foot ulcer?
o: Deep tissue obtained by curettage or biopsy after cleansing and debridement
Superficial swab of undebrided wound exudate
Swab of the surrounding intact skin
Culture of the removed wound dressing
items.e: Superficial swabs grow colonisers and contaminants; deep tissue (or bone) specimens after debridement identify the true pathogens.

items.q: A diabetic with a first, acute, mild infection of a neuropathic ulcer and no prior antibiotics most likely has which pathogens?
o: Aerobic gram-positive cocci such as Staphylococcus aureus and beta-haemolytic streptococci
items.e: Acute mild infections in antibiotic-naive patients are usually gram-positive cocci; polymicrobial gram-negative and anaerobic infections occur in chronic, previously treated or necrotic wounds.

items.q: A chronic diabetic foot wound that is macerated from soaking is particularly likely to be infected with:
items.e: Moist, macerated wounds favour Pseudomonas, so empirical regimens for such wounds should cover it.

items.q: Which measure has most consistently reduced major amputation rates in diabetic foot disease, by roughly half or more?
items.e: Organised multidisciplinary foot care (diabetologist, surgeons, podiatrist, orthotist, nurse) reduces major amputations by about 40-80%; the other measures are adjuncts at best.

items.q: When a total contact cast is used to heal a neuropathic plantar ulcer, it is usually changed:
o: Weekly, to inspect the ulcer and refit as swelling falls
Only when the ulcer has healed
items.e: The cast is changed about every week: oedema reduces quickly and loosening causes shear; healing rates of about 80-90% in 6-8 weeks are reported.

items.q: An 'instant total contact cast' for a neuropathic forefoot ulcer is produced by:
o: Adding a felted foam pad to normal footwear
Wrapping a removable knee-high walker in cast material so it cannot be removed
Moulding a custom insole into an extra-depth shoe
items.e: Rendering a knee-high walker non-removable gives healing comparable to a TCC, because adherence is enforced; removable walkers fail mainly through poor compliance.

items.q: The main rationale for regular sharp debridement of a chronic neuropathic plantar ulcer is that it:
o: Removes callus and necrotic tissue, converting a chronic wound into an acute healing wound
Improves arterial inflow to the foot
items.e: Sharp debridement lowers local pressure from callus, removes biofilm and senescent tissue and stimulates healing; it does not substitute for offloading or revascularisation.

items.q: Becaplermin gel, used as an adjunct for neuropathic diabetic ulcers, is a recombinant form of:
items.e: Becaplermin is recombinant human PDGF-BB, approved for neuropathic lower-extremity diabetic ulcers with adequate blood supply.

items.q: A diabetic has a mild soft-tissue infection of a forefoot ulcer without bone involvement. The usual antibiotic course is:
o: Oral agents covering gram-positive cocci for 1-2 weeks
items.e: Mild diabetic foot infections are treated with oral antibiotics active against staphylococci and streptococci for about 1-2 weeks; longer courses are for osteomyelitis.

items.q: When diabetic forefoot osteomyelitis is treated with antibiotics alone without bone resection, the recommended duration is about:
items.e: IWGDF/IDSA guidance recommends about 6 weeks of antibiotics for non-surgically treated osteomyelitis; much shorter courses suffice after complete resection of infected bone.

items.q: A diabetic has a swollen, tense forefoot with fluctuance, crepitus and gas in the plantar soft tissues on radiographs. The most appropriate management is:
o: Oral antibiotics and review in one week
Application of a total contact cast
Elective angiography and surgery in two weeks
Urgent surgical drainage and debridement with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
items.e: Gas, abscess or necrotising infection is a limb-threatening 'diabetic foot attack' requiring emergency decompression and debridement; revascularisation is planned after source control.

items.q: A neuropathic diabetic has a recurrent ulcer at the tip of a flexible claw second toe. Which procedure best addresses it?
items.e: Apical (tip) ulcers of flexible claw/mallet toes heal and seldom recur after percutaneous flexor tenotomy, a simple office procedure.

items.q: After amputation of the hallux in a diabetic, which problem is most likely to follow?
o: Hallux valgus of the adjacent toe
Transfer ulceration under the lesser metatarsal heads
items.e: Loss of the hallux shifts push-off load to the lesser metatarsal heads, producing transfer ulcers and further amputations.

items.q: Isolated amputation of the second toe in a diabetic commonly leads to:
items.e: The second toe buttresses the hallux; its removal allows the hallux to drift into valgus (a second ray amputation or spacer may be considered).

items.q: Which single ray amputation in a diabetic foot gives the poorest function and highest risk of further breakdown?
items.e: Lateral single ray resections are well tolerated, whereas first ray amputation removes a key weight-bearing and push-off column and often fails.

items.q: The commonest complication after a Syme ankle disarticulation is:
o: Posterior or medial migration of the heel pad
items.e: Heel pad instability and migration is the commonest problem; the pad is anchored to the distal tibia (e.g. via drill holes or Achilles tenodesis) to prevent it.

items.q: A Syme amputation in a diabetic requires a patent:
items.e: The heel pad flap depends on the medial calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery, so its patency is a prerequisite for healing.

items.q: Preserving the knee by performing a transtibial rather than transfemoral amputation is important mainly because the increase in energy cost of walking is approximately:
o: Equal after both levels at about 50%
10-40% after transtibial versus 60-100% after transfemoral amputation
100% after transtibial versus 20% after transfemoral amputation
items.e: Metabolic cost rises far more after above-knee amputation, which many elderly vasculopaths cannot meet; a transtibial level greatly improves the chance of walking.

items.q: The Burgess technique for transtibial amputation in a vascular patient uses:
o: Equal anterior and posterior fish-mouth flaps
A circular guillotine cut closed by secondary intention
items.e: The posterior calf muscles and skin are better perfused than anterior skin, so a long posterior myocutaneous flap is brought forward over the tibial end.

items.q: For an elective transtibial amputation, the ideal tibial length is approximately:
o: 12-15 cm below the knee joint line
At the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the tibia
items.e: About 12-15 cm (roughly 2.5 cm per 30 cm of body height) balances lever arm with a soft-tissue envelope; distal-third stumps have poor coverage.

items.q: Which nutritional and immune parameters are classically required for amputation wound healing in a diabetic?
o: Serum albumin over 1.5 g/dL and lymphocyte count over 500/µL
Serum albumin over 3.0 g/dL and total lymphocyte count over 1,500/µL
Haemoglobin over 14 g/dL and platelets over 400,000/µL
HbA1c below 5% and ESR below 10 mm/h
items.e: Albumin over 3.0 g/dL and total lymphocyte count over 1,500/µL (with adequate perfusion) predict healing of foot and amputation wounds.

items.q: A diabetic at high risk measures foot skin temperatures at home. A difference between the two feet above which value should prompt reduced activity and review?
items.e: A sustained side-to-side difference over 2.2 C (4 F) predicts impending ulceration or Charcot activity; temperature-guided offloading reduces ulcer recurrence.

items.q: A diabetic with loss of protective sensation who has had a previous toe amputation falls into which IWGDF risk category?
items.e: IWGDF category 3 (highest) is LOPS or PAD plus a history of ulcer, any amputation or end-stage renal disease; category 2 is LOPS plus PAD or deformity.

items.q: A diabetic in the highest IWGDF risk category (previous ulcer) should be reviewed by a foot-care professional at intervals of:
items.e: IWGDF recommends screening every 1-3 months for category 3, 3-6 months for category 2, 6-12 months for category 1 and annually for category 0.

items.q: A neuropathic diabetic with good perfusion has recurrent plantar ulcers beneath several metatarsal heads despite custom footwear. Which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: Resection of all lesser (with or without first) metatarsal heads decompresses multiple forefoot plantar ulcers while preserving a functional foot.

items.q: A bedbound, non-ambulatory diabetic with a fixed 60-degree knee flexion contracture needs a major amputation for an unsalvageable foot. The preferred level is:
items.e: In non-walkers with a fixed knee contracture, a below-knee stump would ulcerate against the bed; a through-knee/above-knee level heals better and aids sitting and transfers.

items.q: Which lateral ankle ligament is a thickening of the joint capsule and therefore intracapsular?
items.e: The ATFL is a capsular thickening (intracapsular), whereas the CFL is extracapsular and lies deep to the peroneal tendons.

items.q: The anterior talofibular ligament becomes the primary restraint to inversion when the ankle is in:
items.e: The ATFL is taut in plantarflexion, the position in which most inversion sprains occur; the CFL takes over in neutral and dorsiflexion.

items.q: Which ligament crosses both the tibiotalar and the subtalar joints?
items.e: The CFL runs from the fibular tip to the lateral calcaneus, spanning both joints; the interosseous ligament crosses only the subtalar joint.

items.q: The strongest lateral ankle ligament, which is torn only in frank ankle dislocation, is the:
items.e: The PTFL is the strongest lateral ligament and is rarely injured except in dislocations; the ATFL is the weakest.

items.q: Under the Ottawa foot rules, a foot radiograph is indicated when there is midfoot pain and bone tenderness at the:
o: Cuboid or anterior process of the calcaneus
Navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal
Medial cuneiform or second metatarsal base
items.e: The Ottawa foot rules use navicular or fifth metatarsal base tenderness, or inability to bear weight for four steps.

items.q: In the Ottawa ankle rules, 'inability to bear weight' means the patient cannot take:
o: Four steps both immediately after injury and in the emergency department
Two steps at any time since injury
Ten steps without a limp in the emergency department
items.e: The rules require inability to take four steps (limping allowed) both immediately and at assessment.

items.q: The main reason the Ottawa ankle rules are used in emergency departments is that they:
o: Have specificity above 95%, so a positive rule confirms a fracture
Allow grading of lateral ligament injuries
Have sensitivity close to 100% for significant fractures and reduce radiographs by about 30-40%
items.e: The rules are highly sensitive (safe to rule out fracture) but have low specificity, so a positive rule does not mean a fracture.

items.q: Physical examination for an acute lateral ankle ligament rupture (anterior drawer, tenderness, haematoma) is most accurate when performed:
items.e: Delayed examination at 4-5 days, once pain and swelling settle, gives high sensitivity and specificity (van Dijk).

items.q: In the CAST trial (Lamb et al., Lancet 2009) of severe ankle sprains, which intervention gave faster early recovery than a tubular compression bandage?
o: Primary surgical repair of the ATFL
items.e: A 10-day below-knee cast gave the quickest recovery at 3 months; the Bledsoe boot gave no benefit over the bandage.

items.q: A 24-year-old has recurrent giving way of the ankle on uneven ground, but the anterior drawer and talar tilt are normal and symmetrical. This is best described as:
o: Functional instability due to proprioceptive and peroneal deficits
Mechanical instability due to ATFL and CFL laxity
items.e: Subjective giving way without pathological laxity is functional instability, treated with proprioceptive and peroneal rehabilitation.

items.q: On a varus (talar tilt) stress radiograph, which value suggests lateral ligament insufficiency?
o: Talar tilt over 10°, or over 5° more than the opposite side
items.e: Talar tilt above about 10° absolute or 5° side-to-side difference indicates combined ATFL and CFL insufficiency.

items.q: An anterior drawer stress radiograph is abnormal when the anterior talar translation exceeds the uninjured side by more than about:
items.e: A side-to-side difference over about 3 mm (or over 10 mm absolute) indicates ATFL insufficiency.

items.q: The expected rate of good to excellent results after a modified Broström-Gould repair for chronic lateral ankle instability is about:
items.e: The modified Broström-Gould repair is the gold standard, with good or excellent results in about 85-95%.

items.q: Suture-tape (internal brace) augmentation of a Broström repair is most appropriate in:
o: Poor-quality ligament remnants, generalised laxity or high-demand athletes
items.e: Augmentation adds strength when the native tissue is poor or the demands are high.

items.q: Which non-anatomic lateral ankle stabilisation uses a split peroneus brevis routed through tunnels in the fibula and calcaneus to substitute for both the ATFL and the CFL?
items.e: Chrisman-Snook uses half the peroneus brevis through the fibula to the calcaneus; Evans tenodeses the whole tendon to the fibula alone.

items.q: The first syndesmotic ligament to fail in an external-rotation high ankle sprain is the:
items.e: External rotation of the talus first tears the AITFL, then the interosseous membrane/ligament and finally the posterior structures.
