items.q: Serial radiographs of a patient with lateral foot pain show that the os peroneum has migrated proximally compared with an earlier film. This indicates:
o: Avulsion of the fifth metatarsal base
Rupture of the peroneus brevis tendon
Rupture of the peroneus longus tendon
items.e: The os peroneum lies within peroneus longus at the cuboid; proximal migration means the tendon distal to it has ruptured.

items.q: The os peroneum is a sesamoid lying within the:
o: Peroneus longus tendon, near the cuboid
Peroneus brevis tendon, near the fifth metatarsal
Tibialis posterior tendon, near the navicular
Flexor hallucis longus tendon, near the talus
items.e: The os peroneum is present (ossified) in about 20% and lies in peroneus longus where it turns around the cuboid.

items.q: A 132-kg man is scheduled for primary total knee arthroplasty with no antibiotic allergy. What is the appropriate prophylactic dose of cefazolin?
o: 30 mg/kg IV to a maximum of 2 g
items.e: Cefazolin prophylaxis is 2 g IV, increased to 3 g in patients weighing 120 kg or more. 1 g is underdosing for any adult arthroplasty patient.

items.q: During a long revision hip arthroplasty with modest blood loss, a single dose of cefazolin was given 20 minutes before incision. When should the next intraoperative dose be given?
o: Only if the operation exceeds 8 hours
At wound closure, regardless of duration
After 2 hours, because cefazolin is cleared within one half-life
items.e: Cefazolin is redosed every 4 hours (about two half-lives) of surgery, or earlier if blood loss exceeds 1500 mL. Redosing at closure regardless of duration is not standard.

items.q: After an uncomplicated primary total hip arthroplasty, current guidance (e.g. CDC 2017, AAOS) limits prophylactic antibiotics to:
o: No more than 24 hours after surgery
Until the wound is dry, usually 3-5 days
items.e: Prophylaxis in clean orthopaedic surgery should not extend beyond 24 hours, and CDC 2017 advises no extra doses after closure. Continuing until drain removal adds resistance and C. difficile risk without benefit.

items.q: According to BOAST 4, prophylactic antibiotics for an open tibial fracture should be continued until:
o: 7 days after injury in all cases
Definitive skin closure, however long that takes
72 hours after injury or 24 hours after definitive wound closure, whichever is sooner
items.e: BOAST 4 recommends antibiotics within 1 hour of injury, continued until 72 hours after injury or 24 hours after definitive closure, whichever is sooner. Open-ended courses until closure are not recommended.

items.q: A farmer has a Gustilo IIIA open tibial fracture heavily contaminated with soil and manure. In the classic US regimen, which agent is added to the cephalosporin and aminoglycoside specifically for this contamination?
items.e: Farmyard or faecal contamination raises the risk of Clostridium infection, so penicillin is added to cephalosporin plus aminoglycoside cover. Vancomycin targets MRSA, not the anaerobic clostridial risk.

items.q: Methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus is mediated by:
o: A plasmid-encoded beta-lactamase that hydrolyses cefazolin
An altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) encoded by mecA
Altered D-Ala-D-Lac cell-wall precursors encoded by vanA
An efflux pump that expels beta-lactams
items.e: mecA encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for beta-lactams, so cell-wall synthesis continues despite methicillin or cefazolin. D-Ala-D-Lac alteration (vanA) is the mechanism of vancomycin resistance in enterococci.

items.q: Rifampicin is added to treatment of early staphylococcal periprosthetic infection managed by DAIR, but must never be given alone. Why?
o: It is only bacteriostatic against staphylococci
It antagonises beta-lactams when used alone
Resistance emerges rapidly through single-step mutation of RNA polymerase
items.e: Rifampicin is valued for activity against biofilm-associated staphylococci, but single-point mutations in RNA polymerase cause rapid resistance, so it is always combined with another active agent. It penetrates bone well.

items.q: A patient stable on warfarin is started on rifampicin plus a quinolone for a staphylococcal implant infection. What is the expected effect on anticoagulation?
o: INR rises sharply because rifampicin displaces warfarin from albumin
No change, as rifampicin is renally excreted
INR rises because of reduced vitamin K absorption
INR falls because rifampicin induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
items.e: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer that accelerates warfarin metabolism, lowering the INR and requiring close monitoring and dose increases. It also reduces the efficacy of oral contraceptives.

items.q: A patient on oral linezolid for MRSA osteomyelitis for 4 weeks develops fatigue and bruising. Which adverse effect is most likely?
items.e: Linezolid causes duration-dependent myelosuppression, typically after more than 2 weeks, so weekly blood counts are needed. Raised CK and myopathy are characteristic of daptomycin.

items.q: Which monitoring test is specifically recommended during daptomycin therapy for MRSA bone infection?
items.e: Daptomycin, which depolarises the bacterial cell membrane, can cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, so CK is checked weekly. Trough levels and audiometry relate to vancomycin and aminoglycosides.

items.q: A 72-year-old on oral prednisolone is treated with levofloxacin for a urinary infection. Which musculoskeletal complication is he at particular risk of?
items.e: Fluoroquinolones cause tendinopathy and Achilles rupture; risk is highest over age 60 and with concurrent corticosteroids. Rhabdomyolysis is more typical of statins and daptomycin.

items.q: Flushing, pruritus and hypotension develop during rapid intravenous infusion of vancomycin before arthroplasty. What is the mechanism and remedy?
o: IgE-mediated anaphylaxis; vancomycin is permanently contraindicated
Complement activation by impurities; switch to a different brand
Acute nephrotoxicity; give fluids and stop vancomycin
Direct (non-IgE) mast-cell histamine release; slow the infusion and give an antihistamine
items.e: Vancomycin flushing ('red man') syndrome is a rate-related, non-immunological histamine release; infusing over 1-2 hours and antihistamines prevent it. It is not true allergy, so vancomycin can still be used.

items.q: Which property is required for an antibiotic to be mixed into PMMA bone cement?
o: Heat stability, supplied as a powder
Lipid solubility, supplied as a liquid
items.e: The antibiotic must withstand the exothermic polymerisation and be in powder form, as with gentamicin, tobramycin and vancomycin. Liquid antibiotics weaken the cement.

items.q: For a patient with a remote history of a non-urticarial maculopapular rash to amoxicillin, the recommended prophylactic antibiotic for hip arthroplasty is:
items.e: Cefazolin can be used unless there is a history of severe immediate IgE-mediated reaction; cross-reactivity is only about 1-2%. Clindamycin or vancomycin is reserved for anaphylaxis-type allergy and is less effective against MSSA.

items.q: A known MRSA carrier is listed for total knee arthroplasty. Why is vancomycin usually given together with cefazolin rather than instead of it?
o: Vancomycin inactivates cefazolin unless both are given
Vancomycin is less effective than cefazolin against methicillin-sensitive S. aureus
items.e: Vancomycin is inferior to beta-lactams against MSSA and lacks gram-negative cover, so it is added for MRSA rather than replacing cefazolin. Neither drug inactivates the other.

items.q: Which preoperative regimen is recommended to decolonise a nasal Staphylococcus aureus carrier before elective arthroplasty?
o: Single intranasal povidone-iodine dose 24 h before surgery only
Nasal mupirocin 2% twice daily for 5 days with chlorhexidine body washes
items.e: Standard decolonisation is nasal mupirocin 2% twice daily for 5 days plus chlorhexidine washes. Systemic antibiotics are not used for carriage.

items.q: For hair removal before an orthopaedic incision, best practice is:
items.e: Clipping just before surgery is preferred because razor shaving creates microabrasions that colonise and increase surgical site infection. Shaving the night before is the worst option.

items.q: The PREPARE trial (NEJM 2024) in operatively treated extremity fractures found that, compared with chlorhexidine in alcohol, iodine povacrylex in alcohol:
o: Had more infections in both closed and open fractures
Had fewer surgical site infections in closed fractures, with no difference in open fractures
Had fewer infections only in open fractures
Caused more skin reactions without affecting infection
items.e: PREPARE showed iodine povacrylex in alcohol reduced SSI in closed fractures while open fractures showed no difference. Aqueous-PREP separately found no difference between aqueous preparations in open fractures.

items.q: Seven days after starting enoxaparin for a pelvic fracture, a patient's platelets fall from 280 to 90 x10^9/L and a new DVT appears. Which step is correct?
o: Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
Stop enoxaparin and start warfarin immediately
items.e: This is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; all heparins (including other LMWHs) are stopped and a non-heparin agent (argatroban, fondaparinux or a DOAC) started. Warfarin started early can cause venous limb gangrene and platelet transfusion is avoided.

items.q: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type II is caused by:
o: Direct non-immune platelet aggregation by heparin
IgG antibodies against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex
items.e: HIT type II is immune: IgG binds heparin-PF4 complexes and activates platelets, causing thrombocytopenia with paradoxical thrombosis 5-10 days after exposure. Direct non-immune aggregation describes the benign type I.

items.q: Warfarin skin necrosis and the early procoagulant state at the start of warfarin therapy are explained by:
o: Rapid fall in protein C, which has a short half-life
items.e: Protein C has a short half-life and falls before factors II, IX and X, causing transient hypercoagulability; this is why high-risk patients are bridged with heparin. Prothrombin has the longest half-life and falls last.

items.q: A patient on dabigatran has a displaced hip fracture and needs urgent surgery with normal renal function. Which agent specifically reverses dabigatran?
items.e: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor; dabigatran is also dialysable. Andexanet alfa reverses the anti-Xa agents.

items.q: A patient on apixaban has life-threatening bleeding from a pelvic fracture. Which agent is a specific reversal agent for apixaban?
items.e: Andexanet alfa is a recombinant decoy factor Xa that binds rivaroxaban and apixaban; prothrombin complex concentrate is an alternative. Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran.

items.q: Protamine sulphate reverses the anticoagulant effect of enoxaparin:
o: Completely, as it does for unfractionated heparin
Only after vitamin K is given
Partially, neutralising about 60% of anti-Xa activity
items.e: Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin but neutralises only about 60% of LMWH anti-Xa activity. It has no effect on fondaparinux.

items.q: A patient with creatinine clearance of 22 mL/min needs VTE prophylaxis after hip fracture fixation. Which drug is safest without renal dose concerns?
items.e: Unfractionated heparin is not renally cleared and has a short half-life, so it suits severe renal impairment. Enoxaparin needs dose reduction below 30 mL/min, and fondaparinux and dabigatran accumulate.

items.q: Under ASRA guidance, how long after the last prophylactic dose of LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg once daily) can a spinal anaesthetic be performed?
items.e: ASRA recommends at least 12 hours after prophylactic LMWH and 24 hours after therapeutic-dose LMWH before neuraxial puncture or catheter removal.

items.q: After removal of an epidural catheter following TKA, how soon may the next prophylactic LMWH dose be given according to ASRA (2018)?
items.e: ASRA advises the next LMWH dose at least 4 hours after catheter removal, and the first postoperative dose at least 12 hours after needle placement.

items.q: A patient taking clopidogrel and aspirin for peripheral vascular disease (no coronary stent) is planned for spinal anaesthesia. Per ASRA, what is required?
o: Stop aspirin 7 days before; continue clopidogrel
No change; neither affects neuraxial anaesthesia
Stop clopidogrel 5-7 days before; aspirin alone need not be stopped
items.e: Clopidogrel should be stopped 5-7 days before neuraxial block, whereas aspirin alone is not a contraindication. In patients with recent coronary stents, stopping antiplatelets needs cardiology input.

items.q: According to ASRA, rivaroxaban should be stopped how long before planned neuraxial anaesthesia?
items.e: ASRA recommends stopping rivaroxaban and apixaban about 72 hours before neuraxial block. Shorter intervals of 24-48 hours are used for general anaesthesia without neuraxial techniques.

items.q: Under NICE NG89, a recommended pharmacological VTE prophylaxis option after elective total knee replacement is:
o: LMWH for 10 days then aspirin for 28 days
No pharmacological prophylaxis if mobilised on day 1
items.e: NICE NG89 lists aspirin for 14 days, LMWH for 14 days with stockings, or rivaroxaban after knee replacement. LMWH for 10 days followed by aspirin for 28 days is the hip replacement option.

items.q: After surgery for a hip fracture, NICE NG89 recommends pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH or fondaparinux for:
items.e: For fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur, NICE advises LMWH (from 6-12 h after surgery) or fondaparinux (from 6 h) for 1 month.

items.q: The 2011 AAOS guideline on VTE prevention after hip and knee arthroplasty recommends against:
items.e: AAOS recommends against routine postoperative duplex screening and does not mandate a particular agent. Aspirin was an acceptable option.

items.q: An inferior vena cava filter is most clearly indicated in an orthopaedic trauma patient who:
o: Has an acute proximal DVT and a contraindication to anticoagulation
Has a pelvic fracture, as routine prophylaxis
Is over 75 years old with a hip fracture
Had a previous DVT 10 years ago
items.e: Filters are reserved for established VTE when anticoagulation is contraindicated or has failed. AAOS does not support routine prophylactic filters.

items.q: In EPCAT II (NEJM 2018), all patients received rivaroxaban until postoperative day 5 after THA or TKA and were then randomised. What did the trial show?
o: Rivaroxaban was superior to aspirin for symptomatic VTE
Extended aspirin was non-inferior to continued rivaroxaban
Aspirin caused significantly more major bleeding
Stopping all prophylaxis at day 5 was safe
items.e: EPCAT II found that switching to aspirin 81 mg after 5 days of rivaroxaban was non-inferior to continuing rivaroxaban for preventing symptomatic VTE, with similar bleeding.

items.q: The Pulmonary Embolism Prevention (PEP) trial (Lancet 2000) in hip fracture patients showed that aspirin 160 mg daily for 35 days:
o: Had no effect on venous thromboembolism
Significantly reduced pulmonary embolism and symptomatic DVT compared with placebo
items.e: In over 13,000 hip fracture patients, aspirin reduced PE by about 43% and symptomatic DVT by about 29% compared with placebo, with a small excess of bleeding. It did not compare aspirin with LMWH.

items.q: A patient had a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 3 months ago and requests elective total hip arthroplasty. The best advice is:
o: Proceed after stopping aspirin and clopidogrel for 7 days
Proceed after 30 days from stent insertion
Defer surgery until at least 6 months, ideally 12 months, after stenting
items.e: Elective surgery should be deferred at least 6 (ideally 12) months after a drug-eluting stent, and 30 days after a bare-metal stent, because stopping dual antiplatelet therapy risks stent thrombosis.

items.q: Which connective tissue layer of a peripheral nerve forms the blood-nerve barrier and provides most of its tensile strength?
items.e: The perineurium surrounds each fascicle, maintains the blood-nerve barrier and gives most of the nerve's tensile strength; the endoneurium surrounds individual axons.

items.q: A Sunderland grade II nerve injury differs from grade III in that in grade II:
o: The endoneurial tubes are intact, so complete recovery is expected
items.e: In grade II the axon is disrupted but the endoneurium is intact, so regenerating axons are guided back to their original targets with full recovery; grade III disrupts the endoneurium, giving incomplete recovery.

items.q: In Sunderland's classification of nerve injury, a grade III injury involves disruption of the axon and:
o: Myelin only, with an intact axon
items.e: Grade III disrupts the axon and endoneurium within intact fascicles, causing axonal mismatching and intrafascicular scarring with variable, incomplete recovery.

items.q: Mackinnon added a sixth grade to Sunderland's classification to describe:
o: Root avulsion from the spinal cord
A mixed injury with different grades in different fascicles of the same nerve
items.e: Grade VI describes a mixed injury in which fascicles are injured to different degrees, common in neuromas-in-continuity, requiring selective intraoperative assessment.

items.q: After axonal injury, the longitudinal columns of Schwann cells that guide regenerating axons in the distal stump are called:
items.e: During Wallerian degeneration Schwann cells proliferate and align within the endoneurial tubes as bands of Büngner, providing a scaffold and trophic support for regrowth.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an axonotmetic median nerve injury at the elbow. Recovery of sensation at the fingertips (about 30 cm away) can be expected after approximately:
items.e: Axons regenerate at about 1 mm per day (about an inch a month) after a latent period, so about 300 mm takes roughly 10-12 months.

items.q: Motor recovery after a proximal nerve injury is limited mainly because the motor end plates become irreversibly degenerated after about:
items.e: Motor end plates degenerate irreversibly after about 12-18 months, so axons must reach the muscle before then; this underpins the use of distal nerve transfers for proximal injuries.

items.q: Which factor is associated with a BETTER prognosis after peripheral nerve repair?
o: Distal injury close to the target muscle
items.e: Young age, distal level, sharp clean injury, pure motor or sensory nerves, early repair and short gaps predict better outcomes; the other options worsen prognosis.

items.q: After a nerve injury, electromyography is usually delayed until about 3 weeks because:
o: Nerve regeneration starts only at 3 weeks
Muscle oedema prevents needle insertion before then
Conduction block cannot be detected before 3 months
Wallerian degeneration must occur before denervation potentials appear
items.e: Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves appear only after the distal axon has degenerated, roughly 2-3 weeks after injury, so earlier studies can be falsely reassuring.

items.q: On needle EMG after a nerve injury, fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves at rest indicate:
items.e: Spontaneous fibrillations and positive sharp waves signify denervated muscle fibres; reinnervation shows as nascent, polyphasic motor unit potentials.

items.q: In a recovering peripheral nerve injury, which EMG finding typically precedes visible clinical motor recovery?
o: Giant motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment years later
items.e: Small, polyphasic 'nascent' motor units signal early reinnervation and appear weeks before the patient can visibly contract the muscle.

items.q: After a traction brachial plexus injury, the hand is anaesthetic in the C8-T1 distribution but sensory nerve action potentials from the ulnar nerve are preserved. This indicates:
o: Neurapraxia of the ulnar nerve at the elbow
A lesion distal to the dorsal root ganglion
items.e: The sensory cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion remain connected to the distal axon in a preganglionic lesion, so SNAPs are preserved despite anaesthetic skin; postganglionic lesions abolish the SNAP.

items.q: For a sharp laceration of the ulnar nerve at the wrist, group fascicular repair is particularly appropriate because:
o: The motor and sensory fascicle groups are topographically distinct there
Epineurial repair is contraindicated at the wrist
The ulnar nerve has no epineurium at this level
items.e: At the wrist the deep motor branch fascicles are well defined from sensory fascicles, so aligning groups improves motor outcome; epineurial repair is used where fascicles are not distinct.

items.q: A hollow nerve conduit is generally appropriate for bridging which nerve gap?
o: A 6 cm gap in the median nerve at the forearm
A 10 cm gap in the sciatic nerve
Any motor nerve gap regardless of length
A gap under about 3 cm in a small-calibre sensory (digital) nerve
items.e: Conduits work for short gaps (under about 3 cm) in small sensory nerves; longer or larger mixed-nerve gaps need autograft, classically the sural nerve.

items.q: The gold-standard graft for bridging a large peripheral nerve gap is:
items.e: Autologous sural nerve graft remains the gold standard for large gaps; allografts and conduits are used for shorter, mainly sensory, defects.

items.q: Nerve repair under tension is avoided mainly because elongation of a nerve beyond about 10 percent:
items.e: Stretching a nerve beyond about 8-10 percent significantly reduces intraneural perfusion, impairing regeneration; gaps should be bridged rather than closed under tension.

items.q: In a high ulnar nerve injury, transfer of the terminal anterior interosseous nerve (pronator quadratus branch) is performed in a supercharge end-to-side fashion to the:
o: Dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve
Deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve
items.e: The AIN-to-deep-motor-ulnar transfer delivers motor axons close to the intrinsic muscles, shortening reinnervation time in high ulnar injuries.

items.q: To restore shoulder abduction in an upper brachial plexus injury, a branch of the radial nerve to the triceps is commonly transferred to the:
items.e: The triceps branch (often to the long head) is transferred to the axillary nerve through a posterior approach; the spinal accessory nerve is the usual donor for the suprascapular nerve.

items.q: A closed humeral shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy is usually observed. Which feature is an indication for early exploration of the nerve?
o: Wrist drop with sparing of triceps
Paraesthesia over the first web space
A spiral fracture of the middle third
An open fracture with a penetrating wound
items.e: Most closed injuries are neurapraxia or axonotmesis and recover; open fractures and penetrating injuries carry a high risk of laceration and warrant exploration at debridement.

items.q: The transverse carpal ligament attaches radially to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium, and ulnarly to the:
o: Base of the fifth metacarpal and capitate
items.e: The flexor retinaculum spans from the scaphoid tubercle and trapezial ridge to the pisiform and hook of hamate, forming the roof of the carpal tunnel.

items.q: How many tendons pass through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve?
items.e: The tunnel contains four FDS, four FDP and FPL tendons (nine) plus the median nerve; FCR runs in its own separate sheath in the trapezial groove.

items.q: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in an older man, preceding heart failure with a thickened ventricular wall, should raise suspicion of:
items.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome, often bilateral, frequently precedes cardiac transthyretin amyloidosis by years; amyloid can be identified in tenosynovial biopsy at release.

items.q: Which clinical provocative test is generally regarded as the most sensitive for carpal tunnel syndrome?
items.e: Direct compression over the carpal tunnel (Durkan) has the highest sensitivity among bedside tests; two-point discrimination changes only late in the disease.

items.q: In early carpal tunnel syndrome, which sensory test is most sensitive in detecting compression?
items.e: Threshold tests such as Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments detect early compression; innervation density tests like two-point discrimination become abnormal only with significant axonal loss.

items.q: In carpal tunnel syndrome, the earliest abnormality on nerve conduction studies is usually:
items.e: Sensory fibres are affected first, so prolonged distal sensory latency appears before motor latency prolongation, reduced amplitudes and denervation on EMG.

items.q: In a patient with carpal tunnel syndrome, a good but temporary response to a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel:
o: Indicates that surgery will not be needed
Suggests the diagnosis is pronator syndrome
Predicts a good outcome from surgical release
items.e: Injection is both therapeutic and diagnostic; relief after injection supports the diagnosis and predicts a favourable response to release.

items.q: Compared with open carpal tunnel release, endoscopic release is associated with:
o: Better long-term symptom relief at 5 years
Faster return to work but a higher risk of transient nerve injury
A lower rate of transient nerve injury
Higher rates of pillar pain at 1 year as the main difference
items.e: Long-term results are similar; endoscopic release allows earlier return to work and less early scar tenderness but has a higher rate of transient neurapraxia.

items.q: To minimise risk to the recurrent motor and palmar cutaneous branches in open carpal tunnel release, the skin incision is placed:
o: In line with the radial border of the ring finger
In the thenar crease directly over the thenar muscles
In line with the ulnar border of the little finger
Transversely across the distal wrist crease
items.e: An incision along the axis of the radial border of the ring finger (just ulnar to the thenar crease) keeps away from the palmar cutaneous branch and the recurrent motor branch.

items.q: Which anatomical variation of the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve puts it most at risk during carpal tunnel release?
o: Transligamentous course through the transverse carpal ligament
Subligamentous origin with a recurrent course
Origin from the ulnar side of the median nerve with a normal course
items.e: In about a quarter of hands the branch pierces the ligament (transligamentous) and can be divided when the ligament is incised; the extraligamentous pattern is commonest (about 50 percent).

items.q: The most common cause of persistent symptoms immediately after carpal tunnel release is:
o: Incomplete release of the transverse carpal ligament
items.e: Persistent (never relieved) symptoms are most often due to incomplete division, usually of the distal ligament; recurrence after initial relief is more often due to scarring.

items.q: A 40-year-old has aching in the volar forearm and paraesthesia of the radial three digits AND the thenar palm, without night symptoms; nerve conduction studies are normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Involvement of the palmar cutaneous branch territory places the lesion proximal to the wrist; pronator syndrome typically lacks nocturnal symptoms and has normal NCS.

items.q: The commonest site of median nerve compression in pronator syndrome is:
o: Between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres
items.e: Although the ligament of Struthers, lacertus fibrosus and FDS arch can all compress the nerve, compression between the two heads of pronator teres is commonest.

items.q: A ligament of Struthers compressing the median nerve arises from a supracondylar process located approximately:
o: 8 cm above the medial epicondyle at the medial intermuscular septum
5 cm above the medial epicondyle on the anteromedial humerus
At the coronoid process of the ulna
items.e: The supracondylar process (present in about 1 percent) lies about 5 cm above the medial epicondyle; the arcade of Struthers, a different structure, affects the ulnar nerve about 8 cm proximal.

items.q: In suspected pronator syndrome, reproduction of symptoms with resisted flexion of the middle finger PIP joint implicates compression at the:
o: Fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis
items.e: Resisted middle finger PIPJ flexion tightens the FDS arch; resisted pronation tests pronator teres and resisted elbow flexion in supination tests the lacertus.

items.q: A 35-year-old develops severe shoulder pain for a week, followed by inability to flex the thumb IP joint and index DIP joint, with no sensory loss. The most likely underlying cause is:
items.e: Acute severe pain followed by isolated AIN palsy is typical of brachial neuritis, which often underlies 'AIN syndrome'; it is managed expectantly with most recovering.

items.q: A child with an extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture cannot make an 'OK' sign but has normal sensation in the hand. The injured nerve is the:
items.e: The AIN is the commonest nerve injured in extension-type supracondylar fractures; it supplies FPL and FDP index with no cutaneous territory.

items.q: The most common site of ulnar nerve compression in cubital tunnel syndrome is:
items.e: The arcuate ligament of Osborne, forming the roof of the cubital tunnel between the medial epicondyle and olecranon, is the commonest compression site.

items.q: A 45-year-old develops progressive ulnar nerve palsy decades after a childhood elbow fracture that left cubitus valgus. The original injury was most likely:
o: Non-union of a lateral condyle fracture
Medial epicondyle fracture treated in a cast
items.e: Lateral condyle non-union produces progressive cubitus valgus, which stretches the ulnar nerve causing tardy ulnar nerve palsy; supracondylar malunion usually causes varus.

items.q: The 'ulnar paradox' refers to the observation that:
o: High (elbow) ulnar lesions cause less clawing than low (wrist) lesions
Ulnar lesions spare the hypothenar muscles
Guyon canal lesions cause dorsal hand numbness
Clawing is worse with combined median and ulnar lesions at the elbow
items.e: In high lesions FDP to the ring and little fingers is also paralysed, so the flexion component of the claw is lost; as the nerve recovers distally the claw may paradoxically worsen.

items.q: In ulnar nerve palsy, hyperextension of the thumb MCP joint during key pinch (as the thumb compensates for a weak adductor pollicis) is known as:
items.e: Jeanne sign is compensatory thumb MCPJ hyperextension during pinch; Froment sign is the IPJ flexion from FPL substitution.

items.q: For mild cubital tunnel syndrome, the recommended night splint position of the elbow is:
o: 90 degrees of flexion with full pronation
Relative extension, about 45 degrees of flexion
items.e: Elbow flexion raises cubital tunnel pressure and stretches the nerve, so night splinting holds the elbow relatively extended (about 30-45 degrees of flexion).

items.q: In idiopathic cubital tunnel syndrome with a stable nerve, simple in situ decompression compared with anterior transposition:
o: Is contraindicated in severe McGowan grade III disease
Has similar outcomes with fewer complications
Must always be combined with medial epicondylectomy
items.e: Randomised trials and meta-analyses show equivalent outcomes with fewer wound complications for in situ release; transposition is reserved for a subluxing nerve or failed release.

items.q: A painful neuroma after cubital tunnel surgery most often involves branches of the:
items.e: Branches of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve cross the medial elbow incision and must be identified and protected.

items.q: In the McGowan classification of cubital tunnel syndrome, grade III denotes:
items.e: Grade I is sensory, grade II adds intrinsic weakness and grade III indicates severe weakness or atrophy; higher grades recover less completely.

items.q: The radial (lateral) wall of Guyon's canal is formed by the:
items.e: Guyon's canal has the volar carpal ligament as its roof, the transverse carpal ligament and pisohamate ligament as its floor, the pisiform ulnarly and the hook of hamate radially.

items.q: A long-distance cyclist has numbness of the little finger and ring finger pulp with normal intrinsic strength. The lesion in Guyon's canal is in zone:
o: 1, involving only the dorsal cutaneous branch
items.e: Zone 1 lesions are mixed, zone 2 (deep branch) pure motor and zone 3 (superficial branch) pure sensory; the dorsal cutaneous branch arises proximal to the canal.

items.q: A carpenter who habitually strikes objects with the heel of his hand develops ischaemic cold ulnar fingers and ulnar nerve symptoms. The likely diagnosis is:
o: Hypothenar hammer syndrome (ulnar artery thrombosis or aneurysm)
items.e: Repetitive trauma over the hook of hamate damages the ulnar artery in Guyon's canal, causing thrombosis or aneurysm with digital emboli and ulnar nerve compression.

items.q: A tennis player has lateral forearm pain maximal about 4-5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, worse with resisted middle finger extension, with normal strength and normal NCS. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Radial tunnel syndrome is a pain syndrome without motor weakness, felt over the supinator rather than at the epicondyle; PIN syndrome produces weakness of finger extension.

items.q: The 'leash of Henry' that may compress the posterior interosseous nerve consists of:
o: The fibrous proximal edge of supinator
Fibrous bands over the radial head
items.e: The leash of Henry is the fan of recurrent radial artery and vein branches crossing the nerve; the arcade of Frohse is the proximal edge of supinator.

items.q: A 55-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis suddenly cannot extend the fingers at the MCP joints. Passive wrist flexion produces MCP extension. This indicates:
o: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy rather than extensor tendon rupture
Extensor tendon rupture at the distal ulna
Extensor tendon subluxation into the ulnar gutters
Radial nerve palsy at the spiral groove
items.e: A positive tenodesis effect shows that the extensor tendons are intact, so the inability to extend actively is due to PIN palsy (e.g. from elbow synovitis).

items.q: After falling asleep with his arm over a chair, a man has wrist and finger drop with normal elbow extension. The radial nerve is compressed at the:
o: Distal forearm between brachioradialis and ECRL
items.e: In 'Saturday night palsy' the nerve is compressed in the spiral groove; the branches to triceps arise proximally, so elbow extension is spared, unlike crutch palsy in the axilla.

items.q: The loose areolar tissue that attaches a peripheral nerve to its bed, carries the segmental extrinsic vessels and allows the nerve to glide with joint motion is the:
items.e: The mesoneurium carries segmental vessels into the nerve and permits longitudinal excursion; scarring here causes traction neuritis.

items.q: Fast anterograde axonal transport of neurotransmitter vesicles along microtubules is driven by which motor protein?
items.e: Kinesin moves cargo anterogradely (about 100-400 mm/day); dynein drives retrograde transport towards the cell body.

items.q: Tetanus toxin, rabies virus and poliovirus reach the neuronal cell body from the periphery by:
o: Slow anterograde transport of cytoskeletal proteins
items.e: Retrograde (dynein) transport carries trophic signals such as NGF and is hijacked by tetanus toxin and neurotropic viruses.

items.q: The speed of slow anterograde axonal transport of cytoskeletal proteins, which sets the pace of axonal regeneration, is about:
items.e: Slow anterograde transport of neurofilaments and tubulin runs at roughly 1-6 mm/day, matching the clinical regeneration rate of about 1 mm/day.

items.q: In the peripheral nervous system, a single myelinating Schwann cell:
o: Myelinates internodes of many different axons
Myelinates one internode of a single axon
Myelinates the entire length of one axon
Myelinates axons grouped in a Remak bundle
items.e: One Schwann cell forms one internode on one axon; oligodendrocytes in the CNS myelinate many axons, and Remak bundles are unmyelinated axons sharing a Schwann cell.

items.q: Experimental studies show that intraneural blood flow ceases (complete ischaemia) when a peripheral nerve is elongated by about:
items.e: Venous flow is impaired at about 8% elongation and arterial flow stops at about 15%, which is why nerve repair under tension fails.

items.q: Sustained external compression of about what pressure first impairs epineurial venular flow and axonal transport in a peripheral nerve?
items.e: About 20-30 mmHg impairs venular flow and axonal transport; 30-40 mmHg causes paraesthesia and 50-80 mmHg blocks conduction.

items.q: Afferent fibres from the Golgi tendon organ, which mediate autogenic inhibition, belong to which Lloyd group?
items.e: Golgi tendon organs are supplied by Ib (A-alpha) fibres that sense tension; group Ia supplies the primary spindle ending and group II the secondary ending.

items.q: Gamma (A-gamma) motor neurons supply:
o: Extrafusal fibres of fast-twitch motor units
Intrafusal fibres of the muscle spindle
items.e: Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity by contracting intrafusal fibres; extrafusal fibres are supplied by alpha motor neurons.

items.q: During onset of a peripheral nerve block with local anaesthetic, which function is typically lost first?
items.e: Small fibres are blocked first: B (autonomic), then A-delta and C (pain, temperature), then A-beta (touch), and A-alpha (motor, proprioception) last; recovery is in reverse order.

items.q: Mechanical pressure from a tourniquet tends to block which fibres first?
o: Large myelinated A fibres (motor and proprioception)
items.e: Pressure and ischaemia affect large myelinated fibres first, the reverse of local anaesthetic block, which affects small fibres first.

items.q: Perception of vibration and deep pressure is mediated mainly by which rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor?
items.e: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors for vibration and deep pressure; Merkel discs and Ruffini endings are slowly adapting.

items.q: Static two-point discrimination at the fingertip mainly tests the innervation density of which slowly adapting receptor?
items.e: Static 2PD reflects slowly adapting Merkel discs; moving 2PD reflects rapidly adapting Meissner corpuscles.

items.q: In early carpal tunnel syndrome, which sensibility test is most likely to be abnormal first?
items.e: Threshold tests (monofilaments, vibration) detect early compression; two-point discrimination is an innervation density test that becomes abnormal only after axonal loss.

items.q: Normal static two-point discrimination at the fingertip pulp in an adult is less than about:
items.e: Normal static 2PD at the fingertip is under about 6 mm; values above this suggest axonal loss.

items.q: Mackinnon's addition to the Sunderland classification, grade VI injury, describes:
o: A mixed lesion in which different fascicles have different degrees of injury
Complete transection with a gap over 3 cm
Root avulsion from the spinal cord
An injury involving the nerve and its accompanying artery
items.e: Grade VI is a mixed injury (e.g. some fascicles neurapraxic, others neurotmetic) and is best handled with intraoperative stimulation, repairing only non-functioning fascicles.

items.q: Which is the most severe Sunderland grade of nerve injury that still recovers completely without surgery, even though Wallerian degeneration occurs?
items.e: In grade II the axon is disrupted but the endoneurial tubes remain, guiding axons back to their targets; grade I has no Wallerian degeneration and grade III recovers incompletely.

items.q: After complete transection of a mixed nerve, the distal stump can still be stimulated electrically during surgery for approximately:
items.e: The distal segment conducts for about 3-7 days until Wallerian degeneration is established, so distal stimulation is helpful only in early exploration.

items.q: The bands of Büngner that guide regenerating axons after nerve injury are formed by:
items.e: Schwann cells proliferate, help clear debris and line up within basal lamina tubes (bands of Büngner), secreting NGF, BDNF and GDNF.

items.q: Chromatolysis in the neuronal cell body after axonal injury is characterised by:
o: Dispersal of Nissl substance, cell swelling and an eccentric nucleus
Shrinkage of the soma with a central pyknotic nucleus
Increased neurotransmitter synthesis and vesicle accumulation
items.e: The injured cell body swells, Nissl substance disperses and the nucleus moves to the periphery as the cell switches to making structural proteins.

items.q: The tendency of regenerating axons to grow preferentially towards their distal stump or target organ is termed:
items.e: Neurotropism is directed (chemotactic) growth towards the target; neurotrophism refers to factors that support neuronal survival and growth.

items.q: Motor reinnervation is unlikely to restore useful function if regenerating axons reach the muscle more than about how long after denervation?
items.e: Motor end-plates degenerate and muscle becomes fibrotic after about 12-18 months, whereas sensory receptors tolerate denervation much longer.

items.q: The single most important factor determining the outcome of a peripheral nerve repair is:
o: Choice of epineurial versus fascicular repair
items.e: Age is the most important predictor (children recover best), followed by level, delay, gap and mechanism; fascicular repair has no proven advantage over epineurial repair.

items.q: Among upper limb nerves repaired at a comparable level, which generally has the worst prognosis for motor recovery?
items.e: The usual order of recovery is radial > musculocutaneous > median > ulnar; the ulnar nerve does worst because it supplies many small intrinsic muscles needing precise reinnervation.

items.q: In the lower limb, which nerve has the poorest prognosis for recovery after injury or repair?
items.e: The common peroneal nerve recovers poorly (tethered at the fibular neck, long distance to targets, less soft-tissue cover), whereas the tibial nerve recovers better.

items.q: Nerve conduction studies across a segment of focal demyelination typically show:
o: Markedly reduced amplitude with normal velocity
Absent sensory potentials with normal motor potentials
Prolonged latency and slowed conduction velocity with relatively preserved amplitude
Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves
items.e: Myelin determines conduction velocity, so demyelination slows conduction and prolongs latency; amplitude reflects the number of functioning axons and is relatively preserved.

items.q: Four weeks after a crush injury, motor nerve conduction shows a markedly reduced compound muscle action potential amplitude on distal stimulation with near-normal conduction velocity. This pattern indicates:
items.e: Amplitude reflects the number of conducting axons; a low distal CMAP with preserved velocity after Wallerian degeneration indicates axonal loss. In neurapraxia distal conduction remains normal.

items.q: A 30-year-old with a flail, anaesthetic arm after a motorcycle crash has absent motor responses, but sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) from the anaesthetic hand are preserved. This indicates:
items.e: In a preganglionic injury the dorsal root ganglion cell remains connected to its peripheral axon, so SNAPs persist despite anaesthesia; postganglionic injuries lose both SNAP and CMAP.

items.q: In a patient with a traumatic brachial plexus injury, which clinical sign most strongly suggests avulsion of the C8 and T1 roots?
o: Winging of the scapula on wall push-up
items.e: Horner syndrome reflects injury to the sympathetic outflow at T1 close to the cord, implying preganglionic C8-T1 avulsion. Scapular winging implicates the long thoracic nerve from C5-C7.

items.q: On needle EMG, which is the earliest electrical sign of reinnervation after an axonal nerve injury, often appearing weeks to months before clinical recovery?
o: Nascent, small, polyphasic motor unit potentials
items.e: Nascent polyphasic units appear as the first regenerating axons reach the muscle; large long-duration units appear later after collateral sprouting matures.

items.q: Needle EMG in a primary myopathy typically shows:
o: Large, long-duration motor units with reduced recruitment
Giant motor units with normal recruitment
Small, short-duration polyphasic motor units with early recruitment
items.e: In myopathy each motor unit has fewer functioning fibres, so units are small and short and many must be recruited early; neuropathy produces large units with reduced recruitment.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a crushed, contaminated wound with a lacerated median nerve and ragged nerve ends at the forearm. The best initial management of the nerve is:
o: Tag the nerve ends and perform delayed repair, usually with a graft, at about 2-3 weeks
Primary end-to-end repair under tension at the first debridement
Leave the ends unmarked and observe for 6 months
Immediate nerve transfer from the ulnar nerve
items.e: In crushed or contaminated wounds the zone of injury is not demarcated, so ends are tagged and repaired secondarily (often with a graft) once the zone of injury is clear.

items.q: After a closed fracture with an associated complete nerve palsy, surgical exploration is generally recommended if there is no clinical or EMG evidence of recovery by about:
items.e: Most closed-injury palsies are neurapraxia or axonotmesis, so observation with serial EMG is advised; exploration at 3-6 months allows repair before end-plate loss.

items.q: Which suture is standard for microsurgical epineurial repair of a digital or median nerve?
items.e: Fine non-absorbable 9-0 or 10-0 nylon under magnification allows tension-free epineurial coaptation with minimal foreign-body reaction.

items.q: Group fascicular (perineurial) repair is most justified in which situation?
o: A common digital nerve in the palm
Ulnar nerve at the wrist, where motor and sensory fascicle groups are distinct
items.e: Fascicular repair has no proven superiority in mixed nerves generally; it is used where distinct fascicle groups exist, such as separating the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve at the wrist.

items.q: When a cable nerve autograft is placed, it is usually reversed (distal end of the graft sutured to the proximal stump) in order to:
o: Prevent regenerating axons escaping through the graft's side branches
Allow the graft to be thinner at the distal coaptation
items.e: Reversing the graft points its branches away from the regenerating front so axons are not lost through them.

items.q: Hollow nerve conduits (collagen or polyglycolic acid) are best supported for:
o: Gaps over 6 cm in the sciatic nerve
Short gaps (under about 3 cm) in small-diameter sensory nerves such as digital nerves
Proximal mixed motor nerve gaps of any length
items.e: Conduits work for short sensory gaps (best under 1-2 cm, up to about 3 cm); longer or larger mixed-nerve gaps need autograft, the gold standard.

items.q: A sural nerve graft harvest leaves sensory loss mainly over the:
items.e: The sural nerve supplies the lateral foot and heel border; it is the commonest autograft donor and can give up to about 30-40 cm.

items.q: In the Leechavengvongs (Somsak) nerve transfer to restore shoulder abduction, the donor and recipient are:
o: Spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve
Ulnar nerve FCU fascicle to the biceps branch
Intercostal nerves to the musculocutaneous nerve
Radial nerve branch to the long (or medial) head of triceps to the anterior branch of the axillary nerve
items.e: A triceps branch of the radial nerve is transferred to the anterior branch of the axillary nerve, close to the deltoid, for upper trunk injuries.

items.q: In a high ulnar nerve injury, a supercharged end-to-side transfer to protect the intrinsic muscles uses which donor?
o: Terminal anterior interosseous nerve branch to pronator quadratus
Posterior interosseous nerve to extensor indicis
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
items.e: The AIN branch to pronator quadratus is transferred end-to-side to the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve near the wrist, shortening the regeneration distance.

items.q: The Mackinnon double fascicular transfer for restoring elbow flexion after C5-C6 injury uses donor fascicles from:
o: The radial nerve triceps branches, to the axillary nerve
The ulnar nerve (FCU) and the median nerve (FDS or FCR), to the biceps and brachialis branches
Two intercostal nerves, to the musculocutaneous nerve
The spinal accessory and phrenic nerves, to the suprascapular nerve
items.e: One redundant ulnar fascicle goes to the biceps branch and one median fascicle to the brachialis branch, restoring stronger flexion than a single (Oberlin) transfer.

items.q: When planning a tendon transfer, how much strength does a donor muscle usually lose after transfer?
o: It gains one grade from the new line of pull
items.e: A transferred muscle generally loses about one MRC grade, so the donor should be at least grade 4 (preferably 5) before transfer.

items.q: In the classic tendon transfer set for a high radial nerve palsy, wrist extension is restored by transferring pronator teres to:
items.e: Pronator teres to ECRB gives central wrist extension; FCR or FCU to EDC restores finger extension and palmaris longus to EPL restores thumb extension.

items.q: Targeted muscle reinnervation is mainly used to:
o: Treat or prevent painful neuromas and phantom pain by giving cut nerve ends new motor targets
Restore protective sensation in the sole
Accelerate union of nerve grafts over 10 cm
Replace a damaged muscle with a free functioning flap
items.e: In TMR, transected mixed nerves are coapted to motor branches of nearby muscles, giving regenerating axons a target and reducing neuroma and phantom limb pain.

items.q: In the Zollinger trial, which vitamin C regimen reduced complex regional pain syndrome after wrist fractures?
items.e: Vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days reduced CRPS after distal radius fractures; AAOS guidance supports it, although the evidence has been debated.

items.q: Complex regional pain syndrome type II differs from type I by:
o: Involvement of the lower limb only
The presence of an identifiable peripheral nerve injury
items.e: Type II (causalgia) follows a definable nerve injury; type I has no identifiable nerve lesion. Both are diagnosed with the Budapest criteria.

items.q: According to the sliding filament theory, which part of the sarcomere stays the same length during muscle contraction?
items.e: The A band equals the length of the thick (myosin) filaments and does not change; the I band and H zone shorten as thin filaments slide inwards.

items.q: Which subunit of the troponin complex anchors the complex to tropomyosin?
items.e: Troponin T binds tropomyosin, troponin C binds calcium and troponin I inhibits actin-myosin interaction at rest.

items.q: Rigor mortis develops because, after death:
o: Calcium is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
No ATP is available to detach myosin heads from actin
items.e: ATP binding releases the myosin head from actin; without ATP cross-bridges stay locked.

items.q: Long-term series of high tibial osteotomy for medial compartment osteoarthritis identify which technical factor as the commonest cause of failure and early conversion to TKA?
items.e: Recurrence of varus from inadequate correction is the commonest reason HTO fails; the weight-bearing line must be shifted just lateral to the midline. Hinge fractures and nerve injury are complications but cause fewer failures.

items.q: During a lateral closing-wedge (Coventry) high tibial osteotomy, the fibula must be divided or the proximal tibiofibular joint disrupted. Which structure is chiefly at risk from this part of the operation?
o: Common peroneal nerve and its branches
Anterior tibial artery at the hiatus in the interosseous membrane
items.e: Peroneal nerve palsy is the characteristic complication of closing-wedge HTO because the nerve winds round the fibular neck. Medial opening-wedge HTO avoids the fibula and therefore this risk.

items.q: In a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, to avoid unintentionally increasing the posterior tibial slope, how should the anteromedial opening compare with the posteromedial opening?
o: Both gaps should be equal (a parallel opening)
The anteromedial gap should be wider than the posteromedial gap
The anteromedial gap should be narrower than the posteromedial gap
Gap shape is irrelevant because slope is set by the plate
items.e: Because the medial tibial cortex runs obliquely, an equal or anteriorly wide gap tilts the plateau and increases slope; a trapezoidal gap, wider posteromedially (roughly twice the anterior), keeps slope unchanged.

items.q: For a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, where should the lateral hinge point ideally be placed?
o: Exactly at the lateral cortex so that the cortex is breached
In the centre of the tibia, halfway across the metaphysis
Distal to the tibial tubercle at the level of the fibular neck
About 1 cm medial to the lateral tibial cortex, aimed towards the tip of the fibular head
items.e: Leaving about 1 cm of intact lateral bone at the level of the proximal tibiofibular joint gives a strong, soft-tissue-protected hinge and reduces unstable hinge fractures. A hinge too far medial makes opening difficult.

items.q: In planning a high tibial osteotomy, the Miniaci method is used to:
o: Calculate the correction angle by rotating the planned weight-bearing line about the hinge point
Measure patellar height before and after osteotomy
Classify lateral hinge fractures by their exit point
Grade the severity of medial compartment osteoarthritis
items.e: Miniaci's method draws the desired mechanical axis through the target point, then measures the angle subtended at the hinge to give the wedge required. Takeuchi classifies hinge fractures; Ahlback grades OA.

items.q: A 48-year-old with varus medial compartment OA has a joint line convergence angle (JLCA) of 6 degrees on standing long-leg films. What is the main implication for planning a high tibial osteotomy?
o: The deformity is purely femoral and requires a distal femoral osteotomy
Part of the varus is due to lateral soft-tissue laxity, so a full bony correction risks overcorrection
The patient has an increased posterior tibial slope
It confirms lateral compartment arthritis and contraindicates HTO
items.e: A JLCA over about 2-3 degrees indicates soft-tissue laxity contributing to the deformity; when the limb is loaded after osteotomy the lateral side tightens and the correction overshoots unless this component is subtracted.

items.q: Planning for a 45-year-old with severe varus shows that correcting the limb by a tibial osteotomy alone would leave a medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) of 99 degrees. The best option is:
o: Proceed with a single-level medial opening-wedge HTO
Lateral closing-wedge HTO to the same angle
Double-level osteotomy (femoral and tibial) to keep the joint line near horizontal
items.e: A post-operative MPTA above about 95 degrees creates excessive joint line obliquity and shear across the cartilage; when deformity exists in both bones, correction is shared between femur and tibia.

items.q: Which measurement on a standing long-leg radiograph confirms that a varus knee deformity arises from the proximal tibia and is suitable for correction by a high tibial osteotomy?
o: Mechanical lateral distal femoral angle (mLDFA) of 82 degrees
Joint line convergence angle of 6 degrees
Medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) of 82 degrees
items.e: Normal MPTA is about 87 degrees (85-90); a value below 85 indicates tibial (metaphyseal) varus, which should be corrected in the tibia. An mLDFA of 82 is a femoral valgus deformity.

items.q: A 50-year-old labourer with varus medial OA is assessed for high tibial osteotomy. Which radiographic finding is a contraindication?
o: Medial joint space narrowing to 2 mm (Ahlback grade I)
Varus of 8 degrees from the tibia
Mild osteophytes on the medial patellar facet
items.e: Lateral tibial subluxation over 1 cm indicates instability and advanced disease and is a recognised contraindication to HTO. Medial narrowing, moderate tibial varus and mild patellofemoral change are acceptable.

items.q: Which range-of-motion finding is a contraindication to high tibial osteotomy?
items.e: Candidates for HTO should flex beyond about 90 degrees and have a fixed flexion deformity below about 10-15 degrees; a stiff knee indicates advanced disease and a poor result.

items.q: A 35-year-old has chronic posterior cruciate ligament deficiency with posterior sag, constitutional varus and early medial OA. When performing a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, the posterior tibial slope should be:
o: Decreased, to reduce posterior tibial translation
Increased, to reduce posterior tibial translation
Ignored, because slope does not influence sagittal stability
items.e: Increasing slope shifts the tibia anteriorly and helps a PCL-deficient knee; the reverse (reducing slope) is used for ACL deficiency.

items.q: Which fixation device is most associated with stable fixation of a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, often permitting early weight bearing without bone graft?
o: Single lag screw across the hinge
Angle-stable locking plate (TomoFix type) on the medial tibia
items.e: Long angle-stable locking plates provide strong fixation of opening-wedge osteotomies and allow early loading; staples were used historically for closing-wedge osteotomy.

items.q: During the saw cut for a high tibial osteotomy, the popliteal neurovascular bundle is best protected by:
o: Flexing the knee and placing a blunt retractor subperiosteally behind the tibia
Keeping the knee in full extension
Releasing the tourniquet before the cut
items.e: The popliteal artery lies close to the posterior tibial cortex; knee flexion lets it fall back and a subperiosteal retractor shields it. Extension brings the vessel nearer the bone.

items.q: A 32-year-old has lateral compartment OA with valgus arising from the femur and is undergoing a varus-producing distal femoral osteotomy. What is the usual alignment target?
o: Weight-bearing line through about 62-66% of the plateau width from medial
Weight-bearing line through about the centre of the knee (neutral), without varus overcorrection
Weight-bearing line through the medial tibial spine with 3-5 degrees of varus
Weight-bearing line through the lateral tibial spine
items.e: Unlike HTO, a DFO is not overcorrected; the aim is a neutral axis or very slightly medial, as overloading the medial compartment is unnecessary and poorly tolerated.

items.q: A valgus knee with lateral compartment arthritis is usually corrected by a femoral rather than a tibial osteotomy. The main reason is that tibial correction would:
o: Injure the common peroneal nerve in every case
Require division of the patellar tendon
Create excessive obliquity of the joint line
items.e: Valgus deformity is usually femoral; correcting it in the tibia would leave the joint line tilted superolaterally to inferomedially, causing shear and subluxation.

items.q: A common complaint after a lateral opening-wedge distal femoral osteotomy fixed with a lateral plate is:
o: Iliotibial band irritation over the plate
items.e: The lateral DFO plate lies beneath the iliotibial band and frequently causes irritation requiring removal; peroneal palsy and slope change are features of tibial osteotomies.

items.q: Compared with a lateral opening-wedge distal femoral osteotomy, a medial closing-wedge distal femoral osteotomy has which advantage?
o: Bone-on-bone contact giving greater stability and faster union without graft
No need for any internal fixation
Easier adjustment of correction during surgery
Avoids any change in limb length
items.e: Closing-wedge osteotomies give immediate cortical contact and heal predictably; opening-wedge cuts are easier to adjust but create a gap that may need graft and heals more slowly.

items.q: A 24-year-old presents with a second failure of ACL reconstruction. Lateral radiographs show a posterior tibial slope of 15 degrees. In addition to revision ACL reconstruction, which procedure should be considered?
items.e: A posterior tibial slope above about 12 degrees increases anterior tibial translation and graft strain; an anterior closing-wedge osteotomy reduces slope and protects the revision graft.

items.q: In Noyes's classification of varus in ACL-deficient knees, 'triple varus' differs from 'double varus' by the addition of:
o: Posterolateral corner insufficiency with varus recurvatum
items.e: Primary varus is bony tibiofemoral varus; double varus adds lateral tibiofemoral separation from LCL laxity; triple varus adds posterolateral corner insufficiency producing varus recurvatum.

items.q: With conversion to TKA as the end point, the typical 10-year survivorship of a well-indicated high tibial osteotomy is about:
items.e: Most series report 75-90% survival at 10 years, falling thereafter; results are worse with older age, obesity, advanced arthritis and undercorrection.

items.q: A 30-year-old has lateral patellar facet arthritis and patellar maltracking with an elevated TT-TG distance but a normal tibiofemoral joint. The joint-preserving operation of choice is:
o: Fulkerson anteromedialisation of the tibial tubercle
items.e: Anteromedialisation unloads the lateral and distal patellar facets and corrects lateralised tracking; HTO does not address the patellofemoral joint.

items.q: The randomised sham-controlled trial by Moseley and colleagues (2002) showed that arthroscopic lavage or debridement for knee osteoarthritis:
o: Was superior to sham for at least 5 years
Gave no better pain or function than a sham procedure
Delayed the need for TKA by about 3 years
Helped only patients with mechanical locking
items.e: Moseley's trial, confirmed by Kirkley (2008), found no benefit of arthroscopic lavage or debridement over placebo or physiotherapy, so it is not recommended for degenerative knees.

items.q: The Finnish FIDELITY trial of patients with knee pain and a degenerative medial meniscal tear without established OA found that arthroscopic partial meniscectomy:
o: Was clearly better than sham at 12 months
Increased the rate of TKA at 2 years
Was no better than sham surgery
Benefited only tears with an unstable flap
items.e: FIDELITY compared APM with sham surgery and found no difference in outcome; degenerative tears are managed with exercise therapy first.

items.q: In anteromedial osteoarthritis, the classic pattern suited to Oxford medial UKA, where in the medial compartment is full-thickness cartilage typically preserved?
o: Anteriorly on the medial tibial plateau
Nowhere: the whole compartment is bone-on-bone
Posteriorly on the medial tibial plateau and femoral condyle
items.e: With a functioning ACL, wear is confined to the anterior and central medial plateau and the distal femur; the posterior cartilage is preserved, so the varus corrects in flexion. Posterior wear suggests ACL failure.

items.q: A 63-year-old with medial knee pain has only partial-thickness medial cartilage loss; the medial joint space is preserved on a varus stress radiograph. What is the most appropriate advice about medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty?
o: Avoid UKA: partial-thickness disease has high rates of unexplained pain and revision
Proceed with mobile-bearing UKA as the lateral side is normal
Proceed with fixed-bearing UKA to reduce dislocation
Perform UKA with release of the MCL
items.e: UKA should be reserved for full-thickness (bone-on-bone) loss confirmed on varus stress views; operating on partial-thickness disease gives poor and unpredictable results.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has spontaneous osteonecrosis of the medial femoral condyle with subchondral collapse, an intact ACL and a normal lateral compartment. She has failed non-operative care. The most suitable arthroplasty is:
o: Total knee arthroplasty with a hinged implant
items.e: Spontaneous osteonecrosis (SONK/SIFK) confined to the medial condyle is an accepted indication for medial UKA when the ligaments and other compartments are healthy.

items.q: The Oxford group showed that which feature, listed as a contraindication in the Kozinn and Scott criteria, does not compromise the results of mobile-bearing medial UKA for anteromedial OA?
o: A fixed varus deformity that does not correct
items.e: Goodfellow and Murray broadened indications to include patients regardless of age, weight, activity and chondrocalcinosis; ACL deficiency, lateral disease and non-correctable deformity still contraindicate.

items.q: Which patellofemoral finding is regarded by the Oxford group as a contraindication to medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty?
o: Full-thickness cartilage loss on the medial patellar facet
Lateral facet bone loss with grooving and patellar subluxation
items.e: Medial facet damage and anterior knee pain do not affect results of Oxford UKA; severe lateral patellofemoral damage with bone loss and subluxation does.

items.q: During medial UKA for a correctable varus knee with anteromedial OA, the medial collateral ligament should be:
o: Left unreleased, as its normal tension is restored by the implant
Released from the tibia to balance the knee
Released by pie-crusting of the superficial fibres
Advanced proximally to tighten the medial side
items.e: In anteromedial OA the MCL is of normal length; restoring the lost cartilage thickness re-tensions it. Releasing it causes overcorrection and instability, unlike TKA balancing.

items.q: A routine radiograph 2 years after a cemented Oxford medial UKA shows a thin (under 1 mm), well-defined radiolucent line with a sclerotic margin beneath the tibial component; the patient is pain-free and the line has not changed. Management:
o: Revise the tibial component for aseptic loosening
Reassure and observe: this is a physiological radiolucency, not loosening
Aspirate the knee to exclude infection urgently
Convert to TKA because of impending fracture
items.e: Thin, well-defined, non-progressive lines under the Oxford tibial tray are common and do not indicate loosening; revision for them alone is a recognised cause of unnecessary surgery.

items.q: Overcorrection of the limb into valgus during a medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty most predictably leads to:
o: Progression of arthritis in the lateral compartment
items.e: Alignment should be restored to the pre-disease state, leaving slight varus; overcorrection overloads the lateral compartment and accelerates its degeneration, a leading cause of UKA revision.

items.q: Early periprosthetic tibial plateau fracture after medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty is most often related to:
o: Use of a mobile rather than fixed bearing
An excessively deep vertical saw cut or multiple pin holes weakening the medial plateau
items.e: Breaching the posterior cortex with the vertical cut, or extra pin holes, creates stress risers that lead to medial plateau fracture, usually within the first months.

items.q: Registry analyses of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty show lower revision rates when the surgeon:
o: Uses UKA for at least about 20% of their knee arthroplasties
Uses UKA only for patients over 80 years
Performs fewer than 5 UKAs per year
Uses UKA exclusively in patients with lateral disease
items.e: Low-usage surgeons have high revision rates; usage of about 20% or more (or more than about 13 UKAs a year) is associated with results approaching TKA.

items.q: Compared with TKA, national registry data show that unicompartmental knee arthroplasty has:
o: Lower revision rates and lower mortality
Higher revision rates but lower mortality, VTE and infection rates
Higher revision rates and higher mortality
Equal revision rates and equal complication rates
items.e: UKA is revised about 2-3 times as often as TKA in registries, yet it has lower early mortality, thromboembolism, infection and transfusion rates and faster recovery.

items.q: The higher registry revision rate of UKA compared with TKA is partly explained by:
o: Universally higher infection rates after UKA
A lower threshold for revising a UKA, because revision of a UKA is technically easier
Routine use of UKA in inflammatory arthritis
items.e: A painful UKA is often revised to a primary-type TKA, whereas a painful TKA is less readily revised; revision rate is therefore not a pure measure of implant failure.

items.q: The main design advantage of the Oxford mobile-bearing UKA, with a spherical femoral component articulating with a fully congruent bearing, is:
o: Suitability for any lateral compartment disease
Low contact stress with minimal polyethylene wear
items.e: Full congruity spreads load over a large area and wear rates are very low; the trade-off is dependence on intact ligaments and the risk of bearing dislocation.

items.q: A 45-year-old active man has anteromedial OA with full-thickness medial loss, a correctable varus and chronic ACL deficiency causing instability. The lateral compartment is normal. If partial knee replacement is chosen, which option is most appropriate?
o: Fixed-bearing medial UKA combined with ACL reconstruction
Mobile-bearing medial UKA without ACL reconstruction
items.e: A mobile-bearing UKA in an ACL-deficient knee is prone to bearing dislocation and tibial loosening; in young patients a fixed-bearing UKA with ACL reconstruction is an accepted option.

items.q: In patellofemoral arthroplasty, why have onlay trochlear components largely replaced inlay designs?
o: Onlay designs avoid any bone resection
Onlay designs have fewer patellar maltracking problems, especially with trochlear dysplasia
Inlay designs cause more tibiofemoral progression
Onlay designs can be used with patella baja
items.e: Inlay components sit within the native, often dysplastic trochlea and reproduce its maltracking; onlay components replace the trochlea at the anterior femoral cut, correcting its geometry.

items.q: Which patient is the best candidate for patellofemoral arthroplasty?
o: A 55-year-old with patellofemoral OA and rheumatoid arthritis
A 45-year-old woman with isolated patellofemoral OA secondary to trochlear dysplasia and normal tibiofemoral compartments
A 60-year-old with patellofemoral OA and medial bone-on-bone change
items.e: PFA suits isolated patellofemoral arthritis, typically from dysplasia, in younger patients; inflammatory and tibiofemoral disease are contraindications and predict failure.

items.q: The main proven benefit of robotic-arm-assisted unicompartmental knee arthroplasty over conventional instrumentation is:
o: Elimination of the need for an intact ACL
More accurate and reproducible component positioning
items.e: Randomised trials show more accurate component alignment with robotic UKA; long-term survival benefit has not been established.

items.q: In the Kozinn and Scott (1989) criteria for unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, the upper body-weight limit was:
items.e: Kozinn and Scott recommended UKA for patients over 60 years, weighing under 82 kg, with low demand, good motion and correctable deformity; the Oxford group later abandoned the weight limit.

items.q: A medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy is complicated by a lateral hinge fracture that propagates proximally into the lateral tibial plateau. In the Takeuchi classification this is:
items.e: Takeuchi type I exits within or proximal to the proximal tibiofibular joint (stable), type II exits distal to it and type III extends into the lateral plateau; types II and III are unstable.

items.q: The most important modifiable risk factor for delayed union or non-union after medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy is:
items.e: Smoking markedly increases delayed and non-union after opening-wedge HTO; small corrections with locking-plate fixation usually heal without graft.

items.q: Conversion of a previous lateral closing-wedge high tibial osteotomy to TKA is technically more demanding mainly because of:
o: Increased posterior tibial slope and patella alta
Medial tibial bone loss and MCL laxity
Patella baja, lateral tibial bone loss and offset of the tibial shaft
items.e: Closing-wedge osteotomy removes lateral bone, shortens the patellar tendon region and can offset the metaphysis, complicating exposure and stem placement; opening-wedge HTO preserves bone stock better.

items.q: In the Ahlback radiographic classification of knee osteoarthritis, grade II denotes:
o: Subluxation with bone attrition over 10 mm
items.e: Ahlback grade I is narrowing (under 3 mm), II obliteration, III minor attrition (under 5 mm), IV moderate attrition (5-10 mm), V severe attrition with subluxation; HTO suits grades I-II.

items.q: A patient with painful right knee osteoarthritis is given a walking stick. To unload the knee most effectively it should be held in the:
o: Either hand, as there is no difference
Right hand only when climbing stairs
items.e: A stick in the hand opposite the painful limb reduces the joint reaction force by moving the body's centre of gravity towards the affected side and sharing load during its stance phase.

items.q: Which non-operative measure for knee osteoarthritis has the strongest evidence of benefit and is recommended in AAOS and NICE guidance?
o: Exercise therapy with quadriceps strengthening, plus weight loss if overweight
items.e: Structured exercise and weight loss are core treatments; AAOS does not recommend hyaluronic acid or glucosamine, and lavage is ineffective.

items.q: A 70-year-old with bone-on-bone anteromedial OA, a functioning ACL, a 7-degree passively correctable varus and full-thickness lateral cartilage on a valgus stress view wishes to have surgery. The most appropriate operation is:
items.e: Full-thickness medial disease with an intact ACL and lateral compartment in an older patient is the ideal UKA indication; HTO suits younger patients with partial-thickness disease and tibial varus.

items.q: A 30-year-old footballer has chronic ACL deficiency with recurrent giving way, constitutional tibial varus (MPTA 83 degrees) and early medial compartment OA. The most appropriate surgery is:
o: Medial opening-wedge HTO with slope reduction combined with ACL reconstruction
items.e: In the varus ACL-deficient knee, ACL reconstruction alone tends to fail from varus thrust; combining it with an opening-wedge HTO that corrects alignment and reduces slope addresses both problems.

items.q: A 26-year-old with a meniscus-deficient lateral compartment and valgus alignment is being considered for lateral meniscal allograft transplantation. Which concomitant procedure protects the graft?
items.e: Valgus overloads a lateral meniscal or cartilage graft; correction with a DFO unloads the lateral compartment and is commonly combined with lateral transplant procedures.

items.q: To allow a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy to open, which structure's distal fibres are usually elevated from the tibia?
items.e: The distal insertion of the superficial MCL spans the osteotomy and must be elevated or released for the wedge to open without excessive medial compartment pressure.

items.q: Which investigation is essential for planning the correction of a high tibial osteotomy?
items.e: The mechanical axis, joint orientation angles and correction can only be measured on a standing long-leg film; short films and MRI do not show the whole limb axis.

items.q: Which plain radiograph is most sensitive for early joint space narrowing in the posterior part of the tibiofemoral compartments, often missed on a standing extension AP view?
o: Posteroanterior weight-bearing view in about 45 degrees of flexion (Rosenberg view)
items.e: Cartilage wear often occurs where the femur contacts the tibia in flexion; the flexed weight-bearing PA view reveals narrowing that the extension view misses, important when assessing compartments before HTO or UKA.

items.q: In the Kellgren-Lawrence grading of knee osteoarthritis, grade 2 is defined by:
o: Definite osteophytes with possible joint space narrowing
Multiple osteophytes with definite narrowing and some sclerosis
Large osteophytes, marked narrowing and bone deformity
items.e: KL 1 is doubtful, KL 2 is definite osteophytes with possible narrowing, KL 3 moderate osteophytes with definite narrowing, and KL 4 large osteophytes with marked narrowing, sclerosis and deformity.

items.q: What is the approximate normal value of the medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) used in deformity analysis around the knee?
items.e: The normal MPTA and mechanical LDFA are both about 87 degrees; an MPTA below 85 indicates tibial varus and above 90 tibial valgus.

items.q: When choosing between high tibial osteotomy and medial UKA, which feature favours HTO?
o: Bone-on-bone disease with an intact ACL in a 72-year-old
Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the medial femoral condyle
Intra-articular varus entirely due to cartilage loss
Age under 55 with heavy manual work and constitutional tibial varus
items.e: HTO preserves the joint for young, high-demand patients with metaphyseal varus and less severe disease; UKA suits older patients with full-thickness disease or SONK.

items.q: A lateral closing-wedge high tibial osteotomy, compared with a medial opening-wedge osteotomy, results in:
o: No change in limb length in all cases
items.e: Removing a lateral wedge shortens the limb slightly, whereas opening a medial wedge lengthens it; a closing-wedge needs no graft because the cut surfaces are apposed.

items.q: The usual long-term mode of failure of an isolated patellofemoral arthroplasty is:
o: Progression of tibiofemoral arthritis needing conversion to TKA
items.e: Progressive tibiofemoral OA is the leading cause of revision of modern PFA, with conversion to TKA; maltracking was more common with older inlay designs.

items.q: The developmental origin of an osteochondroma is best explained by:
o: Herniation of physeal cartilage through the perichondral ring (of LaCroix)
Metaplasia of periosteal fibroblasts after trauma
Reactive callus at a tendon insertion
items.e: A fragment of physeal cartilage escapes through the perichondral ring and grows at right angles to the bone, producing a lesion in continuity with the host cortex and medulla.

items.q: A 10-year-old who received total body irradiation for leukaemia at age 3 develops a bony outgrowth in continuity with the distal femoral cortex and medulla. The lesion is most likely:
items.e: Childhood irradiation of a growing physis is a recognised cause of osteochondromas, which behave like sporadic ones; corticomedullary continuity is the defining feature.

items.q: A 16-year-old with a sessile posterior distal femoral osteochondroma develops calf claudication and a pulsatile popliteal swelling after sport. The most likely complication is:
items.e: Osteochondromas of the distal femur or proximal tibia can abrade the popliteal artery, causing pseudoaneurysm or thrombosis.

items.q: An 8-year-old has an osteochondroma whose cartilage cap measures 2.5 cm on MRI, with no pain or growth beyond expected. The best interpretation is:
o: A cap of this thickness can be normal in a growing child
items.e: The 2 cm cap threshold applies to adults; in children caps up to about 3 cm can be normal because the cap is the growth zone.

items.q: To minimise local recurrence when excising a symptomatic osteochondroma, the surgeon must remove:
o: The entire cartilage cap together with its overlying perichondrium
