The cap but leave the perichondrium to protect nearby nerves
Only the protruding part, flush with the bursa
items.e: Recurrence comes from residual cap or perichondrium, so both are excised with the stalk base; surgery is preferably delayed until skeletal maturity.

items.q: The EXT1 and EXT2 genes mutated in hereditary multiple exostoses encode enzymes required for synthesis of:
items.e: EXT1 and EXT2 encode glycosyltransferases for heparan sulphate chain elongation; deficiency disturbs signalling (e.g. Indian hedgehog) at the growth plate.

items.q: EXT2, the second gene implicated in hereditary multiple exostoses, lies on chromosome:
items.e: EXT2 is on 11p (11p11–p12); EXT1 on 8q24 is associated with more lesions and a more severe phenotype.

items.q: A child with hereditary multiple exostoses develops progressive valgus of the ankle. The principal cause is:
o: Relative shortening of the distal fibula
items.e: Distal tibiofibular osteochondromas restrict fibular growth; the short fibula lets the ankle tilt into valgus, often treated with medial distal tibial hemiepiphysiodesis.

items.q: In a 9-year-old with hereditary multiple exostoses and progressive genu valgum from proximal tibial lesions, the least invasive corrective option is:
items.e: Guided growth by medial hemiepiphysiodesis lets the lateral side catch up and corrects valgus while growth remains; tethering the lateral side would worsen it.

items.q: In the Masada classification of forearm deformity in hereditary multiple exostoses, type I is:
o: Radial head dislocation caused by a proximal radial osteochondroma
Distal ulnar osteochondroma with a short ulna and bowed radius, but no radial head dislocation
Distal radial osteochondroma with relative shortening of the radius
items.e: Type I has a short ulna from a distal ulnar lesion without radial head dislocation; it is managed with excision and ulnar lengthening ± radial osteotomy.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy has an intra-articular bony mass arising from the medial side of the talus and distal tibial epiphysis on one leg. Histology would resemble an osteochondroma. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Trevor disease is an epiphyseal osteochondroma, usually on the medial side of one lower limb, commoner in boys; symptomatic lesions are excised while protecting the joint surface.

items.q: A subungual exostosis of the great toe differs from a true osteochondroma because it:
o: Lacks continuity with the medulla of the distal phalanx
items.e: Dupuytren's subungual exostosis is a reactive fibrocartilaginous lesion of the distal phalanx without medullary continuity; it is excised with its cap.

items.q: Which statement about Ollier disease is correct?
o: It is autosomal dominant with full penetrance
It is sporadic, caused by somatic mosaic mutations, and often has unilateral predominance
items.e: Ollier disease is non-inherited (somatic mosaic IDH1/IDH2), commonly predominantly one-sided, with secondary chondrosarcoma in roughly 25–40%.

items.q: Besides chondrosarcoma, patients with Maffucci syndrome have an increased risk of which non-skeletal malignancy?
o: Glioma and ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumour
items.e: Maffucci syndrome (enchondromas + spindle cell haemangiomas, IDH1/IDH2) carries risks of gliomas, ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumours and pancreatic/hepatic tumours.

items.q: In a child with Ollier disease undergoing gradual tibial lengthening with an external fixator, enchondromatous bone within the distraction regenerate typically:
items.e: Lesional cartilage within the distraction zone tends to ossify, so gradual lengthening and deformity correction work well in Ollier disease.

items.q: Within the hand, a solitary enchondroma most commonly involves the:
items.e: The proximal phalanx is the commonest site, followed by the metacarpals and middle phalanges; carpal enchondromas are rare.

items.q: On bone scintigraphy, which finding in a long-bone central cartilage lesion favours an atypical cartilaginous tumour over enchondroma?
o: Uptake greater than that of the anterior iliac crest
Uptake equal to normal femoral shaft
items.e: Enchondromas usually show mild uptake; activity exceeding the anterior iliac crest raises suspicion of chondrosarcoma, though it must be read with radiographs and MRI.

items.q: A 50-year-old has an incidental cartilage lesion with chondroid calcification in the iliac wing. Compared with an identical lesion in the distal femur, the pelvic lesion:
o: Should be regarded as chondrosarcoma until proven otherwise
items.e: Central cartilage tumours of the pelvis and axial skeleton are almost always malignant, so they are treated as chondrosarcoma and resected widely.

items.q: Histologically, which finding helps distinguish an atypical cartilaginous tumour from an enchondroma?
o: Hypocellular lobules encased by lamellar bone
Permeation of the tumour between pre-existing host trabeculae, entrapping them
items.e: Enchondroma lobules are encased by bone, whereas ACT/chondrosarcoma permeates and entraps host trabeculae; cytology alone is unreliable.

items.q: The most frequent site of a periosteal (juxtacortical) chondroma is the:
items.e: Periosteal chondroma is a small surface lesion, commonest at the proximal humerus and in the hand, producing cortical saucerisation with buttressing.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a 2.5 cm periosteal chondroma of the proximal humerus. The recommended treatment is:
o: Marginal en bloc excision including the underlying cortex
items.e: Excision with the underlying saucerised cortex has a low recurrence rate; shelling out the cartilage alone risks recurrence.

items.q: Chondroblastoma of the proximal humeral epiphysis has which eponym?
items.e: Codman described the 'epiphyseal chondromatous giant cell tumour' of the proximal humerus, now chondroblastoma.

items.q: A 15-year-old has a 2 cm lytic lesion in the proximal tibial epiphysis. MRI shows marrow and soft tissue oedema far beyond the lesion with periosteal reaction. This disproportionate oedema is most typical of:
items.e: Chondroblastoma characteristically shows extensive perilesional oedema on MRI, out of proportion to its small size, which can mimic infection.

items.q: A chondroblastoma of the femoral head shows fluid-fluid levels on MRI. This indicates:
items.e: Secondary ABC change occurs in roughly 15–30% of chondroblastomas and is associated with higher local recurrence.

items.q: The characteristic histological features of chondroblastoma include:
o: Physaliferous cells in a myxoid matrix
Polygonal cells with grooved 'coffee-bean' nuclei and pericellular 'chicken-wire' calcification
Small round blue cells with CD99 positivity
Stellate cells in lobules with hypercellular peripheries
items.e: Coffee-bean nuclei and chicken-wire calcification, with osteoclast-like giant cells, characterise chondroblastoma; stellate lobules describe chondromyxoid fibroma.

items.q: After extended curettage, the reported local recurrence rate of chondroblastoma is about:
items.e: Recurrence is roughly 10–20%, higher in the pelvis, hip, talus and with secondary ABC, which is why adjuvants and a careful approach are used.

items.q: In a 13-year-old with a chondroblastoma of the distal femoral epiphysis, the main technical priority during curettage is to:
o: Excise the lesion en bloc with the knee joint
Use radiotherapy as the primary treatment
Fill the cavity with bone cement through the articular surface
Protect the physis and articular cartilage while achieving thorough curettage
items.e: Extended curettage through a metaphyseal or cortical window with burring and adjuvants aims to clear tumour without damaging the growth plate or joint surface.

items.q: In older adults, chondroblastoma arising outside long-bone epiphyses classically involves the:
items.e: In older patients chondroblastoma often affects the hindfoot bones (talus, calcaneus), which behave as epiphyseal equivalents.

items.q: Which benign cartilage tumour typically shows little or no visible matrix calcification on radiographs?
items.e: Chondromyxoid fibroma is usually purely lytic with a scalloped sclerotic rim; visible calcification is uncommon, unlike other cartilage tumours.

items.q: Histology of chondromyxoid fibroma typically shows:
o: Abundant hyaline cartilage with no myxoid change
Lobules with hypocellular centres and hypercellular peripheries of stellate and spindle cells
items.e: CMF lobules have myxoid/chondroid hypocellular centres and cellular peripheries; it can mimic chondrosarcoma histologically.

items.q: Among primary malignant bone tumours, chondrosarcoma ranks:
items.e: Chondrosarcoma accounts for roughly 20–30% of primary malignant bone tumours, second to osteosarcoma (myeloma excluded as a marrow neoplasm).

items.q: The most common site of conventional chondrosarcoma is the:
items.e: Chondrosarcoma favours the pelvis, followed by the proximal femur, proximal humerus, ribs and scapula; hand lesions are rare.

items.q: Conventional chondrosarcoma responds poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy mainly because of:
o: Low mitotic rate, poor vascularity and abundant extracellular matrix
items.e: Slow cell turnover, poor blood supply and a dense matrix barrier limit drug delivery and radiosensitivity, so surgery is the mainstay.

items.q: A 62-year-old has a femoral cartilage lesion with rings-and-arcs calcification and an adjacent purely lytic, cortex-destroying zone. Where should the biopsy be directed?
o: The calcified area, which is most representative
items.e: A lytic area within a calcified cartilage tumour suggests a dedifferentiated, high-grade component; sampling it avoids undergrading.

items.q: On MRI, hyaline cartilage tumours such as chondrosarcoma typically show:
o: Lobulated very high T2 signal with peripheral and septal ('ring-and-arc') enhancement
items.e: High water content gives cartilage lobules very bright T2 signal, and contrast outlines lobule margins and septa.

items.q: A 45-year-old has a 4 cm atypical cartilaginous tumour of the distal femur confined to bone, without soft-tissue extension. Commonly accepted surgical treatment is:
o: Extended intralesional curettage with local adjuvant and filling of the cavity
items.e: Intracompartmental appendicular ACT can be treated by extended curettage with burr and adjuvant (phenol, cryotherapy), with low recurrence and better function than resection.

items.q: In the Enneking-Dunham classification of pelvic resections, zone II refers to the:
items.e: Zone I is ilium, II periacetabular, III pubis/ischium (obturator ring) and IV the sacral extension; zone II resection needs reconstruction or leaves a flail hip.

items.q: A chondrosarcoma of the skull base cannot be resected with adequate margins. The preferred form of radiotherapy is:
items.e: Because chondrosarcoma is radioresistant, high-dose particle therapy (protons or carbon ions) is used for inoperable or incompletely resected skull base and spinal tumours.

items.q: Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is characterised by which gene fusion?
items.e: HEY1-NCOA2 is the characteristic fusion; EWSR1-FLI1 is Ewing sarcoma, a key histological differential since both show small round cells and CD99.

items.q: The typical 5-year survival of dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is about:
items.e: Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, with a high-grade non-cartilaginous component, has the worst prognosis of the chondrosarcoma subtypes.

items.q: The most common site of distant metastasis from chondrosarcoma is the:
items.e: Chondrosarcoma spreads haematogenously, mainly to the lungs; nodal spread is rare.

items.q: Long-term follow-up (10 years or more) is advised after resection of chondrosarcoma because:
o: Local recurrence and lung metastases can occur many years later
Most patients develop a second primary
items.e: Late recurrence and late pulmonary metastases are characteristic, so surveillance continues for a decade or longer.

items.q: After intralesional curettage of a grade 2 chondrosarcoma of the proximal femur, a local recurrence develops. A particular danger of such recurrence is that:
o: The recurrent tumour may be of a higher grade
items.e: Recurrent chondrosarcoma may show higher grade, which is why grade 2–3 tumours need wide en bloc resection at the first operation.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of grade 3 conventional chondrosarcomas metastasise?
items.e: Metastases are rare in grade 1, occur in about 10–30% of grade 2 and in up to about 70% of grade 3 tumours.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a lytic lesion of the femoral head confirmed as clear cell chondrosarcoma. The appropriate surgery is:
o: Wide en bloc resection with reconstruction
items.e: Clear cell chondrosarcoma recurs frequently after curettage, so wide en bloc resection (e.g. proximal femoral replacement) is recommended, with long follow-up.

items.q: Which subtype of chondrosarcoma is treated with Ewing-type chemotherapy in addition to wide resection?
items.e: Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma has a small round cell component that is chemosensitive, so Ewing-type regimens are used.

items.q: Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma arising in the cap of an osteochondroma is usually:
o: Low grade and treated with wide excision
items.e: Most secondary peripheral chondrosarcomas are low grade; wide en bloc excision, not shelling out, is the treatment.

items.q: Primary synovial chondromatosis most commonly involves the:
items.e: It is typically monoarticular in adults, with the knee commonest, then hip, elbow and shoulder.

items.q: A 40-year-old with primary synovial chondromatosis of the knee has symptomatic loose bodies and active nodular synovium. The standard treatment is:
items.e: Removing loose bodies with synovectomy (arthroscopic or open) reduces recurrence (about 10–20%) compared with loose body removal alone.

items.q: The OTA Open Fracture Classification grades five domains. Which of the following is one of them?
items.e: OTA-OFC grades skin, muscle, arterial injury, contamination and bone loss, and is more reproducible than Gustilo-Anderson. Fracture morphology is classified separately by the AO/OTA system.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A man is shot in the forearm with a low-velocity handgun and has an undisplaced ulnar shaft fracture with small entry and exit wounds and no neurovascular deficit. The most appropriate management is:
o: Local wound care with a short antibiotic course and treating the fracture on its own merits
Formal open debridement of the whole bullet track as for a Gustilo IIIB injury
Mandatory exploration to retrieve all bullet fragments
items.e: Low-velocity gunshot fractures behave like low-grade open fractures and are usually managed with wound care, short antibiotics and standard fracture care. Extensive debridement is reserved for high-velocity or close-range shotgun injuries.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A retained bullet lying within the knee joint after a low-velocity gunshot wound should be removed mainly because of the risk of:
o: Bullet migration into the popliteal artery
Lead synovitis, mechanical cartilage damage and systemic lead toxicity
items.e: Synovial fluid dissolves lead, causing lead arthropathy and occasionally plumbism, and the fragment abrades cartilage. Extra-articular fragments in soft tissue can usually be left.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: High-velocity rifle wounds cause far more tissue damage than handgun wounds of the same calibre mainly because of:
o: Heat from the bullet sterilising the track
Temporary cavitation from the high kinetic energy transferred to tissue
items.e: Kinetic energy rises with the square of velocity, and its transfer creates a temporary cavity that damages tissue well beyond the visible track. Such injuries are treated as Gustilo type III with extensive debridement.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A gunshot passes through the descending colon and then fractures the iliac wing. Appropriate orthopaedic management of the bone wound is:
o: A single dose of cefazolin with no surgery
Observation alone as for any low-velocity wound
Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negative and anaerobic organisms with debridement of the bony track
items.e: A missile that passes through bowel before bone carries faecal organisms into the fracture, so broad-spectrum cover and debridement are needed. The usual low-velocity protocol does not apply.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: After reduction of a knee dislocation, the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable but the ankle-brachial index is 0.75. The next step is:
items.e: An ABI under 0.9 after knee dislocation indicates possible popliteal artery injury and requires arterial imaging. A palpable pulse does not exclude an intimal tear.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A Gustilo IIIC open tibial fracture presents with a pale foot 4 hours after injury. The usual sequence in theatre is:
o: Definitive vein graft first, then manipulation and external fixation
Temporary vascular shunt, then skeletal stabilisation, then definitive vascular repair
Internal fixation first, then vascular repair whenever the bone is stable
Fasciotomy and wound closure, with vascular repair delayed to 48 hours
items.e: A shunt restores perfusion quickly, so the skeleton can be stabilised at length without endangering a definitive repair; vascular repair then follows, usually with prophylactic fasciotomy. Repairing the artery first risks disruption during later bony manipulation.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: After revascularisation of a limb that has been ischaemic for 6 hours, which step is usually recommended at the same operation?
o: Application of a tight circumferential cast
Prophylactic fasciotomy of the involved compartments
Elevation of the limb well above heart level
items.e: Reperfusion causes muscle swelling and a high risk of compartment syndrome, so prophylactic fasciotomy is advised after prolonged (over about 4-6 hours) ischaemia. Elevation reduces perfusion pressure and is avoided.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: When measuring intracompartmental pressure in a suspected acute compartment syndrome with a tibial shaft fracture, the catheter tip should be placed:
o: At the ankle, as far from the fracture as possible
In the subcutaneous tissue over the fracture
Within about 5 cm of the fracture level
items.e: Pressure is highest near the fracture, so readings are taken within about 5 cm of it, in the anterior and deep posterior compartments. Readings far from the zone of injury underestimate the pressure.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A patient under general anaesthesia for tibial nailing has an intraoperative diastolic pressure of 50 mmHg (pre-operative diastolic 78 mmHg) and an anterior compartment pressure of 35 mmHg. There are no clinical signs to assess. The correct interpretation is:
o: Use the pre-operative diastolic: delta pressure 43 mmHg, so fasciotomy is not indicated on this reading
Use the intraoperative diastolic: delta 15 mmHg, so immediate fasciotomy
Any reading over 30 mmHg requires fasciotomy regardless of blood pressure
Pressure cannot be measured under anaesthesia
items.e: Anaesthesia lowers diastolic pressure transiently, and calculating delta with intraoperative values can lead to unnecessary fasciotomy; the pre-operative diastolic is used. Here delta is 78 - 35 = 43 mmHg, above the 30 mmHg threshold, so the pressure is monitored after surgery.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: While preparing a patient with a suspected acute compartment syndrome of the leg for fasciotomy, the limb should be positioned:
o: At the level of the heart
items.e: Elevation lowers arterial pressure in the limb and reduces the perfusion gradient, worsening ischaemia. Dressings are split to skin and the limb is kept at heart level.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In acute compartment syndrome of the leg, early sensory loss in the first dorsal web space indicates involvement of which compartment?
items.e: The deep peroneal nerve runs in the anterior compartment and supplies the first web space. Lateral compartment pressure affects the superficial peroneal nerve over the dorsum of the foot.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A young man with a tibial fracture has severe pain on passive toe flexion and a tense leg, but strong dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. This means:
o: There must be an associated arterial injury
Only chronic exertional compartment syndrome is possible
Compartment syndrome is still possible because pulses usually persist until late
items.e: Compartment pressure that compromises capillary perfusion is far below systolic arterial pressure, so distal pulses remain until very late. Loss of pulses suggests a late stage or an arterial injury.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: During the anterolateral incision of a two-incision leg fasciotomy, the nerve at greatest risk is the:
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve runs in the lateral compartment and pierces the fascia in the distal third, near the intermuscular septum. The saphenous nerve is at risk with the posteromedial incision.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The posteromedial incision of a two-incision leg fasciotomy, made about 2 cm behind the medial tibial border, places which structures at risk?
o: Saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein
Sural nerve and small saphenous vein
items.e: The great saphenous vein and saphenous nerve lie in the subcutaneous tissue near the posteromedial border and should be identified and retracted. The superficial peroneal nerve lies on the lateral side.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: For acute compartment syndrome of the thigh, a single lateral incision decompresses which compartments?
o: Anterior and posterior, through the lateral intermuscular septum
items.e: The lateral approach releases the anterior compartment and, through the lateral intermuscular septum, the posterior compartment. The medial (adductor) compartment needs a separate medial incision if involved.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: How many osteofascial compartments are classically described in the hand for compartment syndrome release?
items.e: The hand has 4 dorsal interossei, 3 palmar interossei, thenar, hypothenar and adductor pollicis compartments. They are released through dorsal incisions over the 2nd and 4th metacarpals plus thenar and hypothenar incisions.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: Acute compartment syndrome of the foot most typically follows:
o: A calcaneal fracture or crush injury
items.e: High-energy calcaneal fractures and crush injuries (also Lisfranc injuries) cause foot compartment syndrome; the calcaneal compartment is commonly involved. Missed cases lead to claw toes and chronic pain.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In forearm fasciotomy for acute compartment syndrome, the volar curvilinear incision is usually extended to also release the:
o: Extensor retinaculum and first dorsal compartment
Lacertus fibrosus proximally and the carpal tunnel distally
Arcade of Struthers and cubital tunnel
items.e: The volar Henry-type incision runs from medial to the biceps tendon to the palm, dividing the lacertus fibrosus and the transverse carpal ligament. A dorsal incision is added if the mobile wad or dorsal compartment remains tight.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A man is found 4 days after a crush injury to his leg with a firm, insensate, paralysed leg and established muscle necrosis. Regarding fasciotomy:
o: Fasciotomy should be done through a single small incision
Fasciotomy is generally not advised; manage systemically and plan later reconstruction or amputation
Fasciotomy should be delayed until creatine kinase normalises, then performed
items.e: Opening established dead muscle converts closed necrosis into open infected necrosis, with high infection and amputation rates. Treatment focuses on renal protection and later management of contracture.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: For a moderate established Volkmann ischaemic contracture of the forearm, the procedure that detaches the flexor-pronator origin from the medial epicondyle and ulna and slides it distally is the:
items.e: The flexor origin slide lengthens the contracted flexors as a unit. The Steindler flexorplasty moves the origin proximally to restore elbow flexion, the opposite direction.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the Pedowitz criteria for chronic exertional compartment syndrome, the 1-minute post-exercise compartment pressure that supports the diagnosis is:
items.e: Pedowitz criteria are a resting pressure of 15 mmHg or more, 30 mmHg or more at 1 minute after exercise, or 20 mmHg or more at 5 minutes. Any one supports the diagnosis with a typical history.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A man trapped under rubble for 10 hours with a crushed thigh is about to be freed. The most immediate life-threatening complication when the compression is released is:
items.e: Release washes potassium, myoglobin and acid from necrotic muscle into the circulation; hyperkalaemic arrhythmia can kill within minutes, so IV fluids should start before extrication. Renal failure from myoglobin develops over hours to days, and calcium falls rather than rises.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In the fluid resuscitation of crush syndrome, the usual urine output target is about:
items.e: Generous saline aims for a high urine output (about 200-300 ml/hour) to flush myoglobin and prevent acute kidney injury. 0.5 ml/kg/hour is the routine resuscitation target and is too low here.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: In patients with haemodynamically unstable pelvic ring fractures, the most common source of haemorrhage is:
o: The posterior venous plexus and cancellous fracture surfaces
items.e: About 80-90% of pelvic bleeding is venous or from bone, which is controlled by binder, fixation and preperitoneal packing. Arterial bleeding, most often from the superior gluteal artery, is a minority and is treated by angioembolisation.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A patient with a pelvic fracture has a contrast blush on CT indicating arterial bleeding and is transiently responsive to fluids. The preferred definitive haemorrhage-control method is:
o: Skeletal traction through the distal femur
items.e: A contrast blush indicates arterial extravasation, best treated by selective angioembolisation. Binders and packing mainly control venous and bony bleeding.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: When resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for isolated pelvic haemorrhage, the balloon is placed in:
o: Zone I, the descending thoracic aorta
Zone III, the infrarenal aorta above the bifurcation
Zone II, between the coeliac axis and the renal arteries
The external iliac artery on the injured side
items.e: Zone III occlusion controls pelvic and junctional bleeding while preserving visceral perfusion. Zone I is for intra-abdominal haemorrhage, and Zone II is a no-occlusion zone.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A man with a tetanus-prone open fracture contaminated with soil does not know his immunisation history. Tetanus prophylaxis should be:
o: Tetanus vaccine plus human tetanus immunoglobulin
No prophylaxis if the wound is debrided within 6 hours
items.e: With an unknown or incomplete history and a tetanus-prone wound, active immunisation with a vaccine and passive immunisation with immunoglobulin are both given. Debridement does not replace prophylaxis.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A crushed-limb patient has dark urine, and a urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. This pattern suggests:
items.e: The haem reaction on dipstick also detects myoglobin, so a positive test without red cells points to myoglobinuria. A raised creatine kinase confirms rhabdomyolysis.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: The fracture most commonly complicated by acute compartment syndrome is:
items.e: Tibial diaphyseal fractures account for the largest share of acute compartment syndrome (about 2-10% of these fractures), especially in young men. Open tibial fractures can still develop it.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: A 22-year-old with a Gustilo II open tibial fracture has increasing leg pain on passive toe stretch 12 hours after nailing. Which statement is correct?
o: An open wound excludes compartment syndrome
Open fractures can still develop compartment syndrome because the wound does not decompress all compartments
Compartment syndrome only occurs after closed fractures
Pain on stretch is expected after nailing and needs no assessment
items.e: Compartment syndrome occurs in a recognised proportion of open tibial fractures, because a small wound decompresses at most one compartment. Clinical suspicion and pressure measurement are needed.
items.sub: polytrauma, open fractures and compartment syndrome

items.q: On a short-TE MRI sequence of the shoulder, the supraspinatus tendon shows intermediate signal near its insertion that disappears on the long-TE T2-weighted images of the same region. The most likely explanation is:
o: Magic angle artefact from fibres oriented at about 55 degrees to the main magnetic field
Chemical shift artefact at the fat-tendon interface
Calcific tendinitis in the resorptive phase
items.e: Magic angle effect causes increased signal on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE) in tendons angled about 55 degrees to B0 and disappears on long-TE T2 images; a true tear remains bright on T2.

items.q: MRI is requested to look for loosening and soft-tissue reaction around a cobalt-chrome hip arthroplasty. Which technical change most reduces metal susceptibility artefact?
o: Using gradient-echo sequences with chemical fat saturation
Moving from a 1.5 T to a 3 T scanner
Using fast spin-echo with STIR, wide receiver bandwidth and metal artefact reduction sequences such as MAVRIC or SEMAC
Increasing slice thickness to improve signal-to-noise
items.e: Susceptibility artefact is reduced by fast spin echo, STIR instead of chemical fat-sat, high receiver bandwidth, thin slices, lower field strength and MARS techniques; GRE, fat-sat and 3 T all worsen it.

items.q: Gadolinium-based contrast agents produce enhancement on MRI chiefly because they:
o: Lengthen T2 relaxation so enhancing tissue is bright on T2
Shorten T1 relaxation so enhancing tissue becomes bright on T1-weighted images
Increase proton density in the extracellular space
Attenuate the radiofrequency pulse in vascular tissue
items.e: Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens T1, so enhancing tissue is bright on T1 images, usually viewed with fat suppression.

items.q: A patient with persistent leg pain 18 months after L4-5 discectomy has a contrast MRI. Epidural tissue at the operated level enhances homogeneously throughout after gadolinium. This favours:
items.e: Scar is vascular and enhances uniformly; a recurrent disc is avascular and enhances only at its periphery, the key use of gadolinium after spinal surgery.

items.q: In a patient with severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2), the main concern with older linear gadolinium agents is:
o: Contrast-induced acute tubular necrosis similar to iodinated contrast
items.e: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is linked to linear gadolinium agents in severe renal impairment; macrocyclic agents are safer.

items.q: A welder needs an MRI of his knee. Before scanning, which screening step is most important?
o: Orbital radiographs to exclude an intraocular metallic foreign body
items.e: A metallic foreign body in the orbit is a contraindication to MRI because it can move and injure the eye; metal workers are screened with orbital radiographs.

items.q: During musculoskeletal ultrasound of the Achilles tendon, a segment appears hypoechoic only when the probe is tilted, and becomes normally fibrillar and echogenic when the beam is perpendicular to the fibres. This is:
items.e: Anisotropy makes tendons look falsely hypoechoic when the beam is not perpendicular to the fibres, mimicking tendinopathy; correcting the probe angle restores normal echogenicity.

items.q: For ultrasound-guided injection of the carpal tunnel, the most suitable transducer is:
items.e: Higher frequency gives better resolution but less penetration, ideal for superficial structures such as the median nerve; low-frequency curvilinear probes are for deep structures like the adult hip.

items.q: Technetium-99m used in bone scintigraphy has which physical characteristics?
o: Half-life 6 hours, pure gamma emitter of 140 keV
Half-life 67 hours, gamma emitter of 171 and 245 keV
Half-life 78 hours, beta and gamma emitter
items.e: Tc-99m has a 6-hour half-life and emits a 140 keV gamma photon, ideal for gamma cameras; 67 hours is indium-111 and 110 minutes is fluorine-18.

items.q: A three-phase bone scan of a diabetic foot shows increased activity on the flow and blood-pool phases but diffuse, non-focal activity on the delayed images. This pattern indicates:
items.e: Cellulitis is hot on phases 1 and 2 but not focal on the delayed bone phase; osteomyelitis is positive on all three phases with focal delayed uptake.

items.q: In suspected vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis where MRI is contraindicated, labelled leukocyte scintigraphy is unreliable. Which nuclear medicine study is preferred?
o: Tc-99m sulfur colloid marrow scan alone
Gallium-67 citrate scan or F-18 FDG PET
items.e: Labelled WBC scans often show photopenic areas in spinal infection; gallium-67 (often with SPECT) or FDG-PET is preferred for spondylodiscitis.

items.q: A 65-year-old man with a lytic lesion and anaemia has a normal Tc-99m MDP bone scan despite multiple lytic lesions on skeletal survey. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Myeloma lesions lack osteoblastic activity and are classically cold or normal on bone scan, so a skeletal survey, low-dose whole-body CT or MRI is used instead.

items.q: For suspected periprosthetic joint infection, the most accurate nuclear medicine technique is a combined labelled leukocyte and Tc-99m sulfur colloid marrow scan. Infection is diagnosed when:
o: Both scans show matching (congruent) uptake around the implant
The leukocyte scan shows uptake with no corresponding uptake on the marrow scan
Uptake is present only on the marrow scan
items.e: Incongruent uptake (WBC activity without matching marrow activity) indicates infection; congruent uptake reflects displaced or reactive marrow.

items.q: Which is the strongest single risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip in a newborn?
o: Breech presentation, especially frank breech with the hips flexed and knees extended
items.e: Breech positioning, particularly frank breech with hamstring tension across extended knees, is the strongest single risk factor. First-born status and oligohydramnios raise risk but less strongly.

items.q: DDH affects the left hip in about 60% of unilateral cases. The usual explanation is that:
o: The left femoral head ossifies later than the right
In the common left occiput anterior position the left hip is held adducted against the maternal sacrum
The left acetabulum is normally shallower at birth
The left hip receives a smaller share of the fetal circulation
items.e: In the left occiput anterior fetal position, the left thigh lies against the maternal lumbosacral spine and is forced into adduction. Ossification timing and blood supply do not differ by side.

items.q: A newborn has a fixed, irreducible hip dislocation with stiff joints and absent skin creases at several joints. The hip dislocation is best described as:
o: Typical DDH that will respond to a Pavlik harness
Teratologic, typically associated with arthrogryposis and needing early open reduction
items.e: Teratologic dislocations occur in utero with conditions such as arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele and Larsen syndrome; they are irreducible and resist harness treatment. Typical DDH is reducible in the newborn.

items.q: In the pathoanatomy of a dislocated hip in DDH, the 'pulvinar' refers to:
o: The inverted labrum at the acetabular rim
The hourglass constriction of the capsule
A false acetabulum on the ilium
Fibrofatty tissue filling the floor of the acetabulum
items.e: The pulvinar is fibrofatty tissue occupying the acetabular fossa and blocks deep seating of the head. The inverted labrum is the limbus; the hourglass capsule is caused by the iliopsoas.

items.q: Which of the following is an INTRA-articular obstacle to concentric reduction of a dislocated hip in DDH?
items.e: Intra-articular obstacles are the inverted labrum, hypertrophied ligamentum teres, pulvinar, transverse acetabular ligament and contracted inferior capsule. The iliopsoas and adductor longus are extra-articular.

items.q: In a child with bilateral dislocated hips from DDH, the Galeazzi (Allis) sign is typically:
o: Strongly positive on the side with the higher dislocation only
Negative, because both femora appear equally short
Positive bilaterally with knees at different heights
The most reliable sign of bilateral disease
items.e: The Galeazzi sign compares knee heights with hips and knees flexed; symmetrical bilateral dislocation gives equal knee levels, so the test is falsely negative. Limited abduction and a waddling gait are clues to bilateral disease.

items.q: The Klisic test for a dislocated hip is positive when a line drawn from the greater trochanter through the anterior superior iliac spine:
items.e: Normally the line through the tip of the greater trochanter and ASIS points at or above the umbilicus. A proximally displaced trochanter in a dislocated hip makes it pass below the umbilicus.

items.q: The Ortolani manoeuvre in the newborn is performed by:
o: Adducting the flexed hip while pushing posteriorly to dislocate a located head
Extending the hip and internally rotating it to feel a click
Applying axial pressure along the femur with the hip extended
Gently abducting the flexed hip while lifting the greater trochanter forwards, reducing a dislocated head
items.e: Ortolani reduces a dislocated hip ('out to in') with abduction and anterior lift of the trochanter. Barlow uses adduction with posterior pressure to show that a located hip is dislocatable.

items.q: Barlow and Ortolani tests usually become negative after about 3 months of age in a dislocated hip because:
o: Soft tissues contract and the dislocation becomes fixed and irreducible
The femoral head has ossified and can no longer pass the rim
The acetabulum has remodelled to normal depth
The infant's muscle tone abolishes any clunk
items.e: With time the adductors, iliopsoas and capsule tighten, so the dislocated head can no longer be reduced or dislocated by these manoeuvres. Limited abduction then becomes the key sign.

items.q: During newborn hip screening, a high-pitched 'click' without any sensation of the hip moving in or out of the socket most likely represents:
o: A benign soft-tissue click that is not significant on its own
items.e: Isolated high-pitched clicks arise from ligaments or tendons and do not indicate instability. A clunk of the head entering or leaving the acetabulum is the significant finding.

items.q: In the Graf ultrasound method, the beta angle measures the:
o: Bony roof of the acetabulum relative to the iliac baseline
Percentage of femoral head covered by the acetabulum
Cartilaginous (labral) roof of the acetabulum relative to the iliac baseline
Neck-shaft angle of the proximal femur
items.e: Beta is the angle between the baseline and the cartilaginous roof line through the labrum; it rises as the head displaces. Alpha measures the bony roof, and head coverage is the Terjesen/Morin measure.

items.q: An infant hip ultrasound shows an alpha angle of 46° and a beta angle of 82°. The Graf classification is:
items.e: Alpha 43-49° with beta over 77° is type D, a decentring hip that is about to dislocate. Alpha 43-49° with beta under 77° would be IIc; type IV has alpha under 43° with an inverted labrum.

items.q: A 5-week-old has a Graf ultrasound with an alpha angle of 45° and a beta angle of 70°. The classification and appropriate management are:
o: Type IIc (critical); start a Pavlik harness
Type IIa; repeat ultrasound at 12 weeks
Type III; immediate closed reduction under anaesthesia
items.e: Alpha 43-49° with beta under 77° is the critical type IIc hip, which is treated in a Pavlik harness. Type IIa (alpha 50-59° under 3 months) is observed with repeat scanning.

items.q: In the Graf classification, what distinguishes a type IV hip from a type III hip, given that both have an alpha angle under 43°?
o: Type IV has a beta angle under 55°
In type IV the labrum is inverted (pushed down into the joint), whereas in type III the cartilaginous roof is pushed upwards
Type IV is reducible on dynamic stress, type III is not
Type IV is defined by age over 3 months
items.e: Both are dislocated, but in type III the head displaces the cartilage roof upwards, while in type IV the labrum is inverted between head and acetabulum, which predicts poorer closed treatment results.

items.q: A 4-month-old has an ultrasound alpha angle of 55° with a stable hip. This is classified and managed as:
o: Graf IIb (delayed ossification beyond 3 months); treat in a Pavlik harness
items.e: Alpha 50-59° is type IIa only under 3 months of age; beyond 3 months it is type IIb, regarded as true dysplasia and treated with a harness.

items.q: Ultrasound is the preferred imaging for DDH only up to about 4-6 months of age mainly because after that:
o: The hip becomes too deep to image
The alpha angle normally exceeds 60° in all hips
The femoral head ossific nucleus appears and blocks the ultrasound view of the acetabulum
items.e: Once the femoral head ossific nucleus forms, it casts an acoustic shadow over the medial acetabulum and radiographs become more informative.

items.q: On dynamic ultrasound of the infant hip (Terjesen/Morin method), femoral head coverage by the bony acetabulum is considered abnormal when it is below:
items.e: Bony coverage of under 50% of the femoral head on coronal ultrasound is regarded as abnormal. Normal hips show coverage of about 50-60% or more.

items.q: Under the UK NIPE selective screening programme, which baby should have a hip ultrasound by about 6 weeks of age even with a normal clinical examination?
o: A baby born by elective caesarean in cephalic presentation
A baby in breech presentation at or after 36 weeks of gestation
A baby with a single sacral dimple
A baby with a unilateral talipes calcaneovalgus only
items.e: NIPE selects babies with breech presentation at or after 36 weeks (regardless of delivery mode) or a first-degree family history of childhood hip problems for ultrasound by 6 weeks.

items.q: Compared with selective screening, universal ultrasound screening of newborn hips (as in Austria and Germany) is associated with:
o: Lower treatment rates and fewer late cases
Higher rates of avascular necrosis from late diagnosis
Higher rates of treatment, with possibly fewer late-presenting cases
No change in the number of infants treated
items.e: Universal scanning detects many immature hips that would resolve, increasing treatment, while possibly reducing late diagnosis. The evidence for reduced late dislocation is not conclusive.

items.q: On the AP pelvic radiograph of an infant, Hilgenreiner's line is drawn:
o: Vertically from the lateral edge of the acetabular roof
Along the inferior border of the femoral neck and superior pubic ramus
From the centre of the femoral head to the lateral acetabular edge
items.e: Hilgenreiner's line passes through both triradiate cartilages. Perkin's line is the vertical from the lateral acetabular margin, and Shenton's line runs along the femoral neck and superior pubic ramus.

items.q: In a normal infant hip on an AP radiograph, the femoral head ossific nucleus (or medial metaphyseal beak) lies in which quadrant formed by Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines?
items.e: A normally located head lies below Hilgenreiner's line and medial to Perkin's line. Lateral and superior displacement indicates subluxation or dislocation.

items.q: In a newborn, the acetabular index is generally considered abnormal (dysplastic) when it exceeds approximately:
items.e: The normal acetabular index is under about 30° at birth, falling to under 20-25° by around 2 years. Higher values indicate a shallow, dysplastic acetabulum.

items.q: In a child older than about 5 years, a Wiberg centre-edge angle below which value indicates acetabular dysplasia?
items.e: The Wiberg CE angle becomes reliable from about age 5; values below about 20° indicate dysplasia, with normal values above 20-25°.

items.q: During closed reduction of a hip in DDH, an arthrogram shows a medial dye pool of 3 mm with the hip stable in the safe zone. This indicates:
o: Interposed soft tissue requiring open reduction
An acceptable concentric reduction that can be held in a spica
items.e: A medial dye pool under about 5 mm signifies acceptable concentric reduction. A pool over 5-7 mm suggests interposed tissue and is an indication for open reduction.

items.q: On a hip arthrogram in an infant with DDH, the 'rose thorn' sign indicates:
o: A normal, everted labrum outlined by contrast at the acetabular rim
items.e: The rose thorn is the thin contrast outline of a normal labrum lying over the head. An inverted limbus appears as a filling defect between the head and acetabulum.

items.q: After closed reduction and hip spica application for DDH, the preferred imaging to confirm concentric reduction while avoiding radiation is:
items.e: MRI (or limited-sequence CT) through the spica confirms reduction; MRI is preferred as it avoids ionising radiation. A plain radiograph is unreliable through a cast and in an unossified head.

items.q: In a correctly fitted Pavlik harness, the posterior (abduction) straps should be:
o: Tightened to hold the hips in maximum abduction
Removed entirely after the first week
Loose enough to prevent adduction without forcing the hips into abduction
Used to hold the hips in extension
items.e: The posterior straps block adduction while gravity allows abduction within the safe zone; forced abduction risks avascular necrosis. The anterior straps hold about 100° of flexion.

items.q: Excessive hip flexion (over about 120°) in a Pavlik harness can cause, besides femoral nerve palsy, which type of hip dislocation?
o: Superolateral dislocation into a false acetabulum
items.e: Hyperflexion drives the head inferiorly towards the obturator foramen. Insufficient flexion, by contrast, fails to reduce the hip.

items.q: An infant in a Pavlik harness develops weakness of the arm. The likely cause is:
o: Brachial plexus palsy from shoulder straps that are too tight
Femoral nerve palsy from excess flexion
Cervical cord compression from the chest strap
items.e: Over-tight shoulder straps can compress the brachial plexus. Femoral nerve palsy, from hyperflexion, affects knee extension.

items.q: 'Pavlik harness disease' refers to:
o: Erosion of the posterior acetabular wall from prolonged harness use with a persistently dislocated head
Avascular necrosis caused by forced abduction
items.e: Continuing the harness when the head remains posteriorly dislocated flattens the posterior acetabulum, making later reduction harder. Hence the harness is stopped if the hip is not reduced by 3-4 weeks.

items.q: Which feature predicts FAILURE of Pavlik harness treatment in an infant with DDH?
o: A dislocated hip that is Ortolani-negative (irreducible)
items.e: Harness failure is more likely with irreducible (Ortolani-negative) dislocation, Graf IV hips, bilateral dislocation and starting after about 7 weeks. Barlow-positive and IIc hips respond well.

items.q: The Pavlik harness is generally the first-line treatment for DDH in infants up to about what age?
items.e: The harness works in infants up to about 6 months; beyond that, a stronger and more mobile child usually needs closed reduction and spica.

items.q: During closed reduction for DDH, percutaneous adductor longus tenotomy is performed mainly to:
o: Widen the safe zone so the hip can be held reduced with less abduction
Allow the hip to be held in maximum abduction
items.e: Releasing the tight adductor increases maximum abduction and therefore the Ramsey safe zone, reducing the need for forced abduction that causes avascular necrosis.

items.q: Regarding preliminary skin traction before closed reduction of a dislocated hip in DDH, current evidence shows that:
o: It halves the rate of avascular necrosis
It has not been shown to reduce avascular necrosis or improve reduction and is largely abandoned
It is mandatory in all children over 6 months
It replaces the need for adductor tenotomy
items.e: Prereduction traction was historically used to lower AVN, but studies have not shown a convincing benefit, so it is not routinely used.

items.q: In a 7-month-old with a dislocated hip from DDH and no visible femoral head ossific nucleus, the correct approach to timing of closed reduction is:
o: Delay reduction until the ossific nucleus appears to reduce avascular necrosis
Proceed with reduction; delaying until the ossific nucleus appears is not recommended
Delay until 18 months and perform open reduction
items.e: Most studies show the ossific nucleus has no consistent effect on AVN risk, while delay worsens dysplasia, so reduction should not be postponed.

items.q: After closed reduction for DDH in a 10-month-old, the hip spica is usually maintained for about:
o: 3 months, with a cast change at about 6 weeks, then an abduction brace
items.e: Typically the spica is worn for about 3 months with a change under anaesthesia at 6 weeks, followed by an abduction orthosis while the acetabulum remodels.

items.q: Which arthrographic finding during attempted closed reduction is an indication for open reduction in DDH?
o: A medial dye pool over about 5-7 mm with the hip stable only in extreme abduction
A medial dye pool of 2 mm
A hip stable throughout a wide safe zone
items.e: A wide medial dye pool and the need for excessive abduction indicate interposed tissue and a non-concentric reduction, so open reduction is indicated.

items.q: The Ferguson medial approach for open reduction in DDH differs from the Ludloff approach in that it passes:
o: Anterior to adductor brevis, between it and pectineus
Posterior to adductor brevis, between it and adductor magnus
items.e: Ludloff's approach is anterior to adductor brevis, near pectineus and iliopsoas, whereas Ferguson's goes posterior to adductor brevis. Both are medial approaches used in infants.

items.q: The main advantage of the anterior (Smith-Petersen/bikini) approach over the medial approach for open reduction of a hip in DDH is that it:
o: Avoids any risk to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Gives the most direct access to the transverse acetabular ligament and medial circumflex artery
Allows capsulorrhaphy and a concomitant pelvic osteotomy
Is suitable only for infants under 6 months
items.e: The anterior approach allows plication of the redundant capsule and a pelvic osteotomy, so it suits children over about 12-18 months. The medial approach cannot address the capsule.

items.q: In open reduction of a dislocated hip in a 3-year-old, a femoral shortening osteotomy is added mainly to:
o: Reduce pressure on the reduced femoral head and lower the risk of avascular necrosis and redislocation
items.e: Shortening relieves soft-tissue tension across the reduced hip, lowering AVN and redislocation. Varus and derotation can be added through the same osteotomy if needed.

items.q: A redirectional pelvic osteotomy such as the Salter innominate osteotomy requires which prerequisite?
o: A concentrically reduced, congruent hip with a good range of motion
items.e: Redirection only changes the orientation of the existing acetabulum, so the head must be concentrically reduced and congruent. Incongruent hips need salvage procedures.

items.q: The Salter innominate osteotomy is a single cut through the ilium running from the:
o: Anterior superior iliac spine to the ischial tuberosity
Greater sciatic notch to just above the anterior inferior iliac spine
Triradiate cartilage to the iliac crest
Pubic symphysis to the obturator foramen
items.e: The cut runs from the sciatic notch to the AIIS, and the distal fragment hinges on the pubic symphysis to improve anterolateral coverage.

items.q: The Salter innominate osteotomy can improve the acetabular index by approximately:
items.e: Because it hinges on the symphysis, the Salter osteotomy corrects the acetabular index by about 10-15°. Larger deficiencies need reshaping or triple osteotomies.

items.q: The principal advantage of the Bernese (Ganz) periacetabular osteotomy over a triple innominate osteotomy is that it:
o: Can be done with an open triradiate cartilage
Preserves the posterior column, keeping the pelvic ring stable and allowing early weight bearing
items.e: The PAO keeps the posterior column intact, so the pelvis remains stable and the true pelvis is not narrowed. It is used after triradiate closure, in adolescents and adults.

items.q: A Steel (triple innominate) osteotomy for residual acetabular dysplasia involves osteotomies of the:
o: Ilium only, hinging on the triradiate cartilage
items.e: Triple osteotomy cuts the ilium, ischium and pubis to free the acetabulum for redirection in older children and adolescents.

items.q: An 8-year-old with spastic cerebral palsy has hip subluxation with posterosuperior acetabular deficiency. Which pelvic osteotomy is most suited?
items.e: The Dega is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy hinging on the triradiate cartilage that increases posterolateral coverage, matching the deficiency in neuromuscular dysplasia. The Salter mainly improves anterolateral coverage.

items.q: The Chiari pelvic osteotomy for an incongruent dysplastic hip works by:
o: Redirecting a congruent acetabulum with the symphysis as hinge
Reducing acetabular volume by hinging on the triradiate cartilage
Medially displacing the acetabulum under the ilium so the interposed capsule undergoes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia
Rotating the acetabulum around an intact posterior column
items.e: The Chiari is a salvage osteotomy: the ilium above becomes a roof over the capsule, which converts to fibrocartilage. It does not restore hyaline cartilage coverage.

items.q: A 9-year-old has bilateral high dislocated hips from undiagnosed DDH with no false acetabula and good function. The usual recommendation is:
o: Bilateral open reduction with femoral shortening
Leave the hips unreduced, as function is often better than after failed reduction or avascular necrosis
items.e: Beyond about 8 years for bilateral (about 10 years for unilateral) high dislocations without false acetabula, reduction is usually not attempted; complications of late reduction outweigh benefits.

items.q: In the Kalamchi-MacEwen classification of avascular necrosis after DDH treatment, group II (lateral physeal damage) typically produces:
o: Valgus tilt of the femoral head from lateral growth arrest
Changes in the ossific nucleus only, with no deformity
A short neck with symmetrical trochanteric overgrowth
Complete destruction of the head and physis
items.e: Group II involves the lateral physis, causing lateral tethering and a valgus-tilted head. Group I affects the ossific nucleus only, group III the central physis (coxa breva) and group IV the whole head and physis.

items.q: A 10-year-old has relative greater trochanteric overgrowth and a Trendelenburg gait after avascular necrosis from DDH treatment. A recognised operation is:
o: Greater trochanteric advancement (or epiphysiodesis if younger)
items.e: Trochanteric overgrowth shortens the abductor lever arm; distal and lateral advancement of the trochanter restores tension, and epiphysiodesis can prevent overgrowth in younger children.

items.q: In the Crowe classification of adult DDH, a femoral head subluxed by 75-100% of its height is:
items.e: Crowe grades proximal migration: I under 50%, II 50-75%, III 75-100% and IV over 100% (high dislocation).

items.q: During total hip arthroplasty for a Crowe IV hip, limb lengthening beyond about which amount is associated with a high risk of sciatic nerve palsy, prompting subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy?
items.e: Lengthening beyond about 4 cm risks stretch palsy of the sciatic nerve, so a subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy is used when the cup is placed in the true acetabulum.

items.q: In the Hartofilakidis classification of adult DDH, a 'low dislocation' means:
o: The femoral head articulates with a false acetabulum that partly overlaps the true acetabulum
The head is contained within the true acetabulum despite dysplasia
The head is high on the ilium with no contact with the true acetabulum
The head has migrated medially through the floor
items.e: Hartofilakidis grades dysplasia (head within the true acetabulum), low dislocation (false acetabulum overlapping the true one) and high dislocation (no contact).

items.q: 'Hip-healthy' swaddling of newborns aims to:
o: Hold the hips extended and adducted
Leave the hips free to flex and abduct
Hold the hips in maximum abduction and internal rotation
Immobilise the hips with the knees extended
items.e: Tight swaddling with hips extended and adducted increases DDH risk; allowing flexion and abduction lets the head seat in the acetabulum.

items.q: The low incidence of DDH in many African populations has been attributed mainly to:
o: A low rate of breech delivery
Carrying infants on the back with the hips flexed and abducted
items.e: Carrying infants astride the mother's back keeps the hips flexed and abducted, which favours stability. Cultures that swaddle with extended hips have higher rates.

items.q: An infant has a congenital dislocation of the knee. Which other condition should be specifically screened for?
items.e: Congenital knee dislocation is a 'packaging' condition from intrauterine crowding and has a strong association with DDH, like metatarsus adductus and muscular torticollis.

items.q: Which secondary change of the proximal femur is typical in untreated DDH?
o: Increased femoral anteversion with coxa valga
Shortened femoral neck with coxa vara
items.e: Untreated DDH is associated with increased femoral anteversion and valga, along with an anteverted, shallow acetabulum. Coxa vara is not a feature of typical DDH.

items.q: The most common long-term sequela of DDH in adults is:
o: Early osteoarthritis, a leading cause of hip arthroplasty in younger adults
items.e: Residual dysplasia concentrates load on the acetabular rim, leading to labral tears and early arthritis; DDH is a common indication for THA under 40-50 years.

items.q: In a multicentre RCT of two fixation methods, the next allocation is obtained by telephoning a central computer only after the patient has been enrolled. This step mainly prevents which bias?
items.e: Allocation concealment stops the recruiting surgeon from knowing or influencing which group the next patient enters, preventing selection bias. Blinding (not concealment) addresses performance and detection bias.

items.q: In a surgical RCT where the operating surgeon cannot be blinded, using an independent assessor unaware of group allocation to measure the outcome mainly reduces:
items.e: A blinded outcome assessor prevents the outcome being measured differently between groups (detection bias), the minimum blinding expected in surgical trials.

items.q: Knee flexion (normally distributed) is measured in the same 40 patients before and 6 weeks after a new physiotherapy protocol. The appropriate test to compare the two sets of values is:
items.e: Two related measurements of continuous normally distributed data in the same patients are compared with the paired t-test; the unpaired t-test is for independent groups.

items.q: Length of hospital stay (markedly right-skewed) is compared between two independent groups of hip fracture patients. The appropriate test is:
items.e: Skewed continuous data in two independent groups need a non-parametric test, the Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is for paired data.

items.q: VAS pain scores (ordinal, not normally distributed) are recorded in the same patients before and after a nerve block. Which test is appropriate?
items.e: Paired non-parametric data are analysed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test.

items.q: Mean blood loss (normally distributed) is compared among three independent groups receiving different tranexamic acid regimens. The appropriate initial test is:
items.e: Three or more independent groups of normally distributed continuous data are compared with one-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc tests; repeated t-tests inflate the type I error.

items.q: Oxford knee scores (skewed) are compared among four independent groups of patients receiving different implants. The appropriate test is:
items.e: Kruskal-Wallis is the non-parametric test for three or more independent groups; Friedman is for three or more repeated measures in the same subjects.

items.q: In the same 100 patients, the presence or absence of a positive Lachman test is recorded before and after arthroscopic reconstruction. Which test compares these paired proportions?
items.e: Paired binary (categorical) data in the same subjects are analysed with the McNemar test; chi-square and Fisher's exact assume independent groups.

items.q: Non-normal pain scores are measured in the same patients at 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months after surgery. The appropriate test is:
items.e: Three or more repeated measures of non-parametric data in the same patients are compared with the Friedman test (the parametric equivalent is repeated-measures ANOVA).

items.q: The association between Kellgren-Lawrence grade and WOMAC pain rank in 200 knees is best assessed with:
items.e: Spearman's rho measures association between ordinal or non-normal variables; Pearson's r requires continuous normally distributed data.

items.q: Two surgeons independently classify 80 ankle fractures as Weber A, B or C. Agreement between them, corrected for chance, is measured with:
items.e: Cohen's kappa measures chance-corrected agreement between two observers for categorical data; the ICC is used for continuous measurements.

items.q: Five observers measure the Cobb angle on the same 50 radiographs. Inter-observer reliability of this continuous measurement is best expressed with:
items.e: The ICC quantifies the reliability of continuous measurements such as the Cobb angle; kappa is for categorical data.

items.q: A new smartphone goniometer is compared with a standard goniometer by plotting the difference between the two readings against their mean, with 95% limits of agreement. This is a:
items.e: The Bland-Altman plot assesses agreement between two measurement methods; a correlation coefficient alone can be high even when methods disagree systematically.

items.q: The inter-observer kappa for a fracture classification is 0.52. According to Landis and Koch, this agreement is:
items.e: Kappa 0.41-0.60 is moderate agreement (0.21-0.40 fair, 0.61-0.80 substantial, 0.81-1.00 almost perfect).

items.q: Intra-observer kappa for the Lauge-Hansen classification is reported as 0.74. This is interpreted as:
items.e: On the Landis and Koch scale, kappa 0.61-0.80 indicates substantial agreement.

items.q: In a registry of hemiarthroplasty in patients over 85 years, many patients die before any revision. Using 1 minus Kaplan-Meier survivorship to report cumulative revision rate will:
o: Underestimate revision; the log-rank test is preferred
Give an unbiased estimate because deaths are censored
Overestimate revision; a chi-square test is preferred
Overestimate revision; a cumulative incidence (competing-risk) method is preferred
items.e: Kaplan-Meier treats death as non-informative censoring, so with death as a competing risk it overestimates cumulative revision; the cumulative incidence function (Fine and Gray) is used.

items.q: Two Kaplan-Meier survivorship curves for different cemented stems are compared for a statistically significant difference using the:
items.e: The log-rank test compares two or more survival curves; Cox regression is used when adjustment for covariates is needed.

items.q: Investigators want the risk of revision for a new knee implant adjusted for age, BMI and diagnosis, expressed as a hazard ratio. The appropriate method is:
items.e: Cox proportional hazards regression models time-to-event data while adjusting for covariates and yields hazard ratios.

items.q: A study examines whether diabetes, smoking and obesity independently predict surgical site infection (yes/no). The appropriate multivariable method, which gives adjusted odds ratios, is:
items.e: Logistic regression is used for a binary outcome and gives adjusted odds ratios; linear regression is for a continuous outcome.

items.q: A test for PJI with sensitivity 80% and specificity 90% is applied to 1000 patients with a prevalence of 10%. Its positive predictive value is approximately:
items.e: 100 infected: TP 80, FN 20. 900 uninfected: TN 810, FP 90. PPV = 80/170 = about 47%; low prevalence makes PPV much lower than the specificity.

items.q: A clinical test has sensitivity 80% and specificity 90%. Its positive likelihood ratio is:
items.e: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.8 / 0.1 = 8. The LR- would be 0.2/0.9 = 0.22.

items.q: For a serum marker cut-off with sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.75, the Youden index is:
items.e: Youden index = sensitivity + specificity - 1 = 0.85 + 0.75 - 1 = 0.60; the cut-off with the maximum Youden index is often chosen as optimal.

items.q: On a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, the x-axis represents:
items.e: An ROC curve plots sensitivity (true-positive rate) on the y-axis against 1 - specificity (false-positive rate) on the x-axis across cut-offs.

items.q: A new biomarker for fracture-related infection has an area under the ROC curve of 0.50. This means the test:
items.e: An AUC of 0.5 lies on the diagonal line of no discrimination; 0.8-0.9 is excellent and 1.0 perfect.

items.q: Two diagnostic tests for PJI are combined so that infection is diagnosed only if both are positive (testing in series). Compared with either test alone, this strategy:
items.e: Requiring both tests to be positive reduces false positives (higher specificity) at the cost of missing more true cases (lower sensitivity); parallel testing does the opposite.

items.q: The serum CRP cut-off for diagnosing chronic PJI is lowered from 20 mg/L to 10 mg/L. The expected effect is:
o: No change in sensitivity or specificity
items.e: Lowering the threshold classifies more patients as positive, catching more true infections (sensitivity rises) but creating more false positives (specificity falls).

items.q: A test with very high sensitivity returns a negative result. This result is most useful for:
items.e: SnNout: a highly sensitive test rarely misses disease, so a negative result rules it out; SpPin applies to highly specific tests.

items.q: A study identifies 60 patients with deep infection after TKA and 180 matched patients without infection, then compares prior intra-articular steroid injection. The measure of association reported should be the:
items.e: A case-control study starts from the outcome, so incidence and relative risk cannot be calculated; the odds ratio is the appropriate measure.

items.q: A survey records, at a single time point, how many members of a population currently have symptomatic knee OA. This cross-sectional design measures:
items.e: Cross-sectional studies measure prevalence at one point in time and cannot establish temporal sequence; incidence requires follow-up over time.

items.q: A prospective comparative cohort study of two treatments for scaphoid waist fractures is, by the JBJS hierarchy for therapeutic studies, level:
items.e: Prospective comparative (cohort) studies are level II; retrospective comparative studies and case-control studies are level III.

items.q: A study reviews records of 120 patients treated with plating and 110 treated with nailing for humeral shaft fractures in one hospital over 10 years and compares union rates. Its level of evidence is:
items.e: A retrospective comparative cohort study is level III evidence for therapeutic studies.

items.q: A surgeon reports outcomes of 45 consecutive patients treated with a new tibial plateau plate, without a comparison group. The level of evidence is:
items.e: A case series without a control group is level IV; expert opinion is level V.

items.q: A systematic review pools 9 retrospective comparative studies of hip arthroscopy versus open surgical dislocation. Its level of evidence is:
items.e: A systematic review takes the level of the studies it includes; a review of level III studies is level III.

items.q: Of the Bradford Hill criteria for causation, which one is regarded as essential?
items.e: Temporality, the exposure preceding the outcome, is the only criterion that must be satisfied; the others strengthen but are not essential for a causal inference.

items.q: An observational study uses propensity score matching to compare cemented and uncemented hemiarthroplasty. The main limitation compared with randomisation is that propensity scores:
o: Cannot be used with binary outcomes
Always reduce the sample size to zero
items.e: Propensity scores balance the covariates that were measured; only randomisation balances unknown and unmeasured confounders.

items.q: A trial finds that a new dressing reduces infection markedly in diabetic patients but has no effect in non-diabetics. The varying effect across levels of diabetes is best termed:
items.e: Effect modification is a real difference in treatment effect across subgroups, not a bias; confounding distorts an association through a third variable linked to both exposure and outcome.

items.q: A study performs 10 independent comparisons and applies a Bonferroni correction with an overall alpha of 0.05. The significance threshold for each comparison becomes:
items.e: Bonferroni divides alpha by the number of tests: 0.05/10 = 0.005, limiting the inflation of type I error from multiple comparisons.

items.q: A cohort study reports the relative risk of nonunion in smokers as 1.6 (95% CI 0.9 to 2.8). The correct interpretation is:
o: Smokers have a significantly higher risk because the RR exceeds 1
The result is significant because the CI excludes 0
The result is not statistically significant because the CI includes 1
items.e: For a ratio measure the line of no effect is 1; a 95% CI spanning 1 means the result is not significant at the 5% level.

items.q: An RCT reports a mean difference in KOOS of 4 points (95% CI -1 to 9) favouring a new implant. This means:
o: The difference is significant because the CI excludes 1
The difference is significant because the point estimate is positive
The new implant is proven equivalent to the old
The difference is not statistically significant because the CI includes 0
items.e: For a difference measure the null value is 0; a CI that includes 0 is not significant. Absence of significance does not by itself prove equivalence.

items.q: A sample of 100 patients has a mean age of 70 years with a standard deviation of 10 years. The standard error of the mean is:
items.e: SEM = SD / square root of n = 10/10 = 1 year; SEM reflects the precision of the sample mean and falls as n rises.

items.q: In a normally distributed variable, approximately what proportion of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean?
items.e: About 68% lie within 1 SD, 95% within 1.96 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean.

items.q: Hospital costs after spinal fusion show a long tail to the right. Which statement is correct?
o: Mean equals median, so either summary is suitable
Median is greater than mean, so mean is the better summary
Mean is greater than median, so median is the better summary
Mode is greater than mean in a right-skewed distribution
items.e: In positive (right) skew, mean > median > mode because outliers pull the mean up; the median and interquartile range summarise skewed data better.

items.q: Which of the following is an ordinal variable?
o: Range of knee flexion in degrees
Gustilo-Anderson grade of an open fracture
items.e: Ordinal data are ordered categories with unequal intervals, such as Gustilo grade; blood group and manufacturer are nominal, while range of motion is a ratio variable.

items.q: Body temperature measured in degrees Celsius is an example of which type of data?
items.e: Celsius temperature has equal intervals but no true zero, so it is interval data; blood loss or height (true zero) are ratio data.

items.q: In an RCT, deep infection occurs in 8% of controls and 6% of patients receiving antibiotic-loaded cement. The number needed to treat to prevent one infection is:
Wound complications occur in 20% of patients with standard closure and 15% with a new closure device. The relative risk reduction is:
items.e: RRR = (CER - EER)/CER = (0.20 - 0.15)/0.20 = 25%, while the ARR is only 5%.

items.q: Gastrointestinal bleeding occurs in 2% of controls and 7% of patients given a new anticoagulant. The number needed to harm is:
items.e: Absolute risk increase = 7% - 2% = 5%; NNH = 1/0.05 = 20.

items.q: The odds ratio from a case-control study gives a close approximation to the relative risk when:
items.e: When the outcome is rare, odds and risk are numerically similar, so the OR approximates the RR; with common outcomes the OR exaggerates the RR.

items.q: In a non-inferiority RCT, the investigators report both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses. The per-protocol analysis is also required because intention-to-treat analysis alone in this design:
o: Always favours the new treatment in superiority
Can bias the result towards showing no difference, falsely supporting non-inferiority
Removes the need for a non-inferiority margin
items.e: Crossovers and non-adherence dilute differences, which is conservative in superiority trials but anti-conservative in non-inferiority trials, so both ITT and per-protocol should show non-inferiority.

items.q: Dubousset's 'cone of economy' concept describes:
o: A narrow zone of standing posture within which the body stays balanced with minimal muscular effort
The cone-shaped spinal canal at the conus medullaris
The range of coronal Cobb angles that need no treatment
The arc of pelvic rotation during gait
items.e: The cone of economy is the small range of postural sway in which the head stays over the pelvis with little muscle energy; malalignment pushes the body to the edge of the cone, costing energy and causing fatigue and pain.

items.q: Pelvic incidence is measured as the angle between:
o: The S1 endplate and the horizontal
A line perpendicular to the S1 endplate at its midpoint and a line from that midpoint to the centre of the femoral heads
The vertical and a line from the hip axis to the S1 endplate midpoint
The L1 superior endplate and the S1 endplate
items.e: PI is the angle between the perpendicular to the S1 endplate at its midpoint and the line joining that midpoint to the hip axis; the S1-horizontal angle is sacral slope and the vertical-based angle is pelvic tilt.

items.q: On a standing lateral radiograph a patient has pelvic incidence 62° and pelvic tilt 27°. The sacral slope is:
items.e: PI = PT + SS, so SS = 62 − 27 = 35°; the relatively high PT with low SS indicates a retroverted pelvis.

items.q: Pelvic incidence behaves as a fixed morphological parameter only after skeletal maturity. During childhood it:
o: Changes with sitting and standing like pelvic tilt
Remains exactly the same from birth
items.e: PI rises through childhood and adolescence as the pelvis and sacrum grow, then becomes constant in the adult, unlike PT and SS which change with position throughout life.

items.q: A high pelvic incidence (for example 75°) is most strongly associated with which lumbosacral condition?
o: Lumbar disc herniation in a flat spine
items.e: A high PI increases sacral slope and shear across L5-S1, favouring isthmic spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis and progression of high-grade slips; low PI is linked to flat spines and disc herniation.

items.q: In a normal adult, approximately what proportion of total lumbar lordosis (L1-S1) lies between L4 and S1?
items.e: About two-thirds of lumbar lordosis is concentrated at L4-L5 and L5-S1, which is why restoring segmental lordosis at these levels is critical in lumbar fusion.

items.q: The sagittal vertical axis (SVA) is measured as the horizontal distance between:
o: The C2 plumb line and the centre of the femoral heads
The T1 centroid and the S1 endplate midpoint
The C7 plumb line and the posterosuperior corner of S1
The external auditory meatus and the ankle joint
items.e: SVA uses a plumb line dropped from the C7 vertebral body centroid; its offset from the posterosuperior corner of S1 is recorded, positive when C7 lies anterior.

items.q: The main advantage of the T1 pelvic angle (TPA) over the sagittal vertical axis in assessing global alignment is that TPA:
o: Requires no femoral heads on the radiograph
Is a fixed morphological value like pelvic incidence
Is not affected by postural compensation such as pelvic retroversion or knee flexion
items.e: TPA combines SVA and PT into one angle from the femoral heads to T1 and S1, so it stays the same whether or not the patient compensates by retroverting the pelvis; SVA can be falsely reassuring in a compensated patient.

items.q: In cervical sagittal alignment, which mismatch parameter is analogous to PI-LL in the lumbar spine, with a target below about 20°?
o: Chin-brow vertical angle minus T1 slope
items.e: T1 slope acts like pelvic incidence for the neck: the cervical lordosis needed depends on it, and T1S-CL above about 20° indicates cervical malalignment.

items.q: The chin-brow vertical angle (CBVA) is the angle between:
o: The C2 endplate and the horizontal
A line from the chin to the brow and the vertical, measured with hips and knees extended
The orbitomeatal line and the C7 endplate
items.e: CBVA is measured on a clinical photograph or radiograph with the patient standing with hips and knees extended; it quantifies horizontal gaze and guides the size of osteotomy in ankylosing spondylitis.

items.q: The Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) score proposed by Yilgor differs from absolute SRS-Schwab targets because it:
o: Applies to children with idiopathic scoliosis only
Uses parameters proportioned to the individual's pelvic incidence to predict mechanical complications
Is calculated from CT bone density
