Interposition of the alar ligaments in the fracture
items.e: The junction of the dens and body has a watershed vascular supply and a small cross-sectional area for healing, unlike type III fractures that extend into well-vascularised cancellous body.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a minimally displaced fracture that runs from the base of the dens into the cancellous body of C2. The classification and usual treatment are:
items.e: Fractures extending into the C2 body are Anderson-D'Alonzo type III and usually unite with a collar or halo.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a displaced type II odontoid fracture with the fracture line running obliquely from anterosuperior to posteroinferior (Grauer IIB), an intact transverse ligament and a slim neck. The preferred fixation is:
o: Posterior Gallie wiring alone without graft
items.e: In a Grauer IIB fracture the screw passes perpendicular to the fracture line, compressing it while preserving C1-C2 rotation.

items.q: A type II odontoid fracture runs obliquely from anteroinferior to posterosuperior (Grauer IIC). The preferred operative treatment is:
o: Odontoid excision by a transoral route
items.e: An anterior screw would run parallel to this fracture line and cause it to shear and displace, so posterior C1-C2 fusion is preferred.

items.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to anterior odontoid screw fixation of a type II fracture?
o: Fracture line from anterosuperior to posteroinferior
A barrel chest with a short neck
items.e: A barrel chest, short neck or thoracic kyphosis prevents the steep trajectory needed for the screw. An intact TAL, favourable obliquity and an acute fracture are prerequisites, not contraindications.

items.q: Which feature most increases the risk of non-union when a type II odontoid fracture is treated in a halo vest?
o: Extension of the fracture into the C2 body
Initial displacement of more than 5 mm
items.e: Displacement over about 5 mm, posterior displacement, angulation over 10 degrees, age over 50, smoking and delay all predict non-union.

items.q: In an 84-year-old with a type II odontoid fracture, halo vest immobilisation is generally avoided because it is associated with:
o: High rates of aspiration, pneumonia and death
Inability to insert pins into an elderly skull
A higher non-union rate than no treatment
items.e: Halo vests are poorly tolerated in the elderly, causing dysphagia, aspiration, pneumonia, falls and increased mortality; a rigid collar or posterior C1-C2 fusion is preferred.

items.q: The Harms (Goel-Harms) technique for posterior atlantoaxial fusion uses:
o: C1 lateral mass screws and C2 pedicle or pars screws joined by rods
Sublaminar wires and a structural graft alone
An anterior odontoid screw supplemented by a collar
items.e: Harms' construct uses independent C1 lateral mass and C2 pedicle/pars screws connected with rods, allowing intraoperative reduction; Magerl's technique uses transarticular screws.

items.q: Before Magerl C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation, fine-cut CT is studied mainly to assess:
o: The width of the posterior arch of C1 for wiring
The thickness of the transverse ligament
A high-riding vertebral artery in the C2 isthmus
The height of the C2-C3 disc
items.e: In a proportion of patients the vertebral artery groove encroaches on the C2 pars, leaving no safe corridor for a transarticular screw.

items.q: An advantage of anterior odontoid screw fixation over posterior C1-C2 fusion is preservation of the atlantoaxial joint, which provides approximately what proportion of total cervical rotation?
items.e: About half of cervical axial rotation occurs at C1-C2, which is lost after atlantoaxial fusion.

items.q: A lateral radiograph shows a smooth, round, well-corticated ossicle sitting above a hypoplastic dens, with a gap above the level of the C1-C2 facets. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Os odontoideum has smooth corticated margins and a hypoplastic dens. An acute fracture has irregular non-corticated edges; ossiculum terminale is a small apical ossicle on a normal-height dens.

items.q: A 12-year-old with os odontoideum has 8 mm of sagittal translation on flexion-extension radiographs and new hyperreflexia. The treatment of choice is:
items.e: Instability with neurological signs requires posterior atlantoaxial fusion; an anterior screw has nothing to fix since the ossicle is not an acute fracture.

items.q: In road traffic accidents, traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis is most often caused by:
items.e: Most hangman's fractures in vehicle crashes and diving result from hyperextension and axial load; judicial hanging involves hyperextension with distraction.

items.q: CT shows bilateral C2 pars fractures with severe angulation but minimal translation, and an oblique fracture line. Which manoeuvre should be avoided?
o: Halo immobilisation with gentle compression in extension
items.e: This is a Levine-Edwards type IIA (flexion-distraction) injury; traction widens the disc space and increases angulation.

items.q: A hangman's fracture is associated with bilateral C2-C3 facet dislocation (Levine-Edwards type III). The usual treatment is:
items.e: The dislocated facets cannot be reduced or held by closed means, so open reduction and fusion are needed.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a hangman's fracture with 5 mm translation and 15 degrees of angulation of C2 on C3 (Levine-Edwards type II). The classical non-operative treatment is:
o: Reduction by traction in slight extension, then a halo vest
Traction in flexion followed by a collar
No immobilisation, since the injury is stable
items.e: Type II injuries are reduced with traction (in extension) and held in a halo; type IIA, in contrast, must not be placed in traction.

items.q: In the Subaxial Injury Classification (SLIC) system, a rotation or translation morphology scores:
items.e: Morphology scores 0 (none), 1 (compression), 2 (burst), 3 (distraction) and 4 (rotation/translation).

items.q: A patient has a C6 burst fracture, an intact disco-ligamentous complex on MRI, and an incomplete cord injury with continuing cord compression. The SLIC score and recommendation are:
items.e: Burst morphology 2 + intact DLC 0 + incomplete cord injury 3 + continuous compression with deficit 1 = 6. Scores over 4 favour surgery.

items.q: In the neurological component of the SLIC system, which status scores highest, before adding the continuous-compression modifier?
items.e: Incomplete cord injury scores 3 (complete 2, root 1, intact 0) because it has the greatest potential to benefit from urgent decompression.

items.q: In the Allen-Ferguson mechanistic classification of subaxial cervical injuries, bilateral facet dislocations belong to the category of:
items.e: Distractive flexion injuries range from facet subluxation to unilateral and bilateral facet dislocation and a 'floating' vertebra.

items.q: In the AO Spine subaxial cervical classification, a type C injury denotes:
o: Compression injury of the vertebral body
Failure of the posterior or anterior tension band without translation
Translation of one vertebra relative to another in any direction
items.e: Type A is compression, type B tension band failure, and type C translation or displacement in any plane.

items.q: An intubated patient with a severe head injury has a bilateral C5-C6 facet dislocation on CT. Before any reduction, the next step is:
o: MRI to exclude a disc herniation behind the C5 body
Closed reduction with incremental tong traction
Immediate posterior open reduction without imaging
items.e: A patient who cannot be examined during reduction needs MRI first, because a herniated disc could be pushed into the cord as the facets are reduced.

items.q: Pre-reduction MRI of a C5-C6 bilateral facet dislocation shows a large disc herniation behind the C5 vertebral body. The recommended sequence is:
o: Closed tong traction to reduce the facets first
Anterior discectomy first, then reduction and fusion
Posterior open reduction first, then anterior surgery
Halo vest immobilisation in the dislocated position
items.e: The disc must be removed anteriorly before reduction so that it is not driven into the cord; reduction and stabilisation follow.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a unilateral C5-C6 facet dislocation. The most typical neurological picture is:
o: Radiculopathy of the root at that level
Bilateral upper limb paralysis with sacral sparing
items.e: Unilateral facet dislocation narrows the foramen and commonly produces a root lesion; cord injury is much more frequent with bilateral dislocation.

items.q: On a lateral cervical radiograph, anterior translation of about 50% of the vertebral body width at C5-C6 most likely indicates:
items.e: About 25% anterolisthesis suggests unilateral, and 50% or more bilateral, facet dislocation, which has a high rate of cord injury.

items.q: A diver has a C5 injury with a large triangular anteroinferior body fragment, posterior displacement of the rest of the body into the canal and widened interspinous spaces. He has lost motor power and pain sensation below C5 but retains proprioception. The injury is:
items.e: The flexion teardrop fracture combines anterior body failure with posterior ligament disruption; it is very unstable and typically causes an anterior cord syndrome.

items.q: A 72-year-old falls and hyperextends his neck. CT shows a small triangular fragment avulsed from the anteroinferior corner of C2, with normal alignment and no canal compromise. Treatment is:
items.e: This is an extension teardrop avulsion by the anterior longitudinal ligament, which is usually stable and treated in a collar.

items.q: A labourer feels a sudden pain between his shoulder blades while shovelling heavy clay. Radiographs show an avulsion fracture of the C7 spinous process. Management is:
o: Symptomatic treatment with analgesia and a soft collar
items.e: The clay-shoveler's fracture is a stable spinous process avulsion that heals or forms a painless fibrous union with symptomatic care.

items.q: A 60-year-old with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis and a fixed cervical kyphosis falls and has neck pain. Before imaging, how should the neck be immobilised?
o: In a standard rigid collar in neutral alignment
In skull traction with the neck in extension
It does not need immobilisation, since the spine is fused
In the patient's pre-injury flexed posture, with padding
items.e: Forcing an ankylosed kyphotic neck into neutral or extension can displace an occult fracture and injure the cord; it is immobilised in its usual position.

items.q: Six hours after a C6-C7 transdiscal extension fracture in a patient with ankylosing spondylitis, he develops progressive weakness of all four limbs. The most likely cause is:
o: Central cord syndrome from disc herniation
Vertebral artery dissection with brainstem stroke
items.e: Fractures in ankylosed spines bleed from the cancellous bone and epidural veins, and epidural haematoma with delayed deterioration is characteristic, needing urgent MRI and decompression.

items.q: CT of the neck after a car crash shows a fracture extending through the C3 foramen transversarium. The appropriate further investigation is:
o: CT angiography of the neck vessels
items.e: Fractures through the foramen transversarium and facet dislocations are associated with vertebral artery injury, screened with CT angiography.

items.q: According to the AO Spine 2017 guideline on acute spinal cord injury, high-dose methylprednisolone:
o: Should be given as a 48-hour infusion to all patients
Is recommended for 7 days after penetrating injury
May be offered as a 24-hour infusion if started within 8 hours, but not after 8 hours
Is mandatory for complete cord injuries only
items.e: The guideline suggests a 24-hour infusion as an option within 8 hours of injury and suggests against starting it later; it is not a standard of care.

items.q: The STASCIS study of acute cervical spinal cord injury found that decompression within 24 hours of injury was associated with:
o: Higher rates of wound infection only
Greater odds of improving by two or more AIS grades
items.e: Early surgery was associated with about 2.8 times the odds of at least a two-grade AIS improvement at 6 months, without excess complications.

items.q: In the ISNCSCI (ASIA) motor examination, the key muscle group for the C8 myotome is:
o: Finger flexors to the distal phalanx of the middle finger
items.e: C5 elbow flexors, C6 wrist extensors, C7 elbow extensors, C8 middle finger DIP flexion and T1 little finger abduction.

items.q: In the Herbert classification, a fracture of the scaphoid tubercle is graded as:
items.e: Herbert type A fractures are stable acute injuries: A1 is the tubercle fracture and A2 an incomplete waist fracture. B1 is an unstable distal oblique fracture and C is delayed union.

items.q: An acute fracture through the proximal pole of the scaphoid is placed in which Herbert group?
items.e: Herbert B3 is the proximal pole fracture, an unstable acute type with a high non-union risk. B2 is a complete waist fracture and D1 a fibrous non-union.

items.q: In the Herbert classification, type B4 denotes:
items.e: B4 is the scaphoid fracture that forms part of a trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation. Incomplete waist fractures are A2, and sclerotic non-union (pseudarthrosis) is D2.

items.q: A scaphoid non-union with sclerotic bone ends and cyst formation (pseudarthrosis) is classified by Herbert as:
items.e: Herbert D covers established non-union: D1 is fibrous (stable) and D2 is sclerotic, a pseudarthrosis that tends to progress. C denotes delayed union.

items.q: According to Russe, which orientation of scaphoid fracture line is the least stable because it is subjected to shear forces?
items.e: Russe described horizontal oblique, transverse and vertical oblique fractures; the vertical oblique line is loaded in shear and is the least stable. Horizontal oblique fractures are loaded in compression.

items.q: The most common site of scaphoid fracture in adults is the:
items.e: About two-thirds of adult scaphoid fractures involve the waist. Proximal pole fractures make up roughly 10-20% and distal pole/tubercle fractures about 10-15%.

items.q: In children, scaphoid fractures most commonly involve the:
o: Whole scaphoid as an osteochondral sleeve
items.e: Paediatric scaphoid fractures are usually in the distal third (often tubercle avulsions) and heal well with casting. Waist fractures predominate in adults.

items.q: On CT along the scaphoid axis, which AP (coronal) intrascaphoid angle indicates a humpback deformity?
items.e: Amadio defined humpback deformity as a lateral intrascaphoid angle over 45 degrees or an AP intrascaphoid angle under 35 degrees. Such deformity is linked with poorer outcomes and needs correction with a wedge graft.

items.q: After a scaphoid waist fracture, a lateral radiograph shows a radiolunate angle of 25 degrees of dorsal tilt. This indicates:
o: An unstable fracture with DISI deformity
items.e: A radiolunate angle over 15 degrees of dorsal tilt means the lunate is extended with the proximal fragment (DISI), which is one of the criteria for instability and fixation. The normal radiolunate angle is 0 plus or minus 15 degrees.

items.q: Which factor most increases the risk of non-union after a scaphoid waist fracture?
o: Delay in diagnosis and treatment of more than 4 weeks
items.e: Delayed treatment (over about 4 weeks), displacement, proximal pole location, smoking and associated carpal instability increase non-union risk. Thumb inclusion in the cast has not been shown to improve union.

items.q: Roughly what non-union rate is expected if a displaced scaphoid waist fracture (more than 2 mm) is treated in a cast alone?
items.e: Displaced waist fractures have about a 50% non-union rate with casting, which is why internal fixation is advised. Undisplaced waist fractures unite in over 90% with a cast.

items.q: In scaphoid non-union advanced collapse (SNAC), stage I arthritis affects the joint between:
o: Radial styloid and distal scaphoid fragment
items.e: SNAC progresses in a predictable sequence: stage I radial styloid-distal scaphoid, stage II scaphocapitate, stage III capitolunate. The radiolunate joint is spared until late.

items.q: Why is the radiolunate joint preserved in SNAC wrist?
o: The lunate has a separate dorsal blood supply
The proximal scaphoid fragment stays attached to the lunate and moves with it
The radiolunate joint carries no load
The lunate fossa has thicker cartilage than the scaphoid fossa
items.e: In SNAC the proximal pole remains linked to the lunate by the scapholunate ligament, so the radiolunate articulation stays congruent. Load is transmitted perpendicularly through this spherical joint, protecting it.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a waist non-union with a humpback deformity, and at surgery the proximal pole shows no punctate bleeding. The most suitable graft to correct the deformity and revascularise the pole is:
o: Free vascularised medial femoral condyle graft
items.e: The free medial femoral condyle corticocancellous graft provides structural support to correct the humpback as well as vascularity. The 1,2-ICSRA pedicled graft is small and less able to restore length and angle in humpback deformity.

items.q: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the scaphoid without a preceding fracture is known as:
items.e: Preiser disease is idiopathic scaphoid AVN, often affecting the proximal pole. Kienbock disease is lunate AVN; Kohler and Freiberg affect the navicular and second metatarsal head.

items.q: The Matti-Russe procedure for scaphoid non-union involves:
o: A volar inlay of cancellous bone graft
items.e: Matti-Russe is a historical technique using a cancellous (later corticocancellous) graft inlaid through a volar approach. It does not correct humpback deformity as well as an interpositional wedge graft.

items.q: Proximal row carpectomy for SLAC or SNAC wrist requires which condition to be met?
o: Intact cartilage of the capitate head and lunate fossa
items.e: After PRC the capitate head articulates with the lunate fossa of the radius, so both surfaces must have healthy cartilage. Capitolunate arthritis (stage III) is therefore a contraindication.

items.q: Compared with scaphoid excision and four-corner fusion, an advantage of proximal row carpectomy is that it:
o: Is suitable when the capitate head is arthritic
Does not require bony union and needs shorter immobilisation
Has a lower long-term rate of radiocapitate arthritis
items.e: PRC is simpler, avoids non-union and allows earlier mobilisation. Four-corner fusion tends to preserve grip and durability, and PRC carries a risk of later radiocapitate arthritis.

items.q: During scaphoid excision and four-corner fusion, failure to correct a dorsally tilted (DISI) lunate leads mainly to:
o: Dorsal impingement of the capitate on the radius with limited extension
items.e: If the lunate is fused in extension, the capitate impinges dorsally on the radius rim, limiting extension and causing pain. The lunate should be reduced to neutral before fixation.

items.q: Partial wrist denervation for chronic wrist pain usually involves neurectomy of the:
o: Superficial radial and dorsal ulnar sensory nerves
Median and ulnar nerves at the wrist
Lateral antebrachial cutaneous and palmar cutaneous nerves
items.e: Partial denervation divides the terminal AIN and PIN, which supply much of the wrist capsule, preserving motor function. It is a motion-preserving option for SNAC or SLAC pain.

items.q: Which part of the scapholunate interosseous ligament is the thickest and biomechanically most important?
items.e: The dorsal SLIL is the strongest portion and is key to SL stability; the proximal part is membranous. In contrast, the palmar portion is the strongest part of the lunotriquetral ligament.

items.q: Which portion of the lunotriquetral interosseous ligament is the strongest?
items.e: The palmar LT ligament is strongest, the opposite of the SL ligament where the dorsal portion predominates.

items.q: The radioscapholunate ligament (ligament of Testut) is best described as:
o: The main stabiliser of the scapholunate joint
A dorsal ligament inserting on the triquetrum
A neurovascular conduit with little mechanical strength
items.e: The ligament of Testut carries vessels and nerves to the SL ligament and contributes little to mechanical stability. The radioscaphocapitate is a major palmar stabiliser.

items.q: After complete division of the scapholunate interosseous ligament, which structure acts as an important secondary stabiliser preventing scaphoid flexion?
items.e: Secondary SL stabilisers include the STT ligaments, the dorsal intercarpal and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments, and the radioscaphocapitate ligament. Static DISI develops once these are attenuated.

items.q: The normal capitolunate angle on a lateral wrist radiograph is approximately:
items.e: The capitate, lunate and radius are nearly colinear: capitolunate angle 0-15 degrees and radiolunate 0 plus or minus 15 degrees. The 30-60 degree range is the normal scapholunate angle.

items.q: In the Mayo classification, palmar midcarpal instability is an example of:
items.e: CIND describes abnormal motion between rows (midcarpal) or between radius and carpus with intact intrinsic ligaments. CID involves disruption within a row, such as SL dissociation.

items.q: Carpal malalignment secondary to a dorsally angulated distal radius malunion is classified as:
items.e: An adaptive DISI develops to compensate for dorsal tilt of the radius; the intrinsic ligaments are intact. Corrective osteotomy of the radius restores alignment.

items.q: Ulnar translocation of the carpus in rheumatoid arthritis is a form of:
items.e: Ulnar translocation results from failure of the radiocarpal (extrinsic) ligaments, so it is non-dissociative instability at the radiocarpal level.

items.q: The cortical 'ring sign' of the scaphoid on a PA radiograph is considered abnormal when the distance from the ring to the proximal pole is less than:
items.e: A flexed, foreshortened scaphoid shows its tubercle as a ring; a ring-to-proximal-pole distance under 7 mm suggests scaphoid flexion as in SL dissociation.

items.q: Which radiographic view best demonstrates a dynamic scapholunate gap?
items.e: A clenched-fist PA loads the carpus as the capitate drives into the SL interval, widening a dynamic gap (over 3 mm compared with the other side). Static views may be normal in dynamic instability.

items.q: During wrist arthroscopy, a 2.7 mm arthroscope can be passed from the midcarpal joint through the scapholunate interval into the radiocarpal joint. This Geissler grade is:
items.e: Geissler IV is gross instability with the 'drive-through' sign. In grade III a probe, but not the scope, passes between the bones.

items.q: At arthroscopy the scapholunate ligament shows haemorrhage and attenuation but no carpal incongruity from either joint. The Geissler grade is:
items.e: Geissler I is attenuation or haemorrhage without step-off. Grade II shows incongruity in the midcarpal joint only.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an acute (3-week-old) complete scapholunate ligament tear with a repairable dorsal ligament and reducible alignment. The preferred treatment is:
o: Open repair with suture anchors, K-wire stabilisation and dorsal capsulodesis
items.e: Acute complete tears with repairable tissue are repaired, pinned and often augmented with a dorsal capsulodesis (Blatt or DIC-based). Salvage procedures are for arthritis.

items.q: The three-ligament tenodesis described by Garcia-Elias for chronic reducible scapholunate dissociation uses a strip of:
items.e: The 3LT is a modification of the Brunelli procedure using a distally based strip of FCR passed through the scaphoid and secured to the lunate and dorsal radiotriquetral ligament.

items.q: The RASL procedure for scapholunate dissociation involves:
o: Excision of the scaphoid and fusion of the lunate to the radius
Reduction and fixation of the scaphoid and lunate with a headless screw across the SL joint
items.e: RASL (reduction and association of the scaphoid and lunate) uses a Herbert-type screw across the SL interval to create a fibrous union between the bones.

items.q: A 40-year-old has chronic scapholunate dissociation with a fixed, irreducible rotatory subluxation of the scaphoid and no arthritis. A suitable procedure is:
items.e: When the malalignment cannot be reduced, soft-tissue reconstruction fails, so limited intercarpal fusion (STT or scaphocapitate) is used to hold the scaphoid out of flexion.

items.q: In SLAC wrist, stage II arthritis involves:
o: Only the tip of the radial styloid
items.e: Watson stages: I radial styloid-scaphoid, II whole radioscaphoid fossa, III capitolunate as the capitate migrates into the SL gap. The radiolunate joint is spared.

items.q: A pattern of degenerative arthritis identical to SLAC wrist, with radioscaphoid and STT changes, is classically associated with:
items.e: CPPD (chondrocalcinosis) can disrupt the SL ligament and cause SLAC-type collapse; STT arthritis is also common in CPPD.

items.q: Isolated lunotriquetral ligament injury typically results from a fall on the outstretched hand with:
o: Forced supination with the elbow flexed
Wrist extension, radial deviation and impact on the hypothenar region
items.e: LT tears result from hypothenar impact with the wrist extended and radially deviated, producing ulnar-sided wrist pain.

items.q: A static VISI deformity after lunotriquetral ligament rupture develops only when there is also injury to the:
o: Dorsal radiocarpal and dorsal intercarpal ligaments
items.e: Isolated LT tears do not produce static VISI; the lunate flexes with the scaphoid only when the dorsal extrinsic ligaments are also disrupted.

items.q: A 32-year-old with a chronic lunotriquetral tear and 3 mm positive ulnar variance has failed splinting. A useful procedure that also tensions the ulnocarpal ligaments is:
items.e: Ulnar shortening unloads the ulnar carpus and tightens the ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments, which stabilises the LT joint, especially with positive ulnar variance.

items.q: A young woman with generalised ligamentous laxity has a painful clunk as the wrist moves from radial to ulnar deviation in pronation, and VISI on the resting lateral radiograph. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Palmar midcarpal instability is the commonest CIND: the proximal row stays flexed and then suddenly snaps into extension with a clunk in ulnar deviation. The Lichtman midcarpal shift test reproduces it.

items.q: First-line management of palmar midcarpal instability is:
o: Splinting with a pisiform boost and proprioceptive training of FCU and ECU
items.e: Most patients improve with splints that support the pisiform and with dynamic stabilisation exercises. Capsulodesis or midcarpal fusion is reserved for refractory cases.

items.q: In Mayfield's progressive perilunar instability, stage III corresponds to:
o: Capitolunate dislocation through the space of Poirier
items.e: Mayfield: I SL disruption, II capitolunate dislocation, III LT disruption (perilunate dislocation, lunate remains in the fossa), IV lunate dislocation.

items.q: Transcapitate fracture in which the proximal capitate fragment rotates up to 180 degrees, usually with a scaphoid fracture, is called:
items.e: In scaphocapitate syndrome the capitate head rotates so its articular surface faces distally; it must be reduced and fixed openly. A trans-scaphoid perilunate injury is the de Quervain pattern.

items.q: Perilunate injuries that pass through bone, such as the scaphoid, capitate or triquetrum, are termed:
items.e: Greater arc injuries pass through the bones around the lunate; lesser arc injuries are purely ligamentous. The trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation is the commonest greater arc pattern.

items.q: On the PA radiograph of a lunate dislocation, the lunate appears:
items.e: A volarly rotated lunate projects as a triangle instead of its normal trapezoid on the PA view. Gilula's arcs are disrupted.

items.q: The usual closed reduction manoeuvre for an acute perilunate dislocation is named after:
items.e: The Tavernier manoeuvre uses longitudinal traction, wrist extension and then flexion with pressure on the lunate to reduce the capitate onto it. Definitive treatment is usually open repair.

items.q: A perilunate dislocation is first diagnosed 10 weeks after injury, with cartilage damage on the capitate head and lunate fossa. The most reliable salvage is:
items.e: PRC can be used for chronic perilunate dislocation only if the capitate head and lunate fossa are intact; when both surfaces are damaged, wrist arthrodesis is the reliable option.

items.q: A 4-year-old with nutritional rickets (low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, raised ALP and PTH) has parents who cannot manage daily medication. Under the 2016 Global Consensus recommendations, the appropriate single oral high-dose (stoss) vitamin D treatment is:
items.e: For children over 1 year up to 12 years the consensus single-dose option is 150,000 IU (daily alternative 3,000-6,000 IU for 12 weeks). 50,000 IU is the dose for infants aged 3-12 months and 300,000 IU is for those over 12 years.

items.q: An 8-month-old infant is diagnosed with nutritional rickets. According to the 2016 Global Consensus, the recommended daily oral vitamin D treatment dose and minimum duration are:
o: 400 IU daily for at least 6 weeks
6,000 IU daily for at least 4 weeks
10,000 IU daily for at least 24 weeks
2,000 IU daily for at least 12 weeks
items.e: Infants up to 12 months receive 2,000 IU/day; all age groups are treated for a minimum of 12 weeks. 400 IU/day is the prevention (maintenance) dose for infants, not a treatment dose.

items.q: A 6-week-old infant has hypocalcaemia from maternal vitamin D deficiency. Which vitamin D regimen does the 2016 Global Consensus advise against in this age group?
o: A single oral stoss dose of vitamin D
Daily oral cholecalciferol rather than ergocalciferol
items.e: Single high-dose (stoss) therapy is not recommended under 3 months of age because of the risk of hypercalcaemia; daily 2,000 IU with calcium is used instead.

items.q: While treating nutritional rickets with vitamin D, the 2016 Global Consensus recommends that calcium intake (diet plus supplement) should be at least approximately:
o: 100 mg of elemental calcium per day
500 mg of elemental calcium per day
2,500 mg of elemental calcium per day
No calcium is needed if vitamin D is given
items.e: About 500 mg/day of elemental calcium should accompany vitamin D therapy, since rickets is a combined calcium-vitamin D problem; healing is incomplete with vitamin D alone when dietary calcium is poor.

items.q: For prevention of rickets in a healthy exclusively breast-fed infant in the first year of life, the recommended routine vitamin D supplement is:
items.e: The Global Consensus advises 400 IU/day from birth to 12 months, and 600 IU/day thereafter (or from diet), regardless of feeding mode. 2,000 IU/day is a treatment dose.

items.q: A 5-month-old breast-fed infant with nutritional rickets presents with a generalised seizure. Serum calcium is 1.5 mmol/L. The most appropriate first step is:
o: Intravenous calcium gluconate under cardiac monitoring
Single oral stoss dose of 300,000 IU vitamin D
items.e: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany, laryngospasm) is an emergency treated with IV calcium gluconate first, followed by oral calcium and vitamin D. Phosphate would worsen hypocalcaemia.

items.q: An infant with rickets and hypocalcaemic tetany remains hypocalcaemic despite adequate intravenous calcium. Which additional serum level should be checked and corrected because its deficiency impairs PTH secretion and action?
items.e: Hypomagnesaemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism and PTH resistance, producing refractory hypocalcaemia until magnesium is replaced.

items.q: In a 4-month-old with nutritional rickets, the earliest clinical sign typically found on examination is:
o: Craniotabes: ping-pong softening of the parieto-occipital skull
items.e: Craniotabes is the earliest sign in young infants (under 6 months), before weight-bearing deformities appear. Genu varum and double malleoli need a walking child.

items.q: In a child with rickets, a horizontal groove along the lower chest wall is seen. This Harrison sulcus results from:
o: Premature fusion of the sternal ossification centres
Inward pull of the diaphragm attachment on softened lower ribs
Intercostal muscle hypertrophy from chronic cough
items.e: Harrison sulcus is produced by the diaphragm pulling the soft, poorly mineralised lower ribs inward. Enlarged costochondral junctions form the rachitic rosary, a separate sign.

items.q: In rickets, the clinical finding of 'double malleoli' (Marfan sign) at the ankle is due to:
o: Metaphyseal widening of the distal tibia and fibula
Periosteal new bone from subperiosteal haemorrhage
items.e: Flaring of the distal tibial and fibular metaphyses above the epiphyses gives a palpable double contour at the malleoli, analogous to the widened wrists.

items.q: A 3-year-old with rickets has valgus of one knee and varus of the other, so both knees point to the same side. This deformity is called:
items.e: Windswept knees (genu valgum on one side, genu varum on the other) are typical of rickets. Sabre tibia is anterior tibial bowing associated with congenital syphilis and Paget disease.

items.q: A 2-year-old has wide physes, metaphyseal irregularity and coxa vara resembling rickets, but serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are all normal. The mother has the same short-limbed habitus. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.e: Schmid-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is autosomal dominant, due to COL10A1 mutation, and mimics rickets radiologically with entirely normal mineral biochemistry. PHEX (XLH), CYP27B1 (VDDR 1A) and ALPL (hypophosphatasia) all give abnormal biochemistry.

items.q: An irritable 10-month-old fed only boiled cow's milk refuses to move the legs. Radiographs show a dense white metaphyseal line with a lucent band beneath it, sclerotic rings around the epiphyses and metaphyseal spurs, with a physis of normal width. The deficiency is of:
items.e: These are features of scurvy: Frankel line, Trummerfeld (scurvy) zone, Wimberger ring and Pelkan spurs, with subperiosteal haemorrhage. Unlike rickets, the physis is not widened.

items.q: An 18-month-old has symmetrical bowed legs. Serum calcium, phosphate and ALP are normal. On standing radiographs the metaphyseal-diaphyseal (Drennan) angle is 8 degrees with no medial beaking. The most likely diagnosis and plan is:
o: Physiological genu varum; reassure and observe
items.e: Normal biochemistry, symmetry, age under 2 years and an MDA under 11 degrees indicate physiological varus, which resolves spontaneously. An MDA over 16 degrees with medial beaking suggests Blount disease.

items.q: At the cellular level, why does hypophosphataemia widen the growth plate in rickets?
o: Low phosphate accelerates proliferation of resting zone chondrocytes
Phosphate is needed for apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes, which accumulate when it is low
Low phosphate stimulates osteoclast invasion of the reserve zone
Low phosphate causes premature physeal bar formation
items.e: Phosphate (via the caspase-9 mitochondrial pathway) drives apoptosis of terminally hypertrophic chondrocytes; when it is low these cells persist, so the hypertrophic zone lengthens and provisional calcification fails.

items.q: An infant receiving standard vitamin D prophylaxis develops hypercalcaemia, suppressed PTH, raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and nephrocalcinosis. Loss-of-function mutation of which enzyme gene is most likely?
items.e: CYP24A1 inactivates 25(OH)D and calcitriol; its loss causes idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia with vitamin D hypersensitivity. CYP27B1 and CYP2R1 defects cause vitamin D-dependent rickets with hypocalcaemia.

items.q: The principal cell source of circulating FGF23, the hormone raised in X-linked hypophosphataemia, is the:
items.e: FGF23 is produced mainly by osteocytes (and osteoblasts) in bone; it acts on the kidney with its co-receptor Klotho.

items.q: FGF23 lowers serum phosphate. Which pair of renal actions explains this and the inappropriately low calcitriol seen in XLH?
o: Up-regulation of NaPi-IIa and stimulation of 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Inhibition of the calcium-sensing receptor and stimulation of PTH release
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase and of 24-hydroxylase
Down-regulation of NaPi-IIa/IIc cotransporters and suppression of 1-alpha-hydroxylase
items.e: FGF23 removes sodium-phosphate cotransporters from the proximal tubule (phosphaturia) and suppresses CYP27B1 while stimulating CYP24A1, so calcitriol is low or inappropriately normal despite hypophosphataemia.

items.q: A child with rickets has low serum phosphate. Which urinary index best confirms that the hypophosphataemia is due to renal phosphate wasting?
o: Low tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per GFR (TmP/GFR)
items.e: TmP/GFR, calculated from fasting paired serum and urine phosphate and creatinine, is the renal phosphate threshold; it is low in FGF23-mediated and tubular phosphate wasting. Hypercalciuria is seen only in HHRH.

items.q: A woman with X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX mutation) asks about the risk to her children. The correct counselling is:
o: Only her daughters can be affected
Each child, son or daughter, has a 50% chance of being affected
All her children will be affected
Only her sons can be affected, and all of them
items.e: XLH is X-linked dominant: an affected mother transmits the mutant X to half of her children of either sex, whereas an affected father passes it to all daughters and no sons.

items.q: Two toddlers both have bowed legs and raised ALP. Which clinical feature points to nutritional vitamin D-deficiency rickets rather than X-linked hypophosphataemia?
o: Dental abscesses in teeth without caries
Hypotonia with proximal muscle weakness and delayed walking
An affected father with short stature
items.e: Calcipenic rickets causes hypotonia and proximal myopathy, often with tetany; these are characteristically absent in XLH, which features dental abscesses, family history and normal calcium and PTH.

items.q: A child with X-linked hypophosphataemia develops headaches and an abnormal head shape. Which cranial complication is particularly associated with XLH?
o: Craniosynostosis (often sagittal) with Chiari I malformation
Basilar invagination from occipital condyle hypoplasia
Wormian bones with delayed fontanelle closure
items.e: XLH is associated with premature cranial suture fusion, especially sagittal, and Chiari I malformation; children with headaches or abnormal skull shape need neurosurgical assessment.

items.q: In children with X-linked hypophosphataemia, burosumab is administered by subcutaneous injection at a usual interval of:
items.e: Paediatric burosumab is weight-based and given every 2 weeks; in adults it is given every 4 weeks.

items.q: Conventional therapy for X-linked hypophosphataemia uses oral phosphate given 4-6 times a day. The main reason for such frequent dosing is that:
o: Phosphate is absorbed only in the fasting state at night
Serum phosphate rises only briefly after each dose because renal wasting continues
Once-daily phosphate causes acute nephrocalcinosis within days
items.e: Because FGF23-driven phosphaturia persists, each dose produces only a transient rise in serum phosphate, so divided frequent doses are needed. GI upset and poor compliance follow.

items.q: In conventional treatment of X-linked hypophosphataemia, active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) is combined with oral phosphate chiefly to:
o: Counter the low calcitriol and prevent phosphate-induced secondary hyperparathyroidism
Allow the phosphate to be given once daily
items.e: Phosphate alone lowers ionised calcium and stimulates PTH; active vitamin D improves gut absorption and offsets the FGF23-induced calcitriol deficiency. Combined therapy itself increases the nephrocalcinosis risk.

items.q: A child with hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH, SLC34A3 mutation) is being treated. Which approach is correct?
items.e: In HHRH FGF23 is low and calcitriol already high, causing hypercalciuria; phosphate alone corrects the defect, and calcitriol would worsen hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Burosumab is pointless when FGF23 is suppressed.

items.q: A 2-year-old with failure to thrive, polyuria and photophobia has hypophosphataemic rickets with glycosuria, aminoaciduria and metabolic acidosis. Slit-lamp examination shows corneal crystals. The underlying disorder is:
items.e: Cystinosis is the commonest inherited cause of renal Fanconi syndrome in children; corneal cystine crystals are characteristic. Wilson disease causes Fanconi syndrome later in childhood with Kayser-Fleischer rings.

items.q: A 12-year-old previously treated with ifosfamide for osteosarcoma develops bone pain and pseudofractures with hypophosphataemia, glycosuria and low bicarbonate. The mechanism is:
o: Hepatic enzyme induction degrading vitamin D
items.e: Ifosfamide is nephrotoxic to the proximal tubule and causes Fanconi syndrome with phosphate wasting and osteomalacia, similar to tenofovir in adults.

items.q: A 12-year-old on haemodialysis for chronic kidney disease develops bilateral hip pain and a limp. Radiographs show slipped capital femoral epiphyses. Compared with idiopathic SCFE, the slip in renal osteodystrophy characteristically occurs through the:
o: Zone of proliferating cartilage, unilateral in most cases
Metaphysis, adjacent to the physis, because of secondary hyperparathyroid resorption
items.e: In renal osteodystrophy, subperiosteal and metaphyseal resorption from hyperparathyroidism causes the slip to occur through the metaphyseal side; it is often bilateral and at atypical ages. Treat the metabolic disease and fix in situ.

items.q: A lateral spine radiograph of a patient with chronic kidney disease shows alternating sclerotic bands at the vertebral end plates and lucent mid-vertebral bodies. This sign is called:
items.e: Rugger-jersey spine is the end-plate sclerosis of renal osteodystrophy (secondary hyperparathyroidism). Picture-frame vertebrae are typical of Paget disease and codfish vertebrae of osteomalacia or osteoporosis.

items.q: In long-standing adult osteomalacia, which pelvic and spinal radiographic deformities result from softened bone?
items.e: Soft bone deforms under load: the acetabulum protrudes into the pelvis and the vertebral end plates become biconcave. Squared vertebrae suggest ankylosing spondylitis; iliac horns occur in nail-patella syndrome.

items.q: A woman who had severe rickets in childhood is at increased risk of obstructed labour because of which pelvic deformity?
o: Triradiate pelvis with a contracted outlet
Wide gynaecoid pelvis with hypermobile symphysis
items.e: Softened pelvic bones are compressed by the femoral heads and spine, producing a triradiate (trefoil) pelvis with a narrowed outlet.

items.q: The term 'Milkman syndrome' refers to:
o: Multiple bilateral symmetrical pseudofractures in osteomalacia
Hypercalcaemia from excessive milk and antacid intake
Rickets from cow's milk protein intolerance
Stress fractures of the metatarsals in dairy workers
items.e: Milkman syndrome describes multiple symmetrical Looser zones (Milkman lines). Hypercalcaemia from milk and alkali ingestion is milk-alkali syndrome, a different entity.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman on alendronate for 8 years has thigh pain. Radiographs show a transverse lucent line with focal cortical beaking in the subtrochanteric femur. Which feature favours an atypical femoral fracture over an osteomalacic Looser zone?
o: Location on the medial femoral neck
Low serum phosphate with raised ALP
items.e: Atypical femoral fractures begin on the lateral, tension cortex of the subtrochanteric or diaphyseal femur. Looser zones lie on the medial, compression side, classically the femoral neck, with abnormal mineral biochemistry.

items.q: A lucent transverse line is seen in a bowed femur. Which location suggests a Paget disease pseudofracture rather than an osteomalacic Looser zone?
o: Convex (lateral) cortex of the bowed bone
items.e: Paget fissure fractures occur on the convex, tension side of a bowed bone, whereas Looser zones occur on the concave or medial side.

items.q: A 5-year-old with nutritional rickets has had vitamin D and calcium for 6 months; ALP is falling but has not yet normalised and radiographs show partial metaphyseal healing. The parents request surgery for genu varum. The most appropriate advice is:
o: Continue medical treatment and observe, since most bowing remodels once rickets heals
Long leg bracing to correct the deformity
Guided growth now, before the rickets has healed
items.e: Surgery on active rickets risks poor fixation, non-union and recurrence; most nutritional deformity remodels within 1-2 years of metabolic control. Bracing is ineffective for established deformity.

items.q: After tension-band plate (8-plate) guided growth for rachitic genu valgum in a 9-year-old, the plates are removed once the mechanical axis is neutral. The parents should be warned that the main risk afterwards is:
o: Rebound recurrence of the deformity with continued growth
Avascular necrosis of the femoral condyle
items.e: Guided growth is reversible; after removal, growth may cause rebound, especially in metabolic bone disease and young children, so follow-up is continued and slight overcorrection is sometimes accepted.

items.q: Which statement best describes the timing of definitive corrective osteotomy for lower limb deformity in X-linked hypophosphataemia?
o: It is usually deferred towards skeletal maturity because recurrence after early osteotomy is common
It should be done before age 3 years to prevent bowing
It is contraindicated in XLH at any age
It should be done before starting medical therapy
items.e: In XLH, deformity recurs readily after osteotomy in young children; guided growth is used while growing, and osteotomy is generally deferred until near maturity with metabolic control optimised.

items.q: A 15-year-old with XLH has tibial varus, internal tibial torsion and anterior bowing, with a 4 cm limb length discrepancy. Which technique best allows simultaneous multiplanar correction and lengthening?
o: Single-plane opening wedge osteotomy with a plate
Gradual correction with a hexapod circular external fixator
items.e: Hexapod (computer-assisted) circular fixators allow gradual correction of angulation, rotation and translation with lengthening. Guided growth needs open physes and corrects only coronal or sagittal angulation.

items.q: In deformity planning for rachitic genu varum, the normal medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) on a standing radiograph is approximately:
items.e: Normal MPTA is about 87 degrees (85-90), as is the mLDFA; an MPTA below 85 degrees indicates proximal tibial varus.

items.q: A patient on long-term haemodialysis using aluminium-containing phosphate binders has bone pain and fractures. Bone biopsy shows low turnover with wide osteoid seams and aluminium staining at the mineralisation front. Which agent is used to remove the aluminium?
items.e: Aluminium-induced osteomalacia is a low-turnover form of renal bone disease; desferrioxamine chelates aluminium, and aluminium-containing binders are stopped.

items.q: Which bisphosphonate, when given continuously at high doses for Paget disease, is known to impair mineralisation and cause osteomalacia?
items.e: Etidronate, a first-generation non-nitrogen bisphosphonate, inhibits mineralisation at doses close to its antiresorptive dose and can cause osteomalacia; nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates do not at therapeutic doses.

items.q: The circulating half-life of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which makes it the preferred marker of vitamin D status, is approximately:
items.e: 25(OH)D has a half-life of about 2-3 weeks, reflecting stores over time, whereas 1,25(OH)2D has a half-life of only hours and is tightly regulated by PTH, so it is a poor marker of status.

items.q: A laboratory reports serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D as 40 nmol/L. Under the 2016 Global Consensus classification this child's vitamin D status is:
items.e: Consensus thresholds are sufficient over 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL), insufficient 30-50 nmol/L and deficient under 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL); 40 nmol/L is 16 ng/mL (divide by 2.5).

items.q: For intermittent high-dose vitamin D therapy in nutritional rickets, cholecalciferol (D3) is preferred over ergocalciferol (D2) because D3:
o: Is the active hormone at the receptor
items.e: D3 gives a longer-lasting rise in 25(OH)D than D2, so it is preferred for stoss dosing. Both need hepatic and renal hydroxylation, and both can cause hypercalcaemia in excess.

items.q: In nutritional (calcipenic) rickets, serum phosphate is usually low even though the primary deficiency is vitamin D. The main mechanism is:
o: Excess intestinal phosphate binding by calcium
items.e: Hypocalcaemia stimulates PTH, which promotes renal phosphate excretion; the resulting low phosphate is what ultimately prevents mineralisation at the growth plate.

items.q: Calcitriol promotes mobilisation of mineral from bone mainly by acting on which cell?
o: Osteoclast, through a high-density calcitriol receptor on its surface
items.e: Calcitriol, like PTH, acts on osteoblast-lineage cells to increase RANKL, which then drives osteoclast differentiation and resorption; mature osteoclasts are not its main direct target.

items.q: A 2-year-old with rickets due to complete absence of a functional vitamin D receptor (VDDR type 2) fails to respond to very high doses of oral calcitriol. The most effective next treatment to heal the rickets is:
items.e: When the receptor is absent, intestinal calcium absorption cannot be increased by calcitriol; nocturnal IV calcium bypasses the gut and can heal the rickets, after which high-dose oral calcium may suffice.

items.q: A child with nutritional rickets shows no biochemical or radiological improvement after 3 months of prescribed vitamin D and calcium. The first step is to:
o: Confirm adherence and check serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D
items.e: Non-adherence is the commonest reason for treatment failure; a low 25(OH)D confirms it. If 25(OH)D is adequate, VDDR, XLH or malabsorption should be sought.

items.q: A 60-year-old with osteomalacia has a painful Looser zone in the medial femoral neck. Treatment has started. To prevent displacement, the usual additional measure is:
o: Prophylactic internal fixation of the femoral neck
items.e: Most Looser zones heal with medical treatment, but painful femoral neck pseudofractures at risk of displacement are fixed prophylactically (e.g. cannulated screws or a sliding hip screw).

items.q: A 55-year-old man with adult-onset hypophosphataemic osteomalacia has raised FGF23, but repeated whole-body functional imaging fails to locate a tumour. Which test can help localise the phosphaturic tumour?
items.e: Selective venous sampling with FGF23 gradients can localise an occult phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour after equivocal Ga-68 DOTATATE PET-CT; complete excision is curative.

items.q: Most congenital differences of the upper limb arise during which period of gestation, when the limb bud forms and differentiates?
items.e: The upper limb bud appears at about day 26-28 and limb development is essentially complete by week 8, so most congenital hand differences originate between weeks 4 and 8.

items.q: The apical ectodermal ridge, which controls proximal-to-distal outgrowth of the limb bud, acts mainly through which signalling molecules?
items.e: The AER secretes FGFs that drive proximal-distal growth; its failure produces transverse deficiencies and symbrachydactyly. Sonic hedgehog belongs to the zone of polarising activity (radial-ulnar axis).

items.q: A 12-year-old has hypoplastic, triangular-lunula fingernails, absent patellae and iliac horns on pelvic radiograph. The dorsal-ventral patterning gene mutated in this condition is:
items.e: Nail-patella syndrome results from LMX1B mutation; LMX1B is expressed in dorsal mesoderm under Wnt-7a control and specifies dorsal structures such as nails and patella.

items.q: Which molecule, expressed in the ventral ectoderm of the limb bud, restricts Wnt-7a to the dorsal side so that palmar structures develop normally?
items.e: EN-1 in ventral ectoderm suppresses Wnt-7a; loss of EN-1 allows dorsal signalling ventrally (dorsal dimelia, e.g. palmar nails). LMX1B is a dorsal mesodermal effector, not a ventral suppressor.

items.q: Failure of programmed cell death (apoptosis) of the interdigital tissue at about weeks 6-8 produces which anomaly?
items.e: Digits separate by BMP-mediated apoptosis of the interdigital mesenchyme; failure leaves the digits joined (syndactyly).

items.q: Isolated syndactyly of the hand most commonly involves which web space?
items.e: About half of syndactylies involve the third web, followed by the fourth and second; first web syndactyly is the rarest.

items.q: A 1-year-old has syndactyly of the middle and ring fingers extending to the fingertips, with radiographs showing side-to-side fusion of the distal phalanges but otherwise normal bones. This is best classified as:
items.e: Complete means the union extends to the tip; complex means bony (usually distal phalangeal) fusion. 'Complicated' is reserved for abnormal or accessory bones, as in Apert syndrome or synpolydactyly.

items.q: A child has syndactyly of both the second and third web spaces. Why should the middle finger not have both its radial and ulnar sides released at the same operation?
o: Risk of vascular compromise of the middle finger
Risk of injury to both digital nerves causing complete anaesthesia
Insufficient skin graft donor sites in infancy
Risk of physeal arrest of the middle phalanx
items.e: Releasing both sides of one digit at once may divide or devascularise both digital arterial supplies; adjacent webs are staged at least a few months apart.

items.q: For coverage of the skin deficit after release of complete syndactyly, which graft is generally preferred to reduce web creep and contracture?
o: Split-thickness skin graft from the thigh
Full-thickness skin graft from the groin
items.e: Joined digits share skin so grafts are nearly always needed; full-thickness grafts (groin, antecubital or wrist crease) contract less than split-thickness grafts, which are linked to web creep.

items.q: In release of complete syndactyly with a shared (fused) nail plate, the Buck-Gramcko pulp flaps are used to:
o: Cover the exposed flexor tendon sheath at the base
Create the lateral nail folds of the separated digits
items.e: Synonychia leaves no lateral nail fold; Buck-Gramcko pulp plasty uses flaps from the fingertip pulp to recreate the paronychial folds. The commissure is made with a dorsal rectangular or pentagonal flap.

items.q: A 6-month-old boy has short, webbed fingers on the right hand with hypoplastic middle phalanges and an absent anterior axillary fold on the same side. The chest finding most likely present is:
o: Absence of the clavicular head of pectoralis major
Absence of serratus anterior with winged scapula
Absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major
items.e: Poland syndrome combines unilateral absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major with ipsilateral symbrachydactyly; breast and nipple hypoplasia may coexist.

items.q: An infant has fingertips joined distally with small proximal openings (sinus tracts) between the digits, circumferential grooves on two fingers and an amputated thumb tip. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Acrosyndactyly - distal fusion with fenestrations proximally - together with rings and terminal amputations is characteristic of constriction ring syndrome, which is sporadic rather than genetic.

items.q: In Apert syndrome, the thumb is classically:
o: Triphalangeal and in the plane of the fingers
Short and radially deviated owing to a delta (bracketed) proximal phalanx
Absent with a stable carpometacarpal joint
items.e: Apert hands show a complex 'mitten' syndactyly with symphalangism and a short, radially clinodactylous thumb due to a delta phalanx.

items.q: Suture ligation of a pedunculated postaxial 'nubbin' (type B polydactyly) in the newborn nursery is quick, but its recognised drawback is:
o: Frequent necrosis of the little finger
Ulnar collateral ligament instability of the little finger
A residual bump that may contain a painful neuroma
Growth arrest of the fifth metacarpal
items.e: Type B extra digits have only a skin pedicle; tying them off often leaves a small residual nodule, sometimes with a tender neuroma, which may later need excision.

items.q: A 10-month-old has a well-formed sixth digit articulating with a broad fifth metacarpal head (postaxial type A). Besides removing the extra digit, the excision should include:
o: Fusion of the little finger MCP joint
Release of the fourth web space
Transfer of the extensor indicis to the little finger
Reattachment of the ulnar collateral ligament and abductor digiti minimi to the retained little finger
items.e: In type A postaxial duplication, the ulnar collateral ligament and the hypothenar (ADM) insertion are on the excised digit and must be transferred to the retained little finger to prevent instability.

items.q: In the Wassel classification of thumb duplication, a type V lesion is:
items.e: Odd numbers denote a bifid (partially split) bone and even numbers a complete duplication: I bifid distal phalanx, III bifid proximal phalanx, V bifid metacarpal, VI duplicated metacarpal, VII triphalangeal.

items.q: Thumb duplication in which one or both components are triphalangeal (Wassel VII) should prompt evaluation for which associated condition?
items.e: Triphalangeal thumb components are associated with syndromic radial-ray conditions such as Holt-Oram syndrome and Fanconi anaemia, and with dominantly inherited triphalangeal thumb.

items.q: A child has a bifid distal phalanx with two equally small thumb halves (Wassel I). The procedure that combines both halves by central wedge resection is:
items.e: Bilhaut-Cloquet removes the central tissue and unites the two halves to make one thumb of adequate size; its drawbacks are a nail ridge, physeal mismatch and IPJ stiffness.

items.q: When the smaller radial component of a Wassel IV thumb duplication is excised, which structure must be preserved and reattached to the retained ulnar thumb?
o: Radial collateral ligament of the MCP joint, taken with a periosteal sleeve
Ulnar collateral ligament of the MCP joint
items.e: The radial collateral ligament (and the abductor pollicis brevis insertion) belong to the excised radial thumb; they are raised with a periosteal sleeve and reattached to stabilise the retained thumb.

items.q: A 6-year-old who had excision of a radial thumb duplication in infancy now has a zigzag deformity with deviation at the MCP joint in one direction and the IP joint in the other. The commonest cause is:
o: Overgrowth of the retained distal phalanx
Eccentric (unbalanced) flexor and extensor tendon insertions left uncorrected
Premature closure of the metacarpal physis
Excessive release of the first web space
items.e: Z-deformity is the commonest late problem after duplicated-thumb reconstruction and results from failure to centralise eccentric FPL/EPL insertions, correct the axis and balance the collateral ligaments.

items.q: A newborn has a hand with seven fingers, no thumb, and radiographs showing two ulnae and no radius. Surgical treatment usually involves:
o: Centralisation of the carpus on the ulna
Pollicisation of one digit with excision of excess digits
Observation only, as function is normal
items.e: Mirror hand (ulnar dimelia) results from ZPA/SHH duplication; reconstruction excises surplus digits and pollicises one to make a thumb, often with procedures to improve elbow and wrist motion.

items.q: In the Bayne and Klug classification of radial longitudinal deficiency, a type I deficiency is:
o: A miniature radius with both physes present but growth deficient
Absence of the distal radius with a proximal remnant
A short distal radius due to delayed appearance of the distal radial physis
items.e: Type I = short distal radius; type II = hypoplastic (miniature) radius; type III = partial absence; type IV = complete absence (the commonest).

items.q: In the modified (James) classification of radial longitudinal deficiency, type 0 refers to:
o: Carpal anomalies with normal radial length
Thumb hypoplasia with a normal carpus and radius
items.e: James added type N (isolated thumb hypoplasia, normal carpus and radius) and type 0 (carpal abnormalities with a radius of normal length) to Bayne and Klug's types I-IV.

items.q: A newborn has bilateral radial deficiency with hypoplastic thumbs and a cardiac murmur; echocardiography shows an atrial septal defect, and his father has a similar upper limb difference. The gene most likely involved is:
items.e: Holt-Oram syndrome is autosomal dominant (TBX5) and combines radial-ray anomalies with cardiac septal defects. RBM8A is the TAR syndrome gene.

items.q: In thrombocytopenia-absent radius (TAR) syndrome, the natural history of the platelet count is that it:
o: Is normal at birth and falls at about 6-7 years
Remains severely low throughout life, requiring splenectomy
Is lowest in infancy and usually improves after the first year
Falls with the onset of puberty
items.e: Thrombocytopenia in TAR is most severe in the first year (bleeding risk) and then improves, so limb surgery is usually deferred. Marrow failure developing in mid-childhood is typical of Fanconi anaemia.

items.q: An infant with radial longitudinal deficiency is being screened for VACTERL association. Which investigation is part of the routine screen?
items.e: Screening for VACTERL includes renal ultrasound, echocardiography and spinal radiographs, along with a blood count and chromosomal breakage test for Fanconi anaemia.

items.q: During centralisation for radial longitudinal deficiency, which nerve lies superficially on the radial side of the wrist and is at particular risk?
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve
items.e: The radial nerve usually ends at the elbow in radial deficiency; the median nerve takes over its sensory territory and runs superficially along the radial border, where it is vulnerable.

items.q: Radialisation (Buck-Gramcko) differs from classic centralisation for radial club hand in that it:
o: Excises the distal ulna and fuses the carpus to the radial remnant
Places the carpus over the ulna in overcorrection and transfers the radial wrist extensors to the ulnar side
Uses a vascularised fibular graft to reconstruct the radius
Creates a notch in the carpus to seat the ulna
items.e: Radialisation avoids carpal notching, overcorrects the hand onto the ulna and rebalances it with tendon transfers; centralisation traditionally seats the ulna in a carpal notch.

items.q: The commonest complication after centralisation for radial longitudinal deficiency is:
items.e: Recurrent radial deviation is very common in long-term follow-up; other problems include ulnar physeal injury with growth arrest and wrist stiffness.

items.q: Before centralisation of a type IV radial club hand with a tight radial soft-tissue envelope, many surgeons first perform:
o: Release of the elbow extension contracture
Gradual soft-tissue distraction with an external fixator
items.e: Preliminary distraction stretches the tight radial structures so the carpus can be placed on the ulna without excessive bone resection; pollicisation follows the wrist procedure.

items.q: A child has Blauth type II thumb hypoplasia with thenar muscle deficiency, a narrow first web and an unstable MCP joint. In the Huber opponensplasty used to restore opposition, the transferred muscle is:
o: Flexor digitorum superficialis of the ring finger
items.e: The Huber transfer moves abductor digiti minimi to the thumb, adding bulk to the thenar eminence; the ring FDS transfer is an alternative that can also reconstruct the ulnar collateral ligament.

items.q: In Blauth type III thumb hypoplasia, 'pollex abductus' refers to:
o: Absence of the abductor pollicis brevis alone
An abnormal connection between flexor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis longus
An extra abductor tendon inserting on the proximal phalanx
Fixed abduction from a radial collateral ligament contracture
items.e: Pollex abductus is an anomalous FPL-EPL connection that abducts the thumb on attempted flexion; type III also has a hypoplastic metacarpal and extrinsic tendon anomalies.

items.q: A 1-year-old has a small thumb attached to the hand only by a narrow skin bridge with no bony connection (Blauth type IV). The recommended treatment is:
o: Toe phalanx transfer to stabilise the thumb
Excision of the rudimentary thumb and index pollicisation
items.e: The 'pouce flottant' lacks a stable basal joint and cannot be reconstructed usefully; pollicisation of the index finger gives a far better thumb.

items.q: In pollicisation of the index finger, the index finger's proximal interphalangeal joint comes to function as the new thumb's:
items.e: After shortening, the index metacarpal head acts as the trapezium, the MCP joint as the CMC joint, the PIP joint as the MCP joint and the DIP joint as the IP joint.

items.q: In index pollicisation, the extensor indicis proprius is used to function as the new:
items.e: The tendons are rebalanced: EIP becomes EPL, the index EDC becomes APL, the first dorsal interosseous becomes the abductor and the first palmar interosseous the adductor.

items.q: Compared with radial longitudinal deficiency, ulnar longitudinal deficiency is characteristically:
o: Associated with blood dyscrasias such as Fanconi anaemia
Not associated with systemic syndromes but associated with other limb anomalies such as PFFD and fibular hemimelia
items.e: Ulnar deficiency is 4-10 times rarer than radial deficiency and is not linked with haematological, cardiac or renal syndromes, but it often coexists with other musculoskeletal anomalies.

items.q: In partial ulnar aplasia, a fibrocartilaginous ulnar anlage is excised early because it:
o: Compresses the ulnar nerve at the wrist
Tethers the growing radius, causing progressive bowing and radial head dislocation
Fuses to the carpus and blocks wrist flexion
items.e: The anlage acts as a tight band; excision allows the radius to grow straight. A one-bone forearm is reserved for severe forearm instability.

items.q: In the Bayne classification of ulnar longitudinal deficiency, type IV denotes:
o: Hypoplasia of the ulna with both physes present
items.e: Bayne ulnar types: I hypoplastic ulna, II partial aplasia, III total aplasia, IV radiohumeral synostosis.

items.q: The Snow-Littler procedure is used for:
o: Closure of a typical cleft hand with reconstruction of the first web
Release of a congenital clasped thumb
items.e: Snow-Littler (like the Ueba and Miura techniques) closes the central cleft, transposes the index ray towards the middle position and uses cleft skin to deepen the narrowed first web.

items.q: A child has bilateral central cleft hands, split feet, cleft lip and palate, sparse hair and dental anomalies. The syndrome is:
items.e: EEC syndrome combines split hand/foot malformation with ectodermal dysplasia and orofacial clefting; Poland syndrome is linked with unilateral symbrachydactyly.

items.q: A 1-year-old with unilateral symbrachydactyly has short digital nubbins with small nails and no phalanges. Non-vascularised toe phalanx transfer is best done before about 18 months of age because:
o: The donor toe regrows its phalanx at that age
Tendons are absent after this age
The transferred physis is more likely to survive and keep growing
Nerve repair is unnecessary in infants
items.e: Early free (non-vascularised) phalangeal transfer, ideally under 18 months with the periosteum preserved, has the best chance of physeal survival and continued growth.

items.q: Congenital camptodactyly of the little finger is most often caused by:
o: Volar subluxation of the DIP joint
Delta phalanx of the middle phalanx
items.e: The commonest cause of camptodactyly (PIPJ flexion contracture) is an anomalous lumbrical insertion; FDS anomalies, skin shortage and volar plate contracture also contribute.

items.q: A 2-year-old has a flexible 35-degree flexion contracture of the little finger PIP joint with no functional problem. The first-line treatment is:
o: Volar plate release with skin grafting
items.e: Splinting and stretching are the mainstay of camptodactyly treatment and work best in children under about 3 with flexible contractures; surgical results are unpredictable.

items.q: Late radiographs of long-standing camptodactyly typically show:
o: A C-shaped longitudinal epiphyseal bracket of the middle phalanx
Flattening and notching of the proximal phalangeal neck with a flattened middle phalangeal base
Palmar-radial curvature of the distal phalanx
Bony fusion of the proximal and middle phalanges
items.e: Chronic PIPJ flexion remodels the joint: the proximal phalangeal head flattens with neck notching and the middle phalangeal base flattens, sometimes with volar subluxation.

items.q: A delta phalanx causing clinodactyly is characterised radiologically by:
o: A cone-shaped epiphysis with central physeal fusion
A C-shaped physis (longitudinal epiphyseal bracket) along one side of the bone
An accessory ossicle at the DIP joint
items.e: In a delta phalanx the physis brackets the shaft longitudinally, so growth on one side is tethered and the bone becomes triangular or trapezoidal, causing angulation.

items.q: A 3-year-old has progressive 40-degree clinodactyly of the thumb from a delta proximal phalanx. Excision of the longitudinal bracket with fat interposition (physiolysis) is favoured at this age because:
o: It avoids the need for a later osteotomy in all cases
Subsequent growth can correct the deformity gradually
items.e: Vickers physiolysis interrupts the longitudinal tether; done in young children (under about 6) it allows the remaining growth to straighten the digit.

items.q: Clinodactyly of the little finger due to a short, trapezoidal middle phalanx is most commonly associated with:
items.e: Little-finger clinodactyly is very frequent in trisomy 21; it also occurs with Klinefelter, Turner and Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes.

items.q: A 10-year-old girl develops a painless palmar and radial curvature of the distal phalanx of both little fingers. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Kirner deformity is a palmar-radial bowing of the little finger distal phalanx, usually in girls aged about 8-14; it is managed by observation or osteotomy.

items.q: During open A1 pulley release for a fixed paediatric trigger thumb, which structure is most at risk because it lies superficial and close to the pulley?
o: Ulnar digital nerve of the index finger
Motor branch of the median nerve
Radial digital nerve of the thumb
items.e: The radial digital nerve crosses obliquely and superficially over the A1 pulley region of the thumb and is the structure classically injured during release.

items.q: A 4-year-old has persistent triggering of the ring finger. In paediatric trigger finger, compared with trigger thumb, surgery often requires:
o: A1 release only, as in adults
Excision of one slip of FDS, sometimes with A3 pulley release, in addition to A1 release
items.e: Paediatric trigger fingers often have anatomical anomalies (abnormal FDS decussation or slips, nodules), so isolated A1 release frequently fails.

items.q: An infant holds the thumb flexed across the palm at the MCP joint and cannot extend it actively; passive extension is full. The first-line treatment is:
o: Splinting of the thumb in extension for several months
items.e: Congenital clasped thumb from hypoplastic EPB/EPL usually responds to 3-6 months of extension splinting; tendon transfer is reserved for failures.

items.q: A newborn has a deep constriction ring around the middle finger with a swollen, dusky, cool fingertip distal to it. The appropriate management is:
o: Urgent release of the constriction ring
items.e: A constriction ring causing vascular compromise or progressive distal oedema is a neonatal emergency requiring urgent release with Z- or W-plasty.

items.q: In the OMT classification of congenital upper limb anomalies, constriction ring syndrome is classified as a:
items.e: OMT divides anomalies into malformations (axis formation/differentiation), deformations (e.g. constriction ring), dysplasias (e.g. macrodactyly and tumorous conditions) and syndromes.

items.q: Nerve territory-oriented macrodactyly of the index and middle fingers is associated with lipofibromatous hamartoma of which nerve?
items.e: Macrodactyly in the median nerve territory accompanies lipofibromatous hamartoma of the median nerve; it is now included in the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum.

items.q: Somatic mutation in which gene underlies most cases of isolated true macrodactyly?
items.e: Macrodactyly is part of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS); neurofibromatosis and Proteus syndrome are differential diagnoses.

items.q: A newborn with amyoplasia (classic arthrogryposis) is most likely to show which upper limb posture?
o: Abducted shoulders, flexed elbows and extended wrists
Internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows and flexed, ulnar-deviated wrists
Externally rotated shoulders and supinated forearms
Flail shoulders with normal elbows and wrists
items.e: Amyoplasia gives a symmetrical posture of internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows, flexed ulnarly deviated wrists and thumb-in-palm, with absent skin creases but normal sensation and intelligence.

items.q: A child with arthrogryposis has stiff extended elbows. Once passive flexion has been gained by posterior capsulotomy and triceps lengthening, active flexion can be restored by:
o: Elbow arthrodesis in 90 degrees of flexion
Tendon transfer such as triceps to biceps
items.e: Passive elbow flexion must be achieved first; active flexion is then provided by transfers such as triceps-to-biceps, pectoralis major or latissimus dorsi transfer.

items.q: For congenital radioulnar synostosis with severe fixed pronation, resection of the bony bridge to restore rotation is not recommended because:
o: It causes posterior interosseous nerve palsy in most cases
It destabilises the distal radioulnar joint
It leads to radial head overgrowth
The synostosis reliably re-forms and motion is not regained
items.e: Attempts to mobilise the synostosis fail; the standard is derotational osteotomy through the fusion mass to place the forearm in a functional position.

items.q: A 5-year-old with unilateral congenital proximal radioulnar synostosis has the dominant forearm fixed in 80 degrees of pronation and difficulty with daily tasks. The recommended treatment is:
o: Derotational osteotomy through the synostosis to a slightly pronated position
Excision of the synostosis with interposition of fat
Observation, as the shoulder will compensate
items.e: Severe pronation (over about 60 degrees) causes functional problems; rotational osteotomy brings the dominant forearm to about 10-20 degrees of pronation. Large rotations risk compartment syndrome and vascular compromise.

items.q: A 2-year-old has bilateral posterior radial head dislocation discovered incidentally. Which radiographic feature indicates that the dislocation is congenital rather than traumatic?
o: A concave radial head with a normal capitellum
A convex, dome-shaped radial head with a hypoplastic capitellum
A fracture of the proximal ulna
Periosteal reaction along the radial neck
items.e: Congenital dislocations show a convex radial head and an underdeveloped capitellum because the head has never articulated; a traumatic dislocation preserves a concave head and normal capitellum.

items.q: A 13-year-old girl with short stature and bilateral Madelung deformity is likely to have Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis due to a mutation of which gene?
items.e: Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis (mesomelic short stature with Madelung deformity) is caused by SHOX haploinsufficiency; FGFR3 causes achondroplasia.

items.q: A 44-year-old tennis player feels as if he has been struck in the calf while lunging forward. There is tenderness and bruising over the medial calf at mid-calf level; the Thompson test is normal. Which structure is most likely torn?
o: Medial head of gastrocnemius at its musculotendinous junction
Achilles tendon 2-6 cm above its insertion
Soleus at its origin from the fibula
items.e: 'Tennis leg' is a tear of the medial head of gastrocnemius at the musculotendinous junction in middle-aged players; the intact Thompson test argues against an Achilles rupture. Isolated plantaris rupture was historically blamed but is uncommon.

items.q: In a middle-aged man with sudden medial calf pain and swelling suggestive of 'tennis leg', which first investigation both confirms the muscle injury and excludes the main differential diagnosis?
o: Plain radiograph of the tibia and fibula
items.e: Ultrasound shows the medial gastrocnemius tear and fluid collection, and duplex scanning excludes deep vein thrombosis, the key differential of acute calf pain and swelling.

items.q: During an open Strayer gastrocnemius recession through a posteromedial incision at the distal gastrocnemius aponeurosis, which structure is most at risk?
items.e: The sural nerve (with the short saphenous vein) runs in the midline superficial to the gastrocnemius aponeurosis and must be identified and protected during a Strayer recession.

items.q: Which gastrocnemius recession is performed proximally, by incising the deep (anterior) fascia of the gastrocnemius muscle bellies in the interval between gastrocnemius and soleus through a medial calf incision?
items.e: The Baumann recession divides the gastrocnemius fascia within the muscle bellies (intramuscular, proximal), whereas the Strayer divides the distal gastrocnemius aponeurosis and the Hoke procedure lengthens the Achilles tendon itself.

items.q: What is the main risk specific to a percutaneous triple-hemisection (Hoke) Achilles tendon lengthening compared with a gastrocnemius recession?
o: Injury to the deep peroneal nerve
Overlengthening with weak push-off, calcaneal gait and heel pressure ulceration
items.e: Lengthening the conjoint tendon affects both gastrocnemius and soleus and can overlengthen it, giving weak push-off, calcaneal gait and plantar heel ulcers (a particular concern in neuropathic patients).

items.q: After repeated inversion sprains, a mass of hyalinised fibrous scar tissue forms in the lateral gutter of the ankle between the talus and fibula, causing anterolateral impingement. This was described as the:
items.e: Wolin described a 'meniscoid' fibrous lesion in the lateral gutter as a cause of anterolateral soft-tissue impingement, treated by arthroscopic debridement.

items.q: In anterior bony ankle impingement ('footballer's ankle'), osteophytes form on the anterior distal tibia and the talar neck. Pain is typically reproduced by:
o: Forced passive dorsiflexion of the ankle
Forced passive plantarflexion of the ankle
items.e: The anterior tibial and talar neck osteophytes 'kiss' in dorsiflexion; forced plantarflexion instead provokes posterior impingement (os trigonum).

items.q: An anterocentral portal for ankle arthroscopy is generally avoided because it lies between the extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus tendons, endangering the:
o: Dorsalis pedis artery and deep peroneal nerve
