items.e: The Cunningham technique uses massage and patient relaxation with the arm adducted. FARES uses longitudinal traction with vertical oscillation while abducting; Hippocratic and Kocher methods use traction or leverage.

items.q: After closed reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation, which radiographs are required to confirm concentric reduction?
o: An AP view plus an axillary (or Velpeau axillary) view
items.e: Two orthogonal views (AP plus axillary or Velpeau) are needed, because a dislocation or subluxation can be missed on a single AP view. The Stryker notch view is for Hill-Sachs lesions.

items.q: Compared with a teenager, a 58-year-old after a first-time anterior shoulder dislocation is more likely to develop which problem?
items.e: Recurrence falls sharply with age (about 10-15% after 40), whereas rotator cuff tears (and axillary nerve injury) become common. Persistent weakness after reduction in an older patient is a cuff tear until proved otherwise.

items.q: A 19-year-old rugby player has a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation with a Bankart lesion and no bone loss. Compared with non-operative treatment, primary arthroscopic Bankart repair:
o: Increases later osteoarthritis without reducing recurrence
Has similar recurrence rates at 2 years
Is indicated only after three or more dislocations
items.e: In young contact athletes, recurrence after non-operative treatment is about 80%, compared with roughly 10-15% after primary arthroscopic stabilisation, so early surgery is offered selectively to this group.

items.q: At shoulder arthroscopy, viewed from the anterosuperior portal, the glenoid has the shape of an 'inverted pear'. This indicates:
o: Anteroinferior glenoid bone loss of about 25% or more
items.e: Burkhart described the inverted-pear glenoid as loss of the anteroinferior bone, corresponding to about 25% or more of the inferior glenoid width; isolated Bankart repair then fails frequently and a bone block is indicated.

items.q: In the glenoid track concept, the Hill-Sachs interval (HSI) is the:
o: Width of the Hill-Sachs lesion plus the intact bone bridge between it and the rotator cuff insertion
Distance between the Hill-Sachs lesion and the bicipital groove
Intact glenoid width minus the anterior bone loss
items.e: HSI = width of the Hill-Sachs lesion + the bone bridge to the cuff footprint. If HSI exceeds the glenoid track, the lesion is off-track (engaging).

items.q: On 3D CT, the intact inferior glenoid diameter is 25 mm and the anterior glenoid bone loss is 3 mm. The Hill-Sachs interval is 20 mm. Using glenoid track = 0.83D - d, the lesion is:
o: On-track, so isolated Bankart repair is appropriate
On-track, but a Latarjet is needed because of the bone loss
Off-track, so remplissage should be added to the Bankart repair
items.e: Track = 0.83 x 25 - 3 = 17.75 mm; HSI 20 mm exceeds it, so the lesion is off-track. With only 12% glenoid bone loss, Di Giacomo's algorithm recommends arthroscopic Bankart plus remplissage.

items.q: An 18-year-old competitive rugby player is planned for surgery for recurrent anterior instability. External rotation at the side is 70 degrees, an AP radiograph in external rotation shows a Hill-Sachs lesion, and the glenoid contour is normal. His Instability Severity Index Score is:
items.e: Age under 20 (2) + competitive sport (2) + contact sport (1) + Hill-Sachs on external rotation AP (2) = 7; no hyperlaxity and normal glenoid contour score 0. A score over 6 predicts about 70% recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart, favouring Latarjet.

items.q: In the Instability Severity Index Score, shoulder hyperlaxity (1 point) is defined as:
o: External rotation with the arm at the side over 85 degrees, or Gagey hyperabduction over 90 degrees
A Beighton score of 4 or more
Internal rotation behind the back reaching T4
items.e: Balg and Boileau defined hyperlaxity as external rotation (arm at side) over 85 degrees and/or inferior hyperlaxity with Gagey hyperabduction over 90 degrees. The Beighton score is not part of the ISIS.

items.q: Which radiographic finding scores 2 points in the Instability Severity Index Score?
o: Glenoid retroversion over 10 degrees on CT
Loss of the sclerotic inferior glenoid contour on the AP radiograph
items.e: The two radiographic items, each worth 2 points, are a Hill-Sachs lesion visible on the AP view in external rotation and loss of the inferior glenoid sclerotic contour on the AP view. CT parameters are not used.

items.q: Arthroscopic remplissage for recurrent anterior instability involves:
o: Transfer of the coracoid to the anterior glenoid
Tenodesis of the infraspinatus tendon and posterior capsule into the Hill-Sachs defect
Filling the Hill-Sachs defect with bone cement
items.e: Remplissage ('to fill') is a capsulotenodesis of infraspinatus and the posterior capsule into the Hill-Sachs lesion, making the defect extra-articular so it cannot engage the anterior glenoid rim.

items.q: The main functional cost of adding remplissage to an arthroscopic Bankart repair is:
o: Axillary nerve palsy in most cases
A small loss of external rotation
items.e: Tethering infraspinatus into the defect typically causes a small, usually clinically minor, loss of external rotation (especially in abduction), while greatly reducing recurrence for off-track lesions.

items.q: In the Latarjet procedure, the coracoid graft (about 2-3 cm with the conjoint tendon attached) is passed through a subscapularis split and fixed:
o: With two screws, flush with the glenoid face, below the equator
With one screw, placed vertically at the 12 o'clock position
With suture anchors on the scapular neck medial to the rim
With a buttress plate on the posterior glenoid
items.e: The Latarjet graft is placed flat on the anteroinferior glenoid neck (3-5 o'clock, below the equator), flush with the articular surface, and fixed with two screws. Placement medial to the rim risks recurrence.

items.q: Compared with the Latarjet procedure, the classical Bristow procedure:
o: Uses a tricortical iliac crest graft
Transfers only the coracoid tip, typically fixed with a single screw
Transfers the coracoid with pectoralis minor to the posterior glenoid
Places the graft over subscapularis without splitting it
items.e: The Bristow transfers just the tip of the coracoid (with conjoint tendon), usually placed vertically and fixed with one screw, giving less bone than the Latarjet, which lays the larger coracoid flat with two screws.

items.q: Postoperative CT after a Latarjet shows the coracoid graft protruding 4 mm lateral to the glenoid articular surface. The main long-term risk of this malposition is:
items.e: A laterally overhanging graft abrades the humeral head and leads to glenohumeral arthritis; a graft placed too medially gives an inadequate bony effect and recurrence.

items.q: In Patte's 'triple blocking effect' of the Latarjet, the capsular (Bankart-like) effect is achieved by suturing the capsule to the:
o: Stump of the coracoacromial ligament left on the graft
items.e: The three effects are the bony glenoid extension, the sling effect of the conjoint tendon (most important in abduction-external rotation) and the capsular repair to the coracoacromial ligament stump.

items.q: The Eden-Hybinette procedure for anterior glenoid bone loss uses a:
o: Coracoid transfer with the conjoint tendon
items.e: Eden-Hybinette is a free tricortical iliac crest bone block fixed to the anterior glenoid, used for massive bone loss or after a failed Latarjet.

items.q: For massive anterior glenoid bone loss or a failed Latarjet, a fresh distal tibial allograft is attractive mainly because it provides:
o: A curved osteochondral surface that matches the glenoid
A dynamic tendon sling similar to the conjoint tendon
A lower cost than autologous iliac crest
items.e: The lateral distal tibia has a radius of curvature close to the glenoid and carries articular cartilage, restoring a congruent cartilage-covered glenoid arc; it is non-vascularised and provides no sling effect.

items.q: Thermal capsulorrhaphy for shoulder instability was abandoned mainly because of:
o: Excessive loss of external rotation alone
Capsular necrosis, chondrolysis and high failure rates
items.e: Thermal shrinkage caused capsular thinning and necrosis, glenohumeral chondrolysis, axillary nerve injury and unacceptable recurrence, so it is no longer used.

items.q: Rapid glenohumeral chondrolysis after arthroscopic shoulder stabilisation has been most strongly linked to:
o: Continuous intra-articular local anaesthetic infusion through a pain pump
items.e: Postarthroscopic glenohumeral chondrolysis is strongly associated with intra-articular pain pumps delivering bupivacaine (and with thermal capsulorrhaphy).

items.q: A 40-year-old wakes after a nocturnal seizure with a painful shoulder. The arm is held adducted and internally rotated and cannot be externally rotated; the AP radiograph has been reported as normal. The next step is:
o: An axillary radiograph or CT of the shoulder
Analgesia and a sling for frozen shoulder
Ultrasound for a rotator cuff tear
items.e: This is a posterior dislocation until proved otherwise; 50-80% are missed on the AP view. An axillary view or CT confirms the dislocation and shows the reverse Hill-Sachs lesion.

items.q: On an AP shoulder radiograph, the 'light bulb' appearance of the humeral head is caused by:
o: Anterior dislocation with a large Hill-Sachs lesion
The humeral head being fixed in internal rotation in a posterior dislocation
Avascular necrosis of the humeral head
items.e: In posterior dislocation the head is locked in internal rotation, so the greater tuberosity no longer projects laterally and the head looks symmetrical, like a light bulb; loss of the half-moon overlap is another sign.

items.q: The 'rim sign' of posterior shoulder dislocation on an AP radiograph is positive when the distance between the anterior glenoid rim and the medial humeral head exceeds about:
items.e: A widened gap of more than 6 mm between the anterior glenoid rim and the humeral head suggests posterior dislocation (positive rim sign).

items.q: In the modified McLaughlin (Neer) procedure for a reverse Hill-Sachs lesion involving 25-50% of the articular surface, the defect is filled by transferring the:
o: Lesser tuberosity with the attached subscapularis
items.e: McLaughlin transferred the subscapularis tendon into the anteromedial defect; Neer's modification transfers the lesser tuberosity with subscapularis, giving bone-to-bone healing.

items.q: A 60-year-old has a locked posterior shoulder dislocation of 8 months' duration with a reverse Hill-Sachs lesion involving 55% of the articular surface. The best treatment is:
o: Closed reduction and immobilisation in external rotation
items.e: Defects over about 50%, or dislocations older than about 6 months with cartilage damage, are treated with hemiarthroplasty or total shoulder arthroplasty.

items.q: After an acute posterior shoulder dislocation, the reverse Hill-Sachs lesion involves 15% of the articular surface and the joint is stable after closed reduction. Management is:
o: Immobilisation in neutral to slight external rotation for about 6 weeks
Immobilisation in an internal rotation sling
items.e: Small defects (under about 25%) that are stable after reduction are treated by immobilisation in external rotation, keeping the defect away from the posterior glenoid; an internal rotation sling favours redislocation.

items.q: In a patient with multidirectional instability, a sulcus sign that remains greater than 2 cm with the arm in external rotation indicates incompetence of the:
o: Posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
items.e: External rotation normally tightens the rotator interval structures and reduces the sulcus; persistence in external rotation indicates rotator interval incompetence, which may need interval closure if surgery is required.

items.q: In the Gagey hyperabduction test, passive glenohumeral abduction with the scapula stabilised of more than about 105 degrees indicates laxity of the:
items.e: Normal passive glenohumeral abduction is about 85-90 degrees; over 105 degrees indicates laxity of the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex.

items.q: A 20-year-old with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and multidirectional shoulder instability has persistent symptoms after 6 months of structured rehabilitation. The main consideration regarding surgery is that:
o: Soft-tissue stabilisation has a high failure rate in this condition, so surgery is approached with great caution
Thermal capsulorrhaphy is the preferred procedure
A Latarjet procedure is the treatment of choice
Results of capsular shift match those of traumatic Bankart repair
items.e: Abnormal collagen leads to high failure rates after capsular shift or plication in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; prolonged rehabilitation is the mainstay and surgery is undertaken selectively.

items.q: Among clinical tests for anterior shoulder instability, which is often cited as the most specific?
items.e: In the release test, sudden removal of the posterior relocating force in abduction-external rotation reproduces apprehension; it has high specificity for anterior instability. The jerk test is for posterior instability and the sulcus sign for inferior laxity.

items.q: A 17-year-old swimmer has painless, symmetrical, increased anterior and posterior translation on load-and-shift testing of both shoulders and no history of instability symptoms. This represents:
items.e: Laxity is a physical sign; instability is symptomatic pathological translation. Asymptomatic laxity, common in swimmers, needs no treatment.

items.q: A recognised drawback of open Bankart repair through a subscapularis takedown, compared with arthroscopic repair, is:
o: A higher rate of axillary artery injury
Loss of external rotation and risk of subscapularis insufficiency
items.e: Open Bankart repair gives low recurrence but can cause loss of external rotation and, after subscapularis takedown, subscapularis dysfunction; capsular shift is readily performed in open surgery.

items.q: At arthroscopy, the anteroinferior labroligamentous complex is found healed medially and inferiorly on the scapular neck (ALPSA lesion). The key step in repair is to:
o: Mobilise the sleeve from the glenoid neck and reattach it at the articular margin
Repair it in situ to the scapular neck
Perform an open Latarjet regardless of bone loss
items.e: An ALPSA lesion must be fully mobilised off the glenoid neck and shifted back up to the glenoid articular margin; repairing it in its medialised position leaves the shoulder unstable and recurrence is higher.

items.q: During arm elevation, the ratio of glenohumeral to scapulothoracic motion is approximately:
items.e: Scapulohumeral rhythm is about 2:1 (glenohumeral:scapulothoracic), so of 180 degrees elevation roughly 120 degrees is glenohumeral and 60 degrees scapulothoracic.

items.q: In current clinical practice, the commonest underlying cause of Charcot neuroarthropathy of the foot is:
items.e: Diabetes has replaced tabes dorsalis (the historical commonest cause) as the leading cause of Charcot foot. Syringomyelia mainly produces upper-limb Charcot joints.

items.q: A 35-year-old man with progressive loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape distribution develops a grossly destroyed, painless, swollen shoulder. The underlying condition is most likely:
items.e: Syringomyelia (dissociated sensory loss in a cape distribution) characteristically causes Charcot arthropathy of the shoulder and elbow. Tabes classically affects the knee and hip, diabetes the foot and ankle.

items.q: Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy due to tertiary syphilis (tabes dorsalis) classically involves which joint?
items.e: Tabes dorsalis classically produces a Charcot knee (and hip). The shoulder is typical of syringomyelia and the midfoot of diabetes.

items.q: The 'neurotraumatic' (German) theory of Charcot neuroarthropathy proposes that joint destruction results from:
o: Autonomic hyperaemia causing osteoclastic bone resorption
Haematogenous low-grade infection of subchondral bone
Deposition of glycosylated collagen in articular cartilage
Repetitive unperceived microtrauma to an insensate foot that continues to be loaded
items.e: The German (Volkmann-Virchow) theory blames repeated trauma that the patient cannot feel. The French (Charcot) neurovascular theory instead blames autonomic hyperaemia with bone resorption.

items.q: The 'neurovascular' (French) theory of Charcot neuroarthropathy attributes bone destruction primarily to:
o: Autonomic neuropathy causing arteriovenous shunting, hyperaemia and osteoclastic resorption
Repetitive mechanical microtrauma in an insensate foot
Occlusive tibial artery disease causing bone infarction
items.e: The French theory links sympathetic denervation to increased bone blood flow and osteopenia, weakening bone. Modern thinking unifies both theories via inflammation and the RANKL pathway.

items.q: In the current unifying theory of acute Charcot neuroarthropathy, uncontrolled inflammation after minor trauma leads to osteolysis mainly through:
o: Increased RANKL expression relative to osteoprotegerin, activating osteoclasts
Reduced TNF-alpha production causing osteoclast apoptosis
Excess parathyroid hormone secretion from the parathyroid glands
items.e: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6) up-regulate RANKL, tipping the RANKL/OPG balance towards osteoclast activation; loss of protective pain allows continued loading.

items.q: A 56-year-old diabetic has had a warm, swollen midfoot for 3 weeks. The foot is 4 C warmer than the other side and radiographs show bony debris, fragmentation and dorsal subluxation at the tarsometatarsal joints. The Eichenholtz stage is:
items.e: Eichenholtz stage I combines an active, warm foot with radiographic fragmentation, debris and subluxation. Stage 0 has normal radiographs; stages II and III show healing.

items.q: A diabetic with known Charcot midfoot has decreasing warmth and swelling. Radiographs show absorption of fine debris, sclerosis and fusion of larger fragments. This corresponds to Eichenholtz stage:
items.e: Coalescence (stage II) shows resorption of debris, sclerosis and early fusion of fragments with settling inflammation. Stage III shows remodelling and a cool, stable foot.

items.q: A Charcot foot that is cool, clinically stable and shows remodelled, rounded bone ends with bony ankylosis and a fixed rocker-bottom deformity is in Eichenholtz stage:
items.e: Stage III is the quiescent phase of remodelling and ankylosis, often leaving a permanent deformity such as rocker-bottom foot.

items.q: The complete natural history of an untreated episode of Charcot neuroarthropathy, from acute inflammation to consolidation, typically spans about:
items.e: Each Eichenholtz stage lasts months and the whole process usually takes about 1-2 years; this is why offloading and bracing are prolonged.

items.q: A diabetic with acute Charcot midfoot is treated in a total contact cast. Which objective finding is most commonly used to judge that the active phase has settled and casting can be discontinued?
o: Normalisation of the serum alkaline phosphatase
Complete radiographic fusion of all affected joints
Skin temperature difference from the opposite foot falling below about 2 C
Disappearance of all marrow oedema on MRI
items.e: Serial infrared thermometry is used: casting continues until the side-to-side temperature difference is under about 2 C, after which the patient moves to a CROW. Radiographic fusion or MRI resolution may lag considerably.

items.q: In the Brodsky anatomical classification of Charcot foot, type 2 involvement (subtalar, talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints) is characterised by:
o: The best prognosis and most rapid healing of all types
Isolated avulsion fracture of the calcaneal tuberosity
Involvement limited to the metatarsophalangeal joints
Hindfoot instability and a prolonged time to consolidation
items.e: Brodsky type 2 is hindfoot (Chopart and subtalar) disease, which tends to be unstable and slow to consolidate. Type 3B is the calcaneal tuberosity avulsion.

items.q: A diabetic neuropathic patient develops a painless pathological avulsion fracture of the calcaneal tuberosity with loss of push-off. In the Brodsky classification this is type:
items.e: Brodsky 3B is a pathological fracture of the calcaneal tuberosity, weakening the Achilles insertion and causing loss of push-off and a flattened foot. Type 3A is the ankle.

items.q: In the Sanders and Frykberg classification of Charcot foot, pattern II refers to involvement of the:
items.e: Sanders-Frykberg patterns: I forefoot, II tarsometatarsal, III naviculocuneiform/talonavicular/calcaneocuboid, IV ankle and subtalar, V calcaneus.

items.q: A diabetic has Charcot midfoot with a rocker-bottom deformity and a plantar ulcer, but no osteomyelitis. Using the Rogers and Bevilacqua classification, this is:
items.e: Rogers-Bevilacqua uses location (1 forefoot, 2 midfoot, 3 hindfoot/ankle) plus A no deformity, B deformity, C ulcer, D osteomyelitis; a midfoot ulcer without osteomyelitis is 2C.

items.q: Which weight-bearing lateral radiographic finding is characteristic of a Charcot rocker-bottom midfoot?
o: Increased height of the medial longitudinal arch
Loss or reversal of calcaneal pitch with a plantar-apex (negative) talus-first metatarsal angle
items.e: Midfoot collapse flattens and then reverses the arch: calcaneal pitch is lost or negative and the talus-first metatarsal axis breaks plantarward. A dorsal apex and high calcaneal pitch indicate cavus.

items.q: For a stable, consolidated Charcot midfoot with a recurrent plantar ulcer over a bony prominence, plantar exostectomy gives better results when the prominence is located at the:
items.e: Exostectomy of medial column prominences has a higher success rate than for lateral column (cuboid) prominences, where ulcers recur more often and reconstruction may be needed.

items.q: A 60-year-old diabetic with dense neuropathy presents with a hot, swollen, mildly red foot after a minor twist. There is no ulcer, the foot is 3 C warmer than the other side and radiographs are normal. The most appropriate immediate management is:
o: A 2-week course of oral antibiotics for cellulitis
Offloading in a total contact cast (or non-weight-bearing) and MRI to confirm early Charcot
NSAIDs and normal walking with review in 6 weeks
Compression stockings for presumed venous insufficiency
items.e: A hot swollen neuropathic foot is Charcot until proved otherwise; immediate offloading in stage 0 can prevent collapse. Treating it as cellulitis and allowing walking risks progression to deformity.

items.q: On MRI of a diabetic foot, a bone that is poorly defined on T1-weighted images but reappears clearly on post-contrast T1 images (the 'ghost sign') favours:
items.e: The ghost sign (bone margins disappear on T1 and reappear after gadolinium) favours osteomyelitis, whereas Charcot bone keeps its outline on post-contrast imaging.

items.q: When a labelled leucocyte scan is used to distinguish osteomyelitis from Charcot neuroarthropathy, it is combined with which study to account for displaced or reactive bone marrow?
o: Technetium-99m sulfur colloid bone marrow scan
items.e: Charcot joints contain hyperplastic marrow that takes up labelled leucocytes; a matching sulfur colloid marrow scan identifies marrow, so leucocyte uptake without marrow uptake (discordance) indicates infection.

items.q: The role of bisphosphonates in acute Charcot neuroarthropathy is best described as:
o: They may lower temperature and turnover markers but have not been shown to improve clinical outcome, so they are not routine
They are first-line treatment and replace the need for casting
They halve the time to consolidation and are mandatory
They are contraindicated because they cause rapid fragmentation
items.e: Trials of pamidronate, alendronate and zoledronate show falls in markers and temperature without proven benefit in time to remission or deformity; offloading remains the mainstay.

items.q: After the active phase of Charcot neuroarthropathy settles in a total contact cast, the usual next step in protection is:
o: A Charcot restraint orthotic walker (CROW) for several months, then custom footwear
Removable ankle-foot orthosis worn only at night
items.e: The CROW is a custom full-contact walker used for about 6-12 months after casting, followed by lifelong custom footwear or bracing.

items.q: Which is the strongest indication for surgical reconstruction in Charcot neuroarthropathy of the midfoot?
o: Radiographic fragmentation in a warm but well-aligned foot
A healed, stable rocker-bottom foot without ulceration
An unstable, unbraceable deformity with recurrent ulceration despite offloading
Raised skin temperature in Eichenholtz stage 0
items.e: Surgery is reserved for instability, deformity that cannot be braced, recurrent or non-healing ulcers over prominences, infection or progressive collapse; well-aligned or stable feet are treated non-operatively.

items.q: Traditionally, reconstruction of a Charcot foot was deferred until which phase to reduce the risk of fixation failure?
o: The prodromal phase with normal radiographs (stage 0)
Within 48 hours of the first symptoms
The quiescent consolidation phase, when the foot is no longer warm (Eichenholtz III)
items.e: Classic teaching operated on the cool, consolidated foot because bone is soft and inflamed in stage I. Early surgery for unstable patterns is now accepted when superconstruct fixation is used.

items.q: In realignment arthrodesis of a Charcot midfoot, a 'medial column beam' is:
o: A solid intramedullary bolt passed from the first metatarsal across the cuneiform and navicular into the talus
A plate applied to the dorsum of the second metatarsal
A cerclage wire around the calcaneocuboid joint
items.e: Beaming places a large solid intramedullary screw or bolt along the medial column (first metatarsal into talus), spanning beyond the zone of injury in line with superconstruct principles.

items.q: In Charcot midfoot reconstruction, a plate is preferably placed on the plantar surface because:
o: It avoids injury to the dorsalis pedis artery only
The plantar surface is the tension side of the midfoot during weight-bearing
Plantar bone is denser than dorsal bone in all patients
It allows earlier removal of hardware
items.e: Plantar plating places the implant on the tension side, giving the greatest mechanical advantage, one of the principles of superconstruct fixation.

items.q: A 62-year-old diabetic has an unstable varus Charcot ankle with an open ulcer over the lateral malleolus and MRI evidence of talar osteomyelitis. The most appropriate surgical strategy is:
o: Single-stage retrograde tibiotalocalcaneal nailing through the ulcer
Staged debridement and resection of infected bone, then correction and fusion with circular external fixation
Exostectomy of the lateral malleolus alone
items.e: With an open wound and osteomyelitis, internal fixation carries high infection risk; staged resection with circular (Ilizarov-type) fixation is preferred. Arthroplasty is contraindicated in Charcot.

items.q: A 58-year-old diabetic has an unbraceable, unstable Charcot ankle with intact skin and no infection. A common definitive reconstruction is:
o: Isolated subtalar arthrodesis with a single screw
Supramalleolar osteotomy with preservation of the ankle joint
Tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis with a retrograde intramedullary nail
items.e: TTC arthrodesis with a retrograde nail (often with additional fixation) is standard for an uninfected unstable Charcot ankle; ankle replacement is contraindicated.

items.q: Six months after realignment arthrodesis for Charcot midfoot, CT shows a fibrous rather than bony union, but the foot is plantigrade, stable, braceable and ulcer-free. The best course is:
o: Accept the result and continue protective bracing and footwear
Urgent revision arthrodesis with bone grafting
items.e: In Charcot reconstruction, a stable fibrous union with a plantigrade, ulcer-free foot is an acceptable outcome; revision is needed only for instability, deformity or ulceration.

items.q: Achilles tendon lengthening or gastrocnemius recession is often added to Charcot midfoot reconstruction because it:
o: Restores protective sensation to the sole
Reduces the equinus-driven bending load on the midfoot that promotes collapse
Increases calcaneal pitch by tightening the plantar fascia
Improves arterial flow to the forefoot
items.e: Equinus concentrates load on the midfoot and forefoot; releasing it reduces the force driving rocker-bottom collapse and protects the reconstruction.

items.q: In India, apart from diabetes, an important cause of neuropathic plantar ulceration and Charcot changes in the foot is:
o: Hansen's disease (leprosy) affecting the posterior tibial nerve
items.e: Leprosy damages peripheral nerves, especially the posterior tibial nerve, causing anaesthetic soles, plantar ulcers and tarsal disintegration. Syringomyelia mainly causes upper-limb Charcot joints.

items.q: During prolonged casting of one foot for active Charcot neuroarthropathy, the opposite foot should be closely monitored mainly because:
o: The cast causes sympathetic dystrophy in the opposite limb
Bisphosphonates given for the casted foot weaken the opposite foot
Charcot always spreads by contiguous infection
Increased loading of the contralateral neuropathic foot can trigger Charcot or ulceration there
items.e: Offloading one limb transfers load to the other, which is also neuropathic; contralateral Charcot or ulceration is a recognised complication of treatment.

items.q: A diabetic with a cool, stable, consolidated Charcot midfoot (rocker-bottom) has a recurrent ulcer under a plantar-medial bony prominence despite custom footwear. Joints are stable on stress. The most appropriate operation is:
o: Plantar exostectomy of the prominence, often with Achilles lengthening
Total contact casting for another 12 months
Midfoot realignment arthrodesis with superconstruct fixation
items.e: For a stable, consolidated deformity whose only problem is an ulcer over a prominence, simple exostectomy is effective; realignment arthrodesis is for unstable or unbraceable deformities.

items.q: Charcot neuroarthropathy in a diabetic typically develops in a foot that has:
o: Dense neuropathy with intact, often bounding, pedal pulses
Normal sensation with tibial artery occlusion
items.e: The acute hyperaemic inflammatory phase requires preserved perfusion; Charcot is uncommon in a severely ischaemic foot. The typical patient has a warm, well-perfused, insensate foot.

items.q: Dantrolene, the specific treatment for a malignant hyperthermia crisis during anaesthesia, acts by:
o: Blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor end-plate
Inhibiting calcium release through the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in the sarcolemma
Activating the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA) pump
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is usually due to RYR1 mutations causing uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release; dantrolene binds RYR1 and reduces this release. It has no action at the end-plate receptor.

items.q: Henneman's size principle of motor unit recruitment states that, as the force of a voluntary contraction increases:
o: Large type IIb motor units are recruited first
All motor units are recruited at once and only their firing rate changes
Small motor units with type I fibres are recruited first, then progressively larger units
Motor units are recruited in random order
items.e: Small motor neurones (low threshold, supplying slow oxidative type I fibres) are recruited first; larger fast-twitch units are added as force demand rises.

items.q: The gene defective in Duchenne muscular dystrophy is located at:
items.e: Dystrophin is encoded at Xp21; absent dystrophin causes Duchenne and reduced or abnormal dystrophin causes Becker dystrophy. DMPK on 19q13 is myotonic dystrophy and SMN1 on 5q13 is spinal muscular atrophy.

items.q: A 35-year-old with distal weakness, grip myotonia, early cataracts and a cardiac conduction defect most likely has which genetic abnormality?
o: Expanded CTG trinucleotide repeat in the DMPK gene
items.e: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is autosomal dominant with a CTG repeat expansion in DMPK, showing anticipation, cataracts and conduction defects.

items.q: In facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy with painful scapular winging but a functioning deltoid, the procedure that best improves shoulder elevation is:
o: Pectoralis major transfer to the inferior scapula
Latissimus dorsi transfer to the greater tuberosity
items.e: FSHD (autosomal dominant) weakens the scapular stabilisers while the deltoid is relatively spared; scapulothoracic fusion gives the deltoid a stable base and improves elevation. Tendon transfers fail because donor muscles are also affected.

items.q: Spinal muscular atrophy differs from Duchenne muscular dystrophy in that it:
o: Is due to loss of anterior horn cells from SMN1 deletion, with normal sensation
Causes a very high serum CK of 50-100 times normal
items.e: SMA is autosomal recessive anterior horn cell degeneration due to SMN1 deletion (treatable with nusinersen or onasemnogene); it is a neurogenic, not myopathic, disorder.

items.q: A boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy needs a general anaesthetic. Which agent must be avoided because it can precipitate hyperkalaemic rhabdomyolysis and cardiac arrest?
items.e: Depolarising relaxants (and volatile agents) can cause acute rhabdomyolysis with fatal hyperkalaemia in dystrophinopathies; total intravenous anaesthesia with non-depolarising agents is preferred.

items.q: Which feature best distinguishes Becker from Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
o: Reduced or abnormal (but present) dystrophin with walking usually preserved beyond about 15 years
items.e: Becker is also X-linked but in-frame mutations leave some dystrophin, so the course is milder and ambulation continues past about 15 years; CK is still raised.

items.q: In the first 24 hours after a moderate quadriceps contusion in an athlete, which measure shortens the time to return to sport?
o: Immobilisation of the knee in full extension
Immobilisation of the knee in about 120 degrees of flexion
items.e: Holding the knee in about 120 degrees of flexion for the first day keeps the quadriceps stretched, limits haematoma and stiffness and speeds return; massage increases the risk of myositis ossificans.

items.q: Radiographs of a thigh mass 6 weeks after a football injury show peripheral mineralisation around a lucent centre, separated from the femoral cortex by a clear cleft. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Myositis ossificans shows a zonal pattern with mature bone at the periphery and immature centre, the reverse of parosteal osteosarcoma, which is most mature centrally and attached to the cortex.

items.q: Which hamstring muscle is most commonly injured in sprinting strains?
items.e: The long head of biceps femoris, a two-joint muscle rich in type II fibres, is the commonest site of hamstring strain, typically at the myotendinous junction during eccentric loading in late swing.

items.q: A 40-year-old water-skier has a proximal hamstring avulsion. Which finding is the commonly quoted indication for surgical repair?
o: Avulsion of the semimembranosus alone without retraction
Avulsion of two or more tendons with more than about 2 cm of retraction
items.e: Repair is advised for two- or three-tendon avulsions retracted more than about 2 cm (or in high-demand patients), ideally within about 4-6 weeks, when results are better than with delayed repair.

items.q: Regeneration of new myofibres after skeletal muscle injury depends mainly on activation of:
o: Satellite cells beneath the basal lamina
items.e: Satellite cells are muscle stem cells lying between the sarcolemma and basal lamina; they proliferate and fuse to form new myofibres, while fibroblasts produce competing scar.

items.q: According to the length-tension relationship, a sarcomere develops its maximum active isometric tension when:
o: It is fully shortened so that thin filaments overlap each other
It is stretched until actin and myosin no longer overlap
It is near resting length, where actin-myosin overlap allows the greatest number of cross-bridges
It is at any length, because tension depends only on calcium concentration
items.e: Active tension peaks at optimal overlap near resting length; overstretching reduces cross-bridges and excessive shortening causes filament interference.

items.q: In a boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who has lost ambulation, spinal fusion for scoliosis is generally advised:
o: Only once the curve exceeds 80 degrees
Early, when the curve is about 20-30 degrees and forced vital capacity is still adequate
Never, because bracing controls the curve
Only after the forced vital capacity falls below 20% predicted
items.e: Curves progress relentlessly after loss of walking and respiratory function declines, so fusion is done early while FVC is still above roughly 30-35% predicted; bracing does not halt progression.

items.q: Bisphosphonates resist enzymatic breakdown in the body because their structure contains:
o: A P-C-P bond in place of the P-O-P bond of pyrophosphate
items.e: Replacing the central oxygen of pyrophosphate with carbon (P-C-P) makes bisphosphonates resistant to hydrolysis by phosphatases while keeping strong hydroxyapatite binding.

items.q: Which of the following bisphosphonates has the highest antiresorptive potency?
items.e: Potency order is roughly zoledronate > risedronate > ibandronate > alendronate > pamidronate > clodronate/etidronate.

items.q: The correct instruction for taking weekly oral alendronate 70 mg is:
o: Take with breakfast and a glass of milk to reduce dyspepsia
Take fasting with a full glass of plain water and stay upright for at least 30 minutes before food or other drugs
Take together with a calcium supplement to improve absorption
items.e: Oral bioavailability is under 1% and is abolished by food, calcium or coffee; staying upright reduces the risk of oesophagitis.

items.q: Which oral bisphosphonate has trial evidence for reducing vertebral fractures but no proven reduction in hip fractures?
items.e: In the BONE trial ibandronate reduced vertebral fractures but hip fracture reduction was not demonstrated; alendronate (FIT) and risedronate (HIP) reduced hip fractures.

items.q: The Fracture Intervention Trial (FIT) showed roughly a 50% reduction in both vertebral and hip fractures in women with prior vertebral fractures who received:
items.e: FIT established alendronate's efficacy at the spine and hip; raloxifene (MORE) reduced only vertebral fractures.

items.q: In the HORIZON Pivotal Fracture Trial, yearly zoledronic acid 5 mg reduced morphometric vertebral fractures over 3 years by approximately:
items.e: HORIZON-PFT showed about a 70% reduction in vertebral fractures and about 41% in hip fractures.

items.q: Which serious adverse event signal was reported with zoledronic acid in the HORIZON Pivotal Fracture Trial, although not consistently confirmed later?
items.e: Serious atrial fibrillation was more frequent with zoledronate in HORIZON-PFT; later analyses did not consistently confirm the association.

items.q: After hip fracture surgery, when can the first zoledronic acid infusion be given without compromising its efficacy, according to analysis of HORIZON-RFT?
o: From about 2 weeks after surgery, within the first 90 days
Only after radiological union at 6 months
Not until 12 months after the fracture
items.e: HORIZON-RFT gave the infusion within 90 days of surgery; post hoc analysis found that giving it from about 2 weeks onwards did not reduce efficacy. Vitamin D should be replete first.

items.q: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw is defined as exposed necrotic maxillofacial bone persisting for more than how long in a patient on antiresorptive or antiangiogenic drugs without prior jaw irradiation?
items.e: The accepted definition requires exposed bone (or bone probeable through a fistula) for over 8 weeks with no history of radiation to the jaws.

items.q: Which regimen carries the highest risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw?
o: Denosumab 120 mg monthly for skeletal metastases
Zoledronic acid 5 mg yearly for osteoporosis
items.e: High-dose oncology regimens (zoledronate 4 mg or denosumab 120 mg monthly) carry an ONJ risk around 1%, compared with roughly 1 in 10,000 to 100,000 patient-years at osteoporosis doses.

items.q: A woman develops a painful red eye with blurred vision a few days after her first intravenous zoledronic acid infusion. The most likely drug-related cause is:
items.e: Ocular inflammation (uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis) is a recognised, uncommon adverse effect of bisphosphonates, particularly intravenous ones.

items.q: Continuous high-dose etidronate is avoided mainly because, unlike nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates, it can:
o: Cause atypical femoral fractures within weeks
items.e: Etidronate inhibits mineralisation at doses close to its antiresorptive dose, causing osteomalacia; hence it was given cyclically.

items.q: In children with moderate to severe osteogenesis imperfecta, the established drug treatment that reduces fractures and bone pain and increases vertebral height is:
items.e: Cyclical IV pamidronate (or zoledronate) is standard; teriparatide is contraindicated with open growth plates and denosumab causes rebound hypercalcaemia in children.

items.q: The FLEX extension of FIT, comparing continuation of alendronate for 10 years with stopping after 5 years, found that continuation:
o: Reduced clinical vertebral fractures, with no significant effect on non-vertebral fractures
Had no effect on any fracture outcome
items.e: Women who stopped after 5 years lost little BMD and had similar non-vertebral fracture rates; continuation reduced clinical vertebral fractures, mainly in higher-risk women.

items.q: For a woman who remains at high fracture risk after initial bisphosphonate therapy, the ASBMR task force suggests continuing treatment up to a total of about:
o: 5 years oral or 3 years intravenous, then always stop
items.e: After 5 years oral or 3 years IV, high-risk patients may continue to about 10 years oral or 6 years IV (or switch); low-risk patients may take a 2-3 year holiday.

items.q: Denosumab is best described as a:
o: Fully human IgG2 monoclonal antibody against RANKL
items.e: Denosumab is a fully human IgG2 antibody that binds RANKL, mimicking osteoprotegerin; romosozumab is the humanised anti-sclerostin antibody.

items.q: Apart from hypocalcaemia, which adverse effect was more frequent with denosumab than placebo in the FREEDOM trial?
o: Serious skin infections such as cellulitis, and eczema
items.e: FREEDOM reported more cellulitis (serious skin infections) and eczema with denosumab; acute phase reactions are typical of IV bisphosphonates.

items.q: Denosumab 120 mg given monthly (with loading doses) is approved for which orthopaedic tumour when it is unresectable or resection would cause severe morbidity?
items.e: The giant cells of GCT express RANK and the stromal cells RANKL; denosumab shrinks and ossifies the tumour, though recurrence after stopping is common.

items.q: In the 10-year extension of the FREEDOM trial, continued denosumab therapy was associated with:
o: A plateau in BMD after 3 years
Continued increases in lumbar spine and hip BMD without a plateau, with low fracture rates
Progressive loss of hip BMD after year 5
A rise in atypical femoral fractures to over 1%
items.e: Unlike bisphosphonates, whose BMD gains plateau, denosumab produced continuing BMD gains over 10 years with low fracture incidence.

items.q: The standard dose of teriparatide for osteoporosis is:
items.e: Teriparatide is 20 micrograms SC daily, traditionally for a maximum of 24 months; 80 micrograms daily is abaloparatide, 60 mg six-monthly denosumab and 210 mg monthly romosozumab.

items.q: A recognised limitation of the teriparatide Fracture Prevention Trial (Neer 2001) is that it:
o: Showed no reduction in vertebral fractures
Had no hip fracture endpoint data
Used continuous rather than intermittent PTH
items.e: Teriparatide reduced vertebral fractures by about 65% and non-vertebral by about 53%, but the trial was not able to show an effect on hip fractures.

items.q: The 'anabolic window' of teriparatide refers to the early period of treatment in which:
o: Bone formation markers such as P1NP rise before resorption markers increase
items.e: Intermittent PTH first stimulates formation (P1NP rises within weeks); resorption rises later, so net formation is greatest early in therapy.

items.q: Which adverse effect is recognised with teriparatide, particularly after the first few doses?
items.e: Transient orthostatic hypotension, nausea, leg cramps, transient hypercalcaemia and hyperuricaemia occur with teriparatide; rebound fractures on stopping are characteristic of denosumab.

items.q: The licensed dose of abaloparatide for postmenopausal osteoporosis is:
items.e: Abaloparatide, a PTHrP(1-34) analogue, is 80 micrograms SC daily for up to 2 years.

items.q: In the FRAME trial, 12 months of romosozumab compared with placebo reduced new vertebral fractures by about:
items.e: FRAME showed a 73% reduction in new vertebral fractures at 12 months, after which both groups received denosumab.

items.q: In the ARCH trial of high-risk postmenopausal women, 12 months of romosozumab followed by alendronate, compared with alendronate alone:
o: Reduced vertebral, non-vertebral and hip fractures, but with more serious cardiovascular events
Showed no fracture benefit but greater BMD gain
items.e: ARCH showed superior fracture reduction at all three sites with the romosozumab-first sequence, but an imbalance in serious cardiovascular events led to the warning about recent MI or stroke.

items.q: A non-skeletal benefit of raloxifene that may favour it in a postmenopausal woman with vertebral osteoporosis is:
o: Reduction in invasive oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer
items.e: Raloxifene reduces invasive ER-positive breast cancer; it worsens hot flushes, increases VTE, and RUTH showed a signal for fatal stroke.

items.q: In the Women's Health Initiative, combined oestrogen plus progestogen hormone therapy:
o: Reduced hip and total fractures but increased breast cancer, stroke and venous thromboembolism
Reduced breast cancer and coronary disease
items.e: WHI proved fracture reduction including the hip, but the extraskeletal risks mean HRT is not first-line purely for bone; it is mainly used in younger women with menopausal symptoms.

items.q: Short-term calcitonin may still be used in osteoporosis mainly for:
o: Prevention of glucocorticoid-induced bone loss in children
Its analgesic effect in the first weeks after an acute osteoporotic vertebral fracture
items.e: Calcitonin has an analgesic effect in acute vertebral fractures (about the first 4 weeks); long-term use is restricted because of a malignancy signal.

items.q: Thiazide diuretics have a modest beneficial effect on bone mainly because they:
items.e: Thiazides increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption, lowering urinary calcium and giving modest BMD benefit; loop diuretics do the opposite.

items.q: What daily vitamin D intake is commonly recommended as an adjunct for adults over 50 receiving osteoporosis treatment?
items.e: Most guidelines recommend 800-1,000 IU vitamin D daily with total calcium about 1,000-1,200 mg; very high doses do not prevent and may increase falls.

items.q: Bisphosphonates can be given as 'drug holidays' whereas denosumab cannot, mainly because bisphosphonates:
o: Have no effect on osteoclasts after stopping
Are retained in the skeleton with a half-life of years, so their effect persists after stopping
items.e: Bisphosphonates bind hydroxyapatite and are released slowly, giving a residual effect; denosumab does not bind bone and its effect wears off within months, with rebound turnover.

items.q: A 58-year-old with good soft tissues needs femoral revision for a Paprosky type IV defect (widened, ectatic canal with no isthmus able to provide fixation). Which reconstruction aims to restore femoral bone stock?
o: Impaction allografting with a cemented polished tapered stem
Cement-in-cement revision with a short stem
items.e: Paprosky IV femurs have no isthmus for scratch-fit; impaction grafting (Exeter technique) rebuilds bone stock in younger patients, with APC or proximal femoral replacement as alternatives. Extensively coated stems need at least 4 cm of intact isthmus.

items.q: Fixation failure of extensively porous-coated cylindrical cobalt-chromium stems in femoral revision becomes notably more frequent when the femoral canal diameter exceeds about:
items.e: Large-diameter extensively coated CoCr stems are very stiff and have less isthmus to grip; results deteriorate when the canal is over about 18-19 mm, where tapered fluted titanium stems are preferred.

items.q: On follow-up radiographs of an uncemented femoral stem, new endosteal bone bridging the canal to the porous surface ('spot welds') near the distal end of the coating indicates:
items.e: In Engh's criteria, spot welds (endosteal densification contacting the porous coating) are the key sign of bone ingrowth. Absent spot welds with reactive lines suggest fibrous fixation or loosening.

items.q: Radiographs of an uncemented stem show no spot welds, divergent radiolucent lines around the entire porous surface and a distal endosteal pedestal not touching the stem tip, with progressive subsidence. By Engh's criteria this stem is:
items.e: Progressive subsidence with widening reactive lines around the coated surface and a pedestal indicate an unstable, loose stem. Stable fibrous fixation shows parallel, non-progressive reactive lines without migration.

items.q: Twelve years after an uncemented THA, a patient reports thigh pain on the first few steps after rising that eases as he keeps walking. This 'start-up' thigh pain most suggests:
items.e: Start-up thigh pain is typical of a loose femoral stem; groin or buttock pain points more to the acetabular component. Trochanteric bursitis causes lateral hip pain on lying on the side.

items.q: By the Harris criteria, a cemented femoral stem with a continuous radiolucent line surrounding the entire cement mantle but no migration and no cement fracture is classed as:
items.e: Harris: definite = stem migration, cement fracture or stem fracture; probable = a continuous lucent line around the whole cement mantle; possible = lucency over 50-100% of the interface.

items.q: In the AAOS (D'Antonio) classification of acetabular bone deficiency, type IV denotes:
items.e: AAOS acetabular: I segmental, II cavitary, III combined, IV pelvic discontinuity, V arthrodesis.

items.q: At revision THA the acetabular rim and both columns are supportive, the hip centre has migrated less than 3 cm and the only significant defect is a medial wall deficiency. Paprosky type:
items.e: Paprosky IIC is an isolated medial wall defect with an intact rim and columns; IIA is superomedial cavitation and IIB a superolateral rim defect under one-third. IIIA has over 3 cm superior migration.

items.q: A Paprosky type II acetabular defect (supportive rim and columns, superior migration under 3 cm, teardrop and ischium intact) is usually reconstructed with:
o: A hemispherical uncemented cup with screws, with particulate graft if needed
Acetabular distraction with a jumbo cup
items.e: With supportive columns, a hemispherical porous cup with screw supplementation achieves reliable ingrowth; cages, triflange implants and distraction are for Paprosky IIIB defects and pelvic discontinuity.

items.q: For a chronic pelvic discontinuity, a technique uses an oversized acetabular component to distract the superior and inferior hemipelvis so that elastic recoil compresses the cup. This is called:
o: Cemented cup on a reinforcement mesh
items.e: The acetabular distraction technique (Sporer/Paprosky) uses peripheral distraction and recoil of the discontinuity to give initial stability to a porous cup, often with augments.

items.q: Acetabular impaction bone grafting with a cemented cup (Slooff/Nijmegen technique) is best suited to:
o: Contained cavitary defects, with segmental rim defects first closed by metal mesh
Paprosky IIIB defects with an absent posterior column
Revision in the presence of active infection
items.e: Impaction grafting needs a contained cavity; rim or medial wall segmental defects are converted to contained ones with mesh. Discontinuity and absent columns need cup-cage or triflange solutions.

items.q: On a preoperative AP pelvis for revision THA, severe osteolysis of the ischium mainly indicates deficiency of the:
items.e: In Paprosky's scheme ischial lysis reflects loss of the inferior posterior column and posterior wall; teardrop lysis reflects the medial wall and inferior anterior column.

items.q: A patient with recurrent instability after THA has well-positioned components and functioning abductors. Which bearing choice at revision most reduces re-dislocation while avoiding the mechanical failures of constraint?
o: 28 mm head on a standard liner
22 mm head on an elevated-rim liner
items.e: Dual mobility greatly increases effective head size and jump distance and markedly lowers dislocation after revision. Constrained liners transfer high loads to fixation and fail by dissociation or loosening, so they are reserved for abductor deficiency.

items.q: A constrained acetabular liner at revision THA is most appropriate for:
o: Recurrent dislocation due to a retroverted cup
Recurrent instability from abductor deficiency in a low-demand elderly patient
A young active patient with a first dislocation
items.e: Constraint is a salvage for instability without a correctable cause, typically abductor loss in low-demand patients. Malposition should be corrected by revising the component, and constraint is avoided in the young because of high failure.

items.q: Irreparable abductor deficiency after multiple revision hip procedures can be reconstructed by transferring which muscle to the greater trochanter?
o: Anterior portion of gluteus maximus (with tensor fascia lata)
items.e: Whiteside's technique transfers the anterior part of gluteus maximus (± TFL) to the trochanter to restore abduction; the other muscles are not used for this purpose.

items.q: Cement-in-cement femoral revision is appropriate when:
o: The cement mantle is well bonded to bone and intact, and the stem must be removed (e.g. for acetabular access or a failed taper)
There is gross cement-bone loosening with osteolysis
The cement mantle is fractured with stem subsidence
items.e: A well-fixed intact mantle can be retained and a new polished tapered stem cemented into it, shortening surgery. Loosening at the cement-bone interface, cement fracture or infection need full cement removal.

items.q: During revision TKA the patella cannot be safely mobilised despite synovectomy, re-establishing the gutters and medial tibial release. The first extensile manoeuvre usually recommended is:
o: Releasing the patellar tendon from the tubercle
items.e: The quadriceps snip, an oblique proximal-lateral cut across the quadriceps tendon, is simple and does not alter rehabilitation; TTO and V-Y turndown are reserved for more difficult cases. Patellar tendon avulsion is a catastrophe to avoid.

items.q: A tibial tubercle osteotomy used for exposure in revision TKA should ideally be:
o: About 2 cm long and fixed with one screw
About 6-8 cm long with a distal bony bridge, fixed with wires or screws
About 15 cm long and fixed with a plate
A thin cortical wafer with no fixation
items.e: A long (about 6-8 cm) tubercle osteotomy gives a broad surface for healing and secure wire or screw fixation; short fragments risk fracture and escape.

items.q: Compared with the quadriceps snip, a V-Y quadricepsplasty (turndown) for revision TKA exposure is particularly associated with:
items.e: The turndown detaches the extensor mechanism more extensively and can leave an extensor lag; the snip leaves extensor function largely unaffected. Tubercle non-union relates to TTO.

items.q: In revision TKA, the native joint line typically lies about how far distal to the medial epicondyle?
items.e: The joint line is about 3 cm distal to the medial epicondyle (about 2.5 cm from the lateral epicondyle) and about one fingerbreadth above the fibular head; these help avoid joint-line elevation.

items.q: The classic three-step sequence for component reconstruction in revision TKA is:
o: Re-establish the tibial platform, then the flexion gap (femoral size and rotation), then the extension gap
Balance the extension gap, then the flexion gap, then the tibia
Choose constraint first, then the tibia, then the patella
Size the patella, then the femur, then the tibia
items.e: The tibia sets the platform, then the femur is built to stabilise the flexion gap (size, rotation, posterior augments), and finally the extension gap is matched with distal augments and joint-line position.

items.q: In revision TKA with destroyed posterior femoral condyles, femoral component rotation is best referenced from:
o: The position of the removed femoral component
items.e: With posterior condyles absent, the transepicondylar axis is the most reliable bony landmark for rotation; the posterior condylar axis cannot be used, and the old component may be malrotated.

items.q: At revision TKA a thin, cavitary patellar remnant cannot hold a new button. A technique that osteotomises the remnant longitudinally so it conforms to the trochlea is:
items.e: The gull-wing osteotomy of a deficient patellar shell improves tracking and contact; porous metal patellar augments are another option. The others are tibial tubercle osteotomies.

items.q: After revision TKA, wound breakdown exposes the patellar tendon and proximal tibia. The usual local muscle flap for soft-tissue cover is:
items.e: The medial head of gastrocnemius reaches the proximal tibia and patellar tendon area and is the workhorse flap for knee arthroplasty wounds; soleus covers the middle third of the tibia.

items.q: A knee needing revision TKA has several previous longitudinal incisions. Which should generally be used?
o: A new straight midline incision between them
items.e: The skin of the anterior knee is supplied mainly from the medial side, so using the most lateral usable incision limits a devascularised lateral skin bridge and wound necrosis.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a metaphyseal sleeve from a metaphyseal cone in revision TKA?
o: A cone is attached to the component by a Morse taper, whereas a sleeve is cemented separately
A sleeve is attached to the component by a taper and the bone is prepared by broaching; a cone is a separate porous augment into which the component is cemented
Both are made of cancellous allograft
A sleeve is used only on the patella
items.e: Sleeves are modular parts of the implant, press-fit after broaching. Cones (tantalum or titanium) are impacted into reamed metaphyseal bone and the component is then cemented into the cone. Both give zone 2 fixation.

items.q: In revision TKA, offset couplers are used with press-fit diaphyseal-engaging stems mainly to:
o: Allow a canal-filling stem without forcing the component into overhang or malposition
items.e: Because the canal axis is often not centred under the ideal component position, an offset coupler lets the stem engage the diaphysis while the component sits correctly on the bone.

items.q: A painful TKA has normal alignment, rotation and fixation, a stable joint and a negative infection work-up. What is the expected result of revision surgery for this unexplained pain?
o: Reliable pain relief in most patients
Poor results; revision without a diagnosis is generally not advised
Pain relief only if the patella is resurfaced
items.e: Revision TKA for unexplained pain without a mechanical or infective cause has poor and unpredictable outcomes; a diagnosis should be established first.

items.q: Six weeks after primary TKA, a patient has only 70 degrees of flexion. Infection is excluded and components are well positioned. The first-line intervention is:
o: Revision with a larger polyethylene insert
items.e: Early postoperative stiffness without malposition or infection is treated by manipulation under anaesthesia, most effective within about 12 weeks; revision is reserved for refractory or malpositioned cases.

items.q: When reconstructing a chronic extensor mechanism disruption after TKA with an extensor mechanism allograft or synthetic mesh, the graft should be tensioned:
o: Tightly with the knee in full extension
items.e: Grafts stretch with time, so they are tensioned tight in full extension and protected in extension postoperatively; tensioning in flexion leaves a persistent extensor lag.

items.q: Proximal femoral replacement (megaprosthesis) for massive femoral bone loss in revision hip surgery carries a characteristically high rate of:
items.e: Loss of the greater trochanter and abductor attachment makes dislocation a leading complication of proximal femoral replacement (with infection); constrained or dual-mobility cups and mesh soft-tissue attachment are used to reduce it.

items.q: Silver coating of a megaprosthesis is intended mainly to:
o: Improve bone ingrowth at the stem
items.e: Silver ions are antimicrobial; silver-coated tumour and revision megaprostheses aim to lower the high infection rates of these large implants.

items.q: In a young patient with massive proximal femoral bone loss, an allograft-prosthesis composite is chosen over a proximal femoral replacement mainly because it:
o: Allows biological reattachment of the abductors and soft tissues to the allograft
Can be performed without a long stem
items.e: An APC restores bone stock and allows tendon-to-allograft healing (abductors), improving stability and function in younger patients; it still risks non-union, resorption and infection.

items.q: After Girdlestone resection arthroplasty of the hip for uncontrollable infection, the usual functional result is:
o: Reasonable pain relief but several centimetres of shortening, a Trendelenburg gait and need for walking aids
Complete pain relief with full abductor power
items.e: Resection arthroplasty controls infection and usually relieves pain but leaves a short, unstable hip with abductor weakness and reliance on aids.

items.q: The reported dislocation rate after revision THA is approximately:
items.e: Revision THA has a much higher dislocation rate than primary THA (about 2-3%), up to about 10-15%, because of soft-tissue and abductor compromise; dual mobility and larger heads reduce it.

items.q: In chronic (over 6 weeks) periprosthetic knee infection, the 2018 ICM synovial white cell count threshold suggesting infection is about:
items.e: For chronic PJI the synovial WBC threshold is about 3,000 cells/µL with PMN over 80%; much higher cut-offs (about 10,000/µL, PMN 90%) apply in the acute postoperative period.

items.q: Blood cobalt or chromium above which level was used by the UK MHRA as a threshold for concern and further imaging in metal-on-metal hips?
items.e: The MHRA used 7 ppb (7 µg/L) as the level prompting cross-sectional imaging and closer review; ions alone do not mandate revision.

items.q: In taper corrosion (trunnionosis) at a cobalt-chromium head on a titanium stem in a metal-on-polyethylene THA, the typical blood ion pattern is:
o: Chromium raised far more than cobalt
Normal ions in nearly all cases
items.e: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion releases cobalt preferentially, so cobalt is raised out of proportion to chromium; treatment is head (ceramic with titanium sleeve) and liner exchange when symptomatic.

items.q: Best imaging to detect a pseudotumour (adverse local tissue reaction) around a metal-on-metal hip is:
items.e: MARS MRI shows soft-tissue masses, fluid collections and abductor damage; ultrasound is an alternative. Bone scan and PET are non-specific.

items.q: After uncemented THA, increased periprosthetic uptake on a technetium bone scan can be normal for up to about:
items.e: Remodelling causes increased uptake for 1-2 years (longer for uncemented implants), so a bone scan is non-specific early; a normal scan later makes loosening or infection unlikely.

items.q: The principal early complication of monoblock tapered fluted titanium (Wagner-type) stems used in femoral revision is:
items.e: Monoblock tapered stems must be sized so they engage a long tapered segment; under-sized stems subside, which also increases dislocation. Modular junction fracture belongs to modular designs.

items.q: A recognised failure mode specific to modular tapered titanium revision stems, especially with poor proximal bone support, is:
o: Stem subsidence of over 5 cm in all cases
Fatigue fracture at the modular body-stem junction
items.e: When the proximal femur gives no support, the modular junction bears high cyclic bending loads and can fracture; using large junctions and restoring proximal support reduce this risk.

items.q: A typical long-term radiographic consequence of large-diameter extensively porous-coated cobalt-chromium stems in femoral revision is:
items.e: Stiff, distally fixed stems bypass the proximal femur, causing proximal bone resorption (stress shielding), worse with larger diameters.

items.q: After an extended trochanteric osteotomy in revision THA, the new stem should obtain diaphyseal fixation at least how far distal to the osteotomy?
items.e: At least about 4-6 cm of scratch-fit or tapered fixation below the end of the ETO is needed for stability; the osteotomy fragment is then cabled back.

items.q: Porous tantalum (trabecular metal) acetabular shells and augments help in revision THA mainly because they have:
o: High porosity (about 75-80%), low modulus and high surface friction encouraging initial stability and bone ingrowth
items.e: Highly porous metals give a high coefficient of friction for press-fit stability and ingrowth even against poor host bone, which is why they are used with augments for Paprosky III defects.

items.q: For a Paprosky IIIB acetabular defect with pelvic discontinuity, a porous cup that bridges the defect protected by an ilioischial cage fixed over it is called:
items.e: In the cup-cage, the porous cup achieves biological fixation while the cage offloads it until ingrowth; a cage alone relies on cement and has high long-term failure.

items.q: A revision acetabular implant manufactured from the patient's CT scan with iliac, ischial and pubic flanges, used for massive defects and pelvic discontinuity, is the:
items.e: The custom triflange is a patient-specific implant bridging massive bone loss with three flanges screwed into ilium, ischium and pubis.

items.q: A failed acetabular component has migrated medially through Köhler's line into the pelvis. The essential preoperative investigation is:
o: CT with contrast angiography to define the relation to the iliac vessels
items.e: Intrapelvic components or cement may adhere to the external iliac vessels, ureter or bowel; CT angiography guides whether a retroperitoneal approach and vascular surgery support are needed.

items.q: A 62-year-old has a well-fixed, well-positioned modular uncemented cup but marked polyethylene wear and a large retroacetabular lytic lesion. Appropriate revision:
o: Remove the shell and implant a cup-cage
Exchange the liner, graft the lesion through screw holes or a window, and retain the shell
items.e: A well-fixed, well-positioned shell can be retained: debride and graft accessible lysis and insert a new (highly cross-linked) liner, accepting a higher dislocation risk.

items.q: Peak elbow valgus torque in a baseball pitch (about 64 Nm) is roughly twice the ultimate tensile strength of the ulnar collateral ligament. Which dynamic structure takes much of the remaining load?
items.e: The flexor-pronator mass (especially FCU and FDS overlying the UCL) acts as a dynamic valgus stabiliser, sharing load with the radiocapitellar joint and posteromedial olecranon. Brachioradialis and biceps do not resist valgus significantly.

items.q: The fastest human movement recorded in sport, shoulder internal rotation at up to about 7,000°/second, occurs in which phase of throwing?
items.e: During acceleration the maximally externally rotated shoulder internally rotates explosively. Late cocking is the position of maximum external rotation, and deceleration follows ball release.

items.q: In which phase of throwing do the posterior rotator cuff muscles work most strongly eccentrically to slow the arm?
items.e: After ball release the posterior cuff and scapular muscles contract eccentrically to decelerate the rapidly internally rotating arm, which is why posterior cuff overload occurs in this phase.

items.q: In valgus extension overload of the thrower's elbow, the radiocapitellar joint is subjected to:
o: Compression, predisposing to capitellar osteochondritis dissecans
items.e: Valgus load stretches the medial side, compresses the lateral radiocapitellar joint and shears posteromedially. Lateral compression leads to capitellar OCD, Panner disease and loose bodies.

items.q: In the throwing kinetic chain, approximately what proportion of ball velocity and force is generated by the legs and trunk?
items.e: Roughly half of the kinetic energy comes from the legs and trunk; weakness or poor mechanics there increase the load on the shoulder and elbow.

items.q: Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) in a thrower is usually defined as loss of internal rotation compared with the non-throwing side of more than about:
items.e: GIRD is generally defined as more than about 20° loss of internal rotation (or a loss of total arc) relative to the other shoulder, and it increases shoulder and elbow loads.

items.q: The anterior bundle of the elbow's ulnar collateral ligament inserts on the:
o: Sublime tubercle of the coronoid process
items.e: The anterior bundle runs from the anteroinferior medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle on the medial coronoid. The supinator crest is the insertion of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament.

items.q: Within the anterior bundle of the elbow UCL, which statement about tension is correct?
o: The anterior band is tight in extension and the posterior band is tight in flexion
Both bands are tight only in full extension
The anterior band is tight in flexion and the posterior band in extension
Neither band changes tension with elbow position
items.e: The reciprocal tightening of the anterior band in extension and the posterior band in flexion lets the anterior bundle resist valgus through most of the arc.

items.q: The posterior bundle of the elbow ulnar collateral ligament forms the floor of the cubital tunnel. Its contracture after trauma typically causes:
items.e: The posterior bundle is tight in flexion, so contracture limits flexion; it is released in stiff elbow surgery (with ulnar nerve protection).

items.q: The transverse bundle (Cooper's ligament) of the elbow UCL complex:
o: Is the primary restraint to valgus between 20° and 120°
Is the preferred graft attachment in UCL reconstruction
Runs from coronoid to olecranon and contributes little to valgus stability
Is the main restraint to posterolateral rotatory instability
items.e: The transverse bundle connects two points on the ulna, so it does not cross the joint and adds little to stability. The anterior bundle is the primary valgus restraint.

items.q: With the elbow flexed to 90°, the anterior bundle of the UCL contributes approximately what proportion of resistance to valgus stress?
items.e: At 90° the anterior bundle provides most valgus resistance (about 55-70%). In full extension the anterior capsule, UCL and bony articulation each contribute about one-third.

items.q: In an elbow with a deficient ulnar collateral ligament, which structure becomes the most important secondary restraint to valgus stress?
items.e: The radial head is a secondary valgus stabiliser that becomes critical when the UCL is deficient; excising it in this situation can produce gross valgus instability.

items.q: A pitcher with chronic UCL insufficiency is also likely to report which associated symptom in about 40% of cases?
o: Paraesthesia in the ulnar nerve distribution
items.e: Medial laxity and inflammation stretch the adjacent ulnar nerve, producing ulnar neuritis symptoms in a large minority of throwers with UCL injury.

items.q: The 'milking manoeuvre' for elbow UCL injury is performed by:
o: Applying varus stress with the elbow fully extended
Hooking a finger under the distal biceps tendon
Pulling the patient's thumb to apply valgus with the shoulder abducted and the elbow flexed about 90°
Supinating and axially loading the extended elbow
items.e: Pulling on the thumb with the elbow flexed applies valgus stress to the anterior bundle; medial pain or apprehension suggests UCL injury. The hook test is for the distal biceps and supination/axial loading is the lateral pivot-shift.

items.q: On valgus stress radiographs of a thrower's elbow, which finding suggests UCL insufficiency?
o: Any medial joint opening of 0.5 mm
Posterior subluxation of the radial head
Medial joint opening more than about 3 mm greater than the opposite side
items.e: A side-to-side difference in medial gapping of more than about 3 mm under valgus stress indicates UCL insufficiency; throwers may have slight physiological laxity on the dominant side.

items.q: A 20-year-old college pitcher has a partial undersurface tear of the UCL on MR arthrography. First-line management is:
o: Rest from throwing with a structured rehabilitation programme, with or without PRP injection
items.e: Partial UCL tears are usually treated with 6-12 weeks of rest and rehabilitation of the flexor-pronator and kinetic chain; PRP has been used as an adjunct. Reconstruction is for complete tears or failed rehabilitation.

items.q: Jobe's original 1974 UCL reconstruction ('Tommy John' surgery) involved:
o: A muscle-splitting approach with no nerve handling
Detachment of the flexor-pronator mass and submuscular ulnar nerve transposition
A single humeral tunnel with docked graft limbs
Suture-tape augmentation of a primary repair
items.e: The original technique detached the flexor-pronator origin and routinely transposed the ulnar nerve, with high rates of ulnar neuropathy. Later modifications used a muscle-splitting approach.

items.q: The docking technique (Altchek) for elbow UCL reconstruction is characterised by:
o: Figure-of-eight graft through two humeral and two ulnar tunnels with flexor-pronator detachment
Interference screw fixation on the ulna only
A single humeral tunnel into which the graft limbs are docked and tied over a bone bridge
Primary repair of the native ligament with suture tape
items.e: Docking uses one humeral tunnel with two small exit holes, allowing graft tensioning; it is associated with high return-to-play rates. The figure-of-eight technique is Jobe's.

items.q: If the palmaris longus is absent (about 15% of people), a commonly used alternative autograft for elbow UCL reconstruction is:
items.e: Gracilis (or plantaris, or contralateral palmaris) is used when the ipsilateral palmaris longus is absent. Sacrificing FCR or ECU would weaken the wrist.

items.q: After UCL reconstruction in a professional pitcher, return to the same level of competition is typically achieved in about:
items.e: Most series report return to play in roughly 80-90% after about 12-18 months of graded rehabilitation and an interval throwing programme.

items.q: Primary UCL repair with suture-tape (internal brace) augmentation is best suited to:
o: A professional pitcher with chronic attenuated midsubstance tissue
A young thrower with a proximal or distal avulsion and good ligament tissue
An elderly patient with elbow arthritis
items.e: Augmented repair is indicated for end avulsions with good tissue quality and allows faster return (about 6-7 months); chronic midsubstance degeneration needs reconstruction.

items.q: During the medial approach for UCL reconstruction, which cutaneous nerve is at particular risk?
items.e: Branches of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve cross the medial elbow incision and may form painful neuromas. The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve is at risk in distal biceps repair.

items.q: In valgus extension overload of the elbow, the 'kissing lesion' refers to:
o: A capitellar OCD opposite a radial head lesion
Cartilage damage of the coronoid tip
Impingement of the radial head on the annular ligament
Chondromalacia of the posteromedial trochlea opposite the posteromedial olecranon osteophyte
items.e: Repetitive posteromedial impingement produces an olecranon osteophyte and a matching chondral lesion on the posteromedial trochlea.

items.q: The valgus extension overload test is performed by:
o: Repeatedly forcing the elbow into terminal extension while applying a valgus force, reproducing posteromedial pain
Applying valgus stress with the elbow at 90° while pulling the thumb
Resisting middle finger extension with the elbow extended
Supinating and axially loading the elbow while flexing from extension
items.e: Forced extension with valgus drives the posteromedial olecranon into the fossa; posteromedial pain is positive. The milking manoeuvre tests the UCL at 90°.

items.q: A 7-year-old Little League pitcher has dull lateral elbow pain. Radiographs show fragmentation and irregularity of the entire capitellar ossific nucleus. The most appropriate management is:
o: Rest from throwing and symptomatic treatment, as the condition is self-limiting
Open reduction and internal fixation of the fragments
items.e: This is Panner disease, an osteochondrosis of the whole capitellar ossific nucleus in children under 10, which reossifies spontaneously. Surgery is reserved for capitellar OCD in adolescents.

items.q: Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum in adolescent throwers typically involves which part of the capitellum?
items.e: Capitellar OCD is a focal subchondral lesion of the anterolateral capitellum. Whole ossific nucleus involvement is Panner disease, and the posterior groove is a normal pseudodefect.

items.q: A 12-year-old gymnast has a capitellar OCD lesion with an open capitellar physis, near-full elbow motion and intact overlying cartilage on MRI. Management is:
o: Osteochondral autograft transfer from the knee
Fragment excision and radial head excision
Rest from upper-limb loading for about 3-6 months
items.e: Stable lesions (open physis, good motion, intact cartilage) have a good chance of healing with activity modification. Unstable or failed lesions need surgery.

items.q: A 15-year-old pitcher has an unstable capitellar OCD lesion involving more than half the capitellar width and the lateral margin. The preferred surgical option is:
o: Osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS) from the knee
items.e: Large lesions, especially those involving the lateral margin (which buttresses the radial head), do poorly with debridement and microfracture, so osteochondral autograft is preferred.

items.q: On MRI of an adolescent elbow, a smooth defect at the posterolateral junction of the capitellum and lateral epicondyle with no marrow oedema most likely represents:
items.e: The pseudodefect is a normal non-articular groove at the posterior capitellum and should not be confused with OCD, which affects the anterolateral articular surface.
