items.q: A 13-year-old pitcher has a medial epicondyle avulsion after an elbow dislocation, and radiographs show the fragment lying in the joint. Management is:
o: Open reduction and screw fixation of the fragment
Excision of the fragment and UCL reconstruction
items.e: Incarceration of the medial epicondyle in the joint is an absolute indication for surgery. Fixation also restores the UCL origin.

items.q: In a dominant-arm overhead throwing athlete, operative fixation of a medial epicondyle fracture is often recommended when displacement exceeds about:
items.e: Many surgeons fix medial epicondyle fractures displaced more than about 2 mm in throwers (versus about 5 mm in others) to restore valgus stability.

items.q: Which measure has the best evidence for preventing Little League elbow and shoulder injuries in youth pitchers?
o: Age-based pitch-count limits with mandatory rest and no pitching while fatigued
items.e: Overuse, especially pitching with fatigue, high pitch counts and year-round pitching, is the strongest risk factor. The role of curveballs is controversial.

items.q: In randomised trials of lateral epicondylitis (Bisset, Coombes), corticosteroid injection compared with wait-and-see or physiotherapy showed:
o: Better outcomes at all time points
Better short-term relief but worse outcomes and more recurrences at 1 year
items.e: Steroid injection gives rapid short-term relief but higher recurrence and poorer 1-year outcomes. Most cases resolve within a year with conservative care.

items.q: During open debridement for lateral epicondylitis, posterolateral rotatory instability can be caused iatrogenically by damaging the:
o: Lateral ulnar collateral ligament, by dissecting posterior to the equator of the radial head
items.e: Staying anterior to the radial head equator protects the LUCL; excessive posterior release leads to PLRI. The UCL anterior bundle is on the medial side.

items.q: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) mainly involves the common origin of the:
o: Pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis
Extensor carpi radialis brevis and extensor digitorum
items.e: Golfer's elbow is a tendinosis of the flexor-pronator origin, mainly pronator teres and FCR. Coexisting ulnar neuritis is common and must be sought.

items.q: After a complete distal biceps tendon rupture managed non-operatively, the strength loss is greatest for:
items.e: The biceps is the main supinator, so supination strength falls by about 40-50%, with a lesser loss of flexion strength (about 30%).

items.q: The two-incision (Boyd-Anderson) distal biceps repair is particularly associated with which complication?
o: Heterotopic ossification and proximal radioulnar synostosis
items.e: The posterolateral incision exposes the ulna near the radial tuberosity, so subperiosteal ulnar exposure can lead to heterotopic bone and synostosis; muscle-splitting modifications reduce this.

items.q: A chronic distal biceps rupture of 3 months with a retracted tendon is best treated by:
o: Reconstruction with a tendon graft (such as Achilles allograft)
Primary repair in maximal elbow flexion
Tenodesis of the biceps to the brachialis
items.e: After about 6 weeks the tendon often retracts and cannot be repaired primarily without excessive flexion, so a graft (commonly Achilles allograft) is used.

items.q: In a distal biceps rupture, an intact lacertus fibrosus is clinically important because it:
o: May limit proximal retraction and mask a complete rupture on examination
Must always be repaired to the radius
items.e: The intact bicipital aponeurosis can tether the tendon, limiting retraction and making the deformity less obvious; it can make delayed repair easier.

items.q: A weightlifter on anabolic steroids has posterior elbow pain after a fall on the outstretched hand. A lateral radiograph shows a small bony flake proximal to the olecranon. This 'fleck sign' indicates:
items.e: The fleck sign is a small avulsed piece of olecranon with the triceps insertion, diagnostic of distal triceps rupture; anabolic steroids and local steroid injections are risk factors.

items.q: Posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow results primarily from insufficiency of the:
o: Anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament
items.e: The LUCL, from the lateral epicondyle to the supinator crest, prevents the radius and ulna from rotating off the humerus as a unit. Its failure is commonly after dislocation or iatrogenic injury.

items.q: In the lateral pivot-shift test for posterolateral rotatory instability (O'Driscoll), the examiner applies supination, valgus and axial load as the elbow is flexed from extension. Reduction of the subluxed radius and ulna with a clunk typically occurs at about:
items.e: Subluxation is maximal near extension and reduces with a palpable clunk at about 40° of flexion; the test is most reliable under anaesthesia.

items.q: A patient with suspected posterolateral rotatory instability reports apprehension when pushing up from a chair with the forearms supinated. This test is the:
items.e: Pushing up from a chair with the forearm supinated and elbow flexed reproduces posterolateral subluxation in PLRI. The table-top relocation test is a variant.

items.q: During elbow arthroscopy, which nerve lies closest to the standard (distal) anterolateral portal?
items.e: The radial/posterior interosseous nerve lies about 4-7 mm from the anterolateral portal; joint distension and elbow flexion move it further away. The proximal anterolateral portal is safer.

items.q: Before establishing a proximal anteromedial portal for elbow arthroscopy, the surgeon must check for:
o: Ulnar nerve subluxation or previous ulnar nerve transposition
items.e: The portal is placed about 2 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, anterior to the intermuscular septum; a subluxing or transposed ulnar nerve may lie in its path.

items.q: The direct lateral ('soft spot') portal for elbow arthroscopy is located at the centre of the triangle formed by the:
o: Lateral epicondyle, radial head and olecranon tip
Medial epicondyle, olecranon and radial head
Lateral epicondyle, biceps tendon and radial head
items.e: The soft spot lies between the lateral epicondyle, radial head and olecranon; the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve is the structure at risk.

items.q: The most common complication of elbow arthroscopy is:
items.e: Transient palsies (radial, ulnar or median) are the commonest complications because the nerves lie close to the portals. Infection is less frequent, mainly superficial portal infection.

items.q: Morrey's classic 'functional arc' of elbow motion required for most activities of daily living is:
items.e: Morrey described 30-130° of flexion-extension and 100° of rotation (50° each way); more recent studies suggest modern tasks such as phone use need more.

items.q: During release of a post-traumatic stiff elbow, prophylactic ulnar nerve decompression or transposition is recommended when the preoperative flexion is less than about:
items.e: Gaining substantial flexion stretches the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel; when preoperative flexion is under about 90-100°, the nerve is decompressed to prevent postoperative neuritis.

items.q: The most commonly used donor nerve for interpositional grafting in brachial plexus reconstruction is the:
items.e: The sural nerve provides up to about 30–40 cm of graft per leg with an acceptable sensory deficit; the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is an alternative, often from the injured limb.

items.q: Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) recorded during brachial plexus exploration after stimulating a root are mainly used to:
o: Measure the conduction velocity of the ulnar nerve
Confirm continuity of the root with the spinal cord before using it as a graft source
Measure motor recovery in the biceps
items.e: A cortical SSEP response on stimulation shows the root is still connected to the cord (not avulsed), so it can be used as a proximal stump for grafting.

items.q: The single strongest risk factor for obstetric (birth) brachial plexus palsy is:
items.e: Shoulder dystocia, often with macrosomia (maternal diabetes), is the strongest risk factor; caesarean section greatly reduces but does not abolish the risk.

items.q: Obstetric brachial plexus palsy after breech delivery characteristically differs from that after cephalic delivery with shoulder dystocia by being more often:
o: Bilateral, with avulsion of the upper roots
Confined to the lower roots with Horner syndrome
items.e: Breech deliveries are associated with bilateral upper-root (C5–C6) injuries, often avulsions, with a poorer prognosis.

items.q: The incidence of obstetric brachial plexus palsy is approximately:
items.e: Most series report about 1–2 per 1,000 live births, and most children (especially Narakas I) recover spontaneously.

items.q: An infant has a total flail arm involving C5–T1 with ptosis and a small pupil on the same side. In the Narakas classification this is:
o: Group I, with the best prognosis
Group IV, with the worst prognosis
Group II, with a good prognosis
items.e: Narakas IV is a total C5–T1 palsy with Horner syndrome, indicating lower root avulsion; it has the worst prognosis and warrants early surgery.

items.q: An infant with obstetric brachial plexus palsy has a waiter's tip posture plus wrist drop and absent finger extension, but finger flexion is present and there is no Horner sign. The Narakas group is:
items.e: Adding C7 involvement to an Erb palsy causes loss of wrist and finger extension (extended Erb); finger flexion is preserved because C8–T1 are intact.

items.q: A 3-week-old who is irritable and febrile will not move the right arm, and cries when the shoulder is moved. Before diagnosing obstetric brachial plexus palsy, the most important condition to exclude is:
o: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the shoulder
items.e: Pseudoparalysis from shoulder sepsis (or a clavicle or proximal humeral physeal fracture) mimics plexus palsy; fever and pain on movement point to infection needing urgent investigation.

items.q: The Toronto Test Score used at 3 months in obstetric brachial plexus palsy assesses elbow flexion, elbow extension and wrist, finger and thumb extension. Microsurgical reconstruction is indicated when the score is below:
items.e: A Toronto Test Score under 3.5 (out of 10) at 3 months predicts poor spontaneous recovery and is an indication for plexus exploration.

items.q: In obstetric brachial plexus palsy, the 'cookie test' performed at about 9 months assesses whether the child can:
o: Grasp a small biscuit with a pincer grip
Reach behind the back to hold a biscuit
Bring a biscuit to the mouth with the arm held adducted to the trunk
Hold a biscuit above the head
items.e: Inability to bring the hand to the mouth with the arm adducted (without flexing the neck more than 45°) indicates inadequate elbow flexion and is an indication for surgery.

items.q: The Mallet classification used in children with obstetric brachial plexus palsy grades:
o: Global shoulder function (abduction, external rotation, hand to neck, hand to back, hand to mouth)
items.e: The Mallet score grades five shoulder movements from I to V; glenohumeral deformity is graded by the Waters classification.

items.q: For an infant with obstetric brachial plexus palsy who has no antigravity biceps by 3 months, the usual window for primary microsurgical reconstruction is:
items.e: Primary nerve surgery (neuroma excision, grafting or nerve transfers) is generally done between 3 and 9 months; total palsies with Horner sign are explored earlier, around 3 months.

items.q: A 3-year-old with a residual C5–C6 obstetric palsy has progressive loss of passive external rotation with the arm adducted. The underlying deformity that develops at the glenohumeral joint is:
o: Posterior subluxation of the humeral head with glenoid retroversion
Inferior subluxation with a hypoplastic acromion
Superior migration of the head from cuff tear
items.e: Internal rotation contracture (tight subscapularis, weak external rotators) leads to glenoid retroversion, posterior subluxation and pseudoglenoid formation, graded by Waters.

items.q: In infants with obstetric brachial plexus palsy, glenohumeral dysplasia is best screened for by:
items.e: The largely cartilaginous infant shoulder is well imaged by ultrasound, which detects posterior subluxation early; MRI is used later for Waters grading.

items.q: In obstetric brachial plexus palsy, the main clinical sign to monitor for developing glenohumeral dysplasia is:
o: Loss of passive external rotation with the arm adducted
items.e: Declining passive external rotation in adduction reflects internal rotation contracture and signals posterior subluxation and glenoid deformity.

items.q: A 4-year-old with a C5–C6 obstetric palsy has weak active external rotation and abduction but a congruent glenohumeral joint after contracture release. The tendon transfer commonly performed is:
o: Latissimus dorsi and teres major to the rotator cuff
Flexor carpi ulnaris to the wrist extensors
items.e: Transfer of latissimus dorsi and teres major to the posterosuperior cuff (L'Episcopo/Hoffer) restores external rotation and improves abduction.

items.q: A 9-year-old with obstetric palsy has a fixed internal rotation deformity with severe glenoid dysplasia and an incongruent joint. The preferred procedure is:
o: Latissimus dorsi transfer to the cuff alone
External rotation (derotation) osteotomy of the humerus
items.e: Late cases with severe joint deformity are not reconstructable by soft-tissue procedures, so a humeral external rotation osteotomy repositions the arm in a more functional arc.

items.q: Botulinum toxin is used in infants with obstetric brachial plexus palsy mainly by injecting the:
o: Flexor digitorum profundus to improve grip
Subscapularis and pectoralis major to reduce internal rotation contracture
items.e: Toxin weakens the internal rotators temporarily, allowing stretching and closed reduction to improve external rotation and limit dysplasia.

items.q: When a child with obstetric palsy tries to bring the hand to the mouth, the shoulder abducts so that the elbow rises to the side. This 'trumpet sign' indicates:
o: Weak external rotation of the shoulder
items.e: Without active external rotation, the child abducts the shoulder to clear the hand to the mouth, producing the trumpet posture.

items.q: A recognised elbow complication in children with residual obstetric brachial plexus palsy is:
o: Posterior dislocation of the radial head
items.e: Muscle imbalance (biceps and supinator against paralysed pronators) and contracture can lead to posterior radial head dislocation and elbow flexion contracture.

items.q: A child with residual obstetric palsy has a fixed supination deformity of the forearm. A recognised soft-tissue procedure to convert the biceps into a pronator is:
o: Flexor carpi ulnaris to the extensor digitorum transfer
Biceps rerouting around the radial neck
Pronator teres transfer to the extensor carpi radialis brevis
items.e: Rerouting the biceps tendon around the radius (Zancolli) changes its action from supinator to pronator; fixed deformities may need radial osteotomy.

items.q: A 40-year-old has sudden, severe shoulder pain a week after a viral illness. As the pain settles over 2 weeks, he develops scapular winging and weakness of the spinati. Sensation is largely normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Cervical radiculopathy from C5–C6 disc herniation
items.e: Acute severe pain followed by patchy weakness (often long thoracic, suprascapular, anterior interosseous nerves), with pain resolving before weakness, is typical of neuralgic amyotrophy.

items.q: In a patient with neuralgic amyotrophy and no recovery after many months, high-resolution ultrasound or MRI may show which finding that can be treated surgically?
o: Fibrous bands from a cervical rib
items.e: Hourglass constrictions of fascicles (e.g. within the AIN or radial nerve) are seen in neuralgic amyotrophy; interfascicular neurolysis is considered when recovery fails.

items.q: Years after radiotherapy for breast cancer, a woman develops progressive painless weakness of the upper limb. EMG shows myokymic discharges. The likely diagnosis is:
o: Tumour infiltration of the lower plexus
items.e: Myokymia on EMG, a painless course and upper plexus predominance favour radiation plexopathy; tumour infiltration is typically painful, involves the lower plexus and may cause Horner syndrome.

items.q: A 60-year-old smoker has severe shoulder and medial arm pain, wasting of the hand intrinsics and ipsilateral ptosis with miosis. The most likely cause is:
o: Radiation plexopathy of the upper trunk
Apical lung (Pancoast) tumour invading the lower plexus
items.e: A superior sulcus tumour invades C8–T1 and the sympathetic chain, producing painful lower plexus palsy with Horner syndrome.

items.q: A rugby player has transient burning pain and numbness radiating down one arm after a tackle, resolving within minutes with full strength. Regarding return to play, the usual recommendation is:
o: Immediate return even if weakness persists
Return once symptoms have fully resolved with full painless neck movement and normal strength
Mandatory MRI and 6 weeks off sport after every episode
items.e: Stingers/burners are transient upper trunk traction or root compression injuries; players return when completely asymptomatic; recurrent or persistent episodes need investigation for stenosis.

items.q: The most common primary tumour of the brachial plexus is:
items.e: Schwannomas are the commonest; they are eccentric to the nerve and can usually be enucleated with fascicles preserved, unlike neurofibromas.

items.q: A patient with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a known plexiform neurofibroma of the brachial plexus that has recently enlarged rapidly and become painful. The main concern is:
o: Malignant transformation to a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
items.e: Rapid growth, new pain or neurological deficit in a plexiform neurofibroma suggests MPNST, which should be investigated (PET-CT, MRI, biopsy).

items.q: Compared with supraclavicular brachial plexus injuries, infraclavicular injuries (cords and branches, such as after shoulder dislocation) generally have:
o: A better prognosis because the lesions are postganglionic
The same prognosis as root avulsion
A worse prognosis because they are always avulsions
items.e: Infraclavicular lesions are postganglionic and frequently in continuity, so spontaneous recovery is common and surgical results are better.

items.q: Bilateral Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease occurs in about 10–15% of patients and is characteristically:
o: Commoner in girls than in boys
Symmetrical and simultaneous in both hips
Asynchronous, with the two hips at different stages
items.e: Bilateral Perthes is usually asynchronous; symmetric simultaneous involvement suggests another diagnosis such as multiple epiphyseal dysplasia or hypothyroidism.

items.q: Which finding on investigation is found in about 90% of children with Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease?
items.e: Delayed skeletal maturation is very common in Perthes, along with short stature; inflammatory markers are typically normal.

items.q: At the usual age of onset of Perthes disease (4–7 years), the capital femoral epiphysis is supplied almost entirely by the:
o: Lateral epiphyseal vessels from the medial femoral circumflex artery
items.e: At this age the ligamentum teres artery contributes little and the physis blocks metaphyseal vessels, so the epiphysis depends on the lateral epiphyseal branches of the MFCA.

items.q: The earliest radiographic sign of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, seen on the frog-leg lateral view, is:
items.e: The crescent (Caffey) sign is a subchondral fracture in the initial stage; coxa magna and trochanteric overgrowth are late residual changes.

items.q: In Waldenström's staging of Perthes disease, the stage in which the femoral head is most mechanically vulnerable to deformation is the:
items.e: During fragmentation the necrotic bone is resorbed and the head is soft, so it can extrude and deform; containment aims to protect it during this stage.

items.q: A 3-year-old has irregular, mottled ossification of both femoral capital epiphyses noticed incidentally, with no symptoms and full hip motion. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Meyer dysplasia is delayed, irregular epiphyseal ossification in children under 4, often bilateral and asymptomatic, which resolves spontaneously.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy with Perthes disease limps and complains of knee pain only. The knee pain is explained by referral along the:
o: Femoral cutaneous branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Saphenous nerve from the adductor canal
items.e: The obturator nerve supplies both the hip joint and the medial knee, so hip pathology commonly presents with knee pain in children.

items.q: On examination of a child with Perthes disease, the movements most characteristically restricted are:
items.e: Synovitis and head deformity limit abduction and internal rotation; persistent loss of abduction is a poor prognostic sign.

items.q: In Herring's lateral pillar classification of Perthes disease, the lateral pillar is defined as the:
o: Lateral cortex of the femoral neck
Lateral third of the metaphysis on the frog-leg view
Lateral 15–30% of the femoral epiphysis on the AP radiograph
Lateral half of the acetabular roof
items.e: The epiphysis is divided into lateral (15–30%), central and medial pillars on the AP view; the height of the lateral pillar is compared with the opposite side.

items.q: A 7-year-old with Perthes disease has a lateral pillar maintaining more than 50% of its original height at the start of fragmentation. This is lateral pillar group:
items.e: Group A: pillar intact; group B: over 50% height maintained; B/C border: about 50% or a narrow/poorly ossified pillar; group C: under 50%.

items.q: A 9-year-old with Perthes disease has a lateral pillar maintaining only 30% of its original height. The expected outcome is:
o: Poor, regardless of the treatment chosen
Excellent if treated by abduction bracing
Good, because collapse of the lateral pillar always remodels
items.e: Lateral pillar C hips do poorly in most series irrespective of treatment, particularly in older children.

items.q: Which group in the Herring lateral pillar classification is associated with a good outcome regardless of age at onset?
items.e: An intact lateral pillar (group A) protects the head from collapse, and outcomes are good whatever the age or treatment.

items.q: In Catterall's classification of Perthes disease, involvement of more than 50% of the femoral head with only a small medial and posterior segment spared is:
items.e: Catterall I: anterior head only; II: up to 50% with a central sequestrum; III: over 50%, only medial/posterior parts spared; IV: whole head.

items.q: A major criticism of the Catterall classification of Perthes disease is that it:
o: Ignores the extent of femoral head involvement
Is based on MRI findings only
Applies only to children over 10 years
Has poor interobserver reliability and can only be assigned once fragmentation is advanced
items.e: Catterall grouping relies on the extent of head involvement, which is hard to judge reliably and often cannot be assigned early; the lateral pillar classification is more reliable.

items.q: Which of the following is one of Catterall's 'head-at-risk' signs in Perthes disease?
o: Horizontal orientation of the proximal femoral physis
Widening of the medial joint space in the initial stage
items.e: The head-at-risk signs are Gage sign, lateral calcification, lateral subluxation, a horizontal physis and metaphyseal cysts (diffuse metaphyseal reaction).

items.q: In the Stulberg classification of healed Perthes disease, a femoral head that is ovoid or mushroom-shaped but not flat, with aspherical congruency, is class:
items.e: Stulberg III heads are ovoid with aspherical congruency and carry a risk of mild to moderate arthritis in later adulthood.

items.q: In the Stulberg classification, which class carries the highest risk of early, severe osteoarthritis?
o: Class II: spherical but enlarged head
Class V: flat head with a normal acetabulum (aspherical incongruency)
Class III: ovoid head with aspherical congruency
items.e: Stulberg V hips are incongruent (a flat head in a round acetabulum) and develop severe early arthritis; classes I–II have spherical congruency and a good prognosis.

items.q: A Stulberg class IV hip in healed Perthes disease is defined by:
o: A spherical but enlarged head with a short neck
A flat femoral head in a normal round acetabulum
A spherical femoral head of normal size
A flattened femoral head (over 1 cm flat weight-bearing area) with a correspondingly flat acetabulum
items.e: Class IV is aspherical congruency between a flat head and flat acetabulum, with moderate arthritis typically in middle age; a flat head in a normal acetabulum is class V.

items.q: In the classic cadaveric study of Ramsey and Hamilton, a 1 mm lateral shift of the talus within the ankle mortise reduced the tibiotalar contact area by approximately:
items.e: Ramsey and Hamilton showed that 1 mm of lateral talar shift reduces tibiotalar contact by about 42%, which concentrates load and is the basis for demanding anatomical reduction of the mortise.

items.q: Which structure is the primary restraint against lateral translation of the talus in the ankle mortise?
items.e: The deep deltoid (deep anterior and posterior tibiotalar fibres) is the main restraint to lateral talar shift; the superficial deltoid crosses the subtalar joint and mainly resists hindfoot eversion.

items.q: The posterior malleolus is the bony attachment of which ligament, explaining why fixing a large posterior malleolar fragment can restore syndesmotic stability?
items.e: The PITFL (with its deep inferior transverse part) inserts on the posterior malleolus, so reducing and fixing the fragment re-tensions the posterior syndesmosis; the AITFL attaches to the anterolateral (Chaput) tubercle.

items.q: In the Lauge-Hansen supination-external rotation (SER) mechanism, which structure fails first (stage I)?
o: Fibula at the level of the syndesmosis
items.e: SER progresses AITFL (I), short oblique fibular fracture at the syndesmosis (II), PITFL or posterior malleolus (III), then medial malleolus or deltoid (IV).

items.q: On the lateral radiograph, the fibular fracture of a supination-external rotation injury classically appears as:
o: A short oblique/spiral line running from anteroinferior to posterosuperior at the level of the syndesmosis
A transverse avulsion fracture below the joint line
A high spiral fracture of the proximal fibula
A transverse fracture with lateral comminution above the syndesmosis
items.e: The SER stage II fibular fracture starts at the syndesmosis anteroinferiorly and runs posterosuperiorly (Weber B); a transverse infra-syndesmotic avulsion is supination-adduction and lateral comminution suggests pronation-abduction.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a transverse fibular fracture below the level of the plafond and a near-vertical fracture of the medial malleolus with a small area of medial plafond impaction. Which Lauge-Hansen mechanism produced this?
items.e: Supination-adduction gives a transverse infra-syndesmotic fibular avulsion (stage I) and a vertical shear fracture of the medial malleolus, often with medial plafond impaction (stage II).

items.q: When fixing a vertical medial malleolar fracture from a supination-adduction injury, which step is specifically required?
o: Two screws inserted from the tip of the malleolus perpendicular to the joint line
Elevation and grafting of any medial plafond impaction, then horizontal screws or a medial antiglide plate
items.e: Vertical shear fractures need fixation perpendicular to the fracture (horizontal screws or an antiglide plate), and the impacted medial plafond must be elevated; tip-to-shaft screws are for transverse fractures.

items.q: In the Lauge-Hansen pronation-external rotation (PER) mechanism, the fibular fracture occurs at which stage and level?
o: Stage II, at the level of the syndesmosis
Stage I, below the joint line
Stage IV, at the level of the plafond
items.e: PER injures the medial side first (I), then the AITFL (II), then produces a high spiral fibular fracture above the syndesmosis (III, Weber C), and finally the PITFL or posterior malleolus (IV).

items.q: Radiographs show a transverse medial malleolar fracture and a short transverse fibular fracture just above the syndesmosis with a laterally based comminuted (butterfly) fragment. Which Lauge-Hansen mechanism is most likely?
items.e: Pronation-abduction bends the fibula, giving a transverse or comminuted fracture with lateral comminution at or above the syndesmosis; PER produces a spiral, not a bending, fibular fracture.

items.q: In the Lauge-Hansen system, why are the lateral structures injured first in supination injuries?
o: The lateral malleolus is the weakest bone of the ankle
Supination places the lateral side under tension
The talus rotates internally in supination
The deltoid ligament is relaxed in supination
items.e: The first word describes foot position; the first structure to fail is on the tension side, which is lateral in supination and medial in pronation.

items.q: In the Danis-Weber classification, a type C ankle fracture is defined by:
o: A fibular fracture below the level of the syndesmosis
A fibular fracture at the level of the syndesmosis
A fibular fracture above the syndesmosis, implying syndesmotic disruption
An isolated posterior malleolar fracture with an intact fibula
items.e: Weber classifies by the level of the fibular fracture: A infra-syndesmotic, B trans-syndesmotic, C supra-syndesmotic, where the syndesmosis is torn and must be assessed and usually fixed.

items.q: A 40-year-old has an apparently isolated medial malleolar fracture with a widened medial clear space and tenderness over the proximal fibula, where radiographs show a spiral fracture. Which treatment is standard?
o: Open reduction and plating of the proximal fibula
Exploration of the common peroneal nerve with fibular plating
Reduction and fixation of the syndesmosis, without fixing the proximal fibula
items.e: This is a Maisonneuve injury (PER): treatment is anatomical syndesmotic reduction and fixation with medial fixation as needed; the proximal fibular fracture is not plated because of the peroneal nerve and because it is not needed for stability.

items.q: An ankle fracture-dislocation cannot be reduced closed. The lateral radiograph shows the proximal fibular fragment locked behind the posterolateral ridge of the tibia. What is the diagnosis and its management?
o: Tibial pilon fracture; spanning external fixator
items.e: In a Bosworth injury the fibula is trapped behind the tibia (incisura), which makes closed reduction impossible; urgent open reduction is needed to protect skin and neurovascular structures.

items.q: A Wagstaffe-Le Fort fragment in an adult ankle fracture is an avulsion of the:
o: Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament from the anterolateral tibia
Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament from the anterior fibula
Posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament from the posterior tibia
Calcaneofibular ligament from the fibular tip
items.e: Wagstaffe-Le Fort is AITFL avulsion from the fibular side; Tillaux-Chaput is AITFL avulsion from the tibial (Chaput) tubercle; PITFL avulsion produces a posterior malleolar (Volkmann) fragment.

items.q: On axial CT, the commonest posterior malleolar fracture pattern in the Haraguchi classification is:
o: A fracture extending into the medial malleolus (type II)
items.e: Haraguchi type I, a posterolateral oblique wedge, is the commonest; type II extends medially and type III consists of small shell fragments of the posterior rim.

items.q: Under the Ottawa ankle rules, which finding indicates a foot radiograph series rather than ankle radiographs?
o: Tenderness along the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus
Malleolar pain with inability to bear weight for four steps
Tenderness at the tip of the medial malleolus
Tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal
items.e: Midfoot pain with tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular (or inability to bear weight) triggers a foot series; malleolar posterior-edge or tip tenderness triggers ankle films.

items.q: The mortise view of the ankle is taken with the leg in:
items.e: About 15-20 degrees of internal rotation brings the intermalleolar axis parallel to the cassette so the medial, superior and lateral clear spaces can be assessed.

items.q: Which plain radiographic measurement is considered the most reliable indicator of a distal tibiofibular syndesmotic injury?
o: Tibiofibular clear space over about 6 mm measured 1 cm above the plafond
items.e: The tibiofibular clear space (incisura floor to medial fibular border, 1 cm above the plafond) above about 5-6 mm is the most reliable radiographic sign of syndesmotic disruption; medial clear space reflects deltoid injury.

items.q: Tibiofibular overlap suggesting syndesmotic disruption is defined as:
o: Overlap of more than 10 mm on the AP view
Overlap of less than 6 mm on the lateral view
Overlap of less than 1 mm on the mortise view
Overlap of more than 4 mm on the mortise view
items.e: Reduced tibiofibular overlap (under 6 mm on the AP or under 1 mm on the mortise view) indicates syndesmotic widening; overlap is not assessed on the lateral view.

items.q: The talocrural angle (normally about 83 degrees, plus or minus 4) on the mortise view is used mainly to assess:
o: Integrity of the deep deltoid ligament
items.e: The talocrural angle, between the intermalleolar line and the plafond, changes when the fibula is shortened; comparison with the opposite side checks restoration of fibular length.

items.q: On a mortise radiograph after an ankle injury, a medial clear space of 6 mm that exceeds the superior clear space indicates:
o: Deep deltoid disruption with lateral talar shift
An isolated syndesmotic injury with an intact deltoid
items.e: A medial clear space over about 4-5 mm, or greater than the superior clear space, signifies deep deltoid incompetence and lateral talar shift, i.e. an unstable injury.

items.q: In the randomised trial by Kortekangas and colleagues (BMJ 2019) of stress-test-negative (stable) Weber B ankle fractures, what was the main finding?
o: Six weeks of casting was superior to three weeks
Three weeks of cast or orthosis was non-inferior to six weeks of casting
Operative fixation gave better function than any cast
No immobilisation gave the best outcomes
items.e: In stable Weber B fractures, 3 weeks of cast or orthosis was non-inferior to 6 weeks of casting for function at 52 weeks, supporting shorter immobilisation.

items.q: The AIM trial compared close-contact casting with ORIF in adults over 60 with unstable ankle fractures. Its principal result was:
o: ORIF gave significantly better function at 6 months
Close-contact casting gave equivalent function at 6 months
Casting had lower rates of malunion
items.e: AIM (Willett et al., JAMA 2016) found equivalent Olerud-Molander scores at 6 months with skilled close-contact casting; radiological malunion was actually more frequent with casting.

items.q: Compared with a lateral neutralisation plate, a posterolateral antiglide plate for a Weber B fibular fracture has which recognised drawback?
o: Greater risk to the superficial peroneal nerve
It needs a longer incision over the subcutaneous fibula
Irritation of the peroneal tendons when placed distally
items.e: The posterolateral antiglide plate is biomechanically stronger and less prominent, but a distally placed plate or screw can irritate the peroneal tendons; the superficial peroneal nerve is more at risk with the lateral approach.

items.q: The standard fixation for a displaced transverse medial malleolar fracture with a good-sized fragment is:
o: Two 4.0 mm partially threaded cancellous screws perpendicular to the fracture
A single 6.5 mm fully threaded screw
A one-third tubular plate on the anterior tibia
items.e: Two partially threaded 4.0 mm cancellous lag screws give compression and rotational control; tension-band wiring is used for small or comminuted fragments.

items.q: After anatomical fibular plating and syndesmotic stabilisation of an unstable ankle fracture, fluoroscopy shows a persistently widened medial clear space. The most likely cause is:
o: Interposition of the deltoid ligament or tibialis posterior tendon
items.e: When the lateral side is anatomically restored but the medial clear space will not close, soft tissue (deltoid or tibialis posterior) is usually interposed and medial exploration is indicated.

items.q: Current evidence favours direct fixation of a large posterior malleolar fragment rather than relying on a syndesmotic screw mainly because direct fixation:
o: Avoids the need for fibular fixation
Restores PITFL-mediated syndesmotic stability and incisura congruity more reliably
Removes any risk to the sural nerve
items.e: Fixing the posterior malleolus re-tensions the PITFL and restores the incisura, giving more stable syndesmotic reduction than a transsyndesmotic screw; the posterolateral approach still risks the sural nerve.

items.q: The posterolateral approach to the posterior malleolus develops the interval between:
o: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
The Achilles tendon and flexor hallucis longus
Peroneus tertius and extensor digitorum longus
The peroneal tendons and flexor hallucis longus
items.e: The posterolateral approach passes between the peroneal tendons (superficial peroneal nerve) and FHL (tibial nerve), giving access to the posterior tibia and fibula.

items.q: During the superficial dissection of the posterolateral approach to the ankle, which nerve is most at risk?
items.e: The sural nerve and short saphenous vein run in the subcutaneous tissue between the Achilles tendon and the peroneal tendons and must be protected.

items.q: During a lateral approach to the distal fibula, the superficial peroneal nerve is at risk because it pierces the crural fascia approximately how far above the tip of the lateral malleolus?
o: At the level of the joint line
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve becomes subcutaneous about 10-12 cm proximal to the lateral malleolar tip and crosses obliquely anterior to the fibula, so proximal extension of a lateral incision must protect it.

items.q: The intraoperative Cotton (hook) test assesses:
o: Syndesmotic stability, by lateral pull on the fibula with a bone hook
Stability of a posterior malleolar fragment
items.e: In the Cotton test the fixed fibula is pulled laterally with a bone hook; widening of the tibiofibular space beyond about 2 mm indicates syndesmotic instability needing fixation.

items.q: Which describes recommended syndesmotic screw placement?
o: 8 cm above the joint, perpendicular to the fibula in the coronal plane
From the medial tibia directed posterior to anterior
Through two cortices at the level of the joint line
2-5 cm above the plafond, parallel to the joint, angled about 25-30 degrees anteriorly from posterolateral
items.e: Screws are placed 2-5 cm above the plafond, parallel to it, and directed from posterolateral to anteromedial (about 25-30 degrees) to follow the fibula's position in the incisura.

items.q: The most important determinant of poor functional outcome after operative treatment of an ankle syndesmotic injury is:
o: Choosing 3.5 mm rather than 4.5 mm screws
items.e: CT studies show syndesmotic malreduction in up to 30-50% of cases and it is the main predictor of poor outcome, hence direct visualisation of the incisura; screw size and breakage matter little.

items.q: Compared with syndesmotic screws, suture-button (dynamic) syndesmotic fixation has been associated with:
o: Fewer malreductions and less need for implant removal
Rigid fixation that abolishes physiological fibular motion
items.e: Suture-buttons allow physiological micromotion, tolerate small reduction errors better, and need removal less often; screws are rigid and are sometimes removed.

items.q: Six months after syndesmotic screw fixation, a pain-free patient's radiograph shows the screw broken at the level of the tibiofibular joint. The best management is:
o: Urgent removal of both screw fragments
CT-guided extraction of the tibial fragment
items.e: Broken syndesmotic screws are usually asymptomatic and harmless; they are left alone unless they cause symptoms.

items.q: A 58-year-old with diabetic peripheral neuropathy has a displaced bimalleolar ankle fracture. Which operative strategy is recommended?
o: Standard one-third tubular plate with weight bearing at 2 weeks
Cast treatment with early weight bearing
Primary ankle arthrodesis in all cases
Augmented fixation (longer plates, multiple syndesmotic screws or transarticular pins) with prolonged non-weight-bearing
items.e: Neuropathic diabetic patients have high rates of fixation failure, infection and Charcot change, so 'super-construct' fixation and roughly double the usual period of protected weight bearing are advised.

items.q: An 85-year-old frail diabetic with fragile skin has an unstable ankle fracture-dislocation and cannot comply with non-weight-bearing. Which option allows early weight bearing with minimal soft-tissue disruption?
o: Standard ORIF with a lateral plate
items.e: A retrograde tibiotalocalcaneal nail inserted through small incisions gives a stable construct permitting early weight bearing in very poor bone and skin; standard ORIF risks wound breakdown and loss of fixation.

items.q: A closed bimalleolar fracture presents 3 days after injury with tense swelling and fracture blisters over the medial malleolus. The best plan is:
o: Immediate ORIF through the blistered skin
Reduction, splinting and elevation, with ORIF delayed until swelling settles (about 7-10 days)
items.e: ORIF is done within about 24 hours or after the soft tissues recover; operating through swollen, blistered skin raises wound breakdown and infection, while the fracture remains unstable and needs fixation.

items.q: Non-anatomical lateral ankle reconstructions such as Watson-Jones, Evans or Chrisman-Snook are now rarely used mainly because they:
o: Have higher recurrent instability than a Broström repair in all series
Always injure the superficial peroneal nerve
items.e: Peroneus brevis tenodeses cross the subtalar joint non-anatomically and cause hindfoot stiffness and altered mechanics, so anatomical repair or reconstruction is preferred.

items.q: The talar tilt (inversion stress) test performed with the ankle in neutral mainly assesses the integrity of the:
items.e: Talar tilt in neutral tests the CFL (with the ATFL); the anterior drawer test isolates the ATFL.

items.q: The anterior talofibular ligament is the most frequently injured ankle ligament because it is the weakest lateral ligament and becomes taut in:
items.e: The ATFL is parallel to the long axis of the leg and tight in plantarflexion, the position in which inversion sprains occur; the CFL is tight in dorsiflexion.

items.q: A footballer has pain over the anterolateral distal tibiofibular joint when the foot is externally rotated with the knee flexed to 90 degrees, and pain on squeezing the mid-calf. The most likely injury is:
items.e: Positive external rotation (Kleiger) and squeeze tests localising to the distal tibiofibular joint indicate a syndesmotic sprain, which takes longer to recover and needs stress assessment for instability.

items.q: A snowboarder with a presumed ankle sprain has persistent pain and tenderness just anterior and inferior to the tip of the lateral malleolus; initial radiographs looked normal. Which fracture is classically missed in this setting?
items.e: The snowboarder's fracture of the lateral process of the talus (dorsiflexion, inversion, external rotation) is easily missed on plain films and is best seen on CT.

items.q: Compared with posteromedial osteochondral lesions of the talus, anterolateral lesions are typically:
items.e: Anterolateral talar dome lesions are usually shallow, wafer-like and traumatic, whereas posteromedial lesions are deeper, cup-shaped and often have no clear injury.

items.q: Intramedullary nailing of the fibula is particularly suited to which ankle fracture patient?
o: A young athlete with a Weber A fracture
A Maisonneuve injury with a proximal fibular fracture
An elderly patient with fragile soft tissues and osteoporotic bone
items.e: Fibular nails go in through small incisions and give good fixation in osteoporotic bone, reducing wound complications in elderly or soft-tissue-compromised patients.

items.q: A 35-year-old has an isolated transverse avulsion fracture of the fibula below the plafond, with no medial tenderness and a congruent mortise. The best management is:
o: Walking boot with weight bearing as tolerated
items.e: An isolated Weber A fracture leaves the syndesmosis and deltoid intact and is stable, so functional treatment in a boot with early weight bearing is appropriate.

items.q: A 14-year-old has a Salter-Harris III fracture of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis after an external rotation injury (juvenile Tillaux). Why is this fragment involved?
o: The distal tibial physis closes centrally and medially first, leaving the anterolateral part open to avulsion by the AITFL
The lateral part of the physis closes first
The deltoid ligament avulses the anterolateral epiphysis
The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament avulses it
items.e: The distal tibial physis closes centrally, then medially, and anterolaterally last; during this window the AITFL avulses the still-open anterolateral epiphysis, giving the Tillaux fracture.

items.q: In a triplane fracture of the distal tibia, the fracture lines run in which planes?
o: Coronal through the epiphysis, sagittal through the metaphysis and axial through the physis
Sagittal through the epiphysis, axial through the physis and coronal through the metaphysis
Axial through the epiphysis, coronal through the physis and sagittal through the metaphysis
Coronal through the epiphysis, physis and metaphysis
items.e: A triplane fracture has a sagittal epiphyseal line, an axial physeal component and a coronal metaphyseal line (Salter-Harris IV on the lateral view); CT defines displacement.

items.q: The strongest single risk factor for cerebral palsy is:
items.e: Prematurity and low birth weight are the strongest risk factors; spastic diplegia from periventricular leukomalacia is the classic pattern in preterm infants.

items.q: The brain lesion classically associated with spastic diplegia in a child born at 28 weeks is:
items.e: Periventricular white matter carries the leg fibres of the corticospinal tracts closest to the ventricles, so damage there causes leg-predominant spasticity.

items.q: A child with cerebral palsy following severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia has writhing involuntary movements. Regarding tendon surgery, this type of CP is:
o: A poor candidate because results are unpredictable
Treated mainly with tendon transfers in early childhood
The best candidate for multilevel lengthening
items.e: Kernicterus causes dyskinetic (athetoid/dystonic) CP from basal ganglia injury; fluctuating tone makes soft-tissue surgery unreliable and can produce opposite deformities.

items.q: In spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy, which statement is typical?
o: Hip displacement risk is highest of all CP types
The upper limb is usually more affected than the lower limb and most children walk
Intellectual disability and inability to walk are the rule
Both legs are affected more than the arms
items.e: Hemiplegia involves one side, usually arm worse than leg; nearly all children walk, often by 18-24 months, though seizures are common.

items.q: A 9-year-old with cerebral palsy walks indoors and outdoors on level surfaces but needs a rail for stairs and has difficulty on uneven ground and long distances, without using any walking aid. His GMFCS level is:
items.e: GMFCS II children walk without aids but with limitations; level III requires a hand-held mobility device, and level I has limitations only in advanced skills.

items.q: A 10-year-old with cerebral palsy walks with a posterior walker at school and uses a manual wheelchair for long distances in the community. GMFCS level:
items.e: Walking with a hand-held mobility device, with wheeled mobility for longer distances, defines GMFCS III.

items.q: Which predicts that a child with cerebral palsy is likely to walk?
o: Sitting independently by about 2 years of age
items.e: Independent sitting by 2 years is a good prognostic sign for walking; a child not sitting by about 4 years is unlikely to walk.

items.q: The risk of hip displacement in cerebral palsy correlates most closely with:
items.e: Hip displacement risk rises from near zero in GMFCS I to around 90% in GMFCS V, so surveillance intensity is based on GMFCS level.

items.q: Botulinum toxin A reduces spasticity by:
o: Acting as a GABA-B agonist in the spinal cord
Blocking sodium channels in the muscle membrane
Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
items.e: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and prevents presynaptic acetylcholine release; baclofen is the GABA-B agonist.

items.q: A 3-year-old with spastic diplegia toe-walks; the equinus corrects fully on passive dorsiflexion with the knee extended under slow stretch. The most suitable intervention is:
o: Botulinum toxin A to the gastrocnemius with serial casting or orthoses
items.e: Dynamic equinus in a young child responds to botulinum toxin (effect about 3-6 months) combined with casting and AFOs; surgery is reserved for fixed contracture in older children.

items.q: The duration of clinical effect after a botulinum toxin A injection for spasticity is typically about:
items.e: Nerve terminals sprout and the junction recovers over a few months, so the effect lasts roughly 3-6 months.

items.q: A 13-year-old non-ambulant child with spastic quadriplegia and severe generalised spasticity and dystonia, poorly controlled by oral medication causing sedation, is best treated with:
items.e: Intrathecal baclofen treats generalised spasticity and dystonia in GMFCS IV-V with much less sedation than oral baclofen. SDR is for spastic diplegia without dystonia.

items.q: Selective dorsal rhizotomy for spastic diplegia involves dividing a proportion of the dorsal rootlets from:
items.e: SDR sections a portion of L2-S1 dorsal rootlets, guided by stimulation, to interrupt the afferent limb of the stretch reflex.

items.q: A late problem recognised after selective dorsal rhizotomy is:
o: Loss of sensation in the feet
Progressive hip subluxation or spinal deformity
items.e: SDR permanently lowers tone but may unmask weakness, and later hip migration, scoliosis or spondylolysis can occur, so surveillance continues.

items.q: The rationale for single-event multilevel surgery (SEMLS) in ambulant cerebral palsy is to:
o: Correct all soft-tissue and bony deformities in one operation and avoid repeated yearly surgery
Operate only on the most severe level
items.e: SEMLS, guided by 3D gait analysis and usually done around 6-10 years, prevents the 'birthday syndrome' of annual operations; rehabilitation takes about a year.

items.q: Spastic hip displacement in cerebral palsy is usually in which direction?
items.e: Adductor and iliopsoas overactivity with weak abductors drive the head posterosuperiorly, producing posterosuperior acetabular deficiency, unlike the anterolateral deficiency of DDH.

items.q: Bony features of the hip in spastic cerebral palsy with displacement include:
o: Coxa vara, femoral retroversion and deep acetabulum
Coxa breva with a large femoral head
Coxa valga, increased femoral anteversion and acetabular dysplasia
items.e: Muscle imbalance and lack of weight bearing leave the proximal femur valgus and anteverted, with secondary acetabular dysplasia.

items.q: In children with cerebral palsy, hip surveillance with an AP pelvis radiograph usually begins at about:
items.e: Surveillance programmes start clinical and radiological checks at around age 2, repeated every 6-12 months, more often in GMFCS III-V.

items.q: A Reimers migration percentage of 105% on an AP pelvis radiograph indicates:
items.e: MP over 33% is subluxation and over 100% means the whole femoral head lies lateral to Perkin's line, i.e. dislocated.

items.q: The annual increase in Reimers migration percentage is typically greater in non-ambulant children with CP, at about:
o: 12% per year versus about 2% in ambulant children
2% per year versus 12% in ambulant children
items.e: Non-walkers progress about 12% a year compared with about 2% in walkers; progression over about 10% a year is significant.

items.q: A 4-year-old GMFCS IV child with cerebral palsy has a migration percentage of 35% and limited hip abduction. Appropriate surgery is:
o: Varus derotation osteotomy with Dega osteotomy
Adductor longus and gracilis tenotomy with or without iliopsoas lengthening
items.e: Young children with MP around 30-40% are offered preventive soft-tissue releases; bony reconstruction is for higher MP, older children or failed releases.

items.q: A 9-year-old non-ambulant child with CP has a migration percentage of 60% and acetabular dysplasia but a round femoral head. Recommended surgery is:
o: Observation and repeat X-ray in a year
Varus derotation osteotomy of the proximal femur with a pelvic osteotomy
items.e: Established subluxation in an older child needs reconstruction: VDRO corrects valgus and anteversion, and a Dega or San Diego osteotomy addresses posterosuperior dysplasia.

items.q: Routine anterior obturator neurectomy with adductor release in cerebral palsy has been largely abandoned because it may cause:
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Recurrent adductor spasticity in all cases
items.e: Excessive weakening of the adductors can lead to over-abduction and windswept hips; tenotomy alone is preferred.

items.q: A child with total body involvement CP has one hip adducted and dislocated and the other abducted, with pelvic obliquity and scoliosis. This is termed:
items.e: Windswept deformity combines an adducted (often dislocated) hip on one side with an abducted hip on the other, linked to pelvic obliquity and scoliosis.

items.q: A 10-year-old with spastic diplegia has reduced, delayed peak knee flexion in swing with toe drag. Dynamic EMG shows rectus femoris firing throughout swing. The recommended procedure is:
o: Distal rectus femoris transfer to the semitendinosus or gracilis
items.e: Stiff-knee gait is due to an overactive rectus femoris in swing; transferring its distal tendon behind the knee improves knee flexion more than release alone.

items.q: The Duncan-Ely test in a child with cerebral palsy assesses:
items.e: With the child prone, rapid knee flexion causing the buttock to rise indicates rectus femoris tightness; this supports stiff-knee gait.

items.q: A side effect of hamstring lengthening in a child with cerebral palsy, because the hamstrings also extend the hip, is:
items.e: Weakening the hip extensor action of the hamstrings allows the pelvis to tilt anteriorly; lateral hamstring lengthening also risks recurvatum.

items.q: In the hamstrings of a child with CP, contracture severity is clinically measured by the:
items.e: With the hip flexed to 90°, the angle of residual knee flexion (popliteal angle) quantifies hamstring tightness.

items.q: A 14-year-old with spastic diplegia has severe fixed crouch with a 25° knee flexion contracture and patella alta. The usual surgery is:
o: Distal femoral extension osteotomy with patellar tendon advancement
items.e: Fixed knee flexion contracture with extensor lag needs bony correction by distal femoral extension osteotomy plus patellar tendon shortening or advancement to restore extensor mechanism efficiency.

items.q: Which orthosis is used to help control crouch gait by producing a knee-extending moment in stance?
items.e: A rigid floor-reaction AFO blocks forward tibial progression, creating a knee extension moment that supports the weak plantarflexor-knee-extension couple.

items.q: In the Rodda and Graham sagittal gait classification for spastic diplegia, which pattern combines ankle equinus with knee and hip flexion in stance?
items.e: Jump gait has equinus with flexed knees and hips; apparent equinus has a plantigrade ankle with knee and hip flexion; crouch has excessive dorsiflexion with knee flexion.

items.q: In the hemiplegic child with an equinovarus foot, dynamic EMG shows the tibialis anterior is continuously active in stance and swing. A suitable procedure is:
o: Split anterior tibial tendon transfer to the cuboid
items.e: Overactive tibialis anterior causes swing- and stance-phase varus with supination; the split anterior tibial tendon transfer (SPLATT) balances the foot.

items.q: A 10-year-old with spastic quadriplegia has a flexible planovalgus foot causing pain and poor orthotic fit. A joint-sparing correction is:
items.e: Lateral column lengthening corrects mobile planovalgus while preserving joints; fusion is kept for rigid or severe feet in older children. Dwyer osteotomy corrects varus, not valgus.

items.q: In an adolescent with cerebral palsy, severe hallux valgus associated with planovalgus is best treated by:
items.e: Spastic hallux valgus recurs after soft-tissue or osteotomy procedures; first MTP arthrodesis gives a durable correction.

items.q: Neuromuscular scoliosis in severe cerebral palsy typically shows:
o: A long C-shaped thoracolumbar curve with pelvic obliquity
A short right thoracic curve with normal sitting balance
A sharp angular kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction
A double major curve without pelvic involvement
items.e: Long collapsing C-shaped curves with pelvic obliquity are typical of GMFCS IV-V; they continue to progress after maturity, especially over about 40°.

items.q: In the upper limb of a child with hemiplegic CP, which transfer is used to correct a flexed, ulnarly deviated wrist with good finger extension control?
o: Pronator teres to flexor pollicis longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris to extensor carpi radialis brevis
Palmaris longus to extensor pollicis brevis
items.e: FCU to ECRB (Green transfer) converts a deforming wrist flexor and ulnar deviator into a wrist extensor.

items.q: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by mutation of the dystrophin gene located at:
items.e: Dystrophin lies at Xp21; deletions account for about 65%. SMN1 is at 5q13 and PMP22 at 17p12.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy has frequent falls and toe-walking. To rise from the floor he places his hands on his knees and thighs and pushes himself up. This sign reflects:
o: Proximal pelvic girdle and hip extensor weakness
items.e: Gowers sign indicates weak hip and knee extensors; it is classic in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

items.q: Calf enlargement in Duchenne muscular dystrophy is due to:
o: Replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue (pseudohypertrophy)
items.e: Pseudohypertrophy reflects fatty and fibrous infiltration of degenerating muscle, not increased contractile tissue.

items.q: The usual first diagnostic test to confirm Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a boy with very high creatine kinase is:
o: Genetic testing for dystrophin deletions or duplications (e.g. MLPA)
items.e: Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification detects most dystrophin deletions and duplications; biopsy is reserved for unclear cases.

items.q: Corticosteroid therapy in Duchenne muscular dystrophy:
o: Is contraindicated because it worsens weakness
Has no effect on motor function
Prolongs walking by about 2-3 years and reduces the risk of scoliosis
Cures the disease by restoring dystrophin
items.e: Prednisolone or deflazacort delays loss of walking, lowers scoliosis rates and helps cardiorespiratory function, at the cost of osteoporosis and weight gain.

items.q: In planning spinal fusion for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the forced vital capacity below which surgery carries a much higher cardiopulmonary risk (relative contraindication) is about:
o: 50% of the patient's own value at age 10
items.e: Fusion is preferred while FVC is 50% or more; below about 35% risk rises sharply, which is why early fusion is advised.

items.q: During anaesthesia in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which agent should be avoided because of the risk of hyperkalaemic rhabdomyolysis?
items.e: Depolarising relaxants and volatile agents can trigger rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest in dystrophinopathies; total intravenous anaesthesia is preferred.

items.q: A boy who walks beyond age 16 with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy and reduced (not absent) dystrophin on muscle biopsy has:
items.e: Becker dystrophy involves partially functional dystrophin, later onset and walking into adolescence or beyond; Duchenne has absent dystrophin and loss of walking around 12.

items.q: A teenager has early elbow flexion contractures, tight Achilles tendons, mild humeroperoneal weakness and an ECG showing heart block. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Early contractures (elbows, ankles, neck) and cardiac conduction defects requiring a pacemaker characterise Emery-Dreifuss dystrophy.

items.q: In facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy with painful scapular winging and preserved deltoid strength, the surgical option is:
items.e: Fusing the scapula to the ribs gives the preserved deltoid a stable base, improving shoulder abduction and flexion.

items.q: A child with spinal muscular atrophy has symmetric proximal weakness, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations. Which feature is preserved?
items.e: SMA is an anterior horn cell disease from SMN1 deletion, so sensation and cognition are normal.

items.q: A child with spinal muscular atrophy sits independently but has never stood or walked. This is SMA type:
items.e: Type I never sits, type II sits but never stands, type III (Kugelberg-Welander) achieves walking, and type IV is adult onset.

items.q: In spinal muscular atrophy, disease severity is modified mainly by the number of copies of:
items.e: Homozygous SMN1 loss causes SMA; more SMN2 copies produce more functional SMN protein and a milder phenotype. Nusinersen and risdiplam act on SMN2 splicing.

items.q: A 9-year-old with SMA type II has a painless dislocated left hip and comfortable sitting. Management of the hip is:
o: Open reduction with femoral and pelvic osteotomy
Leave it and focus on sitting posture and the spine
items.e: Hip subluxation in SMA is common and usually painless; reduction attempts often redislocate and add stiffness, so it is generally left alone.

items.q: Spinal surgery for scoliosis in children with SMA receiving intrathecal nusinersen should ideally:
o: Preserve access to the intrathecal space, for example by leaving a lumbar level unfused or creating a window
Fuse from T2 to sacrum with a solid posterior mass at every level
Be delayed until after skeletal maturity regardless of curve size
items.e: Posterior fusion masses block lumbar puncture, so surgeons leave a gap or window to allow continued intrathecal therapy.

items.q: An important intraoperative precaution for children with myelomeningocele is:
items.e: Repeated exposure from bladder catheterisation and surgery makes latex allergy common in spina bifida, so theatres must be latex-free.

items.q: A 7-year-old with myelomeningocele has a dislocated right hip, walks with crutches and AFOs and has a level pelvis with no hip contracture. Management of the hip is:
o: Observation, keeping the hip free of contracture
items.e: In myelomeningocele, reduction of the hip has not improved walking and risks stiffness and redislocation; maintaining a level pelvis and contracture-free hips matters more.

items.q: A child with L4 myelomeningocele develops a calcaneus foot from unopposed tibialis anterior with absent gastrocnemius-soleus. A recognised procedure is:
o: Split anterior tibial tendon transfer to the cuboid
Transfer of tibialis anterior posteriorly to the calcaneus
items.e: Moving the unopposed tibialis anterior through the interosseous membrane to the calcaneus removes the deforming force and adds push-off.

items.q: A child with myelomeningocele has a warm, swollen thigh with low-grade fever after minimal trauma. Radiographs later show abundant callus. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Fractures in anaesthetic limbs present painlessly with warmth, swelling and fever, mimicking infection, and heal with exuberant callus.

items.q: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A is caused by:
items.e: CMT1A, the commonest form, results from PMP22 duplication causing demyelination and slow conduction velocity.

items.q: In a teenager with CMT cavovarus, the Coleman block test shows the hindfoot varus corrects to valgus when the lateral forefoot is on the block. Appropriate surgery includes:
o: Plantar fascia release, first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy and peroneus longus to brevis transfer
items.e: A flexible hindfoot means the deformity is forefoot-driven, so forefoot and tendon balancing procedures are enough; a rigid hindfoot needs a calcaneal osteotomy as well.

items.q: The commonest cause of death in Friedreich ataxia is:
o: Aspiration from bulbar palsy in childhood
items.e: Friedreich ataxia (GAA repeat in frataxin) causes cardiomyopathy, the leading cause of death, plus diabetes, cavovarus feet and scoliosis.

items.q: In the classic amyoplasia form of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, the typical upper limb posture is:
o: Abducted shoulders, flexed elbows and extended wrists
Internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows and flexed wrists
Externally rotated shoulders with flexed elbows
Normal upper limbs with isolated clubfeet
items.e: Amyoplasia gives symmetrical internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows, flexed and ulnar-deviated wrists, with rigid clubfeet and hip and knee contractures.

items.q: In residual poliomyelitis, tendon transfer planning assumes that a transferred muscle will:
o: Lose all power if transferred out of phase
Lose about one grade of power
items.e: A muscle typically loses one MRC grade after transfer, so a donor should be at least grade 4 and preferably in phase.

items.q: The reported incidence of idiopathic clubfoot is highest in which population?
items.e: Clubfoot occurs in about 1-2 per 1,000 births overall, rising to about 7 per 1,000 in Polynesians (Maori, Hawaiians) and lower in Chinese populations.

items.q: Which genetic pathway has been most consistently implicated in idiopathic clubfoot?
items.e: Mutations and copy-number changes in the PITX1-TBX4 hindlimb developmental pathway are linked to familial and idiopathic clubfoot. FGFR3 causes achondroplasia and COL1A1/2 osteogenesis imperfecta.

items.q: A newborn has bilateral rigid clubfeet, 'hitchhiker' thumbs, and swollen cystic ears that later become cauliflower-shaped. The underlying gene defect is in:
items.e: These are features of diastrophic dysplasia, caused by mutations in the SLC26A2 sulphate transporter gene. Its clubfeet are stiff and resistant to treatment.

items.q: A newborn's foot looks inturned but can be passively brought fully into dorsiflexion and eversion with normal creases. The appropriate management is:
o: Ponseti casting from the first week
items.e: A positional (postural) clubfoot from intrauterine moulding is fully correctable and resolves with stretching. Idiopathic clubfoot is rigid and needs Ponseti casting.

items.q: In idiopathic clubfoot, the bone that shows the greatest intrinsic deformity is the:
o: Talus, with medial and plantar deviation of its neck
items.e: The talar neck is deviated medially and plantarly, making the talus the most deformed bone. The navicular is displaced medially on the talar head but is not itself the most deformed.

items.q: In the pathoanatomy of clubfoot, the hindfoot varus results mainly from:
o: Medial rotation and inversion of the calcaneus beneath the talus
items.e: The calcaneus rotates medially under the talus about the interosseous ligament, producing varus and adduction. Ponseti correction abducts the foot so the calcaneus rotates back out from under the talus.

items.q: Arterial anomalies are common in clubfoot. The vessel most often hypoplastic or absent is the:
items.e: The anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis artery is frequently hypoplastic, so the posterior tibial artery may be the dominant supply and must be protected during surgery.

items.q: Which group of signs makes up the hindfoot contracture score of the Pirani system?
o: Posterior crease, empty heel and rigid equinus
Medial crease, curved lateral border and lateral talar head coverage
Cavus, forefoot adduction and heel varus
Calf circumference, foot length and dorsiflexion angle
items.e: The hindfoot score (max 3) is posterior crease, empty heel and rigidity of equinus; the midfoot score (max 3) is curved lateral border, medial crease and uncovering of the lateral talar head.

items.q: The maximum total Pirani score for a severely deformed clubfoot is:
items.e: Six signs are each scored 0, 0.5 or 1, giving a maximum of 6. The Dimeglio system uses a 20-point scale.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of an untreated clubfoot, the talocalcaneal (Kite) angle is typically:
o: Reduced, with the talus and calcaneus nearly parallel
Reversed with the calcaneus medial to the talus by 90 degrees
items.e: Clubfoot shows talocalcaneal parallelism: an AP angle under 20 degrees (normal 20-40) and a reduced lateral angle. Radiographs are not routinely needed for Ponseti treatment.

items.q: Ponseti casts for idiopathic clubfoot are applied as:
o: Below-knee casts with the knee free
Long-leg casts with the knee fully extended
Long-leg casts with the knee flexed to about 90 degrees
items.e: Above-knee casts with 90 degrees of knee flexion control rotation and prevent slipping; below-knee casts slip and lose correction.

items.q: Before Achilles tenotomy is performed in the Ponseti method, the foot should first be abducted to about:
items.e: Equinus is corrected last, after abduction of about 60-70 degrees has corrected adductus and heel varus. Dorsiflexing earlier risks a rocker-bottom deformity.

items.q: After percutaneous Achilles tenotomy in Ponseti treatment, the final cast is usually kept on for about:
items.e: The final cast holds about 60-70 degrees abduction and 15-20 degrees dorsiflexion for 3 weeks while the tendon regenerates, followed by the brace.

items.q: During Ponseti casting, attempting to dorsiflex the foot before adduction and heel varus are corrected most likely results in:
o: A rocker-bottom foot with a midfoot break
Dynamic supination from tibialis anterior overactivity
items.e: Forcing dorsiflexion against a locked, varus calcaneus breaks the midfoot and creates a rocker-bottom foot; equinus must be addressed last.

items.q: Transfer of the tibialis anterior tendon for dynamic supination after Ponseti treatment is generally delayed until:
o: Age 10, when triple arthrodesis is possible
The lateral cuneiform is ossified, around 2.5-3 years or older
items.e: The tendon is fixed to the lateral cuneiform, so it must be ossified; the deformity must also be passively correctable.

items.q: Primary posteromedial release for clubfoot has largely been abandoned mainly because of:
o: Stiffness, overcorrection and pain or arthritis in adulthood
Injury to the tibial nerve in most cases
items.e: Long-term studies of extensive releases show stiff, painful, often overcorrected feet with early arthritis, compared with supple feet after Ponseti treatment.

items.q: A 5-year-old with a relapsed clubfoot has residual forefoot adduction from a long lateral column. Which procedure shortens the lateral column?
o: Dwyer medial opening wedge osteotomy of the calcaneus
Lichtblau resection of the distal calcaneus
items.e: Lateral column shortening (Evans calcaneocuboid fusion or Lichtblau distal calcaneal resection) corrects residual adductus in children of about 4-8 years. Calcaneal lengthening does the opposite.

items.q: Residual fixed heel varus in an older child with treated clubfoot is corrected with:
items.e: The Dwyer lateral closing wedge osteotomy of the calcaneus moves the heel into valgus. Cuneiform osteotomies address midfoot adduction.

items.q: Talectomy is most commonly indicated for:
items.e: Talectomy is a salvage procedure for severe rigid deformity, classically in arthrogryposis or myelomeningocele, where soft-tissue releases fail.

items.q: Joshi's External Stabilisation System (JESS), developed in India, is used in clubfoot mainly for:
o: Gradual distraction correction of neglected or relapsed feet in older children
items.e: JESS uses a mini-external fixator to correct rigid neglected or recurrent clubfoot gradually, avoiding extensive soft-tissue release.

items.q: Which feature distinguishes metatarsus adductus from clubfoot?
o: Normal ankle dorsiflexion with a neutral or valgus hindfoot
items.e: Metatarsus adductus is isolated forefoot adduction with a normal hindfoot and no equinus, whereas clubfoot has equinus and hindfoot varus.

items.q: In the Bleck classification of metatarsus adductus, the heel bisector line in a normal foot passes through:
o: The second web space (between the second and third toes)
Between the fourth and fifth toes
items.e: The heel bisector normally passes between the second and third toes. In moderate deformity it passes between the third and fourth toes, and in severe between the fourth and fifth.

items.q: A heel bisector line passing between the third and fourth toes indicates metatarsus adductus of which Bleck severity?
items.e: Bleck: mild through the third toe, moderate between the third and fourth toes, severe between the fourth and fifth toes.

items.q: An infant with metatarsus adductus should also be examined carefully for:
items.e: Metatarsus adductus, like other moulding deformities, is associated with DDH in about 5-10%, so hip examination or imaging is needed.

items.q: A rigid metatarsus adductus that does not correct past neutral is best treated by serial casting started before about:
items.e: Serial casting is most effective in the first months of life; results decline after about 8 months. Flexible deformities usually resolve spontaneously.

items.q: A 6-year-old has painful, rigid residual metatarsus adductus. The usual procedure is:
o: Medial cuneiform opening-wedge with cuboid closing-wedge osteotomy
items.e: After about 4 years, bony correction with a medial cuneiform opening wedge and cuboid closing wedge (or metatarsal base osteotomies) is used. Capsulotomies have high failure rates.

items.q: A skewfoot (serpentine foot) consists of:
items.e: Skewfoot combines metatarsus adductus with hindfoot valgus and lateral talonavicular subluxation; it may follow casting that pushed the hindfoot into valgus.

items.q: Which gene mutation has been reported in familial isolated congenital vertical talus?
items.e: A HOXD10 mutation has been found in families with isolated CVT. PITX1 is associated with clubfoot.

items.q: The fundamental lesion in congenital vertical talus is:
o: Irreducible dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talar neck
Medial subluxation of the navicular on the talar head
Fusion of the calcaneus and navicular
items.e: In CVT the navicular is dislocated dorsally onto the talar neck with a vertical talus, hindfoot equinus and valgus, producing a rigid rocker-bottom foot.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of congenital vertical talus cases are associated with a neuromuscular or genetic condition?
items.e: About half of CVT is syndromic (arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele, trisomies 13/18), so the spine, hips and neurology should be examined.

items.q: The Dobbs ('reverse Ponseti') method for congenital vertical talus consists of serial casting followed by:
o: Tibialis posterior transfer to the dorsum
Talonavicular pinning and percutaneous Achilles tenotomy
items.e: Casting stretches the foot into plantarflexion and inversion with pressure on the talar head; the reduced talonavicular joint is pinned and the residual equinus treated by tenotomy.

items.q: In open release of a congenital vertical talus, which group of tendons is typically lengthened dorsally?
o: Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and peroneus tertius
items.e: The dorsal and lateral structures are contracted in CVT, so the anterior tibial, toe extensors and peroneus tertius are lengthened along with the dorsal talonavicular capsule and the Achilles.

items.q: A newborn's foot lies against the anterior shin in dorsiflexion and valgus but can be plantarflexed passively beyond neutral. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Postural calcaneovalgus foot is flexible and resolves spontaneously or with stretching. CVT is rigid and the foot cannot be plantarflexed.

items.q: A newborn has a calcaneovalgus foot with a posteromedial bow of the tibia. The main long-term problem is:
o: Persistent bowing needing osteotomy in infancy
Leg-length discrepancy of about 3-4 cm at maturity
items.e: Posteromedial bowing improves spontaneously, but the limb remains short; epiphysiodesis or lengthening may be needed. Anterolateral bowing is the type linked with pseudarthrosis and NF1.

items.q: A 7-year-old has a painless flatfoot in standing. The arch forms when he stands on tiptoe and the heel swings into varus. The appropriate management is:
o: Custom orthoses to correct the arch
items.e: Painless flexible flatfoot is a normal variant; orthoses have not been shown to change its natural history. Surgery is reserved for symptomatic feet that fail conservative care.

items.q: A 12-year-old with a symptomatic flexible flatfoot and a tight gastrocnemius has failed stretching and orthoses. The usual operation is:
o: Calcaneal lengthening (Evans) osteotomy with gastrocnemius recession
Tibialis anterior transfer to the cuboid
items.e: Lateral column lengthening corrects the abduction and valgus while preserving joints; the gastrocnemius contracture is released at the same time.

items.q: Tarsal coalition is usually inherited in which manner?
items.e: Coalitions arise from failure of mesenchymal segmentation and show autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance; about half are bilateral.

items.q: Compared with calcaneonavicular coalition, talocalcaneal coalition usually presents:
o: At birth with a rigid foot
items.e: Talocalcaneal (middle facet) coalitions ossify later and present at 12-16 years; calcaneonavicular coalitions present at about 8-12 years.

items.q: Dorsal beaking of the talar head on a lateral radiograph in a child with talocalcaneal coalition represents:
o: An avulsion fracture of the deltoid ligament
A traction spur from abnormal talonavicular motion
items.e: Talar beaking reflects altered motion and capsular traction because subtalar motion is lost; it is not a sign of arthritis and does not preclude resection.

items.q: A calcaneonavicular coalition is best seen on which plain radiograph?
o: 45-degree internal oblique view of the foot
Harris axial view of the heel
Standing AP view of the ankle
items.e: The 45-degree oblique view shows the bar between the anterior process of the calcaneus and the navicular. The Harris view is used for talocalcaneal coalition.

items.q: After resection of a calcaneonavicular coalition, recurrence is reduced by interposing:
o: The extensor digitorum brevis muscle or fat
items.e: Interposition of EDB (or fat) fills the gap and reduces re-formation of the bar, with good results in symptomatic CN coalitions.
