items.q: Resection of a talocalcaneal coalition is generally recommended only when the coalition involves less than about what proportion of the posterior facet area, without severe valgus or arthritis?
items.e: Resection with fat or FHL interposition works best when the coalition is under about half of the posterior facet area and hindfoot valgus is modest; otherwise arthrodesis is considered.

items.q: The commonest symptomatic type of accessory navicular is:
o: Type I, a sesamoid within the tibialis posterior tendon
Type II, connected to the navicular by a synchondrosis
items.e: Type II ossicles attach by a cartilage bridge that is prone to microtrauma and pain; type I is a sesamoid and type III a fused cornuate navicular.

items.q: The Kidner procedure for a painful accessory navicular involves:
o: Excision of the ossicle and advancement of the tibialis posterior tendon
Transfer of FDL to the navicular with spring ligament repair
items.e: Kidner described excision of the accessory bone with rerouting/advancement of the tibialis posterior; simple excision has comparable results in many series.

items.q: The commonest form of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease causing bilateral cavovarus feet in children is due to:
o: Frataxin GAA repeat expansion on chromosome 9
Dystrophin deletion on the X chromosome
items.e: CMT1A (HMSN I) results from PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17p. Friedreich ataxia (frataxin) also causes cavus but is less common.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a progressive unilateral cavovarus foot. The most important investigation is:
o: Nerve conduction studies of both legs
items.e: A unilateral cavus foot suggests spinal cord pathology (tethered cord, diastematomyelia, syrinx, tumour) until proven otherwise. Bilateral cavus is more often CMT.

items.q: In a child with cavovarus foot, the hindfoot corrects to valgus on the Coleman block test. The hindfoot component is best treated by:
o: Addressing only the forefoot (first metatarsal osteotomy, plantar fascia release, peroneus longus to brevis transfer)
items.e: A correctable hindfoot on the Coleman block is forefoot-driven, so forefoot correction suffices; a hindfoot that fails to correct needs a calcaneal osteotomy as well.

items.q: The Jones procedure for a clawed hallux in cavus foot involves:
o: Transfer of FHL to the proximal phalanx
Transfer of EHL to the first metatarsal neck with interphalangeal joint fusion
Transfer of EDL to the lateral cuneiform
Transfer of tibialis posterior through the interosseous membrane
items.e: The Jones transfer turns the EHL into a first metatarsal elevator and fuses the hallux IP joint to stop it flexing; Hibbs transfers EDL to the lateral cuneiform or cuboid.

items.q: Among organs affected by blood-borne metastasis from carcinomas, bone ranks:
o: First, ahead of lung and liver
Fifth, after lung, liver, brain and adrenal
items.e: Bone is the third commonest site of metastasis after lung and liver. Metastasis is also far commoner than primary sarcoma as a cause of malignant bone destruction.

items.q: Together, which three primary cancers account for about 80% of skeletal metastases?
items.e: Breast, prostate and lung cause about 80% of bone metastases because they are common and bone-seeking. Kidney and thyroid are also bone-seeking but much less common overall.

items.q: Which long bone is most commonly involved by skeletal metastases?
items.e: The proximal femur is the commonest long bone site, after the spine, pelvis and ribs overall, reflecting its red-marrow content. Metastases distal to the elbow and knee are rare.

items.q: Within the spine, metastases most frequently involve the:
items.e: About 70% of spinal metastases are thoracic, about 20% lumbar and about 10% cervical. The thoracic canal is also narrow, so cord compression is common there.

items.q: Spread of prostate cancer to the lumbar spine and pelvis without lung metastases is explained by:
o: Lymphatic spread through the thoracic duct
items.e: Batson's vertebral venous plexus has no valves, so a rise in intra-abdominal pressure can push tumour cells from pelvic veins straight into the vertebral bodies, bypassing the lungs.

items.q: The 'seed and soil' hypothesis, which explains why some tumours prefer bone, was proposed by:
items.e: Stephen Paget (1889) proposed that tumour cells (seed) grow only in a favourable organ environment (soil); in bone this involves marrow chemokines such as CXCL12 binding CXCR4 on tumour cells. Batson described the vertebral venous plexus.

items.q: In osteoblastic prostate cancer metastases, the key factor secreted by tumour cells that stimulates osteoblasts is:
items.e: Prostate cancer cells secrete endothelin-1 (with Wnt proteins and BMPs) to stimulate osteoblasts, producing woven, mechanically weak bone. PTHrP and RANKL drive osteolytic metastases.

items.q: Approximately how much of the bone mineral must be lost at a site before a lytic metastasis becomes visible on plain radiographs?
items.e: About 30-50% of bone mineral must be destroyed before a lytic lesion is visible on radiographs, which is why MRI and bone scanning detect metastases earlier.

items.q: Apart from prostate carcinoma, which tumour is well known for producing sclerotic (osteoblastic) bone metastases?
items.e: Carcinoid, small cell lung cancer, medulloblastoma and treated breast cancer can produce sclerotic metastases. Renal, thyroid and melanoma metastases are typically purely lytic.

items.q: Untreated breast cancer metastases to bone are typically:
items.e: Breast cancer metastases are classically mixed lytic and sclerotic; they may become more sclerotic as they heal after treatment. Expansile blow-out lesions suggest renal or thyroid carcinoma.

items.q: A solitary bone metastasis from differentiated thyroid carcinoma that takes up iodine may respond to:
items.e: Iodine-avid differentiated thyroid metastases can be treated with radioactive iodine; they are also hypervascular, so solitary lesions are often embolised and resected. Radium-223 is used for prostate cancer.

items.q: A patient with a known femoral metastasis previously had only night pain; now the thigh hurts every time she bears weight. This change mainly indicates:
items.e: Night or rest pain is biological, but pain on weight bearing (functional or mechanical pain) shows the bone is failing structurally and is the most important clinical sign of an impending fracture.

items.q: A patient with metastatic renal cancer has hypercalcaemia that has not responded to fluids and zoledronic acid, and has an eGFR of 25 mL/min. A suitable next agent is:
items.e: Denosumab can be used for bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia of malignancy and needs no renal dose adjustment, unlike zoledronic acid. Thiazides raise calcium and must be avoided.

items.q: In severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy, which agent lowers calcium most rapidly (within hours) but loses effect within a few days?
items.e: Calcitonin acts within hours but tachyphylaxis limits it to about 48 hours; it bridges the delay until IV bisphosphonate, which takes 2-4 days to act, becomes effective.

items.q: The earliest symptom in most patients with metastatic spinal cord compression is:
o: Back pain, often band-like and worse lying down
items.e: Back or radicular pain, typically band-like and worse lying flat or on straining, precedes neurological deficit by weeks; sphincter disturbance is a late sign. Recognising the pain early allows MRI before paralysis.

items.q: In trials of bone-targeted agents, a 'skeletal-related event' includes pathological fracture, radiotherapy to bone, surgery to bone and:
items.e: Skeletal-related events are pathological fracture, spinal cord compression, radiotherapy or surgery to bone, and (in some trials) hypercalcaemia. Anaemia and neutropenia are not counted.

items.q: Rougraff's diagnostic strategy for skeletal metastasis of unknown origin (history, examination, laboratory tests, chest radiograph, CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, bone scan and biopsy) identified the primary tumour in about:
items.e: Rougraff's protocol identified the primary in about 85%; in roughly 10-15% the primary is never found (carcinoma of unknown primary). CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis is a key step.

items.q: In Rougraff's series of skeletal metastases of unknown origin, the second commonest primary after lung carcinoma was:
items.e: Lung carcinoma was the commonest occult primary, followed by kidney. Breast and prostate cancers are usually already known or easily found on examination and PSA.

items.q: For staging bone metastases in high-risk prostate cancer, the most sensitive modern investigation is:
items.e: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET-CT is more sensitive and specific than bone scan for prostate cancer metastases. FDG PET-CT is less useful in prostate cancer, which is often not very FDG-avid.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of the thoracic spine, one pedicle is missing at a vertebral level while the opposite pedicle is intact ('winking owl' sign). The most likely cause is:
items.e: Metastases spread from the vertebral body into the pedicle, so pedicle destruction on the AP view suggests metastasis. Myeloma tends to spare the pedicle early, and osteoporotic fractures spare the posterior elements.

items.q: On spinal imaging, which feature best distinguishes vertebral metastasis from pyogenic spondylodiscitis?
o: Preservation of the intervertebral disc space
items.e: Tumours rarely cross the disc, so the disc space is preserved in metastasis, whereas pyogenic infection destroys the disc and both adjacent endplates. Both conditions involve the body and are hot on bone scan.

items.q: MRI of an acute vertebral collapse shows a convex bulge of the posterior vertebral cortex, low T1 signal replacing the whole body, pedicle involvement and an epidural soft-tissue mass. These features suggest:
items.e: A convex posterior cortex, complete marrow replacement, pedicle involvement and an epidural mass favour malignancy. Osteoporotic fractures show band-like oedema with preserved fatty marrow, a retropulsed angular fragment and sometimes a fluid sign.

items.q: On MRI of a collapsed vertebra, a linear fluid-signal collection (the 'fluid sign') or an intravertebral vacuum cleft favours:
items.e: The fluid sign and vacuum cleft indicate osteonecrosis or nonunion within a benign osteoporotic fracture. Malignant collapse more often shows diffuse marrow replacement, a convex posterior wall and posterior element involvement.

items.q: In Mirels scoring, a metastatic lesion involving between one-third and two-thirds of the bone diameter scores:
items.e: Size scores 1 point for under one-third, 2 for one-third to two-thirds and 3 for over two-thirds of the diameter. Each of the four variables scores 1-3, so the total ranges from 4 to 12.

items.q: A metastatic lesion has a Mirels score of 8. The predicted fracture risk and recommendation are:
items.e: Mirels 7 or less carries about 4% risk (radiotherapy), 8 about 15% (judgement) and 9 or more about 33% or higher (prophylactic fixation).

items.q: The main limitation of the Mirels scoring system is that it:
o: Has very low sensitivity, missing most impending fractures
Can only be used in the spine
Has poor specificity, so many lesions scored 9 would not fracture
items.e: Mirels' score is sensitive but not specific, so it overtreats some lesions; CT-based structural rigidity analysis and finite element models are more accurate but less available.

items.q: A metastatic lesion in the humeral shaft is scored using Mirels. The site variable for the upper limb scores:
items.e: Site scores 1 for the upper limb, 2 for the lower limb and 3 for the peritrochanteric region, reflecting the different loads. A lytic, painful, large humeral lesion can still reach a high total score.

items.q: Under Harrington's criteria for prophylactic fixation of a femoral metastasis, which degree of cortical destruction is an indication?
o: 50% or more of the cortex destroyed
items.e: Harrington's criteria are cortical destruction of 50% or more, a proximal femoral lesion of 2.5 cm or more, pathological avulsion of the lesser trochanter and persistent weight-bearing pain after radiotherapy.

items.q: Under Harrington's criteria, what size of lytic lesion in the proximal femur warrants prophylactic fixation?
items.e: A proximal femoral lesion of 2.5 cm or more is one of Harrington's criteria, together with 50% cortical destruction, lesser trochanter avulsion and persistent pain after radiotherapy.

items.q: In the Dutch Femoral Metastases study (Van der Linden et al., 2004), which radiographic measurement best predicted pathological fracture of the femur?
items.e: Axial cortical involvement over 30 mm (or circumferential involvement over 50%) predicted fracture, and lesions below this could be treated with radiotherapy alone. The study found Mirels' score less useful.

items.q: In classic teaching, operative fixation of a long-bone metastasis is generally considered worthwhile when the patient's expected survival is at least about:
items.e: Long-bone surgery is usually justified if survival is expected to exceed about 6 weeks, and spinal surgery about 3 months. Tools such as PATHFx, SPRING and Katagiri scores help estimate survival.

items.q: PATHFx is a tool used in metastatic bone disease to:
o: Estimate patient survival to guide the choice of surgery
Score femoral fracture risk from CT
items.e: PATHFx is a machine-learning tool estimating the probability of survival at set intervals, helping decide between durable reconstruction, simple fixation or non-operative care. Bilsky grades cord compression and Harrington classifies acetabular defects.

items.q: In Gainor and Buchert's study, approximately what proportion of pathological fractures from breast carcinoma united?
items.e: Healing rates were highest in myeloma (about 65-70%), then renal (about 45%) and breast (about 35-40%), and essentially none in lung cancer. Healing needs survival beyond about 6 months.

items.q: Because many pathological fractures never unite, the key principle when fixing a metastatic long-bone lesion is that:
o: The implant must rely on fracture healing within 3 months
Weight bearing should be avoided for 3 months
The construct should be strong enough to last the patient's lifetime without bone healing
Bone grafting is mandatory at every fixation
items.e: Fixation in metastatic disease should allow immediate weight bearing and outlast the patient without relying on union; load-sharing nails, cement augmentation and replacement rather than fixation are used for this.

items.q: Before nailing an impending pathological fracture of the right femur from breast cancer, the surgeon should image:
o: Only the lesion with a single AP radiograph
The lesion and the knee joint
The whole femur and the opposite femur
items.e: The whole femur (and the opposite femur) is imaged to detect other lesions that the implant must protect or that need treatment. A short implant ending in an unrecognised lesion risks a new fracture.

items.q: A 66-year-old with metastatic renal cancer has extensive destruction of the intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric region with loss of the calcar, after previous nailing has failed. The best reconstruction is:
o: Revision to a dynamic hip screw
items.e: Extensive proximal femoral destruction or failed fixation is best treated with a cemented proximal femoral endoprosthesis, which does not depend on bone healing. A dynamic hip screw is unsuitable in pathological bone.

items.q: A patient with metastatic breast cancer has a painful lytic metastasis in the pubic ramus with no fracture. The usual management is:
items.e: Metastases of the non-weight-bearing pelvis (ilium away from the acetabulum, pubic rami) are treated with radiotherapy, analgesia and mobilisation. Surgery is reserved for periacetabular disease threatening hip function.

items.q: A periacetabular metastasis has intact lateral cortices and intact superior and medial walls. In Harrington's classification this is class I, treated by:
o: Harrington pins from the iliac crest
items.e: Class I defects have adequate acetabular bone, so a conventional cemented THA suffices. Class II (medial wall loss) needs a protrusio cage, class III (roof and lateral cortex loss) the Harrington procedure, and class IV resection.

items.q: In Harrington's classification of periacetabular metastases, class IV refers to:
o: A solitary lesion treated for cure, by en bloc resection
items.e: Class IV is a solitary lesion (or discontinuity) treated with curative intent by en bloc resection and reconstruction, for example a solitary renal metastasis. The other classes are treated by THA of increasing complexity.

items.q: After fixation of a pathological femoral fracture, postoperative radiotherapy is usually started:
o: About 2 weeks after surgery, once the wound is healing
After 6 months, if the fracture has not united
items.e: Radiotherapy to the whole implant length is usually begun about 2 weeks after surgery, when the wound is healing, to control local disease. Waiting for nonunion would allow tumour progression around the implant.

items.q: During cemented long-stem hemiarthroplasty for a metastatic femoral neck fracture, sudden hypoxia and hypotension occur on cement insertion. This is most likely:
o: Bone cement implantation syndrome from marrow, fat and tumour embolism
Acute myocardial infarction unrelated to surgery
items.e: Pressurising cement into a long canal can embolise marrow, fat and tumour, causing bone cement implantation syndrome; metastatic patients are at high risk. Canal lavage, venting and careful cementing reduce the risk.

items.q: On axial T2 MRI, epidural tumour deforms the thecal sac and touches the spinal cord without compressing it. The Bilsky grade is:
items.e: Bilsky 1a is epidural impingement without sac deformation, 1b sac deformation without cord contact, 1c cord abutment without compression, 2 cord compression with CSF visible, and 3 compression with no CSF.

items.q: Bilsky grade 3 epidural spinal cord compression is defined as:
o: Thecal sac deformation without cord contact
Cord compression with CSF still visible around the cord
Cord compression with no CSF visible around the cord
items.e: Grade 3 is cord compression with no visible CSF; grade 2 still has CSF around the cord. Grades 2-3 are high-grade compression where surgery is considered for radioresistant tumours.

items.q: In 'separation surgery' for high-grade epidural compression from a radioresistant tumour, the aim is to:
o: Create a gap of about 2-3 mm between tumour and cord so stereotactic radiotherapy can be given safely
Remove the entire vertebra en bloc with clear margins
Inject cement into the vertebral body
items.e: Separation surgery decompresses the epidural tumour (with stabilisation) to create a small margin around the cord, allowing high-dose SBRT to control the tumour. It is not an en bloc resection.

items.q: Which spinal metastasis is considered radioresistant to conventional external-beam radiotherapy?
items.e: Renal cell, thyroid, melanoma, sarcoma, non-small cell lung, colon and hepatocellular carcinoma are relatively radioresistant. Lymphoma, myeloma/plasmacytoma and seminoma are highly radiosensitive.

items.q: In the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS), a lesion at T12 receives the maximum location score of 3 because T12 is:
items.e: Junctional levels (occiput-C2, C7-T2, T11-L1, L5-S1) score 3; mobile segments (C3-C6, L2-L4) score 2; semi-rigid (T3-T10) 1; rigid (S2-S5) 0.

items.q: In SINS, which radiographic alignment finding earns the highest single-component score (4 points)?
items.e: Subluxation or translation scores 4, de novo deformity 2 and normal alignment 0. Collapse over 50% and bilateral posterolateral involvement score 3 each, and a lytic lesion scores 2.

items.q: A spinal metastasis has a SINS score of 14. This is classified as:
items.e: SINS 0-6 is stable, 7-12 indeterminate (potentially unstable) and 13-18 unstable. Surgical consultation is recommended for any score of 7 or more.

items.q: On a weight-bearing lateral radiograph of an adult flatfoot, the talo-first metatarsal (Meary) angle is 20 degrees convex plantarward. This grades the deformity as:
items.e: Meary angle is normally about 0 degrees; plantar-convex 4-15 degrees is mild, 15-30 degrees moderate and over 30 degrees severe flatfoot.

items.q: Weight-bearing CT of a progressive collapsing foot deformity shows subluxation of the middle facet of the subtalar joint and sinus tarsi impingement. In the 2020 consensus classification this component of the deformity is described as:
o: Class C - forefoot varus/medial column instability
items.e: Class D denotes peritalar subluxation or dislocation, for which middle facet uncoverage and sinus tarsi impingement on weight-bearing CT are markers; class E is ankle (valgus) instability.

items.q: A 57-year-old woman has a flexible hindfoot valgus from tibialis posterior insufficiency, but after the hindfoot is held reduced the forefoot remains in fixed supination that cannot be passively corrected. In the Myerson modification of Johnson and Strom this is stage:
items.e: Stage II is the flexible flatfoot; IIC is defined by fixed forefoot varus (supination) after hindfoot correction, needing a medial column procedure such as a Cotton osteotomy. Stage III means the hindfoot itself is rigid.

items.q: In an Evans lateral column lengthening for flexible flatfoot, the tricortical graft inserted into the anterior calcaneal osteotomy is typically about:
items.e: A graft of about 8-10 mm usually corrects talonavicular uncoverage; overlengthening increases lateral column overload and calcaneocuboid pressure.

items.q: A 55-year-old with flexible flatfoot has limited ankle dorsiflexion that does NOT improve when the knee is flexed (negative Silfverskiöld test). The appropriate procedure to correct the equinus is:
items.e: Equinus unchanged by knee flexion means the soleus is also contracted (tendo Achilles tightness), so the whole tendon is lengthened; isolated gastrocnemius tightness (positive Silfverskiöld) is treated by Strayer recession.

items.q: The UCBL (University of California Biomechanics Laboratory) insert used for flexible flatfoot is best described as:
o: A rigid moulded foot orthosis with a deep heel cup and medial and lateral flanges that hold the heel in neutral
A hinged ankle-foot orthosis extending to the calf
A soft accommodative full-length insole with a metatarsal pad
items.e: The UCBL is a rigid shell with a deep heel cup and high side walls that controls hindfoot valgus and forefoot abduction; more advanced deformity needs an ankle-foot orthosis.

items.q: A triple arthrodesis for rigid flatfoot united with the hindfoot in excessive varus. The commonest resulting problem is:
o: Overload of the first metatarsal head with hallux rigidus
Tarsal tunnel syndrome from tibial nerve stretch
Overload of the lateral border of the foot with pain under the fifth metatarsal base and head
items.e: Hindfoot varus locks the transverse tarsal joint and shifts weight laterally, causing lateral foot pain, callosities and ankle stress; about 5 degrees of valgus is the target.

items.q: A 13-year-old with medial midfoot pain has an accessory navicular. Which type (Geist/Veitch classification) is most often symptomatic?
o: Type I - a small sesamoid within the tibialis posterior tendon
Type III - a cornuate navicular fused to the main bone
Type II - a large ossicle joined to the navicular by a synchondrosis
An os supranaviculare on the dorsal talonavicular joint
items.e: Type II is joined by a fibrocartilaginous synchondrosis that is disrupted by tibialis posterior traction, producing pain; type I is a sesamoid (os tibiale externum) and type III a fused prominent (cornuate) navicular.

items.q: A 6-year-old has bilateral flatfeet noticed by his parents. He has no pain, the arches reconstitute on tiptoe standing and subtalar motion is full. The appropriate management is:
o: Custom moulded orthoses until skeletal maturity
items.e: Asymptomatic flexible flatfoot is physiological and usually improves; orthoses do not alter natural arch development and surgery is reserved for painful feet failing non-operative care.

items.q: A 14-year-old with a flexible flatfoot has activity-related pain under the talar head despite orthoses for a year. There is a tight heel cord. The appropriate surgery is:
o: Calcaneal lengthening osteotomy with gastrocnemius recession
items.e: A painful flexible flatfoot with a contracted gastrocnemius-soleus that fails conservative care is treated by lateral column (calcaneal) lengthening plus correction of equinus; arthrodesis is avoided in adolescents.

items.q: In the Jack (Hubscher) toe-raise test, passive dorsiflexion of the hallux in a standing patient restores the medial arch and externally rotates the tibia. This indicates:
o: A flexible flatfoot with an intact windlass mechanism
A rigid flatfoot from tarsal coalition
items.e: Hallux dorsiflexion tightens the plantar fascia (windlass), elevating the arch and inverting the heel; reconstitution of the arch shows the deformity is flexible.

items.q: A 69-year-old man has a painless foot slap when walking. There is a soft swelling at the front of the ankle, weak ankle dorsiflexion and the toes extend strongly as he tries to dorsiflex. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Degenerative tibialis anterior rupture affects older men; the retracted stump forms an anterior lump and the long toe extensors are recruited (substitution), which would be weak in a nerve palsy.

items.q: Results of surgical release for tarsal tunnel syndrome are best when:
o: There is no Tinel sign over the tunnel
A space-occupying lesion such as a ganglion compresses the tibial nerve
items.e: Tarsal tunnel release is less predictable than carpal tunnel release (about 50-75% good results); the best outcomes are when a discrete space-occupying lesion is excised.

items.q: A runner with chronic medial heel pain unresponsive to plantar fascia stretching has selective fatty atrophy of the abductor digiti minimi on MRI. The nerve entrapped is the:
o: Medial calcaneal branch of the tibial nerve
First branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter nerve)
items.e: The inferior calcaneal (Baxter) nerve supplies abductor digiti minimi; its entrapment between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae mimics plantar fasciitis.

items.q: Why is complete plantar fascia release avoided when operating for recalcitrant plantar fasciitis?
o: It causes heel fat pad atrophy
It destabilises the medial arch and causes lateral column pain
It produces a rigid cavus foot
items.e: Release of more than about half of the fascia (the medial third to half is recommended) loses the windlass support of the arch and overloads the lateral column.

items.q: In Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, the muscles that typically weaken earliest in the leg are:
o: Flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus
items.e: The length-dependent neuropathy affects the anterior and lateral compartments first; strong peroneus longus and tibialis posterior then overpower their weak antagonists, producing cavovarus.

items.q: Claw toes in a Charcot-Marie-Tooth cavovarus foot develop mainly because:
o: Weak intrinsics fail to flex the MTP joints while the long extensors are recruited to dorsiflex the ankle
The plantar fascia ruptures and the toes drift dorsally
The peroneus longus pulls the toes into extension
items.e: With intrinsic weakness the long extensors hyperextend the MTP joints (especially when substituting for a weak tibialis anterior) and the long flexors flex the IP joints, producing clawing.

items.q: A lateral ankle radiograph of a patient with cavovarus foot shows a 'double contour' of the talar dome and a posteriorly placed fibula. These findings reflect:
o: Hindfoot varus with external rotation of the talus in the mortise
items.e: In cavovarus the talus is externally rotated relative to the beam so the medial and lateral domes are not superimposed (double talar dome), and the fibula lies posterior.

items.q: The Dwyer osteotomy used for fixed hindfoot varus is:
o: A medially based opening-wedge osteotomy of the talar neck
A dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy of the first metatarsal base
A laterally based closing-wedge osteotomy of the calcaneal body
A plantarflexion osteotomy of the medial cuneiform
items.e: Removing a lateral wedge from the calcaneus swings the tuberosity into valgus; a lateralising translational (Z) calcaneal osteotomy is an alternative.

items.q: The Steindler procedure used in cavus foot surgery consists of:
o: Transfer of the peroneus longus to the peroneus brevis
Stripping the plantar fascia and short plantar muscle origins from the calcaneus
Fusion of the hallux interphalangeal joint
items.e: The Steindler stripping releases the plantar fascia, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi from the calcaneal tuberosity, allowing the arch to drop.

items.q: For a fixed cavus with its apex in the midfoot, the Japas osteotomy differs from a Cole wedge osteotomy in that it:
o: Is performed through the calcaneal tuberosity
Is a V-shaped osteotomy with its apex proximal at the navicular, avoiding shortening of the foot
Corrects deformity by fusing the talonavicular joint
Is an opening wedge in the first metatarsal
items.e: The Japas V-osteotomy rotates the forefoot through a chevron-shaped cut without removing a wedge, whereas the Cole osteotomy removes a dorsal wedge and shortens the foot.

items.q: In the Hibbs procedure for flexible clawing of the lesser toes in a cavus foot, the extensor digitorum longus tendons are:
o: Transferred to the lateral cuneiform or cuboid
items.e: Rerouting EDL proximally to the midfoot removes its hyperextending force on the MTP joints and adds ankle dorsiflexion power; the Girdlestone-Taylor transfer uses the long flexors instead.

items.q: In the Jones transfer for a clawed hallux, why is the interphalangeal joint of the hallux fused?
o: To provide an anchor point for the tendon
To prevent a flexion deformity (droop) of the IP joint after the extensor hallucis longus is moved
items.e: Once EHL is moved to the first metatarsal neck, the unopposed flexor hallucis longus would flex the IP joint, so it is fused.

items.q: A 16-year-old has progressive bilateral cavus feet, scoliosis, ataxic gait, absent ankle reflexes and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The genetic abnormality is:
o: GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin gene
items.e: Friedreich ataxia (autosomal recessive, frataxin, chromosome 9) causes cavovarus feet, scoliosis and cardiomyopathy; PMP22 duplication is CMT1A.

items.q: Eighteen months after a tibial shaft fracture, a man has fixed clawing of the toes, a high arch and loss of plantar sensation. The most likely underlying cause is:
o: Missed deep posterior compartment syndrome with ischaemic contracture
items.e: Ischaemic contracture of the long toe flexors and intrinsics after compartment syndrome (Volkmann-type) produces claw toes and an acquired cavus foot.

items.q: A varus malunion of a talar neck fracture typically produces:
o: A planovalgus foot with forefoot abduction
A cavovarus hindfoot with lateral overload of the foot
items.e: Varus malunion of the talar neck adducts and supinates the foot, producing hindfoot varus and lateral border overload; it reduces subtalar and transverse tarsal motion.

items.q: A runner with a subtle cavovarus foot is at increased risk of which stress fracture?
o: Proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal
items.e: Hindfoot varus overloads the lateral column, predisposing to fifth metatarsal stress fractures, which may fail fixation unless the varus is corrected.

items.q: Nerve conduction studies in a 20-year-old with bilateral cavus feet show markedly reduced motor conduction velocities (about 20 m/s) in all nerves. This pattern suggests:
o: An axonal neuropathy such as CMT type 2
A demyelinating neuropathy such as CMT type 1
items.e: CMT1 is demyelinating with uniformly slowed conduction (below about 38 m/s); CMT2 is axonal with near-normal velocity but reduced amplitudes.

items.q: X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMTX1), a cause of cavovarus feet in males, results from a mutation in:
items.e: CMTX1 is due to GJB1 mutations; PMP22 duplication causes CMT1A, MPZ causes CMT1B and MFN2 causes the axonal CMT2A.

items.q: When planning a tendon transfer to correct foot drop in a cavovarus foot, the surgeon expects the transferred muscle to:
o: Gain one MRC grade after transfer
Lose about one MRC grade of power after transfer
Function only if it is grade 3 or less
items.e: A transferred tendon usually loses about one grade, so the donor should be grade 5 (at least 4) to provide useful function.

items.q: The Bridle procedure for foot drop involves:
o: Fusion of the ankle in neutral
Tibialis posterior transfer through the interosseous membrane with a tri-tendon anastomosis to tibialis anterior and a rerouted peroneus longus
Transfer of peroneus brevis to the base of the fifth metatarsal
items.e: The Bridle anchors the transferred tibialis posterior to both tibialis anterior and peroneus longus, giving balanced dorsiflexion without inversion or eversion bias.

items.q: The normal calcaneal pitch angle on a weight-bearing lateral foot radiograph is approximately:
items.e: Calcaneal pitch is normally about 20-30 degrees; it falls in flatfoot and exceeds about 30 degrees in calcaneocavus.

items.q: On a weight-bearing AP foot radiograph, a talonavicular coverage angle of more than about 7 degrees indicates:
items.e: The talonavicular coverage angle measures lateral displacement of the navicular on the talar head; values above about 7 degrees indicate abduction in flatfoot.

items.q: A 46-year-old has stage I tibialis posterior tenosynovitis with intact tendon length. Pain persists after 3-4 months of boot immobilisation, orthoses and physiotherapy. The next step is:
o: FDL transfer with medialising calcaneal osteotomy
Corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath
items.e: Failed conservative care in stage I is treated by synovectomy and debridement (with repair of any longitudinal split); reconstructive procedures are for stage II deformity.

items.q: The commonest reason for a second operation after subtalar arthroereisis for flexible flatfoot is:
o: Persistent sinus tarsi pain requiring implant removal
items.e: Sinus tarsi pain from the implant is the commonest complication and frequently leads to implant removal.

items.q: A 64-year-old with progressive collapsing foot deformity develops valgus tilt of the talus in the ankle mortise. In the 2020 consensus classification, this component is recorded as class:
items.e: Class E denotes ankle instability (valgus tilt from deltoid insufficiency); A is hindfoot valgus, B midfoot/forefoot abduction, C forefoot varus/medial column instability and D peritalar subluxation.

items.q: The commonest site of an osteoma (dense surface lamellar bone tumour) is the:
items.e: Osteomas arise on the skull and facial bones, most often in the frontal (then ethmoid) sinuses, and are usually asymptomatic.

items.q: A 24-year-old has multiple osteomas of the mandible, epidermoid cysts and a desmoid tumour of the abdominal wall. The most important next investigation is:
items.e: This is Gardner syndrome (APC, chromosome 5q): the colonic polyps have near 100% malignant potential, so colonoscopy is essential.

items.q: Gardner syndrome, with multiple osteomas and colonic polyposis, is caused by a mutation in which gene?
items.e: Gardner syndrome is a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis due to APC mutations; EXT1 causes hereditary multiple exostoses and GNAS fibrous dysplasia.

items.q: A 30-year-old has multiple small round sclerotic foci clustered symmetrically around the hips, knees and shoulders, and yellowish skin papules (connective tissue naevi). The diagnosis is:
items.e: Osteopoikilosis (multiple periarticular bone islands, LEMD3 mutation) combined with dermatofibrosis lenticularis is Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome; lesions are asymptomatic.

items.q: A 35-year-old has limb pain and stiffness. Radiographs show flowing cortical hyperostosis along one side of the radius and the bones of one ray of the hand, like candle wax. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Melorheostosis is a sclerotomal sclerosing dysplasia with 'dripping candle wax' hyperostosis, often with soft tissue contracture; it is not neoplastic.

items.q: A dense intramedullary sclerotic lesion with spiculated margins in the ilium measures 3 cm. It is best termed a:
items.e: A bone island over 2 cm is called a giant bone island; it is usually followed with imaging, and biopsy is reserved for atypical growth or behaviour.

items.q: Which scintigraphic finding helps distinguish a bone island from an osteoblastic metastasis?
o: Bone islands are usually cold or only mildly active, whereas osteoblastic metastases are hot
Bone islands show a double-density sign
Bone islands are intensely hot with a photopenic centre
Metastases are always cold on bone scan
items.e: Most enostoses show little or no uptake; marked uptake raises concern for a blastic metastasis, which in prostate or breast cancer is intensely hot.

items.q: Osteoid osteoma shows which sex distribution?
items.e: Osteoid osteoma occurs mainly between 5 and 25 years with a male to female ratio of about 2-3:1.

items.q: The intense pain of an osteoid osteoma is explained by prostaglandin production in the nidus and by:
o: Compression of a peripheral nerve by the reactive bone
Unmyelinated nerve fibres within the nidus
items.e: The nidus contains unmyelinated axons and produces PGE2 via COX-2, explaining night pain and dramatic relief with NSAIDs.

items.q: A 7-year-old has an osteoid osteoma in the proximal tibial metaphysis close to the physis. A recognised consequence of the untreated lesion is:
o: Overgrowth of the limb with leg-length discrepancy
items.e: Hyperaemia from a lesion near the physis can stimulate growth, causing limb overgrowth, as well as muscle wasting.

items.q: A 13-year-old has a painful scoliosis from an osteoid osteoma of the L3 lamina. Why is early removal of the nidus advised?
o: The nidus has a high risk of malignant change
Removal within about 15 months of symptom onset allows the curve to resolve before it becomes structural
The lesion invariably causes cord compression
Delay leads to vertebral body collapse
items.e: The scoliosis is initially non-structural due to muscle spasm; prolonged duration (more than about 15 months) risks a persistent structural curve.

items.q: During CT-guided radiofrequency ablation of an osteoid osteoma, the nidus is typically heated to about:
items.e: RFA heats the nidus to about 90 degrees C for 4-6 minutes, producing a small sphere of necrosis; primary success is about 90%.

items.q: A 19-year-old has a well-documented osteoid osteoma of the tibial diaphysis; pain is fully controlled by ibuprofen, which he tolerates, and he declines intervention. Which statement about non-operative care is correct?
o: Many lesions burn out within 2-4 years, so long-term NSAIDs are an acceptable option
The lesion will progress to osteoblastoma without treatment
NSAIDs are contraindicated because they mask malignant change
Non-operative care causes progressive cortical destruction
items.e: Osteoid osteoma has a self-limiting natural history; NSAIDs over 2-4 years are acceptable if tolerated, though gastrointestinal and renal side effects limit many patients.

items.q: Surgical excision rather than radiofrequency ablation is preferred for an osteoid osteoma that lies:
o: Within about 1 cm of the skin surface or a nerve root
items.e: Thermal spread risks skin burns and neural injury when the nidus is very close to skin or nerves; surgery is also used when RFA fails or tissue is needed.

items.q: Quantitative MRI perfusion work by Hettrich and colleagues (2010) showed that most of the blood supply to the humeral head comes from the:
items.e: About two-thirds of head perfusion came from the posterior humeral circumflex artery, which helps explain why many displaced fractures keep a viable head; the anterior circumflex was classically regarded as dominant.

items.q: The arcuate artery of Laing, classically described as an important supply of the humeral head, enters the head:
o: At the upper end of the bicipital groove, as the ascending branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery
Through the posteromedial calcar, as a branch of the posterior humeral circumflex artery
Through the rotator interval, as a branch of the suprascapular artery
At the greater tuberosity, as a branch of the thoracodorsal artery
items.e: The anterolateral ascending branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery runs up the lateral side of the bicipital groove and enters the head as the arcuate artery.

items.q: In a displaced greater tuberosity fracture of the proximal humerus, the fragment is typically pulled:
items.e: The supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tuberosity and displace it superiorly and posteriorly.

items.q: In a displaced lesser tuberosity fracture, the fragment is pulled medially by the:
items.e: Subscapularis inserts on the lesser tuberosity and draws the fragment medially.

items.q: In a two-part surgical neck fracture of the humerus, the shaft is usually displaced anteriorly and medially by the pull of the:
items.e: Pectoralis major inserts on the lateral lip of the bicipital groove and pulls the shaft anteromedially.

items.q: During a deltoid-splitting approach to the proximal humerus, the axillary nerve is at risk at approximately what distance below the lateral edge of the acromion?
items.e: The axillary nerve runs transversely on the deep surface of the deltoid about 5-7 cm below the acromion; the split must not extend beyond this without identifying the nerve.

items.q: A 32-year-old volleyball player has an isolated greater tuberosity fracture displaced 7 mm superiorly. The best management is:
o: Open or arthroscopic reduction and fixation
items.e: In young or overhead-active patients, greater tuberosity displacement of over about 5 mm (especially superior) causes subacromial impingement and cuff dysfunction, so fixation is advised.

items.q: The commonest two-part fracture pattern of the proximal humerus in the Neer classification is a fracture of the:
items.e: Displaced surgical neck fractures are the commonest two-part pattern; isolated anatomical neck fractures are rare.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of all proximal humerus fractures are minimally displaced (Neer one-part)?
items.e: Around 80% of proximal humerus fractures do not meet Neer's displacement criteria and are treated non-operatively.

items.q: A valgus-impacted four-part fracture of the proximal humerus has a better prognosis than a classic four-part fracture mainly because:
o: The head always remains dislocated, protecting its blood supply
The medial periosteal hinge is preserved, reducing the risk of avascular necrosis
The rotator cuff is always torn, reducing deforming forces
items.e: In valgus impaction the head is tilted up but the posteromedial periosteum and its vessels stay attached, so AVN is less frequent.

items.q: The ProFHER randomised trial in adults with displaced proximal humerus fractures involving the surgical neck found that, compared with non-operative treatment, surgery:
o: Gave significantly better Oxford Shoulder Scores at 2 years
Gave no significant benefit in patient-reported shoulder function at 2 years
items.e: ProFHER showed no meaningful difference in Oxford Shoulder Score at 2 and 5 years between surgery and sling treatment.

items.q: The commonest complication after locking plate fixation of proximal humerus fractures is:
o: Screw cut-out or intra-articular screw penetration
items.e: Primary or secondary screw penetration of the humeral head, often with varus collapse, is the most frequent complication.

items.q: When a fibular strut allograft is placed in the medullary canal during locking plate fixation of an osteoporotic proximal humerus fracture, its main purpose is to:
o: Allow the plate to be placed more proximally
Provide medial column support and reduce varus collapse
Eliminate the need for tuberosity sutures
items.e: The intramedullary strut buttresses the medial calcar, increases screw purchase and lowers varus collapse and screw cut-out.

items.q: During locking plate fixation of a three-part proximal humerus fracture, heavy sutures are passed through the rotator cuff tendons near their insertions and tied to the plate mainly to:
o: Repair a coexisting full-thickness cuff tear
Increase blood flow to the humeral head
Neutralise the deforming pull of the cuff on the tuberosities
items.e: Tension-band sutures through the supraspinatus, infraspinatus and subscapularis insertions hold the tuberosities reduced against the cuff's pull.

items.q: Compared with curved nails, straight antegrade intramedullary nails for two-part surgical neck fractures reduce postoperative shoulder pain because they:
o: Are inserted through the deltopectoral interval
Do not require proximal locking screws
Enter through the greater tuberosity lateral to the cuff
Enter at the apex of the head through muscle rather than the hypovascular cuff tendon
items.e: The entry point of a straight nail is at the top of the head, medial to the critical zone of the supraspinatus tendon, so the tendon is less damaged.

items.q: In an elderly patient with a four-part proximal humerus fracture, the main functional advantage of reverse shoulder arthroplasty over hemiarthroplasty is that its outcome:
o: Does not depend on healing of the tuberosities
Gives full return of external rotation in all cases
items.e: Reverse arthroplasty relies on the deltoid rather than the cuff, so function is more predictable; tuberosity healing improves rotation but is not essential.

items.q: In hemiarthroplasty for a proximal humerus fracture, the single most important determinant of a good functional outcome is:
o: Healing of the tuberosities in the correct position
items.e: Tuberosity malposition or non-union leaves the cuff non-functional and causes poor elevation; height and version must be restored.

items.q: When performing hemiarthroplasty for a four-part fracture, the top of the prosthetic head should be positioned approximately:
o: Level with the top of the greater tuberosity
20 mm above the top of the greater tuberosity
5-8 mm above the top of the greater tuberosity
5 mm below the top of the greater tuberosity
items.e: A head-to-tuberosity distance of about 5-8 mm restores the cuff's lever arm; a low head or high tuberosity causes impingement and weakness.

items.q: In fracture hemiarthroplasty of the shoulder, the humeral component is usually placed in approximately how much retroversion?
items.e: About 20-30 degrees of retroversion relative to the forearm axis approximates normal anatomy; excess retroversion stresses the greater tuberosity repair.

items.q: The deltopectoral approach to the proximal humerus is an internervous plane between muscles supplied by the:
o: Axillary nerve and the medial and lateral pectoral nerves
items.e: The deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve and the pectoralis major by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves.

items.q: In the deltopectoral approach, the cephalic vein is usually:
o: Retracted medially with the pectoralis major in all cases
items.e: Most surgeons take the vein laterally with the deltoid because most of its tributaries come from the deltoid; it marks the interval.

items.q: A 62-year-old cannot actively elevate her arm 3 weeks after reduction of a first anterior shoulder dislocation; deltoid sensation and EMG of the deltoid are normal. The most likely diagnosis and investigation are:
o: Axillary nerve palsy; repeat EMG in 6 months
Rotator cuff tear; ultrasound or MRI
items.e: After age 40 a traumatic dislocation often tears the rotator cuff; weakness after reduction with an intact axillary nerve calls for cuff imaging.

items.q: The strongest predictor of recurrence after a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation is:
o: Duration of immobilisation in a sling
Presence of a greater tuberosity fracture
Young age at the first dislocation
items.e: Recurrence is inversely related to age, approaching 90% in teenagers; a greater tuberosity fracture actually lowers recurrence.

items.q: The Hill-Sachs lesion of anterior shoulder dislocation is an impaction defect of the humeral head located:
items.e: The posterolateral head impacts on the anteroinferior glenoid rim when the head dislocates anteriorly. An anteromedial defect is a reverse Hill-Sachs lesion of posterior dislocation.

items.q: The Bankart lesion in traumatic anterior shoulder instability is an avulsion of the:
o: Anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament complex from the glenoid
Glenohumeral ligaments from the humeral neck
items.e: The classic Bankart lesion is detachment of the anteroinferior labroligamentous complex; avulsion from the humerus is a HAGL lesion.

items.q: A 58-year-old has an anterior shoulder dislocation with a greater tuberosity fracture. After closed reduction, the tuberosity lies within 3 mm of its bed. The appropriate management is:
items.e: The tuberosity usually reduces with the head; if residual displacement is under about 5 mm it is treated non-operatively. Recurrent instability is uncommon in this pattern.

items.q: An AP radiograph of the shoulder after an electric shock shows the humeral head fixed in internal rotation with a symmetrical, rounded 'lightbulb' appearance. This suggests:
items.e: In posterior dislocation the head is locked in internal rotation and the tuberosities overlap, giving the lightbulb sign.

items.q: The radiographic view most important to avoid missing a posterior shoulder dislocation is the:
items.e: The AP view can look nearly normal in posterior dislocation; the axillary lateral (or a scapular Y or CT) shows the head behind the glenoid.

items.q: A 40-year-old falls from a ladder and presents with his arm held fully abducted above his head, unable to lower it; the humeral head is palpable in the axilla. The diagnosis and a key concern are:
items.e: Inferior dislocation locks the arm in abduction; brachial plexus and axillary artery injuries and cuff tears are common.

items.q: A lateral third clavicle fracture lies medial to the coracoclavicular ligaments, so the medial fragment is no longer held down (Neer type II). The usual treatment in an active adult is:
o: Sling for 3 weeks, because it is stable
Excision of the lateral fragment in all cases
Operative fixation, because non-union rates are high
items.e: Neer type II fractures have a non-union rate of about 30% with non-operative care, so fixation (hook plate, lateral locking plate or CC suspension) is favoured.

items.q: The high non-union rate of Neer type II lateral clavicle fractures is mainly explained by:
o: Loss of coracoclavicular ligament attachment of the medial fragment, which is pulled upward
Poor blood supply of the entire clavicle
Intra-articular extension into the AC joint
items.e: Without its CC ligament restraint, the medial fragment is elevated by the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid while the arm's weight pulls the lateral fragment down.

items.q: A lateral clavicle fracture that extends into the acromioclavicular joint without ligament disruption (Neer type III) is most likely to lead to:
items.e: Neer type III fractures are stable but intra-articular and may cause post-traumatic AC arthritis, treated by distal clavicle excision if symptomatic.

items.q: The Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society (COTS) trial of 2007 in displaced midshaft clavicle fractures found that plate fixation, compared with a sling:
o: Increased non-union because of periosteal stripping
Gave identical outcomes in all measures
Reduced non-union and symptomatic malunion and gave better early function
Was associated with frequent subclavian vessel injury
items.e: Plating lowered non-union and symptomatic malunion and improved early Constant and DASH scores, though later trials found smaller differences.

items.q: Compared with superior plating, anteroinferior plating of a midshaft clavicle fracture has the advantage of:
o: Biomechanically stronger fixation in all loading modes
No need to protect the supraclavicular nerves
Allowing fixation without any soft-tissue dissection
Less hardware prominence, longer screws and drills directed away from the subclavian vessels
items.e: Anteroinferior plates are less prominent and the drill is aimed posteriorly and superiorly, away from the subclavian vessels and plexus.

items.q: A 20-year-old has an apparent posterior sternoclavicular dislocation after a rugby tackle. The injury is likely to be a medial clavicular physeal fracture rather than a true dislocation because the medial clavicular physis:
o: Closes only at about 23-25 years of age
Closes at about 12 years of age
Is the first physis in the body to close
Does not exist, since the clavicle forms by intramembranous ossification only
items.e: The medial clavicular epiphysis is the last to fuse (early to mid-20s), so in young adults 'dislocations' are often physeal separations that remodel well.

items.q: A 35-year-old office worker has a Rockwood type III acromioclavicular joint injury of the non-dominant shoulder. The recommended initial treatment is:
o: Non-operative management with a sling and rehabilitation
items.e: Most type III injuries do well non-operatively; surgery is considered for heavy labourers, overhead athletes or failure of rehabilitation.

items.q: On an axillary radiograph after a fall onto the shoulder, the distal clavicle is displaced posteriorly into the trapezius. The Rockwood type and treatment are:
o: Type IV; operative reduction and stabilisation
items.e: Posterior displacement of the clavicle through the trapezius defines a type IV injury, which is treated surgically.

items.q: A Rockwood type V acromioclavicular injury is characterised by:
o: Clavicle displaced inferior to the coracoid
AC ligaments torn with intact coracoclavicular ligaments
Up to 25% increase in the coracoclavicular distance
A 100-300% increase in the coracoclavicular distance with stripping of the deltotrapezial fascia
items.e: In type V the clavicle is grossly elevated because the deltotrapezial fascia is detached; it is treated operatively.

items.q: The Zanca view for imaging the acromioclavicular joint is taken with the beam tilted:
o: 10-15 degrees cephalad, at about half normal shoulder exposure
items.e: A 10-15 degree cephalic tilt projects the AC joint clear of the scapular spine, and reduced penetration shows the joint clearly.

items.q: The normal coracoclavicular distance on an AP radiograph of the shoulder in an adult is about:
items.e: A normal CC distance is about 11-13 mm; comparison with the opposite side quantifies displacement in AC injuries.

items.q: The Weaver-Dunn procedure for chronic acromioclavicular dislocation involves distal clavicle excision and transfer of the:
o: Coracoid tip with its conjoined tendon to the clavicle
Coracoacromial ligament to the end of the clavicle
Pectoralis minor tendon to the acromion
items.e: The coracoacromial ligament is detached from the acromion and transferred into the resected end of the clavicle; it is now often augmented or replaced by anatomical graft reconstruction.

items.q: In a patient with a scapular body fracture after a motorcycle crash, the most frequently associated injury is:
items.e: Scapular fractures signal high-energy trauma; associated injuries occur in about 80-90%, most commonly rib fractures with pneumothorax or pulmonary contusion.

items.q: Operative fixation of a displaced extra-articular scapular body or neck fracture is generally considered when the glenopolar angle falls below about:
items.e: The normal glenopolar angle is about 30-45 degrees; values under about 20-22 degrees indicate significant glenoid malalignment and are a relative indication for surgery.

items.q: Displaced intra-articular glenoid fossa fractures are usually fixed when the articular step-off exceeds about:
items.e: Step-off over about 4-5 mm or humeral head subluxation are the usual indications for ORIF of glenoid fossa fractures.

items.q: An anterior glenoid rim fracture after a dislocation is best treated by fixation when the fragment involves more than about what proportion of the glenoid articular surface?
items.e: Rim fragments over about 20-25% of the glenoid (or with persistent subluxation) cause instability and should be fixed.

items.q: Which structure forms part of Goss's superior shoulder suspensory complex?
items.e: The SSSC is a ring of the glenoid, coracoid, CC ligaments, distal clavicle, AC joint and acromion; double disruption makes the shoulder unstable.

items.q: After a motorcycle crash, a 24-year-old has a pulseless flail upper limb. The chest radiograph shows the scapula displaced laterally compared with the other side. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Scapulothoracic dissociation is a closed forequarter amputation with lateral scapular displacement, usually with subclavian or axillary artery injury and brachial plexus avulsion.

items.q: A 32-year-old neurologically intact man has an L1 burst fracture after a fall. MRI shows equivocal signal in the interspinous ligament without clear disruption. What is his TLICS score and the implied management?
items.e: Burst morphology scores 2, intact neurology 0 and suspected/indeterminate PLC injury 2, giving 4, the grey zone where either approach is acceptable. A score of 5 or more favours surgery.

items.q: A restrained rear-seat passenger has an L2 flexion-distraction injury through the disc and posterior ligaments, with a clearly disrupted PLC on MRI and normal neurology. The TLICS score is:
items.e: Distraction morphology scores 4, PLC injured 3 and intact neurology 0, totalling 7, well above the surgical threshold.

items.q: In TLICS, how many points are given for a neurological status of cauda equina syndrome?
items.e: Incomplete cord/conus injury and cauda equina injury each score 3, because they have the greatest potential to benefit from decompression; nerve root and complete cord injuries score 2.

items.q: In TLICS, a thoracolumbar injury with an isolated nerve root deficit receives how many neurological points?
items.e: Nerve root injury scores 2, the same as a complete cord or conus injury; intact neurology scores 0.

items.q: In the TLICS morphology component, a fracture showing translation or rotation of one vertebra on another on CT scores:
items.e: Morphology scores are compression 1, burst 2, translation/rotation 3 and distraction 4.

items.q: In Denis's three-column model, which structures form the middle column?
o: Anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior two-thirds of the body
Posterior third of the vertebral body and disc with the posterior longitudinal ligament
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments with the ligamentum flavum
items.e: The middle column is the posterior third of the body and annulus plus the PLL. Denis regarded failure of the middle column (with one other) as the key to instability.

items.q: Why is the thoracolumbar junction (T11-L2) the most frequent site of spinal fractures?
o: It is a transition from the rigid rib-supported thoracic spine with coronal facets to the mobile lumbar spine with sagittal facets
The vertebral bodies here are the smallest in the spine
The spinal canal is widest here
The paraspinal muscles are absent at this level
items.e: Stress concentrates where a stiff kyphotic segment meets a mobile lordotic segment, with the facet orientation changing from coronal to sagittal.

items.q: During a left-sided anterior approach for T12 corpectomy, the surgeon avoids ligating multiple segmental arteries because the great anterior radiculomedullary artery (of Adamkiewicz) usually arises:
o: On the right between C5 and T1
On the left between L3 and L5
On the left between T9 and L2
items.e: The artery of Adamkiewicz arises on the left in about 75% of people, usually between T9 and L2, and supplies the anterior spinal artery to the lower cord.

items.q: Thoracic spine fractures cause complete cord injury more often than lumbar fractures. Which pair of factors explains this?
o: A wide canal and abundant segmental supply
Presence of the cauda equina at thoracic levels
Absence of the dentate ligaments in the thoracic spine
A narrow thoracic canal and a tenuous watershed blood supply at T4-T9
items.e: The cord fills the small thoracic canal leaving little space for displacement, and the mid-thoracic cord has a vascular watershed. Below L1-L2, injury affects the more resilient cauda equina.

items.q: In the AO Spine thoracolumbar classification, a fracture of only one endplate without involvement of the posterior vertebral wall is classified as:
items.e: A1 is a wedge or impaction fracture of a single endplate with an intact posterior wall; A3 adds posterior wall involvement.

items.q: CT shows a coronal fracture line running through the vertebral body and involving both endplates, but the posterior vertebral wall is intact. The AO Spine type is:
items.e: A2 split or pincer fractures involve both endplates without posterior wall involvement; disc may herniate into the gap, increasing non-union risk.

items.q: An L1 fracture involves the superior endplate and the posterior vertebral wall with retropulsion, while the inferior endplate is intact and the PLC is undamaged. The AO Spine type is:
items.e: A3 is a burst fracture of a single endplate plus the posterior wall; A4 involves both endplates and the posterior wall. PLC injury would make it type B.

items.q: A fracture involving both endplates and the posterior vertebral wall, with an intact posterior tension band, is AO Spine type:
items.e: A4 complete burst fractures involve both endplates and the posterior wall. If the posterior tension band were disrupted it would be classified as B.

items.q: A horizontal fracture line passes through the spinous process, laminae, pedicles and vertebral body of L2 with no ligamentous injury. In the AO Spine system this is:
o: B2: ligamentous posterior tension band disruption
B1: transosseous posterior tension band disruption (bony Chance)
items.e: B1 is a monosegmental purely osseous failure of the posterior tension band, the classic bony Chance fracture, which can heal non-operatively if reduced and the patient is intact.

items.q: An L1 incomplete burst fracture is associated with interspinous widening and MRI evidence of ruptured supraspinous ligament and facet capsules. The AO Spine classification is:
o: B2 (posterior ligamentous tension band disruption with an A-type body fracture)
items.e: B2 denotes posterior tension band disruption through ligaments or capsule combined with any type A body injury. M1 is used only when PLC injury is indeterminate.

items.q: A 70-year-old with ankylosing spondylitis falls backwards and sustains a fracture through the T11 disc space that opens anteriorly. In AO Spine terms this is:
items.e: B3 is a hyperextension injury disrupting the anterior tension band, typical of ankylosed spines (AS, DISH), and is highly unstable.

items.q: In the AO Spine thoracolumbar classification, the case-specific modifier M1 is used to indicate:
o: A fracture with indeterminate injury of the posterior tension band on imaging or examination
items.e: M1 flags indeterminate PLC injury, which may tip treatment toward surgery. M2 denotes a patient-specific comorbidity such as ankylosing spondylitis, osteoporosis or burns over the surgical site.

items.q: A neurologically intact patient with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis sustains an A3 thoracolumbar fracture. The AO Spine modifier for the comorbidity that may influence treatment is:
items.e: M2 denotes a patient-specific comorbidity (ankylosing disorders, osteoporosis, skin compromise) that could affect the treatment decision.

items.q: After an L1 fracture, a patient had leg numbness and weakness at the scene that fully resolved by arrival in the emergency department. In the AO Spine neurology grading this is:
o: N3: incomplete cord or cauda equina injury
items.e: N1 indicates a transient deficit that has resolved; it suggests potential instability and should be considered in decision-making.

items.q: An isolated fracture of the L3 transverse process in the AO Spine thoracolumbar classification is:
items.e: A0 covers transverse or spinous process fractures that do not compromise mechanical integrity; they are managed symptomatically, though associated renal or visceral injuries should be sought.

items.q: On the lateral radiograph of a thoracolumbar fracture, which finding most suggests disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex?
o: Loss of 15% of anterior vertebral height
Increased interspinous distance with splaying of spinous processes
Schmorl node at the adjacent endplate
items.e: Widened interspinous spacing, facet diastasis or perched facets indicate posterior tension band failure; mild anterior wedging alone does not.

items.q: On MRI of a thoracolumbar fracture, which finding is most specific for disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex?
o: Bone marrow oedema in the vertebral body on STIR
Discontinuity of the low-signal black stripe of the supraspinous ligament/ligamentum flavum
Disc desiccation at the adjacent level
items.e: Interspinous STIR hyperintensity is sensitive but less specific; a visible break in the continuous low-signal stripe of the supraspinous ligament or ligamentum flavum is more specific for PLC rupture.

items.q: On an AP radiograph after a fall from height, which sign distinguishes an L1 burst fracture from a simple wedge compression fracture?
items.e: Interpedicular widening reflects posterior body and middle column failure with lateral spread of the fragments, typical of burst fractures.

items.q: In the randomised trial by Wood et al. comparing operative (posterior or anterior fusion) and non-operative treatment for neurologically intact stable thoracolumbar burst fractures, the long-term finding was:
o: Operative patients had significantly less pain and better function
Non-operative patients developed late neurological deficits
Operative treatment reduced kyphosis and improved outcome scores
Non-operative patients had similar or better pain and function, with fewer complications
items.e: Wood's RCT showed no advantage for surgery; non-operative patients reported equal or better pain and function scores at long-term follow-up, supporting conservative care for intact burst fractures with an intact PLC.

items.q: In the randomised trial by Bailey and colleagues (2014) of neurologically intact AO A3 thoracolumbar burst fractures treated with a TLSO brace or no brace, the result was:
o: Significantly worse kyphosis without a brace
Higher rate of conversion to surgery without a brace
Better outcomes without a brace but more neurological deficits
Equivalent functional outcomes and kyphosis without a brace
items.e: Early mobilisation without a brace was equivalent to TLSO bracing for function and kyphosis, so bracing is optional in these fractures.

items.q: A neurologically intact patient with an L2 burst fracture and intact PLC has 45% canal compromise from a retropulsed fragment. Regarding the canal fragment, the correct statement is:
o: The fragment will migrate and cause late paraplegia unless removed
Retropulsed fragments tend to resorb and the canal remodels with non-operative care
Ligamentotaxis is required to prevent late stenosis
items.e: In intact patients, canal compromise alone is not an indication for surgery; follow-up CT shows progressive remodelling and resorption of retropulsed fragments.

items.q: Indirect reduction of a retropulsed burst fragment by distraction through pedicle screws (ligamentotaxis) is most likely to succeed when:
o: The PLL is ruptured and the fragment is inverted
The posterior longitudinal ligament is intact and surgery is done within a few days of injury
The posterior wall fragment is rotated 180 degrees
items.e: Ligamentotaxis relies on an intact PLL and annulus to pull the fragment back, and is effective early (within about 4 days); a ruptured PLL or reversed fragment needs direct decompression.

items.q: The McCormack load-sharing classification for thoracolumbar burst fractures awards points for which three features?
o: Comminution of the body, apposition (displacement) of fragments, and kyphosis correction required
Canal compromise, neurology and PLC status
Age, bone density and level of injury
Interpedicular distance, laminar fracture and facet subluxation
items.e: Each factor scores 1-3 (total 3-9). A score of 7 or more predicts failure of short-segment posterior fixation alone and indicates anterior column reconstruction.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a highly comminuted L1 burst fracture with widely displaced fragments requiring 12 degrees of kyphosis correction. Load-sharing score is 8. Short-segment posterior fixation alone carries a high risk of:
o: Implant failure and loss of correction; anterior column reconstruction should be added
Pseudarthrosis of the facet joints with excellent sagittal alignment
items.e: Load-sharing scores of 7 or more indicate a body that cannot share load; anterior corpectomy and reconstruction (or long-segment fixation) is recommended to avoid screw breakage and recurrent kyphosis.

items.q: Why does a lap belt worn without a shoulder strap produce a flexion-distraction (Chance) injury rather than a burst fracture?
o: The axis passes through the posterior elements, causing anterior compression
Axial load passes vertically through the vertebral body
Rotational force is applied across the facets
The axis of flexion moves anterior to the vertebral body, so all three columns fail in tension
items.e: With the lap belt acting as a fulcrum on the anterior abdominal wall, the whole spine lies posterior to the axis and fails in tension from posterior to anterior.

items.q: A 9-year-old restrained by a lap belt has an L2 Chance fracture and a transverse abdominal wall bruise. The most important associated investigation is:
o: Bone scan of the whole skeleton
Contrast CT of the abdomen and surgical review for hollow viscus injury
items.e: Intra-abdominal injuries (bowel perforation, mesenteric tears) accompany about 40-50% of Chance fractures, especially with a seat-belt sign; they may be missed initially.

items.q: A neurologically intact 20-year-old has a purely osseous Chance fracture of L1 that reduces in extension. The most appropriate management is:
o: Hyperextension cast or TLSO with close radiographic follow-up
Bed rest without immobilisation for 12 weeks
items.e: A bony Chance fracture (AO B1) heals reliably bone to bone in an extension orthosis if reduced and the patient is intact; ligamentous injuries do not heal and need fusion.

items.q: A flexion-distraction injury at L1-L2 passes through the interspinous ligament, facet capsules and disc, with no fracture. The recommended treatment is:
items.e: Ligamentous and disc injuries heal poorly and leave instability, so posterior instrumentation in compression with fusion is advised.

items.q: Which thoracolumbar injury pattern carries the highest rate of neurological injury, frequently complete?
items.e: Translation or rotation of one segment on another narrows the canal acutely and is associated with the highest rate of (often complete) cord injury; all require posterior instrumentation.

items.q: An elderly man with ankylosing spondylitis and a fixed thoracic kyphosis falls and has back pain. A thoracolumbar fracture is confirmed. How should he be immobilised before surgery?
o: Flat supine on a hard board to restore lordosis
In a rigid cervical collar with the neck extended
Prone with traction to correct the kyphosis
In his pre-injury kyphotic posture, supported with pillows, not flattened supine
items.e: Forcing a fused kyphotic spine into neutral can displace the fracture and injure the cord; immobilisation in the pre-injury position is recommended.

items.q: Twelve hours after admission with a minimally displaced T10 fracture through an ankylosed spine, a patient develops progressive paraparesis. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Fractures in ankylosed spines bleed from cancellous bone and epidural veins; epidural haematoma with delayed neurological deterioration is a recognised complication needing urgent MRI and decompression.

items.q: For an unstable thoracolumbar fracture through an ankylosed spine (AS or DISH), the usual surgical fixation strategy is:
o: Short-segment fixation one level above and below
Long posterior instrumentation spanning at least 2-3 levels above and below the fracture
items.e: The long lever arms of the fused spine create large forces at the fracture, so multiple fixation points above and below are needed; osteoporotic bone adds to the need.

items.q: A man with ankylosing spondylitis has neck and back pain after a minor fall; a thoracic fracture is seen on radiographs. What imaging is mandatory before treatment?
o: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine only
CT (with or without MRI) of the whole spine to exclude non-contiguous fractures
items.e: Fractures in ankylosed spines are easily missed on radiographs and frequently non-contiguous, so whole-spine CT, often with MRI for occult injury and haematoma, is recommended.

items.q: A 24-year-old who jumped from the fourth floor has saddle anaesthesia and bilateral vertical sacral fractures joined by a transverse fracture at S2 (U-shaped pattern). The recommended fixation is:
o: Lumbopelvic (triangular) fixation with or without sacral decompression
Single iliosacral screw on one side
Pelvic binder and bed rest for 12 weeks
items.e: Spinopelvic dissociation separates the spine and central sacrum from the pelvis; lumbopelvic fixation (pedicle screws in L4/L5 connected to iliac screws) with decompression of sacral roots is the standard.

items.q: The Roy-Camille classification (later modified by Strange-Vognsen) is used to describe:
o: Transverse fractures of the upper sacrum
items.e: Roy-Camille types 1-3 (with type 4 added later) describe kyphotic angulation and displacement of transverse upper sacral fractures, often in spinopelvic dissociation.

items.q: A 30-year-old with a T12 fracture-dislocation and incomplete cord injury is admitted to the ICU. Haemodynamic guidelines recommend maintaining mean arterial pressure at approximately:
items.e: Augmenting MAP to 85-90 mmHg for about a week after acute spinal cord injury is recommended to improve cord perfusion; steroids are not routinely given.

items.q: A patient with an L1 burst fracture has early urinary retention, saddle anaesthesia, absent bulbocavernosus reflex and brisk knee reflexes with some leg weakness. The lesion is best described as:
items.e: Injury at T12-L1 affecting the conus gives mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs with early sphincter loss; cauda equina lesions produce a purely lower motor neuron pattern and have a better recovery.

items.q: A civilian gunshot wound causes an incomplete cauda equina injury with the bullet lodged in the canal at L3. Which statement is correct?
o: Bullet removal from the canal at T12-L5 may improve motor recovery, and steroids should be avoided
Immediate laminectomy at the entry level improves cord recovery in complete injuries
items.e: Removal of bullets within the canal at T12-L5 has shown possible motor benefit in cauda equina injuries; steroids increase complications and are contraindicated in penetrating spinal injury.

items.q: A gunshot passes through the colon before lodging in the L2 vertebral body without neurological deficit. The key management is:
o: Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering bowel flora
Immediate bullet removal through an anterior approach
No antibiotics, as the bullet is sterilised by heat
items.e: Transcolonic spinal gunshot wounds carry a significant infection risk; broad-spectrum antibiotics (for 7-14 days in many protocols) are given, while routine debridement or bullet removal is debated.

items.q: A 15-year-old weightlifter has acute low back pain and L5 radiculopathy. CT shows a small bony fragment displaced posteriorly from the posteroinferior rim of L4 into the canal. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Ring apophysis fractures occur in adolescents, behave like disc herniations, and may need excision of the bony fragment if symptoms persist.

items.q: A 6-year-old sustains a complete thoracic spinal cord injury. Which late spinal deformity is almost inevitable if injury occurs before the adolescent growth spurt?
items.e: Paralytic deformity develops in nearly all children injured before puberty; bracing may delay it but many need fusion later.

items.q: Five years after a T8 fracture with incomplete paraplegia, a patient notices ascending numbness, new hand weakness and loss of pain sensation in the arms. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: A post-traumatic syrinx presents with late, ascending neurological deterioration and dissociated sensory loss; MRI confirms it.

items.q: A patient with painful post-traumatic thoracolumbar kyphosis needs about 35 degrees of sagittal correction at a single level. Which osteotomy provides this amount?
items.e: A pedicle subtraction osteotomy achieves about 30-40 degrees through a closing wedge of all three columns; a Smith-Petersen osteotomy gives about 10 degrees per level.

items.q: Several weeks after a minor fall, a 72-year-old woman develops increasing back pain. Radiographs show collapse of T12 with a horizontal intravertebral gas collection. This is:
o: Kummell disease (vertebral osteonecrosis with intravertebral vacuum cleft)
items.e: Kummell disease is delayed post-traumatic collapse due to avascular necrosis, marked by an intravertebral vacuum cleft that may fill with fluid on MRI.

items.q: The randomised sham-controlled trials by Buchbinder and Kallmes (2009) on vertebroplasty for painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures found that:
o: Vertebroplasty gave no significant benefit over a sham procedure
Vertebroplasty was inferior to sham, with more fractures
Vertebroplasty reduced pain only in fractures over 1 year old
items.e: Both 2009 NEJM trials showed pain improvement in both arms with no difference from sham; later trials such as VERTOS II and IV gave conflicting results.

items.q: A 4-month-old has multiple thoracolumbar compression fractures of different ages without a history of trauma, with normal bone density and biochemistry. The first concern is:
items.e: Multiple vertebral compression fractures in an infant without plausible trauma warrant a skeletal survey and safeguarding assessment; normal density and biochemistry argue against metabolic bone disease.

items.q: In adults, the dominant blood supply to the weight-bearing femoral head comes from the:
o: Inferior metaphyseal branches of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
Lateral epiphyseal (posterosuperior retinacular) branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery
Nutrient artery of the femoral shaft
items.e: The deep branch of the MFCA gives the posterosuperior retinacular (lateral epiphyseal) arteries, the main supply; the ligamentum teres artery contributes little.

items.q: During surgical hip dislocation (Ganz), the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery is protected because it runs posterior to which muscle, which is left intact?
