items.e: The deep branch of the MFCA passes posterior to obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators; preserving obturator externus protects it during the trochanteric flip approach.

items.q: After a traumatic posterior hip dislocation in a young adult, the risk of femoral head osteonecrosis rises significantly when reduction is delayed beyond about:
items.e: Urgent reduction is advised because AVN risk increases markedly when reduction is delayed beyond about 6 hours.

items.q: After corticosteroids, the second commonest cause of non-traumatic femoral head osteonecrosis is:
items.e: Steroids are the commonest and alcohol (dose-dependent) the second commonest non-traumatic cause.

items.q: Under the ARCO 2019 criteria, to classify femoral head osteonecrosis as glucocorticoid-associated, it must be diagnosed within what period after the qualifying steroid exposure?
items.e: ARCO requires over 2 g prednisolone equivalent within 3 months and diagnosis within 2 years of use, with other risk factors excluded.

items.q: Under the ARCO 2019 criteria for alcohol-associated osteonecrosis, the high intake (over 400 mL pure ethanol per week) must have lasted for more than:
items.e: Alcohol-associated ONFH requires over 400 mL pure ethanol per week for more than 6 months, with ONFH diagnosed within 1 year of this intake.

items.q: After complete interruption of blood supply, osteocytes in the femoral head die within approximately:
items.e: Osteocytes die within about 12-48 hours of ischaemia, but radiographs stay normal for weeks to months until repair changes appear.

items.q: In femoral head osteonecrosis, subchondral collapse occurs mainly:
o: At the moment of cell death, from immediate loss of mechanical strength
During the repair phase, when resorption at the dead-living bone junction weakens the subchondral plate
items.e: Dead bone retains its mechanical strength initially; creeping substitution resorbs bone at the reactive interface, leading to subchondral fracture and collapse.

items.q: 'Creeping substitution' in osteonecrosis refers to:
o: Fibrous tissue replacing the entire head
New bone laid down on dead trabeculae followed by resorption of the dead bone
items.e: Repair proceeds from the living margin: new bone is laid on necrotic trabeculae and the dead bone is gradually resorbed.

items.q: In non-traumatic femoral head osteonecrosis, the contralateral hip is involved in approximately:
items.e: Non-traumatic ONFH is bilateral in about 50-80%, so MRI of the other hip is recommended at presentation.

items.q: A patient with known femoral head osteonecrosis develops a sudden increase in hip pain, and MRI now shows extensive bone marrow oedema around the lesion. This oedema most likely indicates:
items.e: Marrow oedema accompanying a known lesion correlates with pain and suggests recent or impending collapse.

items.q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for detecting a subchondral fracture and early collapse in femoral head osteonecrosis when radiographs are equivocal?
items.e: CT best shows the subchondral fracture and early collapse and is more sensitive than radiographs for this; MRI is best for early pre-radiographic necrosis.

items.q: Multifocal osteonecrosis is defined as involvement of at least how many separate anatomical sites?
items.e: Multifocal osteonecrosis (3 or more sites) affects about 3% of patients and is almost always related to steroids or coagulopathy.

items.q: Compared with the earlier ARCO system, the ARCO 2019 revised staging of femoral head osteonecrosis:
o: Added a stage 0 for preclinical disease
Defines stage IV as an MRI-only lesion
items.e: ARCO 2019 removed stage 0 and moved size and location assessment out of the staging; stage I is now MRI-positive with normal radiographs.

items.q: In ARCO 2019 staging, a femoral head with a subchondral fracture and 1.5 mm of head depression is stage:
items.e: Stage IIIA (early) is subchondral fracture or collapse of 2 mm or less; over 2 mm is IIIB.

items.q: A patient with hip pain has normal radiographs but a band-like lesion on MRI of the femoral head. In ARCO 2019 staging this is stage:
items.e: ARCO stage I: radiograph normal, MRI positive. Stage II has radiographic changes (sclerosis, osteolysis) without collapse.

items.q: In the modified Ficat-Arlet classification, joint-space narrowing with acetabular changes indicates stage:
items.e: Ficat IV is secondary osteoarthritis with joint-space narrowing and acetabular involvement; stage III has the crescent sign and collapse.

items.q: In the Japanese Investigation Committee (JIC) classification, which type carries the highest risk of femoral head collapse?
o: Type C2, extending lateral to the acetabular edge
Type A, confined to the medial third
Type B, within the medial two-thirds
Type C1, within the acetabular edge
items.e: JIC C2 lesions extend beyond the acetabular edge laterally and have the highest collapse risk; type A lesions rarely collapse.

items.q: An asymptomatic contralateral femoral head lesion is found on MRI. The modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle is 150 degrees and the lesion is medial. The most appropriate management is:
o: Observation with serial MRI and risk-factor modification
items.e: Small, medial lesions with a combined necrotic angle under 190 degrees have a low collapse risk and can be observed.

items.q: During core decompression of the femoral head, the drill or trephine should be advanced to stop approximately:
o: Through the articular surface into the joint
3-5 mm short of the subchondral plate
items.e: The track should reach the necrotic lesion to within about 3-5 mm of the subchondral plate without breaching the articular surface.

items.q: The main advantage of multiple small-diameter (about 3 mm) percutaneous drillings over a single 8-10 mm trephine core for femoral head osteonecrosis is:
o: Complete removal of all necrotic bone
Ability to insert a vascularised graft
items.e: Multiple small drillings (Mont) decompress the head with less weakening of the lateral cortex, reducing the risk of fracture.

items.q: Porous tantalum rods inserted after core decompression for femoral head osteonecrosis are now largely abandoned because of:
o: High failure rates and difficulty at later conversion to THA
Inability to be seen on radiographs
Excessive cost alone despite excellent results
items.e: Tantalum rod series showed high failure (progression to collapse) and made subsequent arthroplasty more difficult.

items.q: Core decompression of the femoral head gives its poorest results when:
o: The lesion is small and medial
A crescent sign (subchondral fracture) is already present
The radiograph is normal and MRI positive
The patient is symptomatic but pre-collapse
items.e: Core decompression is a pre-collapse procedure; results are poor once collapse has begun (crescent sign, Ficat III).

items.q: Regarding protected weight bearing alone (crutches) in symptomatic femoral head osteonecrosis:
o: It reliably prevents collapse in large lesions
It is the treatment of choice for ARCO IIIB disease
It does not alter the natural history of the disease
It reverses MRI changes within 6 weeks
items.e: Protected weight bearing alone has not been shown to change the natural history; most untreated symptomatic lesions progress.

items.q: A recognised donor-site complication of free vascularised fibular grafting for femoral head osteonecrosis is:
o: Foot drop from tibial nerve injury
items.e: Harvesting the fibula can cause ankle pain, weakness of great toe flexion (flexor hallucis longus) and peroneal nerve symptoms.

items.q: Meyers' muscle-pedicle bone graft for femoral head osteonecrosis uses which muscle, through a posterior approach?
items.e: Meyers described a quadratus femoris muscle-pedicle graft inserted posteriorly into the debrided femoral head.

items.q: In the 'lightbulb' procedure for femoral head osteonecrosis, the necrotic bone is removed and grafted through a window made in the:
o: Lateral femoral cortex below the lesser trochanter
items.e: The lightbulb technique uses a cortical window at the head-neck junction; the trapdoor technique enters through the articular cartilage.

items.q: The Phemister procedure for femoral head osteonecrosis involves:
o: A rotational osteotomy of the femoral neck
Inserting a cortical bone strut graft through a core decompression track
items.e: Phemister grafting places a non-vascularised cortical strut through the core track to support the subchondral bone.

items.q: Sugioka's transtrochanteric anterior rotational osteotomy requires which condition to succeed?
o: Involvement of the entire femoral head
An intact posterior head providing healthy bone for over a third of the weight-bearing area after rotation
items.e: Rotation brings intact posterior head under load; adequate healthy posterior bone (over a third of the weight-bearing surface) is essential.

items.q: Intertrochanteric varus or valgus flexion osteotomy for femoral head osteonecrosis is most suitable for lesions with a combined necrotic angle under about:
items.e: Angular osteotomies can move the lesion out of the loaded zone only when it is limited, typically a combined necrotic angle under about 200 degrees.

items.q: A 45-year-old man has severe hip pain from femoral head osteonecrosis with 4 mm collapse and early acetabular changes. The treatment of choice is:
items.e: Symptomatic collapse over 2 mm (ARCO IIIB) or arthritis (IV) is best treated by THA; modern cementless THA results are close to those for OA.

items.q: Bipolar hemiarthroplasty is not routinely recommended for femoral head osteonecrosis mainly because of:
o: Persistent groin pain and acetabular cartilage erosion
items.e: The acetabular cartilage is often already abnormal; hemiarthroplasty leads to groin pain and acetabular erosion, so THA is preferred.

items.q: During THA for osteonecrosis in sickle cell disease, a specific intraoperative technical hazard is:
o: Soft osteopenic bone that cannot hold cementless implants
Pathological tumour tissue in the femoral canal
Femoral perforation or fracture from sclerotic, obliterated medullary canal
items.e: Bone infarcts make the canal sclerotic and partly obliterated, so reaming and broaching risk perforation and fracture; infection and sickling crises are other risks.

items.q: Before THA in a patient with homozygous sickle cell disease, the recommended preoperative measure to reduce sickling complications is:
o: Transfusion to raise haemoglobin (and lower HbS proportion), with hydration and oxygenation
items.e: Preoperative transfusion, hydration, warmth and oxygenation reduce the risk of sickling crises, acute chest syndrome and other perioperative complications.

items.q: Iloprost has been used in early osteonecrosis and bone marrow oedema because it is a:
items.e: Iloprost, a prostacyclin analogue, is used to reduce marrow oedema and pain; evidence is limited.

items.q: Statins have been proposed to reduce the risk of steroid-associated osteonecrosis because they:
items.e: Statins may lessen steroid-induced fat-cell hypertrophy in the marrow, reducing intraosseous pressure; evidence is observational.

items.q: On MRI, a subchondral insufficiency fracture of the femoral head is distinguished from osteonecrosis by a low-signal subchondral line that is:
o: Concave to the articular surface, enclosing fatty marrow
Located in the femoral neck only
Convex to the articular surface, with surrounding oedema
items.e: Insufficiency fracture lines run convex to (parallel with) the articular surface; the osteonecrosis band is concave to it and encloses the necrotic segment.

items.q: A 62-year-old woman has a spontaneous osteonecrosis (subchondral insufficiency fracture) of the medial femoral condyle. Which lesion size most favours non-operative management with protected weight bearing?
o: Lesion under about 40% of the condylar width on AP radiograph
Lesion over 50% of the condylar width
Lesion with subchondral collapse and a flap
items.e: Small lesions (under about 40% of condylar width, or under about 3.5 square cm) usually settle; large lesions tend to collapse and need arthroplasty.

items.q: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SIFK) is frequently associated with which concurrent meniscal pathology?
o: Bucket-handle tear of the lateral meniscus
Meniscal cyst of the lateral meniscus
items.e: A medial meniscal posterior root tear causes loss of hoop stresses and overload of the medial femoral condyle, predisposing to subchondral insufficiency fracture.

items.q: Apart from the femoral head, the commonest site of non-traumatic osteonecrosis is the:
items.e: The humeral head is the second commonest site of non-traumatic osteonecrosis (steroids, sickle cell, dysbaric).

items.q: A patient with humeral head osteonecrosis has collapse with arthritic involvement of the glenoid (Cruess stage V). The appropriate operation is:
items.e: Cruess V involves the glenoid, so a total shoulder arthroplasty is preferred; hemiarthroplasty or resurfacing suits collapse with an intact glenoid.

items.q: In talar neck fractures, the risk of talar body osteonecrosis is highest with which Hawkins (Canale-Kelly) type?
o: Type IV, with talonavicular subluxation or dislocation in addition
Type III, subtalar and ankle dislocation without talonavicular involvement
items.e: AVN risk increases from type I to IV; type IV (Canale and Kelly addition with talonavicular dislocation) carries the highest risk, approaching 100% in older series.

items.q: Kienbock disease (osteonecrosis of the lunate) is classically associated with which radiographic variant?
items.e: A short ulna (negative ulnar variance) increases load on the lunate and is associated with Kienbock disease; staging is by Lichtman.

items.q: A 7-year-old boy has lateral elbow pain; radiographs show fragmentation and sclerosis of the whole capitellum. The most likely diagnosis and course is:
items.e: Panner disease affects the capitellum in boys under 10 and resolves with rest; capitellar OCD occurs in older adolescent throwers and gymnasts.

items.q: A 5-year-old boy has a limp and medial midfoot pain; the radiograph shows a flattened, sclerotic tarsal navicular. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Kohler disease is osteochondrosis of the tarsal navicular in boys of about 4-6 years and is self-limiting; a cast helps if painful.

items.q: A child has a single uniformly flattened vertebral body (vertebra plana) with preserved disc spaces. This 'Calve disease' is usually due to:
items.e: Vertebra plana in children is most often eosinophilic granuloma, not true osteonecrosis.

items.q: An elderly osteoporotic woman develops delayed collapse of a vertebral body weeks after minor trauma, and CT shows a gas-filled intravertebral cleft. This is:
items.e: Kummell disease is delayed post-traumatic vertebral collapse due to osteonecrosis, with a characteristic intravertebral vacuum cleft.

items.q: The proximal pole of the scaphoid is prone to osteonecrosis after waist fractures because its blood supply:
o: Comes only from the ulnar artery
Enters through the proximal pole from the radiocarpal ligament
Enters distally via dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery and flows retrograde
Is derived from the anterior interosseous artery alone
items.e: About 70-80% of scaphoid blood supply enters distally through dorsal ridge vessels from the radial artery and flows retrograde, so the proximal pole is at risk.

items.q: In infants with sickle cell disease, painful swelling of the hands and feet from infarction of the small tubular bones is called:
items.e: Hand-foot syndrome (sickle dactylitis) is often the first manifestation of sickle cell disease in infancy.

items.q: Which is the commonest site of giant cell tumour of bone?
items.e: GCT occurs most often in the distal femur, then the proximal tibia and distal radius; about half of all cases are around the knee.

items.q: What is the commonest axial location of giant cell tumour of bone?
items.e: The sacrum is the commonest axial site; GCT in the mobile spine above the sacrum is uncommon and tends to involve the vertebral body.

items.q: Giant cell tumour of the distal radius differs from GCT at the knee in that it:
o: Occurs mainly in children with open physes
Behaves more aggressively, with higher local recurrence and more lung implants
Never extends to the subchondral bone
Is usually treated by observation alone
items.e: The distal radius is the third commonest site and the most aggressive, with higher recurrence after curettage and more frequent benign pulmonary implants.

items.q: A 35-year-old has three lytic, giant-cell-rich lesions in the femur, a metacarpal and the mandible. Before labelling this multicentric GCT, which test is most important?
o: Serum alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D only
Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone
items.e: Multiple giant-cell lesions, especially in the jaw or hands, should raise suspicion of brown tumours of hyperparathyroidism, which resolve after parathyroidectomy; true multicentric GCT is rare (under 1%).

items.q: In the Lodwick classification, the typical margin of a giant cell tumour of bone (geographic, well-defined but without a sclerotic rim) is grade:
items.e: Lodwick IA is geographic with a sclerotic rim (slow-growing, e.g. NOF, UBC); IB is geographic without a sclerotic rim (e.g. GCT, myeloma); II is moth-eaten and III permeative.

items.q: On MRI, the solid component of a giant cell tumour of bone typically shows low to intermediate signal on T2-weighted images. This is mainly due to:
items.e: Unlike most tumours, which are bright on T2, GCT often has low-intermediate T2 signal from haemosiderin and collagen; fluid-fluid levels may appear where there is secondary ABC change.

items.q: Which Campanacci grade is the commonest presentation of giant cell tumour of bone?
o: Grade I (latent): sclerotic rim and intact cortex
Grade III (aggressive): indistinct margins with soft tissue mass
Grade II (active): well-defined without sclerotic rim, expanded thinned but intact cortex
items.e: About 70-80% of GCTs are Campanacci grade II; grade I is rare and grade III has cortical breach with soft tissue extension. There is no grade IV.

items.q: Historically, what was the local recurrence rate of giant cell tumour of bone after simple curettage and bone grafting without burring or adjuvants?
items.e: Simple curettage recurred in roughly half of cases; adding a large cortical window, high-speed burring, local adjuvants and cement reduces recurrence to about 10-20%.

items.q: Most local recurrences of giant cell tumour of bone after curettage appear:
items.e: Most recurrences show within 2-3 years, so follow-up with radiographs of the site (and chest imaging) is most frequent in that period.

items.q: When PMMA cement is used to fill a curetted giant cell tumour cavity, the heat of polymerisation is thought to kill residual tumour cells to a depth of about:
items.e: The exothermic reaction causes thermal necrosis of about 2-3 mm of the surrounding bone, acting as a local adjuvant in addition to giving immediate structural support.

items.q: A 28-year-old has a large giant cell tumour of the proximal fibula with a soft tissue mass. The preferred treatment is:
o: En bloc resection of the proximal fibula
items.e: The proximal fibula is an expendable bone, so en bloc resection gives the lowest recurrence with little functional cost (the LCL and biceps are reattached to the tibia); the common peroneal nerve must be protected.

items.q: After en bloc resection of a Campanacci III giant cell tumour of the distal radius, which reconstruction relocates the ulna into the radial defect and fuses it to the carpus?
o: Ilizarov bone transport of the radius
Ulnar translocation (radialisation of the ulna) with wrist arthrodesis
items.e: Ulnar translocation creates a one-bone forearm with radiocarpal (ulnocarpal) arthrodesis; alternatives are osteoarticular proximal fibula autograft or allograft reconstruction.

items.q: What is the standard dosing schedule of denosumab for giant cell tumour of bone?
o: 120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, with extra doses on days 8 and 15 of the first month
items.e: GCT dosing is 120 mg SC every 4 weeks with loading doses on days 8 and 15, plus calcium and vitamin D; 60 mg every 6 months is the osteoporosis dose.

items.q: Denosumab received FDA approval (2013) for giant cell tumour of bone in which group?
o: All patients with Campanacci II GCT before curettage
Adults and skeletally mature adolescents with unresectable GCT or where surgery would cause severe morbidity
Children under 10 years with any GCT
items.e: Approval was for unresectable disease or where resection would be severely morbid, based on phase 2 trials (Thomas 2010, Chawla 2013); it is not routine before curettage of resectable lesions.

items.q: A 40-year-old has been on long-term denosumab for an unresectable sacral giant cell tumour. Which adverse effect becomes more likely with increasing duration of treatment?
items.e: Osteonecrosis of the jaw (about 1-5%) rises with cumulative exposure; hypocalcaemia and atypical femoral fractures are other recognised problems.

items.q: A 17-year-old stops denosumab after 18 months of treatment for a giant cell tumour. A few months later she develops nausea, confusion and polyuria. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Rebound hypercalcaemia after stopping denosumab is a recognised problem in young patients with high bone turnover, as osteoclast activity surges.

items.q: Biopsy of a giant cell tumour after several months of denosumab typically shows:
o: Marked depletion of osteoclast-like giant cells with new woven bone formation
An increased number of giant cells
Complete absence of the H3F3A-mutant stromal cells
items.e: Denosumab removes the RANKL-driven giant cells and allows new bone formation, but the mutant stromal cells persist, which explains regrowth after stopping.

items.q: Which drug class is used as a cheaper adjuvant in giant cell tumour of bone because it also inhibits the osteoclast-like giant cells, although the evidence is weaker than for denosumab?
o: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib
items.e: Bisphosphonates induce apoptosis of giant cells and have been used locally or systemically to reduce recurrence and in unresectable disease.

items.q: Radiotherapy for giant cell tumour of bone is now reserved for unresectable disease mainly because of the risk of:
items.e: Secondary malignant GCT (sarcoma) after radiotherapy was historically reported in up to about 10%; risk is lower with modern megavoltage techniques but radiotherapy is still a last resort.

items.q: A 32-year-old has a large sacral giant cell tumour. Which minimally invasive treatment, sometimes repeated every few weeks, can control the tumour or reduce bleeding before surgery?
o: Percutaneous radiofrequency ablation of the sacral roots
items.e: Serial arterial embolisation is used for sacral and pelvic GCT, either as primary treatment or pre-operatively, along with denosumab, because en bloc sacrectomy risks bladder, bowel and sexual function.

items.q: In which population is giant cell tumour of bone relatively more common?
o: Asian populations, including Indian and Chinese
items.e: GCT makes up a higher proportion of primary bone tumours in Asian (Indian and Chinese) series; it typically affects skeletally mature adults aged 20-40 with slight female predominance.

items.q: On histology, a characteristic feature of conventional giant cell tumour of bone is that:
o: The giant cells cluster around haemorrhage only
The giant cells are evenly distributed and their nuclei resemble those of the mononuclear stromal cells
Abundant chondroid matrix surrounds the giant cells
items.e: In GCT the numerous large giant cells are uniformly scattered and have nuclei similar to the stromal cells; in other giant-cell-rich lesions they tend to be patchy, around haemorrhage.

items.q: Giant cell reparative granuloma, a giant-cell-rich lesion that can mimic GCT histologically, typically affects:
o: The distal femoral epiphysis of adults
The jaws and the small bones of the hands and feet
items.e: Giant cell reparative granuloma involves the jaw and the short tubular bones of the hands and feet, now regarded as part of the solid ABC spectrum.

items.q: Brown tumours of hyperparathyroidism usually:
o: Regress after the hyperparathyroidism is corrected
Require wide resection like a sarcoma
items.e: Brown tumours (osteitis fibrosa cystica) are reactive giant-cell lesions that heal after parathyroidectomy, so the endocrine cause is treated first.

items.q: A primary malignant giant cell tumour of bone is defined as:
o: A high-grade sarcoma juxtaposed with conventional GCT at first presentation
A sarcoma arising at the site of a previously irradiated GCT
A GCT with benign lung implants
A GCT in a patient over 60 years
items.e: Primary malignancy in GCT means a high-grade sarcoma coexisting with benign GCT at diagnosis; secondary malignant GCT arises later at a treated site, usually after radiotherapy.

items.q: What is the male-to-female ratio of unicameral bone cysts?
items.e: Simple bone cysts occur mainly at 5-15 years and are about twice as common in boys.

items.q: Where does a unicameral bone cyst most often occur in an adult?
o: Calcaneus, beneath the angle of Gissane
items.e: In adults, simple cysts typically occur in the calcaneus (the neutral triangle below the angle of Gissane) and the ilium; in children the proximal humerus and femur predominate.

items.q: In a simple bone cyst, which sign refers to a gas bubble that moves to the uppermost (non-dependent) part of the cyst with change of position, confirming a fluid-filled cavity?
items.e: The rising bubble sign is the gas counterpart of the fallen fragment sign; both indicate a fluid-filled cavity rather than a solid lesion.

items.q: A 9-year-old's proximal humeral fracture through a simple bone cyst heals uneventfully in a sling. How often does the cyst itself heal after such a fracture?
items.e: Although the fracture usually heals in about 6 weeks, the cyst heals spontaneously in only a minority, so further management of the cyst is considered afterwards.

items.q: Before injecting methylprednisolone into a suspected unicameral bone cyst (Scaglietti technique), what confirms the diagnosis at the time of aspiration?
o: Frank blood and multiple loculations on contrast
Straw-coloured fluid and a cystogram showing contrast filling a single cavity
items.e: A UBC yields clear straw-coloured fluid and contrast stays in a single cavity; bloody fluid with multiloculated filling suggests an ABC.

items.q: Elastic stable intramedullary nails are used in unicameral bone cysts of long bones because they provide stability and also:
o: Act as a continuous drain decompressing the cyst into the medullary canal
items.e: Flexible nails decompress the cyst (continuous drainage through the canal) as well as splinting the bone, allowing early return to activity.

items.q: A 40-year-old has an incidental well-defined lucent lesion in the neutral triangle of the calcaneus with a central calcified nidus and fat density on CT. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Intraosseous lipoma of the calcaneus has fat attenuation with a central calcification ('cockade' or target appearance); a simple cyst contains fluid. Observation is usual.

items.q: The 'cyst index' used to estimate fracture risk in unicameral bone cysts is calculated as:
o: Cyst area on the radiograph divided by the square of the diaphyseal diameter
Cyst length divided by bone length
Distance from the physis divided by cyst width
Cortical thickness divided by cyst width
items.e: Kaelin and MacEwen's cyst index (area divided by diaphyseal diameter squared) correlates with fracture risk; a high index and a thin cortex predict fracture.

items.q: Recent molecular studies of unicameral bone cysts have identified which recurrent gene fusions?
items.e: NFATC2 fusions have been described in simple bone cysts, whereas USP6 rearrangement defines primary ABC; EWSR1-FLI1 is Ewing sarcoma and SS18-SSX synovial sarcoma.

items.q: The traditional theory of the pathogenesis of a unicameral bone cyst is:
o: Clonal proliferation of osteoclast-like giant cells
Venous obstruction causing accumulation of fluid rich in prostaglandins and bone-resorbing enzymes
items.e: UBCs are thought to arise from blocked venous drainage in the metaphysis, with cyst fluid containing prostaglandins, interleukin-1 and enzymes that resorb bone.

items.q: On a radiograph, which feature favours an aneurysmal bone cyst over a unicameral bone cyst in a child's proximal humerus?
o: A fallen fragment in the dependent part of the cyst
Eccentric expansion wider than the adjacent physis
items.e: A UBC is central and not wider than the physis; an ABC is eccentric, blow-out and may expand wider than the physis, with fluid-fluid levels on MRI.

items.q: In primary aneurysmal bone cyst, the commonest fusion partner of USP6 is:
items.e: The CDH11-USP6 fusion is the commonest rearrangement in primary ABC; USP6 is placed under the strong CDH11 promoter.

items.q: In the spine, aneurysmal bone cysts characteristically arise from the:
o: Posterior elements, often extending into the vertebral body
items.e: Spinal ABCs (about 15-20% of cases) arise in the posterior elements and may spread into the body and adjacent levels, causing pain, scoliosis or neural compression.

items.q: Histology of an aneurysmal bone cyst shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa. Which feature of the septa is characteristic?
o: An endothelial lining like a haemangioma
Reactive woven bone ('blue bone') and osteoclast-like giant cells, without an endothelial lining
items.e: ABC spaces lack an endothelial lining; the septa contain fibroblasts, giant cells and characteristic basophilic 'blue bone'. Malignant cells in the septa would indicate telangiectatic osteosarcoma.

items.q: A 13-year-old has an expansile lytic lesion of the distal femur with fluid-fluid levels. Which MRI feature most suggests telangiectatic osteosarcoma rather than aneurysmal bone cyst?
o: Thick, nodular enhancing septa and solid tissue
items.e: Fluid-fluid levels occur in both; thick nodular septa, solid enhancing areas, cortical destruction and a soft tissue mass favour telangiectatic osteosarcoma and mandate biopsy of the solid parts.

items.q: A 14-year-old has a large aneurysmal bone cyst of the ilium. Which treatment can be used as the primary therapy or before surgery to reduce major intra-operative bleeding?
items.e: Selective arterial embolisation is valuable for pelvic, sacral and spinal ABCs; radiotherapy is avoided because of radiation-induced sarcoma and growth disturbance.

items.q: The 'solid' variant of aneurysmal bone cyst, lacking blood-filled spaces, is histologically similar to:
items.e: Solid ABC and giant cell reparative granuloma share histology (and USP6 rearrangements) and are regarded as one spectrum.

items.q: About what proportion of patients with aneurysmal bone cyst are under 20 years of age?
items.e: Around 80% of ABCs present in the first two decades, with a peak at 10-20 years and roughly equal sex distribution.

items.q: Which statement best describes recurrence after extended curettage with adjuvant for an aneurysmal bone cyst?
o: About 10-20%, higher in young children and lesions close to the physis
items.e: Recurrence is about 10-20% overall, mostly within 2 years, and more common in young children and lesions abutting the physis.

items.q: Which is the commonest presentation of a unicameral bone cyst?
o: Painful night-time swelling relieved by aspirin
Incidental finding on chest radiograph in adults
items.e: About two-thirds to three-quarters of UBCs present with a pathological fracture, most often of the proximal humerus; the rest are incidental.

items.q: Which treatment is recommended for a unicameral bone cyst of the proximal humerus in an older child with a latent lesion, minimal symptoms and low fracture risk?
items.e: Latent cysts that have migrated away from the physis tend to heal and can be observed; intervention is reserved for active, symptomatic or high-fracture-risk cysts.

items.q: In giant cell tumour of bone, what is the reported frequency of pathological fracture at presentation?
items.e: Pathological fracture occurs in roughly 10-30% of GCTs and is not by itself an indication for resection if the joint can be preserved.

items.q: Which is the most important reason not to give denosumab before curettage of a giant cell tumour that is already suitable for joint-preserving surgery?
o: The thick new bone and sclerotic rim it creates hide residual tumour, increasing local recurrence
It causes immediate malignant transformation in most patients
It is contraindicated in skeletally mature patients
items.e: Pre-operative denosumab forms a new bony shell that hides nests of viable stromal cells, and several series show higher recurrence after curettage, so suitable lesions go straight to surgery.

items.q: After treatment of a giant cell tumour of bone, chest imaging is usually repeated every 3-6 months for the first 2-3 years mainly to detect:
o: Benign pulmonary implants (lung metastases), present in about 2-5%
items.e: Lung implants usually appear 2-4 years after diagnosis, often after local recurrence; they are histologically benign and are treated by metastasectomy, observation or denosumab.

items.q: A 3-year-old has disproportionate short stature with shortening mainly of the forearms and legs. This pattern of limb shortening is termed:
items.e: Mesomelic shortening affects the middle segments (forearm and leg), as in Langer and Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis; rhizomelic affects the humerus and femur, as in achondroplasia.

items.q: A short child has a normal-length trunk with short limbs. Which dysplasia is a short-trunk rather than a short-limbed type?
items.e: Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasias and Morquio syndrome involve the spine and produce short-trunk dwarfism; achondroplasia, pseudoachondroplasia and metaphyseal dysplasias are short-limbed.

items.q: Camurati-Engelmann disease is a dysplasia predominantly affecting which part of the long bones?
items.e: Camurati-Engelmann disease (TGF-beta 1 mutation) causes symmetrical diaphyseal cortical thickening with leg pain and a waddling gait.

items.q: FGFR3 normally acts on the growth plate by:
o: Promoting osteoclast resorption of calcified cartilage
items.e: FGFR3 is a negative regulator of physeal growth; activating mutations (achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, thanatophoric dysplasia) therefore suppress endochondral growth.

items.q: Over 95% of achondroplasia is caused by which specific FGFR3 mutation?
o: Asn540Lys in the tyrosine kinase domain
items.e: Achondroplasia is almost always G380R; N540K is the usual hypochondroplasia mutation and R248C/K650E are thanatophoric dysplasia mutations.

items.q: Most children with achondroplasia are born to parents of average stature. The new mutation is associated with:
items.e: About 80% of cases are sporadic new FGFR3 mutations arising in the paternal germline, with increased frequency at older paternal age.

items.q: Two adults with achondroplasia plan a family. The chance that a child will be homozygous for the mutation, which is lethal, is:
items.e: With two heterozygous parents, 25% of children are homozygous (lethal), 50% heterozygous (achondroplasia) and 25% of average stature.

items.q: A child with achondroplasia has hands in which the fingers are short and the middle and ring fingers diverge when the hand is extended. This sign is called:
items.e: The trident hand of achondroplasia reflects short, equal-length fingers with a gap between the middle and ring fingers; the hitchhiker thumb belongs to diastrophic dysplasia.

items.q: An infant with achondroplasia has central apnoea, hypotonia and brisk reflexes. The most important cause to exclude is:
o: Foramen magnum stenosis with cervicomedullary compression
items.e: Foramen magnum stenosis is the main cause of sudden death in infants with achondroplasia; MRI and polysomnography are used, with suboccipital decompression when significant.

items.q: A 9-month-old with achondroplasia has a flexible thoracolumbar kyphosis. The best initial advice is:
o: Avoid unsupported sitting and observe, as most resolve once walking
items.e: Thoracolumbar kyphosis is common in infancy and usually resolves with walking; unsupported sitting is avoided, bracing is used if it persists, and fusion is reserved for progressive rigid curves after about age 3-5.

items.q: A 40-year-old with achondroplasia develops neurogenic claudication. The typical cause is:
o: Lumbar spinal stenosis from short pedicles and narrowing interpedicular distance
items.e: Congenitally narrow lumbar canals make adult spinal stenosis the commonest spinal problem in adult achondroplasia, treated by wide decompression often with fusion.

items.q: Genu varum in achondroplasia is mainly attributed to:
o: Medial tibial physeal arrest as in Blount disease
Ligamentous laxity of the lateral collateral ligament
Relative overgrowth of the fibula compared with the tibia
Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
items.e: Relative fibular overgrowth is the main cause of the bowing in achondroplasia; symptomatic cases are treated by guided growth or osteotomy.

items.q: Vosoritide, approved to increase growth velocity in achondroplasia, acts as:
o: A C-type natriuretic peptide analogue that antagonises FGFR3 downstream signalling
items.e: Vosoritide is a CNP analogue that inhibits the MAPK pathway downstream of FGFR3, increasing annual growth velocity.

items.q: A child has mild short-limbed short stature, a normal face and skull, and radiographs showing only mild lumbar interpedicular narrowing. The likely diagnosis and gene are:
items.e: Hypochondroplasia is the mild FGFR3 dysplasia, resembling achondroplasia without the facial features.

items.q: A stillborn infant has a cloverleaf skull, extremely short limbs, a narrow thorax and curved 'telephone receiver' femora. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Thanatophoric dysplasia (FGFR3) is the commonest lethal skeletal dysplasia and shows telephone-receiver femora and sometimes cloverleaf skull.

items.q: Which cervical abnormality is particularly important to screen for before anaesthesia in pseudoachondroplasia?
items.e: Pseudoachondroplasia, like Morquio and SED congenita, causes odontoid hypoplasia and atlantoaxial instability; foramen magnum stenosis is typical of achondroplasia.

items.q: A 7-year-old has bilateral, symmetrical small irregular femoral epiphyses at the same stage, irregular distal femoral epiphyses and a normal spine. Which feature best distinguishes this from bilateral Perthes disease?
o: Subchondral fracture line on lateral view
Symmetrical involvement at the same stage with involvement of other epiphyses
items.e: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia affects both hips symmetrically and synchronously with other epiphyses involved; bilateral Perthes is asynchronous, with the hips at different stages.

items.q: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia of the dominant type is caused by mutations in genes for:
o: COMP, type IX collagen or matrilin-3
items.e: Dominant MED arises from COMP, COL9A1-3 or MATN3 mutations; the recessive form (SLC26A2) is associated with a double-layered patella.

items.q: A double-layered patella on a lateral knee radiograph is characteristic of:
items.e: The double-layered patella is a hallmark of recessive MED; nail-patella syndrome has absent or hypoplastic patellae.

items.q: The long-term problem that most often leads to surgery in adults with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is:
items.e: The irregular, flattened epiphyses of MED lead to early-onset osteoarthritis, often requiring hip arthroplasty in early adult life.

items.q: Why are myopia and retinal detachment features of spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita?
o: Type I collagen forms the sclera
Fibrillin forms the suspensory ligament of the lens
Type X collagen is present in the retina
Type II collagen is a major component of the vitreous humour
items.e: COL2A1 dysplasias (SED congenita, Kniest, Stickler) affect cartilage, vitreous and inner ear, so annual eye review for retinal detachment is needed.

items.q: A child with SED congenita has myelopathic signs, and flexion-extension radiographs show an os odontoideum with C1-C2 instability. The treatment is:
items.e: Atlantoaxial instability with myelopathy in SED congenita requires posterior upper cervical fusion.

items.q: A boy of 10 presents with back and hip pain; spinal radiographs show platyspondyly with a 'heaped-up' bony mound on the posterior part of the vertebral endplates. His maternal uncle is similar. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: SED tarda (TRAPPC2) is X-linked, presents in late childhood in boys and shows the characteristic posterior heaped-up vertebral bodies.

items.q: A child has short stature, large stiff joints, myopia, cleft palate and dumbbell-shaped femora. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Kniest dysplasia (COL2A1) is characterised by dumbbell-shaped femora, enlarged stiff joints, myopia with retinal detachment risk and cleft palate.

items.q: A neonate with Pierre Robin sequence has high myopia and a family history of early-onset osteoarthritis and retinal detachment. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Stickler syndrome (COL2A1, COL11A1) combines Pierre Robin sequence, high myopia with retinal detachment and premature osteoarthritis.

items.q: An infant has short limbs, cystic swelling of the pinnae, a cleft palate, severely rigid clubfeet and abducted, proximally placed thumbs. The gene involved is:
items.e: Diastrophic dysplasia (autosomal recessive, common in Finland) features hitchhiker thumbs, cauliflower ears and rigid clubfeet.

items.q: Which spinal deformity in diastrophic dysplasia needs close monitoring because it can cause quadriplegia?
items.e: Cervical kyphosis in diastrophic dysplasia may progress and compress the cord; progressive cases are fused.

items.q: The clubfeet of diastrophic dysplasia, compared with idiopathic clubfoot, are typically:
o: Flexible and corrected by stretching alone
Absent at birth and appearing after walking
Rigid and highly resistant to treatment with frequent recurrence
Associated with a vertical talus in most cases
items.e: Diastrophic clubfeet are notoriously stiff; casting gives limited correction and surgical release has a high recurrence rate.

items.q: Cleidocranial dysplasia results from mutation of RUNX2 (CBFA1), whose normal role is:
o: A negative regulator of chondrocyte proliferation
The master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation
items.e: RUNX2 drives osteoblast differentiation; haploinsufficiency mainly affects membranous bone (clavicles, skull) and dentition.

items.q: Which dental feature is characteristic of cleidocranial dysplasia?
o: Premature loss of primary teeth with neutropenia
items.e: Cleidocranial dysplasia features retained primary teeth, delayed eruption and supernumerary teeth; dentinogenesis imperfecta is a feature of osteogenesis imperfecta.

items.q: A 6-year-old with cleidocranial dysplasia has coxa vara with a Hilgenreiner-epiphyseal angle of 65 degrees and a Trendelenburg gait. The appropriate treatment is:
items.e: Coxa vara with an HE angle over 60 degrees is likely to progress and is corrected by valgus osteotomy.

items.q: A 4-year-old has a waddling gait, coxa vara and bowed legs. Radiographs show widened, irregular metaphyses resembling rickets, but serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D are normal. The most likely gene is:
items.e: Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (type X collagen, autosomal dominant) mimics rickets radiologically but has normal biochemistry; PHEX causes X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets.

items.q: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is distinguished from other metaphyseal dysplasias by:
o: Fine sparse hair and immune deficiency
Hypercalcaemia from an activating PTH/PTHrP receptor mutation
items.e: Jansen type is severe and caused by a constitutively active PTH1R, producing hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia.

items.q: An Amish child with short limbs has fine, sparse, light-coloured hair, recurrent infections and Hirschsprung disease. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (RMRP, autosomal recessive) combines metaphyseal dysplasia, sparse hair, T-cell immune deficiency and a raised lymphoma risk.

items.q: A child with metaphyseal chondrodysplasia has fatty stools from pancreatic insufficiency and cyclical neutropenia. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SBDS, autosomal recessive) combines exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, marrow dysfunction (neutropenia) and metaphyseal dysplasia.

items.q: Which mucopolysaccharidosis is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait?
items.e: Hunter syndrome (iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency) is the only X-linked MPS; it resembles Hurler but lacks corneal clouding.

items.q: A 6-year-old with short-trunk dwarfism, pectus carinatum, genu valgum, joint laxity, corneal clouding and normal intelligence has excess urinary keratan sulfate. Before any anaesthetic, the priority is to assess:
o: The craniocervical junction for odontoid hypoplasia and atlantoaxial instability
items.e: Morquio syndrome (MPS IVA, galactose-6-sulfatase deficiency) carries a high risk of odontoid hypoplasia with C1-C2 instability and cord compression; occipitocervical fusion is often needed.

items.q: The enzyme deficient in Hurler syndrome (MPS I) is:
items.e: Hurler syndrome is alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency (autosomal recessive) with coarse facies, intellectual disability, corneal clouding and gibbus; early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the standard.

items.q: On a lateral spinal radiograph, anterior beaking of the vertebral bodies is located centrally in Morquio syndrome, whereas in Hurler syndrome it is typically:
items.e: Dysostosis multiplex includes vertebral beaking - anteroinferior in Hurler (contributing to a thoracolumbar gibbus) and central in Morquio.

items.q: Which group of radiographic features constitutes dysostosis multiplex in the mucopolysaccharidoses?
o: Bone-in-bone vertebrae, Erlenmeyer flask femora and rugger-jersey spine
Wormian bones, beaded ribs and crumpled femora
Oar-shaped ribs, bullet-shaped phalanges and proximally pointed metacarpals
Dumbbell femora, coronal clefts and platyspondyly
items.e: Oar-shaped ribs, bullet-shaped phalanges, pointed metacarpal bases and vertebral beaking are the classic dysostosis multiplex pattern; the bone-in-bone group belongs to osteopetrosis.

items.q: Osteopetrosis results from a failure of:
items.e: Defective osteoclast function (e.g. TCIRG1, CLCN7, carbonic anhydrase II) leaves dense but brittle bone with marrow encroachment.

items.q: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure infantile malignant osteopetrosis because:
o: Osteoclasts are derived from haematopoietic (monocyte-macrophage) precursors
Osteoblasts are derived from marrow stromal cells
It replaces defective type I collagen
It corrects the renal tubular defect
items.e: Osteoclasts arise from the haematopoietic lineage, so donor marrow provides functioning osteoclasts and restores resorption and marrow space.

items.q: Osteopetrosis accompanied by renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification is due to deficiency of:
items.e: Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency (autosomal recessive) produces the triad of osteopetrosis, renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification.

items.q: Which radiographic finding of the spine is characteristic of osteopetrosis?
o: Anterior vertebral wedging with Schmorl nodes
items.e: Sclerotic endplates give the rugger-jersey or sandwich appearance; other signs are bone-in-bone and Erlenmeyer flask deformities.

items.q: When fixing a femoral fracture in an adult with osteopetrosis, the main technical difficulty is:
o: Soft osteoporotic bone with poor screw purchase
A wide medullary canal requiring large nails
Extremely hard, brittle bone that is difficult to drill and ream
items.e: The sclerotic bone with an obliterated canal is very hard to drill; cooled drills and frequent bit changes are needed, and plates are often preferred over nails.

items.q: A short adult has dense bones, an obtuse mandibular angle, persistently open fontanelles and resorption of the terminal phalanges. The enzyme deficient is:
items.e: Pyknodysostosis is caused by cathepsin K deficiency; acro-osteolysis and open fontanelles distinguish it from osteopetrosis.

items.q: Multiple small, round, periarticular sclerotic bone islands found incidentally in an asymptomatic adult suggest:
items.e: Osteopoikilosis is a benign, symmetric, periarticular sclerotic dysplasia of no clinical significance, important only to avoid misdiagnosis as metastases.

items.q: A child has recurrent fractures, short stature and progressive long-bone deformity; the sclerae were blue at birth but are now white, and dentinogenesis imperfecta is present. The Sillence type is:
items.e: Type III is the most severe form compatible with survival, with progressive deformity and sclerae that lighten with age; type I is mild with persistently blue sclerae.

items.q: Hearing loss in osteogenesis imperfecta type I typically begins:
o: In the second to third decades
items.e: Hearing loss (conductive, later mixed) in type I OI usually starts in adolescence or early adulthood, around the second to third decades.

items.q: A child with osteogenesis imperfecta has hyperplastic callus after fractures and calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane restricting rotation. The Sillence type and gene are:
items.e: Type V OI (IFITM5) has normal type I collagen but shows hyperplastic callus, interosseous membrane calcification and radial head dislocation.

items.q: The main benefit of cyclical intravenous pamidronate in children with moderate to severe osteogenesis imperfecta is:
o: Correction of the underlying collagen defect
Improvement in final adult height to normal
Increased bone density with fewer fractures and less pain
items.e: Bisphosphonates inhibit resorption, increasing bone density and reducing fracture rate and bone pain; they do not correct the collagen abnormality.

items.q: For correcting progressive femoral bowing in a 5-year-old with osteogenesis imperfecta, the preferred fixation is:
o: Multiple osteotomies with a locking plate
Multiple osteotomies with a telescoping intramedullary rod (e.g. Fassier-Duval)
items.e: Sofield-Millar osteotomies with telescoping rods that elongate with growth reduce reoperation; plates act as stress risers and are avoided.

items.q: A 6-month-old has three fractures of differing ages. Which finding most supports osteogenesis imperfecta over non-accidental injury?
o: Numerous wormian bones in the skull
items.e: Wormian bones, blue sclerae, osteopenia, dentinogenesis imperfecta and family history suggest OI; classic metaphyseal lesions and posterior rib fractures are highly specific for abuse.

items.q: In neurofibromatosis type 1, which feature distinguishes a dystrophic scoliosis from a non-dystrophic curve?
o: Short, sharp angular curve with rib pencilling and vertebral scalloping
Curve that responds well to bracing
items.e: Dystrophic NF1 curves are short and angular with rib pencilling, scalloping, enlarged foramina and dural ectasia; they progress rapidly and need early combined anterior and posterior fusion.

items.q: A 3-year-old with NF1 has a non-dystrophic 25-degree thoracic scoliosis. The family should be told that:
o: The curve may later acquire dystrophic features (modulation) and needs close follow-up
items.e: Non-dystrophic NF1 curves behave like idiopathic scoliosis but can modulate into dystrophic curves, especially when they appear early.

items.q: Which of the following is a diagnostic criterion for NF1?
o: Coast-of-Maine cafe-au-lait spots with precocious puberty
items.e: Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) are an NF1 criterion; bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2, and a shagreen patch suggests tuberous sclerosis.

items.q: An infant with NF1 has anterolateral bowing of the tibia without fracture. The appropriate management is:
o: Total contact orthosis to protect against fracture
Observation without protection, as it will resolve
items.e: Anterolateral bowing threatens pseudarthrosis; the limb is braced to prevent fracture, and osteotomy to straighten the bow is avoided because it may cause non-union.

items.q: Posteromedial bowing of the tibia in a newborn is typically associated with:
o: Calcaneovalgus foot and later leg-length discrepancy, with spontaneous improvement of the bow
items.e: Posteromedial bowing is benign and remodels, but leaves a leg-length discrepancy that may need epiphysiodesis; anterolateral bowing suggests NF1 and anteromedial bowing fibular hemimelia.

items.q: In NF1, a plexiform neurofibroma that becomes painful and rapidly enlarges should be investigated for:
items.e: Lifetime MPNST risk in NF1 is about 10%; a painful, growing plexiform lesion needs MRI and PET-CT, then biopsy.

items.q: Hereditary multiple exostoses is caused by mutations in:
items.e: Multiple osteochondromas are autosomal dominant, caused by EXT1 (chromosome 8) or EXT2 (chromosome 11); IDH1/2 mutations underlie Ollier and Maffucci.

items.q: A 32-year-old with hereditary multiple exostoses has a new painful enlargement of a pelvic lesion. On MRI, which finding suggests secondary chondrosarcoma?
o: Cortical and medullary continuity with the host bone
Lesion pointing away from the joint
items.e: Pain or growth after maturity and a cartilage cap over about 2 cm in an adult suggest malignant change; corticomedullary continuity defines any osteochondroma.

items.q: A 10-year-old has multiple enchondromas of one side of the body with limb shortening, and also multiple soft-tissue haemangiomas with phleboliths. Compared with Ollier disease, this condition carries:
o: A higher risk of malignancy including non-skeletal tumours such as gliomas
items.e: Maffucci syndrome (enchondromatosis with haemangiomas) carries an even higher chondrosarcoma risk than Ollier disease plus risk of gliomas and gastrointestinal malignancies; both are non-hereditary IDH1/2 mosaic conditions.

items.q: A girl has polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with a shepherd's crook femur, cafe-au-lait spots with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders and precocious puberty. The underlying mutation is in:
items.e: McCune-Albright syndrome results from a mosaic activating GNAS mutation; NF1 cafe-au-lait spots have smooth 'coast of California' borders.

items.q: An infant has short great toes with hallux valgus at birth and later develops painful swellings of the back that ossify. The most important advice is to:
o: Avoid biopsy, surgery and intramuscular injections, which provoke flare-ups
Perform a biopsy to exclude sarcoma
items.e: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (ACVR1) produces heterotopic ossification triggered by trauma; biopsy and surgery cause new ossification.

items.q: A tall 15-year-old has arachnodactyly, scoliosis and a downward dislocation of the lens, with mild intellectual disability and a history of venous thrombosis. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) gives a marfanoid habitus with downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, osteoporosis and thrombosis; Marfan lens dislocation is upward.

items.q: Which hip finding is characteristic of Marfan syndrome in adults?
o: Coxa vara with a triangular fragment
items.e: Protrusio acetabuli is one of the systemic features scored in the Ghent criteria for Marfan syndrome, along with dural ectasia and scoliosis.

items.q: An infant has bilateral congenital knee dislocations, dislocated hips and elbows, a flat face and cervical kyphosis. The syndrome is:
items.e: Larsen syndrome (filamin B) causes multiple large-joint dislocations and cervical kyphosis that may compress the cord.

items.q: A girl with short stature has cubitus valgus, short fourth metacarpals and Madelung deformity. The karyotype is most likely:
items.e: Turner syndrome is associated with cubitus valgus, short fourth metacarpals and Madelung deformity (SHOX haploinsufficiency).

items.q: An adult with spinal deformity has a pelvic tilt of 24°. Which SRS-Schwab pelvic tilt grade applies?
items.e: The SRS-Schwab PT modifier is 0 under 20°, + for 20-30° and ++ over 30°; there is no +++ grade.

items.q: A positive sagittal vertical axis of 7 cm means that:
o: The C7 plumb line falls 7 cm behind the sacrum
The C7 plumb line falls 7 cm anterior to the posterosuperior corner of S1
The femoral heads lie 7 cm anterior to S1
items.e: Positive SVA indicates the C7 plumb line lies anterior to the posterosuperior S1 corner; values over about 5 cm indicate positive sagittal imbalance.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman has pelvic incidence 40° and lumbar lordosis 62°. Her PI-LL value indicates:
o: Normal harmony between pelvis and lumbar spine
Positive sagittal imbalance from loss of lordosis
Relative hyperlordosis for her pelvic morphology (PI-LL about −22°)
items.e: PI-LL = 40 − 62 = −22°, i.e. more lordosis than her low PI needs; the target is LL within about 10° of PI.

items.q: The cervical sagittal vertical axis (C2-C7 SVA) is measured from:
o: A plumb line from the C2 centroid to the posterosuperior corner of C7
A plumb line from C7 to the posterosuperior corner of S1
The external auditory meatus to the C7 spinous process
The opisthion to the T1 endplate
items.e: cSVA is the horizontal offset of the C2 centroid plumb line from the posterosuperior corner of C7; values over about 4 cm correlate with worse neck disability.

items.q: A fixed hip flexion contracture in a patient with an otherwise normal spine typically produces:
o: Pelvic retroversion and loss of lumbar lordosis
Anterior pelvic tilt with increased lumbar lordosis
items.e: To stand upright with flexed hips the pelvis tilts forward and the lumbar spine hyperextends (hyperlordosis); this can mask or mimic spinal pathology in hip-spine syndrome.

items.q: The Ponte osteotomy (wide posterior column resection at several levels) was originally described for correction of:
items.e: Ponte described multilevel posterior column osteotomies for Scheuermann kyphosis; Smith-Petersen's 1945 osteotomy was for rheumatoid/ankylosing spondylitis lumbar kyphosis.

items.q: When a Smith-Petersen opening-wedge osteotomy is performed through a calcified anterior longitudinal ligament in ankylosing spondylitis, a specific danger is:
o: Excessive shortening of the spinal cord
Rupture of the anterior column with stretching of the aorta and great vessels
items.e: Correction hinges open anteriorly and lengthens the anterior column, which can rupture the ossified ALL and stretch or tear major vessels; closing-wedge PSO avoids anterior lengthening.

items.q: During closure of a lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy, an important cause of neurological deficit is:
o: Dural buckling and translation (subluxation) at the osteotomy site compressing neural elements
Injury to the conus because PSO is done at L1
items.e: As the wedge closes the dura can buckle and the segments can sublux, impinging on nerve roots; adequate decompression and controlled closure reduce this.

items.q: After a lumbar fusion restores lumbar lordosis in a patient with sagittal malalignment, the pelvic tilt decreases and thoracic kyphosis increases. This phenomenon is called:
items.e: Correcting the lumbar spine releases compensations: the pelvis anteverts (PT falls) and the unfused thoracic spine regains kyphosis, which must be anticipated to avoid under-correction.

items.q: The inflection point, where thoracic kyphosis changes to lumbar lordosis, normally lies around:
items.e: In a typical spine the transition from kyphosis to lordosis lies near T12-L1; its position varies with Roussouly type.

items.q: Compared with standing, lumbar lordosis in the sitting position normally:
o: Decreases, as the pelvis tilts posteriorly
items.e: On sitting the pelvis retroverts and the lumbar spine flattens; this is why seated films underestimate lordosis and why spinal stiffness affects hip function.

items.q: With normal ageing in asymptomatic adults, which change in sagittal parameters is typical?
o: SVA and pelvic tilt increase, while lumbar lordosis tends to decrease
items.e: Ageing brings increased thoracic kyphosis, decreased lordosis, rising PT and a more positive SVA, which is the basis for age-adjusted targets.

items.q: The normal range of thoracic kyphosis measured from T4 (or T5) to T12 is approximately:
items.e: Thoracic kyphosis of about 20-50° is normal; over about 50° is hyperkyphosis, as in Scheuermann disease.

items.q: The normal range of sacral slope in adults is approximately:
items.e: SS is about 35-45° in most adults; it falls with pelvic retroversion as PT rises because PI = PT + SS.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph the two femoral heads do not superimpose. To measure pelvic incidence, the hip axis is taken as:
o: The centre of the head closer to the film
The centre of the larger head
The tip of the greater trochanter
The midpoint of the line joining the two femoral head centres
items.e: When the heads are not superimposed, the midpoint between their centres is used as the hip axis for PI and PT.

items.q: Low-dose biplanar slot-scanning (EOS) imaging is particularly useful in sagittal alignment assessment because it:
o: Gives simultaneous full-body standing AP and lateral images including the lower limbs at low radiation dose
Shows ligament injury better than MRI
Is taken supine to remove compensation
Measures bone mineral density at the same time
items.e: EOS captures head-to-feet weight-bearing images with low dose, allowing assessment of lower limb compensation (knee flexion, hip extension) along with the spine.

items.q: Glassman's analysis of adult deformity showed that, for the same magnitude, kyphosis in which region is least well tolerated?
items.e: Glassman found positive sagittal balance correlated with symptoms and that lumbar kyphosis was less well tolerated than thoracic kyphosis.

items.q: Besides SVA, Lafage showed that which pelvic parameter correlates significantly with disability in adult spinal deformity?
items.e: High PT reflects compensatory retroversion and correlates with worse health-related quality of life; PI is a fixed morphological value.

items.q: The Roussouly 'type 3 anteverted' variant is characterised by:
o: A high pelvic incidence and retroverted pelvis
A sacral slope over 45° with high PI
A flat back with sacral slope under 25°
A low pelvic incidence with an anteverted pelvis but a type 3 lordosis
items.e: Type 3 anteverted has a low PI with low (sometimes negative) PT, so SS falls in the type 3 range despite the low PI.

items.q: In a long posterior fusion from the thoracic spine to the sacrum in an adult, the main purpose of adding S2-alar-iliac or iliac screws is to:
o: Protect the S1 screws and improve fusion at L5-S1
items.e: Long constructs place large cantilever loads on S1 screws; pelvic fixation reduces S1 screw loosening and L5-S1 pseudarthrosis.

items.q: An advantage of S2-alar-iliac screws over traditional iliac screws is that they:
o: Are in line with the S1 screws and less prominent, with fewer wound problems
items.e: S2AI screws start in line with the S1 pedicle screws, need no offset connectors, sit deeper and cause less implant prominence; they do cross the SI joint.

items.q: Anterior column realignment (ACR) performed through a lateral transpsoas approach achieves lordosis mainly by:
o: Releasing the anterior longitudinal ligament and inserting a hyperlordotic cage
items.e: ACR sections the ALL and inserts a hyperlordotic interbody cage, usually with posterior column osteotomy and fixation, giving segmental lordosis without a PSO.

items.q: After a C7-T1 extension osteotomy for ankylosing spondylitis, the chin-brow vertical angle is over-corrected into extension. The main functional problem will be:
o: Difficulty seeing the ground when walking
items.e: Leaving the gaze slightly downward (about 0-10° of flexion) is preferred; over-correction prevents viewing the floor and hampers walking.

items.q: In adolescent idiopathic thoracic scoliosis, the usual sagittal profile of the thoracic curve is:
items.e: Rotational lordosis of the thoracic apex is typical in AIS; marked thoracic hyperkyphosis should prompt a search for another cause.

items.q: In long fusions to the sacrum for adult deformity, an interbody fusion at L5-S1 is commonly added mainly to:
o: Improve fusion rates and add segmental lordosis at the lumbosacral junction
items.e: L5-S1 is the commonest site of pseudarthrosis in long constructs; anterior column support improves fusion and allows lordosis restoration.

items.q: A pedicle subtraction osteotomy that includes resection of the adjacent disc and endplate (bone-disc-bone osteotomy) corresponds to Schwab grade:
items.e: An extended PSO taking part of the vertebral body plus the adjacent disc is grade 4; grade 3 is a standard PSO and grade 5 a full VCR.

items.q: The normal range of pelvic tilt in asymptomatic adults is approximately:
items.e: PT is normally about 10-20°; over 20° suggests compensatory pelvic retroversion.

items.q: Which spinopelvic parameter determines how much lumbar lordosis an individual needs to remain balanced?
items.e: PI is the fixed morphological parameter that sets the lordosis requirement; LL should approximate PI within about 10°.

items.q: A patient has pelvic incidence 52°, sacral slope 40° and pelvic tilt 12°. Which is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: Measurement error, as PI must exceed PT + SS
items.e: PT 12 + SS 40 = 52 = PI; PT under 20° and SS in the normal range indicate a normally oriented pelvis.

items.q: Pseudarthrosis and rod fracture after a three-column osteotomy most commonly occur:
o: At or adjacent to the osteotomy level
items.e: The osteotomy site carries the highest bending stress and healing demand, so rod fractures cluster there; supplementary rods help.

items.q: A 65-year-old with adult deformity has pelvic incidence 65°, lumbar lordosis 30°, SVA 12 cm and a fused, ankylosed anterior column at L2-L4. Which procedure is most appropriate to correct the sagittal deformity?
o: Multiple Ponte osteotomies through ankylosed levels
Lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy with long posterior instrumentation
items.e: Large fixed malalignment (PI-LL 35°, SVA 12 cm) with a fused anterior column needs a three-column osteotomy; Ponte osteotomies require mobile discs.

items.q: In a fusion for degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4-L5, failure to restore segmental lordosis is most likely to lead to:
o: Adjacent segment degeneration and a positive sagittal balance
items.e: Fusing the lower lumbar spine in hypolordosis increases PI-LL mismatch and loads the adjacent segments, accelerating degeneration.

items.q: In adult spinal deformity surgery, the target T1 pelvic angle is generally below about:
items.e: TPA targets of roughly under 14-20° correspond to an SVA under 4-5 cm and PT under 20-25°.

items.q: Teriparatide given around adult deformity surgery in an osteoporotic patient is used mainly to:
o: Improve screw purchase and reduce proximal junctional failure
items.e: Anabolic therapy improves bone quality and screw fixation and has been shown to reduce screw loosening and junctional failure in osteoporotic spines.

items.q: In a 25-year-old, the normal lumbar lordosis measured from L1 to S1 is approximately:
items.e: Lumbar lordosis is typically about 40-60° (varying with PI), with two-thirds between L4 and S1.

items.q: The normal intermetatarsal angle between the first and second metatarsals on a weight-bearing AP radiograph is less than about:
items.e: An IMA under 9° is normal; 9-11° is mild and over 16° severe in the commonly used grading.

items.q: Clinical hypermobility of the first tarsometatarsal joint, favouring a Lapidus procedure, is suggested by dorsal translation of the first metatarsal over about:
items.e: Dorsal excursion of the first ray greater than about 8-10 mm on examination is the conventional threshold for hypermobility.

items.q: In a distal chevron osteotomy for mild hallux valgus, the metatarsal head can usually be translated laterally by up to about:
items.e: Lateral shift is limited to roughly one-third to one-half of the head width; greater translation risks instability and loss of fixation.

items.q: To reduce the risk of avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head when combining a chevron osteotomy with lateral release, the surgeon should avoid extensive dissection:
o: Dorsolaterally and plantar-laterally around the metatarsal neck
items.e: The head's blood supply enters dorsolaterally (first dorsal metatarsal artery branches) and plantar-laterally; extensive lateral capsular stripping plus an osteotomy can devascularise it.

items.q: Dorsal malunion (elevatus) of the first metatarsal after a proximal osteotomy for hallux valgus typically causes:
o: Transfer metatarsalgia under the lesser metatarsal heads
Sesamoiditis of the fibular sesamoid only
items.e: An elevated first metatarsal shifts load to the second and third metatarsal heads, producing transfer metatarsalgia.

items.q: The acronym MICA in minimally invasive bunion surgery refers to:
o: Minimally invasive chevron and Akin osteotomies performed percutaneously
items.e: MICA (third-generation MIS) combines a percutaneous extra-articular distal chevron osteotomy with an Akin, fixed with screws.

items.q: Which uncorrected element of the deformity is an increasingly recognised cause of hallux valgus recurrence?
items.e: Residual first metatarsal pronation leaves the sesamoids unreduced and is linked to recurrence, along with IMA under-correction, unrecognised DMAA and TMT hypermobility.

items.q: A 60-year-old has a rigid hallux varus with first MTP arthritis after bunion surgery. The preferred treatment is:
items.e: Soft-tissue reconstructions (EHB tenodesis, EHL transfer) are for flexible deformities without arthritis; rigid or arthritic hallux varus is fused.

items.q: As hallux valgus progresses, the abductor hallucis tendon migrates plantarly. The consequence is that it:
o: Loses its abducting power and acts as a flexor and pronator of the hallux
Becomes a strong adductor of the hallux
Becomes an extensor of the MTP joint
items.e: Plantar migration removes the only medial dynamic restraint, so the hallux continues to drift into valgus and pronation.

items.q: In hallux valgus, the sesamoids remain essentially in place while the metatarsal head drifts medially because they are anchored by:
o: The abductor hallucis and medial capsule
The adductor hallucis and the deep transverse metatarsal ligament
items.e: The sesamoid complex is tethered laterally by adductor hallucis and the transverse metatarsal ligament, so the apparent lateral sesamoid displacement is really medial drift of the head.

items.q: In the Coughlin and Shurnas classification of hallux rigidus, grade 4 differs from grade 3 by:
o: Pain in the mid-range of motion with a positive grind test
items.e: Grade 4 has the radiographic changes of grade 3 plus mid-range pain; mid-range pain predicts failure of cheilectomy, so arthrodesis is preferred.

items.q: The synthetic cartilage implant (Cartiva) used for hallux rigidus is:
o: A two-component cobalt-chrome total joint replacement
A resurfacing of the proximal phalanx only with ceramic
A polyvinyl alcohol hydrogel plug implanted into the metatarsal head as a hemiarthroplasty
items.e: Cartiva is a PVA hydrogel hemiarthroplasty for the metatarsal head; early results were promising, but later series show mixed outcomes and a notable conversion rate to fusion.

items.q: The isolated cheilectomy for hallux rigidus gives best results when the patient's pain is:
o: At the extremes of motion, especially dorsiflexion, with preserved mid-range
Throughout the arc with a positive grind test
items.e: Dorsal impingement pain at the end of dorsiflexion responds to osteophyte removal; mid-range pain indicates diffuse arthritis better treated by fusion.

items.q: A 38-year-old premenopausal woman on long-term antiepileptics has a DXA scan. Which result should be used to interpret her bone density?
o: T-score, with osteoporosis at -2.5 or below
Z-score, where -2.0 or below is 'below the expected range for age'
items.e: In premenopausal women, men under 50 and children the Z-score (age-matched) is used; a Z-score of -2.0 or below should prompt a search for secondary causes. The WHO T-score definition applies to postmenopausal women and older men.

items.q: According to the WHO definitions, 'severe (established) osteoporosis' is:
o: A T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 with a fragility fracture
A T-score of -2.5 or below plus one or more fragility fractures
A T-score of -3.5 or below without fracture
items.e: Established osteoporosis is a T-score at or below -2.5 together with a fragility fracture; a hip or vertebral fragility fracture alone also allows a clinical diagnosis of osteoporosis.

items.q: Under US (BHOF/NOF) guidance, pharmacological treatment is recommended for a postmenopausal woman with osteopenia when her FRAX 10-year probability is:
o: Hip fracture 3% or more, or major osteoporotic fracture 20% or more
items.e: The US thresholds for treating osteopenia are FRAX hip 3% or more or major osteoporotic 20% or more; other countries such as the UK use age-dependent thresholds (NOGG).

items.q: Which patient would be classed as 'very high risk' under AACE/ACE 2020 and considered for anabolic therapy first?
o: A 62-year-old with a T-score of -2.6 and no fractures
A 55-year-old with osteopenia and FRAX major fracture risk of 12%
A 70-year-old who sustained a vertebral fracture while taking alendronate
items.e: Very high risk includes fracture on approved therapy, fracture in the past 12 months, multiple fractures, T-score below -3.0, high fall risk or very high FRAX (major over 30%, hip over 4.5%).

items.q: Why do current guidelines favour giving an anabolic agent before, rather than after, an antiresorptive in very-high-risk patients?
o: The anabolic-then-antiresorptive sequence gives larger BMD gains than the reverse order
Anabolics work only in treatment-naive bone
items.e: Prior antiresorptive therapy blunts the anabolic response (and switching from denosumab to teriparatide causes hip bone loss), whereas following an anabolic with an antiresorptive consolidates and extends the gain.

items.q: Three to six months after starting oral alendronate, which test best confirms adherence and biological response?
o: Serum CTX showing suppression of bone resorption
items.e: CTX, a resorption marker, falls substantially within 3-6 months of effective antiresorptive therapy; DXA changes are too small to detect before 1-2 years.

items.q: Treatment failure in osteoporosis, prompting review of adherence and secondary causes and a switch to a more potent or anabolic agent, is defined as:
o: Two or more incident fragility fractures while on therapy
Any decrease in BMD below the least significant change at 6 months
Failure of serum calcium to rise
A single wrist fracture in the first month of treatment
items.e: Failure is two or more incident fractures, or one fracture plus inadequate suppression of turnover markers or significant BMD loss, after adequate adherence.

items.q: After a fragility fracture, the risk of a further fracture is highest:
o: In the 5-10 years after the fracture
items.e: Refracture risk is concentrated in the first 1-2 years, which is the rationale for urgent assessment by a fracture liaison service and for rapidly acting or anabolic drugs.

items.q: The osteoporosis 'treatment gap' refers to the finding that after a fragility fracture:
o: Most patients are over-treated with anabolic drugs
Only about 20-30% or fewer of patients receive osteoporosis treatment
Hip fractures are treated but wrist fractures are not operated on
Men receive more treatment than women
items.e: Most fragility fracture patients leave hospital without assessment or treatment; fracture liaison services (Capture the Fracture, Own the Bone) close this gap.

items.q: Which long-term drug used in breast cancer treatment is a recognised cause of secondary osteoporosis?
items.e: Aromatase inhibitors reduce residual oestrogen and accelerate bone loss; tamoxifen is bone-protective in postmenopausal women.

items.q: Under the ASBMR 2013 revised case definition, an atypical femoral fracture must be located:
o: Between the distal lesser trochanter and the proximal supracondylar flare
In the intertrochanteric region with spiral extension
items.e: AFFs occur along the femoral diaphysis from just distal to the lesser trochanter to just proximal to the supracondylar flare; femoral neck and intertrochanteric fractures are excluded.

items.q: How many of the five major features are required to classify a femoral shaft fracture as atypical under the ASBMR 2013 definition?
items.e: At least four of the five major features are required; minor features (such as bilaterality or prodromal pain) are not required.

items.q: Which fracture is specifically excluded from the definition of an atypical femoral fracture?
o: A transverse subtrochanteric fracture after a fall from standing
A periprosthetic fracture below a hip stem
An incomplete lateral cortical fracture with beaking
items.e: Periprosthetic fractures, pathological fractures from tumour, femoral neck and intertrochanteric fractures with spiral subtrochanteric extension are excluded.

items.q: Which is a MINOR (not major) feature in the ASBMR definition of an atypical femoral fracture?
o: Origin of the fracture at the lateral cortex
Generalised cortical thickening of the femoral diaphysis
items.e: Generalised diaphyseal cortical thickening, prodromal pain, bilaterality, delayed healing and drug exposure are minor features; localised lateral cortical beaking is a major feature.

items.q: After a bisphosphonate is stopped, the risk of atypical femoral fracture:
o: Falls rapidly, by roughly 70% for each year off the drug
items.e: AFF risk is related to duration of exposure and declines quickly after cessation, unlike the protective effect against osteoporotic fractures, which wanes slowly.

items.q: Which patient characteristic increases the risk of atypical femoral fracture during bisphosphonate therapy?
o: Asian ethnicity and lateral femoral bowing
items.e: Asian women and femurs with lateral bowing (higher tensile strain on the lateral cortex) have a markedly higher AFF risk; glucocorticoids and long duration also contribute.

items.q: The proposed mechanism of atypical femoral fractures with long-term bisphosphonates is:
o: Suppressed remodelling impairing repair of microdamage, increasing brittleness at the tensile lateral cortex
items.e: Prolonged suppression of turnover allows microcracks to accumulate and makes mineralisation more homogeneous and brittle, so fatigue fractures start at the lateral (tension) cortex.

items.q: A 66-year-old on alendronate for 9 years has an incidental incomplete lateral cortical lesion of the femoral shaft on a DXA extended femur image. She is pain-free and there is no visible fracture line. Appropriate management is:
o: Continue alendronate and review in 2 years
Stop the bisphosphonate, protected weight bearing, consider teriparatide and nail if no improvement in 2-3 months
items.e: Painless incomplete AFF without a fracture line can be managed conservatively after stopping antiresorptives; painful lesions or a visible 'dreaded black line' merit prophylactic nailing. Denosumab also causes AFF.
