items.q: The preferred fixation for a complete atypical femoral shaft fracture is:
o: Intramedullary nailing, commonly with a cephalomedullary nail
items.e: Load-sharing nails have lower failure rates than plates; cephalomedullary nails protect the femoral neck. Delayed union is common.

items.q: When nailing an atypical femoral fracture in a markedly laterally bowed femur, the main technical hazard is:
o: Iatrogenic fracture or malreduction because the straight nail does not match the bow
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
items.e: A straight nail in a bowed femur risks anterior or lateral cortical perforation, iatrogenic fracture and varus malreduction; entry point and reduction must be adjusted.

items.q: After diagnosing a complete atypical femoral fracture, which investigation is mandatory?
items.e: AFFs are frequently bilateral, so the opposite femur should be imaged with full-length radiographs, MRI or DXA extended femur scan.

items.q: What is the effect of starting a bisphosphonate soon after a fragility fracture on fracture healing?
o: It produces a larger callus with delayed remodelling but no clinically meaningful delay in union
items.e: Animal and clinical data show bigger, slower-remodelling callus without a clinical delay, so bisphosphonates can be started early (HORIZON-RFT).

items.q: A 76-year-old woman with osteoporosis and a creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min needs antiresorptive therapy. Which agent is suitable because it is not cleared by the kidney?
items.e: Denosumab is not renally cleared, but calcium and vitamin D must be checked because severe hypocalcaemia is a risk in advanced CKD. Bisphosphonates are avoided below about 30-35 mL/min.

items.q: Teriparatide is contraindicated in a 19-year-old man with osteoporosis whose radiographs show:
items.e: Open growth plates are a contraindication because of the theoretical osteosarcoma risk seen in rats; others are Paget disease, unexplained high ALP, prior skeletal radiation and skeletal malignancy.

items.q: Raloxifene belongs to which drug class?
items.e: Raloxifene is a SERM: oestrogen agonist on bone and antagonist on breast and endometrium; bazedoxifene is another.

items.q: The acute phase reaction after a first zoledronic acid infusion can be reduced by:
o: Paracetamol given around the time of the infusion
items.e: Paracetamol reduces the flu-like reaction; zoledronate must be infused over at least 15 minutes to protect the kidney.

items.q: Which oral condition is a contraindication to oral bisphosphonates?
o: Gastro-oesophageal reflux controlled with a proton pump inhibitor
items.e: Conditions that delay oesophageal emptying (stricture, achalasia) or inability to stay upright for 30 minutes contraindicate oral bisphosphonates; IV zoledronate or denosumab are alternatives.

items.q: Bisphosphonates should be avoided in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy mainly because they:
o: Cross the placenta and are retained in the skeleton for years
Cause neural tube defects in all exposed fetuses
items.e: Bisphosphonates have prolonged skeletal retention and can be released during pregnancy and cross the placenta, with potential effects on fetal bone and calcium.

items.q: Romosozumab increases bone formation by blocking sclerostin, which is secreted by:
items.e: Sclerostin from osteocytes inhibits Wnt signalling by binding LRP5/6; blocking it releases the brake on bone formation and also reduces resorption.

items.q: What is the commonest cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over the age of 55?
items.e: DCM, an umbrella term including spondylotic myelopathy, OPLL and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy or ossification, is the most common cause of adult spinal cord dysfunction.

items.q: A Torg-Pavlov ratio below which value on a lateral cervical radiograph suggests a congenitally narrow canal?
items.e: The ratio of sagittal canal diameter to vertebral body width is about 1.0 normally; under 0.8 indicates congenital stenosis, a static risk factor for myelopathy.

items.q: An absolute sagittal cervical canal diameter below which value indicates absolute stenosis?
items.e: An AP diameter under 13 mm is relative stenosis and under 10 mm is absolute stenosis; normal subaxial canal is about 17 mm.

items.q: In cervical extension, the spondylotic canal narrows mainly because:
o: The disc bulges posteriorly and the cord lengthens
The ligamentum flavum buckles and the cord is pinched between the posteroinferior vertebral body and the lamina below
items.e: Extension shortens the canal, buckles the ligamentum flavum inwards and creates a pincer between the posteroinferior corner of the upper body and the lamina of the level below.

items.q: An electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine and limbs on neck flexion is called:
items.e: Lhermitte sign reflects dorsal column irritation and occurs in DCM and multiple sclerosis; Spurling reproduces radicular pain with extension, rotation and axial load.

items.q: The Hoffmann sign is elicited by:
o: Pressing on the vertex with the neck extended
Flicking the nail of the middle finger, producing flexion of the thumb and index finger
items.e: A positive Hoffmann sign is an upper motor neurone sign of the upper limb; stroking the sole is the Babinski response.

items.q: Tapping the brachioradialis tendon produces finger flexion with a reduced brachioradialis contraction (inverted radial reflex). This localises the lesion to:
items.e: The C6 reflex arc is interrupted (reduced brachioradialis jerk) while the cord below is released (hyperactive finger flexors, C8): this localises compression to C5-C6.

items.q: A brisk scapulohumeral reflex (scapular elevation and humeral abduction on tapping the scapular spine) in a myelopathic patient suggests cord compression at:
items.e: A hyperactive scapulohumeral reflex indicates an upper motor neurone lesion above the C4 segment, i.e. at or above C3-C4.

items.q: When a patient with cervical myelopathy holds the fingers extended and adducted, the ring and little fingers drift into abduction and flexion within 30 seconds. This is:
o: Wartenberg sign due to ulnar neuropathy only
The finger escape sign of the myelopathy hand
Pronator drift from a cerebral lesion
items.e: Ono's finger escape sign reflects ulnar intrinsic weakness from cervical cord involvement; it is graded by how quickly and how many digits drift.

items.q: In the grip-and-release test for myelopathy, a normal adult can make a full fist and release it at least how many times in 10 seconds?
items.e: Fewer than about 20 cycles in 10 seconds suggests myelopathic hand dysfunction (Ono).

items.q: A 68-year-old has hand clumsiness and spastic gait. Examination shows tongue fasciculations, wasting of the hands and legs, brisk reflexes and no sensory loss. Cervical MRI shows mild spondylosis without cord signal change. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs including the bulbar region (tongue) with no sensory involvement suggest motor neurone disease; EMG confirms widespread denervation.

items.q: A 55-year-old who had bariatric surgery 6 years ago and uses zinc-containing denture cream develops a progressive sensory ataxic myelopathy. MRI shows dorsal column T2 signal without compression and B12 is normal. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Copper deficiency (malabsorption or excess zinc) mimics subacute combined degeneration with dorsal column involvement and should be excluded when imaging shows no compression.

items.q: An elderly man is referred with gait imbalance thought to be myelopathy. He also has urinary incontinence and progressive memory loss, and reflexes are normal in the arms. The diagnosis to exclude with brain imaging is:
items.e: The triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus, an important mimic of DCM.

items.q: Tropical spastic paraparesis, a differential of myelopathy in endemic areas, is caused by:
items.e: HTLV-1-associated myelopathy produces slowly progressive spastic paraparesis with bladder dysfunction, mainly affecting the thoracic cord.

items.q: The maximum total score of the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) scale for cervical myelopathy is:
items.e: The mJOA has 18 points: upper limb motor 5, lower limb motor 7, upper limb sensation 3 and bladder 3; a lower score means worse myelopathy.

items.q: A patient with DCM has an mJOA score of 13. This severity is classified as:
items.e: Mild is 15-17, moderate 12-14 and severe under 12; moderate and severe DCM are indications for surgery under the AO Spine/WFNS guideline.

items.q: Which component of the mJOA score carries the most points?
items.e: Lower extremity motor function is scored 0-7, upper limb motor 0-5, sensation 0-3 and micturition 0-3.

items.q: On MRI in degenerative cervical myelopathy, which intramedullary signal pattern indicates irreversible myelomalacia and predicts a poorer surgical outcome?
o: Faint, poorly defined T2 hyperintensity only
Focal T1 hypointensity with corresponding T2 hyperintensity
items.e: T2 hyperintensity alone may represent reversible oedema, whereas added T1 hypointensity indicates cavitation or necrosis and a worse prognosis.

items.q: Scoliosis is defined radiographically as a lateral spinal curvature, measured by the Cobb method on a standing radiograph, of more than:
items.e: A coronal curve over 10 degrees with vertebral rotation defines scoliosis; smaller asymmetries are spinal asymmetry.

items.q: In the sagittal plane, the thoracic segment of a typical right thoracic adolescent idiopathic curve shows:
o: Normal kyphosis of 40 degrees in all cases
items.e: AIS is a three-dimensional deformity with apical lordosis (hypokyphosis) in the thoracic spine; marked hyperkyphosis with scoliosis should raise suspicion of another cause.

items.q: Early-onset scoliosis is defined as scoliosis of any cause with onset before which age, and its key danger is thoracic insufficiency syndrome?
items.e: EOS is onset before 10 years; most alveolar development occurs before about 8 years, so early deformity can impair lung growth.

items.q: In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, small curves occur almost equally in girls and boys, but among curves large enough to need treatment the female-to-male ratio is about:
items.e: Girls are far more likely to have progressive curves, so treated AIS shows roughly an 8-10:1 female predominance.

items.q: In school screening with a scoliometer during the Adams forward bend test, a reading of about 7 degrees corresponds roughly to a Cobb angle of:
items.e: A scoliometer angle of trunk rotation of 5-7 degrees or more is the usual referral threshold, roughly equivalent to a 20-degree Cobb angle.

items.q: A 12-year-old girl with a 30-degree right thoracic curve has an absent right-sided superficial abdominal reflex with a normal left side. The most appropriate next investigation is:
o: MRI of the whole neural axis to look for a syrinx or Chiari malformation
Bone scan to exclude osteoid osteoma
Nerve conduction studies of the lower limbs
items.e: Asymmetric abdominal reflexes suggest an intraspinal anomaly such as syringomyelia with Chiari malformation, so whole-spine MRI is indicated.

items.q: On the Risser grading of iliac apophyseal ossification (US system), Risser 4 means:
o: Ossification covers 50% of the iliac crest
The apophysis has fused completely to the ilium
The apophysis has ossified along its full length but is not yet fused to the ilium
items.e: Risser 1-4 correspond to 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% excursion of ossification; Risser 5 is fusion to the ilium.

items.q: In girls with AIS, the peak height velocity of the adolescent growth spurt typically occurs:
o: Before Risser 1, while the triradiate cartilage is still open
items.e: Peak growth occurs around Risser 0 with an open triradiate cartilage, so the Risser sign underestimates remaining growth; menarche follows peak height velocity by about a year.

items.q: In the Sanders skeletal maturity staging, based on a hand radiograph, the stage that corresponds to peak height velocity and highest curve progression risk is:
o: Stage 4 (distal phalangeal physes beginning to close)
Stage 8 (all hand and distal radial physes fused)
items.e: Sanders 3, with capping of the phalangeal epiphyses, marks the steepest growth phase and predicts curve progression better than the Risser sign.

items.q: In girls with AIS, menarche usually occurs in relation to peak height velocity:
o: About 2 years before peak height velocity
About 1 year after peak height velocity
At the same time as Risser 5
items.e: Menarche typically follows the peak of the growth spurt by around a year, so a premenarchal girl still has substantial growth and progression risk.

items.q: The most common curve type in the Lenke classification of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is:
items.e: Lenke 1 (structural main thoracic curve only) is the commonest pattern, usually treated by selective thoracic fusion.

items.q: A Lenke curve has both a structural main thoracic curve and a structural thoracolumbar/lumbar curve, with the thoracolumbar/lumbar curve being the larger (major) curve. Its Lenke type is:
items.e: Lenke 6 is a structural TL/L major curve with a structural main thoracic minor curve; Lenke 3 is the same pair with the thoracic curve major.

items.q: In the Lenke lumbar modifier, modifier C means the centre sacral vertical line:
o: Lies entirely medial to (does not touch) the apical lumbar vertebral body
Passes between the pedicles of the apical lumbar vertebra
Touches the apical vertebral body or pedicle
Passes through the L3 spinous process
items.e: Modifier A has the CSVL between the apical pedicles, B touching the apical body or pedicle, and C completely medial to the apical vertebra.

items.q: Besides side-bending of 25 degrees or more, a proximal thoracic or thoracolumbar minor curve is also considered structural in the Lenke system if the regional sagittal kyphosis is:
items.e: Kyphosis of 20 degrees or more at T2-T5 or T10-L2 makes the regional curve structural, which usually means it must be included in the fusion.

items.q: The Nash-Moe method assesses vertebral rotation in scoliosis by:
o: Rib-vertebra angle difference at the apex
Spinous process height on lateral radiographs
Position of the pedicle shadows relative to the vertebral body on the PA radiograph
items.e: Nash-Moe grades apical rotation from the migration of the convex pedicle towards the midline of the vertebral body.

items.q: A 14-month-old boy has a 22-degree left thoracic curve. The apical rib-vertebra angle difference (RVAD) is 25 degrees and the convex rib head overlaps the vertebral body. The best interpretation is:
o: Benign postural curve; no follow-up needed
High risk of progression; treat, for example with serial derotational casting
items.e: In infantile idiopathic scoliosis, an RVAD over 20 degrees and a phase 2 rib head (overlapping the vertebral body) predict progression (Mehta).

items.q: Compared with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, infantile idiopathic scoliosis is more typically:
o: A left thoracic curve in a boy, often with plagiocephaly, and usually resolves
A right thoracic curve in a girl that always progresses
Associated with a unilateral unsegmented bar
items.e: Infantile idiopathic curves are commonly left thoracic in boys, are associated with plagiocephaly and hip dysplasia, and most resolve spontaneously.

items.q: The non-operative technique of serial derotational elongation-flexion casting under general anaesthesia, which can cure progressive infantile idiopathic curves when started early, is associated with:
items.e: Mehta casting applies derotation and elongation through serial casts; started early in infantile scoliosis it can achieve permanent correction.

items.q: A 25-year-old woman with untreated AIS has a 58-degree right thoracic curve. After skeletal maturity, such a curve is expected to:
o: Continue to progress by about 1 degree per year
Progress by about 10 degrees per year
items.e: Thoracic curves over about 50 degrees at maturity continue to progress slowly (about 1 degree per year), whereas curves under 30 degrees rarely progress.

items.q: Untreated thoracic idiopathic curves of greater than about 100 degrees carry a risk of:
o: Cor pulmonale from restrictive lung disease
items.e: Severe thoracic curves cause restrictive pulmonary impairment from about 70-100 degrees and may lead to cor pulmonale beyond about 100 degrees.

items.q: A 12-year-old premenarchal girl, Risser 0, has a 32-degree right thoracic curve. The recommended management is:
items.e: Skeletally immature patients (Risser 0-2) with curves of 25-40 degrees should be braced; surgery is reserved for curves over 45-50 degrees.

items.q: In BrAIST (Weinstein, NEJM 2013), the dose-response analysis showed that brace wear of more than about how many hours per day gave success rates of about 90%?
items.e: Success rose with hours worn; average wear over about 13 hours a day achieved roughly 90% avoidance of progression to the surgical threshold.

items.q: Night-time bending braces such as the Charleston or Providence are best suited to which curve?
o: A double thoracic curve with high left shoulder
A 60-degree thoracic curve in a mature patient
A single thoracolumbar or lumbar curve
A congenital curve from a hemivertebra
items.e: Night-time braces overcorrect while recumbent and work best for single TL/L curves; they are not indicated for large, mature or congenital curves.

items.q: The principal goal of bracing in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is to:
o: Improve pulmonary function in curves over 80 degrees
Prevent progression to the surgical threshold
items.e: Bracing halts or slows progression during growth; at the end of treatment the curve is usually similar to its pre-brace magnitude, not corrected.

items.q: A 15-year-old with a Lenke 1A curve (52-degree main thoracic, nonstructural 30-degree lumbar curve) is planned for surgery. The usual approach is:
o: Selective posterior fusion of the main thoracic curve, allowing the lumbar curve to correct spontaneously
Fusion of both curves from T2 to L4
Anterior fusion of the lumbar curve only
items.e: In Lenke 1 curves with lumbar modifier A or B, only the structural main thoracic curve is fused; the nonstructural lumbar curve corrects spontaneously, preserving lumbar motion segments.

items.q: Which instrumentation construct provides the greatest three-dimensional correction in posterior surgery for AIS?
items.e: Pedicle screws engage all three columns and allow better coronal correction and apical derotation than hook, wire or distraction systems.

items.q: Anterior vertebral body tethering for idiopathic scoliosis relies on:
o: Rigid fusion of the concave side
Distraction of the concave side in a mature spine
Growth modulation of the convex side in a skeletally immature spine
items.e: Tethering compresses the convex physes so that continued growth on the concave side corrects the curve; it needs remaining growth and is still an evolving technique.

items.q: During spinal deformity correction, which neuromonitoring modality gives the earliest warning of compromise to the anterior (motor) cord?
o: Free-running EMG of the abdominal muscles
items.e: MEPs monitor corticospinal tracts and detect motor compromise sooner than SSEPs, which monitor the dorsal columns.

items.q: During AIS correction, transcranial MEPs are lost bilaterally just after rod rotation. Among the first steps is to:
o: Raise mean arterial pressure and release the correction
Complete the procedure and examine the patient next day
items.e: Signal loss is managed by raising MAP, checking anaesthesia, temperature and technical factors, releasing correction and checking screws, with a Stagnara wake-up test if signals do not recover.

items.q: The Stagnara test used during scoliosis surgery is a:
o: Intraoperative wake-up test to check voluntary foot movement
Measurement of pedicle screw breach by stimulation
Test for dural tear by Valsalva
items.e: The Stagnara wake-up test lightens anaesthesia so the patient moves the feet on command; it is now a backup to SSEP/MEP monitoring.

items.q: Two years after posterior fusion for AIS, a girl has low-grade wound discomfort and a draining sinus with negative early blood cultures. The commonest organism in such delayed infections is:
items.e: Late infections after spinal instrumentation are often caused by low-virulence Cutibacterium acnes, which needs prolonged culture incubation.

items.q: A 9-year-old (Risser 0, open triradiate cartilage) undergoes posterior-only fusion with hooks for a progressive curve. Over the next years, rotation and the curve increase despite a solid fusion. This is the:
o: Adding-on phenomenon from fusing too short distally
Crankshaft phenomenon from continued anterior growth
items.e: Continued anterior vertebral growth against a posterior tether causes the spine to rotate and the curve to increase; anterior fusion or pedicle screw constructs reduce this risk.

items.q: After selective thoracic fusion for AIS, the curve below the lowest instrumented vertebra progressively lengthens and increases on follow-up. This complication is called:
items.e: Adding-on is distal extension of the curve below the fusion, usually from choosing too short a lowest instrumented vertebra.

items.q: Loss of lumbar lordosis after scoliosis fusion, with forward stooping and back pain, was classically caused by:
o: Harrington distraction instrumentation into the lower lumbar spine
items.e: Distraction rods extended into the lumbar spine flatten lordosis, producing flatback syndrome.

items.q: A thin 14-year-old girl starts bilious vomiting and abdominal distension 4 days after posterior correction of a large thoracolumbar curve. The most likely cause is:
o: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome compressing the third part of the duodenum
items.e: Lengthening the spine narrows the angle between the SMA and aorta, compressing the duodenum; thin patients are at risk, and treatment is usually decompression and nutrition.

items.q: The drug with the best evidence for reducing blood loss in posterior spinal fusion for scoliosis is:
items.e: Tranexamic acid significantly reduces perioperative blood loss and transfusion in scoliosis surgery.

items.q: Traditional growing rods for early-onset scoliosis are typically lengthened surgically about every:
items.e: Traditional growing rods are lengthened about every 6 months; repeated operations lead to diminishing gains and autofusion, which MCGRs aim to reduce.

items.q: A 4-year-old with congenital fused ribs and a constricted hemithorax has thoracic insufficiency syndrome. The growth-friendly device designed specifically to expand the chest wall is:
items.e: VEPTR attaches to ribs and allows expansion thoracostomy and lengthening, addressing thoracic insufficiency from fused ribs.

items.q: The Shilla system for early-onset scoliosis works by:
o: Lengthening rods with an external magnet
Expanding the ribs through rib cradles
Fusing the apex and allowing rods to slide through screws above and below as the spine grows
items.e: Shilla is a guided-growth construct: the apex is corrected and fused while the proximal and distal screws glide on the rods.

items.q: With repeated lengthenings of traditional growing rods, the gain in length achieved at each lengthening progressively decreases. This is known as:
items.e: Each successive distraction yields less length because of spinal stiffening and autofusion, limiting the duration of growing-rod treatment.

items.q: Compared with AIS, juvenile idiopathic scoliosis (onset 4-10 years):
o: Has a high progression risk, with about 70% needing treatment, and a higher rate of neural axis abnormality
Occurs mainly in boys with left curves that resolve
items.e: Juvenile curves have a long growth period ahead and frequently progress, and MRI is commonly obtained because intraspinal anomalies are more frequent.

items.q: In congenital scoliosis, which vertebral anomaly has the best prognosis with little or no progression?
items.e: A block vertebra grows symmetrically and causes little deformity, whereas a unilateral bar, especially with a contralateral hemivertebra, progresses rapidly.

items.q: A child with congenital scoliosis from a hemivertebra must be screened for associated anomalies. Which pair of tests is mandatory in addition to whole-spine MRI?
o: Hearing test and ophthalmology review only
items.e: Genitourinary (about 20%) and cardiac (about 10-25%) anomalies are common, and intraspinal anomalies occur in about 20-40%, so kidneys, heart and cord are all screened.

items.q: A child has a short neck, low posterior hairline and restricted neck motion with congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae. The associated scapular anomaly commonly seen is:
o: Scapular winging from long thoracic nerve palsy
items.e: The classic Klippel-Feil triad is often accompanied by Sprengel deformity, renal anomalies and hearing loss.

items.q: A 3-year-old has a progressive curve from a single fully segmented lumbar hemivertebra. The preferred surgical treatment is:
o: Posterior hemivertebra excision with short-segment fusion
Long posterior fusion from T4 to the pelvis
items.e: Early excision of an isolated hemivertebra (ideally under about 5 years) with short fusion corrects the deformity and avoids long fusions; bracing does not control rigid congenital curves.

items.q: Convex hemiepiphysiodesis for congenital scoliosis aims to:
o: Lengthen the concave side by distraction
Arrest growth on the convex side while the concave side continues to grow
Excise the hemivertebra through an anterior approach
Fuse the whole spine in situ
items.e: Convex growth arrest combined with ongoing concave growth allows gradual correction in young children with modest curves.

items.q: A toddler has congenital kyphosis from anterior failure of formation (type I) of T11. The main concern and usual management are:
o: High risk of paraplegia; early posterior fusion
Spontaneous anterior fusion; no follow-up needed
items.e: Type I congenital kyphosis progresses and can cause paraplegia, so early posterior fusion is advised; type II (failure of segmentation) is less dangerous.

items.q: A 13-year-old with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy has a 70-degree long C-shaped thoracolumbar curve with marked pelvic obliquity affecting sitting. The fusion should usually extend:
o: Only across the apical three vertebrae
From T10 to L4 without pelvic fixation
From the upper thoracic spine to the pelvis, for example with S2-alar-iliac screws
items.e: Neuromuscular curves with pelvic obliquity require long fusion to the pelvis to level the pelvis and restore sitting balance.

items.q: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, spinal fusion has classically been recommended:
o: Early, once the curve reaches about 20-30 degrees and before FVC falls below about 30-35%
Only after the curve exceeds 90 degrees
Only after the patient is ventilator dependent
items.e: Curves in DMD progress rapidly after loss of ambulation while lung function declines, so early fusion while FVC is adequate was the traditional rule.

items.q: A 12-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a short, sharply angulated thoracic curve with pencilled ribs, vertebral scalloping and dural ectasia. The appropriate management is:
o: Early anterior and posterior spinal fusion
items.e: Dystrophic NF1 curves progress rapidly and respond poorly to bracing; early combined anterior and posterior fusion reduces pseudarthrosis and progression.

items.q: In NF1, a non-dystrophic curve that later acquires dystrophic features such as rib penciling is said to have undergone:
items.e: Modulation of non-dystrophic into dystrophic curves is well recognised in NF1, especially in young children, so close follow-up is needed.

items.q: A main reason that pedicle screw fixation is more difficult in Marfan syndrome scoliosis is:
o: Absent pedicles from failure of segmentation
Dural ectasia with thinned pedicles and laminae
items.e: Dural ectasia erodes the pedicles and laminae, and Marfan curves are larger and more rigid with higher pseudarthrosis and complication rates.

items.q: The normal range of thoracic kyphosis (T5-T12) in adolescents is about:
items.e: Thoracic kyphosis between about 20 and 45 degrees is normal; Scheuermann kyphosis is rigid kyphosis greater than 45 degrees.

items.q: A 15-year-old boy has a 55-degree thoracic kyphosis that corrects fully on prone hyperextension, with no vertebral wedging on radiographs. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Postural roundback is flexible and corrects on extension; Scheuermann kyphosis is rigid with wedging of three adjacent vertebrae.

items.q: A 13-year-old boy (Risser 1) has a 62-degree rigid thoracic Scheuermann kyphosis with mild back pain. The recommended initial treatment is:
o: Bracing with a Milwaukee or modified extension brace
items.e: In skeletally immature patients with Scheuermann kyphosis of about 50-75 degrees, bracing can halt progression; fusion is considered for curves over 75 degrees or refractory pain.

items.q: When fusing a Scheuermann kyphosis posteriorly, the distal fusion level is chosen as the sagittal stable vertebra mainly to avoid:
items.e: Ending the fusion short of the sagittal stable vertebra (the most proximal lumbar vertebra bisected by the posterior sacral vertical line) risks distal junctional kyphosis.

items.q: For a rigid, sharp multiplanar deformity requiring more than 40 degrees of correction at one level, the osteotomy of choice, carrying the highest neurological risk, is:
items.e: VCR removes the whole vertebral segment, allowing large multiplanar corrections at the cost of the highest neurological and blood-loss risk.

items.q: A Ponte (Smith-Petersen) osteotomy can only achieve correction at a level where:
o: The anterior column is solidly fused
The anterior disc space is mobile
A pedicle subtraction osteotomy has already been done
items.e: Posterior column osteotomies hinge on the disc and open it anteriorly, so they need a mobile anterior disc; fused anterior columns require a three-column osteotomy.

items.q: A 13-year-old has a mild lumbar curve on a standing radiograph that disappears when a block is placed under the shorter leg. The curve is best described as:
o: Non-structural compensatory scoliosis from leg-length discrepancy
items.e: Compensatory curves from leg-length inequality are non-structural, lack fixed rotation and correct when the pelvis is levelled.

items.q: Because of inter-observer measurement error, progression of a scoliotic curve on serial radiographs is usually defined as an increase in Cobb angle of more than:
items.e: Cobb measurement error is about plus or minus 5 degrees, so an increase greater than 5 degrees is taken as true progression.

items.q: Ewing sarcoma shows striking ethnic variation in incidence. It is:
o: Commonest in people of European ancestry and rare in people of African ancestry
Commonest in people of African ancestry
Equally common in all ethnic groups
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is much commoner in people of European ancestry and rare in those of African ancestry, partly explained by germline variation at GGAA microsatellites near EGR2.

items.q: Genome-wide association studies of Ewing sarcoma susceptibility identified a GGAA microsatellite enhancer, bound by the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion protein, near which gene?
items.e: Polymorphic GGAA repeats near EGR2 act as enhancers when bound by EWSR1-FLI1; longer repeats in European populations help explain the ethnic difference in incidence. TP53 and RB1 are linked to osteosarcoma, EXT1 to osteochondromas.

items.q: Among primary malignant bone tumours of children and adolescents, Ewing sarcoma ranks:
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is the second commonest primary bone malignancy in the young, after osteosarcoma.

items.q: The commonest single bone affected by Ewing sarcoma is the:
items.e: The femur is the commonest single site, followed by the pelvis (ilium); together pelvis and femur account for about half of cases.

items.q: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma arising in the soft tissues of the trunk or limbs:
o: Is treated with the same multimodal protocol as skeletal Ewing sarcoma
Is benign and treated by marginal excision
Is treated with surgery alone because it is chemoresistant
Does not carry an EWSR1 rearrangement
items.e: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma (about 15-20% of cases) shares the same genetics and behaviour and is treated with induction chemotherapy, local control and consolidation.

items.q: In Ewing sarcoma arising beneath the periosteum, the outer cortex may show a shallow concave erosion caused by external pressure of the tumour. This radiological sign is called:
items.e: Saucerisation is external cortical erosion by a subperiosteal mass; endosteal scalloping arises from within the medullary cavity (as in chondrosarcoma).

items.q: A 15-year-old has an iliac lesion with mixed sclerosis and a large soft-tissue mass. A trainee concludes it must be osteosarcoma because of the sclerosis. The correct statement is:
o: Sclerosis in a pelvic lesion is diagnostic of lymphoma
Reactive sclerosis occurs in up to a third of Ewing sarcomas, especially pelvic ones
Ewing sarcoma always produces tumour osteoid
items.e: Reactive (non-tumour) bone formation makes up to a third of Ewing sarcomas look sclerotic, particularly in flat bones; histology and molecular tests decide. Tumour osteoid is a feature of osteosarcoma, not Ewing.

items.q: At diagnosis, detectable metastases are present in approximately what proportion of patients with Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: About a quarter have overt metastases (lungs commonest, then bone and marrow); micrometastatic disease is assumed in all, so every patient receives chemotherapy.

items.q: With modern multimodal therapy, the approximate 5-year survival for localised Ewing sarcoma is:
items.e: Localised disease has about 70-75% 5-year survival; isolated lung metastases about 40%; bone or marrow metastases under 20-30%.

items.q: Which pattern of metastatic Ewing sarcoma at diagnosis carries the better prognosis?
items.e: Isolated lung metastases have about 40% survival with chemotherapy and whole-lung irradiation, whereas bone or marrow metastases carry under 20-30% survival.

items.q: Which tumour volume threshold is widely used as an adverse prognostic factor in localised Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: Tumour volume over 200 mL (or largest dimension over 8 cm) is associated with poorer outcome and was used to define high-risk localised disease in European trials.

items.q: In patients treated with modern chemotherapy, how does the fusion type (EWSR1-FLI1 versus EWSR1-ERG) affect prognosis in Ewing sarcoma?
o: EWSR1-FLI1 type 1 fusions require no chemotherapy
EWSR1-ERG tumours are chemoresistant and treated by surgery alone
It has no independent prognostic value
items.e: Older data suggested type 1 EWSR1-FLI1 fusions did better, but with current regimens fusion type is not prognostic; metastases, site, volume and histological response are.

items.q: The Children's Oncology Group trial AEWS0031 (Womer et al., 2012) in localised Ewing sarcoma showed that:
o: Giving VDC/IE every 2 weeks instead of every 3 weeks improved event-free survival without more toxicity
High-dose chemotherapy with stem-cell rescue was superior to standard therapy
Radiotherapy alone was equivalent to surgery for local control
items.e: Interval-compressed (2-weekly) VDC/IE improved event-free survival over 3-weekly cycles with similar toxicity, establishing interval compression as standard in North America.

items.q: In the Euro-EWING 99 R2Loc randomised trial (Whelan et al., 2018), high-dose busulfan-melphalan with autologous stem-cell rescue improved event-free survival in which group?
o: High-risk localised disease (poor histological response or large tumour volume)
items.e: BuMel benefited high-risk localised disease. In the R2Pulm arm (lung metastases) it gave no significant benefit over standard chemotherapy plus whole-lung irradiation.

items.q: In standard Ewing sarcoma protocols, definitive local control (surgery and/or radiotherapy) is usually performed:
o: Before any chemotherapy, immediately after biopsy
At the end of all chemotherapy, about 1 year after diagnosis
After induction chemotherapy, at about weeks 12-18
items.e: Local control follows about 12-18 weeks of induction chemotherapy and reassessment imaging, and is followed by consolidation chemotherapy; total treatment lasts about 9-12 months.

items.q: A 14-year-old has a large sacral Ewing sarcoma for which resection would sacrifice bowel and bladder function. The usual local-control approach after induction chemotherapy is:
o: Observation, since chemotherapy alone is curative
items.e: Ewing sarcoma is radiosensitive, so unresectable or functionally unacceptable sites (sacrum, spine, many pelvic tumours) receive definitive radiotherapy around 55-56 Gy, accepting a higher local recurrence rate than surgery.

items.q: A survivor of pelvic Ewing sarcoma treated with radiotherapy 12 years ago develops a new painful destructive lesion within the radiation field. The commonest histology of such a radiation-induced sarcoma is:
items.e: Radiation-associated sarcomas arise in the field after a long latency (often over 5-10 years) and are most often osteosarcoma or undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, with a poor prognosis.

items.q: In survivors of Ewing sarcoma, therapy-related acute myeloid leukaemia or myelodysplasia is most associated with exposure to:
items.e: Topoisomerase II inhibitors (etoposide) and alkylators (cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide) cause secondary leukaemia/MDS; vincristine causes neuropathy.

items.q: A child receiving Ewing sarcoma chemotherapy develops glycosuria, phosphaturia and hypophosphataemic bone changes. Which drug is responsible?
items.e: Ifosfamide causes proximal tubular damage (Fanconi syndrome) leading to hypophosphataemic rickets or osteomalacia; doxorubicin's signature toxicity is cardiomyopathy.

items.q: A 17-year-old has a relapse of Ewing sarcoma 14 months after completing treatment. Which statement is correct?
o: Relapse within 2 years has a better prognosis than late relapse
Relapsed Ewing sarcoma is treated by amputation alone
Relapse is managed with the same induction regimen with excellent cure rates
Early relapse has a very poor prognosis; irinotecan-temozolomide is a common salvage regimen
items.e: Relapse within 2 years carries very poor survival (overall under 15% after relapse). Salvage options include irinotecan-temozolomide, high-dose ifosfamide and high-dose chemotherapy with stem-cell rescue.

items.q: After induction chemotherapy, a 13-year-old has a localised Ewing sarcoma of the fibular diaphysis. The usual surgical management is:
o: Wide resection of the fibular segment without skeletal reconstruction
items.e: Expendable bones (fibula, rib, clavicle, parts of ilium) can be resected widely without reconstruction; the distal fibula is an exception where ankle stability may need addressing.

items.q: In Ewing sarcoma, the second commonest fusion (about 10% of cases) results from which translocation?
items.e: EWSR1-ERG from t(21;22) is the second commonest fusion after EWSR1-FLI1. FUS-DDIT3 is myxoid liposarcoma, SS18-SSX synovial sarcoma, EWSR1-ATF1 clear cell sarcoma.

items.q: Desmoplastic small round cell tumour, an intra-abdominal sarcoma of young males, carries which fusion?
items.e: DSRCT has t(11;22)(p13;q12) fusing EWSR1 to WT1 and shows polyphenotypic staining (keratin plus dot-like desmin).

items.q: Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma, which can mimic Ewing sarcoma because it contains small round cells and may be CD99 positive, is characterised by which fusion?
items.e: HEY1-NCOA2 is characteristic of mesenchymal chondrosarcoma. IDH1/2 mutations occur in conventional chondrosarcoma, EWSR1-NR4A3 in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma, COL1A1-PDGFB in DFSP.

items.q: Which of the following is classified by WHO 2020 as a 'Ewing-like' round cell sarcoma distinct from Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: Undifferentiated round cell sarcomas with CIC rearrangement, BCOR alteration (e.g. BCOR-CCNB3) or EWSR1 fused to non-ETS partners are now separate entities from Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: A 7-year-old has a lytic lesion with a small round cell infiltrate rich in eosinophils. Which immunohistochemical profile confirms Langerhans cell histiocytosis rather than Ewing sarcoma?
items.e: Langerhans cells express CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100; CD99/NKX2.2 suggests Ewing, CD20 B-cell lymphoma, desmin/myogenin rhabdomyosarcoma.

items.q: Primary lymphoma of bone is diagnosed only if, at presentation and for a defined period after diagnosis, there is no nodal or visceral disease. That period is classically:
items.e: Classically there should be no lymphoma elsewhere within 6 months of diagnosis; secondary bone involvement by systemic lymphoma is much commoner than primary bone lymphoma.

items.q: A uniformly dense 'ivory' vertebral body with normal size and contour in a young adult with cervical lymphadenopathy most suggests:
items.e: An ivory vertebra in a young adult suggests Hodgkin lymphoma; in older patients consider osteoblastic metastasis (prostate, breast). Paget disease enlarges the vertebra (picture frame), unlike lymphoma.

items.q: Why can radiographs of primary lymphoma of bone appear nearly normal despite extensive marrow and soft-tissue involvement on MRI?
o: The tumour permeates the cortex through small channels rather than destroying it
The tumour forms dense new bone that hides lysis
The lesion is confined to the epiphysis
items.e: Lymphoma cells spread through Haversian canals, so a large circumferential soft-tissue mass can surround a cortex that looks relatively intact on radiographs.

items.q: The recommended imaging for staging diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of bone under the Lugano classification is:
items.e: DLBCL is FDG-avid and Lugano staging and response assessment use PET-CT.

items.q: With modern rituximab-based chemotherapy, the 5-year survival of localised diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of bone is approximately:
items.e: Localised primary bone DLBCL has a good prognosis, about 70-90% at 5 years with R-CHOP with or without radiotherapy.

items.q: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) progresses to multiple myeloma or a related disorder at a rate of approximately:
items.e: MGUS progresses at about 1% per year lifelong; smouldering myeloma progresses faster (about 10% per year in the first 5 years).

items.q: Osteoblast suppression in multiple myeloma, which explains the normal alkaline phosphatase and lack of bone healing response, is mediated largely by myeloma-cell secretion of:
items.e: DKK1 (and sclerostin) inhibit Wnt signalling and osteoblast function, while increased RANKL and reduced OPG drive osteoclast activity; the result is purely lytic disease.

items.q: The commonest type of monoclonal protein secreted in multiple myeloma is:
items.e: IgG accounts for about half of myelomas, IgA about 20% and light-chain-only about 20%; IgM paraprotein suggests Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.

items.q: Compared with people of European ancestry, multiple myeloma in people of African ancestry is:
items.e: Myeloma (and MGUS) is about twice as common in people of African ancestry, in contrast to Ewing sarcoma which is rare in them.

items.q: The commonest presenting symptom of multiple myeloma is:
items.e: Bone pain, especially back pain from vertebral involvement or collapse, is the commonest presentation; anaemia-related fatigue is also frequent.

items.q: In the IMWG CRAB criteria, the hypercalcaemia threshold that counts as a myeloma-defining event is a serum calcium above:
items.e: Calcium over 2.75 mmol/L (11 mg/dL), or more than 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal, fulfils the C of CRAB.

items.q: For skeletal assessment in suspected multiple myeloma, IMWG now recommends which investigation in preference to the conventional radiographic skeletal survey?
o: Plain radiograph of the lumbar spine only
items.e: Whole-body low-dose CT detects lytic lesions more sensitively than the skeletal survey; PET-CT or whole-body MRI are alternatives. Bone scans miss purely lytic myeloma lesions.

items.q: Multiple small, well-defined lytic lesions throughout the calvarium on a lateral skull radiograph of a 68-year-old describe the:
items.e: Myeloma gives a raindrop or pepper-pot skull; cotton-wool skull is Paget disease, hair-on-end is chronic haemolytic anaemia, and button sequestrum suggests LCH.

items.q: In the International Staging System (ISS) for multiple myeloma, stage III is defined by:
o: Serum beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more
items.e: ISS III is beta-2 microglobulin 5.5 mg/L or more; stage I is beta-2 microglobulin under 3.5 mg/L with albumin 3.5 g/dL or more; stage II is neither. Lesion counts belong to the older Durie-Salmon system.

items.q: Bortezomib, a backbone drug in myeloma regimens such as VRd, acts as a:
items.e: Bortezomib inhibits the proteasome; lenalidomide is the immunomodulator, daratumumab the anti-CD38 antibody, denosumab the RANKL antibody.

items.q: Daratumumab, increasingly added to first-line myeloma regimens, targets:
items.e: Daratumumab is an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody; rituximab targets CD20 (used in lymphoma).

items.q: In the MRC Myeloma IX trial, zoledronic acid compared with clodronate:
o: Had no effect on survival or skeletal events
Reduced skeletal-related events and modestly improved overall survival
items.e: Zoledronic acid reduced skeletal events and gave a modest overall survival benefit, supporting bisphosphonates for all patients with myeloma needing therapy.

items.q: A patient on long-term monthly zoledronic acid for myeloma has exposed necrotic bone in the mandible after a dental extraction. This complication is:
items.e: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw occurs with potent antiresorptives (bisphosphonates, denosumab), especially after dental extraction; a dental review before starting therapy reduces the risk.

items.q: For a painful myeloma deposit in the rib without fracture risk, a commonly used palliative radiotherapy regimen is:
items.e: Myeloma is very radiosensitive, so low-dose regimens (8 Gy single fraction or 20 Gy in 5 fractions) control pain.

items.q: The CAFE randomised trial (Berenson et al., 2011) in patients with painful cancer-related vertebral compression fractures, mostly myeloma, showed that balloon kyphoplasty:
o: Improved pain, function and quality of life compared with non-surgical care
items.e: Kyphoplasty gave rapid, sustained improvement in back pain and function compared with non-surgical management; it did not alter survival.

items.q: After radiotherapy for a solitary plasmacytoma of bone, roughly what proportion of patients progress to multiple myeloma within 10 years?
items.e: Most solitary bone plasmacytomas eventually progress (about 50-70% at 10 years), so follow-up with protein electrophoresis and free light chains is required.

items.q: Extramedullary (soft-tissue) plasmacytoma most commonly arises in the:
items.e: Most extramedullary plasmacytomas occur in the head and neck (nasal cavity, sinuses, nasopharynx); they progress to myeloma less often than solitary plasmacytoma of bone.

items.q: A 62-year-old with myeloma develops bilateral nocturnal hand paraesthesia and macroglossia. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Light-chain (AL) amyloid deposition in the carpal tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome and in the tongue macroglossia.

items.q: A urine dipstick for protein is negative in a patient with light-chain myeloma. Why?
o: Light chains are never excreted in urine
Dipsticks detect mainly albumin and miss Bence Jones light chains
Light chains are destroyed by the kidney
items.e: Dipsticks detect albumin; Bence Jones proteins require urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (and serum free light-chain assay).

items.q: In Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, the single most important clinical prognostic factor is:
o: Age at onset of the disease
items.e: Children under about 6 years at onset have more remodelling potential and generally do well; onset after 8 years carries a poor prognosis.

items.q: Girls with Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease tend to have a worse prognosis than boys of the same age mainly because they:
o: Have a different blood supply to the femoral head
Are usually treated with bracing only
Reach skeletal maturity earlier, leaving less time for remodelling
items.e: Earlier skeletal maturation in girls reduces the remaining growth available to remodel the deformed head.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy (bone age 3 years) has Perthes disease with lateral pillar B involvement and mild loss of abduction. The most appropriate management is:
o: Observation with activity modification and physiotherapy to maintain motion
items.e: Young children (bone age under 6) generally do well without surgery; treatment focuses on symptom control and maintaining range of motion, especially abduction.

items.q: Abduction orthoses and Petrie casts were once widely used to contain the femoral head in Perthes disease. Current evidence suggests that bracing:
o: Is superior to surgical containment in children over 8 years
Has no proven benefit over the natural history and has largely been abandoned
Should be worn until full skeletal maturity
items.e: Studies, including Herring's multicentre study, showed bracing did no better than no treatment, so it is rarely used today.

items.q: A recognised disadvantage of proximal femoral varus osteotomy for containment in Perthes disease, compared with Salter innominate osteotomy, is:
o: Need for a second-stage pelvic procedure in every case
Limb shortening and a Trendelenburg gait from abductor weakness
items.e: Varus osteotomy shortens the limb and reduces abductor lever arm (often with relative trochanteric overgrowth); the Salter osteotomy slightly lengthens the limb.

items.q: Before a Salter innominate osteotomy is performed for containment in Perthes disease, the key prerequisite is that the hip:
o: Is in the residual stage of the disease
Has nearly full abduction with a containable, congruent head
items.e: A Salter osteotomy redirects the acetabulum anterolaterally; it requires a containable head and good abduction, otherwise it increases joint pressure.

items.q: In a child with Perthes disease being considered for containment surgery, dynamic arthrography is principally used to:
o: Assess whether the head can be contained and to detect hinge abduction
Show the extent of marrow oedema
items.e: Arthrography shows the cartilaginous head shape, its congruity and whether abduction contains the head or causes it to hinge on the lateral acetabular edge.

items.q: A 14-year-old with healed Perthes disease has a short neck, a high-riding greater trochanter above the femoral head and a positive Trendelenburg sign. The procedure that best improves abductor mechanics is:
o: Distal and lateral advancement of the greater trochanter
items.e: In the mature hip, trochanteric advancement (Wagner) restores the abductor lever arm and tension; epiphysiodesis only works when done before about 8 years.

items.q: A 20-year-old with healed Perthes disease has a large aspherical femoral head (coxa magna) causing impingement and instability. A procedure that directly reduces the size of the femoral head is:
o: Femoral head reduction osteotomy via surgical hip dislocation
items.e: Femoral head reduction osteotomy (Ganz) removes a central segment of the head through a surgical dislocation with an extended retinacular flap to restore sphericity and congruency.

items.q: Which environmental exposure has been consistently associated with an increased risk of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease?
items.e: Exposure to passive smoking and low socioeconomic status are associated with Perthes disease, possibly through effects on coagulation or vascularity.

items.q: In the initial (avascular) stage of Perthes disease before radiographic changes, a technetium bone scan typically shows:
o: Absent uptake (a photopenic area) in the capital femoral epiphysis
Increased uptake in the acetabulum only
items.e: Avascular epiphyseal bone appears cold on scintigraphy; revascularisation later produces increased uptake, starting laterally (lateral column formation).

items.q: Besides a smaller, sclerotic ossific nucleus, which radiographic sign is seen in the initial stage of Perthes disease?
o: Widening of the medial joint space
items.e: Widened medial joint space (from synovitis, cartilage hypertrophy and a smaller epiphysis) is an early sign; coxa magna and trochanteric overgrowth are late.

items.q: In healed Perthes disease, the term 'coxa magna' refers to:
items.e: Coxa magna is enlargement of the femoral head; coxa plana is flattening, and coxa breva is a short neck.

items.q: Which inherited coagulation abnormality has been reported in association with Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, though the link is controversial?
items.e: Thrombophilic states (factor V Leiden, protein C and S deficiency) have been linked to Perthes, supporting a vascular-occlusive theory; bleeding disorders are not.

items.q: The principle of containment treatment in Perthes disease is to:
o: Keep the femoral head within the acetabulum so that the acetabulum moulds it during fragmentation and reossification
Rest the hip in adduction to relieve the lateral pillar
items.e: Containing the softened head deep in the acetabulum lets it remodel spherically, reducing extrusion and deformity.

items.q: A 10-year-old with Perthes disease and lateral extrusion of the femoral head has a hip that is not suitable for redirectional osteotomy. A procedure that augments lateral acetabular coverage with bone graft is:
items.e: A shelf acetabuloplasty extends the lateral acetabular roof with graft, covering and containing the extruded part of the head.

items.q: In slipped capital femoral epiphysis, the relationship between the epiphysis and the femoral neck is best described as:
o: The epiphysis displaces laterally and the neck medially
The epiphysis and neck displace together with dislocation of the hip
The epiphysis remains in the acetabulum while the metaphysis displaces anteriorly and superiorly (externally rotated)
The epiphysis displaces anteriorly and superiorly out of the acetabulum
items.e: The epiphysis is held in the acetabulum by the ligamentum teres; the neck moves anterosuperiorly and rotates externally, so the epiphysis lies posterior and inferior to it.

items.q: The slip in SCFE occurs through which zone of the physis?
o: Zone of provisional calcification of the metaphysis
items.e: The hypertrophic zone, with large cells and little matrix, is the mechanically weakest region of the physis and is where the slip occurs.

items.q: The strongest risk factor associated with idiopathic slipped capital femoral epiphysis is:
items.e: Most children with SCFE are above the 95th centile for BMI; obesity increases shear forces across the physis.

items.q: The most common endocrine disorder associated with slipped capital femoral epiphysis is:
items.e: Hypothyroidism is the commonest endocrine association; growth hormone deficiency or treatment, hypogonadism and renal osteodystrophy are others.

items.q: A 12-year-old on dialysis for chronic renal failure develops bilateral slipped capital femoral epiphyses. The underlying mechanism is:
o: Renal osteodystrophy with secondary hyperparathyroidism weakening the physis
items.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in renal osteodystrophy disrupts the metaphyseal side of the physis; bilateral involvement is common, so both hips are fixed.

items.q: In the traditional temporal classification of SCFE, a chronic slip is one in which symptoms have been present for longer than:
items.e: Acute slips have symptoms under 3 weeks; chronic slips (the commonest) over 3 weeks, with metaphyseal remodelling; acute-on-chronic slips have an acute exacerbation.

items.q: On an AP radiograph, the Wilson classification grades a slip in which the epiphysis is displaced by 40% of the metaphyseal width as:
items.e: Wilson grading: mild under 33%, moderate 33–50% and severe over 50% displacement relative to the width of the metaphysis.

items.q: Which examination finding is the most sensitive for detecting a slipped capital femoral epiphysis?
o: Loss of internal rotation of the hip
Positive anterior drawer test of the knee
items.e: Loss of internal rotation, particularly in flexion, is the most consistent finding; knee pain is often referred and can mislead the clinician.

items.q: A 12-year-old cannot bear weight after a minor fall and has a shortened, externally rotated leg; SCFE is suspected. Which lateral radiograph should be obtained?
items.e: Frog-leg positioning may displace an unstable slip further, so a cross-table lateral is used when the slip may be unstable.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of a chronic SCFE, the metaphyseal blanch sign of Steel is caused by:
o: Overlap of the posteriorly displaced epiphysis on the metaphysis, producing a crescent of increased density
Periosteal new bone along the femoral neck
A lucent band from physeal widening
items.e: The double density results from the displaced epiphysis superimposed on the metaphysis; it complements Klein's line on the AP view.

items.q: In SCFE, the Capener sign on an AP radiograph refers to:
o: Failure of Klein's line to intersect the epiphysis
Loss of the normal triangular overlap between the medial metaphysis and the posterior acetabular wall
Widening of the physis with metaphyseal rarefaction
A double density at the metaphysis
items.e: Normally the medial metaphysis overlaps the posterior acetabular wall in a triangle; with a slip, the metaphysis moves laterally and the triangle is lost.

items.q: An obese 11-year-old has hip pain, a slightly widened physis on radiographs and no displacement. MRI would most likely show:
o: An effusion with synovial thickening only
Physeal widening with adjacent marrow oedema (a pre-slip)
A crescent sign and epiphyseal fragmentation
items.e: A pre-slip is seen on MRI as physeal widening and oedema without displacement; it is treated like a slip by in situ fixation.

items.q: During in situ screw fixation of a stable SCFE, the screw enters the anterior femoral neck and is directed posteriorly because:
o: A lateral entry would cross the greater trochanteric physis
An anterior entry avoids the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
The anterior cortex is thicker and gives better purchase
The epiphysis lies posterior to the femoral neck, so this trajectory places the screw centrally and perpendicular to the physis
items.e: With the epiphysis displaced posteriorly, a lateral entry would place the screw eccentrically and obliquely; anterior entry achieves a central, perpendicular screw.

items.q: In in situ fixation of SCFE, the screw tip is generally placed how far from the subchondral bone of the femoral head?
o: Within 1 mm, breaching the cartilage slightly for better purchase
items.e: Leaving at least about 5 mm reduces the risk of unrecognised joint penetration and chondrolysis while giving adequate purchase in the epiphysis.

items.q: The 'approach-withdraw' fluoroscopic technique during SCFE screw fixation is used to:
o: Detect unrecognised penetration of the screw into the joint
Assess blood flow to the femoral head
items.e: Rotating the hip under live fluoroscopy shows the screw tip approaching and withdrawing from the subchondral bone, confirming it does not breach the joint.

items.q: In the management of an unstable SCFE, capsular decompression (arthrotomy or aspiration) is performed because it:
o: Allows fixation with a single smooth pin
Reduces intracapsular pressure from the haemarthrosis that may compromise femoral head perfusion
items.e: An unstable slip causes a tense haemarthrosis; decompression is thought to relieve tamponade of the retinacular vessels, although evidence is debated.

items.q: For symptomatic deformity after a healed severe stable SCFE, which osteotomy is safest for the femoral head blood supply but provides only compensatory correction?
items.e: Intertrochanteric osteotomies are far from the retinacular vessels and safest; subcapital osteotomies correct at the deformity but carry the highest AVN risk.

items.q: In a child with a unilateral idiopathic SCFE, a posterior sloping angle of the contralateral hip of over about 12–14° indicates:
o: An increased risk of a contralateral slip, supporting prophylactic pinning
Femoral anteversion that protects the opposite hip
A contralateral pre-slip that requires open reduction
items.e: A raised posterior sloping angle on the lateral view has been associated with later contralateral slip and is one indication for prophylactic fixation.

items.q: Chondrolysis after treatment of SCFE is defined radiographically by narrowing of the hip joint space to less than about:
items.e: Chondrolysis presents as painful stiffness with joint space narrowing to under 3 mm (or half the contralateral side); unrecognised screw penetration is the commonest cause.

items.q: Three months after in situ pinning of an SCFE in which the screw entered the lateral femoral cortex below the level of the lesser trochanter, the child falls and sustains a fracture. The likely fracture is:
o: Femoral neck fracture through the physis
Subtrochanteric fracture through the entry hole
items.e: A lateral entry at or below the lesser trochanter, especially with multiple drill holes, creates a stress riser in the subtrochanteric region.

items.q: In SCFE fixation, which screw position within the epiphysis is particularly associated with avascular necrosis?
o: Screw tip 5 mm from the subchondral bone
items.e: Posterosuperior screw placement may injure the lateral epiphyseal vessels from the MFCA; a central screw on both views is the target.

items.q: Which anatomical factor increases shear stress across the proximal femoral physis and predisposes to SCFE?
items.e: Femoral retroversion and increased physeal obliquity during adolescence raise shear forces across the physis, especially in obese children.

items.q: A 19-year-old who had in situ pinning of a moderate stable SCFE at age 13 now has groin pain on flexion and internal rotation. Radiographs show a 'pistol-grip' head–neck deformity with a preserved joint space. The most appropriate surgical option is:
o: Femoral head–neck osteochondroplasty (arthroscopic or open) to treat cam impingement
items.e: Residual metaphyseal prominence after SCFE causes cam-type FAI; osteochondroplasty restores head–neck offset when the joint is preserved.

items.q: Bilateral involvement in SCFE is particularly common in children with an underlying endocrine or metabolic cause. In idiopathic SCFE, roughly what proportion have bilateral slips at presentation?
items.e: About 20% have bilateral slips at presentation, and further contralateral slips develop in follow-up, giving an eventual bilateral rate of up to 40–60%.

items.q: Compared with a femoral varus osteotomy, Salter innominate osteotomy for containment in Perthes disease has the advantage of:
o: Shortening the limb to offload the head
Slightly lengthening the limb and avoiding further abductor weakness
items.e: The Salter osteotomy gives anterolateral coverage and slightly lengthens the limb, whereas varus osteotomy shortens it and weakens the abductors.

items.q: In the Loder classification of SCFE, a 12-year-old who has severe hip pain but can walk with crutches is classified as having:
items.e: Loder stability depends on weight bearing: a child who can walk, even with crutches, has a stable slip (AVN risk under about 5%).

items.q: The adult intervertebral disc receives most of its nutrition by:
o: Segmental arteries penetrating the nucleus pulposus
Diffusion through the cartilaginous vertebral endplates
Basivertebral veins draining into the annulus
Synovial fluid from the facet joints
items.e: The disc is the largest avascular structure in the body; the nucleus and inner annulus are nourished by diffusion through the endplates, which calcify with age and impair nutrition.

items.q: Which collagen type predominates in the nucleus pulposus of a healthy intervertebral disc?
items.e: The nucleus is rich in type II collagen and aggrecan; the outer annulus is mainly type I collagen, and degeneration increases the type I to type II ratio.

items.q: A 50-year-old with chronic back pain has endplate signal that is high on both T1 and T2-weighted MRI at L4-L5. This Modic change represents:
o: Type I, marrow oedema and inflammation
items.e: Modic II (T1 high, T2 iso or high) is fatty replacement, the commonest and most stable type; type I (T1 low, T2 high) is oedema.

items.q: Endplate changes that are low signal on both T1 and T2 MRI sequences correspond to Modic type:
items.e: Modic III changes are dark on T1 and T2 and represent bony sclerosis, correlating with sclerosis on radiographs.

items.q: Modic type I endplate changes adjacent to a previously herniated disc have been linked, controversially, to low-grade infection with which organism?
items.e: Low-virulence Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes has been proposed as a cause of Modic I change and chronic low back pain, the basis of antibiotic trials (AIM trial negative).

items.q: On MRI, displaced disc material whose dome is wider than its base in any plane is classified as a:
items.e: In an extrusion the displaced material is wider than its neck or migrates beyond the disc space; in a protrusion the base is wider than the dome.

items.q: The commonest location of a symptomatic lumbar disc herniation in the axial plane is:
items.e: About 90% of lumbar herniations are paracentral, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is weakest; foraminal and far lateral account for about 5-10%.

items.q: A 38-year-old has sciatica after lifting. Which single weakness most specifically indicates an L5 radiculopathy?
items.e: EHL is the key L5 muscle; quadriceps is L3-L4, and gastrocnemius-soleus and the ankle jerk are S1.

items.q: A patient has foot drop. Which finding favours an L5 radiculopathy over a common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular neck?
o: Numbness over the first web space
Weakness of hip abduction and ankle inversion
items.e: Gluteus medius (hip abduction) and tibialis posterior (inversion) are L5-innervated but not supplied by the peroneal nerve, so their weakness localises to the root.

items.q: A paracentral L3-L4 disc herniation in a 45-year-old would most likely cause:
o: Reduced ankle jerk and lateral foot numbness
Reduced knee jerk, quadriceps weakness and medial leg numbness
Weak EHL and first web space numbness
items.e: A paracentral L3-L4 herniation compresses the traversing L4 root: knee jerk, quadriceps/tibialis anterior and medial leg sensation.

items.q: In a patient with suspected lumbar disc herniation, which clinical sign is the most specific?
items.e: Crossed SLR, where lifting the asymptomatic leg reproduces pain in the affected leg, is highly specific (though insensitive); the ipsilateral SLR is sensitive but less specific.

items.q: Anterior thigh pain reproduced with the patient prone by flexing the knee and extending the hip suggests compression of which roots?
items.e: The femoral nerve stretch test tensions the L2-L4 roots and is positive in upper lumbar and foraminal herniations.

items.q: Which type of lumbar disc herniation is most likely to regress spontaneously on follow-up MRI?
items.e: Extruded and sequestrated fragments regress most, through neovascularisation, macrophage infiltration and resorption.

items.q: In the SPORT trial for lumbar disc herniation, the as-treated analysis showed that compared with non-operative care, surgery gave:
o: No difference at any time point
Faster and greater improvement in pain and function
Better outcomes only for back pain, not leg pain
items.e: Both groups improved, but surgery gave faster and greater improvement as treated; high crossover made the intention-to-treat analysis inconclusive.

items.q: A 40-year-old with an L4-L5 disc herniation develops progressive weakness of ankle dorsiflexion from grade 4 to grade 2 over 3 days. Bladder function is normal. The best management is:
items.e: Progressive or severe motor deficit is an indication for early decompression, which may improve the chance of motor recovery.

items.q: For a far lateral (extraforaminal) L4-L5 disc herniation, the Wiltse paraspinal approach develops a plane between which muscles?
items.e: The Wiltse muscle-splitting approach between multifidus and longissimus reaches the foramen laterally and avoids a facetectomy.

items.q: Regarding recurrent herniation after lumbar microdiscectomy, which statement is correct?
o: Aggressive subtotal disc removal eliminates recurrence
Recurrence requires fusion in all cases
Recurrence occurs in roughly 3-7% (more in some series), mostly in the first months, and aggressive disc removal does not prevent it
items.e: Recurrence rates of about 3-7% (up to about 15% in some series) are reported, most in the first 6 months; aggressive discectomy increases back pain without reducing recurrence.

items.q: During L4-L5 microdiscectomy, a small dural tear with CSF leak is noticed. The preferred management is:
o: Leave it alone and keep the patient flat for 48 hours only
Primary watertight repair, augmented with sealant or graft if needed
Insert a lumbar drain for two weeks routinely
items.e: Incidental durotomy should be repaired primarily in a watertight fashion if possible, to prevent persistent CSF leak, headache, pseudomeningocele and fistula.

items.q: Shortly after an uneventful-seeming L4-L5 discectomy, the patient becomes hypotensive and tachycardic with no obvious wound bleeding. The surgeon should suspect:
o: Vascular injury from perforation of the anterior annulus, requiring emergency laparotomy
items.e: Instruments passing through the anterior annulus can injure the aorta, iliac vessels or vena cava; unexplained hypotension demands urgent vascular surgical exploration.

items.q: A patient with a massive central disc prolapse has bilateral sciatica, perianal numbness and reduced urinary sensation with a poor stream, but can still void voluntarily. This is classified as:
items.e: CES-I has altered urinary sensation or stream without retention; CES-R is painless retention with overflow and carries a worse prognosis.

items.q: In suspected cauda equina syndrome, a post-void residual bladder volume above about what level raises concern for bladder involvement?
items.e: A post-void residual over about 200 mL is a sensitive but non-specific marker that supports urgent MRI.

items.q: The Ahn meta-analysis of cauda equina syndrome due to disc herniation found significantly better outcomes when decompression was performed:
items.e: Ahn et al. reported better sensory, motor, urinary and rectal outcomes with surgery within 48 hours; current guidance favours decompression at the earliest opportunity, ideally before retention.

items.q: In lateral recess (subarticular) stenosis at L4-L5, the root usually compressed and the structure most often compressing it are:
o: Exiting L4 root by disc osteophyte in the foramen
Traversing L5 root by a hypertrophied inferior articular process of L4 alone
S1 root by the L5-S1 disc
Traversing L5 root by a hypertrophied superior articular process of L5
items.e: The lateral recess lies beneath the superior articular process of the lower vertebra; its hypertrophy compresses the traversing (L5) root at L4-L5.

items.q: Loss of disc height at L5-S1 with posterolateral osteophytes narrowing the neural foramen would most likely compress the:
items.e: Foraminal stenosis compresses the exiting root, which at L5-S1 is L5.

items.q: A 72-year-old man can cycle on an exercise bike for 30 minutes without symptoms but develops bilateral thigh heaviness after walking 200 m, relieved by leaning on a shopping trolley. Pedal pulses are normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar canal stenosis
items.e: Flexed postures (cycling, leaning forward) enlarge the canal and relieve neurogenic claudication; vascular claudication is also provoked by cycling and relieved by standing still.

items.q: On axial MRI, an anteroposterior diameter of the lumbar dural sac/canal below which value is considered absolute central stenosis?
items.e: An AP diameter under 10 mm is absolute stenosis (10-13 mm relative); a dural sac cross-sectional area under about 75-100 mm2 also indicates stenosis.

items.q: On supine axial MRI, nerve roots of the cauda equina that fail to settle to the dependent (dorsal) part of the dural sac at a level of stenosis constitute a positive:
items.e: Normally the roots sediment dorsally with gravity; a positive sedimentation sign (roots suspended) is associated with symptomatic central stenosis.

items.q: The Schizas grading of lumbar central stenosis on axial T2 MRI is based on:
o: Dural sac cross-sectional area measured in mm2
Morphology of the dural sac: the ratio of CSF to rootlets
items.e: Schizas grades A-D describe how much CSF remains around the rootlets; grade D shows no CSF and no visible rootlets (extreme stenosis).

items.q: The LESS trial (NEJM 2014) of epidural injections for lumbar spinal stenosis found that epidural glucocorticoid plus lidocaine, compared with lidocaine alone:
o: Gave minimal or no additional benefit at 6 weeks
Reduced the need for surgery by half
Was superior only in patients with spondylolisthesis
items.e: The LESS trial showed glucocorticoid added to lidocaine offered minimal or no short-term benefit for pain and function in central stenosis.

items.q: The Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study (Forsth, NEJM 2016) compared decompression alone with decompression plus fusion in lumbar stenosis with or without degenerative spondylolisthesis and found:
o: Fusion improved outcomes only in patients without spondylolisthesis
Fusion reduced reoperation rate by half
No added clinical benefit from fusion at 2 and 5 years, with greater cost
Decompression alone had more neurological complications
items.e: Forsth showed no benefit from adding fusion, even in the subgroup with spondylolisthesis, while costs and operative time increased.

items.q: The SLIP trial (Ghogawala, NEJM 2016) in stable grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis found that adding instrumented posterolateral fusion to laminectomy:
o: Gave no difference in any outcome
Was inferior on SF-36 physical component
Gave slightly greater improvement in physical health and fewer reoperations
items.e: SLIP found modestly better SF-36 physical scores and fewer reoperations with fusion, contrasting with the Swedish trial, so fusion decisions are individualised.

items.q: In degenerative spondylolisthesis, which flexion-extension radiographic finding indicates dynamic instability supporting fusion with decompression?
o: More than about 3-4 mm translation or more than 10-15 degrees angular change
Any facet joint effusion on MRI alone
items.e: Translation over about 3-4 mm or angulation over 10-15 degrees on dynamic films indicates instability; facet effusion is a supportive but not sufficient sign.

items.q: Compared with conventional decompression, interspinous process spacers (such as X-Stop) for neurogenic claudication are associated with:
items.e: Trials show similar early outcomes but substantially higher reoperation rates with interspinous spacers, limiting their role.

items.q: Degenerative spondylolisthesis is most typical of which patient and level?
o: Man over 60 at L5-S1 with pars defect
Woman over 50 at L4-L5 with sagittally oriented facets
Child at L3-L4 with dysplastic facets
items.e: Degenerative slip occurs mainly in women over 50 at L4-L5 with an intact pars and sagittally oriented facets; isthmic slip is typically L5-S1.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman with grade I degenerative L4-L5 spondylolisthesis has unilateral leg pain. Which root is most likely compressed and where?
o: L4 root in the L4-L5 foramen
S1 root in the lateral recess
L3 root in the far lateral zone
L5 root in the lateral recess at L4-L5
items.e: With an intact pars the posterior arch of L4 slides forward, narrowing the canal and lateral recess at L4-L5 and compressing the traversing L5 root.

items.q: In adult isthmic spondylolisthesis at L5-S1, radicular leg pain is usually due to compression of the:
o: S1 root in the lateral recess
L5 root in the L5-S1 foramen by fibrocartilaginous pars tissue and disc
L4 root in the L4-L5 foramen
items.e: In isthmic slip the canal is widened (posterior arch stays behind), but the exiting L5 root is compressed in the foramen by the pars fibrocartilage (Gill lesion) and bulging disc.

items.q: In the Wiltse-Newman classification, which type of spondylolisthesis carries the highest risk of cauda equina symptoms because the intact posterior arch is pulled forward with the slipping vertebra?
items.e: In dysplastic slips the posterior arch remains attached to the vertebral body, so even modest slips can tether the sacral roots and cause cauda equina features.

items.q: In the Wiltse classification, an isthmic spondylolisthesis with an elongated but intact pars interarticularis (from repeated healed microfractures) is subtype:
items.e: IIA is a lytic fatigue fracture, IIB an elongated healed pars, and IIC an acute pars fracture; type III is degenerative.

items.q: A lateral radiograph shows L5 slipped forward on S1 by 60% of the S1 endplate width. The Meyerding grade is:
items.e: Meyerding grades rise in 25% steps: I under 25%, II 25-50%, III 50-75%, IV 75-100%, V over 100%.

items.q: Meyerding grade V spondylolisthesis, in which L5 has slipped completely off the sacrum, is termed:
items.e: Grade V (over 100% slip) is spondyloptosis; the inverted Napoleon hat sign is the AP radiographic appearance of a high-grade L5 slip.

items.q: Which spinopelvic parameter is characteristically high in patients with isthmic spondylolisthesis and predisposes to slip progression?
items.e: High pelvic incidence increases sacral slope and shear stress at L5-S1, predisposing to isthmic slip and its progression.

items.q: In a child with isthmic spondylolisthesis, which radiographic measurement greater than about 45-50 degrees predicts progression?
items.e: A high slip angle reflects lumbosacral kyphosis and is a strong predictor of progression in paediatric spondylolisthesis.

items.q: A 12-year-old girl with high-grade L5-S1 spondylolisthesis walks with flexed hips and knees, a short stride and very tight hamstrings. This gait is known as the:
items.e: The Phalen-Dickson sign is the crouched, knee-flexed, hip-flexed gait with hamstring tightness seen in high-grade paediatric spondylolisthesis.

items.q: Direct repair of a pars defect (Buck screw, Scott wiring or pedicle screw-hook construct) is best suited to:
o: A 55-year-old with grade II L5-S1 slip and degenerated disc
A young patient with a symptomatic L3 or L4 spondylolysis, minimal slip and a healthy disc
items.e: Pars repair preserves motion and suits young patients with symptomatic L1-L4 defects, no significant slip and no disc degeneration; otherwise fusion is preferred.

items.q: In a growing child with isthmic spondylolisthesis, in situ fusion is generally indicated when the slip exceeds:
items.e: Slips over 50%, documented progression, or persistent symptoms despite conservative care are indications for fusion (L5-S1 or L4-S1).

items.q: Reduction of a high-grade L5-S1 spondylolisthesis during fusion carries a particular risk of:
o: Cauda equina syndrome from the S4 roots only
L5 nerve root palsy from stretch
