items.e: Reduction lengthens the L5 roots; most L5 deficit occurs in the last half of reduction, so partial reduction and root decompression are used.

items.q: The MRC spine stabilisation trial (Fairbank, BMJ 2005) of chronic low back pain compared lumbar fusion with intensive rehabilitation and found:
o: Rehabilitation superior with fewer complications and better function
Fusion superior only for discogenic pain
No clear clinically significant difference in disability, with fusion carrying surgical risks
items.e: Fairbank found no significant difference in Oswestry Disability Index between fusion and intensive rehabilitation, whereas the Swedish Fritzell trial favoured fusion.

items.q: A 25-year-old has unilateral low back pain. Radiographs show an enlarged L5 transverse process forming a pseudoarthrosis with the sacral ala. This is:
items.e: Bertolotti syndrome is back pain related to a lumbosacral transitional vertebra with an enlarged transverse process articulating with the sacrum or ilium.

items.q: An elderly patient has midline low back pain worse on extension. Radiographs show close approximation and sclerosis of adjacent spinous processes with neoarthrosis. The eponym is:
items.e: Baastrup disease is contact and neoarthrosis between adjacent spinous processes with interspinous bursitis, from excessive lordosis and disc height loss.

items.q: For persistent neuropathic leg pain after technically adequate lumbar surgery (failed back surgery syndrome) with no compressive lesion, which intervention has randomised evidence of benefit over reoperation or medical management?
items.e: Spinal cord stimulation trials (PROCESS, North et al.) showed better leg pain relief than conventional medical management or reoperation in failed back surgery syndrome.

items.q: During TKA trialling, the knee is equally tight in both flexion and extension with rectangular gaps. The simplest correction is to:
items.e: The tibial cut contributes to both gaps, so extra tibial resection loosens flexion and extension equally. Distal femoral resection affects extension only, and femoral size affects flexion only.

items.q: In a valgus knee with a hypoplastic lateral femoral condyle, setting femoral component rotation 3° external to the posterior condylar axis risks:
o: Excessive external rotation and medial flexion laxity
Internal rotation of the femoral component relative to the transepicondylar axis
items.e: The deficient lateral posterior condyle makes the posterior condylar axis itself internally rotated, so referencing from it internally rotates the component; the transepicondylar axis or Whiteside line should be used instead.

items.q: During medial release of a varus knee in TKA, the anterior fibres of the superficial MCL are mainly tight in:
items.e: The anterior part of the superficial MCL tightens in flexion and the posterior part (with the posteromedial capsule) in extension, which guides selective release.

items.q: During lateral retinacular release for patellar maltracking in TKA, which vessel should be preserved to reduce the risk of patellar avascular necrosis?
items.e: The medial arthrotomy has already divided the medial genicular supply, so preserving the superior lateral genicular artery during lateral release protects patellar blood flow.

items.q: A periprosthetic supracondylar femoral fracture above a TKA has a loose femoral component. In the Lewis-Rorabeck classification this is type:
o: II, treated with a locking plate
III, treated by revision arthroplasty (often with distal femoral replacement)
II, treated with a retrograde nail
items.e: Type III has a loose prosthesis regardless of fracture displacement and needs revision. Type I is undisplaced with a stable prosthesis, and type II is displaced with a stable prosthesis.

items.q: Which preoperative factor is among the strongest predictors of dissatisfaction after primary TKA?
o: Pain catastrophising with only mild radiographic arthritis
items.e: About 10-20% of patients are dissatisfied after TKA; poor expectations, pain catastrophising, depression and mild radiographic disease predict dissatisfaction, whereas severe arthritis predicts a good result.

items.q: Eighteen months after a posterior-stabilised TKA, a patient has recurrent effusions, a feeling of giving way when descending stairs and anterior drawer laxity at 90° flexion, with good stability in extension. The likely diagnosis is:
o: Flexion instability from a flexion gap larger than the extension gap
Aseptic loosening of the tibial component
items.e: Flexion instability causes effusions, soft-tissue pain and giving way on stairs, and in PS knees may lead to cam jump. Treatment is revision to balance the gaps, sometimes with more constraint.

items.q: When choosing an incision for TKA in a knee with previous skin incisions, a skin bridge between parallel incisions should ideally be at least about:
items.e: Narrow skin bridges risk necrosis; a bridge of about 5-6 cm is advised, and the most lateral usable incision is chosen because the blood supply comes from the medial side.

items.q: In TKA for a fixed flexion deformity with a balanced flexion gap, the first step to correct the tight extension gap is:
o: Resecting an extra 4 mm of distal femur
Removing posterior osteophytes and releasing the posterior capsule
items.e: Posterior osteophytes tent the capsule; removing them and releasing the posterior capsule often corrects the deformity without raising the joint line. Extra distal femoral resection is a later step.

items.q: In mechanical alignment TKA, the posterior slope of the tibial cut is generally set at about:
items.e: A posterior slope of about 3-7° is typical, with more in cruciate-retaining and less in posterior-stabilised designs; excessive slope opens the flexion gap and can cause instability.

items.q: During TKA, a knee is tight in flexion but balanced in extension in a cruciate-retaining design. Besides downsizing the femur, which step can loosen the flexion gap selectively?
o: Recessing or releasing a tight PCL (or increasing tibial slope)
items.e: A tight PCL limits the flexion gap and causes excessive rollback; recession or increased slope opens flexion without changing extension. Distal femoral resection affects only extension.

items.q: A varus-valgus constrained (condylar constrained, non-linked) TKA is preferred over a rotating hinge when:
o: There is global ligament loss with hyperextension
The collateral ligaments are attenuated but the flexion and extension gaps can still be balanced
A distal femoral replacement is required for tumour
There is complete extensor and collateral disruption
items.e: Condylar constrained implants resist varus-valgus but rely on balanced gaps; global ligamentous deficiency, gross gap mismatch, bone loss needing distal femoral replacement and hyperextension instability need a linked hinge.

items.q: A 30-year-old has diffuse aching of the arm with ulnar-sided paraesthesia and wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis; a cervical rib is seen on radiographs. This wasting pattern is called:
o: Simian hand from carpal tunnel syndrome
items.e: In neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, compression of the lower trunk (C8-T1), often by a band from a cervical rib, causes thenar (APB) wasting with ulnar-sided sensory symptoms: the Gilliatt-Sumner hand.

items.q: The most common type of thoracic outlet syndrome is:
o: Neurogenic, affecting the lower trunk of the brachial plexus
items.e: About 95% of thoracic outlet syndrome is neurogenic and involves the C8-T1 lower trunk. Venous (Paget-Schroetter) and arterial forms are uncommon but more dramatic.

items.q: The Roos (elevated arm stress) test, in which the patient opens and closes the hands for 3 minutes with arms abducted and externally rotated, is used to assess:
items.e: Reproduction of symptoms or early fatigue in the elevated position suggests thoracic outlet compression. Adson and Wright tests are other provocative tests.

items.q: A baseball pitcher has vague posterior shoulder pain, and MRI shows isolated fatty atrophy of teres minor. The structures compressed are the:
o: Suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch
Radial nerve in the triangular interval
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery in the quadrilateral space
Long thoracic nerve at the scalenes
items.e: Quadrilateral space syndrome compresses the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery, often by fibrous bands in throwers; teres minor atrophy is the classic MRI sign.

items.q: Compression of the suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse scapular ligament produces weakness of:
items.e: At the suprascapular notch the nerve has not yet given off its supraspinatus branch, so both muscles are weak; spinoglenoid notch compression affects infraspinatus alone.

items.q: After a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck, a patient has a drooping shoulder and lateral scapular winging. The injured nerve is the:
items.e: The spinal accessory nerve runs superficially across the posterior triangle; trapezius paralysis produces shoulder droop and lateral winging. Long thoracic palsy produces medial winging.

items.q: The 'double-crush' hypothesis states that:
o: Two separate nerves are compressed at the same site
Proximal compression of a nerve (for example cervical radiculopathy) makes its distal part more susceptible to compression
A nerve compressed twice at one site never recovers
Bilateral compression always has a systemic cause
items.e: Upton and McComas proposed that impaired axoplasmic flow from one lesion lowers the threshold for symptoms from a second lesion on the same nerve, such as C6 radiculopathy with carpal tunnel syndrome.

items.q: A patient has a complete ulnar nerve transection at the elbow yet retains good function of the first dorsal interosseous. The most likely explanation is:
o: A Riche-Cannieu anastomosis in the palm
Innervation of the first dorsal interosseous by the radial nerve
A Martin-Gruber anastomosis carrying motor fibres from the median to the ulnar nerve in the forearm
items.e: The Martin-Gruber anastomosis (median or AIN to ulnar in the forearm, in about 15-20%) can carry fibres to ulnar intrinsics, sparing them after a high ulnar lesion. Riche-Cannieu is a palmar communication between the recurrent median branch and the deep ulnar branch.

items.q: The arcade of Struthers, a potential site of ulnar nerve compression, lies approximately:
o: 5 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, arising from a supracondylar process
At the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
8 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, related to the medial intermuscular septum
items.e: The arcade of Struthers is a fascial band about 8 cm above the medial epicondyle that may tether the ulnar nerve after transposition. The ligament of Struthers, from a supracondylar process about 5 cm above the epicondyle, compresses the median nerve.

items.q: On nerve conduction studies, a distal MOTOR latency of the median nerve at the wrist greater than about what value supports carpal tunnel syndrome?
items.e: A median distal motor latency above about 4.5 ms (and sensory latency above about 3.5 ms) is the usual threshold. Sensory latency changes appear first.

items.q: Which feature best distinguishes cubital tunnel syndrome from ulnar nerve compression in Guyon's canal?
o: Sensory loss over the dorsoulnar hand, from the dorsal cutaneous branch that leaves the nerve proximal to the wrist
Clawing of the ring and little fingers
items.e: The dorsal cutaneous branch arises about 5-8 cm proximal to the wrist, so its territory is spared in Guyon's canal lesions but affected at the elbow. Intrinsic weakness and Froment sign occur in both.

items.q: Neurapraxia (Seddon) differs from axonotmesis chiefly in that neurapraxia:
o: Has an intact axon with a local conduction block and no Wallerian degeneration
Shows fibrillation potentials distal to the lesion
items.e: Neurapraxia is a focal demyelinating conduction block without axonal loss, so there is no Wallerian degeneration, no advancing Tinel sign and full recovery within weeks to about 3 months.

items.q: With the elbow in full extension, resistance to valgus stress is shared approximately equally by which three structures?
o: Radial head, annular ligament and LUCL
Flexor-pronator mass, anconeus and interosseous membrane
Anterior capsule, ulnar collateral ligament and the bony articulation
items.e: In extension the anterior capsule, UCL and olecranon-trochlea articulation each provide about one-third of valgus restraint; at 90° the anterior bundle of the UCL dominates.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of patients with lateral epicondylitis improve within one year with conservative management or no treatment?
items.e: Lateral epicondylitis is largely self-limiting; most patients settle within a year, which is why surgery is reserved for symptoms persisting beyond 6-12 months.

items.q: Surgical release or debridement of the ECRB origin for lateral epicondylitis is generally considered after failure of conservative treatment for at least:
items.e: Because most cases resolve within a year, surgery (open, percutaneous or arthroscopic) is considered after about 6-12 months of failed non-operative care.

items.q: A recognised intraoperative or early complication of humeral tunnel drilling in elbow UCL reconstruction is:
items.e: Tunnels in the medial epicondyle can weaken it and lead to fracture, particularly with large or convergent tunnels. Ulnar neuritis remains the commonest complication overall.

items.q: Distal biceps tendon rupture most typically occurs in which patient?
o: A woman aged 70 after a fall on the outstretched hand
A man aged 40-60 lifting with the dominant elbow flexed under eccentric load
items.e: Distal biceps rupture classically occurs in middle-aged men with sudden eccentric loading of the flexed elbow; smoking and anabolic steroids increase risk.

items.q: In elbow arthroscopy, why is the proximal anterolateral portal preferred over the distal anterolateral portal?
o: It lies further from the radial nerve
It gives direct access to the olecranon fossa
It enters through the soft spot
items.e: Moving the anterolateral portal proximally (about 2 cm above and 1 cm anterior to the lateral epicondyle) increases its distance from the radial nerve.

items.q: An adolescent pitcher has persistent posterior elbow pain, and radiographs show a widened olecranon apophysis compared with the other side. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Olecranon apophysitis or stress injury from repetitive triceps traction
items.e: Repetitive triceps traction and posterior impingement in skeletally immature throwers stress the olecranon apophysis, which may fail to fuse. Panner disease affects the capitellum and medial apophysitis the medial epicondyle.

items.q: In the Graf ultrasound method, the alpha angle is formed between the:
o: Iliac baseline and the bony acetabular roof line
Iliac baseline and the labral (cartilage roof) line
Femoral neck and the iliac baseline
Bony roof line and the labral line
items.e: Alpha measures bony roof depth (normal 60° or more); beta measures the cartilaginous roof using the line through the labrum.

items.q: In an infant over 3 months old, hip abduction in flexion below about what value (or obvious asymmetry) suggests a dislocated hip?
items.e: Limited abduction in flexion, under about 60° or asymmetric, is the most reliable sign once Barlow and Ortolani become negative.

items.q: A walking child with bilateral untreated hip dislocations from DDH would typically show:
o: A unilateral Trendelenburg lurch with a positive Galeazzi sign
A circumduction gait with knee hyperextension
A waddling gait with increased lumbar lordosis
items.e: Bilateral dislocation causes bilateral abductor weakness (waddling) and hip flexion posture compensated by hyperlordosis; the Galeazzi sign may be negative because both sides are equal.

items.q: The Staheli shelf procedure for an incongruent dysplastic hip works by:
o: Redirecting the acetabulum around the pubic symphysis
Reducing acetabular volume by hinging on the triradiate cartilage
Medialising the femoral head with a femoral osteotomy
Adding bone graft to the lateral acetabular margin to support the capsule, which undergoes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia
items.e: The shelf is a salvage augmentation: bone graft extends the lateral roof over the capsule, which converts to fibrocartilage. Redirectional osteotomies need a congruent hip.

items.q: In the Kalamchi-MacEwen classification of avascular necrosis after DDH treatment, which group has the best prognosis?
o: Group I, with changes confined to the ossific nucleus
Group II, with lateral physeal damage
Group III, with central physeal damage
Group IV, with total head and physeal involvement
items.e: Group I involves only the ossific nucleus and usually remodels without deformity. Physeal involvement in groups II-IV leads to progressive deformity.

items.q: In total hip arthroplasty for a Crowe III or IV dysplastic hip, the acetabular component should usually be placed:
o: In the false acetabulum to avoid lengthening
In the true acetabulum to restore a low hip centre
High on the ilium with a large cup
items.e: Placing the cup at the true acetabulum restores hip biomechanics and bone stock, often with a small cup and femoral head autograft for superolateral deficiency; a shortening osteotomy may be needed to reduce the femur.

items.q: Female preponderance in DDH (about 4-6:1) has been attributed mainly to:
o: More frequent breech presentation in girls
Earlier ossification of the femoral head in girls
Greater ligamentous laxity of female infants in response to maternal relaxin and oestrogen
items.e: Female infants are more sensitive to maternal hormones such as relaxin, causing capsular laxity. Breech presentation is an independent risk factor.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman has a 9 cm deep thigh mass. Biopsy shows uniform oval cells in a myxoid stroma with a delicate branching capillary network and scattered signet-ring lipoblasts. The characteristic translocation is:
items.e: This is myxoid liposarcoma, defined by FUS-DDIT3 (rarely EWSR1-DDIT3). SS18-SSX is synovial sarcoma and EWSR1-ATF1 clear cell sarcoma.

items.q: The 'chicken-wire' plexiform capillary pattern on histology is a classic feature of which soft-tissue sarcoma?
items.e: Myxoid liposarcoma has a delicate arborising (chicken-wire) capillary network in a myxoid matrix with lipoblasts; myxofibrosarcoma instead has curvilinear vessels.

items.q: In myxoid liposarcoma, a hypercellular round-cell component of more than about 5% of the tumour indicates:
o: High-grade disease with a worse prognosis
Atypical lipomatous tumour that cannot metastasise
items.e: A round-cell (hypercellular) component above about 5% upgrades myxoid liposarcoma to high grade, with a higher risk of metastasis and death.

items.q: Trabectedin, a marine-derived alkylating agent, is particularly active against which soft-tissue sarcoma subtype?
items.e: Trabectedin targets the FUS-DDIT3 transcriptional programme and is especially effective in myxoid/round-cell liposarcoma, and is also used in leiomyosarcoma.

items.q: A 66-year-old has a 15 cm intramuscular fatty thigh mass. Biopsy shows atypical lipomatous tumour with MDM2 amplification and no dedifferentiated areas. The appropriate treatment is:
o: Radical compartmental resection with postoperative radiotherapy
Neoadjuvant doxorubicin-ifosfamide followed by wide excision
Marginal excision without adjuvant therapy, with follow-up for local recurrence
items.e: Atypical lipomatous tumour of the limb does not metastasise; marginal excision is accepted, accepting some local recurrence risk. Chemotherapy and radical surgery are not indicated.

items.q: Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma of soft tissue was previously known as:
items.e: UPS replaced the term malignant fibrous histiocytoma; it is a diagnosis of exclusion when no line of differentiation can be identified.

items.q: A 26-year-old has an ulcerated nodule on the volar forearm. Biopsy shows epithelioid cells positive for keratin and EMA. Loss of nuclear expression of which protein on immunohistochemistry supports epithelioid sarcoma?
items.e: Epithelioid sarcoma characteristically shows loss of INI1 (SMARCB1). TLE1 is a synovial sarcoma marker, myogenin rhabdomyosarcoma, MDM2 amplification atypical lipomatous tumour.

items.q: Tazemetostat, approved for advanced epithelioid sarcoma, acts by inhibiting:
items.e: Loss of INI1 makes epithelioid sarcoma dependent on EZH2; tazemetostat is an oral EZH2 inhibitor. Gamma-secretase inhibition (nirogacestat) is used in desmoid tumours.

items.q: A tumour attached to the Achilles tendon in a 28-year-old is S100, HMB-45 and Melan-A positive. Which test most reliably distinguishes clear cell sarcoma from metastatic melanoma?
o: Detection of an EWSR1-ATF1 (or EWSR1-CREB1) fusion
items.e: Both tumours express melanocytic markers; clear cell sarcoma carries an EWSR1-ATF1 fusion, whereas melanoma does not and often has BRAF mutations.

items.q: Alveolar soft part sarcoma is characterised by which genetic alteration?
items.e: ASPS carries der(17)t(X;17) producing ASPSCR1-TFE3, with nuclear TFE3 staining. PAX3-FOXO1 is alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, a different tumour despite the similar name.

items.q: A 22-year-old has a highly vascular deep thigh mass diagnosed as alveolar soft part sarcoma. In addition to chest CT, staging should include:
items.e: ASPS commonly metastasises to lung and brain, so brain imaging is recommended. Whole-spine MRI is the specific addition for myxoid liposarcoma.

items.q: Which class of systemic therapy has shown notable activity, leading to drug approval, in metastatic alveolar soft part sarcoma?
o: Immune checkpoint inhibitors such as atezolizumab
items.e: ASPS is resistant to conventional chemotherapy but responds to checkpoint inhibitors; atezolizumab was approved for unresectable or metastatic ASPS.

items.q: A leiomyosarcoma of vascular origin most commonly arises from the:
items.e: Vascular leiomyosarcoma arises most often from large veins, especially the IVC; leiomyosarcomas stain for desmin, SMA and h-caldesmon.

items.q: Which pair of immunohistochemical markers best supports the diagnosis of angiosarcoma?
items.e: Angiosarcoma expresses endothelial markers CD31, ERG (and CD34). Desmin/myogenin indicate rhabdomyosarcoma; S100/SOX10 neural or melanocytic tumours.

items.q: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is driven by which fusion, explaining its response to imatinib?
items.e: The t(17;22) COL1A1-PDGFB fusion causes autocrine PDGFB signalling, which imatinib blocks at the PDGF receptor.

items.q: A slowly growing plaque-like dermal tumour on the trunk could be a dermatofibroma or dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. Which immunostain favours DFSP?
items.e: DFSP is typically diffusely CD34 positive and factor XIIIa negative, whereas dermatofibroma is factor XIIIa positive and CD34 negative.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a primary dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans of the trunk with irregular finger-like extensions. Which surgical approach gives the lowest local recurrence?
o: Mohs micrographic surgery or wide excision with complete margin assessment
items.e: DFSP infiltrates with tentacle-like projections, so complete peripheral margin assessment (Mohs or wide excision) minimises recurrence. It rarely metastasises.

items.q: Which nuclear immunohistochemical marker is most specific for skeletal muscle differentiation in rhabdomyosarcoma?
items.e: Myogenin and MyoD1 are nuclear transcription factors specific for skeletal muscle lineage; strong diffuse myogenin is typical of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

items.q: Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma is characterised by rearrangement of which gene?
items.e: EMC carries NR4A3 rearrangements (most often EWSR1-NR4A3). IDH1 mutations occur in conventional cartilage tumours of bone, not in EMC.

items.q: Which chemotherapy agent is particularly active in synovial sarcoma, which is one of the most chemosensitive adult soft-tissue sarcomas?
items.e: Synovial sarcoma responds well to ifosfamide (with or without doxorubicin). Imatinib is for DFSP and GIST; high-dose methotrexate is used in osteosarcoma.

items.q: A biphasic synovial sarcoma is one that contains:
items.e: Synovial sarcoma can be monophasic (spindle cells only), biphasic (spindle plus epithelial glands) or poorly differentiated; all share the SS18-SSX fusion.

items.q: In patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, the lifetime risk of developing a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour is approximately:
items.e: Recent series give an NF1 lifetime MPNST risk of about 8-13% (older figures about 5%), far above the general population; about half of all MPNSTs occur in NF1.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman with an extremity soft-tissue sarcoma had breast cancer at 28; her mother had an adrenocortical carcinoma and her brother a brain tumour in childhood. The most likely germline mutation is in:
items.e: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline TP53) clusters early sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumours and adrenocortical carcinoma. APC is associated with FAP and desmoids.

items.q: Survivors of hereditary (bilateral) retinoblastoma have a markedly increased risk of later bone and soft-tissue sarcomas because of a germline mutation in:
items.e: Germline RB1 loss predisposes to osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcomas, especially (but not only) within radiotherapy fields.

items.q: A 32-year-old with familial adenomatous polyposis develops a growing mesenteric mass after colectomy. The underlying germline mutation predisposing to this desmoid tumour is in:
items.e: Desmoids in FAP/Gardner syndrome arise from germline APC mutations, often intra-abdominal and after surgery. Sporadic desmoids carry somatic CTNNB1 mutations.

items.q: Which immunohistochemical finding supports a diagnosis of desmoid-type fibromatosis?
items.e: Both CTNNB1 and APC alterations stabilise beta-catenin, which accumulates in the nucleus; nuclear beta-catenin is the key supportive stain.

items.q: Which oral multikinase inhibitor improved progression-free survival over placebo in a phase 3 trial (Gounder, NEJM 2018) in progressive or symptomatic desmoid tumours?
items.e: The Alliance trial showed sorafenib significantly prolonged progression-free survival in desmoid tumours. Nirogacestat (DeFi trial) is a gamma-secretase inhibitor alternative.

items.q: After resection of an extra-abdominal desmoid tumour of the shoulder girdle, the margin is microscopically positive. The patient is asymptomatic and function is good. The preferred management is:
items.e: Positive margins in desmoid surgery do not reliably predict recurrence, and many residual tumours stabilise; consensus favours watchful observation rather than morbid re-excision.

items.q: In the WHO classification, desmoid-type fibromatosis is categorised as:
items.e: Desmoids infiltrate locally and recur but never metastasise, placing them in the intermediate locally aggressive category; DFSP is intermediate rarely metastasising.

items.q: Benign soft-tissue tumours outnumber soft-tissue sarcomas by approximately:
items.e: Benign soft-tissue tumours (lipoma being the commonest) are about 100 times more common than sarcomas, which is why red-flag features guide referral.

items.q: The most common anatomical site of soft-tissue sarcoma in adults is the:
items.e: About half to 60% of sarcomas occur in the extremities, the lower limb (especially the thigh) being commonest; the retroperitoneum accounts for about 15%.

items.q: Enucleating ('shelling out') a soft-tissue sarcoma through its pseudocapsule leads to a high local recurrence rate because:
o: The pseudocapsule is made entirely of normal fascia
The reactive zone around the tumour contains satellite tumour cells
Sarcomas never invade beyond their capsule
Blood loss from the capsule seeds the lungs
items.e: Sarcomas compress surrounding tissue into a reactive pseudocapsule that harbours satellite nodules; a marginal plane through it leaves tumour behind, so a cuff of normal tissue is required.

items.q: MRI of a 6 cm mass deep in the thigh of a 45-year-old shows a homogeneous lesion with very high T2 signal that looks like a cyst on non-contrast sequences. The key next step before calling it benign is:
o: Aspiration and reassurance if fluid is obtained
Contrast-enhanced MRI to look for internal solid enhancement
items.e: Myxoid tumours (myxoid liposarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, myxoma) mimic cysts on T2 but enhance internally with gadolinium; a deep 'cyst' should never be dismissed without contrast.

items.q: Fine-needle aspiration cytology is not adequate for the primary diagnosis of a suspected soft-tissue sarcoma mainly because it:
o: Always seeds tumour along the entire limb
Cannot be performed under ultrasound guidance
Gives larger samples than core biopsy
Provides cells without tissue architecture, limiting subtyping and grading
items.e: FNA yields dispersed cells; core needle biopsy preserves architecture for histological subtype, grade and molecular tests and is the standard.

items.q: Sentinel lymph node biopsy may be considered during staging of which extremity soft-tissue tumour?
items.e: Node-seeking subtypes (epithelioid, clear cell, synovial, rhabdomyosarcoma, angiosarcoma) justify nodal assessment; ALT, DFSP and desmoids do not spread to nodes.

items.q: A 25-year-old develops a 2 cm tender subcutaneous forearm nodule that grew over 3 weeks. Histology shows loosely arranged myofibroblasts in a 'tissue-culture' pattern with extravasated red cells. The lesion typically carries which rearrangement?
items.e: This is nodular fasciitis, a self-limiting pseudosarcomatous lesion with MYH9-USP6 fusion; rapid growth can lead to mistaken diagnosis of sarcoma.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia develops several intramuscular soft-tissue masses with very high T2 signal. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Mazabraud syndrome combines fibrous dysplasia with intramuscular myxomas, both linked to GNAS mutations. Maffucci combines enchondromas with haemangiomas.

items.q: A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumour that lies eccentric to the parent nerve and can usually be enucleated while preserving the nerve fascicles is a:
items.e: Schwannomas are encapsulated and eccentric, allowing fascicle-sparing enucleation; neurofibromas grow centrally among fascicles, so excision sacrifices the nerve.

items.q: A 55-year-old on warfarin has a deep thigh 'haematoma' after minor trauma that has not resolved after 6 weeks. The most appropriate next step is:
o: Contrast-enhanced MRI, followed by biopsy if a solid enhancing component is seen
items.e: A persistent haematoma may be a haemorrhagic sarcoma; it needs contrast MRI to look for enhancing solid tissue. Drainage could contaminate tissues.

items.q: When radiotherapy for an extremity soft-tissue sarcoma is given postoperatively, the usual dose is about:
items.e: Postoperative radiotherapy needs about 60-66 Gy over a larger field covering the whole surgical bed, compared with 50 Gy preoperatively; this contributes to greater late toxicity.

items.q: The NCI randomised trial of Yang et al. (1998) of external-beam radiotherapy after limb-sparing surgery for extremity sarcoma showed that radiotherapy:
o: Improved overall survival but not local control
Had no effect on local recurrence
Reduced local recurrence but did not improve overall survival
items.e: Adjuvant radiotherapy significantly lowered local recurrence without a survival difference, establishing radiotherapy's role in local control.

items.q: The EORTC STRASS trial (62092) studied preoperative radiotherapy for retroperitoneal sarcoma and found:
o: A large reduction in distant metastasis
That surgery could be omitted after radiotherapy
No significant improvement in abdominal recurrence-free survival overall
items.e: STRASS showed no overall benefit of preoperative radiotherapy in retroperitoneal sarcoma; any benefit in liposarcoma subgroups remains debated, and en bloc surgery is the mainstay.

items.q: By wet weight, the approximate composition of adult bone is:
items.e: Bone is roughly 60-70% mineral (mainly hydroxyapatite), 20-25% organic matrix (90% type I collagen) and 5-10% water; cells form a tiny fraction.

items.q: The type I collagen molecule in bone is a triple helix composed of:
o: Two alpha-1 chains and one alpha-2 chain
One alpha-1 chain and two alpha-2 chains
Two alpha-1 chains and one alpha-3 chain
items.e: Type I collagen is a heterotrimer of two alpha-1(I) chains (COL1A1) and one alpha-2(I) chain (COL1A2); type II collagen of cartilage is a homotrimer of three alpha-1(II) chains.

items.q: Which amino acid occupies every third position of the collagen chain (Gly-X-Y repeat), and whose substitution underlies most severe osteogenesis imperfecta mutations?
items.e: Glycine, the smallest amino acid, is required at every third residue to fit inside the tight triple helix; glycine substitutions in COL1A1/COL1A2 disrupt helix folding and cause severe OI.

items.q: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis requires which cofactor, whose deficiency causes defective collagen in scurvy?
items.e: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate (and ferrous iron); without hydroxylation the triple helix is unstable, producing the bleeding, subperiosteal haemorrhage and weak osteoid of scurvy.

items.q: Which non-collagenous bone protein, also called SPARC, binds both calcium and collagen and helps regulate mineralisation?
items.e: Osteonectin (SPARC), made by osteoblasts and platelets, links mineral to collagen; osteocalcin is the vitamin K-dependent gla protein and osteopontin an RGD-containing attachment protein.

items.q: Which pair of non-collagenous matrix proteins contains RGD sequences that anchor osteoclasts to bone via integrins?
items.e: Osteopontin and bone sialoprotein carry Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) motifs that bind the osteoclast alpha-v-beta-3 integrin to form the sealing zone.

items.q: In skeletal fluorosis, fluoride substitutes for the hydroxyl group of hydroxyapatite. The resulting bone is:
o: Of normal quality but lower density
Denser and harder but more brittle
Unmineralised with wide osteoid seams only
items.e: Fluorapatite crystals are larger and more stable, so bone becomes dense and hard but brittle, with an increased fracture tendency despite higher density.

items.q: Which transcription factor acts downstream of RUNX2 and is essential for the final commitment of pre-osteoblasts to mature osteoblasts?
items.e: Osterix (SP7) is required downstream of RUNX2 for osteoblast maturation; SOX9 drives chondrocytes and PPAR-gamma adipocytes.

items.q: A child has severe juvenile osteoporosis with fractures and congenital blindness. Loss-of-function mutation of which gene is responsible?
items.e: Loss-of-function of the Wnt co-receptor LRP5 causes osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome (low bone mass and eye abnormalities); gain-of-function LRP5 mutations cause high bone mass.

items.q: Sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease, characterised by progressive skeletal overgrowth and cranial nerve compression, result from loss of function of which gene?
items.e: Loss of sclerostin (SOST) removes a Wnt inhibitor, causing unchecked bone formation; this observation led to the anti-sclerostin antibody romosozumab.

items.q: Multiple myeloma typically produces purely lytic lesions that are often cold on bone scan. Overproduction of which Wnt inhibitor contributes by suppressing osteoblast activity?
items.e: Myeloma cells secrete DKK1, which blocks Wnt signalling and osteoblast function, so lesions lack a reparative blastic response; RANKL excess simultaneously drives resorption.

items.q: Romosozumab differs from teriparatide in that, besides increasing bone formation, it also:
o: Acts as a decoy receptor for RANK
items.e: Blocking sclerostin both stimulates osteoblastic formation and reduces resorption (lower RANKL), a dual effect; teriparatide increases both formation and, later, resorption.

items.q: Why does once-daily teriparatide build bone whereas primary hyperparathyroidism causes bone loss?
o: Intermittent PTH exposure increases osteoblast number and survival, whereas continuous high PTH favours resorption
Teriparatide binds directly to osteoclasts and inhibits them
items.e: Intermittent PTH1R activation is anabolic (osteoblast recruitment, reduced apoptosis, lower sclerostin); sustained elevation increases osteoblast RANKL and net resorption.

items.q: After completing matrix synthesis, the fate of the majority of osteoblasts is to:
items.e: Most osteoblasts die by apoptosis; about 10-20% are entombed as osteocytes and the remainder become flat bone-lining cells. Osteoclasts derive from a different (haematopoietic) lineage.

items.q: Osteocytes communicate with each other and with surface cells through dendritic processes in canaliculi, linked mainly by gap junctions formed of:
items.e: Connexin 43 gap junctions couple the osteocyte network, allowing transmission of mechanical and chemical signals through the lacuno-canalicular system.

items.q: What is the effect of mechanical loading on osteocyte sclerostin production?
o: Loading has no effect on sclerostin
Loading reduces sclerostin, releasing Wnt signalling and increasing formation
items.e: Load-induced fluid shear lowers osteocyte sclerostin, de-repressing Wnt/beta-catenin and bone formation; unloading (bed rest, space flight) raises sclerostin and causes bone loss.

items.q: The phosphaturic hormone FGF23 is produced mainly by which cells?
items.e: Osteocytes secrete FGF23, which with Klotho reduces renal phosphate reabsorption and inhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase; PHEX and DMP1 in osteocytes regulate it.

items.q: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure malignant infantile osteopetrosis because osteoclasts:
o: Are derived from mesenchymal stromal cells
Derive from the haematopoietic monocyte-macrophage lineage
Need transplanted osteoblasts to produce RANKL
items.e: Osteoclasts arise from haematopoietic monocyte-macrophage precursors, so donor marrow supplies functional osteoclasts; this is effective when the defect is intrinsic to the osteoclast.

items.q: Which two factors are both necessary and sufficient for differentiation of osteoclast precursors into mature osteoclasts?
items.e: M-CSF (via c-Fms) supports precursor survival and proliferation, and RANKL (via RANK and NF-kappa-B) drives fusion and activation; OPG inhibits the process.

items.q: A child has osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification. Deficiency of which enzyme is responsible?
items.e: Carbonic anhydrase II supplies protons for osteoclastic acidification and for renal acid handling; its deficiency causes the triad of osteopetrosis, RTA and intracerebral calcification.

items.q: Pyknodysostosis (short stature, dense brittle bones, open fontanelles, acro-osteolysis) is caused by deficiency of:
items.e: Cathepsin K, the osteoclast cysteine protease that digests type I collagen, is deficient in pyknodysostosis; mineral is dissolved but collagen matrix is not degraded.

items.q: Calcitonin reduces bone resorption by:
items.e: Osteoclasts express calcitonin receptors, so calcitonin acts directly to cause rapid loss of the ruffled border and reduced resorption; in contrast osteoclasts lack PTH receptors.

items.q: The shallow resorption pits created by osteoclasts on bone surfaces are called:
items.e: Howship lacunae are the resorption bays beneath active osteoclasts; Haversian and Volkmann canals carry vessels in cortical bone.

items.q: Mutation of which gene is associated with familial Paget disease of bone through enhanced RANK-NF-kappa-B signalling?
items.e: SQSTM1 mutations are the commonest genetic cause of familial Paget disease, increasing osteoclast activity; activating RANK mutations cause familial expansile osteolysis.

items.q: Accelerated bone loss after the menopause is mediated mainly by:
o: An increased RANKL:OPG ratio with longer osteoclast lifespan
items.e: Oestrogen normally increases OPG and limits RANKL and osteoclast survival; its loss raises the RANKL:OPG ratio and cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha), accelerating trabecular resorption.

items.q: A woman stops denosumab after 4 years without starting another agent. Which complication is characteristically reported?
o: Rebound increase in bone turnover with multiple vertebral fractures
Osteonecrosis of the jaw on stopping
items.e: Denosumab's effect is reversible; stopping it causes a rebound surge in turnover and rapid loss of BMD with multiple vertebral fractures, so a bisphosphonate should follow.

items.q: Compared with lamellar bone, woven bone is:
o: Composed of randomly oriented collagen and mechanically isotropic
items.e: Woven bone has coarse, random collagen, is laid down rapidly, is weak and isotropic, and is normal only in the embryo, the metaphysis and fracture callus; lamellar bone is organised and anisotropic.

items.q: Persistence of woven bone in the mature skeleton is characteristic of which condition?
items.e: Woven bone in adults is pathological: Paget disease, fibrous dysplasia ('Chinese letter' trabeculae), osteosarcoma and hyperparathyroidism; osteoporosis has normal lamellar bone in reduced amount.

items.q: Compared with cortical bone, cancellous bone has:
o: Greater surface area and several times faster turnover
items.e: Cancellous bone forms about 20% of skeletal mass but has a large surface area and much higher turnover, so it is lost first in postmenopausal and steroid osteoporosis.

items.q: In cortical bone, which structures mark the outer boundary of an osteon and act as a weak interface where microcracks are arrested?
items.e: Cement (reversal) lines are laid at the end of the resorption phase and bound each osteon; they deflect and stop microcracks. Volkmann canals run transversely linking Haversian canals.

items.q: Sharpey fibres are:
o: Collagen fibres of the endosteum lining the medullary canal
Collagen fibres anchoring tendons, ligaments and the periosteum into bone
items.e: Sharpey (perforating) fibres are extrinsic collagen bundles from the fibrous periosteum, tendons and ligaments embedded in bone.

items.q: In mature long bone, the nutrient artery supplies approximately which part of the diaphyseal cortex?
items.e: The high-pressure nutrient (endosteal) system supplies the inner two-thirds of the cortex, and periosteal vessels the outer third.

items.q: After a displaced diaphyseal fracture or intramedullary reaming, the direction of cortical blood flow changes from:
o: Centrifugal (inside-out) to centripetal (outside-in), with the periosteum dominant
items.e: Normal flow is centrifugal because the medullary system is high pressure; when the endosteal supply is disrupted, flow becomes centripetal from the periosteum, so periosteal stripping should be minimised.

items.q: New bone in the regenerate zone during Ilizarov distraction osteogenesis forms mainly by:
items.e: Under stable fixation, the distraction gap ossifies by direct intramembranous bone formation along tension lines; fracture callus under relative stability is endochondral.

items.q: The usual distraction rate and rhythm in Ilizarov lengthening after a latency of 5-7 days is:
o: 2 mm per day as a single increment
3 mm per day in three increments
1 mm per day in four increments of 0.25 mm
items.e: About 1 mm per day divided into four 0.25 mm steps balances regenerate formation; faster rates risk poor regenerate and slower rates premature consolidation.

items.q: Which secondary ossification centre is normally present at birth in a term infant and is used as a sign of fetal maturity?
items.e: The distal femoral epiphysis appears at about 36-40 weeks' gestation; the femoral head appears at about 4-6 months and the capitellum at about 1 year.

items.q: Defects of matrix production in the reserve (resting) zone of the physis are associated with which condition?
items.e: Reserve-zone disorders include diastrophic dysplasia (sulphate transporter), pseudoachondroplasia, Kniest dysplasia and Gaucher disease; achondroplasia is proliferative-zone and rickets hypertrophic-zone.

items.q: Most physeal (Salter-Harris) fractures propagate through which part of the growth plate?
o: Zone of provisional calcification in the hypertrophic zone
items.e: The hypertrophic zone, with enlarged cells and little matrix, is the weakest; fractures pass through the zone of provisional calcification, leaving the germinal layers with the epiphysis.

items.q: Scurvy and acute haematogenous osteomyelitis both characteristically affect which region of the growing bone?
items.e: The primary spongiosa, where vessels invade calcified cartilage, is affected in scurvy (defective osteoid, Trümmerfeld zone) and is the site of sluggish sinusoidal flow that predisposes to osteomyelitis.

items.q: The ossification groove of Ranvier at the periphery of the physis is responsible for:
o: Growth in width (latitudinal growth) of the physis
Vascular invasion of the hypertrophic zone
items.e: The groove of Ranvier contains chondroprogenitor cells that add cells peripherally and widen the physis; the perichondrial ring of LaCroix provides mechanical support.

items.q: The fibrous perichondrial ring of LaCroix around the physis mainly:
o: Provides mechanical support to the physis against shear
items.e: The ring of LaCroix is a dense fibrous band continuous with the periosteum that buttresses the physis; the groove of Ranvier is the cellular zone for latitudinal growth.

items.q: An activating mutation of the PTH/PTHrP receptor, which delays chondrocyte hypertrophy, causes:
items.e: Constitutive PTH1R activation keeps chondrocytes proliferating and delays hypertrophy (and causes hypercalcaemia): Jansen type; Schmid type is a COL10A1 defect.

items.q: A tall adult man has persistently open physes and osteoporosis despite normal testosterone. Which defect best explains this?
items.e: Oestrogen drives physeal closure and bone mass accrual in both sexes; men lacking aromatase or oestrogen receptor activity keep open physes and grow tall.

items.q: The Hueter-Volkmann law states that, at the physis:
o: Increased compression inhibits growth and tension stimulates it
items.e: Compression slows and reduced compression (tension) accelerates physeal growth; this explains progression of scoliosis and Blount disease and is the basis of guided growth.

items.q: According to the stress-generated (piezoelectric) potentials of loaded bone, which statement is correct?
o: The tension side is electronegative and forms bone
The compression side is electronegative and is associated with bone formation
The compression side is electropositive and resorbed
items.e: Compressed bone becomes electronegative and favours formation; tension sides are electropositive and favour resorption, which is why the cathode is placed at a non-union in electrical stimulation.

items.q: How does bone modelling differ from remodelling?
o: Modelling replaces old bone at the same site with coupled resorption then formation
Modelling changes bone shape with formation and resorption on different surfaces, not coupled
Modelling occurs only in cancellous bone
items.e: Modelling (growth, malunion correction in children) uncouples formation and resorption on different surfaces to alter shape; remodelling is coupled renewal at one site by a basic multicellular unit.

items.q: In the adult bone remodelling cycle (basic multicellular unit), approximate durations of the resorption and formation phases are:
items.e: Osteoclastic resorption is quick (weeks) whereas osteoblastic refilling and mineralisation take months, which is why antiresorptives produce an early BMD gain by closing the remodelling space.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of trabecular and cortical bone, respectively, is remodelled each year in adults?
items.e: Trabecular bone turns over about 25% per year and cortical bone about 2-5%, reflecting the larger surface area of cancellous bone.

items.q: A man has a complete laceration of the median nerve at the wrist, yet abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis remain functional on EMG. The most likely explanation is a:
o: Berrettini anastomosis between common digital nerves
items.e: The Riche-Cannieu anastomosis connects the deep branch of the ulnar nerve with the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve in the palm, so thenar muscles can be ulnar-innervated. Martin-Gruber is a forearm median-to-ulnar connection, and Berrettini is a purely sensory communication.

items.q: During primary TKA for a varus knee, the superficial MCL is inadvertently transected at mid-substance. The generally recommended management is:
o: Accept it and use a thicker standard polyethylene insert
Direct repair of the ligament, considering a more constrained insert and protected bracing
Routine conversion to a rotating-hinge prosthesis
Abandon the TKA and perform a lateral unicompartmental arthroplasty
items.e: Intraoperative MCL injury is managed by primary repair (with or without augmentation), with increased constraint such as a varus-valgus constrained insert considered and a period of bracing. A thicker insert alone leaves the knee unstable, and a hinge is reserved for unreconstructable collateral loss.

items.q: Shenton's line on an AP pelvic radiograph, which is broken when the hip is subluxed or dislocated, is a smooth arc formed by the medial border of the femoral neck and the:
o: Lateral edge of the acetabular roof
Inferior border of the superior pubic ramus
Medial wall of the ischial tuberosity
items.e: Shenton's line runs along the inferomedial femoral neck and continues as the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus (upper margin of the obturator foramen); proximal migration of the femur breaks this arc.

items.q: A 19-year-old pitcher has posterior elbow pain for 4 months; MRI shows an oblique olecranon stress fracture that has not healed despite rest from throwing. The preferred treatment to allow return to throwing is:
o: Excision of the proximal olecranon fragment with triceps advancement
Continued throwing in a hinged elbow brace
Internal fixation with an intramedullary compression screw (with or without bone graft)
items.e: Olecranon stress fractures in throwers that fail rest are fixed with an intramedullary compression screw, giving high union and return-to-play rates. Excision would destabilise the elbow, and UCL reconstruction does not treat the fracture.

items.q: In Salter's criteria for avascular necrosis after treatment of DDH, failure of the femoral head ossific nucleus to appear within what period after reduction indicates AVN?
items.e: Salter's criteria include failure of appearance or growth of the ossific nucleus within 1 year of reduction, broadening of the femoral neck within that year, increased density then fragmentation of the head, and residual deformity after reossification.

items.q: Six months after repair of a median nerve laceration at the forearm, the Tinel sign remains strongly positive at the repair site and has not advanced distally. This most suggests:
o: Normal axonal regeneration ahead of schedule
Failure of axonal regeneration across the repair, such as a neuroma-in-continuity
items.e: A Tinel sign that advances distally at about 1 mm/day signals regenerating axons; a static, strong Tinel at the repair site after months suggests axons are not crossing (neuroma), warranting re-exploration. Neurapraxia does not produce an advancing or static Tinel at a repair.

items.q: On a lateral knee radiograph, how do the tibial plateaus differ in shape?
o: The medial plateau is concave and the lateral plateau is convex
The medial plateau is convex and the lateral plateau is concave
items.e: The lateral plateau is convex and sits higher, whereas the larger medial plateau is concave and bears more load; this helps identify each plateau and its depression on the lateral view.

items.q: Which Schatzker type is the commonest tibial plateau fracture?
items.e: The lateral split-depression (Schatzker II) is the commonest pattern, produced by valgus and axial loading of the lateral plateau. Medial and bicondylar patterns need higher energy.

items.q: A 72-year-old osteoporotic woman steps off a kerb awkwardly and sustains a central depression of the lateral tibial plateau with an intact lateral cortex. The Schatzker type is:
items.e: Pure depression without a lateral split is Schatzker III, typical of osteoporotic bone. Type II has a split as well as depression.

items.q: A 24-year-old with dense bone has a displaced pure lateral wedge (split) fracture of the tibial plateau with no depression. Which soft-tissue problem should particularly be looked for before reduction?
o: Lateral meniscus trapped in the fracture gap
items.e: In Schatzker I splits in young dense bone, the lateral meniscus can be incarcerated in the fracture and block reduction; MRI or arthroscopy/arthrotomy confirms it.

items.q: Which feature defines a Schatzker VI tibial plateau fracture?
o: Dissociation of the metaphysis from the diaphysis
Bicondylar fracture with intact metaphyseal-diaphyseal continuity
Pure depression of the lateral plateau
items.e: Schatzker VI is a plateau fracture with a transverse or oblique metaphyseal component separating the articular block from the shaft; V is bicondylar with the metaphysis still connected to the shaft.

items.q: After a high-energy bicondylar tibial plateau fracture, the foot pulses are palpable but the ankle-brachial index is 0.8. The next step is:
items.e: An ABI below 0.9 indicates possible arterial injury and requires arterial imaging (usually CT angiography) even if pulses are palpable; an ABI of 0.9 or more allows serial clinical examination.

items.q: Which soft-tissue injury most commonly accompanies a lateral tibial plateau fracture?
items.e: Lateral meniscal tears, often peripheral and sometimes incarcerated, are the commonest associated soft-tissue injury, followed by MCL and ACL injuries.

items.q: Which classification of tibial plateau injuries specifically describes fracture-dislocations and is used to predict the risk of neurovascular injury?
items.e: Moore's classification describes fracture-dislocations (split, entire condyle, rim avulsion, rim compression, four-part); neurovascular injury risk rises with type, so these injuries are treated like knee dislocations.

items.q: In Moore's classification of tibial plateau fracture-dislocations, which type carries the highest risk of neurovascular injury (about 50%)?
items.e: The risk of neurovascular injury rises from about 2% in type I split injuries to about 50% in four-part (type V) fracture-dislocations.

items.q: Luo's CT-based three-column classification of tibial plateau fractures was introduced mainly because the Schatzker system:
o: Cannot distinguish medial from lateral fractures
items.e: Schatzker is based on the AP radiograph and misses posterior column fragments, especially posteromedial coronal fractures; Luo's lateral, medial and posterior columns guide approach and plate placement.

items.q: A 50-year-old has a posteromedial coronal-plane shear fragment of the tibial plateau. Which approach gives the best access to buttress it?
o: Lateral approach with fibular head osteotomy
items.e: A posteromedial fragment needs a posteromedial or posterior buttress plate; the Lobenhoffer approach between the medial gastrocnemius and the pes anserinus/semimembranosus gives direct access.

items.q: A randomised trial by Russell and Leighton found that, compared with autogenous iliac crest graft, calcium phosphate cement used to fill the subchondral void after elevation of a depressed tibial plateau fracture:
o: Had a higher rate of deep infection
Caused more non-unions of the metaphysis
Had a lower rate of articular subsidence
items.e: Calcium phosphate cement resists compression and showed less subsidence of the elevated joint surface than iliac crest autograft, while also avoiding donor-site morbidity.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a minimally displaced lateral tibial plateau fracture. Examination under anaesthesia shows 15 degrees of valgus opening with the knee in full extension. The best management is:
o: Operative fixation because the knee is unstable
Hinged brace and early range of motion
items.e: Varus or valgus instability of more than about 10 degrees in full extension is an indication for operative stabilisation, even when articular displacement is small; stability and alignment matter more than a small step-off.

items.q: Which radiological finding in a lateral tibial plateau fracture is generally accepted as an indication for operative treatment?
o: Lipohaemarthrosis on a cross-table lateral view
Condylar widening of more than 5 mm
A fibular head avulsion of 2 mm
items.e: Condylar widening over 5 mm (and step-off over about 2-3 mm, or instability) favours surgery. A lipohaemarthrosis simply confirms an intra-articular fracture.

items.q: During fixation of a Schatzker II fracture through an anterolateral approach, how is the articular surface best visualised directly?
o: Transection of the lateral meniscus at its midbody
Submeniscal arthrotomy with elevation of the lateral meniscus
items.e: A horizontal submeniscal arthrotomy through the coronary ligament allows the meniscus to be lifted and the joint surface seen; the meniscus is repaired back at closure. Cutting the meniscus sacrifices its function.

items.q: After elevating a depressed lateral plateau fragment, what is the purpose of placing several small screws just beneath the subchondral bone parallel to the joint?
o: To provide rotational stability to the diaphysis
To fix the meniscus to bone
To compress the medial and lateral condyles together as lag screws only
To act as a raft supporting the elevated articular surface
items.e: Rafting screws placed immediately below the subchondral plate support the elevated fragments and reduce later subsidence, together with bone graft or substitute in the void.

items.q: During the anterolateral approach to the proximal tibia, the iliotibial band is incised or elevated near its insertion on which landmark?
items.e: The iliotibial band inserts into Gerdy's tubercle on the anterolateral proximal tibia; it is split or elevated, and tibialis anterior is elevated from the lateral metaphysis to place a lateral plate.

items.q: Long-term studies of tibial plateau fractures indicate that the development of post-traumatic osteoarthritis is most strongly related to:
o: The use of a locking rather than a conventional plate
Residual malalignment and instability of the knee
A residual articular step-off of 2 mm
items.e: Retained mechanical malalignment and instability correlate with post-traumatic arthritis more than small residual articular incongruity, which the plateau tolerates relatively well.

items.q: Which tibial plateau fracture type carries the highest risk of acute compartment syndrome?
items.e: High-energy fractures with metaphyseal-diaphyseal dissociation (Schatzker VI) have the highest compartment syndrome rates; low-energy lateral fractures rarely cause it.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a Schatzker VI fracture with tense compartments. Diastolic pressure is 70 mmHg and the anterior compartment pressure is 48 mmHg. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Absolute pressure is below 50 mmHg; no fasciotomy is needed
Delta pressure is 22 mmHg; observe as it is above 20
Delta pressure is 118 mmHg; no action needed
Delta pressure is 22 mmHg; fasciotomy is indicated
items.e: Delta pressure is diastolic minus compartment pressure (70 - 48 = 22 mmHg); a value below 30 mmHg indicates compartment syndrome and the need for four-compartment fasciotomy.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a varus fracture-dislocation of the medial tibial plateau with an avulsion of the fibular head. Which nerve is at particular risk?
items.e: Varus medial plateau fracture-dislocations put the lateral side under tension, causing fibular head avulsion, posterolateral corner injury and common peroneal nerve traction injury.

items.q: A 78-year-old with pre-existing symptomatic tricompartmental osteoarthritis sustains a severely comminuted, depressed tibial plateau fracture in osteoporotic bone. A recognised option to allow immediate weight-bearing is:
o: Acute total knee arthroplasty with augments or stems as needed
items.e: In selected elderly patients with pre-existing arthritis and unreconstructable osteoporotic fractures, primary TKA (often stemmed or augmented) allows early weight-bearing and avoids failed fixation.

items.q: When placing fine tension wires for a circular or hybrid frame for a proximal tibial fracture, why are wires kept at least about 14 mm below the articular surface?
o: To avoid the patellar tendon insertion
To avoid the physis in adults
The joint capsule and synovial reflection extend this far below the joint, so higher wires risk septic arthritis
Because the lateral meniscus attaches there
items.e: The capsular reflection extends about 14 mm below the joint line, especially posterolaterally; wires placed above it are intra-articular and pin-track infection can become septic arthritis.

items.q: Compared with open reduction, arthroscopically assisted reduction and internal fixation (ARIF) of a lateral split-depression plateau fracture particularly allows:
o: Fixation of bicondylar fractures with metaphyseal dissociation
Elimination of the need for bone graft
Avoidance of any risk of compartment syndrome
Direct assessment of the articular reduction and treatment of meniscal injuries with less soft-tissue dissection
items.e: ARIF suits lateral split and depression fractures; it shows the joint surface and menisci with minimal soft-tissue stripping, but fluid extravasation can cause compartment syndrome, so pump pressure is kept low.

items.q: Why are isolated medial tibial plateau fractures usually treated operatively even when displacement seems small?
o: They are inherently unstable and tend to drift into varus
They always involve the anterior cruciate ligament
The medial plateau has no subchondral bone
items.e: The medial plateau bears most of the load and medial fractures often represent fracture-dislocations; they tend to displace into varus, so buttress fixation is usually advised.

items.q: A patient has haemorrhagic (blood-filled) and clear fracture blisters over a tibial plateau fracture. Which statement guides incision placement?
o: Clear blisters are more dangerous than blood-filled blisters
Blood-filled blisters indicate a deeper dermal injury and take longer to re-epithelialise, so incisions should avoid them
Blisters should be unroofed and the incision made through them at once
Blisters have no effect on wound healing
items.e: Haemorrhagic blisters reflect complete separation of the epidermis from the dermis and heal more slowly than clear blisters; incisions are planned away from them and definitive surgery is delayed until the skin has recovered.

items.q: In the AO/OTA classification, a tibial plateau fracture with a split of the lateral condyle combined with depression of the articular surface is coded as:
items.e: 41-B is partial articular proximal tibia: B1 pure split, B2 pure depression, B3 split-depression. 41-C is complete articular, and 43 is the distal tibia.

items.q: Which interval is used for the anteromedial approach to the distal tibia for a pilon fracture?
o: Between extensor digitorum longus and the fibula
Between the Achilles tendon and the peroneal tendons
Between peroneus brevis and flexor hallucis longus
items.e: The anteromedial approach runs just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon over the thin anteromedial skin; it accesses medial and central fragments but has the least soft-tissue cover.

items.q: The anterolateral approach to a pilon fracture, between the extensor digitorum longus/peroneus tertius and the fibula, places which nerve at risk?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve crosses the anterolateral ankle in the superficial tissues and must be identified; this approach gives access to the Chaput fragment and the fibula.

items.q: For the posterolateral approach to the distal tibia in a pilon fracture, which internervous interval is used and which nerve is at risk superficially?
o: Between the Achilles tendon and tibialis posterior; saphenous nerve
Between the peroneal tendons and flexor hallucis longus; sural nerve
Between flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior; tibial nerve
Between tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus; deep peroneal nerve
items.e: The posterolateral approach uses the interval between the peroneals (superficial peroneal nerve) and FHL (tibial nerve), giving access to the Volkmann fragment and fibula; the sural nerve and small saphenous vein lie superficially.

items.q: In a tibial pilon fracture, the anterolateral (Chaput) fragment remains attached to which structure?
items.e: The Chaput (anterolateral) fragment is held by the AITFL, and the Volkmann (posterolateral) fragment by the PITFL; because these ligaments tether them to the fibula, restoring fibular length helps reduce them.

items.q: A fall from height causes a comminuted tibial pilon fracture. Besides the ankle, which injuries must specifically be sought?
o: Scaphoid and distal radius fractures only
items.e: Axial loading from a fall transmits force through the calcaneus and spine; calcaneal, spinal and contralateral limb fractures are commonly associated with pilon fractures.

items.q: In the Rüedi-Allgöwer classification of pilon fractures, a type III injury is:
o: A comminuted and impacted articular fracture
A displaced articular fracture with minimal comminution
items.e: Rüedi-Allgöwer I is undisplaced, II displaced with little comminution, and III comminuted and impacted, with the worst prognosis.

items.q: An AO/OTA 43-C3 fracture of the distal tibia is:
o: Complete articular with articular and metaphyseal comminution
Extra-articular with a simple metaphyseal fracture
items.e: 43 is the distal tibia; A extra-articular, B partial articular, C complete articular. C3 has comminution of the joint surface as well as the metaphysis.

items.q: Which classification grades closed-fracture soft-tissue injury and is often used to time definitive fixation of pilon fractures?
items.e: Tscherne grades closed soft-tissue injury from C0 (minimal) to C3 (extensive crush, degloving or compartment syndrome); Gustilo-Anderson grades open fractures.

items.q: When a spanning external fixator is applied for a pilon fracture, why is a pin often placed into the first metatarsal or medial cuneiform as well as the calcaneus?
o: To correct valgus of the hindfoot
To prevent equinus of the foot
items.e: A calcaneal pin alone allows the forefoot to drop; adding a pin into the first metatarsal or cuneiform holds the foot plantigrade and prevents equinus contracture.

items.q: In the first stage of pilon fracture management, plating the fibula through a poor-quality incision has fallen out of favour partly because:
o: A malreduced fibula prevents later anatomical reduction of the tibia
It increases the risk of compartment syndrome in the thigh
items.e: If the fibula is fixed short or malrotated, the tibial fragments tethered to it cannot be reduced later; fibular fixation at stage one should be done only when the reduction is certain and incisions fit the definitive plan.

items.q: High-energy tibial pilon fractures treated with early ORIF in the 1980s-1990s had deep infection and wound complication rates of up to:
items.e: Early ORIF through swollen soft tissues led to wound breakdown and deep infection in up to 30-40%; the staged protocols of Sirkin and of Patterson and Cole reduced this to under about 5-10%.

items.q: Which is the commonest malunion after a tibial pilon fracture?
items.e: Collapse of the medial column into varus is the commonest malunion, which is why Rüedi-Allgöwer emphasised buttressing the medial tibia.

items.q: A fracture of the distal tibia without a fibular fracture is likely to have collapsed into which deformity?
items.e: With an intact fibula, the lateral side is held out to length, so axial loading typically drives the plafond into varus; a fibular fracture is more often associated with valgus patterns.

items.q: Where does non-union most often occur after a tibial pilon fracture?
items.e: Metaphyseal comminution and bone loss with stripped soft tissues make metaphyseal non-union the usual site; bone grafting the metaphyseal defect is one of the Rüedi-Allgöwer principles.

items.q: Post-traumatic ankle arthritis after a pilon fracture is thought to be determined mainly by:
o: Initial cartilage damage at the time of injury
items.e: Even with good reduction, many patients develop arthritis because of irreversible chondrocyte damage at impact; reduction quality matters but cannot undo the initial injury.

items.q: A 55-year-old diabetic smoker has an unreconstructable, severely comminuted pilon fracture with extensive articular cartilage loss. Which definitive option is reasonable?
items.e: When the plafond cannot be reconstructed, primary ankle arthrodesis (for example with a retrograde nail or plate, or a frame) gives a stable, pain-free ankle; total ankle replacement is contraindicated in acute comminuted fractures.

items.q: What is the primary mechanism of a tibial pilon fracture, distinguishing it from a rotational ankle fracture?
o: Direct blow to the lateral malleolus
Axial loading driving the talus into the plafond
items.e: Pilon fractures result from axial loading (falls, road traffic accidents), with central impaction and metaphyseal comminution; rotational ankle fractures involve the malleoli with little plafond impaction.

items.q: The central impacted articular fragment commonly seen in pilon fractures is described as:
items.e: Axial loading of the talus produces central 'die-punch' impaction of the plafond that must be disimpacted and supported with graft. Tillaux and Wagstaffe fragments are avulsions of the tibial and fibular attachments of the AITFL.

items.q: A Gustilo IIIB open pilon fracture is debrided and stabilised. According to BOAST guidance on open fractures, definitive soft-tissue cover should ideally be achieved within:
items.e: BOAST 4 (open fractures) recommends definitive soft-tissue cover within 72 hours if it is not done at the first debridement; delayed cover increases infection.

items.q: When planning incisions for staged ORIF of a pilon fracture, the traditional recommendation for the minimum skin bridge between two parallel incisions is about:
items.e: A skin bridge of at least about 5-7 cm has traditionally been advised to protect skin perfusion, although some studies suggest narrower bridges are tolerated when incisions are carefully planned.

items.q: What is the typical interval from injury to definitive ORIF in staged management of a high-energy pilon fracture?
items.e: Definitive fixation is delayed until swelling settles, the wrinkle sign returns and blisters re-epithelialise, typically about 1-3 weeks after spanning external fixation.

items.q: A pilon fracture has severe soft-tissue injury and the patient cannot tolerate extensile approaches. A recognised definitive treatment is:
o: Limited internal fixation of the joint with a circular (Ilizarov) or hybrid frame
Early ORIF with an anteromedial plate through the swollen skin
Closed reduction and a below-knee cast
items.e: Fine-wire circular or hybrid frames with percutaneous articular screws neutralise the fracture while sparing the soft tissues; they suit patients whose soft tissues will not tolerate plating.

items.q: An associated fibular fracture is present in approximately what proportion of tibial pilon fractures?
items.e: About three quarters of pilon fractures have a fibular fracture; restoring fibular length helps restore lateral column length and reduce the lateral tibial fragments.

items.q: In adults, haematogenous osteomyelitis most commonly involves which site?
items.e: Adult haematogenous osteomyelitis is uncommon outside the spine; vertebral (spondylodiscitis) involvement predominates, whereas long-bone metaphyses are the typical site in children.

items.q: In the randomised trial by Bernard and colleagues (Lancet 2015) of pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, what was the main finding?
o: 12 weeks of antibiotics halved the relapse rate compared with 6 weeks
6 weeks of antibiotics was non-inferior to 12 weeks
Oral antibiotics were inferior to intravenous antibiotics
Early surgical debridement reduced treatment failure compared with antibiotics alone
items.e: Bernard et al showed that a 6-week course cured as many patients as a 12-week course in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis; the oral-versus-IV question was answered by OVIVA, not this trial.

items.q: Bacteria living in a mature biofilm on dead bone or an implant are approximately how much more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating (planktonic) bacteria?
o: They are no more resistant; only access is reduced
items.e: Biofilm bacteria are metabolically dormant within a glycocalyx matrix and can tolerate antibiotic concentrations up to about 1000-fold higher than planktonic forms, which is why sequestra and loose implants must be removed.

items.q: Why must rifampicin never be used as monotherapy for staphylococcal bone or implant infection?
o: It has no activity against biofilm bacteria
It is bacteriostatic only against Gram-negative organisms
Resistance emerges rapidly through single-step mutation
items.e: Rifampicin is valued for its anti-biofilm activity against staphylococci, but a single point mutation in rpoB rapidly produces resistance, so it is always combined with a second active agent.

items.q: Recurrence of staphylococcal osteomyelitis years after apparently successful treatment is partly explained by small-colony variants. These are:
o: Slow-growing, metabolically inactive phenotypes that persist intracellularly
Highly virulent strains producing Panton-Valentine leukocidin
items.e: Small-colony variants grow slowly, survive inside osteoblasts and other cells, and are tolerant of many antibiotics, allowing late relapse; PVL is a toxin associated with severe acute disease, not dormancy.

items.q: A 28-year-old punches someone in the mouth and presents 3 days later with septic arthritis of the third metacarpophalangeal joint. Besides streptococci and anaerobes, which organism is characteristically isolated?
items.e: A clenched-fist (fight-bite) injury inoculates human oral flora, classically Eikenella corrodens; Pasteurella is typical of cat and dog bites.

items.q: A woman is bitten on the finger by her cat and within 24 hours develops a rapidly progressive flexor tenosynovitis. The most likely organism is:
items.e: Pasteurella multocida is the characteristic pathogen of cat (and dog) bites and produces a rapid inflammatory response within the first day.

items.q: An aquarium keeper has an indolent granulomatous tenosynovitis of the hand. Synovial biopsy for Mycobacterium marinum should be cultured at:
items.e: M. marinum grows best at lower temperatures (around 30-32 C), so the laboratory must be told; routine culture at 37 C may be negative.

items.q: A gardener develops a nodular lesion on the finger after a rose-thorn prick, followed by a chain of nodules along the lymphatics of the forearm. The causative organism is:
items.e: Lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) spread after a thorn injury is typical of the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii.

items.q: A dairy farmer who drinks unpasteurised milk has lumbar spondylitis. MRI shows erosion of the anterosuperior vertebral endplate with preserved vertebral architecture and little paravertebral abscess. This radiological sign is the:
items.e: The Pedro Pons sign (anterosuperior endplate erosion) is characteristic of brucellar spondylitis, which, unlike tuberculosis, tends to preserve vertebral shape and rarely forms large abscesses.

items.q: The recommended antibiotic regimen for brucellar spondylitis is:
o: Doxycycline plus rifampicin (or an aminoglycoside) for about 12 weeks
Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 12 months
items.e: Brucellosis is treated with combination therapy based on doxycycline with rifampicin or streptomycin/gentamicin; spondylitis needs prolonged treatment of about 3 months.

items.q: A boy with recurrent catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections develops vertebral osteomyelitis due to Aspergillus. The underlying immune defect is most likely:
items.e: Chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase defect) predisposes to infections with catalase-positive organisms such as S. aureus, Serratia and Aspergillus, including osteomyelitis.

items.q: A patient with a 20-year history of discharging chronic tibial osteomyelitis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. The most likely cause is:
o: Marjolin ulcer metastasis to the kidney
items.e: Long-standing chronic infection drives persistent serum amyloid A production, leading to AA amyloid deposition, most often presenting with renal involvement.

items.q: In a diabetic patient with a foot ulcer, which ESR value is classically cited as strongly suggesting underlying osteomyelitis?
items.e: An ESR over 70 mm/h, an ulcer larger than 2 cm2 or deeper than 3 mm and a positive probe-to-bone test all increase the likelihood of diabetic foot osteomyelitis.

items.q: Why is a labelled-leucocyte (In-111 or Tc-99m HMPAO) scan of limited value for suspected vertebral osteomyelitis?
o: Leucocytes do not reach the vertebral marrow
It is falsely positive after any spinal surgery only
Spinal infection often appears as a photopenic (cold) defect
Radiation dose to the spinal cord is prohibitive
items.e: In the axial skeleton labelled-leucocyte scans frequently show infection as cold areas and normal marrow uptake confounds interpretation; MRI or FDG PET-CT is preferred.

items.q: Which nuclear imaging technique is most accurate for chronic osteomyelitis of the axial skeleton and is relatively little affected by metal implants?
o: Tc-99m sulphur colloid marrow scan alone
items.e: FDG PET-CT has high sensitivity and specificity for chronic and axial infection; the three-phase bone scan is sensitive but non-specific after surgery or trauma.

items.q: To plan sequestrectomy in chronic osteomyelitis, which investigation best demonstrates sequestra, cloacae and cortical destruction?
items.e: CT gives the best definition of cortical bone and shows dense, sharply marginated sequestra and cloacae; MRI is better for marrow oedema and soft-tissue abscesses.

items.q: Before an elective bone biopsy for suspected chronic osteomyelitis in a clinically stable patient, antibiotics should ideally be withheld for about:
items.e: Stopping antibiotics around 2 weeks before sampling improves culture yield; in a septic patient sampling is done urgently and antibiotics are not delayed.

items.q: Superficial swabs from a sinus tract in chronic osteomyelitis are generally unreliable. For which organism does a sinus isolate correlate reasonably with deep bone culture?
items.e: Sinus swabs are contaminated by colonising flora, but isolation of S. aureus from a sinus correlates reasonably with deep cultures; other organisms correlate poorly.

items.q: In suspected low-grade shoulder implant infection, cultures should be incubated for 10-14 days mainly to detect:
items.e: C. acnes is slow-growing and anaerobic, and extended incubation is required to avoid false-negative cultures; S. aureus grows within 1-2 days.

items.q: During debridement of chronic osteomyelitis, the 'paprika sign' indicates:
