o: Punctate bleeding from viable bone, marking the limit of resection
Rust-coloured pus typical of anaerobic infection
Red discoloration of bone caused by tetracycline labelling
items.e: Debridement continues until healthy bone shows fine punctate bleeding (the paprika sign); inadequate debridement is the commonest cause of recurrence.

items.q: For prophylactic (rather than therapeutic) antibiotic-loaded bone cement, the usual antibiotic dose per 40 g packet of PMMA is about:
items.e: Low-dose cement (about 1 g of antibiotic per 40 g) is used for prophylaxis; treatment spacers and beads use high doses of several grams per packet, accepting reduced mechanical strength.

items.q: After radical debridement of chronic osteomyelitis of the proximal third of the tibia, which local muscle flap is most commonly used for soft-tissue cover?
items.e: The medial gastrocnemius flap reliably covers the proximal third of the tibia; the soleus is used for the middle third and the distal third usually needs a free flap.

items.q: Soft-tissue cover of an exposed debrided bed in the middle third of the tibia is most commonly achieved with a:
o: Split-skin graft directly on cortical bone
items.e: The soleus flap is the workhorse for the middle third; gastrocnemius reaches the proximal third, and bare cortex without periosteum will not accept a skin graft.

items.q: According to the fracture-related infection consensus, the usual antibiotic duration when a stable implant is retained after debridement is about:
items.e: With a retained implant (biofilm likely), around 12 weeks of therapy is recommended, whereas about 6 weeks is usual when the implant is removed or exchanged.

items.q: A patient develops a wound infection 9 days after plating of a tibial plateau fracture; the construct is stable. Under the Willenegger-Roth timing, the preferred approach is:
o: Immediate removal of all implants and external fixation
Debridement, irrigation and implant retention with antibiotics
items.e: Early infections (under 2 weeks) have an immature biofilm, so a stable implant can usually be retained after thorough debridement, with targeted antibiotics until union.

items.q: A tibial fracture plated 5 months ago shows a draining sinus, a loose plate and no healing. The appropriate management principle is:
o: Retain the plate and give 12 weeks of oral antibiotics
Lifelong suppressive antibiotics in a fit young patient
Repeated sinus swabs to guide oral therapy
Remove the implant, debride and restabilise, often with staged reconstruction
items.e: Late infections (over 10 weeks) involve a mature biofilm, and a loose implant provides neither stability nor eradication, so it must be removed with debridement and restabilisation.

items.q: Under the fracture-related infection consensus definition, which finding is only a suggestive (not confirmatory) criterion?
o: A pathogen grown from a single deep tissue sample
A sinus communicating with the implant
The same pathogen in two separate deep samples
items.e: A single positive deep sample may be a contaminant, so it only suggests infection; two phenotypically identical isolates, pus or a communicating sinus are confirmatory.

items.q: When sampling bone and deep tissue at revision for suspected fracture-related infection, the recommended practice is:
o: One large sample sent in a single pot
At least 3, ideally 5, separate samples taken with clean instruments
Swabs of the wound edge and drain tip
Samples taken after the first dose of prophylactic antibiotic is given and the tourniquet released
items.e: Multiple separate deep samples with fresh instruments allow two matching isolates to confirm infection and help distinguish contaminants.

items.q: Which is the strongest recognised risk factor for native-joint septic arthritis in adults?
items.e: Rheumatoid arthritis (damaged joints, immunosuppressive therapy) carries the highest risk and is also associated with polyarticular infection and higher mortality.

items.q: In adult bacterial septic arthritis, synovial fluid glucose is characteristically:
o: Less than 50% of the serum glucose
items.e: Bacterial and leucocyte metabolism lower synovial glucose to typically less than half the serum level, with raised lactate; a normal glucose does not exclude infection.

items.q: In non-gonococcal septic arthritis, an initial synovial Gram stain is positive in approximately:
items.e: Gram stain is positive in only about half of cases, so a negative stain does not exclude septic arthritis; culture is positive in about 80%.

items.q: A 21-year-old woman with suspected gonococcal arthritis of the wrist has a negative synovial culture. The most useful next investigation is:
o: NAAT/culture of urethral, cervical, rectal and pharyngeal swabs
items.e: Synovial cultures are positive in fewer than half of gonococcal arthritis cases, so mucosal sampling with NAAT and culture and blood cultures provide the diagnosis.

items.q: A young man is treated for gonococcal arthritis with intravenous ceftriaxone. Which additional drug is given empirically to cover likely co-infection?
items.e: Chlamydia trachomatis co-infection is common, so doxycycline (or azithromycin) is added, and sexual partners are traced and treated.

items.q: What did Gjika and colleagues (Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 2019) report for adult native-joint septic arthritis after surgical drainage?
o: 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotics was superior to 3 weeks
Arthroscopic lavage was inferior to repeated needle aspiration
2 weeks of antibiotics was non-inferior to 4 weeks
items.e: In this randomised trial, a 2-week antibiotic course after surgical drainage gave cure rates comparable to 4 weeks for native-joint septic arthritis.

items.q: At arthroscopy for septic arthritis of the knee, there is aggressive pannus undermining the cartilage, and radiographs show subchondral osteolysis. The Gachter stage and treatment are:
o: Stage IV; open arthrotomy with synovectomy and debridement
Stage III; arthroscopic lavage without synovectomy
items.e: Gachter stage IV, with pannus infiltrating cartilage and subchondral osteolysis, needs open arthrotomy and synovectomy; stages I-III can usually be managed arthroscopically.

items.q: Arthroscopy for knee septic arthritis shows cloudy fluid with reddened synovium and petechial bleeding, but no fibrin or pus. This corresponds to Gachter stage:
items.e: Stage I is cloudy fluid with synovial redness and possible petechiae; fibrin and pus define stage II, compartmentalisation stage III and cartilage-invading pannus stage IV.

items.q: For septic arthritis of the native hip in an adult, the preferred drainage method is usually:
items.e: The deep hip is difficult to decompress reliably, and raised pressure threatens femoral head perfusion, so open arthrotomy remains the usual approach (arthroscopy is an option in experienced hands).

items.q: Rapid cartilage destruction in septic arthritis within hours is caused mainly by:
o: Bacterial toxins plus neutrophil proteases, MMPs and cytokines such as IL-1
items.e: Bacterial products and the host response (neutrophil enzymes, matrix metalloproteinases, IL-1 and TNF-alpha) degrade proteoglycan and collagen rapidly, hence the urgency of drainage.

items.q: A 76-year-old man on immunosuppressants has septic arthritis of the knee. After aspiration and before Gram stain results, empirical treatment should include an anti-staphylococcal agent plus:
o: Gram-negative cover such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
items.e: Elderly, immunocompromised patients and IV drug users have a higher rate of Gram-negative septic arthritis, so a third-generation cephalosporin is added to staphylococcal cover (vancomycin if MRSA risk).

items.q: Which clinical finding best distinguishes septic prepatellar bursitis from septic arthritis of the knee?
o: Painless passive knee flexion through a reasonable range
items.e: In prepatellar bursitis the joint itself is not inflamed, so gentle knee movement is relatively painless; septic arthritis causes painful restriction of all movements.

items.q: Type II necrotising fasciitis is caused by:
o: A polymicrobial mix of aerobes and anaerobes
Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, with or without S. aureus
items.e: Type I is polymicrobial (often in diabetics or after abdominal surgery), whereas type II is monomicrobial group A streptococcal (sometimes with S. aureus) and can affect healthy young people.

items.q: Clindamycin is added in streptococcal necrotising fasciitis primarily because it:
o: Penetrates necrotic tissue better than any other antibiotic
Is the only drug active against group A streptococcus
Reverses septic shock by blocking nitric oxide synthase
Suppresses bacterial toxin production by inhibiting protein synthesis
items.e: Clindamycin inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis, reducing exotoxin and M-protein production even when the inoculum is large (Eagle effect), complementing a beta-lactam.

items.q: A previously healthy 30-year-old in a tropical region has fever and a painful, woody swelling of the thigh; ultrasound shows a pus collection within the vastus lateralis. The most likely organism is:
items.e: Tropical pyomyositis is a primary muscle abscess caused mostly by S. aureus, typically in large muscles such as the quadriceps or gluteals; treatment is drainage and antibiotics.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with palmoplantar pustulosis has painful swelling of the sternoclavicular joints with hyperostosis; cultures are sterile. The diagnosis is:
o: Pseudomonas osteomyelitis from IV drug use
items.e: SAPHO (synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis) is a sterile inflammatory osteitis typically of the anterior chest wall, treated with NSAIDs, bisphosphonates or biologics.

items.q: In the Cierny-Mader system, a C host is defined as a patient in whom:
o: There is both systemic and local compromise
The infection is caused by MRSA
Treatment would be worse than the disease
items.e: A C host is one in whom the morbidity of curative treatment exceeds that of the infection, so suppressive antibiotics, palliation or amputation are chosen; combined systemic and local compromise is Bls.

items.q: Eighteen months after an intramedullary nail for a tibial fracture that has united, a patient has recurrent infection limited to the medullary canal. In Cierny-Mader terms, the lesion type and key surgical step are:
o: Type II; decortication and local flap
Type III; segmental resection and bone transport
Type I; nail removal and reaming of the medullary canal
items.e: An infected nail with a healed fracture is medullary (type I) osteomyelitis, treated by removing the nail and debriding the canal by reaming (for example with a reamer-irrigator-aspirator), with or without an antibiotic-coated nail.

items.q: Prolonged linezolid therapy (beyond about 4 weeks) for MRSA osteomyelitis requires monitoring mainly for:
o: Myelosuppression and peripheral or optic neuropathy
items.e: Linezolid causes dose- and duration-related thrombocytopenia and anaemia and, with long courses, peripheral and optic neuropathy and lactic acidosis; tendon rupture is linked to fluoroquinolones.

items.q: In acute osteomyelitis, which finding is a recognised indication for surgery rather than continued antibiotics alone?
o: A positive blood culture for S. aureus
Failure to improve clinically within 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
An ESR above 40 mm/h at presentation
Fever on the first day of treatment
items.e: Surgery is indicated for an abscess, necrotic bone, infected implants or failure to respond within 48-72 hours; a positive blood culture alone does not mandate operation.

items.q: Plain radiographs lag behind the clinical onset of acute osteomyelitis because visible lysis requires loss of about:
items.e: Lytic change becomes visible on radiographs only after about 30-50% of mineral is lost, typically 10-21 days after onset; MRI shows marrow oedema much earlier.

items.q: Compared with osteoid osteoma, the pain of an osteoblastoma is typically:
o: A dull ache with less night pain and a poor response to NSAIDs
Severe night pain abolished by aspirin within an hour
Absent, the lesion being found incidentally in most cases
Burning dysaesthetic pain in a dermatomal distribution only
items.e: Osteoblastoma usually causes a dull progressive ache and lacks the dramatic NSAID-responsive night pain of osteoid osteoma, which is driven by intense PGE2 production in a small nidus.

items.q: In the Enneking staging of benign bone tumours, many osteoblastomas, which grow progressively and may breach the cortex, are classified as:
items.e: Osteoblastoma is an intermediate, locally aggressive tumour; lesions that expand and breach the cortex fit Enneking benign stage 3, unlike latent (stage 1) lesions such as most non-ossifying fibromas.

items.q: Radiographs of a spinal osteoblastoma often show an expansile lytic lesion with fluid-fluid levels on MRI. These fluid levels most often reflect:
o: Haemorrhage caused by previous biopsy only
Secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change within the osteoblastoma
items.e: Secondary ABC change is common in osteoblastoma (as in GCT and chondroblastoma); fluid-fluid levels alone do not prove a primary ABC or telangiectatic osteosarcoma, so the solid component must be sampled.

items.q: A 20-year-old has a 3 cm osteoblastoma of the distal tibial metadiaphysis without joint involvement. The usual treatment is:
o: Observation with NSAIDs until it burns out
Extended curettage with a high-speed burr and adjuvant, then bone grafting
items.e: Extended (aggressive) curettage with adjuvants and grafting is standard for accessible osteoblastomas; en bloc resection is reserved for aggressive or spinal lesions, and radiotherapy is avoided because of sarcoma risk.

items.q: After intralesional curettage of an osteoblastoma, the approximate local recurrence rate is:
items.e: Recurrence after curettage of osteoblastoma is about 10-20%, higher for aggressive (epithelioid) lesions, which is why adjuvants or en bloc resection are used.

items.q: Which histological variant of osteoblastoma carries a higher risk of local recurrence?
o: Sclerosing osteoblastoma with abundant mineralised matrix
Epithelioid (aggressive) osteoblastoma with plump epithelioid osteoblasts
Osteoblastoma with secondary ABC change in a long bone
items.e: Epithelioid ('aggressive') osteoblastoma, with large epithelioid osteoblasts, recurs more often and must be distinguished from osteosarcoma.

items.q: The most useful histological feature distinguishing osteoblastoma-like osteosarcoma from a true osteoblastoma is:
o: Presence of osteoblasts rimming woven bone trabeculae
Vascular stroma with scattered osteoclast-like giant cells
Permeation of tumour between and around pre-existing host trabeculae
items.e: Osteoblastoma is well circumscribed and does not permeate host bone; infiltration of the native trabeculae (and a permeative radiographic margin) indicates osteosarcoma. Osteoblastic rimming and giant cells occur in both.

items.q: Osteoblastoma differs from osteoid osteoma in that it:
o: Has no histological similarity to osteoid osteoma
Is almost confined to the femoral neck
Is always associated with surrounding dense reactive sclerosis
Has a progressive growth potential and may cause cord or root compression in the spine
items.e: The two are histologically similar, but osteoblastoma is larger (>1.5-2 cm), grows progressively and can compress neural elements; dense reactive sclerosis is more typical of osteoid osteoma.

items.q: In the foot, a well-recognised site for osteoblastoma is the:
o: Distal phalanx of the lesser toes
items.e: Apart from the spine and long bones, the talus is a classic site of osteoblastoma, often in the neck, sometimes with secondary ABC change.

items.q: A 17-year-old has a 4 cm osteoblastoma involving the lamina, pedicle and part of the body of C5 with radiculopathy. Which statement about management is correct?
o: Long-term NSAIDs are the treatment of choice
Excision (often en bloc or marginal) with stabilisation is indicated, and radiotherapy is avoided
Radiotherapy alone is the preferred definitive treatment
CT-guided radiofrequency ablation is standard for lesions of this size next to the root
items.e: Large spinal osteoblastomas with neural compromise need surgical removal with stabilisation if facet/pedicle resection destabilises the segment; RFA is meant for small nidi away from neural tissue and RT carries sarcoma risk.

items.q: Conventional osteosarcoma is most commonly found, in decreasing frequency, in the:
o: Proximal femur, distal tibia, distal radius
Distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus
Proximal humerus, distal femur, proximal fibula
items.e: Osteosarcoma favours the metaphyses with the fastest growth: distal femur, then proximal tibia, then proximal humerus; about half occur around the knee.

items.q: In osteosarcoma, a 'skip metastasis' is best defined as:
o: A pulmonary nodule detected only on CT
A metastatic lymph node in the popliteal fossa
Tumour that has crossed the physis into the epiphysis
A discontinuous tumour focus in the same bone or across the adjacent joint, separate from the primary
items.e: Skip lesions are separate synchronous medullary foci in the same bone or transarticular bone (about 5-10%); they carry a prognosis similar to metastatic disease and are found on whole-bone MRI.

items.q: Before effective chemotherapy, about 80-90% of patients with apparently localised osteosarcoma treated by amputation alone died of lung metastases. This is explained by:
o: Subclinical micrometastases present at diagnosis in most patients
Tumour seeding from the amputation stump
Late transformation of benign lung nodules
items.e: Although only 15-20% have detectable metastases at presentation, about 80% harbour micrometastases; this is the rationale for systemic chemotherapy in all high-grade osteosarcoma.

items.q: Lymph node metastasis in osteosarcoma is:
o: The commonest site of first metastasis
Rare, as spread is predominantly haematogenous
Present in most patients with tibial tumours
Routinely assessed by sentinel node biopsy
items.e: Osteosarcoma spreads haematogenously, mainly to the lungs and then bone; nodal spread is rare and, when present, is an adverse feature (stage IVB in AJCC).

items.q: The Multi-Institutional Osteosarcoma Study (Link et al., NEJM 1986) is important because it showed that:
o: Limb salvage gave the same survival as amputation
Adding ifosfamide for poor responders improved survival
Adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery dramatically improved relapse-free survival compared with surgery alone
items.e: The MIOS randomised trial showed relapse-free survival of about 66% with adjuvant chemotherapy versus about 17% with observation, establishing chemotherapy as standard; limb salvage equivalence was shown by Simon et al.

items.q: Simon and colleagues (MSTS, JBJS 1986) compared limb salvage with amputation for distal femoral osteosarcoma. They found that:
o: Limb salvage gave better survival because of earlier chemotherapy
Local recurrence was absent after limb salvage
Survival was similar, provided wide surgical margins were achieved
items.e: Limb-sparing surgery with wide margins did not compromise survival compared with amputation, which underpins today's 85-90% limb-salvage rate.

items.q: In EURAMOS-1, good histological responders to MAP were randomised to receive pegylated interferon alfa-2b after chemotherapy. The result was:
o: No significant improvement in event-free survival
A large improvement in overall survival
Improved survival only in pelvic tumours
items.e: Maintenance pegylated interferon gave no significant benefit in good responders, and MAPIE did not help poor responders; MAP remains standard for all.

items.q: For relapsed osteosarcoma that cannot be resected, which drugs have shown modest activity in trials?
o: Multikinase inhibitors such as regorafenib or cabozantinib
items.e: Regorafenib and cabozantinib (multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors) have shown modest progression-free survival benefit in relapsed osteosarcoma; there is no established targeted first-line therapy.

items.q: A child on ifosfamide-containing chemotherapy for relapsed osteosarcoma develops haematuria. Which agent should have been given to prevent this?
items.e: Mesna binds acrolein, the urotoxic metabolite of ifosfamide, preventing haemorrhagic cystitis; dexrazoxane protects against doxorubicin cardiotoxicity and leucovorin rescues methotrexate toxicity.

items.q: Apart from haemorrhagic cystitis, a characteristic renal toxicity of ifosfamide in children is:
o: Proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi-type) with phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemic rickets
items.e: Ifosfamide causes proximal tubular damage (Fanconi syndrome) leading to phosphate, glucose and bicarbonate loss; children can develop hypophosphataemic rickets.

items.q: Osteosarcoma is relatively radioresistant. Radiotherapy, often as protons or carbon ions, is mainly used for:
o: Unresectable axial tumours (skull base, spine, pelvis) or palliation
Routine neoadjuvant treatment of distal femoral tumours
Treatment of skip lesions instead of resection
items.e: Because high doses are needed, radiotherapy is reserved for tumours that cannot be resected with adequate margins or for palliation; particle therapy allows dose escalation near critical structures.

items.q: With modern multimodal treatment, the approximate 5-year survival of localised extremity high-grade osteosarcoma is:
items.e: Neoadjuvant MAP plus wide resection gives about 65-70% 5-year survival for localised disease, compared with 20-30% for metastatic disease; this figure has plateaued since the 1980s.

items.q: A 16-year-old treated for distal femoral osteosarcoma develops two peripheral lung nodules 18 months later, with no other disease. The preferred management is:
o: Surgical resection of the pulmonary metastases (metastasectomy)
items.e: Complete surgical resection of pulmonary metastases is a key part of curative treatment in osteosarcoma and gives meaningful long-term survival when all disease can be removed.

items.q: After proximal tibial resection for osteosarcoma and endoprosthetic replacement, the patellar tendon is reattached and the implant covered with which flap?
o: Latissimus dorsi free flap as routine
items.e: The medial gastrocnemius flap provides soft tissue cover for the prosthesis and a vascularised bed to anchor the extensor mechanism, reducing infection and extensor lag.

items.q: In the Henderson classification of endoprosthetic failure after tumour resection, aseptic loosening is:
items.e: Henderson types: 1 soft tissue failure, 2 aseptic loosening, 3 structural failure (implant or periprosthetic fracture), 4 infection, 5 tumour progression.

items.q: A boy has a Van Nes rotationplasty for a distal femoral osteosarcoma. When he extends his prosthetic 'knee', he is actually performing:
items.e: The leg is rotated 180 degrees so the reversed ankle acts as the knee: plantarflexion produces knee extension and dorsiflexion produces knee flexion.

items.q: The main disadvantage of a Van Nes rotationplasty compared with endoprosthetic replacement is:
o: Phantom limb pain in most patients
The unusual cosmetic appearance of the backward-facing foot
items.e: Rotationplasty gives a durable, active limb without implant failure and with little phantom pain, but its appearance can be psychologically difficult; patients are often very active.

items.q: A relative contraindication to limb salvage for a distal femoral osteosarcoma is:
o: A good histological response to chemotherapy
Tumour extension into the distal femoral epiphysis
Tumour encasement of the femoral vessels and sciatic nerve that cannot be resected and reconstructed
items.e: Limb salvage requires wide margins with a functional limb; unreconstructable neurovascular encasement, gross contamination or infection may necessitate amputation. Epiphyseal extension changes the resection but does not preclude salvage.

items.q: Local recurrence after limb salvage surgery for osteosarcoma occurs in about:
o: 40-50% and is usually curable by re-excision
items.e: Local recurrence is about 5-10%, mainly linked to inadequate margins and poor chemotherapy response, and is strongly associated with subsequent metastasis and death.

items.q: Werner syndrome, associated with premature ageing and an increased risk of osteosarcoma, is due to mutation of:
items.e: Werner (WRN), Bloom (BLM) and Rothmund-Thomson (RECQL4) syndromes are RecQ helicase disorders predisposing to osteosarcoma; EXT1 causes hereditary multiple exostoses.

items.q: Malignant transformation of Paget disease into sarcoma occurs in about what proportion of patients?
items.e: Paget sarcoma develops in roughly 1% of patients (more in polyostotic disease) and has a very poor prognosis, with 5-year survival under about 10-15%.

items.q: According to the Cahan criteria for radiation-induced sarcoma, which condition must be met?
o: The sarcoma must have identical histology to the original tumour
The sarcoma must arise outside the radiation field
The patient must have received chemotherapy
A latent period of several years (classically over 3-4 years) between irradiation and the sarcoma
items.e: Cahan criteria: the sarcoma arises in the irradiated field, after a latency of years, is histologically different from the original lesion, and the bone was normal before irradiation.

items.q: The commonest histological subtype of conventional osteosarcoma is:
items.e: Osteoblastic is the commonest subtype of conventional osteosarcoma; chondroblastic and fibroblastic patterns are also high grade and treated identically. Telangiectatic is a separate variant.

items.q: The histological feature that is essential for a diagnosis of osteosarcoma is:
o: Abundant reactive woven bone at the periphery
Malignant tumour cells producing osteoid directly
Hyaline cartilage matrix with atypical chondrocytes
Small round blue cells with membranous CD99
items.e: Osteosarcoma is defined by malignant cells laying down osteoid directly, even in small amounts; reactive bone at the edge of any lesion does not count.

items.q: A Codman triangle on a radiograph of a long bone indicates:
o: Periosteum elevated by an aggressive process, which is not specific for osteosarcoma
Benign periosteal chondroma in every case
items.e: Codman triangle forms where elevated periosteum lays down bone at the edge of a rapidly growing lesion; it occurs with osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, infection and other aggressive lesions.

items.q: In the AJCC 8th edition, an osteosarcoma with metastases confined to the lungs is staged as:
items.e: M1a denotes lung-only metastases (stage IVA), while M1b denotes other distant sites including bone (stage IVB), which carries a worse prognosis.

items.q: The usual total duration of MAP chemotherapy (neoadjuvant plus adjuvant) for localised osteosarcoma is approximately:
o: 29-30 weeks, with surgery after about 10 weeks
items.e: MAP is given for about 10 weeks before surgery and continued after resection to complete roughly 29-30 weeks of treatment.

items.q: A 12-year-old has a metaphyseal femoral tumour composed of small round cells with lace-like osteoid; CD99 is weakly positive. Which test best excludes Ewing sarcoma?
o: FISH or molecular testing for an EWSR1 rearrangement
items.e: Small cell osteosarcoma can express CD99; the absence of an EWSR1 rearrangement (and the presence of osteoid) supports osteosarcoma over Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: The treatment of a low-grade central osteosarcoma of the distal femur in a 32-year-old is:
o: Neoadjuvant MAP followed by wide excision
items.e: Low-grade central osteosarcoma has excellent prognosis with wide excision alone; curettage (often after misdiagnosis as fibrous dysplasia) leads to recurrence and possible dedifferentiation.

items.q: A parosteal osteosarcoma resected with a marginal margin is at risk of:
o: Immediate lung metastases in most cases
Local recurrence, with possible dedifferentiation to high-grade sarcoma
items.e: Parosteal osteosarcoma must be excised widely; marginal excision often recurs and recurrences can dedifferentiate, which worsens the prognosis.

items.q: When a parosteal osteosarcoma is found to contain a dedifferentiated high-grade component, treatment should be:
o: Wide excision alone as for usual parosteal osteosarcoma
As for conventional high-grade osteosarcoma, with chemotherapy and wide resection
Observation, as dedifferentiation is clinically irrelevant
items.e: Dedifferentiated parosteal osteosarcoma (about 15-25%) behaves like high-grade sarcoma and is treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and wide resection.

items.q: Compared with conventional osteosarcoma and parosteal osteosarcoma, periosteal osteosarcoma has a prognosis that is:
o: Identical to telangiectatic osteosarcoma and better than all others
Better than conventional but worse than parosteal
items.e: Periosteal osteosarcoma is intermediate grade and chondroblastic; its prognosis lies between the low-grade parosteal type and high-grade conventional osteosarcoma.

items.q: High-grade surface osteosarcoma is treated:
o: As conventional osteosarcoma, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and wide resection
By wide excision alone like parosteal osteosarcoma
items.e: Despite its surface location, high-grade surface osteosarcoma is histologically identical to conventional osteosarcoma and has the same metastatic risk, so it is treated identically.

items.q: Which statement about telangiectatic osteosarcoma is correct?
o: It is low grade and treated by curettage
Pathological fracture is common, and its prognosis with chemotherapy is similar to conventional osteosarcoma
It never shows fluid-fluid levels on MRI
It is chemotherapy-resistant with a uniformly fatal outcome
items.e: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma is high grade, purely lytic and haemorrhagic, often presents with pathological fracture, and responds to standard MAP with prognosis similar to conventional disease.

items.q: A 3-year-old has a destructive lytic lesion of the femur. The most likely diagnoses at this age are:
o: Metastatic neuroblastoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis
items.e: Under about 5 years, a destructive bone lesion is usually metastatic neuroblastoma or LCH; osteosarcoma and Ewing peak at 10-25 years, and myeloma or metastasis over 40.

items.q: When performing a needle biopsy of a suspected thigh osteosarcoma, the tract should:
o: Pass between two muscles along an intermuscular plane to avoid contaminating muscle
Pass through the neurovascular bundle to reach the medial cortex
Enter through the knee joint to reach the metaphysis
Pass through a single muscle compartment in line with the planned resection incision
items.e: Mankin's principles: the tract goes through one muscle, in line with the definitive incision, so it can be excised en bloc; intermuscular planes, joints and neurovascular bundles spread contamination.

items.q: In Enneking's terminology, a resection that passes through the reactive zone (pseudocapsule) around a sarcoma is:
items.e: A marginal margin passes through the reactive zone and may leave satellite nodules; a wide margin includes a cuff of normal tissue around the reactive zone, the standard goal for high-grade sarcoma.

items.q: For reconstruction of the distal femur after resection of an osteosarcoma in an adult, the commonest implant used is a modular endoprosthesis with:
items.e: Resection removes the collateral ligaments and capsule, so a constrained rotating-hinge megaprosthesis is used for distal femoral and proximal tibial reconstruction.

items.q: According to the 2016 Warwick Agreement, a diagnosis of femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome requires:
o: Motion- or position-related hip pain, positive clinical signs and cam or pincer morphology on imaging
An alpha angle above 55° on radial MRI, whether or not symptoms are present
A labral tear on MR arthrography in a hip with restricted internal rotation
Pain relief after an intra-articular local anaesthetic injection alone
items.e: Warwick defines FAI syndrome as a triad of symptoms, clinical signs and imaging findings. Cam or pincer morphology alone is not FAI syndrome, because it is common in asymptomatic athletes.

items.q: Isolated pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement is most typically seen in:
items.e: Pincer morphology (acetabular overcoverage) is classically found in middle-aged active women. Cam morphology is typical of young athletic men.

items.q: Among symptomatic patients with femoroacetabular impingement, the most common morphological pattern is:
items.e: Most symptomatic hips (about 70–85% in many series) have combined cam and pincer features. Isolated forms are less common.

items.q: In pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement, a 'contrecoup' chondral lesion is typically found in the:
items.e: Abutment of the neck against the anterior rim levers the head posteroinferiorly, damaging the posteroinferior acetabular cartilage (contrecoup). Anterosuperior delamination is the typical cam lesion.

items.q: On a well-centred AP pelvic radiograph, the line of the posterior acetabular wall passes medial to the centre of the femoral head. This 'posterior wall sign' indicates:
o: Posterior wall deficiency, as seen with acetabular retroversion
Cam deformity of the posterior head–neck junction
items.e: Normally the posterior wall runs through or lateral to the head centre. A wall medial to the centre means posterior undercoverage, typically with acetabular retroversion.

items.q: On an AP pelvic radiograph, the ischial spine is seen projecting medially into the true pelvis on one side. This 'ischial spine sign' suggests:
items.e: A prominent ischial spine on a neutral AP pelvis is a marker of a retroverted hemipelvis and acetabulum. It correlates with the crossover sign.

items.q: On an AP pelvic radiograph, the medial margin of the femoral head lies medial to the ilioischial line. This describes:
items.e: In protrusio, the femoral head itself crosses medial to the ilioischial line. In coxa profunda only the floor of the acetabular fossa touches or crosses the line.

items.q: The alpha angle used to quantify cam morphology is measured between the femoral neck axis and a line from the femoral head centre to:
o: The lateral edge of the acetabular sourcil
The tip of the greater trochanter
The point where the physeal scar meets the anterior cortex
The point where the head–neck contour first exceeds the radius of a best-fit circle around the head
items.e: Nötzli's alpha angle marks where the head loses its sphericity. A larger angle means the aspherical bump extends further from the head, as in cam morphology.

items.q: On a cross-table lateral radiograph of the hip, a head–neck offset ratio below about which value suggests cam morphology?
items.e: The anterior head–neck offset ratio (offset divided by head diameter) below about 0.17 indicates reduced offset typical of cam FAI.

items.q: On an AP pelvis, a 32-year-old woman with groin pain has a Tönnis (acetabular roof) angle of −5°. This indicates:
o: Acetabular dysplasia with a steep roof
items.e: The normal Tönnis angle is 0–10°. A negative value means a horizontal or inward-sloping roof, i.e. overcoverage. Above 10° indicates dysplasia.

items.q: The anterior centre-edge angle, used to assess anterior acetabular coverage, is measured on the:
items.e: Lequesne's false-profile view shows the anterior acetabular coverage. An anterior centre-edge angle under about 20° indicates anterior undercoverage.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman with hip pain has a lateral centre-edge angle (Wiberg) of 23°. This is best described as:
items.e: LCEA is normal at 25–40°, borderline dysplastic at 20–25°, dysplastic below 20° and overcovered above 40°.

items.q: In a hip with borderline acetabular dysplasia, the femoro-epiphyseal acetabular roof (FEAR) index is mainly used to:
o: Help distinguish an unstable hip from a stable impinging one
Quantify the size of a cam lesion
items.e: The FEAR index compares the inclination of the physeal scar with the acetabular roof. It helps decide whether a borderline dysplastic hip behaves as unstable (favouring PAO) or stable (favouring arthroscopy).

items.q: On an AP pelvic radiograph, excessive anterior pelvic tilt (coccyx far from the symphysis) is a source of error because it:
o: Makes the lateral centre-edge angle appear smaller
Makes the acetabulum appear retroverted, producing a false crossover sign
Hides the posterior wall sign by projecting the wall laterally
items.e: Anterior pelvic tilt rotates the anterior wall laterally, so a normally anteverted acetabulum can show a false crossover sign. A standardised film has the coccyx tip about 1–3 cm above the symphysis.

items.q: The FADIR (flexion–adduction–internal rotation) test in suspected femoroacetabular impingement is best described as:
o: Highly specific but of low sensitivity
Both highly sensitive and highly specific
Highly sensitive but of low specificity
items.e: A negative FADIR makes intra-articular impingement unlikely, but a positive test is non-specific and is found in many other hip disorders.

items.q: Pain in the groin on resisted active straight-leg raising with the knee extended (Stinchfield test) mainly suggests:
items.e: Resisted hip flexion loads the joint through iliopsoas compression of the anterior capsule and head. Groin pain points to an intra-articular source.

items.q: With the patient supine and the leg extended, the examiner internally rotates the limb and releases it; the leg rolls out into excessive external rotation without a firm endpoint. This positive dial test indicates:
items.e: Passive external rotation beyond about 45° from vertical without a firm endpoint suggests iliofemoral ligament or capsular laxity. Such hips need capsular repair or plication if operated.

items.q: Pain deep in the posterior hip when the hip is extended and externally rotated with the patient supine at the edge of the couch most suggests:
o: Posterior impingement, as from a pincer contrecoup lesion
items.e: The posterior impingement test (extension plus external rotation) loads the posteroinferior acetabulum, typical of posterior overcoverage or contrecoup damage.

items.q: A footballer has groin pain thought to be from FAI, but the examination also suggests adductor and lumbar pathology. The most useful step to confirm that the hip joint is the source of pain is:
o: Repeating the FADIR test after physiotherapy
Image-guided intra-articular injection of local anaesthetic
items.e: Relief of pain after an intra-articular anaesthetic injection confirms an intra-articular source and predicts a better response to hip arthroscopy.

items.q: A 25-year-old with cam morphology has markedly limited internal rotation in flexion. CT shows femoral version of −5°. How does this femoral version affect his impingement?
o: It protects against impingement but predisposes to instability
It has no effect, because only acetabular version matters
It indicates acetabular dysplasia requiring periacetabular osteotomy
Femoral retroversion worsens impingement by bringing the cam into contact earlier in flexion and internal rotation
items.e: Femoral retroversion reduces internal rotation clearance and aggravates cam and pincer impingement. Excessive anteversion, in contrast, tends towards instability.

items.q: In the Hetsroni classification of anterior inferior iliac spine morphology, a type III AIIS is one that:
o: Extends distally below the level of the anterosuperior acetabular rim
Lies above the acetabular rim with a smooth iliac wall between them
Reaches down to the level of the acetabular rim
Has been avulsed with the rectus femoris and not united
items.e: Type I: AIIS above the rim; type II: extends to the rim; type III: extends below the rim. Types II and III are associated with subspine impingement.

items.q: Before hip arthroscopy is offered for symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement with a preserved joint space, non-operative treatment (activity modification, physiotherapy, NSAIDs) should usually be tried for at least about:
items.e: A structured trial of conservative care for at least about 3 months is generally recommended before surgery for FAI syndrome.

items.q: During hip arthroscopy, how much joint distraction is usually needed to enter the central compartment safely?
items.e: About 8–10 mm of distraction allows instruments to enter without scuffing the cartilage. More force or time increases traction neurapraxia.

items.q: To reduce the risk of traction-related nerve injury during hip arthroscopy, continuous traction time is generally kept below about:
items.e: Traction-related neurapraxia (pudendal, sciatic, femoral) increases with traction time and force. Limiting traction to under about 2 hours and releasing it for peripheral work reduces risk.

items.q: When the posterolateral portal is made during hip arthroscopy, the leg should be kept in neutral or slight internal rotation because external rotation:
o: Brings the femoral artery closer to the portal
Brings the sciatic nerve closer to the portal
Tightens the iliotibial band over the greater trochanter
Increases the risk of lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury
items.e: The posterolateral portal passes near the sciatic nerve. External rotation moves the greater trochanter posteriorly and the nerve closer, so neutral or internal rotation is maintained.

items.q: During hip arthroscopy, the femoral neurovascular bundle is avoided by keeping all portals:
o: Medial to a vertical line from the anterior superior iliac spine
Below the level of the lesser trochanter
Lateral to a vertical line drawn distally from the anterior superior iliac spine
items.e: Portals placed lateral to the vertical line from the ASIS keep clear of the femoral nerve, artery and vein, which lie medially.

items.q: In hip arthroscopy, the anterolateral portal is usually established first because it:
o: Is the only portal that allows access to the peripheral compartment
Gives the best view of the posterior labrum without fluoroscopy
Lies centrally within the safe zone and is placed under fluoroscopy to view the others
items.e: The anterolateral portal has the most room between neurovascular structures. It is established first under fluoroscopic guidance, then used to view and place the other portals.

items.q: Repair of the acetabular labrum is preferred to debridement in hip arthroscopy mainly because the intact labrum:
o: Seals the joint, maintaining fluid pressurisation that protects cartilage and adds stability
Is the main blood supply of the femoral head
Carries most of the weight-bearing load in stance
items.e: The labral seal keeps a pressurised fluid layer between the cartilage surfaces and resists distraction. Repair restores this and gives better outcomes than debridement.

items.q: A 28-year-old has persistent hip pain after a previous arthroscopic labral debridement; at revision arthroscopy the labrum is deficient and irreparable, with a preserved joint space. The preferred procedure is:
o: Labral reconstruction with an allograft or iliotibial band autograft
items.e: In young patients without arthritis, a deficient labrum is reconstructed with graft to restore the suction seal. Further debridement does not restore function.

items.q: During arthroscopic acetabular rim trimming for pincer impingement, resection is limited so that the lateral centre-edge angle remains above about:
items.e: Over-resection of the rim creates iatrogenic dysplasia and instability. The LCEA should remain at or above about 25° after rim trimming.

items.q: During arthroscopic labral repair for pincer impingement, the labrum is often taken down from the rim before acetabuloplasty and then:
o: Excised completely to prevent recurrent crushing
Left detached to heal by scar
Replaced routinely with a fascia lata graft
Re-fixed to the trimmed rim with suture anchors
items.e: The labrum is detached, the rim trimmed, and the labrum re-fixed with suture anchors to preserve the suction seal.

items.q: In pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement, the first structure to be damaged by the linear contact between the femoral neck and the rim is usually the:
o: Anterosuperior acetabular cartilage away from the rim
Femoral head cartilage at the fovea
items.e: In pincer FAI the labrum is crushed first and degenerates, sometimes ossifying. Deep cartilage damage is more limited than in cam FAI, which shears the cartilage from the labrum.

items.q: Haematogenous spread of tuberculosis to the paradiscal regions of adjacent vertebrae is classically attributed to which pathway?
o: Lymphatic drainage from the para-aortic nodes
Direct extension from the cerebrospinal fluid
Retrograde spread along the spinal nerve roots
items.e: Batson's valveless vertebral venous plexus allows retrograde haematogenous seeding of the vertebral bodies (arterial spread to the metaphyses also occurs). Lymphatic and CSF routes are not the classical explanation.

items.q: Of all sites of skeletal tuberculosis, the spine accounts for approximately:
items.e: The spine is the commonest site of osteoarticular tuberculosis, accounting for about half of cases; the hip and knee follow.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a single collapsed mid-thoracic vertebral body with preserved discs above and below. Biopsy shows caseating granulomas. This central type of spinal tuberculosis is clinically important because it:
o: Is the commonest pattern of spinal tuberculosis
Mimics a neoplasm such as metastasis or lymphoma
Always produces a large psoas abscess
items.e: Central (vertebral body) tuberculosis causes concertina collapse with disc preservation and is easily mistaken for a tumour; biopsy is needed. The paradiscal type is the commonest.

items.q: A radiograph shows erosion of the anterior surfaces of four contiguous vertebral bodies (anterior scalloping) with largely intact discs. The tuberculous lesion responsible is the:
o: Central type, with vertebral body collapse
Paradiscal type, with early disc destruction
Anterior (subperiosteal) type, with abscess tracking under the anterior longitudinal ligament
items.e: Anterior-type disease spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament and periosteum, eroding the front of several vertebrae (scalloping). Central disease collapses one body; posterior disease involves the arch.

items.q: Tuberculosis confined to the posterior elements (lamina, pedicle, spinous process) differs from the paradiscal type in that it:
o: Tends to cause early neurological deficit despite little deformity
Is the commonest pattern in adults
items.e: Posterior element tuberculosis is uncommon, causes little kyphosis, but abscess and granulation tissue lie directly on the dura, so neurological deficit occurs early and the diagnosis is often delayed.

items.q: A 25-year-old with lumbar tuberculosis presents with a painless fluctuant swelling in the upper thigh below the inguinal ligament and a fixed flexion of the hip. The swelling is most likely:
o: A psoas cold abscess tracking along the psoas sheath into the femoral triangle
Tuberculous lymphadenitis of the deep inguinal nodes
items.e: Lumbar tuberculous pus tracks within the psoas sheath and points in the femoral triangle below the inguinal ligament; psoas spasm produces a flexed hip (pseudo-flexion deformity).

items.q: A chest radiograph in a patient with mid-thoracic tuberculosis shows a fusiform soft-tissue shadow on both sides of the spine. This represents:
o: A paravertebral cold abscess (the 'bird nest' appearance)
items.e: A fusiform paravertebral shadow bulging on both sides of the thoracic spine is the classic radiographic sign of a paravertebral cold abscess in thoracic tuberculosis.

items.q: A cold abscess from thoracolumbar tuberculosis that tracks posteriorly and points in the loin between latissimus dorsi, external oblique and the iliac crest emerges through:
items.e: Posteriorly tracking pus may point in the inferior lumbar triangle of Petit, bounded by latissimus dorsi, external oblique and the iliac crest.

items.q: A 40-year-old with cervical spine tuberculosis develops difficulty in swallowing and noisy breathing. The most likely cause is:
o: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy from mediastinal nodes
items.e: In cervical tuberculosis, pus collects in front of the vertebrae as a retropharyngeal abscess, causing dysphagia and stridor.

items.q: Histology of a CT-guided vertebral biopsy in spinal tuberculosis characteristically shows:
o: Caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells
Sheets of neutrophils with gram-positive cocci
items.e: Tuberculosis produces caseating granulomas of epithelioid cells with Langhans giant cells. Non-caseating granulomas with asteroid bodies suggest sarcoidosis.

items.q: Plain radiographs may be normal early in spinal tuberculosis because a lytic lesion becomes visible only after loss of approximately:
items.e: About 30-40% of bone mineral must be lost before a lesion is visible on radiographs, so MRI is the investigation of choice for early disease.

items.q: In India, a strongly positive Mantoux test in an adult with back pain and a vertebral lesion:
o: Supports but does not confirm the diagnosis, because latent infection is common
items.e: In endemic areas many adults have latent infection, so tuberculin and IGRA tests are only supportive; confirmation needs histology, culture or nucleic acid amplification.

items.q: Pus from a tuberculous paravertebral abscess is sent for liquid culture (MGIT). The typical time to a positive result is about:
items.e: Liquid (MGIT) culture usually becomes positive in 2-6 weeks, faster than solid Lowenstein-Jensen culture (4-8 weeks); GeneXpert gives a result within hours.

items.q: Compared with the original Xpert MTB/RIF, the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay is particularly useful for vertebral biopsy samples because it has:
o: The ability to detect isoniazid resistance
items.e: Ultra has a lower limit of detection and therefore greater sensitivity for paucibacillary samples such as bone and pus; like the original assay it detects rifampicin (rpoB) resistance only.

items.q: A 28-year-old with spinal tuberculosis is started on isoniazid-containing therapy. Pyridoxine is added to prevent:
items.e: Isoniazid causes pyridoxine depletion and peripheral neuropathy; pyridoxine supplementation prevents this. Optic neuritis is due to ethambutol.

items.q: Two months into antitubercular therapy for spinal TB, a patient notices difficulty distinguishing red from green. The drug most likely responsible is:
items.e: Ethambutol causes dose-related optic (retrobulbar) neuritis, with loss of red-green colour discrimination and reduced acuity; it should be stopped and vision assessed.

items.q: A young woman on antitubercular therapy for spinal TB becomes pregnant despite taking an oral contraceptive. The drug interaction responsible is due to:
o: Rifampicin inducing hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
items.e: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer that accelerates oestrogen metabolism and makes oral contraceptives unreliable; a non-hormonal or alternative method is advised.

items.q: A patient on the intensive phase of antitubercular therapy develops an acutely painful swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint with a raised serum urate. The drug most likely responsible is:
items.e: Pyrazinamide reduces renal urate excretion, causing hyperuricaemia and occasionally acute gout; it is also hepatotoxic.

items.q: An older antitubercular injectable used in some MDR regimens for spinal TB requires audiometric monitoring because of the risk of:
items.e: Aminoglycosides such as streptomycin (and amikacin) are ototoxic and nephrotoxic, requiring audiometry and renal monitoring.

items.q: Under India's National TB Elimination Programme, the continuation phase for drug-sensitive spinal tuberculosis consists of:
items.e: NTEP uses daily HRE (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol) in the continuation phase, extended for extrapulmonary sites such as the spine; WHO regimens use HR alone.

items.q: In a patient with spinal tuberculosis shown by GeneXpert to be rifampicin-resistant, the newer all-oral regimens for MDR-TB are built around:
items.e: Current WHO and NTEP regimens for MDR/RR-TB are all-oral and bedaquiline-based (often with pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin in the shorter BPaLM regimen).

items.q: A patient on antitubercular therapy develops jaundice and serum ALT 6 times the upper limit of normal. The appropriate action is to:
o: Continue all drugs and repeat tests in a month
Stop the hepatotoxic drugs and reintroduce them sequentially after liver function recovers
items.e: ALT over 5 times normal (or over 3 times with symptoms or jaundice) indicates drug-induced hepatitis: stop isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide, then rechallenge sequentially once liver function normalises. Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic.

items.q: Three weeks after starting antitubercular therapy for confirmed drug-sensitive thoracic TB, MRI shows enlargement of the paravertebral abscess, but the patient feels better and is neurologically intact. The most likely explanation and action is:
o: Drug resistance; switch immediately to an MDR regimen
Paradoxical reaction; continue the same therapy and monitor
items.e: A transient worsening of lesions after starting effective therapy (paradoxical reaction, immune-mediated) is well recognised; therapy is continued unless neurology deteriorates or other evidence suggests failure.

items.q: On follow-up MRI after antitubercular therapy, which finding best indicates healing of a tuberculous vertebral lesion?
o: Increased T2 signal throughout the vertebral bodies
New rim enhancement around the paravertebral collection
Increasing height loss with new endplate erosion
Replacement of marrow oedema by fat signal (high signal on T1) with resolution of the abscess
items.e: Healing is shown by resolution of oedema and abscess and fatty marrow replacement (T1 hyperintense), sometimes with fusion; persistent oedema and enhancement suggest activity.

items.q: In spinal tuberculosis, the degree of kyphotic deformity on a lateral radiograph is classically measured by:
o: Cobb's lateral angle on the AP view
items.e: Konstam's method measures the kyphotic angle formed by lines drawn along the vertebrae immediately above and below the diseased segment. Meyerding grades spondylolisthesis; Pavlov's ratio assesses canal stenosis.

items.q: According to Rajasekaran, kyphosis in a child with spinal tuberculosis is at high risk of severe progression when how many 'spine-at-risk' signs are present?
o: None, as long as more than one vertebra is involved
items.e: Two or more of the four spine-at-risk signs (facet separation, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation, toppling) predict severe progression, and surgery should be considered.

items.q: A 6-year-old with thoracic tuberculosis has a lateral radiograph showing the posterior cortex of the involved vertebral segment displaced backwards into the canal. This Rajasekaran spine-at-risk sign is:
items.e: Retropulsion of the posterior fragment into the canal on the lateral view is one of the four spine-at-risk signs; the others are facet dislocation/separation, lateral translation on the AP view and toppling of the upper vertebra.

items.q: An AP radiograph of a child with thoracolumbar tuberculosis shows the vertebral column above the lesion shifted sideways relative to the column below, beyond the pedicle line. This sign is:
items.e: Lateral translation is seen on the AP film when the vertical line through the pedicles of the lower vertebra does not touch the pedicle of the upper vertebra, indicating gross instability.

items.q: Compared with adults, kyphosis due to spinal tuberculosis in children is particularly worrying because:
o: It can continue to increase after the disease has healed, owing to growth
It never progresses once treatment starts
Neurological deficit is impossible in children
Children do not form cold abscesses
items.e: In children, deformity may progress during and after healing because of continued growth and loss of anterior growth potential; adults usually stop progressing once healed.

items.q: Early-onset Pott's paraplegia (during active disease) has a relatively good prognosis because the compression is usually caused by:
o: An internal gibbus of dense healed bone
Abscess, granulation tissue, caseous material or sequestra that can be removed
Thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery
items.e: Active-disease paraplegia is usually from soft, removable or drug-responsive tissue, so recovery is good; bony ridges, fibrosis and atrophy cause late-onset paraplegia with a poor prognosis.

items.q: A rare cause of sudden, complete paraplegia in active spinal tuberculosis, carrying a very poor prognosis for recovery despite decompression, is:
o: Infective thrombosis or endarteritis of the anterior spinal artery
items.e: Vascular infarction of the cord from tuberculous endarteritis or thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery causes sudden paraplegia that does not respond to decompression.

items.q: A patient with thoracic tuberculosis is bedridden with paraplegia in flexion, flexor spasms, sensory loss over 50% and bladder involvement. In Tuli's grading this is:
items.e: Tuli grade IV is grade III (non-ambulatory paraplegia) plus severe sensory loss, flexor spasms or paraplegia in flexion, or sphincter involvement. Grades I-II are ambulatory.

items.q: A patient with thoracic tuberculosis can walk with a stick, but has brisk reflexes, clonus and mild weakness he is aware of. In Tuli's grading this is:
items.e: Grade II: the patient is aware of the deficit but remains ambulatory (with or without support). Grade I is a deficit found only on examination; grade III is non-ambulatory paraplegia in extension.

items.q: In an adult with healing thoracic tuberculosis, surgical correction is advised to prevent late-onset paraplegia when the kyphosis exceeds about:
items.e: Adult kyphosis over about 60 degrees (or progressive deformity) is a surgical indication because of the risk of late cord stretching over the internal gibbus and of cardiopulmonary compromise.

items.q: The Medical Research Council (MRC) Working Party trials of spinal tuberculosis in the 1970s-1980s showed that:
o: Bed rest in hospital for 6 months was essential for cure
Plaster jackets significantly improved outcomes over ambulatory treatment
Debridement alone without grafting gave the best results
Ambulatory chemotherapy was highly effective, while radical debridement with strut grafting gave less kyphosis and earlier fusion
items.e: The MRC trials showed outpatient chemotherapy works without bed rest or casts; the Hong Kong radical operation reduced kyphosis and sped fusion compared with simple debridement.

items.q: Titanium pedicle screws and cages are considered safe in active spinal tuberculosis mainly because:
o: Mycobacterium tuberculosis adheres poorly to metal and forms little biofilm
Antitubercular drugs are concentrated within implants
Tuberculosis never involves the vertebral body
items.e: Mycobacteria produce little glycocalyx and adhere poorly to implants, so instrumentation in active TB (with ATT) does not perpetuate infection, unlike staphylococcal biofilm.

items.q: A key advantage of a single-stage posterior transpedicular approach for thoracolumbar tuberculosis, compared with an anterior approach alone, is that it:
o: Gives better visualisation of the anterior vertebral body than thoracotomy
Allows decompression, kyphosis correction and pedicle screw stabilisation through one approach without opening the chest or abdomen
Avoids the need for antitubercular therapy
Is the only approach that permits strut grafting
items.e: The posterior approach permits debridement of the anterior column through the pedicle, three-column stabilisation and deformity correction, avoiding transthoracic or retroperitoneal morbidity.

items.q: A 22-year-old with healed childhood thoracic tuberculosis has a rigid 95-degree angular kyphosis with progressive myelopathy. The procedure most likely to achieve both decompression and correction is:
o: Posterior vertebral column resection with instrumentation
items.e: A rigid severe angular kyphus needs a three-column osteotomy such as vertebral column resection (or closing-opening wedge osteotomy) to decompress and correct; laminectomy alone worsens instability and Ponte osteotomies give little correction.

items.q: A 48-year-old intravenous drug user develops lumbar spondylodiscitis. Besides Staphylococcus aureus, which organism should be particularly considered?
items.e: Intravenous drug users have a recognised association with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (and Candida) spondylodiscitis, as well as S. aureus.

items.q: A 72-year-old man develops lumbar spondylodiscitis three weeks after a urinary tract infection following catheterisation. The most likely organism is:
items.e: Gram-negative spondylodiscitis, especially E. coli, follows urinary tract infection or instrumentation, spreading via Batson's plexus; the elderly are most at risk.

items.q: Blood cultures in a patient with spondylodiscitis grow Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) group. In addition to treating the spine, which investigation is mandatory?
items.e: Streptococcal (and enterococcal) bacteraemia with spondylodiscitis warrants echocardiography for endocarditis; S. gallolyticus also mandates colonoscopy for colorectal neoplasia.

items.q: Brucella spondylitis is treated with which antibiotic combination?
items.e: Spinal brucellosis needs prolonged combination therapy: doxycycline plus rifampicin, often with an aminoglycoside initially, for at least 3 months.

items.q: In adult pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, infection characteristically begins in the:
o: Nucleus pulposus, which is richly vascular in adults
Spinal canal, spreading outwards to the bone
Subchondral endplate region supplied by segmental arterial branches
items.e: In adults the disc is avascular, so bacteria lodge in the end-arterial subchondral bone near the endplate and spread to the disc and adjacent vertebra.

items.q: Primary discitis without vertebral osteomyelitis occurs in young children rather than adults because:
o: The paediatric disc still has vascular channels through the endplate
Children have more Batson's plexus valves
items.e: In children, vascular channels perforate the cartilage endplate into the disc, allowing direct haematogenous seeding of the disc; these disappear in adolescence.

items.q: The most common region affected by adult pyogenic spondylodiscitis is the:
items.e: Haematogenous pyogenic spondylodiscitis most often involves the lumbar spine, followed by the thoracic and then cervical spine.

items.q: In pyogenic spondylodiscitis, blood cultures identify the organism in approximately:
items.e: Blood cultures are positive in about half to two-thirds of patients, so they are taken first; if negative, CT-guided biopsy is performed.

items.q: During antibiotic treatment of pyogenic spondylodiscitis, the most useful laboratory marker for monitoring response is:
items.e: CRP falls quickly with effective treatment and is used to monitor response; ESR falls more slowly and the white cell count is often normal.

items.q: A 68-year-old with suspected lumbar spondylodiscitis is hypotensive, febrile at 39.5 °C and has a lactate of 5 mmol/L. After blood cultures, the next step is:
o: Start empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately without waiting for biopsy
Withhold antibiotics until a CT-guided biopsy is obtained
Arrange an MRI and start antibiotics only if an abscess is seen
Perform an open biopsy before any antibiotic
items.e: Antibiotics are delayed for biopsy only in stable patients; in sepsis or septic shock empirical therapy starts immediately after blood cultures.

items.q: A 45-year-old has a Schatzker V bicondylar plateau fracture. After a spanning external fixator, when is definitive internal fixation usually performed?
o: Within 6 hours regardless of the soft tissues
Only after the fracture has united in the frame
When swelling has settled and skin wrinkles return, usually about 7-14 days
items.e: Staged management uses a knee-spanning frame for length and alignment; definitive plating waits for soft-tissue recovery, typically 7-14 days, which lowers wound complications.

items.q: Which vascular anatomy explains the popliteal artery's vulnerability in medial and bicondylar tibial plateau fracture-dislocations?
o: It lies freely mobile within the popliteal fat throughout
It runs anterior to the tibia at the joint line
It is surrounded by the popliteus muscle and protected
It is tethered proximally at the adductor hiatus and distally at the soleal arch
items.e: Being fixed at the adductor hiatus and at the fibrous arch of soleus, the popliteal artery cannot move away when the proximal tibia displaces, so it is stretched or torn.

items.q: A 60-year-old with a lateral split-depression plateau fracture in osteoporotic bone is fixed with a lateral plate. Which construct best resists loss of reduction of the elevated joint surface?
o: Locking plate with subchondral rafting screws and calcium phosphate cement in the void
Lateral non-locking plate with no subchondral support
Two cannulated screws without void filling
items.e: In osteoporotic bone, fixed-angle locking screws acting as a raft beneath the subchondral bone, with a compression-resistant void filler such as calcium phosphate cement, best prevent subsidence.

items.q: A Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society randomised trial compared ORIF with circular fine-wire fixation for bicondylar tibial plateau fractures. Which finding is correct?
o: Circular fixation gave a shorter hospital stay and quicker early recovery, with similar 2-year outcomes
Both groups had identical early range of motion and hospital stay
Circular fixation had a much higher rate of non-union
items.e: The COTS trial found shorter hospitalisation and faster early return of function with circular fixation; at 2 years functional outcomes were similar between the groups.

items.q: A 28-year-old has a closed tibial plateau fracture and needs a fasciotomy for compartment syndrome. How should the incisions be planned?
o: A single midline anterior incision over the tibial crest
Two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy placed so that it does not compromise later fixation approaches
items.e: Four compartments are released through medial and lateral incisions; the lateral incision is positioned so that later anterolateral plating is still possible, and wounds are closed or covered later.

items.q: A pilon fracture is approached through the anterior interval between extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus. Which structures lie in or near this interval and must be protected?
o: Great saphenous vein and saphenous nerve
Sural nerve and small saphenous vein
Posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve
Anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve
items.e: The anterior neurovascular bundle (anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve) lies deep near the EHL at the ankle; it is retracted with care during the anterior approach to the plafond.

items.q: Which posterior distal tibial fragment of a pilon fracture is attached to the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament?
items.e: The posterolateral Volkmann fragment stays attached to the PITFL and therefore to the fibula; when fibular length is restored it often reduces partly by ligamentotaxis.

items.q: Which approach allows a posteriorly placed buttress plate for a large posterolateral pilon fragment together with fixation of the fibula?
o: Anterolateral approach lateral to peroneus tertius
Posterolateral approach between the peroneal tendons and FHL
Medial approach over the medial malleolus
Anteromedial approach medial to tibialis anterior
items.e: The posterolateral approach reaches both the posterior tibia and the posterior border of the fibula through one incision, with the patient prone or lateral.

items.q: Rüedi and Allgöwer emphasised buttressing which side of the distal tibia in pilon fracture fixation to prevent the commonest deformity?
items.e: Their fourth principle is a medial buttress to stop collapse into varus, the commonest malunion; in modern practice the plate is placed where the fracture pattern needs it.

items.q: A 32-year-old has a comminuted pilon fracture with a large metaphyseal defect after articular reconstruction. According to Rüedi-Allgöwer principles, the defect should be:
o: Filled with an antibiotic spacer permanently
Ignored because it does not affect union
items.e: Grafting the metaphyseal defect supports the reconstructed joint surface and reduces metaphyseal non-union; it is the third Rüedi-Allgöwer principle.

items.q: Which imaging study best defines fracture lines, fragment number and the position of the die-punch fragment before definitive pilon fixation?
o: CT with axial, sagittal and coronal reconstructions
items.e: CT, ideally after the spanning frame has restored length, shows the primary fracture lines (often Y-shaped), the main fragments and central impaction, and guides the choice of approaches.

items.q: In tibial plateau fractures, why is restoring the mechanical axis and stability considered more important than perfect articular congruity?
o: Articular step-off of any size always remodels
The knee tolerates small residual step-off, but malalignment and instability overload the joint and lead to arthritis
Alignment does not affect knee loading
The tibial plateau cartilage regenerates completely
items.e: Clinical series show that small residual step-off is well tolerated, whereas mechanical malalignment and instability are associated with post-traumatic arthritis and poorer function.

items.q: In high-energy bicondylar tibial plateau fractures, definitive ORIF through swollen soft tissue in the first few days is especially associated with:
items.e: Early extensile approaches through compromised soft tissue in high-energy bicondylar fractures led to high rates of wound breakdown and deep infection, which staged management reduces.

items.q: A 68-year-old with end-stage renal failure on regular haemodialysis, otherwise stable, is listed for elective hip arthroplasty. His ASA physical status is:
items.e: End-stage renal disease on scheduled dialysis is an ASA example of severe systemic disease (ASA III). ASA IV requires disease that is a constant threat to life, such as an MI within 3 months or sepsis.

items.q: Which of the following is one of the six predictors in the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee)?
items.e: The RCRI items are high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes and creatinine above 2 mg/dL. Age, hypertension and AF are not RCRI items.

items.q: Before elective arthroplasty, which total lymphocyte count is a recognised marker of malnutrition associated with wound complications and periprosthetic infection?
items.e: Serological malnutrition markers are albumin under 3.5 g/dL, transferrin under 200 mg/dL and total lymphocyte count under 1500 cells/mm3. A count under 500 is severe lymphopenia, not the screening threshold.

items.q: A patient who received an intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the hip is planning a total hip arthroplasty. To limit the risk of periprosthetic infection, surgery is usually deferred until at least how long after the injection?
items.e: Arthroplasty within about 3 months of an ipsilateral intra-articular steroid injection is associated with a higher rate of periprosthetic joint infection; beyond that the excess risk is not seen.

items.q: According to the WHO, anaemia in non-pregnant adult women and in adult men is defined as a haemoglobin respectively below:
items.e: WHO thresholds are Hb under 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women and under 13 g/dL in men. Preoperative anaemia should be investigated and treated (often with IV iron) before elective surgery.

items.q: A healthy 60-year-old with a well-functioning total knee arthroplasty needs a routine dental extraction. Under current AAOS/ADA guidance, antibiotic prophylaxis is:
o: Amoxicillin 2 g one hour before, lifelong
Required only within 2 years of the arthroplasty
items.e: The AAOS/ADA position is that routine antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is generally not recommended for patients with joint replacements; active dental sepsis should still be treated before arthroplasty.

items.q: Tranexamic acid reduces surgical blood loss by:
o: Increasing the release of von Willebrand factor
Blocking the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen so it cannot bind fibrin
items.e: TXA is a synthetic lysine analogue that occupies lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing fibrinolysis. Release of von Willebrand factor is the action of desmopressin.

items.q: The 2018 AAOS/AAHKS/ASRA/AHS clinical practice guidelines concluded that, compared with intravenous tranexamic acid in primary hip and knee arthroplasty, oral tranexamic acid:
o: Reduces blood loss and transfusion to a similar degree
Is ineffective because of poor absorption
Carries a higher risk of venous thromboembolism
Is effective only in knee arthroplasty
items.e: The guidelines found IV, topical and oral TXA all reduce blood loss and transfusion with no clear difference between routes, and TXA did not increase VTE in the general arthroplasty population.

items.q: The FOCUS trial (NEJM 2011) compared liberal (Hb under 10 g/dL) with restrictive (symptoms or Hb under 8 g/dL) transfusion in elderly hip fracture patients with cardiovascular risk. It showed:
o: No difference in death or inability to walk independently at 60 days
Better walking at 60 days with liberal transfusion
items.e: FOCUS found no difference in its primary outcome (death or inability to walk across a room unaided at 60 days), supporting restrictive thresholds of about 8 g/dL in patients with cardiovascular disease.

items.q: Intraoperative cell salvage is generally avoided in which of the following operations?
o: Revision hip arthroplasty for aseptic loosening
Posterior spinal fusion for idiopathic scoliosis
Hip arthroplasty in a Jehovah's Witness
items.e: Cell salvage is traditionally contraindicated in malignancy (risk of reinfusing tumour cells) and infection. It is valuable in large aseptic revisions and scoliosis surgery, and many Jehovah's Witnesses accept it in a continuous circuit.

items.q: Three hours after receiving fresh frozen plasma during spinal fusion, a patient develops acute hypoxaemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with a normal central venous pressure and no evidence of fluid overload. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: TRALI is non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6 hours of transfusion, often after plasma-rich products, and is a leading cause of transfusion-related death. TACO would show fluid overload with raised venous pressure.

items.q: Compared with a femoral nerve block, the main advantage of an adductor canal block for analgesia after total knee arthroplasty is that it:
o: Largely preserves quadriceps strength, reducing fall risk
Also blocks the sciatic nerve to the posterior knee
Gives longer analgesia because the canal is avascular
Eliminates any risk of local anaesthetic toxicity
items.e: The adductor canal block targets mainly the saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis, giving comparable analgesia while sparing most quadriceps motor function. Posterior knee analgesia needs an additional IPACK or sciatic technique.

items.q: A man with severe COPD is listed for arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. The main respiratory concern with an interscalene brachial plexus block is:
o: Ipsilateral hemidiaphragmatic paresis from phrenic nerve block
Bronchospasm caused by the local anaesthetic
items.e: Standard-volume interscalene blocks almost always spread to the phrenic nerve, paralysing the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, which may be poorly tolerated in severe lung disease. Horner syndrome and hoarseness are usually harmless.

items.q: A child given codeine after a fracture becomes profoundly drowsy with respiratory depression because he converts it unusually fast to morphine. Which enzyme is responsible for this conversion?
items.e: Codeine (and tramadol) are activated by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers produce excess morphine and risk toxicity, which is why codeine is contraindicated in children under 12. Poor metabolisers get little analgesia.

items.q: A woman taking sertraline is given tramadol after an ankle fracture fixation. She becomes agitated and febrile with tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake, so combining it with an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome, characterised by clonus and hyperreflexia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine antagonists and causes lead-pipe rigidity with slow onset.

items.q: Local anaesthetic infiltrated into an abscess cavity before drainage often gives poor anaesthesia. The reason is that the acidic tissue:
o: Increases the ionised fraction of the drug, so less crosses the nerve membrane
Accelerates plasma cholinesterase metabolism of amides
Converts the drug to its unionised form, which cannot bind the sodium channel
Causes vasoconstriction that prevents drug spread
items.e: Local anaesthetics are weak bases; only the unionised form crosses the axonal membrane. Acidic infected tissue increases ionisation, so less drug reaches the intracellular binding site on the sodium channel.

items.q: True allergic reactions to local anaesthetics are most often caused by which agent, because of its para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite?
items.e: Ester local anaesthetics such as procaine are hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase to PABA, which is allergenic. Lidocaine, bupivacaine and ropivacaine are amides metabolised in the liver and rarely cause true allergy.

items.q: For infiltration in a 70-kg adult, the commonly quoted maximum safe dose of lidocaine WITH adrenaline is about:
items.e: The commonly quoted maximum for lidocaine with adrenaline is 7 mg/kg, giving about 490 mg for 70 kg. Plain lidocaine is limited to about 3-4.5 mg/kg.

items.q: Which of the following is appropriate for intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block) of the forearm?
items.e: Prilocaine (or plain dilute lidocaine) is used for Bier block because of its low systemic toxicity. Bupivacaine has caused fatal cardiotoxicity after cuff release and must never be used, and adrenaline-containing solutions are not given intravenously.

items.q: After injecting the local anaesthetic for a Bier block, the tourniquet should not be deflated, even if the procedure is very short, until at least:
items.e: The cuff must remain inflated for at least 20-30 minutes so the drug becomes tissue-bound; earlier deflation releases a toxic intravenous bolus. Two hours is the upper limit of tourniquet time, not the minimum.

items.q: Shortly after an interscalene block with bupivacaine, a patient complains of perioral tingling, then has a seizure followed by ventricular arrhythmia. Besides airway support and benzodiazepines, the specific treatment is:
o: 20% lipid emulsion, 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by an infusion
items.e: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is treated with 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion), with reduced adrenaline doses and avoidance of vasopressin. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia.
