items.q: A 25-year-old had shoulder arthroscopy with an intra-articular pain pump. Over the next year he develops progressive pain, stiffness and complete loss of glenohumeral joint space. Aspirate cultures and inflammatory markers are normal. The most likely cause is:
o: Avascular necrosis of the humeral head
items.e: Postarthroscopic glenohumeral chondrolysis is linked to continuous intra-articular infusion of local anaesthetic, especially bupivacaine, which is dose- and time-dependently chondrotoxic. AVN would show subchondral collapse rather than uniform joint-space loss.

items.q: One hour after a digital block with lidocaine and adrenaline (WALANT), a healthy patient's fingertip remains white with poor capillary refill. Which drug, injected locally, reverses the vasoconstriction?
items.e: Phentolamine, an alpha-adrenergic antagonist, reverses adrenaline-induced vasoconstriction in the digit. Adrenaline in dilute concentrations (1:100,000-1:200,000) is otherwise safe in healthy fingers.

items.q: The sibling of a patient who had a malignant hyperthermia crisis wants to know whether she is susceptible. The reference diagnostic test is:
o: In vitro caffeine-halothane contracture test on a muscle biopsy
items.e: The in vitro contracture test on fresh muscle exposed to caffeine and halothane is the reference test; RYR1 genetic testing can confirm a known familial mutation. A normal CK does not exclude susceptibility.

items.q: A child with lumbar myelomeningocele is scheduled for tendon transfer surgery. Which theatre precaution is specifically important?
items.e: Children with spina bifida have a high prevalence of latex sensitisation and anaphylaxis, so they are managed in a latex-free environment from birth. Dantrolene prophylaxis is not indicated.

items.q: In the HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial, yearly IV zoledronic acid started within 90 days after hip fracture repair reduced new clinical fractures and also reduced:
items.e: HORIZON-RFT showed a reduction in new clinical fractures and in all-cause mortality with zoledronic acid after hip fracture. Atrial fibrillation was a safety concern in the earlier pivotal trial, not a benefit.

items.q: Denosumab can shrink and ossify giant cell tumour of bone because:
o: The giant cells are the neoplastic population and express sclerostin
The tumour secretes PTH-related protein that denosumab neutralises
Denosumab directly kills H3F3A-mutant cells by antibody-dependent cytotoxicity
The neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells express RANKL that recruits the osteoclast-like giant cells
items.e: In GCT the H3F3A-mutant stromal cells are neoplastic and overexpress RANKL, recruiting reactive osteoclast-like giant cells; blocking RANKL removes the giant cells, but the stromal cells persist and recurrence can follow withdrawal.

items.q: Which of the following patients with severe osteoporosis should NOT be given teriparatide?
o: A woman who had pelvic radiotherapy for cervical cancer
A woman with two previous vertebral compression fractures
A man on long-term prednisolone for asthma
A woman with a hip T-score of -3.5
items.e: Because of osteosarcoma in rat studies, teriparatide is avoided after prior skeletal radiotherapy, in Paget disease, with open physes, unexplained raised ALP or bone malignancy. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and prior vertebral fractures are indications.

items.q: Romosozumab should be avoided in a patient who has had which event within the past year?
items.e: In the ARCH trial romosozumab was superior to alendronate but had more serious cardiovascular events, so it is avoided after MI or stroke in the preceding year. Previous fragility fractures are indications for it.

items.q: A postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis two years ago. Which treatment should be avoided?
items.e: Raloxifene, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, increases VTE risk. It reduces vertebral but not hip fractures, and also lowers the risk of invasive breast cancer.

items.q: A woman treated with denosumab for 2 years is switched directly to teriparatide. The expected effect on bone density is:
o: A larger gain than with teriparatide alone
No change because denosumab effects persist for years
An immediate gain in cortical bone only
Progressive or transient bone loss, particularly at the hip
items.e: Switching from denosumab to teriparatide (DATA-Switch) caused bone loss, especially at the hip, because denosumab withdrawal triggers rebound resorption. Anabolic therapy first, then an antiresorptive, gives the greatest gain.

items.q: Which radiographic finding is a major feature of an atypical femoral fracture in the ASBMR task force definition?
o: Localised periosteal thickening of the lateral cortex ('beaking') at the fracture site
Fracture starting at the medial cortex
items.e: Major features include a subtrochanteric or diaphyseal location, minimal trauma, a transverse line starting at the lateral cortex, a medial spike if complete, minimal comminution and localised lateral cortical beaking. Spiral comminuted fractures are typical fragility fractures.

items.q: A woman on alendronate for 8 years is diagnosed with a complete atypical femoral shaft fracture. Besides stopping the bisphosphonate and fixing the fracture, which investigation is essential?
o: Bone scintigraphy of the whole skeleton
Dual-energy CT of the lumbar spine
items.e: Atypical femoral fractures are frequently bilateral, so the other femur must be imaged (radiograph, and MRI or isotope scan if painful) to detect an incomplete fracture that may need prophylactic nailing.

items.q: In a lower-risk patient, a bisphosphonate 'drug holiday' is usually considered after about how long of yearly intravenous zoledronic acid?
items.e: Guidelines suggest reassessment and a possible drug holiday after about 5 years of oral or 3 years of IV bisphosphonate in patients who are not at high fracture risk, to limit atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw risk.

items.q: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab every 2 weeks is planned for TKA. Per ACR/AAHKS 2022 guidance, the correct plan is to:
o: Stop methotrexate 2 weeks before and continue adalimumab
Stop both drugs 3 months before surgery
Continue methotrexate, withhold adalimumab and operate in week 3 after the last dose
items.e: Conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate are continued, while biologics are withheld so surgery falls at the end of the dosing cycle; they are restarted once the wound has healed (about 14 days) without infection.

items.q: A patient on tofacitinib for psoriatic arthritis is planned for elective hip arthroplasty. ACR/AAHKS 2022 guidance advises withholding it for how long before surgery?
items.e: JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) are short-acting and withheld for 3 days before elective arthroplasty, then restarted after wound healing.

items.q: A patient with lupus on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for several years is listed for TKA, with no history of adrenal crisis. ACR/AAHKS guidance on perioperative steroids is to:
o: Stop prednisolone a week before to reduce infection risk
Continue the usual daily dose without routine supraphysiological stress dosing
Give hydrocortisone 100 mg 8-hourly for 3 days routinely
Double the dose for 2 weeks before surgery
items.e: The guidance recommends continuing the current daily glucocorticoid dose rather than routine stress dosing; extra cover is given if hypotension occurs or adrenal insufficiency is known. Abrupt cessation risks adrenal crisis.

items.q: The pelvic inlet radiograph, taken with the beam angled caudally, is used mainly to assess:
o: Anteroposterior displacement and rotation of the hemipelvis
The sacral foramina seen en face
items.e: The inlet view looks down the pelvic brim and shows anterior/posterior translation and internal/external rotation of the hemipelvis. Vertical displacement and the sacral foramina are best seen on the outlet view.

items.q: The pelvic outlet radiograph, taken with the beam angled cephalad about 40-45°, best shows:
o: Vertical displacement of the hemipelvis and the sacral foramina
Anteroposterior translation of the sacroiliac joint
items.e: The outlet view is perpendicular to the sacrum, showing the foramina and any cranial migration of a hemipelvis. AP translation and rotation are inlet-view findings.

items.q: A small avulsion fracture of the ischial spine on CT of a pelvic ring injury indicates disruption of the:
items.e: The sacrospinous ligament attaches to the ischial spine, so its avulsion signals sacrospinous failure and a rotationally unstable ring. The sacrotuberous ligament attaches to the ischial tuberosity.

items.q: In an adult, the normal width of the pubic symphysis on an AP pelvis radiograph is up to about:
items.e: The normal symphysis is under about 5 mm wide. A gap over 2.5 cm implies sacrospinous and anterior SI ligament failure (APC II or worse).

items.q: When angiography is performed for arterial bleeding after a posterior pelvic ring disruption, the artery most commonly found injured is the:
items.e: The superior gluteal artery, exiting through the greater sciatic notch, is the commonest arterial bleeder, followed by the internal pudendal and obturator arteries. Arterial sources account for only about 10-15% of pelvic haemorrhage.

items.q: Of the following Young-Burgess patterns, which carries the highest blood loss and transfusion requirement?
items.e: APC III (complete anterior and posterior SI disruption) opens the pelvic volume most and has the highest transfusion needs. LC I is a stable impaction injury.

items.q: A side-impact injury shows ipsilateral pubic rami fractures and a fracture of the posterior iliac wing that runs into the sacroiliac joint (crescent fracture). The Young-Burgess type is:
items.e: LC II adds a posterior iliac (crescent) fracture or posterior SI disruption to the lateral compression rami fractures. LC I has only sacral buckle plus rami fractures.

items.q: After being rolled over by a vehicle, a patient has one hemipelvis internally rotated (lateral compression) and the opposite hemipelvis externally rotated (open book). This 'windswept pelvis' is Young-Burgess:
items.e: LC III is the windswept pelvis: lateral compression on the impact side with an APC-type open book on the contralateral side.

items.q: In the Tile classification, a pelvic ring injury that is rotationally unstable but vertically stable is type:
items.e: Tile B injuries (open book, ipsilateral or contralateral lateral compression) are rotationally unstable with an intact posterior vertical restraint. Tile C is rotationally and vertically unstable.

items.q: Tile type C3 pelvic injury denotes:
o: A rotationally and vertically unstable ring injury associated with an acetabular fracture
An avulsion of the anterior superior iliac spine
items.e: Tile C1 is unilateral, C2 bilateral and C3 a vertically unstable ring injury with an associated acetabular fracture. Bucket-handle injuries are Tile B3.

items.q: A lateral compression injury in which the posterior disruption is on one side and the anterior rami fractures are on the opposite side ('bucket-handle') is Tile type:
items.e: Tile B3 is the contralateral (bucket-handle) lateral compression pattern; B2 is ipsilateral lateral compression and B1 the open book.

items.q: Compared with anteroposterior compression pelvic injuries, lateral compression injuries are more frequently associated with:
items.e: Lateral (side-impact) mechanisms transmit force to the head and thorax, so these injuries accompany LC patterns. APC injuries bleed more and are more often linked with urethral and vascular injury.

items.q: A Denis zone I sacral fracture (through the ala, lateral to the foramina) with an associated nerve injury most often affects the:
items.e: The L5 root crosses the sacral ala and can be trapped by an upward alar fragment (traumatic far-lateral syndrome). Bowel and bladder dysfunction is typical of zone III.

items.q: A 25-year-old who jumped from a height has a U-shaped sacral fracture with kyphosis, separating the upper sacrum and spine from the pelvis. The usual definitive stabilisation is:
o: Lumbopelvic (triangular) fixation from the lower lumbar pedicles to the ilium
items.e: U/H-type fractures cause spinopelvic dissociation, which needs fixation connecting the lumbar spine to the pelvis (lumbopelvic or triangular osteosynthesis). Anterior devices do not control this posterior instability.

items.q: A pelvic binder should be applied with particular caution, because it may over-compress and worsen deformity, in which pattern?
o: Lateral compression with an internally rotated hemipelvis
Open-book injury with symphysis diastasis of 4 cm
items.e: Binders close the pelvic volume by internally rotating the hemipelves, which helps APC injuries but can over-reduce an already internally rotated lateral compression injury.

items.q: In bleeding trauma patients (CRASH-2), tranexamic acid gives benefit only when the first dose is given within:
items.e: CRASH-2 showed reduced bleeding deaths when TXA was started within 3 hours; later administration was associated with harm.

items.q: A hypotensive patient with an APC III pelvic injury remains unstable despite a binder and massive transfusion. FAST is negative and angiography is not immediately available. The most appropriate next step is:
o: Preperitoneal pelvic packing with pelvic external fixation
Definitive open reduction and plating of the SI joint
CT angiography and observation in the ward
items.e: Venous bleeding predominates, and preperitoneal packing with skeletal stabilisation controls it quickly when angioembolisation is unavailable. A negative FAST argues against laparotomy.

items.q: Supra-acetabular (AIIS) pins for anterior pelvic external fixation give better control than iliac crest pins but specifically endanger the:
items.e: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve passes near the ASIS and AIIS and is the structure classically at risk with supra-acetabular pins. The femoral nerve lies more medially under the inguinal ligament.

items.q: The main danger of applying a posterior pelvic C-clamp is:
o: Injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Pins penetrating through the greater sciatic notch or thin iliac wing into the pelvis
items.e: The C-clamp pins are placed on the posterior ilium near the SI joint; an inferior or anterior placement can enter the greater sciatic notch and injure gluteal vessels and nerves, or perforate a fractured ilium.

items.q: During percutaneous iliosacral S1 screw insertion, a screw that breaches the anterior cortex of the sacral ala endangers the:
o: Superior gluteal artery at the notch
items.e: The L5 root lies on the anterior surface of the sacral ala; an anterior breach injures it. A screw that enters the S1 foramen endangers the S1 root.

items.q: Which radiographic feature suggests upper sacral segment dysmorphism, which narrows the safe corridor for a transverse S1 iliosacral screw?
o: A residual (rudimentary) disc space between S1 and S2 with mammillary processes
Fused sacroiliac joints from ankylosing spondylitis
items.e: Dysmorphic sacra show a residual S1-S2 disc, mammillary processes, an upper sacrum collinear with the iliac crests, and irregular S1 foramina; the S2 corridor is usually larger in these patients.

items.q: Symphyseal diastasis in an APC II injury is usually fixed through:
o: A Pfannenstiel incision with plating of the superior surface of the symphysis
The lateral window of the ilioinguinal approach
items.e: A Pfannenstiel approach exposes the symphysis, and a plate on its superior surface restores the anterior ring. The lateral ilioinguinal window exposes the internal iliac fossa, not the symphysis.

items.q: A man with an APC pelvic injury has blood at the urethral meatus and a perineal haematoma. Before bladder drainage, the next step is:
items.e: Blood at the meatus suggests urethral injury, so a retrograde urethrogram is done before any urethral catheter; a suprapubic catheter is used if the urethra is disrupted.

items.q: In men with pelvic fractures, urethral injury most often involves the:
o: Prostatic urethra at the bladder neck
Posterior urethra at the membranous-bulbar junction
items.e: The posterior urethra is tethered at the urogenital diaphragm, so shear disruption occurs at the membranous-bulbar junction. Straddle injuries without a pelvic fracture usually affect the bulbar (anterior) urethra.

items.q: A pelvic fracture is accompanied by an intraperitoneal bladder rupture on CT cystography. Management is:
o: Urethral catheter drainage alone for 2 weeks
items.e: Intraperitoneal ruptures leak urine into the peritoneum and need operative repair. Most uncomplicated extraperitoneal ruptures heal with catheter drainage alone.

items.q: A pelvic ring fracture has an associated perineal laceration communicating with the rectum. Apart from debridement and skeletal stabilisation, the key step is:
o: Primary closure of the perineal wound
items.e: Faecal diversion reduces contamination and pelvic sepsis in open pelvic fractures with rectal or perineal wounds, which carry high mortality.

items.q: A Morel-Lavallée lesion over the greater trochanter after pelvic trauma is best described as:
o: A haematoma within the gluteus medius muscle
An avulsion of the anterior superior iliac spine
A closed degloving injury separating subcutaneous tissue from the underlying fascia
items.e: Shear separates the skin and fat from the fascia, creating a cavity filled with blood, lymph and fat that easily becomes infected; it is drained and debrided before or with fixation.

items.q: An 82-year-old woman with a low-energy lateral compression fragility fracture of the pelvis still cannot mobilise because of pain after a week of analgesia, and repeat CT shows progression to bilateral sacral ala fractures. Best management is:
o: Continue the same analgesia and mobilisation plan
Percutaneous sacral (iliosacral or transsacral) screw fixation
items.e: In fragility fractures of the pelvis, failure to mobilise or fracture progression is the indication for minimally invasive posterior fixation; prolonged bed rest is harmful in the elderly.

items.q: The classification of fragility fractures of the pelvis (FFP types I-IV) in the elderly was described by:
items.e: Rommens and Hofmann classified low-energy pelvic insufficiency fractures by increasing instability, from anterior-only (FFP I) to bilateral posterior (FFP IV) injuries.

items.q: The iliac oblique Judet view of the acetabulum best shows:
o: The anterior column and posterior wall
The posterior column and anterior wall
The obturator ring and posterior rim
The teardrop and acetabular roof only
items.e: The iliac oblique lies the iliac wing flat, showing the posterior column (greater sciatic notch to ischium) and the anterior wall. The obturator oblique shows the anterior column and posterior wall.

items.q: On an AP pelvis radiograph, disruption of the ilioischial line indicates involvement of the:
items.e: The ilioischial line represents the posterior column (and quadrilateral surface); the iliopectineal line represents the anterior column.

items.q: Of the following associated acetabular fracture types in Letournel's classification, the most common is:
items.e: Both-column fractures are the commonest associated pattern; posterior column with posterior wall and T-type fractures are less frequent.

items.q: The only elementary acetabular fracture type in Letournel's classification that crosses both the anterior and posterior columns is the:
items.e: A transverse fracture divides the innominate bone into an upper iliac and lower ischiopubic segment, crossing both columns, yet it is classed as elementary because it is a single fracture line.

items.q: The defining feature of an associated both-column acetabular fracture is that:
o: Both the iliopectineal and ilioischial lines are broken
No part of the articular surface remains attached to the intact ilium and axial skeleton
A vertical stem passes through the obturator foramen
The posterior wall is fractured as well
items.e: Both lines are also broken in transverse and T-type fractures; what defines a both-column fracture is complete separation of all articular segments from the intact posterior ilium (hence the spur sign).

items.q: A transverse acetabular fracture with an additional vertical limb that splits the quadrilateral plate and exits through the obturator foramen is classified as:
items.e: The T-type is a transverse fracture plus a vertical stem separating the anterior and posterior columns below the transverse line, usually through the obturator foramen and ischiopubic ramus.

items.q: Matta's roof arc angles cannot be used to judge whether the weight-bearing dome is intact in which fracture?
items.e: Roof arcs measure the distance of a fracture line from the dome and are invalid for posterior wall (and both-column) fractures; those are judged on CT and hip stability.

items.q: In a displaced acetabular fracture through the weight-bearing dome, operative fixation is generally indicated when articular displacement exceeds about:
items.e: A step or gap over about 2 mm in the dome predicts post-traumatic arthritis and is the usual operative threshold.

items.q: After closed reduction of a posterior hip dislocation, CT shows a non-concentric joint with an osseous fragment trapped in the joint. Appropriate management is:
o: Removal of the incarcerated fragment (open or arthroscopic) with fixation of any wall fracture as needed
Repeated closed reduction attempts under sedation
items.e: An incarcerated intra-articular fragment causes non-concentric reduction and abrades cartilage; it is an operative indication. Traction does not dislodge it.

items.q: Open reduction of an acetabular fracture becomes much harder, with poorer reduction quality, once surgery is delayed beyond about:
items.e: Acetabular fractures are ideally fixed within about 2 weeks; after about 3 weeks early callus and organised haematoma make anatomical reduction much more difficult.

items.q: During a Kocher-Langenbeck approach, tension on the sciatic nerve is reduced by keeping the limb in:
items.e: Extending the hip and flexing the knee slackens the sciatic nerve throughout the procedure; hip flexion with knee extension maximally stretches it.

items.q: During a Kocher-Langenbeck approach, which muscle should be preserved to protect the deep (ascending) branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery?
items.e: The deep branch of the MFCA runs deep to quadratus femoris and over obturator externus; keeping quadratus femoris intact protects femoral head blood supply.

items.q: In the ilioinguinal approach, the middle window lies between:
o: The iliac crest and the iliopsoas
The iliopsoas with femoral nerve laterally and the external iliac vessels medially
The external iliac vessels and the spermatic cord
The two heads of rectus abdominis
items.e: The middle window, created by dividing the iliopectineal fascia, lies between the iliopsoas/femoral nerve and the external iliac vessels and exposes the pelvic brim and quadrilateral surface.

items.q: A 74-year-old has an anterior column with posterior hemitransverse acetabular fracture and a medially displaced quadrilateral plate after a fall. Which approach gives the most direct access to buttress the quadrilateral plate?
items.e: The modified Stoppa approach works from inside the pelvis along the pelvic brim and quadrilateral surface, allowing infrapectineal plating of medially displaced fragments.

items.q: In an elderly patient with an acetabular fracture, the 'gull sign' on radiographs indicates:
o: Superomedial dome impaction, predicting a poor result after fixation alone
items.e: The gull sign reflects impaction of the superomedial roof; it predicts early failure of ORIF and is a common indication for acute THA combined with fixation.

items.q: Prophylaxis against heterotopic ossification after acetabular fixation through a posterior approach is usually given with:
items.e: NSAIDs (classically indomethacin) or a single low-dose radiotherapy fraction reduce HO after posterior and extensile approaches.

items.q: The most important surgeon-controlled factor predicting long-term outcome after open reduction of an acetabular fracture is:
o: The accuracy of articular reduction (residual displacement 1 mm or less)
The use of heterotopic ossification prophylaxis
items.e: Matta and Letournel showed that anatomical reduction (under 1 mm) gives the best long-term hip function; post-traumatic arthritis is the commonest late complication of malreduction.

items.q: After a fall with the hip forced into abduction, the injured limb lies flexed, abducted and externally rotated. The likely injury is:
items.e: Anterior dislocations present with flexion, abduction and external rotation and endanger the femoral nerve and vessels; posterior dislocations are flexed, adducted and internally rotated.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a posterior hip dislocation with a femoral head fracture fragment above (cephalad to) the fovea that remains displaced after reduction. Appropriate treatment is:
o: Open reduction and internal fixation, via a Smith-Petersen approach or surgical hip dislocation
items.e: This is Pipkin II: the fragment is weight-bearing, so it is fixed anatomically. Excision is reserved for small infrafoveal (Pipkin I) fragments.

items.q: Which Pipkin type of femoral head fracture carries the worst prognosis, particularly for avascular necrosis?
items.e: Pipkin III combines a head fracture with a femoral neck fracture, giving the highest AVN rate; older patients usually need arthroplasty.

items.q: In cervical spondylotic myelopathy, the single most frequently compressed disc level is:
items.e: C5-C6 (then C6-C7) is the most mobile segment of the subaxial spine and degenerates first. C2-C3 and C7-T1 are relatively stiff and rarely the primary level.

items.q: The commonest morphological type of cervical OPLL on lateral radiographs and CT is the:
o: Continuous type, spanning several bodies and discs
Segmental type, confined behind individual vertebral bodies
Circumscribed type, confined to the disc space
Mixed type, with continuous and segmental parts
items.e: Of the four Tsuyama types (continuous, segmental, mixed, circumscribed), segmental OPLL lying behind each vertebral body is the most common. It may keep some motion, so it can progress dynamically.

items.q: Cervical OPLL is classically most prevalent in which population?
items.e: OPLL is found in about 2-4% of Japanese adults, much more often than in Western populations. It is also linked to DISH, diabetes and obesity.

items.q: Which metabolic bone disease is associated with diffuse enthesopathy and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament causing myelopathy in adults?
items.e: Adults with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets develop widespread enthesopathy, including OPLL and ligamentum flavum ossification, which can compress the cord. Hyperparathyroidism causes resorption, not ligament ossification.

items.q: On axial CT of cervical OPLL, a 'double-layer sign' (ossified mass and a separate ossified rim with a central lucent layer) suggests:
o: Ossification of the dura, with a high risk of dural tear and CSF leak during anterior removal
Calcified disc herniation rather than OPLL
items.e: The double-layer sign indicates dural ossification. Removing the mass anteriorly is likely to cause a dural defect and CSF leak, so floating the mass or a posterior approach may be preferred.

items.q: For multilevel cervical OPLL with an occupying ratio of 65% and a hill-shaped mass, outcomes are generally better with:
o: Anterior decompression (corpectomy or anterior floating) and fusion
Non-operative care with a soft collar
items.e: An occupying ratio over about 60% and hill-shaped ossification predict poor recovery after laminoplasty because dorsal drift cannot clear a large anterior mass. Direct anterior decompression gives better neurological recovery.

items.q: The K-line used to choose the approach in cervical OPLL is drawn on a neutral lateral radiograph between:
o: The posterior-inferior corners of C2 and C7 bodies
The tips of the C2 and C7 spinous processes
The midpoints of the spinal canal at C2 and C7
The anterior arch of C1 and the C7 spinous process
items.e: The K-line joins the midpoints of the canal at C2 and C7. If the OPLL stays anterior to it (K-line positive), laminoplasty can decompress the cord; if it crosses it (K-line negative), anterior or posterior fusion surgery is needed.

items.q: In the anterior 'floating' technique for cervical OPLL, the surgeon:
o: Removes the whole ossified mass en bloc from the dura
Performs a laminoplasty and leaves the anterior mass untouched
Resects the posterior arch and floats the cord dorsally
Thins the ossified ligament and detaches it so it migrates anteriorly, without excising it from the dura
items.e: Anterior floating (Yamaura) thins the OPLL to a shell and frees it so it drifts forward with the expanding dura. It lowers the risk of dural tear and CSF leak compared with direct excision, especially with dural ossification.

items.q: On axial T2-weighted MRI in DCM, symmetrical bright foci in both anterior horns of the grey matter ('snake-eyes' appearance) indicate:
o: Cystic necrosis of the anterior horns and a poorer prognosis for recovery
Reversible cord oedema that usually resolves after surgery
Demyelinating plaques typical of multiple sclerosis
items.e: Snake-eyes (owl-eyes) represent cystic necrosis and neuronal loss in the anterior horns. They are associated with persistent amyotrophy and a poorer surgical outcome.

items.q: A cord compression ratio (sagittal diameter divided by transverse diameter of the cord at the tightest level) below about 0.4 on MRI in cervical myelopathy suggests:
o: A poorer prognosis for neurological recovery after surgery
A dynamic rather than static compression
items.e: The compression ratio describes cord flattening; a value below about 0.4 reflects severe flattening and is associated with poorer recovery. A normal cord is a flattened oval with a clearly higher ratio.

items.q: According to the AO Spine/WFNS 2017 guideline, a 62-year-old with DCM and an mJOA score of 16 should be offered:
o: Surgery only if the MRI shows a T2 signal change
Observation only, as mild myelopathy never progresses
Either surgery or a supervised trial of structured rehabilitation, with surgery if he deteriorates
A rigid collar worn for 6 months as definitive treatment
items.e: mJOA 15-17 is mild DCM. The guideline offers surgery or a supervised structured rehabilitation trial, converting to surgery if function worsens or fails to improve.

items.q: A 50-year-old with neck pain has no myelopathic symptoms or signs and no radiculopathy, but MRI shows a disc bulge compressing the cord at C5-C6 without signal change. The AO Spine/WFNS guideline recommends:
o: Repeat MRI every 3 months with surgery when signal change appears
No prophylactic surgery; counsel about warning symptoms and follow up clinically
items.e: Asymptomatic cord compression without radiculopathy does not justify prophylactic surgery. Patients are educated about myelopathic symptoms and reviewed clinically.

items.q: Which finding in a patient with MRI cord compression but no myelopathy most increases the risk of developing clinical myelopathy?
o: Clinical or electrophysiological evidence of cervical radiculopathy
A positive Spurling test in the absence of root signs
items.e: Among non-myelopathic patients with cord compression, those with clinical or electrophysiological radiculopathy are at higher risk of developing myelopathy, so they are counselled about surgery or close review.

items.q: The AO Spine CSM-North America and International prospective studies showed that surgical decompression for DCM:
o: Benefited only patients with severe myelopathy
Improved mJOA, Nurick grade and quality-of-life scores at follow-up in mild, moderate and severe disease
Gave no better outcome than the natural history
Improved pain but not neurological function
items.e: These multicentre cohorts (Fehlings) found significant improvements in mJOA, Nurick, NDI and SF-36 after surgery across all severity groups, supporting surgery for moderate and severe DCM.

items.q: Which is the strongest predictor of a worse functional outcome after surgery for DCM?
o: Long duration of symptoms with severe preoperative myelopathy
items.e: Longer symptom duration and greater preoperative severity (lower mJOA) consistently predict poorer recovery, along with older age, smoking, gait impairment and T1 hypointense cord signal.

items.q: In the CSM-Protect randomised trial, perioperative riluzole in patients undergoing surgery for moderate-to-severe DCM:
o: Reduced C5 palsy rates by half
Was stopped early because of hepatotoxicity
Did not improve the primary outcome (mJOA at 1 year), although some secondary pain outcomes favoured it
items.e: CSM-Protect (Fehlings, Lancet Neurology 2021) found no difference in 1-year mJOA change. Riluzole, a sodium-channel blocking glutamate antagonist, showed only secondary benefits such as reduced neck/arm pain.

items.q: A 40-year-old has slowly progressive wasting and weakness of the deltoid and biceps on one side over a year, with no sensory loss and no long-tract signs. MRI shows C4-C5 foraminal and ventral cord compression. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Cervical spondylotic amyotrophy (Keegan type) causes painless proximal muscle wasting from ventral root or anterior horn compression, without sensory loss or myelopathy. ALS would show widespread denervation and UMN signs beyond one segment.

items.q: An 18-year-old man has slowly progressive weakness and wasting of the forearm and hand on one side, sparing brachioradialis, with no sensory loss. Flexion MRI of the neck shows forward shift of the posterior dural wall with lower cervical cord flattening. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Hirayama disease affects young males, with oblique amyotrophy of C7-T1 muscles. Flexion MRI shows anterior displacement of the posterior dura and cord compression; treatment is often a cervical collar to avoid flexion.

items.q: A patient with suspected cervical myelopathy has 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders with preserved touch and proprioception. This dissociated sensory loss suggests:
items.e: A central syrinx interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibres in the anterior commissure, giving suspended, dissociated pain/temperature loss with intact dorsal columns.

items.q: Axial T2 MRI of the cervical cord in a patient with a sensory ataxic myelopathy and macrocytic anaemia shows symmetrical high signal in the dorsal columns (inverted-V sign). The most likely cause is:
items.e: Subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency affects the dorsal columns (and lateral corticospinal tracts), producing the inverted-V or 'rabbit ears' sign. Anterior spinal artery infarction spares the dorsal columns.

items.q: Which electrodiagnostic finding best supports amyotrophic lateral sclerosis rather than DCM in a patient with hand wasting and hyperreflexia?
o: Active denervation in the thoracic paraspinal muscles and tongue, outside the compressed cervical segments
Reduced sensory nerve action potentials in the hands
Normal needle EMG in all limbs
items.e: ALS produces widespread denervation including bulbar and thoracic paraspinal muscles, which cervical compression cannot explain. Sensory potentials are preserved in ALS, and a prolonged median latency suggests carpal tunnel syndrome.

items.q: A patient with DCM has a Nurick grade of 5. This means:
o: Root signs only, with a normal gait
Gait difficulty that does not prevent full-time work
Able to walk only with someone else's help or a frame
items.e: Nurick grades: 0 root signs only; 1 cord signs, normal gait; 2 gait difficulty but full-time work; 3 gait difficulty preventing full-time work; 4 walks only with help or a frame; 5 chairbound or bedridden.

items.q: In a patient with DCM, a C2-C7 sagittal vertical axis above about which value on standing radiographs is associated with worse disability and poorer surgical outcomes?
items.e: A C2-C7 SVA over about 40 mm correlates with worse NDI and myelopathy severity (Tang, Ames). Sagittal imbalance should be addressed when planning decompression and fusion.

items.q: A 70-year-old with DCM has local kyphosis of 20 degrees across the compressed segments. Posterior laminoplasty is likely to give poor results mainly because:
o: Laminoplasty cannot be performed at more than three levels
Kyphosis increases blood loss during posterior surgery
The lateral mass screws cannot be inserted
The cord cannot drift dorsally away from anterior compression in a kyphotic spine
items.e: Laminoplasty decompresses indirectly by allowing dorsal cord drift, which needs lordotic or neutral alignment. Local kyphosis over about 13 degrees predicts poor recovery; anterior or combined surgery is preferred.

items.q: In an open-door (Hirabayashi) cervical laminoplasty, the hinge is created on one side by:
o: Thinning the dorsal cortex at the lamina-lateral mass junction, leaving the ventral cortex intact as a greenstick hinge
Cutting through both cortices on both sides
Splitting the spinous processes in the midline
Removing the facet joint capsule completely
items.e: One side is cut through both cortices to open the door, and the other side is gutted through the dorsal cortex only to act as a hinge. The French-door (Kurokawa) technique instead splits the spinous processes in the midline with bilateral hinges.

items.q: During open-door laminoplasty, the open side is usually placed on:
o: The left side in all patients
The side with the worse radicular symptoms or foraminal stenosis
The side opposite the worse symptoms, to protect the root
The side of the vertebral artery dominance
items.e: Opening on the more symptomatic side allows foraminotomy and direct root decompression on that side, while the hinge is made on the less affected side.

items.q: Which technical step during cervical laminoplasty is thought to reduce postoperative axial neck pain and loss of lordosis?
o: Routinely including C2 in the laminoplasty
Prolonged rigid collar immobilisation for 3 months
Preserving the muscle attachments to the C2 and C7 spinous processes
items.e: Preserving the semispinalis cervicis insertion on C2 and the nuchal ligament/muscle attachments on C7 reduces axial pain and kyphotic change. Prolonged collar use worsens stiffness and pain.

items.q: When placing a lateral mass screw by the Magerl technique, the screw is directed:
o: Straight anteriorly, perpendicular to the posterior lateral mass
Caudally, perpendicular to the facet joint
About 25 degrees laterally and parallel to the facet joint (cranially angled)
items.e: Magerl: entry slightly medial and cranial to the centre of the lateral mass, aiming about 25 degrees lateral and parallel to the facet. Roy-Camille: centre entry, 10 degrees lateral, perpendicular to the lateral mass.

items.q: Lateral mass screws are angled laterally in the subaxial cervical spine mainly to avoid the:
o: Vertebral artery in the transverse foramen
Exiting nerve root in the foramen
items.e: The vertebral artery lies anterior and medial to the lateral mass, so lateral angulation keeps the screw away from it. Too cranial or anterior a trajectory risks the exiting root.

items.q: Pedicle screws are often used at C7 in posterior cervical fusions because C7 has a thin lateral mass and:
o: The vertebral artery usually does not run in the C7 transverse foramen
C7 pedicles are larger than lumbar pedicles
items.e: The vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen at C6 in about 90% of people, so it usually lies outside the C7 foramen. With a relatively large C7 pedicle and thin lateral mass, pedicle screws give better purchase.

items.q: In the Smith-Robinson anterior approach to the cervical spine, the deep interval is developed between:
o: The carotid artery and the internal jugular vein
The carotid sheath laterally and the trachea and oesophagus medially
The longus colli and the vertebral body
items.e: After dividing platysma and the investing fascia along sternocleidomastoid, the pretracheal fascia is opened between the carotid sheath (lateral) and the visceral column (medial), reaching the prevertebral fascia and longus colli.

items.q: A palpable surface landmark at the level of C6 used to plan an anterior cervical incision is the:
o: Carotid (Chassaignac) tubercle and the cricoid cartilage
items.e: The cricoid cartilage and the carotid tubercle on the C6 transverse process lie at C6. The hyoid is about C3 and the thyroid cartilage about C4-C5.

items.q: After an anterior approach to C3-C4, a singer notices voice fatigue and inability to reach high notes, with normal vocal cord movement on laryngoscopy. The nerve most likely injured is the:
o: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
items.e: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery near C3-C4 and supplies cricothyroid; injury lowers pitch and causes voice fatigue. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness from vocal cord palsy.

items.q: Postoperative Horner syndrome after an anterior cervical discectomy results from injury to the sympathetic chain, which lies:
o: On the anterior surface of the longus colli, behind the carotid sheath
Behind the vertebral body in the epidural space
Within the transverse foramen with the vertebral artery
items.e: The cervical sympathetic trunk runs on the front of longus colli. Excessive lateral dissection or retractor blades placed on top of longus colli can injure it.

items.q: Which structure is particularly at risk with a left-sided low anterior approach to C7-T1?
items.e: The thoracic duct arches over the left subclavian artery at the root of the neck to enter the left venous angle, so it can be injured in left-sided cervicothoracic approaches, causing a chylous leak.

items.q: Two hours after a three-level ACDF, a patient becomes stridulous with a tense anterior neck swelling. The immediate management is:
o: CT of the neck to confirm a haematoma
Nebulised adrenaline and return to theatre next morning
Open the wound at the bedside to evacuate the haematoma, then secure the airway
items.e: An expanding retropharyngeal haematoma can rapidly obstruct the airway. Opening the skin, platysma and deep layers at the bedside decompresses it; delaying for imaging can be fatal.

items.q: Use of recombinant BMP-2 in anterior cervical fusion is discouraged mainly because of:
o: Prevertebral soft-tissue swelling causing dysphagia and airway compromise
items.e: The FDA issued a public health notification about life-threatening cervical swelling with off-label rhBMP-2 in anterior cervical fusion. BMP increases fusion rates rather than pseudarthrosis.

items.q: Hilibrand's long-term study of patients after anterior cervical arthrodesis reported symptomatic adjacent segment disease at a rate of about:
o: 3% per year, about one-quarter of patients by 10 years
10% per year, most patients by 10 years
Only in the first 2 years after surgery
items.e: Hilibrand (1999) found new symptomatic adjacent-level disease at about 2.9% per year, with a predicted 25.6% prevalence at 10 years; whether it reflects fusion or natural history is debated.

items.q: After a two-level anterior cervical corpectomy with a strut graft and anterior plate alone, graft or plate dislodgement most often occurs at the:
o: It never occurs with a plate
items.e: Long anterior strut constructs fail most often at the caudal end by kick-out. For corpectomy over two levels, supplementary posterior fixation is recommended.

items.q: During anterior cervical corpectomy, the vertebral artery is best protected by:
o: Extending the decompression lateral to the uncovertebral joints
Keeping the trough between the uncovertebral joints, about 15-16 mm wide
items.e: The vertebral artery runs lateral to the uncovertebral joints. Using the uncinate processes as the lateral limit and keeping the trough to about 15-16 mm reduces the risk of arterial injury.

items.q: Following posterior cervical decompression, a C5 palsy is most often managed and expected to behave as follows:
o: Observation with physiotherapy; most patients recover over 6-12 months
Immediate reoperation to remove the instrumentation
High-dose steroids with expected permanent paralysis
items.e: Postoperative C5 palsy (deltoid ± biceps weakness, often delayed by a day or more) usually recovers with time. Reoperation is considered only if imaging shows a correctable cause such as a malpositioned screw or residual foraminal stenosis.

items.q: The commonest complication specific to cervical total disc arthroplasty that can reduce motion at the treated level over time is:
o: Prosthesis subsidence into the vertebral body
items.e: Heterotopic ossification (graded by the McAfee classification) occurs in a large proportion of cervical disc arthroplasties and can lead to spontaneous fusion. NSAIDs are sometimes used to reduce it.

items.q: Which is a contraindication to cervical disc arthroplasty for a patient with one-level cervical myelopathy?
o: Compression from OPLL behind the vertebral body
Preserved segmental motion on flexion-extension films
items.e: Disc arthroplasty suits soft disc or osteophyte compression at the disc level with preserved motion. OPLL, significant facet arthropathy, instability, kyphosis and osteoporosis are contraindications.

items.q: A 45-year-old has right arm pain radiating to the thumb with weakness of wrist extension and a reduced brachioradialis reflex. Which disc is most likely herniated?
items.e: Wrist extension, the brachioradialis reflex and thumb sensation indicate the C6 root, which exits at C5-C6 in the cervical spine (the root takes the number of the lower vertebra).

items.q: Extension and rotation of the neck towards the painful side with axial compression reproduces a patient's radiating arm pain. This test is the:
items.e: Spurling's manoeuvre narrows the foramen and is quite specific for cervical radiculopathy. Adson's test is used for thoracic outlet syndrome.

items.q: A 40-year-old has 8 weeks of C7 radicular pain with mild triceps weakness and an MRI showing a soft posterolateral foraminal disc at C6-C7 without instability. If surgery is chosen, an option that avoids fusion is:
items.e: A posterior foraminotomy decompresses a foraminal soft disc or osteophyte without fusion and preserves motion. It is unsuitable for central compression or instability.

items.q: Ossification of the ligamentum flavum causing myelopathy is most commonly found in the:
items.e: Ossified ligamentum flavum mainly affects the lower thoracic levels (around T9-T12), producing thoracic myelopathy; it is common in East Asians and may coexist with cervical OPLL.

items.q: A patient with severe multilevel cervical myelopathy needs general anaesthesia. The safest airway technique to minimise cord injury is:
o: Direct laryngoscopy with full neck extension
Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure and extension
Blind nasal intubation with forced flexion
Awake fibreoptic intubation with the neck kept neutral
items.e: Hyperextension narrows the spondylotic canal and can worsen myelopathy. Fibreoptic or video-assisted intubation with neutral positioning (and neuromonitoring at positioning) limits this risk.

items.q: A diabetic patient taking empagliflozin is scheduled for elective spinal fusion. The drug is withheld for 2-3 days beforehand mainly to avoid:
items.e: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose during fasting and surgical stress, so they are stopped a few days before surgery. Lactic acidosis is the classic concern with metformin.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture. Which of the following is one of Lafontaine's predictors that the reduction will be lost in a cast?
o: Negative ulnar variance on the uninjured side
items.e: Lafontaine's instability factors are dorsal angulation over 20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular extension, an associated ulnar fracture and age over 60; three or more predict loss of reduction. Sex and hand dominance are not among them.

items.q: On a true lateral radiograph of the wrist, the normal teardrop angle of the distal radius (the angle between the axis of the volar rim 'teardrop' and the radial shaft) is about:
items.e: The teardrop angle is normally about 70 degrees; a value below about 45 degrees indicates dorsal rotation of the volar lunate facet that needs correction. 22 and 11 degrees are the normal radial inclination and volar tilt.

items.q: The Fernandez classification of distal radius fractures is based on mechanism. A depressed 'die-punch' fracture of the lunate facet produced by axial loading through the lunate is Fernandez type:
items.e: Fernandez III is a compression fracture of the articular surface such as a die-punch fragment. Type I is a bending (Colles or Smith) metaphyseal fracture, II a shearing rim fracture (Barton) and IV an avulsion with radiocarpal fracture-dislocation.

items.q: A volar Barton fracture (volar rim fracture with volar carpal subluxation) is classified by Fernandez as which mechanism type?
items.e: Barton rim fractures, volar or dorsal, are shearing fractures (Fernandez II) and are unstable, needing a buttress plate. Bending fractures are the extra-articular Colles and Smith patterns.

items.q: In the AO/OTA (2018) classification, a volar rim (volar Barton) fracture of the distal radius is coded as:
items.e: 2R3B is a partial articular fracture: B1 radial styloid (sagittal), B2 dorsal rim and B3 volar rim. A codes are extra-articular and C codes complete articular fractures.

items.q: In Melone's classification of intra-articular distal radius fractures, the 'medial complex' that is key to restoring the joint consists of:
o: The radial styloid and scaphoid facet
The dorsal and palmar fragments of the lunate facet
The ulnar styloid and TFCC insertion
The metaphyseal shaft fragment and Lister's tubercle
items.e: Melone described four parts: shaft, radial styloid, and the dorsal-medial and palmar-medial lunate facet fragments, the latter two forming the medial complex that carries the lunate and sigmoid notch. The ulnar styloid is not one of the four parts.

items.q: In the Frykman classification of distal radius fractures, an associated ulnar styloid fracture is indicated by:
o: An odd-numbered type (I, III, V, VII)
An even-numbered type (II, IV, VI, VIII)
items.e: Frykman types I-VIII progress from extra-articular to radiocarpal, DRUJ and combined involvement, and each even number adds an ulnar styloid fracture to the preceding odd type.

items.q: On a PA wrist radiograph, radial inclination is the angle between a line perpendicular to the radial shaft axis and a line drawn from the tip of the radial styloid to the:
o: Ulnar corner of the lunate fossa (sigmoid notch margin) of the radius
items.e: Radial inclination (normally about 22 degrees) is measured from the radial styloid tip to the ulnar corner of the distal radial articular surface. The ulnar styloid is used for none of the standard radial parameters.

items.q: Ulnar variance on a PA wrist radiograph becomes more ulnar positive when the radiograph is taken with the forearm:
o: Pronated with a tight power grip
In neutral rotation with the shoulder abducted 90 degrees
Supinated with the wrist radially deviated
items.e: Pronation and gripping draw the radius proximally relative to the ulna, increasing ulnar variance, so the standard is a neutral-rotation PA with shoulder abducted and elbow flexed 90 degrees. Supination makes the variance more negative.

items.q: After volar locking plate fixation, the surgeon wants to confirm that the distal screws have not entered the radiocarpal joint. The appropriate image is a lateral view with the forearm:
o: Elevated about 20 degrees off the table to align the beam with the radial inclination
In full wrist flexion with the beam along the forearm axis
items.e: Because the articular surface is inclined about 22 degrees on the PA, an inclined (20-degree) lateral profiles the joint and shows intra-articular screw penetration that a true lateral can hide. The beam along the flexed wrist is the dorsal tangential view, used for dorsal screw prominence.

items.q: After volar plating, which intraoperative image best detects distal screw tips protruding through the dorsal cortex into the extensor compartments?
o: Dorsal tangential (skyline) view with the wrist hyperflexed
items.e: The dorsal tangential view looks along the dorsal radial cortex with the wrist flexed and shows screw tips beyond Lister's tubercle and the compartments that are missed on the lateral because of the cortical contour. Prominent dorsal tips can rupture EPL or EDC.

items.q: In the UK DRAFFT trial of adults with dorsally displaced distal radius fractures needing surgery, the comparison of percutaneous K-wire fixation with volar locking plate fixation showed:
o: Significantly better 12-month function with volar plates
More malunions needing revision with volar plates
Higher deep infection rates with volar plates
No clinically important difference in patient-rated wrist function at 12 months
items.e: DRAFFT found similar PRWE scores at 12 months, with K-wires cheaper; earlier slight advantages of plates did not persist. Malunion needing revision was not more frequent with plates.

items.q: The WRIST trial randomised patients aged 60 or more with unstable distal radius fractures to volar locking plate, external fixation, percutaneous pinning or casting (non-randomised arm). The main finding at 12 months was:
o: No clinically meaningful difference in Michigan Hand Questionnaire scores between groups
Clearly superior function with external fixation
Worse grip strength in all operative groups
A higher complication rate after volar plating than casting
items.e: WRIST showed similar 12-month patient-reported outcomes despite worse radiographic alignment in the cast group; plating gave slightly faster early recovery. This supports non-operative treatment in many older patients.

items.q: To reduce the incidence of complex regional pain syndrome after a distal radius fracture, the AAOS guideline (moderate evidence) supports:
o: Vitamin C 500 mg daily for about 50 days
Vitamin D 1000 IU daily for 3 months
items.e: Trials by Zollinger and others found vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days reduced CRPS after wrist fractures, though later trials conflicted. Gabapentin, calcitonin and vitamin D are not recommended for this purpose.

items.q: Rupture of EPL after an undisplaced distal radius fracture is thought to result mainly from:
o: A sharp fracture spike lacerating the tendon at injury
Plate prominence in the fourth compartment
Raised pressure and ischaemia of the tendon in an intact third compartment over Lister's tubercle
Traction injury from the posterior interosseous nerve
items.e: With an undisplaced fracture the extensor retinaculum stays intact, so haematoma in the tight third compartment compromises the tendon's watershed blood supply over Lister's tubercle, with attrition rupture weeks later. Plate prominence does not apply to a cast-treated fracture.

items.q: Through the modified Henry (FCR) approach to the distal radius, the dissection stays radial to the FCR tendon mainly to avoid injury to the:
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
items.e: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve runs ulnar to the FCR tendon, so working through the floor of the FCR sheath and retracting the tendon ulnarly protects it and the median nerve. The radial artery lies radial to the FCR.

items.q: In the volar (FCR) approach to the distal radius, after retracting FPL the surgeon exposes the fracture by elevating which muscle from its radial insertion?
items.e: Pronator quadratus is detached from the radial border of the distal radius in an L-shape and elevated ulnarly to expose the metaphysis. Pronator teres inserts at mid-shaft and brachioradialis at the styloid.

items.q: In a comminuted distal radius fracture, which muscle acts as the principal deforming force on the radial styloid fragment and may be released to restore radial length?
items.e: Brachioradialis inserts on the radial styloid and pulls it proximally and radially; a step-cut or release of its tendon aids reduction. APL and ECRL do not insert on the styloid.

items.q: In the Soong grading of volar plate position on the lateral radiograph, a grade 2 plate is one that:
o: Stays dorsal (proximal) to the critical line tangential to the volar rim
Lies volar to the critical line but proximal to the volar rim
Lies directly on or beyond the volar rim of the distal radius
Lies within the concavity proximal to the pronator quadratus line
items.e: Soong grade 0 is behind the critical line, grade 1 volar to it but proximal to the rim, and grade 2 on or beyond the rim; grade 2 carries the highest FPL rupture risk, so plate removal after union is advised.

items.q: After volar plating of an intra-articular distal radius fracture, the small volar ulnar ('critical corner') lunate facet fragment was not captured. The expected complication is:
o: Dorsal subluxation of the ulnar head
Volar subluxation of the carpus with the fragment
items.e: The volar lunate facet is the key buttress for the carpus; if this small distal fragment escapes the plate the lunate and carpus slide volarly. Fragment-specific hook plates, spring wires or rim plates are used to capture it.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with polytrauma and a highly comminuted intra-articular distal radius fracture will need to use a walking frame. Which fixation best allows early weight bearing through the wrist?
o: Dorsal spanning (bridge) plate to the second or third metacarpal
Volar locking plate with early mobilisation
items.e: A dorsal distraction bridge plate holds length across severe comminution and tolerates load through a platform walker; it is removed after union at about 12 weeks. K-wires and casts will not tolerate weight bearing.

items.q: After volar plating of a distal radius fracture there is a displaced fracture at the base of the ulnar styloid. What should be done next?
o: Routinely fix every ulnar styloid base fracture with a tension band
Test DRUJ stability in pronation, neutral and supination and fix the styloid or repair the TFCC only if unstable
Immobilise in an above-elbow cast for 12 weeks regardless of stability
items.e: Most ulnar styloid fractures need no fixation; a base fracture can carry the foveal TFCC insertion, so DRUJ stability is tested after the radius is fixed, and only an unstable DRUJ needs styloid fixation or TFCC repair.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a symptomatic extra-articular distal radius malunion with 25 degrees of dorsal tilt and 4 mm of radial shortening. The appropriate operation is:
o: Darrach resection of the distal ulna
Opening-wedge corrective osteotomy with a volar plate and bone graft
items.e: Dorsal angulation and shortening are corrected by an opening-wedge radial osteotomy, filled with graft and fixed with a volar plate. Ulnar shortening alone is used when the only problem is positive ulnar variance with acceptable tilt.

items.q: For intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block) to reduce a distal radius fracture, the preferred local anaesthetic is:
items.e: Prilocaine has the best safety margin if the tourniquet fails; bupivacaine is contraindicated because of cardiotoxicity and adrenaline-containing solutions are not used intravenously. The cuff is kept inflated for at least about 20 minutes.

items.q: Immobilising a reduced Colles fracture in the Cotton-Loder position (marked wrist flexion and ulnar deviation) is avoided mainly because it:
o: Raises carpal tunnel pressure and can produce median nerve compression
Leads to ulnar nerve palsy in Guyon's canal
items.e: Extreme flexion sharply increases carpal tunnel pressure, causing median neuropathy and stiffness. A neutral or slightly flexed position with three-point moulding is used instead.

items.q: A 55-year-old golfer has hypothenar pain after a mis-hit shot. Plain radiographs are normal. Which tendon is at risk of attritional rupture if a hook of hamate fracture goes unrecognised?
o: Flexor digitorum profundus to the little finger
items.e: The little (and ring) finger FDP tendons glide against the radial side of the hook of hamate and can fray and rupture over a non-united hook. FCU inserts on the pisiform and is not at risk.

items.q: A baseball player has a symptomatic non-union of the hook of hamate 4 months after injury. The usual treatment with the quickest return to sport is:
o: Open reduction and screw fixation as the standard
items.e: Excision of the hook reliably relieves pain and allows return to sport in 6-8 weeks with little loss of grip. Fixation is possible but has higher complication and non-union rates.

items.q: A fall on the outstretched hand produces a small flake of bone seen only on the lateral radiograph dorsal to the proximal carpal row. The most likely injury and treatment are:
o: Lunate body fracture needing screw fixation
Scaphoid proximal pole fracture needing fixation
Capitate neck fracture needing open reduction
Dorsal triquetral chip fracture, treated with short splintage for symptom relief
items.e: The dorsal triquetral chip (avulsion or impaction by the ulnar styloid) is the second commonest carpal fracture and is best seen on the lateral; it heals well with brief immobilisation.

items.q: A fracture of the ridge of the trapezium is best demonstrated on which plain radiograph?
items.e: The carpal tunnel view profiles the trapezial ridge and hook of hamate. The ridge gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum and the fracture may irritate the adjacent FCR tendon.

items.q: A 30-year-old has Kienböck disease with lunate collapse and a fixed flexed scaphoid showing a cortical ring sign and a radioscaphoid angle of 65 degrees. Which Lichtman stage and treatment are appropriate?
o: Stage IIIB; proximal row carpectomy or scaphotrapeziotrapezoid/scaphocapitate fusion
Stage II; vascularised bone graft alone
items.e: Fixed scaphoid rotation (ring sign, radioscaphoid angle over 60 degrees) defines stage IIIB, where joint-levelling no longer helps and salvage by PRC or STT/SC fusion is used. Stage IIIA has collapse with normal carpal alignment.

items.q: In Kienböck disease, the radiographic finding that separates Lichtman stage IIIA from IIIB is:
o: Fixed flexion (rotatory malalignment) of the scaphoid
Degenerative change of the radiocarpal joint
items.e: Both stage III subtypes show lunate collapse; IIIB adds fixed scaphoid flexion with a ring sign and radioscaphoid angle over 60 degrees. Pancarpal arthritis is stage IV.

items.q: To revascularise the lunate in early Kienböck disease, the most widely used pedicled graft from the dorsal distal radius is based on the:
o: Anterior interosseous artery branch to pronator quadratus via the palmar carpal arch
items.e: The 4,5-ECA graft has a long retrograde pedicle that reaches the lunate easily; the 1,2-ICSRA graft is better suited to the scaphoid. The descending genicular artery supplies the free medial femoral condyle flap.

items.q: A 52-year-old manual labourer has Kienböck disease with lunate collapse and degenerative change of the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints. The most reliable treatment is:
items.e: Stage IV with pancarpal arthritis needs salvage; for a heavy labourer total wrist fusion gives durable pain relief. PRC requires healthy capitate and lunate fossa cartilage, and joint-levelling or revascularisation are early-stage procedures.

items.q: Biomechanically, the most stable position for a headless compression screw in a scaphoid waist fracture is:
o: Along the central axis of the scaphoid, as long as possible
Perpendicular to the long axis of the scaphoid
Short screw confined to the distal fragment
items.e: A long screw in the central third of both fragments gives greater stiffness, load to failure and faster union than an eccentric screw. Placing it entirely in one fragment gives no compression across the fracture.

items.q: For percutaneous volar fixation of a scaphoid waist fracture, the guidewire is introduced at the:
o: Proximal pole just radial to the scapholunate ligament with the wrist flexed
Radial styloid through the first extensor compartment
Distal pole through the scaphotrapezial joint with the wrist extended and ulnarly deviated
Scaphoid tubercle with the wrist flexed and radially deviated
items.e: The volar route enters at the distal pole via the scaphotrapezial joint (part of the trapezium may obstruct the line) with the wrist extended over a bolster. The dorsal route through the proximal pole needs wrist flexion.

items.q: A free vascularised medial femoral condyle corticocancellous flap is used for proximal pole scaphoid non-union with avascular necrosis and collapse. Its vascular pedicle is the:
items.e: The medial femoral condyle flap is supplied by the articular branch of the descending genicular artery (or the superomedial genicular artery), giving a robust structural graft for collapsed proximal poles.

items.q: On a normal PA wrist radiograph, Gilula's arc III is formed by the:
o: Proximal articular surfaces of the capitate and hamate
Proximal surfaces of the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum
Distal surfaces of the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum
Distal articular surface of the radius and ulna
items.e: Arc I follows the proximal convexities of the proximal row, arc II their distal concavities and arc III the proximal curves of the capitate and hamate. A break in any arc suggests carpal dislocation or instability.

items.q: On the lateral radiograph of a dorsal perilunate dislocation (without lunate dislocation), the expected appearance is:
o: The lunate is displaced volarly out of its fossa with the capitate aligned to the radius
The lunate stays in the lunate fossa of the radius while the capitate lies dorsal to it
The lunate is displaced dorsally out of its fossa
The capitate and lunate are colinear with the radius
items.e: In perilunate dislocation the lunate keeps its relation to the radius and the rest of the carpus dislocates, usually dorsally. In lunate dislocation (Mayfield IV) the lunate tips volarly out of the fossa ('spilled teacup') while the capitate lines up with the radius.

items.q: In open treatment of an acute perilunate dislocation through combined dorsal and volar approaches, the volar approach is mainly used to:
o: Fix the radial styloid with a buttress plate
Release the carpal tunnel and repair the volar capsular tear through the space of Poirier
Harvest bone graft from the distal radius
items.e: The volar incision decompresses the median nerve, allows reduction of the lunate and repair of the volar capsular rent at the space of Poirier; the dorsal scapholunate ligament is repaired through the dorsal approach.

items.q: At wrist arthroscopy, probing the TFCC articular disc shows it has lost its normal taut, springy rebound (negative 'trampoline test'). This most suggests:
o: Central perforation of the disc, Palmer 1A
Radial detachment from the sigmoid notch, Palmer 1D
Ulnar impaction with chondromalacia of the lunate, Palmer 2B
Peripheral (ulnar) detachment of the TFCC, Palmer 1B
items.e: The trampoline effect depends on the peripheral attachment of the disc; loss of tension indicates a peripheral or foveal detachment that should be repaired. A central perforation keeps the rim tension intact.

items.q: A 25-year-old has ulnar-sided wrist pain after a fall and arthroscopy shows an isolated small central traumatic perforation of the TFCC articular disc with a stable DRUJ (Palmer 1A). The treatment is:
o: Arthroscopic debridement of the unstable flap, preserving the peripheral rim
Open foveal reattachment with suture anchors
Darrach resection of the ulnar head
items.e: The central disc is avascular and does not heal, so 1A tears are debrided, leaving the peripheral 2 mm rim and radioulnar ligaments intact for DRUJ stability. Peripheral 1B tears are vascularised and repairable.

items.q: In the Palmer classification of degenerative TFCC lesions (ulnar impaction), stage 2D is defined by:
o: TFCC wear without perforation or chondromalacia
TFCC perforation, lunate or ulnar head chondromalacia and lunotriquetral ligament perforation
TFCC perforation with chondromalacia but an intact lunotriquetral ligament
items.e: Class 2 progresses A wear, B wear with chondromalacia, C perforation with chondromalacia, D plus LT ligament perforation, E plus ulnocarpal arthritis.

items.q: The primary stabilisers of the distal radioulnar joint are the:
o: Dorsal and palmar radioulnar ligaments of the TFCC
Interosseous membrane distal oblique bundle and pronator teres
items.e: The dorsal and palmar radioulnar ligaments, attaching to the fovea and ulnar styloid, are the main DRUJ restraints; the ECU subsheath, pronator quadratus and distal oblique bundle are secondary. The ulnocarpal ligaments stabilise the carpus on the ulna.

items.q: A 30-year-old has chronic painful DRUJ instability after a TFCC injury, with an irreparable TFCC but normal sigmoid notch and articular cartilage. The recommended reconstruction is:
o: Darrach resection of the distal ulna
Anatomical radioulnar ligament reconstruction with a palmaris longus graft (Adams-Berger)
items.e: The Adams-Berger technique passes a tendon graft through tunnels in the distal radius and ulnar fovea to reconstruct both radioulnar ligaments and restore stability. The resection procedures are for arthritic DRUJs.

items.q: The most frequent problem after a Darrach resection of the distal ulna in a younger active patient is:
o: Painful instability and convergence (impingement) of the ulnar stump against the radius
items.e: Excising the ulnar head removes the DRUJ support, and the stump can become unstable and impinge on the radius under load; hence Darrach is reserved mostly for low-demand older patients.

items.q: Palmer and Werner measured ulnocarpal load transmission in cadaver wrists. With neutral ulnar variance the ulna bears about 18% of the axial load; lengthening the ulna by 2.5 mm increases this to approximately:
items.e: A 2.5 mm increase in ulnar length raised ulnocarpal load from about 18% to 42%, whereas 2.5 mm of shortening reduced it to about 4%. This underlies ulnar impaction syndrome and joint-levelling procedures.

items.q: With increasing dorsal angulation of a distal radius malunion, load transmission across the wrist changes so that:
o: Load concentrates on the volar lunate facet
The ulnocarpal load falls to almost zero
Load shifts towards the ulna and onto the dorsal part of the scaphoid fossa
Load distribution remains unchanged until 45 degrees
items.e: Short and Palmer showed ulnocarpal load rising from about 21% to 67% as dorsal tilt increases to 45 degrees, with load concentrated dorsally in the scaphoid fossa; this contributes to ulnar-sided pain and arthritis.

items.q: In volar locking plate fixation of an osteoporotic distal radius fracture, the distal locking screws or pegs give best support to the articular surface when placed:
o: In the metaphysis about 10 mm proximal to the joint
Through the radiocarpal joint into the lunate
Bicortically with tips protruding 2 mm dorsally
Just beneath the subchondral bone, within about 2-4 mm of the joint
items.e: Subchondral placement of the distal row supports the articular fragments like a scaffold and resists collapse; more proximal screws allow settling and loss of tilt. Dorsal protrusion endangers the extensor tendons.

items.q: In the three-column concept of the distal radius and ulna (Rikli and Regazzoni), the intermediate column consists of the:
o: Lunate fossa and sigmoid notch, the main load-bearing column
Lister's tubercle and the dorsal cortex
items.e: The radial column (styloid and scaphoid fossa) acts as a lateral buttress, the intermediate column (lunate fossa and sigmoid notch) carries most axial load, and the ulnar column (distal ulna and TFCC) is a secondary stabiliser for the DRUJ.

items.q: In Kapandji's technique for an extra-articular dorsally displaced distal radius fracture, the K-wires are:
o: Passed from the radial styloid across the fracture into the ulna
Introduced into the fracture site and levered to restore tilt, then driven into the opposite cortex as buttresses
Inserted across the radiocarpal joint into the carpus
Placed through the ulna to the radius to transfix the DRUJ
items.e: Intrafocal pinning places wires through the fracture line, levers the distal fragment into position and leaves them as buttresses that resist redisplacement. Transfixing the joint or DRUJ is not part of the technique.

items.q: By approximately how much does the patella increase the moment arm of the quadriceps mechanism?
items.e: The patella displaces the extensor mechanism anteriorly, increasing the quadriceps moment arm by roughly 30-50%; this is why patellectomy weakens extension substantially.

items.q: The patellofemoral joint reaction force during a deep squat is approximately:
items.e: PFJ reaction force is about 0.5 x body weight in level walking, 3-4 x on stairs and 7-8 x in squatting, rising with flexion and quadriceps force.

items.q: A normal patella, lying lateral to the trochlea in full extension, first engages the trochlear groove at about:
items.e: The patella enters the trochlea at about 20-30 degrees of flexion, so instability occurs in early flexion, when soft-tissue restraints such as the MPFL are most important.

items.q: The odd facet of the patella comes into contact with the medial femoral condyle at about:
items.e: The odd (most medial) facet articulates only in deep flexion, about 120-135 degrees, when it contacts the lateral border of the medial femoral condyle.

items.q: On the patella, the medial patellofemoral ligament inserts mainly onto the:
o: Distal third of the lateral border
Proximal two-thirds of the medial border
Inferior pole at the patellar tendon origin
Centre of the anterior patellar surface
items.e: The MPFL fans out to insert on the proximal two-thirds of the medial patellar border; patellar sockets or anchors for reconstruction are placed there.

items.q: In a skeletally immature adolescent with a first lateral patellar dislocation, the MPFL is most often torn at its:
items.e: In children and adolescents the MPFL characteristically fails at the patellar attachment (sometimes as a small bony avulsion), whereas in adults femoral-side tears are frequently described.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of the restraining force against lateral patellar translation near full extension is provided by the MPFL?
items.e: Sectioning studies (Conlan, Desio) show the MPFL contributes about 50-60% of the medial restraint in 0-30 degrees of flexion, making it the primary soft-tissue stabiliser.

items.q: Beyond about 30 degrees of knee flexion, the main stabiliser of the patella against lateral displacement is the:
o: Bony geometry of the trochlear groove
items.e: Once the patella is seated in the trochlea, the bony trochlear walls (especially the lateral facet) become the main restraint; this is why trochlear dysplasia is so important.

items.q: In asymptomatic knees, the tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance on CT is typically about:
items.e: Normal TT-TG is about 10-13 mm; values over 20 mm are found in most patients with objective patellar instability (Dejour) and are considered abnormal.

items.q: Compared with CT, the TT-TG distance measured on MRI in the same knee is generally:
items.e: MRI values tend to be about 2-4 mm smaller than CT values (different landmarks and positioning), so CT-derived thresholds such as 20 mm should be applied cautiously to MRI.

items.q: The tibial tubercle-posterior cruciate ligament (TT-PCL) distance is considered abnormal when it exceeds about:
items.e: Seitlinger described the TT-PCL distance, with values over 24 mm indicating tubercle lateralisation; it is unaffected by trochlear morphology.

items.q: The normal Q angle in women, measured with the knee extended, is approximately:
items.e: Typical normal Q angles are about 14 degrees in men and 17 degrees in women; higher values reflect a greater lateral pull on the patella.

items.q: The Q angle of the knee is formed by lines drawn from the:
o: Femoral head centre to the knee centre, and from the knee centre to the ankle centre
Anterior superior iliac spine to the patellar centre, and from the patellar centre to the tibial tubercle
Anterior inferior iliac spine to the tibial tubercle, and from the tibial tubercle to the ankle
Greater trochanter to the patellar centre, and from the patellar centre to the fibular head
items.e: The Q angle uses the ASIS-patella line (the quadriceps line of pull) and the patella-tibial tubercle line (patellar tendon); the hip-knee-ankle lines define the mechanical axis instead.

items.q: On a Merchant axial view, trochlear dysplasia is suggested by a sulcus angle greater than about:
items.e: The normal sulcus angle is about 137-138 degrees; a value over 145 degrees indicates a shallow, dysplastic trochlea.

items.q: On a Merchant axial view, which congruence angle indicates lateral patellar subluxation?
items.e: Merchant's normal congruence angle is about -6 degrees (patellar ridge slightly medial to the sulcus bisector); values over +16 degrees indicate lateral subluxation.

items.q: The Merchant axial (skyline) view of the patellofemoral joint is taken with the knee flexed to about:
items.e: Merchant's view uses 45 degrees of knee flexion with the beam angled 30 degrees from horizontal; Laurin's view uses 20 degrees.

items.q: Patella alta is indicated when the Blackburne-Peel ratio exceeds about:
items.e: The Blackburne-Peel ratio (perpendicular height of the inferior articular pole above the tibial plateau line divided by articular length) is normally about 0.8; over 1.0 indicates alta.

items.q: Why is the Insall-Salvati ratio unsuitable for confirming correction of patellar height after a distalising tibial tubercle osteotomy?
o: It depends on the femoral trochlear length
It cannot be measured on a lateral radiograph
The patellar tendon length, on which it depends, is unchanged by the osteotomy
It only applies to skeletally immature knees
items.e: Insall-Salvati is patellar tendon length over patellar length; moving the tubercle does not alter the tendon, so indices referenced to the tibial plateau such as Caton-Deschamps are used to plan and assess distalisation.

items.q: A true lateral radiograph of an unstable knee shows a crossing sign only, and the axial view shows a shallow trochlea with preserved shape and a sulcus angle of 150 degrees. Which Dejour type of trochlear dysplasia is this?
items.e: Dejour type A is a crossing sign with a shallow but normally shaped trochlea; type B adds a supratrochlear spur, type C a double contour, and type D all three with a cliff.

items.q: A lateral radiograph shows a crossing sign and a prominent supratrochlear spur but no double contour; the trochlea is flat on axial MRI. This is Dejour type:
items.e: Type B dysplasia combines a crossing sign with a supratrochlear spur (bump) and a flat or convex trochlea; a double contour would make it type C or D.

items.q: A lateral radiograph shows a crossing sign and a double contour without a supratrochlear spur; axial MRI shows a convex lateral facet and a hypoplastic medial facet. This is Dejour type:
