items.e: Dejour type C has a crossing sign with a double contour (representing the hypoplastic medial facet) and facet asymmetry but no spur; adding a spur and a vertical cliff gives type D.

items.q: On a true lateral knee radiograph, the 'double contour' sign of trochlear dysplasia represents:
o: A hypoplastic medial trochlear facet projected below the lateral facet
An osteochondral loose body in the suprapatellar pouch
items.e: The double contour is the hypoplastic medial facet lying below (posterior to) the lateral facet outline; it is a feature of Dejour types C and D. A truly rotated film must be excluded by superimposing the posterior condyles.

items.q: Trochlear dysplasia is present in approximately what proportion of patients with recurrent objective patellar instability?
items.e: Dejour found trochlear dysplasia (crossing sign) in about 85-96% of patients with objective patellar instability, making it the most important anatomical risk factor.

items.q: The typical mechanism of a lateral patellar dislocation in sport is:
o: Forced external rotation of the femur on a fixed tibia in full extension
A direct posterior blow to the proximal tibia with the knee flexed
Hyperextension with a varus force on a straight knee
Twisting with the foot planted, the femur internally rotating on the tibia with the knee flexed in valgus
items.e: Most dislocations occur when the foot is planted and the femur internally rotates on the externally rotated tibia with the knee flexed and in valgus, so the quadriceps pulls the patella laterally.

items.q: After an acute lateral patellar dislocation, tenderness over the medial epicondyle region at the femoral attachment of the MPFL is known as:
items.e: Bassett sign is tenderness at the adductor tubercle/medial epicondyle region indicating MPFL femoral injury; Fairbank is the apprehension test, Clarke the patellar grind test and Wilson a test for osteochondritis dissecans.

items.q: With the knee at about 30 degrees of flexion, an examiner pushes the patella laterally and the patient contracts the quadriceps and resists in fear. This is:
items.e: The Fairbank apprehension test reproduces the sensation of impending lateral dislocation; it is the most useful clinical sign of lateral patellar instability.

items.q: On the patellar glide test with the knee in 20-30 degrees of flexion, which degree of lateral translation suggests incompetent medial restraints?
o: Three or more quadrants of the patellar width
items.e: Dividing the patella into four longitudinal quadrants, lateral glide of three or more quadrants indicates incompetent medial restraints; a medial glide of one quadrant or less suggests a tight lateral retinaculum.

items.q: With the knee extended, the examiner cannot lift the lateral border of the patella to the horizontal (neutral) position. This finding indicates:
items.e: A negative passive patellar tilt test (lateral facet cannot be raised to neutral) indicates excessive lateral tension; if surgery is required, lateral retinacular lengthening rather than isolated release is preferred.

items.q: Osteochondral fractures complicate acute lateral patellar dislocation in approximately:
items.e: Osteochondral injury occurs in roughly a quarter to a half of first-time dislocations, so MRI is advised when there is a haemarthrosis or a fragment is suspected.

items.q: During an acute lateral patellar dislocation, the commonest source of an osteochondral fragment is the:
items.e: As the patella relocates, the medial patellar facet strikes the lateral femoral condyle; the inferomedial patellar facet is the commonest donor site, followed by the lateral femoral condyle.

items.q: After a first-time lateral patellar dislocation treated non-operatively, the overall rate of recurrent instability is approximately:
items.e: Recurrence after a first dislocation averages about 15-45% overall but rises to about 70% in skeletally immature patients with trochlear dysplasia.

items.q: Which patient has the highest risk of recurrence after a first lateral patellar dislocation?
o: A 30-year-old man injured by a direct blow with normal trochlear anatomy
A 13-year-old girl with open physes, trochlear dysplasia and patella alta
A 25-year-old rugby player with a normal trochlea and Caton-Deschamps index of 1.0
A 45-year-old woman with normal patellar height and a TT-TG of 12 mm
items.e: Young age with open physes, trochlear dysplasia and patella alta together confer recurrence risks above 50-70%; a dislocation from a direct blow in a normal knee has a low recurrence risk.

items.q: During MPFL reconstruction, the graft is usually tensioned and fixed with the knee flexed to about:
o: 120 degrees, with the patella pulled medially
30-60 degrees, with the patella centred in the trochlea
items.e: Fixing the graft at about 30-60 degrees with the patella seated avoids over-tensioning; the MPFL is a checkrein, not a tether, and over-tensioning causes medial overload and loss of flexion.

items.q: In MPFL reconstruction, placing the femoral tunnel too distal (posterior-inferior) to the anatomical point makes the graft:
o: Tight in extension and lax in flexion
Tight in flexion and lax in extension
items.e: A distal femoral tunnel causes the graft to slacken as the knee flexes (tight in extension, loose in flexion); a proximal tunnel does the opposite and overloads the medial facet in flexion.

items.q: In a skeletally immature patient undergoing MPFL reconstruction, the femoral attachment of the MPFL lies:
o: Several centimetres proximal to the physis
Within the physis itself, on its lateral side
Just distal to the distal femoral physis
items.e: The MPFL femoral origin lies a few millimetres distal to the distal femoral physis, so sockets are drilled in the epiphysis angled distally, or physeal-sparing soft-tissue techniques are used.

items.q: Patellar fracture after MPFL reconstruction is best avoided by:
o: Fixing the graft in full extension
Drilling a large transverse tunnel through the centre of the patella
Using suture anchors or short blind sockets instead of transverse tunnels across the patella
items.e: Full-width transverse patellar tunnels act as stress risers; anchors or short sockets in the medial border reduce fracture risk.

items.q: Compared with MPFL reconstruction, isolated repair of the torn MPFL for recurrent patellar instability results in:
o: Identical outcomes in all published series
A lower recurrence rate but more stiffness
A higher rate of recurrent instability
items.e: Repair of an attenuated, often chronically stretched ligament has higher redislocation rates than reconstruction with a tendon graft, which is the preferred procedure.

items.q: When performing a medialising (Elmslie-Trillat) tibial tubercle osteotomy for a TT-TG of 24 mm, the target postoperative TT-TG is about:
items.e: The aim is a normal TT-TG of about 10-15 mm; correction to zero or below over-medialises the tubercle.

items.q: Excessive medialisation of the tibial tubercle during realignment surgery leads to:
o: Increased medial patellofemoral and medial tibiofemoral contact pressures
items.e: Over-medialisation shifts load to the medial patellar facet and medial tibiofemoral compartment, causing pain and arthritis and occasionally medial patellar instability.

items.q: Anteromedialisation (Fulkerson) of the tibial tubercle is relatively contraindicated when the patellar chondral lesion is located in the:
items.e: Anteromedialisation shifts load proximally and medially, unloading the distal and lateral patella; it therefore worsens proximal or medial facet lesions.

items.q: Six weeks after an anteromedialising tibial tubercle osteotomy, a patient who resumed full weight bearing early feels a crack in the proximal leg. The most likely complication is:
items.e: The oblique osteotomy weakens the proximal tibia; fractures typically occur around 6-12 weeks, especially with early unrestricted weight bearing, so protected weight bearing is advised.

items.q: The Hauser procedure for patellar instability was abandoned mainly because it:
o: Required the use of allograft tendon
Moved the tubercle anteriorly, causing skin necrosis
Could only be performed in children
Moved the tubercle posteromedially, raising patellofemoral pressure and causing arthritis
items.e: Hauser transfer posteriorised as well as medialised the tubercle, increasing patellofemoral joint reaction force and causing a high rate of patellofemoral arthritis.

items.q: An 11-year-old with open physes and recurrent lateral patellar dislocation needs a distal realignment. Which procedure avoids the tibial tubercle apophysis?
o: Roux-Goldthwait transfer of the lateral half of the patellar tendon
items.e: The Roux-Goldthwait procedure transfers the lateral half of the patellar tendon medially without disturbing the tubercle apophysis, so it can be used in children.

items.q: A tibial tubercle osteotomy performed before closure of the proximal tibial physis risks which deformity?
items.e: Damage to the anterior part of the proximal tibial physis (tubercle apophysis) causes anterior growth arrest with progressive recurvatum, so osteotomy is contraindicated with open physes.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman has recurrent lateral patellar dislocation. Long-leg standing films show 9 degrees of mechanical valgus; TT-TG is 14 mm and the trochlea is mildly dysplastic. Besides MPFL reconstruction, which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: Genu valgum beyond about 5 degrees increases the lateral vector on the patella; a distal femoral varus osteotomy corrects it at its usual site. TT-TG is normal, so medialisation is not indicated.

items.q: A 6-year-old child's patella dislocates laterally every time the knee is flexed and relocates on extension. The child received repeated thigh injections in infancy. The underlying cause is:
o: Contracture of the vastus lateralis and iliotibial band
items.e: Habitual (obligatory) dislocation is due to a shortened quadriceps, usually the vastus lateralis or iliotibial band, sometimes after intramuscular injections; treatment is quadriceps lengthening with realignment.

items.q: A child with an irreducible congenital patellar dislocation also has dysplastic fingernails, iliac horns on the pelvic radiograph and proteinuria. The gene involved is:
items.e: Nail-patella syndrome (hereditary onycho-osteodysplasia) is due to LMX1B mutation and features hypoplastic or absent patellae, nail dysplasia, iliac horns and nephropathy.

items.q: For a 24-year-old with patellofemoral pain syndrome and no instability, which intervention has the best evidence as first-line treatment?
o: Hip abductor/external rotator and quadriceps strengthening
items.e: Patellofemoral pain is a diagnosis of exclusion managed with exercise therapy; combined hip and knee strengthening has the best evidence, and surgery has no role.

items.q: In Coughlin's radiographic classification of bunionette (tailor's bunion) deformity, type 2 is characterised by:
o: Lateral bowing of the distal fifth metatarsal diaphysis
An enlarged fifth metatarsal head or lateral condyle
An increased fourth–fifth intermetatarsal angle with a straight shaft
Degenerative arthritis of the fifth MTP joint
items.e: Type 1 is an enlarged head/lateral exostosis, type 2 lateral bowing of the distal shaft and type 3 a widened 4-5 intermetatarsal angle; the type guides whether a distal or a more proximal fifth metatarsal osteotomy is needed.

items.q: The hallux valgus interphalangeus angle, measured between the long axes of the proximal and distal phalanges, is normally less than about:
items.e: An interphalangeal angle above about 10° indicates hallux valgus interphalangeus, which is corrected with an Akin osteotomy of the proximal phalanx rather than by metatarsal surgery.

items.q: A 45-year-old has recurrent forefoot pain after a dorsal-approach excision of a third web-space Morton neuroma; a stump neuroma is suspected. Many surgeons prefer which approach for the revision neurectomy?
o: Repeat dorsal incision with release of the deep transverse metatarsal ligament only
Medial hindfoot incision for tarsal tunnel release
Plantar longitudinal incision between the metatarsal heads
Percutaneous radiofrequency ablation through the first web space
items.e: A plantar approach gives direct access to the retracted stump, which lies plantar and proximal to the metatarsal heads, allowing resection well proximal to the weight-bearing area; dorsal re-exploration through scar is more difficult.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman has advanced Freiberg disease of the second metatarsal head with collapse of the dorsal articular surface but preserved plantar cartilage. Which joint-preserving operation is most appropriate?
o: Excision of the base of the proximal phalanx
Dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy of the metatarsal head (Gauthier)
items.e: Freiberg necrosis mainly affects the dorsal head; a dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy rotates the healthy plantar cartilage up into the articulation. Lesser MTP arthrodesis is poorly tolerated and phalangeal base excision destabilises the toe.

items.q: In Coughlin's anatomical grading of lesser MTP plantar plate tears, grade 4 refers to:
o: An extensive tear with a buttonhole defect, usually with MTP dislocation
Attenuation or discolouration of the plate without a tear
A transverse distal tear involving less than 50% of the plate
A medial or lateral tear involving less than 50% of the plate
items.e: Grades run from 0 (attenuation) through 1-2 (transverse distal tears below or above 50%) and 3 (extensive transverse/longitudinal tear) to 4, an extensive buttonhole tear typically with dislocation, where repair is less predictable.

items.q: In the 'paper pull-out' test of a lesser toe, the patient is unable to grip a strip of paper beneath the toe against a gentle pull. This indicates:
o: Loss of toe purchase from plantar plate insufficiency
items.e: The plantar plate and intrinsics provide toe purchase; inability to resist withdrawal of a paper strip is a simple sign of plantar plate failure at the MTP joint.

items.q: A child has a congenital overlapping fifth toe that is dorsiflexed, adducted and externally rotated over the fourth toe and is causing shoe pain. The classic soft-tissue correction is:
o: Hibbs transfer of EDL to the cuneiform
Butler procedure through a double racquet incision
Akin osteotomy of the proximal phalanx
items.e: Butler's operation uses a dorsal and plantar racquet incision to release the dorsomedial contracture and reposition the toe; Girdlestone-Taylor transfer is used for flexible claw/hammer toes.

items.q: For first MTP arthrodesis, the recommended position of the hallux in the transverse (coronal) plane is approximately:
items.e: About 10-15° of valgus with neutral rotation keeps the hallux clear of the second toe and matches shoe wear; varus causes IP and shoe problems and excessive valgus impinges on the second toe.

items.q: During a modified Lapidus (first tarsometatarsal) arthrodesis, the first metatarsal should be fixed in:
items.e: Joint preparation shortens and tends to elevate the first ray; fixing it in slight plantarflexion avoids elevatus and transfer metatarsalgia under the lesser metatarsal heads.

items.q: The Mitchell osteotomy for hallux valgus is a distal step-cut osteotomy of the first metatarsal. Its characteristic drawback is:
o: High rate of avascular necrosis of the medial cuneiform
Shortening of the first metatarsal causing transfer metatarsalgia
Inability to correct any intermetatarsal angle
Routine need for first MTP fusion
items.e: The Mitchell step-cut deliberately shortens the first metatarsal while shifting the head laterally; excessive shortening or dorsal displacement overloads the lesser metatarsal heads.

items.q: A young woman has hallux valgus with a congruent first MTP joint and a distal metatarsal articular angle of 18°. The Reverdin procedure addresses this by:
o: Lateral soft-tissue release of the adductor hallucis
A medial closing-wedge osteotomy in the distal metatarsal that realigns the articular surface
items.e: Reverdin-type distal metatarsal osteotomies reorient an increased DMAA; lateral soft-tissue release in a congruent joint with high DMAA would make the joint incongruent.

items.q: A soft corn (heloma molle) of the lesser toes most commonly forms in the:
o: Plantar aspect of the fifth metatarsal head
Fourth web space between the fourth and fifth toes
items.e: Soft corns form where adjacent bony condyles press toe against toe and moisture macerates the keratosis, typically in the fourth web space; hard corns form on exposed dorsal or lateral surfaces.

items.q: A hard corn (heloma durum) of the fifth toe typically lies over:
o: The dorsolateral aspect of the head of the proximal phalanx (PIP joint)
The tip of the distal phalanx
The base of the fifth metatarsal
items.e: Shoe pressure on the prominent lateral condyle at the fifth toe PIP joint causes the dorsolateral hard corn; treatment is shoe modification or condylectomy.

items.q: Joplin neuroma is a perineural fibrosis of the:
o: Common digital nerve of the third web space
Medial plantar proper digital nerve of the hallux
Superficial peroneal nerve at the ankle
Sural nerve at the fifth metatarsal base
items.e: Joplin neuroma involves the plantar-medial digital nerve of the great toe, typically from shoe pressure or previous bunion surgery; Morton neuroma involves the common digital nerve, usually of the third web space.

items.q: Congenital brachymetatarsia most commonly affects the:
items.e: Brachymetatarsia from premature physeal closure most often involves the fourth metatarsal, is commoner in females and is frequently bilateral.

items.q: When lengthening a short fourth metatarsal by gradual distraction (callotasis), complications such as MTP stiffness and subluxation increase if the gain exceeds roughly:
items.e: Lengthening beyond about 40% of the original length is associated with MTP stiffness, subluxation and poor regenerate; one-stage grafting is limited to smaller gains.

items.q: Dudley Morton described a forefoot that overloads the second metatarsal head because of:
o: A tight plantar fascia with hindfoot varus
items.e: Morton's foot is a congenitally short first metatarsal (often hypermobile), which shifts load to the second metatarsal head; it is distinct from Morton's interdigital neuroma.

items.q: Which radiographic view best shows the position of the sesamoids relative to the metatarsal crista and the pronation of the first metatarsal head?
items.e: The tangential sesamoid view looks along the plantar metatarsal head and shows sesamoid subluxation off the crista and head pronation; Broden and Harris views assess the subtalar joint and calcaneus.

items.q: In the lateral (distal) soft-tissue release of a modified McBride procedure, the key tendon released from the fibular sesamoid and lateral base of the proximal phalanx is the:
items.e: The oblique and transverse heads of adductor hallucis insert as a conjoined tendon on the fibular sesamoid and proximal phalanx and are a major deforming force; FHL and EHL are preserved.

items.q: The tendon running between the two sesamoids of the hallux, beneath the intersesamoid ligament, is the:
items.e: The sesamoids lie within the two heads of flexor hallucis brevis, and FHL runs in the groove between them; peroneus longus inserts more proximally on the first metatarsal base.

items.q: Excision of the tibial (medial) sesamoid alone for intractable sesamoid pain particularly predisposes to:
items.e: Removing the tibial sesamoid weakens the medial flexor hallucis brevis and capsule so the hallux drifts into valgus; isolated fibular sesamoid excision risks hallux varus.

items.q: In Smillie's staging of Freiberg infraction, stage V is characterised by:
o: A fissure fracture in the ischaemic epiphysis
Flattening and deformity of the metatarsal head with degenerative arthrosis
Central depression of the articular surface
A loose body formed from the separated fragment
items.e: Smillie stages progress from a fissure fracture (I) to central depression (II-III), separated loose body (IV) and finally flattening with arthrosis (V).

items.q: Approximately how much first MTP dorsiflexion is needed for normal walking?
items.e: Normal gait requires roughly 60° of hallux dorsiflexion at push-off; loss of this in hallux rigidus causes pain and a supinated, laterally loaded gait.

items.q: One explanation for the predilection of Morton neuroma for the third web space is that the common digital nerve here:
o: Runs dorsal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament
Is supplied only by the deep peroneal nerve
Receives a communicating branch from the lateral plantar nerve, making it thicker
items.e: The third common digital nerve is often joined by a branch of the lateral plantar nerve and is tethered between the more mobile fourth and fixed third rays; it lies plantar to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament.

items.q: In a longstanding claw toe, metatarsalgia develops partly because the plantar fat pad:
o: Is pulled distally by the hyperextended proximal phalanx, uncovering the metatarsal head
items.e: MTP hyperextension drags the plantar plate and fat pad distally so the metatarsal head is pushed plantarward with less cushioning, causing plantar callosity and pain.

items.q: When planning surgery for adolescent hallux valgus, it is relevant that the physis of the first metatarsal lies:
o: At its distal head, like the lesser metatarsals
At its proximal base, unlike the lesser metatarsals whose physes are distal
At both ends of the bone
items.e: The first metatarsal (like the phalanges) has a proximal physis, so proximal osteotomies or basal hemiepiphysiodesis must respect it; the lesser metatarsal physes are at the heads.

items.q: In foot anatomy, the 'first ray' consists of:
o: The navicular and medial cuneiform only
The first metatarsal and hallux phalanges only
The medial cuneiform and first metatarsal
The talus, navicular and first metatarsal
items.e: The first ray is the functional unit of the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal; first ray hypermobility refers to excess motion at the first tarsometatarsal joint.

items.q: A 25-year-old with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy has a painful, progressive hallux valgus. The most reliable surgical option is:
o: Distal chevron osteotomy with lateral release
items.e: In spastic neuromuscular hallux valgus, muscle imbalance makes osteotomies and soft-tissue repairs recur; first MTP arthrodesis gives durable correction.

items.q: During arthroscopic femoral osteochondroplasty for cam FAI, resection at the posterosuperior (about 12 o'clock and posterior) head–neck junction is avoided mainly to protect the:
o: Retinacular (lateral epiphyseal) branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery
items.e: The lateral epiphyseal vessels from the deep branch of the MFCA run in the posterosuperior retinaculum. Damaging them risks avascular necrosis of the head.

items.q: In Ganz surgical hip dislocation, the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery is preserved mainly by:
o: Detaching the short external rotators from the greater trochanter
A posterior approach splitting gluteus maximus with release of quadratus femoris
A trochanteric flip osteotomy, staying anterior to the short external rotators, with the intact obturator externus protecting the vessel
Dividing the ligamentum teres before dislocating the head anteriorly
items.e: The trochanteric flip leaves the short external rotators intact. The deep MFCA branch passes posterior to obturator externus, which shields it during anterior dislocation.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman has symptomatic global acetabular overcoverage with protrusio acetabuli and a cam lesion that extends posteriorly. The most suitable procedure is:
o: Open surgical hip dislocation (Ganz) with rim trimming and osteochondroplasty
items.e: Global overcoverage and posterior deformities are hard to reach arthroscopically. Surgical dislocation gives 360° access to the rim and head–neck junction.

items.q: Which oral prophylaxis is commonly used after arthroscopic femoral osteochondroplasty to reduce heterotopic ossification?
o: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as naproxen
items.e: NSAID prophylaxis (e.g. naproxen for a few weeks) reduces heterotopic ossification after femoroplasty.

items.q: Shortly after a prolonged hip arthroscopy that included an iliopsoas tenotomy, the patient becomes hypotensive with a tense, distended abdomen. The most likely cause is:
o: Femoral artery injury from the anterior portal
Intra-abdominal fluid extravasation causing abdominal compartment syndrome
items.e: Arthroscopy fluid can track along the psoas into the retroperitoneum and abdomen. Risk factors include iliopsoas release, high pump pressure and long surgery.

items.q: The most common reason for revision hip arthroscopy after surgery for femoroacetabular impingement is:
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Residual impingement from under-resection of the deformity
items.e: Inadequate correction of cam or pincer morphology is the most frequent cause of persistent symptoms and revision.

items.q: Excessive acetabular rim resection during arthroscopic treatment of pincer FAI may lead to:
o: Heterotopic ossification of the ligamentum teres
Iatrogenic instability or dislocation from reduced coverage
items.e: Over-resecting the rim converts the hip towards dysplasia and can cause subluxation or dislocation, especially if the capsule is not repaired.

items.q: At hip arthroscopy, a 26-year-old has a 1.5 cm² well-contained full-thickness chondral defect of the anterosuperior acetabulum with a normal joint space. A commonly used treatment is:
items.e: Small, contained full-thickness acetabular lesions in young patients are commonly treated with microfracture.

items.q: Tears of the ligamentum teres found at hip arthroscopy are particularly associated with:
o: Hip instability, including dysplasia and capsular laxity
items.e: The ligamentum teres acts as a secondary stabiliser. Tears are common in unstable, dysplastic or hyperlax hips.

items.q: At hip arthroscopy, numerous small, uniform, smooth cartilaginous loose bodies are found with synovial proliferation. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral head
items.e: Synovial chondromatosis produces many similar-sized cartilaginous bodies from metaplastic synovium. Treatment is removal with synovectomy, which arthroscopy can achieve.

items.q: A 66-year-old woman has lateral hip pain and a Trendelenburg gait after 6 months of physiotherapy. MRI shows a full-thickness tear of the gluteus medius tendon from the greater trochanter with little fatty atrophy. The best treatment is:
o: Endoscopic or open repair of the gluteus medius tendon to the greater trochanter
items.e: Gluteus medius and minimus form the 'rotator cuff of the hip'. A full-thickness tear with poor function after conservative care is repaired endoscopically or open.

items.q: In the LEAP randomised trial of gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome), which intervention gave the best outcomes?
o: Education with a progressive loading exercise programme
items.e: LEAP (Mellor, BMJ 2018) found education plus loading exercise superior to corticosteroid injection and to wait-and-see at 8 weeks.

items.q: A 40-year-old has deep buttock pain radiating down the posterior thigh, worse on sitting, with normal lumbar MRI. MRI of the pelvis shows fibrous bands around the sciatic nerve near the piriformis. The condition and treatment are:
o: Ischiofemoral impingement, treated by lesser trochanter resection
Deep gluteal syndrome, treated by endoscopic sciatic nerve decompression if conservative care fails
Proximal hamstring avulsion, treated by repair
Greater trochanteric pain syndrome, treated by ITB release
items.e: Deep gluteal syndrome is entrapment of the sciatic nerve in the subgluteal space by piriformis or fibrous bands. Endoscopic release is used for refractory cases.

items.q: The Doha agreement (2014) classifies groin pain in athletes into defined clinical entities according to:
o: Duration of symptoms: acute, subacute and chronic
Imaging appearance on MRI: grades 1 to 4
Anatomical source: adductor-, iliopsoas-, inguinal- and pubic-related groin pain
Type of sport: kicking, running and contact
items.e: The Doha agreement defines adductor-, iliopsoas-, inguinal- and pubic-related groin pain, plus hip-related and other causes.

items.q: A 24-year-old female marathon runner has groin pain. MRI shows a stress fracture on the superolateral (tension) side of the femoral neck. The correct management is:
o: Protected weight bearing with crutches for 6 weeks
Activity modification and calcium/vitamin D only
items.e: Tension-side femoral neck stress fractures are prone to displacement and AVN, so they are fixed urgently. The athlete should also be assessed for RED-S.

items.q: A runner has a compression-side (inferomedial) femoral neck stress fracture. Internal fixation rather than protected weight bearing is indicated when the fracture line on MRI involves more than about:
items.e: Compression-side fractures are usually managed with protected weight bearing, but fixation is advised when the fracture extends beyond about half the neck width or when displacement develops.

items.q: A dancer has a visible, painful snapping over the lateral hip that has not responded to 6 months of stretching and injections. The usual surgical treatment is:
o: Fractional lengthening of the iliopsoas tendon
Release or Z-lengthening of the posterior iliotibial band over the greater trochanter
items.e: External snapping hip is caused by the posterior iliotibial band or gluteus maximus catching on the greater trochanter. Refractory cases are treated by ITB release or Z-plasty.

items.q: After arthroscopic release of the iliopsoas tendon for painful internal snapping hip, the most expected postoperative effect is:
items.e: Iliopsoas tenotomy commonly causes transient hip flexion weakness, which usually recovers over a few months.

items.q: A 21-year-old woman with hip pain has a lateral centre-edge angle of 14°, a Tönnis angle of 16° and a preserved joint space. The most appropriate surgical procedure is:
items.e: This is frank acetabular dysplasia. PAO reorients the acetabulum to restore coverage; isolated arthroscopic surgery may worsen instability.

items.q: A 19-year-old with posterior hip pain, increased internal rotation and a sense of instability has femoral anteversion of 40° and normal acetabular coverage. If conservative treatment fails, the procedure that addresses the underlying abnormality is:
items.e: Excessive femoral anteversion causes posterior impingement and anterior instability rather than classic anterior impingement. A derotation osteotomy corrects the version.

items.q: Radiographs of a 48-year-old woman with long-standing pincer impingement show a separate bony fragment at the anterosuperior acetabular rim. This most often represents:
o: An avulsion of the rectus femoris reflected head
Ossification of the degenerate acetabular labrum
items.e: Chronic labral crushing in pincer FAI can lead to labral ossification or rim fragments (os acetabuli), which further deepen the socket.

items.q: The term 'pistol-grip deformity' of the proximal femur, now recognised as a cam morphology, was originally attributed to:
o: A subclinical slipped capital femoral epiphysis
items.e: Stulberg described the pistol-grip deformity and attributed it to a silent SCFE. It is now regarded as cam morphology, often caused by loading of the growing physis in sport.

items.q: The investigation of choice to show an acetabular labral tear in a young adult with suspected FAI is:
o: Plain radiography with a Dunn view
items.e: Gadolinium MR arthrography (or high-resolution 3T MRI) best demonstrates labral tears and chondral damage. Plain films show bony morphology but not the labrum.

items.q: A 30-year-old has an acutely painful, hot, swollen hip; aspiration shows pus with Gram-positive cocci, and radiographs are normal. Which surgical option is accepted for joint debridement?
o: Arthroscopic washout and debridement of the hip
items.e: Arthroscopic lavage and debridement is an effective, less invasive alternative to open arthrotomy for native-hip septic arthritis, combined with antibiotics.

items.q: Arthroscopic or open synovectomy of the hip is the mainstay of treatment for which condition?
o: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (pigmented villonodular synovitis)
items.e: Diffuse TGCT (PVNS) is treated by thorough synovectomy, which can be done arthroscopically or open depending on extent.

items.q: Post-less distraction techniques for hip arthroscopy were developed mainly to avoid:
o: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury from the anterior portal
Pudendal nerve injury and perineal soft-tissue damage
items.e: A perineal post acts as a fulcrum for traction and can compress the pudendal nerve and the perineal skin. Post-less systems use friction on the table instead.

items.q: On an AP pelvic radiograph, the floor of the acetabular fossa touches the ilioischial line while the femoral head remains lateral to it. This appearance is called:
items.e: Coxa profunda describes a deep fossa reaching the ilioischial line. If the femoral head itself is medial to the line, it is protrusio. Coxa profunda is now regarded as a weak marker of overcoverage.

items.q: Which structure can be inspected only in the central compartment of the hip, under traction?
items.e: The central compartment (within the labrum) contains the ligamentum teres, acetabular fossa and articular surfaces. The head–neck junction, synovial folds and zona orbicularis are peripheral.

items.q: In the Seldes classification of acetabular labral tears, a type 1 tear is:
o: One or more cleavage planes within the substance of the labrum
A detachment of the labrum from the articular cartilage at the chondrolabral junction
A complete ossification of the labrum
A radial flap tear of the free edge of the labrum
items.e: Seldes type 1 is a separation at the chondrolabral transition zone (typical of cam FAI). Type 2 is an intrasubstance cleavage tear.

items.q: In cam-type femoroacetabular impingement, the cam lesion is most commonly located at the:
o: Inferomedial femoral neck near the lesser trochanter
items.e: The cam bump usually lies anterosuperiorly (about 12 to 3 o'clock), which is why it impinges in flexion and internal rotation.

items.q: A 27-year-old has pincer symptoms. AP pelvis shows a crossover sign plus a positive posterior wall sign, and CT confirms global acetabular retroversion with posterior wall deficiency. The preferred treatment is:
items.e: Trimming the anterior rim in true retroversion would worsen the already deficient posterior coverage. A reverse PAO reorients the acetabulum into anteversion.

items.q: A femoral head extrusion index above about 25% on an AP pelvis indicates:
o: Lateral undercoverage of the femoral head
items.e: The extrusion index is the proportion of the head lying lateral to the acetabular roof. Values above about 25% mean the head is uncovered, as in dysplasia.

items.q: Before applying traction for hip arthroscopy, the joint is often vented with a spinal needle under fluoroscopy. This makes distraction easier because it:
o: Breaks the negative intra-articular pressure of the labral suction seal
items.e: Introducing air or fluid releases the suction seal, so less traction force is needed to distract the head from the acetabulum.

items.q: In cam-type femoroacetabular impingement, the characteristic mechanism of chondral damage is:
o: Linear crushing of the labrum between the neck and an overcovering rim
Inside-out pressure from a deep acetabular fossa
An 'outside-in' shear as the aspherical head is forced into the socket, separating cartilage from the labrum
Repetitive traction injury of the ligamentum teres
items.e: The cam is jammed under the labrum in flexion, shearing the anterosuperior cartilage from the subchondral bone and causing chondrolabral separation. Labral crushing is the pincer mechanism.

items.q: At revision THA the cup has migrated more than 3 cm superolaterally ('up and out'), Köhler's line is intact, ischial and teardrop lysis are moderate and about 40% of the superolateral rim is deficient. The usual reconstruction is:
o: Large hemispherical porous cup with a porous metal augment filling the superolateral defect
Cemented cup on impaction graft alone
Antiprotrusio cage without a porous cup
items.e: This is a Paprosky IIIA defect: the columns still give partial support, so a jumbo porous cup with a trabecular metal augment (or structural graft) for the superolateral segment is standard. Triflanges and cages are reserved for IIIB defects and pelvic discontinuity.

items.q: In the AORI classification of bone loss at revision TKA, a type 2B femoral defect means:
o: Intact metaphysis with only small contained defects
Damaged metaphyseal bone involving one condyle
Damaged metaphyseal bone involving both condyles
Deficient metaphysis with detachment of a collateral ligament
items.e: AORI 2 means damaged metaphyseal cancellous bone: 2A affects one condyle or plateau, 2B both. Type 1 has an intact metaphysis and type 3 a deficient metaphysis, often with collateral or tendon detachment.

items.q: At revision TKA the metaphysis is intact and the only defects are small, contained and a few millimetres deep (AORI type 1). They are usually managed with:
o: Cement (with or without screws) or particulate graft and standard components
items.e: AORI 1 defects do not compromise component stability and are filled with cement, screws-and-cement or morsellised graft. Cones, sleeves and replacement prostheses are for type 2B and 3 metaphyseal loss.

items.q: Three years after an uncemented THA a 66-year-old has new groin pain and a possibly loose cup on radiographs. Before planning revision, the first investigation should be:
o: CT scan to measure acetabular version
Serum ESR and CRP, followed by aspiration if raised or suspicion is high
items.e: Every failing arthroplasty is presumed infected until proved otherwise, and ESR and CRP are the recommended screening tests, with aspiration when they are raised or clinical suspicion is high. A bone scan cannot distinguish septic from aseptic loosening.

items.q: Loosening of the acetabular component after THA typically presents with pain in the:
o: Lateral thigh on lying on that side
items.e: Acetabular loosening classically causes groin or buttock pain, whereas start-up mid-thigh pain suggests femoral stem loosening. Pain on lying on the side suggests trochanteric bursitis.

items.q: On the AP pelvis before revision THA, which finding most strongly suggests chronic pelvic discontinuity?
o: Superolateral cup migration of under 3 cm with an intact teardrop
A fracture line through both columns with medial translation of the inferior hemipelvis relative to the superior hemipelvis
Isolated lysis in DeLee-Charnley zone I
items.e: Pelvic discontinuity is separation of the superior and inferior hemipelvis through the acetabulum; signs include a visible fracture line through both columns, a broken Köhler line and medial shift or rotation of the inferior hemipelvis (obturator ring asymmetry).

items.q: When removing a cement mantle at revision THA with an ultrasonic cement-removal device, the specific hazard to guard against is:
o: Thermal injury to bone and nearby soft tissues, including nerves
Metallosis from shedding of the device tip
Galvanic corrosion of the new stem
items.e: Ultrasonic devices soften cement by generating heat, so continuous irrigation and short bursts are needed to avoid thermal necrosis of bone and thermal nerve injury; cortical perforation is the other recognised risk.

items.q: During femoral revision a cortical perforation occurs in the diaphysis. The new stem should bypass the perforation by at least about:
o: The length of the femoral head
Two cortical (outer) diameters of the femur
items.e: A cortical window or perforation is a stress riser; standard teaching is to bypass it by at least two femoral cortical diameters (and graft it) to reduce the risk of fracture.

items.q: At revision TKA, the extension gap is balanced but the flexion gap is loose. The correct way to address this is to:
o: Increase the femoral component size, using posterior condylar augments or an offset stem
items.e: Femoral size and posterior position affect only the flexion gap, so upsizing (with posterior augments or offset) tightens flexion alone. A thicker insert tightens both gaps and would make extension tight.

items.q: At revision TKA, the flexion gap is balanced but the extension gap is loose because of distal femoral bone loss. The appropriate correction is:
o: Distal femoral augments to bring the component distally
Further resection of the proximal tibia
items.e: Distal femoral augments affect only the extension gap and restore the joint line. A thicker insert would tighten flexion too and raise the joint line; upsizing affects only flexion.

items.q: Monoblock tapered titanium revision stems of the Wagner type achieve rotational stability mainly through:
o: A cement mantle in the diaphysis
Longitudinal ribs (flutes) that cut into the endosteal cortex
items.e: Wagner-type stems have a conical taper (about 2 degrees) for axial stability and longitudinal ribs that engage the diaphyseal cortex to resist rotation; they are uncemented and do not use locking screws.

items.q: Femoral impaction bone grafting with a cemented polished tapered stem (Exeter technique) for revision THA is particularly associated with:
o: Fatigue fracture at a modular junction
Stem subsidence and periprosthetic femoral fracture
Pedestal formation at the stem tip
items.e: The best-recognised problems of femoral impaction grafting are excessive subsidence of the stem within the graft and intra- or postoperative femoral fracture, especially when the cortices are thin.

items.q: A painful TKA has instability. Isolated exchange of the tibial polyethylene insert is most likely to succeed when:
o: The femoral component is internally rotated by 8 degrees
There is flexion-extension gap mismatch from a malpositioned femoral component
Components are well fixed, correctly aligned and rotated and the problem is insert wear or a correctable gap
The medial collateral ligament is incompetent
items.e: Isolated insert exchange for instability has a high failure rate unless the components are well positioned and well fixed; malrotation, gap mismatch from malposition and ligament incompetence need component revision and often more constraint.

items.q: After THA a patient has groin pain on active straight-leg raising and resisted hip flexion. CT shows the anterior rim of the cup overhanging the anterior acetabular wall. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Aseptic loosening of the femoral stem
items.e: An anteriorly prominent or retroverted cup can impinge on the iliopsoas tendon, causing groin pain on resisted flexion; treatment is cup revision when overhang is marked, or iliopsoas tenotomy.

items.q: In pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, which of Kanavel's signs is considered the earliest and most sensitive?
o: Pain on passive extension of the digit
Fusiform swelling of the whole digit
items.e: Pain along the sheath on passive extension appears early and is the most sensitive of Kanavel's four signs; the others are semiflexed posture, fusiform swelling and sheath tenderness.

items.q: After drainage of a hand infection the hand is splinted in the 'safe' (intrinsic-plus) position. This is:
o: Wrist neutral, MCP joints extended, IP joints flexed 90 degrees
Wrist extended about 30 degrees, MCP joints flexed 70-90 degrees, IP joints fully extended
Wrist flexed 30 degrees, MCP and IP joints all extended
Wrist extended 30 degrees, all finger joints flexed 90 degrees
items.e: The safe position keeps the MCP collateral ligaments and IP volar plates at length, preventing extension contracture of the MCPs and flexion contracture of the IPs.

items.q: Why are the MCP joints splinted in 70-90 degrees of flexion during treatment of a hand infection?
o: The MCP collateral ligaments are at their longest in flexion, so they cannot shorten
It relaxes the flexor tendons and prevents adhesions
It closes the deep palmar spaces and limits spread
It relieves pressure on the digital nerves
items.e: The cam-shaped metacarpal head makes the collateral ligaments taut in flexion; immobilising them stretched avoids an MCP extension contracture.

items.q: A patient with a pus collection in the palm has the most visible swelling on the dorsum of the hand. This is because:
o: The infection has tracked through the interosseous membrane
Palmar pus always spreads dorsally through the web spaces
Lymphatic drainage of the palm runs to the dorsum, where the skin is loose
items.e: Lymphatics drain from the palm to the dorsum and the loose dorsal skin swells readily, so dorsal oedema occurs even when the infection is palmar; the dorsum should not be incised for this.

items.q: A 30-year-old has an acute paronychia with pus visible beneath the nail plate (subungual abscess). The appropriate treatment is:
o: Oral antibiotics and warm soaks alone
Elevation of the nail fold with removal of the overlying part of the nail plate
items.e: When pus has tracked under the nail, the involved part of the nail plate must be removed to drain it; soaks and antibiotics alone are for early cellulitis, and marsupialisation is for chronic paronychia.

items.q: A 'run-around' infection of the finger refers to:
o: Flexor tenosynovitis spreading to the radial and ulnar bursae
Cellulitis encircling the whole digit at the base
A felon extending into the DIP joint
Paronychia spreading around the eponychium to involve both lateral nail folds
items.e: A run-around infection is a paronychia that spreads from one lateral fold across the eponychium to the other side, encircling the nail.

items.q: A 68-year-old has a 'chronic paronychia' of the thumb for 8 months with a longitudinal brown streak in the nail and nail-fold destruction despite antifungals. The next step is:
o: A longer course of oral antifungal treatment
Partial nail plate removal and topical steroid
Biopsy of the nail bed and fold
items.e: A persistent unexplained paronychia, especially with pigmentation, must be biopsied to exclude subungual melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma before any further 'infection' treatment.

items.q: A felon of the thumb is to be drained through a high mid-axial incision. On which side of the thumb should it be placed?
items.e: Mid-axial felon incisions are placed on the non-contact side: radial for the thumb and little finger, ulnar for the index, middle and ring fingers, to keep the scar away from pinch surfaces.

items.q: Which incision for a felon should be avoided because it leaves a painful scar and an unstable pulp?
o: Volar longitudinal incision over the point of maximal fluctuance
High lateral incision on the non-contact side
Short mid-axial incision dividing the septa
items.e: Fish-mouth and through-and-through incisions devascularise the pulp and leave a painful, unstable tip; a mid-axial or volar longitudinal incision is preferred.

items.q: The pressure complications of a felon (pulp necrosis, osteomyelitis of the distal phalanx) occur because the pulp is:
o: Continuous with the flexor tendon sheath
Drained only by the dorsal veins
Divided into closed compartments by fibrous septa running from skin to the periosteum
items.e: Vertical septa anchor the pulp skin to the distal phalanx and create closed compartments; swelling raises pressure, causing necrosis, osteomyelitis, septic DIP joint or sheath infection.

items.q: When draining a felon, the incision should be kept distal to the DIP flexion crease mainly to avoid:
items.e: The flexor sheath ends just proximal to the distal pulp; extending the incision proximal to the DIP crease risks contaminating the sheath and causing flexor tenosynovitis.

items.q: A dental hygienist has burning pain in the index fingertip followed by clusters of clear vesicles on a red base; the pulp is not tense. Management is:
o: Protective dressing, with oral aciclovir if seen within 48-72 hours; no incision
Urgent incision and drainage of the pulp
Unroofing of the vesicles and topical antibiotics
items.e: This is herpetic whitlow, which is self-limiting over about 3 weeks. Incision is contraindicated because it can cause secondary bacterial infection and viraemia.

items.q: A Tzanck smear of the fluid from a fingertip vesicle in suspected herpetic whitlow would show:
items.e: Multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear support herpes simplex infection; PCR or viral culture confirms it.

items.q: A 3-year-old with herpetic gingivostomatitis develops painful vesicles on the thumb. The most likely mode of infection is:
items.e: Herpetic whitlow in children typically follows autoinoculation from oral HSV lesions by thumb or finger sucking; in adults it is classically an occupational infection of healthcare workers.

items.q: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has fever, migratory polyarthralgia, a few pustules on the limbs and tenosynovitis over the dorsum of the wrist. The likely organism and treatment are:
items.e: This is the disseminated gonococcal infection triad of polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustular dermatitis; a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is the treatment.

items.q: For closed catheter irrigation (Neviaser technique) of a finger flexor sheath infection, the two incisions are made:
o: At the A2 and A4 pulleys over the proximal and middle phalanges
Over the radial bursa at the wrist and at the A1 pulley
On both mid-axial lines of the proximal phalanx
Proximally at the A1 pulley in the palm and distally at the A5 pulley/DIP crease level
items.e: A proximal palmar incision opens the sheath at the A1 pulley for the catheter and a distal mid-axial incision near the A5 pulley lets the irrigant out, limiting exposure while flushing the whole sheath.

items.q: Flexor tenosynovitis of the little finger is likely to spread into the:
o: Midpalmar space only through the lumbrical canal
items.e: The little finger sheath is usually continuous with the ulnar bursa, and the thumb sheath with the radial bursa; the index, middle and ring sheaths usually end at the A1 pulley.

items.q: A patient presents 18 hours after a puncture wound with only some of Kanavel's signs, mild swelling and no systemic upset. Reasonable initial management is:
o: Immediate open debridement through Bruner incisions
IV antibiotics, splinting and elevation, with review in 12-24 hours and drainage if not improving
Oral antibiotics and outpatient review in a week
items.e: Very early, equivocal flexor sheath infection can respond to IV antibiotics, splintage and elevation, but it must be reassessed within 12-24 hours and drained if it does not improve.

items.q: The commonest complication after treatment of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis is:
items.e: Adhesions and stiffness are the most frequent sequelae; tendon necrosis, rupture and amputation are less common and associated with diabetes, vascular disease and late presentation.

items.q: In Pang's classification of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, the group with the highest amputation rate is characterised by:
o: No subcutaneous purulence and no risk factors
Digital ischaemia with subcutaneous purulence, often with age over 43, diabetes, vascular disease or renal failure
Isolated Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin
items.e: Pang showed that subcutaneous purulence, digital ischaemia and comorbidity (older age, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, renal failure) predict poor outcome; the group with ischaemia had the highest amputation rate.

items.q: A labourer has a painful hand with loss of the normal palmar concavity, dorsal swelling and pain on moving the middle and ring fingers. The infected space is the:
items.e: Midpalmar space infection lies deep to the flexor tendons of the middle, ring and little fingers and causes loss of palmar concavity; thenar space infection holds the thumb abducted.

items.q: The thenar and midpalmar spaces are separated by:
o: The oblique (midpalmar) septum running from the palmar fascia to the third metacarpal
items.e: A fibrous septum from the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal divides the radial thenar space from the ulnar midpalmar space.

items.q: Infection of the radial and ulnar bursae has spread into Parona's space; the patient now has numbness in the median nerve distribution of the fingers. Drainage should include:
o: Fasciotomy of the dorsal forearm compartment only
Release of the carpal canal (carpal tunnel decompression) with drainage of the distal forearm space
items.e: Parona's space lies between pronator quadratus and FDP; pus there can cause acute carpal tunnel syndrome, so drainage is combined with carpal tunnel release.

items.q: Two days after a punch, a man has a small wound over the dorsum of the fourth MCP joint. Which examination point is most important for finding deep injury?
o: Examine only with the fingers fully extended to relax the extensor
Inspect the wound with the fist clenched, because the extensor tendon and capsule wounds move proximally when the fingers extend
Test grip strength before inspecting the wound
Probe the wound with the hand flat to look for a foreign body
items.e: At the moment of injury the MCP joint was flexed; when the finger is extended the tendon and capsular lacerations slide proximal to the skin wound and are missed, so the injury must be reproduced in the clenched position.

items.q: A fight-bite wound over the third MCP joint has penetrated the joint capsule. The correct management is:
o: Surgical exploration, joint irrigation and debridement, wound left open, and co-amoxiclav
Primary skin closure and oral flucloxacillin
Oral antibiotics and outpatient review in a week
Primary closure of the capsule and skin with a dorsal splint
items.e: Clenched-fist injuries carry mixed oral flora including Eikenella and anaerobes; joint penetration needs formal irrigation and debridement, the wound is not closed primarily, and amoxicillin-clavulanate covers the likely organisms.

items.q: A 50-year-old man who had a splenectomy develops fulminant sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation a day after a dog bite to the hand. The most likely organism is:
items.e: Capnocytophaga canimorsus from dog saliva causes overwhelming sepsis in asplenic patients, alcoholics and the immunocompromised.

items.q: Twelve hours after a cat bite on the finger, a woman has rapidly spreading cellulitis with lymphangitis. The most likely organism is:
items.e: Pasteurella multocida infection after cat or dog bites characteristically appears very quickly, often within 12-24 hours; cat bites are deep punctures and become infected more often than dog bites.

items.q: A penicillin-allergic patient needs empirical oral antibiotics after an infected dog bite to the hand. A suitable combination is:
items.e: Pasteurella is poorly covered by flucloxacillin, cefalexin, clindamycin and erythromycin; in penicillin allergy, doxycycline (or a fluoroquinolone or co-trimoxazole) is combined with anaerobic cover such as metronidazole or clindamycin.

items.q: A pet-shop worker bitten on the hand by a rat develops fever, migratory polyarthritis and a maculopapular rash on the hands and feet. The likely organism is:
items.e: Rat-bite fever is caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis (or Spirillum minus in Asia), with fever, rash and polyarthritis; penicillin is the treatment.

items.q: A child scratched by a kitten has a papule on the hand followed by tender epitrochlear and axillary lymphadenopathy. The causative organism is:
items.e: Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae and produces a primary papule with regional lymphadenopathy, usually self-limiting.

items.q: In India, a stray dog bites through the skin of a man's hand, drawing blood (WHO category III exposure). In addition to tetanus prophylaxis, management is:
o: Rabies vaccine only, if the dog cannot be observed
Wound washing and observation of the dog for 10 days before deciding
Thorough wound washing, rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound and a full course of rabies vaccine
Primary wound closure and rabies immunoglobulin alone
items.e: Category III exposures (transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin) need wound washing, rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound, and the full vaccine course; vaccination is not delayed while the animal is observed.

items.q: A farmer bitten on the hand by a Russell's viper has a tense, swollen forearm. Which statement about fasciotomy is correct?
o: Fasciotomy should be performed routinely in all viper bites with swelling
Fasciotomy is the first-line treatment before antivenom
Fasciotomy is contraindicated even with measured high pressure
Fasciotomy is done only if raised compartment pressure is measured despite antivenom, as true compartment syndrome is uncommon
items.e: Snake envenomation often causes dramatic swelling that mimics compartment syndrome; polyvalent antivenom is the mainstay, and fasciotomy is reserved for objectively raised pressures, as coagulopathy makes surgery hazardous.

items.q: The earliest clinical clue that a hand and forearm soft-tissue infection may be necrotising fasciitis is:
o: Pain out of proportion to the visible skin findings
items.e: Severe pain disproportionate to the appearance is the earliest feature; bullae, crepitus, dusky skin and anaesthesia are late signs of established necrosis.

items.q: Type II (monomicrobial) necrotising fasciitis, which may be accompanied by toxic shock, is typically caused by:
items.e: Type I is polymicrobial (commonest, diabetics and drug users), type II is group A streptococcal with or without S. aureus, and type III is caused by Vibrio vulnificus or clostridia.

items.q: A man with liver cirrhosis cuts his hand while cleaning fish and develops rapidly spreading necrotising infection with haemorrhagic bullae and septic shock. The likely organism is:
items.e: Vibrio vulnificus from seawater or seafood causes fulminant necrotising infection, especially in patients with liver disease; M. marinum causes a slow granulomatous infection instead.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the LRINEC score for necrotising fasciitis?
items.e: LRINEC uses CRP, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; lactate is not part of the score.

items.q: A patient with a rapidly spreading forearm infection and severe pain has a LRINEC score of 4. The surgeon is clinically worried about necrotising fasciitis. The best course is:
o: Treat as cellulitis because the score is under 6
Proceed to urgent surgical exploration, as a low LRINEC score does not exclude the diagnosis
Repeat the score in 48 hours before deciding
Order an MRI and wait for the report before any surgery
items.e: LRINEC has poor sensitivity; clinical suspicion takes precedence, and exploration with the finger test is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Delay increases mortality.

items.q: Acute indirect muscle strains in athletes most often occur at the:
items.e: The myotendinous junction is the weak link during eccentric contraction of two-joint muscles, so most strains occur there.

items.q: Regeneration of new myofibres after a muscle injury comes mainly from which cells?
items.e: Satellite cells are the resident muscle stem cells that proliferate and fuse to form new myofibres during the repair phase. Fibroblasts lay down the competing scar.

items.q: In the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC), the suffix 'c' indicates an injury that is:
o: Myofascial, at the periphery of the muscle
A complete rupture of the muscle
Intratendinous, with longer return to play and higher re-injury rate
items.e: BAMIC uses a for myofascial, b for musculotendinous and c for intratendinous injuries; 'c' injuries take longer to return and recur more often.

items.q: A 34-year-old water-skier has a complete proximal hamstring avulsion. Which finding is the usual indication for surgical repair in an active patient?
o: Avulsion of all three tendons, or of two tendons retracted more than 2 cm
A partial tear retracted less than 1 cm
Persistent pain after 12 months of physiotherapy only
items.e: Repair is advised for three-tendon avulsions or two-tendon injuries with more than 2 cm retraction in active patients, ideally within about 4-6 weeks, as early repair gives better results.

items.q: Proximal hamstring avulsion typically results from which mechanism?
o: Forced knee flexion with the hip extended
Forced hip flexion with the knee extended
Direct blow to the posterior thigh
Forced hip abduction with external rotation
items.e: Sudden hip flexion with the knee held straight, as when a water-skier is pulled forward, maximally stretches the hamstrings and avulses them from the ischial tuberosity.

items.q: In the PEACE & LOVE approach to acute soft-tissue injury, the 'A' in PEACE stands for:
items.e: PEACE is Protection, Elevation, Avoid anti-inflammatories, Compression, Education; NSAIDs are avoided early because they may impair tissue healing.

items.q: Delayed-onset muscle soreness after unaccustomed eccentric exercise typically appears:
items.e: DOMS results from eccentric microtrauma and peaks at about 24-72 hours; it is self-limiting and may be accompanied by a raised CK.

items.q: A footballer has a firm thigh mass 4 weeks after a quadriceps contusion. Which imaging feature favours myositis ossificans over a parosteal or extraskeletal osteosarcoma?
o: Mature peripheral ossification with a less mineralised centre
Dense central ossification with an immature periphery
Cortical destruction with a soft-tissue mass
items.e: Myositis ossificans shows zonal maturation, with mature bone at the periphery; osteosarcoma shows the reverse pattern with the densest bone centrally.

items.q: Symptomatic myositis ossificans of the thigh is best excised:
o: Within the first 2 weeks to prevent ossification
After the lesion has matured, usually 6-12 months, when the bone scan is cold
As soon as calcification is seen on radiographs
Never, because excision always causes recurrence
items.e: Excising an immature lesion risks recurrence; surgery is delayed until maturation (about 6-12 months), shown by a cold bone scan and mature radiographic appearance.

items.q: A military recruit collapses with dark urine after an intense training run in heat; CK is 45,000 U/L. Which inherited condition is a recognised risk factor for exertional rhabdomyolysis?
items.e: Sickle cell trait predisposes to exertional rhabdomyolysis and collapse, especially with heat and dehydration.

items.q: The first-line treatment of exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria is:
items.e: Aggressive IV fluids maintain urine output and prevent myoglobin-induced acute kidney injury; NSAIDs are avoided because they add renal risk.

items.q: Normal tendon is composed predominantly of which collagen type?
items.e: Type I collagen forms about 95% of tendon collagen. Type III appears early in healing and type II is the main cartilage collagen.

items.q: During the proliferative phase of tendon healing, the collagen initially laid down is mainly:
items.e: Type III collagen predominates in the proliferative phase and is gradually replaced by type I during remodelling; healed tendon reaches only about 70-80% of normal strength.

items.q: Histology of chronic Achilles tendinopathy typically shows:
o: Dense neutrophil infiltrate in the paratenon
Disorganised collagen, increased ground substance and neovascularisation with few inflammatory cells
Uniform parallel type I collagen with normal cellularity
items.e: Tendinopathy is a failed healing response (tendinosis) rather than inflammation: disorganised collagen, more ground substance and vessels with nerve ingrowth that cause pain.

items.q: In the continuum model of tendinopathy (Cook and Purdam), the three stages are:
o: Acute tendinitis, subacute tendinitis, chronic tendinitis
Reactive tendinopathy, tendon disrepair, degenerative tendinopathy
items.e: Cook and Purdam described reactive tendinopathy, tendon disrepair and degenerative tendinopathy as a continuum that load changes can move a tendon along.

items.q: A 74-year-old on oral prednisolone is prescribed ciprofloxacin. Which tendon is at greatest risk of rupture?
items.e: Fluoroquinolone tendinopathy most often affects the Achilles tendon, with risk increased by age over 60, concurrent corticosteroids and renal impairment.

items.q: The commonest site of stress fracture overall in athletes is the:
items.e: The compression-side posteromedial tibia is the commonest stress fracture site and is low risk; the anterior tibial cortex is a high-risk tension-side site.

items.q: An elite volleyball player has 6 months of anterior shin pain. A lateral radiograph shows a horizontal lucent line in the anterior cortex of the mid-tibia that has not healed despite rest. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: Further 6 weeks of rest in a walking boot
items.e: The 'dreaded black line' is a tension-side high-risk stress fracture prone to non-union and complete fracture; reamed IM nailing is advised when it fails to heal.

items.q: Tarsal navicular stress fractures typically occur in the central third of the bone because this region:
o: Is the site of tibialis posterior insertion
Is covered by the talonavicular capsule
items.e: The central third of the navicular has a relatively poor blood supply and is subject to shear between the talus and cuneiforms, making these fractures high risk.

items.q: A non-displaced navicular stress fracture in an athlete is most reliably treated non-operatively with:
o: Weight-bearing as tolerated in a soft shoe
A short period of rest followed by return to running at 2 weeks
items.e: Strict non-weight-bearing cast immobilisation for 6-8 weeks gives better union than limited weight-bearing; screw fixation is an alternative in elite athletes.

items.q: A professional footballer has a Jones (zone 2) fracture of the proximal fifth metatarsal. Preferred treatment for early return to play is:
o: Hard-soled shoe and weight-bearing as tolerated
items.e: Zone 2-3 fractures lie in a watershed area with high non-union rates; intramedullary screw fixation gives faster, more reliable union in athletes.

items.q: On the Fredericson MRI grading of tibial bone stress injury, grade 1 corresponds to:
o: Marrow oedema on both T1 and T2 images
Periosteal oedema only, without marrow change
items.e: Fredericson grade 1 is periosteal oedema alone; marrow oedema appears in grades 2-3, and grade 4 shows intracortical signal or a fracture line.

items.q: In ballet dancers, a high-risk stress fracture classically occurs at the:
items.e: Dancing en pointe loads the base of the second metatarsal at the Lisfranc joint; these fractures heal slowly and are considered high risk.

items.q: An army recruit has forefoot pain after a long march; radiographs at 3 weeks show periosteal callus around the second metatarsal shaft. The appropriate management is:
o: Relative rest with a stiff-soled shoe and gradual return
items.e: The 'march fracture' of the second or third metatarsal shaft is a low-risk stress fracture that heals with relative rest and activity modification.

items.q: Which MRI finding best distinguishes medial tibial stress syndrome from a tibial stress fracture?
o: A low-signal fracture line on T1
Extensive marrow oedema on T1 and T2
Periosteal oedema along the posteromedial tibia without a fracture line or significant marrow oedema
A focal cortical defect in the anterior tibia
items.e: MTSS shows diffuse periosteal oedema along the distal two-thirds of the posteromedial tibia without the marrow oedema or fracture line of a stress fracture.

items.q: During lateral compartment fasciotomy for chronic exertional compartment syndrome, which nerve is at risk where it pierces the deep fascia about 10-12 cm above the lateral malleolus?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve emerges through the crural fascia in the distal third of the lateral leg and must be protected during the release.

items.q: A 22-year-old runner has calf claudication with exercise and loss of pedal pulses on active plantarflexion. The usual anatomical cause is:
o: A cystic adventitial disease of the femoral artery
An anomalous medial head of gastrocnemius compressing the popliteal artery
A fabella compressing the common peroneal nerve
items.e: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, usually from an abnormal course or insertion of the medial gastrocnemius head, causes exertional claudication in young athletes.

items.q: External iliac artery endofibrosis causing exertional thigh pain and weakness is classically seen in:
items.e: Repeated hip flexion and high flow in elite cyclists cause intimal thickening of the external iliac artery, producing exercise-related leg pain.

items.q: Low energy availability in athletes is usually defined as dietary energy intake minus exercise energy expenditure of less than about:
o: 45 kcal per kg body weight per day
15 kcal per kg body weight per day
60 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day
30 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day
items.e: An energy availability below about 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day disrupts hormonal and bone metabolism; about 45 is considered optimal.

items.q: Compared with the female athlete triad, the IOC concept of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S):
o: Applies to both sexes and affects many body systems beyond bone and menstrual function
Applies only to female athletes with eating disorders
Requires a stress fracture for diagnosis
Is defined by a BMI below 17.5
items.e: RED-S (IOC 2014, updated 2023) broadens the triad to male and female athletes and includes metabolic, haematological, cardiovascular, immune, psychological and performance effects.

items.q: When assessing bone density by DXA in a 20-year-old amenorrhoeic runner, the result should be expressed as a:
o: T-score, with osteoporosis defined as -2.5 or lower
Z-score, with values below -1.0 warranting further evaluation in athletes
T-score, with values below -1.0 indicating osteopenia
Z-score, with only values below -3.0 considered abnormal
items.e: Z-scores (age-matched) are used in premenopausal women and young athletes; in weight-bearing athletes a Z-score below -1.0 is concerning and below -2.0 is low BMD for age.

items.q: In an amenorrhoeic athlete with low energy availability and low BMD, why is the combined oral contraceptive pill not first-line treatment?
o: It induces withdrawal bleeds that mask amenorrhoea without restoring bone density
items.e: The OCP does not correct the hypothalamic cause or improve BMD and hides the warning sign; treatment is to increase energy intake, with transdermal oestrogen if needed.

items.q: According to the 2022 Amsterdam concussion consensus, the Child SCAT6 is intended for children aged:
items.e: The Child SCAT6 is used for 8-12 year olds; the SCAT6 is for those aged 13 and older.

items.q: A rugby player is concussed during a match. Which finding is a red flag requiring immediate removal and emergency referral?
items.e: Neck pain or tenderness raises concern for cervical spine injury and is a red flag; other red flags include double vision, limb weakness, seizure, vomiting and deteriorating consciousness.

items.q: Second impact syndrome, a rare and often fatal complication of a repeat head injury before recovery from concussion, is due to:
o: Acute extradural haematoma from a skull fracture
Diffuse cerebral swelling from loss of autoregulation
Hypoxic brain injury from airway obstruction
items.e: A second impact before recovery can trigger malignant diffuse cerebral oedema, mainly in adolescents, which is why early return to play is forbidden.

items.q: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy linked to repetitive head impacts in contact sports is pathologically characterised by:
o: Diffuse amyloid-beta plaques with neuritic tangles in the hippocampus
Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra
Perivascular deposits of hyperphosphorylated tau at the depths of cortical sulci
items.e: CTE is a tauopathy with characteristic perivascular p-tau accumulation at the depths of sulci.

items.q: For a 14-year-old recovering from sport-related concussion, current consensus advises:
o: Return to full-contact sport before returning to school
Strict dark-room rest for at least 2 weeks
Clearance by CT scan before any activity
Return to school learning before full return to sport
items.e: Children and adolescents should complete a graded return to learn before full return to sport, with a more conservative approach than in adults.

items.q: In the first 24-48 hours after a sport-related concussion, current guidance recommends:
o: Relative rest with light activity that does not worsen symptoms
Complete bed rest in a dark room for one week
Return to contact training if symptoms are mild
items.e: Relative rest for 24-48 hours, with light symptom-limited activity, is encouraged; strict prolonged rest is no longer advised.

items.q: In the United States, the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young competitive athletes has classically been reported as:
items.e: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is classically cited as the leading cause in US athletes, whereas ARVC is prominent in Italian series.

items.q: In the Veneto region of Italy, the cardiomyopathy most often found in young athletes with sudden cardiac death is:
items.e: Italian data (Veneto) highlight ARVC as a leading cause, which partly motivated mandatory ECG screening in Italy.

items.q: Commotio cordis in a young cricketer struck on the chest by a ball results from:
o: Complete heart block from septal contusion
Ventricular fibrillation triggered by impact during the vulnerable phase of repolarisation
items.e: An impact just before the T-wave peak triggers VF in a structurally normal heart; survival depends on immediate CPR and defibrillation.

items.q: On screening ECG of an asymptomatic trained athlete, which finding is abnormal and needs further cardiac investigation?
o: T-wave inversion in leads V5 and V6
Sinus bradycardia of 45 beats per minute
Isolated QRS voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy
items.e: Lateral T-wave inversion can indicate cardiomyopathy; bradycardia, first-degree block and isolated voltage criteria are normal training-related findings.

items.q: A marathon runner collapses with confusion and a rectal temperature of 41.5 C. The most important immediate treatment is:
o: Immediate transfer to hospital without cooling
items.e: Exertional heat stroke (core above 40 C with CNS dysfunction) is treated by 'cool first, transport second', ideally with cold-water immersion.

items.q: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia in endurance events is most often caused by:
o: Excessive salt loss without fluid intake
items.e: Overdrinking water or hypotonic sports drinks beyond sweat losses dilutes serum sodium; it can cause confusion, seizures and death.

items.q: Before participating in contact sports, athletes with Down syndrome have traditionally been screened for:
items.e: Ligamentous laxity in Down syndrome can cause atlantoaxial instability, which is the classic pre-participation concern (e.g. Special Olympics).

items.q: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was founded in:
items.e: WADA was established in 1999 after the Festina scandal at the 1998 Tour de France.

items.q: India's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) was set up in:
items.e: NADA was established in 2005; its testing is supported by the National Dope Testing Laboratory in New Delhi.

items.q: Anti-doping in India was given a statutory basis by the:
items.e: The National Anti-Doping Act, 2022 gave legal backing to NADA and the National Dope Testing Laboratory.

items.q: Final appeals in international anti-doping cases are heard by the:
items.e: The Court of Arbitration for Sport in Lausanne hears appeals against anti-doping decisions.

items.q: The 'strict liability' principle of the World Anti-Doping Code means that:
o: An athlete is responsible for any prohibited substance found in their sample, whatever the intent
The doctor alone is responsible for prescribed medicines
Only intentional use is an anti-doping rule violation
The team is responsible rather than the individual athlete
items.e: Under strict liability, presence of a prohibited substance is a violation regardless of intent or negligence, though fault can affect the sanction.

items.q: Under the World Anti-Doping Code, the standard period of ineligibility for an intentional violation involving a non-specified substance is:
items.e: An intentional violation with a non-specified substance carries 4 years; 2 years applies when intent is not established.

items.q: An athlete's urine shows a testosterone/epitestosterone ratio above 4. Which test confirms exogenous testosterone?
items.e: IRMS detects the different carbon-13/carbon-12 ratio of synthetic testosterone compared with endogenous steroid.

items.q: Under the WADA Prohibited List, pseudoephedrine is:
o: Prohibited at all times at any concentration
Permitted and only on the monitoring programme
Prohibited only in shooting and archery
Prohibited in competition only, above a urinary threshold of 150 µg/mL
items.e: Pseudoephedrine is an in-competition stimulant (S6) with a urinary threshold of 150 µg/mL; ephedrine's threshold is 10 µg/mL.

items.q: The classic triad of spinal epidural abscess (back pain, fever and neurological deficit) is present at initial presentation in approximately:
items.e: The full triad is present in a minority (under about 20%) at presentation, which is why diagnosis is often delayed; back pain is the commonest early symptom.

items.q: The usual clinical progression of an untreated spinal epidural abscess (Heusner) is:
o: Paralysis first, followed by back pain
Fever, then sudden paralysis without pain
Back pain, then radicular pain, then motor weakness, then paralysis
Sphincter loss, then radicular pain, then back pain
items.e: Heusner described four stages: focal back pain, radicular pain, weakness (with sensory and sphincter disturbance) and finally paralysis; outcome depends on the stage at surgery.

items.q: In a spinal epidural abscess, motor recovery after decompression is unlikely when complete paralysis has been present for longer than about:
items.e: Paralysis lasting more than about 24-36 hours rarely recovers; the pre-operative neurological status and its duration are the strongest predictors of outcome.

items.q: A neurologically intact 50-year-old with a lumbar epidural abscess is considered for antibiotics alone. Which feature predicts failure of medical management?
items.e: Recognised predictors of failure of non-operative treatment include diabetes, MRSA, CRP over about 115 mg/L, WBC over 12,500, positive blood cultures and age over 65.

items.q: A patient with a thoracic epidural abscess has had complete paraplegia for 5 days and has severe comorbidities. A reasonable approach is:
o: Emergency decompression to restore motor function
Intravenous antibiotics alone, since surgery is unlikely to restore function
items.e: Medical management may be chosen for patients unfit for surgery or with complete paralysis beyond about 72 hours, when decompression is unlikely to improve neurology (surgery may still be needed for sepsis or instability).

items.q: The reported rate of surgical site infection after instrumented spinal fusion is approximately:
