items.e: SSI after spinal surgery is about 1-4%, higher with instrumentation, posterior long fusions, obesity, diabetes, trauma and especially neuromuscular scoliosis.

items.q: Three weeks after an instrumented L4-S1 fusion, a patient has wound discharge and raised CRP; the implants are radiologically secure. The recommended management is:
o: Surgical debridement and irrigation with retention of the implants, cultures and antibiotics
Removal of all implants at once
items.e: Early deep infection is treated by thorough debridement and irrigation with retention of stable implants (which are needed for fusion), plus culture-directed antibiotics; vacuum dressings may help.

items.q: Two years after a solid posterior thoracolumbar fusion, a patient has a low-grade painful sinus over the rods with Cutibacterium acnes on culture. The appropriate surgical treatment is:
o: Retaining the implants and adding new screws
Removal of the instrumentation and debridement
Extending the fusion two more levels
items.e: Late infections are often due to low-virulence biofilm organisms; once the fusion is solid, implants are no longer needed and are removed with debridement.

items.q: When Cutibacterium acnes is suspected in a delayed spinal implant infection, the laboratory should be asked to:
o: Extend anaerobic culture incubation to about 14 days
items.e: C. acnes is a slow-growing anaerobe; prolonged incubation (about 10-14 days) of multiple tissue samples is needed to isolate it.

items.q: Local intrawound vancomycin powder in spinal surgery is used to:
o: Reduce the risk of surgical site infection
items.e: Vancomycin powder placed in the wound before closure has been reported in many (mostly retrospective) studies to reduce SSI, particularly staphylococcal; evidence from RCTs is mixed.

items.q: After an uncomplicated lumbar discectomy, the serum CRP normally:
o: Peaks at about 2-3 days and returns to near normal by about 2 weeks
items.e: CRP peaks about 2-3 days after spinal surgery and normalises within about 2 weeks; a persistent or secondary rise suggests infection. ESR stays elevated for weeks and is less useful.

items.q: Five weeks after an L4-L5 discectomy, a patient has severe, mechanical, unremitting back pain and a raised CRP. MRI shows disc T2 hyperintensity with enhancement of both adjacent endplates. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Modic type I degenerative change without infection
items.e: Postoperative discitis presents weeks after surgery with severe back pain and raised inflammatory markers; MRI shows disc and endplate enhancement. A rising CRP helps distinguish it from benign postoperative or Modic changes.

items.q: A 2-year-old refuses to walk or sit, and cries when the nappy is changed; she has a low-grade fever and holds her back stiffly. MRI shows narrowing and enhancement of the L3-L4 disc. The most likely organisms are:
items.e: Paediatric discitis typically affects children aged 1-5 years; S. aureus and Kingella kingae are the usual causes.

items.q: A 3-year-old has MRI-confirmed lumbar discitis and blood cultures are negative. The usual management is:
o: Anti-staphylococcal antibiotics and rest or bracing, without routine biopsy
items.e: Paediatric discitis responds to empirical anti-staphylococcal antibiotics and rest; biopsy is reserved for atypical cases or failure to respond.

items.q: On MRI, which feature favours metastatic disease rather than infection of the spine?
o: Preservation of the intervertebral disc with pedicle involvement
Disc destruction with enhancement of both endplates
A large thin-walled paraspinal abscess with subligamentous spread
Early disc space narrowing with an epidural abscess
items.e: Metastases generally spare the disc and often involve the pedicle (radiographic 'winking owl' sign); infection crosses or destroys the disc.

items.q: In spinal infection, calcification within a large paraspinal abscess on CT most strongly suggests:
items.e: Calcification within a paraspinal abscess is characteristic of tuberculous (chronic) cold abscess and is rare in pyogenic infection.

items.q: In tuberculous spondylitis, subligamentous spread on MRI typically appears as:
o: An abscess confined to the disc space
Epidural gas at a single level
Pus extending beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament over three or more vertebral levels
items.e: Tuberculous pus spreads beneath the anterior or posterior longitudinal ligament across several levels; pyogenic infection rarely spreads so extensively.

items.q: A typical difference in symptom duration at presentation between tuberculous and pyogenic spondylodiscitis is that tuberculosis usually presents after:
o: Symptoms that always begin after trauma
items.e: Tuberculosis has an insidious course over months with constitutional symptoms; pyogenic infection presents acutely over days to weeks.

items.q: A cold abscess in spinal tuberculosis is so called because:
o: It lacks the redness, heat and acute tenderness of a pyogenic abscess
It is always found at low body temperature
It occurs only in winter months
items.e: Tuberculous abscesses develop slowly with little acute inflammation, so the overlying skin is not warm or red.

items.q: When aspirating a superficial tuberculous cold abscess, the needle is introduced obliquely through healthy skin at a non-dependent site to:
o: Reduce the risk of a persistent discharging sinus
Avoid the need for antitubercular therapy
Allow the abscess to drain spontaneously
items.e: Entering obliquely through healthy skin away from the most dependent, thinned area reduces leakage and formation of a chronic sinus, which may become secondarily infected.

items.q: A large tuberculous psoas abscess persists despite 6 weeks of antitubercular therapy in a patient without neurological deficit or instability. The usual first intervention is:
o: Posterior instrumentation from T10 to the pelvis
items.e: Large or symptomatic abscesses not responding to drugs can usually be managed by ultrasound- or CT-guided percutaneous drainage; major surgery is reserved for neurological deficit, instability or deformity.

items.q: A 30-year-old with thoracic tuberculosis develops new paraparesis while on antitubercular therapy, with MRI showing anterior epidural pus and granulation tissue compressing the cord. The appropriate treatment is:
o: Continuing drugs alone and reassessing at 6 months
Stopping therapy as the drugs have failed
Surgical decompression and stabilisation while continuing therapy
items.e: Neurological deficit that develops or worsens on adequate therapy is a clear indication for decompression (with stabilisation) under drug cover.

items.q: Spinal tuberculosis with paraplegia in a patient with HIV infection is treated with the same antitubercular regimen, and antiretroviral therapy is usually started:
o: As soon as possible, within about 2 weeks of starting antitubercular treatment
Only after antitubercular treatment is completed
Before any antitubercular drug is given
items.e: Current WHO guidance is to start ART as soon as possible within 2 weeks of starting TB treatment regardless of CD4 count (TB meningitis excepted), watching for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and rifampicin interactions.

items.q: A 55-year-old with a long-term central venous catheter and recent broad-spectrum antibiotics develops slowly progressive lumbar spondylodiscitis with negative bacterial cultures. The organism most suspected is:
items.e: Fungal (Candida) spondylodiscitis occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with central lines, prolonged antibiotics or intravenous drug use; it has an indolent course.

items.q: In a patient with pyogenic spondylodiscitis, which situation is an indication for surgery rather than antibiotics alone?
o: Progressive neurological deficit from an epidural abscess
items.e: Surgery is indicated for neurological deficit or compression, instability or progressive deformity, failure of medical treatment, or diagnostic uncertainty; uncomplicated cases respond to antibiotics.

items.q: A 60-year-old with L2-L3 pyogenic spondylodiscitis and an epidural abscess needs debridement for neurological deficit. Regarding pedicle screw instrumentation in this actively infected field:
o: It is absolutely contraindicated until the infection has healed
It must be combined with lifelong antibiotics
It can be used only if the organism is Gram-negative
It is acceptable and helps stabilise the spine, with antibiotics continued
items.e: Thorough debridement with instrumentation (including titanium cages and pedicle screws) is safe in active pyogenic infection when combined with appropriate antibiotics and improves stability and alignment.

items.q: In the Pott's spine literature, 'paraplegia in flexion' is clinically significant because it:
o: Indicates a severe, more complete cord lesion with extrapyramidal involvement and poorer prognosis
Is the earliest and mildest sign of cord compression
Is seen only in lumbar tuberculosis
items.e: Paraplegia in flexion reflects severe cord damage with involvement of both pyramidal and extrapyramidal tracts and has a worse prognosis than paraplegia in extension.

items.q: Spinal tuberculosis most commonly involves which region of the spine?
o: The thoracolumbar junction (lower thoracic and upper lumbar)
items.e: The lower thoracic and upper lumbar (thoracolumbar) region is the commonest site; cervical disease is less frequent but more dangerous.

items.q: A 3-year-old child with active thoracic tuberculosis and progressive kyphosis is assessed by Rajasekaran's signs. When the posterior facets of the involved segment have lost contact and dislocated at the apex, the sign is called:
items.e: Separation (dislocation) of the facet joints at the apex of the kyphosis indicates instability and is one of the four spine-at-risk signs.

items.q: In the classification of Pott's paraplegia, late-onset paraplegia caused by healed disease is managed mainly by:
o: Bed rest in a plaster bed
Anterior decompression with resection of the internal gibbus and stabilisation
items.e: Late-onset paraplegia is due to a bony ridge (internal gibbus) or fibrosis; anterior or anterolateral decompression of the ridge with stabilisation is required, though prognosis remains poorer.

items.q: In suspected spinal tuberculosis, which specimen gives the highest diagnostic yield for GeneXpert and culture?
o: Pus or tissue from CT-guided biopsy of the lesion
Sputum in a patient with a normal chest radiograph
items.e: Direct sampling of the lesion (pus, granulation tissue or bone) by image-guided biopsy gives the best yield for histology, AFB stain, culture and nucleic acid amplification.

items.q: Tuberculosis of the craniovertebral junction (atlanto-axial region) typically presents with:
o: Suboccipital neck pain and stiffness, with risk of atlanto-axial instability and quadriparesis
items.e: Craniovertebral tuberculosis causes neck pain and torticollis, retropharyngeal abscess and ligamentous destruction leading to atlanto-axial instability and high cord compression.

items.q: Lymphocytosis on the full blood count with a modestly raised ESR in a patient with insidious back pain is most suggestive of:
o: A chronic granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis
items.e: Spinal tuberculosis often shows relative lymphocytosis with raised ESR; acute pyogenic infection more often shows neutrophilia and markedly raised CRP.

items.q: In Tuli's 'middle path regimen', patients without neurological deficit are treated initially with:
o: Immediate radical anterior debridement in all patients
Drugs for 3 weeks followed by mandatory fusion
Antitubercular drugs and rest or bracing, with surgery reserved for specific indications
items.e: The middle path combines chemotherapy with rest and gradual mobilisation in a brace; operative treatment is used for failure of response, neurological deficit, instability or diagnostic doubt.

items.q: A 12-year-old has thigh pain and a lucent lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis that sends a serpiginous lucent tract across the physis, with no central mineralisation. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: A serpiginous lucent tract, often crossing the physis, without nidus calcification is typical of Brodie abscess (subacute osteomyelitis); an osteoid osteoma has a round nidus that may calcify centrally.

items.q: On a technetium bone scan, the 'double-density sign' of osteoid osteoma refers to:
o: Two separate lesions in the same bone
A small focus of intense uptake (nidus) within a larger area of less intense reactive uptake
Uptake in both the nidus and the contralateral bone
Photopenic nidus surrounded by a hot rim
items.e: The hot nidus sits within a less intense zone of reactive sclerosis, giving the double-density sign, which helps distinguish osteoid osteoma from other causes of focal uptake.

items.q: MRI of a suspected femoral neck osteoid osteoma shows extensive marrow oedema and joint effusion, raising concern about infection or a malignant tumour. Which MRI technique best identifies the nidus?
o: Dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging showing early arterial enhancement of the nidus
items.e: Oedema can obscure the nidus and mislead; dynamic gadolinium imaging shows early arterial-phase enhancement of the hypervascular nidus, though thin-section CT remains the investigation of choice.

items.q: The commonest site of osteoid osteoma is the:
o: Proximal femur (femoral neck and intertrochanteric region)
items.e: The proximal femur is the commonest site, followed by the tibia; about 10% occur in the posterior elements of the spine, mainly lumbar.

items.q: After CT-guided radiofrequency ablation of an osteoid osteoma, the approximate primary clinical success rate is:
o: About 90%, and recurrent lesions can be re-ablated
About 50%, with frequent need for open excision
items.e: RFA achieves about 90% primary success with recurrence around 5-10%; a repeat ablation is usually effective, making RFA the treatment of choice for accessible lesions.

items.q: Osteopoikilosis, with multiple symmetrical bone islands around joints, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in:
items.e: LEMD3 mutations cause osteopoikilosis and Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome; GNAS is linked to fibrous dysplasia and FGFR3 to achondroplasia.

items.q: The most common radiographic type of osteoid osteoma is:
o: Medullary with a large expansile lytic lesion
Cortical, with a small lucent nidus and marked cortical thickening
Intra-articular with a dense sclerotic rim
items.e: Most osteoid osteomas are cortical in the diaphysis or metaphysis, with fusiform cortical thickening that can hide the nidus; intramedullary and intra-articular types have less sclerosis.

items.q: In Paget disease of a long bone, the advancing lytic front seen on radiographs is described as a:
items.e: Lytic Paget disease begins at one end of a long bone and advances along the shaft with a V-shaped 'blade of grass' front; sunburst and onion-skin reactions are features of malignant tumours.

items.q: In a patient treated for osteosarcoma whose serum alkaline phosphatase was raised at diagnosis and normalised after surgery, a later rise in ALP may suggest:
items.e: When raised at diagnosis, ALP falls after successful treatment and a subsequent rise can herald local or metastatic relapse; LDH and ALP elevation are also adverse prognostic markers.

items.q: Pathological fracture occurs at presentation in approximately what proportion of patients with osteosarcoma?
items.e: Pathological fracture complicates about 5-10% of osteosarcomas (more in telangiectatic); with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and careful immobilisation, limb salvage is often still possible.

items.q: Recycled autograft reconstruction after resection of a diaphyseal osteosarcoma involves:
o: Transplanting a vascularised fibula from the opposite leg only
Sterilising the resected tumour-bearing segment (e.g. liquid nitrogen freezing, irradiation or pasteurisation) and re-implanting it
Filling the defect with bone cement permanently
items.e: The resected bone is treated to kill tumour cells (extracorporeal irradiation, liquid nitrogen or pasteurisation) and replaced, giving an anatomical fit with no allograft-related disease transmission.

items.q: After completing treatment for localised osteosarcoma, surveillance for lung metastases in the first two years is usually by:
items.e: Most relapses occur in the lungs within the first 2-3 years, so CT chest is performed about every 3 months in years 1-2, with decreasing frequency up to about 10 years.

items.q: Long-term survivors of osteosarcoma treated with doxorubicin need periodic surveillance for:
items.e: Doxorubicin causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy that can appear years later; survivors need echocardiographic surveillance. Bleomycin, not used for osteosarcoma, causes pulmonary fibrosis.

items.q: In the WHO 2020 classification of osteogenic tumours, osteoblastoma is categorised as:
items.e: WHO 2020 lists osteoma and osteoid osteoma as benign, osteoblastoma as intermediate (locally aggressive) and osteosarcoma subtypes as malignant.

items.q: Myositis ossificans after a muscle injury usually shows peripheral mature ossification on radiographs or CT after about:
items.e: Mineralisation appears at 2-4 weeks and a mature peripheral rim (zonal pattern) is established by about 6-8 weeks; serial imaging helps avoid an unnecessary biopsy that can mimic sarcoma.

items.q: A 15-year-old has an expansile lytic lesion of the proximal humerus with fluid-fluid levels on MRI, thought to be an aneurysmal bone cyst. The most important step before curettage is:
o: Biopsy with histology of the septa and any solid tissue
items.e: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma can mimic ABC on imaging; an apparent ABC should never be curetted without histological confirmation, especially if septa are thick and nodular.

items.q: A 14-year-old's osteosarcoma biopsy shows predominantly chondroid differentiation with malignant cells directly forming osteoid in areas. This tumour is:
o: Conventional chondrosarcoma, treated by surgery alone
Chondroblastic osteosarcoma, treated like any conventional osteosarcoma
items.e: Any direct osteoid production by malignant cells makes it osteosarcoma; the chondroblastic subtype is high-grade and treated with MAP and wide resection, unlike chondrosarcoma which is chemoresistant.

items.q: Osteosarcoma arising in the pelvis or spine, compared with extremity tumours, is associated with:
o: Better prognosis because of earlier diagnosis
Worse prognosis, partly because wide margins are harder to obtain
items.e: Axial osteosarcomas occur in older patients, present larger and are difficult to resect widely, so local control and survival are poorer.

items.q: Mifamurtide, an adjunct for resected non-metastatic osteosarcoma, has which regulatory status?
o: Approved by the US FDA but not in Europe
Approved in Europe but not by the US FDA
items.e: Mifamurtide (liposomal MTP-PE) improved overall survival in INT-0133 (debated analysis) and is approved by the EMA, but the FDA did not approve it.

items.q: Plasma methotrexate levels are monitored after each high-dose infusion in osteosarcoma treatment because:
o: Delayed clearance predicts severe renal, mucosal and marrow toxicity and guides leucovorin dosing
Low levels predict poor tumour necrosis
Levels determine the dose of doxorubicin
Methotrexate is cardiotoxic at high levels
items.e: Delayed elimination increases toxicity; levels guide leucovorin rescue and hydration, and glucarpidase is used if levels remain dangerously high with renal impairment.

items.q: A small, well-defined lucent lesion in the anterior tibial cortex of a runner shows a linear lucency running perpendicular to the cortex on CT. This favours:
items.e: A stress fracture shows a linear lucency perpendicular or oblique to the cortex, whereas osteoid osteoma shows a round or oval nidus, often with central mineralisation.

items.q: The skeletal site most frequently involved by metastatic carcinoma is the:
items.e: The vertebral column is the commonest site of skeletal metastasis, followed by the pelvis, ribs and proximal long bones, reflecting red marrow distribution and venous drainage.

items.q: The region of the spine most commonly affected by metastatic disease and cord compression is the:
items.e: About 70% of symptomatic spinal metastases and most cases of MSCC are thoracic, where the canal is narrow relative to the cord.

items.q: The tendency of prostatic carcinoma to metastasise to the lumbar spine and pelvis is explained mainly by:
o: The valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus)
Arterial embolisation through the lumbar arteries
items.e: Batson's valveless epidural venous plexus communicates with pelvic veins; raised intra-abdominal pressure diverts blood and tumour cells into the vertebrae.

items.q: Within a vertebra, haematogenous metastases usually begin in the:
o: Posterior part of the vertebral body
items.e: Metastases seed the red marrow of the posterior vertebral body and spread into the pedicle; pedicle destruction is seen radiographically, but the body is involved first.

items.q: On MRI, a feature that favours metastatic tumour rather than pyogenic spondylodiscitis is:
o: Disc space narrowing with fluid signal
Endplate erosion on both sides of a disc
Paraspinal abscess crossing the disc level
items.e: Tumour rarely crosses the disc, whereas pyogenic infection characteristically destroys the disc and adjacent endplates.

items.q: Before surgery for a spinal metastasis, pre-operative embolisation is most strongly indicated when the primary is:
items.e: Renal cell and thyroid carcinoma metastases are highly vascular; embolisation shortly before surgery reduces blood loss substantially.

items.q: Pre-operative embolisation of a hypervascular spinal metastasis should ideally be done:
items.e: Surgery is performed within about 24-48 hours of embolisation, before recanalisation and collateral flow restore tumour vascularity.

items.q: The commonest intramedullary spinal cord tumour in adults is:
items.e: Ependymoma is the commonest intramedullary tumour in adults, while astrocytoma predominates in children; meningioma is intradural extramedullary.

items.q: A 45-year-old has radicular pain and a 'dumbbell' mass that widens the C6-C7 neural foramen on imaging. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: A dumbbell lesion extending through and enlarging the foramen is typical of a nerve sheath tumour (schwannoma or neurofibroma), the commonest intradural extramedullary tumour.

items.q: A 55-year-old woman has a thoracic intradural extramedullary tumour with a dural tail and calcification on imaging. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Spinal meningiomas typically affect middle-aged women in the thoracic spine and show a broad dural attachment, dural tail and sometimes calcification.

items.q: A 30-year-old with retinal and cerebellar lesions has an intramedullary cervical cyst with a brightly enhancing mural nodule. The likely spinal lesion and syndrome are:
items.e: A cyst with an enhancing mural nodule is the classic haemangioblastoma appearance; multiple haemangioblastomas with retinal angiomas indicate von Hippel-Lindau disease.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph, a vertebral haemangioma typically shows:
items.e: Thickened vertical trabeculae give the corduroy or jail-bar pattern, corresponding to the polka-dot appearance on axial CT.

items.q: A vertebral haemangioma is more likely to be aggressive (and symptomatic) when MRI shows:
o: High T1 and T2 signal confined to the body
Low T1 signal with extension into the posterior elements and epidural soft tissue
items.e: Typical, inactive haemangiomas are fatty (T1 bright); aggressive haemangiomas have less fat (T1 low), involve the whole body and posterior elements, and may extend into the epidural space.

items.q: A 14-year-old has an expansile lesion of the posterior elements of T10 extending into the body, with multiple fluid-fluid levels on MRI. Which is a recognised treatment option?
o: Selective arterial embolisation or curettage with grafting
Radiotherapy as first-line in all cases
Total en bloc spondylectomy as the only option
items.e: Spinal aneurysmal bone cysts can be treated by embolisation (alone or before surgery), curettage and grafting with stabilisation if needed, sclerotherapy, or denosumab in selected cases.

items.q: The commonest site of giant cell tumour in the spinal column is the:
items.e: Most axial giant cell tumours occur in the sacrum, often eccentric and involving the upper segments; denosumab is useful when resection would cause major morbidity.

items.q: A 6-year-old has back pain. Lateral radiograph shows uniform collapse of one thoracic vertebral body to a thin wafer with preserved disc spaces. The usual management is:
o: Observation or a brace, as the lesion usually heals with partial height restoration
items.e: Vertebra plana in a child is classically Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma); most heal with conservative care, and biopsy is done if the appearance is atypical.

items.q: In multiple myeloma, a technetium bone scan is often normal despite extensive lytic lesions because:
o: The lesions are too small to detect
Technetium is excreted by myeloma cells
Osteoblastic activity is suppressed, so there is little reactive bone formation
items.e: Myeloma inhibits osteoblasts (e.g. via DKK1), so lesions are 'cold'; whole-body low-dose CT, MRI or PET-CT are used for skeletal assessment.

items.q: On axial MRI or CT, a vertebral solitary plasmacytoma can show thickened cortical struts within a lytic lesion, called the:
items.e: The 'mini-brain' appearance, with curvilinear thickened trabeculae resembling sulci, is characteristic of vertebral plasmacytoma.

items.q: Solitary plasmacytoma of a vertebra without instability or significant cord compression is primarily treated with:
items.e: Plasmacytoma is highly radiosensitive; definitive radiotherapy gives excellent local control, and surgery is reserved for instability or neurological compromise.

items.q: Chordoma most commonly arises in the:
items.e: About half of chordomas are sacrococcygeal and about a third arise at the clivus (spheno-occipital), with the mobile spine less often involved.

items.q: Which immunohistochemical marker is most specific for chordoma?
items.e: Brachyury (TBXT), a notochordal transcription factor, is nuclear-positive in chordoma and distinguishes it from chondrosarcoma; physaliferous (bubbly) cells are the histological hallmark.

items.q: The best chance of cure for a sacral chordoma is achieved by:
o: En bloc resection with wide margins, with particle radiotherapy as an adjunct when needed
Intralesional debulking followed by conventional radiotherapy
items.e: Chordoma is chemoresistant and relatively resistant to conventional radiotherapy; wide en bloc resection gives the lowest local recurrence, with proton or carbon-ion therapy as adjuvant or definitive treatment when resection is not possible.

items.q: A 65-year-old man has sacral pain and constipation. CT shows a lytic midline destructive lesion of S3-S5 with a large anterior soft tissue mass containing calcification. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: A midline lytic sacral lesion with a large soft tissue mass in an older man is typical of chordoma; GCT is usually eccentric in the upper sacrum of younger adults.

items.q: A 50-year-old has a solitary renal cell carcinoma metastasis in T11, the primary has been removed, there is no other disease and her performance status is good. The procedure that aims at local cure is:
items.e: For solitary, radioresistant metastases (renal, thyroid) with long expected survival, Tomita's total en bloc spondylectomy can achieve local control; it uses a threadwire saw through the pedicles to remove the vertebra in two pieces.

items.q: In a patient with spinal metastases, pain that is worse on sitting up or loading and relieved by lying still suggests:
items.e: Mechanical pain with movement or loading indicates instability (scores 3 in SINS) and responds poorly to radiotherapy, whereas biological night pain responds to steroids and radiotherapy.

items.q: NICE guidance for a patient with known cancer and suspected metastatic spinal cord compression with neurological symptoms recommends:
o: Whole-spine MRI immediately (within 24 hours at most)
Plain radiographs first, then MRI within a week
items.e: Whole-spine MRI is the investigation of choice; it should be done immediately when neurological signs are present and within 24 hours if MSCC is suspected, because outcome depends on neurological status at treatment.

items.q: In suspected metastatic spinal cord compression, the usual initial corticosteroid regimen is:
o: Dexamethasone 16 mg daily with gastric protection
Methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg bolus as for acute spinal cord injury
items.e: Dexamethasone 16 mg daily (with a proton pump inhibitor) is started as soon as MSCC is suspected, then tapered after definitive treatment.

items.q: In Blazina's staging of patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee), stage IV denotes:
o: Complete rupture of the patellar tendon
Pain during and after activity that impairs performance
Pain during and after activity without loss of performance
items.e: Blazina stages: I pain after activity, II pain during and after activity without functional limitation, III pain that impairs performance, IV complete tendon rupture.

items.q: In a bipartite patella, the accessory fragment is most commonly located at the:
items.e: Saupe type III (superolateral) accounts for about three-quarters of bipartite patellae; it is usually bilateral and asymptomatic, and must not be mistaken for a fracture.

items.q: A 10-year-old cannot actively extend the knee after a jump. The lateral radiograph shows patella alta and a tiny fleck of bone at the inferior pole. The most likely injury is:
items.e: A sleeve fracture avulses a large cartilaginous sleeve from the inferior pole with only a small bony fleck visible; it disrupts the extensor mechanism and needs open reduction and fixation.

items.q: A patient has disabling medial patellar instability after an isolated lateral retinacular release. The most appropriate surgical treatment is:
o: Repair or reconstruction of the lateral retinaculum (lateral patellofemoral ligament)
Further lateral release including the vastus lateralis
items.e: Iatrogenic medial instability follows over-release of the lateral restraints (often with detachment of vastus lateralis obliquus); treatment restores the lateral restraint by repair or tendon-graft reconstruction.

items.q: When a tight lateral retinaculum needs to be addressed during patellar stabilisation, lateral retinacular lengthening is preferred to release because it:
o: Avoids the need for an arthrotomy
Gives a greater medial shift of the patella
Reduces lateral tension while preserving a lateral restraint, lowering the risk of medial instability
items.e: Lengthening (e.g. Z-plasty of the superficial and deep layers) decreases tilt while keeping lateral continuity; randomised data (Pagenstert) showed less medial instability than release.

items.q: The Bereiter trochleoplasty is characterised by:
o: Elevating the lateral facet with an anterior bone wedge
Excising a wedge of bone beneath the trochlea to recess the supratrochlear spur without changing its shape
Raising a thin (about 2 mm) flexible osteochondral flap and pressing it into a deepened groove
Removing the trochlear cartilage and resurfacing with a prosthesis
items.e: Bereiter's technique uses a thin flexible osteochondral flap moulded into a newly created groove; Albee elevates the lateral facet and Goutallier's recession wedge lowers a prominent trochlea.

items.q: A trochleoplasty that elevates the lateral trochlear facet with an underlying bone wedge, rather than deepening the groove, is the:
items.e: The Albee lateral facet elevation increases the height of the lateral wall but raises patellofemoral contact pressure; it is now rarely used.

items.q: Recession wedge trochleoplasty (Goutallier) is designed mainly to address:
o: A shallow trochlea with a normal height
A hypoplastic lateral trochlear facet only
items.e: Removing a wedge of bone beneath the trochlea recesses a prominent supratrochlear spur and reduces patellofemoral pressure in early flexion, without changing trochlear shape.

items.q: When measuring the TT-TG distance on superimposed axial CT slices, the two points are projected perpendicular to which reference line?
o: A line across the anterior trochlear facets
The posterior condylar line of the femur
The posterior border of the tibial plateau
items.e: The deepest point of the trochlear groove and the centre of the tibial tubercle are each projected onto the posterior condylar line, and the distance between them is the TT-TG.

items.q: The oblique fibres of the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO) are angled from the long axis of the femur by about:
items.e: Lieb and Perry showed the VMO fibres run at about 50-55 degrees, giving it a medial vector to resist lateral patellar displacement; the vastus medialis longus runs at about 15-18 degrees.

items.q: The 'miserable malalignment syndrome' associated with anterior knee pain and patellar maltracking consists of:
o: Femoral retroversion, patella baja, genu varum and cavus feet
Coxa vara, genu recurvatum and internal tibial torsion
Increased femoral anteversion, squinting patellae, genu valgum, external tibial torsion and pronated feet
items.e: James described this combination of femoral anteversion with compensatory external tibial torsion and foot pronation; it increases the lateral pull on the patella.

items.q: A woman with recurrent patellar instability stands with her feet pointing forward, and both patellae face inwards ('squinting patellae'). This sign suggests:
items.e: Inward-facing patellae with forward-facing feet indicate excessive femoral internal torsion (anteversion), measured on a rotational-profile CT; derotation osteotomy is considered if it is over about 25-30 degrees.

items.q: Patella alta predisposes to lateral patellar instability mainly because it:
o: Delays engagement of the patella in the trochlear groove until greater flexion
items.e: A high-riding patella remains above the trochlea for longer, so the bony restraint is lost through a wider arc of early flexion.

items.q: When a distalising tibial tubercle osteotomy is performed for patella alta, the usual target Caton-Deschamps index is about:
items.e: Distalisation is usually considered when the Caton-Deschamps index exceeds about 1.2-1.3, and the tubercle is moved to bring the index to about 1.0; over-distalisation causes patella baja.

items.q: The main consequence of over-distalising the tibial tubercle is:
o: Patella baja with loss of flexion and patellofemoral pain
items.e: Excessive distalisation produces patella infera, which overloads the patellofemoral joint, restricts flexion and causes anterior knee pain.

items.q: Using the Grelsamer-Meadows modified Insall-Salvati ratio (distance from the inferior patellar articular margin to the tibial tubercle divided by articular surface length), patella alta is defined by a value above:
items.e: The modified Insall-Salvati index is normally about 1.5; a value over 2.0 indicates patella alta. It accounts for variable patellar morphology such as a long inferior nose.

items.q: Among Dejour's principal (major) factors predisposing to patellar instability, abnormal patellar tilt on CT is defined as greater than:
items.e: Dejour's four factors are trochlear dysplasia, patella alta (Caton-Deschamps over 1.2), TT-TG over 20 mm and patellar tilt over 20 degrees measured on CT with the quadriceps relaxed.

items.q: Which of the following is one of the four principal anatomical factors described by Henri Dejour for objective patellar instability?
items.e: Dejour's principal factors are trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, increased TT-TG and patellar tilt; Q angle, laxity and foot posture are minor or secondary factors.

items.q: The 'J sign' in a patient with patellar instability refers to:
o: Sudden lateral deviation of the patella as the knee reaches terminal extension
Medial displacement of the patella in deep flexion
Tenderness tracking along the patellar tendon
items.e: In the J sign, the patella follows an inverted-J path, jumping laterally as it leaves the trochlea near full extension; it suggests trochlear dysplasia, patella alta or a lateral vector.

items.q: The proximal fibres of the medial patellofemoral complex that insert onto the quadriceps tendon rather than the patella are called the:
items.e: The medial patellofemoral complex includes the MPFL and the more proximal medial quadriceps tendon-femoral ligament (MQTFL); some surgeons reconstruct to the quadriceps tendon to avoid patellar tunnels.

items.q: The graft most commonly used for MPFL reconstruction is:
items.e: A gracilis (or semitendinosus) autograft has sufficient strength (greater than the native MPFL) with low donor morbidity and is the commonest choice.

items.q: On a rotational-profile CT, femoral anteversion is measured as the angle between the femoral neck axis and the:
o: Posterior condylar line of the distal femur
items.e: Femoral version is the angle between the femoral neck axis and the posterior condylar (or transepicondylar) axis; tibial torsion is the angle between the proximal tibial and transmalleolar axes.

items.q: In a patient with recurrent patellar instability and marked external tibial torsion, the deformity may be corrected by:
o: Internal rotational (derotation) osteotomy of the tibia
External rotational osteotomy of the femur
items.e: External tibial torsion lateralises the tubercle and the patellar tendon vector; a supramalleolar or proximal tibial internal derotation osteotomy corrects it.

items.q: Which chromosomal disorder is classically associated with ligamentous laxity and a high rate of patellar instability, including chronic or permanent dislocation?
items.e: Patellar instability affects a notable proportion of children with Down syndrome because of generalised laxity and hypotonia.

items.q: A 22-year-old with previous Osgood-Schlatter disease still has pain on kneeling over a prominent tibial tubercle; radiographs show a separate ossicle. After skeletal maturity, the treatment of choice for persistent symptoms is:
o: Fixation of the ossicle with a screw
Excision of the ossicle with tubercle recontouring
items.e: An unfused ossicle within the patellar tendon can remain painful after maturity; excision (open or endoscopic) with smoothing of the prominent tubercle gives good results.

items.q: Dejour's 'à la carte' approach to recurrent patellar instability means:
o: Treating all patients with trochleoplasty first
Correcting each anatomical abnormality that exceeds its threshold
Performing the same combined operation on every patient
Choosing surgery according to patient preference alone
items.e: Each factor (MPFL insufficiency, TT-TG, patellar height, trochlear dysplasia, rotation, valgus) is assessed against its threshold and corrected individually.

items.q: When drilling the posterior tibial cortex during tibial tubercle osteotomy, which structures are at risk?
o: Saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein
Popliteal artery and tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve
Superficial peroneal nerve and lesser saphenous vein
items.e: Over-penetration through the posterolateral cortex endangers the anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve as they pass through the interosseous membrane; drills should be stopped at the far cortex.

items.q: On axial MRI, trochlear dysplasia is indicated by a lateral trochlear inclination angle of less than about:
items.e: Carrillon described the lateral trochlear inclination angle (lateral facet relative to the posterior condylar line); less than 11 degrees indicates dysplasia.

items.q: Pfirrmann defined trochlear dysplasia on axial MRI as a trochlear depth of less than:
items.e: Trochlear depth below 3 mm (measured 3 cm above the joint line) indicates dysplasia; facet asymmetry (medial/lateral facet width) under 40% is another criterion.

items.q: The patellotrochlear index (Biedert) on sagittal MRI measures:
o: Patellar tendon length divided by patellar length
The angle between the trochlear facets
The overlap of patellar and trochlear cartilage as a proportion of patellar cartilage length
The distance from the tibial tubercle to the PCL
items.e: The patellotrochlear index assesses functional patellar height by cartilage engagement; under about 12.5% indicates patella alta.

items.q: A 16-year-old has an acute lateral patellar dislocation with a tense haemarthrosis but normal radiographs. The most appropriate next investigation is:
items.e: Radiographs miss many chondral and osteochondral injuries; MRI identifies loose fragments needing fixation or removal and shows MPFL injury and trochlear morphology.

items.q: In MPFL reconstruction, the femoral tunnel position is routinely confirmed intraoperatively using:
o: A perfect lateral fluoroscopic image with the posterior condyles superimposed
An anteroposterior radiograph of the knee in full extension
items.e: Schöttle's radiographic point is defined on a true lateral view; a rotated image leads to tunnel malposition, the commonest technical error.

items.q: The patellar tendon in a Roux-Goldthwait procedure is managed by:
o: Splitting it and transferring the lateral half medially beneath the medial half
Detaching the whole tendon with a bone block from the tubercle
items.e: The lateral half of the patellar tendon is detached distally and passed medially under the medial half to the medial tibia, medialising the force vector without an osteotomy.

items.q: In the Galeazzi semitendinosus tenodesis for paediatric patellar instability, the semitendinosus tendon is:
o: Harvested and fixed to the adductor tubercle as a free graft
Used to reinforce the lateral retinaculum
Left attached distally and passed through an oblique tunnel in the patella
items.e: The Galeazzi procedure keeps the semitendinosus insertion, divides it proximally and threads it through the patella, creating a static medial tether without crossing physes.

items.q: An 18-year-old has recurrent lateral patellar dislocation with a TT-TG of 14 mm, Caton-Deschamps index of 1.1, mild Dejour type A dysplasia and normal limb rotation. The most appropriate operation is:
o: MPFL reconstruction with tibial tubercle medialisation
items.e: With no major bony factor beyond its threshold, isolated MPFL reconstruction is appropriate; TT-TG is normal, patellar height is normal and type A dysplasia does not need trochleoplasty.

items.q: A 25-year-old has recurrent lateral instability with a TT-TG of 23 mm, Caton-Deschamps index of 1.45 and a normal trochlea. The best combination is:
o: Tibial tubercle osteotomy with medialisation and distalisation, with MPFL reconstruction
items.e: Both TT-TG and patellar height exceed their thresholds, so the tubercle is moved medially and distally, usually combined with MPFL reconstruction.

items.q: Under absolute stability, direct contact healing, in which cutting cones cross the fracture line without an intermediate woven-bone stage, requires the fragments to be in contact or separated by a gap of less than about:
items.e: Contact healing needs a gap below about 0.01 mm with interfragmentary strain under 2%. Gaps up to about 0.8-1 mm heal by gap healing, where the gap fills with bone first and is then remodelled by cutting cones.

items.q: A transverse tibial fracture fixed under absolute stability is left with a stable gap of about 0.5 mm. This gap heals by:
o: Endochondral ossification through a cartilaginous external callus
Gap healing: bone first fills the gap at right angles to the long axis, then cutting cones remodel it longitudinally
Periosteal bridging callus alone, with no intracortical remodelling
items.e: Small stable gaps (under about 0.8-1 mm) heal by gap healing: the gap fills with transversely orientated bone, which Haversian remodelling then realigns along the long axis. No external callus forms because there is no motion.

items.q: The cartilaginous soft callus that forms about 2-3 weeks into secondary bone healing is made mainly of which collagen type?
items.e: Chondrocytes in the soft callus make type II collagen. Type I collagen appears later in woven and lamellar bone of the hard callus, and type X is produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes as the cartilage calcifies.

items.q: A transverse tibial fracture has a 1 mm gap, and the fragments move 0.5 mm relative to each other under load. By Perren's strain theory, the interfragmentary strain and the tissue that can form in this gap are:
o: 50%: only cartilage or fibrous tissue, not bone
items.e: Strain is the change in gap length divided by the original gap (0.5/1 = 50%). Bone forms only below about 10% strain, so at 10-100% strain only cartilage or fibrous tissue can survive.

items.q: According to Perren's strain theory, a multifragmentary diaphyseal fracture treated with relative stability tolerates more overall motion than a simple transverse fracture because:
o: The total displacement is shared among several fracture gaps, so strain at each gap is lower
The periosteum is always intact in comminuted fractures
Comminuted fractures release more BMP, which overrides strain
Small fragments act as a structural strut that removes all motion
items.e: Strain equals displacement divided by gap length. Spread across several gaps, the same movement produces lower strain at each one, which callus can tolerate. A simple fracture with a small gap concentrates all the motion in one place.

items.q: Bone's piezoelectric property is used to explain Wolff's law. In a bone loaded in bending, the electrical charge and tissue response on the concave (compression) side are:
items.e: On the compression side, the bone becomes electronegative and bone is laid down. On the tension side it becomes electropositive and bone is resorbed. Electrical stimulation devices therefore place the cathode (negative) at the fracture.

items.q: Giannoudis' 'diamond concept' of fracture healing adds which factor to the classic triad of osteogenic cells, an osteoconductive scaffold and osteoinductive growth factors?
items.e: The diamond concept holds that cells, scaffold and growth factors are not enough without an appropriate mechanical environment. Vascularity and host factors were later added to it.

items.q: Bone morphogenetic proteins induce osteoblastic differentiation by binding which receptors and signalling through which intracellular pathway?
o: Tyrosine kinase receptors, signalling through JAK-STAT
Nuclear hormone receptors acting directly on DNA
Serine-threonine kinase receptors, signalling through SMAD proteins
items.e: BMPs belong to the TGF-beta superfamily. They bind type I and II serine-threonine kinase receptors, which phosphorylate SMADs 1, 5 and 8. These SMADs then form complexes with SMAD4 and move into the nucleus.

items.q: In the BESTT trial of open tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing, adding rhBMP-2 (1.5 mg/mL) on an absorbable collagen sponge led to:
o: Fewer secondary interventions for delayed union or non-union and faster healing
More deep infections than standard care
No difference in any outcome compared with standard care
Higher rates of heterotopic ossification needing excision in most patients
items.e: BESTT found that 1.5 mg/mL rhBMP-2 lowered the risk of secondary interventions and sped fracture and wound healing, with fewer infections in Gustilo III injuries. This trial supported its FDA approval for open tibial fractures treated with a nail.

items.q: Off-label use of rhBMP-2 in anterior cervical spine fusion is particularly associated with which serious early complication?
o: Acute pseudogout of the facet joints
Severe prevertebral soft-tissue swelling with dysphagia and airway compromise
Spinal cord ischaemia from the BMP binding to vessels
items.e: rhBMP-2 causes an intense local inflammatory reaction. In the anterior neck this can lead to life-threatening swelling, dysphagia and airway obstruction, which prompted an FDA warning.

items.q: Which bone graft material is truly osteogenic, meaning it contains living cells that can form bone?
items.e: Only autograft and bone marrow aspirate carry viable osteoprogenitor cells. DBM is osteoinductive and osteoconductive, allograft is mainly osteoconductive (with some osteoinduction), and ceramics are osteoconductive only.

items.q: Demineralised bone matrix used as a graft extender is best described as:
o: Osteoconductive only, with no osteoinductive activity
Osteoinductive and osteoconductive, but not osteogenic
items.e: Acid demineralisation exposes the BMPs in the allograft matrix, which makes it osteoinductive (with variation between batches), and the collagen scaffold is osteoconductive. It contains no living cells.

items.q: A non-vascularised cortical autograft used to bridge a defect is mechanically at its weakest at about:
items.e: Cortical grafts are incorporated by osteoclastic resorption first and new bone formation second. This makes them porous and weak between about 6 weeks and 6 months, so they need protection then.

items.q: Cancellous autograft is incorporated faster than cortical autograft mainly because:
o: It must be fully resorbed before any new bone forms
New bone is laid directly onto its necrotic trabeculae before they are resorbed (appositional creeping substitution)
It has a higher elastic modulus
items.e: In cancellous graft, osteoblasts lay down new bone on the dead trabeculae, and resorption follows. The graft therefore gains strength early. Cortical graft is resorbed first and is slower.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a 9 cm segmental tibial defect after debridement of an infected non-union. The bed is scarred. Which reconstructive option is classically indicated?
items.e: Defects larger than about 6 cm, especially in a poorly vascularised or scarred bed, suit a vascularised fibula, which heals like a fracture and hypertrophies with loading. Bone transport or the Masquelet technique are alternatives. Non-structural fillers alone will fail.

items.q: In the Masquelet induced-membrane technique, the usual interval between placing the PMMA cement spacer and grafting the membrane-lined cavity is about:
items.e: The membrane that forms around the spacer is most active biologically (rich in VEGF, TGF-beta and BMP-2) at about 4-8 weeks. The spacer is then removed and the cavity is filled with cancellous autograft, often RIA graft.

items.q: In observational studies of tibial shaft fractures, which patient factor most consistently prolongs healing and increases the risk of non-union?
o: Early protected weight-bearing after stable nailing
Use of a reamed rather than unreamed nail
items.e: Nicotine causes vasoconstriction and inhibits osteoblasts, and smoking substantially raises the risks of delayed union, non-union and infection. Reaming and early weight-bearing after stable nailing tend to help union.

items.q: NSAIDs are thought to impair fracture healing mainly by:
o: Directly blocking the vitamin D receptor on osteoblasts
Inhibiting COX-2-dependent prostaglandin synthesis needed for mesenchymal cell differentiation and osteogenesis
Chelating calcium at the mineralisation front
items.e: COX-2 derived prostaglandins (especially PGE2) are needed in the early phase of healing. COX-2 inhibition delays healing in animal models. Short courses are probably safe, but they are best avoided in patients at high risk of non-union.

items.q: Before elective fracture surgery, which pair of results most strongly suggests malnutrition that may impair wound and fracture healing?
o: Serum albumin below 5.0 g/dL and lymphocyte count below 4,000 cells/mm³
Haemoglobin below 13 g/dL and platelets below 300,000/mm³
Serum albumin below 3.5 g/dL and total lymphocyte count below 1,500 cells/mm³
Serum calcium below 10 mg/dL and phosphate below 5 mg/dL
items.e: Serum albumin below 3.5 g/dL and total lymphocyte count below 1,500/mm³ are standard markers of malnutrition. Transferrin below 200 mg/dL is another. All are linked to wound complications and impaired healing.

items.q: Brinker and colleagues screened patients with unexplained non-unions and found metabolic or endocrine abnormalities in most of them. The commonest abnormality was:
items.e: In Brinker's series, vitamin D deficiency was by far the commonest abnormality. Calcium imbalance, hypogonadism and thyroid or parathyroid problems also occurred. An endocrine screen is part of the work-up of an unexplained non-union.

items.q: The TRUST trial (BMJ 2016) studied low-intensity pulsed ultrasound in adults with tibial shaft fractures treated by intramedullary nailing. It found that LIPUS:
o: Did not improve functional recovery or speed radiographic healing
Halved the time to radiographic union
Reduced non-union rates by about two-thirds
items.e: TRUST was a large sham-controlled trial. It showed no benefit of LIPUS for patient-important function or radiographic healing after tibial nailing, and it led guidelines to recommend against routine use.

items.q: A woman on long-term alendronate sustains a distal radius fracture. Compared with patients not on bisphosphonates, the effect on fracture healing is best described as:
o: Failure of callus formation and a high risk of non-union
A larger callus with delayed remodelling, but no clinically important delay in union
Faster union because of increased osteoblast activity
items.e: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts, so callus forms normally but remodels more slowly and is often larger. Clinical union is not significantly delayed, so they need not routinely be stopped after a fracture.

items.q: The US FDA definition of a fracture non-union, often used in trials, is a fracture that:
o: Is at least 9 months old and has shown no progressive signs of healing for 3 consecutive months
items.e: The FDA defines non-union as a fracture at least 9 months old with no visible progressive signs of healing for 3 months. In clinical practice, non-union is often diagnosed earlier when healing has clearly stalled.

items.q: Eleven months after plating of a humeral shaft fracture, radiographs show no callus, with rounded, pencilled and sclerotic bone ends and a gap. Infection markers are normal. The appropriate treatment is:
o: Exchange of the plate for a stiffer plate without grafting
Functional bracing for a further 3 months
Debridement to bleeding bone, autologous bone grafting and stable compression fixation
items.e: This is an atrophic non-union. Biology is poor, so the ends must be freshened to bleeding bone and graft or biologics added, along with stable fixation. Stability alone is enough only for hypertrophic non-unions.

items.q: In the Weber-Cech classification, an oligotrophic non-union is characterised by:
o: Little or no callus despite viable ends, usually from displacement or distraction of the fragments
Abundant 'elephant foot' callus that fails to bridge the gap
items.e: Oligotrophic non-unions are biologically viable (they take up isotope on bone scan) but form little callus, usually because the fragments are displaced or distracted. Treatment combines restoring contact and stability, often with graft.

items.q: A long-standing mobile tibial non-union is suspected to be a synovial pseudarthrosis. On a technetium bone scan, the characteristic finding is:
o: Uniformly increased uptake across the whole non-union
A cold cleft between two areas of increased uptake at the bone ends
Uniformly absent uptake over the whole bone segment
A single central hot spot in the non-union gap
items.e: In a synovial pseudarthrosis, the fluid-filled false joint does not take up tracer (a cold cleft) between hot, active bone ends. Treatment involves excision of the pseudocapsule, opening the canal, grafting and stable fixation.

items.q: Before revising an apparently aseptic tibial non-union, the most reliable way to identify low-grade infection is:
o: A swab from the skin over the fracture
Multiple deep tissue samples taken at surgery for culture (and histology)
The absence of a sinus on examination
items.e: Normal CRP or ESR does not exclude infection in a non-union. Several deep intraoperative samples, taken with separate instruments and cultured for longer, are the most reliable test. Superficial swabs are misleading.

items.q: Exchange reamed nailing has a high success rate for aseptic femoral shaft non-union. It is least likely to succeed in which situation?
o: A hypertrophic femoral shaft non-union after a small unreamed nail
An oligotrophic mid-shaft femoral non-union with good alignment
A transverse femoral shaft non-union with a broken locking screw
A tibial non-union with a large segmental bone defect
items.e: Exchange nailing works best in diaphyseal non-unions with good bone contact. Its results are poorer in the tibia when there is bone loss, and in metaphyseal non-unions, which usually need grafting, plating or bone transport.

items.q: In distraction osteogenesis by the Ilizarov method, the regenerate bone that forms in the distraction gap ossifies mainly by:
o: Endochondral ossification through a cartilage anlage
items.e: Under stable distraction at the correct rate, the regenerate forms by intramembranous ossification. Longitudinal collagen bundles mineralise directly from the centre outwards. Instability or overly fast distraction leads to cartilage and fibrous tissue instead.

items.q: During adult tibial lengthening with a circular frame, the healing (external fixation) index used to estimate frame time is typically about:
items.e: In adults, the frame usually stays on for roughly 1 month (about 30-45 days) per cm gained, covering both distraction and consolidation. Children consolidate faster.

items.q: During bone transport, distraction is carried out at 2 mm per day instead of the standard 1 mm per day. The most likely effect on the regenerate is:
o: A thin, poorly mineralised regenerate with fibrous tissue in the gap
No change, as the rate does not affect regenerate quality
items.e: Distraction that is too fast outpaces new vessel and bone formation. This gives a thin, hourglass or fibrous regenerate. Distraction that is too slow risks premature consolidation.

items.q: For distraction osteogenesis, an Ilizarov corticotomy is performed with a low-energy technique, for example with multiple drill holes and an osteotome rather than a power saw. The main reason is to:
o: Produce a perfectly transverse cut for compression
Preserve the periosteal and medullary blood supply and avoid thermal necrosis
items.e: Regenerate quality depends on a preserved periosteal (and, where possible, endosteal) blood supply. Low-energy division avoids heat necrosis and stripping, both of which impair new bone formation.

items.q: Tensioned thin wires in an Ilizarov circular frame are usually tensioned to about:
items.e: Thin (1.5-1.8 mm) wires are tensioned to roughly 90-130 kg, with less tension in children and soft bone. This gives stiffness in bending and torsion while allowing some axial micromotion.

items.q: Tensioned-wire circular frames are said to promote healing through a 'trampoline effect', meaning that they:
o: Hold the fracture completely rigid in all planes
Allow controlled axial micromotion while resisting shear, bending and torsion
Allow free rotation at the fracture
Shield the fracture completely from axial load
items.e: Tensioned wires let the bone move a little along its axis under cyclic loading, which stimulates callus. They resist the shear and torsion that would harm healing.

items.q: A 28-year-old has transverse mid-shaft fractures of both the radius and ulna. To fix them with 3.5 mm compression plates under absolute stability, AO recommends a minimum of how many cortices on each side of each fracture?
items.e: Diaphyseal forearm compression plating usually needs at least three bicortical screws (six cortices) in each main fragment. This gives the rigid, absolutely stable fixation needed for primary healing.

items.q: A long oblique fracture is fixed with a single independent lag screw. Which screw orientation gives maximum interfragmentary compression?
o: Perpendicular to the long axis of the bone
At 15 degrees to the long axis
items.e: Compression is greatest when the screw is perpendicular to the fracture, but a screw perpendicular to the bone resists axial shear better. A screw bisecting the two angles is a common compromise when only one screw can be used.

items.q: When a partially threaded cancellous screw is used as a lag screw by design across a metaphyseal fracture, interfragmentary compression is achieved only if:
o: All the threads lie beyond the fracture line in the far fragment
The threads cross the fracture line
The near cortex is tapped for the full thread diameter
items.e: Threads that cross the fracture engage both fragments and hold them apart, so no compression results. The smooth shank must span the fracture so that only the far fragment is pulled towards the screw head.

items.q: The pull-out strength of a bone screw in a given bone depends most on:
o: Its outer (major) diameter and thread depth
The design of the screw head
The length of the unthreaded shank
items.e: Pull-out strength rises with the volume of bone captured between the threads, which depends on outer diameter, thread depth and pitch, and bone density. Bending and fatigue strength depend on the core diameter.

items.q: In a Weber B oblique distal fibular fracture fixed with an interfragmentary lag screw and a one-third tubular plate, the plate is functioning as a:
items.e: The lag screw provides interfragmentary compression. The plate protects that fixation from bending and torsion, which is neutralisation. A posteriorly placed fibular plate would instead act as an antiglide plate.

items.q: A volar plate applied to a volar shearing (volar Barton) fracture of the distal radius works mainly as a:
items.e: In a volar Barton fracture, the volar rim fragment shears proximally and volarly with the carpus. A volar plate placed against it resists this shear and axial load, which is buttressing.

items.q: When plating a femoral shaft fracture, the plate should be placed on the tension side of the bone to act as a tension band. This is the:
items.e: Because the femur bows and body weight acts medially, the lateral cortex is under tension. A lateral plate turns tensile forces into compression at the medial cortex. A plate placed medially would be loaded in tension and fail.

items.q: In tension band wiring of a transverse patellar fracture, the tensile forces on the anterior surface are converted to compression at the articular surface during:
o: Isometric hamstring contraction with the knee extended
items.e: The wires lie on the anterior (tension) surface. When the knee flexes, the quadriceps and patellar tendon forces bend the patella over the femur, and the band converts this into compression at the articular side.

items.q: Compared with the original dynamic compression plate, the main biological advantage of the limited-contact DCP (LC-DCP) is that its undercut design:
o: Allows screws to lock into the plate at a fixed angle
Reduces the plate-bone contact area and so preserves periosteal blood flow
Removes the need for eccentric screw placement
items.e: Undercuts on the under-surface cut plate-bone contact, reducing periosteal damage and the cortical porosity seen beneath DCPs. They also give more even stiffness along the plate. Locking is a feature of LCP combi-holes.

items.q: When a screw is inserted eccentrically (in the load position) in one hole of a 4.5 mm dynamic compression plate, the fragment is displaced towards the fracture by about:
items.e: In a DCP hole, a screw placed eccentrically slides down the inclined hole as it is tightened. This moves the bone about 1 mm towards the fracture and compresses it. Another eccentric screw can add further compression.

items.q: When a straight compression plate is applied to a transverse diaphyseal fracture, it is slightly over-bent (pre-bent) beforehand mainly to:
o: Compress the far cortex as well as the near cortex, avoiding a gap opposite the plate
Make the plate stronger in fatigue
Reduce the number of screws needed
items.e: Tightening a straight plate compresses the cortex under the plate but opens a gap in the far cortex. Pre-bending so that the plate stands slightly off the bone at the fracture brings the far cortex into compression too.

items.q: A 78-year-old woman has a comminuted fracture just above a well-fixed knee arthroplasty, with a short, osteoporotic distal segment. The main mechanical reason a locking plate is preferred over a conventional plate is that it:
o: Compresses the fracture more than any other plate
Gives fixed-angle stability that does not rely on friction between plate and bone
Does not need any screws in the distal fragment
Is less stiff than a conventional plate
items.e: Conventional plates depend on screw purchase to press the plate onto bone. This often fails in osteoporotic or short segments. Locking screws form a fixed-angle construct (an internal fixator) that resists pull-out and toggling.

items.q: A simple transverse distal femoral shaft fracture is bridged with a long locking plate, with locking screws in every hole next to the fracture. At 9 months there is little callus and the plate has broken. The most likely mechanical cause is:
o: Too much motion from too few screws
Galvanic corrosion between the plate and screws
A construct that was too stiff, with a short working length, which suppressed callus
Stress shielding of the whole femur
items.e: Locking constructs with a short working length are very stiff. For a simple fracture this keeps strain too low for callus but too high for primary healing, so the plate fails by fatigue. Longer working lengths, far-cortical locking or dynamic locking screws make the construct more flexible.

items.q: For bridge plating of a comminuted diaphyseal fracture, the AO guideline for the ratio of plate length to fracture length (plate span ratio) is at least about:
items.e: Long plates spread the load over more bone and reduce pull-out forces on the screws. A plate span ratio of over 2-3 for comminuted fractures (more for simple ones) is recommended, with low screw density.

items.q: In bridge plating, 'screw density' (the number of screws inserted divided by the number of holes in the plate) should ideally be:
items.e: Filling fewer than half the holes, with screws spread towards the ends of the plate and near the fracture left empty, reduces stiffness and stress concentration. This favours callus formation.

items.q: A 5-year-old with septic arthritis of the hip lies with the hip held in which position, and why?
o: Flexion, abduction and external rotation, because capsular volume is greatest
Extension, adduction and internal rotation, because the capsule is most relaxed
Full extension and neutral rotation, because the ligaments are slack
Flexion, adduction and internal rotation, because the psoas is spasmodic
items.e: The child holds the hip in flexion, abduction and external rotation, the position of maximum intracapsular volume and least pressure; flexion-adduction-internal rotation is the posture of posterior dislocation.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Why is septic arthritis of the hip in a child regarded as a surgical emergency in particular?
o: The hip cannot be aspirated under ultrasound
Raised intracapsular pressure can tamponade the retinacular vessels and cause femoral head AVN
Antibiotics do not penetrate the hip joint
The hip capsule is the commonest source of PVL toxin
items.e: The femoral head blood supply runs within the capsule along the neck; tense effusion can occlude it, adding avascular necrosis to enzymatic cartilage destruction.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In a child aged 6 years, metaphyseal osteomyelitis usually spreads to form a subperiosteal abscess rather than entering the epiphysis because:
o: Transphyseal vessels carry pus away from the epiphysis
The periosteum is firmly bound to the cortex
The physis acts as a barrier and the thick periosteum is loosely attached
The medullary canal is filled with fatty marrow that resists spread
items.e: After about 18 months the physis blocks epiphyseal spread, and the loosely attached paediatric periosteum is easily lifted; in adults the periosteum is adherent so infection spreads within the canal.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Following effective treatment of acute osteomyelitis in a child, the C-reactive protein typically:
o: Peaks at 2 weeks and normalises after 6 weeks
Remains raised for 3 months regardless of response
Does not rise until radiographic changes appear
Peaks at about 48 hours and returns to normal within about a week
items.e: CRP rises within 6-8 hours, peaks around 2 days and falls quickly with effective therapy, so it is the best marker of response; ESR peaks later and takes weeks to normalise.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Compared with CRP, the ESR in childhood acute osteomyelitis:
o: Peaks around days 3-5 and may stay raised for 3-4 weeks despite effective treatment
Normalises within 48 hours of starting antibiotics
Is never raised in Staphylococcus aureus infection
Rises before CRP and falls before it
items.e: The ESR rises and falls slowly, so it is a poor marker of early response; CRP is preferred for monitoring and for deciding on oral switch.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In children with acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, blood cultures are positive in approximately:
o: Every case caused by S. aureus
items.e: Blood cultures identify the organism in only about a third to a half of cases, so direct aspiration of bone or joint is valuable.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Using the Kocher criteria for an irritable hip, a child with exactly two of the four predictors has a predicted probability of septic arthritis of approximately:
items.e: Kocher's probabilities were about 0.2%, 3%, 40%, 93% and 99.6% for 0-4 predictors; two criteria represent intermediate risk needing aspiration.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In Caird's prospective study of the irritable hip, which single variable was the best independent predictor of septic arthritis?
items.e: Caird added CRP above 2 mg/dL to Kocher's criteria and found fever above 38.5 C to be the strongest single predictor.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 4-year-old with an irritable hip and a low-grade fever has a hip ultrasound showing no effusion. What does this mean for the diagnosis of septic arthritis of the hip?
o: It makes septic arthritis of the hip very unlikely
It confirms transient synovitis and excludes osteomyelitis
It is uninformative, as effusions are seen only after 10 days
It confirms septic arthritis because pus is echogenic
items.e: The absence of a hip effusion on ultrasound makes septic arthritis very unlikely, although adjacent osteomyelitis of the femur or pelvis must still be considered.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Empirical treatment of confirmed Kingella kingae septic arthritis should not rely on which antibiotics, to which the organism is typically resistant?
items.e: K. kingae is usually susceptible to beta-lactams but intrinsically resistant to glycopeptides and often to clindamycin, so MRSA-directed regimens alone may fail.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Kingella kingae reaches the bones and joints of toddlers mainly from which reservoir?
o: The oropharynx, often after a viral upper respiratory infection
items.e: K. kingae colonises the oropharynx of young children and invades during viral stomatitis or URTI, which explains the typical history and the 6 months-4 years age group.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In the Finnish randomised trial of childhood septic arthritis by Peltola and colleagues, a total antibiotic duration of about 10 days compared with 30 days was:
o: Associated with twice the rate of recurrence
Associated with more femoral head AVN
Effective only when combined with arthrotomy of every joint
items.e: Peltola's group showed a 10-day course, with a short IV phase and early oral switch, was as effective as 30 days for uncomplicated paediatric septic arthritis.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 7-year-old with acute tibial osteomyelitis started on IV cefazolin 3 days ago is now afebrile with less pain. Which laboratory change supports switching to oral antibiotics?
o: CRP has fallen by about 50% from its peak
White cell count has risen to 15,000/mm3
items.e: Current practice switches to high-dose oral therapy after a few days once the child is clinically improving and CRP has fallen substantially (around half); the ESR lags behind.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In which child with acute osteomyelitis is a prolonged antibiotic course of 6 weeks or more most appropriate?
o: A 7-year-old with MSSA distal femoral osteomyelitis improving within 48 hours
A neonate with multifocal MRSA infection
A 9-year-old whose CRP normalised within a week
A 5-year-old with Kingella infection responding promptly
items.e: Longer courses are reserved for neonates, MRSA, complicated, multifocal, pelvic or spinal infection and slow responders; uncomplicated AHO needs about 3-4 weeks.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 9-year-old with distal tibial osteomyelitis has an ultrasound showing a 6 mm subperiosteal fluid collection. The next step is:
o: Continue IV antibiotics and repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks
Surgical drainage of the abscess with drilling of the cortex
Apply a long-leg cast for 6 weeks
items.e: A subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess is an indication for surgical drainage; the cortex is drilled to decompress the metaphysis, and antibiotics are continued.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: During surgical drainage of a child's metaphyseal osteomyelitis, the cortex is drilled mainly to:
o: Obtain bone marrow for haematological assessment
Insert a drain into the physis
Decompress intramedullary pus and relieve intraosseous pressure
items.e: Drilling the metaphyseal cortex releases pus under pressure within the medulla and improves antibiotic delivery to ischaemic bone.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: After drainage of extensive femoral diaphyseal osteomyelitis in a 6-year-old, the radiographs show a long segment of destroyed cortex. Which complication should be specifically protected against?
o: Pathological fracture, with a cast or splint
items.e: Extensive osteomyelitis weakens bone and pathological fracture is a recognised complication, so the limb is protected with a cast until the involucrum and cortex are sound.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In chronic osteomyelitis of a child's tibia with a large sequestrum, sequestrectomy should be timed:
o: Within 24 hours of diagnosis, before involucrum develops
After a strong involucrum has formed to support the limb
Never; sequestra in children always resorb
items.e: Removing the sequestrum before the involucrum can bear load risks fracture or a segmental defect, so surgeons wait for a mature involucrum unless sepsis demands earlier surgery.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: The Choi classification is used to describe:
o: Sequelae of septic arthritis of the hip in infancy
items.e: Choi (and Hunka) classified the residual deformities of the femoral head and neck after neonatal or infantile septic hip, guiding reconstruction.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: The Roberts classification describes:
o: Sequelae of septic arthritis of the hip
Subacute osteomyelitis by location and radiographic appearance
items.e: Roberts classified subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess and related forms) by site and appearance, some types mimicking tumours and needing biopsy.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 10-year-old has recurrent episodes of bone pain affecting the medial clavicle, distal tibial metaphysis and a vertebra, with palmoplantar pustulosis. Bone cultures are sterile. First-line treatment is:
items.e: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis is an autoinflammatory, sterile condition; NSAIDs are first line, with bisphosphonates or anti-TNF agents for refractory disease, not prolonged antibiotics.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Which imaging study is most useful to map the extent of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, including clinically silent lesions?
items.e: Whole-body MRI (STIR) detects multiple, often asymptomatic, lesions and avoids radiation, supporting the diagnosis and monitoring of CRMO.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 2-year-old suddenly refuses to walk or sit and prefers lying down, with mild fever and raised CRP. MRI shows narrowing of the L3-L4 disc space with adjacent endplate oedema. Management is usually:
o: Urgent open biopsy and anterior debridement
Anti-staphylococcal antibiotics with rest or bracing; biopsy rarely needed
items.e: Childhood discitis is usually treated empirically with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics and rest or a brace; biopsy is reserved for atypical cases or failure to respond.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Why does discitis occur as a primary disc infection in toddlers but rarely in adults?
o: Toddlers have an open neural arch
The nucleus pulposus is calcified in children
Adults have no Batson venous plexus
The disc is vascularised in young children
items.e: Blood vessels penetrate the disc in early childhood, allowing primary haematogenous seeding; in adults the disc is avascular and infection begins in the vertebral endplate.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 13-year-old has fever, buttock pain and a limp. Hip movements are relatively free, but pain is reproduced by flexion, abduction and external rotation of the hip with pressure on the opposite pelvis. The most likely site of infection is the:
items.e: Pyogenic sacroiliitis presents with buttock or groin pain and a positive FABER (Patrick) test while hip rotation is relatively painless; MRI confirms it.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 10-year-old develops forefoot osteochondritis from a Pseudomonas aeruginosa nail-puncture wound through a sports shoe. Optimal management is:
o: Surgical debridement plus an anti-pseudomonal antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin
items.e: Pseudomonas osteochondritis usually requires surgical debridement of infected cartilage and bone combined with ciprofloxacin or ceftazidime; flucloxacillin has no anti-pseudomonal activity.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: An 8-month-old with sickle cell anaemia has painful, symmetrical swelling of the hands and feet with low-grade fever. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) in infants with sickle cell disease is due to bone infarction and is often the first manifestation of the disease.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: When osteomyelitis is suspected in a child with sickle cell disease, the empirical antibiotic regimen should specifically cover:
o: Salmonella, for example with ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin
