items.e: Salmonella is disproportionately common in sickle cell disease, so empirical therapy combines anti-staphylococcal activity with Salmonella cover such as a third-generation cephalosporin.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Septic arthritis due to Haemophilus influenzae in young children has become rare mainly because of:
items.e: Before Hib conjugate vaccines, H. influenzae type b was a leading cause of septic arthritis in children under 2 years; it is now seen mainly in unvaccinated children.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 3-year-old in India has a painless, fusiform swelling of a proximal phalanx; radiographs show an expanded, ballooned diaphysis with thin cortices. This is called:
items.e: Spina ventosa is tuberculous dactylitis, in which granulation tissue expands the short tubular bone like a balloon of air; it is commonest in young children.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In suspected childhood osteoarticular tuberculosis, the advantage of GeneXpert (CBNAAT) on tissue or pus over culture is that it:
o: Distinguishes M. bovis BCG from all other mycobacteria by colony morphology
Is the only test that shows caseating granulomas
Gives a rapid result and detects rifampicin resistance
items.e: GeneXpert MTB/RIF is a cartridge PCR giving results within hours and detecting rpoB mutations for rifampicin resistance, whereas culture takes weeks.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: The commonest cause of an acutely painful hip with limp in a child aged 3-8 years, often following a viral illness and resolving within 1-2 weeks, is:
items.e: Transient synovitis is the commonest cause of acute hip pain in this age group; children are usually well, can bear some weight and have near-normal markers.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In an endemic area, a 9-year-old has a large, relatively painless knee effusion with little fever, weeks after a tick bite and a spreading target-shaped rash. The diagnosis is best confirmed by:
o: Borrelia serology (ELISA with Western blot) or synovial PCR
items.e: Lyme arthritis causes a large effusion with less pain and fever than bacterial septic arthritis; diagnosis is serological with two-tier testing or PCR of joint fluid.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 3-week-old in the NICU, who had an umbilical venous catheter, is irritable and does not move the left arm. There is no fever. The most likely explanation is:
o: Osteomyelitis or septic arthritis of the shoulder causing pseudoparalysis
items.e: Neonatal osteoarticular infection often presents with pseudoparalysis and few systemic signs; the line is a risk factor, and new-onset reduced movement differs from a birth palsy present from delivery.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A premature infant with a long-term central venous catheter and parenteral nutrition develops multifocal osteomyelitis with negative routine cultures. Besides bacteria, which pathogen should be considered?
items.e: NICU infants with central lines, prematurity and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure are at risk of Candida osteoarticular infection, often multifocal.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Neonatal osteoarticular infection differs from that in older children because it is more often:
o: Accompanied by high fever and toxicity
Multifocal, with combined osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
items.e: Neonates show few systemic signs, frequently have multiple sites, and transphyseal vessels allow metaphyseal infection to involve the epiphysis and joint.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: On a Tc-99m bone scan in a child with severe acute osteomyelitis, a photopenic (cold) area at the affected metaphysis usually indicates:
o: Compromised blood flow from raised intraosseous pressure or thrombosis, a sign of severe infection
items.e: Severe infection can render bone avascular, giving a cold defect; such cold osteomyelitis has been associated with more aggressive disease and a greater need for surgery.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: The earliest finding on plain radiographs in acute osteomyelitis of a child's femur is usually:
o: Deep soft-tissue swelling with displacement or loss of fat planes
Metaphyseal lysis with a sclerotic rim
items.e: Within the first few days only deep soft-tissue swelling and blurring of muscle fat planes may be seen; periosteal reaction and lysis take about 10-14 days.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 6-year-old with acute osteomyelitis grows an erythromycin-resistant, clindamycin-susceptible S. aureus. Before using clindamycin, the laboratory should perform which test?
items.e: Erythromycin-resistant strains may carry inducible erm-mediated resistance that causes clindamycin failure; the D-zone test detects this.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In a region where community MRSA is prevalent, empirical IV treatment of severe acute osteomyelitis in a child should include:
o: Vancomycin (or clindamycin where local resistance is low)
items.e: Where MRSA rates are significant, empirical cover adds vancomycin or clindamycin to anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam therapy until cultures and susceptibilities are known.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 4-year-old has a painful limp, fever and pain on hip movement, but ultrasound shows no hip effusion. MRI shows an abscess in the obturator internus muscle. This condition is:
o: Pelvic pyomyositis mimicking septic arthritis of the hip
items.e: Pyomyositis of the obturator internus or externus (usually S. aureus) can closely mimic a septic hip; MRI is diagnostic and an absent effusion is a clue.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 12-year-old has fever and a diaphyseal femoral lesion with permeative destruction and lamellated periosteal reaction; both Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis are considered. During biopsy, the safest practice is:
o: Send tissue for culture only, as infection is commoner
Send tissue for both histology and culture
Avoid biopsy and treat with 6 weeks of antibiotics
Perform an excisional resection of the lesion
items.e: Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis may look alike clinically and radiologically, so the rule is to culture every biopsy and biopsy every culture.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 14-year-old has a well-defined lytic lesion with a sclerotic rim in the proximal tibial epiphysis. Subacute osteomyelitis is one possibility; which tumour is the main differential in this location?
items.e: An epiphyseal lucency in a skeletally immature patient suggests chondroblastoma or an epiphyseal Brodie abscess; non-ossifying fibroma is metaphyseal and cortical.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: After arthrotomy and washout of a septic knee in a 6-year-old, the best postoperative regimen for the joint is:
o: Strict bed rest until ESR normalises
Brief splinting for comfort followed by early mobilisation
items.e: Short splintage relieves pain, but early movement helps cartilage nutrition and prevents stiffness once symptoms settle.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 4-year-old with Kingella kingae septic arthritis of the knee typically shows which pattern of investigations?
o: Mild illness, normal or slightly raised CRP and WBC, and a lower synovial cell count
High fever, WBC above 25,000/mm3 and synovial WBC above 150,000/mm3
Positive Gram stain in most cases
Growth on routine agar plates within 24 hours
items.e: Kingella causes a milder picture with modest inflammatory markers and lower synovial counts, so the Kocher criteria perform poorly; PCR is the key test.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In a 2-year-old, a 'septic hip' with an associated adjacent proximal femoral metaphyseal abscess is commonly encountered because:
o: The hip capsule inserts distal to the lesser trochanter
Transphyseal vessels and the intracapsular metaphysis allow spread between bone and joint
Infants have a non-ossified femoral head that resists infection
Kingella preferentially infects bone rather than joint
items.e: In infants and young children, infection can pass between metaphysis, epiphysis and joint, and the proximal femoral metaphysis lies within the capsule, so osteomyelitis and septic arthritis coexist.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A child is started on first-line antituberculous therapy for tuberculous arthritis of the knee. Which drug requires monitoring of visual acuity and colour vision?
items.e: Ethambutol can cause dose-related optic neuritis, so visual acuity and red-green colour vision are checked; isoniazid causes neuropathy and hepatotoxicity.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: An 11-year-old boy has had acute tibial osteomyelitis treated successfully. Which late complication is the main reason for follow-up until skeletal maturity?
o: Physeal arrest causing limb-length discrepancy or angular deformity
items.e: Infection adjacent to the physis can cause partial or complete growth arrest, so children are followed to detect leg-length discrepancy and angular deformity.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In septic arthritis of the knee in an otherwise healthy 7-year-old, which drainage method is an acceptable alternative to open arthrotomy?
o: No drainage, antibiotics only, in every case
items.e: Unlike the hip, superficial joints such as the knee can be adequately drained arthroscopically (or, in selected cases, by repeated aspiration) with antibiotics.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: The most common site of a solitary osteochondroma is the:
items.e: Osteochondromas arise from the fastest-growing physes, so the region around the knee (distal femur, then proximal tibia) and the proximal humerus are the commonest sites.

items.q: On radiographs, a pedunculated metaphyseal osteochondroma typically:
o: Points away from the adjacent joint
Crosses the physis into the epiphysis
items.e: The stalk grows away from the joint as the physis moves away with growth; lesions pointing towards the joint suggest other entities such as metachondromatosis.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a long-standing knee osteochondroma that has recently become a soft, enlarging swelling. MRI shows a thin cartilage cap with a fluid-filled sac over it. The most likely explanation is:
o: Exostosis bursata (adventitial bursa over the cap)
items.e: An adventitial bursa can form over the cap and enlarge, mimicking growth; a thin cap and simple fluid argue against malignant transformation, which shows a thick (>1.5-2 cm) cap.

items.q: An osteochondroma of the proximal fibular neck in a teenager is particularly likely to cause:
o: Common peroneal nerve palsy with foot drop
Tibial nerve palsy with claw toes
items.e: The common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck and is easily compressed by an exostosis there; popliteal vascular complications are linked to posterior distal femoral lesions.

items.q: The approximate lifetime risk of chondrosarcoma developing in a patient with hereditary multiple exostoses is:
items.e: Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma arises in roughly 1-5% of HME patients, higher than the under 1% risk of a solitary osteochondroma but well below the risk in Ollier disease.

items.q: Hereditary multiple exostoses is inherited in which pattern?
items.e: HME is autosomal dominant (EXT1 or EXT2) with near-complete penetrance; about 10% of cases are new mutations.

items.q: The typical proximal femoral morphology in hereditary multiple exostoses is:
o: Coxa vara with a short neck
Coxa breva with a retroverted head
Normal neck-shaft angle with a narrow neck
Coxa valga with a broad femoral neck
items.e: Metaphyseal remodelling failure widens the femoral neck, and coxa valga with acetabular dysplasia can lead to hip subluxation in HME.

items.q: The approximate lifetime risk of malignant transformation of enchondromas to chondrosarcoma in Ollier disease is:
items.e: Large series report chondrosarcoma in roughly a quarter to a half of Ollier patients (about 40% in some), with risk highest for lesions of the pelvis and long bones.

items.q: A characteristic feature of the distribution of lesions in Ollier disease is:
o: Involvement of the skull vault only
items.e: Ollier enchondromatosis tends to affect one side of the body, causing limb shortening and angular deformity; the hands and feet are often involved.

items.q: Conventional primary central chondrosarcoma most commonly presents at what age?
items.e: Conventional chondrosarcoma is a tumour of middle-aged and older adults; a central cartilage tumour in a child is rarely malignant, whereas mesenchymal and clear cell variants affect younger patients.

items.q: When biopsying a suspected chondrosarcoma, the biopsy tract must be planned so that it can be excised with the tumour because:
o: Cartilage tumours are highly vascular and bleed
The biopsy usually overgrades the tumour
Frozen section is mandatory for diagnosis
Cartilage tumour cells implant readily and seed the tract
items.e: Chondrosarcoma cells survive and grow in soft tissue, so contamination causes implantation recurrence; the tract is placed in the line of the definitive incision and excised en bloc.

items.q: The classical histological grading of conventional chondrosarcoma into grades 1–3, based on cellularity, nuclear atypia and mitoses, was described by:
items.e: Evans grading (1977) is still the basis of chondrosarcoma grading and predicts metastasis; Enneking is a surgical staging system and Huvos grades chemotherapy-induced necrosis in osteosarcoma.

items.q: In dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, the high-grade non-cartilaginous component is most often:
items.e: A low-grade cartilage tumour abruptly juxtaposed with a high-grade sarcoma, commonly UPS or osteosarcoma (sometimes fibrosarcoma), defines dedifferentiation.

items.q: Detection of the same IDH1 mutation in both the cartilaginous and high-grade components of a dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma indicates:
o: A collision of two unrelated tumours
A common clonal origin of the two components
That the tumour arose from an osteochondroma
items.e: Shared IDH mutations show that both components derive from one precursor clone; osteochondroma-derived peripheral tumours usually lack IDH mutations.

items.q: IDH1/IDH2 mutations, typical of central cartilage tumours, are usually absent in:
o: Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma arising from an osteochondroma
items.e: Peripheral chondrosarcomas arising in osteochondromas relate to EXT1/EXT2 loss, whereas enchondromas, central chondrosarcomas and Ollier/Maffucci lesions carry IDH mutations.

items.q: Chondromyxoid fibroma is characterised by recurrent rearrangement or promoter swapping involving which gene?
items.e: GRM1 activation is found in most chondromyxoid fibromas; H3F3A is typical of giant cell tumour, COL1A1-PDGFB of dermatofibrosarcoma and USP6 of aneurysmal bone cyst.

items.q: In Milgram's classification of primary synovial chondromatosis, phase II refers to:
o: Active intrasynovial disease together with free loose bodies
Free loose bodies with quiescent synovium
items.e: Phase I is active synovial disease without loose bodies, phase II is transitional with both, and phase III has loose bodies with inactive synovium; synovectomy matters most in phases I and II.

items.q: Compared with primary synovial chondromatosis, loose bodies in secondary synovial chondromatosis due to osteoarthritis are typically:
o: Fewer, of varying size and with concentric laminated growth rings
items.e: Secondary osteochondral bodies arise from degenerate joints, grow by layered accretion and vary in size; primary disease produces numerous uniform nodules from metaplastic synovium.

items.q: Chondrosarcoma arising in the short tubular bones of the hand, compared with long-bone chondrosarcoma of the same grade, typically:
o: Rarely metastasises and has a better prognosis
items.e: Hand chondrosarcomas often look worrying histologically but behave indolently, with local recurrence more likely than metastasis; ray or digital resection usually suffices.

items.q: In adults, the most common primary malignant tumour of the anterior chest wall and sternum is:
items.e: Chondrosarcoma predominates in the costochondral junctions and sternum of adults; Ewing sarcoma is the usual chest wall malignancy in children (Askin tumour).

items.q: After intralesional curettage of an atypical cartilaginous tumour of the distal femur, which local adjuvant is commonly used to reduce recurrence?
items.e: Cryotherapy or phenol extends the margin of curettage before grafting or cementing; steroid and marrow injections are used for unicameral bone cysts, and denosumab is systemic therapy for giant cell tumour.

items.q: Extraskeletal (soft-tissue) chondroma most commonly arises in the:
items.e: Soft-tissue chondromas are small, well-defined lesions of the hands and feet, especially the fingers; they are benign and treated by marginal excision.

items.q: Metachondromatosis, with multiple osteochondromas pointing towards the joints and enchondromas, is caused by mutations in:
items.e: Metachondromatosis is an autosomal dominant disorder due to loss-of-function PTPN11 mutations; EXT1 causes HME, IDH1 Ollier/Maffucci and GNAS fibrous dysplasia.

items.q: The approximate 5-year survival for grade 1 chondrosarcoma (atypical cartilaginous tumour) is:
items.e: Low-grade cartilage malignancies rarely metastasise and survival is about 90%, falling substantially for grade 3 and to 10-25% for dedifferentiated tumours.

items.q: Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma accounts for approximately what proportion of all chondrosarcomas?
items.e: Roughly one in ten chondrosarcomas is dedifferentiated; it typically affects older adults in the femur, pelvis and humerus and carries a poor prognosis.

items.q: Malignant transformation of an osteochondroma is more likely when the lesion is located in the:
items.e: Proximal, axial-girdle sites such as the pelvis, scapula and proximal femur have higher rates of secondary chondrosarcoma, and these lesions are also hard to monitor clinically.

items.q: A juxtacortical cartilage tumour of the femoral metaphysis is being evaluated. Which size favours periosteal chondrosarcoma over periosteal chondroma?
o: Size is irrelevant to the distinction
items.e: Periosteal chondromas are usually under 3 cm, while lesions of 5 cm or more favour periosteal chondrosarcoma, which needs wide excision.

items.q: In hereditary multiple exostoses, the region most frequently involved is the:
items.e: HME lesions are often bilateral and commonest around the knee, followed by the proximal humerus, forearm and ankle; the skull is spared as it forms by intramembranous ossification.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a mildly symptomatic distal femoral osteochondroma near the physis. When feasible, excision is preferably deferred until near skeletal maturity because:
o: The lesion always disappears by adulthood
Recurrence and physeal injury are more likely during active growth
Malignant change is common in children
Excision requires an open physis for healing
items.e: Excising an osteochondroma close to an active physis risks physeal damage and recurrence from residual perichondrium; earlier surgery is reserved for significant symptoms such as nerve or vascular compression.

items.q: In selective ligament-sectioning studies (Butler et al.), the ACL provides approximately what share of the total restraint to anterior tibial translation at 30 and 90 degrees of knee flexion?
items.e: The ACL is the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation, contributing about 85% of the restraining force; the collaterals, capsule and iliotibial band supply the remainder.

items.q: The tibial attachment of the ACL lies between the tibial spines and blends with which structure, which can be damaged if the tibial tunnel is reamed too laterally?
o: Posterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Anterior horn (root) of the lateral meniscus
Posterior horn of the medial meniscus
items.e: The ACL tibial footprint is intimately related to the anterior root of the lateral meniscus; tunnel reaming that strays laterally can injure this root. The posterior horns and meniscofemoral ligaments are posterior structures.

items.q: On the medial wall of the lateral femoral condyle, which bony landmark separates the femoral footprints of the anteromedial and posterolateral bundles of the ACL?
items.e: The lateral bifurcate ridge runs perpendicular to the lateral intercondylar ridge and divides the AM and PL bundle footprints. The lateral intercondylar (resident's) ridge marks the anterior limit of the whole footprint.

items.q: The mechanoreceptors in the ACL, thought to contribute to proprioception, are supplied mainly by:
o: Posterior articular branches of the tibial nerve
Recurrent branch of the common peroneal nerve
Infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve
items.e: The ACL is innervated by posterior articular branches of the tibial nerve, which supply mechanoreceptors (Ruffini, Pacinian, Golgi-like endings). The infrapatellar saphenous branch supplies skin over the anterior knee.

items.q: A 24-year-old footballer twists his knee and has a tense effusion within 2 hours. Aspiration yields blood without fat droplets. What is the most likely structural injury?
items.e: About 70% of acute traumatic haemarthroses in adults are due to ACL rupture. Grade I MCL sprains are extra-articular and do not cause haemarthrosis; patellar dislocation and peripheral meniscal tears are less frequent causes.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of ACL ruptures occur through a non-contact mechanism such as cutting, deceleration or landing?
items.e: Most ACL injuries (about 70%) are non-contact, occurring during deceleration, cutting, pivoting or landing with the knee near extension in valgus and rotation.

items.q: In an awake patient with an acute ACL tear, the anterior drawer test at 90 degrees is less sensitive than the Lachman test partly because:
o: The posterior horn of the medial meniscus wedges against the femoral condyle and blocks anterior translation
The posterolateral bundle is tight at 90 degrees
The iliotibial band lies anterior to the axis of rotation at 90 degrees
The MCL is the primary restraint to anterior translation at 90 degrees
items.e: At 90 degrees the posterior horn of the medial meniscus acts as a 'doorstop' and hamstring guarding resists translation, so the drawer is often falsely negative acutely. The MCL is only a secondary restraint to anterior translation.

items.q: A pivot shift may be falsely negative in an ACL-deficient knee when there is an associated:
o: Posterior root tear of the lateral meniscus
items.e: The pivot shift needs an intact MCL (medial hinge) and iliotibial band to produce subluxation and reduction; a complete MCL tear abolishes it. A Segond fracture, lateral root tear and high slope all tend to increase the pivot.

items.q: Which structured neuromuscular warm-up programme has been shown in randomised trials to reduce lower-limb injuries, including ACL ruptures, in footballers?
items.e: FIFA 11+ (like the PEP programme) combines running, strength, plyometric and balance work and reduces non-contact ACL injury. Alfredson is for Achilles tendinopathy, Thrower's Ten for the shoulder and McKenzie for the back.

items.q: The notch width index, a low value of which is associated with non-contact ACL injury, is defined as the ratio of:
o: Intercondylar notch width to bicondylar width at the level of the popliteal groove
Lateral femoral condyle width to medial femoral condyle width
items.e: The notch width index (Souryal) is notch width divided by bicondylar width at the popliteal groove on a tunnel view; values under about 0.20 indicate notch stenosis, which is more common in female athletes.

items.q: A Segond fracture, which is strongly associated with ACL rupture, is an avulsion from the lateral tibial plateau by:
items.e: The Segond fragment is a lateral capsular avulsion at the attachment of the anterolateral ligament, just posterior to Gerdy's tubercle. The LCL, biceps and popliteofibular ligament insert on the fibula (arcuate fracture).

items.q: Which is a recognised secondary (indirect) MRI sign of complete ACL rupture?
o: Bone bruising of the medial patellar facet and lateral femoral condyle
Anterior translation of the tibia by more than about 5-7 mm relative to the lateral femoral condyle
Posterior translation of the medial tibial plateau
items.e: Anterior tibial translation, an uncovered posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, a buckled PCL and pivot-shift bone bruises are secondary signs. Medial patellar facet and lateral condylar bruising indicates lateral patellar dislocation.

items.q: Which ligament is most commonly injured together with the ACL?
items.e: The MCL is the most frequently associated ligament injury in ACL rupture, reflecting the common valgus-rotation mechanism; most associated MCL injuries heal non-operatively.

items.q: After ACL reconstruction with a bone-patellar tendon-bone graft, bone-to-bone healing of the bone plugs in the tunnels is usually achieved by about:
items.e: Bone plugs heal in their tunnels by about 6-8 weeks, faster than soft-tissue (hamstring) graft-to-tunnel healing, which needs about 8-12 weeks.

items.q: Registry and cohort data show higher revision rates after hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction when the graft diameter is less than about:
items.e: Hamstring grafts under 8 mm diameter are associated with higher failure, especially in young patients; options include adding a third tendon, tripling/quintupling or using another graft.

items.q: Allograft ACL reconstruction has higher failure rates in young active patients, particularly when the allograft has been sterilised with gamma irradiation in doses above about:
items.e: Irradiation above about 2.5 Mrad damages collagen cross-links and weakens the graft; low-dose or non-irradiated, fresh-frozen grafts are preferred, and allografts are best avoided in patients under about 25.

items.q: Tunnel widening after ACL reconstruction is most typical of:
o: Hamstring soft-tissue grafts with cortical suspensory fixation
BPTB grafts fixed with aperture interference screws
Quadriceps bone-block grafts fixed with interference screws
items.e: Graft motion within the tunnel ('bungee' and 'windshield-wiper' effects) with distant suspensory fixation of soft-tissue grafts causes tunnel enlargement; bone-block grafts with aperture fixation widen less.

items.q: A late complication of BPTB autograft harvest that can cause patellofemoral pain and restricted flexion is:
o: Patella baja from shortening of the patellar tendon
items.e: Scarring and shortening of the harvested patellar tendon can produce patella baja (infera), with patellofemoral pain and loss of motion. Patellar fracture and tendon rupture are the other specific harvest-site risks.

items.q: Compared with anatomic single-bundle ACL reconstruction, double-bundle reconstruction has:
o: Halved the graft failure rate in all trials
Not shown a consistent clinical advantage in patient-reported outcomes or graft failure
items.e: Despite slightly better rotational laxity in some studies, double-bundle reconstruction has not shown consistent clinical superiority over anatomic single-bundle reconstruction and is technically more demanding.

items.q: If the tibial tunnel in ACL reconstruction is placed too posteriorly, the most likely consequence is:
o: Roof impingement in extension with a cyclops lesion
A graft that is tight in flexion and limits flexion
A vertical graft that controls rotation poorly and may impinge on the PCL
Injury to the anterior root of the lateral meniscus
items.e: A posterior tibial tunnel makes the graft vertical, giving poor rotational control and possible PCL impingement. An anterior tibial tunnel causes roof impingement; an anterior femoral tunnel makes the graft tight in flexion.

items.q: When drilling the femoral tunnel in ACL reconstruction, placing the tunnel too far posteriorly (too deep) risks:
o: Injury to the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve
Blow-out of the posterior femoral cortex, compromising interference screw fixation
items.e: Back-wall blow-out removes the posterior cortex against which an interference screw gains purchase; the surgeon may redirect the tunnel or switch to cortical suspensory fixation.

items.q: Which intraoperative measure has been associated in large cohort studies with a marked reduction in septic arthritis after hamstring ACL reconstruction?
o: Soaking (wrapping) the graft in vancomycin solution before implantation
Leaving a suction drain for 48 hours
items.e: Pre-soaking the graft in vancomycin (for example 5 mg/mL) has been associated with a large fall in post-ACLR infection in several series; it is now widely adopted.

items.q: The most common organism isolated in septic arthritis after ACL reconstruction is:
items.e: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (followed by Staphylococcus aureus) are the commonest pathogens after ACL reconstruction, reflecting skin flora contaminating the graft.

items.q: Ten days after hamstring ACL reconstruction a patient has fever, a hot tense effusion and an aspirate with 80,000 white cells/mm3. At arthroscopy the graft is intact and well fixed. Best management:
o: Immediate removal of the graft and fixation devices
Arthroscopic lavage and debridement with graft retention plus culture-directed intravenous antibiotics
items.e: Early post-ACLR infection is treated by prompt arthroscopic washout (repeated if needed) and IV antibiotics; the graft can usually be retained when it is intact and functional. Graft removal is reserved for failure of this approach or late infection with a non-viable graft.

items.q: In the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort (Grindem et al., 2016), for each month that return to sport was delayed up to 9 months after ACL reconstruction, the knee reinjury rate fell by about:
items.e: Grindem found a 51% reduction in reinjury rate for each month return to sport was delayed until 9 months, and that meeting return-to-sport criteria also reduced reinjury.

items.q: Criteria-based return to pivoting sport after ACL reconstruction usually requires quadriceps strength and hop-test limb symmetry index of at least:
items.e: Most return-to-sport test batteries require a limb symmetry index of 90% or more for quadriceps strength and hop tests, together with psychological readiness, and not before about 9 months.

items.q: In young athletes returning to sport after ACL reconstruction, the risk of a contralateral ACL tear compared with ipsilateral graft rupture is:
o: Similar, or even higher in some series
items.e: Long-term studies (e.g. Webster, Wright) show that young athletes have a substantial contralateral ACL injury rate, similar to or exceeding the graft rupture rate, reflecting shared risk factors.

items.q: In the Meyers and McKeever classification of tibial eminence fractures, a type II fracture is one in which:
o: The anterior part of the fragment is elevated but the posterior hinge is intact
The fragment is completely separated from its bed
items.e: Type I is undisplaced, type II hinged with anterior elevation and an intact posterior hinge, type III completely displaced (IIIB rotated) and type IV (Zaricznyj) comminuted.

items.q: Closed reduction in extension of a displaced tibial eminence fracture in a child fails. The structure most commonly entrapped beneath the fragment is the:
o: Anterior horn of the medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament
items.e: Interposition of the anterior horn of the medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament blocks reduction and is an indication for arthroscopic or open reduction and fixation.

items.q: An 11-year-old has an undisplaced (type I) tibial eminence fracture. The usual treatment is:
o: Immobilisation in a long-leg cast or brace in extension or slight flexion for about 4-6 weeks
items.e: Type I and reducible type II fractures are treated closed with immobilisation near extension; displaced (III/IV) or irreducible fractures need arthroscopic or open fixation with sutures or screws.

items.q: When performing a transphyseal ACL reconstruction in an adolescent with some growth remaining, the risk of growth disturbance is reduced by using:
o: A BPTB graft with bone blocks bridging the physis
Small, more vertical, central tunnels filled with soft-tissue graft, with no bone block or fixation hardware across the physis
Large oblique tunnels to reduce physeal stress
Interference screws placed across the physis
items.e: Physeal damage is minimised by small central vertical tunnels, soft-tissue grafts and avoiding bone plugs or hardware across the physis, especially on the lateral femoral side.

items.q: The tibial attachment of the PCL is:
o: In a depression (PCL facet) on the posterior tibia about 1-1.5 cm below the joint line
Anterior to the medial tibial spine
On the articular surface of the medial plateau
items.e: The PCL inserts extra-articularly into a central posterior depression of the tibia about 1-1.5 cm below the articular surface, which is the site of PCL bony avulsions.

items.q: Compared with the ACL, the PCL is:
o: Wider and about twice as strong
items.e: The PCL is about 13 mm wide and roughly twice as strong as the ACL; both cruciates are intra-articular but extrasynovial.

items.q: The meniscofemoral ligaments (Humphrey and Wrisberg) run from the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to:
o: The medial wall of the lateral femoral condyle
The lateral wall of the medial femoral condyle
The PCL facet on the posterior tibia
items.e: Both meniscofemoral ligaments pass from the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle, Humphrey anterior and Wrisberg posterior to the PCL; at least one is present in about 90% of knees.

items.q: The PCL provides about what share of the restraint to posterior tibial translation?
items.e: The PCL is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation (about 90-95%), and a secondary restraint to external rotation together with the posterolateral corner.

items.q: On the dial test, the injured side shows more than 10 degrees of additional external rotation at both 30 and 90 degrees of knee flexion. This indicates:
o: Combined posterolateral corner and PCL injury
items.e: Asymmetry only at 30 degrees indicates isolated PLC injury; asymmetry at both 30 and 90 degrees indicates PLC plus PCL injury. An MCL injury can mimic a positive dial test, so it must be examined.

items.q: On kneeling posterior stress radiographs, a side-to-side difference in posterior tibial displacement of more than about 12 mm suggests:
o: A PCL tear combined with posterolateral or posteromedial corner injury
items.e: Isolated complete PCL tears usually give about 8-11 mm of side-to-side posterior displacement; more than about 12 mm suggests an associated corner injury.

items.q: During a posterior drawer test, posterior tibial translation of 0-5 mm with the medial tibial plateau still anterior to the femoral condyle corresponds to which grade of PCL injury?
items.e: PCL grade I = 0-5 mm with the tibia still anterior to the condyles, grade II = 5-10 mm with the tibia flush, grade III = over 10 mm with the tibia behind the condyles (suggesting combined injury).

items.q: Rehabilitation of an acute isolated grade II PCL tear commonly uses a brace that:
o: Locks the knee at 90 degrees of flexion
Applies a varus moment to the knee
Applies a dynamic anterior force to the proximal tibia to counter posterior sag
items.e: Dynamic PCL braces (such as the Jack brace) push the proximal tibia anteriorly, reducing posterior sag while the ligament heals, alongside quadriceps-dominant rehabilitation.

items.q: Long-standing untreated PCL deficiency is particularly associated with degeneration of the:
o: Lateral patellar facet only with the medial compartment spared
items.e: Posterior tibial subluxation increases patellofemoral contact force and medial compartment load, so chronic PCL deficiency leads to medial and patellofemoral arthritis.

items.q: The tibial inlay technique for PCL reconstruction was developed mainly to:
o: Avoid the acute 'killer turn' of the graft at the posterior exit of a transtibial tunnel
items.e: In tibial inlay, a bone block is fixed directly into the PCL facet through a posterior approach, avoiding the sharp turn that abrades the graft at the posterior tibial tunnel exit in transtibial techniques.

items.q: During transtibial PCL tunnel drilling, the popliteal artery is best protected by:
o: Keeping the knee flexed to about 90 degrees, guarding the guide-pin tip and viewing through a posteromedial portal
Extending the knee fully while drilling
items.e: Flexion moves the neurovascular bundle posteriorly away from the tibia; a curette or guard over the pin tip, fluoroscopy and direct posteromedial-portal viewing further reduce the risk of popliteal artery injury.

items.q: In the posterior (Burks and Schaffer) approach to fix a PCL tibial avulsion, the popliteal neurovascular bundle is protected by:
o: Retracting the lateral head of gastrocnemius medially
Routinely detaching the medial head of gastrocnemius from the femur
Retracting the medial head of gastrocnemius laterally
items.e: The approach develops the interval between the medial head of gastrocnemius and semimembranosus; retracting the medial gastrocnemius laterally shields the popliteal vessels and tibial nerve.

items.q: The posterolateral corner of the knee is the primary restraint to:
o: Varus and external rotation of the tibia, especially near 30 degrees of flexion
items.e: The LCL, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament resist varus and external rotation, maximally near 30 degrees of flexion; the PCL contributes more at 90 degrees.

items.q: Common peroneal nerve injury accompanies posterolateral corner injuries of the knee in about:
items.e: The peroneal nerve is injured in about 15-30% of PLC injuries because of its course around the fibular neck; it must be documented before and after surgery.

items.q: An AP knee radiograph after a hyperextension-varus injury shows a small avulsed fragment from the fibular styloid (arcuate sign). This indicates:
items.e: The arcuate sign is avulsion of the fibular styloid by the popliteofibular, arcuate and fabellofibular ligaments; it indicates PLC injury, often with cruciate injury.

items.q: Varus laxity of the knee at full extension (0 degrees), as well as at 30 degrees, indicates:
o: Posterolateral corner injury combined with cruciate injury
items.e: In extension the cruciates and posterior capsule also resist varus; gapping at 0 degrees therefore means PLC injury plus cruciate (and capsular) damage, whereas isolated PLC injury opens only at 30 degrees.

items.q: A Schenck KD IV knee dislocation involves:
o: Both cruciates with both the medial and the posterolateral corner/collateral structures
items.e: KD I single cruciate plus collateral, KD II both cruciates, KD III both cruciates plus MCL (M) or PLC (L), KD IV both cruciates and both collaterals, KD V fracture-dislocation.

items.q: After reduction of a knee dislocation, the foot pulses are palpable but the ankle-brachial index is 0.8. The next step is:
o: CT angiography and vascular surgical assessment
items.e: Palpable pulses do not exclude popliteal artery injury; an ABI under 0.9 mandates arterial imaging (CT angiography) and vascular consultation, whereas an ABI of 0.9 or more allows serial examination.

items.q: After revascularisation of a popliteal artery injury in a knee dislocation with several hours of ischaemia, what should usually be done?
o: Immediate ligament reconstruction in the same sitting
Fasciotomy only if compartment pressure exceeds 60 mmHg
items.e: Reperfusion after prolonged ischaemia causes compartment syndrome, so prophylactic four-compartment fasciotomy is performed at revascularisation; ligament surgery is staged.

items.q: On T1-weighted MRI, early osteonecrosis of the femoral head characteristically shows:
o: Diffuse homogeneous low signal of the whole head and neck
A single serpiginous low-signal band outlining a segment that may retain fat signal
Complete absence of signal in the acetabulum
items.e: The T1 hallmark is a well-defined serpiginous low-signal line (the reactive interface) demarcating the necrotic segment, which often keeps normal fat signal; diffuse oedema without a band suggests transient osteoporosis.

items.q: Histologically, the earliest reliable evidence of osteocyte death in osteonecrotic bone is:
items.e: Dead osteocytes leave empty lacunae in the trabeculae; repair features such as granulation tissue and appositional new bone appear later.

items.q: In the first weeks after the femoral head becomes ischaemic, plain radiographs are typically:
o: Normal, because dead bone looks the same as living bone until repair begins
Showing diffuse osteopenia of the whole pelvis
items.e: Radiographic changes (sclerosis, cysts) arise only from the repair process over weeks to months, so early necrotic bone is radiographically normal; MRI detects it.

items.q: In children aged about 4-7 years, the femoral head epiphysis is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia because it depends almost entirely on the:
o: Lateral epiphyseal vessels from the medial femoral circumflex artery
Metaphyseal vessels crossing the open physis
items.e: At this age the lateral epiphyseal (posterosuperior retinacular) vessels supply most of the head; the ligamentum teres contributes little and metaphyseal vessels do not cross the open physis.

items.q: In the adult hip, the artery of the ligamentum teres usually arises from the:
o: Obturator artery (or medial femoral circumflex artery)
items.e: The foveal artery is a branch of the obturator artery (sometimes the MFCA); it supplies only a small area around the fovea and cannot sustain the head alone.

items.q: Osteonecrosis is a recognised skeletal complication of HIV infection, attributed partly to:
o: Direct viral infection of osteocytes only
items.e: HIV patients have an increased risk of osteonecrosis, linked to protease inhibitors and hyperlipidaemia as well as steroids and coagulopathy.

items.q: A 34-year-old with bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis has no steroid or alcohol exposure. A thrombophilia screen is most likely to reveal:
o: Factor V Leiden or another prothrombotic or hypofibrinolytic abnormality
items.e: Idiopathic and multifocal osteonecrosis are associated with thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid antibodies, raised lipoprotein(a)) and hypofibrinolysis.

items.q: In osteonecrosis associated with an inherited thrombophilia, which drug has been studied in small series to slow progression of early lesions?
items.e: Small studies (Glueck) suggested that low-molecular-weight heparin can arrest early osteonecrosis in patients with thrombophilia or hypofibrinolysis; evidence is limited.

items.q: A 45-year-old treated with pelvic radiotherapy for cervical carcinoma develops hip pain with collapse of the femoral head. The underlying cause is best described as:
items.e: Radiation damages osteocytes and small vessels, producing osteonecrosis (and insufficiency fractures) in the irradiated field.

items.q: After renal transplantation, femoral head osteonecrosis is common mainly because of:
items.e: Post-transplant osteonecrosis is chiefly related to glucocorticoid dosing, especially pulsed treatment for rejection.

items.q: Osteonecrosis has been associated with acute pancreatitis, the proposed mechanism being:
o: Fat necrosis and circulating lipase causing intraosseous fat emboli and necrosis
items.e: Pancreatitis releases lipase that causes intramedullary fat necrosis and fat embolism, a recognised cause of osteonecrosis.

items.q: Transient osteoporosis of the hip in a pregnant woman is managed with protected weight bearing mainly to prevent:
o: Femoral neck fracture through the osteopenic bone
items.e: The condition is self-limiting over 6-12 months, but the osteopenic femoral neck can fracture, so protected weight bearing and analgesia are advised.

items.q: A 45-year-old man has transient bone marrow oedema of the right hip that resolves; a year later the left knee and then the ankle are affected in turn. This pattern is called:
o: Complex regional pain syndrome type II
items.e: Transient osteoporosis that moves from joint to joint is termed regional migratory osteoporosis; each episode is self-limiting.

items.q: Apart from women in late pregnancy, transient osteoporosis of the hip classically affects:
items.e: Transient osteoporosis occurs in women in the third trimester and in middle-aged men.

items.q: In a patient with known femoral head osteonecrosis, the radiographic view most likely to reveal a subtle crescent sign is the:
items.e: The crescent (subchondral fracture) lies in the anterosuperior weight-bearing head, best shown on the frog-leg lateral view.

items.q: A 55-year-old man with a large lesion of spontaneous osteonecrosis (subchondral insufficiency fracture) of the medial femoral condyle and varus alignment, but a healthy lateral compartment, is very active. A joint-preserving option is:
o: High tibial osteotomy, with or without drilling or grafting
items.e: In younger active patients, valgus high tibial osteotomy unloads the medial compartment and may be combined with drilling or grafting; older patients with collapse generally need UKA or TKA.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has a large, collapsed spontaneous osteonecrosis of the medial femoral condyle with an intact lateral compartment and ACL. A suitable operation is:
items.e: Collapsed medial condyle SONK in an older patient with a healthy lateral compartment and intact ACL is a good indication for medial UKA (or TKA).

items.q: Six weeks after arthroscopic medial meniscectomy, a 58-year-old has new severe medial knee pain; MRI shows a subchondral lesion in the medial femoral condyle. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Post-arthroscopic osteonecrosis (subchondral insufficiency fracture) of the knee
items.e: Post-arthroscopic osteonecrosis occurs weeks after meniscectomy or chondroplasty, usually in the medial femoral condyle, from increased subchondral stress after meniscal loss.

items.q: A 30-year-old on steroids has collapsed secondary osteonecrosis of the knee extending into the distal femoral metaphysis. During TKA, a specific consideration is:
o: Stemmed components may be needed because of poor metaphyseal bone
Core decompression should be performed first
items.e: Secondary knee osteonecrosis often involves the metaphysis and diaphysis, so stems and augments may be needed for fixation; UKA is unsuitable because lesions are multiple.

items.q: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee is staged radiographically by the systems of:
items.e: Koshino and Aglietti described radiographic stages of SONK; Ficat is used for the hip, Lichtman for Kienbock and Cruess for the humeral head.

items.q: A 40-year-old with steroid-induced humeral head osteonecrosis has collapse of the articular surface but a normal glenoid (Cruess stage IV). The appropriate operation is:
items.e: With head collapse but intact glenoid, hemiarthroplasty or resurfacing suffices; total shoulder arthroplasty is reserved for stage V with glenoid involvement.

items.q: Humeral head osteonecrosis is often better tolerated than femoral head osteonecrosis because:
o: The humeral head has a dual blood supply that always regenerates
Collapse never occurs in the humerus
The shoulder is a non-weight-bearing joint
items.e: Being non-weight-bearing, the shoulder often tolerates necrosis and even some collapse with fewer symptoms than the hip.

items.q: After a talar neck fracture with collapsed, painful osteonecrosis of the talar body and subtalar arthritis, a salvage procedure is:
items.e: Collapse of the talar body with ankle and subtalar arthritis is salvaged by tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis (historically the Blair tibiotalar fusion); talar replacement is an alternative in selected cases.

items.q: Absence of the Hawkins sign at 8 weeks after a talar neck fracture means:
o: Osteonecrosis is certain and the talus will collapse
Osteonecrosis is possible but not proven
The blood supply is definitely intact
items.e: The Hawkins sign (subchondral lucency) indicates intact vascularity; its absence is suggestive of, but not diagnostic of, osteonecrosis, and MRI can clarify.

items.q: Sever disease of the calcaneus is best classified as:
o: A traction apophysitis rather than a true osteonecrosis
A stress fracture of the calcaneal body
items.e: Sever disease is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis at the Achilles insertion in children aged about 8-12 years, not an ischaemic necrosis.

items.q: In sickle cell disease, the vertebral bodies may show central endplate depressions giving a characteristic appearance known as:
items.e: Infarction of the central endplate (supplied by end arteries) with preserved periphery produces H-shaped vertebrae; picture-frame vertebrae suggest Paget disease and rugger-jersey spine renal osteodystrophy.

items.q: In a patient with sickle cell disease, painful bone crisis and acute osteomyelitis are difficult to distinguish because:
o: Both cause pain, fever, swelling and raised inflammatory markers
Osteomyelitis never occurs in sickle cell disease
Only osteomyelitis causes marrow change on MRI
items.e: Infarction and infection both present with pain, fever and raised markers; blood cultures, MRI and ultrasound-guided aspiration help, and infarction is far commoner.

items.q: Before total hip arthroplasty in a patient with Gaucher disease and femoral head osteonecrosis, particular preparation is needed because of:
items.e: Gaucher disease causes hypersplenism with thrombocytopenia and coagulation abnormalities, so bleeding risk must be addressed; enzyme replacement therapy also helps.

items.q: A free vascularised fibular graft for femoral head osteonecrosis is best indicated in:
o: A young patient with a medium to large pre-collapse or early-collapse (ARCO IIIA) lesion
items.e: The vascularised fibula suits young patients with larger lesions before or just after early collapse, in experienced centres; arthritis needs THA and small asymptomatic lesions are observed.

items.q: The 'trapdoor' procedure for femoral head osteonecrosis differs from the 'lightbulb' procedure in that the necrotic bone is approached through:
o: A window at the femoral head-neck junction
A flap of articular cartilage on the femoral head
items.e: In the trapdoor technique the hip is dislocated and a cartilage flap is lifted to debride and graft the lesion; the lightbulb technique uses a window at the head-neck junction.

items.q: A recognised disadvantage of proximal femoral (intertrochanteric) osteotomy for femoral head osteonecrosis is that it:
o: Can make subsequent total hip arthroplasty technically more difficult
Always causes leg lengthening of over 5 cm
Is contraindicated in patients under 40 years
items.e: Osteotomy alters proximal femoral anatomy, making later THA more demanding (stem positioning, hardware removal); this is a major reason it is less used outside Japan.

items.q: Hip resurfacing is limited in femoral head osteonecrosis mainly because:
o: A large necrotic segment leaves inadequate bone to support the femoral component
Resurfacing implants are only available in small sizes
items.e: The femoral component relies on the head bone stock; extensive necrosis risks loosening and femoral neck fracture, besides metal-on-metal concerns.

items.q: Compared with THA for primary osteoarthritis, modern cementless THA for femoral head osteonecrosis has:
o: A failure rate exceeding 50% at 5 years
Far better survival than THA for osteoarthritis
Similar implant survival in recent series, though young age and some aetiologies increase risk
No role, since joint preservation is always preferred
items.e: Older cemented series showed poor results, but modern cementless THA for osteonecrosis gives survivorship comparable with osteoarthritis; sickle cell disease, renal failure and transplant patients do worse.

items.q: Femoral head osteonecrosis most typically presents in which age group?
o: Under 10 years, with a female predominance
items.e: Non-traumatic femoral head osteonecrosis typically affects adults in the third to fifth decades, more often men, making joint preservation important.

items.q: A child with myopia, retinal detachment, a flat midface, cleft palate and early-onset arthritis has a mutation in the gene for the main collagen of articular cartilage. The gene is:
items.e: This is Stickler syndrome type 1, caused by COL2A1 mutations affecting type II collagen, the main collagen of hyaline cartilage and vitreous. FGFR3 causes achondroplasia and COMP causes pseudoachondroplasia/multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.

items.q: Which component of the adult articular cartilage matrix has the slowest turnover, with a half-life measured in decades to more than a century?
items.e: The type II collagen network is turned over extremely slowly (half-life well over 100 years), so collagen damage in OA is essentially irreversible. Aggrecan is replaced much faster, over months to years.

items.q: Which zone of articular cartilage has collagen fibres aligned parallel to the joint surface, flattened chondrocytes, and the greatest tensile stiffness to resist shear?
items.e: The superficial zone has densely packed fibres parallel to the surface and elongated cells, giving the highest tensile strength. The deep zone has perpendicular fibres and the highest proteoglycan content, resisting compression.

items.q: In which zone of articular cartilage are the chondrocytes spherical and the collagen fibres obliquely or randomly oriented, forming a transition between the surface and the deep layer?
items.e: The middle (transitional) zone, the thickest uncalcified zone after the deep zone, has round cells and oblique, randomly arranged fibres. Deep-zone cells are arranged in columns perpendicular to the surface.

items.q: Compared with normal ageing, early osteoarthritis is distinguished by which change in the water content of articular cartilage?
o: Water content falls only in the calcified zone
items.e: In early OA, damage to the collagen network lets proteoglycans swell, raising water content and permeability and reducing stiffness. With ageing, cartilage water content decreases.

items.q: Chondrocytes in cartilage explants are subjected to different loading regimens. Which regimen suppresses proteoglycan and collagen synthesis?
items.e: Static compression lowers matrix synthesis, whereas dynamic (cyclic) loading at physiological frequencies stimulates it, which is the basis for early motion in cartilage healing.

items.q: Which cytokine is regarded as the principal catabolic mediator in osteoarthritic cartilage, inducing MMPs and aggrecanases and suppressing matrix synthesis?
items.e: IL-1 beta (with TNF-alpha) drives chondrocyte catabolism by up-regulating MMP-13, ADAMTS-4/5 and nitric oxide. IL-10, IL-4 and TGF-beta are anti-inflammatory or anabolic.

items.q: A full-thickness articular cartilage defect that penetrates the subchondral bone fills with repair tissue made predominantly of:
o: Hyaline cartilage rich in type II collagen
Calcified cartilage rich in type X collagen
Dense scar rich in type III collagen only
Fibrocartilage rich in type I collagen
items.e: Penetration of subchondral bone (as in microfracture) brings marrow mesenchymal cells and a fibrin clot that matures into fibrocartilage, mostly type I collagen, which is mechanically inferior to hyaline cartilage.

items.q: The swelling pressure that allows articular cartilage to resist compressive loads arises mainly from:
o: Fixed negative charges on the glycosaminoglycan chains drawing in water and counter-ions
Covalent cross-links between type II collagen fibrils
Active pumping of water into the matrix by chondrocytes
Hydrostatic pressure transmitted from the subchondral bone
items.e: The densely packed sulphated GAG chains of aggrecan carry a high fixed negative charge density, creating a Donnan osmotic swelling pressure; the collagen network restrains this swelling.

items.q: A 40-year-old has early-onset arthritis of the spine and large joints, dark ear cartilage, and urine that darkens on standing. At arthrotomy the articular cartilage is black. The deficient enzyme is:
items.e: Alkaptonuria (ochronosis) is caused by homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency; homogentisic acid polymer deposits in cartilage make it black and brittle. HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan, ALP deficiency hypophosphatasia, glucocerebrosidase deficiency Gaucher disease.

items.q: In haemophilic arthropathy, progressive cartilage destruction after recurrent haemarthroses is mainly driven by:
o: Urate crystal deposition within the synovium
Autoantibodies directed against type II collagen
Iron (haemosiderin) deposition causing synovial hypertrophy and chondrocyte injury
items.e: Repeated bleeds deposit iron in the synovium, causing a proliferative inflammatory synovitis that releases catabolic cytokines and enzymes; iron and blood products are also directly toxic to chondrocytes.

items.q: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour typically carries a translocation, often t(1;2) involving COL6A3, that leads to overexpression of:
items.e: The translocation places CSF1 under a strong promoter; a minority of neoplastic cells overexpress CSF1, recruiting the bulk CSF1R-bearing macrophage-like cells, the rationale for CSF1R inhibitors. PDGFB fusion (COL1A1-PDGFB) characterises dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

items.q: The acid-fast staining property of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is due mainly to the cell wall's high content of:
items.e: Long-chain mycolic acids make the waxy cell wall resist decolourisation by acid-alcohol after carbol fuchsin staining. Teichoic acids are features of Gram-positive bacteria and LPS of Gram-negative bacteria.

items.q: Isoniazid is a prodrug. It must first be activated within the mycobacterium by:
items.e: KatG activates isoniazid, which then inhibits InhA and mycolic acid synthesis; katG mutations give high-level isoniazid resistance, while inhA mutations give low-level resistance and cross-resistance to ethionamide.

items.q: Bedaquiline, a core drug in regimens for MDR-TB, acts by inhibiting:
items.e: Bedaquiline is a diarylquinoline that blocks the proton pump of mycobacterial ATP synthase; QT prolongation is its key toxicity. DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolone target, 50S ribosome the linezolid target, arabinosyl transferase the ethambutol target.

items.q: Four months into a BPaLM regimen for MDR tuberculosis of the knee, a patient develops numb, burning feet, blurred vision and anaemia with thrombocytopenia. The drug most likely responsible is:
items.e: Linezolid causes dose- and duration-related myelosuppression, peripheral neuropathy and optic neuropathy, which often require dose reduction. Bedaquiline mainly prolongs the QT interval.

items.q: A woman on anticoagulation and the combined oral contraceptive pill starts rifampicin-containing ATT for tuberculosis of the wrist. The main interaction to anticipate is:
o: Increased bleeding from inhibition of warfarin metabolism
Rifampicin toxicity from reduced hepatic clearance
Reduced efficacy of both drugs from hepatic cytochrome P450 induction
Reduced absorption of rifampicin from the gut
items.e: Rifampicin is a potent CYP450 inducer, lowering levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, protease inhibitors and many other drugs; non-hormonal contraception and closer INR monitoring are needed.

items.q: A 9-year-old with early tuberculosis of the hip (stage of synovitis) has an effusion in the joint. The typical attitude of the limb is:
o: Flexion, adduction and internal rotation with apparent shortening
Extension, adduction and external rotation with true shortening
Flexion, abduction and external rotation with apparent lengthening
items.e: In the synovitis stage the hip assumes flexion, abduction and external rotation, the position of maximal capsular capacity, with pelvic tilt producing apparent lengthening. Flexion, adduction and internal rotation with apparent shortening indicates early arthritis.

items.q: An HIV-positive patient with tuberculosis of the knee is on an antiretroviral regimen containing a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor. To avoid a major drug interaction, rifampicin is usually replaced by:
items.e: Rifabutin is a much weaker CYP3A4 inducer than rifampicin and can be given (with dose adjustment) alongside boosted protease inhibitors. Rifapentine is also a strong inducer, and rifaximin is not absorbed systemically.

items.q: Which antitubercular drug should be avoided in a pregnant woman with osteoarticular tuberculosis because it can cause congenital deafness in the fetus?
items.e: Aminoglycosides such as streptomycin cross the placenta and cause fetal eighth-nerve damage. Isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol (and generally pyrazinamide) are considered safe in pregnancy.

items.q: The main advantage of the automated liquid culture system (BACTEC MGIT 960) over Lowenstein-Jensen medium for tissue from a suspected tuberculous joint is that it:
o: Detects growth faster, typically within about 1-3 weeks
Distinguishes M. tuberculosis from M. bovis by colony colour
items.e: Liquid culture is more sensitive and faster (mean around 10-14 days) than solid LJ culture (4-8 weeks); drug-susceptibility testing can follow. Molecular assays such as Xpert identify resistance mutations.

items.q: An aquarium keeper has a chronic, painless flexor tenosynovitis of the index finger after a minor cut; histology shows granulomas. For culture the laboratory should be asked to incubate the sample at:
o: 42 degrees C, to suppress contaminating flora
37 degrees C in carbon dioxide only
4 degrees C, to enrich for slow growers
30-32 degrees C, because Mycobacterium marinum grows poorly at 37 degrees C
items.e: M. marinum, a fish-tank and swimming-pool organism, causes indolent hand tenosynovitis and grows best at 30-32 degrees C; routine incubation at 37 degrees C may give a false-negative culture.

items.q: In advanced tuberculosis of the knee, wedge-shaped areas of necrotic bone may be seen on both sides of the joint facing each other. These are called:
items.e: Kissing sequestra on opposing articular surfaces are a described feature of tuberculous arthritis, particularly of the knee. Ring sequestra form around pin tracts, and button sequestra are typical of skull lesions such as eosinophilic granuloma.

items.q: A patient on haemodialysis is diagnosed with tuberculosis of the ankle. Which first-line drugs need their dosing frequency reduced to three times weekly (after dialysis) because they are renally excreted?
items.e: Ethambutol and pyrazinamide (metabolites) are cleared by the kidney and accumulate in renal failure, so they are given three times weekly; isoniazid and rifampicin are mainly hepatically cleared and need no change.

items.q: Which of the following is one of the NEXUS low-risk criteria that must all be met to clear the cervical spine clinically without imaging?
o: Ability to walk at any time since the injury
items.e: NEXUS requires no midline tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication and no painful distracting injury. Age, ambulation and delayed-onset pain are elements of the Canadian C-spine rule.

items.q: In the Anderson-Montesano classification of occipital condyle fractures, which type is a potentially unstable avulsion of the condyle by the alar ligament?
items.e: Type I is an impaction (comminuted) fracture from axial load, type II is an extension of a basilar skull fracture, and type III is an alar ligament avulsion that may accompany craniocervical instability. There is no type IV.

items.q: On an open-mouth odontoid view after a C1 ring fracture, the transverse atlantal ligament is likely to be ruptured (rule of Spence) when the combined overhang of the C1 lateral masses over C2 exceeds about:
items.e: A combined lateral mass displacement greater than about 6.9 mm (8.1 mm allowing for radiographic magnification) suggests TAL rupture; MRI now directly assesses the ligament.

items.q: On a lateral cervical radiograph of an adult, the upper limit of the normal atlanto-dens interval is about:
items.e: An adult ADI over 3 mm suggests transverse ligament incompetence (up to 5 mm is accepted in children); over 10 mm implies failure of all the ligamentous restraints.

items.q: Steel's 'rule of thirds' describes the sagittal diameter of the canal at the level of the atlas as being occupied by:
o: One-third cord, one-third CSF and one-third ligamentum flavum
One-third dens, one-third transverse ligament and one-third cord
Two-thirds cord and one-third free space
One-third dens, one-third spinal cord and one-third free space
items.e: The free third acts as a safety zone, allowing some atlantoaxial displacement before cord compression; once ADI exceeds about 10 mm this space is used up.

items.q: A 7-year-old has a painful torticollis with the head tilted to one side and rotated to the other ('cock robin') after a minor fall. Dynamic CT shows fixed rotation of C1 on C2 with no anterior displacement of C1. The Fielding-Hawkins type is:
items.e: Type I, the commonest, is rotatory fixation without anterior shift (intact transverse ligament). Type II has 3-5 mm anterior displacement, type III more than 5 mm, and type IV posterior displacement.

items.q: A 9-year-old develops painful torticollis a week after tonsillectomy, with no history of trauma. CT shows atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation. This condition is known as:
items.e: Grisel syndrome is non-traumatic atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation after pharyngeal infection or head-and-neck surgery, attributed to inflammatory ligamentous laxity via pharyngovertebral venous drainage.

items.q: A 70-year-old with cervical spondylosis falls forwards and strikes his forehead. He has marked weakness of the hands and arms, milder leg weakness and urinary retention; radiographs show no fracture. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Hyperextension of a spondylotic canal causes central cord syndrome, the commonest incomplete cord injury, with upper limbs more affected than lower limbs because the arm fibres are more central in the corticospinal tracts.

items.q: Among incomplete cervical cord injury patterns, which carries the best prognosis for independent walking?
o: Complete injury with zone of partial preservation
Central cord syndrome in an elderly patient
items.e: Over 75-90% of Brown-Sequard patients regain independent ambulation. Anterior cord syndrome has the worst prognosis of the incomplete syndromes, and older patients with central cord syndrome recover less well.

items.q: After a flexion injury of the cervical spine, a patient has complete motor paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion but preserved proprioception and vibration. The syndrome and its prognosis are:
o: Anterior cord syndrome, with poor motor recovery
Central cord syndrome, with good recovery
Posterior cord syndrome, with good motor recovery
items.e: Injury to the anterior two-thirds of the cord (anterior spinal artery territory or retropulsed fragment) spares the dorsal columns; it has the poorest prognosis of the incomplete syndromes.

items.q: In a patient with an acute cervical spinal cord injury, the end of spinal shock is usually marked by the return of the:
items.e: Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex, usually within 24-48 hours, signals the end of spinal shock; if no motor or sensory function below the level has returned by then, the injury is considered complete.

items.q: After a C5 complete cord injury, a patient has a blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg, a pulse of 50 per minute and warm, dry peripheries. The most likely cause is:
o: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone
items.e: Interruption of sympathetic outflow (T1-L2) above T6 causes vasodilatation and unopposed vagal bradycardia; hypovolaemic shock gives tachycardia and cold peripheries. Spinal shock refers to loss of reflexes, not haemodynamics.

items.q: When applying a halo ring in an adult, the anterior pins are placed about 1 cm above the orbital rim over the lateral third of the eyebrow, mainly to avoid:
o: The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves medially and the temporalis muscle laterally
items.e: This safe zone, below the equator of the skull, keeps the pins lateral to the supraorbital/supratrochlear nerves and anterior to the thin temporal bone and temporalis muscle, where pins loosen and impair chewing.

items.q: The recommended insertion torque for halo pins in an adult is about:
items.e: Adult halo pins are tightened to about 8 in-lb (0.9 Nm) and retightened once at 24-48 hours; young children need more pins at lower torque (about 2-4 in-lb, finger-tight).

items.q: When applying Gardner-Wells tongs for closed reduction of a bilateral facet dislocation, placing the pins slightly posterior to the external auditory meatus will:
o: Apply a flexion moment that helps unlock the facets
Rotate the head towards the side of the pins
items.e: Pins in line with the external auditory meatus give neutral traction; posterior placement creates flexion (useful to unlock jumped facets) and anterior placement creates extension.

items.q: In the ASIA impairment scale, a patient with an incomplete cord injury in whom more than half of the key muscles below the neurological level have a grade less than 3 is classified as:
items.e: ASIA B has sensory but no motor function preserved below the level (including S4-5); ASIA C has motor function with more than half of key muscles below grade 3; ASIA D has at least half of key muscles grade 3 or more.

items.q: A 30-year-old has neck pain after a rear-end collision. Examination shows reduced range of motion and point tenderness, but normal neurology and no fracture. In the Quebec Task Force classification of whiplash-associated disorders this is grade:
items.e: Grade I is neck pain/stiffness without physical signs, grade II adds musculoskeletal signs, grade III adds neurological signs and grade IV is a fracture or dislocation.

items.q: On a lateral cervical radiograph of an adult, prevertebral soft-tissue thickness at the level of C2 is considered abnormal when it exceeds about:
items.e: At C2 the upper limit is about 6-7 mm, and at C6 about 22 mm (below the pharynx, where the oesophagus lies). Swelling suggests haematoma from an occult injury, though a normal value does not exclude one.

items.q: A 6-year-old has transient paraesthesiae and weakness of all limbs after a car crash; cervical radiographs and CT are normal. The most appropriate next investigation is:
o: Flexion-extension radiographs in the emergency department
items.e: Spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality (SCIWORA) is commoner in children because of ligamentous laxity; MRI shows cord or ligament injury and guides immobilisation and prognosis.

items.q: In the AO/OTA classification of proximal humerus fractures, group 11C denotes:
o: An articular fracture involving the anatomical neck
A fracture-dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint
items.e: 11C injuries are articular (anatomical neck) fractures, which carry the highest risk of humeral head avascular necrosis; 11A and 11B are extra-articular patterns.

items.q: The proximal humeral physis contributes approximately what proportion of the longitudinal growth of the humerus, explaining the great remodelling potential of these fractures in children?
items.e: About 80% of humeral growth comes from the proximal physis, so substantial angulation and displacement remodel in young children; remodelling capacity falls as skeletal maturity approaches.

items.q: In a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture, the medial fragment is typically displaced superiorly by the pull of the:
items.e: The sternocleidomastoid lifts the medial fragment, while the weight of the arm pulls the lateral fragment down and pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi draw it medially, causing shortening.

items.q: In the Allman classification, the most common site of clavicle fracture, accounting for about 80% of cases, is the:
items.e: Group I midshaft fractures make up about 80%, lateral third (group II) about 15% and medial third (group III) about 5%.

items.q: The serendipity view for sternoclavicular joint injuries is taken with the beam centred on the manubrium and tilted cephalad by about:
items.e: Rockwood's serendipity view uses a 40 degree cephalic tilt; a posteriorly dislocated medial clavicle appears lower than the opposite side. CT is now the investigation of choice.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a posterior sternoclavicular dislocation with dysphagia. Closed reduction under general anaesthesia is planned. The appropriate set-up is:
o: In the emergency department under sedation, with direct downward pressure on the medial clavicle
Without anaesthesia, using a figure-of-eight bandage alone
After 3 weeks, to allow the swelling to settle
In theatre, with a bolster between the scapulae, traction in abduction and a cardiothoracic surgeon available
items.e: The medial clavicle lies close to the great vessels, trachea and oesophagus, so reduction (abduction-traction over an interscapular bolster, plus a towel clip if needed) is done in theatre with thoracic surgical back-up.

items.q: In a Rockwood type VI acromioclavicular dislocation, the distal clavicle is displaced:
o: Inferiorly, into a subacromial or subcoracoid position
Superiorly with a 100-300% increase in coracoclavicular distance
items.e: Type VI is a rare inferior dislocation beneath the acromion or coracoid, usually from severe hyperabduction trauma, and needs operative reduction. Type IV is posterior and type V markedly superior.

items.q: A Rockwood type II acromioclavicular joint injury consists of:
o: Sprain of the acromioclavicular ligaments only, with no displacement
Torn acromioclavicular ligaments with intact coracoclavicular ligaments
Torn acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments with 25-100% superior displacement
Posterior displacement of the clavicle into the trapezius
items.e: In type II the AC ligaments are torn and the joint is subluxed, but the CC ligaments are intact (sprained), so the CC distance is normal or only slightly increased; types I-II are treated non-operatively.

items.q: The commonest site of non-union of the acromial ossification centres (os acromiale) is between the:
items.e: Of the acromial ossification centres, failure of fusion is most frequent at the meso-acromion/meta-acromion junction, near the AC joint level; os acromiale is best seen on an axillary view.

items.q: In reverse shoulder arthroplasty, scapular notching is reduced mainly by:
o: Inferior positioning of the glenosphere with slight inferior tilt or lateralisation
Increasing humeral component retroversion to 60 degrees
Using a smaller glenosphere placed centrally
items.e: Notching results from impingement of the humeral cup on the inferior scapular neck in adduction; placing the baseplate flush with the inferior glenoid rim, with inferior overhang or lateralisation, reduces it.

items.q: An 80-year-old with a four-part proximal humerus fracture is being considered for reverse shoulder arthroplasty. Which finding is a contraindication?
o: Complete axillary nerve palsy with a non-functioning deltoid
items.e: The reverse prosthesis relies on the deltoid to elevate the arm; without a functioning deltoid it will not work and is prone to instability. It is designed to function despite a deficient cuff and poor tuberosities.

items.q: In Balg and Boileau's Instability Severity Index Score for recurrent anterior shoulder instability, a score above which value predicts a high recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart repair, favouring a Latarjet procedure?
items.e: The ISIS (0-10 points: age, sport level and type, hyperlaxity, Hill-Sachs on external rotation radiograph, loss of glenoid contour) above 6 is associated with about 70% recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart.

items.q: The 'sling effect' that contributes to stability after a Latarjet coracoid transfer is provided by:
o: The coracoacromial ligament tightening over the humeral head
The pectoralis minor transferred to the glenoid rim
The long head of biceps tenodesed to the glenoid
The conjoint tendon reinforcing the inferior subscapularis and anteroinferior capsule in abduction and external rotation
items.e: The 'triple blocking' effect combines the conjoint tendon sling (dominant in abduction-external rotation), the bone block extending the glenoid arc, and repair of the capsule to the coracoacromial ligament stump.

items.q: In arthroscopic remplissage for an engaging Hill-Sachs lesion, the defect is filled by tenodesis of the:
items.e: Remplissage ('filling') sutures the posterior capsule and infraspinatus into the posterosuperior Hill-Sachs defect, making it extra-articular; the McLaughlin procedure instead fills a reverse Hill-Sachs with subscapularis or lesser tuberosity.

items.q: Lewinnek's 'safe zone' for acetabular component position in THA, described to reduce dislocation, is:
items.e: Lewinnek (1978) found fewer dislocations with radiographic inclination 30-50 degrees and anteversion 5-25 degrees. Later work shows many dislocations occur within this zone, so spinopelvic factors also matter.

items.q: During the direct anterior approach to the hip, a leash of vessels crossing the deep interval between rectus femoris and gluteus medius must be coagulated or ligated. These are branches of the:
o: Ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
items.e: The ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery and its venae comitantes cross the deep part of the Hueter interval and are ligated. The medial circumflex artery is met posteriorly, near quadratus femoris.

items.q: Eight months after an uncemented THA, a 62-year-old has groin pain on active hip flexion, such as lifting the leg into a car. Components are well fixed, inflammatory markers are normal, and CT shows the anterior rim of the cup projecting beyond the anterior acetabular wall. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: An anteriorly prominent or retroverted cup irritates the iliopsoas tendon, causing pain on active flexion. An ultrasound-guided iliopsoas sheath injection supports the diagnosis; treatment is tenotomy or cup revision.

items.q: While impacting a press-fit uncemented femoral stem, the surgeon sees a fine undisplaced longitudinal crack in the medial calcar. The best management is to:
o: Continue impaction until the stem is fully seated
Abandon the THA and perform a hemiarthroplasty
Convert to a cemented stem without further fixation
Remove the stem, place a cerclage wire or cable below the crack, then reinsert the stem
items.e: A recognised intraoperative calcar crack is controlled with cerclage before reseating the stem, preventing propagation. Continuing impaction alone risks extending the fracture and losing stem stability.

items.q: Which complication is unique to dual-mobility acetabular components?
o: Intraprosthetic dislocation of the small head out of the mobile polyethylene liner
Fracture of the ceramic femoral head
Taper corrosion at the head-neck junction
