items.e: In intraprosthetic dislocation, wear of the liner's retentive rim lets the inner head escape, and the liner then articulates directly with the metal shell. The other options occur with conventional bearings too.

items.q: In Charnley's functional classification of patients undergoing THA, class B indicates:
o: One hip affected and the other hip normal
Multiple joint disease or another condition limiting walking
Both hips affected, with no other condition limiting walking
A previous failed arthroplasty on the same side
items.e: Charnley A is unilateral hip disease, B is bilateral hip disease, and C is multiple joint involvement or a medical condition limiting walking. Outcome scores of class C patients must be interpreted with this in mind.

items.q: During a posterior approach to the hip, which limb position helps to relax the sciatic nerve and reduce traction injury?
o: Hip abducted with the knee extended
Hip flexed, adducted and knee extended
items.e: The sciatic nerve is slackened by hip extension and knee flexion. Hip flexion with knee extension (straight-leg position) puts the nerve under maximal tension.

items.q: Six months after a THA through a direct lateral (Hardinge) approach, a patient has a Trendelenburg gait, lateral hip pain and a palpable gap over the greater trochanter. MRI shows the anterior gluteus medius detached from the trochanter, with no fatty atrophy of the muscle. The most likely cause is:
items.e: A palpable defect and tendon detachment with preserved muscle bulk indicate dehiscence of the abductor repair. Superior gluteal nerve injury would cause denervation with fatty atrophy rather than a tendon gap.

items.q: In obese patients with a large abdominal pannus, the main approach-specific disadvantage of the direct anterior approach for THA is a higher rate of:
o: Wound complications in the groin crease
items.e: The DAA incision lies in a moist skin fold under the pannus, which leads to more wound healing problems and superficial infection in obese patients. Posterior dislocation and sciatic palsy are more associated with the posterior approach.

items.q: A patient with a metal-on-metal THA has new hip pain and a soft-tissue swelling. Besides serum cobalt and chromium levels, the imaging investigation of choice for an adverse local tissue reaction is:
o: MRI with metal artefact reduction sequence (MARS)
items.e: MARS MRI shows pseudotumours, fluid collections and abductor damage around metal implants. Ultrasound is an alternative; plain radiographs and bone scans do not show the soft-tissue reaction.

items.q: Most dislocations after primary THA occur:
o: Within the first 3 months after surgery
items.e: Early dislocations, usually in the first few months, predominate while the soft tissues heal. Late dislocations occur but are often due to polyethylene wear or soft-tissue laxity.

items.q: A patient finds that when he flexes the thumb IP joint, the index finger DIP joint flexes as well, and he has pain on the radial side of the distal forearm. This is caused by:
o: Congenital absence of FDS to the index finger
A juncturae tendinum between index and middle fingers
An anomalous tendinous connection between FPL and the index FDP (Linburg-Comstock)
Adhesion of the EPL to Lister's tubercle
items.e: In Linburg-Comstock syndrome, a slip between FPL and index FDP links thumb and index flexion and can cause tenosynovitis. Release of the connection relieves symptoms if they are troublesome.

items.q: In the Elson test, the PIP joint is flexed 90 degrees over the edge of a table and the patient tries to extend the middle phalanx against resistance. An acute central slip rupture is indicated by:
o: Rigid extension of the DIP joint during the attempt
A floppy DIP joint during the attempt
items.e: With the central slip ruptured, extension force is transmitted through the lateral bands, so the DIP joint becomes rigid in extension. With an intact central slip the lateral bands are slack and the DIP joint stays floppy.

items.q: The Pulvertaft weave is mainly used to:
o: Repair a zone II flexor tendon laceration
Reattach FDP to the distal phalanx
Join a donor tendon to a recipient tendon in tendon transfer or grafting
items.e: The Pulvertaft technique interlaces one tendon through slits in another and is the standard strong junction for tendon transfers and proximal graft junctions. It is too bulky for repair within the digital sheath.

items.q: Adhesions after flexor tendon repair are mainly the result of:
o: Intrinsic healing by tenocytes within the tendon
Extrinsic healing by cells from the sheath and surrounding tissues
items.e: Extrinsic healing brings in fibroblasts and inflammatory cells from the surroundings, which form adhesions. Early mobilisation encourages intrinsic healing and reduces adhesions.

items.q: A key advantage of performing a zone II flexor tendon repair under wide-awake local anaesthesia no tourniquet (WALANT) is that the surgeon can:
o: Ask the patient to actively flex the finger to check for gapping and pulley catching
items.e: Active flexion during surgery shows whether the repair gaps or catches on the pulleys, so the repair or pulley venting can be adjusted. It does not replace a strong repair or a protective splint.

items.q: The Duran rehabilitation protocol after flexor tendon repair is based on:
o: Controlled passive flexion and extension of the DIP and PIP joints to give a few millimetres of tendon glide
Active flexion against a rubber band
Immobilisation in a cast for 4 weeks
items.e: Duran showed that 3-5 mm of passive tendon excursion prevents adhesions. The Kleinert protocol, by contrast, uses active extension with rubber-band passive flexion.

items.q: Spontaneous rupture of EPL after an undisplaced distal radius fracture is mainly attributed to:
o: Direct laceration by a sharp fracture fragment
Steroid injection into the first dorsal compartment
Ischaemia and attrition of the tendon in the tight third compartment at Lister's tubercle
items.e: The EPL has a poorly vascularised segment at Lister's tubercle; fracture haematoma raises pressure in the unyielding third compartment. The intact periosteum in undisplaced fractures keeps the compartment tight.

items.q: In adults with trigger finger, which factor is associated with a poorer response to corticosteroid injection?
items.e: Diabetic patients, especially insulin-dependent ones with multiple digits involved, respond less well to injection and more often need A1 pulley release. Short symptom duration predicts a better response.

items.q: A knife laceration over the dorsum of the PIP joint of the middle finger divides the central slip. In the Verdan/Kleinert extensor zone system this is zone:
items.e: Odd-numbered extensor zones lie over joints: I over DIP, III over PIP, V over MCP, VII over the wrist. Zone IV lies over the proximal phalanx.

items.q: In the spiral oblique retinacular ligament (SORL) reconstruction for chronic mallet finger with swan-neck deformity, the tendon graft passes:
o: Dorsal to both the PIP and DIP joint axes
Dorsal to the DIP joint axis and volar to the PIP joint axis
Through the A2 and A4 pulleys
items.e: Like the natural oblique retinacular ligament, the graft runs from the dorsal distal phalanx, spirals volar to the PIP axis and attaches to the opposite side of the proximal phalanx. PIP extension then tightens the graft and extends the DIP joint while restraining PIP hyperextension.

items.q: In a zone II laceration of both FDS and FDP, which step is an accepted way of reducing repair bulk under the pulleys?
o: Repairing FDP and only one slip of FDS
Repairing FDS and leaving FDP unrepaired
Repairing both tendons with a single shared core suture
items.e: Repairing FDP with one FDS slip (or leaving FDS in tight areas) reduces bulk and friction while preserving some FDS function. FDP is the priority tendon; complete A2 excision risks bowstringing.

items.q: A distal femoral osteosarcoma has a large extraosseous soft-tissue mass. For a core needle biopsy, the preferred target is:
o: The sclerotic intramedullary part, through a cortical window
items.e: The soft-tissue component is usually viable, representative and easy to sample without making a cortical hole, which avoids weakening the bone and fracture. Codman's triangle is reactive bone and often non-diagnostic.

items.q: When biopsying a bone lesion in which both infection and tumour are possible, the correct practice is to:
o: Send tissue for both histology and culture
items.e: The adage 'culture every biopsy and biopsy every culture' applies because osteomyelitis and tumours such as Ewing sarcoma mimic each other. Antibiotics before sampling reduce culture yield.

items.q: The main advantage of a coaxial technique for image-guided core biopsy of a suspected sarcoma is that it:
o: Allows several cores through a single tract, limiting contamination
Avoids the need for image guidance
Gives a definitive margin around the tumour
items.e: An outer cannula stays in place while the cutting needle is passed several times, so only one tract needs to be excised later. Multiple separate passes would contaminate more tissue.

items.q: The histological grading of conventional chondrosarcoma (Evans) is based on:
o: The percentage of necrosis after chemotherapy
Cellularity, nuclear atypia and mitotic activity
items.e: Evans graded chondrosarcoma by cellularity, nuclear size and atypia, and mitoses; grade is the main predictor of metastasis. IDH mutations are diagnostic, not a grading criterion.

items.q: The MSTS (Enneking) functional rating score after limb-salvage surgery has a maximum score of:
items.e: It uses 6 domains (pain, function, emotional acceptance and three limb-specific items), each scored 0-5, for a maximum of 30, often expressed as a percentage.

items.q: A core biopsy of a suspected bone sarcoma will need molecular testing (FISH or sequencing). Which processing step is most likely to make the sample unsuitable?
o: Freezing a portion of fresh tissue
items.e: Strong acid decalcification degrades DNA and RNA, ruining molecular tests. EDTA decalcification or keeping a non-decalcified soft portion preserves nucleic acids.

items.q: A biopsy is planned for a permeative lesion suspected to be primary lymphoma of bone. A portion of the tissue should be sent:
o: Fresh and unfixed for flow cytometry
Only in formalin after acid decalcification
items.e: Flow cytometry needs fresh, viable cells to establish clonality and subtype; formalin fixation prevents it. Discussing handling with the pathologist before biopsy avoids repeat procedures.

items.q: A 58-year-old treated for breast cancer 10 years ago now has a solitary lytic lesion of the proximal femur. Before definitive surgery, the correct step is to:
o: Fix it with an intramedullary nail as a presumed metastasis
Perform a biopsy, because a new primary bone tumour must be excluded
Perform a wide resection without tissue diagnosis
items.e: A solitary lesion, especially after a long disease-free interval, may be a primary sarcoma or a different cancer, and nailing a sarcoma contaminates the whole femur. Tissue diagnosis comes first.

items.q: In Mankin's 1996 follow-up study of biopsy in musculoskeletal tumours, diagnostic errors and biopsy-related complications were:
o: Several times more frequent when the biopsy was done at the referring hospital than at the treating tumour centre
Equally frequent at referring hospitals and tumour centres
Eliminated by using needle rather than open biopsy
items.e: Mankin's repeat study showed problems were several-fold more common when the biopsy was performed outside the treating centre. Hence the rule that the surgeon who will do the resection should plan the biopsy.

items.q: The PICO method for quantifying anterior glenoid bone loss uses:
o: The glenoid width on a plain axillary radiograph
The distance from the bare spot to the posterior rim at arthroscopy
A best-fit circle on en-face CT of both glenoids, comparing the missing area with the circle area
items.e: On bilateral en-face 3D CT, the circle drawn on the intact glenoid is transferred to the injured side and the missing area is expressed as a percentage. The bare-spot method is an arthroscopic estimate.

items.q: In the Rowe score for shoulder instability, which domain carries 50 of the 100 points?
items.e: The Rowe score allots 50 points to stability, 20 to motion and 30 to function. Recurrence therefore dominates the score.

items.q: In Neer's open inferior capsular shift for multidirectional instability, the capsule is:
o: Released from the glenoid and left unrepaired
Plicated arthroscopically with suture anchors at the glenoid rim
Opened with a humeral-based T incision and the inferior flap shifted superiorly to reduce the axillary pouch
items.e: Neer's shift detaches the capsule laterally from the humerus, splits it in a T, and advances the inferior flap upward to obliterate the redundant inferior pouch. Thermal capsulorrhaphy was abandoned because of chondrolysis.

items.q: The West Point axillary radiograph is mainly used to show:
o: A bony lesion of the anteroinferior glenoid rim
items.e: With the patient prone, the arm abducted and the beam angled 25 degrees medially and downward, the anteroinferior glenoid rim is shown in profile. The Stryker notch view is used for Hill-Sachs lesions.

items.q: The Stryker notch view, taken supine with the hand on the head and the beam angled about 10 degrees cephalad, is best for showing:
items.e: The Stryker notch view profiles the posterolateral humeral head, where the Hill-Sachs impaction lies. Glenoid rim lesions are better seen on the West Point view or CT.

items.q: During a Latarjet procedure, which structure is detached completely from the coracoid rather than kept with the graft?
o: A stump of the coracoacromial ligament
items.e: Pectoralis minor is released from the medial coracoid. The conjoint tendon (short head of biceps and coracobrachialis) stays on the graft for the sling effect, and a coracoacromial ligament stump is kept for capsular repair.

items.q: During arthroscopic inferior capsular plication, the axillary nerve lies closest to the glenoid rim at about which clock-face position?
items.e: The axillary nerve passes just below the inferior capsule, closest to the glenoid at the 6 o'clock position (about 1-1.5 cm away). Deep capsular bites here risk injury.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of posterior shoulder dislocations are missed at the first presentation?
items.e: Posterior dislocations are missed in roughly 50-79% of cases because the AP view can look nearly normal. An axillary view or CT is required whenever external rotation is blocked.

items.q: The most frequent radiological finding of the bone graft in medium-term follow-up after a Latarjet procedure is:
o: Osteolysis of the superior part of the coracoid graft
Complete graft non-union with screw breakage
items.e: Partial osteolysis, mainly of the superior graft around the proximal screw where it is less loaded, is common. Non-union and hardware failure occur but are less frequent.

items.q: During the relocation test in an overhead athlete, posterior pressure on the humeral head relieves pain rather than apprehension. This response most suggests:
o: Anterior instability from a Bankart lesion
items.e: Relief of apprehension is the specific sign of anterior instability. Relief of posterior pain in abduction-external rotation suggests internal impingement between the cuff undersurface and the posterosuperior glenoid.

items.q: At arthroscopy, the anterosuperior labrum is absent and the middle glenohumeral ligament is thick and cord-like, attaching directly to the superior labrum. The correct management is:
o: Repair the anterosuperior labrum to the glenoid with anchors
Leave it alone as a normal variant (Buford complex)
Convert to an open Bankart repair
items.e: The Buford complex is a normal variant; reattaching the cord-like MGHL to the glenoid causes painful loss of external rotation. It must not be mistaken for a labral tear.

items.q: Closure of the rotator interval in multidirectional shoulder instability is intended mainly to reduce:
o: Anterior translation in abduction and external rotation
Superior migration of the humeral head
items.e: The rotator interval structures (SGHL and coracohumeral ligament) resist inferior translation in adduction; experimental closure also reduced posterior translation. The anterior band of the IGHL is the restraint in abduction-external rotation.

items.q: Of the pelvic floor ligaments, the one that principally resists vertical shear and flexion of the hemipelvis is the:
items.e: The sacrotuberous ligament, running vertically from sacrum to ischial tuberosity, resists vertical shear and flexion; the sacrospinous ligament resists external rotation.

items.q: The stability of the pelvic ring depends chiefly on the:
items.e: The posterior SI and interosseous ligaments are the strongest in the body and form the posterior tension band; posterior integrity matters more than anterior.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a vertical shear pelvic injury with 3 cm cranial displacement of the hemipelvis. Pending definitive posterior fixation, the best temporary measure to restore and hold length is:
o: Distal femoral (or proximal tibial) skeletal traction on the injured side
items.e: Binders and anterior frames do not control vertical displacement; longitudinal skeletal traction on the injured limb reduces and maintains the cranially migrated hemipelvis.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a minimally displaced LC I injury (sacral buckle fracture and oblique pubic rami fractures) and is haemodynamically stable. Management is:
o: Open reduction and internal fixation of the rami
Mobilisation with weight bearing as tolerated
items.e: LC I injuries are stable and treated with analgesia and early mobilisation; fixation is considered only if pain prevents mobilisation or displacement progresses.

items.q: In the Thompson-Epstein classification of posterior hip dislocation, type V is a dislocation with:
o: A large single posterior rim fragment
A fracture of the femoral head
items.e: Type I has no or a minor fracture, II a large posterior rim fragment, III a comminuted rim, IV an acetabular floor fracture and V a femoral head fracture (subdivided by Pipkin).

items.q: To reduce the risk of avascular necrosis, a traumatic hip dislocation should ideally be reduced within:
items.e: AVN risk rises sharply when reduction is delayed beyond about 6 hours because of prolonged tension and kinking of the retinacular vessels.

items.q: After a dashboard injury causing posterior hip dislocation, which associated injury is particularly easy to miss?
o: Anterior cruciate ligament tear from hyperextension
Ipsilateral knee injury such as a PCL tear or patellar fracture
Lisfranc injury of the opposite foot
items.e: The dashboard strikes the flexed knee, driving the tibia back (PCL injury) and fracturing the patella as the force travels up the femur to dislocate the hip.

items.q: A 76-year-old with pre-existing hip osteoarthritis falls and sustains a displaced acetabular fracture with marked superomedial dome impaction. The most suitable treatment is:
o: Open reduction and internal fixation alone
Acetabular fixation combined with acute total hip arthroplasty
items.e: Pre-existing arthritis and dome impaction predict failure of ORIF in the elderly, so 'fix and replace' allows early weight bearing and avoids a second operation.

items.q: On the AP radiograph of the acetabulum, the medial limb of the radiographic teardrop corresponds to the:
items.e: The teardrop's lateral limb is the floor of the acetabular fossa and its medial limb is the anteroinferior quadrilateral surface; it moves with the posterior column in many fractures.

items.q: During dissection along the quadrilateral plate in a modified Stoppa approach, apart from the corona mortis, the structure most at risk is the:
items.e: The obturator nerve and vessels run along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator canal, directly over the quadrilateral surface exposed in the Stoppa approach.

items.q: During a Kocher-Langenbeck approach, the superior gluteal neurovascular bundle is most at risk when:
o: Extending exposure toward the greater sciatic notch
Detaching the short external rotators near the femur
items.e: The superior gluteal vessels and nerve exit the greater sciatic notch above piriformis; superior dissection or retraction there can injure them, causing bleeding or abductor weakness.

items.q: An isolated iliac wing fracture (Duverney fracture) that does not disrupt the pelvic ring is Tile type:
items.e: Tile A injuries are stable and include avulsions and iliac wing fractures that spare the ring; they are usually treated non-operatively.

items.q: A 15-year-old sprinter feels a pop in the groin while starting a race. Radiographs show avulsion of the anterior superior iliac spine. The muscle responsible is:
items.e: Sartorius (with tensor fasciae latae) arises from the ASIS; rectus femoris avulses the AIIS and iliopsoas the lesser trochanter. Most heal with rest.

items.q: The most common long-term mode of failure requiring revision after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty is:
items.e: Glenoid component loosening (and polyethylene wear) is the dominant long-term problem after anatomic TSA; humeral loosening is much rarer.

items.q: After reverse shoulder arthroplasty, a stress fracture through the scapular spine medial to the acromioclavicular joint is classified by Levy as type:
items.e: Levy type I involves the acromion distal to the AC joint, type II the acromion at the AC joint level, and type III the scapular spine medial to the AC joint; type III is the most disabling.

items.q: In the Wright and Cofield classification of periprosthetic humeral fractures around a stemmed shoulder implant, a fracture lying entirely distal to the stem tip is type:
items.e: Type A is centred at the tip and extends proximally, type B is at the tip with little proximal extension, and type C is distal to the tip; type C is usually treated like a shaft fracture.

items.q: When Cutibacterium acnes infection is suspected after shoulder arthroplasty, intraoperative tissue cultures should be incubated for about:
items.e: C. acnes is slow growing and anaerobic, so cultures are held for about 14 days; standard 5-day cultures miss many cases.

items.q: When fixing the glenoid baseplate in reverse shoulder arthroplasty, the superior locking screw is ideally directed into the:
o: Scapular spine at the spinoglenoid notch
items.e: The best bone for the superior screw is the coracoid base, while the inferior screw goes into the scapular pillar. Screws heading toward the spinoglenoid or suprascapular notch put the suprascapular nerve at risk.

items.q: A 70-year-old has glenohumeral arthritis with an irreparable massive rotator cuff tear and superior migration of the humeral head. Anatomic TSA should be avoided mainly because:
o: Eccentric superior loading rocks and loosens the glenoid component
The humeral stem cannot be cemented
items.e: Without a cuff to centre the head, the humerus rides up and loads the glenoid edge ('rocking-horse' effect), causing early glenoid loosening; reverse arthroplasty is preferred.

items.q: In anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty, the humeral head cut is commonly made in roughly how much retroversion relative to the forearm axis?
items.e: Native humeral retroversion averages about 20-30° and the cut is usually made there or matched to the patient's anatomy; 0° anteverts the component relative to the native head and risks anterior instability.

items.q: Radiolucent lines around a pegged glenoid component after anatomic TSA are graded with the:
items.e: Lazarus grades glenoid radiolucency from 0 (none) to 5 (gross loosening). Sirveaux grades scapular notching after RTSA, Walch grades glenoid morphology and Hamada grades cuff tear arthropathy.

items.q: The 'ream-and-run' procedure for glenohumeral arthritis in a young, active patient consists of:
o: Reverse arthroplasty with a lateralised glenosphere
Humeral hemiarthroplasty with concentric glenoid reaming and no glenoid component
Glenoid resurfacing with a biological interposition graft only
items.e: Matsen's ream-and-run reams the glenoid to a single concavity and relies on fibrocartilage to cover it, avoiding a polyethylene glenoid that may loosen in active patients.

items.q: A 74-year-old has painful anterosuperior escape and pseudoparalysis 3 years after a hemiarthroplasty for fracture, with resorbed tuberosities. The preferred revision is:
o: Revision to a larger humeral head
items.e: Tuberosity resorption leaves a functionally cuff-deficient shoulder, so conversion to RTSA, which relies on the deltoid, gives the most predictable gain in elevation.

items.q: Plantar fibromatosis occurring with Dupuytren disease is known as:
items.e: Ledderhose disease is plantar fascial fibromatosis; Peyronie disease affects the penile tunica albuginea and Garrod pads are knuckle pads, all ectopic manifestations of the Dupuytren diathesis.

items.q: Which feature is part of Hueston's 'Dupuytren diathesis', predicting aggressive disease and recurrence?
o: Ectopic lesions such as knuckle pads or plantar fibromatosis
Unilateral involvement of the little finger only
items.e: The diathesis comprises early onset (under 50), positive family history, bilateral disease, ectopic lesions and male sex (often with radial-side involvement); late onset and limited disease are favourable.

items.q: The lateral cord in Dupuytren disease, which can cause PIP and DIP contracture and displace the neurovascular bundle toward the midline, develops from the:
items.e: The lateral digital sheet (superficial fascia lateral to the neurovascular bundle) becomes the lateral cord; the pretendinous band forms the pretendinous cord causing MCP contracture.

items.q: A commonly accepted indication to treat a Dupuytren contracture is:
o: A painless palmar nodule without contracture
An MCP contracture of about 30° or more, or any significant PIP contracture
items.e: Treatment is offered when contracture affects function, usually an MCP contracture of about 30° (positive tabletop test) or any PIP contracture, which becomes harder to correct the longer it persists.

items.q: A 45-year-old man with a strong Dupuytren diathesis has recurrent PIP contracture with skin involvement after previous fasciectomy. The procedure with the lowest recurrence rate is:
items.e: Excising the involved skin with the diseased fascia and replacing it with a full-thickness graft gives the lowest recurrence and is favoured for recurrent disease or a strong diathesis.

items.q: A rheumatoid swan-neck finger has full PIP flexion when the MCP joint is flexed, but limited PIP flexion when the MCP joint is held extended; joint surfaces are preserved (Nalebuff type II). Appropriate surgery is:
o: Intrinsic release (with correction of MCP disease as needed)
items.e: Type II swan-neck is caused by intrinsic tightness, so the intrinsics are released along with treatment of any MCP subluxation; arthrodesis or arthroplasty is for destroyed joints (type IV).

items.q: A rheumatoid index finger has a fixed boutonniere deformity with a destroyed PIP joint. Preferred treatment is:
o: Extensor tenotomy over the middle phalanx (Fowler)
items.e: With a fixed deformity and a destroyed joint, soft-tissue procedures fail; PIP arthrodesis gives a stable index finger for pinch, where arthroplasty would be weakened by lateral pinch forces.

items.q: The most common deformity of the rheumatoid thumb is:
o: Nalebuff type I (boutonniere: MCP flexion with IP hyperextension)
Nalebuff type III (swan-neck from CMC disease)
items.e: Type I boutonniere thumb, from MCP synovitis attenuating the extensor mechanism, is the commonest; type III swan-neck is second.

items.q: A rheumatoid patient has triggering of the middle finger due to flexor tenosynovitis. The preferred surgical treatment is:
o: Release of the A1 and A2 pulleys
Flexor tenosynovectomy, preserving the A1 pulley
items.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, triggering is due to synovial or nodular bulk, and A1 release removes a restraint against ulnar drift; tenosynovectomy and, if needed, excision of one FDS slip are preferred.

items.q: The randomised RIDD trial in early-stage Dupuytren disease tested intranodular injection of:
items.e: Nanchahal's RIDD trial showed that intranodular adalimumab softened and reduced the size of Dupuytren nodules, targeting TNF-driven myofibroblast differentiation.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of the wet weight of a normal adult meniscus is water?
items.e: Meniscal fibrocartilage is roughly 70% water; most of the dry weight is collagen, predominantly type I.

items.q: Most of the collagen in the dry weight of the meniscus is:
items.e: About 90% of meniscal collagen is type I, whereas hyaline articular cartilage is dominated by type II.

items.q: The cells that synthesise and maintain the meniscal extracellular matrix are:
items.e: Meniscal cells are fibrochondrocytes, with features of both fibroblasts and chondrocytes; hypertrophic chondrocytes belong to the calcified cartilage and growth plate.

items.q: Radially oriented 'tie' fibres in the meniscus mainly function to:
o: Carry most of the hoop stress
Provide channels for the perimeniscal capillaries
Anchor the meniscus to the joint capsule
Resist longitudinal splitting between the circumferential collagen bundles
items.e: Radial fibres bind the dominant circumferential bundles together and resist longitudinal splitting; hoop stress is borne by the circumferential fibres.

items.q: Excursion of the medial meniscus during knee motion is only about 2-5 mm, compared with about 9-11 mm for the lateral meniscus. The main anatomical reason the medial meniscus is torn more often is that it:
o: Is firmly attached to the capsule and the deep MCL, limiting its mobility
Carries a greater share of its compartment load than the lateral meniscus
items.e: Its capsular and deep MCL attachments make the medial meniscus less mobile, so it is trapped and torn more easily; the lateral meniscus actually carries a greater share (about 70%) of its compartment load.

items.q: At the popliteal hiatus, the lateral meniscus:
o: Is firmly attached to the fibular collateral ligament
Gives origin to the ligament of Humphrey
items.e: The popliteus tendon passes through the hiatus, where the lateral meniscus has no capsular attachment; the fibular collateral ligament never attaches to the lateral meniscus.

items.q: The meniscofemoral ligament that runs from the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the medial femoral condyle POSTERIOR to the PCL is the ligament of:
items.e: Wrisberg passes posterior and Humphrey anterior to the PCL; both connect the lateral meniscal posterior horn to the medial femoral condyle.

items.q: The blood supply of the adult menisci comes mainly from:
o: The anterior and posterior tibial recurrent arteries
The medial, lateral and middle genicular arteries through a perimeniscal capillary plexus
items.e: Branches of the genicular arteries form a perimeniscal capillary plexus that penetrates only the peripheral 10-30% of the meniscus.

items.q: A vertical longitudinal meniscal tear lies 4 mm from the meniscosynovial junction. It lies in the:
o: Red-white zone, with intermediate healing potential
Red-red zone, with excellent healing potential
White-white zone, with poor healing potential
Synovial fringe, containing no meniscal tissue
items.e: Under 3 mm from the rim is red-red, 3-5 mm red-white (intermediate) and over 5 mm white-white (avascular).

items.q: Approximately what proportion of the load across the knee is transmitted through the menisci at 90 degrees of flexion?
items.e: The menisci carry about 50% of the load in extension and about 85-90% in flexion.

items.q: In an ACL-deficient knee, which structure is the most important secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation?
o: Anterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Posterior horn of the medial meniscus
items.e: The posterior horn of the medial meniscus acts as a wedge against anterior tibial translation, which is why it tears in chronic ACL deficiency.

items.q: Total meniscectomy increases peak tibiofemoral contact stress by roughly:
items.e: Loss of the meniscus reduces the contact area, increasing peak contact stress by about 2-3 times (up to about 235%).

items.q: Fairbank (1948) described radiographic changes after meniscectomy. They are:
o: Anteroposterior ridge (osteophyte) formation, flattening of the femoral condyle and joint-space narrowing
Subchondral cysts, sclerosis and loose bodies
Chondrocalcinosis of the meniscal remnant and tibial spurs
Squaring of the lateral femoral condyle and cupping of the lateral plateau
items.e: Fairbank's triad is ridging, condylar flattening and joint-space narrowing; squaring and cupping are radiographic signs of a discoid lateral meniscus.

items.q: Lateral meniscectomy has worse long-term outcomes than medial meniscectomy mainly because:
o: The lateral meniscus carries less of its compartment load
The convex lateral femoral condyle sits on a convex lateral plateau, so the compartment depends more on the meniscus
The lateral meniscus is less mobile than the medial
The lateral compartment is concave-on-concave and inherently congruent
items.e: Convex-on-convex lateral geometry and the roughly 70% load share of the lateral meniscus explain the rapid lateral degeneration after its removal.

items.q: Sagittal MRI after a twisting injury shows an unusually tall anterior horn of the lateral meniscus and a small, truncated posterior horn. The most likely explanation is:
o: A displaced flap of the posterior horn flipped anteriorly (flipped meniscus)
items.e: The 'double anterior horn' or flipped meniscus sign indicates posterior horn tissue displaced next to the anterior horn; a discoid meniscus is enlarged in both horns.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman felt a painful 'pop' in the medial knee while squatting. Radiographs were normal. MRI six weeks later shows a medial meniscus posterior root tear, extensive marrow oedema of the medial femoral condyle and a subchondral low-signal line. The diagnosis is:
o: Bone bruise from a pivot-shift injury
Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee
items.e: SIFK (formerly SONK) typically affects older women in the medial femoral condyle, often after a medial root tear, with a subchondral low-signal line and marrow oedema.

items.q: The initial management of a subchondral insufficiency fracture of the medial femoral condyle without collapse is:
o: Protected weight bearing with analgesia and follow-up imaging
items.e: Most early SIFK lesions are managed with protected weight bearing; arthroplasty is reserved for subchondral collapse.

items.q: Which clinical finding is the most sensitive for a meniscal tear?
o: A palpable click on the McMurray test
Pain on the Apley grind test
items.e: Joint-line tenderness is the most sensitive sign, although it is not very specific; locking is specific but uncommon.

items.q: In the Thessaly test, the patient stands on the affected leg and rotates the body with the knee flexed to about:
items.e: Karachalios described the test at 5 and 20 degrees; the 20-degree version is the more accurate one.

items.q: During the McMurray test, a painful click as the knee is extended from full flexion with the tibia held in external rotation suggests a tear of the:
o: Posterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Anterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Posterior horn of the medial meniscus
items.e: External rotation of the tibia loads the posterior horn of the medial meniscus; internal rotation tests the lateral meniscus.

items.q: The Apley grind test for a meniscal tear is performed with the patient:
o: Prone, knee flexed to 90 degrees, applying axial compression while rotating the tibia
Supine, knee extended, applying valgus stress
Standing on one leg with the knee in 20 degrees of flexion
Sitting with the hip flexed and the leg hanging free
items.e: Apley compressed and rotated the tibia with the patient prone and the knee at 90 degrees; pain on compression (not distraction) suggests a meniscal lesion.

items.q: The 'two-slice-touch' rule in MRI of the menisci states that:
o: A tear requires two separate meniscal fragments to be visible
A tear is diagnosed with high positive predictive value when abnormal signal contacting the articular surface is seen on at least two images
Extrusion over 2 mm on two slices indicates a root tear
A bow-tie seen on only two slices is normal
items.e: De Smet showed that surface-contacting signal on two or more images is highly predictive of a tear, whereas signal on a single image is less reliable.

items.q: On sagittal MRI, a linear band of high signal between the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus and Hoffa's fat pad can mimic a tear. This pseudotear is caused by the:
items.e: The transverse (intermeniscal) ligament joins the anterior horns and its junction with the anterior horn can mimic a tear; popliteus and Wrisberg pseudotears involve the posterior horn.

items.q: The ESCAPE trial (van de Graaf et al., JAMA 2018) of patients aged 45-70 with non-obstructive degenerative meniscal tears found that physical therapy was:
o: Superior to partial meniscectomy at 24 months
Equivalent to sham surgery but inferior to repair
Non-inferior to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for knee function at 24 months
items.e: ESCAPE supports physiotherapy first for degenerative tears; it compared physical therapy with partial meniscectomy, not with sham surgery (which was FIDELITY).

items.q: In a 52-year-old with a degenerative medial meniscal tear, which feature is the clearest indication for arthroscopic partial meniscectomy?
o: True mechanical locking from a displaced fragment
items.e: Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy is reserved for true mechanical symptoms or failure of conservative care; an MRI tear alone is not an indication.

items.q: Meniscal repairs heal better when performed with concurrent ACL reconstruction mainly because:
o: The reconstructed knee is immobilised for longer
Tunnel drilling releases blood, marrow-derived cells and growth factors into the joint
ACL graft harvest denervates the meniscus
The meniscus is unloaded permanently after reconstruction
items.e: The haemarthrosis and marrow elements from tunnel drilling provide a biological boost; isolated repairs can be augmented by notch marrow venting.

items.q: The traditional gold-standard technique for repair of a mid-body to posterior horn longitudinal meniscal tear, allowing multiple vertical mattress sutures, is:
items.e: Inside-out repair through a posteromedial or posterolateral safety incision is the benchmark for mid-body and posterior tears.

items.q: The outside-in meniscal repair technique is best suited to tears of the:
o: Posterior horn of the lateral meniscus near the root
items.e: Outside-in suturing gives easy access to the anterior horn, which is hard to reach with inside-out or all-inside devices.

items.q: When an all-inside device is used close to the root of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, the structure at greatest risk if the needle penetrates too deeply is the:
o: Infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve
items.e: The popliteal neurovascular bundle lies directly behind the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus near the midline, so depth-limiters and angling away from the midline are used.

items.q: During the posteromedial safety incision for inside-out repair of the medial meniscus, the nerve that must be protected is the:
o: Saphenous nerve and its sartorial branch
items.e: The saphenous nerve runs with the sartorius posteromedially; the peroneal nerve is at risk on the lateral side.

items.q: In the posterolateral exposure for inside-out lateral meniscal repair, the common peroneal nerve is protected by:
o: Retracting the biceps femoris anteriorly and working posterior to the lateral gastrocnemius
Dividing the fibular collateral ligament for access
Retracting the biceps femoris posteriorly and placing the retractor between the lateral head of gastrocnemius and the posterior capsule
Working medial to the biceps tendon within the popliteal fossa
items.e: The nerve lies posterior to the biceps; working anterior to the lateral gastrocnemius on the capsule, with biceps retracted posteriorly, keeps it out of harm.

items.q: Which is an accepted biological augmentation for an isolated meniscal repair in the red-white zone?
o: Radiofrequency ablation of the tear edges
Twelve weeks of immobilisation in full extension
An exogenous fibrin clot placed into the repair
items.e: Fibrin clot, notch marrow venting and rasping or trephination bring cells and growth factors to the repair; steroid and ablation impair healing.

items.q: After repair of a posterior horn meniscal tear, patients are usually advised to avoid deep squatting beyond 90 degrees of flexion for about:
items.e: Deep flexion loads the posterior horn and can disrupt the repair, so loaded flexion beyond 90 degrees is limited for about 3-4 months.

items.q: Which meniscal repair has the lowest expected healing rate?
o: A lateral repair with concurrent ACL reconstruction
An isolated medial meniscal repair in an ACL-deficient knee that is left unreconstructed
A medial repair with concurrent ACL reconstruction
An acute peripheral lateral repair in a stable knee
items.e: Repairs fail more often medially, when isolated and when the knee remains unstable; lateral repairs with ACL reconstruction do best.

items.q: Transtibial pull-out repair of a medial meniscus posterior root tear is most appropriate in:
o: A 68-year-old with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4 medial osteoarthritis
A 55-year-old with bone-on-bone medial narrowing and 8 degrees of varus
A 45-year-old with an acute traumatic root tear and Kellgren-Lawrence grade 0-1 changes
A 70-year-old with subchondral collapse of the medial femoral condyle
items.e: Root repair slows extrusion and arthritis progression only in knees without advanced osteoarthritis or uncorrected malalignment.

items.q: Which longitudinal tear length is generally regarded as most suitable for meniscal repair?
o: Any length within the white-white zone
items.e: Peripheral vertical tears of about 1-4 cm repair best; very short stable tears can be left alone, and long complex tears fare worse.

items.q: Discoid lateral meniscus is notably more prevalent in:
items.e: Prevalence is about 3-5% overall but reaches up to about 15% in East Asian populations.

items.q: Discoid lateral meniscus is bilateral in roughly:
items.e: About a fifth of discoid menisci are bilateral, so the contralateral knee should be examined.

items.q: In the Watanabe classification, an incomplete discoid lateral meniscus with normal posterior attachments that does not cover the whole plateau is type:
items.e: Type I is complete, type II incomplete and type III the Wrisberg variant lacking posterior meniscotibial attachment; there is no type IV in Watanabe's scheme.

items.q: Which radiographic finding suggests a discoid lateral meniscus in a child?
o: Narrowing of the medial joint space
An ossicle in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus
Widened lateral joint space with squaring of the lateral femoral condyle
items.e: Widening of the lateral joint space, a squared lateral condyle and cupping of the lateral plateau suggest a discoid meniscus.

items.q: On 5-mm sagittal MRI slices, discoid lateral meniscus is suggested when the continuous 'bow-tie' meniscal body is seen on:
items.e: A normal meniscus shows the bow-tie on two slices; three or more contiguous slices suggest a discoid meniscus, and fewer than two suggests a displaced bucket-handle tear.

items.q: Total meniscectomy for a torn discoid lateral meniscus in a child is avoided because it predisposes to:
o: Early lateral compartment arthritis and osteochondritis dissecans of the lateral femoral condyle
items.e: Saucerisation leaving a 6-8 mm rim is preferred because removal of the whole meniscus leads to early lateral degeneration and lateral condyle OCD.

items.q: A discoid lateral meniscus is found incidentally on MRI in an asymptomatic 10-year-old. Management is:
items.e: Asymptomatic discoid menisci are observed; surgery is reserved for symptoms such as pain, snapping or locking.

items.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to meniscal allograft transplantation?
o: Diffuse Outerbridge grade IV changes in the involved compartment
items.e: MAT needs a compartment with minimal arthritis; ACL reconstruction can be performed at the same time to provide stability.

items.q: In lateral meniscal allograft transplantation, the graft is usually fixed with a single bone bridge (keyhole or slot) rather than two separate bone plugs because:
o: The anterior and posterior horn attachments of the lateral meniscus lie close together
The lateral meniscus is much thicker than the medial
The lateral plateau is too soft to hold plugs
items.e: The lateral horns insert close together, so a bridge preserves their anatomical relationship; medial grafts are often fixed with separate bone plugs.

items.q: Radiographic sizing of a meniscal allograft from calibrated AP and lateral radiographs is classically done by the:
items.e: Pollard described meniscal width and length estimation from plateau dimensions on radiographs; the other methods relate to patellar height or the femoral roof line.

items.q: Survival of meniscal allograft transplants at 10 years is roughly:
items.e: About 70-80% of grafts survive at 10 years, with better results laterally; shrinkage, extrusion and tears are common.

items.q: A 32-year-old has medial knee pain after total medial meniscectomy, minimal arthritis, a stable knee and 7 degrees of varus. Before or with a medial meniscal allograft, he needs:
items.e: Uncorrected varus overloads a medial graft, so alignment is corrected with a valgus high tibial osteotomy.

items.q: Collagen meniscus implants and polyurethane scaffolds for partial meniscal loss require:
o: An intact peripheral rim and intact horn attachments
items.e: Scaffolds fill segmental defects and depend on the remaining rim and horns for fixation and hoop stress; total loss needs an allograft.

items.q: Type X collagen in articular cartilage is found mainly in the:
o: Calcified cartilage zone, associated with hypertrophic chondrocytes
items.e: Type X collagen marks hypertrophic chondrocytes in the calcified layer (and the growth plate hypertrophic zone).

items.q: Which collagen type is bound to the surface of type II fibrils and cross-links them in articular cartilage?
items.e: Type IX cross-links type II fibrils, type XI regulates fibril diameter and type VI is pericellular.

items.q: During an extensile posterior approach for THA, the gluteus maximus tendon insertion on the femur is partly released to improve femoral exposure. Which vessel is at risk of troublesome bleeding during this release?
o: Ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
First perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery
items.e: The first perforating artery runs close to the gluteal tuberosity and is cut if the release is taken too close to bone. The ascending lateral circumflex branch is met in the anterior approach.

items.q: A 55-year-old has a large cartilage tumour of the ilium with cortical destruction and a soft-tissue mass on CT. Core biopsy reports 'benign cartilage tumour, consistent with enchondroma'. The best interpretation is:
o: The tumour is benign and can be observed
The biopsy is discordant with imaging and may be unrepresentative; manage at the sarcoma MDT as chondrosarcoma unless proven otherwise
Repeat biopsy is never useful in cartilage tumours
items.e: Cartilage tumours are histologically heterogeneous and cores often under-grade them; aggressive imaging features outweigh a bland core. Discordance is resolved at the multidisciplinary meeting, usually treating as chondrosarcoma.

items.q: In the WHO 2020 classification, the term 'atypical cartilaginous tumour' rather than 'chondrosarcoma grade 1' is used for a low-grade central cartilage tumour located in the:
o: Appendicular skeleton (long and short tubular bones)
items.e: Grade 1 lesions of the limb bones are called atypical cartilaginous tumour because they rarely metastasise and are treated by curettage. In the axial skeleton (pelvis, scapula, skull base) the term chondrosarcoma grade 1 is kept because outcomes are worse.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM preoperative scoring for PJI, a raised plasma D-dimer earns 2 points when it exceeds:
items.e: D-dimer above 860 ng/mL (or serum CRP above 1 mg/dL) scores 2 points; the usual 500 ng/mL VTE cut-off is not the ICM threshold.

items.q: A synovial alpha-defensin test counts as positive in the 2018 ICM criteria when the signal-to-cutoff ratio is above:
items.e: A signal-to-cutoff ratio above 1.0 is positive and scores 3 points.

items.q: A patient with an inconclusive preoperative ICM score has a combined pre- and intraoperative score of 5. This is interpreted as:
o: Inconclusive, needing further molecular or clinical assessment
Infected only if the ESR exceeds 100 mm/h
items.e: With intraoperative findings added, 6 or more is infected, 4-5 is inconclusive and 3 or less is not infected.

items.q: Before aspirating a painful knee arthroplasty for suspected PJI, antibiotics should ideally be stopped for at least:
items.e: Stopping antibiotics at least 2 weeks beforehand reduces false-negative cultures, a common cause of culture-negative PJI.

items.q: When low-virulence organisms such as Cutibacterium acnes are suspected, periprosthetic cultures should be incubated for about:
items.e: Extended incubation of 10-14 days is needed to grow slow-growing C. acnes and other fastidious organisms.

items.q: At revision for suspected PJI, the recommended intraoperative microbiology sampling is:
o: A single swab from the wound edge
Two swabs from the joint fluid
One large tissue sample divided in the laboratory
About five separate periprosthetic tissue samples taken with separate instruments
items.e: Three to six (usually five) tissue samples with clean instruments allow two matching positive cultures to define infection; swabs have poor sensitivity.

items.q: Bacteria within a mature implant biofilm can be up to how many times more resistant to antibiotics than planktonic bacteria?
items.e: Sessile biofilm bacteria may be up to about 1,000 times more resistant, which is why chronic PJI usually needs implant removal.

items.q: Which perioperative blood glucose level is commonly cited as increasing the risk of PJI after joint arthroplasty?
items.e: Perioperative hyperglycaemia above about 200 mg/dL, and HbA1c above about 7.5-8%, are associated with higher PJI rates.

items.q: A 62-year-old has persistent pain 3 years after a cementless TKA, with no fever or wound problem. The best first investigation for PJI is:
items.e: ESR and CRP are sensitive screening tests in every painful arthroplasty; if raised or suspicion is high, aspiration follows.

items.q: Cutibacterium acnes shoulder arthroplasty infection is most common in which patient group?
o: Patients with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy
Young men, especially after previous shoulder surgery
items.e: C. acnes colonises the sebaceous axilla and is commoner in men, younger patients and those with prior shoulder surgery.

items.q: The main blood supply to the proximal pole of the scaphoid comes from:
o: Dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery entering at the dorsal ridge and flowing retrograde
Superficial palmar branch entering at the tubercle
Anterior interosseous artery through the radioscapholunate ligament
Ulnar artery through the scapholunate ligament
items.e: Gelberman showed dorsal ridge vessels supply about 70-80% of the scaphoid, including the proximal pole, by retrograde flow, explaining proximal pole AVN.

items.q: A 24-year-old has snuffbox tenderness after a fall but normal scaphoid series radiographs. The investigation of choice to confirm or exclude an occult fracture is:
items.e: MRI has near 100% sensitivity and specificity for occult scaphoid fracture and allows early decisions; bone scan is sensitive but not specific and needs about 72 hours.

items.q: On sagittal CT of a scaphoid fracture, which measurement indicates a humpback deformity?
o: Lateral intrascaphoid angle less than 20 degrees
Lateral intrascaphoid angle greater than 45 degrees
items.e: A lateral intrascaphoid angle above 45 degrees (or height-to-length ratio of 0.65 or more) indicates flexion collapse; normal is about 24 degrees.

items.q: On sagittal CT, a scaphoid height-to-length ratio of which value indicates a humpback deformity?
items.e: A height-to-length ratio of 0.65 or more indicates flexion (humpback) deformity, which predicts poorer function if left uncorrected.

items.q: The SWIFFT trial (Dias et al., 2020) compared surgery with casting for adults with undisplaced or minimally displaced scaphoid waist fractures. It found:
o: No meaningful difference in wrist function at 1 year, with early fixation of non-unions in the cast group
Surgery gave much better function at 1 year
items.e: Patient-reported function at 52 weeks was similar; casting with prompt fixation of detected non-unions is a reasonable standard.

items.q: For a headless compression screw in a scaphoid waist fracture, the best mechanical outcome is achieved by placing the screw:
o: Along the central axis of the scaphoid
items.e: Central placement gives greater stiffness, more load to failure and faster union than eccentric placement.

items.q: Why is the volar approach preferred for fixation of scaphoid waist fractures?
o: It gives the best access to the proximal pole
It avoids the radial artery entirely
It preserves the dorsal ridge blood supply
It allows screw insertion with the wrist flexed
items.e: The volar approach avoids the dorsal ridge vessels that supply most of the scaphoid; the dorsal approach with wrist flexion is used for proximal pole fractures.

items.q: For a scaphoid waist non-union with a humpback deformity and a viable proximal pole, the standard reconstruction is:
o: Dorsal inlay cancellous graft without fixation
Volar wedge corticocancellous iliac crest graft with screw fixation (Fisk-Fernandez)
items.e: An interposition volar wedge graft restores scaphoid length and corrects the flexion deformity; screw fixation stabilises it.

items.q: The 1,2-intercompartmental supraretinacular artery (1,2-ICSRA) graft used for scaphoid non-union is a:
o: Pedicled vascularised graft from the dorsal distal radius
Free vascularised graft from the medial femoral condyle
Pedicled graft from the pronator quadratus on the volar radius
items.e: Described by Zaidemberg, the 1,2-ICSRA runs on the dorsal distal radius between the first and second extensor compartments and gives a pedicled vascularised graft.

items.q: In the Watson scaphoid shift test for scapholunate instability, the examiner presses on the scaphoid tubercle while moving the wrist from:
items.e: In radial deviation the scaphoid tries to flex; thumb pressure pushes it dorsally over the rim, and releasing the pressure gives a painful clunk.

items.q: A scapholunate gap seen on a PA radiograph (Terry Thomas sign) is considered abnormal when it measures more than:
items.e: A gap above 3 mm, especially on a clenched-fist view and compared with the other side, suggests scapholunate dissociation.

items.q: The space of Poirier, through which the capitate escapes in a perilunate dislocation, lies between which ligaments?
items.e: The space of Poirier is a weak palmar area over the capitolunate joint between the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments.

items.q: On a lateral wrist radiograph after a fall, the lunate is tipped palmarly and displaced in front of the radius, with the capitate in line with the radius. This 'spilled teacup' sign indicates:
items.e: In stage IV the dorsal radiolunate ligament fails and the lunate is extruded palmarly into the carpal tunnel, often compressing the median nerve.

items.q: The commonest greater-arc perilunate injury is:
items.e: The trans-scaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation (de Quervain) is the commonest perilunate injury pattern passing through bone.

items.q: Which clinical test is designed to detect lunotriquetral ligament instability?
items.e: The Reagan test translates the triquetrum against the stabilised lunate; pain or laxity suggests LT injury.

items.q: The Dimeglio classification of clubfoot grades severity using a scale with a maximum score of:
items.e: Dimeglio scores four grades (benign to very severe) on a 20-point scale; the Pirani score has a maximum of 6.

items.q: In the Ponseti foot abduction brace for unilateral clubfoot, the recommended external rotation is:
o: About 30 degrees for the clubfoot and 60 degrees for the normal foot
About 60-70 degrees for the clubfoot and 30-40 degrees for the normal foot
items.e: The affected foot is set at about 60-70 degrees and the normal foot at 30-40 degrees, on a bar the width of the shoulders.

items.q: The commonest cause of relapse after successful Ponseti treatment is:
o: Starting treatment after 2 weeks of age
Non-compliance with the foot abduction brace
items.e: Relapse is several times more frequent when bracing is not followed; good compliance keeps relapse rates low.

items.q: 'Kite's error' in clubfoot casting refers to:
o: Using the calcaneocuboid joint, rather than the lateral talar head, as the fulcrum for abduction
Pronating the forefoot to correct cavus
Using above-knee rather than below-knee casts
items.e: Pressure at the calcaneocuboid joint blocks calcaneal abduction under the talus, so heel varus cannot correct; Ponseti uses the lateral talar head as the fulcrum.

items.q: In an atypical (complex) clubfoot, which change to the standard Ponseti technique is recommended?
o: Abducting to 90 degrees in the first cast
Limiting abduction to about 40 degrees and correcting cavus with thumbs under the metatarsal heads
Using below-knee casts to avoid slippage
items.e: Complex clubfeet (short, fat, stiff with deep creases) need limited abduction, knee hyperflexion in the cast and simultaneous plantar pressure to correct cavus.

items.q: In a newborn with a rigid rocker-bottom foot, which radiograph distinguishes congenital vertical talus from congenital oblique talus?
items.e: In vertical talus the talonavicular dislocation persists on forced plantarflexion lateral (talar axis stays plantar to the first metatarsal); in oblique talus it reduces.

items.q: The 'anteater nose' sign on a lateral foot radiograph indicates:
items.e: An elongated anterior process of the calcaneus reaching toward the navicular signifies calcaneonavicular coalition.

items.q: A continuous C-shaped line formed by the medial outline of the talar dome and the sustentaculum tali on a lateral radiograph suggests:
items.e: The 'C sign' reflects a middle-facet talocalcaneal coalition; CT confirms its extent.

items.q: A 5-year-old boy has a limp and medial midfoot pain. The navicular is flattened and sclerotic on radiographs. The prognosis of this condition is:
o: Poor, with talonavicular arthritis by adolescence
Excellent, with spontaneous reconstitution of the navicular
Usually progresses to rigid flatfoot needing fusion
items.e: Kohler disease (osteochondrosis of the navicular) is self-limiting; a short-leg walking cast for 6-8 weeks shortens symptoms.

items.q: A 10-year-old footballer has activity-related heel pain with pain on medial-lateral squeeze of the posterior calcaneus. Radiographs are normal. Management is:
o: Activity modification, heel cups and calf stretching
items.e: Sever disease (calcaneal apophysitis) of children aged about 8-12 is self-limiting and treated symptomatically.

items.q: Persistent symptomatic curly toes in a 4-year-old are best treated by:
items.e: Curly toes result from tight FDL/FDB; simple flexor tenotomy is as effective as flexor-to-extensor transfer and is simpler.

items.q: A symptomatic overlapping fifth toe (digitus minimus varus) in a child is commonly corrected by:
o: Butler procedure with a double racquet incision and dorsal capsular release
items.e: The Butler procedure releases the dorsomedial contracture and repositions the toe through a double racquet incision.

items.q: Surgery for symptomatic adolescent hallux valgus is usually delayed until skeletal maturity because:
o: Bone healing is poor in children
Metatarsal osteotomy is impossible before maturity
Recurrence is high while the physes are open
Adolescent hallux valgus never causes pain
items.e: Recurrence after correction is high with open physes; lateral first metatarsal hemiepiphysiodesis is an option in younger children.

items.q: Congenital hallux varus is classically associated with which anomaly of the first ray?
items.e: Congenital hallux varus often accompanies a longitudinal epiphyseal bracket, a short broad first metatarsal and preaxial polydactyly.

items.q: Under the WADA programme, caffeine is currently:
o: Not prohibited, but included in the monitoring programme
items.e: Caffeine was removed from the Prohibited List in 2004 and is now monitored, along with nicotine and some other stimulants.

items.q: Which analgesic has been prohibited in competition by WADA since 1 January 2024?
items.e: Tramadol was added to S7 narcotics from 2024; codeine, paracetamol and NSAIDs remain permitted.

items.q: Under the WADA Prohibited List, which cannabinoid is permitted?
items.e: All natural and synthetic cannabinoids are prohibited in competition except cannabidiol; THC has a urinary threshold of 150 ng/mL.

items.q: Clenbuterol, often found in contaminated meat cases, is classified on the WADA Prohibited List as:
o: A stimulant prohibited only in competition
An anabolic agent (S1), prohibited at all times
items.e: Although a beta-2 agonist, clenbuterol is listed under S1 'other anabolic agents' and is prohibited at all times.

items.q: Roxadustat, an oral drug for anaemia of chronic kidney disease, is prohibited by WADA because it is a:
items.e: HIF activators such as roxadustat stimulate endogenous EPO and are listed under S2 with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.

items.q: An athlete with glaucoma needs a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Which preparation is permitted without a TUE?
items.e: Topical dorzolamide and brinzolamide are specifically permitted; systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are prohibited as diuretics/masking agents.

items.q: Inhaled formoterol is permitted by WADA up to a maximum delivered dose of:
items.e: Formoterol is permitted up to 54 µg/24 h; salbutamol up to 1,600 µg/24 h and salmeterol up to 200 µg/24 h.

items.q: An unconscious international athlete with anaphylaxis is given intravenous hydrocortisone in the emergency department during competition. The correct anti-doping step is to:
o: Withdraw from all competition for 4 years
Do nothing, as emergency drugs are exempt automatically
Report it as a whereabouts failure
Apply for a retroactive Therapeutic Use Exemption
items.e: Emergency treatment is never withheld; a retroactive TUE can be granted when urgent treatment with a prohibited substance was needed.

items.q: An athlete asks whether an over-the-counter 'muscle-building' supplement is safe to take. The main anti-doping concern to explain is that:
o: Supplements may be contaminated with anabolic agents or stimulants, and strict liability still applies
Supplements are always permitted if bought from a pharmacy
Only supplements made outside India are tested
A positive test from a supplement never leads to a sanction
items.e: Contamination with undeclared prohibited substances is common; the athlete remains responsible, though contamination may reduce the sanction.

items.q: The test recommended by the IOC Medical Commission to diagnose exercise-induced bronchoconstriction in athletes is:
items.e: Eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea is the preferred bronchial provocation test; a fall in FEV1 of 10% or more supports the diagnosis.

items.q: On CT of a talar fracture, Inokuchi's criterion separates neck from body fractures by where the fracture line exits on the inferior surface. A fracture is classed as a talar NECK fracture when this line exits:
o: Through or posterior to the lateral process, into the posterior subtalar facet
Anterior to the lateral process, into the sinus tarsi
Through the medial tubercle of the posterior process
Through the articular surface of the talar head
items.e: A neck fracture exits inferiorly anterior to the lateral process (sinus tarsi), sparing the posterior facet; a line through or behind the lateral process involves the posterior subtalar facet and defines a body fracture, which carries worse joint prognosis.

items.q: The lateral process of the talus, injured in the 'snowboarder's fracture', bears articular surfaces for:
o: The medial malleolus and the sustentaculum tali
The lateral malleolus and the posterior facet of the calcaneus
The anterior calcaneal facet and the cuboid
items.e: The wedge-shaped lateral process articulates dorsolaterally with the fibula and inferomedially with the posterior calcaneal facet, so fractures involve both the ankle and subtalar joints and can cause subtalar arthritis if displaced.

items.q: During dual-incision ORIF of a talar neck fracture, the anterolateral incision (lateral to the extensor digitorum longus, in line with the fourth ray) places which nerve most at risk?
items.e: Branches of the superficial peroneal nerve cross the anterolateral ankle and are at risk with this incision; the saphenous nerve and vein are at risk with the anteromedial incision.

items.q: The anteromedial approach for ORIF of a talar neck fracture is developed in the interval between:
o: Tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior tendons
Extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus
Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
Peroneus tertius and extensor digitorum longus
items.e: The anteromedial incision runs medial to tibialis anterior, above tibialis posterior, giving access to the medial neck while sparing the deltoid branch; the saphenous vein and nerve lie in this field.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of talar neck fractures are open injuries at presentation?
items.e: Talar neck fractures are high-energy injuries and about one in five is open; open fractures carry higher infection and avascular necrosis rates.

items.q: After fixing a talar neck fracture, the surgeon plans to use MRI to assess talar body viability at 3 months. Which screw material best permits this?
items.e: Titanium produces far less susceptibility artefact than stainless steel or cobalt-chromium, so MRI of the talar body after fixation remains interpretable.

items.q: In a lateral subtalar (peritalar) dislocation, the foot typically appears:
o: Adducted and inverted, like an acquired clubfoot, with the talar head prominent dorsolaterally
Fixed in equinus with a prominent posterior heel
Normally aligned, with deformity only at the ankle mortise
Abducted and everted, like an acquired flatfoot, with the talar head prominent medially
items.e: In lateral dislocation the calcaneus and forefoot displace laterally, so the foot is abducted and everted with the talar head palpable medially; the 'clubfoot' appearance is typical of medial dislocation.

items.q: Following closed reduction and cast treatment of a closed subtalar dislocation, the commonest long-term problem is:
o: Subtalar stiffness and post-traumatic subtalar arthritis
Avascular necrosis of the talar body
items.e: Loss of subtalar motion and arthritis are the main sequelae; because the tibiotalar joint stays located and talar soft-tissue attachments are largely preserved, AVN is uncommon and recurrence is rare.

items.q: An elongated lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process, which can cause posterior ankle impingement in dancers, is called the:
items.e: A Stieda process is a long but fused lateral tubercle; an os trigonum is the same ossification centre that has failed to fuse, giving a separate ossicle.

items.q: Fractures of the talar head most commonly result from:
o: Forced dorsiflexion driving the talar neck against the anterior tibia
Inversion avulsion by the anterior talofibular ligament
Axial compression transmitted through the navicular with the foot plantarflexed
Forced plantarflexion compressing the posterior process against the tibia
items.e: The talar head is crushed by axial load along the forefoot through the navicular with the foot plantarflexed; forced dorsiflexion produces neck fractures and forced plantarflexion produces posterior process fractures.

items.q: Which structures lie in the calcaneal (deep central) compartment of the foot, a compartment often involved after calcaneal fracture?
o: Abductor hallucis and flexor hallucis brevis
Quadratus plantae and the lateral plantar neurovascular bundle
items.e: The calcaneal compartment contains quadratus plantae and the lateral plantar vessels and nerve and communicates with the deep posterior compartment of the leg; adductor hallucis has its own compartment and the interossei lie in the four interosseous compartments.

items.q: For acute compartment syndrome of the foot, decompression of all compartments is classically achieved through:
o: Two dorsal incisions over the second and fourth metatarsals plus a medial hindfoot incision
A single lateral incision along the fifth metatarsal
A single plantar midline incision through the plantar fascia
A posterior midline incision beside the Achilles tendon
items.e: Two dorsal incisions decompress the interosseous and adductor compartments, while a medial incision releases the medial, superficial, lateral and calcaneal compartments without a plantar scar.

items.q: In an open intra-articular calcaneal fracture from a fall, the wound is most often located:
o: On the lateral wall beneath the fibula
On the medial side of the heel
On the plantar weight-bearing heel pad
Over the dorsum of the midfoot
items.e: The sharp inferomedial spike of the primary fracture line (sustentacular fragment) usually pierces the medial skin, so open calcaneal wounds are typically medial.

items.q: CT of an acute joint-depression calcaneal fracture shows a small fleck of bone avulsed from the posterolateral rim of the distal fibula. This most likely indicates:
o: Avulsion of the calcaneofibular ligament from the calcaneus
Avulsion of the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament
Avulsion of the superior peroneal retinaculum with dislocation of the peroneal tendons
A fracture of the lateral process of the talus
items.e: This 'fleck sign' marks a superior peroneal retinaculum avulsion; peroneal tendon dislocation accompanies a substantial minority of intra-articular calcaneal fractures and should be reduced and the retinaculum repaired at surgery.

items.q: The Essex-Lopresti manoeuvre for a displaced tongue-type calcaneal fracture involves:
o: An extensile lateral L-shaped approach with a lateral locking plate
Primary subtalar arthrodesis through a sinus tarsi incision
Application of a spanning ankle external fixator only
Inserting a Steinmann pin into the tongue fragment from posterior and levering it plantarward to reduce the posterior facet
items.e: Essex-Lopresti used a pin driven into the tongue fragment as a joystick to restore the posterior facet and heel height, then advanced it across the fracture; it is a percutaneous technique suited to tongue-type fractures.

items.q: When developing the vertical limb of the extensile lateral approach to the calcaneus, which nerve is at risk at the proximal end of the incision?
items.e: The sural nerve runs with the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus and toward the fifth metatarsal base, so it is at risk at both ends of the L-shaped incision.

items.q: The sinus tarsi approach to the calcaneus runs from the tip of the lateral malleolus toward the:
items.e: The small sinus tarsi incision runs from just below the fibular tip toward the fourth metatarsal base, exposing the posterior facet and anterior process with fewer wound complications than the extensile approach.

items.q: With a depressed posterior facet fragment after a calcaneal fracture, the lateral radiograph typically shows:
o: An increased Böhler angle and a reduced critical angle of Gissane
A reduced Böhler angle and a reduced critical angle of Gissane
A reduced Böhler angle and an increased critical angle of Gissane
Normal angles with an isolated double density sign
items.e: Depression of the posterior facet flattens the tuber-joint line, lowering Böhler's angle (normal 20-40 degrees), and opens the angle of Gissane (normal about 95-105 degrees).

items.q: In a randomised trial of Sanders type IV calcaneal fractures (Buckley et al., 2014), ORIF alone was compared with ORIF plus primary subtalar arthrodesis. The main finding was:
o: Clearly better function with ORIF alone
Clearly better function with primary arthrodesis
An unacceptable non-union rate after primary arthrodesis
Similar patient-reported outcomes at 2 years, with some ORIF-alone patients needing later fusion
items.e: Outcomes were similar in both groups; primary fusion avoided a second operation that some ORIF-alone patients needed for subtalar arthritis, so it is a reasonable option for highly comminuted fractures.

items.q: Two years after a non-operatively treated calcaneal fracture, a patient has painful isolated subtalar arthritis. Heel height and talar declination are preserved and there is no anterior ankle impingement. The best operation is:
items.e: With height preserved, a simple in situ subtalar fusion is sufficient; bone-block distraction is reserved for loss of height with a horizontal talus and anterior ankle impingement, and exostectomy does not treat arthritis.

items.q: A military recruit has 3 weeks of heel pain after long marches. The most typical radiographic finding of a calcaneal stress fracture is:
o: A double density sign of the posterior facet
A sclerotic band in the posterior tuberosity running roughly parallel to its posterior border
A flattened Böhler angle with lateral wall blow-out
A lytic lesion with a sclerotic rim in the neutral triangle
items.e: Healing stress fractures appear as a vertical sclerotic line across the trabeculae in the posterior tuberosity; radiographs can be normal early, when MRI is more sensitive.

items.q: An anterior process fracture of the calcaneus is best treated by ORIF when:
o: Any fragment is seen on the oblique foot radiograph
The fragment is smaller than 1 cm and undisplaced
A displaced fragment involves more than about 25% of the calcaneocuboid joint surface
The injury occurred by an inversion-plantarflexion mechanism
items.e: Most anterior process avulsions are small and treated in a boot; large displaced fragments that disrupt the calcaneocuboid joint are fixed, and symptomatic small non-unions can be excised.

items.q: A 58-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic who smokes and has peripheral vascular disease sustains a displaced Sanders III calcaneal fracture. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: ORIF through an extensile lateral approach once the wrinkle sign appears
Primary subtalar arthrodesis through an extensile lateral approach
Non-operative care with elevation, early range of motion and non-weight bearing
items.e: Diabetes, smoking and vascular disease greatly increase wound breakdown and infection after calcaneal surgery, so non-operative treatment is preferred; late subtalar fusion remains available if needed.

items.q: Months after a calcaneal fracture, a patient has burning plantar pain and paraesthesia with a positive Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus. The most likely cause is:
o: Tibial nerve entrapment in the tarsal tunnel
items.e: Medial displacement, callus and scarring after calcaneal fractures can compress the tibial nerve or its branches in the tarsal tunnel, giving plantar burning pain and a positive Tinel sign medially.

items.q: A fracture of the posterior talar body is approached through a posterolateral incision. The deep interval used lies between:
o: Flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus
Peroneus brevis and flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus
Extensor digitorum longus and peroneus tertius
items.e: The posterolateral approach passes between the peroneal tendons and FHL; staying lateral to FHL protects the posteromedial neurovascular bundle, and the sural nerve is at risk superficially.

items.q: A 40-year-old has collapse of the talar body from avascular necrosis together with symptomatic arthritis of both the ankle and subtalar joints. The most suitable salvage is:
o: Excision of the talar dome fragments only
items.e: With both joints involved and a collapsed, avascular talar body, fusion across the ankle and subtalar joints (often with a hindfoot nail and graft) gives a stable plantigrade foot; ankle replacement is contraindicated by talar AVN.

items.q: The term 'basketball foot' refers to:
o: Lateral process fracture of the talus
Jones fracture of the fifth metatarsal
items.e: Medial subtalar dislocation was described in basketball players landing on an inverted foot; it accounts for about 80% of subtalar dislocations.

items.q: Broden's views for assessing the posterior subtalar facet are taken with the:
o: Leg internally rotated about 40 degrees and the beam angled cephalad at 10 to 40 degrees, centred on the lateral malleolus
Foot in maximum equinus, pronated 15 degrees, with the beam 75 degrees cephalad
Foot dorsiflexed and the beam angled 45 degrees to the plantar surface of the heel
Ankle externally rotated 45 degrees with a horizontal beam
items.e: Broden views show successive parts of the posterior facet and are used intraoperatively to check reduction; the Canale view images the talar neck and the Harris axial view shows tuberosity varus and width.

items.q: A 32-year-old has a symptomatic varus malunion of a talar neck fracture without arthritis of the ankle or subtalar joint. The preferred joint-sparing correction is:
o: Medial opening-wedge osteotomy of the talar neck with bone graft
Dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal alone
items.e: Restoring medial neck length with an opening-wedge osteotomy corrects the hindfoot varus and forefoot adduction at the site of deformity; fusion is reserved for established arthritis.

items.q: The term 'lover's fracture' traditionally describes:
o: A Lisfranc injury from landing on tiptoe
A lateral process of talus fracture from snowboarding
A calcaneal fracture from a fall from height
A fracture of the posterior talar process from forced plantarflexion
items.e: The name comes from the image of someone jumping from a window to escape and landing on the heels, producing an axial-load calcaneal fracture; associated lumbar spine fractures should be sought.

items.q: Closed reduction of a displaced Hawkins type II talar neck fracture with subtalar dislocation is usually attempted by:
o: Pure eversion of the heel without traction
No attempt; immediate application of a backslab
Longitudinal traction with plantarflexion of the forefoot and correction of varus or valgus
items.e: Plantarflexing the foot under traction realigns the head with the body and reduces the subtalar joint; dislocations should be reduced urgently, while definitive fixation can wait for the soft tissues.

items.q: During ORIF of a displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture, a Schanz pin inserted into the posteroinferior tuberosity is mainly used to:
o: Pull the tuberosity out of varus and restore height and length relative to the sustentacular fragment
