Elevate the depressed posterior facet fragment directly
Reduce the anterior process to the cuboid
Distract the ankle joint to inspect the talar dome
items.e: The tuberosity fragment usually displaces into varus, shortening and loss of height; traction and valgus through a tuberosity pin reduce it to the constant sustentacular fragment before the facet is reconstructed.

items.q: Restoration of which calcaneal parameter during fracture fixation most directly prevents late subfibular impingement and peroneal tendon problems?
o: Calcaneal width (reduction of the lateral wall blow-out)
items.e: Lateral wall bulging after a calcaneal fracture widens the heel and impinges against the fibular tip and peroneal tendons; restoring width avoids this, whereas pitch and height relate more to talar declination and ankle impingement.

items.q: Avulsion fractures of the anterior process of the calcaneus are produced by traction from which ligament during inversion and plantarflexion?
items.e: The bifurcate ligament runs from the anterior process to the navicular and cuboid; inversion-plantarflexion avulses its origin, producing a fracture that is often mistaken for an ankle sprain.

items.q: In the 'tie-arch' model of the distal humerus, the trochlea functions as the:
o: Tie-beam linking the medial and lateral columns
items.e: The distal humerus is a triangle of two diverging columns joined distally by the trochlea, the 'tie'. Restoring both columns and trochlear width is the aim of fixation.

items.q: The distal end of the medial column of the humerus is formed by the:
items.e: The medial column ends in the medial epicondyle, which is non-articular, with the trochlea projecting distal to it. The lateral column ends in the articular capitellum.

items.q: Under the AO/OTA classification, a distal humerus fracture with a simple articular split and a multifragmentary metaphysis is type:
items.e: 13C1 is simple articular and simple metaphyseal; 13C2 simple articular with metaphyseal comminution; 13C3 articular multifragmentary. 13B fractures are partial articular.

items.q: Which is one of O'Driscoll's technical principles for plating intra-articular distal humerus fractures?
o: Use short unicortical screws distally to avoid the joint
Fix only the lateral column and leave the medial column to heal
Avoid compression across the supracondylar level
Place as many long screws as possible in the distal fragments, passing through plates and interdigitating
items.e: O'Driscoll's principles maximise distal fixation: every screw through a plate, as long as possible, engaging fragments from the opposite column and interdigitating, with plates applied to achieve supracondylar compression.

items.q: The preferred olecranon osteotomy for exposure of an intra-articular distal humerus fracture is:
o: A chevron osteotomy with the apex pointing distally, at the bare area of the trochlear notch
A transverse osteotomy at the tip of the olecranon
A chevron osteotomy with the apex pointing proximally, through the coronoid
An oblique osteotomy through the proximal ulnar shaft
items.e: A distally pointing chevron at the non-articular bare area gives rotational stability and a larger surface for healing, with less articular damage than a transverse cut.

items.q: In the Bryan-Morrey approach to the elbow, the triceps is:
o: Split in the midline down to the olecranon
Reflected from medial to lateral in continuity with the anconeus and forearm fascia
Left completely attached, working on each side of it
items.e: Bryan-Morrey is a triceps-reflecting approach: after identifying the ulnar nerve, the triceps-anconeus sleeve is elevated from the olecranon medial to lateral. Alonso-Llames is the triceps-sparing (paratricipital) approach.

items.q: When a total elbow arthroplasty is performed for an unreconstructable distal humerus fracture, the triceps can often be left attached because:
o: The ulnar component is inserted from distally
The procedure is done through an anterior approach
The fractured condyles can be excised, giving access to the canals on either side of the triceps
A hemiarthroplasty never needs ulnar access
items.e: Excising the comminuted condylar fragments creates room to prepare the humerus and ulna working on both sides of the intact triceps, avoiding triceps insufficiency. Loss of the condyles has little effect on a linked implant.

items.q: In the randomised trial by McKee and colleagues (2009) in women over 65 with comminuted intra-articular distal humerus fractures, total elbow arthroplasty compared with ORIF:
o: Had a significantly higher reoperation rate
Gave worse Mayo Elbow Performance Scores at 2 years
Was abandoned because of early loosening
Gave better early functional scores, and several ORIF patients were converted to arthroplasty intra-operatively
items.e: TEA produced better Mayo and DASH scores early, with reoperation rates not significantly different. About a fifth of the ORIF group could not be fixed adequately and were converted to TEA in theatre.

items.q: A frail, 90-year-old nursing home resident with dementia has a comminuted distal humerus fracture. A recognised option is:
o: Non-operative 'bag of bones' treatment with early movement as pain allows
Bicolumnar locking plate fixation with olecranon osteotomy
items.e: In very low-demand or medically unfit patients, brief support followed by early motion (Eastwood's 'bag of bones') gives a pain-free, functional, if unstable, elbow. Prolonged casting causes stiffness.

items.q: On a lateral elbow radiograph after a fall, a 'double-arc sign' is seen. This indicates a:
o: Radial head fracture with posterior dislocation
Coronal shear fracture of the capitellum extending into the lateral trochlea
items.e: The double arc represents the subchondral bone of the displaced capitellum and lateral trochlear ridge, typical of a capitellotrochlear (McKee type IV) shear fracture.

items.q: A Hahn-Steinthal (Bryan-Morrey type I) capitellar fracture is:
o: A thin shell of articular cartilage with little subchondral bone
A large osteochondral fragment containing much of the capitellar bone
An avulsion of the lateral epicondyle
items.e: Type I (Hahn-Steinthal) involves a large bony capitellar fragment, amenable to screw fixation. Type II (Kocher-Lorenz) is a thin osteochondral shell; type III is comminuted; type IV (McKee) extends into the trochlea.

items.q: A displaced Hahn-Steinthal capitellar fracture in a 30-year-old is best treated with:
o: Excision of the fragment and early motion
Closed reduction and above-elbow cast for 6 weeks
Open reduction and fixation with headless compression screws (anterior-to-posterior) or posterior-to-anterior screws
items.e: Large capitellar fragments are fixed through a lateral approach with buried headless screws or posterior-to-anterior lag screws, allowing early motion. Excision is reserved for small unfixable fragments.

items.q: After closed reduction of a simple posterior elbow dislocation, the joint is stable through a full arc. The recommended management is:
o: A short period of splinting followed by active motion within the first 1-2 weeks
Primary repair of both collateral ligaments
items.e: Stable simple dislocations do well with early active motion. Immobilisation beyond about 3 weeks is associated with stiffness and loss of extension without improving stability.

items.q: After reduction of a simple elbow dislocation with a lateral collateral ligament injury, in which forearm position is the elbow most stable?
items.e: Pronation tightens the remaining lateral soft tissues and resists posterolateral rotatory subluxation in an LCL-deficient elbow. If the MCL is the main injury, supination is more stabilising.

items.q: The commonest long-term sequel of a simple elbow dislocation in adults is:
items.e: Most patients regain a functional arc but often lose 5-15 degrees of extension. Recurrent instability after a simple dislocation is uncommon.

items.q: In operative treatment of a terrible triad injury through a lateral approach, the usual sequence of steps is:
o: Coronoid or anterior capsule fixation, then radial head fixation or replacement, then LCL repair; MCL repair or hinged fixator only if still unstable
LCL repair first, then MCL repair, then radial head excision
Radial head excision, then coronoid fixation, then hinged fixator
MCL repair first, then coronoid fixation, then LCL repair
items.e: Work deep to superficial: fix the coronoid (exposed through the radial head defect), restore the radial head (never excise), then repair the LCL to the lateral epicondyle. Persistent instability is managed by MCL repair or a hinged fixator.

items.q: In terrible triad injuries, the lateral collateral ligament complex most commonly fails by:
o: Avulsion from its origin on the lateral epicondyle
Avulsion from the supinator crest of the ulna
items.e: The LCL usually strips off the lateral epicondyle, leaving a 'bald spot'. It is repaired back to the isometric point with suture anchors or transosseous sutures.

items.q: After fixing the coronoid and radial head and repairing the LCL in a terrible triad, the elbow still subluxes at 40 degrees of flexion. The next step is:
o: Accept it and cast in full extension for 6 weeks
Repair the MCL and/or apply a hinged external fixator
Perform a primary total elbow arthroplasty
items.e: Residual instability after lateral-sided reconstruction is treated by MCL repair through a medial approach or a hinged external fixator allowing protected motion.

items.q: In the Regan-Morrey classification of coronoid fractures, type II is a fracture involving:
o: Only the tip of the coronoid
More than 50% of the coronoid height
Up to 50% of the coronoid height
items.e: Regan-Morrey: I tip avulsion, II up to 50%, III over 50% of the coronoid. O'Driscoll classifies by location: tip, anteromedial facet and basal.

items.q: The primary restraint to valgus stress at the elbow between 30 and 120 degrees of flexion is the:
o: Anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament
items.e: The anterior bundle of the MCL is the primary valgus stabiliser; the radial head is a secondary stabiliser, important when the MCL is deficient.

items.q: The lateral ulnar collateral ligament inserts on the:
o: Lateral epicondyle only, without an ulnar attachment
items.e: The LUCL runs from the lateral epicondyle, blending with the annular ligament, to the supinator crest of the ulna. Its insufficiency allows posterolateral rotatory instability.

items.q: In the lateral pivot-shift test for posterolateral rotatory instability, the examiner applies:
o: Forearm pronation and varus while extending the elbow from flexion
Valgus stress with the elbow at 90 degrees and the forearm pronated
Axial load in full extension with the forearm in neutral
Forearm supination, valgus and axial load while flexing the elbow from extension, producing a reduction clunk at about 40 degrees
items.e: O'Driscoll's pivot-shift: supination, valgus and axial compression subluxate the radius and ulna off the humerus near extension; as the elbow flexes past about 40 degrees, the joint reduces with a clunk. It is easiest under anaesthesia.

items.q: A patient with suspected posterolateral rotatory instability pushes up from a chair with the forearms supinated and experiences apprehension or dislocation. This is the:
items.e: The chair push-up test loads the supinated elbow axially with valgus, reproducing PLRI symptoms. The moving valgus stress test and milking manoeuvre assess the MCL.

items.q: An iatrogenic cause of posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow is:
o: Medial epicondylectomy for cubital tunnel syndrome
Aggressive release of the common extensor origin for lateral epicondylitis extending posterior to the radial head equator
Anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve
Distal biceps repair through a single anterior incision
items.e: Excessive lateral release or a Kocher approach carried too far posteriorly can divide the LUCL. Keeping the dissection anterior to the equator of the radial head protects it.

items.q: Chronic symptomatic posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow is best treated with:
o: Anconeus transfer to the medial epicondyle
Reconstruction of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament with a tendon graft
items.e: Chronic PLRI usually needs LUCL reconstruction (palmaris longus or gracilis) from the isometric point on the lateral epicondyle to the supinator crest. Acute cases may be repaired directly.

items.q: A 32-year-old has a Mason type I radial head fracture with a tense painful haemarthrosis. The best management is:
o: Aspiration with local anaesthetic, check for a mechanical block, then early active motion
items.e: Aspiration relieves pain and allows testing for a block to rotation. Undisplaced fractures do well with a sling for comfort and early movement.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a comminuted radial head fracture with four fragments and an associated elbow dislocation. The best management of the radial head is usually:
items.e: Comminuted fractures with more than three fragments have poor results after ORIF (Ring). With elbow instability the head must be preserved or replaced, never excised.

items.q: When sizing the height of a radial head prosthesis, the proximal surface of the implant should lie at the level of the:
o: Tip of the coronoid process with the implant 3 mm above it
Proximal edge of the lesser sigmoid notch
Distal edge of the annular ligament
items.e: The native radial head articular surface lies near the proximal edge of the lesser sigmoid notch, just below the coronoid tip. Placing the implant higher overstuffs the radiocapitellar joint.

items.q: Overstuffing of the radiocapitellar joint after radial head arthroplasty typically results in:
o: Capitellar erosion, lateral elbow pain and loss of flexion
items.e: Too long a prosthesis increases radiocapitellar contact pressure, causing capitellar wear, pain and reduced flexion.

items.q: Radial head excision without replacement is contraindicated in a patient with a comminuted radial head fracture and:
o: An isolated radial head fracture in an 80-year-old low-demand patient
No other injury and a stable elbow
Tenderness over the distal radioulnar joint with interosseous membrane disruption
items.e: With interosseous membrane and DRUJ injury (Essex-Lopresti), excision allows the radius to migrate proximally. Excision is contraindicated also with MCL or coronoid injuries and elbow instability.

items.q: During radial head surgery, a 'radius pull test' shows over 3 mm of proximal migration of the radius with the head resected. This suggests:
o: Disruption of the interosseous membrane (longitudinal forearm instability)
items.e: With the radial head removed, a pull of the radius producing more than about 3 mm of migration indicates IOM injury; larger migration suggests additional TFCC/DRUJ injury. The radial head should then be replaced.

items.q: The central band of the forearm interosseous membrane, the key longitudinal stabiliser after radial head loss, has fibres running:
o: Obliquely from proximal on the ulna to distal on the radius
Obliquely from proximal on the radius to distal on the ulna
Transversely at right angles to both bones
items.e: The central band runs distally and ulnarward from the radius to the ulna, transferring load from the radius to the ulna. It is the target of IOM reconstruction in chronic Essex-Lopresti injuries.

items.q: In an acute Essex-Lopresti injury, the recommended management is:
o: Radial head excision and early motion
Radial head fixation or replacement, with assessment and stabilisation of the DRUJ
Ulnar shortening osteotomy as the first procedure
items.e: Restoring the radial head prevents proximal migration of the radius; the DRUJ is reduced and pinned in supination or repaired if unstable. Excision worsens longitudinal instability.

items.q: In the Kocher approach to the radial head, the internervous plane is between:
o: Extensor carpi radialis brevis and extensor digitorum communis
Anconeus (radial nerve) and extensor carpi ulnaris (posterior interosseous nerve)
items.e: Kocher uses the anconeus-ECU interval; anconeus is supplied by the radial nerve and ECU by the PIN. Kaplan's approach uses the ECRB-EDC interval, closer to the PIN.

items.q: During a lateral approach to the radial head and neck, the posterior interosseous nerve is best protected by:
o: Placing retractors around the radial neck
items.e: Pronation moves the PIN anteriorly and medially away from the operative field. Retractors around the radial neck can compress the nerve against the bone.

items.q: In the proximal part of the anterior (Henry) approach to the radius, the posterior interosseous nerve is protected by:
o: Pronating the forearm and splitting the supinator
Supinating the forearm and detaching the supinator from its insertion, reflecting it laterally
Dividing the pronator teres from its origin
items.e: Full supination brings the supinator insertion into view and moves the PIN laterally; elevating the supinator off the radius from its insertion keeps the nerve within the reflected muscle.

items.q: The 'leash of Henry', which must be ligated in the proximal anterior approach to the radius, consists of branches of the:
items.e: The recurrent radial artery and its venae comitantes cross the field near the supinator, tethering brachioradialis; they must be ligated to mobilise the muscle and expose the proximal radius.

items.q: The dorsal (Thompson) approach to the radial shaft develops the interval between:
o: Extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris
Extensor carpi radialis brevis and extensor digitorum communis
items.e: Thompson's dorsal approach uses the ECRB-EDC interval proximally; the posterior interosseous nerve must be identified and protected within the supinator.

items.q: The ulnar shaft is approached through its subcutaneous border, between:
o: Extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris
Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis
Anconeus and extensor carpi radialis brevis
Pronator quadratus and flexor digitorum profundus
items.e: The ulna is subcutaneous along its whole length; dissection between ECU (PIN) and FCU (ulnar nerve) is a true internervous plane. Distally the dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve is at risk.

items.q: When plating an adult diaphyseal forearm fracture, the usual minimum fixation on each side of the fracture with a 3.5 mm compression plate is:
items.e: Classic guidance is at least six cortices proximal and distal to the fracture with 3.5 mm LC-DCP or similar plates; good bone and compression allow early motion.

items.q: In adult both-bone forearm fractures, Schemitsch and Richards showed that restoration of which parameter correlates with recovery of forearm rotation?
o: Ulnar length relative to the humerus
Magnitude and location of the maximum radial bow
items.e: The maximum radial bow normally lies at about 60% of the radial length from its proximal end. Restoring its magnitude and position correlated with better rotation and grip strength.

items.q: A 25-year-old had both-bone forearm fractures fixed through a single dorsal incision after a delay of 3 weeks, with a head injury. He now has no forearm rotation. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Single-incision exposure of both bones, head injury, high-energy trauma and delayed surgery increase the risk of synostosis. Excision with interposition is considered once the bridge has matured.

items.q: After union of an adult forearm shaft fracture fixed with plates, routine plate removal is discouraged mainly because of:
o: The risk of refracture and nerve injury
The high rate of metal allergy
Plates commonly loosen on their own
Removal causes synostosis in most patients
items.e: Refracture through screw holes or the original fracture is reported after removal, especially early or with larger plates, and the PIN or superficial radial nerve can be injured. Removal is reserved for symptomatic implants.

items.q: An isolated ulnar shaft ('nightstick') fracture can be treated non-operatively if the displacement is less than:
o: 100% with less than 30 degrees of angulation
50% of the shaft width with less than 10 degrees of angulation
75% with less than 20 degrees of angulation
items.e: Stable isolated ulnar shaft fractures with under 50% displacement and under 10 degrees of angulation heal well in a functional brace. Greater displacement suggests instability and is plated.

items.q: In the Bado classification, a Monteggia lesion with an anterior radial head dislocation and fractures of both the radius and ulna is type:
items.e: Bado I anterior dislocation with an apex-anterior ulnar fracture; II posterior; III lateral; IV anterior dislocation with fractures of both bones at the same level.

items.q: A lateral (Bado III) Monteggia lesion is most commonly seen:
o: In elderly osteoporotic women with olecranon comminution
In adults with distal-third radial fractures
In children, with a metaphyseal fracture of the proximal ulna
items.e: Bado III lesions involve lateral or anterolateral radial head dislocation with a proximal ulnar metaphyseal fracture and occur mainly in children.

items.q: Under the Jupiter subclassification of posterior (Bado II) Monteggia fractures, type IIA is a fracture of the ulna:
o: At the level of the trochlear notch involving the coronoid
At the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction distal to the coronoid
Extending along most of the ulnar length
items.e: Jupiter: IIA involves the trochlear notch and coronoid; IIB is at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction; IIC is diaphyseal; IID is comminuted over the proximal third to half. Coronoid involvement needs fixation.

items.q: After plate fixation of the ulna in an adult Monteggia injury, the radial head remains subluxated. The most common reason is:
o: Imperfect reduction of the ulnar fracture (residual angulation or shortening)
items.e: The radial head usually reduces once ulnar length and alignment are restored. Persistent subluxation first suggests ulnar malreduction; if the ulna is anatomical, an interposed annular ligament or capsule may need open removal.

items.q: In streptococcal necrotising fasciitis, clindamycin is added to the beta-lactam mainly because it:
o: Suppresses bacterial toxin production by inhibiting protein synthesis
Covers MRSA more reliably than vancomycin
Penetrates necrotic tissue better than any beta-lactam
items.e: Clindamycin inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis, reducing streptococcal exotoxin and M-protein production regardless of bacterial growth phase (the Eagle effect limits penicillin in large inocula).

items.q: At exploration for suspected necrotising fasciitis of the forearm, which finding supports the diagnosis (a positive 'finger test')?
o: Brisk bleeding from the incised subcutaneous fat
Thick creamy pus confined to a single cavity
The fascia separates easily from the subcutaneous tissue on blunt finger dissection, with little bleeding and grey 'dishwater' fluid
Firm adherence of the fascia to the overlying fat
items.e: Loss of normal resistance to finger dissection along the fascial plane, absent bleeding and thin dishwater fluid indicate necrotising fasciitis; a localised creamy collection suggests a simple abscess.

items.q: After the first radical debridement for necrotising fasciitis of the upper limb, the patient should have:
o: Delayed primary closure the next morning
A planned return to theatre within 24-48 hours for re-look and further debridement
A single debridement followed by vacuum dressing for 2 weeks
Hyperbaric oxygen as the definitive treatment
items.e: Necrosis often progresses beyond the first debridement margins, so planned re-look debridement every 24-48 hours is standard until the tissues are healthy; hyperbaric oxygen is only an unproven adjunct.

items.q: Intravenous immunoglobulin is used as an adjunct in necrotising soft-tissue infection mainly when there is:
items.e: IVIG may neutralise streptococcal superantigens and is used as an adjunct in group A streptococcal toxic shock; evidence is limited.

items.q: A rose gardener has a painless ulcerated nodule on the finger after a thorn prick, followed by a chain of nodules along the forearm lymphatics. Treatment of choice is:
items.e: Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii) causes nodular lymphangitic (sporotrichoid) spread after thorn injuries and is treated with itraconazole.

items.q: A 3-year-old has a painless, spindle-shaped swelling of the proximal phalanx; radiographs show an expanded, ballooned bone with a thin cortex. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Spina ventosa is tuberculous dactylitis in young children, producing a fusiform swelling and an expanded, 'blown-out' short tubular bone; it is treated with antitubercular therapy.

items.q: In leprosy, the peripheral nerve most commonly involved in the upper limb is the:
o: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
items.e: The ulnar nerve near the elbow is the commonest thickened and paralysed nerve in leprosy, giving a claw hand; combined ulnar and median palsy produces a total claw hand.

items.q: Tendon transfers to correct claw hand in leprosy should be performed:
o: During an acute type 1 reaction to prevent progression
After the disease is inactive and neuritis has settled, with supple joints
Only if sensation in the hand is normal
items.e: Reconstructive surgery (e.g. Brand or Fritschi transfers) is done when the disease is inactive, nerve function has been stable and contractures are corrected, so that results are not undone by ongoing neuritis.

items.q: A sheep farmer has a solitary, firm, red-violet nodule with a central umbilication on the index finger after lambing. It is likely to:
items.e: Orf is a parapoxvirus infection acquired from sheep and goats; it is self-limiting over weeks and needs only wound care.

items.q: A worker presents 2 hours after a high-pressure paint gun injected oil-based paint into his non-dominant index fingertip. The finger looks almost normal apart from a pinhole wound. Management is:
o: Urgent surgical decompression and wide debridement of the tracked material
Elevation, oral antibiotics and review the next day
Observation unless the finger becomes pale
items.e: The trivial entry wound hides extensive tracking along sheaths and planes; emergency debridement (ideally within about 6 hours) reduces amputation risk.

items.q: In high-pressure injection injuries of the hand, which injected material is associated with the highest amputation rate?
items.e: Oil-based paints and organic solvents cause intense chemical inflammation and necrosis with amputation rates up to about half; water and air are least damaging and grease is intermediate.

items.q: Which factor increases the amputation risk after a high-pressure injection injury?
o: Injection of water at low pressure
Entry into the palm with early surgery
Injection into a digit rather than the palm, with delay to debridement over 6-10 hours
items.e: Amputation risk rises with organic solvents, higher pressure, injection into the confined space of a digit and delayed debridement.

items.q: An intravenous drug user who licks the needle before injecting into the dorsum of the hand develops an abscess. Besides Staphylococcus aureus, which organism is particularly associated with this habit?
items.e: Eikenella corrodens is an oral commensal, so it is seen in human bites and in drug users who lick needles; MRSA is also common in this group.

items.q: Compared with healthy patients, deep hand infections in diabetics are more often:
o: Polymicrobial, including Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, with a higher amputation rate
items.e: Diabetic hand infections are frequently polymicrobial, present atypically, need broad-spectrum cover and tight glucose control, and have worse outcomes including amputation.

items.q: After drainage of a hand abscess in a region with high community-acquired MRSA, a reasonable oral antibiotic pending cultures is:
items.e: Community-acquired MRSA is increasingly common in hand abscesses; co-trimoxazole, doxycycline or clindamycin (where susceptible) are usual oral options, while penicillins and first-generation cephalosporins do not cover MRSA.

items.q: A patient with hand cellulitis treated with IV antibiotics and elevation has not improved after 48 hours. The most likely explanation to exclude first is:
o: An undrained abscess, so the hand should be imaged with ultrasound or explored
items.e: Cellulitis should improve within 24-48 hours; failure suggests a collection needing drainage (or a resistant organism or atypical infection).

items.q: A wool sorter has a painless papule on the hand that becomes a black necrotic eschar surrounded by marked non-pitting oedema. The likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) from animal hides or wool gives a painless black eschar with extensive oedema; it is treated with antibiotics, not surgery.

items.q: A dairy farmer develops painless red-purple nodules on the fingers after milking cows with teat lesions. The diagnosis and management are:
items.e: Milker's nodules are caused by a parapoxvirus from cattle and resolve spontaneously, like orf from sheep and goats.

items.q: The commonest cause of fingernail onychomycosis and its usual oral treatment are:
items.e: Dermatophytes, chiefly Trichophyton rubrum, cause most onychomycosis; oral terbinafine for about 6 weeks (fingernails) is first-line.

items.q: A diabetic presents 6 days after a finger puncture with established flexor sheath infection, purulent drainage and a necrotic-looking flexor tendon. The most appropriate surgery is:
o: Closed catheter irrigation through A1 and A5 incisions
Aspiration of the sheath with a needle
Open debridement of the sheath through Bruner or mid-axial incisions, excising necrotic tendon
items.e: Closed catheter irrigation suits earlier infection; late or severe infection with necrotic tendon needs wide open debridement, and amputation may be required.

items.q: Cat bites to the hand become infected more often than dog bites mainly because they:
o: Produce deep puncture wounds that inoculate tendon sheaths and joints
items.e: Cats' fine, sharp teeth produce deep punctures that are hard to clean and often enter joints and sheaths, giving infection rates up to about 30-50%; dog bites more often cause crush and laceration.

items.q: A man with a soil-contaminated hand laceration cannot recall any tetanus vaccination. Appropriate tetanus prophylaxis is:
o: Tetanus immunoglobulin plus a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine, completing a primary course
No prophylaxis if the wound is cleaned within 6 hours
items.e: A tetanus-prone wound in an unimmunised or unknown-status patient needs both passive (immunoglobulin) and active (vaccine course) immunisation.

items.q: An abscess in the dorsal subaponeurotic space of the hand, deep to the extensor tendons, is drained through:
o: Longitudinal dorsal incisions (e.g. over the second and fourth metacarpals)
Incision across the first web space
A volar zig-zag incision over the ring finger
items.e: The dorsal subaponeurotic space lies under the extensor tendons on the metacarpals; it is drained through one or two longitudinal dorsal incisions, avoiding exposure of the tendons in a single wide flap.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an acutely hot, swollen wrist without trauma. Aspiration should be sent for Gram stain, culture and:
o: Serum uric acid only, without fluid analysis
items.e: Septic arthritis of the wrist (including gonococcal) must be distinguished from crystal arthritis such as gout or CPPD, so the aspirate is examined for crystals as well as organisms.

items.q: A chronic, culture-negative tenosynovitis of the hand is suspected to be mycobacterial or fungal. The most useful diagnostic step is:
o: Synovial biopsy for histology and cultures for mycobacteria and fungi, with M. marinum cultures at about 30-32 C
items.e: Atypical infections need tissue: histology shows granulomas, and cultures must be specifically requested and incubated appropriately (lower temperature for M. marinum).

items.q: Early acute paronychia with nail-fold redness and swelling but no fluctuance is best treated with:
o: Warm soaks and oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotics
items.e: Before an abscess forms, soaks, elevation and antibiotics covering S. aureus usually settle acute paronychia; drainage is needed only when pus collects.

items.q: Physeal fractures in children usually propagate through which zone of the growth plate?
items.e: The hypertrophic zone has the least matrix and is the weakest; the germinal cells stay with the epiphysis, which is why most physeal fractures grow normally.

items.q: In a Salter-Harris type II fracture, the periosteum usually remains intact on:
o: The opposite (tension) side of the fragment
The side of the metaphyseal (Thurston-Holland) fragment, which acts as the hinge for reduction
items.e: The fracture opens on the tension side and the periosteum tears there; the intact periosteum on the compression side with the Thurston-Holland fragment provides a hinge for reduction.

items.q: A child's ankle is grazed by a lawnmower, removing the periphery of the distal tibial physis. Rang's type VI physeal injury typically causes:
o: Uniform cessation of growth and pure shortening
A peripheral physeal bar with progressive angular deformity
No growth disturbance because the injury is extra-articular
items.e: Type VI is injury to the perichondral ring (of LaCroix); the peripheral bar tethers one side of the physis, producing angular deformity.

items.q: Peterson type I physeal injury, seen most often in the distal radius, is:
o: A crush of the entire physis
A loss of part of the physis from an open injury
A fracture through the physis and epiphysis only
A transverse metaphyseal fracture with a longitudinal extension into the physis
items.e: Peterson added type I (transverse metaphyseal fracture extending into the physis) and type VI (open loss of part of the physis) to the Salter-Harris types.

items.q: Two years after a distal femoral physeal fracture, Park-Harris growth arrest lines are parallel to the physis medially but converge on it laterally. This indicates:
o: A lateral physeal bar tethering growth
items.e: Growth arrest lines parallel to the physis mean symmetrical growth; lines that converge on or are tethered to the physis indicate a bar on that side.

items.q: The best investigation for mapping the size and location of a physeal bar before resection is:
items.e: MRI (or thin-section CT) maps the bar and estimates the percentage of physeal area involved, which decides between bar resection and completion of the arrest.

items.q: After reduction of an elbow dislocation in a 6-year-old, a small ossified fragment lies within the joint at the level of the trochlea; the trochlear ossification centre has not yet appeared. The fragment is most likely:
items.e: By the CRITOE sequence the medial epicondyle (about 5-7 years) ossifies before the trochlea (about 7-9); an ossified fragment in the joint before the trochlea appears must be the medial epicondyle.

items.q: After reduction of a supracondylar humerus fracture, the Baumann angle measures 64 degrees compared with 74 degrees on the normal side. This suggests:
o: Malrotation only, with normal coronal alignment
items.e: Baumann angle (about 70-75 degrees) should be within about 5 degrees of the other side; a decrease means varus angulation, which leads to cubitus varus.

items.q: A Gartland III extension supracondylar fracture with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment (proximal spike piercing anteromedially) puts which structures at highest risk?
items.e: With posterolateral displacement the proximal fragment's spike goes anteromedially toward the brachial artery and median nerve; posteromedial displacement threatens the radial nerve.

items.q: A 7-year-old has an extension supracondylar fracture with posteromedial displacement of the distal fragment. The nerve most at risk is the:
items.e: In posteromedial displacement the proximal spike pierces anterolaterally, endangering the radial nerve.

items.q: A child falls on the point of a flexed elbow and sustains a flexion-type supracondylar humerus fracture. The nerve most commonly injured is the:
items.e: Flexion-type injuries (about 3%) displace the distal fragment anteriorly and most often injure the ulnar nerve.

items.q: When a medial pin is needed in crossed-pin fixation of a supracondylar fracture, ulnar nerve injury is best avoided by:
o: Extending the elbow and making a small medial incision to place the pin directly on bone
Inserting the pin with the elbow hyperflexed
Inserting it percutaneously from posterior to anterior
Using a smooth pin through the olecranon
items.e: In hyperflexion the ulnar nerve can sublux anterior to the medial epicondyle; extending the elbow and using a mini-open approach reduces iatrogenic injury.

items.q: With lateral-entry pinning of a displaced supracondylar fracture, stability is maximised by:
o: Two parallel pins crossing at the fracture site
A single lateral pin up the medial column
Two or three divergent pins that are widely separated at the fracture site and engage both fragments' cortices
Pins that cross each other at the fracture line
items.e: Divergent lateral pins maximally spread across the fracture (engaging medial and lateral columns) give stability comparable to crossed pins without the ulnar nerve risk; pins converging at the fracture are weak.

items.q: After closed reduction and pinning of a supracondylar fracture, the hand becomes cold and white with poor capillary refill. The next step is:
o: Observation with the elbow flexed for 24 hours
Urgent open exploration of the brachial artery
Remove the pins and recheck the next morning
items.e: A white, poorly perfused hand after reduction means arterial compromise (entrapment, spasm, intimal tear or transection) and needs urgent exploration through an anterior approach.

items.q: After reduction of a supracondylar fracture the hand is pink and warm but pulseless, and the child now has a new median nerve palsy. Management is:
o: Exploration of the antecubital fossa for entrapment of the artery and nerve
Observe for 3 months for nerve recovery
Repeat closed manipulation in more flexion
items.e: A pink pulseless hand can be observed, but an associated (especially new) median nerve deficit suggests the artery and nerve are tethered or entrapped in the fracture, and exploration is indicated.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a symptomatic cubitus varus deformity after a healed supracondylar fracture. The commonly used corrective procedure is:
o: Hemiepiphysiodesis of the lateral distal humeral physis
items.e: Cubitus varus is a malunion; it is corrected with a lateral closing-wedge (French) or dome osteotomy. Guided growth cannot correct it because it is not a growth disturbance.

items.q: A supracondylar fracture that is unstable in both flexion and extension under image intensification because the periosteal hinge is completely torn is classified as:
items.e: Type IV fractures are multidirectionally unstable; they are often recognised only under the image intensifier and are reduced and pinned by rotating the C-arm rather than the arm.

items.q: Which radiographic view most accurately shows the true displacement of a lateral condyle fracture of the humerus?
items.e: The fracture fragment is posterolateral; the internal oblique view shows it in profile and reveals displacement underestimated on the AP view.

items.q: During ORIF of a displaced lateral condyle fracture, dissection is kept away from the posterior aspect of the fragment because:
o: The radial nerve crosses the posterior condyle
The posterior capsule must be preserved to prevent dislocation
The ulnar collateral ligament inserts posteriorly
The blood supply to the lateral condyle enters posteriorly and stripping it causes avascular necrosis
items.e: The vascular supply of the lateral condyle (capitellum) enters posteriorly; posterior soft-tissue stripping risks AVN, so exposure is anterolateral.

items.q: The nerve most commonly injured in Monteggia fracture-dislocations is the:
items.e: The PIN winds around the radial neck under the arcade of Frohse and is stretched by anterior or lateral radial head dislocation. It usually recovers after reduction.

items.q: The radiocapitellar line used to detect a radial head dislocation is drawn:
o: Along the anterior humeral cortex, passing through the middle third of the capitellum
From the olecranon tip to the coronoid tip
Along the ulnar shaft through the trochlea
Along the axis of the radial neck and head, and should pass through the capitellum in all views
items.e: A line along the radial shaft and neck should bisect the capitellum on every view. Failure to do so indicates radial head dislocation, as in Monteggia injuries. The anterior humeral line relates to supracondylar fractures.

items.q: A Galeazzi fracture is described as a 'fracture of necessity' because:
o: Closed treatment in adults gives poor results, so ORIF of the radius is required
items.e: Closed reduction cannot hold the radius against the deforming forces of brachioradialis, pronator quadratus and the thumb muscles, so adults need plate fixation and DRUJ assessment.

items.q: In Galeazzi-type injuries, DRUJ instability is more likely when the radial shaft fracture lies within about how far of the radial articular surface?
items.e: Rettig and Raskin found that radial fractures within 7.5 cm of the midarticular surface of the distal radius were much more often associated with DRUJ instability than more proximal fractures.

items.q: After anatomical plating of a Galeazzi fracture, the DRUJ is reducible but unstable in all positions except supination. The appropriate management is:
o: Immobilise in supination, or pin the radius to the ulna in supination, for about 4-6 weeks
Proceed directly to ulnar head replacement
items.e: A reducible but unstable DRUJ is held in the stable position (usually supination) with an above-elbow splint or transfixing K-wires, ± TFCC/ulnar styloid repair. Irreducible joints need open reduction.

items.q: After plating a Galeazzi fracture, the DRUJ cannot be reduced closed. The structure most commonly found interposed is the:
items.e: An irreducible DRUJ usually has the ECU tendon (or its sheath) trapped in the joint; open reduction through a dorsal approach is needed.

items.q: A displaced, transverse olecranon fracture with an intact ulnohumeral joint in a fit 40-year-old is classified in the Mayo system as type:
items.e: Mayo: I undisplaced, II displaced but with a stable ulnohumeral joint, III displaced and unstable; each subdivided into A (non-comminuted) and B (comminuted). There is no type IV.

items.q: During tension-band wiring of an olecranon fracture, K-wire back-out can be reduced by:
o: Leaving the wires within the medullary canal only
Directing the wires to engage the anterior ulnar cortex distal to the coronoid
Avoiding bending of the proximal wire ends
items.e: Bicortical purchase in the anterior cortex reduces migration; the proximal ends are bent and impacted beneath the triceps. Wires must not protrude far anteriorly, where they can impinge on rotation or injure the anterior interosseous nerve.

items.q: Tension-band wiring is a poor choice for which olecranon fracture?
o: A simple transverse fracture at the midpoint of the notch
A transverse fracture in a young adult
An oblique fracture extending distal to the midpoint of the trochlear notch
A transverse fracture with good bone stock
items.e: Tension banding needs a transverse, non-comminuted fracture where triceps pull can be converted to compression. Oblique, comminuted or distal fractures and fracture-dislocations need a plate.

items.q: In a randomised trial (Duckworth, 2017) of patients aged 75 or older with displaced olecranon fractures, operative fixation compared with non-operative treatment:
o: Gave significantly better DASH scores at 1 year
Reduced the rate of non-union to zero with no added surgery
Gave no better functional outcome but had more complications, and the trial stopped early
items.e: Non-operative care gave similar function despite frequent radiographic non-union, while the fixation group had a high rate of complications and reoperation, prompting early termination.

items.q: In the Hastings and Graham classification of heterotopic ossification of the elbow, class III indicates:
o: Bony ankylosis of the elbow or forearm
items.e: Class I is radiographic only; class II limits motion (IIA flexion-extension, IIB rotation, IIC both); class III is ankylosis.

items.q: A 58-year-old with suspected spinal cord compression has a mediastinal mass and no tissue diagnosis; lymphoma is suspected. What is the main caution regarding steroids?
o: Steroids may be withheld until biopsy if neurology allows, because they can make lymphoma tissue non-diagnostic
Steroids must be doubled to 32 mg to treat the lymphoma
Steroids are contraindicated in all cases of cord compression
Steroids are harmless to biopsy yield and should always be given first
items.e: Corticosteroids are lymphocytolytic and can shrink lymphoma, rendering biopsy non-diagnostic; if neurological status permits, steroids are deferred until tissue is obtained.

items.q: In the Bilsky epidural spinal cord compression scale, grade 1b means:
o: Epidural tumour deforms the thecal sac without abutting the cord
Cord compressed with no CSF visible around it
Epidural tumour abutting the cord without compression
items.e: Grade 0 is bone only; 1a epidural impingement without thecal sac deformation; 1b thecal sac deformed without cord abutment; 1c cord abutment without compression; 2 compression with CSF visible; 3 compression with no CSF.

items.q: A patient has Bilsky grade 3 compression from a renal cell carcinoma metastasis, a stable spine and good systemic status. Under the NOMS framework, management is:
o: Decompression (separation) surgery followed by stereotactic radiotherapy
items.e: High-grade (2-3) compression from a radioresistant tumour in a fit patient needs surgical decompression, usually separation surgery followed by SBRT; conventional radiotherapy would control renal cell disease poorly.

items.q: Which tumour metastasising to the spine is considered radiosensitive to conventional external beam radiotherapy?
items.e: Breast, prostate, lymphoma, myeloma and seminoma are radiosensitive; renal cell, melanoma, thyroid, sarcoma, colon and NSCLC are relatively radioresistant to conventional fractionation.

items.q: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for spinal metastases differs from conventional radiotherapy mainly in that it:
o: Delivers high ablative doses precisely to the tumour while sparing the cord, overcoming relative radioresistance
Treats the whole spine in a single field
Is used only for radiosensitive tumours
items.e: SBRT gives high biologically effective doses in one or a few fractions with steep dose gradients, achieving local control even in 'radioresistant' histologies such as renal cell carcinoma and melanoma.

items.q: In the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS), a lesion at T12 scores how many points for location?
items.e: Junctional levels (occiput-C2, C7-T2, T11-L1 and L5-S1) score 3; mobile spine (C3-C6, L2-L4) 2; semi-rigid (T3-T10) 1; rigid sacrum (S2-S5) 0.

items.q: In SINS, a lesion at T6 scores how many points for location?
items.e: T3-T10 is the semi-rigid thoracic spine stabilised by the rib cage, scoring 1 point for location.

items.q: In SINS, the bone lesion quality is scored as:
items.e: Lytic lesions weaken the vertebra most and score 2; mixed lesions score 1 and purely blastic lesions 0.

items.q: In SINS, which radiographic alignment finding receives the highest score (4 points)?
items.e: Subluxation or translation scores 4, de novo deformity (kyphosis or scoliosis) 2 and normal alignment 0.

items.q: In SINS, vertebral body collapse of more than 50% scores:
items.e: Collapse over 50% scores 3, under 50% scores 2, no collapse but over 50% of the body involved scores 1, and none of these 0.

items.q: In SINS, bilateral involvement of the posterolateral elements (facets, pedicles or costovertebral joints) scores:
items.e: Bilateral posterolateral involvement scores 3, unilateral 1 and none 0.

items.q: A breast cancer patient has a lytic L3 metastasis (mobile spine) with mechanical pain, normal alignment, collapse under 50% and unilateral pedicle involvement. Her SINS is:
items.e: Location L3 = 2, mechanical pain = 3, lytic = 2, normal alignment = 0, collapse under 50% = 2, unilateral posterolateral = 1; total 10, within 7-12 (indeterminate), which merits surgical consultation.

items.q: In SINS, the threshold at or above which a surgical consultation is recommended is:
items.e: Scores 0-6 are stable, 7-12 indeterminate and 13-18 unstable; any score of 7 or more should prompt a surgical opinion.

items.q: Which item is a component of the revised Tokuhashi score?
items.e: Tokuhashi includes general condition, number of extraspinal bone metastases, number of vertebral metastases, visceral metastases, primary site and severity of paralysis.

items.q: The Tomita score for spinal metastases is based on:
o: Bilsky grade, SINS and performance status
Age, ambulatory status and serum albumin
Growth rate of the primary tumour, visceral metastases and bone metastases
items.e: Tomita scores primary tumour growth (slow, moderate, rapid), visceral metastases (none, treatable, untreatable) and number of bone metastases; low scores favour wide or marginal excision and high scores palliation.

items.q: For major surgery for metastatic spinal cord compression, patients are generally expected to have a life expectancy of at least about:
items.e: Patchell's trial and most guidelines required an expected survival of at least about 3 months, so that the patient benefits from surgery and recovers from it.

items.q: A 64-year-old has a single lytic vertebral lesion and no known primary. Before CT-guided spinal biopsy, which workup is most appropriate?
o: Serum protein electrophoresis, free light chains, CT chest-abdomen-pelvis and PSA
items.e: Myeloma and an accessible primary (lung, kidney, prostate, breast) should be sought first; the primary or a more accessible lesion may give the diagnosis without a spinal biopsy.

items.q: Which was an exclusion criterion in the Patchell trial of surgery plus radiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone for metastatic spinal cord compression?
items.e: Patchell excluded radiosensitive tumours (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma, germ-cell), paraplegia over 48 hours, multiple discrete levels of compression, cauda equina-only lesions and expected survival under 3 months.

items.q: Among patients who were not ambulatory at entry to the Patchell trial, the proportion who regained the ability to walk was:
o: About 62% with surgery plus radiotherapy versus 19% with radiotherapy alone
items.e: Surgery plus radiotherapy restored walking in 62% of non-ambulatory patients versus 19% with radiotherapy alone; overall, 84% versus 57% were ambulatory after treatment.

items.q: For painful uncomplicated spinal bone metastases without cord compression, the standard palliative radiotherapy regimen with equivalent pain relief is:
o: Radiotherapy is not effective for bone pain
items.e: A single 8 Gy fraction gives pain relief equivalent to multi-fraction schedules for uncomplicated bone metastases, with a slightly higher retreatment rate.

items.q: The SCORAD III trial in metastatic spinal cord compression compared:
o: Single-fraction 8 Gy with 20 Gy in 5 fractions of radiotherapy
items.e: SCORAD III compared single 8 Gy with 20 Gy/5 fractions for MSCC; single fraction was not shown to be non-inferior overall for ambulation at 8 weeks, though differences were small, so short-course RT remains common.

items.q: Why is decompressive laminectomy without instrumentation avoided for metastatic cord compression arising from the vertebral body?
o: It removes the remaining posterior support and causes progressive kyphosis and instability
items.e: With anterior column destroyed by tumour, removing the posterior elements leaves no stable column; modern practice is posterior decompression with instrumented stabilisation.

items.q: A 70-year-old with myeloma has a painful L2 pathological compression fracture without retropulsion or epidural disease. A randomised trial (CAFE) supports:
o: Balloon kyphoplasty for rapid pain and function improvement
items.e: The CAFE trial showed balloon kyphoplasty significantly improved back-specific function and pain at 1 month in cancer patients with painful vertebral compression fractures compared with non-surgical care.

items.q: A relative contraindication to vertebroplasty for a painful metastatic vertebral fracture is:
o: Posterior wall destruction with epidural tumour and cord compression
Lytic lesion in the vertebral body
Pain localised to the fractured level
items.e: Cement can leak through a deficient posterior wall into the canal and worsen compression; vertebral augmentation is for painful fractures without significant canal compromise.

items.q: A patient on denosumab for spinal metastases should be monitored especially for:
o: Hypocalcaemia and osteonecrosis of the jaw
items.e: Denosumab and zoledronic acid reduce skeletal-related events; denosumab can cause significant hypocalcaemia (calcium and vitamin D supplementation are needed), and both can cause osteonecrosis of the jaw.

items.q: The strongest predictor of being able to walk after treatment for metastatic spinal cord compression is:
o: Number of vertebral levels involved on bone scan
items.e: Patients who walk at the start of treatment usually remain ambulant; those who are paraplegic rarely recover, which is why rapid diagnosis matters.

items.q: In metastatic spinal cord compression, which pattern of neurological deterioration has the worst prognosis for recovery?
o: Slow progression of weakness over several weeks
Rapid onset of motor deficit over hours to a few days
items.e: A rapid onset of deficit (often from vascular compromise or collapse) predicts poor recovery, whereas slowly developing deficits recover better after treatment.

items.q: Which spinal tumour typically arises in the vertebral body rather than the posterior elements?
items.e: Haemangioma, chordoma, myeloma, GCT and metastases favour the vertebral body, while osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma and ABC usually arise in the posterior elements.

items.q: In a painful scoliosis caused by a spinal osteoid osteoma, the lesion is usually located:
o: On the convex side at the end vertebra
On the concave side near the apex of the curve
In the vertebral body at the junction of the curve
In the disc at the apex
items.e: Muscle spasm on the side of the lesion produces a curve concave towards the nidus, which usually lies in the posterior elements near the apex.

items.q: On MRI, an ependymoma of the spinal cord typically shows:
o: An eccentric infiltrative mass without a plane
A dural-based mass with a dural tail
A central, well-circumscribed enhancing mass with a haemosiderin cap at its poles
A dumbbell lesion widening the foramen
items.e: Ependymomas arise from the central canal lining, are central and well demarcated, and often show haemosiderin caps from previous haemorrhage; they can usually be resected completely.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a lytic destructive lesion of the L2 vertebral body with a large soft tissue mass, fever and raised ESR. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with CD99 positivity. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Ewing sarcoma affects children and adolescents, involves the vertebral body or sacrum with a large soft tissue mass and can mimic infection; small round cells with membranous CD99 and an EWSR1 rearrangement confirm it.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman with osteoporosis and no cancer history has an acute L1 compression fracture. Which MRI feature favours a benign osteoporotic fracture over a metastatic one?
o: Preserved normal fat signal in part of the body with a fluid sign and a retropulsed posterior fragment
Convex bulging of the posterior vertebral border
Involvement of the pedicle with an epidural mass
Diffuse low T1 signal replacing the whole body and posterior elements
items.e: Osteoporotic fractures often retain fatty marrow, show a fluid or linear band sign and a retropulsed angular fragment; metastatic fractures replace marrow diffusely, bulge the posterior border and involve the pedicle and epidural space.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a 6 cm eccentric, expansile lytic lesion of S1-S2 without matrix mineralisation. Biopsy shows osteoclast-like giant cells evenly distributed in mononuclear stroma. Wide resection would sacrifice sacral nerve roots. A useful medical treatment is:
items.e: Sacral giant cell tumour is often unresectable without major morbidity; denosumab, a RANKL inhibitor, shrinks the tumour and is used to downstage or control it.

items.q: In the NOMS framework for metastatic spine disease, the 'M' component refers to assessment of:
items.e: NOMS = Neurological (Bilsky grade and myelopathy), Oncological (radiosensitivity), Mechanical (instability, assessed by SINS) and Systemic (fitness and extent of disease).

items.q: A patient with known prostate cancer has back pain and diffuse sclerotic lesions in several vertebrae with no compression. Which treatment best addresses the systemic disease and reduces skeletal events?
o: Androgen deprivation therapy with a bone-targeted agent
items.e: Prostate metastases are hormone-sensitive and radiosensitive; androgen deprivation plus zoledronic acid or denosumab, with radiotherapy for painful sites, is the mainstay.

items.q: A patient with spinal metastasis from differentiated thyroid carcinoma has iodine-avid disease. Besides surgery and embolisation, a systemic treatment option is:
items.e: Differentiated thyroid carcinoma metastases that take up iodine can be treated with I-131 after thyroidectomy; they are hypervascular and should be embolised before surgery.

items.q: The approximate proportion of patients with cancer who develop metastatic spinal cord compression is:
items.e: About 5-10% of patients with cancer develop MSCC; it is the presenting feature of cancer in about a fifth of cases.

items.q: In metastatic spinal cord compression, sphincter disturbance is typically:
o: The earliest symptom in most patients
A late feature associated with poorer prognosis
A sign of radicular involvement only
items.e: Back pain is the earliest and commonest symptom (about 90%); bladder and bowel dysfunction usually appear late and predict poor functional recovery.

items.q: Percutaneous (minimally invasive) pedicle screw fixation in metastatic spine disease is especially useful for:
o: Bilsky grade 3 compression needing circumferential decompression
Solitary metastasis needing en bloc resection
Mechanical instability without high-grade cord compression in frail patients, with less blood loss and earlier radiotherapy
items.e: Percutaneous stabilisation reduces wound complications and blood loss, allowing radiotherapy to start sooner; when decompression is required, it can be combined with a mini-open approach.

items.q: A myxopapillary ependymoma of the filum terminale in a young adult typically presents with:
o: Low back pain and sciatica-like symptoms, sometimes with bladder dysfunction
Painless foot drop with no back pain
items.e: Myxopapillary ependymomas arise in the conus or filum and present with back pain and radicular or cauda equina symptoms; en bloc removal without capsule violation lowers recurrence.

items.q: A 40-year-old has an aggressive vertebral haemangioma of T7 causing progressive myelopathy from epidural extension. A commonly used treatment approach is:
o: Radiotherapy is contraindicated and observation is advised
Pre-operative embolisation and/or vertebroplasty, followed by decompression and stabilisation
items.e: Symptomatic aggressive haemangiomas are hypervascular; embolisation and intraoperative or pre-operative vertebroplasty reduce bleeding before decompression, and radiotherapy is an option for pain without major deficit.

items.q: Which primary tumour carries the shortest survival after spinal metastasis among the following?
items.e: Lung cancer (and gastrointestinal, liver and unknown primaries) carry poor survival after spinal metastasis, while thyroid, prostate and breast metastases have much better prognosis.

items.q: Which group of primary tumours accounts for the majority of adult spinal metastases?
items.e: Breast, prostate and lung together account for well over half of spinal metastases; kidney and thyroid complete the classic list of bone-seeking carcinomas.

items.q: Which feature on a radiograph of a vertebra with a solitary lesion is most suggestive of metastasis rather than a primary benign lesion in a 60-year-old?
o: Destruction of a pedicle with a soft tissue mass
A small sclerotic focus with spiculated margins
Uniform diffuse sclerosis with vertebral enlargement
items.e: Pedicle destruction and a soft tissue mass suggest metastasis; vertical striations suggest haemangioma, a spiculated sclerotic focus a bone island, and enlargement with sclerosis Paget disease.

items.q: Paget disease involving a vertebra classically produces a radiographic appearance of:
o: A 'picture frame' vertebra with cortical thickening and enlargement
items.e: Pagetic vertebrae are enlarged with thickened peripheral cortex (picture frame) or diffuse sclerosis (ivory vertebra); unlike blastic metastasis, the vertebra is expanded.

items.q: An 'ivory vertebra' (uniform dense sclerosis of one vertebral body) in a 65-year-old man is most commonly due to:
o: Osteoblastic prostate metastasis, Paget disease or lymphoma
items.e: A diffusely sclerotic vertebra suggests blastic metastasis (prostate, breast), Paget disease (enlarged) or Hodgkin lymphoma; myeloma and haemangioma do not usually cause uniform sclerosis.

items.q: The Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini (WBB) classification is primarily used to:
o: Plan en bloc resection of primary spinal tumours by mapping their extent in the axial plane
items.e: WBB maps tumour extent in 12 radiating sectors and 5 layers on axial imaging, guiding whether en bloc vertebrectomy, sagittal resection or posterior arch resection can achieve margins.

items.q: For a primary malignant spinal tumour such as chondrosarcoma, which surgical strategy gives the lowest local recurrence?
o: En bloc resection with a wide or marginal margin (Enneking appropriate)
items.e: Chondrosarcoma is resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy; en bloc resection with appropriate margins is the main determinant of local control and survival, while intralesional surgery leads to high recurrence.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has a slowly growing thoracic intradural extramedullary tumour causing myelopathy. During resection, which monitoring is standard?
o: Intraoperative neuromonitoring with motor and somatosensory evoked potentials
items.e: Intradural tumour surgery is performed with MEP and SEP neuromonitoring to warn of cord injury; D-wave monitoring is useful for intramedullary tumours.

items.q: On T2-weighted MRI, a spinal schwannoma may show a 'target sign', which consists of:
o: A low-signal centre (fibrous) surrounded by a high-signal periphery (myxoid)
items.e: The target sign reflects central fibrocollagenous tissue (low T2) and peripheral myxoid tissue (high T2) and is typical of nerve sheath tumours, especially neurofibromas and schwannomas.

items.q: Which statement about spinal intramedullary astrocytomas is correct?
o: They are always benign and well encapsulated
They are the commonest intramedullary tumour in adults
They are usually eccentric and infiltrative, so complete resection is often impossible
items.e: Astrocytomas infiltrate the cord without a clear plane, so the aim is safe debulking and biopsy, in contrast to ependymomas, which have a cleavage plane allowing gross total resection.

items.q: A 68-year-old with known metastatic lung cancer is paraplegic for 5 days from a T8 metastasis, with multiple visceral metastases and a performance status of 4. The most appropriate treatment is:
items.e: Paraplegia over 48 hours, short expected survival and poor performance status predict no benefit from surgery; palliative radiotherapy for pain and supportive care are appropriate.

items.q: Which tumour is NOT generally considered hypervascular requiring pre-operative embolisation before spinal surgery?
items.e: Renal, thyroid and hepatocellular carcinomas (plus some others like melanoma and paraganglioma) are hypervascular; osteoblastic prostate metastases are not.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a 2 cm vertebral body lesion that is T1 and T2 hyperintense with suppression on fat-saturated images and no soft tissue component. Appropriate management is:
o: Reassurance; no treatment for a typical incidental haemangioma
items.e: A fatty, typical haemangioma is a common incidental finding (about 10% of autopsies) and needs no treatment or follow-up unless symptomatic.

items.q: In separation surgery for metastatic epidural compression, the bone of the vertebral body is:
o: Replaced with cement only without decompression
Removed with the adjacent discs and rib heads to wide margins
Not necessarily resected; the aim is circumferential epidural decompression and stabilisation, leaving gross tumour to SBRT
items.e: Separation surgery aims to create a margin of about 2-3 mm between tumour and cord, via a posterolateral approach with instrumentation; tumour in the body is treated by subsequent SBRT rather than radical resection.

items.q: After a knee dislocation there is a transverse skin dimple and puckering over the medial joint line, and closed reduction fails. The most likely cause is:
o: The lateral femoral condyle trapped in the iliotibial band
The medial femoral condyle buttonholed through the medial capsule and retinaculum
The patella locked in the intercondylar notch
Interposition of the popliteus tendon laterally
items.e: The 'dimple sign' marks an irreducible posterolateral knee dislocation, in which the medial femoral condyle buttonholes through the medial capsule; repeated closed attempts risk skin necrosis, so urgent open reduction is needed.

items.q: Which is the most common direction of traumatic knee dislocation?
items.e: Anterior dislocation from hyperextension is the commonest pattern, followed by posterior; medial, lateral and rotatory dislocations are less frequent.

items.q: In knee dislocation, how is the popliteal artery typically injured in a posterior dislocation compared with an anterior one?
o: Posterior: intimal tear only; anterior: transection
Posterior: frank transection or complete disruption; anterior: traction with intimal tear
Neither injures the artery because it is mobile
items.e: Anterior dislocation stretches the artery and causes intimal tears, whereas posterior dislocation is more likely to transect it directly; either way serial vascular assessment is essential.

items.q: The popliteal artery is particularly vulnerable in knee dislocation because:
o: It is tethered proximally at the adductor hiatus and distally at the fibrous arch of soleus
It is protected only by subcutaneous fat
It lies anterior to the femur
It passes through the iliotibial band
items.e: Fixation of the artery at the adductor hiatus and soleal arch means it cannot move away from displacing bone ends, so it stretches or tears.

items.q: For a multiligament knee injury without vascular compromise, current evidence generally favours:
o: Operative repair/reconstruction, often within about 3 weeks
Delaying all surgery by at least 6 months
items.e: Surgical treatment, particularly early single-stage or staged repair/reconstruction, gives better stability and function than non-operative management; arthrofibrosis is the main risk.

items.q: Which mechanism classically produces combined rupture of the ACL, the posterior capsule and then the PCL?
o: Valgus, flexion and external rotation while cutting
A direct blow to the anterior patella with the knee flexed
A fall onto the flexed knee with the foot plantarflexed
items.e: Hyperextension tears the ACL first, then the posterior capsule and PCL, and is the usual mechanism of anterior dislocation. A fall onto the flexed knee with the foot plantarflexed typically causes isolated PCL injury.

items.q: The anterolateral ligament of the knee attaches distally on the tibia:
o: About midway between Gerdy's tubercle and the fibular head
On the fibular head with the LCL
items.e: The ALL runs from near the lateral epicondyle to the anterolateral tibia, inserting roughly midway between Gerdy's tubercle and the fibular head, the site of the Segond fracture.

items.q: In a modified Lemaire lateral extra-articular tenodesis, a strip of iliotibial band left attached to Gerdy's tubercle is:
o: Passed superficial to the LCL and fixed to the fibular head
Passed through the femoral ACL tunnel
Sutured to the lateral border of the patella
Passed deep to the LCL and fixed to the femur proximal and posterior to the lateral epicondyle
items.e: The ITB strip is routed under the fibular collateral ligament and fixed to the femoral metaphysis just proximal and posterior to the lateral epicondyle, tensioned in neutral rotation at about 60 degrees of flexion.

items.q: On the lateral femoral condyle, the femoral attachment of the popliteus tendon lies:
o: Proximal and posterior to the fibular collateral ligament
Anterior and distal to the attachment of the fibular collateral ligament
Above the origin of the lateral gastrocnemius
items.e: LaPrade showed the popliteus inserts about 18 mm anterior and distal to the FCL femoral attachment, which lies slightly proximal and posterior to the lateral epicondyle; this guides anatomic PLC reconstruction tunnels.

items.q: The fibular collateral (lateral collateral) ligament of the knee inserts distally on the:
o: Lateral aspect of the fibular head
items.e: The FCL runs from just proximal and posterior to the lateral epicondyle to the lateral aspect of the fibular head, where it blends with the biceps femoris insertion.

items.q: During hamstring harvest at the pes anserinus, deep to the sartorius fascia, the gracilis tendon lies in which position relative to semitendinosus?
items.e: Under the sartorial fascia the gracilis is the upper (proximal) tendon and semitendinosus the lower; recognising this avoids harvesting the wrong tendon.

items.q: Premature amputation of the semitendinosus during harvest with a closed tendon stripper is most often caused by failing to release:
o: Its fibrous accessory bands to the fascia of the medial head of gastrocnemius
items.e: Semitendinosus has one or more strong accessory bands to the medial gastrocnemius fascia; if not divided, the stripper is deflected and cuts the tendon short.

items.q: In biomechanical testing, which ACL graft has the highest ultimate tensile load?
items.e: A quadrupled hamstring graft fails at about 4,000 N, compared with about 2,900 N for a 10 mm BPTB graft and about 2,000 N for the native ACL; a single strand of semitendinosus is much weaker.

items.q: The ultimate tensile load of the native ACL in young human specimens (Woo et al.) is approximately:
items.e: Woo measured about 2,160 N in young specimens (about 1,725 N in Noyes' older work), which grafts are designed to exceed to allow for loss of strength during incorporation.

items.q: After ACL reconstruction with a tendon graft, the correct sequence of graft biological incorporation is:
o: Avascular necrosis, revascularisation, cellular repopulation, remodelling (ligamentisation)
items.e: Grafts first become necrotic, then are revascularised and repopulated by host cells before remodelling into ligament-like tissue over 1-2 years; they are weakest at about 6-12 weeks.

items.q: On sagittal MRI with the knee in extension, the intact ACL normally runs:
o: Roughly parallel to, or steeper than, Blumensaat's line
items.e: The normal ACL parallels the intercondylar roof (Blumensaat's line); a torn ACL often lies flatter (more horizontal) than this line.

items.q: For complete ACL tears, the sensitivity of MRI compared with arthroscopy is approximately:
items.e: MRI is highly accurate for complete ACL tears, with sensitivity and specificity above about 90%; partial tears and ramp lesions are less reliably detected.

items.q: On Lachman testing, an anterior translation 6-10 mm greater than the uninjured side is graded as:
items.e: Lachman grading: grade 1 = 3-5 mm, grade 2 = 6-10 mm, grade 3 = over 10 mm greater translation than the normal side; endpoint quality (firm or soft) is also recorded.

items.q: In IKDC grading of the pivot shift, a definite 'clunk' of reduction is graded as:
items.e: The pivot shift is graded as glide (1), clunk (2) or gross with momentary locking (3); higher grades point to additional anterolateral injury and favour adding LET.

items.q: A 38-year-old manual worker has chronic ACL deficiency with instability, medial compartment osteoarthritis and varus malalignment. The best surgical option is:
o: High tibial osteotomy, combined with or followed by ACL reconstruction if instability persists
items.e: Varus malalignment overloads the medial compartment and strains the reconstructed ACL; correcting alignment with HTO (with or without ACL reconstruction) addresses both pain and instability in this age group.

items.q: A medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy tends to change the posterior tibial slope in which way, which matters in ACL-deficient knees?
o: Increases it, increasing anterior tibial translation and ACL graft load
Always converts it to an anterior slope
items.e: Unless the wedge is opened more posteriorly (trapezoidal gap), opening-wedge HTO increases posterior tibial slope, which raises anterior tibial translation; slope can be reduced deliberately in ACL deficiency.

items.q: Primary ACL repair (with or without augmentation) is best suited to which tear pattern?
o: Proximal femoral avulsion with good tissue quality
Chronic tear over 1 year old with a resorbed stump
Tear with a retracted, degenerate stump
items.e: Modern ACL repair is considered mainly for acute proximal (Sherman type I) avulsions with good-quality tissue; midsubstance and chronic tears do not heal reliably.

items.q: The most common complication after ACL reconstruction is:
o: Loss of motion (arthrofibrosis), especially loss of extension
items.e: Loss of motion, particularly extension, is the commonest complication and is linked to early surgery on a swollen stiff knee, tunnel malposition and cyclops lesions; infection and early graft failure are uncommon.

items.q: In the 'over-the-top' route used in some ACL reconstructions (for example the physeal-sparing iliotibial band technique), the graft passes:
o: Through a tunnel across the distal femoral physis
Around the posterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle without a femoral tunnel
Over the anterior surface of the patella
items.e: In the over-the-top position the graft exits the notch posteriorly around the lateral femoral condyle and is fixed laterally, avoiding the femoral physis.

items.q: In the Micheli-Kocher physeal-sparing ACL reconstruction, the iliotibial band graft is fixed on the tibial side by passing it:
o: Under the intermeniscal ligament and through a groove in the anteromedial proximal tibial epiphysis
Through a tibial tunnel crossing the physis
items.e: The ITB graft, left attached to Gerdy's tubercle, goes over the top of the lateral condyle, through the knee, under the intermeniscal ligament and into a small epiphyseal groove, where it is sutured to periosteum.

items.q: The femoral attachment of the PCL is on the:
o: Medial wall of the lateral femoral condyle, posteriorly
Lateral wall of the medial femoral condyle, anteriorly in the notch
items.e: The PCL arises from the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle in the anterior notch; the ACL arises from the medial surface of the lateral condyle posteriorly.

items.q: The posterior drawer test is repeated with the foot externally rotated about 15 degrees, and the lateral tibial plateau rotates posteriorly more than the medial. This is the:
o: Posterolateral drawer test, indicating posterolateral corner injury
items.e: In the posterolateral drawer test, excessive posterolateral rotation of the lateral plateau in external rotation indicates PLC injury; it is performed with the knee at about 80-90 degrees.

items.q: For an acute high-grade posterolateral corner injury, comparative studies show that:
o: Primary repair has a lower failure rate than reconstruction
Anatomic reconstruction has a lower failure rate than primary repair
Both repair and reconstruction fail in over 90%
items.e: Primary repair of torn PLC structures has a high failure rate (around 40% in some series); reconstruction, or repair with augmentation, is more reliable, especially for midsubstance tears.

items.q: Complete common peroneal nerve palsy after knee dislocation:
o: Has a poor prognosis, with fewer than about half regaining useful function
Recovers fully within 6 weeks in almost all
Recovers only if the ligaments are reconstructed
items.e: Traction injuries of the peroneal nerve over long segments recover poorly; many patients need an ankle-foot orthosis or later tibialis posterior transfer.

items.q: In the Schenck classification of knee dislocation, the suffix 'C' denotes:
items.e: The modifiers C (circulatory/arterial injury) and N (nerve injury) are added to the KD grade; KD V denotes a fracture-dislocation.

items.q: Spanning external fixation is most clearly indicated in a knee dislocation that has:
o: Vascular repair, an open wound, or a knee that cannot be held reduced
items.e: A spanning fixator protects a vascular repair, allows wound care in open injuries and holds unstable reductions; stable closed injuries can be braced before ligament surgery.

items.q: ACL injury rates in female athletes have been reported to be higher in which phase of the menstrual cycle?
o: There is no cycle phase in which risk differs
items.e: Several studies report more ACL injuries in the preovulatory phase, possibly from oestrogen effects on ligament laxity and neuromuscular control, although the evidence is not conclusive.

items.q: Which bony morphological factor is associated with increased risk of ACL injury and graft failure?
items.e: A steeper lateral posterior tibial slope increases anterior tibial translation and ACL strain; a narrow notch and small ACL are also risk factors.

items.q: In the early postoperative period after hamstring ACL reconstruction, the weakest link of the fixation construct is usually:
o: The midsubstance of the quadrupled graft
Tibial fixation of the soft-tissue graft in metaphyseal bone
items.e: Soft-tissue graft fixation on the tibia relies on relatively soft cancellous metaphyseal bone and is the weakest point until tendon-to-bone healing occurs at 8-12 weeks.

items.q: When harvesting a BPTB autograft, the usual width of the central patellar tendon taken is about:
items.e: A 9-11 mm central-third strip with patellar and tibial bone blocks is typical; taking more than about a third weakens the residual tendon.

items.q: In the KANON trial (Frobell), roughly what proportion of young active adults assigned to rehabilitation with optional delayed reconstruction had not undergone ACL reconstruction by 5 years?
items.e: About 51% of the optional-delayed group avoided reconstruction over 5 years, with similar KOOS outcomes to early reconstruction.

items.q: Regarding osteoarthritis after ACL injury:
o: Reconstruction eliminates the long-term risk of OA
