OA occurs only in non-reconstructed knees
Reconstruction has not been shown to prevent later OA, and associated meniscectomy increases the risk
Meniscal status has no effect on OA risk
items.e: Post-traumatic OA is common after ACL injury whether or not the knee is reconstructed; meniscal loss and chondral damage at injury are the strongest predictors.

items.q: A longitudinal midline incision used for digital fasciectomy in Dupuytren disease is usually closed with multiple Z-plasties mainly to:
o: Break up the straight scar and prevent a longitudinal scar contracture across the flexion creases
Increase blood supply to the neurovascular bundles
Reduce the risk of collagen recurrence in the cord
Allow the wound to heal by secondary intention
items.e: A straight scar crossing flexion creases contracts and recreates a flexion deformity; Z-plasties redirect the scar and lengthen the skin. Open-palm (secondary intention) healing is a separate technique.

items.q: A rheumatoid swan-neck finger has full PIP flexion whatever the MCP position, with no intrinsic tightness and a normal PIP joint (Nalebuff type I). A suitable procedure is:
o: DIP arthrodesis or an FDS tenodesis (sublimis sling) to limit PIP hyperextension
items.e: Type I deformities are flexible, so the aim is to correct the DIP flexion and block PIP hyperextension (DIP fusion, dermadesis or FDS tenodesis); arthrodesis or arthroplasty of the PIP is for destroyed joints.

items.q: A relative contraindication to total wrist arthroplasty in a rheumatoid patient is:
o: Dependence on crutches or a walker for walking
items.e: Loading the wrist through walking aids overloads the implant and leads to loosening, so arthrodesis is preferred in these patients. Bilateral disease is actually a reason to keep motion in at least one wrist.

items.q: The lateral (first) window of the ilioinguinal approach, developed lateral to the iliopsoas, gives access to the:
o: Internal iliac fossa, anterior sacroiliac joint and upper pelvic brim
items.e: Elevating the iliacus from the inner table exposes the iliac fossa up to the anterior SI joint; the middle window reaches the pelvic brim and quadrilateral surface, and the medial window reaches the symphysis and space of Retzius.

items.q: Tomita's total en bloc spondylectomy removes the vertebra in two main pieces. The posterior element is separated from the vertebral body by cutting through the:
items.e: In TES the T-saw is passed around each pedicle to divide it, allowing en bloc removal of the posterior arch (laminectomy en bloc) and then the vertebral body (corpectomy en bloc) with the dura protected.

items.q: In hybrid plating, a fragment is to be fixed with both a conventional (compression or lag) screw and locking screws. The correct order of insertion is:
o: The conventional screw first, then the locking screws
The locking screws first, then the conventional screw
Either order, as the result is the same
Locking screws only, as the two types cannot be combined
items.e: A conventional screw pulls bone towards the plate or compresses the fracture, and it cannot do this once locking screws have fixed the bone-plate distance. Hence the rule 'lag (or compress) before you lock'.

items.q: A surgeon replaces a 10 mm solid intramedullary nail with a 12 mm nail of the same material and design. The bending stiffness increases by a factor of about:
items.e: For a solid cylinder, bending stiffness is proportional to the fourth power of the radius. (12/10)^4 is about 2.1, so a 2 mm larger nail is roughly twice as stiff.

items.q: Immediately after reamed intramedullary nailing of a tibial shaft fracture, the blood supply to the diaphyseal cortex is affected in which way?
o: Endosteal and periosteal flow both increase
Periosteal flow falls and endosteal flow increases
Endosteal flow falls, and periosteal flow increases to compensate
items.e: Reaming destroys much of the endosteal circulation, so the inner cortex is temporarily ischaemic. Periosteal flow increases, and the endosteal supply revascularises over weeks. Reaming debris also acts as local autograft.

items.q: The SPRINT trial compared reamed with unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures. Its main finding was that reamed nailing:
o: Clearly increased infection in open fractures
Clearly increased non-union in closed fractures
May benefit closed fractures by reducing reoperations, with no clear difference in open fractures
items.e: In SPRINT, reamed nailing lowered the primary composite outcome in closed fractures, mainly through fewer autodynamisations. It showed no significant difference in open fractures. Waiting at least 6 months before reoperating for delayed union was also supported.

items.q: A length-stable transverse femoral shaft fracture fixed with a statically locked nail shows delayed union at 4 months, with an intact nail. A simple first step to stimulate healing is:
o: Dynamisation by removing the locking screws from the longer fragment, or using the dynamic slot
Removing the nail and applying a cast
items.e: Removing the static screws on one side allows axial compression with weight-bearing, which can promote union in axially stable patterns. Dynamisation is avoided in comminuted or length-unstable fractures, which would shorten.

items.q: During nailing of a proximal-third tibial shaft fracture, the proximal fragment tends to drift into valgus. To prevent this, an anteroposterior blocking (Poller) screw is placed in the proximal fragment:
o: Medial to the intended path of the nail
Lateral to the intended path of the nail
Posterior to the intended path of the nail
In the distal fragment, medial to the nail
items.e: Blocking screws are placed in the metaphyseal fragment on the concave side of the deformity, which narrows the canal and guides the nail centrally. For valgus, the concavity is lateral, so the screw sits lateral to the nail path. An anterior-posterior deformity (procurvatum) would need a mediolateral screw placed posteriorly.

items.q: In a unilateral external fixator, which change increases construct stiffness?
o: Moving the pins further from the fracture
Using fewer pins in each fragment
Moving the connecting rod closer to the skin and bone
Moving the pins in each fragment closer together
items.e: Stiffness increases as the bar moves closer to the bone (shorter pin lever arm), as pins are placed near the fracture and spread widely within each fragment, with more pins, and with stacked bars or a second plane. Larger pin diameter has the biggest effect.

items.q: In an elderly patient with osteoporotic bone needing a spanning external fixator for several months, hydroxyapatite-coated pins are chosen mainly because they:
o: Remove the need for pin-site care
Increase the stiffness of the connecting bars
Improve pin-bone fixation and reduce pin loosening
items.e: Hydroxyapatite coating promotes bone ongrowth onto the pin. This increases extraction torque and reduces loosening, which is especially useful in cancellous or osteoporotic bone and during long frame times.

items.q: The most common complication of external fixation is:
items.e: Pin-tract infection affects a large proportion of patients with external fixators. It is mostly superficial and treated with pin care and oral antibiotics. Loosening worsens it, and persistent infection may need pin removal and debridement.

items.q: For tibial shaft external fixation, half-pins are most safely inserted through which surface to avoid neurovascular structures?
o: The lateral surface through the anterior compartment
The posteromedial surface through the soleus
items.e: The anteromedial face of the tibia is subcutaneous and lies within a safe corridor, well away from the anterior and posterior tibial neurovascular bundles. Pins passed through muscle compartments also tether muscle and increase pin-site problems.

items.q: A 4.5 mm plate on a humeral shaft fracture breaks 5 months after surgery. The fracture has not united, and the plate shows beach marks at the fracture site. The mechanism of failure is:
o: A single overload exceeding ultimate tensile strength
Fatigue failure from repeated cyclic loading below the yield strength
items.e: Implants are designed to share load only until the bone heals. If union is delayed, cyclic loading leads to fatigue cracks, seen as beach marks, and eventually fracture: the 'race between healing and implant failure'.

items.q: Which combination of implant metals in direct contact carries the greatest risk of galvanic corrosion?
o: A titanium alloy plate with titanium alloy screws
A stainless steel plate with stainless steel screws
A cobalt-chromium plate with cobalt-chromium screws
A 316L stainless steel plate with cobalt-chromium screws
items.e: Galvanic corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals with different electrochemical potentials touch in body fluids. Stainless steel is the least resistant and should not be combined with cobalt-chromium or titanium. Implants of the same alloy do not set up a galvanic couple.

items.q: Which of the following is one of the four AO principles of fracture management?
o: Preservation of the blood supply to soft tissues and bone through gentle handling
Rigid compression fixation of all diaphyseal fractures
Primary bone grafting of every open fracture
items.e: The four AO principles are fracture reduction to restore anatomy, stability suited to the fracture (absolute or relative), preservation of blood supply, and early safe mobilisation. Compression is not used for every fracture, and immobilisation is avoided.

items.q: In the first hours after a fracture, the main initial source of PDGF and TGF-beta in the fracture haematoma is:
items.e: Platelets in the clot release PDGF and TGF-beta, which attract inflammatory cells and mesenchymal stem cells. Macrophages then add IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha and further growth factors.

items.q: When a locking plate is used on an osteoporotic diaphysis, bicortical rather than unicortical locking screws are recommended mainly because unicortical screws:
o: Cause thermal necrosis of the far cortex
Have poor torsional strength and pull-out resistance in the thin cortex
Are much more likely to break by bending
items.e: In osteoporotic bone the cortex is thin, and a unicortical screw has only a short working thread. This weakens resistance to torsion and pull-out. Bicortical locking screws greatly improve torsional strength, especially in the humerus and femur.

items.q: Which lipid-lowering drug has a modest uricosuric effect and can help reduce serum urate in a patient with gout and hypertriglyceridaemia?
items.e: Fenofibrate increases renal urate excretion and lowers serum urate by about 20-30%. Niacin (nicotinic acid) does the opposite, raising urate and potentially precipitating gout.

items.q: A patient with gout takes 75 mg aspirin daily for secondary cardiac prevention. The effect of this low dose on serum urate is:
o: A slight rise, because low-dose salicylate reduces renal urate excretion
A marked fall, because it is strongly uricosuric
A fall caused by xanthine oxidase inhibition
items.e: Low-dose salicylate causes urate retention by the kidney and raises serum urate slightly. Only high anti-inflammatory doses (above about 3 g/day) are uricosuric. Cardioprotective aspirin is usually continued, and urate-lowering therapy is adjusted.

items.q: A suspected tophus is excised from the olecranon bursa. To show the urate crystals on histology, the specimen should be sent:
o: Fixed in absolute alcohol (non-aqueous fixative) rather than formalin
Frozen in liquid nitrogen after decalcification
In saline for decalcification in acid
items.e: Monosodium urate crystals dissolve in aqueous fixatives such as formalin, leaving only empty clefts. Alcohol fixation preserves the needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals for polarised microscopy.

items.q: The typical histological appearance of a gouty tophus is:
o: Lobules of hyaline cartilage with chondrocyte atypia
Sheets of plasma cells with amyloid
Amorphous urate deposits surrounded by histiocytes and foreign-body giant cells (a granulomatous reaction)
Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells and acid-fast bacilli
items.e: A tophus consists of masses of urate crystals (amorphous after formalin) surrounded by a foreign-body granuloma of macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. Caseation and acid-fast bacilli point to tuberculosis instead.

items.q: Colchicine relieves acute gouty inflammation mainly by:
o: Increasing renal urate excretion through URAT1
Binding tubulin and inhibiting microtubule polymerisation, which impairs neutrophil migration and inflammasome activation
items.e: Colchicine binds tubulin and disrupts microtubules. This reduces neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly. It does not lower serum urate.

items.q: A man taking colchicine for gout flare prophylaxis is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. A few days later he develops diarrhoea, myopathy and pancytopenia. The interaction is due to:
o: Inhibition of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein by clarithromycin, raising colchicine levels
Induction of colchicine metabolism by clarithromycin
items.e: Colchicine is cleared through CYP3A4 and the P-glycoprotein efflux pump. Strong inhibitors such as clarithromycin, ketoconazole, ciclosporin and some calcium channel blockers can cause fatal colchicine toxicity. The dose must be reduced or the drug avoided.

items.q: A patient with chronic gout who takes azathioprine after a renal transplant is started on allopurinol at the usual dose without adjustment. The main risk is:
o: Acute rejection due to lowered azathioprine levels
Severe bone marrow suppression, because xanthine oxidase normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine
items.e: Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which xanthine oxidase inactivates. Allopurinol blocks this pathway and can cause life-threatening myelosuppression unless the azathioprine dose is cut to about a quarter, or the combination is avoided.

items.q: Gout is rare in premenopausal women mainly because:
o: Oestrogen increases renal urate excretion, keeping serum urate lower
Women have lower dietary purine intake
items.e: Oestrogen has a uricosuric effect, so serum urate is lower in premenopausal women. After the menopause, urate rises and gout incidence in women approaches that in men, often with diuretic use and renal impairment.

items.q: High intake of fructose-sweetened soft drinks raises serum urate mainly because hepatic fructose metabolism:
o: Blocks the urate transporter ABCG2 in the gut
Rapidly consumes ATP, increasing AMP breakdown through the purine pathway to urate
items.e: Fructokinase phosphorylates fructose rapidly and depletes ATP. The resulting AMP is degraded through inosine and hypoxanthine to uric acid. Fructose also reduces renal urate excretion.

items.q: Polarised microscopy of synovial fluid shows spherical structures with a 'Maltese cross' birefringence pattern. These are most likely:
items.e: Lipid spherules give a Maltese cross pattern. They can occur in traumatic effusions (for example with fat from an intra-articular fracture) and are occasionally linked to acute arthritis. Urate crystals are needles, CPP crystals are rhomboids and cholesterol forms notched plates.

items.q: A 50-year-old has 9 months of shoulder pain from a dense, well-defined supraspinatus calcific deposit despite physiotherapy and an injection. Which non-invasive treatment has the best randomised evidence for pain relief and deposit resorption?
items.e: High-energy ESWT works better in calcific than non-calcific tendinopathy and improves pain, function and deposit size in trials. Ultrasound-guided barbotage is the main alternative before arthroscopic removal.

items.q: Benzbromarone is a potent uricosuric that works even in moderate renal impairment, but it has been withdrawn in many countries because of:
items.e: Benzbromarone blocks URAT1 and lowers urate effectively, but rare cases of fulminant hepatotoxicity led to its withdrawal or restriction. HLA-B*58:01-related severe skin reactions are linked to allopurinol.

items.q: During a straight-leg raise in a patient with suspected lumbar disc herniation, radicular pain is classically considered a positive Lasègue sign when it is reproduced between hip flexion angles of about:
items.e: Below about 30 degrees there is little root excursion. Above about 70 degrees, pain usually comes from the hamstrings, hip or sacroiliac joints rather than the root. A positive test reproduces leg pain below the knee within this range.

items.q: During an L5-S1 microdiscectomy, the surgeon finds two nerve roots leaving the dural sac through a single sleeve. The most important implication of this conjoined root is:
o: It can mimic a disc herniation on MRI and is easily injured during retraction
It is always the cause of the patient's symptoms
It means the procedure must be converted to fusion
It is always associated with a tethered cord
items.e: A conjoined nerve root is the commonest lumbosacral root anomaly and usually occurs at L5-S1. It is less mobile, may look like a sequestrated fragment on imaging, and is at risk if mistaken for disc or retracted forcefully.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has unilateral L5 radicular pain. MRI shows a cyst arising from an arthritic L4-L5 facet joint and compressing the lateral recess, with a 5 mm degenerative anterolisthesis. This lesion is best described as:
o: A facet synovial (juxtafacet) cyst associated with degenerative instability
An aneurysmal bone cyst of the pedicle
items.e: Juxtafacet synovial cysts are commonest at L4-L5 and are linked to facet arthropathy and degenerative spondylolisthesis. Because of the instability, cyst excision with decompression is often combined with fusion when there is a slip. Tarlov cysts arise from sacral root sleeves.

items.q: A 45-year-old obese man on long-term oral prednisolone develops neurogenic claudication. Axial MRI shows the thecal sac compressed into a 'Y' shape by excess posterior epidural fat. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Epidural lipomatosis is linked to exogenous steroids, Cushing syndrome and obesity. Excess fat compresses the dural sac into a Y shape. First-line treatment is weight loss and reducing steroids, with decompression reserved for refractory cases.

items.q: On sagittal T2 MRI of a patient with chronic low back pain, a small bright focus is seen in the posterior annulus of the L4-L5 disc, brighter than the nucleus and separate from it. This 'high-intensity zone' (Aprill and Bogduk) is thought to represent:
items.e: A high-intensity zone is a bright signal within the posterior annulus that represents a fissure with granulation tissue. It was linked to concordant pain on provocative discography, but it is also common in people without symptoms.

items.q: Lee's MRI grading of lumbar foraminal stenosis on sagittal images classifies a foramen as grade 3 (severe) when:
o: The nerve root shows morphological change or collapse
Perineural fat is obliterated in only one direction
Perineural fat is obliterated in four directions without root change
items.e: Grade 1 is perineural fat obliteration in two opposing directions (vertical or transverse). Grade 2 is obliteration in all four directions without change in the root. Grade 3 is root collapse or change in its shape.

items.q: A 66-year-old with typical neurogenic claudication from L4-L5 stenosis is noted to have brisk knee reflexes, a positive Hoffmann sign and clumsy hands. Before planning lumbar decompression, the next step is:
o: MRI of the cervical spine to look for tandem stenosis with myelopathy
Proceeding with lumbar decompression, since upper motor neuron signs are expected in lumbar stenosis
items.e: Upper motor neuron signs are not caused by lumbar stenosis and suggest cervical (or thoracic) cord compression. Tandem cervical and lumbar stenosis is not rare. The cervical myelopathy may need treatment first.

items.q: Chemonucleolysis with chymopapain for lumbar disc herniation fell out of use mainly because of which serious complication?
items.e: Chymopapain is a foreign protein, and anaphylaxis occurred in about 1% of patients, more often in women. Transverse myelitis was also reported. These risks and the success of microdiscectomy led to its withdrawal.

items.q: After lumbar microdiscectomy in patients with a large annular defect, an annular closure device implanted at surgery has been shown in a randomised trial to:
o: Remove the need for any discectomy
Reduce symptomatic recurrent herniation and reoperation
items.e: Large annular defects carry a high risk of reherniation. A randomised trial of a bone-anchored annular closure device showed fewer symptomatic reherniations and reoperations. Its cost and the risk of endplate changes limit its use to selected patients.

items.q: After an uncomplicated lumbar discectomy, C-reactive protein normally:
o: Peaks at about 2-3 days and returns to normal within about 2 weeks
Peaks at 2 weeks and normalises by 6 weeks
items.e: CRP peaks early and falls quickly after uncomplicated spinal surgery, whereas ESR stays raised for several weeks. A secondary rise in CRP or a failure to fall, with worsening back pain, suggests postoperative discitis.

items.q: According to NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica, epidural injections of local anaesthetic and steroid should be considered for:
o: Neurogenic claudication from central spinal stenosis
items.e: NG59 recommends considering epidural local anaesthetic and steroid for people with acute and severe sciatica. It advises against them for neurogenic claudication due to central canal stenosis.

items.q: The PRECISE trial (NEJM 2017) studied pregabalin in patients with acute or chronic sciatica. It found that pregabalin:
o: Was better than surgery for disc herniation
Did not significantly reduce leg pain compared with placebo at 8 or 52 weeks, and caused more adverse effects
items.e: PRECISE showed no meaningful benefit of pregabalin over placebo for sciatica at 8 weeks or 1 year, and more adverse events such as dizziness. NICE advises against gabapentinoids for sciatica.

items.q: A 15-year-old weightlifter has acute back and leg pain like a disc herniation. CT shows a small curvilinear bony fragment displaced into the canal from the posterior-inferior margin of the L4 vertebral body. The diagnosis is:
o: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
items.e: In adolescents, the posterior ring apophysis can avulse with attached disc. This gives a bony and cartilaginous fragment that MRI may miss but CT shows. Surgery needs removal of the bony fragment, not just the soft disc.

items.q: The EORTC 62931 randomised trial of adjuvant doxorubicin-ifosfamide after resection of adult soft-tissue sarcoma showed:
o: A 20% absolute improvement in overall survival
No significant improvement in relapse-free or overall survival
Reduced local recurrence but worse overall survival
Improved survival only in retroperitoneal sarcoma
items.e: EORTC 62931 (Woll, Lancet Oncol 2012) found no benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy, which is why adjuvant treatment for adult STS remains controversial and is reserved for selected high-risk tumours.

items.q: The 2008 updated Sarcoma Meta-analysis Collaboration (Pervaiz) of doxorubicin-based adjuvant chemotherapy for localised resectable soft-tissue sarcoma found:
o: A large survival benefit with single-agent doxorubicin
A small reduction in local and distant recurrence, with a marginal survival benefit mainly when ifosfamide was added
items.e: The meta-analysis showed modest benefits in recurrence and a small overall survival advantage for doxorubicin plus ifosfamide, supporting its selective use in high-risk, chemosensitive tumours.

items.q: The ISG-STS 1001 trial of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in high-risk extremity and trunk soft-tissue sarcoma showed that, compared with standard epirubicin-ifosfamide, histotype-tailored regimens:
o: Were superior in every histological subtype
items.e: Gronchi et al. (Lancet Oncol 2017) found histotype-tailored chemotherapy did not improve outcomes over full-dose anthracycline plus ifosfamide, which remains the reference neoadjuvant regimen.

items.q: In the phase 3 trial of eribulin versus dacarbazine in advanced liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma, the overall survival benefit of eribulin was seen mainly in:
items.e: Schöffski et al. (Lancet 2016) showed improved overall survival with eribulin, with the benefit driven by the liposarcoma subgroup; eribulin is therefore approved for advanced liposarcoma.

items.q: Gemcitabine combined with docetaxel is a commonly used regimen in advanced soft-tissue sarcoma, particularly for:
items.e: Gemcitabine-docetaxel has activity in leiomyosarcoma (especially uterine) and UPS; ALT and DFSP are treated surgically (imatinib for unresectable DFSP).

items.q: A 30-year-old has a rapidly growing (4 weeks) 2 cm subcutaneous forearm nodule. Histology shows a tissue-culture-like proliferation of myofibroblasts with extravasated red cells. Which genetic finding supports the benign diagnosis?
items.e: Nodular fasciitis is a self-limiting transient clonal lesion driven by USP6 rearrangement (often MYH9-USP6); its rapid growth and mitoses can mimic sarcoma.

items.q: Kaposi sarcoma is causally linked to infection with:
items.e: HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus) is present in all forms of Kaposi sarcoma, including the HIV-associated epidemic form.

items.q: Occupational exposure to vinyl chloride monomer is associated with which sarcoma?
items.e: Vinyl chloride (PVC manufacturing), Thorotrast and arsenic are classic causes of hepatic angiosarcoma.

items.q: Werner syndrome, an adult progeria with a raised risk of sarcomas, is caused by mutation of:
items.e: Werner syndrome is due to WRN (a RecQ helicase) mutation and predisposes to soft-tissue sarcomas, osteosarcoma and other cancers; TP53 is Li-Fraumeni and APC is FAP/Gardner.

items.q: On MRI, which feature most reliably identifies a simple lipoma?
o: Large size over 10 cm and deep location
Homogeneous fat signal that suppresses completely on fat-saturated sequences with only thin septa
Non-fatty enhancing nodules within the mass
items.e: A lipoma follows subcutaneous fat on all sequences and suppresses uniformly; thick or nodular septa, non-fatty enhancing areas, size and depth suggest atypical lipomatous tumour.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of distant metastases from soft-tissue sarcoma involve the lungs?
items.e: Haematogenous spread to the lungs accounts for most (about 80%) metastases, which is why chest CT is the standard staging and surveillance test.

items.q: What proportion of soft-tissue sarcomas arise in the retroperitoneum?
items.e: Extremities account for about 50-60% (thigh commonest), the retroperitoneum about 15%, and the trunk wall, head and neck and viscera the rest.

items.q: For a lump deep to the fascia that is larger than 5 cm, the approximate likelihood of malignancy is:
items.e: Most lumps are benign, but deep lumps over 5 cm carry a malignancy risk of about 10% or more, so they warrant MRI and specialist assessment before any intervention.

items.q: In a soft-tissue lump referral pathway such as the UK NICE pathway, the first-line investigation for a superficial palpable lump is usually:
items.e: Ultrasound triages superficial lumps; features such as heterogeneity, vascularity, depth or size over 5 cm prompt MRI and referral to a sarcoma service.

items.q: Excisional biopsy of a soft-tissue mass without prior core biopsy is generally acceptable only when the lesion is:
items.e: For small superficial lesions, excision can serve as biopsy because a re-excision would be straightforward; deep or large masses should have imaging then core biopsy.

items.q: When performing a core needle biopsy of a large soft-tissue sarcoma, the sample should ideally be taken from the:
o: Enhancing, viable periphery identified on contrast MRI
items.e: Necrotic central areas are non-diagnostic; targeting enhancing solid tissue gives the most representative sample for grading and molecular tests.

items.q: After surgery for soft-tissue sarcoma, which factor is the most important predictor of local recurrence?
items.e: Margin status is the strongest predictor of local recurrence, whereas histological grade is the strongest predictor of distant metastasis and survival.

items.q: A soft-tissue sarcoma is scored with FNCLCC differentiation 2, 5 mitoses per 10 high-power fields and less than 50% necrosis. The FNCLCC grade is:
items.e: Differentiation 2 + mitotic score 1 (0-9 mitoses) + necrosis 1 (under 50%) = 4; total scores of 4-5 are grade 2.

items.q: Under the AJCC 8th edition, a 12 cm grade 3 thigh sarcoma with no nodal or distant metastasis is stage:
items.e: A tumour over 10 cm up to 15 cm is T3; a T3 or T4, N0, M0 high-grade sarcoma is stage IIIB. T2 high-grade tumours are IIIA.

items.q: In Enneking's surgical margin terminology, removal of the entire anatomical compartment containing the sarcoma is a:
items.e: A radical margin removes the whole compartment from origin to insertion; a wide margin passes through normal tissue with a cuff around the reactive zone, which is the usual aim today.

items.q: Which tissue acts as a relatively strong anatomical barrier to sarcoma spread, allowing a close but adequate margin when left intact on the tumour surface?
o: Fascia (such as muscle fascia or periosteum)
items.e: Fascia, periosteum, epineurium and vessel adventitia resist tumour infiltration, so a thin intact fascial layer is considered equivalent to a thicker cuff of fat or muscle.

items.q: With modern multimodal treatment, limb-salvage surgery is possible in approximately what proportion of extremity soft-tissue sarcomas?
items.e: Combined wide excision and radiotherapy allows limb salvage in over 90% of extremity sarcomas, with survival equivalent to amputation (Rosenberg 1982).

items.q: After an unplanned 'whoops' excision of a soft-tissue sarcoma, residual tumour is found in the re-excision specimen in approximately:
items.e: Residual disease is found in roughly half of re-excisions, so the entire tumour bed and scar should be re-excised with wide margins after MRI and staging.

items.q: Major wound complications after preoperative radiotherapy for extremity soft-tissue sarcoma are most frequent in tumours of the:
items.e: In NCIC SR2 most wound complications occurred in lower-limb, especially thigh, tumours; planned plastic surgical closure with flaps reduces this risk.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the thigh soft tissues. Treatment follows:
o: Surgery alone, as for adult-type sarcoma
Ewing sarcoma multi-agent chemotherapy protocols with local control by surgery and/or radiotherapy
items.e: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma behaves like its bone counterpart and is treated with the same intensive chemotherapy (VDC/IE-type) plus local control.

items.q: The risk of dedifferentiation in a well-differentiated liposarcoma / atypical lipomatous tumour is:
o: Higher in the retroperitoneum than in the limbs
Higher in subcutaneous limb tumours than in the retroperitoneum
items.e: Dedifferentiation is much more frequent in retroperitoneal well-differentiated liposarcoma than in limb ALT, which is one reason the limb lesion has a different name and is managed by marginal excision.

items.q: A dedifferentiated liposarcoma differs from a pleomorphic liposarcoma in that dedifferentiated liposarcoma:
o: Is a low-grade tumour that does not metastasise
items.e: Dedifferentiated liposarcoma arises from well-differentiated liposarcoma and keeps MDM2/CDK4 amplification; pleomorphic liposarcoma is a high-grade tumour with pleomorphic lipoblasts and no MDM2 amplification.

items.q: Which immunohistochemical panel best supports a diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma?
o: Cytokeratin, EMA and loss of INI1
Desmin, smooth muscle actin and h-caldesmon
items.e: Smooth-muscle markers (desmin, SMA, h-caldesmon) support leiomyosarcoma; vascular markers indicate angiosarcoma, melanocytic markers clear cell sarcoma, and INI1 loss epithelioid sarcoma.

items.q: Primary cutaneous angiosarcoma not related to radiation or lymphoedema most commonly arises in the:
o: Scalp and face of elderly people
Sole of the foot of young adults
items.e: Cutaneous angiosarcoma classically presents as bruise-like, multifocal lesions of the scalp and face in the elderly; it is aggressive with a poor prognosis.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a soft, compressible intramuscular calf mass that swells on dependency. Radiographs show several small round calcifications with lucent centres. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Phleboliths (calcified thrombi with lucent centres) and positional change in size are characteristic of venous malformation/haemangioma; synovial sarcoma calcification is amorphous and stippled.

items.q: After gadolinium on MRI, a ganglion cyst typically shows:
items.e: A true cyst enhances only at its wall; internal or nodular enhancement in a 'cyst' suggests a myxoid tumour, which must be biopsied rather than aspirated or excised.

items.q: After treatment of a high-grade extremity soft-tissue sarcoma, surveillance for recurrence is usually performed:
o: Every 3-4 months for the first 2-3 years, then less often to 5 years and annually thereafter
items.e: Most recurrences occur in the first 2-3 years, so clinical review with imaging of the primary site and chest is done 3-4 monthly early, then 6-monthly to 5 years and annually later.

items.q: Sarculator, used in extremity soft-tissue sarcoma, is a:
o: Nomogram predicting overall survival and distant metastasis from age, size, grade and histology
items.e: Sarculator is a validated nomogram that estimates individual 10-year overall survival and distant metastasis risk, helping select patients for perioperative chemotherapy.

items.q: In active surveillance of an asymptomatic extra-abdominal desmoid tumour, the first follow-up MRI is usually performed at:
o: Only if the patient becomes symptomatic
1-2 months after diagnosis, then every 3-6 months
items.e: The global consensus advises early MRI at 1-2 months to establish behaviour, then 3-6-monthly imaging; treatment starts only with persistent progression or symptoms.

items.q: A high-grade thigh sarcoma abuts but does not encase the sciatic nerve on MRI. The usual surgical management of the nerve is:
o: Epineurial dissection, sacrificing the epineurium as the margin
Routine resection of the sciatic nerve
Leaving tumour on the nerve and giving radiotherapy alone
items.e: When a nerve is abutted rather than encased, the epineurium acts as a barrier and can be removed with the tumour, preserving the nerve fascicles.

items.q: A high-grade thigh sarcoma encases the superficial femoral artery but spares the nerves and bone. The usual approach is:
o: En bloc resection including the artery with vascular graft reconstruction
Intralesional excision leaving tumour on the vessel
items.e: Encased major vessels can be resected en bloc and reconstructed with a synthetic or vein graft, preserving a functional limb; amputation is reserved for unreconstructable involvement.

items.q: Which criteria are commonly used to diagnose a radiation-associated sarcoma?
o: Arising within a previous radiation field after a latency of several years, with histology different from the original tumour
Any sarcoma in a patient who has had a CT scan
A sarcoma diagnosed within 6 months of radiotherapy
items.e: Cahan's criteria (modified) require origin within the field, a latent period (usually over 3-5 years) and histological proof differing from the primary; angiosarcoma and UPS are typical.

items.q: For an adolescent with extremity rhabdomyosarcoma, assessment of regional lymph nodes is important because:
o: Rhabdomyosarcoma never spreads to lymph nodes
It replaces the need for chest CT
Nodal involvement is relatively common and changes radiotherapy and staging
It is required only for retroperitoneal tumours
items.e: Extremity (often alveolar) rhabdomyosarcoma frequently involves regional nodes, so nodal sampling or sentinel node biopsy is part of staging and determines nodal irradiation.

items.q: Synovial sarcoma usually requires longer follow-up than many other sarcomas because:
o: Metastases may appear late, even after 5-10 years
It converts to a benign tumour
items.e: Synovial sarcoma is known for late local and distant recurrence, so surveillance is often extended beyond 5 years.

items.q: An intramedullary nail with a full-length longitudinal slot (open section) differs from an otherwise identical closed tube mainly by having a much lower:
items.e: Opening the section of a tube drastically reduces its torsional rigidity while bending stiffness is less affected, which is why slotted nails twist more. The material's modulus is unchanged by geometry.

items.q: Corrosion that develops in the narrow, oxygen-poor gap between a screw head and the countersink of a plate is termed:
o: Pitting corrosion of an exposed free surface
items.e: In a confined crevice, oxygen depletion and acidification prevent repassivation of the oxide layer and corrosion accelerates. Galvanic corrosion needs two dissimilar metals.

items.q: Porous tantalum ('trabecular metal') used in revision acetabular components has which property?
o: About 10% porosity with a modulus similar to cobalt-chromium
A low coefficient of friction against bone, reducing initial stability
About 75-80% porosity with an elastic modulus close to cancellous bone
items.e: Porous tantalum is highly porous (about 75-80%), has a modulus near cancellous bone and a high friction coefficient that gives strong initial scratch-fit stability. It is ductile, not brittle.

items.q: For bone ingrowth into a porous-coated cementless implant, the generally accepted optimal pore size is approximately:
items.e: Pores of roughly 50-400 micrometres (optimal 100-400) allow bone ingrowth; very small pores admit only fibrous tissue and very large pores reduce strength and contact.

items.q: Bone ingrowth into a cementless femoral stem fails and a fibrous membrane forms when early interface micromotion exceeds approximately:
items.e: Micromotion below about 20-40 micrometres allows osseointegration, while motion above about 150 micrometres leads to fibrous fixation. Hence initial press-fit stability is essential.

items.q: A carbon-fibre-reinforced PEEK plate offers which particular advantage over titanium in fixation of pathological fractures?
o: Higher bending stiffness than stainless steel
Radiolucency allowing assessment of healing and tumour imaging with little artefact
Ability to be contoured repeatedly in theatre
Superior osseointegration on its untreated surface
items.e: CFR-PEEK is radiolucent and causes minimal MRI/CT artefact and radiotherapy scatter, which helps follow-up of metastatic disease. It cannot be bent intraoperatively and is not osteoconductive untreated.

items.q: Vacuum mixing (or centrifugation) of PMMA bone cement improves its fatigue life mainly by:
o: Increasing the molecular weight of the polymer
items.e: Air bubbles act as stress risers where fatigue cracks start; removing them by vacuum mixing or centrifugation increases fatigue strength. The exothermic reaction and monomer content are not materially altered.

items.q: A retrieved tibial polyethylene insert that had been gamma-sterilised in air and stored for years shows a white band 1-2 mm below the articular surface with delamination. The cause is:
o: Excessive cross-linking by ethylene oxide sterilisation
Oxidation of free radicals generated by irradiation in air
items.e: Gamma irradiation in air leaves free radicals that oxidise over time, with a subsurface peak about 1-2 mm deep; this embrittles the polyethylene and causes fatigue delamination in knees. Ethylene oxide does not generate free radicals.

items.q: In McKellop's classification of wear modes, wear between the back of a modular polyethylene liner and its metal shell is:
items.e: Mode 1 is wear between the intended bearing surfaces, mode 2 a bearing surface against a non-intended surface, mode 3 third-body wear, and mode 4 two non-bearing secondary surfaces rubbing, such as backside or taper wear.

items.q: With conventional polyethylene in total hip arthroplasty, periprosthetic osteolysis becomes uncommon when the linear wear rate is below approximately:
items.e: Clinical series show that osteolysis is rare when linear wear is under about 0.1 mm per year and increases sharply above it, related to particle load.

items.q: Audible squeaking after a ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty is most associated with:
o: Use of a cemented femoral stem
Edge loading from acetabular component malposition
A 28 mm femoral head with ideal cup position
items.e: Squeaking is linked to edge loading, stripe wear and loss of fluid-film lubrication, commonly with excessive cup inclination or anteversion; it does not occur with polyethylene bearings.

items.q: Molybdenum is added to 316L stainless steel implants chiefly to:
o: Reduce the elastic modulus towards bone
items.e: Molybdenum strengthens the passive layer against chloride-induced pitting. Chromium forms the passive oxide film and nickel stabilises the austenitic (non-magnetic) structure.

items.q: A plate's bending stiffness depends on its thickness. If plate thickness is doubled, bending stiffness increases approximately:
items.e: Area moment of inertia of a rectangular section is bh^3/12, so stiffness rises with the cube of thickness (2^3 = 8). Fourth-power dependence applies to the radius of a circular rod.

items.q: A plate breaks by fatigue 4 months after fixation of a comminuted femoral fracture. The failure is most likely to start at:
o: A screw hole filled with a locked screw far from the fracture
An empty screw hole adjacent to the fracture gap
The plate end in contact with intact bone
The midpoint of a hole-free plate segment far from the fracture
items.e: An unfilled hole over or next to an unsupported fracture concentrates stress and strain under cyclic bending, so fatigue cracks initiate there. Filled holes far from the fracture see little strain.

items.q: The metal most commonly responsible for cutaneous hypersensitivity, and therefore asked about before implanting stainless steel or cobalt-chrome devices, is:
items.e: Nickel is the commonest metal sensitiser (about 10-15% of the population), followed by cobalt and chromium. Titanium and tantalum rarely cause hypersensitivity.

items.q: The Thacher Rickets Severity Score, used to grade and monitor nutritional rickets, is calculated from radiographs of the:
items.e: The Thacher score grades metaphyseal changes of the distal radius and ulna and of the femur and tibia at the knee on a 10-point scale.

items.q: The earliest radiological change of rickets at a growing physis is:
o: Loss of the sharp zone of provisional calcification with physeal widening
Looser zones in the femoral neck
items.e: Failure of mineralisation first blurs the zone of provisional calcification and widens the physis, followed by cupping, splaying and fraying of the metaphysis. Looser zones are a feature of osteomalacia.

items.q: After starting vitamin D treatment for nutritional rickets, the first radiological evidence of healing, usually within 2-4 weeks, is:
o: A dense line of provisional calcification appearing in the metaphysis
items.e: Mineralisation resumes at the zone of provisional calcification, seen as a white line separated from the metaphysis, which then fills in. Deformity correction takes months to years.

items.q: A 3-year-old with rickets-like bone changes and early loss of deciduous teeth with intact roots has a very low serum alkaline phosphatase. The diagnosis and treatment are:
o: Hypophosphatasia (ALPL mutation); enzyme replacement with asfotase alfa
Nutritional rickets; stoss vitamin D therapy
items.e: Low ALP with raised pyridoxal-5-phosphate characterises hypophosphatasia, due to ALPL mutations; asfotase alfa is the targeted therapy. All other rickets types have high ALP. Vitamin D is avoided because of hypercalcaemia risk.

items.q: A child has rickets with low serum calcium, high PTH, normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D and low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The defect and treatment are:
o: Vitamin D receptor mutation; very high-dose calcitriol
CYP27B1 (1-alpha-hydroxylase) deficiency; physiological doses of calcitriol
items.e: VDDR type 1A results from CYP27B1 mutation, so 25-OHD is converted poorly to calcitriol; it responds to replacement doses of calcitriol or alfacalcidol. VDR defects (type 2) have high calcitriol.

items.q: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours causing tumour-induced osteomalacia frequently carry which recurrent gene fusion?
items.e: About half of phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours carry FN1-FGFR1 (or FN1-FGF1) fusion driving FGF23 overproduction. The other fusions define Ewing sarcoma, synovial sarcoma and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

items.q: A woman given repeated intravenous iron infusions for menorrhagia develops bone pain and pseudofractures with severe hypophosphataemia. The responsible preparation and mechanism are:
o: Iron sucrose, causing renal tubular acidosis
Ferric carboxymaltose, raising intact FGF23 by reducing its cleavage
Ferric carboxymaltose, causing vitamin D malabsorption
items.e: Ferric carboxymaltose inhibits FGF23 cleavage, raising intact FGF23 and causing renal phosphate wasting and low calcitriol; repeated doses can produce osteomalacia. Other iron forms carry a much lower risk.

items.q: Autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets is caused by mutations in which gene?
o: FGF23, making the hormone resistant to proteolytic cleavage
items.e: ADHR results from FGF23 mutations at its cleavage site so the active hormone persists; it can present variably and worsen with iron deficiency. PHEX causes XLH, DMP1 autosomal recessive HR and SLC34A3 HHRH.

items.q: Which set of biochemical findings is typical of vitamin D-deficiency osteomalacia in an adult?
o: High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH, high urinary calcium
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, low ALP, low PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, normal ALP, suppressed PTH
Low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH, low urinary calcium
items.e: Vitamin D deficiency reduces calcium absorption, triggering secondary hyperparathyroidism with phosphaturia, raised ALP and low urine calcium. High calcium with high PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: Iliac crest biopsy after double tetracycline labelling confirms osteomalacia by showing:
o: Thickened osteoid seams with a prolonged mineralisation lag time
Reduced osteoid with increased bone formation rate
Woven bone with mosaic cement lines
Increased osteoclast numbers with tunnelling resorption alone
items.e: Osteomalacia is defined histologically by increased osteoid seam width and a mineralisation lag time over about 100 days, measured from the gap between tetracycline labels. Mosaic cement lines are typical of Paget disease.

items.q: Long-term phenytoin or phenobarbital therapy predisposes to osteomalacia mainly by:
o: Inducing hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that accelerate vitamin D catabolism
Causing renal phosphate wasting through FGF23
items.e: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants increase hepatic breakdown of vitamin D to inactive metabolites, lowering 25-OHD, and may impair intestinal calcium absorption.

items.q: Metabolic bone disease (rickets) of prematurity is mainly due to:
o: Inadequate phosphate and calcium supply after missing third-trimester mineral accretion
items.e: About 80% of fetal mineral accretion happens in the third trimester, and preterm infants on unfortified breast milk receive too little phosphate and calcium. Phosphate supplementation and fortified feeds prevent it.

items.q: Children in parts of Nigeria and Bangladesh develop rickets despite near-normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. The main cause and treatment are:
o: Inherited FGF23 excess; treat with burosumab
Fluoride toxicity; treat with defluoridated water
Very low dietary calcium; treat with calcium supplementation
items.e: Thacher's studies showed that dietary calcium deficiency causes rickets in these children and that calcium alone (with or without vitamin D) heals it better than vitamin D alone.

items.q: In the AO Spine Thoracolumbar Injury Score (TL AOSIS), a type C (translational) injury is given how many morphology points?
items.e: TL AOSIS gives A0-A3 0-3 points, A4 and B1 5, B2 6, B3 7 and C 8; with neurology and modifiers added, a score over 5 favours surgery. A C injury alone therefore indicates operative stabilisation.

items.q: In short-segment posterior pedicle screw fixation of a thoracolumbar burst fracture, adding screws into the fractured vertebra (intermediate screws) mainly:
o: Allows the fractured vertebral body to be removed
Improves kyphosis correction and reduces loss of correction
Removes the need to protect the PLC
Increases the risk of neurological injury by indirect reduction
items.e: Intermediate screws create a six-screw construct with greater stiffness, better sagittal correction and less late kyphosis, comparable to longer constructs.

items.q: A patient with a T4 fracture-dislocation and complete cord injury has a blood pressure of 75/40 mmHg and a heart rate of 50 per minute with warm peripheries. The most likely cause is:
o: Haemorrhagic shock from a pelvic fracture
Spinal shock with loss of reflexes
Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic outflow
items.e: Injuries above about T6 interrupt sympathetic outflow, causing hypotension with bradycardia and warm vasodilated skin; haemorrhage causes tachycardia and cold peripheries. Spinal shock refers to loss of reflexes, not haemodynamics.

items.q: A thoracic spine fracture associated with a displaced sternal fracture should be regarded as highly unstable because:
o: The sternum carries the anterior longitudinal ligament
Sternal fractures always cause aortic injury
The sternum is part of Denis's middle column
The sternum and rib cage act as a 'fourth column' supporting the thoracic spine
items.e: The intact rib cage and sternum markedly stiffen the thoracic spine; combined sternal and thoracic fractures lose this support and tend to progress to kyphosis and translation.

items.q: Compared with thoracolumbar junction burst fractures, burst fractures of L4 differ mainly in that:
o: Neurological deficit is less common and preservation of lumbar lordosis is the key treatment goal
They usually cause complete cord injury
They are best treated with long kyphosis-inducing posterior constructs
items.e: The capacious lumbar canal contains cauda equina roots, so deficits are uncommon; non-operative care or fixation must preserve segmental lordosis, since flat-back alignment causes pain.

items.q: In neurologically intact patients with thoracolumbar burst fractures treated without decompression, follow-up CT of the retropulsed fragment typically shows:
o: Remodelling with progressive reduction of canal compromise over months
Late neurological deterioration in most patients
items.e: Spontaneous canal remodelling occurs, with canal compromise often reduced by about half over the first year, so initial canal encroachment alone does not mandate decompression.

items.q: After a fall from height, CT confirms an L1 burst fracture. Imaging of the entire spine is advised because non-contiguous spinal fractures occur in approximately:
items.e: About one in ten patients with a spinal fracture has another non-contiguous level injured, so the whole spine is imaged, usually with CT in major trauma.

items.q: In Denis's classification of burst fractures, the most common subtype involves:
items.e: Denis type B, a burst of the superior endplate, is the commonest, typically at the thoracolumbar junction; type A involves both endplates, C the inferior endplate, D rotation and E lateral flexion.

items.q: Holdsworth's two-column classification of thoracolumbar fractures was important because it first emphasised that spinal stability depends largely on:
o: The integrity of the posterior ligamentous complex
items.e: Holdsworth described anterior and posterior columns and stressed that rupture of the posterior ligament complex makes an injury unstable; Denis later added the middle column.

items.q: A stable L5 burst fracture is managed in a brace. To control motion at the L5-S1 level, a standard TLSO should be:
o: Shortened to end at the iliac crests
Extended with a thigh cuff (hip spica extension) on one side
Replaced by a soft lumbar corset
items.e: A TLSO alone poorly controls the lumbosacral junction and may even increase L5-S1 motion; adding a thigh extension immobilises the low lumbar segments.

items.q: In an acute thoracolumbar cord injury, the end of spinal shock is usually marked by return of the:
items.e: Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex signals the end of spinal shock; only then can a complete injury be confirmed by absent sacral sparing. Hyperreflexia appears weeks later.

items.q: Percutaneous K-wires inserted through the radial styloid for distal radius fixation most commonly injure the:
o: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
Dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
items.e: The superficial radial nerve branches cross the styloid region, so a small incision, blunt dissection and a drill sleeve are advised. Painful neuroma is a recognised complication.

items.q: In clinical research, union of a scaphoid fracture on CT is commonly defined as bridging trabeculae across at least:
items.e: Partial union of at least about 50% bridging on CT is generally accepted as sufficient for mobilisation and return to activity; radiographs are unreliable for this.

items.q: A pisiform fracture is best demonstrated on which plain radiograph?
o: Supinated (reverse) oblique view of about 30 degrees
items.e: The 30-degree supinated oblique (and the carpal tunnel view) profiles the pisiform and pisotriquetral joint; on standard PA and pronated views it overlaps the triquetrum.

items.q: A boxer has a coronal fracture of the hamate body. The injury most commonly associated with it is:
o: Dorsal fracture-dislocation of the fourth and fifth carpometacarpal joints
items.e: Axial load through the ring and little metacarpals shears the dorsal hamate body and dislocates the CMC joints dorsally; CT defines the fragment for open reduction and fixation.

items.q: An isolated fracture through the capitate waist carries a notable risk of avascular necrosis of the capitate head because:
o: The capitate has no articular surfaces
The capitate head is supplied only by the dorsal radiocarpal ligament
The fracture always injures the deep palmar arch
The proximal pole is supplied by retrograde intraosseous vessels entering distally
items.e: Like the scaphoid, the capitate head is largely intra-articular and supplied retrogradely from distal vessels, so a waist fracture can devascularise it.

items.q: Gelberman's study of the intraosseous blood supply of the lunate found that the most common pattern is:
o: Single dorsal vessel with no palmar contribution
items.e: About 60% of lunates have a Y pattern, about 30% an I pattern and about 10% an X pattern; the I pattern, with a single vessel, is thought to predispose to Kienböck disease.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman sustains a distal radius fracture from a fall from standing height. Apart from treating the fracture, the most important additional step is:
o: Routine MRI of the contralateral wrist
Assessment for osteoporosis with fracture risk (FRAX) and DXA
items.e: A low-energy distal radius fracture is often the first fragility fracture and predicts later hip and vertebral fractures, so a fracture liaison service should assess bone density and treat.

items.q: The Youm carpal height ratio (carpal height divided by the length of the third metacarpal) is normally about:
items.e: The normal carpal height ratio is 0.54 plus or minus 0.03; it falls with carpal collapse such as Kienböck disease, SLAC and SNAC wrist.

items.q: A 'die-punch' fracture of the distal radius refers to:
o: A radial styloid fracture from a direct blow
A volar rim fracture with carpal subluxation
A depressed fragment of the lunate facet driven proximally by the lunate
items.e: Axial load through the lunate impacts the lunate fossa, depressing a fragment that often cannot be reduced by traction and needs elevation and subchondral support.

items.q: In Thomas's classification of Smith fractures, the type II pattern is:
o: An intra-articular oblique fracture with volar carpal displacement, i.e. a volar Barton fracture
items.e: Thomas type I is extra-articular transverse, type II intra-articular oblique (volar Barton) and type III extra-articular oblique; all are volarly displaced and usually need a volar buttress plate.

items.q: Among the medial soft-tissue stabilisers of the patella, which become relatively more important in deeper knee flexion (beyond about 60-90 degrees) as the MPFL contribution falls?
o: Medial patellotibial and medial patellomeniscal ligaments
items.e: The MPFL dominates near extension, whereas the medial patellotibial and patellomeniscal ligaments contribute more in deeper flexion and to patellar tilt and rotation; trochlear bone geometry is the main restraint once engaged.

items.q: In articular cartilage, the aggrecan core protein is attached to the hyaluronic acid backbone of the proteoglycan aggregate by:
items.e: Link protein stabilises the binding of aggrecan to hyaluronan; lubricin is a surface lubricant.

items.q: The compressive stiffness of articular cartilage derives mainly from:
o: The tensile strength of type II collagen fibrils
Negatively charged glycosaminoglycans that attract water and create swelling pressure
items.e: Fixed negative charges on chondroitin and keratan sulphate draw in water; type II collagen mainly provides tensile strength.

items.q: The superficial (tangential) zone of articular cartilage is characterised by:
o: Collagen parallel to the surface, the highest water content and the lowest proteoglycan content
Collagen perpendicular to the surface and the highest proteoglycan content
Round cells arranged obliquely with intermediate composition
Type X collagen and hypertrophic chondrocytes
items.e: Parallel fibres in the superficial zone resist shear; the deep zone has perpendicular fibres and the most proteoglycan.

items.q: Which zone of articular cartilage has the highest proteoglycan concentration and the lowest water content?
items.e: The deep zone, with collagen perpendicular to the surface and columns of chondrocytes, has the most proteoglycan and resists compression.

items.q: Boundary lubrication of articular cartilage is provided mainly by:
items.e: Lubricin, secreted by superficial chondrocytes and synoviocytes, coats the surface for boundary lubrication; fluid-film and weeping mechanisms act under load.

items.q: Normal ageing of articular cartilage, as distinct from osteoarthritis, is associated with:
items.e: With ageing, water falls, keratan sulphate rises and cartilage stiffens; increased water, falling keratan sulphate and enzyme up-regulation are features of OA.

items.q: Which change distinguishes early osteoarthritic cartilage from normally aged cartilage?
items.e: Disruption of the collagen network in early OA allows swelling and a rise in water, whereas aged cartilage loses water and stiffens.

items.q: In osteoarthritic cartilage, compared with normal cartilage:
o: Both keratan and chondroitin sulphate increase
Keratan sulphate increases and chondroitin sulphate decreases
Keratan sulphate decreases and chondroitin sulphate (chondroitin-4) increases
items.e: OA reverses the ageing pattern: keratan sulphate falls and chondroitin-4-sulphate rises, with overall proteoglycan loss.

items.q: The principal collagenase responsible for degrading type II collagen in osteoarthritic cartilage is:
items.e: MMP-13 cleaves type II collagen; ADAMTS-4 and -5 are aggrecanases, and TIMPs inhibit metalloproteinases.

items.q: Clusters of proliferating chondrocytes ('cloning') on histology are characteristic of:
o: Chondrocyte death after intra-articular local anaesthetic
items.e: Early OA chondrocytes proliferate into clusters in an attempt at repair; ageing reduces chondrocyte number.

items.q: A partial-thickness chondral injury that does not cross the tidemark:
o: Heals with hyaline cartilage within weeks
Does not heal, because marrow-derived cells cannot reach it
Heals with fibrocartilage from the marrow
items.e: Without penetration of the subchondral plate there is no access to marrow cells, and local chondrocytes cannot repair the defect.

items.q: In the Outerbridge classification, grade II chondral damage is:
o: Fissuring or fragmentation in an area under about 1.5 cm in diameter
Erosion down to exposed subchondral bone
items.e: Grade I is softening, II fissuring under 1.5 cm, III over 1.5 cm and IV exposed subchondral bone.

items.q: In Steadman's microfracture technique, the awl holes are made:
o: About 1 cm apart and 1 cm deep
About 1 mm apart and 10 mm deep
About 6-8 mm apart and 1 mm deep
About 3-4 mm apart and 2-4 mm deep
items.e: Holes 3-4 mm apart preserve the subchondral plate between them while releasing marrow elements.

items.q: During microfracture, the calcified cartilage layer at the base of the defect is removed with a curette mainly to:
o: Improve attachment and fill of the marrow-derived repair tissue
Reduce bleeding from the subchondral bone
items.e: Removing the calcified layer while preserving the subchondral plate improves adherence of the clot and repair tissue.

items.q: The clinical results of microfracture for focal chondral defects tend to:
items.e: The fibrocartilaginous repair tissue is mechanically inferior to hyaline cartilage, and results decline after a few years.

items.q: Microfracture gives its best results in:
o: Patients over 60 with large patellar lesions
Patients under about 40 with small (under 2-4 cm²) femoral condyle lesions
Large osteochondral defects with bone loss
items.e: Young patients with small condylar defects do best; large, patellofemoral or osteochondral defects need other techniques.

items.q: Previous microfracture may compromise a later autologous chondrocyte implantation because of:
o: Intralesional osteophytes and subchondral bone overgrowth
items.e: Subchondral overgrowth after marrow stimulation is associated with higher failure rates of subsequent ACI.

items.q: During osteochondral autograft transfer, a plug left 1 mm proud of the surrounding cartilage results in:
o: High contact pressures on the plug and the opposing surface
items.e: Proud plugs concentrate load and degenerate; recessed plugs become covered with fibrocartilage, so flush placement is the goal.

items.q: The commonest donor-site problem after harvesting osteochondral autograft plugs from the knee is:
items.e: Plugs are taken from the trochlear margin or notch, and donor-site patellofemoral symptoms limit the size of defect OATS can treat.

items.q: In autologous chondrocyte implantation, cultured chondrocytes are usually implanted about:
o: On the same day as the biopsy
items.e: ACI is a two-stage procedure: arthroscopic harvest, laboratory expansion over several weeks, then implantation.

items.q: Third-generation (matrix-associated) autologous chondrocyte implantation differs from earlier generations because:
o: A periosteal patch is sutured over injected cells
It is a single-stage marrow stimulation technique
The cells are seeded onto a collagen matrix before implantation
items.e: First-generation ACI used periosteum, second generation a collagen membrane over injected cells, and MACI pre-seeds cells onto a matrix.

items.q: The SUMMIT trial (Saris et al., 2014) compared MACI with microfracture for symptomatic knee chondral defects of 3 cm² or more. At 2 years:
o: MACI gave significantly better KOOS pain and function
There was no difference between the groups
MACI had a higher failure rate
items.e: SUMMIT showed MACI was superior to microfracture for larger defects on the co-primary KOOS pain and function outcomes.

items.q: The long-term (15-year) follow-up of Knutsen's randomised trial of autologous chondrocyte implantation versus microfracture showed:
o: No significant difference in clinical outcome or failure rate
items.e: Knutsen found no significant differences at 2, 5 and 15 years between ACI and microfracture for medium-sized defects.

items.q: Fresh osteochondral allografts are:
o: Stored refrigerated (about 4°C) and implanted within about 28 days of harvest
items.e: Refrigerated storage preserves chondrocyte viability, which falls with time; freezing and irradiation kill chondrocytes.

items.q: HLA or blood-group matching is not required for fresh osteochondral allografts mainly because:
o: Chondrocytes do not express HLA antigens
The graft is irradiated before use
The bony portion is removed before implantation
Chondrocytes are shielded within the avascular matrix from host immune surveillance
items.e: The dense matrix isolates chondrocytes from the immune system; the bone portion is incorporated by creeping substitution.

items.q: Subchondral drilling of exposed bone as a marrow-stimulation technique was introduced by:
items.e: Pridie described drilling; Steadman microfracture, Johnson abrasion arthroplasty and Hangody mosaicplasty.

items.q: A 12-year-old with open physes has a stable osteochondritis dissecans lesion of the medial femoral condyle on MRI. First-line treatment is:
items.e: Juvenile stable lesions heal non-operatively in about 50-75% of cases; surgery is for failure or instability.

items.q: A stable juvenile OCD lesion of the knee has not healed after 3-6 months of activity restriction. The next step is usually:
items.e: Drilling creates vascular channels to stimulate healing of a stable lesion with intact cartilage.

items.q: In adults, the MRI sign most indicative of an unstable osteochondritis dissecans fragment of the knee is:
o: Low T1 signal within the fragment
Mild marrow oedema around the lesion
A high T2 signal line (fluid-like) at the interface behind the fragment
items.e: A fluid-intensity rim behind the fragment, cysts beneath it, an articular fracture line or a fluid-filled defect indicate instability.

items.q: A 17-year-old has an unstable but intact, salvageable OCD fragment of the medial femoral condyle with good subchondral bone. The preferred treatment is:
o: Fixation of the fragment with compression screws or bioabsorbable implants
Excision of the fragment and observation
items.e: Salvageable unstable fragments are fixed; unsalvageable fragments are excised and the defect restored.

items.q: Ramp lesions at the posteromedial meniscocapsular junction are best seen at arthroscopy by:
o: Viewing from the anterolateral portal with the knee in extension
Passing the arthroscope through the notch between the PCL and medial femoral condyle into the posteromedial compartment
Using a 30-degree scope from the anteromedial portal only
items.e: The transnotch (Gillquist) view, often with a posteromedial portal, reveals ramp lesions hidden from standard anterior views.

items.q: During reaming of the ACL tibial tunnel, which meniscal attachment is at risk because its fibres blend with the ACL tibial footprint?
o: Posterior root of the medial meniscus
Posterior root of the lateral meniscus
Anterior root of the lateral meniscus
Anterior root of the medial meniscus
items.e: The anterior horn of the lateral meniscus inserts immediately adjacent to, and partly under, the ACL footprint.

items.q: The median age at diagnosis of neuroblastoma is about:
items.e: Most neuroblastomas present under 5 years, median about 17-18 months, so it is the leading cause of bony metastases in young children.

items.q: Neuroblastoma arises from:
o: Neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain
Primitive mesenchymal stem cells of bone
items.e: Neuroblastoma is a neural crest tumour of the sympathetic nervous system, most often adrenal.

items.q: The commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood is:
items.e: Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour; brain tumours are the commonest solid tumours overall.

items.q: A toddler has a limp, rapid chaotic eye movements and jerky limb movements. The underlying tumour to search for is:
items.e: Opsoclonus-myoclonus is a paraneoplastic syndrome of neuroblastoma.

items.q: A 10-month-old infant has neuroblastoma with metastases limited to the skin, liver and a small fraction of the marrow. This stage:
o: Is stage M with a uniformly poor prognosis
Is stage L1 and curable by surgery alone
Requires amputation of the affected limb
Is stage MS (formerly 4S) and may regress spontaneously
items.e: Stage MS applies to children under 18 months with limited skin, liver and marrow spread, and many such tumours regress.

items.q: The functional imaging of choice for the primary tumour and skeletal or marrow metastases of neuroblastoma is:
items.e: MIBG is taken up by catecholamine-producing cells and is more specific than a bone scan for neuroblastoma.

items.q: Besides MYCN amplification, which feature carries an adverse prognosis in neuroblastoma?
items.e: 11q loss is adverse; hyperdiploidy, young age and favourable histology are good prognostic features.

items.q: A child treated with laminectomy and radiotherapy for a thoracic 'dumbbell' neuroblastoma extending through the neural foramen is at particular long-term risk of:
items.e: Post-laminectomy instability and radiation-induced asymmetric growth arrest cause spinal deformity, so follow-up of the spine is needed.

items.q: A child with neuroblastoma has ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on one side. The primary tumour most likely lies in the:
o: Cervical or upper thoracic sympathetic chain
items.e: Horner syndrome reflects involvement of the cervicothoracic sympathetic chain.

items.q: The commonest histological subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma is:
items.e: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is commonest, affects younger children and has a better prognosis than alveolar.

items.q: A 2-year-old girl has a grape-like mass protruding from the vagina. Biopsy shows small round cells with desmin and myogenin positivity. The diagnosis is:
items.e: The botryoid variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma forms grape-like masses beneath mucosal surfaces.

items.q: Besides t(2;13) PAX3-FOXO1, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma may carry:
items.e: PAX7-FOXO1 is the less common alveolar fusion; the others define Ewing sarcoma, synovial sarcoma and myxoid liposarcoma.

items.q: The standard chemotherapy backbone for rhabdomyosarcoma is:
items.e: VAC is the rhabdomyosarcoma backbone; MAP is for osteosarcoma, R-CHOP for lymphoma and VRd for myeloma.

items.q: In staging an extremity rhabdomyosarcoma, which step is recommended because of its propensity for nodal spread?
o: Regional lymph-node evaluation, such as sentinel node biopsy
items.e: Rhabdomyosarcoma, especially alveolar and extremity tumours, spreads to regional nodes, so nodal evaluation guides radiotherapy fields.

items.q: Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma typically affects:
items.e: Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma is a high-grade sarcoma of adults; embryonal affects young children and alveolar adolescents.

items.q: Giant cell tumour of bone accounts for roughly what proportion of all primary bone tumours in Western series?
items.e: GCT makes up about 5% of primary bone tumours and about 20% of benign bone tumours, with a higher relative frequency in Asian (including Indian and Chinese) populations.

items.q: Pulmonary metastases ('benign pulmonary implants') develop in about what proportion of patients with conventional giant cell tumour of bone?
items.e: Lung implants occur in about 2-5%, typically 2-4 years after diagnosis and often after local recurrence, especially from the distal radius; they are usually indolent.

items.q: After extended curettage of a giant cell tumour with high-speed burring, a local adjuvant and PMMA cement, the expected local recurrence rate is approximately:
items.e: Extending the margin with burr and adjuvant lowers recurrence from the historical 40-60% after simple curettage to about 10-20%.

items.q: On follow-up radiographs after curettage and cementation of a giant cell tumour, local recurrence typically appears as:
o: A progressive, expanding lucency at the cement-bone interface
A thin, stable sclerotic rim around the cement
Periosteal reaction distant from the cement
items.e: A thin, stable sclerotic rim (about 1-2 mm) is a normal reaction; an enlarging lucent zone at the cement-bone interface signals recurrence, one of the advantages of cement over graft.

items.q: When liquid nitrogen cryotherapy is used as an adjuvant after curettage of a giant cell tumour, the main specific complication is:
o: Postoperative fracture through devitalised bone, along with skin necrosis
items.e: Cryotherapy freezes bone to a depth of up to 1-2 cm, so fracture, wound/skin necrosis and nerve injury are its recognised complications; protective fixation and grafting reduce fracture risk.

items.q: Compared with extended intralesional curettage, en bloc resection of a giant cell tumour gives:
o: Lower local recurrence but worse function
items.e: Wide resection lowers recurrence to about 0-10% but sacrifices the joint, so it is reserved for unsalvageable joints, large soft-tissue masses, recurrent tumours and expendable bones.

items.q: According to Arata's criteria, a non-ossifying fibroma has a high risk of pathological fracture when it:
o: Involves 25% of the diameter and is 10 mm long
Involves more than 50% of the transverse diameter on both AP and lateral views and is longer than 33 mm
Lies in the distal femoral metaphysis
items.e: Arata found fractures occurred in NOFs occupying over 50% of the bone width on both views and longer than 33 mm; such lesions may warrant prophylactic curettage and grafting.

items.q: Non-ossifying fibromas are now known to carry activating mutations in which pathway?
items.e: Recent sequencing shows KRAS and FGFR1 mutations, activating the MAPK pathway, in NOF. GNAS is mutated in fibrous dysplasia, H3F3A in GCT and EXT genes in osteochondromas.

items.q: Fibrous cortical defects (small cortical NOFs) are found incidentally on radiographs in about what proportion of children?
items.e: Fibrous cortical defects are very common (about 30% of children), usually in the distal femoral or tibial metaphysis, and regress spontaneously, so they are 'don't touch' lesions.

items.q: In monostotic fibrous dysplasia, which site is most frequently involved?
items.e: Monostotic FD most commonly affects the ribs, followed by the proximal femur and craniofacial bones; spinal, distal radial and calcaneal involvement is uncommon.

items.q: Fibrous dysplasia is caused by:
o: A post-zygotic activating mutation of GNAS
A germline inactivating mutation of GNAS
items.e: FD results from a somatic mosaic activating GNAS (Gs-alpha, R201) mutation, so it is not inherited. Germline inactivating GNAS mutations cause Albright hereditary osteodystrophy; COL1A1 mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta.

items.q: Malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia is:
o: Under 1%, and more likely in McCune-Albright syndrome and after radiotherapy
Usually to chondrosarcoma in about half of cases
items.e: Sarcomatous change (mostly osteosarcoma or fibrosarcoma) is rare, under 1%; radiotherapy increases the risk and is avoided in FD.

items.q: In painful polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, intravenous bisphosphonates (pamidronate or zoledronate) are used mainly to:
o: Reduce bone pain, without reliably healing the lesions
items.e: Bisphosphonates reduce bone turnover and pain in FD, but the lesions do not heal and deformity is not prevented.

items.q: A 6-year-old has osteofibrous dysplasia of the anterior tibial cortex with mild anterior bowing and no pain. Usual management is:
o: Observation, with bracing if needed, delaying any surgery until after about age 15
Early wide resection with intercalary allograft
items.e: OFD is benign and often stabilises or regresses after puberty; early excision frequently recurs, so surgery is deferred until about skeletal maturity unless deformity or fracture demands it.

items.q: A 30-year-old has biopsy-proven adamantinoma of the tibial diaphysis. The treatment of choice is:
o: Wide en bloc resection with intercalary reconstruction (or amputation)
items.e: Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant tumour resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy; wide resection is needed because intralesional surgery recurs and late lung and nodal metastases occur.

items.q: A skull radiograph of a 7-year-old with Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows:
o: A punched-out lytic lesion with bevelled edges ('hole within a hole')
items.e: Uneven destruction of the inner and outer tables gives the bevelled-edge, 'hole within a hole' appearance, sometimes with a button sequestrum.

items.q: Radiographic healing of a treated unicameral bone cyst is commonly graded using the:
items.e: Neer and modified Cole/Capanna criteria classify cysts as healed, healed with residual radiolucency, persistent or recurrent; Campanacci grades GCT and Lodwick describes lesion margins.

items.q: Radiotherapy for aneurysmal bone cyst is avoided mainly because of:
o: Risk of radiation-induced sarcoma and growth disturbance in children
items.e: Radiotherapy does control ABC but carries risks of secondary sarcoma, physeal arrest and myelopathy in the spine, so it is a last resort.

items.q: USP6 gene rearrangement is shared by primary aneurysmal bone cyst and which other lesions?
items.e: USP6-rearranged 'transient neoplasia' includes primary ABC, nodular fasciitis, myositis ossificans and fibroma of tendon sheath; chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma give secondary ABC change without USP6.

items.q: Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome (multiple non-ossifying fibromas with café-au-lait spots) is now generally regarded as part of the spectrum of:
items.e: Most patients with Jaffe-Campanacci have NF1 mutations and other NF1 features, so it is considered a variant of NF1 rather than a separate entity.

items.q: Before elective surgery for fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome, which metabolic problem should be specifically sought and treated to reduce failure of fixation?
items.e: FD tissue secretes FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting and osteomalacia, which worsens fractures and fixation failure; phosphate and calcitriol are given, and other endocrinopathies corrected, before surgery.

items.q: A 14-year-old has a progressive shepherd's crook deformity from fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur. The preferred surgical treatment is:
o: Curettage and autologous cancellous grafting alone
Lateral plate and screws without osteotomy
Valgus osteotomy with a load-sharing cephalomedullary nail
items.e: Valgus osteotomy corrects the varus deformity and intramedullary cephalomedullary fixation protects the whole femur over the long term; autograft alone is replaced by dysplastic bone and plates tend to fail.

items.q: En bloc resection of an aneurysmal bone cyst is best reserved for:
o: Spinal ABCs with no neurological deficit
Small lesions in the proximal humerus
Lesions in expendable bones such as the fibula or rib, or recurrent aggressive lesions
items.e: Most ABCs are treated with curettage plus adjuvant or sclerotherapy; resection is chosen where function is not lost (fibula, rib) or after multiple recurrences.

items.q: A biopsy-confirmed solitary eosinophilic granuloma of the femoral diaphysis in a 10-year-old, without impending fracture, is usually treated by:
