o: Observation or intralesional methylprednisolone; biopsy itself often triggers healing
items.e: Solitary bone LCH is self-limiting; observation, curettage or intralesional steroid suffice. Systemic chemotherapy (vinblastine and prednisolone) is for multisystem or high-risk disease.

items.q: In fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur, the thick sclerotic margin surrounding the lesion is called the:
items.e: The 'rind' is a thick sclerotic border typical of FD; the fallen fragment sign belongs to UBC, the crescent sign to AVN, and Codman's triangle to aggressive periosteal reaction.

items.q: Histology of a non-ossifying fibroma typically shows:
o: Chinese-letter woven bone trabeculae without osteoblastic rimming
Epithelial nests in a fibro-osseous stroma
Spindle fibroblasts in a storiform pattern with scattered giant cells, haemosiderin and foamy macrophages
Sheets of small round blue cells
items.e: NOF shows storiform fibroblasts, osteoclast-like giant cells, haemosiderin and foam cells; Chinese-letter trabeculae are FD, epithelial nests adamantinoma and small round cells Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: After any of the common treatments for a unicameral bone cyst (steroid, marrow injection or curettage), persistence or recurrence occurs in about:
items.e: No method heals every UBC; recurrence or persistence after injection or curettage is about 20-40%, higher in active cysts in young children.

items.q: In a 52-year-old, a peroneus brevis split tear is found at surgery to involve more than 50% of the usable tendon, with the peroneus longus intact. Usual treatment:
o: Excision of the diseased segment and tenodesis of the brevis to the longus
items.e: When over 50% of the brevis is non-viable, the diseased segment is excised and the stumps tenodesed to peroneus longus; tears under 50% are debrided and tubularised.

items.q: Non-operative treatment of an acute first-time peroneal tendon dislocation in a below-knee cast succeeds in about what proportion of patients?
items.e: Cast immobilisation succeeds in roughly half, so early SPR repair is often preferred in athletes; chronic recurrent dislocation needs SPR repair with groove deepening.

items.q: An os peroneum within the peroneus longus tendon at the cuboid is present in about what proportion of feet?
items.e: The os peroneum is present in about 20% of feet (ossified in a smaller proportion); fracture, diastasis or proximal migration indicates painful os peroneum syndrome.

items.q: Which systemic condition is a recognised risk factor for spontaneous Achilles tendon rupture?
o: Chronic renal failure with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Asthma treated only with an inhaled salbutamol reliever
items.e: Renal failure, hyperparathyroidism, inflammatory arthritis, gout, systemic or local corticosteroids and fluoroquinolones all predispose to Achilles rupture.

items.q: In open repair of an acute Achilles tendon rupture, which layer is closed separately over the repaired tendon to reduce adhesions and help healing?
items.e: Careful closure of the paratenon over the repair restores the gliding layer and blood supply and protects the wound; a full-thickness skin flap is also preserved.

items.q: In the meta-analysis by Ochen et al. (BMJ 2019), when accelerated functional rehabilitation was used, operative repair of acute Achilles rupture reduced the absolute re-rupture risk compared with non-operative treatment by about:
o: 0%, with non-operative treatment having fewer re-ruptures
items.e: Ochen found a risk difference of about 2.8% in favour of surgery, which must be weighed against higher complication rates (wound problems, sural nerve injury).

items.q: The commonest cancer of childhood is:
items.e: ALL is the commonest childhood cancer, and musculoskeletal pain is a frequent presenting feature.

items.q: A 5-year-old has migratory joint pain, night pain out of proportion to the joint swelling, mild anaemia and a low platelet count. Steroids are being considered for juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The next step is:
o: Perform knee arthroscopy and synovial biopsy
Examine a peripheral blood smear (and marrow if indicated) before any steroid
items.e: Leukaemia often mimics JIA; steroids can mask it and compromise treatment, so a smear must be checked first.

items.q: A 6-year-old with back pain has diffuse osteopenia and several vertebral compression fractures without trauma. The diagnosis that must be excluded first is:
items.e: Atraumatic vertebral collapse with osteopenia in a child is a classic presentation of leukaemia.

items.q: Why should part of a biopsy from a suspected small round cell tumour of bone be sent fresh rather than all in formalin?
o: To allow molecular tests (FISH, RT-PCR, sequencing), flow cytometry and culture
To reduce the risk of tract contamination
items.e: These tumours look alike on H&E, so fresh tissue is needed for molecular diagnosis, lymphoma flow cytometry and culture to exclude infection.

items.q: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positivity in Ewing sarcoma cells reflects their content of:
items.e: Ewing cells contain glycogen in their scant cytoplasm, which stains with PAS and is diastase-sensitive.

items.q: A small round cell tumour is strongly CD99 positive but also TdT and CD79a positive. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: CD99 is not specific for Ewing sarcoma; TdT and B-cell markers identify precursor B-lymphoblastic lymphoma.

items.q: The peripheral blood film in multiple myeloma typically shows:
items.e: The paraprotein reduces red cell repulsion, causing stacking (rouleaux) and a very high ESR.

items.q: In a patient with myeloma bone disease and significant renal impairment, the bone-targeted agent usually preferred is:
items.e: Denosumab is not renally cleared, whereas bisphosphonates need dose reduction or avoidance in renal impairment.

items.q: Under the IMWG 2014 criteria, multiple myeloma requires clonal bone marrow plasma cells of at least ___ (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event.
items.e: Clonal marrow plasma cells of 10% or more, or a plasmacytoma, plus a CRAB feature or SLiM biomarker define myeloma.

items.q: Among the IMWG 'SLiM' biomarkers, the MRI criterion is more than one focal lesion measuring at least:
items.e: More than one focal marrow lesion of 5 mm or more on MRI counts as a myeloma-defining event even without bone destruction.

items.q: The commonest site of primary lymphoma of bone is the:
items.e: The femur is most often affected, followed by the pelvis, humerus, tibia and spine.

items.q: A 66-year-old with myeloma has a painful lytic lesion in the femoral diaphysis at high risk of fracture. The preferred surgical stabilisation is:
o: A short plate spanning only the lesion
A locked intramedullary nail protecting the whole femur
items.e: Myeloma is multifocal, so a long intramedullary device protects the entire bone; such fractures have high healing rates.

items.q: A 66-year-old smoker has a lytic vertebral lesion. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with nuclear moulding that are TTF-1 and synaptophysin positive. The diagnosis is:
items.e: In older adults, metastatic small cell carcinoma joins lymphoma and myeloma in the round cell differential; TTF-1 and neuroendocrine markers identify it.

items.q: The commonest cause of end-stage ankle arthritis is:
items.e: About 70-80% of end-stage ankle arthritis is post-traumatic, typically after rotational ankle fractures or chronic instability.

items.q: Which intervention has the best evidence for reducing recurrent lateral ankle sprains in athletes with a previous sprain?
items.e: Balance and neuromuscular training substantially reduce recurrence after a sprain; prolonged casting delays recovery.

items.q: Osteochondral lesions of the talar dome that are deep, cup-shaped and often without a clear history of trauma are typically located:
items.e: Medial lesions are deeper and often atraumatic, whereas lateral lesions are shallow, wafer-shaped and usually traumatic.

items.q: Compared with juvenile osteochondritis dissecans of the knee, adult OCD (closed physes) usually:
o: Heals with activity restriction in most cases
Requires surgical treatment because non-operative healing is unlikely
items.e: Juvenile lesions heal non-operatively in about 50-75%, but adult lesions rarely do and usually need fixation or restoration.

items.q: Type VI collagen in articular cartilage is concentrated in the:
items.e: Type VI collagen forms the pericellular matrix (chondron) linking chondrocytes to the surrounding matrix; type X is found in the calcified zone.

items.q: The subscapularis muscle is innervated by the:
o: Suprascapular nerve from the upper trunk
Axillary nerve from the posterior cord
Upper and lower subscapular nerves from the posterior cord
Thoracodorsal nerve from the posterior cord
items.e: Subscapularis receives the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5-6, posterior cord); supraspinatus and infraspinatus are supplied by the suprascapular nerve and teres minor by the axillary nerve.

items.q: At the suprascapular notch, the relationship of the suprascapular nerve and artery to the superior transverse scapular ligament is:
o: The artery passes below the ligament and the nerve passes above it
The nerve passes below the ligament and the artery passes above it
items.e: The nerve runs through the notch beneath the ligament while the artery usually runs over it ('the army goes over the bridge, the navy under'); ossification or thickening of the ligament can compress the nerve.

items.q: In the drop arm test, the examiner passively abducts the patient's arm to 90 degrees and asks the patient to lower it slowly. A sudden drop of the arm suggests:
items.e: Inability to control lowering from abduction indicates loss of the supraspinatus contribution, typically a large full-thickness tear; frozen shoulder restricts passive motion rather than causing a drop.

items.q: In the belly-press test, a patient with a subscapularis tear typically substitutes for internal rotation by:
o: Abducting the shoulder and externally rotating the arm
Flexing the wrist and extending the shoulder so that the elbow drops behind the trunk
Extending the wrist with the elbow held well forward
Shrugging the shoulder while keeping the wrist straight
items.e: Without subscapularis, the patient presses using wrist flexion and shoulder extension (the 'Napoleon sign'); a normal subscapularis keeps the wrist straight and the elbow in front of the trunk.

items.q: An unfused acromial ossification centre is regarded as an os acromiale if it persists beyond about what age?
items.e: The acromial ossification centres normally fuse by about 22-25 years; persistence beyond this defines an os acromiale, most commonly at the meso-acromion/meta-acromion junction.

items.q: In Neer's three stages of subacromial impingement, stage III is characterised by:
o: Rotator cuff tears and bony changes such as acromial spurs, usually after age 40
Reversible oedema and haemorrhage of the cuff in patients under 25
Fibrosis and tendinitis in patients aged 25-40
Calcium hydroxyapatite deposition in the supraspinatus
items.e: Neer described stage I (oedema and haemorrhage, under 25), stage II (fibrosis and tendinitis, 25-40) and stage III (tears and bone changes, over 40).

items.q: In the Hamada radiographic classification of massive rotator cuff tears, grade 3 is defined by:
o: An acromiohumeral interval of 6 mm or more
Acetabularisation of the acromion (concave undersurface) in addition to a narrowed acromiohumeral interval
Narrowing of the glenohumeral joint without acromial changes
items.e: Hamada grade 1 has AHI 6 mm or more, grade 2 AHI 5 mm or less, grade 3 adds acetabularisation, grade 4 glenohumeral narrowing and grade 5 humeral head collapse (cuff tear arthropathy).

items.q: Serial imaging studies after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair show that most re-tears occur:
o: At 2-3 years, once the patient returns to heavy work
After 5 years, as part of degenerative progression
Within the first 3-6 months after surgery
At random times with no particular pattern
items.e: Most repairs that fail do so early, before tendon-bone healing is mature (about 12-16 weeks); this is why rehabilitation protects the repair during the first months.

items.q: After single-row arthroscopic rotator cuff repair, the commonest re-tear pattern (Cho type 1) is:
o: Failure at the musculotendinous junction medial to the anchors
Pull-out of the anchors with a large greater tuberosity fracture
An interstitial split within an intact repair
Failure at the tendon-bone interface, leaving little or no tendon on the footprint
items.e: Type 1 failure at the footprint predominates after single-row repair, whereas type 2 failure medial to the medial row, with tendon left on the footprint, is more typical of double-row constructs.

items.q: Which pair of factors most consistently predicts re-tear after rotator cuff repair?
o: Increasing patient age and larger tear size
Use of an absorbable rather than metal anchor and a lateral portal
Repair performed arthroscopically rather than mini-open
items.e: Age (especially over 65) and tear size/retraction are the most consistent predictors, along with fatty infiltration; arthroscopic and mini-open repairs have similar outcomes.

items.q: In a typical rehabilitation protocol after repair of a medium full-thickness supraspinatus tear, resisted strengthening is usually started at about:
items.e: A sling with passive motion is used for about 4-6 weeks, active motion follows, and strengthening begins at about 12 weeks when early tendon-bone healing has occurred.

items.q: Before latissimus dorsi transfer for an irreparable posterosuperior cuff tear, which condition must be met?
items.e: The transfer works as a humeral head depressor and external rotator in concert with the deltoid, so deltoid deficiency (for example axillary nerve palsy) is a contraindication, as is subscapularis deficiency.

items.q: In lower trapezius transfer for an irreparable posterosuperior cuff tear, the muscle is extended to the greater tuberosity using:
o: A fascia lata strip left attached to the iliac crest
items.e: The lower trapezius tendon is too short to reach the tuberosity, so Elhassan's technique uses an Achilles allograft to bridge the gap; the spinal accessory nerve supplies the transferred muscle.

items.q: During pectoralis major transfer for an irreparable subscapularis tear, routing the tendon deep to the conjoint tendon places which nerve at particular risk?
items.e: The musculocutaneous nerve enters coracobrachialis a few centimetres below the coracoid, so passing the transfer under the conjoint tendon risks compression or traction; the route is chosen because it reproduces the subscapularis line of pull.

items.q: In superior capsular reconstruction for an irreparable supraspinatus tear, the graft is fixed:
o: Medially to the coracoid and laterally to the lesser tuberosity
Medially to the superior glenoid and laterally to the greater tuberosity
Medially to the acromion and laterally to the greater tuberosity
Medially to the scapular spine and laterally to the deltoid tuberosity
items.e: The graft recreates the superior capsule from the superior glenoid rim to the greater tuberosity, resisting superior translation of the humeral head; it is usually supplemented by side-to-side sutures to infraspinatus posteriorly.

items.q: A 72-year-old with cuff tear arthropathy has pseudoparalysis and a positive hornblower sign with gross fatty infiltration of teres minor. To improve function after reverse shoulder arthroplasty, the surgeon should consider:
o: Superior capsular reconstruction instead of arthroplasty
Combining the reverse arthroplasty with a latissimus dorsi (with or without teres major) transfer
Pectoralis major transfer to the lesser tuberosity
items.e: A reverse prosthesis restores elevation but not active external rotation when infraspinatus and teres minor are absent; adding a latissimus dorsi transfer (modified L'Episcopo) restores external rotation.

items.q: In Uhthoff's description of calcific tendinitis as a cell-mediated process, the precalcific stage is characterised by:
o: Vascular invasion with macrophage phagocytosis of calcium
Formation of a dense, chalk-like deposit
items.e: Fibrocartilaginous metaplasia precedes calcification; the calcific stage has formative, resting and resorptive phases (resorption is the painful phase), followed by postcalcific reconstitution of the tendon.

items.q: Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff differs from dystrophic calcification in a degenerate tendon because it:
o: Is an active, cell-mediated process that often resorbs spontaneously, followed by tendon healing
Occurs mainly in tendons with full-thickness tears
Is most common in men over 70
Is caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition
items.e: Calcific tendinitis typically affects women aged 30-50, involves hydroxyapatite formed by metaplastic cells and tends to resolve; dystrophic calcification occurs in degenerate tissue at the insertion and does not resorb.

items.q: Which statement about the Gärtner radiographic types of calcific tendinitis and spontaneous resorption is correct?
o: Cloudy, translucent type III deposits rarely resorb spontaneously
Dense, sharply outlined type I deposits rarely resorb spontaneously
Type II deposits virtually always disappear within 6 weeks
The Gärtner type bears no relation to the likelihood of resorption
items.e: Dense, well-defined type I deposits are in the formative or resting phase and rarely resorb on their own, so they are more likely to need barbotage or excision; cloudy type III deposits are usually resorbing.

items.q: Histologically, the capsular tissue in adhesive capsulitis shows proliferation of which cell type, resembling Dupuytren disease?
items.e: Fibroblasts and contractile myofibroblasts lay down type III collagen in the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament; the process is fibroproliferative rather than inflammatory, which explains its association with Dupuytren disease.

items.q: The UK FROST trial (Rangan et al., Lancet 2020) compared arthroscopic capsular release, manipulation under anaesthesia and early structured physiotherapy with steroid injection for frozen shoulder. It concluded that:
o: Arthroscopic capsular release gave clinically important superior results at 1 year
Physiotherapy with steroid injection was clearly superior to both surgical options
Manipulation under anaesthesia caused humeral fractures in about 10%
None was clinically superior, and manipulation under anaesthesia was the most cost-effective
items.e: All three groups improved substantially with no clinically important difference between them; capsular release had more serious adverse events and higher cost, making manipulation the most cost-effective procedure.

items.q: Regarding the natural history of idiopathic adhesive capsulitis:
o: It usually passes through freezing, frozen and thawing phases over about 1-3 years, though some patients keep mild residual stiffness
It almost always resolves completely within 6 weeks
It progresses inexorably to glenohumeral arthritis
It typically recurs in the same shoulder within 2 years
items.e: Most patients recover substantially over 1-3 years, but a proportion have persistent mild restriction; recurrence in the same shoulder is rare, although the other shoulder may later be affected.

items.q: At arthroscopy, a bucket-handle tear of the superior labrum is found with an intact, firmly attached biceps anchor. In Snyder's classification this is type III, and it is usually treated by:
o: Repair of the biceps anchor to the glenoid with suture anchors
Excision (debridement) of the unstable bucket-handle fragment
items.e: In type III the biceps anchor is stable, so removing the displaced labral fragment suffices; type II (anchor detached) and type IV (tear extending into the biceps) may need repair or tenodesis.

items.q: A 45-year-old manual worker has a symptomatic type II SLAP lesion that has failed rehabilitation. The procedure most often preferred at his age is:
items.e: SLAP repair in patients over about 35-40 has higher rates of stiffness and failure, so biceps tenodesis is generally preferred; repair is reserved for young overhead athletes.

items.q: Subcoracoid impingement, associated with anterior shoulder pain and subscapularis tears, is suggested on axial MRI when the coracohumeral distance is less than about:
items.e: The normal coracohumeral interval is roughly 8-11 mm; a distance under about 6 mm suggests subcoracoid narrowing that can abrade the subscapularis and biceps pulley.

items.q: During arthroscopic repair of a retracted subscapularis tear, the 'comma sign' (Lo and Burkhart) refers to:
o: An arc of tissue formed by the torn medial biceps sling (superior glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments) that marks the superolateral corner of the retracted subscapularis
A comma-shaped labral tear extending into the biceps root
A curved calcific deposit in the subscapularis footprint
The appearance of the long head of biceps dislocated over the lesser tuberosity
items.e: The comma tissue stays attached to the upper border of the retracted subscapularis and is a reliable landmark for finding and mobilising the tendon back to the lesser tuberosity.

items.q: Codman's 'rent' test for a full-thickness rotator cuff tear is performed by:
o: Resisting abduction in the scapular plane with the thumb down
Palpating through the deltoid just anterior to the acromion while the arm is extended and rotated, feeling for a defect at the greater tuberosity
Passively abducting the arm to 90 degrees and asking the patient to lower it slowly
Measuring the acromiohumeral interval on a true AP radiograph
items.e: With the arm extended, the greater tuberosity rotates out from under the acromion so that a sulcus (rent) and prominent tuberosity can be palpated through the deltoid; it is a simple and fairly accurate bedside test.

items.q: An isolated traumatic tear of the subscapularis in a young adult is most typically caused by:
o: A direct blow to the superior shoulder
Repetitive overhead throwing with the arm in abduction-external rotation
Forced external rotation or hyperextension of the adducted arm
A fall onto the point of the elbow with the arm flexed
items.e: Sudden forced external rotation or extension with the arm at the side loads the subscapularis eccentrically; repetitive throwing produces internal (posterosuperior) impingement rather than subscapularis tears.

items.q: For an elderly, low-demand patient with a massive irreparable rotator cuff tear and preserved deltoid, a structured non-operative programme focuses on:
o: Immobilisation in a sling for 3 months
Isolated strengthening of the torn supraspinatus
Passive stretching only, avoiding active elevation
Progressive anterior deltoid strengthening, starting supine and moving to upright
items.e: The anterior deltoid programme retrains the deltoid and remaining cuff to elevate the arm, starting supine where gravity is minimised; many patients regain useful overhead function.

items.q: Goutallier's CT-based grading of rotator cuff fatty infiltration was adapted for MRI by:
items.e: Fuchs and colleagues showed that Goutallier's five grades could be applied on sagittal oblique MRI; Thomazeau described the occupation ratio, Patte the retraction stages and Hamada the cuff arthropathy grades.

items.q: Thomazeau's occupation ratio on sagittal oblique MRI measures:
o: The acromiohumeral distance divided by the humeral head diameter
The cross-sectional area of the supraspinatus muscle divided by that of the supraspinatus fossa
The width of the greater tuberosity footprint covered by tendon
The ratio of glenoid width to humeral head width
items.e: A ratio near 1 is normal and falling ratios indicate supraspinatus atrophy; together with fatty infiltration this predicts reparability and outcome.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a symptomatic PASTA lesion involving more than 50% of the supraspinatus thickness. Besides completing the tear and repairing it, the other accepted arthroscopic option is:
o: Transtendon (in situ) repair of the articular-sided tear to the footprint
items.e: High-grade (Ellman grade 3) partial tears are repaired; the transtendon technique reattaches the torn articular fibres while preserving the intact bursal layer, whereas debridement alone suits tears under 50%.

items.q: Nyffeler's acromion index describes the lateral extension of the acromion relative to the humeral head. A high acromion index is associated with:
items.e: A laterally extended acromion increases the upward shear vector of the deltoid, which is linked to degenerative cuff tears; this concept was later developed into the critical shoulder angle.

items.q: Burkhart's partial repair of a massive rotator cuff tear, without closing the supraspinatus defect, aims mainly to:
o: Restore a balanced transverse force couple by repairing the infraspinatus posteriorly and the subscapularis anteriorly
Fully cover the humeral head with tendon
Increase the acromiohumeral interval by acromioplasty
Prevent the need for postoperative rehabilitation
items.e: If the anterior and posterior cuff are balanced, a stable fulcrum allows elevation despite a residual superior defect, which is why partial repair can relieve pain and improve function.

items.q: Burkhart's 'deadman' principle for suture anchor placement during rotator cuff repair recommends inserting anchors at an angle of about:
o: 90 degrees to the line of pull of the tendon
45 degrees or less to the line of pull of the tendon
120 degrees to the line of pull of the tendon
135-150 degrees to the line of pull of the tendon
items.e: An anchor angled at 45 degrees or less to the tendon's line of pull was proposed to increase resistance to pull-out and reduce suture tension; later studies have questioned whether the angle matters greatly in good bone.

items.q: The ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion because:
o: The deltoid ligament is slack in dorsiflexion
The talar dome is wider anteriorly and wedges into the mortise
The posterior malleolus blocks talar rotation only in dorsiflexion
The fibula moves distally in dorsiflexion
items.e: The trochlea of the talus is broader anteriorly, so in dorsiflexion it fills the mortise tightly; in plantarflexion the narrower posterior part allows play, which is why sprains occur in plantarflexion.

items.q: On an AP or mortise radiograph after ankle fracture fixation, an unbroken curve between the subchondral line of the lateral talar process and the recess at the tip of the fibula (the dime sign) indicates:
items.e: Disruption of the dime sign suggests a shortened fibula; along with the talocrural angle it is used to confirm restoration of fibular length.

items.q: In the Lauge-Hansen pronation-external rotation mechanism, stage I injury involves:
o: The medial malleolus or deltoid ligament
items.e: In pronation the medial side is under tension, so the medial malleolus or deltoid fails first (stage I), followed by the AITFL, the high fibular fracture and finally the PITFL or posterior malleolus.

items.q: The Broström-Gould procedure for chronic lateral ankle instability consists of:
o: Anatomical repair of the ATFL (and CFL) reinforced with the inferior extensor retinaculum
Rerouting the whole peroneus brevis through the fibula and talus
Free hamstring graft tenodesis through the calcaneus only
Subtalar arthrodesis with lateral ligament excision
items.e: The Gould modification augments the anatomical Broström ligament repair by advancing the inferior extensor retinaculum to the fibula, also limiting subtalar inversion.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a symptomatic anterolateral osteochondral lesion of the talus measuring 1 cm2 after failed non-operative treatment. The usual first-line operation is:
o: Osteochondral allograft transplantation of the whole dome
items.e: Lesions under about 1.5 cm2 (or under 15 mm in diameter) respond well to arthroscopic debridement and marrow stimulation; larger or cystic lesions need osteochondral grafting or other cartilage procedures.

items.q: The anterior drawer test of the ankle, performed in slight plantarflexion, mainly assesses the:
items.e: Anterior translation of the talus tests the ATFL, which is taut in plantarflexion; the talar tilt test assesses mainly the CFL.

items.q: The tibiofibular clear space used to assess syndesmotic integrity is measured on the AP view at what level?
o: About 1 cm above the tibial plafond
At the tip of the medial malleolus
At the level of the talar dome
items.e: The clear space between the medial border of the fibula and the lateral border of the posterior tibial tubercle is measured 1 cm above the plafond; over about 5-6 mm suggests syndesmotic injury.

items.q: When reducing the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis with a pointed reduction clamp, malreduction is best avoided by placing the clamp:
o: As anterior as possible on the fibula
Along the anatomical transmalleolar axis, with direct inspection of the incisura
Perpendicular to the foot axis with maximum compression
Across the talus to hold the ankle in plantarflexion
items.e: An off-axis clamp can malrotate or over-compress the fibula in the incisura; aligning it with the transmalleolar axis and checking the incisura directly (or with intraoperative CT) reduces malreduction.

items.q: After an inversion injury with the foot plantarflexed, a patient thought to have an ankle sprain has persistent tenderness about 2 cm anterior and 1 cm distal to the ATFL. Which missed fracture is most likely?
o: Anterior process of the calcaneus (bifurcate ligament avulsion)
items.e: Inversion with plantarflexion can avulse the anterior calcaneal process via the bifurcate ligament; it is easily missed on ankle views and seen on oblique foot radiographs or CT.

items.q: Traumatic dislocation of the peroneal tendons over the lateral malleolus results from injury to which structure?
items.e: Forced dorsiflexion with peroneal contraction tears or strips the superior peroneal retinaculum from the fibula, allowing the tendons to sublux anteriorly; a small fibular rim avulsion (fleck sign) may be seen.

items.q: The Bartonicek-Rammelt classification of posterior malleolar fractures is based mainly on the relationship of the fragment to the:
items.e: This CT-based classification considers whether the fragment involves the fibular notch (incisura), which is important for syndesmotic stability and the choice of approach.

items.q: During a medial approach to fix a medial malleolar fracture, which nerve and accompanying vein are at risk in the subcutaneous tissue?
o: Sural nerve and small saphenous vein
Saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein
Tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels
items.e: The saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein run anterior to the medial malleolus and must be protected during medial incisions.

items.q: Approximately what proportion of total body calcium is stored in the skeleton?
items.e: About 99% of body calcium and about 85% of phosphate are stored in bone, which acts as the reservoir for serum calcium homeostasis.

items.q: In direct (primary) bone healing under absolute stability, the fracture is crossed by:
o: Endochondral ossification of a cartilaginous callus
Cutting cones of osteoclasts followed by osteoblasts forming new osteons
items.e: Under compression with minimal gap, osteoclastic cutting cones tunnel across the fracture and osteoblasts behind them lay down new Haversian systems, without visible callus.

items.q: According to Frost's mechanostat theory, when bone strain stays below the minimum effective strain threshold, the result is:
o: Disuse-mode remodelling with net bone loss
items.e: Frost proposed strain windows: below the threshold remodelling removes bone (disuse), within the adapted window mass is maintained, and above it modelling adds bone; excessive strain causes microdamage.

items.q: Which serum measurement best reflects vitamin D status?
items.e: 25(OH)D has a long half-life and reflects stores; 1,25(OH)2D is tightly regulated by PTH and can be normal or even raised in deficiency.

items.q: FGF23 acts on the kidney together with which co-receptor to cause phosphaturia?
items.e: FGF23 requires the co-receptor alpha-Klotho to signal through FGF receptors, reducing proximal phosphate reabsorption and inhibiting 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

items.q: Burosumab is used to treat X-linked hypophosphataemia and tumour-induced osteomalacia because it:
items.e: Burosumab is a monoclonal antibody against FGF23, restoring renal phosphate reabsorption and 1,25(OH)2D production in FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia.

items.q: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis is characterised by:
o: Pure increase in osteoclast activity with preserved osteoblast function
Cortical loss alone, sparing trabecular bone
Reduced osteoblast formation and lifespan with early trabecular (vertebral) bone loss
No increase in fracture risk during the first year of therapy
items.e: Glucocorticoids suppress osteoblastogenesis and increase osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis, so trabecular bone is lost rapidly in the first months and vertebral fracture risk rises early.

items.q: Bone morphogenetic proteins signal intracellularly mainly through which proteins?
items.e: BMPs bind type I and II serine-threonine kinase receptors that phosphorylate SMAD 1/5/8; beta-catenin belongs to the Wnt pathway and NF-kappa-B to RANK signalling.

items.q: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is caused by an activating mutation of which gene?
items.e: A recurrent activating mutation in ACVR1, a BMP type I receptor, causes progressive heterotopic ossification of muscle and connective tissue, typically with malformed great toes.

items.q: In 2008 the FDA issued a warning about off-label use of rhBMP-2 in which procedure because of life-threatening complications?
o: Open tibial fracture nailing, because of infection
Anterior cervical spine fusion, because of soft-tissue swelling and airway compromise
Posterolateral lumbar fusion, because of nonunion
Scaphoid nonunion grafting, because of avascular necrosis
items.e: rhBMP-2 in the anterior cervical spine caused marked prevertebral swelling with dysphagia and airway compromise, prompting the FDA public health notification.

items.q: The immunogenicity of fresh bone allograft is mainly due to:
o: Marrow and other cellular elements expressing MHC class I and II antigens
items.e: Cellular components, especially marrow, carry the MHC antigens; freezing, freeze-drying and removing marrow reduce immunogenicity.

items.q: Vosoritide is used in children with achondroplasia because it:
o: Inhibits sclerostin to increase bone formation
Is a C-type natriuretic peptide analogue that counteracts FGFR3 signalling
items.e: Activating FGFR3 mutations suppress proliferative-zone chondrocytes; the CNP analogue vosoritide inhibits the downstream MAPK pathway and increases growth velocity.

items.q: Empirical antibiotics for suspected osteoarticular infection in a 3-week-old neonate should cover S. aureus plus:
o: Group B streptococcus and Gram-negative enteric bacilli, for example by adding cefotaxime
items.e: Neonatal infections are caused by S. aureus, group B streptococcus and Gram-negative enteric organisms, so an anti-staphylococcal agent is combined with a third-generation cephalosporin (or an aminoglycoside).
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: For open drainage of a septic hip in a child, the anterior approach is generally preferred to a posterior approach because it:
o: Gives better access to the acetabular roof
Avoids damage to the medial circumflex femoral vessels that supply the femoral head
Avoids the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve completely
items.e: The main femoral head blood supply runs posteriorly from the medial circumflex femoral artery; a posterior capsulotomy risks AVN and posterior instability.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 5-year-old has a limp and bone pain that wakes him at night, mild fever, and pallor. Blood count shows anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and radiographs show transverse metaphyseal lucent bands. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Leukaemia commonly mimics osteoarticular infection; cytopenias, night pain and metaphyseal lucent (leukaemic) lines should prompt a blood film and bone marrow examination.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In childhood acute osteomyelitis, pus escapes from the metaphyseal medulla to the subperiosteal space mainly through:
o: The growth plate's zone of Ranvier
Haversian and Volkmann canals of the cortex
items.e: Rising intramedullary pressure forces pus through the Haversian and Volkmann canal system to lift the loose periosteum, forming a subperiosteal abscess.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: Which feature favours juvenile idiopathic arthritis over septic arthritis in a child with a swollen knee?
o: Several weeks of morning stiffness with a relatively well child
High fever and refusal to bear weight
CRP rising to 150 mg/L within 24 hours
items.e: JIA is more chronic, with morning stiffness, often other joints, and a well child; acute toxicity and very high synovial counts favour sepsis. Children with JIA need uveitis screening.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 7-year-old with femoral osteomyelitis has persistent fever and pain after 72 hours of appropriate IV antibiotics. The next step is:
o: MRI to look for an abscess, followed by surgical drainage if present
Add a second antistaphylococcal beta-lactam and wait another week
items.e: Failure to respond within 48-72 hours suggests an undrained abscess, sequestrum, adjacent septic arthritis or resistant organism; MRI guides surgical drainage.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In a stable child with suspected acute osteomyelitis, the optimal timing of antibiotics relative to sampling is:
o: Start antibiotics first and sample only if there is no response after 1 week
Withhold antibiotics until MRI is performed, even if this takes several days
Take blood cultures and, if it does not cause undue delay, aspirate bone or joint before starting antibiotics
Sample only after 2 weeks off antibiotics, as in chronic osteomyelitis
items.e: Cultures before antibiotics improve organism identification, but in children empirical treatment must not be delayed significantly, especially in the septic child.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 6-year-old has an irritable hip diagnosed as transient synovitis after septic arthritis has been reasonably excluded. Appropriate management is:
o: Rest, NSAIDs and review, with a return visit if symptoms worsen or persist
items.e: Transient synovitis is self-limiting over 1-2 weeks; NSAIDs and rest with safety-netting are appropriate, and persistent symptoms prompt re-evaluation for sepsis or Perthes disease.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In experimental septic arthritis, the earliest change in articular cartilage is:
items.e: Neutrophil and bacterial enzymes deplete proteoglycan within hours, followed by collagen degradation over days, which is why delayed drainage leads to permanent damage.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 3-year-old with clinical discitis has normal lumbar radiographs on day 3 of symptoms. Radiographic narrowing of the disc space usually becomes visible after about:
items.e: Disc-space narrowing and endplate irregularity lag behind symptoms by about 2-3 weeks; MRI shows changes much earlier.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 6-year-old develops severe pain, fever and a swollen knee during recovery from chickenpox. The organism of particular concern is:
items.e: Varicella skin lesions are a portal for invasive group A streptococcal infection, including septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and necrotising fasciitis.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 2-week-old with septic arthritis of the hip has a radiograph showing lateral displacement of the proximal femoral metaphysis. This most likely represents:
o: A physeal fracture from birth trauma
Pathological subluxation of the hip caused by a tense effusion
items.e: A large purulent effusion in a neonate can push the unossified femoral head out of the acetabulum, causing pathological subluxation or dislocation; urgent drainage is required.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: A 20-month-old refuses to walk but examination cannot localise the problem and radiographs are normal. To localise a possible osteoarticular infection, which investigation is particularly useful?
items.e: When the site is unclear or multifocal disease is suspected, a bone scan (or whole-body MRI where available) localises the lesion; focused MRI then defines it.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: In a child with suspected septic arthritis, which synovial fluid finding most strongly supports the diagnosis?
o: WBC above 50,000/mm3 with more than 75% neutrophils
Glucose equal to serum glucose with WBC 500/mm3
items.e: High cell counts with neutrophil predominance indicate bacterial infection, although counts may be lower in early infection and Kingella.
items.sub: bone and joint infection in children

items.q: During the second stage of the Masquelet technique for an infected tibial defect, which graft harvesting device provides a large volume of autologous cancellous bone from the femoral canal?
items.e: RIA harvests a large volume of osteogenic cancellous bone and marrow from the femoral canal, useful to fill the induced membrane when iliac crest graft is insufficient.

items.q: During bone transport for an infected tibial defect, the docking site commonly causes problems because:
o: The docking site always becomes reinfected
Bone transport cannot be performed through a scarred bed
The bone ends are often sclerotic and covered with fibrous tissue, so union may need freshening and grafting
items.e: Docking site nonunion is common; ends are often sclerotic with interposed soft tissue, and many surgeons freshen the ends and graft when the segment arrives.

items.q: Histological examination of bone in chronic osteomyelitis typically shows:
o: Lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibrosis and necrotic bone with empty lacunae
Sheets of neutrophils only with viable osteocytes
items.e: Chronic infection shows a mononuclear infiltrate, fibrosis and dead bone with empty osteocyte lacunae; granulomas suggest TB or fungal infection and biopsy also excludes malignancy.

items.q: Deep samples from a suspected bone infection are culture-negative, but the patient has received antibiotics. Which molecular test can help identify the organism?
items.e: 16S rRNA PCR amplifies conserved bacterial DNA and can identify organisms in culture-negative samples, especially after antibiotic exposure.

items.q: The mortality of adult native-joint bacterial septic arthritis is approximately:
o: 10%, higher with polyarticular disease and rheumatoid arthritis
items.e: Septic arthritis carries a mortality of about 10% overall, increasing substantially with polyarticular infection, rheumatoid arthritis and old age.

items.q: In adult septic arthritis, blood cultures are positive in approximately:
o: A third to a half of patients
items.e: Blood cultures should always be taken because they identify the organism in roughly a third to a half of cases, sometimes when synovial culture is negative.

items.q: A 70-year-old with delayed treatment of septic arthritis of the hip later develops collapse of the femoral head. The most likely mechanism is:
o: Avascular necrosis from raised intracapsular pressure plus enzymatic cartilage destruction
items.e: Tense effusion compromises retinacular blood flow within the capsule, causing AVN in addition to chondrolysis; delay in drainage predicts poor outcome.

items.q: In an elderly patient too unwell for anaesthesia, septic arthritis of an accessible joint such as the knee can be managed by:
o: Repeated closed needle aspiration to dryness with antibiotics
items.e: Repeated aspiration is an accepted option in selected patients and accessible joints, with outcomes comparable to surgical drainage in some series; failure to improve requires surgical lavage.

items.q: Salter's experimental work on septic arthritis in rabbits showed that, compared with immobilisation, continuous passive motion:
o: Spread the infection to adjacent bone
items.e: Salter showed that CPM improved cartilage nutrition and clearance of harmful enzymes, protecting cartilage in septic arthritis.

items.q: On MRI, acute osteomyelitis typically shows marrow signal that is:
o: High on T1 and low on T2
Low on both T1 and T2
Normal on T1 with signal void on T2
Low on T1 and high on T2/STIR
items.e: Inflammatory oedema replaces fatty marrow, lowering T1 signal and increasing T2/STIR signal; a normal MRI essentially excludes osteomyelitis.

items.q: Which property of antibiotic-loaded PMMA beads explains why they are usually removed or exchanged?
o: They are non-absorbable and elute most antibiotic in the first days, then act as a foreign body
They dissolve within 48 hours causing hypercalcaemia
They release antibiotic at a constant rate for 5 years
They conduct bone ingrowth like autograft
items.e: Most elution from PMMA occurs early; once depleted, the beads can become a surface for biofilm, so they are removed or exchanged at a planned second stage.

items.q: The earliest clinical clue that distinguishes necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis is often:
o: Pain out of proportion to the visible skin changes
items.e: Deep fascial infection causes severe pain before skin signs develop; bullae, skin necrosis, crepitus and anaesthesia are later features.

items.q: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis underlying a chronic ulcer is typically:
o: Polymicrobial, including S. aureus, streptococci, Gram-negatives and anaerobes
items.e: Chronic diabetic foot infections are usually polymicrobial, so bone biopsy guides targeted therapy rather than empirical treatment based on superficial swabs.

items.q: A 4-year-old with limb pain and a limp is suspected of having juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Which laboratory finding should instead raise suspicion of acute leukaemia?
o: Raised serum LDH and uric acid
items.e: High cell turnover in leukaemia raises LDH and uric acid; these, with cytopenias or blasts, are red flags before treating as JIA.

items.q: A 30-year-old with chronic lateral ankle instability has a fixed hindfoot varus that does not correct on the Coleman block test. At the time of ligament reconstruction, the hindfoot is best addressed with:
items.e: Uncorrected hindfoot varus overloads the lateral ligaments and causes repair failure; a lateralising calcaneal osteotomy shifts the weight-bearing axis.

items.q: On axial CT of a trimalleolar ankle fracture, the posterior malleolar injury consists of one or more small shell-like flakes along the posterior tibial rim. In the Haraguchi classification this is:
items.e: Haraguchi type I is a posterolateral oblique wedge (commonest), type II extends transversely into the medial malleolus, and type III comprises small shell-shaped rim fragments; there is no type IV.

items.q: A displaced medial malleolar fracture with a small, osteoporotic distal fragment too small for two lag screws is best fixed with:
o: A single 6.5 mm fully threaded screw
An antiglide plate on the fibula only
items.e: Tension-band wiring converts the pull of the deltoid into compression and suits small or osteoporotic fragments where two partially threaded screws would not hold.

items.q: With ageing, long-bone diaphyses partly preserve their bending strength despite cortical thinning because:
o: Periosteal apposition increases the external diameter while the endosteum resorbs
Trabecular bone in the canal thickens
items.e: Endosteal resorption is accompanied by periosteal apposition, moving bone away from the neutral axis and increasing the area moment of inertia, partly compensating for thinner cortices.

items.q: Peak bone mass, a major determinant of later osteoporotic fracture risk, is normally reached at about which age?
o: Immediately after skeletal maturity at 16 years in both sexes, with no later gain
items.e: Bone mass accrues rapidly through adolescence and peaks in the third decade, mostly determined by genetics but also by exercise, calcium intake and sex hormones; bone is lost slowly thereafter.

items.q: Ten years after an untreated, displaced lateral condyle fracture of the humerus, a 16-year-old has a valgus elbow and numbness of the little finger. The underlying cause is:
o: Non-union of the lateral condyle with cubitus valgus and tardy ulnar nerve palsy
Malunion of a supracondylar fracture with cubitus varus
Medial epicondyle non-union with ulnar neuritis
Radial head dislocation compressing the ulnar nerve
items.e: Lateral condyle non-union allows progressive cubitus valgus, which stretches the ulnar nerve and causes a tardy ulnar palsy years later.

items.q: A lateral condyle fracture whose line enters the trochlear groove, so that the elbow is unstable and may subluxate, is classified as:
items.e: In Milch I the line is lateral to the trochlear groove (capitellotrochlear), leaving the elbow stable; in Milch II it extends into the trochlear groove and the elbow can sublux.

items.q: A 12-year-old's elbow dislocation is reduced, but the medial epicondyle fragment remains trapped within the joint. Management is:
o: Open reduction and fixation of the medial epicondyle
Valgus stress manipulation under sedation only, then mobilise
items.e: Incarceration of the medial epicondyle in the joint is the absolute indication for surgery; most other displaced medial epicondyle fractures can be managed non-operatively.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a radial neck fracture angulated 70 degrees that does not reduce with closed manipulation. The preferred technique before considering open reduction is:
o: Intramedullary reduction with a pre-bent elastic nail (Metaizeau technique) or percutaneous joystick reduction
items.e: Percutaneous joystick and Metaizeau intramedullary reduction achieve good alignment while avoiding the stiffness, AVN and synostosis associated with open reduction; radial head excision is not done in children.

items.q: The commonest complication after treatment of a displaced paediatric radial neck fracture is:
items.e: Loss of motion, especially pronation-supination, is the commonest sequela; AVN of the radial head and radioulnar synostosis occur more often after open reduction.

items.q: An 8-year-old has a radial head that has been dislocated for 9 months after a missed Monteggia injury, with pain and loss of motion. The usual reconstruction is:
o: Closed reduction and above-elbow cast in supination
Ulnar osteotomy with lengthening and angulation, open reduction of the radial head and annular ligament reconstruction
items.e: Chronic Monteggia lesions need correction of the ulnar deformity (osteotomy, often overcorrected and lengthened) to allow radial head reduction, usually with annular ligament reconstruction; radial head excision is avoided in growing children.

items.q: The paediatric equivalent of a Galeazzi fracture-dislocation is a radial shaft fracture with:
items.e: In children the distal ulnar physis fails before the DRUJ ligaments, so a Galeazzi-equivalent is a distal radial fracture with an ulnar physeal separation.

items.q: After cast treatment of a greenstick midshaft forearm fracture, a recognised problem is refracture in about:
o: 5% of cases, particularly if the greenstick is not completed or the cast is removed early
50% of cases if the child is under 5
items.e: Diaphyseal greenstick fractures heal slowly on the compression side; refracture occurs in about 5%, so the cast is kept on long enough and some surgeons complete the fracture.

items.q: A 12-year-old's Salter-Harris II distal radius fracture has lost some position at the 10-day review, with 15 degrees of dorsal angulation. Management is:
o: Accept and allow remodelling, as late re-manipulation risks physeal damage
items.e: Re-manipulating a physeal fracture after about 5-7 days risks growth arrest; with growth remaining, the distal radius remodels well in the sagittal plane.

items.q: The more successful reduction manoeuvre for a pulled elbow (radial head subluxation) in a 2-year-old is:
o: Valgus stress with the elbow extended
items.e: Hyperpronation has a higher first-attempt success rate and appears less painful than supination-flexion; both reduce the annular ligament subluxation.

items.q: In a 4-year-old with a proximal humeral physeal fracture, closed treatment is acceptable with angulation of up to about:
items.e: The proximal humeral physis provides about 80% of humeral growth, so young children remodel very large deformities; tolerance falls to about 30 degrees by age 12-13.

items.q: A 17-year-old rugby player has a posteriorly displaced medial clavicular physeal injury with dysphagia. Which is correct?
o: It is a sternoclavicular dislocation and should be ignored if asymptomatic
The medial clavicular physis has fused by 15, so this is a ligament injury
CT is needed, and closed or open reduction is done in theatre with a thoracic surgeon available
items.e: The medial clavicular physis is the last to close (about 23-25 years), so 'sternoclavicular dislocations' in young people are usually physeal injuries; posterior displacement can compress mediastinal structures.

items.q: A painless, non-tender swelling of the middle third of the right clavicle has been present since birth; radiographs show a gap between rounded bone ends and no callus. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Congenital pseudarthrosis is almost always right-sided, painless and without callus; a birth fracture is tender, shows abundant callus within weeks and heals.

items.q: A 6-year-old has neurological deficit after a road accident but normal radiographs and CT of the spine. The investigation of choice is:
items.e: Spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality (SCIWORA) reflects the elastic paediatric spine; MRI shows cord or ligamentous injury.

items.q: On a lateral cervical radiograph of a 5-year-old, C2 appears 3 mm anterior to C3 in flexion. The spinolaminar line of C2 lies within 1 mm of the posterior cervical (Swischuk) line. This most likely represents:
items.e: Pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3 (and C3 on C4) up to about 4 mm is normal in young children; a spinolaminar line deviating 2 mm or more from the Swischuk line suggests true injury.

items.q: To immobilise the cervical spine of a 3-year-old on a backboard in neutral, the board should have:
o: Elevation of the head end by 30 degrees
An occipital recess or a pad under the shoulders
A cervical collar only, without a board
items.e: The child's relatively large occiput flexes the neck on a flat board; an occipital cut-out or shoulder roll restores neutral alignment.

items.q: A child restrained by a lap belt alone has a flexion-distraction (Chance) fracture of L2. The associated injury that must be sought is:
items.e: Lap-belt flexion-distraction injuries are associated with intra-abdominal (especially bowel and mesenteric) injuries in up to half of cases; the 'seat-belt sign' is a clue.

items.q: An adolescent sprinter has an ischial tuberosity avulsion. Surgical fixation is usually considered when displacement exceeds about:
items.e: Most pelvic apophyseal avulsions heal with rest, but ischial tuberosity fragments displaced more than about 1.5-2 cm may give painful non-union or hamstring weakness and are often fixed.

items.q: A 64-year-old has an isolated avulsion fracture of the lesser trochanter after minimal trauma. The most important next step is:
o: Reassure, as this is a typical athletic avulsion
Investigate for a pathological fracture, such as metastasis
items.e: Lesser trochanter avulsion in an adult is pathological until proved otherwise; it is an important sign of metastatic disease of the proximal femur.

items.q: The most common type of paediatric hip fracture in the Delbet classification is:
items.e: Transcervical fractures make up about 45-50% of paediatric hip fractures and carry an AVN risk around 50%; type I is rarest with the highest AVN risk.

items.q: Besides urgent anatomical reduction and stable fixation, which step is commonly recommended in displaced paediatric femoral neck fractures to reduce the risk of AVN?
o: Avoiding any fixation across the physis even if unstable
Delaying surgery for 1 week until swelling settles
items.e: Intracapsular haematoma may tamponade the retinacular vessels; capsulotomy or aspiration is often combined with urgent reduction. Stability takes priority over sparing the physis.

items.q: A 3-month-old has a femoral shaft fracture after a well-documented accidental fall (abuse excluded). The usual treatment is:
o: Pavlik harness or a simple splint
items.e: Under about 6 months, femoral shaft fractures heal rapidly and remodel; a Pavlik harness or splint is enough.

items.q: Why is about 1-2 cm of overlap accepted when a 5-year-old's femoral shaft fracture is treated in a spica cast?
o: Femoral fractures in children aged about 2-10 overgrow by roughly 1-2 cm
The tibia compensates by slowing its growth
Shortening is fully corrected by remodelling at the hip
items.e: Hyperaemia after a femoral fracture stimulates the physes, producing overgrowth of about 1-2 cm in this age group; reduction to end-to-end may lead to overlengthening.

items.q: For flexible titanium elastic nailing of a paediatric femoral shaft fracture, each of the two nails should be about what proportion of the narrowest canal diameter?
items.e: Two balanced, pre-bent nails each about 40% of the canal (combined about 80%) provide three-point fixation; undersized nails risk malunion.

items.q: For a 13-year-old (60 kg) with a femoral shaft fracture treated with a rigid intramedullary nail, the entry point should be:
o: Piriformis fossa, for straight nail alignment
Intercondylar notch (retrograde) through the open physis
Lateral trochanteric, to avoid the piriformis fossa and the ascending branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery
items.e: Piriformis-entry nailing in adolescents risks AVN of the femoral head by damaging the retinacular branches of the MFCA; lateral trochanteric entry nails are used instead.

items.q: A 9-year-old (35 kg) has a long spiral comminuted femoral shaft fracture that is length-unstable. Suitable fixation is:
items.e: Elastic nails cannot control length in comminuted or long oblique fractures and in heavier children; submuscular bridge plating or external fixation is preferred.

items.q: Distal femoral physeal fractures in children have a growth disturbance rate of about:
items.e: Even Salter-Harris I and II fractures of the undulating distal femoral physis disturb growth in about 40-50%; families are warned and growth is followed for 1-2 years.

items.q: A tibial eminence fracture in which the fragment is completely displaced from its bed without contact is Meyers-McKeever type:
items.e: Type I is undisplaced, II has an anterior elevation with an intact posterior hinge, III is completely displaced (IIIB rotated) and IV (Zaricznyj) is comminuted; III and irreducible II need fixation.

items.q: A 10-year-old cannot actively extend the knee after a jump; radiographs show patella alta and only a small fleck of bone at the inferior pole. The diagnosis and treatment are:
o: Patellar sleeve fracture; open reduction and fixation
items.e: A sleeve fracture avulses a large cartilaginous sleeve with a small bony fragment, so radiographs underestimate it; loss of extension and patella alta indicate the need for ORIF.

items.q: A displaced Salter-Harris fracture of the proximal tibial physis carries a particular risk of:
o: Common peroneal nerve neurapraxia from the fibular head
items.e: The popliteal artery is tethered near the trifurcation behind the proximal tibia, so posterior displacement of the metaphysis can injure it; careful vascular assessment is needed.

items.q: The distal tibial physis closes over about 18 months in adolescence. The order of closure is:
items.e: Closure begins centrally (Kump's bump), then medially and finally laterally, which explains transitional fractures such as the juvenile Tillaux.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a Salter-Harris IV fracture of the medial malleolus with 2 mm displacement. Without anatomical reduction, the main long-term risk is:
o: A medial physeal bar causing progressive varus deformity
items.e: Medial malleolar SH III and IV fractures cross the physis and often form a medial bar, tethering medial growth and causing ankle varus; anatomical reduction and fixation are needed.

items.q: Which deformity after a paediatric fracture is least likely to remodel?
o: Sagittal angulation near the distal radial physis
Shortening of a femoral shaft fracture in a 5-year-old
Angulation in the plane of motion of the adjacent hinge joint
items.e: Remodelling is best in young children, near active physes and in the plane of joint motion; rotational deformity and intra-articular step-offs do not remodel.

items.q: Plastic deformation (bowing without a visible fracture line) in children occurs most commonly in the:
items.e: Plastic deformation is commonest in the ulna (and fibula); it can block reduction of the partner bone or a dislocated radial head and may need correction under anaesthesia.

items.q: The proximal humeral physis contributes approximately what proportion of the longitudinal growth of the humerus?
items.e: The proximal humeral physis gives about 80% of humeral growth, which is why proximal humeral fractures remodel so well; the distal humerus contributes only about 20%.

items.q: Approximately how much longitudinal growth does the distal femoral physis contribute each year before skeletal maturity?
items.e: The distal femur grows about 9-10 mm a year (about 70% of femoral length) and the proximal tibia about 6 mm a year, figures used in timing epiphysiodesis.

items.q: Posterior rib fractures in an infant are highly specific for abuse because they result from:
o: Direct falls onto the back from standing height
Anteroposterior squeezing of the chest, levering the posterior ribs over the transverse processes
items.e: Forceful squeezing of the thorax levers the posterior rib necks over the transverse processes; CPR in infants rarely causes posterior rib fractures.

items.q: In a 10-month-old being investigated for suspected non-accidental injury, the skeletal survey is repeated after about:
items.e: A follow-up survey at about 11-14 days shows healing of fractures that were occult initially (e.g. rib and metaphyseal fractures) and helps date injuries.

items.q: Acceptable angulation for a midshaft forearm fracture in a 7-year-old treated in a cast is up to about:
items.e: Children under about 9 accept up to about 15 degrees of angulation (and up to 45 degrees of malrotation) in the shaft; older children accept about 10 degrees.

items.q: A neonate after a difficult delivery does not move the right arm; there is crepitus and tenderness over the midclavicle. Radiographs show a clavicle fracture. Management is:
o: Reassurance and gentle handling, perhaps pinning the sleeve to the vest for comfort; it heals in a few weeks
items.e: Birth fractures of the clavicle cause pseudoparalysis and heal rapidly without specific treatment; persisting weakness after the fracture becomes painless suggests an obstetric brachial plexus palsy.

items.q: Medial epicondyle fractures in children are associated with an elbow dislocation in about:
o: Almost none, as they are isolated avulsions
items.e: The medial epicondyle is avulsed by the flexor-pronator mass and ulnar collateral ligament; about half occur with an elbow dislocation, which may leave the fragment incarcerated.

items.q: Injury to the triradiate cartilage in a young child's acetabular fracture may later produce:
o: A shallow acetabulum with progressive hip subluxation
items.e: Premature closure of the triradiate cartilage, especially under about 10 years, arrests acetabular growth, giving a shallow dysplastic acetabulum and lateral subluxation.

items.q: In the Garden classification, what distinguishes a type IV from a type III femoral neck fracture?
o: In type IV the head is fully displaced, so its trabeculae realign with those of the acetabulum
In type IV the fracture is incomplete
In type IV the fracture is valgus impacted
In type IV the head is rotated so its trabeculae lie at an angle to the acetabular trabeculae
items.e: In Garden III the partially displaced head is rotated into varus with trabeculae malaligned with the acetabulum; in Garden IV the head is completely detached and returns to its anatomical position in the acetabulum.

items.q: A young adult's femoral neck fracture line makes an angle of 40 degrees to the horizontal. In the Pauwels classification this is type:
items.e: Pauwels I is under 30 degrees, II is 30-50 degrees and III is over 50 degrees; increasing verticality increases shear and failure rates.

items.q: When fixing an undisplaced femoral neck fracture with three cannulated screws, the recommended configuration is:
o: An inverted triangle, with the inferior screw along the calcar and the posterior screw against the posterior neck cortex
A triangle with its apex inferior and all screws in the centre of the neck
Three screws converging at the head centre
Screws starting below the level of the lesser trochanter for better purchase
items.e: Parallel screws in an inverted triangle supported by the inferior and posterior cortices resist varus and posterior collapse; starting points below the lesser trochanter create a subtrochanteric stress riser.

items.q: NICE guidance on hip fracture recommends that surgery should be performed:
o: Within 6 hours of arrival in the emergency department
Within 7 days, once the patient is medically optimised
On the day of, or the day after, admission
Only after a formal echocardiogram in every patient
items.e: Surgery on the day of or day after admission, with correction of treatable comorbidities, reduces mortality and complications; routine echocardiography should not delay surgery.

items.q: A technetium-99m bone scan in a man with prostate cancer shows intense, uniform uptake throughout the axial skeleton with faint or absent renal and soft-tissue activity. This 'superscan' most likely indicates:
o: A normal scan with a technical error in tracer injection
Renal failure from ureteric obstruction only
items.e: Widespread metastases take up so much tracer that little reaches the kidneys, so the skeleton looks uniformly 'bright' with absent renal activity; metabolic bone disease (hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy) can produce a similar pattern.

items.q: A 62-year-old with renal cell carcinoma has a painful purely lytic lesion in the iliac wing on CT, yet the technetium-99m bone scan shows no increased uptake there. The best explanation is:
o: Aggressive lytic metastases with little osteoblastic response may be cold on bone scintigraphy
The lesion must be benign because metastases are always hot
Renal metastases are always photopenic because of embolisation
The scan was performed too late after tracer injection
items.e: Bone scans detect osteoblastic reaction, so purely lytic, rapidly destructive lesions (renal, thyroid, myeloma) can be falsely negative; CT, MRI or PET-CT is more reliable for these.

items.q: A patient with bone metastases has received denosumab and it is then stopped without any follow-on treatment. The main skeletal concern is:
o: Permanent suppression of bone turnover lasting decades
Immediate osteonecrosis of the jaw on withdrawal
Rapid rebound bone resorption with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures
Severe hypocalcaemia developing weeks after stopping
items.e: Denosumab's effect wears off quickly, and stopping it causes a surge of osteoclast activity (rebound) that can lead to multiple vertebral fractures, so a bisphosphonate is often given afterwards; bisphosphonates, by contrast, stay bound in bone for years.

items.q: Before starting high-dose zoledronic acid or denosumab for bone metastases, which step most reduces the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw?
o: Dental assessment and completion of necessary dental treatment
items.e: Invasive dental procedures during therapy are the main trigger for osteonecrosis of the jaw, so dental review and extractions before starting treatment, plus good oral hygiene, are recommended.

items.q: A woman with breast cancer has received monthly zoledronic acid for 5 years for bone metastases. She now has prodromal thigh pain, and radiographs show focal lateral cortical thickening ('beaking') in the subtrochanteric femur with a faint transverse lucency. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: A new lytic metastasis of the femur
Stress reaction from osteoarthritis of the hip
items.e: Long-term antiresorptive therapy predisposes to atypical femoral fractures that start in the lateral cortex with beaking and a transverse lucency; an impending fracture is usually treated with intramedullary nailing.

items.q: In the phase III trial by Fizazi and colleagues (Lancet 2011) in castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases, denosumab compared with zoledronic acid:
o: Improved overall survival by about 1 year
Delayed the time to the first skeletal-related event
Reduced the incidence of osteonecrosis of the jaw to zero
Was less effective in preventing skeletal-related events
items.e: Denosumab delayed the first skeletal-related event by several months compared with zoledronic acid, but overall survival and disease progression were similar; osteonecrosis of the jaw occurred with both agents.

items.q: The CAFE trial (Berenson et al., Lancet Oncology 2011) in cancer patients with painful vertebral compression fractures showed that balloon kyphoplasty compared with non-surgical management:
o: Increased the risk of adjacent fractures sevenfold
Gave no difference in pain or function at 1 month
Rapidly improved pain and back-specific function
items.e: Kyphoplasty produced rapid, clinically meaningful improvement in Roland-Morris disability and pain at 1 month that was sustained; it is suitable for painful pathological fractures without significant epidural disease or instability.

items.q: A recognised complication specific to stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for spinal metastases, more than with conventional radiotherapy, is:
o: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
Vertebral compression fracture of the treated level
items.e: High-dose SBRT causes vertebral compression fractures in a significant minority of treated levels, especially with lytic lesions, existing collapse and spinal malalignment; radiation-induced sarcoma takes years to develop.

items.q: A patient has a metastatic deposit destroying the T9 vertebral body with epidural cord compression. Why is laminectomy alone contraindicated?
o: Removing the intact posterior elements further destabilises a spine whose anterior column is already destroyed and does not address anterior compression
Laminectomy cannot be performed in the thoracic spine
The posterior elements are always involved first and are already absent
Laminectomy causes immediate tumour seeding of the cerebrospinal fluid
items.e: In metastatic disease the compressing tumour is usually anterior in the vertebral body; laminectomy without stabilisation removes the remaining posterior support and can worsen deformity and neurology, so decompression is combined with instrumentation.

items.q: A patient has a solitary spinal metastasis from slow-growing thyroid carcinoma, no visceral metastases and no other bone lesions. The Tomita score is 2. The recommended surgical strategy is:
o: Wide or marginal excision, such as total en bloc spondylectomy, for long-term local control
items.e: Tomita scores of 2-3 indicate long expected survival and favour wide or marginal excision; 4-5 marginal or intralesional excision, 6-7 palliative surgery and 8-10 supportive care.

items.q: A patient with spinal metastases has a revised Tokuhashi score of 7. The predicted survival and broad treatment recommendation are:
o: Six months or more; palliative surgery
One year or more; excisional surgery
Less than 6 months; conservative or palliative treatment
items.e: In the revised Tokuhashi score, 0-8 predicts survival under 6 months, 9-11 six months or more, and 12-15 one year or more, guiding increasingly aggressive surgery.

items.q: In a patient with metastatic spinal cord compression and neurological deficit, the usual immediate dose of dexamethasone recommended in UK practice is:
o: Methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg bolus followed by 5.4 mg/kg/h
items.e: Dexamethasone 16 mg daily (with gastric protection) reduces cord oedema while definitive treatment is arranged; very high bolus doses add side effects without proven benefit, and the methylprednisolone infusion regimen belongs to traumatic cord injury trials.

items.q: Which chemokine axis is important in homing of breast and prostate cancer cells to the bone marrow, supporting Paget's 'seed and soil' hypothesis?
items.e: Marrow stromal cells express CXCL12, attracting CXCR4-expressing tumour cells to bone; RANKL/OPG governs osteoclast activation once the tumour is established, and sclerostin and FGF23 relate to other pathways.

items.q: A patient with a hypervascular renal cell metastasis in the proximal femur is scheduled for curettage, cementation and nailing. Preoperative arterial embolisation should ideally be performed:
o: Only if intraoperative blood loss exceeds 2 litres
items.e: Embolisation reduces intraoperative bleeding, but collateral flow and recanalisation develop over days, so surgery should follow within about 1-3 days.

items.q: A child has a renal tumour that has spread to multiple bones. Which childhood renal tumour is characteristically bone-metastasising?
o: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney
items.e: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney is known as the 'bone-metastasising renal tumour of childhood'; Wilms tumour usually metastasises to lung and liver and rarely to bone.

items.q: Compared with fixation after a completed pathological fracture, prophylactic fixation of an impending pathological fracture of a long bone is associated with:
o: Shorter hospital stay, less blood loss, quicker return to walking and longer survival
Higher rates of fat embolism and longer hospital stay
items.e: Retrospective series consistently show that fixing impending fractures is easier and gives better function and survival than fixing completed fractures, which is why lesions at risk should be identified and stabilised early.

items.q: A 60-year-old with metastatic breast cancer has extensive destruction of the distal femoral metaphysis and condyles with a pathological fracture, and an expected survival of over a year. The most suitable reconstruction is:
o: Two crossed Kirschner wires and radiotherapy
items.e: When periarticular bone is destroyed, fixation is likely to fail because pathological fractures heal poorly; resection and endoprosthetic replacement allow immediate weight bearing and a durable result in patients with reasonable survival.

items.q: A metastatic lesion in the humeral diaphysis is mixed lytic-blastic, causes moderate pain and involves more than two-thirds of the bone diameter. What is the Mirels score?
items.e: Upper limb 1 + moderate pain 2 + mixed lesion 2 + size over two-thirds 3 = 8, which carries about a 15% fracture risk and calls for clinical judgement.

items.q: A lytic metastasis in the femoral diaphysis (not peritrochanteric) causes pain on walking and involves about half the bone diameter. What is the Mirels score and the recommendation?
items.e: Lower limb 2 + functional pain 3 + lytic 3 + size one-third to two-thirds 2 = 10; a score of 9 or more predicts a fracture risk of about a third or more and warrants prophylactic fixation.

items.q: A patient has a lytic L3 metastasis with mechanical pain, normal alignment, less than 50% vertebral body collapse and unilateral pedicle involvement. What is the SINS score and category?
items.e: Mobile spine (L2-L4) 2 + mechanical pain 3 + lytic 2 + normal alignment 0 + under 50% collapse 2 + unilateral posterolateral 1 = 10, in the 7-12 indeterminate band, which warrants surgical consultation.

items.q: In the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score, a metastasis at T6 receives a location score of:
items.e: Location scores are junctional (occiput-C2, C7-T2, T11-L1, L5-S1) 3, mobile (C3-C6, L2-L4) 2, semi-rigid (T3-T10) 1 and rigid (S2-S5) 0; the rib cage stabilises the mid-thoracic spine.

items.q: On axial T2 MRI, epidural tumour from a breast cancer metastasis deforms the thecal sac but does not reach the spinal cord (Bilsky 1b). The spine is stable. The usual treatment is:
o: Radiotherapy (conventional or stereotactic) without decompressive surgery
items.e: Bilsky 0-1 are low-grade compression and are treated with radiation; decompression is considered for high-grade (2-3) compression, particularly with radioresistant tumours, or for instability.

items.q: The main dose-limiting toxicity of strontium-89 or samarium-153 used for palliation of painful sclerotic bone metastases is:
items.e: These bone-seeking beta emitters irradiate the adjacent marrow, causing myelosuppression; they palliate pain but, unlike radium-223, have not been shown to prolong survival.

items.q: Lutetium-177 PSMA-617 therapy, which improved survival in the VISION trial, is used for:
items.e: Lu-177-PSMA delivers beta radiation to cells expressing prostate-specific membrane antigen; patients are selected by PSMA PET imaging.

items.q: In classic teaching, surgical decompression and stabilisation for metastatic spinal disease is generally offered only when expected survival is at least about:
items.e: Patchell's trial included patients with an expected survival of 3 months or more, and this threshold is widely used for spinal surgery (about 6 weeks for long-bone fixation).

items.q: In which cause of hypercalcaemia of malignancy are glucocorticoids particularly effective?
o: Squamous cell lung cancer secreting PTHrP
items.e: Steroids inhibit the 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity of lymphoma cells and are also useful in myeloma; PTHrP- and PTH-mediated hypercalcaemia respond to fluids and antiresorptives instead.

items.q: Overall, the commonest mechanism of hypercalcaemia in patients with cancer is:
o: Ectopic secretion of true parathyroid hormone
Humoral secretion of PTH-related peptide by the tumour
items.e: About 80% of hypercalcaemia of malignancy is humoral (PTHrP), typical of squamous, renal and breast cancers; local osteolysis accounts for most of the rest, while calcitriol production and ectopic PTH are rare.

items.q: Six weeks after starting effective hormonal therapy for breast cancer, a follow-up bone scan shows increased intensity of known lesions while the patient's pain is improving. This is most likely:
o: The flare phenomenon, reflecting an osteoblastic healing response
Definite disease progression requiring a change of therapy
items.e: In the first few months after successful treatment, healing bone increases tracer uptake; this flare should not be mistaken for progression, so scans are best reassessed later or interpreted with other imaging.

items.q: After curettage of a metastatic lesion before fixation, the defect is usually filled with PMMA cement rather than bone graft because cement:
o: Is osteoinductive and encourages new bone formation
