items.e: STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery) is an inversion recovery sequence that nulls fat signal and is the most sensitive for marrow oedema (bone bruises, infection, occult fractures). It is also more robust near metal than chemical fat-saturated sequences.

items.q: On an MRI of the ankle, the peroneal tendons appear to have increased signal intensity on T1-weighted images as they curve around the lateral malleolus, but appear normal on T2-weighted images. This phenomenon is likely due to:
items.e: The magic angle effect occurs when collagen fibres are oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the static magnetic field (B0). This causes increased signal on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE) which mimics pathology but disappears on long-TE sequences (T2).

items.q: Which of the following conditions is most likely to appear as a 'cold' (photopenic) lesion on a Technetium-99m MDP bone scan?
items.e: Multiple myeloma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and purely lytic metastases (such as from renal or thyroid cancer) often appear as cold lesions because they do not trigger a sufficient osteoblastic response. Osteoid osteoma and Paget's disease typically show intense 'hot' uptake.

items.q: During a prolonged spinal fusion surgery for scoliosis, at what point should the anaesthetist redose the prophylactic cefazolin, assuming no massive haemorrhage has occurred?
o: Only if the case exceeds 12 hours
items.e: Standard guidelines recommend redosing cefazolin every 4 hours during surgery to maintain adequate tissue levels. Redosing is also indicated if blood loss exceeds 1500 mL.

items.q: Which regional anaesthetic technique is preferred for postoperative analgesia in total knee arthroplasty because it provides effective pain relief while better preserving quadriceps strength for early mobilisation?
items.e: The adductor canal block is a sensory-dominant block that preserves quadriceps motor strength better than a femoral nerve block, thereby reducing the risk of falls and facilitating early mobilisation after TKA.

items.q: A 4-year-old child is brought with painless, fusiform swellings of the proximal phalanges and metacarpals of the hand. Radiographs show ballooned, expanded short tubular bones with marked cortical thinning ('spina ventosa') without sequestra. Which statement regarding tuberculous dactylitis is correct?
o: It affects long bones of the leg more commonly than short tubular bones of the hand
Massive sequestra formation and dense sclerosis are classic early radiological findings
Surgical curettage and bone grafting are mandatory first-line treatment in all children
Syphilitic dactylitis, an important differential, is characteristically bilateral and symmetrical
items.e: Tuberculous dactylitis (spina ventosa) affects the short tubular bones of the hand more than the foot in young children and responds to antitubercular chemotherapy. Syphilitic dactylitis is typically bilateral and symmetrical, which helps differentiate it.

items.q: All of the following are classic, typical anatomical locations for Looser zones (pseudofractures) in osteomalacia EXCEPT:
o: Medial aspect of the femoral neck
Convex (lateral) cortex of the subtrochanteric femoral shaft
items.e: Looser zones in osteomalacia occur typically on the concave/compression side of bones (such as the medial femoral neck, axillary border of the scapula, and pubic rami). Pseudofractures on the convex (lateral) cortex of the femoral shaft suggest atypical femoral fractures or Paget's disease.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for chronic musculoskeletal aches and fatigue. Hand radiographs show subperiosteal cortical resorption along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers. Which biochemical profile is expected?
o: Low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, elevated PTH
Normal serum calcium, normal serum phosphate, markedly elevated ALP
Low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, low PTH
High serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated PTH
items.e: Radial-sided subperiosteal resorption of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers is characteristic of primary hyperparathyroidism, which shows high calcium, low phosphate and inappropriately elevated PTH.

items.q: A 68-year-old man with known extensive polyostotic Paget disease presents with a 2-month history of intense, new-onset pain in his left pelvis accompanied by a rapidly enlarging local soft-tissue mass. Radiographs confirm cortical destruction. Which histopathological entity accounts for the majority of secondary malignant transformations in Paget disease?
items.e: Pagetic sarcomatous transformation occurs in under 1% of patients and carries a very poor prognosis. Osteosarcoma is the most common histological subtype arising in pagetic bone.

items.q: Which of the following skeletal dysplasias is characterised by histopathological abnormalities predominantly in the reserve (resting) zone of the physis?
items.e: Reserve-zone disorders include diastrophic dysplasia, Kniest dysplasia, pseudoachondroplasia and Gaucher disease. Achondroplasia affects the proliferative zone; rickets and Schmid chondrodysplasia affect the hypertrophic zone.

items.q: A 72-year-old male is undergoing a total knee replacement for osteoarthritis. Analysis of the non-osteoarthritic, age-matched portion of his articular cartilage would most likely show which of the following changes compared to a 20-year-old?
items.e: With normal aging, keratan sulfate increases while chondroitin-4 sulfate, water content, and chondrocyte number decrease. This results in a decreased chondroitin:keratan sulfate ratio.

items.q: A 28-year-old male sustains a high-velocity gunshot wound to the thigh. During exploration of the sciatic nerve, the surgeon notes a 'neuroma-in-continuity' where the nerve is visibly enlarged but the epineurium is intact. Despite waiting for 4 months, there has been no clinical recovery and the Tinel sign has not advanced. This injury corresponds to which Sunderland grade?
items.e: Sunderland Grade IV is a neuroma-in-continuity where the axons, endoneurium, and perineurium are disrupted, but the epineurium remains intact. Unlike grades II and III, it does not show an advancing Tinel sign and requires surgical excision and repair.

items.q: In the physiological classification of nerve fibres, which of the following fibres is the first to be blocked by local anaesthetics?
items.e: Local anaesthetics block small, myelinated fibres first. The typical order is B (preganglionic autonomic) > A-delta and C (pain, temperature) > A-beta (touch) > A-alpha (motor). Pressure/tourniquets block large fibres first.

items.q: A 68-year-old man needs fixation of an intertrochanteric hip fracture. He had a myocardial infarction 6 weeks ago and has ongoing exertional angina. Ignoring any emergency modifier, what is his ASA physical status class?
items.e: ASA IV is severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; the ASA examples include a recent (under 3 months) myocardial infarction or ongoing cardiac ischaemia. ASA V is a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation.

items.q: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with an infected tibial nonunion with a through-and-through cortical defect and a mechanically unstable construct. How is this staged in the Cierny-Mader classification?
items.e: Anatomical type IV is diffuse osteomyelitis with mechanical instability (e.g. infected nonunion). Diabetes is a systemic host compromise, making him a Bs host; Bl denotes local compromise such as lymphoedema or venous stasis.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with chronic low back pain and a swollen right knee that has been painful for the past 4 months. Baseline ESR is 65 mm h⁻¹ and Mantoux induration is 15 mm. Synovial fluid analysis shows 18 000 WBC/mm³, predominantly lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Synovial fluid culture on Lowenstein–Jensen medium
MRI of the knee with contrast
items.e: GeneXpert MTB/RIF on a biopsy or tissue sample provides rapid detection of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance. Synovial cultures are slow and often negative in paucibacillary disease, while MRI is useful for extent but not diagnosis.

items.q: A 7-year-old has a 4-month history of hip pain with night cries and a limp but no fever. Which early radiographic pattern most favours tuberculous over pyogenic arthritis?
o: Rapid early joint-space loss with subchondral sclerosis
Juxta-articular osteopenia with peripheral (marginal) erosions and a relatively preserved joint space
Symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis with periarticular osteopenia
items.e: Phemister's triad of tuberculous arthritis is juxta-articular osteoporosis, peripheral osseous erosions and gradual joint-space narrowing; cartilage is preserved relatively long, unlike in pyogenic arthritis where proteolytic enzymes destroy it early.

items.q: GeneXpert MTB/RIF on a synovial biopsy from a chronic monoarthritis detects M. tuberculosis with rifampicin resistance. Mutations in which gene does this assay detect?
items.e: Xpert MTB/RIF detects mutations in the 81-bp rifampicin-resistance-determining region of rpoB. katG and inhA mutations confer isoniazid resistance and embB ethambutol resistance.

items.q: A 2-year-old child presents with bowed legs, widened wrists and delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle. Serum 25(OH)D is 10 ng/mL, calcium 8.5 mg/dL, phosphate 2.0 mg/dL and PTH 80 pg/mL. Which disorder best explains this profile?
items.e: Low 25(OH)D with secondary hyperparathyroidism, low phosphate and low-normal calcium is the classic picture of nutritional vitamin D deficiency. Calcium-deficiency rickets and VDR defects have normal 25(OH)D, and XLH has normal PTH.

items.q: A 5-year-old with progressive genu varum, short stature and recurrent spontaneous dental abscesses has low serum phosphate, normal calcium, normal PTH and an inappropriately normal 1,25(OH)2D level. Which circulating hormone is most likely elevated?
items.e: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (PHEX mutation) raises FGF23, which causes renal phosphate wasting and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so 1,25(OH)2D is inappropriately normal or low despite hypophosphataemia.

items.q: In a child with hypophosphataemic rickets, which measurement best confirms renal phosphate wasting?
o: TmP/GFR calculated from paired fasting urine and serum phosphate and creatinine
items.e: A low tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per GFR (TmP/GFR) in the presence of hypophosphataemia confirms renal phosphate wasting, as in FGF23-mediated rickets.

items.q: Which laboratory feature differentiates hypophosphatasia from other forms of rickets and osteomalacia?
items.e: Hypophosphatasia is caused by ALPL mutations reducing tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, so serum ALP is low, whereas other rickets/osteomalacia have raised ALP. Pyridoxal-5-phosphate and pyrophosphate accumulate.

items.q: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman with no previous fracture has a femoral neck T-score of -2.8. She has normal renal function and no oesophageal disease. Which drug is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
items.e: For osteoporosis without very-high-risk features, an oral bisphosphonate such as alendronate is first-line. Anabolic agents (teriparatide, romosozumab) are reserved for very high fracture risk, and calcitonin is no longer recommended.

items.q: Below which creatinine clearance are alendronate and zoledronic acid generally contraindicated in the treatment of osteoporosis?
items.e: Bisphosphonates are renally excreted; alendronate and zoledronic acid are not recommended when creatinine clearance is below 35 mL/min. Denosumab is not renally cleared and can be used instead.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical adverse effect of IV zoledronate administered as a 5‑mg infusion?
o: Acute phase reaction with fever and myalgia
Hypocalcaemia in patients with inadequate vitamin D
items.e: Oesophageal ulcers are associated with oral bisphosphonates; IV zoledronate does not cause oesophageal irritation.

items.q: A 58-year-old man has an acute first MTP joint flare with aspirate showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals, but his serum urate during the attack is 6.2 mg/dL. When should serum urate be rechecked to assess hyperuricaemia?
o: Within 24 hours, before starting anti-inflammatory treatment
Immediately after the first dose of colchicine
About 2-4 weeks after the flare has settled
Only after 6 months of urate-lowering therapy
items.e: Serum urate may be normal or falsely low during an acute gout flare, so it should be remeasured a few weeks (about 2-4 weeks) after the flare has resolved.

items.q: Under compensated polarised light microscopy, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals typically appear as:
o: Rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence, blue when parallel to the compensator axis
Needle-shaped crystals with strong negative birefringence, yellow when parallel to the compensator axis
Non-birefringent clumps seen only on alizarin red staining
items.e: CPPD crystals are rhomboid or rod-shaped, weakly positively birefringent and blue when parallel to the compensator. Needle-shaped strongly negative crystals are urate; non-birefringent clumps staining with alizarin red are basic calcium phosphate.

items.q: A patient with chronic tophaceous gout develops a sudden, painful, swollen right elbow. Synovial fluid contains urate crystals and more than 70,000 WBC/mm³. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Send Gram stain and culture and treat as septic arthritis until excluded
Reassure, since crystals confirm an acute gout flare
items.e: Crystals do not exclude coexisting infection, and very high synovial WBC counts overlap with septic arthritis, so Gram stain and culture are sent and the joint is treated as septic until excluded.

items.q: In suspected calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, chondrocalcinosis on plain radiographs is most commonly sought in the knee menisci, the pubic symphysis and which other structure?
o: Triangular fibrocartilage complex of the wrist
items.e: Chondrocalcinosis in CPPD is classically seen in fibrocartilage: knee menisci, the triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist and the pubic symphysis, which form the usual radiographic screening set.

items.q: A 52-year-old man with recurrent gout starts allopurinol 100 mg daily and develops a flare on day 10. What is the correct management?
o: Stop allopurinol until the flare resolves
Continue allopurinol, treat the flare (e.g. colchicine) and maintain anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for 3-6 months
items.e: Urate-lowering therapy is not stopped during a flare; the flare is treated and prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine, NSAID or prednisone) is given for 3-6 months after starting ULT, with allopurinol titrated gradually from a low starting dose.

items.q: Serum calcium is usually normal in Paget disease of bone. In which situation does hypercalcaemia typically develop in a patient with extensive Paget disease?
o: During prolonged immobilisation, e.g. after a fracture
items.e: Pagetic bone has very high turnover; when a patient is immobilised, resorption is uncoupled from formation and hypercalcaemia (and hypercalciuria) can develop. Otherwise calcium is normal, and hypercalcaemia should prompt a search for hyperparathyroidism or malignancy.

items.q: A 70-year-old man with active Paget disease of the pelvis and proximal femur is scheduled for total hip arthroplasty. Which perioperative problem is characteristically increased because of the pagetic bone?
items.e: Active pagetic bone is hypervascular, so THA carries increased blood loss; other recognised problems are heterotopic ossification, deformity causing malposition, and hard sclerotic bone. Preoperative bisphosphonate treatment reduces vascularity.

items.q: An MRI of a patient with suspected early osteonecrosis of the femoral head shows a serpiginous low‑signal band on T1 and a double‑line appearance on T2. What does the inner high‑signal line represent?
o: Granulation tissue forming the reactive interface.
Residual necrotic bone with fatty marrow.
Synovial fluid tracking into the subchondral region.
items.e: The inner hyperaemic granulation tissue (high‑signal on T2) borders the outer low‑signal sclerotic bone, giving the classic double‑line sign of osteonecrosis.

items.q: Which of the following **is not** a common non‑traumatic cause of osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Alcohol consumption >400 ml pure ethanol per week
items.e: Radiation is a recognised but uncommon cause; the most frequent non‑traumatic etiologies are steroids, alcohol, and haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease.

items.q: In osteonecrosis of the femoral head, the size and location of the necrotic lesion on MRI are the most important predictors of which outcome?
items.e: Large lesions (over about 30% of the head, or a high necrotic angle) and lateral weight-bearing location strongly predict progression to collapse, whereas small medial lesions often remain stable.

items.q: A 45-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has periarticular osteopenia on hand radiographs. Which cell, activated via RANKL from synovial fibroblasts and T cells, is primarily responsible?
items.e: Inflamed rheumatoid synovium expresses RANKL, which activates osteoclasts, producing periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions.

items.q: Compared with normal aging of articular cartilage, early osteoarthritic cartilage characteristically shows:
items.e: Osteoarthritic cartilage has increased water content (from collagen network disruption) and decreased proteoglycans, whereas aging cartilage has decreased water and increased keratan sulfate.

items.q: Which glycoprotein, secreted by synoviocytes and superficial-zone chondrocytes, is the principal boundary lubricant of articular cartilage?
items.e: Lubricin (proteoglycan 4) coats the articular surface and provides boundary lubrication; hyaluronic acid adds viscosity. Aggrecan and type II collagen are matrix components, and MMP-13 is a collagenase.

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the role of pericellular type VI collagen in articular cartilage?
o: Forms the bulk of the matrix giving compressive strength
Anchors collagen fibrils to the subchondral bone
Surrounds chondrocytes and regulates their function
Cross‑links aggrecan aggregates to resist shear stress
items.e: Type VI collagen is a pericellular matrix protein that surrounds individual chondrocytes, influencing cell–matrix interactions and signaling. It is not a bulk structural component.

items.q: A 22-year-old undergoes microfracture for a 1.5 cm² full-thickness chondral defect of the medial femoral condyle. The repair tissue is predominantly:
o: Hyaline cartilage rich in type II collagen
Fibrocartilage rich in type I collagen
items.e: Microfracture releases marrow mesenchymal cells into the defect, which form fibrocartilage composed mainly of type I collagen, mechanically inferior to native hyaline cartilage.

items.q: The Donnan osmotic pressure in articular cartilage is primarily generated by:
o: Fixed negative charges of proteoglycan GAGs attracting cations
Positive charge of type II collagen fibers
Calcium crystals in the calcified zone
Synovial fluid pH changes during loading
items.e: Proteoglycan GAGs carry negative charges that create an osmotic swelling pressure, counterbalanced by the collagen network and responsible for compressive stiffness.

items.q: Which collagen type is characteristic of the hypertrophic zone of the physis and is mutated in Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia?
items.e: Hypertrophic chondrocytes produce type X collagen, which is involved in matrix mineralisation; COL10A1 mutations cause Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia.

items.q: On quantitative MRI of early osteoarthritic cartilage, T2 relaxation time is prolonged. This mainly reflects:
o: Disruption of the collagen network with increased free water
Thickening of the calcified cartilage layer
items.e: T2 mapping is sensitive to collagen organisation and water content; collagen network breakdown and increased water in early OA prolong T2. Proteoglycan loss is assessed better with dGEMRIC or T1rho.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man with a stable distal femur fracture is being planned for intramedullary nailing. The surgeon decides to use a titanium alloy nail. What is the most likely consequence of this choice in terms of stress shielding?
o: Greater stress shielding than a steel nail
Less stress shielding than a steel nail
Stress shielding only occurs with cobalt‑chrome implants
items.e: Titanium alloy (E≈110 GPa) is closest to cortical bone (E≈15‑20 GPa) and therefore produces the least stress shielding compared with a higher‑modulus steel nail.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old female presents with an isolated 5th metatarsal base fracture. Which fracture pattern is most compatible with the tensile‑force mechanism described for this bone?
items.e: The 5th metatarsal base is commonly fractured by a transverse, avulsion pattern due to tensile loading at its base.

items.q: Medialising the acetabular component in total hip arthroplasty reduces the hip joint reaction force mainly by:
items.e: In single-leg stance the abductors balance body weight times its moment arm; medialising the hip centre shortens the body-weight moment arm, so less abductor force and a lower joint reaction force are needed.

items.q: In cemented total hip arthroplasty, PMMA bone cement functions primarily as:
o: A grout that transfers load by mechanical interlock with bone and implant
An adhesive that chemically bonds to bone
A material strongest in tension and shear
A stiffer interface than cortical bone
items.e: PMMA has no adhesive properties; it acts as a grout filling the space between implant and bone and interlocking with cancellous bone. It is strongest in compression, weak in tension and shear, and has a low modulus (about 2-3 GPa).

items.q: On a stress–strain curve of a metallic alloy, the region where the slope is linear and deformation is fully recoverable is known as the:
items.e: The elastic region is linear, with stress directly proportional to strain; deformation is reversible upon unloading.

items.q: Which material property best describes the ability of an implant to absorb energy before breaking?
items.e: Toughness is defined as the area under the stress–strain curve, indicating how much energy an implant can absorb before failure.

items.q: A 28-year-old has foot drop after prolonged compression at the fibular head. Nerve conduction shows a focal conduction block with normal distal amplitudes and sensation is largely preserved. What explains the predominantly motor loss?
o: Wallerian degeneration of the whole nerve
Injury to the dorsal root ganglion
Focal demyelination preferentially affecting large myelinated motor fibres (neurapraxia)
items.e: Compression neurapraxia causes focal demyelination with conduction block and no axonal loss; large myelinated motor fibres are most susceptible, so motor loss exceeds sensory loss and recovery is complete within weeks to months.

items.q: In a randomised trial comparing two shoulder arthroplasty techniques, what is the main purpose of concealed allocation (e.g. central web-based randomisation)?
o: It blinds the surgeon to the operation being performed
It prevents selection bias by keeping the next assignment unknown to those enrolling patients
It allows a relative risk to be calculated instead of an odds ratio
items.e: Allocation concealment stops recruiters from predicting or influencing the next allocation, protecting against selection bias at enrolment; it is different from blinding after allocation.

items.q: A meta-analysis of five RCTs of an osteoarthritis drug shows widely varying effect estimates with minimally overlapping confidence intervals and I² of 80%. Under GRADE, the evidence is downgraded for:
items.e: Inconsistency is unexplained heterogeneity of results across studies (variable point estimates, poorly overlapping CIs, high I²). Imprecision refers to wide confidence intervals around the pooled estimate.

items.q: A registry follows a cohort of patients after shoulder arthroplasty for 10 years. It reports a 5% revision rate. Which of the following is a limitation of using a registry for evaluating implant survivorship?
o: It lacks a control group for comparative analysis
Revision is a crude endpoint with limited clinical detail
It is susceptible to recall bias
items.e: Retrospective registry data provide revision rates but often miss detailed clinical information such as reasons for revision or early functional outcomes.

items.q: A cohort study compares early versus delayed mobilisation after knee replacement, but 25% of patients are lost to follow-up, more in one arm. Which bias is most likely?
items.e: Loss to follow-up, especially when unequal between groups, causes attrition bias because those remaining may differ systematically from those lost.

items.q: A PA chest radiograph gives an effective dose of about 0.02 mSv. The effective dose of a CT scan of the lumbar spine is closest to:
items.e: A lumbar spine CT delivers roughly 5-6 mSv, several hundred times a chest radiograph and comparable to about two years of natural background radiation.

items.q: During fluoroscopy for a hand fracture, the C-arm X-ray tube is placed under the table and the image intensifier above. Why does this reduce radiation to the surgeon?
o: The photoelectric effect predominates at low kVp
Scatter is greatest on the beam-entrance (tube) side, so the tube below directs most scatter away from the surgeon's upper body
The inverse square law does not apply to scatter
It allows the use of lower mAs
items.e: Most scatter arises where the beam enters the patient, so keeping the tube under the table directs scatter towards the floor and away from the operator's eyes, thyroid and hands.

items.q: The effective dose of a DXA scan of the hip and lumbar spine is closest to:
items.e: DXA uses a very low tube current and narrow beam, giving a few microsieverts, less than a day of natural background radiation and lower than a chest radiograph.

items.q: Which interaction dominates photon attenuation in soft tissues at the kVp settings typically used for plain radiography (80–120 kVp)?
items.e: At 80–120 kVp, Compton scattering is the predominant interaction in soft tissue, responsible for image fog and most of the occupational dose to staff.

items.q: During routine pre‑operative assessment, a patient is identified as a former smoker who quit 18 days ago. Which statement best reflects the evidence regarding smoking cessation and surgical wound healing?
o: Smoking must be stopped at least 12 weeks prior to surgery to reduce wound complications.
Quitting 4‑6 weeks before surgery is sufficient to lower infection risk.
Smoking cessation has no measurable impact on postoperative outcomes.
Only current smokers, not former smokers, are at increased risk.
items.e: The guideline recommends stopping smoking at least 4 weeks (ideally 6–8) before surgery to optimise wound healing; 18 days is insufficient to reap full benefits.

items.q: A patient with a history of recent stent placement is scheduled for elective knee arthroplasty. Which of the following statements about peri‑operative antiplatelet therapy is correct?
o: Aspirin should be stopped 7 days before surgery and restarted on the day of the operation.
Dual antiplatelet therapy can be continued without interruption in all patients.
If the patient had a bare‑metal stent, elective surgery should be delayed for at least 30 days unless cardiology advises otherwise.
Tapering the dose of aspirin to 81 mg is adequate to avoid bleeding complications.
items.e: Bare‑metal stents require at least 30 days of dual therapy; drug‑eluting stents need 6–12 months. Cardiologist input is essential before any change.

items.q: A 45-year-old has leg pain, low-grade fever and a sinus draining from the medial aspect of the leg. Radiographs of the tibia show a dense, sharply marginated fragment of bone lying in a lucent cavity, surrounded by thick periosteal new bone. What is the diagnosis?
o: Chronic osteomyelitis with sequestrum and involucrum
items.e: A dense dead bone fragment (sequestrum) within a cavity, surrounded by reactive periosteal new bone (involucrum), with a sinus, indicates chronic osteomyelitis.

items.q: In the Cierny‑Mader system, which treatment implication is associated with a type III (localised) osteomyelitis?
items.e: Type III lesions can be excised without compromising structural stability; the standard plan is debridement with dead‑space management.

items.q: Which organism is most commonly implicated in septic arthritis of the knee in an immunocompetent adult?
items.e: Staphylococcus aureus accounts for the majority of septic arthritis cases in the adult knee.

items.q: A staphylococcal fracture-related infection is treated with debridement, retention of a stable plate and antibiotic therapy. According to FRI consensus, the regimen should be:
o: Rifampicin combined with a second active agent (e.g. a fluoroquinolone), for about 12 weeks in total
items.e: Rifampicin penetrates biofilm on retained implants but rapidly selects resistance if used alone, so it is always combined with another active agent; with implant retention, about 12 weeks of therapy is recommended.

items.q: A 50-year-old with a 20-year history of chronic discharging osteomyelitis of the femur develops heavy proteinuria and peripheral oedema. What is the most likely cause?
items.e: Long-standing chronic inflammation such as chronic osteomyelitis can cause secondary AA amyloidosis, which typically presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman from a high-TB-burden area has chronic right hip pain, night sweats, weight loss and a soft fluctuant swelling in the anterolateral thigh. Radiographs show juxta-articular osteopenia and peripheral erosions with a preserved joint space. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis quickly?
o: Joint aspiration for Gram stain and routine culture
GeneXpert MTB/RIF on image-guided biopsy tissue or abscess pus
MRI of the hip with contrast
items.e: Nucleic acid amplification (Xpert MTB/RIF) on tissue or pus gives rapid microbiological confirmation of osteoarticular TB and detects rifampicin resistance; MRI shows extent but does not confirm the organism.

items.q: A BCG-vaccinated woman with rheumatoid arthritis is about to start an anti-TNF agent. Which test is preferred to screen for latent tuberculosis?
items.e: IGRAs are preferred for latent TB screening before biologics in BCG-vaccinated patients because, unlike the tuberculin skin test, they are not confounded by BCG. Serology is not recommended and sputum smear detects active pulmonary disease only.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy with genu varum and short stature has low serum phosphate, normal calcium, inappropriately normal 1,25(OH)2D, very high FGF23 and a PHEX mutation. Which therapy directly targets the underlying mechanism?
items.e: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets is driven by excess FGF23; burosumab, a monoclonal antibody against FGF23, restores renal phosphate reabsorption and 1,25(OH)2D production. Conventional therapy is oral phosphate with calcitriol.

items.q: Which of the following is the principal adverse effect that limits the use of intravenous zoledronate in patients with renal impairment?
items.e: IV zoledronate is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is <35 mL/min because of risk of renal toxicity; this limits its use in patients with moderate to severe renal impairment.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman is prescribed risedronate 35 mg weekly. She is advised to take the tablet with a full glass of water while upright. What is the primary reason for this instruction?
o: To enhance absorption in the stomach
To avoid interaction with calcium supplements
items.e: Oral bisphosphonates have <1 % bioavailability; taking them on an empty stomach with water and staying upright for 30–60 minutes reduces oesophageal irritation and maximises absorption.

items.q: Which of the following is true regarding denosumab in osteoporosis management?
o: It has a long skeletal half‑life allowing a drug holiday
It is contraindicated in patients with creatinine clearance <30 mL/min
It binds to RANKL, preventing RANK activation
items.e: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds RANK‑L, blocking its interaction with RANK on osteoclast precursors. It has no significant renal clearance issue, is given every 6 months, and does not allow a drug holiday.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old man presents with deep aching hip pain and progressive bowing of the distal femur. Plain radiograph shows a widened cortical thickness with a “blade of grass” lytic front. Which laboratory finding best reflects the activity of his bone disease?
items.e: Paget disease is characterised by a markedly raised bone‑specific alkaline phosphatase that tracks disease activity; calcium and phosphate remain normal and CTX may be mildly elevated but is not the primary marker.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old man with polyostotic Paget disease develops sudden high‑output congestive heart failure. The most likely pathophysiological mechanism is:
o: Left ventricular hypertrophy due to hypertension
items.e: Extensive pagetic bone causes many arteriovenous shunts, increasing cardiac output and leading to high‑output heart failure.

items.q: In a monostotic Paget lesion of the femur with normal serum calcium and phosphate, an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is indicative of:
items.e: In monostotic disease the alkaline phosphatase rise reflects the active remodeling phase; calcium/phosphate remain normal unless immobilized.

items.q: In the early lytic phase of Paget disease of the skull, a large, well-demarcated lytic area seen on radiographs is called:
items.e: Osteoporosis circumscripta is the lytic phase of Paget disease in the skull; the later mixed/sclerotic phase gives the cotton-wool skull. The blade-of-grass sign is the advancing lytic front in long bones, and picture-frame vertebrae are seen in the sclerotic phase.

items.q: A 48‑year‑old patient with sickle cell disease presents with right hip pain. MRI shows the classic double‑line sign with a central area of bone marrow oedema. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of osteonecrosis in sickle cell disease?
o: Direct marrow cell toxicity by steroids
Intravascular occlusion by sickled red cells
items.e: In sickle cell disease, sickled erythrocytes occlude the femoral head vasculature, causing ischemia and osteonecrosis.

items.q: A 4-year-old has hypoplastic clavicles, a persistently open anterior fontanelle and delayed dentition due to a RUNX2 loss-of-function mutation. RUNX2 acts upstream of which transcription factor that is essential for osteoblast differentiation?
items.e: Cleidocranial dysplasia is caused by RUNX2 haploinsufficiency; RUNX2 induces osterix, both required for osteoblast differentiation. SOX9 drives chondrogenesis, PPAR-gamma adipogenesis and NFATc1 osteoclastogenesis.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman on long‑term glucocorticoids has elevated serum CTX but normal serum osteocalcin. Which cellular event is most responsible for the rise in CTX?
o: Increased osteoclast fusion mediated by RANKL
Decreased alkaline phosphatase activity in osteoblasts
items.e: Glucocorticoids up‑regulate RANKL expression on osteoblasts/osteocytes, promoting osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption, thereby elevating CTX.

items.q: Which of the following proteoglycans is the main core protein that carries chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains in articular cartilage?
items.e: Aggrecan is the predominant large proteoglycan in cartilage, with extensive GAG side chains forming the aggregates that confer compressive stiffness.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between water content and mechanical properties of intact articular cartilage?
o: Higher water content increases compressive stiffness
Higher water content increases permeability but reduces strength
Water content is irrelevant to cartilage mechanics
Water content decreases permeability under load
items.e: Increased water content raises permeability and lowers compressive strength; loss of proteoglycans early in OA reduces water retention and compromises cartilage integrity.

items.q: Which zone of articular cartilage contains the highest density of chondrocytes?
items.e: The superficial zone has the highest chondrocyte density, contributing to shear resistance and lubrication through lubricin secretion.

items.q: A surgeon fixes a comminuted metadiaphyseal fracture in osteoporotic bone with a locking plate. Which biomechanical feature of the locking construct is primarily exploited?
o: Compression of the plate against bone to generate friction
Interfragmentary compression by lag screws through the plate
Conversion of the plate into a tension band
A fixed-angle construct (internal fixator) that does not rely on plate-bone friction
items.e: Locking screws thread into the plate, creating a fixed-angle construct that transmits load through the screw-plate interface rather than plate-bone friction, which preserves periosteal blood supply and resists screw toggling in osteoporotic bone.

items.q: Regarding a cortical screw hole in a long-bone shaft, which statement is FALSE?
o: The hole acts as a stress riser
An open-section defect reduces torsional strength far more than a round hole
The stress concentration is independent of the shape of the defect
The stress-riser effect persists until the hole fills with new bone
items.e: Stress concentration depends on defect geometry: an open-section (slot) defect reduces torsional strength dramatically, while a small round hole has a smaller effect; the stress riser remains until the hole remodels.

items.q: After a crush injury of the wrist with median nerve palsy, tapping over the nerve 3 weeks later produces tingling in the index finger; over the next 4 weeks the point of maximal tingling moves distally. This advancing Tinel sign indicates:
o: Wallerian degeneration of the distal stump
Regenerating axons advancing after an axonotmetic injury
items.e: An advancing Tinel sign tracks regenerating axon sprouts (about 1 mm/day) and is a favourable sign seen in axonotmesis (Sunderland II-III); a static Tinel suggests a neuroma.

items.q: Which peripheral nerve fibre type transmits the primary afferent signal from a muscle spindle that initiates the stretch reflex?
items.e: Primary spindle afferents are large, myelinated Ia fibres, classed as A‑alpha.

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between the perineurium and nerve compression injuries?
o: Damage to the perineurium always results in loss of all fascicles
The perineurium provides the primary tensile strength of the nerve
The perineurium acts as a blood‑nerve barrier but does not influence mechanical strength
Cutting the perineurium leads to immediate axonal regeneration of all fascicles
items.e: The perineurium is the main source of tensile strength and maintains intrafascicular pressure; it also forms the blood‑nerve barrier.

items.q: A systematic review includes only cohort studies that report an adjusted odds ratio for implant loosening. According to GRADE, how should the quality of the evidence initially be rated?
items.e: Observational studies start as low‑grade evidence in GRADE.

items.q: A clinician asks whether a newly developed joint replacement implant is likely to be at least as effective as the standard implant within a 5% margin. Which trial type is appropriate?
items.e: A non‑inferiority trial tests that the new treatment is not worse than the standard by more than a predefined margin.

items.q: An orthopedic trainee notes that the scatter dose to the surgeon’s hands is negligible when a lead apron is worn. What is the most accurate statement regarding hand exposure?
o: Lead gloves completely eliminate hand dose
Hands are safest when kept outside the primary beam
Scatter dose to the hand is always lower than to the chest
The apron provides no protection to the arms
items.e: Hands must stay out of the primary beam; otherwise the x‑ray tube increases output to maintain image quality, raising the overall dose. Lead gloves are ineffective and can be misleading.

items.q: Which physical interaction contributes most to image contrast in conventional radiography of bone?
items.e: The photoelectric effect (probability ∝ Z³/E³) is dominant at the low energies used for bone imaging and provides differential absorption that forms image contrast.

items.q: A 66-year-old woman listed for elective total knee arthroplasty has an HbA1c of 8.6%. What is the most appropriate step to reduce her periprosthetic joint infection risk?
o: Proceed with surgery using a perioperative insulin sliding scale
Defer surgery and optimise glycaemic control before proceeding
Proceed and extend prophylactic antibiotics to 7 days
items.e: Poor glycaemic control (HbA1c above roughly 7.5-8%) increases PJI and wound complications, so elective arthroplasty should be postponed while control is optimised. Prolonged antibiotics do not reduce PJI.

items.q: During the induction of general anaesthesia for a total joint replacement, the surgeon asks you to administer a perioperative antibiotic. The patient has a documented penicillin allergy with a history of non‑severe rash only. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
o: Cefazolin 2 g IV plus vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV
items.e: Cefazolin can be safely used in patients with non‑severe penicillin allergy; cross‑reactivity is low. The other options are unnecessary or adjunctive.

items.q: What is the mechanism of red man (vancomycin flushing) syndrome?
o: Rapid renal clearance of the drug
Non-IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells related to infusion rate
IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity in all cases
items.e: Rapid vancomycin infusion directly degranulates mast cells, releasing histamine and causing flushing, pruritus and hypotension; slowing the infusion (over at least 60 minutes) and antihistamines prevent it.

items.q: In the Cierny-Mader host classification, which is a LOCAL (Bl) compromising factor?
items.e: Local (Bl) factors include chronic lymphoedema, venous stasis, major vessel disease, extensive scarring and radiation fibrosis; diabetes, renal or hepatic failure and malnutrition are systemic (Bs) factors.

items.q: An MRI of the lumbar spine shows a large, thin‑walled paraspinal abscess extending across three vertebral bodies with sparing of the intervertebral disc. Which diagnosis does this imaging feature most strongly suggest?
items.e: Tuberculous spondylitis characteristically forms large, well‑defined, thin‑walled abscesses that spread under the anterior longitudinal ligament and skip vertebrae, while pyogenic infection produces smaller, thick‑walled, ill‑defined collections.

items.q: Which of the following is a contraindication for starting an oral bisphosphonate?
o: Achalasia with inability to stay upright for 30 min
items.e: Achalasia precludes the required upright position after ingestion; this is an absolute contraindication.

items.q: A 52‑year‑old man presents with sudden, excruciating pain and swelling of the second metatarsophalangeal joint after a night of heavy beer consumption. His serum urate is 7.2 mg/dL. Which of the following investigations would conclusively confirm the diagnosis?
o: Synovial fluid analysis under compensated polarised light microscopy
items.e: Synovial fluid analysis with compensated polarised light microscopy is the gold standard; it will show negatively birefringent, needle‑shaped MSU crystals in gout.

items.q: What is the most common neurological complication of Paget disease of the skull?
items.e: Hearing loss (conductive from ossicular involvement and sensorineural from cochlear/petrous bone involvement) is the commonest neurological complication of skull Paget disease; basilar invagination and cranial nerve palsies are less common.

items.q: Pagetic bone is enlarged yet mechanically weaker than normal bone. What best explains this?
o: Disorganised mosaic woven and lamellar bone from chaotic, uncoupled remodelling
items.e: Excessive osteoclastic resorption followed by rapid disorganised formation produces a mosaic pattern of woven and lamellar bone with cement lines, which is bulky but structurally weak and prone to bowing and fissure fractures.

items.q: When is a bone biopsy indicated in a patient with suspected Paget disease?
items.e: Biopsy is performed only if sarcoma, metastasis or diagnostic uncertainty is suspected.

items.q: Which radiographic sign is NOT a feature of Paget disease of bone?
items.e: Rugger-jersey spine (endplate sclerosis) is a sign of renal osteodystrophy/secondary hyperparathyroidism. Picture-frame vertebra, cotton-wool skull and the blade-of-grass (flame) lytic front are classic Paget signs.

items.q: Which of the following laboratory investigations is most appropriate to screen for an underlying coagulopathy in a patient with multifocal osteonecrosis?
o: Coagulation profile with factor V Leiden PCR
Serum calcium with vitamin D level
items.e: A coagulation profile including factor V Leiden (and other thrombophilias) is essential in multifocal osteonecrosis to identify underlying hypercoagulable states.

items.q: In isolated osteoblast cultures, the addition of an antibody that blocks sclerostin leads to:
items.e: Sclerostin antagonises the Wnt/LRP5/6 pathway; blocking it restores beta‑catenin signalling, thereby stimulating osteoblast proliferation and activity.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman stops denosumab after 4 years without any follow-on therapy. Nine months later she sustains multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures. What explains this?
o: Development of neutralising antibodies to denosumab
Rebound surge in osteoclast activity after loss of RANKL inhibition
Excess osteoid accumulation from osteoblast overactivity
items.e: Denosumab's effect wanes within months of the last dose, causing rebound high bone turnover and rapid bone loss with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures; a bisphosphonate should be started when denosumab is stopped.

items.q: During bone mineralisation, matrix vesicles from osteoblasts initiate formation of which mineral that is then deposited in the hole zones of collagen fibrils?
items.e: Matrix vesicles concentrate calcium and phosphate (and contain alkaline phosphatase, which removes the inhibitor pyrophosphate) to nucleate hydroxyapatite crystals, which then grow in the gap zones of type I collagen.

items.q: A 6‑month‑old girl with hypophosphataemic rickets shows mutation in which gene coding for a protein that regulates osteocyte‑derived FGF23?
items.e: Mutations in PHEX impair degradation of FGF23, causing increased phosphaturia and hypophosphataemic rickets.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a major catabolic cytokine involved in cartilage matrix degradation?
items.e: TGF‑β is an anabolic cytokine that promotes matrix synthesis; the others stimulate MMPs and aggrecanases.

items.q: A patient with primary synovial chondromatosis will most likely exhibit which of the following histological findings?
o: Calcified bone fragments embedded in synovial fluid
Cartilage nodules arising from synovial lining
items.e: Synovial cells undergo metaplasia into cartilage nodules that detach and later calcify.

items.q: A simple diaphyseal fracture fixed with a bridging locking plate has an interfragmentary strain of about 8%. According to Perren's strain theory, the fracture will heal by:
o: Fibrous tissue only, non-union is inevitable
items.e: Strain below about 2% allows primary bone healing, 2-10% allows secondary healing via callus (cartilage tolerates up to about 10%), and strain above 10% permits only granulation tissue.

items.q: Cobalt-chrome alloy is chosen for the femoral component of a total knee arthroplasty mainly because of which property?
items.e: Cobalt-chrome is hard, polishes well and resists scratching, so it gives low polyethylene wear as a bearing surface; titanium is softer and prone to scratching, so it is not used as an articulating surface.

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between axonal diameter and conduction velocity?
o: Velocity increases with increasing diameter only in unmyelinated fibres.
Velocity is independent of diameter in myelinated fibres.
Velocity increases with increasing diameter and myelination.
items.e: Conduction velocity rises with both axonal diameter and the degree of myelination; larger, well‑myelinated axons conduct fastest.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the difference between an explanatory and a pragmatic randomized controlled trial?
o: Explanatory trials use placebo controls; pragmatic trials do not
Explanatory trials test efficacy under ideal conditions; pragmatic trials test effectiveness in routine practice
Pragmatic trials randomise only healthy volunteers; explanatory trials randomise patients
Explanatory trials are always non‑inferiority; pragmatic trials are superiority
items.e: Explanatory trials assess whether an intervention works in controlled, ideal settings, whereas pragmatic trials evaluate how it performs in real‑world clinical practice.

items.q: In a prospective cohort study, investigators match patients on age but not on gender. Which bias is now most likely to affect the association between the exposure and the outcome?
items.e: Matching on age controls for that confounder, but gender remains unbalanced and can confound the exposure‑outcome relationship.

items.q: A 68-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day, with well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c 6.9%) and a BMI of 30, is listed for elective total hip arthroplasty. Which preoperative step most reduces his risk of wound complications and periprosthetic infection?
o: Smoking cessation at least 4 weeks before surgery
Starting an additional oral hypoglycaemic 1 week before surgery
items.e: Stopping smoking at least 4 weeks before surgery improves tissue oxygenation and reduces wound complications and surgical site infection; his diabetes is already well controlled.

items.q: A surgeon prepares a local‑depot antibiotic‑laden cement spacer for a two‑stage revision of a knee prosthesis infected with *Staphylococcus aureus*. The spacer contains 1 g of vancomycin per 40 g of cement. Which statement best describes the expected pharmacokinetics of vancomycin released from this preparation?
o: It will remain fully active for at least 6 months
It releases a peak concentration in the first 24 h and then declines rapidly
It provides systemic levels equivalent to intravenous dosing
It is ineffective because heat‑stable antibiotics cannot be mixed with cement
items.e: Vancomycin is heat‑stable and is released from cement immediately after setting, with a high peak in the first 24 h that then declines; it does not achieve systemic levels comparable to IV therapy.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old IV drug user develops fever and a swollen knee. Synovial fluid analysis shows 150 000 WBCs/µl, predominantly polymorphs, and Gram stain reveals Gram‑negative rods. Which organism is most likely?
items.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic pathogen in septic arthritis of IV drug users, especially causing acute, painful, swollen joints.

items.q: Which statement about chronic osteomyelitis is FALSE?
o: A sequestrum is an avascular fragment of dead bone
An involucrum is reactive periosteal new bone surrounding the dead bone
A cloaca is an opening in the involucrum through which pus discharges
Sinus tracts always arise from the periosteal surface without communicating with the medullary cavity
items.e: Sinus tracts in chronic osteomyelitis communicate with the infected medullary cavity, usually through cloacae in the involucrum; the other statements are correct definitions.

items.q: An adolescent girl from a rural area with short stature, scoliosis and a history of delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle is diagnosed with rickets. Which laboratory investigation is most useful to decide the next step in management?
items.e: Serum 25(OH)D is the best marker of vitamin D status and guides supplementation. It is more useful than 1,25(OH)₂D in nutritional rickets.

items.q: A 38-year-old man with no family history has 2 years of progressive bone pain and proximal muscle weakness. Radiographs show a femoral pseudofracture. Serum phosphate is low, calcium normal, 1,25(OH)2D low and FGF23 raised. What is the most likely cause?
items.e: Adult-onset hypophosphataemic osteomalacia with high FGF23 and low 1,25(OH)2D and no family history suggests tumour-induced osteomalacia, usually from a small phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour located with Ga-68 DOTATATE PET; excision is curative.

items.q: Which of the following statements BEST describes the defect in vitamin D–dependent rickets type 1A?
o: Defect in the vitamin D receptor
items.e: VDDR 1A is due to a recessive mutation in CYP27B1, the enzyme that converts 25(OH)D to the active 1,25(OH)₂D. Resistance to calcitriol is seen in type 2, not type 1A.

items.q: A 65-year-old woman on alendronate 70 mg weekly develops new dysphagia and odynophagia. What is the most likely cause and appropriate action?
o: Osteonecrosis of the jaw; refer for dental implant
Atypical femoral fracture; obtain full-length femur radiographs
Pill oesophagitis; stop alendronate and switch to a parenteral agent such as zoledronate or denosumab
Acute phase reaction; give an antihistamine before the next dose
items.e: Oral bisphosphonates can cause erosive oesophagitis, especially if not taken upright with plenty of water; with symptoms the drug should be stopped and a parenteral agent used instead.

items.q: Which patient is the most appropriate candidate for first-line anabolic therapy such as teriparatide?
o: 58-year-old man with T-score -2.4 and no fractures
70-year-old woman with T-score -1.8, no fractures and low FRAX
80-year-old woman with multiple prior vertebral fractures and T-score -3.2
62-year-old woman with T-score -2.6 and no fractures
items.e: Anabolic agents are prioritised for very high fracture risk: multiple or recent fragility fractures, T-score below -3.0, or very high FRAX. The others are managed with antiresorptives or observation.

items.q: Which of the following imaging techniques is best for detecting monosodium urate deposits when aspiration is impractical?
items.e: DECT colour‑codes the urate deposits, providing a sensitive and specific imaging method for gout when joint aspiration cannot be performed.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man presents with thigh pain that worsens at night. X‑ray of the femur shows bowing with a transverse ‘banana‑shaped’ fracture. His serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised, calcium and phosphate normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The classic ‘banana’ fracture (transverse subtrochanteric) in a patient with high ALP and normal calcium/phosphate points to Paget disease where the bone is enlarged yet weak.

items.q: Which complication of Paget disease most often improves with bisphosphonate therapy, sometimes avoiding surgery?
o: Spinal stenosis/cord compression from pagetic vertebrae
items.e: Neurological compromise from pagetic vertebrae is partly due to hypervascular bone and vascular steal, so bisphosphonates often improve it; established deformity and deafness do not reverse.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old patient with progressive femoral bowing develops a painful, incomplete fracture on the convex side. Which statement best describes this fracture?
o: It is an osteoporotic wedge fracture
items.e: In Paget-affected long bones, the convex (tension) side is prone to fissure or stress fractures, which are painful and precede complete breakage.

items.q: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman on denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 3 years abruptly discontinues the injections. Eight months after her last dose, she presents with severe back pain due to multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures. To avoid this known rebound effect, which protocol should be instituted upon stopping denosumab?
o: Transition to an antiresorptive agent such as zoledronate approximately 6 months after the last dose
Institute an obligatory 2- to 3-year drug holiday
Re-evaluate DXA at 1 year and start raloxifene only if T-score falls
items.e: Discontinuing denosumab causes a rebound surge in bone turnover, rapid bone mineral density loss, and an increased risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures within months. Denosumab should never be stopped without follow-on antiresorptive therapy, typically an infusion of zoledronate given about 6 months after the last denosumab injection.

items.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as alendronate and zoledronate reduce bone resorption predominantly by inhibiting which of the following biochemical targets?
o: Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway
Carbonic anhydrase type II in the osteoclast ruffled border
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases essential for osteoclast ruffled border maintenance and survival, leading to osteoclast apoptosis.

items.q: Romosozumab is a dual-action monoclonal antibody targeting sclerostin that promotes bone formation while decreasing bone resorption. Based on clinical trials, it is contraindicated in patients with:
o: Estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min
Myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding 12 months
Pre-existing osteopenia with prior deep venous thrombosis
Unexplained elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase
items.e: In the ARCH trial, romosozumab significantly reduced fracture risk but demonstrated an imbalance in serious cardiovascular adverse events (myocardial infarction and stroke). Consequently, it is contraindicated in patients who have had a myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding 12 months.

items.q: In which landmark clinical trial did an annual infusion of zoledronic acid (5 mg IV) administered after surgical repair of a low-trauma hip fracture demonstrate a significant reduction in all-cause mortality as well as new clinical fractures?
items.e: The HORIZON-RFT (Recurrent Fracture Trial) evaluated annual 5 mg zoledronic acid infusions initiated within 90 days of surgical fixation of a low-trauma hip fracture. It demonstrated a 35% reduction in new clinical fractures and a 28% reduction in all-cause mortality.

items.q: Regarding sequential osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, which of the following drug transitions causes a progressive or transient loss of bone mineral density, particularly at the hip, as demonstrated in the DATA-Switch trial?
o: Switching from denosumab to teriparatide monotherapy
items.e: The DATA-Switch study showed that transitioning patients from denosumab to teriparatide monotherapy leads to a transient or progressive decline in BMD, especially at cortical-rich sites like the hip. Conversely, anabolic therapy followed by an antiresorptive agent (teriparatide followed by denosumab) preserves and further increases BMD.

items.q: According to the ASBMR guidelines on osteoporosis management, at what treatment duration should low-to-moderate risk patients routinely be reassessed for a bisphosphonate 'drug holiday'?
o: After 5 years of oral or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
After 3 years of oral or 5 years of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
After 2 years of oral or 1 year of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
After 10 years of oral or 6 years of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
items.e: The ASBMR Task Force recommends reassessing fracture risk after 5 years of oral bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronate). If the patient is not at high risk (femoral neck T-score > -2.5 and no incident fractures), a drug holiday of 2 to 3 years can be considered.

items.q: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute severe neck pain, rigid cervical stiffness, and a low-grade fever mimicking meningitis. Cervical CT reveals curvilinear calcification around the odontoid process involving the transverse atlantal ligament (crowned dens syndrome). Analysis of synovial fluid from a concomitant acute arthritis of her knee is most likely to demonstrate which type of crystal?
o: Needle-shaped crystals with strongly negative birefringence
Rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence
Non-birefringent crystal aggregates staining positive with alizarin red S
Bipyramidal envelope-shaped crystals with positive birefringence
items.e: Crowned dens syndrome is an axial manifestation of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) caused by CPP crystal deposition around the odontoid process. CPPD crystals are characteristically rhomboid- or rod-shaped and exhibit weak positive birefringence under polarised light microscopy.

items.q: Which of the following radiographic abnormalities is characteristic of chronic tophaceous gout and helps distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
Marginal erosions localized strictly to synovial bare areas
items.e: Chronic gout classically produces punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic borders and overhanging margins (Martel sign or 'rat-bite' erosions). In contrast to rheumatoid arthritis, gout characteristically preserves the joint space until late stages and lacks periarticular osteopenia.

items.q: A 55-year-old man with severe, refractory chronic tophaceous gout is being evaluated for therapy with pegloticase. Which of the following baseline laboratory tests is mandatory before starting pegloticase to prevent life-threatening haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia?
items.e: Pegloticase is a recombinant uricase that oxidises uric acid to allantoin and produces hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct. Patients with G6PD deficiency are at high risk of severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, making baseline G6PD screening essential before therapy.

items.q: In the staging of calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff described by Uhthoff, during which stage does the patient typically experience the most severe, excruciating pain?
items.e: The resorptive phase of the calcific stage is characterised by vascular and macrophage invasion with a toothpaste-like deposit under high pressure. This marked inflammatory reaction makes the resorptive phase the most painful clinical stage, often leading to spontaneous bursal rupture.

items.q: Under compensated polarised light microscopy, which optical characteristic correctly identifies monosodium urate (MSU) crystals?
o: Blue coloration when aligned parallel to the compensator axis (positive birefringence)
Yellow coloration when aligned perpendicular to the compensator axis (negative birefringence)
Blue coloration when aligned perpendicular to the compensator axis (positive birefringence)
Yellow coloration when aligned parallel to the compensator axis (negative birefringence)
items.e: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and show strong negative birefringence; they appear yellow when aligned parallel to the slow axis of the compensator and turn blue when perpendicular. In contrast, calcium pyrophosphate crystals are weakly positively birefringent and turn blue when parallel.

items.q: On musculoskeletal ultrasound examination of an inflamed joint, the 'double contour sign' is characteristic of which underlying pathology?
o: Monosodium urate crystals coating the outer surface of hyaline cartilage
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals embedded within the mid-substance of hyaline cartilage
Basic calcium phosphate deposition within the deep substance of the rotator cuff tendon
Linear calcification along the triangular fibrocartilage complex of the wrist
items.e: The 'double contour sign' on ultrasound is produced by a hyperechoic band of monosodium urate crystals coating the superficial surface of articular hyaline cartilage, overlying the deeper hyperechoic subchondral bone. In CPPD, crystal deposition occurs within the cartilage layer rather than on its surface.

items.q: A 62-year-old man presents with deep, aching pelvic pain that is worse at night. Radiographs reveal coarse trabecular thickening and an enlarged iliopectineal line ("brim sign"). Genetic analysis identifies a mutation in the SQSTM1 gene encoding p62. This protein plays a critical regulatory role in which of the following osteoclastic signalling pathways?
items.e: SQSTM1 encodes sequestosome-1 (p62), an important scaffold protein in the RANK/NF-kappa-B pathway of osteoclasts. Mutations in SQSTM1 are found in approximately 40% of familial and 5-10% of sporadic cases of Paget disease.

items.q: A 74-year-old woman with active polyostotic Paget disease sustains an acute, displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture following a minor fall. What is the recommended definitive management for this specific injury in pagetic bone?
o: Dynamic hip screw with a derotation screw
items.e: Femoral neck fractures in pagetic bone carry an exceptionally high rate of non-union and delayed union with internal fixation. Therefore, arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty) is the preferred management rather than osteosynthesis.

items.q: The landmark PRISM trial (Langston et al., 2010) evaluated intensive bisphosphonate therapy aimed at normalising serum alkaline phosphatase versus symptom-directed therapy in Paget disease. What did this trial establish?
o: Intensive therapy significantly reduced fracture risk and the need for orthopaedic surgery
Intensive therapy arrested the progression of sensorineural deafness
Intensive therapy significantly improved clinical quality of life and pain scores
There was no clinical benefit in treating asymptomatic patients simply to normalise alkaline phosphatase
items.e: The PRISM trial demonstrated that intensive bisphosphonate treatment aiming to normalise ALP did not reduce fractures, orthopaedic surgery, hearing loss, or improve quality of life compared with symptomatic treatment. Consequently, international guidelines do not recommend treating asymptomatic Paget disease purely to normalise biochemical markers.

items.q: A 54-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on maintenance haemodialysis sustains a low-energy metatarsal fracture. Transiliac bone biopsy demonstrates low bone turnover, diminished cellular activity, and reduced osteoid volume without aluminium accumulation. Which histological subtype is currently the commonest form of renal osteodystrophy in this setting?
items.e: Adynamic bone disease has become the commonest histological subtype of renal osteodystrophy in dialysis patients. It is characterised by low bone turnover and suppressed parathyroid hormone levels, often exacerbated by dialysis, diabetes, and over-suppression from calcium and active vitamin D therapy.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with persistent thigh pain and is diagnosed with an incomplete lateral subtrochanteric pseudofracture. Laboratory evaluation shows an abnormally low total serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) along with elevated urinary phosphoethanolamine. Which of the following treatments is strictly CONTRAINDICATED in this condition?
items.e: The patient has adult hypophosphatasia (mutation in ALPL). Bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogues that further inhibit bone mineralisation, worsening the mineralisation defect and predisposing to atypical or complete fractures; they are strictly contraindicated.

items.q: A 52-year-old man from an endemic region presents with axial stiffness, reduced chest expansion, and progressive compressive myelopathy. Radiographs reveal diffuse osteosclerosis of the spine and pelvis. Which of the following imaging features is characteristic of skeletal fluorosis and helps distinguish it from other osteosclerotic entities?
o: Subperiosteal resorption on the radial aspect of the middle phalanges
Expansion of the vertebral body with thick peripheral cortices ("picture frame" vertebra)
Calcification and ossification of the interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg
Sclerotic endplate bands with a radiolucent central vertebral body ("rugger-jersey" spine)
items.e: Skeletal fluorosis typically manifests with diffuse osteosclerosis along with prominent calcification and ossification of ligaments and interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg. Subperiosteal resorption indicates hyperparathyroidism, picture-frame vertebrae indicate Paget disease, and rugger-jersey spine indicates renal osteodystrophy.

items.q: During surgical dislocation of the hip via the Ganz approach, safe preservation of the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) relies on its consistent anatomical path. What is the relationship of this vessel to the surrounding musculature?
o: It runs anterior to the obturator externus and posterior to the short external rotators
It passes posterior to the obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators
It passes superior to the piriformis and anterior to the gluteus minimus
It courses inferior to the quadratus femoris and superficial to the obturator internus
items.e: The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) passes posterior to the obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators (gemelli and obturator internus). This precise relationship forms the anatomical basis of the Ganz surgical dislocation approach, preserving femoral head perfusion.

items.q: A 36-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with deep groin pain after high-dose corticosteroid therapy. Plain radiographs of the pelvis are unremarkable. Which MRI feature, if present, is pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: A T2 double-line sign consisting of an inner high-signal band and an outer low-signal band
Diffuse marrow oedema extending from the femoral head down into the intertrochanteric line
A subchondral low-signal fracture line that is convex toward the articular surface
Homogeneous high T1 signal intensity throughout the entire femoral epiphysis
items.e: On T2-weighted MRI, the 'double-line sign' is pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head. It consists of an inner high-signal line of hyperaemic granulation tissue adjacent to an outer low-signal line of sclerotic bone.

items.q: A 32-year-old man has pre-collapse osteonecrosis of the femoral head. To assess the risk of subchondral collapse, the modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle is measured on MRI. Which necrotic angle threshold designates a 'high risk' of collapse?
items.e: The modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle sums the necrotic arcs on mid-coronal and mid-sagittal MRI. An angle under 190 degrees represents low risk, 190–239 degrees indicates intermediate risk, and 240 degrees or greater designates a high risk of collapse.

items.q: A 29-year-old woman in her 34th week of pregnancy presents with acute left hip pain. Radiographs demonstrate subtle regional osteopenia. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema throughout the femoral head and neck extending into the intertrochanteric region, with no focal subchondral band or double-line sign. What is the management of choice?
o: Urgent core decompression combined with autologous bone marrow aspirate concentrate
Protected weight bearing and analgesia with observation
items.e: The presentation and imaging are classic for transient osteoporosis of the hip, which typically occurs in the third trimester of pregnancy and shows diffuse marrow oedema without a focal subchondral band or double line. It is self-limiting over 6–12 months, and management is conservative with protected weight bearing to prevent femoral neck fracture.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman presents with sudden, severe medial knee pain and night pain. Weight-bearing radiographs show subtle focal flattening of the medial femoral condyle. What is a well-established clinicopathological feature of spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK / SIFK)?
o: It is characterised by multiple bilateral lesions extending into the metaphysis and diaphysis
It is a true primary ischaemic necrosis that most commonly affects patients under 45 years of age
Lesions involving under 40% of condylar width invariably collapse and require total knee arthroplasty
It represents a subchondral insufficiency fracture and is frequently associated with a medial meniscus posterior root tear
items.e: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK) is pathologically a subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIFK) rather than primary ischaemic necrosis. It classically affects women over 55–60 years and is frequently associated with posterior root tears of the medial meniscus.

items.q: A 12-year-old child presents with limping and hip pain, diagnosed with Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE). Disruption of the physis in this condition typically occurs primarily through which zone?
items.e: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), Rickets, and standard Salter-Harris fractures predominantly occur through the hypertrophic zone (specifically the zone of provisional calcification), which is the mechanically weakest region of the growth plate.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with severe juvenile osteoporosis and visual impairment due to ocular vascular developmental defects. Genetic analysis reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) gene. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
items.e: Loss-of-function mutations in LRP5 impair Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome. In contrast, gain-of-function LRP5 mutations lead to high bone mass, loss of sclerostin (SOST) causes sclerosteosis/Van Buchem disease, and RUNX2 mutations cause cleidocranial dysplasia.

items.q: A 30-year-old male sustains a displaced midshaft femoral fracture and undergoes reamed intramedullary nailing. How does cortical bone blood flow change immediately following reaming of the medullary canal?
o: Flow reverses from centrifugal to centripetal, relying on periosteal supply
Flow reverses from centripetal to centrifugal, relying on endosteal supply
Endosteal flow increases fourfold with complete cessation of periosteal flow
Both endosteal and periosteal blood flow cease completely
items.e: Normal cortical bone blood flow is centrifugal (inside-to-outside), supplied primarily by the high-pressure endosteal nutrient system (inner two-thirds). Displaced fractures or reaming disrupt the endosteal supply, reversing blood flow to centripetal (outside-to-inside) as the periosteal supply (outer one-third) takes over.

items.q: A 6-month-old infant with osteopetrosis is found to have a homozygous mutation in the TCIRG1 gene encoding the a3 subunit of the vacuolar H+ ATPase proton pump. This specific defect directly impairs bone resorption by disrupting the function of which osteoclast structure?
items.e: The vacuolar H+ ATPase proton pump is localized to the ruffled border of osteoclasts to acidify the resorption compartment. Mutations in TCIRG1 or CLCN7 disrupt proton pump and chloride channel function at the ruffled border, preventing mineral dissolution and causing osteopetrosis.

items.q: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis starts antiresorptive therapy. To monitor treatment adherence and early biological response, which pair of turnover markers is recommended by the IOF and IFCC as standard reference markers?
o: Serum bone-specific ALP and urinary hydroxyproline
items.e: The International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF) and International Federation of Clinical Chemistry (IFCC) recommend serum procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (P1NP) as the standard formation marker and serum C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX) as the standard resorption marker.

items.q: A 35-year-old male undergoes the first-stage procedure of the Masquelet induced-membrane technique for a 7 cm segmental tibial defect using a PMMA spacer. At what timeframe does the bioactivity and growth factor release of the induced membrane peak for placing the secondary bone graft?
items.e: In the Masquelet induced-membrane technique, the foreign body membrane formed around the PMMA spacer reaches peak vascularity and bioactivity (releasing VEGF, TGF-beta, and BMP-2) between 4 and 8 weeks, which is the optimal window for secondary cancellous autografting.

items.q: A spine surgeon evaluates recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) for off-label use in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). Which severe complication led to a specific FDA warning against using rhBMP-2 in this region?
items.e: rhBMP-2 can induce marked local inflammatory soft-tissue swelling and seroma formation. In anterior cervical spine surgery, this swelling can cause life-threatening airway compromise and severe dysphagia, prompting an FDA safety warning.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete undergoes microfracture for a full-thickness chondral defect on the medial femoral condyle. Which predominant tissue type forms to repair the defect following marrow stimulation?
o: Fibrocartilage composed primarily of Type I collagen
Hyaline cartilage composed primarily of Type II collagen
Elastic cartilage composed of Type II collagen and elastin
Calcified cartilage rich in Type X collagen
items.e: Marrow stimulation procedures breach the subchondral bone plate, releasing bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells that form a clot maturing into fibrocartilage (composed mostly of type I collagen). Fibrocartilage is mechanically inferior to hyaline cartilage (type II collagen) and degrades over time.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes Type A synoviocytes located in the intimal layer of the synovial membrane?
o: They are mesenchymal fibroblast-like cells that produce hyaluronic acid and lubricin.
They form tight junctions sitting on a continuous basement membrane.
They secrete large amounts of fibrinogen into normal non-inflammatory synovial fluid.
They are bone marrow-derived cells of monocyte lineage that perform phagocytic functions.
items.e: Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-like cells derived from bone marrow monocytes (expressing CD68) that function in phagocytosis and antigen presentation. Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like mesenchymal cells that synthesize hyaluronic acid and lubricin.

items.q: A 58-year-old man presents with acute knee pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis shows cloudy yellow fluid with a WBC count of 38,000/mm³. Polarised light microscopy reveals weakly positive, blue birefringent, rod- and rhomboid-shaped crystals when aligned parallel to the compensator axis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals are rhomboid or rod-shaped with weak positive birefringence (appearing blue when parallel to the red compensator axis). Monosodium urate crystals in gout are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel).

items.q: Which zone of articular cartilage contains round chondrocytes arranged in vertical columns, collagen fibrils oriented perpendicular to the surface, the highest proteoglycan content, and the lowest water content?
items.e: The deep (radial) zone makes up about 30% of articular cartilage and features round chondrocytes in vertical columns with perpendicular collagen fibrils. It contains the highest proteoglycan content and lowest water content to resist compressive forces.
