items.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent atraumatic bloody knee effusions. Gradient-echo MRI demonstrates nodular synovial masses with low signal intensity on T1 and T2 images and prominent 'blooming' artifact. Cytogenetics reveals a translocation causing CSF1 overexpression. What is the diagnosis?
o: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (Pigmented villonodular synovitis)
items.e: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS) is driven by a CSF1 gene translocation that overexpresses CSF1. Haemosiderin accumulation from recurrent haemorrhagic effusions produces characteristic low T1/T2 MRI signals with blooming artifacts on gradient-echo sequences.

items.q: During dynamic joint motion under high cyclic loading, which mode of fluid-film lubrication is considered the primary mechanism preventing direct cartilage contact by generating fluid pressurisation as cartilage deforms?
o: Boundary lubrication mediated by hyaluronic acid
items.e: Elastohydrodynamic lubrication is the main mode of fluid-film lubrication during dynamic joint motion. The deformable nature of articular cartilage increases contact area under load and traps a pressurized fluid film between moving joint surfaces.

items.q: Specific catabolic enzymes drive cartilage matrix degradation in osteoarthritis. Which enzyme is primarily responsible for the enzymatic cleavage and breakdown of Type II collagen fibrils?
items.e: MMP-13 (collagenase-3) is the principal matrix metalloproteinase responsible for degrading type II collagen fibrils in articular cartilage. ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5 are aggrecanases that specifically cleave aggrecan proteoglycans.

items.q: A 65-year-old male with symptomatic right hip osteoarthritis is advised on non-operative management strategies to decrease hip joint reaction forces during walking. Which of the following recommendations is biomechanically correct?
o: Hold a walking cane in the ipsilateral (right) hand
Hold a walking cane in the contralateral (left) hand
Carry heavy grocery bags in the contralateral (left) hand
Lean the torso toward the contralateral side during stance phase
items.e: Holding a walking cane in the contralateral hand provides a long lever arm relative to the hip joint, reducing the required abductor muscle force and decreasing joint reaction force by up to 40–60%. Conversely, carrying loads in the contralateral hand increases joint reaction force, while holding loads in the ipsilateral hand reduces it.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon is assembling a monoplanar external fixator for an unstable open tibial shaft fracture. To achieve the single most effective increase in construct bending stiffness, which modification should be implemented?
o: Increase the diameter of the Schanz pins
Place the connecting bar further away from the bone
Decrease the distance between the two pins within the proximal fragment
items.e: Increasing pin diameter provides the greatest increase in external fixator stiffness because bending stiffness is proportional to the pin radius to the fourth power (r^4). Placing the connecting bar closer to bone and spreading pins wider apart within each fragment also increase stiffness.

items.q: According to Perren's strain theory, what interfragmentary strain environment is required to stimulate secondary (indirect) bone healing with callus formation?
items.e: Interfragmentary strain between 2% and 10% promotes secondary (indirect) bone healing with callus under conditions of relative stability. Strain under 2% leads to primary bone healing, whereas strain exceeding 10% results in non-union and tissue breakdown.

items.q: Stress shielding around joint replacements occurs when load is preferentially borne by a stiff implant rather than host bone. Which metallic biomaterial has a Young's modulus of elasticity closest to that of cortical bone (~15–20 GPa)?
items.e: Titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) has a Young's modulus of elasticity of approximately 110 GPa, which is the lowest among common implant metals and closest to cortical bone (15–20 GPa), thereby reducing stress shielding. Stainless steel (~190–200 GPa), Cobalt-chromium (~210–230 GPa), and Alumina (~350–400 GPa) are substantially stiffer.

items.q: During the processing of highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) for total hip arthroplasty, thermal treatment above the melting point (remelting) is performed after irradiation. What is the primary mechanical disadvantage of remelting?
o: Reduces fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength of the material
Leaves abundant residual free radicals causing rapid oxidation and delamination
Increases adhesive and abrasive wear rates compared to conventional non-irradiated polyethylene
Triggers an acute cytotoxic immune response upon joint implantation
items.e: Remelting HXLPE above its melting point eliminates residual free radicals (preventing oxidation), but it alters the crystalline structure, thereby reducing mechanical properties such as fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength. Annealing below the melting point preserves strength but leaves residual free radicals.

items.q: A 70-year-old male with a total hip arthroplasty (modular CoCr femoral head on a titanium alloy stem) presents with hip discomfort. Diagnostic workup reveals mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC / trunnionosis) at the head-neck taper. Which serum ion pattern is classic for this condition?
o: Isolated elevation of serum titanium ions only
Serum cobalt elevation significantly greater than serum chromium elevation
Serum chromium elevation significantly greater than serum cobalt elevation
Equal elevation of serum nickel and iron ions with normal cobalt
items.e: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC / trunnionosis) at a modular taper interface (CoCr head on Ti stem) characteristically causes preferential release of cobalt into the circulation, resulting in elevated serum cobalt levels that are significantly higher than serum chromium levels.

items.q: When performing a biopsy of a long bone tumor, creating an open-section longitudinal rectangular cortical window drastically reduces structural strength. Which loading mode suffers the most severe reduction in strength (up to 90%) from an open-section defect?
items.e: An open-section defect (a longitudinal cortical slot or window) severely impairs the bone's cross-sectional geometry and polar moment of inertia, reducing torsional strength by up to 90%. For this reason, biopsy defects should ideally be round or oval with rounded margins to limit stress concentration.

items.q: Which connective tissue layer of a peripheral nerve contains tight junctions forming the blood-nerve barrier and provides the primary source of tensile strength of the nerve?
items.e: The perineurium surrounds individual nerve fascicles and contains tight junctions that constitute the blood-nerve barrier. It is the primary contributor to the tensile strength of a peripheral nerve and maintains intrafascicular pressure.

items.q: A 22-year-old motorcyclist sustains a traction injury to the brachial plexus, causing complete sensory loss in the C6 dermatome. Electrodiagnostic testing at 4 weeks post-injury shows a completely preserved sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude for the superficial radial nerve. Where is the lesion located?
o: Preganglionic root avulsion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Upper trunk distal to the dorsal root ganglion
items.e: In a preganglionic (root avulsion) injury, the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and sensory cell bodies remain intact and attached to the peripheral axon. Consequently, distal sensory axonal degeneration does not occur, leaving the SNAP preserved despite complete clinical anaesthesia in the dermatome.

items.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a closed midshaft humeral fracture and an complete radial nerve palsy. Closed reduction and functional bracing are performed. What is the most appropriate initial management for the nerve injury?
o: Immediate operative exploration and primary nerve repair
Electromyography (EMG) on post-injury day 1 to assess axonal disruption
Clinical observation with serial examination and electrodiagnosis at 3 to 4 weeks
Operative exploration and sural nerve autografting at 2 weeks
items.e: Closed injuries associated with nerve palsies are predominantly neurapraxias or axonotmeses, with high spontaneous recovery rates (70-90% for radial palsy in closed humerus fractures). Initial observation is indicated, with EMG delayed to 3-4 weeks to accurately distinguish neurapraxia from axonal loss.

items.q: A 16-year-old male undergoing open reduction of a femur fracture under general anaesthesia develops a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, generalized muscle rigidity, and severe tachycardia. What is the underlying pathophysiology of this condition?
o: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Antibodies directed against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum due to an RYR1 receptor gene mutation
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the RYR1 gene (ryanodine receptor), leading to uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when exposed to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine. A rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 is the earliest clinical sign.

items.q: In accordance with Henneman's size principle, which motor units are recruited first during a gradually increasing voluntary isometric muscle contraction?
o: Large motor units containing Type IIB fast glycolytic fibres
Small motor units containing Type I slow oxidative fibres
Intermediate motor units containing Type IIA fast oxidative-glycolytic fibres
Large motor units containing Type IIA fibres
items.e: Henneman's size principle dictates that smaller motor units containing Type I (slow oxidative, fatigue-resistant) muscle fibres are recruited first at low force levels, while larger motor units containing Type II fibres are progressively recruited as force requirements increase.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon conducts a prospective study following two cohorts of patients: one group treated with an intramedullary nail and another with a locking plate for proximal humerus fractures. Patients are followed for 2 years to assess nonunion rates. According to the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (JBJS) levels of evidence for therapeutic studies, what level of evidence does this study represent?
items.e: Prospective comparative (cohort) studies represent Level II evidence according to the JBJS hierarchy for therapeutic studies. In contrast, retrospective comparative cohort studies and case-control studies are classified as Level III, whereas high-quality RCTs represent Level I.

items.q: A research group evaluates functional recovery using the Oxford Knee Score before surgery and at 1-year follow-up in 30 patients undergoing total knee replacement. The score distribution is non-normally distributed (skewed). Which statistical test is most appropriate to evaluate if there is a significant change in scores postoperatively?
items.e: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test, used for comparing two paired or related measurements when data are skewed or ordinal. The Mann-Whitney U test is used for comparing two independent non-parametric groups.

items.q: Which of the following reporting guidelines should be followed when preparing a manuscript for a systematic review and meta-analysis of orthopaedic interventions?
items.e: PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) is the standard reporting guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. CONSORT is used for randomised controlled trials, STROBE for observational studies, and STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies.

items.q: A diagnostic blood test for prosthetic joint infection has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. If this test is applied in a tertiary revision unit with a high disease prevalence rather than a community setting with a low disease prevalence, how will the test statistics behave?
o: Sensitivity increases and Positive Predictive Value (PPV) decreases
Sensitivity and Specificity remain unchanged, while PPV increases
Specificity increases and Negative Predictive Value (NPV) increases
Both PPV and NPV will increase simultaneously
items.e: Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios are intrinsic properties of a test and do not change with disease prevalence. Predictive values depend heavily on prevalence: as prevalence rises, the Positive Predictive Value (PPV) increases and the Negative Predictive Value (NPV) decreases.

items.q: In a randomised controlled trial comparing two surgical techniques for distal radius fractures, which design feature is specifically effective at controlling for both known and unknown confounding variables at baseline?
items.e: Randomisation is the only methodological technique that balances both known and unknown confounding variables between groups at baseline. Allocation concealment prevents selection bias, whereas blinding prevents performance and detection bias.

items.q: A trial reports that a novel wound dressing reduces the risk of surgical site infection after total joint arthroplasty from 10% in the control group to 5% in the intervention group. What is the Number Needed to Treat (NNT) to prevent one surgical site infection?
items.e: The Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) is calculated as Control Event Rate (10%) minus Experimental Event Rate (5%), which equals 5% (0.05). The Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.05 = 20.

items.q: When conducting a long-term survivorship analysis of joint replacement implants in an elderly population, patient death acts as a competing risk. If standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis is used without accounting for competing risks, what is the impact on the reported revision rate?
o: It underestimates the cumulative revision rate
It overestimates the cumulative revision rate
It has no effect on the revision rate estimate
It invalidates the log-rank test p-value
items.e: In survival analysis of elderly cohorts, death prevents the occurrence of implant revision (competing risk). Standard Kaplan-Meier analysis treats dead patients as censored, which artificially overestimates the cumulative revision rate over time; the Cumulative Incidence Function (Fine and Gray method) should be used instead.

items.q: According to current International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) recommendations, what is the annual occupational equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye in a radiation worker?
o: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
items.e: The ICRP annual limit for the lens of the eye for occupational workers is 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (with no single year exceeding 50 mSv). The limit for skin, hands, and feet is 500 mSv per year, and for the general public, it is 1 mSv per year.

items.q: A patient undergoes computed tomography (CT) for a complex intra-articular fracture. When assessing tissue attenuation values on the scan, which pairing of tissue to Hounsfield Units (HU) is correct?
items.e: Acute blood measures approximately +50 to +80 HU on CT. Water is defined as 0 HU, air is -1000 HU, fat is -100 to -50 HU, and cortical bone measures +1000 HU or more.

items.q: A 35-year-old tennis player undergoes MRI of the shoulder. Signal hyperintensity is noted in the supraspinatus tendon on short-TE (T1 and proton density) sequences, which completely disappears on long-TE (T2-weighted) sequences. What artefact explains this non-pathologic finding?
items.e: The magic angle effect occurs when collagen fibres are oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the main magnetic field (B0), resulting in increased signal intensity on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE) that disappears on long-TE (T2-weighted) sequences.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman undergoes Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) for osteoporosis evaluation. Which of the following factors is most likely to produce a falsely high areal bone mineral density (BMD) reading at the lumbar spine?
items.e: Degenerative osteophytes, facet joint arthritis, aortic calcification, and vertebral compression fractures add extra mineralised tissue in the 2D projection path of DEXA, causing a falsely elevated lumbar spine BMD.

items.q: A Tc-99m methylene diphosphonate (MDP) triple-phase radionuclide bone scan is requested for diagnostic workup. Which of the following skeletal conditions typically manifests as a 'cold' (photopenic) lesion on the delayed phase?
items.e: Multiple myeloma produces purely lytic lesions with minimal or no osteoblastic activity, typically appearing photopenic or 'cold' on a Tc-99m MDP bone scan. Osteoid osteoma, Paget disease, and CRPS characteristically demonstrate increased ('hot') radionuclide uptake.

items.q: During musculoskeletal ultrasound examination of the Achilles tendon, an image artefact causes a normal tendon structure to appear falsely hypoechoic when the transducer beam strikes the tissue at a non-perpendicular angle. What is this artefact called?
items.e: Anisotropy occurs in linear fibrillar structures like tendons and ligaments when the ultrasound beam is not perpendicular (90 degrees) to the fibres, leading to a false hypoechoic appearance mimicking a tear or tendinopathy.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding X-ray physics and interactions with biological tissue is correct?
o: Approximately 99% of electron kinetic energy at the anode target is converted into heat, with only about 1% converted into X-rays
Increasing peak kilovoltage (kVp) increases image contrast by enhancing the photoelectric effect
Compton scatter is the dominant interaction producing contrast at low photon energies in high atomic number tissue like bone
Aluminium filtration is used in the tube assembly to absorb high-energy photons to protect the digital detector
items.e: In an X-ray tube, about 99% of kinetic energy is converted into heat at the tungsten anode, with only ~1% converted to X-rays. Increasing kVp increases penetration and scatter while decreasing contrast; the photoelectric effect dominates at low energies in high atomic number tissues, and filtration removes low-energy photons to lower patient skin dose.

items.q: A 65-year-old patient undergoing revision total hip arthroplasty for chronic staphylococcal prosthetic joint infection is prescribed oral rifampicin for its biofilm-clearing property. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Direct inhibition of bacterial RNA polymerase
items.e: Rifampicin acts by inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase and is uniquely active against staphylococcal biofilm in implant infections. It must never be used as monotherapy due to rapid emergence of resistance.

items.q: During closed reduction of a distal radius fracture under intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block), which local anaesthetic agent is strictly contraindicated due to severe cardiotoxicity?
items.e: Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic agent and is strictly contraindicated for intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block). Prilocaine is the agent of choice for Bier block, while lidocaine is also used.

items.q: A 72-year-old postmenopausal female with severe osteoporosis is being evaluated for osteoanabolic treatment. She sustained an ischemic stroke 8 months ago. Which medication is contraindicated due to an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events?
items.e: Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin with dual anabolic and antiresorptive action; results from the ARCH trial showed an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events, leading to a warning against its use in patients with a myocardial infarction or stroke within the past year.

items.q: A 68-year-old male receiving prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) following total knee arthroplasty exhibits a 60% drop in platelet count on postoperative day 7, along with a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
o: Switch LMWH to therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion
Discontinue LMWH and initiate argatroban or fondaparinux
Transfuse pooled random donor platelets immediately
Discontinue LMWH and immediately start oral warfarin loading
items.e: This clinical picture represents Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT Type II). Management requires stopping all heparin products immediately and initiating a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux; platelet transfusions and starting warfarin prior to platelet recovery are contraindicated.

items.q: According to the ACR/AAHKS guidelines for elective total joint arthroplasty in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, which medication should be CONTINUED uninterrupted through the perioperative period?
items.e: Current ACR/AAHKS perioperative guidelines recommend continuing conventional synthetic DMARDs like methotrexate, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine. Biologic agents (e.g., adalimumab) should be withheld until the end of their dosing cycle, and JAK inhibitors (e.g., tofacitinib, upadacitinib) should be stopped 3 days before surgery.

items.q: During elective posterior spinal instrumentation under general anaesthesia with volatile anaesthetic agents, what is the EARLIEST clinical sign of malignant hyperthermia?
items.e: The earliest manifestation of malignant hyperthermia is an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 (capnography elevation), often accompanied by sinus tachycardia and masseter spasm. Hyperthermia is a late sign of the disorder.

items.q: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a high-energy motor vehicle accident. He has a clinically unstable pelvis. If the patient has arterial bleeding from the posterior pelvic complex, which vessel is most likely involved?
items.e: While 80-90% of pelvic bleeding is venous, the superior gluteal artery (branch of the internal iliac) is the most common arterial source of bleeding, especially in posterior ring disruptions.

items.q: In the radiographic evaluation of a pelvic ring injury, which specific view is most diagnostic for assessing vertical displacement (migration) of a hemipelvis?
items.e: The pelvic outlet view, taken with the beam angled 40-45 degrees cephalad, is the best view to demonstrate vertical displacement and sacral foraminal anatomy.

items.q: A patient sustains a sacral fracture that passes medial to the sacral foramina, involving the central spinal canal. According to the Denis classification, what is the most likely clinical finding associated with this injury zone?
items.e: Denis Zone III fractures involve the central sacral canal and carry a high risk (approx. 57%) of neurological deficit, specifically bowel, bladder, and sexual dysfunction.

items.q: During the evaluation of a complex acetabular fracture, the presence of a 'spur sign' on the obturator oblique radiograph indicates that the fracture is a:
items.e: The spur sign represents the posterior-superior ilium which is no longer attached to the articular surface; it is pathognomonic for a both-column fracture.

items.q: A 76-year-old active female sustains a displaced femoral neck fracture (Garden IV). According to the HEALTH trial and NICE guidelines, which management plan is most appropriate for a patient who is medically fit and walks independently outdoors?
items.e: For active, independent, and cognitively intact elderly patients with displaced neck fractures, total hip arthroplasty (THA) is recommended over hemiarthroplasty for better functional outcomes. The WHiTE 5 trial supports using cemented stems to reduce pain and periprosthetic fracture risk.

items.q: Regarding the blood supply to the adult femoral head, which of the following statements is correct based on the applied anatomy of the proximal femur?
o: The artery of the ligamentum teres provides the majority of the blood supply in adults.
The lateral femoral circumflex artery is the primary source via its posterosuperior branches.
The lateral epiphyseal branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery provide the main supply.
Intracapsular fractures rarely disrupt the retinacular vessels due to their protected location.
items.e: The medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), specifically its lateral epiphyseal (retinacular) branches running up the posterosuperior neck, is the primary blood supply to the femoral head. Intracapsular fractures often disrupt these vessels, leading to high rates of AVN.

items.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a vertical femoral neck fracture following a high-velocity motor vehicle accident. The fracture line is oriented at 65 degrees from the horizontal. Which of the following is true regarding this injury?
o: It is a Pauwels Type I fracture with a low risk of non-union.
It represents a Pauwels Type III fracture, which carries the highest risk of vertical shear and fixation failure.
Primary treatment should be a cemented hemiarthroplasty within 48 hours.
The fracture is considered stable and can be managed with protected weight bearing.
items.e: A fracture angle >50 degrees from the horizontal is classified as Pauwels Type III. This represents a vertical shear pattern with the highest risk of non-union and fixation failure in young patients, necessitating urgent anatomical reduction and stable fixation.

items.q: In the management of intertrochanteric fractures, which fracture characteristic is considered a contraindication for the use of a sliding (dynamic) hip screw (DHS)?
o: Presence of a simple two-part A1.1 pattern
Intact lateral wall thicker than 25 mm
Posteromedial comminution limited to the lesser trochanter
items.e: The DHS is contraindicated in reverse obliquity fractures because the fracture line allows the femoral shaft to slide medially along the lag screw axis, leading to failure. Cephalomedullary nails are the treatment of choice for these unstable patterns.

items.q: A 72-year-old patient on long-term bisphosphonate therapy for osteoporosis presents with prodromal thigh pain. Radiographs reveal a transverse, non-comminuted subtrochanteric fracture with a distinct lateral cortical 'beaking'. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Increase the dose of bisphosphonates and prescribe bed rest
Perform a total hip arthroplasty with a long uncemented stem
Stop bisphosphonates, consider teriparatide, and proceed with intramedullary nailing
Apply a hip spica cast for 12 weeks to allow secondary bone healing
items.e: These are features of an Atypical Femoral Fracture (AFF). Management includes stopping the bisphosphonate, supplementing with Vitamin D/Calcium, considering teriparatide to stimulate bone healing, and surgical fixation (usually an intramedullary nail).

items.q: During the surgical fixation of a subtrochanteric fracture, the surgeon notes that the proximal fragment is flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the flexion deformity of this fragment?
items.e: In subtrochanteric fractures, the proximal fragment is deformed by the iliopsoas (flexion), gluteus medius/minimus (abduction), and short external rotators (external rotation). The distal fragment is typically adducted by the adductors.

items.q: Which of the following is considered a 'Major' criterion in the Gurd and Wilson classification for the diagnosis of Fat Embolism Syndrome following a femoral shaft fracture?
o: Petechial rash in the axilla or conjunctiva
items.e: Gurd and Wilson's major criteria for Fat Embolism Syndrome include respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs (not explained by other causes), and a petechial rash (typically found in the axilla, neck, or conjunctiva). Tachycardia and pyrexia are minor criteria.

items.q: To minimize the risk of 'cut-out' when fixing an intertrochanteric fracture with a lag screw, what is the recommended Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) according to Baumgaertner?
items.e: The Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) is the sum of the distance from the tip of the lag screw to the apex of the femoral head on both AP and lateral views. A TAD of less than 25 mm is the strongest predictor of preventing mechanical cut-out.

items.q: A patient with a high-energy Schatzker Type VI tibial plateau fracture is being evaluated in the emergency department. The leg is grossly swollen. The Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) is measured at 0.85. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Application of a long leg cast and elevation
Four-compartment fasciotomy based on ABI alone
items.e: According to the source notes, an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) of less than 0.9 in high-energy tibial plateau fractures (especially Schatzker IV and VI) necessitates an arterial study to rule out popliteal artery injury.

items.q: Which of the following soft tissue injuries is most frequently associated with lateral tibial plateau fractures?
items.e: Lateral meniscus tears are the most common associated soft-tissue injury in lateral tibial plateau fractures; these tears are often peripheral and can sometimes become incarcerated within the fracture site.

items.q: A 35-year-old patient sustains a high-energy pilon fracture. The surgeon decides to follow the staged protocol. What is the primary goal of the first stage of management?
o: Definitive fixation of the tibial plafond to allow early range of motion
Application of a spanning external fixator to restore length and alignment via ligamentotaxis
Primary ankle arthrodesis to prevent post-traumatic arthritis
Immediate bone grafting of the metaphyseal defect
items.e: The staged protocol for pilon fractures begins with an urgent spanning external fixator to restore length, alignment, and rotation through ligamentotaxis, allowing soft tissues to settle before definitive ORIF.

items.q: In the classic four-step reconstruction of a pilon fracture described by Rüedi and Allgöwer, which step is performed first?
o: Reconstruction of the distal tibial articular surface
items.e: The Rüedi-Allgöwer principles for pilon ORIF follow a specific sequence: (1) restore fibular length, (2) reconstruct the articular surface, (3) bone graft the metaphyseal defect, and (4) buttress the medial tibia.

items.q: A CT scan of a complex tibial plateau fracture shows a large shear fragment in the posteromedial column. Which surgical approach is specifically indicated to address and buttress this fragment?
items.e: The three-column concept identifies posterior column fragments (especially posteromedial) that are often missed by Schatzker classification. These require a posteromedial approach (such as the Lobenhoffer) for direct visualization and buttress plating.

items.q: During the ORIF of a pilon fracture, the surgeon identifies the anterolateral articular fragment that is attached to the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL). This is known as the:
items.e: The Chaput fragment is the anterolateral fragment of the distal tibia attached to the AITFL. The Volkmann fragment is the posterolateral fragment attached to the PITFL.

items.q: A 32-year-old male presents with a trimalleolar fracture. Intraoperatively, the surgeon notes a residual lateral talar shift of 1 mm after fibular fixation. According to the classic study by Ramsey and Hamilton, this residual shift reduces the tibiotalar contact area by approximately:
items.e: Ramsey and Hamilton demonstrated that just 1 mm of lateral talar shift results in a 42% reduction in the contact area of the tibiotalar joint, which provides the biomechanical basis for the requirement of anatomical reduction.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman sustains an ankle injury after a fall. Radiographs reveal a short oblique fibular fracture at the level of the syndesmosis, running from anteroinferior to posterosuperior. According to the Lauge-Hansen classification, which of the following represents the correct sequence of injury for this pattern?
o: I: Medial malleolus fracture -> II: AITFL rupture -> III: Fibula fracture -> IV: PITFL rupture
I: AITFL rupture -> II: Spiral fibula fracture -> III: PITFL or posterior malleolus fracture -> IV: Medial malleolus fracture/deltoid rupture
I: AITFL rupture -> II: PITFL rupture -> III: Fibula fracture -> IV: Medial malleolus fracture
I: Medial malleolus fracture -> II: Fibula fracture -> III: AITFL rupture -> IV: PITFL rupture
items.e: This describes a Supination-External Rotation (SER) injury (Weber B). The sequence is Stage I: AITFL; Stage II: short oblique/spiral fibula at the level of the syndesmosis; Stage III: PITFL or posterior malleolus; Stage IV: medial malleolus fracture or deltoid rupture.

items.q: A patient presents with a Weber A fibular avulsion fracture and a vertical fracture of the medial malleolus with associated impaction of the medial tibial plafond. Which Lauge-Hansen mechanism is most likely responsible for this injury pattern?
items.e: Supination-Adduction (SAD) injuries typically result in a transverse fibular avulsion (Weber A) in Stage I, followed by a vertical medial malleolus fracture and medial plafond impaction in Stage II.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of the ankle, which of the following measurements, taken 1 cm above the tibial plafond, is considered the most reliable radiographic indicator of a syndesmotic injury?
items.e: While multiple measurements exist, the tibiofibular clear space (measured on the AP view, 1 cm above the plafond) being over 5-6 mm is considered the most reliable radiographic indicator of syndesmotic injury.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete sustains a trimalleolar fracture. CT shows a posterolateral oblique fragment involving 30% of the articular surface with associated posterior talar subluxation. Which of the following is the preferred management for the posterior malleolar fragment according to current evidence?
o: Indirect reduction and fixation with an anterior-to-posterior screw
Direct fixation via a posterolateral approach
Conservative management as it will reduce automatically with the fibula
items.e: Current evidence favors direct fixation of larger posterior malleolar fragments (over 25-30% or with subluxation) via a posterolateral approach, as it restores syndesmotic stability and incisura congruity better than indirect methods.

items.q: A 50-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with an ankle fracture-dislocation. Despite multiple attempts, closed reduction is unsuccessful. Radiographs show the proximal fibular fragment trapped behind the posterolateral tibia in the incisura. This injury is known as:
items.e: A Bosworth fracture-dislocation occurs when the fibula is trapped behind the posterior tibial tubercle (incisura). It is irreducible by closed means and represents a surgical emergency for open reduction.

items.q: A 62-year-old diabetic patient with peripheral neuropathy sustains an unstable bimalleolar ankle fracture. Which of the following management strategies is recommended to minimize the risk of fixation failure and Charcot arthropathy?
o: Standard ORIF and immediate weight bearing at 2 weeks
Super-construct fixation (e.g., longer plates, multiple syndesmotic screws) and prolonged non-weight bearing
Primary ankle arthrodesis with an intramedullary nail
items.e: Diabetic patients with neuropathy require "super-constructs" (more robust fixation) and often double the standard non-weight-bearing time (e.g., 12 weeks instead of 6) to prevent complications like Charcot and loss of fixation.

items.q: During the lateral approach to the fibula for an ankle fracture, which nerve is at greatest risk as it pierces the crural fascia approximately 10-12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus and crosses the surgical field obliquely?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the crural fascia approximately 10-12 cm above the lateral malleolus and crosses the lateral surgical field obliquely, making it susceptible to injury during the lateral incision for fibular fixation.

items.q: Regarding the blood supply to the proximal humerus, recent studies (e.g., Hettrich et al.) have revised classical teaching. Which artery is now considered to provide the majority (approximately 64%) of the blood supply to the humeral head?
o: Ascending branch of the profunda brachii
items.e: Classically, the anterior humeral circumflex and its arcuate branch were considered the main supply, but modern studies show the posterior humeral circumflex artery provides the majority (64%) of the head's blood supply.

items.q: An 82-year-old female sustains a displaced two-part surgical neck fracture of the humerus. She is relatively sedentary. Based on the findings of the ProFHER trial (2015), what is the most appropriate management?
o: Non-operative management with a sling and early pendulum exercises
items.e: The ProFHER trial showed no significant difference in clinical outcomes at 2 and 5 years between surgery and non-operative care for displaced proximal humerus fractures involving the surgical neck in elderly patients.

items.q: A 75-year-old male sustains a four-part proximal humerus fracture with significant comminution of the tuberosities. Which surgical option is currently preferred in this age group due to more predictable functional outcomes?
o: Open reduction and internal fixation with a locking plate
items.e: In elderly patients (typically >70 years) with four-part fractures, RTSA is preferred over hemiarthroplasty because functional outcomes in RTSA do not strictly depend on tuberosity healing, which is often poor in the elderly.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a lateral third clavicle fracture. Radiographs show that the medial fragment is detached from the coracoclavicular ligaments (Neer Type II). What is the most likely clinical concern regarding this specific fracture pattern?
o: High risk of subclavian artery injury
Spontaneous healing is expected with a sling
items.e: Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures are unstable because the medial fragment is detached from the CC ligaments, leading to a high non-union rate (about 30%) if treated non-operatively.

items.q: A 30-year-old mountain biker sustains an acromioclavicular joint injury. Radiographs show a 50% increase in the coracoclavicular (CC) distance compared to the contralateral side. Which Rockwood grade is this, and what is the recommended initial management?
items.e: Rockwood Type III involves a 25-100% increase in CC distance. Current consensus recommends initial non-operative management for most Type III injuries, reserving surgery for high-demand athletes or failed conservative care.

items.q: According to the revised ASBMR Task Force case definition for atypical femoral fractures (AFF), which of the following is classified as a MINOR feature rather than a major feature?
o: Origin at the lateral cortex with substantially transverse orientation
Localised periosteal or endosteal thickening ('beaking') at the fracture site
Non-comminuted or minimally comminuted fracture line
items.e: The 5 major features of atypical femoral fractures include minimal trauma, lateral cortical origin with transverse orientation, complete/incomplete extension without comminution, and localised cortical beaking/thickening. Minor features include prodromal thigh or groin pain, diaphyseal cortical thickening, and bilaterality.

items.q: A 48-year-old man presents with acute pseudogout of the right knee. Because he is younger than 60 years, he is screened for metabolic predispositions. Which of the following conditions represents one of the classic '4 H's' associated with calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease?
items.e: The classic metabolic associations ('4 H's') that predispose to CPPD disease are Haemochromatosis, Hyperparathyroidism, Hypomagnesaemia, and Hypophosphatasia (characterised by low alkaline phosphatase). Patients under 60 years presenting with CPPD should be screened for these secondary causes.

items.q: A 4-year-old child with autism and a highly restricted diet presents with limb pain, irritability, and painful subperiosteal swelling. Radiographs reveal a dense zone of provisional calcification (white line of Frankel) and an underlying radiolucent Trummerfeld zone. What is the fundamental cellular mechanism underlying this bone disorder?
o: Defective osteoid production due to impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine
Impaired mineralisation of newly formed osteoid caused by calcium-phosphate deficiency
Hyperactive osteoclastic bone resorption driven by circulating PTHrP
Inhibition of hydroxyapatite crystal formation by accumulated inorganic pyrophosphate
items.e: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) causes defective hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen synthesis, leading to osteoblast dysfunction and failure of osteoid production. It is a defect in osteoid formation, not a mineralisation defect.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman is found to have asymptomatic hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, and an elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is planned. Which anatomical site demonstrates the greatest preferential loss of bone mineral density in this condition?
items.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism preferentially causes cortical bone catabolism over trabecular bone loss. Consequently, bone mineral density drops most dramatically at cortical-predominant sites such as the distal radius (forearm), while trabecular sites like the lumbar spine are relatively preserved.

items.q: A surgeon is performing intraoperative fluoroscopy for distal locking of a femoral intramedullary nail. Which of the following technical setups will minimise radiation exposure to both the patient and operating room staff?
o: Place the X-ray tube above the table and the image intensifier below
Position the image intensifier as close to the patient as possible
Stand on the X-ray tube side of the patient when acquiring lateral views
Routine use of magnification (zoom) mode to lower tube voltage output
items.e: To minimise scatter and patient dose, the image intensifier should be placed close to the patient while keeping the X-ray tube as far away as possible under the operating table. Scatter is highest on the tube side, so staff should stand on the intensifier side, and magnification modes increase dose.

items.q: During cement insertion for a hemiarthroplasty, an 84-year-old female experiences a fall in systolic blood pressure from 130 mmHg to 70 mmHg (SBP drop > 40%) along with an oxygen saturation drop to 85%. According to the Donaldson classification, which grade of Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS) is present?
items.e: Donaldson Grade 2 BCIS is defined by severe hypoxia (SpO2 < 88%), severe hypotension (systolic blood pressure fall > 40%), or unexpected loss of consciousness. Grade 1 involves moderate hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) or hypotension (20–40% fall), while Grade 3 involves cardiac collapse requiring CPR.

items.q: A 28-year-old female sustains a posterior hip dislocation. Post-reduction CT reveals a femoral head fracture located cephalad to the fovea capitis (weight-bearing portion) and an associated femoral neck fracture. This is classified as a Pipkin Type:
items.e: Pipkin Type III fractures involve a femoral head fracture (Type I or II) associated with a concomitant femoral neck fracture; this pattern has the worst prognosis.

items.q: A 42-year-old male presents with a valgus-load injury to the knee. Radiographs reveal a split of the lateral tibial plateau accompanied by a central articular depression. According to the Schatzker classification, which type is this, and what is its clinical significance?
o: Type I; most common in osteoporotic bone
Type II; most common tibial plateau fracture pattern
Type III; associated with the highest risk of compartment syndrome
Type IV; often involves a fracture-dislocation mechanism
items.e: Schatzker Type II is a lateral split-depression fracture and is the most common tibial plateau fracture pattern. Type III is typically seen in osteoporotic bone, while Type IV and VI carry higher risks of neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome respectively.

items.q: An 80-year-old female with known osteoporosis sustains a low-energy fall. Radiographs show a pure depression of the lateral tibial plateau without an associated split or wedge fragment. What is the classification and recommended surgical technique?
o: Schatzker II; lateral buttress plating only
Schatzker III; elevation through a cortical window and subchondral grafting
items.e: Schatzker Type III is a pure lateral depression fracture typically seen in elderly, osteoporotic patients. Treatment involves elevating the depressed articular surface through a cortical window and supporting it with bone graft or substitute and raft screws.

items.q: A 17-year-old rugby player sustains his first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, which is reduced and treated non-operatively. What is the approximate risk of recurrent instability?
items.e: Recurrence is inversely related to age at first dislocation; in patients under 20 years treated non-operatively recurrence rates of up to 90% are reported, falling below 20% after 40 years.

items.q: A 25-year-old patient sustains a closed midshaft humeral shaft fracture following a fall. Clinical examination reveals an inability to extend the wrist and fingers. What is the most appropriate next step in management for the nerve injury?
o: Immediate surgical exploration of the radial nerve
Observation and expectant management for 3-4 months
items.e: Radial nerve palsy in closed humeral shaft fractures is usually a neurapraxia. Spontaneous recovery occurs in 70-90% of cases, so observation for 3-4 months is the standard of care before considering EMG or exploration.

items.q: A 78-year-old woman with osteoporosis sustains a highly comminuted, intra-articular distal humerus fracture (AO/OTA 13C3). Based on the McKee trial findings for this patient group, which management strategy is likely to provide better early functional outcomes?
o: Open reduction and internal fixation with parallel plates
External fixation with early range of motion
items.e: In the McKee RCT (patients over 65 with displaced comminuted intra-articular distal humerus fractures), primary TEA gave better Mayo Elbow Performance and early DASH scores than ORIF; about a quarter of ORIF cases had to be converted to TEA intraoperatively, and reoperation rates were similar.

items.q: When performing an open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a radial shaft fracture in an adult, restoring the 'radial bow' is critical for forearm rotation. At what location along the radius (from the proximal end) is the maximal radial bow normally found?
items.e: Restoring the radial bow is essential for full forearm rotation; the maximal radial bow is located at approximately 60% of the length of the radius measured from the proximal end.

items.q: A 35-year-old male sustains a displaced, non-comminuted transverse fracture of the olecranon. The ulnohumeral joint remains stable. What is the most common complication associated with the standard surgical treatment (tension-band wiring) for this injury?
items.e: According to the Mayo classification, this is a Type IIA fracture. Tension-band wiring (TBW) is the standard treatment, but symptomatic hardware is the most common complication, with removal rates reported between 50-80%.

items.q: A patient presents with elbow instability following a previous lateral release for tennis elbow. On examination, a 'clunk' is felt at 40 degrees of flexion while applying a valgus load, axial load, and supination. Insufficiency of which structure is responsible for this finding?
items.e: The description defines a positive lateral pivot-shift test (O'Driscoll), which is diagnostic of posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) caused by LUCL insufficiency.

items.q: Regarding Monteggia fracture-dislocations in the adult population, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Bado Type I (anterior dislocation) is the most common pattern in adults
Bado Type II (posterior dislocation) is the most common pattern in adults
Non-operative management of the ulnar fracture is the treatment of choice
The radial head should be excised immediately to prevent stiffness
items.e: While Bado Type I is most common in children, Bado Type II (posterior Monteggia, often involving a radial head fracture) is the most common pattern in adults. Treatment requires anatomical ulnar plating to reduce the radial head.

items.q: A 55-year-old active woman falls on an outstretched hand. Radiographs show a distal radius fracture with 25° dorsal angulation, dorsal metaphyseal comminution and a 3 mm intra-articular step-off. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
o: Closed reduction and below-elbow cast for 6 weeks
Open reduction and volar locking plate fixation
Bridging external fixation as definitive treatment
items.e: Dorsal angulation over 20°, dorsal comminution and intra-articular extension are Lafontaine instability factors predicting loss of reduction in plaster, and a step-off over 2 mm needs anatomical reduction; volar locking plate fixation achieves both.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman has an undisplaced extra-articular distal radius fracture with 1.5 mm radial shortening, 20° radial inclination, neutral volar tilt and no articular step-off. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Below-elbow cast for about 4-6 weeks with check radiographs at 1-2 weeks
items.e: All parameters are within acceptable limits (shortening under 3 mm, no step-off, tilt not dorsal beyond 10°), so cast immobilisation with early check radiographs to detect late displacement is sufficient.

items.q: A patient with a displaced distal radius fracture treated by closed reduction and cast develops progressive median nerve paraesthesia and pain that do not improve after the cast is split and the wrist is brought out of flexion. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue observation and re-examine at 2 weeks
Nerve conduction studies before any intervention
Urgent carpal tunnel release with fracture reduction and stabilisation
Oral corticosteroids and a wrist splint
items.e: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome that persists after releasing the cast and removing wrist flexion needs urgent carpal tunnel decompression, with the fracture reduced and stabilised at the same sitting.

items.q: A 27-year-old man has a Gustilo-Anderson type IIIB open tibial shaft fracture. According to the BOAST open fracture standard, definitive soft-tissue cover should ideally be achieved:
o: At the first debridement within 12 hours in every case
Only after the fracture has united
After at least three planned relook debridements over 2 weeks
Within 72 hours of injury, ideally at the same sitting as definitive internal fixation
items.e: BOAST recommends definitive soft-tissue cover within 72 hours of injury if not achieved at the primary debridement, preferably combined with definitive fixation ('fix and flap'), because delayed cover increases deep infection and flap failure.

items.q: A 32-year-old man sustains a closed mid-shaft tibial fracture fixed with a reamed intramedullary nail. Which biomechanical environment does this construct provide for secondary bone healing?
o: Relative stability allowing interfragmentary strain of about 2-10%
Absolute stability with lag screw compression
Rigid fixation with interfragmentary strain below 2%
items.e: Intramedullary nailing provides relative stability; interfragmentary strain of roughly 2-10% permits cartilage and callus formation, the hallmark of secondary (indirect) healing.

items.q: According to Perren's interfragmentary strain theory, lamellar bone can form directly in a fracture gap only when the strain is below about:
items.e: Granulation tissue tolerates strain up to about 100%, fibrocartilage about 10% and lamellar bone only about 2%; absolute stability keeps strain under 2% for direct healing, whereas 2-10% favours callus.

items.q: A 20-year-old has a displaced transverse midshaft radius fracture fixed anatomically with a dynamic compression plate giving interfragmentary compression. Which type of bone healing is expected?
o: Endochondral ossification with abundant external callus
Intramembranous ossification with periosteal callus only
Primary (direct) bone healing by cutting cones
items.e: Anatomical reduction with compression gives absolute stability and strain below 2%, so healing is direct: osteoclast-led cutting cones cross the fracture followed by osteoblasts laying down lamellar bone, without visible callus.

items.q: A 60-year-old diabetic had a distal femoral fracture fixed with a locking plate 9 months ago. Radiographs show a persistent gap with rounded, osteopenic bone ends, no callus and an intact, stable construct; infection markers are normal. In the Weber-Cech classification this non-union is:
items.e: Atrophic non-unions show no callus with resorbed, rounded bone ends and poor biology and need biological stimulation (debridement and grafting), whereas hypertrophic non-unions have abundant callus and need only more stability.

items.q: In the Masquelet induced-membrane technique for a 6 cm segmental tibial defect, what is the main role of the membrane that forms around the PMMA spacer?
o: It acts as a permanent load-bearing strut
It releases antibiotic for months after the spacer is removed
It must be excised at the second stage to expose bleeding bone
It is vascularised and secretes growth factors (VEGF, TGF-beta, BMP-2) that nourish the second-stage graft and limit its resorption
items.e: The foreign-body membrane induced by the cement spacer over 6-8 weeks is vascular and rich in growth factors; at the second stage it is incised and preserved, the spacer removed and the cavity filled with cancellous graft.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an aseptic oligotrophic non-union of a femoral shaft fracture previously treated with a 10 mm intramedullary nail. How does exchange nailing promote union?
o: It converts the construct to absolute stability with primary healing
Over-reaming and a larger, stiffer nail improve stability while reaming debris acts as local autograft
It shortens the femur to compress the non-union
It removes the nail to allow functional bracing
items.e: Exchange nailing reams the canal 1-2 mm larger and inserts a nail at least 1 mm bigger, improving stiffness and fit (still relative stability) while the reamings act as osteogenic graft and stimulate periosteal blood flow.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has taken alendronate 70 mg weekly for 6 years. She reports several weeks of dull aching pain in her left lateral thigh. Which diagnosis must be excluded first?
items.e: Prodromal thigh or groin pain in a long-term bisphosphonate user suggests an incomplete atypical femoral fracture; bilateral full-length femoral radiographs (and MRI if needed) are required, and the bisphosphonate is stopped if confirmed.

items.q: A 66-year-old woman at low-to-moderate fracture risk (no fractures, hip T-score now -2.0) has completed 5 years of oral alendronate. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Switch to denosumab 60 mg every 6 months indefinitely
Stop alendronate for a drug holiday and reassess fracture risk in 2-3 years
items.e: For patients not at high risk after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate (or 3 years of zoledronate), a drug holiday with reassessment after 2-3 years is advised, since the drug persists in bone and prolonged use raises atypical femoral fracture risk.

items.q: A 55-year-old man taking prednisolone 10 mg daily for a year for rheumatoid arthritis has no prior fracture, a T-score of -2.0 and a glucocorticoid-adjusted FRAX of 14% for major osteoporotic fracture and 1.8% for hip fracture. According to ACR guidance, what is the preferred treatment?
o: Continue observation with calcium and vitamin D only
items.e: This is moderate risk (FRAX major 10-19% or hip 1-3%); ACR guidance prefers an oral bisphosphonate such as alendronate with calcium and vitamin D, reserving anabolic agents for very high risk.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with untreated vitamin D deficiency receives her first infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg. Which biochemical abnormality is the most important adverse effect to anticipate in the following days?
items.e: By abruptly suppressing osteoclastic resorption, IV bisphosphonates can cause symptomatic hypocalcaemia, especially with vitamin D deficiency, which should be corrected before infusion.

items.q: A 52-year-old man has a hot, swollen first MTP joint, temperature 38.6 °C and raised blood WBC. Aspirate is turbid with 60,000 WBC/mm³ and negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. What is the most important next step?
o: Gram stain and culture of the fluid, treating as possible septic arthritis until excluded
items.e: Crystals do not exclude coexisting septic arthritis; with fever and a very high synovial count, Gram stain and culture (and empirical antibiotics if suspicion remains) take priority over anti-inflammatory treatment.

items.q: A haemodynamically unstable patient with an open-book pelvic injury needs a pelvic circumferential compression device in the emergency department. Where should the binder be centred?
o: At the level of the anterior superior iliac spines
Over the lower abdomen at the umbilicus
items.e: Centring the binder over the greater trochanters gives the most effective reduction of the pelvic volume; placement over the iliac crests or abdomen is a common error that is less effective and can widen the injury.

items.q: In a Galeazzi-type injury, radial shaft fractures located within what distance of the mid-articular surface of the distal radius are most often associated with DRUJ instability (Rettig and Raskin)?
items.e: Rettig and Raskin found DRUJ instability in about 55% of radial shaft fractures within 7.5 cm of the distal radial articular surface versus about 6% of more proximal fractures.

items.q: A 35-year-old man has a displaced vertical (Pauwels type III) femoral neck fracture. Which fixation construct is biomechanically superior in resisting shear for this pattern?
o: Three parallel cannulated screws in an inverted triangle
Sliding hip screw with an additional antirotation screw
Single cannulated screw along the calcar
items.e: Vertical Pauwels III fractures are dominated by shear forces; a fixed-angle device such as a sliding hip screw with an antirotation screw resists shear and varus collapse better than parallel cannulated screws.

items.q: What was the main finding of the FAITH trial comparing sliding hip screw with multiple cancellous screws for low-energy femoral neck fractures in patients aged 50 or older?
o: Sliding hip screw halved the reoperation rate in all patients
Cancellous screws had a significantly lower avascular necrosis rate
Sliding hip screw had higher mortality
No significant difference in reoperation rate at 24 months
items.e: FAITH found no overall difference in reoperation at 24 months, though avascular necrosis was more frequent with the sliding hip screw and subgroups (smokers, displaced or basicervical fractures) may benefit from it.

items.q: In the HEALTH trial comparing total hip arthroplasty with hemiarthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures in ambulatory older patients, what was the primary outcome result?
o: No significant difference in unplanned secondary hip procedures at 24 months
Hemiarthroplasty had a significantly higher dislocation rate
THA had higher mortality at 24 months
items.e: HEALTH (NEJM 2019) showed no significant difference in secondary procedures; THA gave a small, not clinically important, improvement in function and quality of life with slightly more dislocations.

items.q: In the FLOW trial on irrigation of open fractures, which finding influenced practice?
o: High-pressure irrigation reduced infection compared with low pressure
Castile soap irrigation had a higher reoperation rate than normal saline
Very low pressure irrigation increased nonunion
items.e: FLOW (NEJM 2015) showed similar reoperation rates across irrigation pressures, but soap had a higher reoperation rate than saline, supporting low-pressure saline irrigation.

items.q: What did the SPRINT trial conclude about reamed versus unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures?
o: Unreamed nailing reduced events in closed fractures
Reaming significantly increased infection in open fractures
Reaming may benefit closed fractures, with no difference in open fractures
Reaming increased fat embolism and mortality
items.e: SPRINT found a possible benefit of reamed nailing in closed fractures, mainly fewer reoperations such as dynamisation, and no difference between techniques in open fractures.

items.q: The UK DRAFFT trial compared K-wire fixation with volar locking plate fixation for dorsally displaced distal radius fractures in adults. What was the result?
o: Volar plating gave much better PRWE at 12 months
K-wires had a significantly higher tendon rupture rate
No clinically significant difference in PRWE at 12 months
items.e: UK DRAFFT (JAMA 2016) found no clinically important difference in the Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation at 12 months, with K-wires being cheaper, supporting K-wires where closed reduction is possible.

items.q: In the ProFHER trial of displaced proximal humerus fractures involving the surgical neck in adults, what was found?
o: No significant difference in Oxford Shoulder Score at 2 years between surgery and non-operative treatment
Locking plate fixation gave superior Oxford Shoulder Scores
Hemiarthroplasty was superior to non-operative care
Non-operative care had a higher complication rate
items.e: ProFHER (JAMA 2015) showed no significant differences in Oxford Shoulder Score, complications or mortality at 2 years, questioning routine surgery for these fractures.

items.q: The Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society trial (2007) on displaced midshaft clavicle fractures in adults compared plate fixation with sling treatment. What did it show?
o: No difference in nonunion between groups
Plating reduced nonunion and symptomatic malunion and improved early function
Sling treatment gave better Constant scores
Plating doubled the infection rate without functional benefit
items.e: Plate fixation improved Constant and DASH scores, shortened time to union and reduced nonunion and symptomatic malunion compared with sling treatment.

items.q: In the UK Heel Fracture Trial on displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures, operative treatment compared with non-operative treatment resulted in:
o: Significantly better Kerr-Atkins scores at 2 years
No improvement in Kerr-Atkins score at 2 years and more complications
items.e: UK HeFT (BMJ 2014) found no functional benefit from open reduction and internal fixation at 2 years, with a higher risk of complications and reoperation.

items.q: In the AIM trial of unstable ankle fractures in adults over 60, close contact casting compared with ORIF showed:
o: Equivalent Olerud-Molander function at 6 months, with more malunion in the casting group
items.e: AIM (JAMA 2016) found close contact casting non-inferior to surgery for function at 6 months, with fewer infections but more radiological malunion.

items.q: The WOLLF trial studied negative pressure wound therapy after debridement of open lower limb fractures. What was the finding?
o: No difference in disability (DRI) at 12 months or deep infection compared with standard dressings
NPWT reduced time to flap cover
items.e: WOLLF (JAMA 2018) showed no difference in Disability Rating Index at 12 months or in deep infection, so NPWT is not superior to standard dressings.

items.q: In the LEAP study of severe lower-extremity trauma, what was learned about absent plantar sensation at presentation?
o: It reliably predicted the need for amputation
More than half of insensate limbs managed by salvage regained sensation by 2 years
It indicated complete tibial nerve transection in most cases
It was the strongest predictor of final outcome
items.e: In LEAP, over 50% of initially insensate salvaged limbs recovered plantar sensation, so absent plantar sensation should not be used as an indication for amputation.

items.q: In the LEAP study, which amputation level had the worst functional outcomes and slowest walking speed?
items.e: Through-knee amputees had the worst Sickness Impact Profile scores and slowest walking speeds, while below-knee amputees did best.

items.q: A coronal-plane fracture of the posterior part of the lateral femoral condyle, often missed on AP radiographs, is called a:
items.e: A Hoffa fracture is a coronal-plane fracture of the femoral condyle, most often lateral; CT is often needed and fixation uses anterior-to-posterior or posterior-to-anterior lag screws perpendicular to the fracture.

items.q: The Lisfranc ligament, whose avulsion produces the 'fleck sign', connects:
o: The medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal
The base of the first metatarsal to the base of the second metatarsal
The middle cuneiform to the base of the first metatarsal
The lateral cuneiform to the base of the third metatarsal
items.e: The Lisfranc ligament runs obliquely from the lateral surface of the medial cuneiform to the medial base of the second metatarsal; there is no intermetatarsal ligament between the first and second metatarsal bases.

items.q: A high-energy tibial pilon fracture is treated with a spanning external fixator. Which clinical finding indicates that the soft tissues are ready for definitive internal fixation?
o: Return of skin wrinkles over the ankle
Ankle swelling that pits on pressure
Reduction of pain on passive toe stretch
items.e: Staged management waits (usually 7-21 days) until swelling settles and the wrinkle sign returns, which lowers wound complication rates after definitive plating.

items.q: During a two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg, which nerve is most at risk with the anterolateral incision?
items.e: The anterolateral incision releases the anterior and lateral compartments; the superficial peroneal nerve pierces the fascia in the distal third and must be protected.

items.q: In patients with femoral shaft fractures, the associated ipsilateral femoral neck fracture is typically:
o: An avulsion of the lesser trochanter
items.e: Ipsilateral femoral neck fractures occur in a few percent of femoral shaft fractures and up to a third are missed initially because they are vertical, basicervical and undisplaced; dedicated imaging of the neck is required.

items.q: Which of the following is a major criterion in Gurd's criteria for fat embolism syndrome?
items.e: Gurd's major criteria are respiratory insufficiency, cerebral involvement and petechial rash; tachycardia, pyrexia, retinal changes, renal changes and fat in urine are minor criteria.

items.q: Which finding places a polytrauma patient in Pape's 'borderline' category, favouring damage control orthopaedics for femoral shaft fixation?
o: Bilateral lung contusion on the initial chest radiograph
items.e: Borderline patients include those with ISS over 40, ISS over 20 with thoracic trauma, bilateral lung contusion, hypothermia below 35 °C, or raised pulmonary artery pressure; early total care risks a second hit.

items.q: In the AO Spine thoracolumbar classification, a burst fracture involving both endplates with posterior wall involvement and an intact posterior tension band is type:
items.e: A3 is an incomplete burst involving one endplate, whereas A4 is a complete burst involving both endplates; B types involve posterior tension band failure.

items.q: A Levine-Edwards type IIA traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 (hangman's fracture) is characterised by significant angulation with minimal translation. Which management step must be avoided?
items.e: Type IIA results from flexion-distraction, so traction widens the disc space and worsens displacement; reduction is by gentle extension and compression followed by halo immobilisation.

items.q: In a type II odontoid fracture, which factor most strongly predicts nonunion with non-operative halo treatment?
o: Displacement of the dens more than 5 mm
items.e: Nonunion risk rises with displacement over about 5 mm, age over 50, posterior displacement and angulation over 10°, which favour surgical fixation.

items.q: On an open-mouth odontoid view of a Jefferson fracture, a combined overhang of the C1 lateral masses over C2 exceeding about how much suggests transverse atlantal ligament rupture (Spence rule)?
items.e: Spence's rule states that a total lateral mass overhang over 6.9 mm (about 8.1 mm allowing for radiographic magnification) indicates rupture of the transverse ligament and instability.

items.q: During surgery for a terrible triad injury of the elbow, what is the usual sequence of repair from deep to superficial?
o: Lateral collateral ligament, then coronoid, then radial head
Radial head, then medial collateral ligament, then coronoid
Coronoid or anterior capsule, then radial head, then lateral collateral ligament complex
Medial collateral ligament, then lateral collateral ligament, then radial head
items.e: The coronoid (or anterior capsule) is fixed first, the radial head repaired or replaced, and the LCL complex repaired to the lateral epicondyle; the MCL is repaired or a hinged fixator applied only if instability persists.

items.q: A fracture of the anteromedial facet of the coronoid process with a lateral collateral ligament tear produces which pattern of instability?
items.e: O'Driscoll anteromedial facet fractures result from varus and posteromedial rotation with LCL disruption and usually need buttress fixation of the facet to prevent varus subluxation and arthrosis.

items.q: The term 'floating shoulder' classically describes which injury combination?
o: Ipsilateral clavicle fracture and scapular (glenoid) neck fracture
Proximal humerus fracture with glenoid rim fracture
items.e: A floating shoulder is a double disruption of the superior shoulder suspensory complex (Goss), most commonly an ipsilateral clavicle and glenoid neck fracture.

items.q: Why do Neer type II lateral clavicle fractures have a high nonunion rate?
o: The fracture is intra-articular at the acromioclavicular joint
The coracoclavicular ligaments are detached from the medial fragment, which is pulled upward
The lateral fragment has no periosteal blood supply
The medial fragment is displaced downward by pectoralis major
items.e: In Neer II fractures the medial fragment loses its coracoclavicular attachment and is elevated by trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, while the arm weight pulls the lateral fragment down, causing high nonunion rates.

items.q: In Mayfield's progressive perilunar instability, stage III represents disruption of which structure?
o: Dorsal radiocarpal ligament allowing lunate dislocation
items.e: Mayfield stages progress from scapholunate disruption (I) to capitolunate (II), lunotriquetral (III) and finally lunate dislocation (IV) through failure of the dorsal radiocarpal ligament.

items.q: The principal blood supply to the proximal pole of the scaphoid enters through:
o: Volar tubercle branches of the ulnar artery
Branches of the anterior interosseous artery entering the proximal pole
Dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery, flowing retrograde
items.e: About 70-80% of the scaphoid, including the entire proximal pole, is supplied retrograde by dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery, explaining avascular necrosis after waist and proximal fractures.

items.q: In a Bennett fracture-dislocation, which muscle is chiefly responsible for proximal and radial displacement of the metacarpal shaft?
items.e: The volar-ulnar fragment stays attached to the anterior oblique (beak) ligament, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally and radially and adductor pollicis adducts it.

items.q: In a trial, 20% of control patients and 15% of treated patients have a deep infection. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one infection?
items.e: The absolute risk reduction is 20% - 15% = 5%, and NNT is 1/ARR = 1/0.05 = 20.

items.q: A new test for periprosthetic joint infection gives 90 true positives, 10 false negatives, 30 false positives and 170 true negatives. What is its positive predictive value?
items.e: PPV = true positives / all positives = 90/(90+30) = 75%; sensitivity is 90%, specificity 85% and NPV about 94%.

items.q: A study is designed with 80% power. What does this mean?
o: The probability of a type I error (alpha) is 0.20
There is an 80% chance the null hypothesis is true
80% of patients will show the treatment effect
The probability of a type II error (beta) is 0.20
items.e: Power is 1 - beta, the probability of detecting a true difference of the specified size; 80% power accepts a 20% chance of a false-negative (type II) result.

items.q: The 'fragility index' of a randomised trial with a significant dichotomous outcome is defined as:
o: The minimum number of patients whose outcome would need to change from non-event to event to make the result non-significant
The number of patients lost to follow-up
The ratio of the confidence interval width to the effect size
The number of trials needed to overturn a meta-analysis
items.e: A small fragility index (often below the number lost to follow-up) shows that a statistically significant result is fragile; many orthopaedic RCTs have indices under 5.

items.q: On MRI, normal tendons can show falsely increased signal on short-TE sequences when oriented at about what angle to the main magnetic field (magic angle effect)?
items.e: The magic angle artefact occurs when collagen fibres lie about 55° to B0 on short-TE (T1, PD, gradient echo) sequences, mimicking tendinopathy; it disappears on long-TE T2 images.

items.q: On CT, subcutaneous fat typically measures approximately how many Hounsfield units?
items.e: The Hounsfield scale sets water at 0 and air at -1000; fat measures around -50 to -150 HU, and dense cortical bone around +1000 HU or more.

items.q: On musculoskeletal ultrasound, a normal tendon appears falsely hypoechoic when the beam is not perpendicular to its fibres. This artefact is called:
items.e: Anisotropy is the loss of echogenicity in fibrillar structures (tendons, ligaments) when the beam is angled; it can mimic a tear and is corrected by angling the probe.

items.q: During fluoroscopy, a surgeon doubles his distance from the X-ray source. His radiation exposure falls to approximately:
items.e: By the inverse square law, intensity is proportional to 1/distance squared, so doubling the distance reduces exposure to about one quarter.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman wishes to stop denosumab after 4 years of treatment. What is recommended to prevent rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures?
o: Start a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid about 6 months after the last denosumab dose
Halve the denosumab dose for 1 year before stopping
items.e: Denosumab withdrawal causes rapid rebound resorption and risk of multiple vertebral fractures, so a bisphosphonate should be given when the next dose would be due.

items.q: Romosozumab should not be started in a patient with which history?
o: Myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding year
items.e: Romosozumab, an anti-sclerostin antibody given monthly for 12 months, carries a boxed warning for myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death.

items.q: Abaloparatide, used as an osteoanabolic agent, is an analogue of which molecule?
items.e: Abaloparatide is a synthetic PTHrP(1-34) analogue acting on the PTH1 receptor, whereas teriparatide is recombinant PTH(1-34).

items.q: The CARES trial compared febuxostat with allopurinol in gout patients with cardiovascular disease. What did it show?
o: Higher cardiovascular and all-cause mortality with febuxostat
Higher rates of Stevens-Johnson syndrome with febuxostat
items.e: Although febuxostat was non-inferior for the composite endpoint, cardiovascular death and all-cause mortality were higher than with allopurinol, leading to a boxed warning.

items.q: Before starting allopurinol in a patient of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry, which genetic test is recommended to reduce the risk of severe cutaneous reactions?
items.e: HLA-B*5801 carriage strongly predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome and SJS/TEN; HLA-B*5701 is the abacavir hypersensitivity marker.

items.q: In urate-lowering therapy for gout without tophi, what is the target serum urate level?
items.e: Guidelines (ACR, EULAR) recommend treat-to-target below 6 mg/dL (360 µmol/L), and below 5 mg/dL in severe or tophaceous gout.

items.q: In the ARCO 2019 classification of femoral head osteonecrosis, stage IIIA is defined by subchondral fracture with femoral head depression of:
o: Any depression with joint space narrowing
items.e: ARCO 2019 stage III is subchondral fracture or collapse, subdivided into IIIA (early, depression up to 2 mm) and IIIB (late, more than 2 mm); stage IV is osteoarthritis.

items.q: In the modified Kerboul method for femoral head osteonecrosis, a combined necrotic angle greater than which value predicts a high risk of collapse?
items.e: Summing the necrotic arcs on mid-sagittal and mid-coronal MRI, angles under 190° carry low risk while angles over 240° predict a high risk of collapse.

items.q: Which zone of adult articular cartilage has the highest proteoglycan concentration and the lowest water content?
items.e: Water content is highest superficially and lowest in the deep zone, where proteoglycan content is highest and collagen fibres run perpendicular to the surface.

items.q: Lubricin, a boundary lubricant of articular cartilage, is encoded by which gene, whose mutation causes camptodactyly-arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis syndrome?
items.e: Lubricin (proteoglycan 4) is secreted by superficial zone chondrocytes and synoviocytes and provides boundary lubrication; PRG4 mutations cause CACP syndrome.

items.q: Which cells of the synovial lining secrete hyaluronic acid into synovial fluid?
items.e: Type A synoviocytes are phagocytic macrophage-like cells, whereas type B fibroblast-like synoviocytes produce hyaluronan and lubricin.

items.q: Which of the following implant materials has the lowest elastic modulus, closest to cortical bone?
items.e: Titanium alloy has a modulus of about 110 GPa versus about 200 GPa for stainless steel, 210-230 GPa for cobalt-chromium and around 380 GPa for alumina; cortical bone is about 15-20 GPa.

items.q: Which screw characteristic most strongly determines pull-out strength in bone?
items.e: Pull-out strength depends on the area of bone captured by the threads, chiefly the outer diameter and thread depth, plus bone density; core diameter mainly governs bending and torsional strength.

items.q: If the thickness of a plate is doubled while its width is unchanged, its bending stiffness increases by a factor of about:
items.e: Plate bending stiffness is proportional to the cube of its thickness (area moment of inertia = width x thickness^3/12), so doubling thickness increases it eightfold.

items.q: A ligament held under a constant load continues to elongate over time. This viscoelastic behaviour is called:
items.e: Creep is increasing deformation under constant load; stress relaxation is falling stress under constant deformation, and hysteresis is energy lost during a load-unload cycle.

items.q: In Sunderland's classification of nerve injury, a fourth-degree injury involves:
o: Disruption of endoneurium and perineurium with only epineurium intact
