items.e: Absolute indications for clavicle ORIF include open fractures, neurovascular injury, and skin tenting with impending perforation. Shortening > 2 cm and 100% displacement are relative indications supported by the COTS trial to reduce non-union.

items.q: A 35-year-old man sustains a closed transverse midshaft humeral fracture in a motor vehicle accident. On examination, he has a complete radial nerve palsy. What is the most appropriate initial management of the nerve palsy?
o: Immediate surgical exploration of the radial nerve
Functional bracing of the humerus and observation of the nerve
Early EMG/NCV studies at 1 week to assess prognosis
Tendon transfers for wrist and finger extension
items.e: Radial nerve palsy associated with a closed humeral shaft fracture is typically a neurapraxia with a high rate of spontaneous recovery (70-90%). The recommended management is observation for 3-4 months before considering exploration or EMG.

items.q: A 60-year-old male sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation which is reduced in the emergency department. One week later, he reports persistent weakness in shoulder abduction. What is the most likely cause of this weakness in this age group?
items.e: In patients over 40 years of age, the incidence of rotator cuff tears following an anterior shoulder dislocation increases significantly. Persistent weakness after reduction in an older patient should be evaluated for a cuff tear via MRI or ultrasound.

items.q: During the surgical management of a 'terrible triad' injury of the elbow, which of the following reflects the correct sequence of stabilization when using a lateral approach?
o: Radial head replacement -> LUCL repair -> Coronoid fixation
Coronoid fixation -> Radial head fixation/replacement -> LUCL repair
LUCL repair -> Radial head replacement -> MCL repair -> Coronoid fixation
MCL repair -> LUCL repair -> Radial head fixation
items.e: The recommended sequence for terrible triad injuries is (1) coronoid fixation or anterior capsule repair, (2) radial head fixation or replacement, (3) LCL (LUCL) repair, and finally (4) MCL repair or external fixator if still unstable.

items.q: A 40-year-old patient presents with a comminuted radial head fracture. Clinical examination and imaging suggest an associated interosseous membrane disruption and distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) tenderness. Which procedure is strictly contraindicated in this patient?
o: Stabilization of the DRUJ with K-wires
items.e: In an Essex-Lopresti injury (radial head fracture + IOM disruption + DRUJ injury), the radial head must never be excised as it is a critical longitudinal stabilizer. It must be fixed or replaced.

items.q: A patient undergoes ORIF with a 3.5 mm LC-DCP for a distal-third radial shaft fracture. Intraoperative testing reveals that the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) is reducible but remains unstable even when the forearm is placed in full supination. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Perform an open reduction of the DRUJ to check for ECU interposition
Pin the radius to the ulna with the forearm in supination
Apply a volar buttress plate to the distal ulna
Immediate active range of motion exercise
items.e: According to the notes, if the DRUJ is reducible but remains unstable after radial fixation, the radius should be pinned to the ulna in supination. If it were stable in supination, early motion would be the next step.

items.q: A 52-year-old active woman sustains a distal radius fracture after a fall. Post-reduction radiographs show a radial height of 11 mm, a radial inclination of 18 degrees, and a dorsal tilt of 5 degrees. Based on acceptable radiographic parameters for an active adult, which of the following is correct?
o: The radial height indicates excessive shortening.
The alignment is within acceptable limits.
The dorsal tilt is unacceptable and requires re-reduction.
items.e: Acceptable parameters after reduction in an active adult include shortening under 3-5 mm (normal height is 11-12 mm), radial inclination over 15 degrees, and dorsal tilt under 10 degrees (or neutral/volar tilt).

items.q: Which of the following is a primary predictor of instability in distal radius fractures according to the Lafontaine criteria?
items.e: Lafontaine's instability predictors include dorsal angulation >20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular involvement, associated ulnar fracture, and age over 60. Initial shortening >5 mm is also a predictor.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient with severe left hip osteoarthritis is evaluated for conservative gait modifications prior to joint replacement. Which of the following actions will INCREASE the joint reaction force across the affected hip joint?
o: Using a walking cane in the contralateral hand
Carrying a heavy briefcase in the contralateral hand
Leaning the trunk over the affected side during stance (Trendelenburg lurch)
Carrying a heavy load in the ipsilateral hand
items.e: Carrying a load in the contralateral hand increases the body weight moment arm relative to the hip, thereby requiring a greater abductor muscle force and increasing the overall joint reaction force (JRF). Conversely, using a cane in the contralateral hand reduces hip JRF by up to 40–60%, and carrying loads in the ipsilateral hand or leaning over the affected hip (Trendelenburg lurch) reduces abductor muscle demand and JRF.

items.q: A surgeon reviews hospital records to compare the 5-year implant survivorship of two different femoral stem designs used in patients who underwent total hip arthroplasty between 2010 and 2015. Surgical details and outcomes were gathered retrospectively from patient charts. According to the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (JBJS) hierarchy for therapeutic studies, what level of evidence does this study represent?
items.e: A retrospective comparative cohort study and a case-control study are classified as Level III evidence. Prospective comparative cohort studies represent Level II evidence, whereas non-comparative case series represent Level IV evidence.

items.q: An investigator is analysing 15-year implant survivorship of a total knee arthroplasty system in an elderly cohort (mean age 78 years at index surgery). During long-term follow-up, a significant proportion of subjects die before requiring revision surgery. If the investigator performs a standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis treating death as a censored event, what is the effect on the estimated cumulative revision rate?
o: It overestimates the cumulative revision rate
It underestimates the cumulative revision rate
It eliminates loss to follow-up bias completely
It provides an unbiased adjusted hazard ratio
items.e: When death acts as a competing risk (preventing the event of interest, revision), standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis overestimates the cumulative revision rate because it assumes censored patients would experience revision at the same rate as surviving patients. To handle competing risks accurately in elderly populations, the cumulative incidence function (Fine and Gray) should be used.

items.q: According to the ASRA guidelines, what is the minimum recommended duration that prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) should be held prior to performing a spinal anaesthesia block?
items.e: According to ASRA guidelines, a minimum of 12 hours must elapse between the last prophylactic dose of LMWH and spinal/epidural needle placement or catheter removal. For therapeutic LMWH, 24 hours is required.

items.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding coronal plane fractures of the femoral condyle (Hoffa fractures)?
o: They are extra-articular fractures classified as AO Type 33A
The medial condyle is more commonly involved than the lateral
They are best visualized on a lateral radiograph or CT scan
They are typically fixed with transverse lag screws from medial to lateral
items.e: Hoffa fractures are coronal plane partial articular fractures (AO Type 33B3). The lateral condyle is more commonly involved. They are often missed on AP views and require lateral views or CT; they are fixed with anteroposterior (AP) lag screws.

items.q: When evaluating the anatomy and common injury patterns of the tibial plateau, which of the following statements is correct?
o: The lateral plateau is concave and lower than the medial plateau
The medial plateau is convex and frequently undergoes pure depression fractures
The lateral plateau is convex and higher than the medial plateau
The medial plateau is smaller and carries less load than the lateral plateau
items.e: The lateral plateau is convex and higher, while the medial plateau is concave, larger, and stronger as it carries more load. Lateral fractures are more common due to the typical valgus-axial load mechanism.

items.q: A 76-year-old woman with an unreconstructable, osteoporotic AO/OTA 13C3 distal humerus fracture is treated with primary total elbow arthroplasty. What lifelong lifting restriction is she usually counselled to follow?
o: No lifting more than 10 kg in a single effort
No repetitive lifting of more than about 1 kg (single lifts up to about 5 kg)
No repetitive lifting of more than about 10 kg
No restriction once the wound has healed
items.e: Linked total elbow arthroplasty carries a lifelong restriction of roughly 1 kg (2 lb) for repetitive lifting and about 5 kg (10 lb) for a single lift, to limit polyethylene bushing wear and aseptic loosening.

items.q: To protect the posterior interosseous nerve during the Kocher (anconeus-ECU) approach to a radial head fracture, the forearm should be held in:
items.e: Pronation moves the PIN anteriorly and medially, away from the operative field of lateral elbow approaches; supination brings it closer to the radial neck.

items.q: A 24-year-old male presents with pain in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall. Initial radiographs are negative, but an MRI confirms an undisplaced fracture of the scaphoid waist. According to the results of the SWIFFT trial (2020), what is the most appropriate management?
o: Percutaneous headless compression screw fixation to allow early return to work
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation with a volar approach
Above-elbow cast immobilization for 6 weeks followed by a brace
items.e: The SWIFFT trial (2020) showed no long-term functional or clinical benefit of early surgical fixation over cast immobilization for undisplaced or minimally displaced (under 2 mm) scaphoid waist fractures.

items.q: A patient presents with a 'spilled teacup' appearance on a lateral wrist radiograph after a high-energy injury. This finding is characteristic of which Mayfield stage of perilunate instability?
items.e: Mayfield Stage IV represents a volar lunate dislocation, where the lunate is displaced and tilted volarly, resembling a spilled teacup on the lateral view. Stage I is scapholunate disruption, Stage II is lunocapitate, and Stage III is lunotriquetral disruption (perilunate dislocation).

items.q: Regarding the anatomy of the scaphoid, which statement is true?
o: The proximal pole receives its main blood supply from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
About 80% of the scaphoid surface is covered by articular cartilage
The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters through the proximal pole
Distal pole fractures carry the highest risk of avascular necrosis
items.e: About 80% of the scaphoid is articular. Its main supply (70-80%) is retrograde from dorsal carpal branches of the radial artery entering at the dorsal ridge near the waist, so proximal pole fractures carry the highest AVN risk.

items.q: A 26-year-old polytrauma patient with bilateral femur fractures and a severe pulmonary contusion undergoes temporary spanning external fixation on admission. In the ICU, the patient improves. According to damage control orthopaedics (DCO) principles, which time window is considered optimal for definitive conversion to intramedullary nailing, and which period should strictly be avoided?
o: Optimal window is within days 2–4; avoid days 4/5–10/14
Optimal window is days 4/5–10/14; avoid days 2–4
Optimal window is within 24–48 hours; avoid days 5–7
Optimal window is after day 14; avoid days 1–3
items.e: In damage control orthopaedics, definitive conversion is performed during the 'window of opportunity' between days 4/5 and 10/14 once physiology recovers. Days 2–4 must be avoided because the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) peaks, increasing the risk of ARDS and multiple organ failure from a 'second hit'.

items.q: A 24-year-old male undergoes intramedullary nailing of a closed tibial shaft fracture. Six hours postoperatively, he complains of severe leg pain out of proportion to the injury, markedly increased by passive stretch of the great toe. Distal dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable. His blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. Anterolateral compartment pressure measured with a slit catheter is 36 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Immediate emergent four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg
Elevate the limb above the heart and monitor compartment pressures hourly
CT angiography to investigate potential anterior tibial artery occlusion
Administer IV regional block and reassess in 2 hours
items.e: Delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus intracompartmental pressure) is 60 - 36 = 24 mmHg. A delta pressure under 30 mmHg confirms acute compartment syndrome and mandates urgent fasciotomy; distal pulses are typically preserved until very late.

items.q: Regarding severe open lower limb injuries and the indications for limb salvage versus primary amputation established by the Lower Extremity Assessment Project (LEAP) study, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Loss of plantar sensation at initial presentation is an absolute indication for primary amputation
Limb salvage demonstrates significantly superior functional outcomes (Sickness Impact Profile) at 2 and 7 years compared to amputation
A Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) of 7 or higher reliably predicts the need for amputation and should be used as the sole decision criterion
Absent plantar sensation at presentation does not mandate amputation, as approximately half of these limbs regain sensation by 2 years
items.e: The LEAP study demonstrated that initial plantar insensation is not an absolute indication for amputation, as about half of initially insensate limbs regain sensation by 2 years. Furthermore, salvage and amputation resulted in comparable functional outcomes (Sickness Impact Profile) at 2 and 7 years.

items.q: Contact (direct) bone healing without callus requires which of the following conditions?
o: Relative stability with a gap under 0.8 mm
Absolute stability with interfragmentary compression and a gap under about 0.01 mm
Any gap size provided the implant is rigid
A bridging plate with a gap under 1 mm
items.e: Contact healing occurs when the fragments are compressed under absolute stability with a gap of less than about 0.01 mm and interfragmentary strain under 2%, allowing cutting cones to cross the fracture directly.

items.q: A fracture fixed with absolute stability is left with a 0.5 mm gap. How does this gap heal?
o: Contact healing, with cutting cones crossing the fracture line directly
Gap healing: lamellar bone fills the gap perpendicular to the long axis and is later remodelled by Haversian systems, without callus
Endochondral ossification through an external bridging callus
It does not heal and progresses to fibrous non-union
items.e: Under absolute stability, gaps smaller than about 0.8-1 mm undergo gap healing, a form of direct (primary) healing: woven/lamellar bone fills the gap transversely and is secondarily remodelled by osteons, with no callus.

items.q: Synovial type non‑union is best described as:
o: A bleeding bone surface with extensive callus
Fluid‑filled false joint surrounded by fibrous tissue
A rigid fused segment with no motion
An avascular bone end with no callus
items.e: Pseudarthrosis (synovial) presents as a fluid‑filled ‘false joint’ where persistent motion keeps the ends from uniting.

items.q: Nine months after plating of a tibial shaft fracture, radiographs show a persistent fracture line with abundant flared callus at the bone ends ('elephant foot') and a loose screw. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Revision to stable fixation (compression plating or exchange nailing) without bone grafting
Decortication with autologous iliac crest bone grafting
Resection of the non-union and Ilizarov bone transport
items.e: An elephant-foot hypertrophic non-union (Weber-Cech) is biologically active; it lacks only mechanical stability, so stable fixation alone usually achieves union without grafting.

items.q: During stage‑1 of the Masquelet technique, which component is essential for membrane induction?
items.e: A polymethylmethacrylate cement spacer is placed inside the defect to induce a vascularized membrane rich in growth factors.

items.q: Which statement best reflects the biological qualities of cancellous autograft harvested from the iliac crest?
o: Cortical strength but no osteogenic potential
Lacks osteoinductive factors but provides rapid structural support
items.e: Cancellous autograft contains living cells (osteogenic), BMPs (osteoinductive) and provides a scaffold (osteoconductive).

items.q: A 48‑year‑old male presents after a motorcycle collision. He is alert, has midline cervical tenderness but no focal neurological deficit. According to the NEXUS criteria, which of the following is the sole reason imaging is required?
items.e: Only the presence of midline cervical tenderness mandates imaging under NEXUS.

items.q: A restrained back-seat passenger wearing only a lap belt sustains an L1 flexion-distraction (Chance) fracture. Which associated injury is most frequently found?
o: Small bowel or other hollow viscus injury
items.e: Lap-belt flexion-distraction injuries are associated with intra-abdominal injury in up to about half of cases, most commonly hollow viscus (small bowel) and mesenteric injuries, so a high index of suspicion is needed.

items.q: A 27-year-old woman has complete paraplegia after a fall. CT shows the T12 vertebral body translated laterally and anteriorly relative to L1. According to the AO Spine thoracolumbar classification, this injury is type:
items.e: Any displacement or translation of the cranial spine relative to the caudal spine in any plane is an AO Spine type C injury, the most unstable morphology; type C has no further subtypes.

items.q: A 62-year-old man has progressive gait imbalance and clumsy hands, with hyperreflexia, a positive Hoffmann sign and an inverted brachioradialis reflex. MRI shows a single-level disc-osteophyte complex compressing the cord at C6-C7, with preserved cervical lordosis. Which operation is most appropriate?
o: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) at C6-C7
items.e: Single- or two-level anterior compression in a lordotic spine is best treated anteriorly; ACDF directly removes the compressing disc-osteophyte. Posterior procedures suit multilevel disease with lordosis, and foraminotomy treats radiculopathy, not myelopathy.

items.q: An MRI of a 54-year-old woman with cervical myelopathy shows a T2 hyperintense signal in the cord without T1 hypointensity. What does this imply for prognosis after decompression?
o: Poor, because any intramedullary signal change indicates irreversible damage
Relatively good, because isolated T2 change often represents reversible oedema or gliosis
Poor, because T2 change indicates syrinx formation
Irrelevant, because only the operative approach determines outcome
items.e: Isolated T2 hyperintensity may reflect oedema and can regress after decompression, whereas combined T1 hypointensity indicates myelomalacia or necrosis and predicts a poorer outcome.

items.q: During planning for multilevel cervical OPLL, the K-line is negative on the neutral lateral radiograph. Which procedure is LEAST likely to achieve adequate decompression?
items.e: A K-line negative OPLL extends beyond the line joining the canal midpoints at C2 and C7, so the cord cannot drift back enough after laminoplasty alone; anterior decompression (or posterior fusion with correction) is preferred.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old patient with a 3‑year history of neck pain and hand numbness has an mJOA score of 11. According to AO Spine guidelines, the most appropriate management is:
o: Surgical decompression with or without fusion
items.e: An mJOA under 12 constitutes severe DCM; guidelines recommend surgery to prevent further decline.

items.q: Which of the following is a static factor contributing to cervical cord compression in degenerative cervical myelopathy?
o: Radiculopathy from a central disc herniation
items.e: Static factors are anatomical; a low Torg‑Pavlov ratio indicates a congenitally stenotic canal.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old woman presents with chronic low back pain unrelieved by NSAIDs for 8 weeks. MRI of the lumbar spine shows a L4‑L5 disc with a Pfirrmann grade IV appearance and a Modic type I change of the adjacent endplate. According to current consensus, the most likely explanation for her pain is:
o: Inflammatory oedema in the vertebral marrow
items.e: Modic type I changes (low T1, high T2) represent oedema/inflammation in the vertebral endplate and are the imaging correlate most often linked to chronic low back pain.

items.q: In the SPORT spinal stenosis study (degenerative lumbar stenosis without spondylolisthesis), the as-treated analysis showed that:
o: Non-operative care gave superior long-term outcomes to decompression
Decompression produced significantly greater improvement in pain and function, maintained through 4-year follow-up
There was no difference between the groups at any time point
The early benefit of decompression had disappeared by 1 year
items.e: In SPORT, patients treated surgically for spinal stenosis had significantly greater improvement in bodily pain, function and disability than those treated non-operatively, and the benefit persisted at 4 years.

items.q: A 48-year-old man presents with saddle anaesthesia, urinary urgency and reduced anal tone; bladder scan shows a post-void residual of 250 ml. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine followed by urgent decompression if compression is confirmed
Elective myelography and a trial of conservative treatment
items.e: Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs emergency MRI to confirm the level and cause, followed by urgent decompression; operating without imaging risks the wrong level and steroids have no role.

items.q: A 13-year-old girl (Risser 1) has a 34° right thoracic idiopathic curve. According to the BrAIST trial, which management best reduces progression to the surgical threshold of 50°?
o: Full-time rigid TLSO, with benefit increasing with hours of wear
items.e: BrAIST (2013) showed rigid bracing reduced progression to 50° (72% success vs 48% with observation), with a dose-response: wear of about 13 hours or more a day gave success rates of 90-93%.

items.q: In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, which radiographic assessment best predicts remaining growth and the timing of peak height velocity?
o: Cobb angle on the standing PA radiograph
Risser grade of the iliac apophysis
Sanders skeletal maturity stage on a hand radiograph
Nash-Moe grade of apical vertebral rotation
items.e: The Sanders stage (based on the hand phalangeal and metacarpal epiphyses) correlates better with peak height velocity and curve progression risk than Risser grade; Sanders stage 3 coincides with peak height velocity.

items.q: During posterior spinal fusion of a Lenke 1 curve, a sudden loss of motor evoked potentials (MEPs) is noted. The first intra‑operative step should be:
o: Proceed to a Stagnara wake‑up test
items.e: MEP loss is treated first by raising MAP to restore perfusion and checking anesthesia; only then are correction forces adjusted.

items.q: Which of the following is true regarding early‑onset scoliosis (EOS) before age 10?
o: It primarily causes kyphosis rather than scoliosis
Thoracic insufficiency syndrome is a major long‑term risk
Growth of the spine is not a concern
items.e: EOS patients are at risk of thoracic insufficiency syndrome because lung and chest wall growth are disrupted.

items.q: A 14-year-old girl with a 52° Lenke 1 thoracic curve is planned for posterior spinal fusion. Which construct gives the greatest correction of apical vertebral rotation?
o: Hybrid construct of hooks and screws
All-pedicle-screw segmental construct with direct vertebral rotation
items.e: Segmental pedicle screws grip all three columns and allow direct vertebral derotation, giving better coronal and axial (rotational) correction than hook, hybrid, wire or Harrington constructs.

items.q: A 2-year-old has a progressive left thoracic infantile idiopathic curve. Which examination finding most strongly suggests an underlying intraspinal anomaly requiring MRI of the whole neuraxis?
o: Plagiocephaly on the same side as the convexity
Asymmetric or absent superficial abdominal reflexes
items.e: Asymmetric abdominal reflexes are a neurological red flag for syringomyelia or Chiari malformation; plagiocephaly and a left thoracic curve are typical of benign infantile idiopathic scoliosis.

items.q: A 9‑year‑old boy with rapidly progressive kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction shows separation of facets and posterior retropulsion on imaging. Which of the following is the most likely indication for surgical intervention?
o: Presence of a painless cold abscess
items.e: Two or more Rajasekaran “spine‑at‑risk” signs predict severe kyphosis progression; surgery is indicated in such children.

items.q: Which laboratory test is most specific for diagnosing spinal tuberculosis in an endemic setting?
items.e: GeneXpert MTB/RIF on biopsy provides rapid, specific detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance, the most definitive test in endemic areas.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of the thoracic spine in a patient with metastatic breast carcinoma, one pedicle outline is absent. What is this sign called?
items.e: Metastases spreading from the vertebral body destroy the pedicle early, so its loss on the AP view gives the 'winking owl' sign. Corduroy is haemangioma, rugger-jersey is renal osteodystrophy and picture-frame is Paget disease.

items.q: In the NOMS decision‑making framework for metastatic spinal disease, which component assesses tumour radiosensitivity?
items.e: The ‘Oncological’ arm of NOMS evaluates whether the tumour is radiosensitive or radioresistant, guiding the choice between surgery, radiotherapy or both.

items.q: The classic axial CT appearance of a typical asymptomatic haemangioma is described as:
items.e: On axial CT a haemangioma shows a punctate or ‘polka‑dot’ pattern due to thickened vertical vessels within the affected vertebral body.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman with adult spinal deformity has a pelvic incidence of 60°, lumbar lordosis of 30° and SVA of 8 cm. In the SRS-Schwab classification her PI-LL modifier is:
o: Cannot be graded without pelvic tilt
items.e: PI-LL = 60 - 30 = 30°, which exceeds 20° and is graded '++'. Her SVA of 8 cm (over 9.5 cm is '++') is graded '+' for global alignment.

items.q: Which Roussouly type corresponds to a sacral slope below 35° and a lumbar lordosis that is short and low?
items.e: Type 1 has SS<35° and a short, low lordosis, often predisposing to disc degeneration at the thoracolumbar junction.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man is found to have elevated serum CTX and normal serum osteocalcin. Which cell‑type is primarily responsible for the rise in CTX?
items.e: CTX is a degradation product of type‑I collagen cleaved by osteoclast‑derived cathepsin K; hence osteoclasts are the main source.

items.q: During normal bone remodeling, which of the following pathways is indispensable for driving osteoblast differentiation from mesenchymal progenitors?
items.e: Wnt ligands bind Frizzled/LRP5‑6, stabilising β‑catenin and up‑regulating RUNX2, the master transcription factor for osteogenesis.

items.q: Osteocalcin is a major non‑collagenous protein in bone. Which statement is true regarding its regulation?
o: It requires vitamin C for γ‑carboxylation
Its expression is suppressed by 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D
It binds the RANKL receptor on osteoclasts
It is a bone‑formation marker secreted by osteoblasts
items.e: Osteocalcin is a vitamin K‑dependent protein produced by osteoblasts and used as a serum marker of bone formation.

items.q: A mutation that abolishes the function of the CLCN7 chloride channel results in which of the following skeletal phenotypes?
items.e: CLCN7 loss impairs osteoclast acidification, causing a form of osteopetrosis; mental retardation and renal tubular acidosis are not seen.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the inorganic mineral phase of bone?
items.e: Osteocalcin is an organic matrix protein, not part of the mineral phase.

items.q: Which collagen type is concentrated in the pericellular matrix immediately surrounding chondrocytes in articular cartilage?
items.e: Type VI collagen forms the pericellular network of the chondron and anchors chondrocytes to the matrix; type II is the main interterritorial collagen and type X is found in the calcified zone.

items.q: Which biomechanical property of articular cartilage is primarily responsible for its ability to off‑load a joint during a single gait cycle?
o: Elastic modulus in the superficial zone
Fluid pressurisation in the solid‑fluid biphasic model
items.e: Under load, the fluid phase initially carries >90 % of the joint load, protecting the solid matrix.

items.q: Compared with type II collagen, turnover of aggrecan in adult articular cartilage is:
o: Much faster, so proteoglycan loss is potentially reversible early in OA
Much slower, taking more than a century
Absent once skeletal maturity is reached
items.e: Type II collagen has a half-life of over 100 years, whereas aggrecan turns over in years or less, so early proteoglycan depletion can recover while collagen network damage is essentially permanent.

items.q: When the biceps flexes the elbow to lift a weight in the hand, the elbow is the fulcrum and the biceps insertion lies between the fulcrum and the load. This is which class of lever?
o: It does not act as a lever
items.e: With the effort applied between the fulcrum and the load, the elbow flexors form a third-class lever, which favours speed and range of motion over mechanical advantage.

items.q: Five years after cementless THA with a large-diameter, extensively porous-coated cobalt-chromium stem, radiographs show a well-fixed stem with proximal calcar rounding and cortical thinning but distal cortical hypertrophy. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Stress shielding due to stem stiffness
items.e: A stiff, distally fixed stem transfers load distally and unloads the proximal femur, producing adaptive proximal bone loss (stress shielding); stem stiffness rises with diameter and modulus, so large cobalt-chromium stems are worst.

items.q: A 55-year-old man has a persistent femoral shaft non-union after intramedullary nailing. At 12 months the nail breaks at the level of the non-union. What is the most likely failure mechanism?
o: Fatigue failure from repeated cyclic loading below the ultimate strength
Creep of the nail under constant load
Crevice corrosion of the nail surface
items.e: Implants protect a fracture only until union; with a non-union, cyclic sub-ultimate loading causes fatigue cracks, often at stress risers such as screw holes, until the nail breaks.

items.q: The fastest conducting peripheral nerve fibers are:
items.e: A‑alpha fibers (70–120 m/s) are the fastest, carrying alpha motor neuron and proprioceptive Ia/Ib signals.

items.q: Which receptor type in muscle provides the rapid adjustment of muscle length during a stretch reflex?
items.e: The muscle spindle detects sudden length changes and initiates the stretch reflex.

items.q: In a prospective cohort study investigating the effect of a new brace on wrist fracture healing, which of the following measures of association is most appropriate?
items.e: Prospective cohort designs allow direct calculation of incidence; relative risk compares the proportion of events in exposed vs unexposed groups.

items.q: A properly randomised controlled trial of 120 patients comparing two surgical techniques has 85% follow-up and reports a significant difference in the primary functional outcome. According to the JBJS levels of evidence for therapeutic studies, this is:
items.e: A high-quality randomised controlled trial with at least 80% follow-up is Level I; an RCT with poor follow-up or methodology drops to Level II.

items.q: A systematic review of 8 randomized controlled trials on postoperative pain management found high heterogeneity (I² = 68 %). Which GRADE factor would most likely lead to downgrading the certainty of evidence?
items.e: High heterogeneity reflects inconsistency among study results, a GRADE downgrading criterion.

items.q: An observational cohort study claims that a drug reduces fracture risk, but the exposed group had a different history of falls. Which analytic method best balances such measured confounders between exposed and unexposed patients?
o: Sensitivity analysis of losses to follow-up
items.e: Propensity score matching pairs exposed and unexposed patients with similar probabilities of exposure based on measured covariates (such as fall history), reducing confounding in observational data; it cannot correct unmeasured confounders.

items.q: A meta‑analysis of 12 studies on a new fixation device shows a funnel plot that is symmetric. Which bias is least likely to affect the pooled estimate?
items.e: Symmetry in a funnel plot generally indicates an absence of publication bias.

items.q: In an RCT evaluating two rehabilitation protocols, the primary outcome is the change in a functional score measured at 6 months. Which intention‑to‑treat principle applies?
o: Patients are analysed according to the protocol they actually followed
Patients are analysed according to the treatment they received
All randomised patients are analysed in the groups they were randomised to
items.e: Intention‑to‑treat analysis includes all participants in the groups to which they were randomised, regardless of adherence.

items.q: A technologist increases the kVp for a hand radiograph to shorten the exposure, and image contrast falls. The loss of contrast is mainly due to a relative decrease in which interaction?
items.e: Photoelectric absorption, which depends strongly on atomic number (about Z³/E³), creates bone-soft tissue contrast; at higher photon energies it falls sharply and Compton scatter dominates, reducing contrast.

items.q: During fluoroscopy, a theatre nurse steps back from 1 m to 2 m from the patient and the measured scatter dose rate falls to about one quarter. Which principle explains this?
items.e: Radiation intensity from a point source is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, so doubling the distance reduces dose to one quarter.

items.q: Which SI unit expresses the energy absorbed per unit mass of tissue during a DEXA scan?
items.e: Absorbed dose is measured in gray (1 J/kg); the sievert expresses equivalent or effective dose weighted for radiation and tissue type, the becquerel measures radioactivity and the roentgen measures exposure in air.

items.q: Compared with a standard C-arm, using a mini C-arm for hand and wrist surgery offers which advantage?
o: Higher patient skin entrance dose for better image quality
Lower scatter radiation to the surgeon and theatre staff
Higher tube output allowing faster imaging
No difference in dose but a larger field of view
items.e: Mini C-arms use lower tube current and a smaller field, so patient dose and scatter to staff are much lower, provided the surgeon's hands are kept out of the direct beam.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old diabetic patient scheduled for elective total knee replacement is on insulin therapy. What is the recommended peri‑operative glucose target to minimise wound‑infection risk?
items.e: Current peri‑operative guidelines and evidence from orthopaedic studies recommend maintaining glucose <180 mg/dL to reduce infection risk. A target <140 mg/dL is unnecessarily stringent and may predispose to hypoglycaemia; >200 mg/dL is associated with higher infection rates.

items.q: In a patient with a known MRSA colonisation, the attending surgeon wants to give peri‑operative antibiotic prophylaxis. Which of the following gives the best coverage and is most appropriate to add to cefazolin?
items.e: Cefazolin is the standard for clean orthopedic surgery; vancomycin is added for MRSA colonisation or high‑risk situations.

items.q: Which pharmacological property makes fluoroquinolones useful for oral treatment of bone and joint infections?
o: Excellent bone penetration and high oral bioavailability
Low risk of tendon rupture in elderly patients
items.e: Fluoroquinolones achieve good bone concentrations and near-complete oral bioavailability, allowing oral therapy (often combined with rifampicin for staphylococci), but they increase the risk of tendinopathy and tendon rupture, especially over 60 years.

items.q: When a patient with a history of chronic steroid use undergoes a total hip replacement, which of the following peri‑operative interventions is most important to reduce the risk of periprosthetic joint infection?
o: Avoid intra‑articular steroid injections within 3 months pre‑op
items.e: Intra‑articular steroids within 3 months increase infection risk; thus they should be avoided pre‑operatively.

items.q: Which drug should NOT be used as monotherapy for treatment of a staphylococcal implant infection due to its rapid resistance development?
items.e: Rifampicin alone induces resistance rapidly; it must be paired with another agent.

items.q: In an elderly patient with a simple pertrochanteric fracture (AO 31A1), the surgeon measures the tip‑apex distance (TAD) of the lag screw on postoperative AP and lateral radiographs. The sum is 28 mm. What is the most likely clinical implication?
o: Adequate fixation with low risk of failure
Risk of varus collapse but low cut‑out risk
items.e: Typical cut‑out risk rises sharply when TAD exceeds 25 mm; 28 mm indicates a high probability of mechanical failure.

items.q: A 57‑year‑old woman sustains a Weber B fracture of the fibula with a posterior malleolar fragment involving 28% of the articular surface. Which fixation strategy is most appropriate?
o: Lag screw only for the fibula and close‑wedge cast for the posterior fragment
Posterior malleolar fragment fixed with a buttress plate via the posterolateral approach and fibula fixed with lateral plating
Open reduction of the posterior facet with a screw and fibula fixed with an intramedullary nail
Closed reduction and casting of both fragments
items.e: Current evidence favours direct fixation of the posterior fragment when it is >25–30%; a posterolateral buttress plate restores syndesmotic stability simultaneously.

items.q: A 22-year-old has a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation; MRI shows a posterosuperolateral humeral head impaction. Which associated lesion is most likely?
o: Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion of the anteromedial head
items.e: In young patients, anterior dislocation characteristically produces a Bankart lesion of the anteroinferior labrum together with the posterosuperolateral Hill-Sachs impaction; rotator cuff tears become common mainly after age 40.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old female presents with a displaced, transverse fracture of the olecranon that is non‑comminuted but is displaced more than 2 mm. Sensory exam of the ulnar nerve is normal. What is the most appropriate surgical fixation?
o: Tension‑band wiring using two parallel K‑wires and a figure‑of‑eight wire
Anterior plating with a volar plate
items.e: A transverse, non‑comminuted olecranon fracture >2 mm is best fixed by tension‑band wiring, which converts triceps pull into compressive forces across the fracture.

items.q: A 78-year-old woman with osteoporosis has a comminuted, low intercondylar AO/OTA 13C3 distal humerus fracture judged unreconstructable. Which treatment gives the most predictable early function?
o: Parallel medial and lateral locking plates
items.e: In elderly patients with unreconstructable osteoporotic distal humerus fractures, primary linked total elbow arthroplasty gives better early function and fewer reoperations than ORIF, at the cost of lifelong lifting restrictions.

items.q: A 27‑year‑old male presents with a comminuted open tibial shaft fracture (Gustilo–Anderson type IIIB) after a bicycle accident. He is haemodynamically stable but has a diastolic BP of 88 mmHg and a lactate of 3.2 mmol/L. According to the early appropriate care (EAC) criteria, when may definitive intramedullary nailing be safely performed?
o: Once lactate is <4 mmol/L, pH >7.25, and BE >‑5.5
Only after completion of a 24‑hour course of broad‑spectrum antibiotics
items.e: EAC allows definitive fixation within 36 h once physiological parameters are favourable – lactate <4 mmol/L, pH ≥7.25 and base excess >‑5.5.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a Gustilo-Anderson type III open tibial fracture. Which antibiotic regimen is traditionally recommended for the first 24-72 hours?
o: Cefazolin plus gentamicin (5 mg/kg once daily)
items.e: Type III open fractures need gram-positive and gram-negative cover, classically a first-generation cephalosporin plus an aminoglycoside (adding penicillin for farmyard contamination), continued until 24-72 hours after wound closure.

items.q: What is the main advantage of reamed over unreamed intramedullary nailing for a closed femoral shaft fracture?
o: Higher union rates, from a larger stiffer nail and reaming debris acting as local graft
Preservation of the endosteal blood supply
Absolute stability leading to primary bone healing
items.e: Reaming allows a larger-diameter nail with better cortical contact and deposits osteogenic debris at the fracture, giving higher union rates; it damages endosteal blood supply temporarily and healing remains secondary, with callus.

items.q: A 23-year-old falls from a bicycle at low speed and has neck pain. He is alert, has no high-risk factors and is sitting in the emergency department. According to the Canadian C-spine rule, he can be cleared without imaging if he:
o: Had a dangerous mechanism of injury
Can actively rotate his neck 45° to the left and right
items.e: In patients without high-risk factors (age 65 or more, dangerous mechanism, limb paraesthesia) who have a low-risk factor, the ability to actively rotate the neck 45° to each side allows clinical clearance without radiography.

items.q: A 32-year-old has a traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis after a car crash: bilateral C2 pars fractures with 4 mm translation and some angulation, without a widened C2-C3 disc posteriorly (Levine-Edwards type II). Initial management is usually:
o: Open reduction and C1-C3 posterior fusion
Closed reduction with traction and extension, then a halo vest
Anterior C2-C3 discectomy and fusion as first-line
items.e: Levine-Edwards type II hangman's fractures are usually reduced with axial traction and slight extension and held in a halo; type IIA must not be placed in traction, and type III needs open reduction and fixation.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man with a high‑speed MVC has a C3–C4 transverse fracture‑distraction. The SLIC score is 5. Treatment should be:
items.e: SLIC ≥5 mandates surgery; a transverse distractive injury needs posterior fusion.

items.q: In a patient with segmental OPLL spanning C4–C6, what imaging sign predicts that posterior decompression alone is likely to fail?
o: Presence of double‑layer sign on CT
items.e: When the OPLL occupies >60% of the canal (occupying ratio), posterior decompression alone usually fails, prompting consideration of an anterior approach or posterior fusion.

items.q: A 70‑year‑old man with a mild mJOA score of 16 has a 4‑month history of progressive hand clumsiness but no gait disturbance. According to AO Spine recommendations, what is the initial management strategy?
o: Structured supervised rehabilitation for a limited period
items.e: With mild DCM (mJOA 15‑17) and no significant deficits, the guideline recommends a trial of supervised rehabilitation, with surgery reserved if symptoms worsen.

items.q: Which Pfirrmann grade on lumbar disc MRI indicates the most advanced degeneration?
items.e: Pfirrmann grading is I–V; grade V represents the most severe changes—complete loss of disc height and signal.

items.q: Which clinical sign is the most specific for a lumbar disc herniation causing radiculopathy?
items.e: The crossed straight-leg raise (sciatica reproduced in the affected leg when the opposite leg is raised) has high specificity (about 90%) but low sensitivity; the ipsilateral SLR is sensitive but less specific.

items.q: Which patient with a lumbar disc herniation most clearly warrants early surgical discectomy rather than continued conservative care?
o: 4 weeks of sciatica with mild neurogenic claudication
L4-L5 herniation with a progressive dense foot drop despite 6 weeks of treatment
Asymptomatic disc protrusion found on MRI
Non-radiating low back pain with Modic I changes
items.e: A progressive or severe motor deficit (and cauda equina syndrome) is an indication for early decompression; most patients with sciatica alone improve and surgery mainly offers faster relief.

items.q: What is the most frequent complication after microdiscectomy for lumbar disc herniation?
items.e: Recurrent disc herniation occurs in roughly 3–7 % of cases, most often within the first six months; it is the most common postoperative problem.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old man with thoracolumbar TB develops paraplegia after 10 months of ATT. He has a posterior element disease with retropulsion of the pedicle. Which surgical approach is most indicated?
o: Anterior radical debridement and strut grafting
Posterior pedicle screw fixation with transpedicular debridement
items.e: Posterior element disease with neurological deficit necessitates posterior debridement and instrumentation; it allows decompression, correction of kyphosis, and stabilization.

items.q: A 25-year-old with C3-C4 tuberculous spondylodiscitis develops a large cold abscess in the retropharyngeal space. Its most likely presenting feature is:
items.e: Upper cervical TB abscesses collect in the retropharyngeal space and present with dysphagia, hoarseness or stridor; they may need drainage through the mouth or a lateral neck approach.

items.q: The Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) gives a total of 15 for a patient with a T12 lytic metastasis, significant mechanical pain, and a 50% collapse of the vertebral body. According to current guidelines, what is the recommended next step?
items.e: A score of 15 (unstable) mandates surgical consultation for decompression and stabilization, as non‑operative options are unlikely to relieve instability or neurological deficit.

items.q: A 52‑year‑old female with a known thyroid carcinoma presents with sudden onset of back pain. MRI reveals a single, intensely enhancing, lytic lesion in L2 with soft‑tissue mass extending into the canal. According to the NOMS framework, which component is least likely to influence the treatment decision?
items.e: Primary tumour size on CT is not part of the NOMS framework; the decision is based on neurological grade, radiosensitivity, mechanical stability and systemic disease.

items.q: A raised urinary deoxypyridinoline level indicates increased activity of which cell?
items.e: Deoxypyridinoline is a collagen cross-link released when osteoclasts degrade type I bone collagen, so it is a marker of bone resorption, like CTX and NTX.

items.q: During bone mineralisation, matrix vesicles released by osteoblasts perform several functions. Which of the following is NOT a role of these vesicles?
o: Providing a site for hydroxyapatite nucleation
items.e: Matrix vesicles concentrate Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻, provide nucleation sites and release ALP to hydrolyse pyrophosphate; they do not directly increase collagen fibril thickness.

items.q: A child with a loss-of-function RUNX2 mutation is most likely to show which skeletal feature?
o: Hypoplastic or absent clavicles with delayed closure of the fontanelles
Generalised dense bones with Erlenmeyer flask femora
items.e: RUNX2 haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia: absent or hypoplastic clavicles, open fontanelles, retained primary and supernumerary teeth and a widened pubic symphysis.

items.q: Which of the following best explains how sclerostin regulates bone remodeling?
o: It binds RANKL, preventing it from interacting with RANK
It blocks Wnt/β‑catenin signalling in osteocytes
It increases alkaline phosphatase activity in osteoblasts
items.e: Sclerostin, secreted by osteocytes, antagonises Wnt signaling, thereby inhibiting osteoblast activity and bone formation.

items.q: How is water distributed through the depth of normal adult articular cartilage?
o: Lowest at the surface and highest in the deep zone
Highest at the surface (about 80%) and decreasing towards the deep zone (about 65%)
Highest in the calcified cartilage zone
items.e: Water makes up 65-80% of cartilage wet weight, with the highest concentration in the superficial zone, decreasing with depth as proteoglycan concentration rises.

items.q: A tissue-engineered scaffold for meniscal repair should be based mainly on which collagen type to replicate the native meniscus?
items.e: The meniscus is fibrocartilage whose dry weight is mostly type I collagen, arranged circumferentially to resist hoop stresses; type II predominates in hyaline cartilage.

items.q: In the superficial zone of articular cartilage, collagen fibrils are arranged in parallel to the surface. What mechanical property does this orientation primarily support?
items.e: Parallel collagen alignment in the superficial zone resists shear and tensile forces applied parallel to the joint surface.

items.q: A 35-year-old has wrist drop after a closed humeral shaft fracture. Nerve studies at 3 weeks show conduction block across the fracture site with a normal compound muscle action potential on stimulating the radial nerve distally. What type of injury is this?
items.e: A focal conduction block with preserved distal amplitude beyond the time needed for Wallerian degeneration means the axons are intact (Seddon neurapraxia, Sunderland I), and full recovery is expected.

items.q: A randomized controlled trial comparing two postoperative pain regimens includes only patients who eventually received the allocated treatment. The analysis is performed excluding those who deviated from the protocol. This approach is known as:
items.e: Per‑protocol analysis includes only patients who completed the treatment as randomised.

items.q: Which of the following is a true statement about allocation concealment?
o: It is the same as blinding.
It is only necessary in pharmacological trials.
It stops the enrolling clinician from knowing the next assignment.
items.e: Allocation concealment hides the next assignment from the enroler, preventing selection bias.

items.q: For a lumbar spine radiograph, the radiographer raises the tube voltage from 80 kVp to 92 kVp and halves the mAs to keep image density constant (15% rule). What is the effect?
o: Higher contrast and higher patient dose
Lower contrast and higher patient dose
Lower contrast and lower patient dose
items.e: A more penetrating beam reduces photoelectric absorption, so contrast falls, but the halved mAs means fewer photons are absorbed by the patient and dose is reduced.

items.q: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.2%) is listed for elective primary TKA. What is the most appropriate action to reduce his infection risk?
o: Proceed after a nasal mupirocin course alone
Defer surgery and optimise glycaemic control, aiming for HbA1c below about 7.5-8%
Proceed and give 30 days of oral antibiotics afterwards
items.e: HbA1c above about 7.5-8% is associated with higher rates of periprosthetic joint infection and wound complications, so elective arthroplasty is usually postponed until control improves.

items.q: A 37-year-old is hypotensive after a motorcycle crash; the AP pelvis shows symphyseal diastasis of 3 cm with intact posterior structures on CT (APC II). What is the most appropriate initial step?
o: Immediate open fixation of the symphysis
Pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters with the legs internally rotated
items.e: An open-book (APC) injury increases pelvic volume; a binder centred on the greater trochanters, with the feet strapped in internal rotation, reduces volume and controls venous bleeding while resuscitation continues.

items.q: During a modified Stoppa approach, the corona mortis is typically found crossing the superior pubic ramus at about what distance lateral to the symphysis?
items.e: The corona mortis (an obturator-external iliac/inferior epigastric anastomosis) crosses the superior pubic ramus on average about 6 cm (range 3-9 cm) from the symphysis and must be ligated to avoid troublesome bleeding.

items.q: An 82-year-old with a displaced Garden IV femoral neck fracture is planned for hemiarthroplasty. Which statement about stem fixation is supported by current evidence?
o: Bipolar heads give clearly better function than total hip arthroplasty
Cementless stems have lower periprosthetic fracture rates in osteoporotic bone
All patients should receive a unipolar head regardless of activity
Cemented stems reduce periprosthetic fracture and residual thigh pain compared with cementless stems
items.e: Trials and registries (e.g., WHiTE 5, NICE guidance) show cemented stems give better function and fewer periprosthetic fractures than cementless stems in hip fracture patients; cement implantation syndrome is the main risk.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman with osteoporosis sustains a low‑energy fall. AP knee films reveal a purely depressed lateral tibial plateau with a 4 mm articular step‑off. What is the best indication for surgical intervention?
items.e: For osteoporotic, comminuted fractures a step‑off >2 mm (and >5 mm condylar widening) mandates surgery – option B.

items.q: A 45-year-old has a displaced, comminuted olecranon fracture extending distal to the coronoid base. What is the best fixation method?
o: Tension-band wiring with two K-wires and a figure-of-eight wire
Excision of fragments and triceps advancement
items.e: Tension-band wiring needs an intact anterior cortex and is unsuitable for comminuted fractures or those extending to the coronoid; a precontoured dorsal plate restores length and stability and allows early motion.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old comes with a posterior elbow dislocation, a fractured radial head, and a Regan‑Morrey type III coronoid fracture with intact MCL. The surgical priority order should be:
o: LCL repair, radial head replacement, coronoid fixation
Coronoid fixation, radial head reconstruction, LCL repair
Radial head excision, coronoid fixation, LCL repair
LCL repair, coronoid fixation, radial head replacement
items.e: Fix the coronoid first to restore the hinge, then address the radial head (reconstruction or replacement), and finally repair the LCL to restore posterolateral stability.

items.q: When fixing an intertrochanteric fracture with a sliding hip screw, which lag screw position in the femoral head (AP and lateral views) carries the highest risk of cut-out?
o: Inferior on AP, centre on lateral
Superior on AP, anterior on lateral
Inferior on AP, posterior on lateral
items.e: Superior and anterior placement leaves the screw in weak bone close to the subchondral surface and gives the highest cut-out rate; centre-centre or inferior-centre positions with a tip-apex distance under 25 mm are recommended.

items.q: In tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) fracture-dislocations, the metatarsal bases most commonly displace dorsally because:
o: The dorsal tarsometatarsal ligaments are weaker than the plantar ligaments
Tibialis anterior pulls the first metatarsal dorsally
Peroneus longus pulls the lateral rays dorsally
The intermetatarsal ligament between the first and second metatarsals is the strongest
items.e: The plantar ligaments, including the plantar part of the Lisfranc ligament, are stronger than the dorsal ligaments, so failure and displacement occur dorsally; there is no intermetatarsal ligament between the first and second metatarsals.

items.q: A polytrauma patient has the following highest Abbreviated Injury Scale scores: head 4, chest 3, abdomen 2 and lower extremity 3. What is the Injury Severity Score?
items.e: ISS is the sum of the squares of the highest AIS scores in the three most severely injured body regions: 4² + 3² + 3² = 16 + 9 + 9 = 34.

items.q: A haemodynamically stable 28-year-old has ipsilateral closed femoral and tibial shaft fractures (floating knee). What is the most commonly preferred definitive fixation?
o: Definitive external fixation of both fractures
Femoral nail and cast treatment of the tibia
Retrograde femoral nail and antegrade tibial nail through a single knee incision
items.e: Operative fixation of both fractures allows early knee motion; nailing both bones, often retrograde femoral and antegrade tibial nails through one incision, gives high union rates, whereas cast treatment of the tibia leads to stiffness and malunion.

items.q: After closed reduction of a posterior hip dislocation in a 25-year-old, CT shows a small osteochondral fragment within the joint with widening of the joint space. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Removal of the incarcerated fragment by arthroscopy or arthrotomy
Skeletal traction for 6 weeks and repeat CT
items.e: A non-concentric reduction caused by an intra-articular fragment damages the articular cartilage and needs early removal of the fragment, arthroscopically or by open surgical dislocation.

items.q: A 45-year-old has a transverse patellar fracture with 1 mm displacement and 1 mm articular step-off, and can perform a straight-leg raise. What is the best management?
o: Knee brace in extension with weight bearing as tolerated
items.e: Non-operative treatment in extension is appropriate when the extensor mechanism is intact, displacement is under 3 mm and step-off under 2 mm; surgery is indicated beyond these limits or if the patient cannot straight-leg raise.

items.q: The SPRINT trial comparing reamed and unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures found that:
o: Reamed nailing may benefit closed fractures, with no difference between techniques in open fractures
Unreamed nailing reduced reoperations in closed fractures
Reamed nailing significantly increased deep infection in open fractures
Reaming increased the rate of compartment syndrome in closed fractures
items.e: In SPRINT (2008), reamed nailing reduced the composite reoperation outcome in closed fractures (largely fewer dynamisations for delayed union) and showed no difference in open fractures; reaming did not increase infection or compartment syndrome.

items.q: A snowboarder has lateral ankle pain after a fall with tenderness just below the tip of the lateral malleolus; radiographs are reported as normal. Which fracture is commonly missed in this setting?
o: Posterior process of the talus (Shepherd fracture)
items.e: Lateral talar process fractures ('snowboarder's fracture') are often mistaken for ankle sprains; CT confirms the diagnosis, and displaced fragments are fixed or excised to prevent subtalar arthritis.

items.q: A 40-year-old has an inversion injury with a minimally displaced avulsion fracture of the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal (zone 1). What is the best treatment?
o: Hard-soled shoe or walking boot with weight bearing as tolerated
items.e: Zone 1 tuberosity avulsions heal reliably with symptomatic treatment and early weight bearing; zone 2 (Jones) fractures lie in a vascular watershed and have a higher non-union risk.

items.q: Which alignment is generally accepted for non-operative functional brace treatment of a humeral shaft fracture?
o: Up to 5° varus and 1 cm shortening
Up to 10° anterior angulation and no shortening
Up to 20° anterior angulation, 30° varus and 3 cm shortening
Up to 45° varus and 5 cm shortening
items.e: Shoulder and elbow motion compensate well, so up to 20° anterior angulation, 30° varus/valgus and 3 cm shortening are acceptable for humeral shaft fractures treated in a functional brace.

items.q: According to Hertel's criteria, which combination of features best predicts humeral head ischaemia after a proximal humerus fracture?
o: Posteromedial metaphyseal head extension under 8 mm and medial hinge displacement over 2 mm
Greater tuberosity displacement over 5 mm with a valgus-impacted head
Isolated surgical neck fracture with 50% translation
Lesser tuberosity fracture with a head-split under 10%
items.e: Hertel found that a short posteromedial metaphyseal extension (under 8 mm) together with a disrupted medial hinge (over 2 mm) was the best predictor of ischaemia, reflecting loss of the posterior humeral circumflex supply.

items.q: A displaced distal-third clavicle fracture in which the coracoclavicular ligaments remain attached to the lateral fragment but not the medial fragment (Neer type II) is significant because it:
o: Is best treated with a figure-of-eight bandage
Has a high non-union rate with non-operative treatment
items.e: In Neer type II fractures the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid while the lateral fragment stays with the scapula, so non-union rates are high (up to about 30%) and fixation is often advised in active patients.

items.q: A lateral elbow radiograph after a fall shows a 'double-arc' sign anteriorly. This most suggests:
o: Radial head fracture with an anterior fat pad
Coronal shear fracture of the capitellum extending into the trochlea
items.e: The double-arc sign represents the subchondral bone of the displaced capitellum and lateral trochlear ridge, typical of a coronal shear capitellum fracture extending into the trochlea; CT defines it before fixation.

items.q: In an isolated radial head fracture, which finding is the clearest indication for operative treatment?
o: A mechanical block to forearm rotation persisting after aspiration and intra-articular local anaesthetic
An elbow effusion with a positive posterior fat pad
1 mm displacement of a fragment involving 20% of the head
items.e: A block to motion confirmed after aspirating the haemarthrosis and injecting local anaesthetic indicates a displaced fragment needing fixation or excision; minimally displaced fractures without block do well with early motion.

items.q: In compression plating of an adult diaphyseal forearm fracture with a 3.5 mm plate, the recommended minimum fixation on each side of the fracture is:
items.e: At least three bicortical screws (six cortices) on each side of the fracture with a 3.5 mm compression plate gives stable fixation, with union rates over 95%.

items.q: In a Galeazzi fracture, which radial fracture location is most associated with instability of the distal radioulnar joint after radial fixation?
o: Proximal third of the radial shaft
Junction of the proximal and middle thirds
Within 7.5 cm of the distal radial articular surface
items.e: Rettig and Raskin found that radial shaft fractures within 7.5 cm of the distal radial articular surface were much more likely to have DRUJ instability needing stabilisation.

items.q: A 22-year-old has an undisplaced fracture of the proximal pole of the scaphoid on CT. What is the preferred treatment?
o: Thumb spica cast for 8 weeks and review
Headless compression screw fixation, usually from a dorsal approach
items.e: Proximal pole fractures rely on a tenuous retrograde blood supply and have high non-union and AVN rates with casting, so early screw fixation is recommended even when undisplaced.

items.q: In a Bennett fracture-dislocation of the thumb metacarpal base, the small volar-ulnar fragment stays in place because it is attached to the:
items.e: The anterior oblique ligament holds the volar-ulnar fragment to the trapezium, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the metacarpal shaft proximally and radially and adductor pollicis adducts it.

items.q: A 70-year-old has a lateral compression type I pelvic injury: an anterior sacral buckle fracture with ipsilateral superior and inferior rami fractures. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the initial management?
o: Analgesia and mobilisation with weight bearing as tolerated
items.e: LC-I injuries are usually mechanically stable and are managed with analgesia and early mobilisation; fixation is considered if pain prevents mobilisation or the fracture displaces.

items.q: A patient with a pelvic ring injury remains hypotensive despite a pelvic binder and blood products; contrast CT shows an active arterial blush from the superior gluteal artery. What is the next step?
o: Definitive open reduction and internal fixation of the pelvis
items.e: An arterial blush with ongoing instability indicates arterial bleeding best controlled by angioembolisation; preperitoneal packing mainly addresses venous and bony bleeding.

items.q: In Letournel's series, which is the most common elementary acetabular fracture pattern?
items.e: Posterior wall fractures are the commonest elementary pattern (about a quarter of acetabular fractures), usually from dashboard injuries with posterior hip dislocation; both-column is the commonest associated pattern.

items.q: A construction worker falls 6 m onto his feet. CT shows bilateral vertical sacral fractures joined by a transverse fracture at S2 (U-type). The preferred fixation is:
o: Lumbopelvic (spinopelvic) fixation, with or without iliosacral screws
items.e: U-type sacral fractures cause spinopelvic dissociation, separating the spine and upper sacrum from the pelvis; lumbopelvic or triangular fixation restores stability and allows early mobilisation.

items.q: A patient with a C6 spinal cord injury has preserved sacral sensation and voluntary anal contraction, and at least half of the key muscles below the neurological level are grade 3 or stronger. The ASIA Impairment Scale grade is:
items.e: Motor incomplete injuries are AIS C if fewer than half of the key muscles below the neurological level reach grade 3 and AIS D if at least half do; AIS B has sensory but no motor sparing below the level.

items.q: A neurologically intact 35-year-old has an L1 burst fracture; MRI shows an intact posterior ligamentous complex. What is his TLICS score and the suggested management?
items.e: TLICS scores burst morphology 2, intact neurology 0 and intact PLC 0, giving 2; scores of 3 or less suggest non-operative care, 4 is indeterminate and 5 or more suggests surgery.

items.q: The most common complication of halo-vest immobilisation is:
items.e: Pin loosening (about a third of patients) and pin-site infection are the commonest halo complications; abducens palsy and dural penetration are rare.

items.q: On a lateral cervical radiograph, anterior translation of one vertebral body on the next by about 25% of its AP depth, with rotation of the spinous processes, most suggests:
items.e: Unilateral facet dislocation typically produces about 25% anterolisthesis with rotational malalignment, whereas bilateral facet dislocation produces about 50% translation.

items.q: A 65-year-old with ankylosing spondylitis has new neck pain after a minor fall; cervical radiographs show no obvious fracture. What is the next step?
o: CT of the whole spine (with MRI if needed), immobilised in his usual posture
items.e: Fractures of the ankylosed spine are often occult on radiographs, are highly unstable and may be non-contiguous, so whole-spine CT and/or MRI is needed; forcing the neck into neutral can cause cord injury.

items.q: Three weeks after an uneventful L4-L5 microdiscectomy, a patient develops severe mechanical back pain and a rising CRP; the wound looks healthy. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Postoperative discitis typically presents 1-4 weeks after surgery with severe back pain, paraspinal spasm and raised ESR/CRP; contrast MRI and image-guided biopsy confirm it.

items.q: A 75-year-old has worsening back pain 2 months after a minor fall with initially normal radiographs; now there is vertebral collapse with an intravertebral gas cleft. This is:
items.e: Kümmell disease is delayed post-traumatic avascular necrosis of a vertebral body with an intravertebral vacuum cleft and progressive collapse; intravertebral gas argues against infection or tumour.

items.q: Six hours after a lumbar laminectomy, a patient develops rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness and saddle numbness. What is the best management?
o: Urgent MRI and emergency evacuation of an epidural haematoma
High-dose steroids and review the next morning
items.e: A postoperative epidural haematoma causing progressive deficit is a surgical emergency; outcome is best with evacuation within hours, and MRI is used if it does not delay surgery.

items.q: A posterolateral C5-C6 disc herniation most likely causes:
o: Weak triceps, reduced triceps jerk and numbness of the middle finger
Weak wrist extension and elbow flexion, reduced brachioradialis jerk and numbness of the thumb
Weak finger flexion and numbness of the little finger
Weak hand intrinsics and numbness of the medial forearm
items.e: In the cervical spine the root numbered below the disc is compressed, so a C5-C6 disc affects C6: wrist extensors, biceps, brachioradialis reflex and thumb/index sensation.

items.q: A patient with cervical radiculopathy finds relief by resting the affected hand on top of the head. This finding is called the:
items.e: Shoulder abduction reduces tension on the compressed cervical root and relieves radicular pain, helping distinguish radiculopathy from shoulder pathology; Spurling's manoeuvre provokes the pain.

items.q: A 70-year-old with leg pain on walking can cycle for 30 minutes without symptoms, is relieved by sitting or bending forward and has palpable foot pulses. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar canal stenosis
items.e: Lumbar flexion (cycling, leaning on a trolley) enlarges the canal and relieves neurogenic claudication, whereas vascular claudication occurs with any leg exercise and is relieved simply by standing still.

items.q: After an acute traumatic cervical spinal cord injury, current guidelines suggest maintaining mean arterial pressure at:
o: Any level provided systolic pressure exceeds 90 mmHg
items.e: To optimise spinal cord perfusion and limit secondary injury, guidelines recommend a MAP of 85-90 mmHg for about the first week after acute spinal cord injury, using fluids and vasopressors.

items.q: An adolescent has a round ossicle separated from a short, hypoplastic dens by a wide gap with smooth cortical margins, and C1-C2 instability on flexion-extension films. The diagnosis and usual treatment are:
o: Acute type II odontoid fracture; halo vest
Type III odontoid fracture; rigid collar
items.e: Os odontoideum appears as a well-corticated ossicle separated from a short dens; symptomatic or unstable cases need C1-C2 fusion. Ossiculum terminale is a small stable tip ossicle above the transverse ligament.

items.q: In the revised Tokuhashi score for spinal metastases, a total of 12-15 predicts a survival of:
items.e: Revised Tokuhashi: 0-8 predicts survival under 6 months, 9-11 six months or more, and 12-15 a year or more, which favours excisional surgery.

items.q: During muscle contraction, which part of the sarcomere stays the same length?
items.e: The A band equals the length of the thick (myosin) filaments and stays constant; the I band and H zone shorten as thin filaments slide over thick filaments and the Z discs approach each other.

items.q: Type I skeletal muscle fibres are characterised by:
o: Fast contraction, glycolytic metabolism and rapid fatigue
Slow contraction, oxidative metabolism, high mitochondrial and myoglobin content and fatigue resistance
Large motor units recruited mainly for sprinting
Low capillary density and pale colour
items.e: Type I (slow-twitch, red) fibres are oxidative and fatigue resistant, with many mitochondria, myoglobin and capillaries; they predominate in postural muscles and endurance athletes.

items.q: Calcitonin lowers serum calcium mainly by:
o: Directly inhibiting osteoclasts through calcitonin receptors
items.e: Calcitonin from thyroid C cells binds receptors on osteoclasts and rapidly inhibits bone resorption; the effect wanes with continued use (escape phenomenon).

items.q: Which serum measurement best reflects a patient's vitamin D stores?
items.e: 25-hydroxyvitamin D has a half-life of about 2-3 weeks and reflects stores; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is tightly regulated by PTH and may be normal or even raised in deficiency.

items.q: Why is technetium bone scintigraphy unreliable for detecting multiple myeloma lesions?
o: The lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic response
Myeloma cells take up technetium so avidly that lesions are masked
The lesions are too small to be resolved by a gamma camera
The tracer is excreted too quickly in renal failure
items.e: Technetium-MDP uptake depends on osteoblastic activity; myeloma suppresses osteoblasts, so lesions are often cold or normal on bone scan. Whole-body low-dose CT or MRI is preferred.

items.q: On MRI, a STIR sequence is particularly useful in musculoskeletal imaging because it:
o: Makes fat bright to show marrow anatomy
Suppresses fat signal so that marrow oedema and fluid appear bright
Gives the best detail of cortical bone
items.e: Short tau inversion recovery nulls fat signal, so oedema, fluid and many lesions stand out brightly against dark marrow, making it sensitive for stress injury, infection and tumour.

items.q: During ultrasound of the rotator cuff, a normal tendon appears falsely hypoechoic when the probe is not perpendicular to the fibres. This artefact is called:
items.e: Anisotropy makes tendons look hypoechoic when the beam is not perpendicular to the fibrils and can mimic tendinopathy or tear; adjusting the probe angle corrects it.

items.q: Which of the following is most suitable for mixing into PMMA bone cement as a local antibiotic?
items.e: Antibiotics for cement should be heat stable, water soluble, broad spectrum and in powder form (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin, vancomycin); rifampicin inhibits polymerisation and liquids weaken the cement.

items.q: Shortly after bupivacaine injection for an interscalene block, a patient has a seizure followed by a ventricular arrhythmia. Besides airway and seizure control, the specific treatment is:
o: 20% lipid emulsion, bolus about 1.5 mL/kg then infusion
items.e: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is treated with 20% lipid emulsion (about 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion) and modified ACLS with reduced adrenaline doses.

items.q: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium is most often due to a mutation in which gene, and is treated with which drug?
items.e: Most malignant hyperthermia susceptibility is due to RYR1 ryanodine receptor mutations causing uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release; dantrolene blocks this release.

items.q: An 80-year-old taking warfarin has a hip fracture with an INR of 3.2 and needs surgery urgently. Which gives the most rapid and sustained reversal?
o: Prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K
items.e: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate reverses warfarin within minutes and IV vitamin K sustains the effect; protamine reverses heparin, and waiting for the INR to drift down delays hip fracture surgery.

items.q: In a trial, deep infection occurred in 6% of controls and 2% of patients given antibiotic-loaded cement. The number needed to treat to prevent one infection is:
items.e: Absolute risk reduction = 6% - 2% = 4%; NNT = 1/0.04 = 25.

items.q: A new test for scaphoid fracture is positive in 45 of 50 patients with a fracture and in 20 of 100 patients without a fracture. Its sensitivity and specificity are:
items.e: Sensitivity = 45/50 = 90%; specificity = true negatives/all without fracture = 80/100 = 80%. The 69% and 94% figures are the positive and negative predictive values.

items.q: Agreement between two surgeons classifying the same fractures, corrected for agreement expected by chance, is best expressed by:
items.e: Cohen's kappa measures agreement between two raters on categorical data beyond chance (0.61-0.80 substantial, over 0.80 almost perfect); Cronbach's alpha measures internal consistency of a scale.

items.q: In Bone's randomised trial of femoral shaft fractures in multiply injured patients, early (within 24 hours) compared with delayed stabilisation resulted in:
o: Fewer pulmonary complications such as ARDS, fat embolism and pneumonia, and shorter ICU stay
Higher rates of fat embolism syndrome
items.e: Bone et al. (1989) showed early femoral stabilisation reduced pulmonary complications, ICU stay and hospital costs; later damage control concepts reserve delayed fixation for patients who are physiologically unstable.

items.q: A 30-year-old basketball player cannot actively extend his knee after landing from a jump. The lateral radiograph shows a high-riding patella with an Insall-Salvati ratio of 1.5. What is the diagnosis?
o: Tibial tubercle avulsion in an adolescent
items.e: Patellar tendon rupture, typical under 40 years, produces patella alta (Insall-Salvati over 1.2); quadriceps tendon rupture occurs mainly over 40 and gives a low-lying patella.

items.q: A 40-year-old has an acute Achilles tendon rupture. Compared with operative repair, non-operative treatment with accelerated functional rehabilitation (Willits trial) results in:
o: Lower strength at all time points and worse function
Similar re-rupture rates and function, with fewer complications
items.e: Willits et al. (2010) found that with early weight bearing and functional rehabilitation, non-operative treatment gave re-rupture rates and functional outcomes similar to surgery, without wound complications.

items.q: For ORIF of a displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture, which approach is associated with fewer wound complications than the extensile lateral L-shaped incision?
items.e: The sinus tarsi (limited lateral) approach gives direct access to the posterior facet with markedly fewer wound complications than the extensile lateral approach, whose flap depends on the lateral calcaneal artery.

items.q: Compared with syndesmotic screw fixation, dynamic suture-button fixation of an unstable ankle syndesmosis has been shown to give:
o: Fewer syndesmotic malreductions and implant removals
A greater need for routine implant removal
items.e: Randomised trials (e.g., Andersen 2018) found suture-button fixation produced fewer malreductions, fewer reoperations for implant removal and slightly better function than screws.

items.q: A civilian sustains a low-velocity handgun injury causing an undisplaced fracture of the radial shaft with small entry and exit wounds and no neurovascular injury. Which management is appropriate?
o: Formal extensive debridement and 72 hours of IV triple antibiotics
Amputation if bone loss is present
Local wound care with a short course of antibiotics, treating the fracture as a closed injury
Mandatory exploration of the radial nerve
