items.e: Sample size rises with smaller effect size, greater variance, lower alpha and higher power.

items.q: Patients who are offered surgery choose it; those who decline are treated non-operatively and their outcomes are compared. The main threat to validity is:
items.e: When treatment is chosen rather than randomised, prognostic differences between groups confound the comparison.

items.q: In a forest plot, a horizontal line crossing the vertical line of no effect indicates:
o: The individual study result is not statistically significant
items.e: Each line is a study's confidence interval; if it crosses 1 (for ratios) or 0 (for differences), the result is not significant.

items.q: An ordinal outcome scale where the distance between grades is not equal, such as Kellgren-Lawrence grades, should be summarised with:
items.e: Ordinal data lack equal intervals, so medians and IQRs and non-parametric tests are appropriate.

items.q: In skeletal muscle, the energy system predominating in a sustained 30-minute run is:
items.e: Phosphocreatine powers the first seconds, anaerobic glycolysis up to about 2 minutes, and aerobic metabolism thereafter.

items.q: After a period of endurance training, skeletal muscle shows:
o: Conversion of type I to type II fibres
Increased fibre cross-sectional area as the main change
items.e: Endurance training increases mitochondria, oxidative enzymes and capillaries; strength training mainly causes fibre hypertrophy.

items.q: Muscle strength gains in the first weeks of resistance training are mainly due to:
o: Neural adaptation with better motor unit recruitment
items.e: Early strength gains reflect neural factors; hypertrophy contributes after about 6-8 weeks.

items.q: Anabolic steroid misuse by athletes is associated with an increased risk of:
items.e: Muscle strength increases faster than tendon adaptation and steroids alter collagen, leading to tendon ruptures.

items.q: Which hormone, raised in hyperthyroidism, increases bone turnover with net bone loss?
items.e: Excess thyroid hormone accelerates remodelling with resorption exceeding formation, increasing fracture risk; over-replacement has the same effect.

items.q: Long-term unfractionated heparin can cause:
items.e: Prolonged heparin, particularly unfractionated, reduces bone formation and increases resorption; LMWH carries lower risk.

items.q: The hypoglossal nerve is at risk during the anterior approach to which cervical levels?
items.e: High anterior approaches (C2-C3) put the hypoglossal and superior laryngeal nerves at risk.

items.q: C2 pedicle screw placement is relatively contraindicated when imaging shows:
o: A high-riding vertebral artery with a narrow pedicle/isthmus
items.e: A high-riding vertebral artery narrows the C2 isthmus; translaminar screws are an alternative.

items.q: During C1 lateral mass screw insertion, troublesome bleeding typically comes from:
o: The vertebral artery in all cases
The venous plexus around the C2 nerve root
items.e: A large perivenous plexus surrounds the C2 root below the C1 posterior arch; the C2 root may be sacrificed for exposure.

items.q: Thermal necrosis during pin insertion for an external fixator is reduced by:
o: Predrilling and using sharp drills at low speed with irrigation
items.e: Bone necrosis occurs above about 50-55 degrees Celsius; heat causes ring sequestra and loosening.

items.q: Hyperthyroidism and excessive thyroxine replacement both increase fracture risk mainly by:
o: Accelerating bone remodelling with resorption exceeding formation
items.e: Thyroid hormone shortens the remodelling cycle and increases resorption, leading to net bone loss.

items.q: In a cross-sectional study, prevalence of hand osteoarthritis is measured at a single point in time. Such a design cannot establish:
o: Temporal sequence between exposure and outcome
items.e: Because exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously, cross-sectional studies cannot show which came first.

items.q: A statistically significant result with a very large sample may still be clinically unimportant because:
o: Large samples detect very small differences that may be below the MCID
Large samples increase type II error
p-values are invalid in large samples
items.e: Statistical significance reflects precision; clinical importance depends on whether the effect exceeds the minimal clinically important difference.

items.q: The commonest site of spinal cord compression in thoracic metastatic disease arises from:
o: Vertebral body tumour extending posteriorly into the canal
items.e: Haematogenous metastases seed the vascular vertebral body and then extend into the anterior epidural space.

items.q: Thoracic pedicle screws breaching the anterior vertebral body on the left in the mid-thoracic spine endanger the:
items.e: The descending aorta lies anterolateral to the left side of the mid-thoracic vertebral bodies; overlong left-sided screws risk it.

items.q: Fracture callus mineralisation is impaired most specifically by deficiency of:
items.e: Vitamin D is needed for calcium and phosphate supply to mineralise osteoid; vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen formation instead.

items.q: Schmorl's nodes are:
o: Herniations of nucleus pulposus through the vertebral endplate into the body
Osteophytes at the anterior vertebral margin
items.e: Intravertebral disc herniations through weak endplates are common incidental findings and a feature of Scheuermann disease.

items.q: A peripheral nerve's response to slow, chronic compression (as in carpal tunnel syndrome) first involves:
o: Breakdown of the blood-nerve barrier with endoneurial oedema and demyelination
items.e: Chronic compression causes ischaemia, oedema and segmental demyelination first, with axonal loss only in severe late stages.

items.q: Bisphosphonates such as alendronate have a skeletal half-life of many years because they:
o: Are not excreted by the kidney
Bind avidly to hydroxyapatite and are released only when bone is resorbed
items.e: Unbound drug is excreted renally within hours, but drug bound to bone mineral persists for years (about 10 years for alendronate), which underlies drug holidays.

items.q: Pathogens such as rabies virus, herpes simplex, and poliovirus, as well as neurotrophic signals like nerve growth factor (NGF) and tetanus toxin, travel from the axon terminal back to the neuronal cell body via which transport mechanism and motor protein?
o: Saltatory transport using sodium channel currents
items.e: Retrograde axonal transport moves vesicles, trophic signals (such as NGF), and specific neurotropic viruses and toxins from the peripheral axon terminal to the cell body using the motor protein dynein. Fast anterograde transport uses kinesin to move neurotransmitters and membrane vesicles away from the cell body.

items.q: A 28-year-old man undergoes an Oberlin nerve transfer to restore elbow flexion following a proximal brachial plexus avulsion injury. Which donor nerve component is harvested to reinnervate the motor branch of the biceps muscle?
o: A motor fascicle of the ulnar nerve destined for the flexor carpi ulnaris
The entire main trunk of the median nerve
The anterior interosseous nerve branch supplying pronator quadratus
A motor fascicle of the radial nerve supplying the long head of triceps
items.e: The classic Oberlin nerve transfer uses a redundant motor fascicle of the ulnar nerve (specifically one supplying the flexor carpi ulnaris) transferred directly end-to-end to the biceps motor branch of the musculocutaneous nerve to restore active elbow flexion.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon evaluates a patient with a closed nerve injury 4 weeks after trauma. Electromyography (EMG) is performed to assess for axonal degeneration. How long after an acute nerve injury do spontaneous fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves typically first appear at rest on EMG in denervated skeletal muscle?
items.e: Spontaneous fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves indicate active axonal denervation of muscle and typically appear 2 to 3 weeks (10 to 21 days) following nerve injury. Electromyography is usually delayed until 3 to 4 weeks post-injury to accurately distinguish neurapraxia from axonal disruption.

items.q: According to the sliding filament theory of skeletal muscle contraction, which band or zone of the sarcomere maintains a CONSTANT length during active cross-bridge cycling and shortening?
items.e: The A band corresponds to the total length of the thick myosin filaments and remains constant in length during muscle contraction. As actin filaments slide over myosin toward the M line, the I band and H zone shorten and the Z lines move closer together.

items.q: During general anaesthesia for open reduction and internal fixation, a patient with underlying central core disease develops muscular rigidity, rapid hypercapnia (rising end-tidal CO2), and a severe temperature spike following succinylcholine administration. This acute reaction is caused by a genetic mutation affecting which sarcoplasmic reticulum structure?
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant pharmacogenetic disorder linked to mutations in the ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1) gene on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Exposure to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine triggers uncontrolled calcium release into the sarcoplasm, leading to hypermetabolism, rigidity, hypercapnia, and hyperthermia; it is managed urgently with dantrolene.

items.q: A track athlete presents with an acute tear of the biceps femoris long head at the myotendinous junction sustained during terminal swing phase while sprinting. Which type of muscle contraction generates the HIGHEST peak force and carries the greatest risk of structural muscle strain injury?
items.e: Eccentric contractions (where the muscle actively lengthens under load) produce the highest total force across the muscle unit, making them the primary cause of acute muscle strains and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), particularly at the myotendinous junction of two-joint muscles.

items.q: A surgeon evaluates a new serum biomarker for diagnosing prosthetic joint infection (PJI). When applying this test in a high-prevalence tertiary revision centre compared to a low-prevalence primary joint registry population, which of the following diagnostic parameters will increase?
items.e: Positive predictive value (PPV) depends directly on disease prevalence; as prevalence increases, PPV rises while negative predictive value (NPV) falls. Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios are intrinsic properties of the test and remain unchanged by disease prevalence.

items.q: An orthopaedic researcher aims to investigate potential risk factors for an extremely rare postoperative complication (incidence < 0.01%) following total ankle arthroplasty. Which study design is most appropriate and efficient for this objective?
items.e: Case-control studies start with the outcome (cases vs controls) and look backward for prior exposures, making them the most efficient design for studying rare diseases or rare outcomes. Prospective cohort studies and RCTs are inefficient for rare events because they would require unfeasibly large sample sizes.

items.q: During recruitment for a multicentre surgical trial, investigators use a central web-based randomisation service so that the enrolling clinician cannot foresee the upcoming treatment assignment. This procedure specifically ensures allocation concealment to prevent which type of bias?
items.e: Allocation concealment prevents enrolling clinicians from knowing or predicting the next treatment assignment, thereby preventing selection bias. Detection bias is prevented by blinded outcome assessment, performance bias by blinding care providers/patients, and attrition bias by maintaining high follow-up and intention-to-treat analysis.

items.q: A clinical trial compares non-normally distributed Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain scores recorded at 6 weeks postoperatively between two independent treatment groups of 20 patients each. Which statistical test is most appropriate for comparing these two groups?
items.e: The Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is the non-parametric statistical test used to compare non-normally distributed continuous or ordinal data between two independent groups. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are reserved for paired or repeated measures within the same subjects.

items.q: In a randomised trial evaluating a new antibiotic-impregnated bone cement for open tibia fractures, the deep infection rate is 15% in the standard control group and 5% in the experimental treatment group. What is the Number Needed to Treat (NNT) to prevent one deep infection?
items.e: The Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) is the Control Event Rate minus the Experimental Event Rate (15% - 5% = 10% or 0.10). The Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is calculated as 1 / ARR (1 / 0.10 = 10).

items.q: When calculating long-term implant survivorship of a total hip prosthesis in an elderly population, using standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in the presence of death as a competing risk leads to which of the following statistical errors?
o: Underestimation of the cumulative revision rate
Overestimation of the cumulative revision rate
Falsely low hazard ratio in Cox regression
items.e: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis censors subjects who die before revision, assuming they remain at risk of revision. In elderly cohorts where death is a major competing risk, Kaplan-Meier overestimates the cumulative revision rate; a cumulative incidence function (Fine and Gray method) should be used instead.

items.q: Two orthopaedic surgeons independently grade 50 proximal humerus fractures using the Neer classification system. Which statistical metric is most appropriate for evaluating inter-observer reliability for this categorical classification?
items.e: Cohen's kappa coefficient measures agreement between two observers for categorical data while correcting for agreement occurring by chance alone. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) is used to assess reliability for continuous quantitative variables.

items.q: An orthopaedic researcher is preparing a manuscript reporting a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing hemiarthroplasty with total hip arthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures. Which reporting guideline checklist must be followed?
items.e: PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) is the mandatory reporting guideline checklist and flow diagram for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. CONSORT is used for randomised controlled trials, STROBE for observational studies, and STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies.

items.q: According to the ICRP guidelines for radiation protection, what is the annual effective dose limit for an occupational radiation worker (averaged over 5 years) and the specific annual limit for the lens of the eye?
o: 20 mSv per year (effective dose) and 20 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
50 mSv per year (effective dose) and 150 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
20 mSv per year (effective dose) and 500 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
1 mSv per year (effective dose) and 20 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
items.e: ICRP recommendations set the occupational limit for annual effective dose to 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (not exceeding 50 mSv in any single year). The dose limit for the lens of the eye was lowered in 2011 to 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years to reduce the risk of radiation-induced cataracts.

items.q: During CT evaluation of a complex intra-articular fracture, attenuation values are measured in Hounsfield Units (HU). Which of the following tissue/material pairs is correctly matched with its typical HU value?
o: Fat: -100 to -50 HU; Cortical bone: +1000 HU or more
items.e: On the Hounsfield scale, water is defined as 0 HU and air is -1000 HU. Fat has negative values (-100 to -50 HU), whereas cortical bone has high attenuation (+1000 HU or more); cancellous bone typically ranges between +300 and +700 HU.

items.q: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman undergoes DEXA scanning. Her T-score at the femoral neck is -2.8, and she has no prior history of low-energy fractures. According to the WHO criteria, how should her bone density be categorized?
items.e: According to WHO criteria based on T-scores in postmenopausal women, a score of -1.0 or higher is normal, between -1.0 and -2.5 is osteopenia, and -2.5 or lower defines osteoporosis. Severe (established) osteoporosis requires a T-score of -2.5 or lower combined with one or more fragility fractures.

items.q: During a musculoskeletal ultrasound examination of the patellar tendon, a dark, hypoechoic area is observed. Tipping the transducer slightly (heel-toe maneuver) so that the sound beam meets the tendon fibres at a 90-degree angle restores normal hyperechoic fibrillar architecture. What artefact was present initially?
items.e: Anisotropy occurs when an ultrasound beam strikes ordered fibrillar structures (like tendons or ligaments) at a non-perpendicular angle, causing sound waves to reflect away from the transducer and creating a false hypoechoic appearance. Angling the probe perpendicular to the fibres resolves the artefact.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes X-ray interactions with human tissue during clinical orthopaedic radiography?
o: Compton scatter probability is directly proportional to atomic number cubed (Z cubed)
Photoelectric absorption is dominant in bone at lower photon energies and is responsible for image contrast
The photoelectric effect is the main source of occupational scatter radiation dose to operating theatre personnel
Compton scatter occurs when an incident photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron
items.e: The photoelectric effect involves complete absorption of photons by inner-shell electrons and is proportional to Z cubed / E cubed, making it dominant at lower energies in high-atomic-number materials like bone (calcium), which creates radiographic image contrast. Compton scatter involves outer-shell electron interactions and is the main source of occupational scatter dose to operating room staff.

items.q: A 68-year-old female is prescribed annual intravenous zoledronic acid following surgical fixation of a fragility hip fracture. What is the specific cellular enzymatic mechanism by which nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates induce osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis?
o: Competitive inhibition of carbonic anhydrase II
Direct inhibition of farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway
Antagonism of the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL)
Formation of toxic ATP analogues within the osteoclast cytoplasm
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (such as zoledronate and alendronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, preventing protein prenylation and causing osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis. Non-nitrogen bisphosphonates form toxic ATP analogues, while denosumab targets RANKL.

items.q: During a total knee arthroplasty performed under nerve blocks, a patient suddenly develops perioral tingling, tinnitus, a metallic taste, followed by generalised tonic-clonic seizures. What is the recommended lipid resuscitation protocol for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)?
o: 20% lipid emulsion: 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min
10% lipid emulsion: 3.0 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 0.5 mL/kg/min
20% lipid emulsion: 5.0 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 1.0 mL/kg/min
10% lipid emulsion: 0.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 0.1 mL/kg/min
items.e: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) presents with early CNS excitation (perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, seizures) followed by cardiovascular collapse. Management includes airway control and administration of 20% lipid emulsion as a 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min.

items.q: Which of the following antimicrobial agents exerts its antibacterial effect by inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase and is specifically used as adjunctive therapy in staphylococcal implant-associated orthopaedic infections due to its activity against biofilm?
items.e: Rifampicin acts by inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase and possesses specific activity against staphylococcal biofilm in implant infections. It should never be used as monotherapy due to the rapid development of resistance.

items.q: During spine surgery under general anaesthesia using volatile anaesthetics, the anaesthetist notes an unexplained, rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, followed by generalized muscle rigidity and masseter spasm. Which targeted therapeutic agent must be immediately administered?
o: Protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units IV
items.e: An unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 is the earliest clinical sign of malignant hyperthermia (commonly caused by RYR1 mutations triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine). Immediate management includes stopping triggers, hyperventilation, and IV dantrolene at 2.5 mg/kg, which blocks calcium release from the ryanodine receptor.

items.q: Romosozumab is a sclerostin-inhibiting monoclonal antibody that exerts a dual action of increasing bone formation and decreasing bone resorption. Which of the following clinical scenarios represents an absolute contraindication to initiating romosozumab?
o: History of myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding year
Unexplained elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase
Presence of open physes or Paget disease of bone
Renal impairment with CrCl below 35 mL/min
items.e: Romosozumab was shown in the ARCH trial to carry an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events compared to alendronate. Therefore, it is contraindicated and should be avoided in patients who have suffered a myocardial infarction or stroke within the past year.

items.q: During local anaesthetic administration for peripheral nerve blockade, nerve fibres are blocked in a characteristic sequence based on axonal diameter and myelination. Which of the following nerve fibre types is blocked LAST by local anaesthetics?
items.e: Local anaesthetics block small, thinly myelinated or unmyelinated fibres first and large, heavily myelinated fibres last. The sequence of blockade sensitivity is B (autonomic) > A-delta and C (pain, temperature) > A-beta (touch, pressure) > A-alpha (motor and proprioception), meaning A-alpha fibres are blocked last and recover first.

items.q: During cementation of a femoral stem in an elderly patient undergoing hemiarthroplasty for a hip fracture, the patient develops severe intraoperative hypoxia with an SpO2 of 86% and a 45% fall in systolic blood pressure. According to the Donaldson classification, which grade of Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS) is present?
items.e: Under the Donaldson classification for Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS), Grade 1 involves moderate hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) or a systolic BP fall > 20%. Grade 2 is defined by severe hypoxia (SpO2 < 88%), a systolic BP fall > 40%, or unexpected loss of consciousness. Grade 3 involves cardiovascular collapse requiring CPR.

items.q: After removal of an epidural catheter in a patient receiving prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin following total hip arthroplasty, ASRA guidelines recommend waiting at least how long before giving the next prophylactic LMWH dose?
items.e: ASRA advises that the next LMWH dose be given no sooner than 4 hours after catheter removal; the catheter itself is removed at least 12 hours after the last prophylactic dose.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old male presents with a vertical shear pelvic injury following a motor‑vehicle collision. CT shows a vertical displacement of the right hemipelvis with an ipsilateral L5 transverse process avulsion. Which of the following is most likely to be true about this fracture pattern?
o: The posterior sacroiliac ligaments are intact
The anterior sacroiliac ligaments are torn
The injury is marginally stable with a small (≤2 cm) symphyseal widening
items.e: Vertical shear (VS) fractures involve disruption of both the anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments and are characterized by a complete vertical displacement of the hemipelvis. L5 transverse process avulsion is a classic indicator of vertical instability.

items.q: A haemodynamically unstable patient has an APC II pelvic injury with 3.2 cm symphyseal diastasis. What is the preferred immediate non-invasive measure to reduce pelvic volume and tamponade venous bleeding?
o: Pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters
Skeletal traction through the distal femur
items.e: A circumferential binder placed at the level of the greater trochanters (not the iliac crests) closes the open-book pelvis, reduces pelvic volume and tamponades venous and cancellous bleeding.

items.q: During a Kocher-Langenbeck approach for a posterior wall acetabular fracture, which limb position minimises tension on the sciatic nerve throughout the procedure?
items.e: Keeping the hip extended and the knee flexed (at least 60-90 degrees) slackens the sciatic nerve, reducing traction neurapraxia, the commonest nerve complication of the Kocher-Langenbeck approach.

items.q: Which imaging study is the standard for characterising posterior pelvic ring injuries such as sacral fractures and sacroiliac joint disruption?
o: CT scan of the pelvis with reconstructions
items.e: Plain films frequently miss or underestimate posterior ring injury; CT with multiplanar and 3D reconstructions defines sacral fracture pattern, SI joint displacement and guides fixation.

items.q: An 82-year-old woman has a displaced pertrochanteric femoral fracture. CT shows the lateral femoral wall thickness to be 15 mm. Which implant is most appropriate?
items.e: A lateral wall thinner than about 20.5 mm (Hsu) predicts lateral wall fracture and failure with a sliding hip screw, so an intramedullary cephalomedullary nail is preferred.

items.q: A 76-year-old woman has a comminuted, depressed lateral tibial plateau fracture with osteoporotic bone. Which factor most strongly favours acute total knee arthroplasty over ORIF?
o: An intact lateral meniscus on MRI
A simple split fracture without depression
items.e: Acute TKA is considered in elderly, low-demand patients with osteoporotic comminution and pre-existing arthritis, where ORIF is likely to fail and post-traumatic arthritis would require arthroplasty anyway.

items.q: A 24-year-old has a supination-external rotation ankle injury: a Weber B fibular fracture at the syndesmosis and a displaced medial malleolar fracture, with talar shift on the mortise view. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Closed reduction and weight-bearing cast for 6 weeks
ORIF of the fibula and medial malleolus
items.e: This is a bimalleolar (SER IV equivalent) unstable fracture with talar shift; anatomical ORIF of both malleoli restores the mortise and is the standard treatment.

items.q: During fixation of a two‑part surgical‑neck fracture in a young adult, the surgeon places a locking plate from the anterolateral aspect. Which technical point is most critical to avoid varus collapse?
o: Using screws that cross the articular surface
Fixing the plate as high as possible on the shaft
Including an inferomedial calcar screw for medial support
Drilling the screws at a 45° angle to the shaft
items.e: Medial calcar support is essential; loss of this leads to varus collapse and screw cut‑out.

items.q: A 25-year-old woman has a positive apprehension test after a first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. Which soft-tissue lesion is most likely present?
items.e: The Bankart lesion, avulsion of the anteroinferior labrum with the IGHL complex, is present in the large majority of traumatic anterior dislocations and underlies recurrent instability.

items.q: An elderly patient with a comminuted distal humerus fracture (AO 13C3) who is low demand and osteoporotic is best managed with:
o: Locked plating with a lateral plate only
items.e: In osteoporotic, irreconstructable C3 fractures, a total elbow arthroplasty provides early pain relief and functional restoration.

items.q: In a radial head fracture (Mason type III) associated with a medial collateral ligament tear, the recommended treatment is:
items.e: The radial head must be preserved or replaced as a secondary stabiliser to valgus forces when the MCL is deficient.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a comminuted radial head fracture with wrist pain and tenderness over the distal radioulnar joint. Radial head excision alone would risk proximal migration of the radius mainly because of disruption of which structure?
o: Central band of the interosseous membrane
items.e: This is an Essex-Lopresti injury: longitudinal radioulnar instability from disruption of the central band of the interosseous membrane and DRUJ, so the radial head must be fixed or replaced.

items.q: A 72-year-old low-demand woman has a displaced distal radius fracture. Which statement about operative versus non-operative treatment in patients over 65 is best supported by current evidence?
o: Volar plating produces substantially better long-term function than casting
Casting gives comparable functional outcomes despite poorer radiographic alignment
Surgical fixation is mandatory to regain useful wrist motion
Casting is contraindicated if radial shortening exceeds 2 mm
items.e: In older patients, randomised trials and meta-analyses (e.g. CROSSFIRE, Arora) show similar patient-reported function at 1 year after casting and plating, even though radiographic parameters are worse with casting; AAOS reflects this.

items.q: In an active 45-year-old, which post-reduction finding of a distal radius fracture falls OUTSIDE the AAOS-accepted limits and favours operative fixation?
items.e: AAOS recommends operative fixation when post-reduction radial shortening exceeds 3 mm, dorsal tilt exceeds 10 degrees or intra-articular displacement exceeds 2 mm; 18 degrees of dorsal tilt is unacceptable.

items.q: Which of the following is one of Lafontaine's criteria predicting redisplacement of a distal radius fracture treated in a cast?
o: Initial dorsal angulation greater than 20 degrees
items.e: Lafontaine's criteria are dorsal angulation over 20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular fracture, associated ulnar fracture and age over 60; three or more predict loss of reduction.

items.q: When placing distal locking screws through a volar distal radius plate, screw length is limited relative to which structure to avoid extensor tendon irritation or rupture?
o: The dorsal cortex of the distal radius
items.e: Distal screws should stop short of the dorsal cortex (about 2 mm), because protruding tips irritate or rupture EPL and other dorsal extensors; the watershed line instead governs distal plate placement to protect FPL.

items.q: A 22-year-old has a heavily contaminated Gustilo-Anderson IIIB open tibial shaft fracture. After resuscitation and IV antibiotics, what is the most appropriate first surgical step?
o: Immediate reamed intramedullary nailing and primary wound closure
Thorough debridement and temporary spanning external fixation with planned definitive coverage
Irrigation in the emergency department and above-knee cast
items.e: Heavily contaminated IIIB injuries need radical debridement and temporary stabilisation, with definitive fixation and flap coverage ideally within 72 hours (BOAST 4) once the wound is clean.

items.q: A trauma patient has a heart rate of 145/min, systolic BP 70 mmHg, negligible urine output and is lethargic. According to ATLS, what is the estimated blood loss?
items.e: Class IV haemorrhage (over 40% loss) shows marked tachycardia, markedly reduced systolic pressure, negligible urine output and depressed consciousness, and needs massive transfusion and haemorrhage control.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old male sustains a closed transverse midshaft tibial fracture. Radiographs show a 2‑mm gap after reduction. Which fixation principle best promotes secondary bone healing in this case?
o: Rigid cast immobilisation with no motion
Immediate open reduction with plating and compression screw
items.e: Secondary healing requires relative stability; an intramedullary nail allows axial compression and allows micromotion (strain 2‑10%) to stimulate callus formation.

items.q: During exchange nailing of an aseptic femoral diaphyseal non-union, the canal is over-reamed by 1-2 mm. What is the main mechanical purpose of this step?
o: To remove all fibrous tissue from the non-union
To allow insertion of a larger-diameter, stiffer nail
To create a distraction gap for regenerate
items.e: Over-reaming permits a larger, stiffer nail that improves stability; reaming also deposits osteogenic debris (autograft) at the non-union and stimulates periosteal blood flow.

items.q: On the lateral cervical radiograph of a polytrauma patient, the Powers ratio is 1.3 and the basion-dens interval is 14 mm. What is the most accurate conclusion?
items.e: A Powers ratio above 1 indicates anterior atlanto-occipital dissociation and a basion-dens interval over 12 mm on radiographs (Harris rule of 12) corroborates it; this is a highly unstable injury.

items.q: A neurologically intact 28-year-old has a T12 burst fracture with 15 degrees of kyphosis and 30% canal compromise; MRI shows an intact posterior ligamentous complex. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Posterior pedicle screw fixation with interbody fusion
Non-operative care with early mobilisation, with or without a thoracolumbar orthosis
items.e: A burst fracture with intact PLC and no deficit scores 2 on TLICS, so non-operative treatment with early mobilisation is indicated; trials show bracing adds little over mobilisation alone.

items.q: CT of a seat-belt restrained driver shows a horizontal fracture line through the spinous process, laminae, pedicles and vertebral body of L1 without facet dislocation. Which injury is this?
items.e: A horizontal fracture through all three columns from the posterior elements forwards is the bony Chance fracture, caused by flexion-distraction about an axis anterior to the spine, as with a lap belt.

items.q: A 70-year-old osteoporotic woman has progressive collapse of L2 weeks after a minor fall. Imaging shows an intravertebral vacuum cleft. Which condition is this?
items.e: An intravertebral vacuum cleft in a delayed osteoporotic collapse is the hallmark of Kummell disease (avascular necrosis of the vertebral body); it argues against infection or tumour.

items.q: Which imaging modality is most useful for assessing the extent and type of OPLL and detecting a double‑layer sign before deciding on a surgical approach?
items.e: CT accurately delineates OPLL morphology and the double‑layer sign indicating dural ossification.

items.q: A patient has cervical spondylosis with a disc‑osteophyte complex compressing the cord at C6‑C7. He is 58 years old with mild spastic paresis. What is the optimal surgery according to current guidelines?
items.e: For a single‑level anterior compression in a 58‑year‑old, ACDF provides direct decompression and is the guideline‑recommended procedure.

items.q: In degenerative cervical myelopathy, which modified JOA (mJOA) score range defines severe myelopathy?
items.e: mJOA grades myelopathy as mild (15-17), moderate (12-14) and severe (11 or less); AO Spine guidelines recommend surgery for moderate and severe disease (18 is normal).

items.q: During an anterior approach to the cervical spine, which nerve is most at risk of injury, leading to hoarseness?
items.e: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve has a longer and more variable course, making it most vulnerable during anterior cervical surgery.

items.q: Which of the following findings is NOT a sign of cervical myelopathy?
o: Grip-and-release test of 30 cycles in 10 seconds
items.e: Healthy people achieve 20 or more grip-and-release cycles in 10 seconds; fewer than 20 suggests myelopathy, so 30 cycles is normal.

items.q: A patient with mild DCM (mJOA 16) and T2 hyperintensity on MRI opts for structured physiotherapy. Which event would warrant proceeding to surgery?
o: Worsening of hand clumsiness after 3 months
items.e: If symptoms worsen (e.g., hand clumsiness) or fail to improve after a trial, guideline recommends surgical decompression.

items.q: In a left‑sided L4‑L5 paracentral disc herniation, which root is most likely to be compressed?
items.e: A paracentral L4‑L5 herniation sits posterolaterally and compresses the traversing L5 root; exiting L4 root is spared.

items.q: A 38‑year‑old woman has a left‑sided L5‑S1 far‑lateral herniation. The first‑step surgical approach that avoids facetectomy is:
items.e: The Wiltse muscle‑splitting approach targets the far‑lateral foramen and preserves the facet joint, avoiding the need for facetectomy.

items.q: The most reliable imaging sequence to rule out a syrinx or Chiari malformation in a patient with a left thoracic curve is:
o: Prone CT of the thoracic spine
Supine MRI of the whole spine
items.e: Left thoracic curves raise suspicion for occult cord anomalies; a whole‑axis MRI is the investigation of choice to exclude syrinx, Chiari, or tethered cord.

items.q: In infantile idiopathic scoliosis, a rib-vertebra angle difference (RVAD) greater than 20 degrees, or a phase 2 rib head (rib head overlapping the apical vertebra), predicts:
items.e: Mehta showed that an RVAD over 20 degrees and phase 2 rib heads predict progression, whereas phase 1 curves with RVAD under 20 degrees usually resolve spontaneously.

items.q: Vertebral body tethering for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in a skeletally immature patient is performed by:
o: Posterior instrumented fusion of the curve
Anterior placement of vertebral body screws and a flexible tether on the convexity of the curve
Anterior screws and tether on the concavity of the curve
items.e: VBT is a non-fusion growth-modulation technique: through an anterior (often thoracoscopic) approach, screws are placed in the vertebral bodies on the convex side and tensioned with a tether to slow convex growth (Hueter-Volkmann).

items.q: A 26‑year‑old man presents with insidious back pain, night sweats and a 10‑kg weight loss. Plain radiographs show loss of height of the upper thoracic vertebrae and a mild kyphotic angulation. Which imaging modality is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis?
items.e: MRI is the investigation of choice for spinal TB as it shows early marrow oedema, paradiscal involvement with relatively preserved disc and paraspinal abscesses.

items.q: A 12‑year‑old boy with spinal tuberculosis at the thoracolumbar junction shows separation of the facet joints and posterior retropulsion of the vertebral body. According to Rajasekaran’s "spine‑at‑risk" signs, what should be considered?
items.e: Two or more spine‑at‑risk signs predict severe kyphosis; early surgery is advised to prevent progression.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman with thoracic spinal tuberculosis is started on antitubercular therapy. Two weeks later her back pain worsens and she develops progressive paraparesis. Which surgical indication does this represent?
items.e: Neurological deficit that appears or worsens on adequate ATT (or fails to improve after a few weeks) is a standard indication for surgical decompression in spinal tuberculosis.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old man with spinal TB has a paravertebral abscess detected on MRI. Which surgical approach is most commonly used today to decompress, obtain tissue and stabilize?
o: Anterior radical debridement with strut grafting
Posterior transpedicular debridement with pedicle screws
Deformity correction with vertebral column resection
items.e: Posterior transpedicular debridement with pedicle screw fixation allows decompression, fixation and can be done in a single stage.

items.q: Which investigation is the most rapid and can detect rifampicin resistance in spinal TB?
items.e: GeneXpert MTB/RIF detects MTB and rifampicin resistance within a few hours.

items.q: A standing full-length radiograph of a 45-year-old man shows a sagittal vertical axis (SVA) of 6.2 cm and a T1 pelvic angle (TPA) of 22 degrees. Which statement is correct?
o: He is sagittally balanced because SVA is under 7 cm
TPA is irrelevant when lumbar lordosis is normal
SVA is unaffected by pelvic tilt compensation
items.e: An SVA over 4-5 cm (SRS-Schwab) and a TPA above about 20 degrees indicate positive sagittal malalignment; TPA has the advantage of being independent of postural compensation such as pelvic retroversion.

items.q: A postoperative radiograph after primary THA shows acetabular cup inclination of 55 degrees and anteversion of 5 degrees. What is the most concerning early complication?
items.e: Both values lie outside the Lewinnek safe zone (40 +/- 10 inclination, 15 +/- 10 anteversion); a steep, under-anteverted cup predisposes to early instability, particularly posterior dislocation, and edge loading.

items.q: Two years after revision THA, a 55-year-old has a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis. Aspiration shows 4,000 WBC/microL with 90% neutrophils and a positive alpha-defensin. According to the 2018 ICM criteria, the case is classified as:
o: Infected only if intraoperative cultures are positive
items.e: A sinus tract communicating with the joint is a major criterion; one major criterion alone establishes periprosthetic joint infection, regardless of the minor criteria score.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old man with a THA presents with a 3‑month history of pain and limited range of motion, normal ESR and CRP, but a synovial fluid WBC of 3 200 cells/µL with 82 % PMNs. Which additional test would most likely confirm a periprosthetic joint infection?
items.e: Alpha‑defensin has high specificity and remains positive even with negative systemic markers, making it the best confirmatory test here.

items.q: A 64-year-old has groin pain 8 years after THA with a 36 mm cobalt-chromium head on highly cross-linked polyethylene and a titanium stem. Radiographs are unremarkable. Serum cobalt is 6 microg/L and chromium 1 microg/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and repeat blood tests in 2 years
items.e: In a metal-on-polyethylene THA, a raised cobalt disproportionate to chromium suggests head-neck taper corrosion (trunnionosis); MARS MRI is used to look for an adverse local tissue reaction.

items.q: A 55-year-old has groin pain 5 years after metal-on-metal hip resurfacing, with raised serum cobalt and chromium and a periarticular soft-tissue mass on MARS MRI. Which histological finding is characteristic of ALVAL in this setting?
o: Foreign-body giant cells around polyethylene particles
Acute fibrinoid necrosis without inflammatory cells
items.e: ALVAL (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion) is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction showing dense perivascular T and B lymphocyte cuffing, often with necrosis, around metal debris.

items.q: In a THA, a 36 mm head is used with a highly cross-linked polyethylene liner only 4 mm thick at its thinnest point. What is the main concern with this construct?
o: Reduced wear from lower contact stress
items.e: Larger heads leave thinner polyethylene; very thin HXLPE (under about 4-6 mm), which has reduced fatigue strength, is at risk of rim cracking and liner fracture, especially with impingement or malposition.

items.q: In revision TKA, the tibia shows an AORI type 2B defect (metaphyseal bone loss involving both condyles). Which tibial reconstruction is most appropriate?
o: Standard primary tibial tray without a stem
Cement filling alone with a primary tray
Metaphyseal sleeve or cone with a stemmed tibial component
Structural allograft-prosthetic composite of the whole proximal tibia
items.e: AORI 2B defects involve both condyles; metaphyseal cones or sleeves with stems provide metaphyseal fixation and load transfer, while allograft-prosthetic composites are reserved for type 3 loss with collateral ligament compromise.

items.q: During two-stage revision of an infected THA, a well-fixed extensively porous-coated cementless femoral stem must be removed. Which technique gives the safest access?
o: Cortical window at the stem tip only
items.e: An extended trochanteric osteotomy exposes the bone-implant interface for controlled division (with Gigli saw and trephines), reducing the risk of uncontrolled femoral fracture or perforation, while leaving diaphysis for distal fixation.

items.q: In reverse shoulder arthroplasty, which design modification has been shown to reduce the incidence of scapular notching?
items.e: Lateralising the glenoid side or using a larger glenosphere moves the humeral cup away from the inferior scapular neck, lowering notching rates.

items.q: Which of the following is the most specific indication for a medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty?
o: Isolated medial compartment osteoarthritis with intact ligaments and varus malalignment <10°
Mixed medial and lateral compartment osteoarthritis with moderate bone loss
Knee instability requiring cruciate ligament reconstruction
Severe patellofemoral arthritis with mild tibiofemoral disease
items.e: UKA is reserved for patients with isolated medial compartment disease, intact collateral and cruciate ligaments and varus alignment less than about 10°.

items.q: In a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, postoperative patella baja is best minimised by:
o: A single transverse cut distal to the tibial tubercle
A biplanar osteotomy with a descending anterior cut that leaves the tubercle on the proximal fragment
Placing the lateral hinge at the joint line
items.e: In a uniplanar opening wedge the tubercle stays on the distal fragment and moves distally, lowering the patella; a descending (distally directed) frontal cut keeps the tubercle with the proximal fragment and preserves patellar height.

items.q: After a laceration over the dorsoradial wrist, a patient has numbness over the dorsum of the first web space but normal thumb extension and abduction. Which nerve is injured?
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
items.e: The superficial radial nerve is purely sensory and supplies the dorsal first web space; the PIN is motor to the extensors, and the dorsal ulnar branch supplies the dorso-ulnar hand.

items.q: In Dupuytren disease, which cell type expressing alpha-smooth muscle actin is chiefly responsible for contraction of the diseased cords?
items.e: Myofibroblasts, which contain alpha-smooth muscle actin, predominate in the proliferative and involutional phases and generate the contractile force that produces the flexion contracture.

items.q: Vibration sense tested with a tuning fork is carried predominantly by which peripheral nerve fibre type?
items.e: Vibration and light touch are carried by large myelinated A-beta fibres from Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles; A-alpha serves motor and proprioception, while A-delta and C carry pain and temperature.

items.q: The immediate sharp, well-localised pain felt at the moment of a fracture is transmitted mainly by which fibres?
items.e: Fast, sharp, well-localised pain is carried by thinly myelinated A-delta fibres; the later dull, poorly localised ache is carried by unmyelinated C fibres.

items.q: Which observational study design best establishes that an exposure (for example a surgical technique) preceded the outcome?
items.e: A prospective cohort identifies exposure first and follows patients forward, establishing temporality; case-control and cross-sectional designs cannot reliably do so.

items.q: A study reports a 10‑year revision rate of 4.2% for a new total knee implant using a large registry. Which of the following is *not* a limitation inherent to registry data for this question?
o: Loss to follow‑up may bias results
High internal validity due to randomisation
items.e: Registries are observational; they lack randomisation, so internal validity is limited, not high.

items.q: During the design of a surgical RCT for a new cementless femoral stem, the investigators decide to use a stratified randomisation block of size 4 based on patient's sex. Why is this method preferred over simple randomisation?
o: It guarantees equal numbers of male and female participants overall
It ensures blinding of the surgeon
It balances prognostic factors during enrolment
items.e: Stratified block randomisation keeps groups balanced for a key prognostic factor (sex) at every stage of enrolment.

items.q: A randomized trial of two rehabilitation protocols after ACL reconstruction shows a mean IKDC score of 78 (SD 7) in group A and 81 (SD 9) in group B. The investigators plan a non‑inferiority trial with a margin of 5 points. Which analysis is mandatory to support non‑inferiority?
items.e: In a non‑inferiority trial, both ITT and per‑protocol analyses must demonstrate non‑inferiority, as ITT alone may be overly conservative.

items.q: Which bias is most likely introduced if the surgeon in a surgical RCT is aware of the patient’s allocation but the outcome assessor remains blinded?
items.e: Performance bias occurs when the surgeon behaves differently based on the allocated treatment, despite a blinded assessor.

items.q: An orthopedic study uses propensity score matching to compare patients receiving a new graft‑free ACL repair with historical controls. What key limitation remains despite this matching?
o: Unknown confounders cannot be adjusted for
The study becomes a randomized trial
It removes the need for a control group
items.e: Propensity matching only balances measured covariates; unmeasured confounders may still bias the results.

items.q: A prospective cohort of 500 patients examined the incidence of non‑union after tibial plafond fracture fixation. Over 3 years, 58 patients experienced non‑union. What statistical measure best describes this occurrence?
items.e: Incidence proportion is calculated as number of events divided by total cohort at risk (58/500).

items.q: While obtaining a lumbar spine radiograph, which change in exposure factors most reduces image contrast (producing a longer grey scale)?
items.e: Higher kVp produces a more penetrating beam with less photoelectric absorption and more Compton scatter, narrowing attenuation differences between tissues and lowering contrast; mAs mainly controls density and dose.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the strength of a lead apron and its effectiveness in reducing scattered radiation to the operator’s torso?
o: 0.25 mm lead equivalent blocks 50 % of scatter
0.5 mm lead equivalent blocks about 95 % of scatter
Lead thickness has no effect beyond 0.1 mm
The apron must be in direct contact with the skin for it to work
items.e: A 0.5 mm lead‑equivalent apron attenuates roughly 95 % of scattered photons, providing the most commonly recommended protective level.

items.q: The ICRP (2011) occupational equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye, relevant to orthopaedic surgeons using fluoroscopy, is:
o: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
50 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
items.e: ICRP reduced the lens limit from 150 mSv to 20 mSv per year (averaged over 5 years, no single year above 50 mSv) because of radiation cataract risk, so lead glasses are recommended.

items.q: For digital templating before THA, a 25 mm calibration ball placed at the level of the hip measures 30 mm on the radiograph. What is the radiographic magnification?
items.e: Magnification = (measured - actual) / actual = (30 - 25) / 25 = 20%; templates or measurements must be scaled down accordingly.

items.q: A 125‑kg female patient is to receive routine prophylactic cefazolin during her elective femoral fracture fixation. What is the recommended dose?
items.e: The protocol stipulates 3 g IV for patients ≥120 kg, administered within 60 minutes before incision.

items.q: When vancomycin is used for surgical prophylaxis in orthopaedic surgery, the infusion should begin within what time before incision?
items.e: Because vancomycin must be infused slowly (over at least 60 minutes to avoid vancomycin infusion reaction), guidelines advise starting it within 120 minutes before incision, versus 60 minutes for cefazolin.

items.q: Low‑dose antibiotic‑loaded cement is used prophylactically in primary arthroplasty. Which agent is appropriate for this purpose?
items.e: Gentamicin (and tobramycin) are heat‑stable powders used in low doses (~1 g per 40 g cement) for prophylaxis.

items.q: Which modifiable risk factor is associated with an increased risk of surgical site infection and should ideally be resolved at least 4 weeks pre‑operation?
items.e: Stopping smoking ≥4 weeks before surgery reduces nicotine‑induced vasoconstriction and improves wound healing.

items.q: Cefazolin is now considered safe for surgical prophylaxis in most patients with a reported penicillin allergy. What is the main reason for the low cross-reactivity?
o: Cefazolin has a unique R1 side chain not shared with penicillins
Cefazolin is excreted unchanged by the kidney
items.e: Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is mainly driven by similar R1 side chains; cefazolin's side chain is dissimilar, so allergic cross-reaction is rare.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old man falls from height and sustains a Ruedi‑Allgower type III tibial pilon fracture with a prominent central die‑punch impaction.  Which staged protocol is most suitable?
o: Immediate ORIF with limited ankle arthrotomy
Spanning external fixator followed by definitive fixation after soft‑tissue recovery
Conservative management with a walking cast
items.e: High‑energy, comminuted pilon fractures (Ruedi‑Allgower III) are best managed with an initial spanning external fixator to restore length and alignment, followed by ORIF once the soft tissues have healed.

items.q: Which CT-based tibial plateau fracture classification specifically identifies posterior column fractures that may need a posterior approach?
items.e: Luo's three-column concept divides the plateau on axial CT into lateral, medial and posterior columns, highlighting posterior fragments that the radiograph-based Schatzker system misses.

items.q: Which fragment type is defined by an anterolateral tibial plafond avulsion from the AITFL?
items.e: The Tillaux‑Chaput fragment is an anterolateral tibial plafond fragment avulsed by the AITFL, seen in supination‑external rotation injuries.

items.q: After reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation, which single radiographic view most reliably confirms concentric reduction of the humeral head on the glenoid?
items.e: The axillary lateral view shows the humeral head relative to the glenoid face directly, confirming reduction and revealing posterior dislocation or glenoid rim fractures that AP views miss.

items.q: A 38-year-old has a radial head fracture comminuted into more than three fragments, with elbow instability after a dislocation. The most appropriate treatment is:
items.e: Ring showed poor results with ORIF of radial head fractures with more than three fragments; in an unstable elbow, replacement restores the radial column, which excision would sacrifice.

items.q: A 28-year-old has a volar shearing (volar Barton) fracture with a small volar lunate facet fragment. If this fragment is not captured by fixation, the most likely complication is:
items.e: The volar lunate facet is the 'critical corner' that buttresses the carpus; failure to fix it lets the carpus sublux volarly with the fragment despite a well-placed volar plate.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old male is brought to the trauma bay after a high‑speed road traffic crash. Primary survey reveals a systolic BP of 78 mmHg and a heart rate of 140 bpm. Which resuscitative strategy is most appropriate at this stage?
o: Permissive hypotension with a target systolic 80–90 mmHg
Aggressive crystalloid bolus to achieve MAP > 90 mmHg
Immediate definitive fixation of all long‑bone fractures
Administration of only saline and no blood products
items.e: In haemorrhagic shock class III, permissive hypotension (systolic 80–90 mmHg) protects against further injury while maintaining organ perfusion.

items.q: In the CRASH-2 trial of bleeding trauma patients, tranexamic acid reduced death from bleeding only when started within what time of injury?
items.e: CRASH-2 showed benefit when TXA (1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours) was given within 3 hours; administration after 3 hours increased bleeding deaths.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old male sustains an isolated mid‑shaft humeral fracture. The fracture is perfectly aligned and the patient is keen for a quick return to work. What type of fixation will most likely provide primary bone healing?
items.e: Compression plating with lag screws gives absolute stability and interfragmentary compression, allowing primary bone healing with no callus.

items.q: During a routine follow‑up of a femoral shaft fracture fixed with an intramedullary nail, the radiograph shows a well‑formed, broad, bony bridge across the fracture site. The most likely mechanism of healing is:
o: Secondary bone healing via endochondral ossification
Secondary bone healing via intramembranous ossification
items.e: Intramedullary nails provide relative stability; the substantial callus indicates secondary bone healing through endochondral ossification.

items.q: Recombinant BMP-2 applied at a tibial non-union contributes which biological property?
items.e: BMP-2 is an osteoinductive growth factor that recruits mesenchymal cells and drives their differentiation into osteoblasts; it supplies no cells (osteogenesis) or scaffold (osteoconduction) by itself.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the primary biological role of a Masquelet spacer in the management of a segmental bone defect?
o: Provides immediate structural support to the defect
Acts as a vascularized bone graft
Induces a membrane rich in VEGF and BMP‑2
Delivers local antibiotics to the defect site
items.e: The spacer chiefly induces a growth‑rich induced membrane; later, autograft placed within this membrane promotes healing.

items.q: An awake, cooperative 45-year-old has bilateral C5-C6 facet dislocations with an incomplete cord injury. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Posterior fusion in situ without reduction
Rapid closed reduction with Gardner-Wells tong traction and serial neurological examination
items.e: In an awake, examinable patient with incomplete injury, early closed reduction with incremental tong traction and serial neurological checks decompresses the cord; pre-reduction MRI is reserved for those who cannot be examined or fail reduction.

items.q: A 70-year-old has a type II odontoid fracture with 2 mm displacement and no angulation, treated non-operatively. Which factor most increases the risk of non-union?
items.e: Risk factors for non-union of type II odontoid fractures are age over 50, displacement of 5 mm or more (especially posterior), angulation over 10 degrees and comminution; age is the relevant factor here.

items.q: A 23‑year‑old athlete presents with a hangman’s fracture type I after a bike crash. What is the recommended initial treatment?
items.e: Type I hangman’s fracture has minimal translation (<3 mm) and no angulation; it is treated non‑operatively with a rigid cervical collar.

items.q: A neurologically intact 28-year-old has a T12 fracture with a TLICS score of 5. According to TLICS, management should be:
o: Either operative or non-operative at surgeon's discretion
items.e: TLICS of 3 or less suggests non-operative care, 4 is indeterminate, and 5 or more indicates surgery.

items.q: A 65-year-old neurologically intact woman has a T12 fracture involving the superior endplate and the posterior vertebral wall, with the inferior endplate intact and an intact posterior tension band on MRI. The AO Spine thoracolumbar classification is:
items.e: An A3 incomplete burst involves the posterior wall and a single endplate; involvement of both endplates would make it A4, and PLC disruption would make it a type B injury.

items.q: In neurologically intact patients with thoracolumbar burst fractures and an intact posterior ligamentous complex, randomised trials comparing a thoracolumbosacral orthosis with no brace (e.g. Bailey et al.) found:
o: Significantly better pain scores with bracing
More kyphosis requiring surgery without a brace
Bracing was mandatory to prevent neurological deterioration
items.e: Bailey et al. (2014) showed that early mobilisation without a brace gave equivalent pain, function and kyphosis to TLSO treatment for AO A3 fractures in neurologically intact patients.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old female with long‑standing neck pain has an AP canal diameter of 12 mm on a lateral radiograph. Her Torg‑Pavlov ratio is 0.75. Which statement is true regarding her risk of developing myelopathic symptoms?
o: She is automatically free of compression and needs no further work‑up
The canal is considered absolutely obstructed; surgery is indicated
The canal is relatively stenotic; she should be monitored for progression
The canal size suggests severe kyphosis which defines her prognosis
items.e: An AP diameter under 13 mm indicates relative stenosis; a ratio below 0.8 indicates congenital narrowing. The patient is at risk of progressive compression but does not yet require surgery unless symptoms develop.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a poor prognostic indicator for functional recovery after surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy?
o: Presence of T1 hypointensity on MRI
items.e: Younger age (< 40 years) is associated with better neurological recovery. The other three factors—long symptom duration, severe baseline dysfunction, and irreversible cord changes—are recognized poor prognostic markers.

items.q: A 42-year-old with axial low back pain has an MRI showing low T1 and high T2 signal in the vertebral endplates adjacent to a degenerate L4-L5 disc. These Modic type I changes represent:
o: Bone marrow oedema and inflammation with fissured endplates
items.e: Modic I (low T1, high T2) reflects marrow oedema and inflammation and correlates most strongly with discogenic pain; Modic II (high T1, high T2) is fatty change and Modic III (low on both) is sclerosis.

items.q: During decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis, removal of more than about what proportion of both facet joints at one level significantly increases the risk of iatrogenic instability?
items.e: Biomechanical studies show that resecting more than about 50% of both facets (or a complete unilateral facetectomy) destabilises the motion segment, so fusion is usually added.

items.q: A 12-year-old from a TB-endemic area has insidious back pain, night sweats and a thoracolumbar kyphosis. Which imaging feature most favours tuberculous over pyogenic spondylodiscitis?
o: Early disc destruction with a thick, irregular enhancing abscess wall
Relative preservation of the disc early with paradiscal bone destruction
Vertebral sclerosis with bony fusion at presentation
Involvement confined to a single facet joint
items.e: TB spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament and spares the avascular disc until late, producing paradiscal destruction, skip lesions and thin, smooth-walled abscesses; pyogenic infection destroys the disc early.

items.q: A 25-year-old with T12-L1 tuberculosis has a large paraspinal abscess and mild epidural compression but no neurological deficit or instability. According to Tuli's 'middle path' regimen, initial management is:
o: Immediate anterior radical debridement and strut grafting
Antitubercular therapy with rest and bracing, surgery reserved for failure or neurological deficit
items.e: The middle path regimen relies on ATT with rest and bracing, reserving surgery for non-response, neurological deficit, instability or diagnostic doubt.

items.q: Using the NOMS framework, a patient with high-grade (Bilsky 3) epidural cord compression from a radioresistant renal cell carcinoma metastasis, without mechanical instability and with good systemic status, is best treated by:
o: Separation surgery followed by stereotactic body radiotherapy
items.e: In NOMS, high-grade compression from radioresistant tumours needs separation surgery to create a margin around the cord, followed by SBRT; radiosensitive tumours are treated with radiotherapy regardless of compression grade.

items.q: Which feature on a plain AP radiograph of a thoracic vertebra is an early red flag for a vertebral metastasis rather than a simple compression fracture?
o: Pedicle erosion giving a “winking owl” sign
Collapse of the anterior vertebral body with vertebral height loss
Lateral translation of the vertebral body >3 mm
items.e: Metastatic lesions often erode the posterior elements, producing the classic “winking owl” appearance due to pedicle destruction.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old man with renal cell carcinoma undergoes pre‑operative angiography for a suspected T10 vertebral metastasis. What is the primary reason for embolisation?
items.e: Renal cell tumours are hypervascular. Embolisation limits intra‑operative bleeding and facilitates safer resection.

items.q: A standing lateral radiograph shows a sacral slope of 50 degrees with a long, curved lumbar lordosis involving many vertebrae. According to Roussouly, the sagittal type is:
items.e: Roussouly type 4 has a sacral slope over 45 degrees with a long, highly curved lordosis; types 1 and 2 have sacral slope under 35 degrees and type 3 between 35 and 45 degrees.

items.q: Which of the following is the investigation of choice to confirm progressive loss of lumbar lordosis after multi‑level posterior instrumented fusion?
o: CT scan of the thoracic spine
items.e: Serial full‑length standing radiographs are preferred to document changes in lumbar lordosis and sagittal balance over time.

items.q: Which THA approach, performed supine, uses the internervous interval between tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal nerve) and sartorius (femoral nerve)?
items.e: The direct anterior approach exploits the true internervous plane between TFL and sartorius superficially; the Watson-Jones interval between TFL and gluteus medius is intermuscular but not internervous.

items.q: In a primary THA in a patient with marked abductor deficiency, which implant choice best reduces the risk of dislocation while avoiding the high failure rates of constraint?
items.e: Dual mobility gives a large effective head with greater jump distance and arc of motion; small heads, reduced offset and unrepaired capsule all increase instability, while constrained liners carry high mechanical failure rates.

items.q: The most common specific complication of a conventional greater trochanteric osteotomy used for exposure in complex primary THA is:
items.e: Trochanteric non-union and escape occur in a notable proportion of cases and cause abductor weakness, limp, pain from wires and instability.

items.q: In mechanically aligned TKA, the distal femoral cut is made perpendicular to the mechanical axis. Relative to the intramedullary (anatomical) femoral axis this is typically set at:
items.e: The femoral anatomical and mechanical axes differ by about 5-7 degrees, so the intramedullary guide is set at that valgus angle (more with a large neck-shaft offset or short femur).

items.q: What is the principal goal of kinematic alignment in TKA?
o: Neutral mechanical axis in every patient
Restoring the patient's pre-arthritic joint lines and constitutional alignment
Femoral component in 3 degrees external rotation to the posterior condylar axis in all cases
Tibial component in routine 3 degrees of varus
items.e: Kinematic alignment resurfaces the knee to restore the native pre-arthritic joint lines and limb alignment, aiming to minimise soft-tissue release, unlike mechanical alignment which targets a neutral axis.

items.q: Which landmark is generally considered the most reliable reference for femoral component rotation in TKA?
items.e: The surgical transepicondylar axis (lateral epicondyle to medial sulcus) approximates the flexion-extension axis and is used as the reference; the PCA is unreliable with condylar hypoplasia or wear.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT considered a major patient‑related risk factor for periprosthetic joint infection?
o: Prior intra‑articular steroid injection within 3 months
items.e: Risk increases with poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c >7.5 %) but not when glycaemia is well controlled.

items.q: Which laboratory threshold is generally applied to identify an early postoperative (within 4 weeks) prosthetic joint infection?
items.e: Early post‑operative infection is characterized by synovial WBC >10,000 cells/µL (and CRP >100 mg/L); lower thresholds apply to chronic cases.

items.q: Compared with a cobalt-chromium head, a ceramic femoral head on a highly cross-linked polyethylene liner particularly reduces the risk of:
o: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion at the head-neck taper
items.e: Ceramic heads do not undergo the fretting corrosion seen at CoCr head-neck tapers, avoiding trunnionosis and cobalt-related adverse local tissue reactions; squeaking and fracture are ceramic-specific concerns.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old man undergoes a total hip resurfacing with a cobalt‑chromium femoral component. Two years post‑op he develops a pseudotumour. Blood tests reveal cobalt concentration of 12 µg/L. Which statement best describes the threshold for closer surveillance in a unilateral resurfacing?
items.e: For unilateral resurfacing, a cobalt level above about 7 µg/L warrants close monitoring for adverse reactions to metal debris.

items.q: Delamination and pitting of polyethylene, seen far more in TKA than THA, are caused mainly by which wear mechanism?
o: Fatigue wear from high subsurface contact stress
items.e: Low-conformity knee articulations produce high cyclic subsurface stresses causing fatigue cracks, delamination and pitting, made worse by oxidation of gamma-in-air sterilised polyethylene.

items.q: During revision TKA, a metaphyseal bone defect involving only the medial femoral condyle is found. According to the AORI classification this is:
items.e: AORI type 1 has intact metaphyseal bone, type 2A metaphyseal loss of one condyle or plateau, type 2B both, and type 3 deficient metaphysis with collateral or tendon attachment compromise.

items.q: During anatomic TSA in an active 55-year-old with a B2 glenoid, CT shows 20 degrees of retroversion. Which glenoid strategy best reduces the risk of component loosening?
o: Implant the glenoid in its native retroversion without correction
Eccentric high-side reaming to neutral regardless of bone loss
Limited eccentric reaming combined with a posteriorly augmented glenoid component
items.e: Eccentric reaming alone corrects only about 10-15 degrees before excessive vault bone loss and peg perforation; beyond that, augmented components or bone grafting restore version and reduce eccentric loading (rocking-horse loosening).

items.q: A 72-year-old with cuff tear arthropathy is planned for reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Which is an absolute prerequisite for a functional outcome?
o: Intact axillary nerve and functioning deltoid
Pre-operative passive forward flexion over 90 degrees
items.e: RTSA depends on the deltoid as the motor for elevation, so axillary nerve palsy or deltoid deficiency is a contraindication; subscapularis and teres minor status affect stability and rotation but are not absolute.

items.q: In a patient undergoing an anatomic TSA, the surgeon chooses a pegged all‑polyethylene glenoid component. Which statement best explains why this design is preferred?
o: It allows for greater glenoid bone loss before revision
It reduces the incidence of postoperative scapular notching
It has a lower rate of radiolucent lines compared to keeled designs
It enables the use of larger glenosphere diameters
items.e: Pegged all‑polyethylene components show fewer radiolucencies (i.e., lower loosening) than keeled designs, making them the preferred choice.

items.q: A new MRI protocol for occult scaphoid fracture is tested against CT: 90 true positives, 10 false negatives, 20 false positives and 80 true negatives. What is the sensitivity of the MRI protocol?
items.e: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) = 90 / 100 = 90%; specificity would be TN / (TN + FP) = 80 / 100 = 80%.

items.q: The statistical power of a clinical trial is best defined as:
o: The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
The probability of a type I error
The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false (1 - beta)
The proportion of patients completing follow-up
items.e: Power = 1 - beta, the probability of detecting a true difference; it is usually set at 80-90% and rises with sample size, effect size and alpha.

items.q: Using the JBJS levels of evidence for therapeutic studies, a well-designed randomised controlled trial with only 70% follow-up is graded as:
items.e: An RCT with less than 80% follow-up, improper randomisation or no blinding is downgraded from Level I to Level II.

items.q: Three independent groups of patients with normally distributed Oxford Hip Scores are compared after three different approaches for THA. The appropriate test is:
items.e: One-way analysis of variance compares means of three or more independent groups with normally distributed continuous data; Kruskal-Wallis is the non-parametric equivalent.

items.q: In a Kaplan-Meier survivorship analysis of a hip implant with revision as the endpoint, a patient who dies with the implant still in place at 6 years is:
o: Censored at the time of death
Counted as a failure at 6 years
Imputed as revised at the mean revision time
items.e: Patients who die or are lost to follow-up without reaching the endpoint are censored at that time; they contribute to the at-risk population until then.

items.q: On CT, normal adipose tissue has an attenuation of approximately:
items.e: Fat measures about -50 to -100 HU, air -1000 HU, water 0 HU and dense cortical bone up to about +1000 HU or more.

items.q: Which complication is most common after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion?
items.e: Transient dysphagia is the most frequent complication after ACDF, related to oesophageal retraction and soft-tissue swelling; perforation and vertebral artery injury are rare.

items.q: Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR) with exchange of modular components is most appropriate for which periprosthetic infection?
o: Chronic infection at 2 years with a sinus tract and loose stem
Acute postoperative infection 2 weeks after TKA with well-fixed components
Fungal infection with a loose cup
Infection with a draining sinus and extensive osteolysis
items.e: DAIR is indicated for early postoperative (within about 4 weeks) or acute haematogenous infection with symptoms under 3 weeks, well-fixed implants and healthy soft tissues; chronic or loose cases need staged or one-stage revision.

items.q: The H-reflex, recorded from soleus after submaximal tibial nerve stimulation, is most useful in assessing which nerve root?
items.e: The H-reflex is the electrical equivalent of the ankle jerk, travelling via Ia afferents and the S1 root; a prolonged or absent H-reflex supports S1 radiculopathy.

items.q: Myostatin (GDF-8), a member of the TGF-beta superfamily, acts on skeletal muscle by:
o: Stimulating satellite cell proliferation and hypertrophy
Inhibiting muscle growth and limiting hypertrophy
Converting type II to type I fibres
items.e: Myostatin is a negative regulator of muscle mass; loss-of-function mutations cause marked muscle hypertrophy, and it is a therapeutic target in muscle wasting.

items.q: In a stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial of a new hip fracture pathway, the defining feature is that:
o: All clusters start as controls and cross over to the intervention at randomly assigned, staggered times
Each patient receives both treatments in random order
Only half the clusters ever receive the intervention
items.e: In a stepped-wedge design every cluster eventually receives the intervention, with the timing of crossover randomised; it suits interventions believed beneficial or rolled out gradually.

items.q: A randomised trial of a new bone graft substitute is stopped early at an interim analysis because of an apparently large benefit. The main concern with interpreting this result is that:
o: The type II error rate is increased
Trials stopped early for benefit tend to overestimate the treatment effect
items.e: Truncated trials stopped for benefit, especially with few events, systematically exaggerate effect sizes because they stop at a random high point.

items.q: A diagnostic test for periprosthetic infection has a positive likelihood ratio of 10. If the pre-test probability is 50% (pre-test odds 1:1), the post-test probability after a positive result is about:
items.e: Post-test odds = pre-test odds x LR = 1 x 10 = 10; probability = 10 / 11, about 91% (Bayes' theorem).

items.q: A registry study finds that countries with higher national bisphosphonate sales have higher rates of atypical femoral fracture and concludes that individual patients on bisphosphonates are at risk. This reasoning is an example of:
items.e: The ecological fallacy is inferring individual-level associations from group-level (population) data, which may be confounded.

items.q: In a multivariable regression analysis of risk factors for non-union, two predictors (BMI and body weight) are very highly correlated with each other. This problem is called:
o: Overfitting due to too few variables
items.e: Multicollinearity inflates standard errors and makes individual coefficients unstable; one of the correlated variables is usually removed or combined.

items.q: Deep infection occurs in 6% of diabetic and 2% of non-diabetic patients after ankle ORIF. The attributable risk (risk difference) due to diabetes is:
items.e: Attributable risk = risk in exposed - risk in unexposed = 6% - 2% = 4%; the relative risk would be 3.

items.q: A patient-reported outcome score shows that 30% of patients score the lowest possible value before surgery. This limitation is known as:
items.e: A floor effect occurs when many patients score at the minimum, so further deterioration (or differences between the worst patients) cannot be detected; usually more than 15% is considered significant.

items.q: A Morel-Lavallee lesion over the greater trochanter is found in a patient needing acetabular fixation through a Kocher-Langenbeck approach. Why is it important?
o: It indicates an underlying femoral neck fracture
It contraindicates any surgery for 6 months
It is associated with a high rate of bacterial colonisation and wound infection if operated through
items.e: The closed degloving cavity contains necrotic fat and haematoma, and up to a third are culture-positive; it should be debrided and drained before or during acetabular surgery through that area.

items.q: In the LEAP study of severe lower extremity trauma, which factor was the strongest predictor of poor functional outcome at 2 and 7 years in both amputation and salvage groups?
o: Patient factors such as low education, poverty, smoking and poor self-efficacy
items.e: LEAP found similar outcomes after salvage and amputation; outcome was driven mainly by socioeconomic and psychosocial factors (education, income, insurance, smoking, self-efficacy, social support).

items.q: In the Checketts-Otterburn classification of pin site infection, a pin site with serous discharge, redness and pain that responds to oral antibiotics is graded as:
